[Validate multipart boundaries and enforce file-size/content-type limits on OpenAI-compat tool/file endpoints]
description:
Motivation: several incidents and flaky E2E runs showed that tool/file uploads to the OpenAI-compat endpoints could hang or be accepted with malformed boundaries or incorrect content-type headers, leading to streaming stalls and memory spikes on private deployments. This PR tightens validation for multipart/form-data and chunked transfer uploads, adds enforcement of default file-size limits, and surfaces explicit compatibility-layer error codes so downstream SDKs and clients can handle rejections cleanly. Summary of changes: - Add a multipart boundary presence and consistency check early in request parsing; reject requests missing a boundary with 422 MALFORMED_MULTIPART. - Enforce Content-Type whitelist for tool/file payloads (application/octet-stream, image/*, text/*, application/json, multipart/form-data). Requests with disallowed content-types now return 400 INVALID_CONTENT_TYPE. - Introduce Content-Length and chunked streaming guards. For chunked uploads we now apply per-chunk size ceiling and an aggregate max (default 25MB) and return 413 FILE_TOO_LARGE when exceeded. Limit is configurable via service config and Dedicated/Private can override per-tenant. - Update the OpenAI-compat adapter to normalize incoming form-data to internal file objects, while preserving streaming semantics. Old behavior accepted missing boundary on some clients; new behavior rejects those requests but includes a compatibility hint header (X-Compat-Error) to aid callers. - Add a small in-memory streaming parser for boundary edge-cases to avoid allocating large buffers when boundaries come in split TCP frames. - Bake in tests: unit tests for malformed boundary paths, integration tests with chunked transfer encoding (nginx-style split chunks), e2e test that runs against the compatibility layer. - Documentation: api changelog + compatibility notes and SDK test expectations. Risk & rollout: - Backwards compatible at the protocol level for well-formed clients; some malformed clients will be rejected. To soften rollout we emit the X-Compat-Error hints and a telemetry metric (compat.multipart.reject_count) for 2 weeks before flipping enforcement in some private installs where customers asked for a grace period. - Default file-size cap is conservative (25MB); customers can configure via config.service.file_upload.max_size_bytes. Related: ENG-4132 (multipart resilience), PM-291 (compat ergonomics).

review_comments:
Marco Ruiz: We should document the default max_size_bytes in the config file; otherwise Private customers will be surprised. - ACK, added to config/service_defaults.yaml.
Aisha Thompson: Can we avoid a hard 25MB constant in the runtime? Make sure it's read from the service config with a sensible default. - Done: reads config and falls back to 25MB.
Devon Li: The X-Compat-Error header value should be stable. Use short tokens (e.g., MALFORMED_BOUNDARY) so SDKs can pattern-match. - Updated to use stable tokens in adapters.
Marco Ruiz (follow-up): I hit a flaky test on CI where a boundary split across two frames caused a buffer growth; the streaming parser fix looks good but add a targeted unit test. - Added test and CI passes.
Priya Nair (author): Responded to all review comments and pushed the additional tests and docs updates.

release_notes:
- Enforce multipart boundary and return 422 MALFORMED_MULTIPART for missing/mismatched boundaries.
- Enforce allowed content-types on tool/file endpoints (400 INVALID_CONTENT_TYPE).
- Default file upload size cap of 25MB with 413 FILE_TOO_LARGE error for overage (configurable).
- Compatibility layer emits X-Compat-Error header to help client migration.

[multipart: add per-part/file size guards, content-type validation, and OpenAI-compat field mapping]
description:
Motivation: customers using the OpenAI-compatibility layer and the tool/function-calling endpoints were able to upload large multipart payloads and malformed parts which caused OOMs and destabilized streaming. This PR centralizes multipart validation into the API gateway handler and adds explicit per-part and total payload limits, content-type sniffing, and dual-field support for OpenAI-compat clients (accept both 'file' and 'files' form fields). The change is intentionally conservative: we validate before handing off to the streaming runtime so we can guarantee early rejection and deterministic error responses instead of mid-stream failures. Implementation highlights: 1) api/handlers/multipart_handler.py implements a two-pass scan: fast header-only pass to enforce per-part size and type heuristics, followed by a streaming handoff that preserves the original stream for allowed parts. 2) Introduced config flags (env) for PART_MAX_BYTES and MULTIPART_TOTAL_MAX_BYTES with sane defaults (10MB per part, 50MB total) and runtime metrics emitted for rejected uploads. 3) Content-type safety: we perform lightweight sniffing (magic bytes + declared header) to avoid accepting text/plain labeled binary blobs; for non-whitelisted types we respond 415 with structured error payload. 4) OpenAI-compat: map legacy form names and accept arrays and singletons to reduce client breakage. 5) Added unit and integration tests covering edge cases and a small e2e run that exercises the streaming generation + tool-call with an uploaded schema file. Checklist: - [x] Implement server-side validation and env flags - [x] Add metrics and structured error responses - [x] Add unit tests and integration e2e - [x] Update docs/compatibility and API reference - [x] Add a hotfix note for incident INT-4421 in changelog

review_comments:

Priya Kaur: I kept defaults slightly higher (10MB) after spike showed tokenized schema files often exceed 8MB; but made it configurable via env so infra can match historic behavior.
Marta Gomez: Please add a log line at INFO for rejected uploads with the rejection_reason tag; it will help SRE triage.
Priya Kaur: Added metric + structured log in latest commit c5a2f90.
Samir Patel: Security nit: make sure we don't emit file contents in logs.

discussion_resolution:
Addressed reviewer feedback: defaults configurable, metrics/logs added, no file contents logged

release_notes:
Server: multipart uploads now enforce per-part and total payload limits and validate content-type; clients that upload larger files should set PART_MAX_BYTES or switch to external storage and pass URLs. OpenAI-compat field mapping reduces client breakage for legacy integrations.

notes:
This PR was motivated by an incident (INT-4421) where malformed multipart uploads caused worker OOMs. Post-merge, SLO for streaming stability improved in the subsequent canary run. Ops should consider setting stricter PART_MAX_BYTES in high-throughput clusters.

[add multipart/form-data handling, strict content-type validation, and payload limit enforcement for API tool/file inputs]
description:
Motivation: users integrating tool/function calling and file uploads via the OpenAI-compatibility endpoints were sending a wide variety of content-types and very large multipart requests which caused inconsistent runtime behavior, high memory pressure, and unexpected acceptance of unsupported payloads. This PR introduces a focused, backwards-compatible implementation for multipart/form-data parsing on the OpenAI-compatibility path, strict Content-Type validation for tool/file inputs, and deterministic payload limits both per-file and per-request. Summary of changes: 1) Add a streaming-safe multipart parser that yields parts rather than buffering entire requests; 2) Validate Content-Type of each part (whitelist: text/*, image/*, application/json, application/octet-stream with explicit size checks); 3) Enforce configurable limits: max_file_size (default 10MiB), max_total_request_size (default 50MiB), max_parts_count (default 20). These defaults are conservative and documented; they can be overridden at tenant or route level via API config. 4) Hook validation into the OpenAI-compat layer so existing client integrations get predictable errors (400/413) with structured error bodies when inputs are rejected. 5) Add detailed unit and integration tests and end-to-end tests for streaming uploads and for the dedicated Dedicated/Private ingress paths. Backwards compatibility notes: this does not change the non-multipart JSON body semantics. Existing users who relied on accepting arbitrary large file uploads should update their tenant config or use Redwood Dedicated with higher quotas. Rollout plan: feature-flagged behind feature.enable_multipart_input (off by default); staged rollout to internal dogfood tenants, then gradual roll to 10%, 50%, 100% via config rollout. Checklist: - [x] Streaming-safe multipart parser implemented - [x] Content-Type whitelist + validation errors - [x] Per-file and per-request size enforcement + configurable defaults - [x] OpenAI-compat error mapping and structured error shapes - [x] Tests: unit, integration, e2e - [x] Docs: compatibility notes and config guide - [x] Telemetry: counters for rejected parts and throttled requests - [x] Migration & rollout plan included Testing notes: the multipart parser uses a small constant memory footprint for each active part and yields part metadata to the handler; large parts trigger a streaming drain with early termination (413 response) to avoid OOM. Integration tests exercise combination of binary and text parts, wrong content-types, and boundary cases around the configured limits. Telemetry: added metrics api.multipart.rejected_content_type, api.multipart.rejected_size, api.multipart.accepted_parts and a hist for part sizes. Implementation details: - parser: runtime/multipart/stream_parser.py - validator: api/validation/multipart_validator.py - compat layer: api/openai_compat/input_adapter.py - config: config/defaults/multipart.yaml - docs: docs/openai-compat/multipart.md - tests: tests/unit/test_multipart_parser.py, tests/integration/test_openai_compat_multipart.py Error shape examples (structured output): when a part is rejected we return 413 with a JSON body {"error":{"type":"request_too_large","message":"part exceeds max_file_size","meta":{"part_name":"file","limit_bytes":10485760}}} and 400 for unsupported content-types with type unsupported_media_type. Observability: trace spans added around parse->validate->route dispatch to help pinpoint latency regressions. Related items: Linear ENG-2728 (multipart uploader stability), PM-146 (OpenAI compat feature parity).

review_thread:
Liam Chen: key question — do we need to special-case application/pdf? many partners send PDFs as application/pdf; current whitelist would block it. Suggest adding application/pdf or making whitelist configurable per-tenant.
Aisha Patel: replied — agreed, added application/pdf to tenant_whitelist in config and made default conservative. Added test case + note in docs explaining why binary blobs should be limited.
Ravi Singh: please ensure the validator surfaces clear errors for multipart boundary parsing failures; I saw a flaky crash in an initial run.
Aisha Patel: replied — parser now catches malformed boundary exceptions and returns a 400 with error.type=malformed_multipart and includes low-signal debug id for tracing; updated tests.
Sofia Alvarez: approved — addressed my comments about metrics naming and added a suggestion to include counter tags for tenant_id and route_id.
CI Bot: integration-tests failed on first run due to test harness timeout; rerun completed successfully.
QA: noted an edge case where client SDK retries might double-submit large files; added a recommendation in docs and an optional idempotency header support in adapter.

release_notes:
Added multipart/form-data support on OpenAI-compat API paths with strict content-type validation and configurable per-file and per-request size limits. Default limits: 10MiB per file, 50MiB per request. Feature is behind a feature flag and can be enabled per-tenant. See docs/openai-compat/multipart.md for migration steps.

[Enforce MIME sniffing and chunking limits for tool/file uploads (OpenAI-compat layer)]
description:
Motivation: Tool integrations and file attachments coming through the OpenAI-compatibility proxy were accepting overly permissive Content-Type headers and arbitrarily large streaming chunks which caused downstream model handlers to OOM or misclassify payloads. This PR adds deterministic MIME sniffing, per-tool attachment quotas, and streaming chunk size enforcement at the proxy layer so tool authors and user clients get immediate, deterministic rejections instead of opaque runtime errors.

What this changes: - Add a MIME sniffing pass for multipart and single-part uploads that normalizes Content-Type to a safe set and rejects unknown/binary blobs when a tool opts into textual input only. - Implement per-tool max_upload_bytes and max_chunks settings surfaced through the tools registry; defaults applied when not configured. - Enforce max_chunk_bytes for streaming/transfer-encoding style uploads so a single chunk cannot exceed safety limits. - Map legacy OpenAI style headers ("OpenAI-File-Name", "openai-content-type") into our normalized metadata to keep compatibility with existing clients. - Return structured JSON error payloads compatible with OpenAI-compat error shapes (error.code, error.message, error.type) so SDKs can handle programmatic failures. - Add unit and integration tests that exercise multipart boundaries, chunked streams, and header-based compatibility fallbacks.

Checklist: - [x] Add MIME sniffing implementation and canonicalizer in api/proxy/upload_validator.go - [x] Add per-tool config + defaults in services/tools/registry - [x] Add streaming chunk enforcement in streaming/handler.go - [x] Preserve OpenAI compatibility headers and map to internal metadata - [x] Add tests for multipart streaming, single-part file uploads, and header fallbacks - [x] Update docs: redwood-docs/api/file-uploads.md

Compatibility notes: This change preserves behavioral compatibility for existing clients that set Content-Type correctly. Clients relying on implicit server-side assumptions (e.g. sending mixed binary/text under text/plain) will now receive a structured 400 with guidance. Ops: rollout is safe behind a feature flag (features.validate_tool_uploads). Default is off for 48 hours to allow canary release, then on cluster-wide by default.

References: Linear ENG-7382 (upload hardening), incident SUP-4127 (tool-run OOM on binary attachment), and a related follow-up PR will add per-tenant overrides for enterprise Private deployments.

Notes on testing and observations: integration tests found a tokenizer mismatch when content-type was incorrectly marked as "text/plain; charset=utf-16"; MIME canonicalizer now strips charset and uses content sniffed encoding detection for tokenization. CI: one flaky streaming test needed a 200ms backoff retry; I renamed the test to reflect expected semantics.

review_comments:
Marco Liu: Can we add a short-circuit for tools that explicitly accept binary? reasoning: avoid double-copy when proxied to dedicated GPU pool.
Priya (author): Added allow_binary flag per-tool and short-circuit path; added unit tests for the fast path.
Elena Garcia: Please ensure errors follow OpenAI shape and include a "type" that SDKs can switch on. Also confirm 400 vs 415 semantics.
Priya (author): Error payloads now include code/message/type and we return 415 for unsupported media types and 400 for malformed multipart frames.
Samir Patel: lgtm after docs update and a note in the changelog about the 48h feature-flag rollout.

release_notes:
Harden file and tool upload handling: MIME sniffing, per-tool upload quotas, streaming chunk limits, and improved OpenAI-compat error shapes. Feature gated rollout (features.validate_tool_uploads).

[multipart: robust streaming + tool/file payload limits + content-type validation]
description:
Problem: Streaming endpoints and the OpenAI-compat layer accepted mixed content payloads inconsistently which led to silent truncation and misrouting of tool/file attachments, and unclear behavior when callers combined streaming with multipart uploads. This PR: 1) Adds a rigorous multipart/form-data validation layer for streaming and non-streaming endpoints that enforces Content-Type and boundary checks, rejects ambiguous content types, and returns clear 4xx errors with machine-readable error codes. 2) Implements per-file and per-request limits for tool/file attachments (configurable via service-level flags and per-customer overrides) with graceful backpressure for streaming uploads. 3) Fixes streaming stability issues for chunked multipart bodies by introducing a streaming parser that can handle interleaved event frames and large binary parts without buffering the whole part in memory. 4) Extends the OpenAI compatibility shim so that tool calling semantics match expected types when files are present (file->tool reference translation, and deterministic multipart ordering). 5) Adds E2E tests for Python/TS SDKs, unit tests for the parser, integration tests exercising the compatibility layer, and examples in quickstarts and docs. Migration notes: Clients that previously relied on loosely typed content-types (e.g., sending application/json with a binary body) will now receive 400 errors and should switch to multipart/form-data or application/octet-stream. Checklists: - [x] parser and validation implementation - [x] config flags and per-customer overrides - [x] OpenAI-compat mapping updates - [x] SDK tests and quickstart examples - [x] docs and release notes

Priya Patel: Addressed in a1c3b9f and added tests for CRLF/LF; expanded comment in multipart_stream_parser.rs.

[Ephemeral stall mitigator and heartbeat leak patch]
release_notes:
Fix: mitigate transient control-plane stalls caused by heartbeat drift and KV checkpoint leak; add telemetry and canary rollout for health-gate state changes.

description:
Context and motivation: We observed intermittent regional stalls during high churn where control-plane health gates would hold requests open while a small subset of connections leaked KV cache checkpoints and failed to close cleanly. This manifested as a temporary spike in inflight slowpath requests and cascading per-tenant latency regressions despite available GPU capacity. The goal of this PR is to close the KV checkpoint leak, add a bounded stall mitigator on the health-gate path, and strengthen telemetry so SRE can detect recurrence quickly. Changes summary: 1) Introduce a lightweight stall mitigator state machine that limits per-connection slowpath retention with exponential backoff and a capped token budget; 2) Add a checkpoint-finalizer to runtime/kv to ensure in-flight KV checkpoints are reconciled on connection termination; 3) Harden the health_gate state transitions to tolerate transient heartbeat jitter and avoid sticky 'degraded' states; 4) Add telemetry tags and metrics (health_gate.state_changes, kv.checkpoint_finalized, stall_mitigator.evictions) and traces for the slowpath; 5) Add an integration test that simulates high-connection-churn and validates no stall persists beyond the configured quorum window; 6) Canary rollout plan via the helm values change to enable the mitigator by default in staging and 10% of production nodes. Commits (high-level): - 1a2b3c: initial refactor of health_gate to extract transition hooks and add unit tests - 2b3c4d: implement token-bucket stall mitigator and eviction logic - 3c4d5e: kv checkpoint finalizer and safe-reconcile flow with retry/backoff - 4d5e6f: telemetry and tracing annotations; update metric names and tag schema - 5e6f7g: integration test harness and canary helm values - 6f7g8h: fix for race condition found during CI run and test flake suppression Changed areas (high level): - services/controlplane/health_gate.go: refactor state machine, add transition hooks, integrate stall mitigator - runtime/kv/checkpoint_finalizer.go: ensure checkpoint is finalized on connection close - runtime/kv/persist.go: small reconciliation loop and retry policy - telemetry/metrics.go: new metrics and tag dimensions - tests/integration/ephemeral_stall_test.go: e2e simulation for churn - helm/values/staging.yaml: enable mitigator in staging - docs/operational/health-gate.md: operational notes and runbook (small doc additions) Checklist: - [x] Add unit tests for state transitions - [x] Integration test that simulates churn and verifies eviction within SLO window - [x] Telemetry + dashboard notes included - [x] Canary rollout values added - [x] Documentation and runbook updated Review conversation summary: - Marco Liu (SRE): "Observed pattern matches reported SUP-912; +1 on adding metrics but request to expose a percentile of stall duration and a labeled counter for evictions by reason." Author reply (Aisha): "Added stall_mitigator.duration_p50/p95 and stall_mitigator.eviction_reason tag in telemetry patch; included queries for the dashboard." - Sophie Kramer (Backend): "Refactor looks fine but please ensure the health_gate transition logging is not too verbose at scale." Author reply: "Switched to sampling logs at INFO for initial state changes and DEBUG for every transition; added a fail-safe to limit per-node transition logging to 5 events/sec." - Devon Brooks (Runtime): "Race on kv.persist noted in initial CI; suggest defensive nil-checks and a single reconcile goroutine per-connection." Author reply: "Applied single-goroutine reconcile and added an atomic guard; re-ran unit tests." CI summary: - Initial CI run: unit tests failed on a timing-sensitive test (race detected in kv persist); fixed in commit 6f7g8h. - Second CI run: all unit and integration tests passed. - E2E perf-canary job: passed with mitigator enabled in canary mode. Merge and rollout notes: - Merge method: squash and merge. - Merged to main and immediately deployed to staging via the helm/staging values update. - Production plan: progressive canary at 10% nodes for 24h with telemetry alerts (health_gate.state_flaps and stall_mitigator.evictions) and an automated rollback job if evictions exceed threshold for tenant fairness. Post-merge follow-ups: - Add a Grafana dashboard panel to surface eviction_reason breakdown (ENG-4821). - Run a 12-hour soak in staging and collect p50/p95 stall duration metrics (ENG-4873). - If any tenant sees >3 evictions/hour, trigger rollback and open an incident runbook (SUP-912). Rationale for this approach: The root cause is a combination of heartbeat jitter and unreconciled KV checkpoints; purely increasing timeouts hid the issue and allowed slowpath buildup. This mitigator restricts retention time, forces checkpoint finalization, and gives SRE the signals to act before customer-visible SLOs are impacted. Metrics added are intentionally low-cardinality with an eviction_reason tag to allow fast aggregation. Backwards compatibility and safety: The change is non-breaking; the mitigator is toggleable via helm values and defaults to off in legacy clusters. We validated the reconciler under load in the perf-canary harness and verified no regression in throughput. Merge outcome: merged via squash, closed associated Linear tickets as part of the merge commit message, and created a follow-up task to add an incident-runbook snippet to docs.

[introduce-server-timebox-and-idempotent-cancel-fallbacks-for-streaming-compat]
description:
Context: production customers observed cases where long lived streaming sessions (tool calls + structured output) were left in indeterminate states after a client network disconnect or a client-initiated Cancel. Motivation: we need a predictable server-side safety net that bounds resource residency time, ensures tool-call idempotency when retries/resume occur, and provides a clear fallback path (trimmed response + final event) that OpenAI-compatible clients can rely on. This PR implements a server-side streaming timebox (configurable per-route) that gracefully converts oversized/inflight streams into a final 'timeboxed' terminal event, augments client-cancel handling to be idempotent across reconnect/resume windows, and plumbs a compact resume token that includes tool-call idempotency metadata. Summary of changes: 1) stream manager: add configurable timebox_ms and a deterministic finalization path that emits a structured terminal event ("__redwood_timeboxed__") with a compact summary; 2) openai adapter: interpret Cancel events as idempotent markers tied to resume tokens; retries within the resume window will deduplicate tool calls using a request-level id; 3) tooling: map function-call invocations to idempotency keys and persist minimal call metadata to the stream checkpoint to support safe resume; 4) API: extend the OpenAI-compat streaming spec with two optional fields in the final event (timeboxed=true, resume_hint) without breaking existing clients; 5) tests & docs: integration tests for flaky network simulated disconnects and release notes for the behavior and recommended operational knobs. Rollout plan: feature guarded behind a runtime flag and route-level config. Backwards compatibility: default behavior is unchanged unless a route opts-in. Checklist: [x] unit tests for stream finalizer [x] integration test that simulates disconnect + resume [x] docs page and compatibility notes [x] change log entry. Related: ENG-1023 (stream lifecycle SLO), SUP-4572 (customer incident replicant).

commits:
stream: add timebox lifecycle and finalizer logic (runtime)
compat: interpret cancel as idempotent marker with resume token (openai adapter)
stream: persist minimal tool-call idempotency metadata to checkpoints
api: add 'timeboxed' and 'resume_hint' flags to streaming final event schema
tests: integration tests for disconnect/resume/timebox behavior
docs: add streaming-lifecycle/timebox operational runbook

Server-side streaming timebox (route-configurable) that guarantees a graceful terminal event when streams exceed a configured residency time. Client Cancel events are now idempotent within a short resume window; resume tokens include minimal idempotency hints to avoid duplicated tool/function executions on reconnect. Default behavior unchanged unless enabled per-route.

[signal-fencing-client-abort-edge-reconnect-policy-openai-compat]
description:
Motivation: Production customers continue to hit intermittent tailcases when clients disconnect mid-stream or issue a cancel while the server is still reconciling long-running tool calls. This leads to 'zombie' leases on backend resources, double-tool-invocations after reconnects, and confusing metrics spikes. This PR introduces a signal-fencing model paired with an edge-side reconnect policy to ensure client cancels and disconnects are handled deterministically while preserving OpenAI-compatible streaming semantics. Design summary: 1) Signal fencing: a short-lived fencing token is issued per streaming session lease. When a client sends a cancel/abort or disconnect occurs, the token moves the session into a quarantined state for a configurable grace window (default 30s). The server will honor idempotent tool-call markers only if the token is active; reconnects negotiate a fresh token plus an optional continuation handle. 2) Edge reconnect policy: the edge proxy supports a three-stage reconnect state machine (ACCEPT, QUARANTINE, REJECT) driven by lease expiry and backend load signals. Clients attempting to reconnect during QUARANTINE receive structured instructions (JSON payload) indicating whether to resume, re-request, or start a new session. 3) Tool/function calling semantics: function/tool invocations are gated by an invocation-id + token pair; duplicate requests outside the token window are rejected to prevent double-execution. 4) OpenAI adapter compatibility: kept existing streaming frames unchanged; the adapter injects a compatible control frame type ("x-control-signal") that downstream OpenAI-compat clients will ignore if not understood. 5) Rollout: feature-flag default off for hosted; enabled for dedicated/private on request for initial customers. Backwards compatibility: clients that don't understand the control frame will continue to operate normally; tool idempotency is strongly recommended but not required to adopt immediately. Implementation highlights: - server: src/server/streaming/orchestrator.py implements session fencing and state transitions, includes new metrics (fenced_sessions, resume_requests, quarantine(evictions)). - runtime: src/server/streaming/lease_manager.rs adds compact lease fingerprints and lease negotiation RPCs to support quick fencing checks. - adapter: api/openai/stream_adapter.go maps the new control frame to the OpenAI-compatible stream envelope. - client docs and examples: docs/api/streaming-lifecycle.md and examples/ts/reconnect-guides.md show recommended client backoff and token negotiation. Testing: new integration tests tests/integration/stream_quarantine_test.py simulate disconnects during in-flight tool invocations and assert single-execution and correct client instructions. Security/ops: KMS-backed token signing added so fences cannot be spoofed; audit logs now capture fence transitions. Release notes: see field below. This description string is continuous and contains checklist, design, testing, and rollout guidance for reviewers.

[Observability: add context-grokker service and tiered noise-gating for alerts]
body:
Motivation: Production SLO noise from long-running multi-turn chat and high-entropy embeddings has been driving alert churn for several tenants. We need a higher-fidelity signal that explains whether a cost/latency spike is meaningful or just context-driven noise. This PR introduces a lightweight observability component named 'context-grokker' that synthesizes per-invocation contextual anchors (prompt shape, token-phase profile, kv-cache hit heuristic, tenant burstiness score, embed-similarity bucket) and attaches a stable anchor id to spans and metrics so downstream alerting can make smarter decisions.\n\nSummary of changes: Implement context-grokker service that ingests invocation metadata and emits context.anchor tags; add proto metric definitions for anchor-backed rollups; enrich traces with anchor IDs; add a tiered noise-gating alert adapter that dynamically widens alert thresholds when anchors indicate known noisy patterns; ship console panels and a feature flag; add integration tests and a short runbook for operators.\n\nKey behavioral notes (what this does at runtime): The grokker computes an invocation-context score (0..1) and a discrete set of tags (prompt_shard, phase_profile, kv_warm, embed_cohort). The score aggregation is cheap (microsecond-level shim) and emitted as anchor.score metric. Alerts wired through the noise-gate adapter consult the anchor tags over a 5m sliding window: low score -> strict alerts, mid score -> dampened alerts (15-40% threshold widen depending on historical volatility), high score + known noisy cohort -> suppress duplicate alerts and surface a single summary. There is a hard fallback that never suppresses severity=P1.\n\nCommits (high level): - Add context-grokker core and API (service.go, README) - Add anchor proto and metric names (anchor.proto) - Trace enricher: attach anchor_id to span tags (anchor_linker.go) - Noise-gate adapter and alert tiering logic (noise_gate.go) - Console: dashboard + feature flag opt-in (context-grokker-overview.json, observability_flags.go) - Tests: integration harness and lightweight unit tests (context_grokker_test.go) - Docs: ops runbook and tuning guidelines (observability-noise-gating.md)\n\nFiles changed (high-level diff): - observability/grokker/service.go: New service and batching ingestion; core scoring function, 320 lines added. - telemetry/metrics/anchor.proto: new metric /tag definitions for anchor.score, anchor.cohort. - tracing/span_enricher/anchor_linker.go: span enrichment hook to attach anchor_id and anchor.score to existing spans. - alerts/noise_gate/noise_gate.go: alert adapter that consults recent anchors and applies tiered thresholding and dedup rules. - console/dashboards/context-grokker-overview.json: New dashboard with anchor cohort explorer, noise-decay meter, sample trace overlay. - integration-tests/observability/context_grokker_test.go: end-to-end checks including collision detection and alert-flow. - docs/ops/observability-noise-gating.md: operator runbook and rollout checklist.\n\nReview conversation (summary): Zoe: "Please add a unit test for anchor ID collisions and clarify lifetime semantics of anchor IDs for multi-stage invocations." -> Priya: "Added collision test and documented anchor TTL (10m by default, configurable via feature flag)." Liam: "Noise gate looks good but quantify how we pick widen factors per tenant." -> Priya: "Added tenant volatility estimator and defaults in the runbook; the console panel surfaces the recommended multiplier for each tenant so SREs can tune per-account." Andre: "Add a safety valve to always emit the raw token-cost metric (so we can audit suppression)." -> Priya: "Noise-gate preserves raw metrics in a hidden namespace (raw.*) and adds a suppression_reason tag; updated tests."\n\nCI and rollout notes: First CI run failed due to flaky integration test (timing-sensitive assert in context_grokker_test); I adjusted the test to use eventual consistency with a 15s retry window and reran. Subsequent CI passed (unit/integration/lint). Feature flag default is OFF; rollout plan is staged opt-in: enable for internal tenants first, then opt-in for a cohort of external tenants using feature flag gating. Metrics names are namespaced under observability.anchor.* to avoid collision.\n\nOperational impact and telemetry: New high-cardinality tags are limited to a small enumerated set (cohort buckets, prompt_shard) to avoid explosion; anchor_id is stable but ephemeral (TTL) and stored only on sampled traces and rollups; core metrics exposed: observability.anchor.score, observability.anchor.cohort, observability.anchor.ttl, observability.anchor.suppression_rate. We also added a dashboard and a short playbook for tuning the tiered wideners.\n\nRollback plan: Flip feature flag off, which immediately disables enrichment and returns all alerts to the existing static thresholds; docs include a quick remediation section for mis-suppressed P2/P3 alerts.\n\nRelease notes: Adds an optional observability component (context-grokker) that improves alert quality by tagging invocations with contextual anchors and enabling tiered noise-gating. Opt-in behind feature flag; no customer-facing API changes.\n\nMerge: Squash merged after approvals from reviewers; all CI green.\n

release_notes:
Optional context-grokker service to tag invocations with contextual anchors and a tiered noise-gating adapter to reduce alert churn. Opt-in behind a console feature flag. New metrics: observability.anchor.*

[Ordered Toolcall Reconciliation & Disconnect Splay for Streaming Resilience (OpenAI compat)]
description:
Motivation: customers running multi-tool conversations saw non-deterministic toolcall ordering after client disconnect + rapid reconnects which caused out-of-order side effects in third-party systems. This PR introduces server-side ordering guarantees for tool/function calls across reconnect/resume boundaries plus a client disconnect splay (randomized small backoff applied server-side to accept/reconcile reconnects) to avoid thundering reconnections. Design: 1) Sequence numbers: each stream session assigns a monotonic sequence number to each emitted event that can invoke a tool. Sequence numbers are signed by the server lease and attached to events sent to the client. 2) Reconciliation window: on reconnect the client can provide latest-acked-seq; server replays pending events in-order and drops duplicates. 3) Idempotency + ordered-apply: tool call invocations include an ordered_id composed of session_id:seq so downstream adapters (and the OpenAI compat shim) can apply tools in sequence. 4) Disconnect splay: when many clients disconnect during scale events we introduce a small randomized acceptance delay (0-300ms configurable) before reattaching the session lease to avoid simultaneous inflight reconnections overwhelming the tool adapters. 5) Config and compatibility: the OpenAI compatibility layer now accepts and emits ordered_toolcalls metadata on streaming endpoints and falls back to previous behavior when the flag is off. 6) Safety: added checks so that a resumed stream with an older lease is rejected; client must re-negotiate if server lease id mismatches. Rollout plan: feature gated behind streaming.reconnect.ordered_toolcalls, enabled for canary customers for 48 hours, metric-driven rollouts tied to toolcall error-rate and tail-latency. Tests: unit tests for seq assignment and validation, integration tests simulating N concurrent reconnects with artificial clock skew, e2e tests validating toolcall ordering against a mock adapter. Docs: docs/streaming/reconnect.md updated with semantics and migration steps. Implementation notes: implementation touches the session manager, ack manager, and OpenAI adapter layers to wire ordered ids into structured output. Commits are small and focused to ease bisecting. Backwards compatibility: when the client does not provide ordered metadata we maintain existing behavior; SDKs are updated to opt into the new behavior. Observability: added metrics streaming.reconnect.splay_applied and streaming.reconcile.ordered_replays to monitor adoption. 

release_notes:
Adds ordered reconciliation for tool/function calls during stream reconnects and introduces a randomized disconnect splay to reduce reconnect storms. OpenAI compatibility layer now preserves toolcall ordering and surfaces deterministic idempotency tokens. Behavior is opt-in via streaming.reconnect.ordered_toolcalls config; rollout staged behind a feature flag.

review_comments:
Ethan Cole: Nice focused change. Can we ensure the sequence number fits in 64 bits across long-lived sessions? Also request an extra unit test for seq wrap-around detection.
Maya Patel (author): Seq is u64 currently; added a test for wrap-around detection and defensive error path that forces session renewal when seq would overflow.
Ravi Singh: The disconnect splay param seems low for high fan-out events. Suggest making the upper bound configurable per deployment and exposing metric when splay is applied.
Maya Patel (author): Made upper bound configurable via streaming.reconnect.splay_max_ms and added streaming.reconnect.splay_applied metric and dashboards in observability pack.
Priya Nair: Integration test flaked in the first run due to timing; can we add a deterministic clock or retries to stabilize? Also ensure SDK changes have clear migration notes.
Maya Patel (author): Switched integration harness to use fake clock for deterministic behavior and added migration note in docs/streaming/reconnect.md. Marking as ready-for-merge after CI green.

merge_outcome:
Merged via squash on 2026-02-24 by Maya Patel after approvals from reviewers. Feature gated; no immediate global rollout. Canary enabled for 3% of streaming traffic and monitored for 48 hours.

notes:
Behavior is opt-in via streaming.reconnect.ordered_toolcalls; default remains backwards compatible.
SDKs: python/ts updated to include helpers for reconstructing ordered toolcall ids; patch released in minor versions.
Observability: new metrics added; dashboards updated in observability-pack repo.
Operational: when enabling globally, consider raising tool-adapter concurrency limits for first 24 hours to absorb ordered replays.

[Develop interactive tone derivatives and Kappa elevation scale for data grids]
description:
Objective: Create a deterministic system for producing interactive color derivatives (hover/focus/pressed/disabled) from the base semantic palette and introduce a physics-inspired elevation scale ("Kappa") tuned for dense data surfaces such as DataGrid, compact tables, and inline action bars.

Scope:
- Define algorithmic transforms to derive interactive tones from semantic base tokens (primary, neutral, success, caution, critical). The transforms must preserve WCAG contrast for actionable states and offer predictable deltas for designers and engineers.
- Introduce a Kappa elevation token family (kappa-0..kappa-6) with mapped umbra/penumbra/ambient values and matching colorized overlays for dark/light themes optimized for high-density rows.
- Propose spacing/radius adjustments for compact rows to align with new elevation cues while retaining hit-target accessibility.
- Update Figma token library and token spec (CSS vars + JSON token artifacts) and provide migration guidance for DataGrid, Table, Button, and InlineAction components.

Goals & Acceptance criteria:
1) Token spec: produce a stable token spec file (design JSON) that includes base palette, interactive derivatives (e.g., color.interactive.primary.hover), and elevation.kappa.{0..6} with explicit shadow parameters.
2) Implementation-ready: frontend repo receives a tokens PR implementing variables; DataGrid and Table components consume new tokens behind a feature flag.
3) Accessibility: automated contrast checks pass for all interactive states against 3:1 where applicable and 4.5:1 for primary actionable text.
4) Visual regression: add per-component visual snapshots and tolerances; no regressions beyond approved deltas.
5) Figma: updated design kit with tokenized components and guidance notes.
6) Rollout plan: canary on internal analytics dashboards -> staged rollout -> full migration with a fallback.

Design notes and trade-offs:
- Algorithmic derivation reduces token sprawl (fewer manual swatches) but requires deterministic tuning. We will prefer per-hue perceptual adjustments (Lab-space tweaks) over fixed lightness deltas to avoid color shifts across hues.
- Kappa elevation prioritizes subtle penumbra for dense rows; larger elevations are intentionally muted to avoid visual clutter. This might reduce perceived separation in extreme cases; provide an override token for high-contrast surfaces.
- Implementation should use runtime CSS variables for quick theming and a build-time compiled fallback for older clients. There are performance trade-offs when shipping many tokens; we will group tokens under semantic prefixes to keep runtime size manageable.

Migration plan:
1) Finalize tokens in design JSON and Figma (this ticket).
2) Engineered tokens PR (feature-flagged).
3) Update DataGrid/Table to read tokens; create opt-in toggle for compact Kappa mode.
4) Run automated visual diffs and accessibility scans.
5) QA and UAT with PM/Analytics team, then canary-release on internal dashboards for 2 weeks before full rollout.

Links and artifacts: see attachments.

[Compact density: inversion-safe token set and component overrides for high-density dark variants]
description:
Scope: Define a compact-density token set and corresponding component overrides that remain visually stable under color inversion or extreme contrast settings. This work is targeted at console views where high information density is required (dense tables, narrow sidebars, mini-charts) and where brand theming must not break readability or interaction affordances in dark or high-contrast environments. Outcome: a documented token subset, component override rules for buttons/tables/charts, implementation guidance for designers and engineers, and a migration path for existing console screens.

acceptance_criteria:
Token set includes neutral elevation tokens, two inversion-safe foreground scales, and two tint-preserving brand accents for dense UI
Buttons (primary/secondary/ghost) render legible labels at 12px/14px across contrast modes and pass WCAG AA text contrast for normal text sizes
Table zebra and grid separators adapt to dark dense surfaces without introducing perceptual noise; delta between row backgrounds adheres to contrast guidance
Mini line and sparkline charts maintain stroke visibility against inverted backgrounds and when overlaid on density surfaces
Design tokens are documented in Figma and exported JSON mapping for engineering with clear fallback rules and platform hints
Migration guide and rollout checklist published; can toggle new tokens behind a UI feature flag for experimentation

Use inverted-neutral tokens (surface-02..surface-04) rather than single 'surface' token to avoid mid-tone banding on mini-charts
Prefer semi-transparent overlays for separators (alpha over surface) instead of hard color shifts to preserve texture on dense rows
Brand accents for compact mode will map to two saturation tiers: accent-compact and accent-compact-muted, with explicit luminance targets for dark variants
Do not change existing global token names; supply a 'compact' token namespace (compact.surface-1, compact.fg-1) and migration aliases handled in runtime

[Construct composable token matrix and elevation presets]
description:
Problem: The current token set for color, radius, spacing and elevation has drifted after multiple ad-hoc fixes. This causes inconsistent shadows across cards, irregular radius combinations in dense tables, and duplicated semantic tokens (eg. surface-01 vs card-surface). Goal: Deliver a composable, ingredient-based token matrix that unifies color ramps, a 5-step radius scale, spacing cadence, and a deterministic elevation preset set (shadows + uplift) that maps to physical spacing and z-index usages. The deliverable includes token names, recommended usage guidelines, a migration mapping for components (buttons, tables, charts, cards), Figma styles, and a staged rollout plan with a compatibility layer for existing tokens.

acceptance_criteria:
1) Token matrix documented in Confluence with canonical names and rationale for each axis (hue, chroma, ramp, neutral ramp).
2) Elevation presets: 4 canonical elevations (surface, raised, overlay, modal) with exact shadow stacks and opacity steps.
3) All core components updated in Figma and a migration table mapping old tokens to new tokens.
4) Implementation guidance for engineering (CSS variables and JSON token export) and a migration PR created in the tokens repo.
5) Accessibility checks validated: contrast ratios meet AA for text on interactive surfaces and focus outlines preserved.

decisions:
- Adopt 4 semantic elevation presets (surface / card, raised / interactive, overlay / popover, modal / full-screen) instead of the previous 6-step physical ramp to reduce implementation complexity.
- Use rem-based spacing tokens with base 4px grid expressed as 0.25rem increments for consistency with existing CSS architecture.
- Radius scale standardized to 5 values: 0, 2, 6, 12, 24 (px) and exposed as token names radius-0..radius-4.
- Prefer semantic color tokens (bg-surface, bg-muted, accent-primary) backed by neutral and chromatic ramps rather than component-specific color names.
- Keep backward-compatibility aliases for 3 releases (aliases: card-surface -> bg-surface) and introduce a codemod to assist migration.

migration_plan:
Phase 1 (Week 1): Finalize token names and Figma styles. Phase 2 (Week 2): Export token JSON, open tokens repo PR with aliases and tests. Phase 3 (Week 3-4): Component spec updates (buttons, tables, charts) and small canary rollout in Console QA. Phase 4 (Week 5): Fleetwide migration, deprecate aliases after two releases.
Notes: Engineering will use a compatibility flag (feature flag 'new-tokens') to toggle usage during rollout.

[00:50] Miguel Alvarez: Miguel here. Cloud Commerce metering / billing integrations. Happy to go deep on dimensions, aggregation, rounding, and what reviewers will look for.

[01:01] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. Quick context: we’re replacing legacy listings. We now have Hosted API usage-based, Dedicated capacity, and Private deployment. We want the marketplace SKUs to map cleanly to our internal billing meters. The primary issues we want to avoid are dimension mismatches and the buyer gets invoiced for something weird.

[01:20] Miguel Alvarez: Yeah. The big thing is consistency. Dimension names and IDs in the offer need to match what you’re sending in metering events. And be careful if you’re changing them later—customers don’t like it and it can break reporting.

[01:35] Cole Summers: That’s exactly what we’re trying to nail. Let me outline what we were thinking and you can tell us what’s realistic. For Hosted, we meter “tokens generated” and “input tokens” internally, but we can expose it as “tokens” total if that’s simpler. We also have embeddings measured as “embedding units” (basically per 1K tokens equivalent). For Dedicated, we have reserved GPU capacity, which internally is monthly commit + overage. Private is more of a platform fee plus support tier.

[02:05] Miguel Alvarez: Okay. So in Cloud Marketplace, you can do usage-based dimensions and you can do subscription pricing models, and you can also do committed-use style constructs depending on the product type. Most SaaS partners keep it simple: one or a small number of usage dimensions, like “1K tokens” or “1M tokens”, and then for a base subscription you do a seat or a flat monthly fee.

[02:29] Nadia Rahman: Quick question on granularity. If we do “1K tokens” as the unit, do you see partners reporting fractional quantities? Like 123.456 units? Or is it recommended to round?

[02:41] Miguel Alvarez: You can send decimal quantities, but you should document how you compute it and be consistent. The most common pattern is you aggregate per hour or per day and send integer quantities. But for token meters, lots of folks send decimals, just be explicit. Rounding differences between your UI and the invoice is where support tickets come from.

[03:02] Ben Carter: On the onboarding side, we have this subscription -> entitlement -> Redwood org provisioning. One issue we see on AWS is entitlements sometimes take a few minutes to show up. Is that also a thing on GCP?

[03:14] Anika Desai: Yep. It’s not usually super long, but there can be propagation delay. The UX expectation is you handle “pending” gracefully. Like, don’t show a scary error that says “you are not entitled.” Instead say “we’re still syncing your subscription, retry in a few minutes” and maybe a refresh button.

[03:32] Stephanie Nguyen: That’s helpful. We’ve got an entitlement verification endpoint and a sync job; we can make sure the UI does the “pending” messaging.

[03:41] Priya Shah: Also important: the marketplace reviewers will click through the onboarding. If they hit a dead end, that’s friction during review. Provide a support link and clear instructions.

[03:53] Chris Osei: Got it. Maybe we jump into identifiers. Anika, can you talk about what we should store and what we can expect to receive? We’ve seen “consumer ID” in docs but there are like multiple names for it.

[04:07] Anika Desai: Yeah. So, you’ll have a procurement account / buyer account. When a customer subscribes, there’s an entitlement created. Depending on your integration, you’ll get a consumerId and entitlement name or resource. Your system should treat that as the source of truth for “is this customer subscribed” and also for mapping metering events to the right buyer.

[04:30] Cole Summers: For metering, we need a stable key to associate usage to the marketplace customer. We also have our internal “org_id”. So our thought was: marketplace entitlement maps to Redwood org, and then that org has one or more projects / API keys. Usage is aggregated at org level and then billed.

[04:49] Miguel Alvarez: That’s typical. Just ensure you don’t mix multiple entitlements into a single org without clear logic. If a customer buys two subscriptions, you need to decide whether that’s two entitlements attached to one org or two orgs. Reviewers will look for correct allocation.

[05:06] Ben Carter: We have an edge case: existing Redwood customers may subscribe later through marketplace for procurement reasons. So they want to link the marketplace subscription to an already-existing org.

[05:17] Anika Desai: That’s also common. UX expectation: you allow linking to an existing account. But ensure authentication is done. And avoid a scenario where someone can claim an entitlement that isn’t theirs.

[05:31] Stephanie Nguyen: Right. We require sign-in, then they paste an entitlement or we detect via login? We were thinking detect via a “claim token” page in our console.

[05:42] Anika Desai: Either works. Most partners do a redirect back with parameters, or they ask the user to input the entitlement ID. Redirect flows are nicer but more work. For review, either is acceptable as long as it’s documented.

[06:00] Chris Osei: For this phase we’re doing a marketplace-specific entrypoint in our console. It will prompt for “GCP marketplace subscription” and then run entitlement verification.

[06:10] Miguel Alvarez: That’s fine. On billing: I want to zoom in on the dimension list. Can you share what you propose?

[06:18] Cole Summers: We don’t have final IDs yet, but draft is something like:
- Hosted: “hosted_tokens_1k” and “hosted_embeddings_1k”
- Rerank: “rerank_requests_1k” (maybe)
- Dedicated: “dedicated_gpu_hour” or “dedicated_capacity_unit”
- Private: “private_platform_month”
- Add-ons: “compliance_pack_month”, “extended_audit_log_retention_month”
The big question is whether “Dedicated” should be a usage dimension or a subscription SKU.

[06:55] Miguel Alvarez: Dedicated capacity tends to fit better as subscription / contract. Usage metering for “gpu hours” works, but you need to align it with what you’re actually providing. If it’s truly reserved, then a monthly subscription fee is clearer. If there’s burst/overage, you can meter overage separately.

[07:16] Nadia Rahman: We can do either. Internally we track reserved pool size and then tokens anyway, but the contract is the key. If you recommend subscription for reserved, then our metering is mostly for overage.

[07:29] Priya Shah: From a procurement standpoint, enterprise buyers usually prefer a predictable subscription line item. Then usage-based Hosted is more PLG.

[07:41] Stephanie Nguyen: That matches what we’re seeing. One thing we’re worried about: we want three clear “paths” in the listing—Hosted, Dedicated, Private. But under the hood GCP constructs are not always “three products.” It’s one listing with plans, right?

[07:57] Priya Shah: Exactly. You typically have one product listing and multiple plans. You can describe the three modes in the copy, but technically it’s one product with pricing plans.

[08:12] Ben Carter: On the onboarding, would you expect different landing pages for different plans? Like, if someone buys Private, they shouldn’t be dropped into “create API key and call the hosted endpoint” because their next step is networking and deployment.

[08:26] Anika Desai: That’s a good point. Ideally yes: after entitlement, route them to the appropriate next steps. But you can also have a general landing page that asks “what did you purchase?” or reads the plan from the entitlement.

[08:43] Cole Summers: Reading the plan from entitlement is doable if the entitlement includes plan name. We just need to be careful with plan rename.

[08:52] Miguel Alvarez: Plan rename is okay if you keep the underlying plan ID stable. Don’t key logic off display name.

[09:01] Chris Osei: Noted. We’ll key off ID.

[09:05] Stephanie Nguyen: Let’s talk about reviewer expectations on the metering payload. Miguel, can you share what they check?

[09:14] Miguel Alvarez: Sure. They’ll check: (1) you’re using the correct API endpoints, (2) the consumerId or entitlement is valid, (3) the dimension is a valid one configured in your offer, (4) the quantity is non-negative and within reason, (5) timestamps are sane (not future by a day), (6) idempotency—you don’t double bill on retry.

[09:40] Nadia Rahman: On idempotency: we have an internal “usage_event_id” and we can keep a ledger. If we retry, we send the same event id. Is that a pattern you like to see?

[09:52] Miguel Alvarez: Yes. Exactly. Store the request ID and mark it as sent. Most of the “billing mismatch” issues are duplicate sends during outages.

[10:05] Ben Carter: Do you have any advice on how to validate end-to-end that metering is going to show up for the customer? Like, in AWS we can see it in the buyer account pretty quickly.

[10:15] Miguel Alvarez: On GCP, you can see metering records in the partner console and via reports, but it’s not always instant. For testing, you want to confirm your API calls succeed and then use the console to verify the usage events are recorded. Anika can share the checklist.

[10:33] Anika Desai: Yeah, I can send a link. There’s a “test buyer” flow too. You procure with a test account, then you validate that entitlement is created and your backend can resolve it.

[10:47] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. Another question: dimension naming constraints. We saw some limitations around character length and allowed characters.

[10:56] Miguel Alvarez: Keep it short, alphanumeric plus underscore usually. Avoid spaces. If you have to include a version, don’t. Better to keep the same dimension and change the price model rather than changing the dimension name.

[11:13] Cole Summers: That’s helpful. We were going to do “hosted_tokens_1k” rather than “hosted_input_tokens_1k” and “hosted_output_tokens_1k” to keep it one dimension. We can still show the breakdown in our console for observability, but bill as total tokens.

[11:32] Miguel Alvarez: That’s a good compromise.

[11:35] Stephanie Nguyen: And embeddings we can keep separate.

[11:38] Miguel Alvarez: Yes.

[11:40] Chris Osei: I want to make sure we cover onboarding UX expectations. Ben, can you describe what we’re building and get GCP feedback?

[11:49] Ben Carter: Sure. So in our console, when you click “Get started”, there will be a “Purchased via marketplace?” path. If they choose GCP marketplace, we ask them to sign in. Then we try to auto-detect entitlements tied to that user, and if we can’t, we allow them to paste an entitlement ID. If entitlement is found, we show “link to existing org” or “create new org.” After that, we prompt them to create first API key for Hosted, or if the plan is Dedicated/Private, we route to request provisioning steps.

[12:24] Anika Desai: That’s pretty aligned with what we like to see. Two things: (1) make it very clear what to do if they’re not the person who purchased. Sometimes procurement buys and engineering uses. So include instructions like “ask the billing admin to invite you” or “forward this entitlement ID.” (2) include a retry experience for pending entitlements.

[12:50] Ben Carter: Yep. We have an error state “Entitlement not found” that currently suggests contacting support. We can change that to “may take a few minutes” and include refresh.

[13:02] Priya Shah: Also include support SLA information and the right support channel for marketplace customers. It doesn’t have to be complex, but the listing should say how to get help.

[13:12] Stephanie Nguyen: We’ll incorporate that into listing FAQs. On testing: we need a clear test plan. Chris, we have some draft steps; can we align with GCP?

[13:22] Chris Osei: Yeah. Proposed test checklist:
1) Subscribe to plan in GCP Marketplace using test buyer
2) Verify entitlement exists (via API/console)
3) In Redwood console, run entitlement verification and link/create org
4) Generate an API key
5) Send a small set of inference requests (chat/text and embeddings)
6) Verify metering calls succeed and appear under correct dimension
7) Cancel subscription and verify access behavior (grace period?)
8) Re-subscribe / plan change and verify entitlements update
9) Negative tests: wrong entitlement, cross-org linking, delayed propagation

[14:03] Miguel Alvarez: That’s good. On cancellation: define your policy. Some partners cut off immediately, some allow a grace period. But it needs to match your listing terms and how you interpret the entitlement state.

[14:18] Cole Summers: Our default is to stop accepting billable traffic if entitlement is inactive, but we may allow a short grace if the cancellation is accidental. For marketplace we probably keep it strict.

[14:31] Anika Desai: During review, they’ll test cancel and see if your UI reflects it. If there’s a grace, document it.

[14:40] Nadia Rahman: On entitlement state changes, how quickly do we see “active -> cancelled”? That’s a potential race.

[14:49] Anika Desai: It’s usually quick, but again, you should poll or have a scheduled sync. Don’t assume immediate.

[15:00] Ben Carter: We have a sync job that runs every few minutes and on-demand verification. We can tighten it during onboarding.

[15:08] Miguel Alvarez: Just be careful with rate limits. If you have everyone spamming “verify entitlement” you might hit quotas. But for normal scale it’s okay.

[15:19] Stephanie Nguyen: One more thing: our SKUs include compliance add-ons (like extended audit log retention, compliance pack). Is it common to have add-ons as separate dimensions or separate plans?

[15:34] Priya Shah: It depends. If it’s truly an add-on, separate plan can be complicated. Some do “bundle plans” (base + add-on). Others handle add-ons off-marketplace. If you want it procured via marketplace, bundling plans is usually easiest.

[15:54] Miguel Alvarez: If you do it as a usage dimension, that’s weird for a monthly compliance pack. Better as subscription line item. But you can create a plan called “Hosted + Compliance” and so on.

[16:09] Cole Summers: That increases plan combinatorics. We were trying to keep it minimal.

[16:14] Stephanie Nguyen: For enterprise procurement, it might be okay. We can do a small number: Hosted, Hosted+Compliance, Dedicated, Dedicated+Compliance, Private. Something like that.

[16:26] Priya Shah: Exactly. Keep it manageable.

[16:29] Chris Osei: Let’s capture that as an open decision: add-ons as bundles vs separate plans.

[16:35] Ben Carter: If it’s bundled, onboarding can still read plan ID and show the right “features enabled” banner.

[16:42] Anika Desai: Yep.

[16:44] Miguel Alvarez: For dimensions, fewer is better. If you have too many, it’s harder to validate.

[16:52] Nadia Rahman: Another metering nuance: we do streaming responses. Tokens get generated over time. We aggregate at end of request. That means we may emit one usage record per request or per batch. Is that okay?

[17:07] Miguel Alvarez: That’s okay. The marketplace doesn’t care if you batch, as long as it’s accurate and you can explain your aggregation. Many partners aggregate per hour to reduce volume.

[17:19] Cole Summers: We can aggregate per hour per org per dimension. That’s probably a good default.

[17:26] Miguel Alvarez: Yes.

[17:28] Stephanie Nguyen: Any pitfalls with multi-region? Our hosted API runs in multiple regions. If a GCP marketplace buyer uses us in EU, does billing care?

[17:39] Priya Shah: Billing doesn’t care, but listing and security docs might. If you claim data residency, make sure it’s accurate. The marketplace reviewers may look at your data handling statements.

[17:52] Chris Osei: We’re preparing a security packet; we’ll align wording.

[17:57] Anika Desai: From onboarding side, if you route them to a region selection, ensure it’s clear. Some customers think marketplace implies region-specific. It doesn’t necessarily.

[18:10] Ben Carter: We plan to ask region at org creation and default to the closest region, but allow override.

[18:18] Stephanie Nguyen: Great.

[18:20] (brief crosstalk)

[18:22] Stephanie Nguyen: Miguel, can we ask about “dimension mismatch” issues you’ve seen? We had one on AWS where our internal meter name didn’t match the marketplace dimension and we billed wrong. We’re trying to prevent it.

[18:37] Miguel Alvarez: Yeah, common. It’s usually one of: using display name instead of dimension ID, or typos, or changing the offer and not updating code. The best practice: keep a single source config file for mapping, version it, and add automated tests that validate the dimension list against what’s configured in marketplace.

[18:57] Cole Summers: We have a billing catalog config in code. We can add a test that asserts “these dimensions are the only allowed ones.” But we can’t programmatically query the marketplace config easily.

[19:10] Miguel Alvarez: You can still do a manual gate before launch: export the dimension list and compare. And once stable, don’t change often.

[19:21] Nadia Rahman: We also emit telemetry events in our pipeline. We can alert on unknown dimension errors.

[19:28] Miguel Alvarez: Perfect. Set alerts on 4xx responses from metering API.

[19:35] Chris Osei: Okay. Let’s do a quick pass on what GCP needs for submission beyond billing: screenshots, support, security docs, etc. Priya?

[19:46] Priya Shah: You’ll need: final listing copy, pricing plans configured, support contact info, a privacy policy link, and security documentation depending on the category. For enterprise oriented products, we often see SOC 2 statements, encryption, retention, audit logging. You don’t need to paste the whole report, but your claims must be accurate.

[20:10] Stephanie Nguyen: Understood. We’ll provide a marketplace security overview and pointers to evidence under NDA.

[20:18] Anika Desai: Reviewers like diagrams. Even a simple data flow diagram helps.

[20:23] Ben Carter: We have a diagram showing subscription -> entitlement -> Redwood control plane -> inference runtime. We’ll use it.

[20:31] Chris Osei: Back to testing. Anika, you mentioned a test buyer flow. Can you outline quickly? Just so we know if we need special accounts.

[20:40] Anika Desai: Typically you’ll have a partner test project and a test buyer project. You procure your own product as a test buyer. Then you verify that your integration receives the entitlement. If you’re using the Cloud Commerce Partner API, you can query entitlements. If you’re using webhooks, ensure those are wired. Since you’re doing a console-based claim flow, you can also validate by retrieving entitlement status from your backend.

[21:08] Cole Summers: We’re using the partner API and a sync job, plus on-demand verify endpoint. Webhook we considered but didn’t want to rely solely on it.

[21:19] Miguel Alvarez: That’s fine. Webhook can be flaky if not retried. Polling plus retry is okay, just mind quotas.

[21:30] Nadia Rahman: For quotas, do you have ballpark? Like requests per minute? We’re not huge but we want to be safe.

[21:38] Miguel Alvarez: It depends on the project and API. I’ll send the doc. But generally, if you do a sync every 5 minutes and on-demand for onboarding, you’re fine.

[21:53] Stephanie Nguyen: Great.

[21:55] (pause)

[21:56] Ben Carter: A small UX question: when entitlement is not found, do you recommend we show “wait 10 minutes” or “wait 2 minutes”? We don’t want to over-promise.

[22:06] Anika Desai: I’d say “a few minutes” and allow retry. And show a timestamp “last checked at” to reassure them you’re doing something.

[22:18] Ben Carter: Nice idea.

[22:20] Chris Osei: Another edge case: procurement might buy in a different Google identity than the engineer uses (like billing@company.com). That means auto-detect entitlements won’t work.

[22:31] Anika Desai: Exactly. That’s why inputting entitlement ID is helpful, or a separate “admin invites user” workflow.

[22:41] Stephanie Nguyen: We’ll make sure docs call that out.

[22:45] Miguel Alvarez: On billing, one more thing: if you’re doing token usage, define what “token” means. Different models count differently. You should base it on what you count internally, but documentation should say it’s per model tokenizer.

[23:01] Cole Summers: Good point. Our API already reports token usage per request in the response metadata. We can use that as source of truth.

[23:10] Nadia Rahman: And we can expose daily usage summaries in console to match marketplace billing.

[23:15] Miguel Alvarez: That’s helpful for customer trust.

[23:19] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay. Let’s talk about dimension naming and plan structure. It sounds like recommended is:
- Hosted plan with usage dimensions (tokens, embeddings)
- Dedicated plan as subscription, possibly with an overage usage dimension
- Private plan as subscription
- Compliance add-on as bundle plans (Hosted+Compliance etc)
Is that fair?

[23:44] Priya Shah: Yes.

[23:46] Miguel Alvarez: Yes, that would be a clean structure.

[23:49] Cole Summers: For Dedicated overage, would we meter tokens or something else? Because customers might still care about tokens, not GPU hours.

[23:59] Miguel Alvarez: If the overage is “extra usage beyond included”, tokens is okay. If it’s “extra capacity”, maybe hours. But tokens is more straightforward given your product.

[24:12] Cole Summers: Great. We’ll think through included vs overage.

[24:16] Chris Osei: I want to make sure we leave with concrete outputs. Cole will send a proposed mapping table and example payloads. Anika and Miguel will send docs and constraints. Ben will share screenshots/wireframes.

[24:31] Stephanie Nguyen: One question: in GCP marketplace, do customers expect to get credits / trial? We offer free credits on our website; does marketplace support that?

[24:41] Priya Shah: Marketplace trials exist in some contexts but not universally. Many partners handle trials outside marketplace or do a low-cost starter plan. If you want a trial, we can discuss, but it may complicate approval.

[24:56] Stephanie Nguyen: We’ll keep it simple for now.

[24:59] Ben Carter: Another thing: we have a dedicated onboarding docs page. Is it okay to link external docs from the listing?

[25:07] Priya Shah: Yes, you can link to documentation. Just make sure it’s stable URLs.

[25:12] Chris Osei: We’re finalizing vanity redirects for marketplace. Okay.

[25:16] (minor audio glitch)

[25:18] Nadia Rahman: Can we ask about time window for metering submissions? Like can we send usage events delayed by a day?

[25:26] Miguel Alvarez: There is a window; don’t send extremely late. A few hours delay is okay. A day is sometimes okay but not ideal. Send as close to real time as possible. Again, I’ll send guidance.

[25:43] Nadia Rahman: Got it.

[25:45] Cole Summers: For retry logic, if API errors, we retry with exponential backoff. If it fails for a long time, we queue. We can cap backlog.

[25:54] Miguel Alvarez: That’s fine. But make sure you don’t exceed the allowed backfill window.

[26:02] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay.

[26:04] Priya Shah: Any other questions from Redwood before we wrap?

[26:09] Stephanie Nguyen: I have one more: procurement question. Some buyers will ask “does buying through marketplace change the support terms / SLAs?” We have dedicated support tiers. Do you see any constraints on what we can say?

[26:23] Priya Shah: You can state support terms clearly. Just avoid promising things you can’t deliver. If there’s a premium SLA, you can make it a plan or an add-on, but it should be consistent.

[26:37] Ben Carter: We’ll align with our support team.

[26:40] Chris Osei: Okay. Let’s do a quick recap and next steps.

[26:45] Chris Osei: Recap:
- Dimension strategy: keep Hosted usage-based with a small set of dimensions (tokens, embeddings), use subscription plans for Dedicated/Private, consider bundled plans for compliance add-ons.
- Use stable IDs, don’t key logic off display names.
- Handle entitlement propagation delays with friendly UI + retry.
- Implement idempotency for metering events and alert on 4xx errors.
- Run staging test: subscribe -> entitlement -> org link -> API key -> sample traffic -> verify metering -> cancellation/plan change.

[27:21] Stephanie Nguyen: And action items: Cole will send draft mapping + payload examples, Ben will send UX screens, Anika/Miguel will send docs on quotas/rounding/validation.

[27:33] Anika Desai: Yep.

[27:35] Miguel Alvarez: Yep, I’ll send the metering validation checklist and rounding recommendations.

[27:40] Priya Shah: And once you’ve done the staging test, we can do a short follow-up to review results and any issues.

[27:48] Stephanie Nguyen: Perfect. Thanks everyone.

[27:51] (call continues with scheduling chatter)

[28:00] Chris Osei: I’ll send the notes and propose a follow-up next week.

[28:05] Priya Shah: Great.

[28:07] Meeting ended (recording continued briefly)

summary:
