[Edge switch ARP proxying leads to VPN client IP duplication and intermittent routing to wrong host]
description:
Issue summary: Several users reporting intermittent loss of access to internal services while connected to corporate VPN. Symptoms include duplicate IP conflict alerts on endpoints, frequent VPN re-auth events, and traffic appearing to be routed to a different on-prem host (service 10.23.5.12). Impact: ~8% of VPN sessions in us-west over the last 48h experienced short blackholes (30-90s) impacting git pushes, internal CI jobs, and ssh sessions. Scope: affects users on Wi-Fi SSID 'Redwood-Corp' behind specific edge switches in building SF2 rack 7.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Connect laptop to 'Redwood-Corp' Wi-Fi in SF2 building (tested on macOS 13 and Ubuntu 22.04)
2) Establish VPN session to redwood-vpn-usw.redwood.net (WireGuard-based corporate VPN)
3) Trigger continuous ping to an internal host (ping -i 0.2 10.23.5.12)
4) Observe intermittent duplicate IP warnings on client and packets forwarded to an unexpected MAC on the L2 domain
5) Reproduce frequency increases when there is a short burst of multicast/mDNS traffic on the same AP's radio

observed_logs_and_artifacts:
Client syslog excerpt: 'kernel: arp: IP address 10.23.8.45 claimed by 00:11:22:33:44:55 (conflict)'
Switch (edge-sw-7) log: 'proxy-arp conflict detected for 10.23.8.45, source 00:66:77:88:99:AA bridging-port 5'
Packet capture (pcap) snippet: ARP reply for 10.23.8.45 with two different source MACs within 120ms
VPN server metrics: client rekey count spike (client 10.23.8.45) correlated to timestamp 2026-03-12T14:12Z
Internal service (10.23.5.12) reported TCP reset spikes aligning with client blackholes

investigation_notes:
Hypothesis 1: Edge switch proxy-arp configured for legacy NAT path is responding to ARP for VPN-assigned addresses from an overlapping DHCP pool, causing two active ARP entries on the LAN.
Hypothesis 2: A misconfigured VXLAN/bridge on edge-sw-7 is advertising ARP for the VPN subnet into the campus L2 segment when multicast bursts occur.
What we tried: - Disabled proxy-arp on edge-sw-7 port-channel to AP group temporarily (no immediate reduction). - Isolated a suspect AP by moving a test client to a different AP (blackhole persisted only when client served by AP-7A). - Captured pcap on AP, switch uplink, and VPN server concurrently for correlated timestamps (pcaps saved to /mnt/logs/INT-460811/pcaps/).
Preliminary find: ARP 'gratuitous' replies with VPN client IP are being injected by the switch's 'proxy-arp' feature only when the AP's multicast queue exceeds threshold. The switch returns ARP for the same IP with a different MAC that matches a spare management interface in rack 7 (00:66:77:88:99:AA).

impact_summary:
Intermittent connectivity loss for internal developer workflows (git/ssh/CI). Approximately 8% of VPN sessions in the SF2 us-west site affected in the window; potential for data-transfer retries and CI flakiness. No customer-facing outage but notable developer productivity hit.

initial_triage_actions:
1) Placed affected edge switch (edge-sw-7) in monitoring schedule and enabled debug logging for proxy-arp events.
2) Temporarily increased DHCP lease affinity for VPN pool for clients in SF2 to reduce the window for IP reuse.
3) Asked campus networking team to disable 'proxy-arp' global feature on a staging switch and observe (ongoing).
4) Notified platform reliability and CI owners of potential re-run needs for impacted jobs (Slack #incidents and #platform-alerts).

comments:
2026-03-11 09:18 - Jonah Reed: Assigned to network; will coordinate switch config changes and gather pcaps. Next action: schedule maintenance window if we need to push config rollback.
2026-03-12 15:25 - Priya Shah (campus-net): Reproduced proxy-arp responses on edge-sw-7 when AP multicast queue > 70%. Suspect firmware 1.2.3 on these switches has a known misc bridging bug. Opened ticket with vendor (TAC-889233).
2026-03-13 08:52 - Jonah Reed: Vendor TAC confirmed the switch may respond to ARP for non-local subnets under multicast overload in 1.2.3. Recommended immediate mitigation: set 'proxy-arp disable' on VRF for AP VLANs and upgrade firmware to 1.2.6.
2026-03-14 07:30 - Aisha Malik: Applied 'proxy-arp disable' to edge-sw-7 in staged maintenance window (07:00-07:15). Monitoring: VPN rekey spikes reduced from 47/hr to 2/hr for affected clients in the first 24h.
2026-03-14 10:02 - Jonah Reed: Confirming RFC and rollout plan for global fix. Proposed follow-up: firmware upgrade across SF2 rack 4-9, audit for proxy-arp enabled on other edge switches, and update config baseline to explicitly disable proxy-arp for VPN/DHCP subnets.

root_cause:
Switch firmware (1.2.3) bug caused proxy-arp behavior under high multicast load leading to ARP advertisements for VPN-assigned addresses. This created ephemeral duplicate IP assignments on the L2 domain and caused VPN clients to experience routing blackholes and rekeys.

resolution_notes:
Mitigation applied: 'proxy-arp disable' set on edge-sw-7 AP VLANs during maintenance window 2026-03-14 07:00-07:15.
Temporary workaround: increased DHCP lease affinity and moved high-multicast APs to separate RF profile to reduce multicast bursts.
Permanent fix: planned firmware upgrade to 1.2.6 across SF2 edge switches (racks 4-9) and config baseline change to disable proxy-arp for VPN/DHCP subnets. Vendor TAC provided patch notes and recommended upgrade path.
Follow-ups: - Create change request CR-2026-0415 for firmware rollout. - Run campus-wide audit script to detect 'proxy-arp' enabled instances and remediate. - Add regression test to onboarding checklist for AP multicast stress.
Status: Partial fix applied and validated; full remediation scheduled (see CR-2026-0415).

[Intermittent SF HQ Wi-Fi disconnects and corporate VPN DNS resolution failures (split-tunnel)]
description:
Issue summary:
Multiple SF office users report intermittent Wi-Fi disconnects over the past 48 hours. Users who subsequently reconnect via the corporate VPN experience DNS resolution failures for internal services (e.g., vault.redwood.local, internal-console.redwood.local). Root cause unknown; appears correlated with a configuration change on the office firewall or DHCP/DNS behavior when clients switch networks.

Impact:
- ~12-18 users affected sporadically during business hours (engineering, sales desks on 4th floor).
- Developers cannot access internal-only services after connecting to VPN until DNS cache/route is cleared or laptop rebooted.
- Productivity impact: medium-high during intermittent windows.

Environment:
- SF HQ office Wi-Fi (SSIDs: Redwood-Employee, Redwood-Guest) managed by Meraki MS/ MR stack behind Palo Alto PA-5260 firewall.
- Corporate VPN: OpenVPN server cluster (private), split-tunnel enabled for internet traffic; internal subnets routed via VPN.
- Timeframe first reports: 2026-03-09 09:40 PST.

Observed behavior:
- Wi-Fi disconnects: client reports 'Disconnected' then reconnects to same SSID; DHCP lease renewals logged on Meraki controller.
- After rejoin and VPN connect: client resolves public DNS but not internal short names; nslookup against 10.0.0.10 (internal DNS) times out intermittently.
- Some clients require ipconfig/flushdns + dhclient restart or full reboot to restore internal name resolution.

Expected behavior:
- Seamless reconnection to Wi-Fi and VPN without loss of internal DNS resolution; split-tunnel should still route internal domains to 10.0.0.10 DNS.

Temporary workaround:
- Instruct affected users to run: "sudo systemd-resolve --flush-caches" (Linux) or "ipconfig /flushdns" (Windows) and then restart the VPN client. Reboot if that fails.

Notes about scope:
- Guest SSID is unaffected. Wired clients do not report issues. Problem appears tied to Wi-Fi client state transitions and DNS server reachability immediately after VPN bring-up.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Connect a laptop to Redwood-Employee SSID in SF HQ (4th floor).
2) Authenticate and obtain DHCP lease.
3) Establish OpenVPN connection with split-tunnel enabled.
4) Attempt to resolve an internal hostname (vault.redwood.local) or access internal-console URL.
5) If Wi-Fi disconnects and reconnects during the session, note DNS failures immediately after reconnection.

Observed: DNS timeouts or NXDOMAIN for internal names until local cache cleared or network restarted.

logs:
Meraki event snippets (times in PST):
- 2026-03-09T09:38:12: Client AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF association failure: DHCP timeout
- 2026-03-09T09:38:19: Client AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF re-associated, DHCP assigned 10.88.45.102

OpenVPN client log (example):
- Tue Mar 09 09:39:05 2026 ERROR: RESOLVE: Cannot resolve host address: 10.0.0.10: DNS lookup failed
- Tue Mar 09 09:39:07 2026 NOTE: sequence of routes added: 10.0.0.0/16 -> tun0
- Tue Mar 09 09:39:08 2026 WARNING: DNS push failed, fallback to system resolver

System DNS resolution trace (from affected laptop):
- dig +short @10.0.0.10 vault.redwood.local -> ;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached
- dig +short @1.1.1.1 vault.redwood.local -> 203.0.113.50 (public) -> incorrect; internal name leaked to public resolver

investigation_notes:
- 2026-03-10: Support confirmed 12 initial reports from SF; reproduced on MacBook Pro (macOS 13.6) and Ubuntu 22.04.
- Hypothesis 1: Meraki controller DHCP reassignments are briefly dropping local route advertisement; clients rebind with DNS search domain lost.
- Hypothesis 2: Palo Alto firewall policy update (2026-03-09 02:00 UTC) altered NAT rules for split-tunnel, causing internal DNS traffic to be NATed to public interface resulting in dropped packets.
- Collected packet captures from affected client (pcap attached to INT-4102) showing DNS queries leaving tun0 but no replies from 10.0.0.10 during failure window.
- Verified OpenVPN server config pushes DNS 10.0.0.10 and route 10.0.0.0/16; server logs show successful push but some clients log 'DNS push failed'.
- Meraki telemetry shows spikes in DHCP handshake failures coincident with the times users reported drops (see Meraki dashboard link).
- Quick test: creating a temporary static DNS entry in laptop /etc/hosts allowed access to internal-console immediately after reconnect, indicating name resolution is primary failure, not routing entirely.

comments:
Aisha Patel (2026-03-10 10:02 PST): Notified office support desk to collect affected MACs and seat locations. Pls escalate to networking team - several engineers blocked.
Diego Alvarez (2026-03-10 11:45 PST): I pulled PA firewall audit logs for 2026-03-09 01:30-03:30 UTC. Found a config commit at 2026-03-09 02:05 UTC titled 'egress nat policy tweak' by network-admin. Will coordinate rollback window.
Morgan Chen (SRE) (2026-03-10 12:10 PST): Packet captures received (linked INT-4102). I see DNS queries to 10.0.0.10 with no response; traceroutes show tun0 present. Suggest testing with split-tunnel disabled to confirm whether issue is DNS over VPN only.
Diego Alvarez (2026-03-11 09:08 PST): Rolled back the egress NAT change in a controlled window (09:00-09:15 PST). Post-rollback initial checks show fewer DNS timeouts; monitoring continues.
Riley Brooks (Office IT) (2026-03-12 16:20 PST): Collected additional user reports after rollback — two users still had problems after afternoon hotspot maintenance. We swapped APs for those desks; both recovered. Could be flaky AP and concurrent firewall change made it visible.
Diego Alvarez (2026-03-14 08:39 PST): Follow-up: request to schedule a deeper config audit for Meraki <-> Palo Alto interactions and to add a health-check monitor for internal DNS reachability over VPN. Assigned INT-4199 for monitoring task.

1) Run controlled tests with split-tunnel disabled on a set of affected clients to confirm DNS behavior (SRE + Networking).
2) Audit Meraki DHCP lease churn on 4th floor APs and check for firmware updates; replace flaky APs (Office IT).
3) Add active health check that queries internal DNS (10.0.0.10) over VPN for SF office and alert on failures (Monitoring / Observability).
4) Create a firewall rule test plan: replay NAT change in staging and validate DNS packet handling (Network team).
5) Follow-up ticket INT-4199 created for long-term monitoring and INT-4200 for Meraki firmware rollout.

resolution:
In progress - temporary rollback of egress NAT rule reduced incidents. Ongoing follow-ups: AP replacements and DNS health-checks scheduled. No permanent root-cause confirmed yet.

[IPv6 privacy address rotation breaks WireGuard peer rekey and SSH sessions]
description:
Issue summary: Several engineers reported losing long-lived SSH sessions to internal hosts after laptops moved between access points or after system suspend/resume. Root cause appears to be IPv6 temporary (privacy) address rotation causing the endpoint observed by the WireGuard peer to change, triggering a rekey and leaving in-flight TCP sessions (SSH) stalled until a manual restart of the VPN interface or agent.

Impact: Intermittent session drops for ~10-20% of laptop handoffs and after suspend/resume. Affects internal engineering teams in SF office on corporate Wi‑Fi using the zero-trust WireGuard client. Not customer-facing but high productivity impact for on-site devs.

Observed behavior: On move/suspend event the laptop obtains a new IPv6 privacy address. WireGuard peer sees endpoint change and performs handshake/rekey. Some existing TCP connections are not NAT-translated correctly by the office AP/NAT path during the transition, causing SSH connections to hang (no packet flow). "Restart wg" or disabling IPv6 temporary address on the host restores connectivity.

Expected behavior: WireGuard rekey should be seamless and preserve TCP sessions or zero-trust agent should gracefully migrate NAT mappings so SSH and other long-lived connections survive address rotation.

Additional context: Several ticketed occurrences correlate to AP handoffs within the same SSID (fast BSS transition) and to kernel privacy address regeneration events (net.ipv6.conf.*.use_tempaddr).

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Boot laptop and connect to corporate Wi‑Fi (office sf).
2) Establish long-lived SSH session to internal bastion (ssh -T -o TCPKeepAlive=yes).
3) Trigger suspend/resume or force AP roam (move between desks/rooms).
4) Observe that laptop acquires a new IPv6 temporary address (ip -6 addr show).
5) Observe WireGuard rekey/handshake on the server side (wg show / journalctl -u wg-quick).
6) Verify that SSH stalls and packets are not forwarded until wg-quick restart or zero-trust-agent restart.

logs:
Client: ip -6 addr show dev wlp3s0 -> inet6 2601:XXXX:YYYY:ABCD:ZZZZ:ZZZZ:ZZZZ:1234/64 scope global temporary dynamic
Server: wg show peer <peer-key> endpoint 2601:XXXX:YYYY:ABCD:ZZZZ:ZZZZ:ZZZZ:5678:51820 latest-handshake: 24s ago
journalctl -u zero-trust-agent: Mar 11 09:12:04 kernel: ipv6: duplicate address detected, veering?
tcpdump on AP: no TCP packets from old client IPv6 when endpoint changes (only ICMPv6 RA/NS seen)
ssh client stuck: application shows stall but connection not reset (no TCP RST observed)
wg show conf: persistent-keepalive = 25s on client, handshake initiated but NAT binding timed out on path.

investigation_notes:
Confirmed privacy address rotation coincident with suspend/resume and with network roam events using tcpdump and ip -6 addr history.
WireGuard triggers a handshake when endpoint changes; handshake succeeds but the NAT/flow state on the AP and edge NAT sometimes does not translate ephemeral old TCP state to new source address quickly enough.
Observed that disabling temporary addresses (sysctl net.ipv6.conf.all.use_tempaddr=0) prevents the problem but is not acceptable as a permanent policy due to privacy requirements on managed devices.
Hypothesis: AP/edge NAT implementation drops existing TCP conntrack entries when it sees a new source IPv6 address from the same MAC/4-tuple; the zero-trust-agent/wg-client does a rekey which new packets arrive on different source address before NAT has remapped flows.
Reproduced against a lab AP (same vendor) and confirmed gap ~2-15s between handshake completion and application-level recovery leading to hung SSH sessions.
Checked kernel logs for RFC 4941 rotation triggers and verified rotation interval is default (hourly) but rotation also occurs at link events and resume which explains higher incidence.

comments:
Morgan Li (reporter) -- 2026-03-10: Noticed multiple engineers lose SSH after coming back from lunch or moving floors. Restarting the VPN client fixes immediately.
Diego Ramos (assignee) -- 2026-03-10: Collected tcpdump and wg show from affected laptop and office AP. Early suspicion: IPv6 privacy rotation + AP NAT behavior.
DevOps (SRE) -- 2026-03-11: Reproduced in lab with controlled roam. Need to know AP vendor/model to test NAT behavior across firmware.
Network Eng (Aisha Khan) -- 2026-03-11: SF office uses Aruba APs with controller-managed NAT; opening ticket with Aruba to confirm NAT/conntrack behavior on IPv6 source change.
Diego Ramos -- 2026-03-12: Temporary mitigation deployed to cohort of volunteer laptops: configure systemd-networkd drop-in to set net.ipv6.conf.*.use_tempaddr = 2 (prefer stable with temporary allowed). Monitoring for side effects.

resolution:
Mitigation: Configured a managed profile that sets net.ipv6.conf.<ifaces>.use_tempaddr=2 on enrolled corporate devices to prefer a stable IPv6 address while still allowing temporary addresses as fallback. In parallel, increased WireGuard persistent-keepalive to 45s for volunteers to reduce rekey frequency.

Long-term fix: Tracking two parallel workstreams: 1) Engage with networking vendor (Aruba) to adjust AP/edge NAT conntrack behavior on IPv6 source changes and to evaluate firmware that preserves TCP flows during address migration; 2) Update zero-trust agent to implement a graceful migration mode that maintains NAT mappings by sending a short-burst of translated traffic and re-issuing TCP keepalive-like packets on address change to reestablish conntrack state.

Follow-ups: Create a hardware compatibility note in internal KB, add a sysctl profile for managed devices, and push an engineering task to add graceful-migration support in the zero-trust agent.

[Roaming between APs causes corporate VPN to stay bound to stale interface; internal connections fail until client restart]
summary_detail:
Multiple engineers reported that after walking between floors or moving across AP groups, their Redwood corporate VPN client continued to route via the old (disconnected) virtual interface. Internal traffic (SSH, gRPC to internal clusters) stalled with TCP RSTs or timeouts until the VPN client was restarted or routes were manually flushed.

impact:
Intermittent loss of connectivity to internal services for engineers on corporate Wi-Fi while on the corporate VPN. Blocks developer workflows, remote debugging, and can cause failed job submissions. Affects both macOS and Windows users but more frequent on Windows 10/11 with aggressive roaming enabled.

environment_detail:
Corp Wi-Fi: WPA2-Enterprise with 802.11k/r enabled on Aruba APs, DHCP via internal DHCP clusters; VPN: corporate WireGuard-based client (rw-vpn), version 1.2.3 on Windows and 1.2.1 on macOS. Observed mostly in us-east office floors where AP density and roaming handoffs occur frequently.

steps_to_reproduce:
Connect laptop to corporate Wi-Fi on floor A and establish rw-vpn connection to internal gateway
SSH into an internal jump host or maintain an active gRPC stream to a dev service
Walk (or force roaming) to an adjacent AP on floor B causing Wi-Fi reassociation
Observe that VPN client reports connection still active but internal traffic stalls
Restart rw-vpn client or run 'sudo ip route flush' / 'wg-quick down && wg-quick up' to restore connectivity

observed_behavior:
Existing TCP sessions to internal hosts either hang (no packets forwarded) or receive immediate RSTs. System network stack shows old tun/tap interface still present with routes pointing to a previous gateway. The VPN client logs show no clear disconnect event and does not auto-rebind to the new underlying physical interface.

expected_behavior:
On underlying network interface change (Wi-Fi reassociation), VPN client should detect link change, rebind/tunnel across the new adapter, and preserve or gracefully re-establish active sessions where possible.

logs_and_traces:
Windows 10 client netstat: stale route via "rw-vpn0" and no outbound packets after roam (logs attached to ticket)
WireGuard debug: no handshake errors logged; last handshake timestamp unchanged despite change of physical interface
tcpdump on client NIC: reassociation to new AP followed by ARP retries; VPN encapsulated traffic stops after roaming
Core router logs: no apparent drop on VPN gateway side; peer remains active

investigation_notes:
Hypothesis 1: VPN client does not subscribe to OS netlink events on Windows, so it misses interface index changes and keeps binding socket to old interface handle.
Hypothesis 2: Quick roaming causes a short DHCP renewal and interface index remap which leaves existing tun/tap bindings invalid until process restart.
Reproduced locally: Sophie reproduced on Windows 11 with a scripted AP switch; verified that restarting the VPN client restores proper routes immediately.
Checked AP configuration: 802.11k/r enabled and transition thresholds set to aggressive values. DHCP lease times are short in the affected VLAN (60s) which may accelerate rebinding issues.
No server-side rate limiting or gateway termination observed; peer remains listed in WireGuard peers table at the gateway during failures.
Related prior internal tickets checked: none match this exact symptom; see linked runbook for VPN client restart procedure.

workaround:
In the short term, users should restart the rw-vpn client after roaming or run the provided PowerShell script (attached) to flush stale routes and reinitialize the tunnel. IT can also ask users to disable aggressive fast-roaming in Wi-Fi adapter properties as a temporary mitigation.

proposed_fix:
Engineering to update rw-vpn client to handle interface change events (netlink on Linux/macOS, Windows Network List Manager or RegisterNetworkChangeNotification on Windows) and rebind sockets dynamically. Also add an optional 'rebind-on-network-change' flag to the client config.

resolution_timeline:
Investigation started 2026-03-12. Engineering prioritization discussion scheduled 2026-03-13. Short-term mitigation (doc + PowerShell) published same day. Long-term client fix targeted for 1.3.x release in April 2026.

comments:
Marcus Li (2026-03-12): Filed after 3 engineers on floor 4 reported dropped SSH sessions while moving between desks. Collected client logs and tcpdumps.
Sophie Nguyen (2026-03-12): Reproduced locally with AP simulator. Confirmed restart of rw-vpn client restores connectivity. Adding (vpn-client) component.
IT Network Team (2026-03-12): Noted AP roaming thresholds currently set to aggressive for performance. Can temporarily relax thresholds if required.
Eng (2026-03-13): Created tech task to add network-change listeners and rebind logic in rw-vpn client. Assigned to eng-infra backlog; PR referenced above.
Marcus Li (2026-03-13): Published quick workaround to #it-support Slack and attached PowerShell script. Marking status In Progress while engineering work proceeds.

[Dual-NIC route priority creates split-tunnel blackhole after macOS sleep/resume]
description:
Issue summary:
Dual-NIC laptops (docked Ethernet + Wi‑Fi) intermittently lose access to internal services after waking from sleep. Traffic destined for internal subnets is routed to the wrong interface causing a silent blackhole — the OS chooses the Wi‑Fi gateway but the corporate split-tunnel policy expects WireGuard bound to the Ethernet interface.

Impact:
- Multiple engineers in the SF office reported inability to reach internal CI, internal dashboards, and LDAP-protected services after resume.
- Symptoms: TCP connections hang (no RST), SSH sessions freeze, and http requests timeout despite VPN status 'connected'.
- Affects ~5–10% of docked macOS laptops (M1/M2) observed over the past week.

Environment:
- Client: macOS Monterey/Big Sur variations (12.x/11.x), Redwood wireless + wired docked setups.
- VPN: WireGuard-based zero-trust agent (internal build r2026.03.01).
- Network: Office LAN with split-tunnel routes provisioned by agent.
- Affected region: us-west (SF office).

Steps to reproduce (observed):
1) Dock MacBook to ethernet dock while on corporate Wi‑Fi.
2) Agent starts and establishes WireGuard tunnel bound to the Ethernet adapter.
3) Put laptop to sleep (close lid).
4) Wake laptop, rejoin Wi‑Fi; OS sometimes reorders interface metrics and moves default route to Wi‑Fi before agent rebinds tunnel.
5) Requests to 10.0.0.0/8 (internal) show routing to Wi‑Fi gateway instead of WireGuard, resulting in packet loss.

Observed network state example (post-resume):
- netstat -nr shows default route via 192.168.1.1 (Wi‑Fi) with metric 100
- WireGuard interface wg0 present with peer handshake OK, but route for 10.20.0.0/16 is missing or points to wrong dev

Sample traceroute to internal app (user machine):
1  192.168.1.1  1.2 ms  1.1 ms  1.1 ms
2  * * *

Logs collected from client (attached in ticket):
- /var/log/wg-agent.log excerpt: 
  [2026-03-10T08:12:02Z] wg-agent: peer handshake OK
  [2026-03-10T08:12:03Z] wg-agent: applied routes: 0 entries (expected 3)
  [2026-03-10T08:12:03Z] wg-agent: interface bound to en0 (Ethernet)
  [2026-03-10T08:12:04Z] netlink: interface change: en1 metric 50

Expected behavior:
- After resume, the agent should re-apply split-tunnel routes and ensure internal prefixes are routed through wg0 regardless of default route metric changes. WireGuard should bind to the active interface used for corporate traffic or use policy-based routing.

Temporary workaround used by users:
- Manually run: sudo wg-agent restart && sudo route -n add -net 10.20.0.0/16 -interface wg0
- Toggling Wi‑Fi off briefly restores correct routing.

Notes:
- Issue appears racey: sometimes agent reapplies routes correctly. Suspect timing between OS network stack reordering interfaces and agent's post-resume handler.
- A small subset of affected machines are using third-party 'Ethernet Dock' drivers that modify interface metrics on attach.


comments:
2026-03-10 | Support triage - Priortized by Alex Kim: Confirmed multiple reports from SF office. Repro steps requested from affected user. Assigned to Jordan Patel.
2026-03-11 | Customer (internal user) - Rahul S: Attached tcpdump and wg-agent logs. I reproduced by closing lid for ~30s. Toggling Wi‑Fi off fixed it for me.
2026-03-12 | Jordan Patel (SRE): Collected additional traces. Observed netlink events where en1 (Wi‑Fi) gets metric 50 and becomes default before wg-agent reapplies routes. Hypothesis: agent listens to sleep/wake but race with OS route update. Planning to instrument a test build that delays route application until stable network state is observed.
2026-03-13 | Jordan Patel (SRE): Deployed instrumented agent to 3 volunteers. Initial data: in 6 resume cycles where issue would have occurred, delayed reapply fixed 5. One failure correlated with third-party dock drivers changing metrics after 10s post-resume.
2026-03-14 | Alex Kim (Support): Notifying desktop platform team to escalate dock driver compatibility. Opening follow-up internal ticket for packaging vendor communication.

investigation_notes:
Collected artifacts: tcpdump, wg-agent logs, netstat -nr, route outputs from 7 affected devices.
Hypothesis: race between OS network reorder and agent route application. Agent assumes active interface immediately after wake; sometimes the system updates interface metrics afterward.
Confirmed: restart of wg-agent or toggling Wi‑Fi forces correct routing. Suggests route application is the corrective action.
Repro rate on instrumented devices: ~83% prevented by delaying route apply until no netlink changes for 5s.
Edge case: docks that hotplug drivers modify metric after we consider 'stable' - need driver-aware probe or retry loop.

resolution:
(In Progress) Workaround: users can run 'wg-agent restart' or toggle Wi‑Fi until fix published.
Next steps: 1) Engineering to ship agent patch that waits for netlink stability (5–10s) before applying split-tunnel routes and adds a retry loop for late metric changes. 2) Desktop team to contact dock vendor to confirm driver behavior; consider vendor-specific mitigation. 3) Add telemetry to detect prevalence and log metric-change timelines.
Planned rollout: staged canary to 5% of macOS fleet 2026-03-20, full rollout if no regressions by 2026-03-25.

[GPU CI credential rotation and image promotion safety kit]
Summary

Purpose
This document defines a safety-first pattern for: (1) rotating CI credentials used by GPU provisioning and image-promotion pipelines, and (2) promoting GPU runtime images (golden bundles) to production pools with provable checks and fast rollback paths. The kit bundles Terraform/IaC patterns, CI job templates, runtime verification checks, SLO-driven gating, and an operator runbook for emergency credential revocation.

Why this matters
- Credential rotation without careful orchestration can leave running inference pools unable to pull images, causing degraded capacity and failed deployments.
- Image promotion (CI -> staging -> prod) must be atomic and verifiable: a mismatched image in a GPU pool can produce model-regression incidents.
- Past incidents show the majority of image-promotion outages occur during key rotation + cross-account image copy windows. This doc reduces blast radius.

Scope
Applies to: all CI pipelines that build GPU runtime images, the Terraform modules that provision tenant GPU hosts and warm pools, and the image-signing/attestation services used by Redwood Inference.

Owner and contacts
- Owner team: engineering (Infra Reliability)
- Primary oncall for rollout windows: infra-oncall@redwood.com
- Escalation: Diego Ramos (Lead - GPU Infra), Priya Shah (Security), Evan Liu (CI/CD)

Terminology
- Golden image: signed OCI image bundle used for production inference nodes.
- Image promoter: CI job that signs, copies, and tags artifacts into the production registry.
- Promotion window: the short period where an image transitions from staging to prod and cross-account copies may be in-flight.

Safety principles (high level)
1) Always sign images with key versioning (KMS key alias + key-id). Verification must include key version metadata.
2) Use a promotion plan that stages in-region canaries before full fleet promotion.
3) Make credential rotation a two-phase operation: preflight (test) then swap (cutover) with automatic rollback on failure.
4) Prefer short-lived credentials (ephemeral IAM role / signed cert) for CI agents; store long-term secrets only in HSM-backed KMS.
5) Maintain an explicit PROMOTION SAFETY MATRIX mapping signals to actions (below).

Promotion safety matrix\
| Signal | Threshold | Action | Rollback trigger |
|--------|-----------:|--------|-----------------|
| Canary 99th latency increase | +40% vs baseline | Halt promotion, mark image suspect, run deeper perf trace | Auto-revert to previous tag in 15m if >2 buckets exceed threshold |
| Error rate (5xx) | >0.5% absolute | Re-route 100% traffic off canary nodes, abort promotion | Full fleet rollback if persisted for 10m |
| Tokenization mismatch (new tokenizer failure) | any runtime error | Halt; capture failing prompt, block image | Manual rollback after investigation |
| Image signature verification failures | any | Stop promotion, alert security, revoke CI key version | Block until signature chain validated |
| Pull auth errors across >=2 regions | >=3% pull failures | Pause promotion; force ephemeral credential refresh | If persists 10m, automated rollback and revoke ephemeral role |

Preflight checklist (CI + Terraform)
1) CI builds image and signs with signing service (key alias: kms/gpu-image-signer). Artifact metadata must include key-version and build-id.
2) CI runs integration smoke: small inference harness against a staging warm pool (tag: staging-smoke). Verify latency and correctness metrics.
3) Terraform plan for registry permissions and cross-account roles is generated and reviewed via tfsec/gate. Module names referenced: tf-modules/registry-crosscopy, tf-modules/ephemeral-ci-role, tf-modules/warm-pool-provisioner.
4) Register promotion intent in the promotion ledger (tagged Git commit + promotion ticket).

CI pipeline example (GitHub Actions / Buildkite style)
- name: build-and-sign-gpu-image
  runs-on: ubuntu-22.04
  steps:
    - checkout
    - run: |
        docker build -t staging-gpu:${{GIT_SHA}} -f infra/Dockerfile .
        docker push staging-gpu:${{GIT_SHA}}
    - uses: redwood/sign-image-action@v1
      with:
        image: staging-gpu:${{GIT_SHA}}
        kms-key: projects/redwood/locations/global/keyRings/gpu/cryptoKeys/gpu-image-signer
    - run: |
        curl -X POST https://signing.redwood.internal/attest -d '{"image":"staging-gpu:${{GIT_SHA}}","key_version":"v3"}'

Promotion job (partial)
- name: promote-to-canary
  env:
    EPHEMERAL_ROLE_ARN: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/ci-ephemeral-publisher
  steps:
    - assume-role $EPHEMERAL_ROLE_ARN --duration 900
    - run: |
        ./scripts/cross-account-copy --src staging-gpu:${{GIT_SHA}} --dst prod-gpu:${{PROMOTION_TAG}} --regions us-west-2,eu-west-1
    - run: |
        terraform -chdir=infra/promotion apply -auto-approve -var='image_tag=${PROMOTION_TAG}'

Terraform patterns and recommendations
- Module: registry-crosscopy
  - Purpose: declaratively model cross-account ECR/GCR copy permissions and a short-lived promotion task.
  - Inputs: src_repo, dst_repo, allowed_regions, promotion_role_arn
  - Outputs: promotion_task_id, crosscopy_logs_s3
- Module: ephemeral-ci-role
  - Purpose: create an IAM role the CI system assumes for promotion. Short-lived session only; require MFA for manual triggers. Use OPA policy to prevent wide-scoped permissions.
- Remote state gating: the promotion apply must assert a remote state lock and include a semaphore key in a central tfstate bucket to avoid concurrent promotions.

Credential rotation protocol (two-phase)
Phase A: Preflight (no live swap)
1) Provision new KMS key version and create alias kms/gpu-image-signer -> key-vN.
2) Deploy CI adapters (sign-image-action) to use key-vN in a feature-flagged mode and run 100% test-signings that do not change promotion ledger. Verify that attestation services accept key-vN signatures.
3) Run shadow cross-account copy with ephemeral role using new signing metadata. Confirm copies succeed across all target regions.
4) Monitor for 24h (or 3 release windows) for any unexpected pull auth regressions.

Phase B: Cutover (the swap)
1) Schedule change window (SLO: <30m blind window).
2) Update alias kms/gpu-image-signer -> key-vN (atomic alias swap).
3) Revoke short-lived CI credentials associated with key-v(N-1) after 5m grace. Rotate ephemeral role sessions.
4) Promote a canary image signed with key-vN. Verify canary health for 20m across latency/error metrics.
5) Proceed to full fleet promotion if no triggers fired; otherwise, revert alias to key-v(N-1) and mark key-vN as revocation-pending for forensic review.

Emergency rollback runbook (oncall steps)
1) Detect: Pager fires for pull auth failures or mass pod CrashLoopBackOff when pulling prod images.
2) Immediate action (within first 5 minutes):
   - Confirm via cross-region registry metrics whether pull auth errors are present and their percentage.
   - If pull auth failures >=3% across >=2 regions, run: ./scripts/revoke-ci-ephemeral-sessions --role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/ci-ephemeral-publisher
   - If image signature mismatch reported, quarantine the image tag: mark in the promotion ledger as blocked.
3) If problems persist >10m:
   - Revert registry image tag on affected warm pools to previous production tag via terraform apply -var='image_tag=${PREV_TAG}'
   - Recreate node groups (if nodes are stuck) by triggering warm-pool rolling-replace job.
4) Post-incident: open an incident review, attach promotion ledger entries, CI logs, KMS audit trail, and the short-lived session token logs.

Observability and SLOs to enforce
- Canary latency delta SLO: canary 99th must stay within +25% of baseline during canary window.
- Image pull success: >=99.5% successful pulls within 1m of request at steady state.
- Promotion lead time: preflight checks must finish within 90 minutes for standard releases; emergencies may use expedited path with manual approver.

Telemetry dashboards (must include)
- Registry pull success rate by region and account (1m and 5m windows)
- Image signature verification failures by key-version
- Promotion job success/failure histogram (by commit)
- Canary latency and error rate trends vs baseline (auto-annotate promotion events)

Automation safety checks (required CI gates)
- Signatures must be validated by attestation service and include key-version metadata. Job fails on mismatches.
- OPA admission check in promotion Terraform that asserts promotion_task_id is unique and no concurrent promotions are in progress.
- Pre-promotion smoke harness that runs 100 inference prompts and validates outputs against a golden-response set (fuzzy matching allowed; threshold 95% similarity).

FAQ and edge cases
Q: What if a region's image copy lags by more than 30 minutes?
A: Pause promotion and trigger a manual crosscopy re-run. If unable to copy within 60 minutes, postpone full promotion and continue with a limited regional promotion strategy.

Q: Who can manually trigger expedited promotions?
A: CI admins with MFA + a signed approval from the Release Lead and Security. The ephemeral role requires an MFA assertion to be assumed for manual flows.

Appendix A — Example Terraform stub for ephemeral role
resource "aws_iam_role" "ci_ephemeral_publisher" {
  name               = "ci-ephemeral-publisher-${var.env}"
  assume_role_policy = data.aws_iam_policy_document.assume.json
  tags = { team = "gpu-infra", created_by = "ci-pipeline" }
}

# OPA policy (promotion gate) — high level
# deny if concurrent_promotion == true
package promotion.gate

default allow = false

allow {
  not input.concurrent_promotion
}

- 2024-06-03: Updated safety thresholds and rollback timing after postmortem lessons (review: Priya Shah)

[Golden GPU Worker Images: Build, Versioning, Patch Cadence, and Rollbacks]
## Overview
Golden GPU worker images are the default OS + driver/toolkit baseline for Redwood’s Kubernetes GPU fleets (Hosted, Dedicated, and internal perf clusters).

This page defines:
- The end-to-end image build pipeline and promotion flow
- Versioning and pinning policy (per pool / per region)
- CVE patch cadence and emergency patch handling
- Supported driver/CUDA/NCCL matrix by GPU type
- Rollback procedure with blast-radius controls and auditability

**Goals**
- Reduce provision-to-ready time and post-provision break/fix work by standardizing node configuration.
- Ensure repeatable fleet bring-up across regions/GPU types with explicit compatibility contracts.
- Make changes safe: staged promotion, rapid rollback, and clear operator visibility.

**Non-goals**
- Defining Kubernetes cluster architecture or scheduler behavior.
- Customer-facing documentation (this is internal).  

## Ownership and on-call
**Primary owners**
- Release Engineering (pipeline + image publishing): **Sahana Iyer**
- Infra/Fleet (consumers + rollout policy): **Vanessa Ortiz**

**Consulted**
- Security hardening / vulnerability response: **Fiona McCarthy**

**Where to ask / escalate**
- #eng-infra for rollout questions
- #eng-releases for pipeline failures
- SRE on-call for fleet-wide readiness regressions

---

## Definitions
- **Golden image**: A versioned machine image used for GPU worker nodes (OS + kernel + NVIDIA driver + CUDA userspace + container runtime + kubelet config + hardening).
- **Image channel**: Promotion tier used to control blast radius.
  - **candidate**: Newly built; used only for staged rollouts.
  - **stable**: Approved for broad rollout; default for new capacity.
  - **pinned**: Explicitly pinned version (bypasses channel following).
- **Pool**: A logical group of nodes (e.g., Dedicated customer pool, shared capacity pool) that shares rollout controls.

---

## Image build pipeline (high level)
We build images in a reproducible pipeline with provenance. Builds are triggered by:
- Scheduled patch cadence (weekly/monthly)
- Dependency bumps (driver/CUDA/NCCL/kernel)
- Emergency security response
- Explicit request (approved by Infra + Release Eng)

### Pipeline stages
1) **Source and change control**
   - Image definitions live in Git (infra-images repo) and are reviewed via PR.
   - Required approvals:
     - Release Eng (required)
     - Infra/Fleet (required)
     - Security (required for kernel, sshd, auth, hardening deltas)

2) **Build (packer/AMI) with locked inputs**
   - Base OS: Ubuntu LTS (currently 22.04) unless otherwise noted.
   - Kernel: pinned minor release per train (see versioning below).
   - NVIDIA driver: pinned version (no “latest”).
   - CUDA userspace: pinned minor version.
   - NCCL: pinned version matching CUDA + driver policy.

3) **Provision baseline configuration**
   The bake applies the baseline from **Node Configuration Baseline (GPU Workers)**, including:
   - containerd + registry/cgroup settings
   - kubelet flags (eviction thresholds, reserved resources)
   - time sync (chrony) and NTP sanity
   - ulimits and sysctl (file descriptors, conntrack where applicable)
   - disk layout + mount options (noexec where appropriate)
   - log forwarding agent + node validation agent bootstrap

4) **Hardening + security checks**
   - CIS-aligned SSH configuration (no password auth, restricted ciphers)
   - OS package minimization; remove unused services
   - Image-level vulnerability scan + SBOM generation
   - Secrets check: ensure no credentials/keys baked into image

5) **Smoke tests in an isolated test cluster**
   Before publishing to **candidate**, we run:
   - `nvidia-smi` health and driver enumeration
   - Container runtime GPU passthrough test
   - CUDA sample kernel run (sanity)
   - Network and storage reachability checks required for cluster join
   - K8s node join test (kubelet + CNI) in a staging environment

6) **Publish artifacts + provenance**
   For each build we publish:
   - Image ID(s) per region
   - SBOM (SPDX or CycloneDX)
   - Build attestation (builder identity, commit SHA)
   - Release notes (what changed; compatibility notes)

7) **Promotion workflow**
   - Build outputs land in **candidate**.
   - Promotion from **candidate → stable** is gated by fleet readiness metrics and validation success rates (see “Promotion criteria”).

---

## Naming, versioning, and pinning policy
### Image naming
Images are named for quick inspection and traceability:

`rwi-gpu-worker-ubuntu2204-nv<DRIVER>-cuda<CUDA>-nccl<NCCL>-k<kernel>-<YYYYMMDD>.<build>-<gitsha>`

Example:
`rwi-gpu-worker-ubuntu2204-nv550.54.14-cuda12.4-nccl2.21.5-k6.5.0-20251012.2-a1b2c3d`

### Version semantics
- **Date/build**: identifies the release train build.
- **gitsha**: identifies the exact image definition commit.
- Dependencies are explicitly recorded in image metadata tags.

### Pinning and rollout controls (per pool)
Pools select images using one of the following:

1) **Follow a channel (default)**
- Most pools track **stable**.
- Staged rollouts track **candidate** explicitly (time-boxed).

2) **Pinned version**
- Used when a pool must remain on a known-good image during an investigation or customer freeze.
- Pinning requires an owner and an unpin date or review checkpoint.

### Where pinning is configured
- Terraform module outputs expose:
  - `image_channel` (stable/candidate)
  - `image_version` (optional explicit pin)
- The provisioning orchestrator reads these settings and selects the correct regional image ID.

---

## Promotion criteria (candidate → stable)
An image may be promoted to **stable** when all are true:
- Bake-time tests passed in staging.
- Provision-to-ready validations show acceptable success rates on staged capacity.
- No open P0/P1 incidents attributed to the image.

**Minimum rollout exposure before promotion**
- At least one region and one GPU type in staged rollout.
- At least 200 node-hours of runtime in production-like conditions.

**Quality thresholds (promotion gates)**
- Post-provision validation success rate: **≥ 99.0%** over the staged window.
- NCCL smoke test pass rate: **≥ 98.5%** (flakes tracked; consistent failures block promotion).
- No regression in time-to-ready P95 greater than **+15%** compared to current stable.

**Approvals**
- Release Eng (Sahana Iyer) confirms artifacts + provenance.
- Infra/Fleet (Vanessa Ortiz or delegate) confirms operational readiness.
- Security sign-off required when:
  - Kernel changes
  - SSH/auth changes
  - Base OS bump

---

## CVE patch cadence and emergency response
### Regular cadence
- **Weekly (every Tuesday)**: patch Tuesday-style rebuilds for:
  - High/critical CVEs in kernel, OpenSSL, glibc, sshd, container runtime
  - NVIDIA driver security updates (when applicable)
- **Monthly (first full week of the month)**: full dependency refresh window for:
  - OS package updates (non-critical)
  - Monitoring/agent updates
  - Minor kubelet/containerd config improvements

### Emergency patch policy
If a critical vulnerability is identified with practical exploitability:
- Target **candidate build within 24–48 hours**.
- Target promotion to **stable within 72 hours**, assuming staged validations pass.
- If validations cannot be completed safely, we will:
  - Pin pools to last-known-good stable
  - Apply compensating controls (e.g., network policy, package removal) where feasible
  - Communicate risk + mitigation to stakeholders

### Scanning and evidence
- Image scan results are retained per build.
- SBOM is generated for every release and stored alongside build artifacts.
- Exceptions (known vulns accepted temporarily) require:
  - Owner
  - Expiration date
  - Documented mitigation

---

## Supported driver/CUDA/NCCL matrix
This matrix is the compatibility contract for fleet images.

**Notes**
- We avoid mixing GPU families in a single pool when possible.
- For multi-tenant/shared pools, we prioritize stability and deterministic perf.
- Driver upgrades are staged and must pass NCCL + perf canary checks.

### Current supported combinations (2025-Q4)
| GPU type | Image train | NVIDIA driver | CUDA userspace | NCCL | Intended use | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| A100 (80GB) | stable | 550.54.14 | 12.4 | 2.21.5 | Dedicated + shared | Default stable train. |
| H100 (80GB) | stable | 550.54.14 | 12.4 | 2.21.5 | Dedicated (high-throughput) | Requires fabric/NCCL validation; stricter canary thresholds. |
| L4 | stable | 535.161.07 | 12.2 | 2.20.5 | Cost-optimized / burst | Keeps older driver for compatibility with fleet baseline. |
| A10 | candidate | 535.161.07 | 12.2 | 2.20.5 | Legacy capacity | Candidate only until join/validation flake rate is reduced. |

### Upgrade principles
- Upgrade only one major axis at a time when possible:
  - driver OR CUDA minor OR kernel
- NCCL changes require:
  - NCCL all-reduce smoke test
  - Perf canary (inference throughput/latency) comparison vs current stable

---

## Rollback strategy (blast-radius controlled)
Rollbacks must be safe, fast, and auditable. There are two rollback types:

1) **Channel rollback** (preferred)
- Move **stable** pointer back to previous stable version.
- Pools following stable will converge automatically on next node cycle.

2) **Pool pin rollback** (targeted)
- Pin a specific pool (or region/GPU slice) to a known-good image version.
- Used when an issue is isolated (single region, single customer pool).

### Rollback triggers
A rollback is recommended when any are true and attributable to the image:
- Provision-to-ready validation failure rate increases by **> 2x** baseline.
- Nodes are stuck in **Validating** or **Provisioning** with a common signature linked to the image.
- NCCL smoke test shows consistent failures (not flakes) in a region/GPU type.
- Kernel/driver regressions: elevated GPU Xid errors, ECC error spikes, or repeated device resets.
- Metric/telemetry regressions that block safe operations (e.g., cardinality explosion).

### Blast-radius controls
- Candidate rollouts are limited by policy:
  - Max **5%** of nodes per pool OR **20 nodes**, whichever is smaller.
  - Single region + single GPU type during first stage.
- Stable rollout is phased:
  - 25% → 50% → 100% per region/GPU type, with a minimum observation window between steps.

### Automated rollback hooks (guardrails)
When enabled for a staged rollout, the orchestrator will auto-stop and recommend rollback if:
- Validation failure rate exceeds threshold for 30 minutes (configurable per stage).
- Time-to-ready P95 exceeds threshold for 1 hour.
- Quarantine count exceeds a fixed cap (to prevent capacity shortfalls).

---

## Rollback procedure (operator playbook)
Follow this process to minimize impact and preserve evidence.

### Step 0 — Confirm scope and symptom
1. Identify affected slice:
   - region, GPU type, pool ID, image version
2. Check readiness dashboards and validation artifacts:
   - failure reasons by step
   - quarantine reasons and counts
3. Confirm whether the issue reproduces on new nodes only (provisioning) or also on existing nodes (runtime).

### Step 1 — Stop the bleeding
Choose the smallest effective intervention:
- If issue is limited: **pin the affected pool** to last-known-good stable.
- If issue is broad: **rollback stable pointer** to previous stable.

Operational notes:
- Prefer pinning a single pool before moving stable for the entire fleet.
- If a customer Dedicated pool is impacted, coordinate with Capacity Ops and Support on expected throughput impact.

### Step 2 — Control node churn safely
- For nodes already serving traffic:
  - Do not mass-reboot unless required.
  - Use standard drain/cordon procedures.
- For nodes failing readiness:
  - Quarantine automatically after retry budget is exceeded.
  - Reimage only after pin/rollback is in place (to avoid reintroducing the bad image).

### Step 3 — Verify recovery
- Provision a small batch (e.g., 5–10 nodes) on the rolled-back image and confirm:
  - time-to-ready returns to baseline
  - validation pass rate returns to normal
  - NCCL smoke tests pass
- Keep staged rollout flags disabled until root cause is understood.

### Step 4 — Preserve evidence and follow up
- Attach logs/artifacts to the tracking ticket:
  - image version and build metadata
  - validation outputs and failure signatures
  - GPU health stats (Xid, ECC)
- File follow-ups:
  - fix forward PR
  - test coverage gaps
  - promotion gate adjustments (if needed)

---

## Operational FAQs
### How long do we keep old images?
- Keep at least **N-2 stable** images per region (minimum) for rapid rollback.
- Keep **all candidate images for 30 days** for forensics.

### Can we have different stable images per region?
- Yes, but only with an explicit reason (region-specific driver/fabric constraints).
- Document the divergence and plan to converge.

### What if validations are flaky and block promotion?
- Do not lower gates by default.
- Instead:
  - isolate flakes by region/GPU type
  - tune timeouts/backoff
  - fix root causes (network jitter, disk warm-up, NCCL timeouts)

### Who can change image channel/version for a pool?
- Restricted to Infra/Fleet and Release Eng roles.
- All changes must emit an audit event (see control-plane audit logging) and include:
  - requester
  - reason
  - scope (pool/region/GPU)
  - rollback plan

---

## Change log (recent)
- 2025-10-18: Clarified promotion thresholds and emergency patch timeline; updated matrix for L4 and A10; added blast-radius caps for candidate rollouts.
- 2025-10-08: Added requirement to publish SBOM + build attestation for every image.
- 2025-09-29: Initial version for Provision-to-ready automation sprint.


[GPU CI Dependency Graph and Promote Safety Net]
Summary

This document defines the GPU CI dependency graph, the artifact promotion pipeline used to move GPU images and runtime bundles from CI -> QA -> Staging -> Production, and the safety net (telemetry, automatic rollback, manual gates) we use to prevent costly regressions. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and release engineers running GPU workloads and maintaining image/driver compatibility.

Goals

- Make promotion deterministic and auditable: every promoted artifact must show test/telemetry evidence and a signed provenance record.
- Minimize production regressions introduced by GPU runtime, kernel, or driver changes.
- Provide an automated safety net that can (a) prevent promotion, (b) enable safe canaries, and (c) rollback quickly if regressions are detected.

Scope

Applies to: GPU images, runtime bundles, kernel-module artifacts, operator charts, and IaC modules that directly affect GPU scheduling or networking. Not in scope: model checkpoints, evaluation-only artifacts.

Architecture overview (text diagram)

CI (pre-merge) -> Build/Packaging -> Artifact Signing -> QA Cluster (gpu-e2e) -> Promote Orchestrator -> Staging Canary -> Canary Telemetry Collector -> Production Rollout

Components

- ci-gpu-runner: GitHub Actions/self-hosted runners that execute GPU integration tests.
- gpu-builder: build job that runs container build, multi-arch packaging, and outputs layered artifacts to artifact-bucket.
- artifact-bucket: S3/GCS bucket with object-lock lifecycle for provenance.
- signer-keyring: cosign/keys managed in KMS used to sign artifacts and provenance metadata.
- promotion-orchestrator: internal service (k8s Job + controller) that applies promotion policies and records audits.
- telemetry-collector: Prometheus + Loki collection for canary runs and gpu-run metrics (nvml, kernel oops, host-cpu, memory).
- warm-pool-priming: warm GPU VMs/containers to stabilize first-request latency metrics.

Dependency graph generation

We generate a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of artifact dependencies at build time. Each node includes: artifact_id, base_image_sha, driver_version, kernel_compat_matrix (hash of supported kernels), build_tags, and signed_provenance_uri. The DAG is produced by the gpu-builder and committed as metadata alongside artifacts:

Example metadata snippet (JSON, stored as object "<artifact>.meta.json"):

{
  "artifact_id": "gpu-runtime-2025-02-12-abc123",
  "base_image_sha": "sha256:...",
  "driver_version": "540.XX",
  "kernel_compat_matrix": "kcm:v1:linux-5.4,linux-5.10,linux-6.1",
  "build_tags": ["nightly","cuda-12"],
  "signed_provenance_uri": "s3://artifact-bucket/provenance/gpu-runtime-2025-02-12.sig"
}

Promotion gates and pass criteria (text table)

Gate | Purpose | Owner | Pass criteria
-----|---------|-------|----------
Unit tests | Verify build integrity | ci-team | 100% required, flaky tests documented (<=1 flake/week)
Container CVE scan | Prevent known vuln regression | security | No critical or high CVEs with active exploits
Driver smoke | Ensure driver loads and NVML enumerates devices | eng-infra | NVML device_count == expected, no OOMs in 5 runs
E2E throughput | Validate throughput on a small workload | gpu-qe | >= 90% of baseline throughput (within window)
Warm-start latency | Ensure first-token latency for runtime path | product-slo | p95 <= 250ms for main workload
Telemetry sanity | No kernel OOPS, no memory leak signatures | SRE | Zero kernel oops, stable resident memory for 30m
Sign-off | Manual sign-off for major changes | release-owner | Release owner acknowledges changes and checks notes

Promotion workflow (step-by-step)

1) Pre-merge CI: Pull request must include build matrix metadata. Commands run:
   - ./ci/run-gpu-unit.sh --profile=presubmit
   - ./ci/build-and-publish.sh --bucket artifact-bucket --tag $PR_SHA

2) Artifact signing and DAG publish:
   - cosign sign --key kms://projects/redwood/keys/signer-keyring \n       s3://artifact-bucket/gpu-runtime:$PR_SHA
   - aws s3 cp <artifact>.meta.json s3://artifact-bucket/meta/$ARTIFACT_ID.json --acl bucket-owner-full-control

3) QA cluster verification (gpu-e2e):
   - promotion-orchestrator will schedule a qa-run job with the artifact.
   - telemetry-collector collects GPU metrics with labels: job=qa-run, artifact=$ARTIFACT_ID
   - if any gate fails, orchestrator returns promotion_failed and posts to #gpu-ci-alerts with artifact link.

4) Staging canary: automated canary of 5% of traffic with accelerated telemetry retention. Canary runs for a minimum of 2 hours and must meet the telemetry SLOs.

5) Production rollout: phased rollout (5%, 25%, 100%) with automatic pause on SLO breach.

Telemetry and SLOs (metric names and thresholds)

- gpu_nvml_device_count{job="qa-run"} == expected_device_count (no drift)
- gpu_host_memory_rss_bytes{service="runtime"}  (stable, no >10% growth over 30m)
- gpu_first_infer_latency_ms{pctl="p95"} < 250
- kernel_oops_count{host=~".*"} == 0
- node_restarts_total{job="kubelet"} increase > 0 triggers P0

Alerting and dashboards

- Dashboards: ci/gpu/promotion-overview, ci/gpu/canary-health, infra/gpu-driver-compatibility.
- Alerts:
  - ALERT:GPU_CANOARY_LATENCY (p95 > 250ms for 10m) -> Pager to oncall infra (severity: P1)
  - ALERT:GPU_KERNEL_OOPS (any increase) -> Pager P0 and auto-rollback trigger
  - ALERT:ARTIFACT_SIGN_MISSING (un-signed artifact) -> Slack #release-ops (warning)

Safety net behavior (automatic actions)

- If a P0 kernel oops is detected during staging or production canary, promotion-orchestrator triggers an immediate rollback to last_good_artifact and pauses the pipeline.
- For latency regressions that meet threshold (p95 > 250ms for 10m), the orchestrator pauses rollout, scales down canary to 0 traffic, and pages SRE.
- Any security-critical CVE discovered after promotion triggers immediate freeze of promotion queue and a required patch release.

Rollback playbook (quick steps)

1) Identify last_good_artifact via promotion-orchestrator UI or:
   - curl -s "$PROMO_API/latest_good?service=runtime" | jq .artifact_id
2) Trigger rollback:
   - ./promotionctl rollback --artifact $LAST_GOOD --env production --reason "kernel-oops-detected"
3) Confirm node health: check kernel_oops_count and node_restarts_total; run nvml smoke: ./tools/nvml-smoke.sh
4) Run a canary re-deploy with warm-pool priming for 30m; monitor dashboards.
5) Postmortem: open incident in PagerDuty + link to release and attach trace logs.

Canary tuning and warm pools

- Warm-pool-priming must ensure one container per target GPU is pre-initialized before canary traffic. Warm pools reduce first-request jitter and make telemetry signals less noisy.
- Warm pool size default: min(2, anticipated_canary_replicas). Increase for heavy model init (>2s).

[CI/CD for GPU-Optimized Images and IaC Modules]
Overview

This document describes Redwood's standard CI/CD patterns for building, testing, scanning, and publishing GPU-optimized container images plus the companion Terraform / IaC modules that provision GPU capacity and networking for inference clusters. It covers pipeline topology, gating tests (functional, perf, quantization), image signing and SBOM generation, module publishing, rollback processes, and runbook steps for common failures.

Goals

- Ensure reproducible, auditable GPU images with verified runtime characteristics (CUDA/cuDNN, kernel compatibility, quantization variant artifacts).
- Keep build times and costs predictable: median pipeline time < 12 minutes for incremental builds; < 40 minutes for full image builds.
- Prevent regressions in latency/cost by running lightweight perf checks as part of CI.
- Automate safe rollout of new images to Hosted/Dedicated pools with canaries and automated fallback.

Scope

Included: Docker container images for inference runtime (Torch/Triton/TF), multi-variant artifacts (fp16, int8/quantized), Helm charts, Terraform modules for cluster/ASG, VPC and subnet modules, and pipeline templates.
Excluded: Model training pipelines, third-party marketplace build processes.

Pipeline architecture (recommended)

1) Source push / PR triggers pipeline in CI system (we use Buildkite for infra-sensitive pipelines).
2) Stages (parallel where safe):
   - Lint & static analysis (Dockerfile, IaC linting: tflint, checkov)
   - Unit tests (python unit tests, infra module unit tests via terratest)
   - Build image variants (cache layer: base-image digest + buildkit)
   - SBOM generation and image signing (syft + cosign)
   - Vulnerability scan (trivy)
   - Lightweight perf smoke against local emulation or small Dedicated dev pool (latency, memory, kv-cache warmup)
   - Publish to internal registry (artifact tag: semantic + commit + build id)
   - IaC module publish (registry and git tag)
   - Release gating: QA approval or automatic canary rollout to 5% traffic

Diagram (text)

[PR] -> [Buildkite pipeline] -> parallel: [Lint, Unit tests] -> [Image builds -> SBOM/Sign -> Scan] -> [Perf smoke] -> [Publish registry + Tag IaC] -> [Canary deploy]

Pipeline conventions and naming

- Image tag: redwood/<service>:v{major}.{minor}.{patch}-{commit_sha_short}-{variant} e.g. redwood/inference-runtime:v2.4.1-ab12f3-int8
- Terraform module versioning: semantic vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH with module-test/CHANGELOG in module repo root.
- Buildkite pipeline naming: infra-ci/<service>/<variant>
- Secrets stored in Vault paths: secret/ci/buildkite/<service> and secret/ci/docker-creds/<registry>

Preconditions & permissions

- Service account for CI with minimal IAM: storage writer to registry bucket, ECR push (or GCR/ACR equivalent), KMS encrypt/decrypt only for signing keys, and Terraform state write access to the specific backend bucket.
- Vault policy: ci-build can read signing key path and docker credentials; rotate keys quarterly.

Example Buildkite YAML (snippet)

steps:
  - label: ":docker: build runtime int8"
    commands:
      - "./ci/build-image.sh --variant=int8 --tag=${BUILDKITE_COMMIT:0:7}"
    agents:
      - queue=ci-small
    env:
      - IMAGE_REGISTRY=registry.internal.redwood.com

ci/build-image.sh (excerpts)

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
VARIANT=$1
TAG=$2
# Use buildkit + cache-from to speed up repeated builds
docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
  --build-arg VARIANT=${VARIANT} \
  --cache-from=type=registry,ref=${IMAGE_REGISTRY}/base:cache \
  --tag ${IMAGE_REGISTRY}/${SERVICE}:${TAG}-${VARIANT} \
  --push .

SBOM + Signing + Scan sample commands

syft ${IMAGE_REGISTRY}/${SERVICE}:${TAG}-${VARIANT} -o json > build/sbom.json
cosign sign --key k8s://projects/redwood/secrets/signing-key ${IMAGE_REGISTRY}/${SERVICE}:${TAG}-${VARIANT}
trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL,HIGH ${IMAGE_REGISTRY}/${SERVICE}:${TAG}-${VARIANT} || echo 'VULNERABILITY_FAIL'

Gating tests (must pass before publish)

- Lint and unit tests: exit on any failure.
- Trivy vulnerability check: block if CRITICAL vulnerabilities found. For HIGH vulnerabilities, policy depends on whitelist and CVSS comments.
- Perf smoke: must meet baseline threshold calculated from last successful release. Baseline stored in /infra/perf-baselines (internal). Failure triggers automatic rollback of publish step and notifies owners.

Terraform / IaC module publishing flow

1. Module PR -> tests (tflint, terratest) -> merge to main.
2. CI runs module validation and increments module patch version (via semantic-release or manual tag).
3. Publish module artifact to module-registry (internal) and update module CHANGELOG.
4. Notify downstream stacks via automatic pull request with pinned version bump.

IaC module requirements table

| Field | Requirement | Rationale | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| module_name | prefix: rdw- | Identify Redwood modules in registry | infra-iac-team |
| inputs | explicit, no implicit region defaults | Avoid accidental cross-region deployments | infra-iac-team |
| outputs | standardized tagging outputs (service, env, owner) | For observability and cost allocation | platform-observability |
| tests | terratest + tfsec | Prevent regressions | infra-iac-team |

Canary rollout and rollback policy (images)

- Canary phases: 5% -> 25% -> 60% -> 100% with 10–30 minute observation windows depending on traffic.
- Automated health checks during canary: 200 OK rate, p95 latency within baseline +20%, error budget burn < 2% per window.
- If any check fails, the pipeline triggers an automated rollback to the previous image and opens an incident in PagerDuty (see Runbook: Canary Failure).

Runbooks (high-level)

1) Build fails on buildkite (common causes: cache miss, base image change, low disk)
   - Owner: infra-ci oncall
   - Steps:
     1. Inspect Buildkite logs and the buildkite-agent machine: tail /var/log/buildkite-agent.log
     2. Check cache hit rate: registry API for cache layer digest mismatch. If cache miss, rebuild base-image and re-run.
     3. If machine disk pressure: trigger ephemeral agent reprovisioning: aws ec2 reboot or delete instance in the ci-agent autoscaling group.
     4. If base-image change detected, validate base digest and coordinate with base-image owner to cut a compatible patch.

2) Image scan returns CRITICAL vulnerabilities
   - Owner: security-engineering & infra-ci
   - Steps:
     1. Gate publish: image is not pushed to prod registry (pipeline should prevent).
     2. Retrieve SBOM and vuln report: build/sbom.json and trivy output.
     3. Triage: if fixable by package upgrade, patch Dockerfile and re-run. If requires upstream OS rebuild, escalate to security for policy decision.
     4. Record incident and add CVE to vulnerability backlog with severity and ETA.

3) Canary health check failed after rollout
   - Owner: infra-sre + service owning the image
   - Steps:
     1. Abort further rollout. Trigger rollback to previous image tag via deployment controller.
     2. Attach perf traces and logs (tracing link) to incident.
     3. Run local repro steps against canary instances: reproduce request patterns used in health checks.
     4. If root cause is infra (node kernel, NV driver), follow GPU fleet runbook (see related page).

Operational metrics and SLOs for pipelines

- Build success rate: >= 98% (weekly rolling).
- Median incremental build time: <= 12 min.
- Median full build time: <= 40 min.
- Time-to-publish after merge (automated): <= 30 minutes for non-manual releases.
- Image scanning block on CRITICAL vulnerabilities: 100%

Secrets and signing keys management

- Cosign keys stored in KMS-backed Vault path: secret/signing/ci, rotated quarterly.
- SBOMs persisted alongside artifact metadata in the artifact registry for reproducibility.

Owner & contact matrix

- infra-ci team (primary): infra-ci@redwood.internal
- infra-iac-team (modules): infra-iac@redwood.internal
- security-engineering: security-eng@redwood.internal
- SRE oncall: see rota in PagerDuty

Onboarding checklist for a new service to adopt the pipeline

1. Create service repo with Dockerfile following runtime base-image guidelines.
2. Add pipeline.yaml using template (contrib/pipeline-templates/ci-image.yaml).
3. Add module.tf referencing rdw-gpu-cluster module with explicit inputs.
4. Run `./ci/local-smoke.sh` and push PR for infra review.

Troubleshooting tips and FAQs

Q: My perf smoke is flaky across runs.
A: Use a fixed random seed, control concurrency, and warm KV cache before measuring. Capture the full p95 distribution for 50 runs instead of a single run.

Q: How do I test int8/quantized runtime locally?
A: Use the small dedicated dev-pool (namespace: rdw-dev-gpu-small) and limit traffic via k8s patch to avoid consuming production capacity.

Appendix: Useful commands and links

- Publish a module locally: `make module-publish MODULE=rdw-gpu-cluster VERSION=0.3.1`
- Force-retry a failed Buildkite job: `buildkite-agent build retry <build-id>`
- View SBOM for image: `curl -s https://artifact-registry.internal.redwood.com/sbom/<image-tag>.json`
- Internal wiki links:
  - GPU node sizing: /confluence/eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity/gpu-node-sizing-guidance
  - Module publishing standards: /confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/module-publishing-standards

Change log
