- 2024-06-03: Added SBOM/signing flow and trivy policy (Marcus Lee).
- 2024-11-02: Updated canary observation windows and perf gating thresholds (Sasha Patel).

[GPU Kernel Rollout and Telemetry Gating — Runbook]
Summary

This runbook describes the safe rollout pattern for kernel-level changes (CUDA kernels, custom fused kernels, or runtime micro-optimizations) that affect the GPU serving runtime. The goal is to deploy new kernels with a telemetry gating strategy that minimizes user impact while enabling quick rollback if regressions are detected.

When to use this runbook

- Any change that modifies low-level GPU kernels, JIT codepaths, or scheduling hooks that could influence latency, error surface, or memory usage.
- Binary changes to the runtime Docker image that include optimized kernels.
- Enabling/disabling a kernel feature flag that affects model inference execution.

Prerequisites

- Owner: runtime-team (oncall rotation listed in Team Roster page).
- CI: Buildkite job "gpu-kernel-bake" configured and green.
- Canary pool: "gpu-canary-pool" (tagged fleet with 2 x A100-80GB and 4 x A10s).
- Telemetry: Prometheus -> Cortex metrics available for these targets and Grafana dashboard "GPU Runtime / Canary".
- Tracing: distributed traces visible in Jaeger with sampling for canary requests (tag: kernel_canary=true).
- Infra automation: terraform module ref module.kernel_canary (see appendix).

Key services referenced

- gpu-runtime (service): api endpoints /v1/generate, /v1/stream
- kernel-deployer (CI/CD job): build -> sign -> image-promote
- telemetry-pipeline: prometheus-cortex-grafana + alerts in OpsPager
- kcache (KV cache service): used by runtime; watch cache hit/miss curves during rollout

Telemetry gating criteria (explicit, measurable)

Set a baseline window of 60 minutes prior to rollout. Compute baseline values for each metric. Abort and rollback if any of the following gating conditions are met for 5 continuous minutes during canary traffic unless marked as "investigating":

1) Error surface
- HTTP 5xx rate for /v1/generate > baseline * 3 OR absolute 5xx > 0.5% of requests.

2) Latency regressions
- p95 latency increases by > 40ms compared to baseline AND p99 increases by > 80ms.
- For short-sequence workloads (<=64 tokens) p50 increases > 20ms is also significant.

3) Memory/oom
- GPU memory OOM events > 0 (immediate abort).
- Resident set size (RSS) increase > 20% sustained for 3 minutes.

4) Throughput degradation
- Aggregate tokens/sec across canary nodes drops > 25% while request count is steady.

5) Model-quality signals (if available)
- Automated eval harness reports embedding cosine degradation > 0.03 or generation BLEU/ROUGE-drop beyond configured thresholds.

Gating thresholds are intentionally conservative for kernel changes; teams may request temporary relaxation with explicit risk signoff documented in the PR.

Rollout plan (recommended stepwise procedure)

1. Pre-rollout checks (Run by owner)
- Confirm baseline metrics for 60 minutes.
- Confirm CI artifacts are signed and provenance recorded.
- Run local perf sanity: ./tools/gpu-smoketest --image sha:abcd1234 --workload shortseq
- Announce a 15-minute maintenance window to #runtime-alerts channel and OpsPager.

2. Bake stage (private canary) — 0% external traffic (10–20m)
- Deploy image to gpu-canary-pool with k8s label kernel_canary=true.
- Run synthetic load: 1000 requests/min across short/long seq profiles and RTT measurements.
- Validate: no gating triggers for 10 minutes, p95 within 20ms of baseline.

3. Shadow traffic stage — mirrored (15m)
- Enable proxy mirroring of 5% of production traffic into canary instances (mirror only, do not return to end users).
- Validate guards: error surface ~0, trace sampling consistent, kcache hit ratio unchanged (+/-2%).

4. Progressive traffic-shift (canary) — controlled traffic ramp (30–90m)
- Traffic plan: 1%, 5%, 10%, 25% with at least 10 minutes at each step.
- Automated gate check at each step via CI job gate-check-canary which queries Prometheus and returns pass/fail.
- If gate fails: immediately scale traffic to 0% and trigger rollback.

5. Promote (full)
- After 25% sustained for 30 minutes with no gate failures, schedule a promotion to production images across autoscaling groups in a rolling fashion (max 10% of nodes concurrently).

Rollback procedure (immediate)

1. If any gating criterion fires:
- Kernel-deployer: cut traffic to canary pool to 0% using traffic-shift API: 
  curl -X POST "https://orchestrator.internal/api/traffic-shift" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d '{"pool":"gpu-canary-pool","percent":0}'
- Trigger image reversion: kernel-deployer promote --pool gpu-canary-pool --image sha:previous
- Create incident in PagerDuty channel and mark the rollout PR with "reverted".

2. Post-rollback checks:
- Verify baseline metrics return within 30 minutes.
- Collect heap, GPU memory profiles and kernel traces; upload to shared S3 bucket s3://redwood-telemetry/kernel-rollbacks/$(date +%F_%H%M).tar.gz
- Owner opens a postmortem stub in /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/postmortems with tag kernel-rollback.

Post-rollout verification (observability checklist)

- Confirm p50/p95/p99 metrics match baseline within tolerance for 60m.
- Verify no new 5xx spikes in the error histogram.
- Confirm kcache hit ratio and LRU churn metrics are stable.
- Confirm trace spans for hot paths have similar duration distributions.
- Verify that release notes and SLSA provenance are attached to image metadata.

Ownership & escalation

- Primary owner: runtime-team (oncall rotation).
- Secondary owner: infra-sre.
- Escalation path: runtime-owner -> infra-sre -> head of eng-infra -> CTO on call.
- PagerDuty playbook: PD escalation policy "kernel-rollout".

Runbook automation (CI/CD examples)

- Buildkite snippet (simplified):

  steps:
    - label: "gpu-kernel-bake"
      command: "scripts/bake-and-promote.sh $BUILDKITE_COMMIT"
      agents: {gpu: "true"}

- Gate checker (bash) example:
  # gate-check-canary.sh
  BASELINE_P95=$(promql 'histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{env=\"prod\"}[5m])) by (le))')
  CANARY_P95=$(promql 'histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{env=\"canary\"}[5m])) by (le))')
  delta=$((CANARY_P95 - BASELINE_P95))
  if [ $delta -gt 0.04 ]; then echo "FAIL"; exit 1; fi

Appendix: recommended Terraform variables and module example

| variable | type | default | description |
|---------|------|---------|-------------|
| canary_pool_name | string | "gpu-canary-pool" | Name of the canary node group |
| canary_instance_types | list(string) | ["a100-80gb", "a10"] | Heterogeneous instance list for canary |
| canary_max_percent | number | "25" | Max traffic percent for canary stage |

Example module usage (HCL snippet):

module "kernel_canary" {
  source = "git::ssh://git.internal/repo/terraform/modules/kernel_canary.git?ref=v1.2.0"
  name   = var.canary_pool_name
  instance_types = var.canary_instance_types
  max_percent = var.canary_max_percent
  health_check = { type = "prometheus", endpoint = "/metrics" }
}

Payment/Cost considerations

- Canary pools are charged to "runtime-canary" cost center. Keep canary duration under 4 hours when possible to limit cost.

FAQ & common failure modes

- Q: "Can I skip the shadow stage?"
  A: Only with explicit approval from infra-sre and a documented risk mitigation plan.

- Common issues:
  * Synthetic load mismatch: ensure test client uses correct request shape and sequence lengths.
  * Burst scaling masks regressions: use rate-limited synthetic load to approximate production steady-state.

Postmortem / followup requirements

- If rollback occurs, owner must file a full postmortem within 72 hours with root cause, timeline, and remediation steps. Add labels: kernel, rollback, postmortem.

Document history & change log

- 2024-11-05: Created by Priya Natarajan.
- 2024-12-02: Added memory OOM immediate-abort rule (reviewer: Miguel Alvarez).
- 2025-01-12: Tightened latency gating thresholds for short-sequence workloads (reviewer: Dana Park).

Related references

- /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/kv-cache-reconstruction-and-eviction-resilience-runbook
- /confluence/eng-infra/ci-cd-and-build/gpu-image-promotion-canary-cd-playbook

[Private upgrades technical deep dive (design partner) - upgrade plan, backups, rollback]
summary:
Northstar walked through current pain points upgrading their on-prem Redwood Private environment: upgrades are high-touch, require manual sequencing between control plane components and data plane, and rollback is mostly 'restore from VM snapshot and hope'. They emphasized air-gapped constraints (no outbound internet), strict change windows, and audit evidence requirements.

Redwood reviewed the planned upgrade workflow (preflight checks -> plan generation -> backup -> staged rollout -> verification) and discussed which prechecks should block vs warn (storage headroom, DB connectivity, OIDC reachability). Backup approach was discussed across CSI snapshots and logical DB dumps, with Northstar noting they do not have consistent snapshot support across clusters.

Key concerns were around schema migrations (lock timeouts, partial upgrades), deterministic rollback hooks, and how artifacts are verified offline (checksums/signatures). The call ended with agreement on beta prerequisites, a rollback drill, and a short list of environment details Northstar will provide.

topics:
Current on-prem upgrade workflow and failure modes
Air-gapped artifact delivery and verification (checksums/signing)
Preflight checks: cluster health, storage, RBAC/SSO, networking/DNS/TLS, DB readiness
Backup/restore: CSI snapshots vs logical dumps, encryption/KMS expectations
Rollback semantics: partial upgrade handling, schema migration guardrails
Beta timeline, success criteria, and a rollback drill

transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-05-28
Time: 4:03pm - 5:00pm PT
Duration: 57 minutes
Call type: Technical deep dive

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Markus Klein, Fatima Noor, Bruno Silva, Irene Choi, Sean Gallagher
Northstar Health Systems: Priya Raman, Evan Wu, Marisol Chen, Jake Miller

---

[00:00] Markus Klein: Cool, I think we’re recording. Um, thanks everyone for making time. Goal today is to go deeper on the upgrade and rollback stuff for Private, especially for on-prem, air-gapped. We’ve got Fatima, Bruno, Irene, Sean here.

[00:15] Priya Raman: Sounds good.

[00:16] Markus Klein: Priya, do you wanna start with what you all do today for upgrades and, like, where it’s painful?

[00:24] Priya Raman: Yeah. So currently our process is basically, we schedule a maintenance window, we… we download the new package from our internal mirror, we do a Helm upgrade, and then it’s like, fingers crossed. The ordering is not obvious. We’ve had one incident where control plane came up but data plane got stuck because of… I think it was a migration? And rollback was manual.

[00:47] Jake Miller: The rollback is basically, we restore etcd snapshots and PV snapshots where we can, but not all clusters have the same storage. Sometimes we revert the whole node pool image. It’s… it’s messy.

[01:01] Evan Wu: Yeah and the charts have hooks but they don’t always run in the order we expect. Like pre-upgrade jobs time out and then Helm rolls back but the DB already got migrated.

[01:16] Sean Gallagher: Yep, that’s the exact class of issue we’re trying to kill. Partial upgrades + schema migration side effects.

[01:23] Markus Klein: Great context. Fatima, do you wanna give the 2-minute overview of the new approach we’re implementing?

[01:30] Fatima Noor: Sure. So the direction is: the installer generates an upgrade plan first, it’s a versioned artifact that lists stages and steps. Before doing anything, we run preflight checks—cluster health, storage headroom, DNS/TLS, RBAC, database connectivity, and also artifact availability. Then we orchestrate backups. After that we execute the plan in phases: control plane first, then data plane, with readiness gates. If something fails, we have deterministic rollback entry points that use stored state from the plan execution.

[02:05] Priya Raman: When you say installer—this is the redwood-private-installer CLI, right? Not Helm itself?

[02:10] Fatima Noor: Correct. Helm still does the actual apply of charts, but we wrap it with an orchestrator so we can be consistent and auditable.

[02:19] Marisol Chen: Auditable meaning we can show, like, exactly what checks ran and what was backed up?

[02:24] Fatima Noor: Exactly. Plan output persisted, precheck results, backup IDs, and upgrade start/stop events.

[02:31] Irene Choi: And timestamps, plus versions: current version, target version, and what artifacts were used.

[02:39] Marisol Chen: Okay.

[02:41] Markus Klein: Evan, can you describe your on-prem constraints? Like how air-gapped are we talking.

[02:47] Evan Wu: Fully. No outbound internet. We have an internal artifact mirror for container images and we can host a chart repo internally, but it’s manual. Also we need checksums for everything. Our security team won’t allow “curl random thing during upgrade.”

[03:06] Marisol Chen: And signatures if possible. Checksums alone are… better than nothing, but ideally there’s a signing chain.

[03:13] Fatima Noor: Yep. So we’re adding bundle verification: manifest, checksums, and optional signatures. The installer will fail early if the bundle doesn’t match.

[03:24] Priya Raman: Can it operate with, like, a USB drop? We sometimes do physical transfer to the restricted enclave.

[03:30] Fatima Noor: That’s a supported model. The bundle is basically a directory or tarball with a manifest file plus all referenced artifacts.

[03:40] Bruno Silva: And on the Terraform side for VPC it’s a bit different, but for on-prem we’ll document “offline registry endpoint” variables too, so the installer knows where to pull from without going to the public registry.

[03:54] Evan Wu: Okay. Biggest pain for us is, if Helm upgrade fails, we don’t know what state we’re in. Like, was the database migrated? Was it halfway? And then we get stuck.

[04:08] Sean Gallagher: Right. So we’re defining “rollback hooks” as part of the plan. The critical part is: schema migrations have to be guarded. We’re implementing idempotency checks and lock timeouts. Also, we’re biasing to backwards-compatible changes when possible so rollback doesn’t require “un-migrating” data.

[04:28] Jake Miller: That’s good in theory but we’ve seen migration jobs hold locks for a long time.

[04:32] Sean Gallagher: Yep. We’ve been tuning defaults—like statement timeouts and lock timeouts—so a bad migration doesn’t freeze the cluster. And the precheck will also test DB connectivity and maybe space.

[04:45] Priya Raman: Can we dig into prechecks? Which ones are blocking? Because we don’t want the system to block over something we accept risk on.

[04:52] Fatima Noor: For beta, we’re proposing a mix. Blocking: unsupported version jump, missing artifacts, DB not reachable, insufficient storage headroom for backups, and cluster not healthy (like nodes NotReady). Warning: OIDC reachability maybe, depending on your setup, and DNS latency, stuff like that.

[05:15] Marisol Chen: OIDC reachability as a warning seems dangerous? If auth breaks, we can’t log in.

[05:21] Irene Choi: The nuance is, some customers have break-glass local admin. If you have that, we can make it warn; if you don’t, it should block.

[05:30] Jake Miller: We do have break-glass but it’s painful and audited.

[05:35] Priya Raman: Our preference is: block if OIDC is required for operator access. If it’s only for end-user, maybe warning.

[05:44] Fatima Noor: That’s fair; we can make it configurable, like policy.

[05:50] Markus Klein: Marisol, what would you need from an audit standpoint for “we ran prechecks”?

[05:56] Marisol Chen: We need a record of what ran, outcome, and ideally configuration and versions. Also backup encryption verification. And who initiated it.

[06:06] Markus Klein: Got it.

[01:40] Daniel Ruiz: We avoid key reuse by including tenant id in the KMS context, and cache keys are stored with tenant prefix. Also, we support audit logs for cache gets/puts tied to request ids for SOC2 evidence.
[01:52] Ethan Yu: Walk us through a cache-key example we can implement on our side.
[01:57] Daniel Ruiz: Example: cobalt-123::gptx-8k::session-9f3a::prompthash-<sha256>. That's the Redis key. The value is serialized KV tensors or compressed prompt metadata. We also store a tiny header with model_version, quantization_profile, and boolean 'is_prefix_cached' so the runtime can validate compatibility.
[02:20] Tom Berger: About eviction — what's recommended? LRU, TTL, or hybrid? Our sessions are often short but a small fraction are long-lived.
[02:28] Daniel Ruiz: Hybrid usually works best. TTL for session-based prefixes (e.g., 30–120 minutes), plus LRU within each tenant shard to avoid thundering herd scenarios. We also recommend a maximum shard size to bound worst-case memory usage.
[02:42] Maya Patel: And for hit-rate objectives — what's realistic? Some customers we see 40–60% for generic chat workloads, but with strong session affinity you can push 70–85% for system/prompt-heavy apps. For Cobalt's case (structured clinician templates), I'd aim for 60% baseline.
[02:58] Aisha Khan: That aligns with our goals. How should we measure hit/miss? Do you expose metrics?
[03:04] Kira Wong: Yup — Console exposes token-level cost, cache hits/misses per model, and per-tenant histograms. We can also emit debug-level dumps for a POC run.
[03:14] [03:15] Daniel Ruiz: On quantization — if you quantize model weights/tensors, that will change the exact bytes you cache. So you must include quantization profile in the cache key header (we mention model_version:quant_profile). Otherwise you risk cache poisoning where a cached tensor produced under int8 is used against a float16 execution path and causes mismatch.
[03:33] Tom Berger: Is there any loss of correctness with quantized cached KV pairs? Because some of our prompts are medically precise.
[03:40] Daniel Ruiz: In general, quantization is deterministic per kernel, but lower-bit quantization can introduce small numeric drift. For prompt continuation tasks it's usually fine, but for exact retrieval / measurement tasks you may prefer higher precision. For Cobalt, if clinical correctness is critical, keep precache at higher precision or add a small QA evaluation set to monitor regression.
[03:58] Aisha Khan: Great, noted. Next, multi-tenant safety — we want strong isolation. Options you discussed earlier were per-tenant Redis logical DBs, key prefixing, or full shard separation. Tradeoffs?
[04:10] Daniel Ruiz: Right: prefixing is simplest and works well in practice, but if one tenant has a noisy workload it can evict keys for others in the same Redis instance. Logical DBs help a bit, but they still share memory at the instance level. Full shard separation (dedicated Redis shard per customer or a group of customers) gives the best isolation at cost. We often recommend grouping tenants into shard pools based on traffic tier.
[04:34] Tom Berger: Cost-wise, dedictated shards per tenant for hundreds of tenants is expensive. We'd likely group by tier. How do you decide shard buckets?
[04:42] Daniel Ruiz: Use percentile of peak concurrent sessions + average cached size per session to compute expected memory. We can provide a sizing script: e.g., 95th-percentile concurrent sessions * avg bytes per session * safety factor 1.5. That gives shard assignment thresholds.
[04:59] Maya Patel: We'll attach the sizing spreadsheet after the call — that's one of the next steps.
[05:04] Ethan Yu: On local node caches vs centralized Redis — any guidance for on-prem?
[05:10] Kira Wong: For on-prem or VPC, you can do node-local RocksDB per inference node to reduce network hops and get lower P95 latencies. But node-local complicates coherence and increases duplication — hit rate per node may drop if traffic isn't sticky. Centralized Redis gives easier global hit rate but higher network RTT. For low-latency SLOs we'd recommend a two-tier cache: node-local L1 for the hottest prefixes + Redis L2 for shared.
[05:35] Tom Berger: Is that pattern supported in Redwood out of the box?
[05:38] Daniel Ruiz: Yes, Redwood Runtime supports a two-tier cache with async fallbacks. We maintain a small L1 in-memory cache and then query L2 Redis. The runtime handles consistency semantics and can do async warm-ups to L1 when Redis returns a hit.
[05:51] [06:00] Aisha Khan: About batching — what's the typical batching window you recommend? We're worried about adding latency by waiting to batch.
[06:06] Daniel Ruiz: It depends on request distribution. For interactive chat you want small batching windows: 5–20ms at the runtime level with aggressive microbatching. For high-throughput background inference, you can go up to 50–100ms. Batching reduces per-token cost but increases P95; we let you set per-route SLOs.
[06:25] Tom Berger: So combining batching with cache — if a prefix is found in cache, that request short-circuits and avoids batching latency, right?
[06:32] Daniel Ruiz: Correct. Cache hits often bypass large parts of the pipeline and return low single-digit-millisecond latency depending on network. That's why hit rate is so valuable.
[06:39] Lina Park: Audit logs again — we need to prove cache gets/puts for compliance. What metadata is kept and for how long?
[06:46] Kira Wong: We can log request id, tenant id, key hash (not raw prompt), operation (GET/PUT/EVICT), and model version. Retention is configurable; for enterprise plans we can store logs for 12+ months in a tamper-evident store.
[06:58] [07:05] Ethan Yu: Any gotchas with the hash of the prompt? If we store only the hash, is there risk we can't reconstruct for debug?
[07:12] Daniel Ruiz: For privacy, we avoid storing raw prompts when customers require it. For debug, you can opt-in to store (encrypted) raw prompts with strict access controls. Alternatively, store reversible metadata: e.g., prompt template id + parameterization which is safe.
[07:27] Aisha Khan: About collisions again — do you ever prefix with time-based salts to avoid stale collisions?
[07:33] Daniel Ruiz: Time salts would reduce cacheability. We prefer to encode session TTLs and versioning in the key meta rather than changing the hash. If you need to invalidate a prefix, use a namespace version or bump model_version/quant_profile.
[07:46] Tom Berger: What about fallback policies? If primary model/cache path is unavailable, what's Redwood's approach?
[07:52] Daniel Ruiz: We support policy-driven fallback: fallback to a smaller model variant, route to a different region, or bypass cache and use stateless token-limited mode. For critical paths you can configure synchronous fallback or asynchronous best-effort.
[08:05] Maya Patel: Also worth noting: cache poisoning mitigation — we verify compatibility flags in the header and only accept cached entries that match runtime model fingerprint. We also rate-limit cache writes per tenant to prevent noisy writes.
[08:19] Aisha Khan: For the POC, can we simulate 10,000 tenants with mixed burstiness and see hit-rate per tenant?
[08:25] Daniel Ruiz: Absolutely — our SE toolkit includes a synthetic workload generator. We'll provide the script and expected baseline metrics.
[08:33] Tom Berger: On the encryption front — for private deployment, do you recommend TLS to Redis and should we use mutual TLS?
[08:39] Kira Wong: Yes — mTLS to Redis, and if it's across VPC peering, enforce network ACLs. Also, consider private Redis instances inside the customer's subnet so there are no public IPs.
[08:50] Lina Park: Any special notes about on-prem hardware or NVMe-backed RocksDB sizing?
[08:55] Daniel Ruiz: RocksDB with NVMe is solid for high throughput. For cold-starts and evictions, tune compaction and set max_background_jobs appropriately. Also provide headroom for memtable size — we can share our recommended defaults.
[09:08] [09:15] Ethan Yu: I have one last question about measuring regression from quantized cache hits — what's the best practice?
[09:20] Daniel Ruiz: Keep a small validation set of critical prompts and compare outputs (exact string match or semantic similarity) across float32 vs quantized runs. Hook Redwood Optimize to alert when quality drops below threshold.
[09:33] Maya Patel: Alright let's recap next steps quickly — Maya to share cache-key-spec, Daniel to provide Redis sizing and scripts, Cobalt runs synthetic benchmark, then we meet the week of 2025-06-23.
[09:45] Aisha Khan: That works. Also please include sample Redis ACLs and firewall checklist.
[09:50] Kira Wong: We'll include a checklist and a hardened default Redis config in the spec doc.
[09:56] Maya Patel: Great — thanks everyone, we'll follow up.

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker attribution mismatches and small transcription errors (e.g., 'K V cache' vs 'KV cache'). Original recording link: (internal) redwood://recordings/ff-20250609-ck-7892

Meeting header

Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Luca (SE), Samir (SE), Rosa (CISO), Ethan (Platform Lead), Nadia (Security Architect), Tom (Compliance)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, uh thanks for taking the time. Quick roll call, we have Pegasus security and platform on the line, and we'll focus on the on-prem private deployment questions and audit prep.
[00:18] Rosa: Thanks Maya, need to confirm we want a tight perimeter, minimal egress, and full auditability. We're SOC 2 preparing so everything needs to be demonstrable.
[00:30] Luca: Got it. We'll walk through the network zoning and egress patterns we support, plus KMS options. Quick note, transcription may garble K V cash references, sorry about that.
[00:42] Ethan: The main constraints: no direct outbound from compute nodes, everything must route through our proxy, and keys need to be customer-managed, ideally in a hardware module.
[00:55] Samir: We support BYOK via CloudHSM or customer HSM appliance for Private. We also let customers hold keys in an HSM that's on their side and we do a secure handshake for the control plane. There are a few permutations.
[01:12] Nadia: When you say control plane, is that ever exposed to internet? We need to know the minimal egress flows.
[01:20] Maya: Good question. For Redwood Private we can run a customer-managed control plane inside the VPC/on-prem; however some optional telemetry requires outbound to our ops endpoints unless you opt for air-gapped mode. We should map those exact endpoints for you.
[01:35] Rosa: Air-gapped is preferred but we need to understand the tradeoffs for maintenance and security updates. Is there a patch pipeline you can hand over?
[01:46] Luca: Yes — for air-gapped there's an offline package model and signed artifacts. For on-prem with limited egress, we support an egress proxy pattern where only a small set of endpoints are allowed.
[01:58] Tom: Also need to understand logging: we must ingest all audit logs into Splunk and retain them for two years per policy. Can Redwood ship logs or do we pull?
[02:10] Samir: Both. We can push logs into your SIEM via forwarder, or you can pull via SFTP or API. The log schema includes request metadata, model version, tokens, and actor identity. Heads up the token field is redacted by default.
[02:27] Ethan: On RBAC: we want SSO integration (SAML/SCIM) and mapping to our internal groups. Service accounts used by apps should get scoped roles, not full admin.
[02:39] Maya: We'll show role mappings and least-privilege templates. For service accounts we recommend short-lived credentials mapped to an internal service principal.
[02:51] Nadia: How's key rotation handled if we use BYOK? Our compliance requires quarterly rotation and audit trails.
[02:58] Samir: With BYOK on CloudHSM, rotation can be orchestrated via a key policy and AWS KMS lifecycle. For on-prem HSM we provide a procedure and a signed rotation step that you run; Redwood captures the rotation event in the audit log. We'll provide the signed payload examples.
[03:15] Rosa: Any additional certification artifacts you can share? We need IAM diagrams and control mappings for SOC 2 Type II.
[03:22] Maya: We'll send our SOC 2 letter and a control-mapping template that shows which Redwood control corresponds to Pegasus control objectives.
[03:30] 
[03:30] (Segue into topology discussion)
[03:35] Luca: Let me sketch the recommended network layout. Slide link in chat: https://redwood-internal.example/diagrams/private-network-layout.pdf (note - we're using an example link for artifacts).
[03:50] Luca: Suggested zones: management, inference, cache, and egress/proxy. Management hosts are put into a separate VLAN and only reachable from your bastion. Inference nodes have no direct internet; egress is via the egress gateway.
[04:05] Ethan: For egress gateway are you okay if we use a proxy that performs TLS inspection? That might conflict with healthcare regs though.
[04:12] Nadia: We try to avoid TLS inspection where PHI might be involved; prefer mTLS to enforce mutual auth.
[04:19] Samir: We support mTLS between the inference runtime and your egress proxy, and we can do header-based allow lists so payloads are restricted.
[04:30] Rosa: What's the recommended firewall policy? Stateful security groups plus NACLs?
[04:35] Luca: Typically we do security groups for east-west controls and NACLs for broader subnet-level deny lists. Use host-based firewalls on critical nodes for defense in depth.
[04:46] Tom: IDS/IPS integration? We have a network sensor and want to correlate alerts with model activity.
[04:52] Samir: We can forward flow logs and application logs to your SIEM. Also expose webhook alerting for anomalous inference patterns. We recommend hooking both network IDS and application-layer anomaly into the same Splunk index.
[05:08] (brief cross-talk)
[05:15] Rosa: What about data residency — logs and model artifacts must remain in our datacenter. Does Redwood store any persistent data outside the cluster?
[05:24] Maya: In Private mode we do not store customer data on Redwood-hosted storage. There's an optional control plane telemetry; if you disable it, nothing leaves your cluster. We will provide configuration flags that ensure no snapshot or checkpoint is sent offsite.
[05:41] Ethan: Are there any built-in protections for model parameter exfiltration? We need to assess risks where model weights or KV caches could leak.
[05:50] Luca: Model weights are read-only, stored on encrypted disks; we never transmit weights off the node unless packaging for a signed upgrade. KV cache may include prefixes of user data — we encrypt caches at rest and recommend short TTLs and strict ACLs to isolate customers.
[06:09] Nadia: Can we run inference entirely behind an internal LB with no public endpoints?
[06:13] Samir: Yes — we support internal-only load balancers and integration with your IP allow lists. The management plane can be internal-only as well.
[06:22] Rosa: For audit evidence, can you provide sample log entries and an example of a rotation record?
[06:29] Maya: Yes, Samir will produce sample payloads. We'll also provide the mapping doc for SOC 2 controls.
[06:37] (15-minute mark moved into egress specifics)
[15:02] Luca: Ok focusing on egress: many customers use an outbound proxy that terminates TLS and performs allowlisting, but as Nadia said, for PHI we prefer mTLS where the proxy only routes encrypted traf and does not inspect content.
[15:22] Ethan: We can do mTLS. Question: how does the Redwood runtime validate certificates?
[15:28] Samir: The runtime supports a local trust store and can be configured to validate via an internal CA. We also support cert rotation via your PKI and short-lived certs distributed by your SSO/PKI system.
[15:40] Rosa: If we use an HSM appliance, what's the handshake flow? Does Redwood have a connector that talks to on-prem HSM or do we mount a service?
[15:49] Luca: Two patterns: (1) Redwood connects to your HSM via a dedicated TLS tunnel with mutual auth and remote attestations; (2) a local key proxy runs in your network that signs/decrypts requests for the runtime. Pattern 2 keeps HSM traffic entirely internal to your DC.
[16:06] Ethan: For pattern 2, do we need additional software from Redwood?
[16:10] Samir: We provide a lightweight keyproxy binary with minimal dependencies, signed by Redwood. You run it behind your firewall. The runtime calls the keyproxy over mTLS and receives wrapped keys.
[16:19] Nadia: How do you attest that the binary is the right one? We need reproducible builds and a checksum.
[16:24] Maya: We'll provide signed checksums, and if needed we can do an SBOM and reproducible build artifacts.
[16:31] Tom: Back to logging retention. Does Redwood offer configurable retention for local audit stores before forwarding?
[16:36] Samir: Yes, you configure retention per index locally. Logs can be kept in the node for X days and forwarded; default is 30 days but it's fully configurable.
[16:44] Rosa: Any out-of-band admin access? Who can escalate to root?
[16:49] Luca: Escalation follows your RBAC. Redwood support requires an explicit support session and limited-time access tokens that you approve. There is no standing root access for Redwood engineers in Private unless you enable a timeframe-limited session via your admin console.
[17:05] (customer asks about emergency access)
[17:08] Maya: We have an emergency access playbook; access is logged, requires 2-man approval, and all actions are captured in audit logs. We'll attach that playbook.
[17:18] (brief pause)
[17:21] Ethan: On the topic of network blocking: can we get an allowlist of the minimal endpoints Redwood control plane needs for updates/metrics if we want partial egress?
[17:31] Maya: Yes — action item. We'll provide an endpoint list and port matrix. There are optional endpoints for telemetry — those can be disabled.
[17:40] Nadia: How are service accounts represented in logs? We want to trace back from a model call to a user or service principal.
[17:49] Samir: Each request includes an actor id, origin (IP/host), and the model version. We also include a request-id for trace correlation. If you use SSO/SCIM mapping the actor id will be your internal principal id.
[17:59] Rosa: Is there PII or PHI ever included in logs? We need to avoid storing user content unredacted.
[18:06] Luca: By default, user content is redacted in logs. You can opt in for content retention but that's discouraged for regulated workloads.
[18:15] Tom: For SOC 2 evidence, we need to show config snapshots and change history for firewall rules. Do you keep change history?
[18:23] Samir: Yes, the platform records config diffs and stores signed snapshots for a configurable period. Those snapshots can be exported as evidence.
[18:33] (crosstalk about snapshot format)
[18:40] Ethan: One more: can we run offline security scans of the container images Redwood uses?
[18:45] Maya: We'll provide SBOMs and signed artifact lists, and you can run your own scanning pipeline against the images before deploying.
[18:54] (30 minute mark - dive into pilot details)
[30:01] Luca: Proposed pilot: small cluster behind Pegasus egress proxy, single model, generate synthetic loads, verify no outbound connections other than the allowlisted endpoints, and validate log ingestion into Splunk. Duration 2 weeks.
[30:14] Ethan: That works. We'll need a playbook for onboarding and a checklist for network changes.
[30:21] Maya: We'll send the onboarding checklist and a sample ansible playbook for firewall rules.
[30:30] Nadia: About encryption in transit: does Redwood support mTLS for internal service-to-service and enable cipher suite minimums?
[30:36] Samir: Yes — mTLS everywhere supported and we default to TLS1.3 with a restricted cipher suite list.
[30:46] Rosa: Any requirement for kernel-level hardening or specific OS images?
[30:50] Luca: We recommend minimal distro images with CIS benchmarks applied. We'll share our hardened AMI/container baseline.
[31:00] (small tangent about patch windows)
[31:12] Tom: About evidence, can we get a runbook that maps Redwood's control IDs to SOC 2 criteria? We need that for our auditors.
[31:20] Maya: Yes, we'll attach a mapping doc—action item Samir.
[31:28] Ethan: One operational detail: do you support NAT sticky rules so ephemeral nodes reuse the same outbound IP for allowlisting?
[31:36] Samir: We can configure SNAT with consistent egress IPs via the egress gateway or via NAT pools so your allowlists remain stable.
[31:44] Nadia: Are there known limitations for high throughput models when running with strict egress?
[31:50] Luca: The main constraint is telemetry/metrics throughput — if you completely block metrics and telemetry, debugging is harder. But for inference throughput itself, as long as the egress gateway has enough bandwidth it's fine. We'll size accordingly.
[32:06] (40 minute mark - discussion of key rotation and HSM)
[40:05] Rosa: Let's deep-dive on KMS options. CloudHSM vs on-prem appliances?
[40:12] Samir: CloudHSM is convenient for hybrid clouds with AWS; if you're fully on-prem an HSM appliance is recommended. The appliance gives you full physical control. We support both and have integration guides for common vendors (Thales, Gemalto).
[40:26] Ethan: If we do on-prem HSM, can Redwood still sign updates? How do you verify update packages?
[40:33] Luca: All updates are signed with Redwood's code signing key and we provide verifiable signatures. You can require a chain-of-trust attestation before applying any update.
[40:43] Nadia: What about dual-control for rotations? We require two approvers for key rotation.
[40:49] Samir: We can support a dual-signature rotation flow where two authorized operators sign off on the new key before it becomes active. Rotation events are recorded in the audit log.
[40:59] Rosa: Splunk ingestion — do you accept forwarded JSON or do we need a HEC token?
[41:06] Samir: Both supported: HEC tokens are easiest, or you can forward via syslog. We'll provide sample connectors.
[41:16] Tom: For evidence, auditor may ask for a snapshot of the HSM policies. Can you produce a sample policy?
[41:23] Maya: Yes — we'll include a sample HSM policy in the KMS doc set.
[41:30] (50 minute mark - risks and mitigations)
[50:02] Ethan: Are there any common gotchas customers run into during SOC 2 audits with Redwood Private?
[50:09] Maya: Common items: missing evidence for ephemeral token rotation, not capturing config diffs, and relying on default retention. We recommend explicit retention configs and periodic export of snapshots.
[50:22] Nadia: Any known performance hit with encryption and HSM round trips for decryption?
[50:28] Luca: There's added latency for HSM ops but we use key-wrapping and cache unwrapped keys in memory with short TTLs to minimize calls. We'll provide numbers from our benchmark: typical per-request overhead under 8ms for wrapped-key flow.
[50:46] Rosa: That seems acceptable.
[50:49] Tom: Final question: can you provide a sample SOC 2 evidence bundle after pilot?
[50:55] Maya: Yes — after pilot we can produce an evidence bundle with logs, config snapshots, and the mapping doc.
[51:04] (closing minutes)
[51:10] Maya: Quick recap — Redwood to send: KMS architecture + BYOK options, endpoint allowlist, onboarding checklist, SOC 2 mapping doc, and Splunk examples. Pegasus to share firewall export and agree pilot dates.
[51:25] Ethan: We'll aim to get the firewall export and schedule the pilot.
[51:30] Rosa: Please include the signed checksum and SBOM for the keyproxy binary.
[51:36] Samir: Will do.
[51:40] (small social)
[51:45] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites and the docs.
[51:50] Rosa: Thanks all.

[03:44] Carlos: TLS is end-to-end. For private endpoint peering TLS terminates at the service endpoint inside the Redwood VPC; for an on-prem runtime you hold certs. We can also integrate with your KMS for key material if you run private.
[03:58] Lena: Okay, can you quickly sketch the data path for the two approaches?
[04:02] Priya: Sure — handing off to quick sketch: Option A: Private endpoints/peering to Redwood-managed runtime. You establish VPC peering or Transit Gateway to Redwood VPC. Traffic hits private endpoint, traverses peering link to Redwood runtime in the same cloud region, model runs, tokens and KV cache handled by Redwood runtime. Egress IPs provided by Redwood NAT. Option B: Customer-hosted runtime (Redwood Private): we ship a runtime image, it runs in your VPC or on-prem, control plane optionally sits in Redwood's control plane with an encrypted control channel, or you can opt to host control plane as well in your VPC. No external egress needed except for optional metrics/log shipping.
[04:45] Maya: If we host the runtime, does the control plane still need to talk back to Redwood?
[04:50] Priya: You can choose a 'private control plane' where the control plane API is in a customer network — that eliminates most calls outbound. We do require a bootstrap connection for updates unless you opt for air-gapped. We have an on-prem package for that flow.
[05:03] Samir: What about performance tuning: batching and the KV cache you mentioned. How is that impacted when runtime is outside Redwood cluster?
[05:11] Priya: If runtime is in your VPC, batching and KV cache behave the same as in our hosted environment because it's the same runtime. The only difference is networking latency between your app and the runtime. That's why we recommend colocating the runtime in the same region and AZ as the callers.
[05:27] Lena: For ACLs — we use very strict NACLs. Is there a minimal set of ports/protocols we need to open?
[05:33] Priya: Mostly TCP for gRPC/HTTPS on TLS. We'll provide a minimal port matrix. For peering you'll need to accept certain prefixes and routes; for Transit Gateway there's an extra step for route tables. We'll send a port/route checklist.
[05:47] Carlos: I also want to call out quotas and rate limiting. If you put throughput behind the peering link, you may need to account for connection limits. For Dedicated we can reserve capacity with SLA to avoid throttling.
[05:58] Maya: How does Dedicated compare price-wise vs private-hosted?
[06:02] Carlos: Dedicated is a Redwood-managed reserved pool in our infra — cheaper ops for you but data flows through Redwood infrastructure. Private-hosted is you pay for infra and manage network but gives full control. We'll share a price delta spreadsheet — Priya will drop the numbers.
[06:14] Priya: I'll prepare a rough delta later today.
[06:17] Samir: On the security compliance side we need to run a vulnerability scan on any images you ship for the runtime. Are runtime images signed?
[06:26] Priya: Yes, runtime images are signed — and we can provide SBOM and vulnerability scan reports. For customers who run their own runtime we recommend you run an additional internal scan; we can also provide an attestation.
[06:38] Lena: There's also procurement constraints — we need an enterprise contract with data residency clauses and indemnities. Who do we talk to?
[06:45] Carlos: Our commercial team will loop in legal — I'll include our standard enterprise addendum, and we can highlight residency clauses. That'll be in the package I send.
[06:54] Maya: One operational question: how do upgrades happen for a customer-hosted runtime?
[07:00] Priya: We have a controlled rollout process: we produce a signed artifact, you can opt into automatic updates or manual approval. Rollouts can be canaryed across nodes; we also support A/B traffic splitting if you run multiple runtime versions.
[07:14] Samir: For observability we need trace correlation and per-request IDs so our SIEM can stitch requests back to user IDs.
[07:21] Priya: We emit trace headers and request IDs; we can forward them with logs and provide a tracing hook. We'll add the sample tracing config to the runbook.
[07:31] Lena: Let's talk about our DR model — during failover we may redirect some traffic to our AWS DR region. If Redwood region is eu-west-2 and you don't have capacity there, I don't want silent routing to US. How are failovers surfaced?
[07:44] Priya: We surface failover behavior in the route configuration. By default some customers enable automatic fallback, but for strict residency you would disable fallback and instead surface explicit error. Alternatively you can create an exception route for DR traffic that goes to a pinned region in AWS. We'll walk through route policies in the next session.
[08:05] Carlos: Quick poll — is the team leaning toward peering-first or hosting runtime in-house as the long-term plan?
[08:12] Lena: Short-term peering with private endpoints to prove connectivity. Long-term possible on-prem/private runtime to avoid egress.
[08:20] Maya: Agreed. We want to run a pilot with a few endpoints and then measure latency and cost.
[08:25] Samir: Also want to do a security review — can you provide SOC2 and any ISO certs you have?
[08:31] Carlos: Yes, SOC2 report and ISO certs. I'll attach them to the follow-up email.
[08:36] Lena: For the pilot we need to know the expected token throughput — can Redwood give us guidance on instance sizing for our expected QPS?
[08:44] Priya: Absolutely — share your current QPS, avg seq len, and concurrency targets and we'll map to a recommended profile (GPU type, batch config, quantization). We'll include a sizing worksheet.
[08:56] Maya: We'll put together a quick traffic profile doc.
[09:00] Priya: One last nuts-and-bolts: when you set up VPC peering to a Redwood VPC, you must ensure route propagation for the prefixes we provide. For Transit Gateway there's a slightly different setup and you can do centralized egress. If you're using cloud express connectivity (Interconnect / Direct Connect), that also works through transit.
[09:18] Lena: We're on GCP Interconnect for our onprem -> cloud. Do you support partner interconnect routes?
[09:23] Priya: Yes, Partner Interconnect is fine as long as the route reaches your VPC — it's just the regular IP reachability. We'll work with your network team to validate.
[09:32] Samir: A question about secrets — if we have to pass keys to the runtime, do we want Redwood to manage them or do we hold them in our KMS?
[09:40] Priya: If you're running runtime in your VPC you can host keys; for Redwood-managed runtime we offer KMS integrations and envelope encryption so you retain control over keys in your KMS. We'll add a doc on KMS integration patterns.
[09:52] Carlos: Alright, looks like good alignment. Quick recap of next steps: I'll send security docs and legal starter packet; Priya will send region capacity and price delta; Lena will share network diagram and traffic profile; we schedule a tech deep dive next week.
[10:08] Maya: Sounds good. Thanks Carlos and Priya.

transcript:
Header: 2028-04-17 16:00 UTC | Duration: 52m | Attendees: Alex Morales (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Evan Liu (Redwood), Dr. Sara Lin (CTO - NexisHealth), Marcus Hale (ML Lead), Anita Verma (Infra), Tom Ruiz (Product), Jing Park (Data Eng)

0:00 Alex Morales: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros from our side - I'm Alex, AE, Priya is our systems SE, Evan helps on benchmarks.
0:18 Dr. Sara Lin: Hi all, thanks. we'll be pretty focused, Marcus will cover the ML requirements, Anita our infra constraints.
0:30 Alex Morales: Great, goal of today's chat is to decide hosting approach for embeddings + rerank pilot and surface networking/security blockers.
0:45 Priya Kapoor: Quick agenda — current infra, embedding volumes/dimensions, expected qps and p99 SLOs, vector DB integration options, rerank placement, and next steps.
1:10 Marcus Hale: To give context — we run a search product for clinicians. Queries/day ~ 1.2M, peak qps around 140; expected pilot 200k/day but bursty. Typical query returns top 100 candidates from our vector DB then we do a rerank with a small 2B-ish model.
1:38 Alex Morales: When you say 2B-ish, is that an off-the-shelf model or custom? and is rerank done with the same embeddings or with separate features?
1:50 Marcus Hale: It's a fine-tuned open model — we currently run it on a single A10 box in prod for low-volume. Features: embedding dim 1536 (from our current encoder), some metadata features. We want the rerank to be fast — p95 under 120ms if possible.
2:12 Priya Kapoor: Ok p95 120ms is ambitious when you're doing a vector fanout plus rerank. Two general options: 1) embeddings and rerank served by Redwood near the app (hosted/dedicated) with local rerank to avoid network RTT to the vector DB, or 2) keep embeddings in customer VDB (Pinecone/Milvus) and call Redwood only for the rerank model or do hybrid — embed externally and rerank in Redwood.
2:42 Dr. Sara Lin: Security wise, we prefer data not to leave our region for PHI. So private or dedicated with VPC peering + KMS is preferable. Hosted API might be hard for compliance unless we have enterprise controls.
3:05 Anita Verma: Also, we have strict egress rules — any hosted option needs a clear list of IPs or private link.
3:18 Alex Morales: Understood. For dedicated we can allocate reserved GPU pools within a region and offer VPC peering; Private option provides a customer-managed control plane with on-prem or VPC deployment and brings KMS integration. We'll include SOC2 docs.
3:35 Tom Ruiz: Cost is big. For rerank, we care about cost per 1k reranks and cost per 1M embeddings. We're trying to model economics vs latency.
3:48 Priya Kapoor: Some quick numbers — if you quantize the rerank model to int8 or int4 we can reduce memory footprint and increase throughput by 1.8-3x, but there is a small accuracy impact; similarly embedding dims: moving 1536 -> 768 halves storage and retrieval costs but may change recall.
4:15 Marcus Hale: We did a quick A/B and 768 lost about 1.2% recall on our testset for top-10. Might be acceptable.
4:28 Evan Liu: For throughput, what matters is how you batch. If you do synchronous rerank per query with 100 candidates, batching across queries can amortize kernel launches. Redwood runtime supports continuous batching & KV cache for prefix hits which helps chat-like flows; for rerank the pattern is more bursty.
4:53 Marcus Hale: Our pattern is bursty; morning clinical hours are huge spikes. We need autoscaling that can handle 3x baseline for a 10-minute window.
5:06 Priya Kapoor: Dedicated pools support quick scaling and burst capacity; Private gives you control but autoscaling may depend on the customer's infra. We can pre-warm and keep a small committed pool to hit p95s.
5:28 Jing Park: For vector DB we currently use Pinecone managed; we'd either keep that or consider migrating to Milvus self-hosted if needed. How does Redwood integrate with an external vector DB?
5:45 Alex Morales: Two options: 1) Redwood calls your VDB as part of the pipeline (we call Pinecone for top K)** — this adds network latency; 2) you fanout vectors to both VDB and Redwood cache/index and run rerank locally in Redwood. Many customers do a hybrid where retrieval is done in VDB but rerank co-located.
6:09 Marcus Hale: If we keep the VDB external, what's a realistic p95 add?
6:16 Priya Kapoor: Depends on region and VDB average RTT; ballpark +30-80ms just for fanout roundtrips if cross-network. Coupled with rerank compute, could push p95 over 200ms.
6:30 Dr. Sara Lin: So for strict p95 under 120ms we probably must co-locate rerank with retrieval or keep a warm cache of candidates inside Redwood.
6:44 Alex Morales: Right — you can store a hot index or cache in Redwood via prefix/KV cache; or we can run embeddings + vector index on your private deployment so everything is intra-vpc with single-digit ms network calls.
7:03 Anita Verma: If we go private, how is KMS handled? We need to ensure keys never leave our KMS/HSM.
7:12 Priya Kapoor: Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and we can keep keys in your cloud KMS; Redwood will not have raw key material. We'll send the KMS integration guide.
7:26 Marcus Hale: What's the deployment time for private vs dedicated?
7:32 Alex Morales: Dedicated reserved pools can be provisioned in 2-4 weeks depending on capacity and region. Private VPC deployment (managed) typically 4-8 weeks — longer if on-prem air-gapped.
7:45 Tom Ruiz: Timeline wise, we want pilot in 6 weeks. Is that feasible?
7:50 Alex Morales: Pilot in 6 weeks is tight but possible with dedicated + peering; private might be risky unless we start immediately.
8:03 Priya Kapoor: For a pilot we recommend starting with Dedicated — gives predictable throughput and easier onboarding. If compliance is strict we can do a dedicated in your VPC via peering, or start with dedicated and migrate to private later.
8:22 Marcus Hale: Sounds ok. For benchmarks — we want end-to-end: query fanout to top 100, rerank top 100 with our 2B model quantized to int8, 1536 embeddings. Can Redwood simulate that?
8:38 Evan Liu: Yes, we'll run a synthetic workload matching your histograms. We'll need the dataset sample and the spike profile. We'll test hosted vs dedicated vs private (if possible) but private will require your infra access.
8:51 Jing Park: We can share a 100k subset and traffic histogram. One caveat: our dataset includes PHI, so we need an NDA for data transfer.
8:59 Alex Morales: Noted — we'll use synthetic anonymized data for initial runs. For PHI we'll follow your compliance process; enterprise/legal already discussed NDAs previously.
9:12 Marcus Hale: Another question: vector dimension reductions — is there tooling to project to smaller dims on the fly?
9:20 Priya Kapoor: We don't do dimensionality reduction as a managed service but we can recommend approaches — knowledge distillation, PCA or training a new encoder. Many customers keep high-dim embeddings for recall and then use compact embeddings for latency-sensitive endpoints.
9:38 Tom Ruiz: Regarding rerank model size — are there options to split the model? e.g., two-stage rerank where a small model filters then a bigger model re-scores top 20.
9:48 Priya Kapoor: Absolutely, that's common. Two-stage reduces cost and latency; Redwood supports multi-model rollouts and routing policies, so you can run light model inline and heavy model for fallback / periodic re-score.
10:05 Dr. Sara Lin: What's the failure/fallback story? If dedicated nodes are saturated, do you fallback to hosted or a smaller model?
10:14 Alex Morales: We support graceful degradation policies: fallback to a smaller model or to an older model variant, and routing by latency policy; can also reroute to another region or capacity tier. We'll show examples in the runbook.
10:30 Anita Verma: Monitoring — what observability do we get? We need token-level latency + per-route P95 + audit logs for each request with request IDs.
10:42 Priya Kapoor: Redwood Console has per-route dashboards, token/latency breakdowns, trace hooks and 6 months of audit logs (longer retention as add-on). We can tie logs to your SIEM via syslog or S3 export.
10:57 Marcus Hale: How's the per-token pricing handled for rerank? If we do large rerank batches, cost could spike.
11:05 Alex Morales: Pricing can be usage-based plus reserved capacity. For rerank we meter token compute and model runtime. We'll include examples: cost per 1k reranks at different batch sizes, and committed discounts.
11:20 Tom Ruiz: Any caveats around embeddings stored in external VDB re: freshness and consistency?
11:26 Priya Kapoor: If you're writing embeddings to an external VDB there's eventual consistency and sync latency; for near-real-time you can write to both VDB and Redwood cache synchronously or use streaming replication. We have connectors/recipes for common VDBs.
11:44 Jing Park: On the topic of connectors, does Redwood do vector sharding or routing for high-throughput retrievals?
11:51 Evan Liu: Redwood doesn't replace your VDB sharding; we can operate with sharded VDBs and implement hybrid top-k routing. For rerank-heavy workloads we recommend sharding embeddings across dedicated pools and using consistent routing to reduce cross-node fanout.
12:09 Marcus Hale: curious about caching — can we keep a hot set of candidate vectors in Redwood to avoid VDB roundtrip for popular queries?
12:17 Priya Kapoor: Yes, prefix/KV cache for hot items is supported; works very well for repeated patterns. It reduces network roundtrip and significantly lowers p95 latency.
12:28 Dr. Sara Lin: Let's talk security specifics — SSO, RBAC, and audit — we need SAML + SCIM provisioning and role based access.
12:36 Alex Morales: We support SAML SSO, SCIM for user provisioning and fine-grained RBAC. We'll include our security pack with SOC2, ISO docs and the IAM mappings examples.
12:50 Anita Verma: For private we need to ensure no egress to internet aside from approved endpoints. How is software patching handled?
12:58 Priya Kapoor: For private managed we coordinate patch windows; we can do offline package delivery for air-gapped. For VPC you can restrict outbound and we provide a list of endpoints to allow for telemetry.
13:15 Marcus Hale: Ok shifting to cost modeling — Alex, can you walk through an example with our numbers?
13:20 Alex Morales: Sure — rough calc: assume 200k queries/day during pilot, top100 candidates, average rerank tokens 200, quantized int8; dedicated with reserved capacity gives X dollars per month — we'll attach a spreadsheet but short version: dedicated reduces per-call cost vs pure hosted at scale by about 20-40% depending on utilization.
13:43 Tom Ruiz: We need that spreadsheet. Also want to see committed capacity tiers and breakpoints where dedicated becomes cheaper.
13:50 Alex Morales: We'll send it.
13:55 Jing Park: For the benchmark, can you also include tail-latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99) and warm vs cold start numbers?
14:04 Evan Liu: Absolutely; we'll run cold start, warm steady-state, and burst spike tests. We'll include CPU/GPU utilization and memory for the model variants.
14:18 Priya Kapoor: One more note on quantization — int4 is attractive but requires validation. Some models degrade more than others. We'll validate accuracy tradeoffs during bench runs.
14:30 Marcus Hale: Are there customers who've done a similar migration from Pinecone managed to Redwood private/dedicated?
14:36 Alex Morales: Yes, a healthcare customer migrated retrieval into a dedicated pool with VPC peering and kept Pinecone as cold store; they reduced p95 by ~60ms and cut per-query cost ~25%. We'll anonymize and share that case study.
14:51 Dr. Sara Lin: Good. Any blockers from our side for pilot?
14:55 Anita Verma: Need to verify outbound rules for peering and provide a SID for the network team. Also legal needs updated SOC2 docs.
15:04 Alex Morales: We'll send the SOC2, KMS guide, and network checklist tonight.
15:10 Tom Ruiz: Quick question — for experiments, can we do AB testing between reranking variants?
15:16 Priya Kapoor: Yes, Redwood supports canary/A-B rollouts and automatic fallback if the model underperforms; metrics tie into our evals so you can compare recall and latency.
15:30 Marcus Hale: Good. Regarding data residency, is dedicated deployed in multiple regions or single?
15:36 Alex Morales: Dedicated pools can be provisioned per region; for multi-region failover we set up cross-region routing and replicate models. For strict residency you can pin workloads to a specific region.
15:52 Dr. Sara Lin: Let's capture final decisions: for pilot we lean toward Dedicated in our region with VPC peering, quantized int8 rerank, keep embeddings initially in Pinecone but push hot set to Redwood cache, run benchmarks, then evaluate Private if compliance requires.
16:12 Alex Morales: Excellent summary — we'll create a pilot plan doc reflecting that and include timelines.
16:20 Evan Liu: Action items: we'll need the sample dataset, traffic histograms and infra constraints.
16:28 Jing Park: We'll provide dataset and histograms by Friday, and Anita will provide network rules.
16:35 Priya Kapoor: We'll prepare benchmark configs and propose test windows; expect a first pass within 5 business days after we have the data.
16:45 Alex Morales: Any other concerns?
16:49 Marcus Hale: Only that we validate the 1.2% recall drop if we try 768 dims in a side experiment.
16:57 Priya Kapoor: We'll include that experiment in the bench plan.
17:05 Dr. Sara Lin: Thanks everyone. We'll look out for the pricing and pilot doc.
17:12 Alex Morales: Thanks all — we'll follow up with pricing, SOC2, and schedule the deep technical VPC/KMS dive next week.
17:20 Meeting end.

[Access-to-Award: Company-wide Playbook for Access, Change, Procurement and Vendor Workflows]
Overview

This playbook, "Access-to-Award", defines the end-to-end company policies and prescriptive procedures for: access and permissions, change management, data handling, procurement and expenses, vendor management, travel approvals, and the set of canonical internal templates. It is intended for all employees, hiring managers, procurement requesters, and approvers.

Scope

Applies to: all Redwood employees, contractors with corporate accounts, and any supplier integrations that interact with Redwood infrastructure or corporate data.

Objectives

- Reduce time-to-approve for common procurements to <= 5 business days for requests under $10k.
- Centralize access requests with auditable approvals and 90-day revalidation cycles.
- Ensure vendor onboarding includes a standardized risk assessment and an assigned contract owner.
- Minimize unapproved configuration changes by enforcing change windows and pre-deployment checklists.

Key Roles and Responsibilities

- Requester: Submits the procurement or access request and provides business justification.
- Approver: Team manager or cost center owner who validates business need.
- Procurement Owner (Finance): Reviews supplier terms, price reasonableness, and tax/compliance checks.
- Security Reviewer: Assesses data access, required controls, and required legal addenda.
- IT/Cloud Ops: Implements access and provisioning tasks.
- Contract Owner: Maintains the vendor contract and renewal calendar.

Section 1 — Access and Permissions (Access-to-Award phase A)

Policy statements:
- Principle of least privilege enforced by default. Access is granted for a defined purpose and expiry.
- All privileges that allow data egress, escalation, or production writes require a business justification and Security approval.

Process (Steps):
1) Requester files an Access Request via the Access Portal (access.redwood.internal). Include duration, scope, and justification.
2) Manager approves or rejects within 3 business days.
3) Security performs risk review for sensitive scopes (PII, Billing, Secrets).
4) IT provisions access with a time-limited role and records audit entry.
5) Revalidation reminder triggered at 60 days, mandatory reapproval at 90 days.

Access tiers and examples:
- Tier 0: Public docs; no request required.
- Tier 1: Internal non-sensitive services (read-only dashboards). Manager approval.
- Tier 2: Sensitive systems (billing, PII). Manager + Security approval.
- Tier 3: Privileged operations (deploy write access, infra admin). Manager + Security + SRE approval.

Section 2 — Change Management

Change types:
- Routine: Configuration changes that are reversible, low risk. No CAB required if change < 15 min impact and tested in staging.
- Scheduled: Feature releases, infra scaling with >15 min expected impact — requires standard CAB review.
- Emergency: Outage mitigation — documented post-facto to CAB within 24 hours.

Change windows and SLA:
- Normal change window: Mon–Fri 09:00–17:00 UTC for non-critical services. Night/weekend windows are reserved for scheduled infra changes with pre-approved rollback plans.
- Rollback capability must be demonstrable in <= 30 minutes for any change classified as Scheduled.

Pre-deployment checklist (required):
- Link to runbook and test results.
- Smoke test plan and rollback steps.
- Impacted services and owners listed.
- Performance and observability queries included.

Section 3 — Data Management

Data classification categories: PUBLIC, INTERNAL, CONFIDENTIAL, RESTRICTED. All datasets must be labeled in the data catalog.

Handling rules (high level):
- RESTRICTED: Encryption at rest + in transit, limited to named principals, storage audited monthly.
- CONFIDENTIAL: MFA enforced for access, export controls applied.

Data retention & deletion:
- Default retention for logs: 90 days (hot), 2 years (cold).
- Sensitive PII: retention only as long as required by the business process; data owner must document retention justification.

Data sharing with vendors:
- Data sharing requires: Data Processing Agreement (DPA), approved SOC/ISO evidence, and a Data Access Justification form. No PII is shared without encryption and contractual protections.

Section 4 — Procurement and Expense Approval (Access-to-Award phase B)

Purchase thresholds and path: 
| Amount range | Required approvals | Procurement path | Typical SLA |
|--------------|--------------------|------------------|-----------|
| <$1,000      | Manager            | Self-serve expense | 3 business days |
| $1,000–$25,000 | Manager + Finance  | Procurement ticket | 5–7 business days |
| >$25,000     | Manager + Finance + VP | Procurement + Contract review | 10–20 business days |

Request process (summary):
1) Create a Purchase Request in the Procurement Portal with line-item estimates and vendor info.
2) Finance validates budgets and tax implications.
3) Procurement negotiates terms and issues PO.
4) Contract Owner finalizes legal terms for >$25k or if data will be accessed by vendor.

Expense policy highlights:
- Travel expenses require pre-approval for airfare > $1,000 or international travel.
- Per diem caps and class of travel are defined in the Travel section template.

Section 5 — Vendor Management and Onboarding

Vendor risk assessment: score vendors on Security (30%), Financial stability (20%), Strategic dependency (20%), Legal/Compliance (30%). A vendor with a calculated score > 75 requires an executive sponsor and quarterly reviews.

Onboarding checklist (must be completed before production access):
- Signed contract and DPA.
- Completed vendor security questionnaire and evidence (SOC2/ISO/etc).
- Assigned Contract Owner and renewal date entered into vendor ledger.
- Technical contact, escalation path, and SLOs documented.

Sample vendor scorecard (CSV-friendly):
vendor_name,security_score,financial_score,dependency_score,legal_score,total_score,contract_owner,renewal_date
AcmeAI,85,70,60,90,76,FinOps Team,2029-05-12

Section 6 — Travel Policy (summary and pre-approval workflow)

- Business travel requires a Travel Request form with justification, estimated cost, and itinerary.
- Manager must approve domestic travel; VP approval required for international travel or events with budget > $5,000.
- Preferred booking channels: corporate travel portal; exceptions require Finance approval.

Section 7 — Templates and Forms (Appendix)

Included templates (canonical):
- Access Request Form (fields: resource, scope, duration, justification, manager)
- Procurement Request (vendor, line items, cost center, budget code, business case)
- Vendor Onboarding Checklist (contract steps, evidence required)
- Change Request Template (description, rollback plan, test plan, owners)
- Travel Request Template (dates, justification, estimated cost)

Example: Procurement request YAML snippet
---
requester: aisha.patel@redwood.com
vendor: AcmeAI
items:
  - sku: ACME-ENT-1
    description: Enterprise model endpoint (12 months)
    unit_cost: 8500
    quantity: 1
cost_center: ENG-PLATFORM
justification: Production inference capacity for Redwood Dedicated testing
---

Escalation matrix (quick):
- Day 0–3: Manager approval queue (auto-reminder).
- Day 4–7: Procurement owner escalates to Finance Lead.
- Day 8+: VP review required for unresolved high-priority requests.

Audit and Compliance

- Monthly reports: open access grants, expiring vendor contracts, pending procurements > $10k.
- Quarterly audits: random sample of access revalidation, procurement approvals, and vendor evidence.

Operational Metrics (tracked):
- Median time to approve access requests.
- % of scheduled changes with successful rollback tests.
- Time from procurement request to PO issuance.
- Vendor risk score distribution.

Change history and governance

This playbook is maintained by Finance-Legal with Security and IT as primary reviewers. Major revisions follow a documented change request and will be ratified by the Governance Board.

Contact and escalation

- Procurement Queue: procurement@redwood.internal
- Security Review: security-review@redwood.internal
- Finance Owner: finops@redwood.internal

References and links

- Internal Access Portal: https://access.redwood.internal
- Procurement Portal: https://procure.redwood.internal
- Vendor Ledger: https://vendors.redwood.internal

Revision notes

2027-09-01: Initial draft authored by Aisha Patel.
2028-05-14: Published with updated procurement thresholds and vendor risk scoring formula.


[Workplace Access, Change, and Global Travel Playbook]
Overview:

This playbook consolidates company-wide policies and step-by-step procedures for: access and permissions (entitlement lifecycle), change management, data handling and classification, procurement & expenses, vendor onboarding, and global travel. It is intended for requesters, approvers, line managers, and process owners. The document includes practical templates and runnable examples for frequently used workflows.

Scope and applicability:

- Applies to all Redwood Inference employees, contractors, and approved external vendors.
- Covers systems and services under Redwood control, including cloud accounts, internal admin consoles, payroll/expense systems, and external vendor portals when acting on Redwood’s behalf.
- Does not replace service-specific runbooks (see related pages).

Owners and escalation:

- Primary owner: People Ops (policy maintenance, approvals cadence).
- Access control steward: Security & Compliance (RBAC design, periodic audits).
- Procurement owner: Finance & Legal (PO policy, vendor contracts).
- Travel owner: People Ops (policy, corporate card governance).
- Escalation path: requestor -> direct manager -> owner_team contact -> People Ops director.

1) Access & Permissions (Entitlement Lifecycle)

Purpose: Ensure least-privilege access while enabling productive work.

Roles and definitions:

- Requestor: employee requiring access.
- Approver: direct manager or role owner.
- Role Owner: team or service owner responsible for role definitions (e.g., "infra-admin", "billing-reader").
- Provisioning system: Identity Provider (IdP) + SCIM automation feeding our access orchestration service.

Entitlement matrix (summary):

- Day-to-day access (<= 30 days): Manager approval required. Examples: temporary dev credentials, test cluster access.
- Project access (> 30 days): Manager + Role Owner sign-off. Examples: service-specific production access.
- Admin-level access: Manager + Role Owner + Security approval. Examples: core infra, secrets-management admin.
- Vendor/contractor access: Manager + Security + Procurement (term-limited).

Request workflow (standard):

1. Requestor files an Access Request via the Access Portal (template below).
2. Automated check: IdP verifies group mappings; if matching policy, auto-approve for low-risk roles.
3. Manager receives approval email with 48-hour SLA to approve/deny.
4. If Role Owner approval required, routed to them after manager approval.
5. Provisioning automation grants access and records audit event (SAML/SCIM).
6. Access review occurs at 90-day cadence for all non-service accounts; owners must certify access or trigger revocation.

Emergency access (break-glass):

- Use the emergency escalation channel with multifactor confirmation (Slack private channel + ticket).
- Emergency admin sessions are limited to 4 hours and must be logged; postmortem required within 48 hours.

Example Access Request template (JSON payload for automation):

{
  "requester_email": "alice@example.com",
  "requested_role": "service-readonly",
  "justification": "Onboarding for analytics project",
  "duration": "90d",
  "manager_approval": "pending"
}

2) Change Management

Purpose: Reduce risk while enabling regular changes to services, infra, and policy.

Change types and approvals:

- Standard change: Pre-authorized, repeatable, low-risk (no CAB). Owner: service team. Examples: scheduled library upgrades per policy.
- Normal change: Requires Change Advisory Board (CAB) review for medium/high risk. Owner: service team + change manager.
- Emergency change: Go-to state for outages or critical fixes. Owner: incident commander; post-implementation review mandatory.

CAB composition and meeting cadence:

- Weekly CAB for scheduled normal changes. Members: Change Manager, 2 SRE reps, 1 Security rep, Finance/Compliance as needed.
- Emergency CAB: ad-hoc with rota-defined on-call staff.

Change submission checklist (minimum):

- Change ID and owner
- Rollout window and blackout windows
- Backout/rollback plan with exact commands or scripts
- Monitoring & verification steps (metrics to observe)
- Impacted services and stakeholders
- Test plan or pre-production verification evidence

Rollback template (example commands):

- Step 1: Halt rollout: ./deploy stop --change-id CHG-2025-1234
- Step 2: Revert to last good artifact: ./deploy revert --artifact v2025.01
- Step 3: Verify service health via: curl -fsS https://status.internal/service/health || echo "health-fail"

3) Data Management and Classification

Classification tiers:

- Public: Data safe for external distribution.
- Internal: Company-only, non-sensitive operational data.
- Confidential: Customer PII, model training datasets with contractual restrictions. Access requires documented business justification and DPA alignment.
- Restricted: Secrets, private keys, and regulated data. Access is strictly controlled and audited.

Data access request flow:

1. Request submitted to Data Catalog (include dataset, purpose, and retention).
2. Data steward reviews classification and returns decision within 5 business days.
3. For Confidential/Restricted data, Security performs a privacy review and approves technical controls.

Retention and deletion:

- Default retention for internal logs: 90 days.
- Product telemetry: 365 days unless otherwise specified.
- Customer data: per contract; default 30 days post-termination unless extended by customer agreement.
- Data deletion requests must produce a deletion certificate stored with the ticket.

Storage and encryption requirements:

- All Confidential/Restricted datasets must be stored encrypted at rest with KMS-managed keys.
- Secrets must be stored in approved Secrets Manager only.

4) Procurement & Expenses

Thresholds and approvals (summary):

- <= $2,000: Manager approval.
- $2,001 - $25,000: Manager + Finance approval.
- > $25,000: Manager + Finance + Legal (contract review) + Procurement team.

Preferred vendors and purchase channel:

- Use the Procurement Portal for all SaaS subscriptions and hardware purchases.
- Use approved vendor list (AVL) maintained by Procurement - exceptions require Procurement approval.

Purchase Order (PO) process (steps):

1. Requestor fills Purchase Request template in Procurement Portal (fields below).
2. Finance validates budget availability and routes to Legal for contract review if > $25k.
3. Procurement issues PO; vendor must acknowledge before order.

Purchase Request template (fields):

- project_code
- vendor_name
- business_justification
- estimated_amount
- requested_delivery_date
- approver_manager

Expense reimbursement guidelines:

- Use Concur for expense submissions. Attach receipts > $25 and itemize airfare and hotel nights.
- Meal per diem: $75/day domestic; regional caps for international (see Travel section).
- Corporate card: allowed for travel-related expenses; reconcile within 7 business days.

Example PO JSON (automation-friendly):

{
  "project_code": "ENG-PLATFORM-Q2",
  "vendor_name": "FastInfra Inc",
  "amount": "12000",
  "description": "Dedicated support contract"
}

5) Vendor Management and Onboarding

Onboarding checklist:

1. Procurement issues initial SOW/PO.
2. Legal & Security complete vendor risk assessment (VRM questionnaire).
3. Finance verifies payment terms and tax forms.
4. Security (if access required) defines least-privilege access and term-limits.
5. Procurement adds vendor to AVL and assigns vendor owner.

Vendor re-assessment cadence:

- High-risk vendors: quarterly review.
- Medium-risk vendors: semi-annual.
- Low-risk vendors: annual.

Security controls required for vendors with system access:

- Unique vendor accounts (no shared generic logins).
- MFA enabled on all vendor accounts.
- Access timeboxes (e.g., 30/90 days) and automated expiry.
- Contract clause for data handling, breach notification (72 hours), and audit rights.

6) Global Travel Policy

Booking and approvals:

- Domestic travel: Manager approval required for trips longer than 2 consecutive nights or > $1,000 total.
- International travel: Manager + People Ops travel approval; certain countries require Security clearance (see Travel Restrictions matrix).
- Use corporate travel portal or approved travel agencies; exceptions require People Ops pre-approval.

Per diems and allowable expenses:

- Domestic per diem: $75/day for meals & incidentals.
- International per diem: determined by country band (see appendix table).
- Ground transportation: rideshare or taxi; use lowest-cost safe option.

Safety and emergency procedures:

- All travelers must register trip in the Travel Tracker and share itinerary with People Ops.
- Emergency contact: People Ops on-call + Security on-call.
- Medical evacuations: covered for business travel with corporate insurance when pre-approved.

Travel Restrictions matrix (examples):

- High-risk jurisdictions: require Security clearance and written approval from People Ops director.
- Sanctioned countries: travel is prohibited unless Legal provides specific written exception.

Expense claim timeline:

- Submit expense reports within 10 business days of trip completion. Delays > 30 days require manager justification.

7) Templates and Quick Artifacts

Included templates (accessible in Templates library):

- Access Request (web form + JSON payload)
- Purchase Request (Procurement Portal template + PO JSON sample)
- Vendor Onboarding checklist (CSV checklist)
- Change Request form (CAB submission HTML form)

Change Request quick checklist (bullet list for CAB submission):

- CHG-Id assigned
- Owner and rollback owner listed
- Verified pre-prod test results attached
- Monitoring metric thresholds listed

Appendix: contacts and SLAs

- People Ops (policy inbox): people-ops@redwood.ai (SLA: 3 business days for policy questions)
- Procurement: procurement@redwood.ai (SLA: 2 business days on purchase requests)
- Security/Access steward: security-ops@redwood.ai (SLA: 5 business days for non-emergency access reviews)
- Emergency change channel: #emergency-changes (instant)
