[Advance Payments & Retainers: Controls, Procurement Flow, and Revenue Recognition Guidance]
Overview:

This guidance establishes Redwood Inference’s required controls, procurement flow, contract language, and accounting treatment for advance payments (including retainers and prepaid service arrangements). Purpose is to reduce revenue recognition risk, improve cash-to-revenue transparency, and standardize procurement and legal review for prepayment scenarios.

Scope:

- Applies to all negotiating parties that obligate Redwood to accept or disburse advance payments, retainers, deposits, or prepaid service fees across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private offerings.
- Includes customer-facing contracts, reseller/partner agreements, and vendor prepayment arrangements.

Key definitions:

- Advance payment: Any cash or cash-equivalent received prior to full delivery of contracted goods or services.
- Retainer: An upfront payment to secure availability of services for a defined period.
- Deferred revenue: Liability recorded when cash is received before satisfaction of performance obligations.
- Prepaid expense: Payment made in advance for goods or services Redwood will consume (vendor prepayment).

High-level policy statements:

1) All customer advance payments must be captured and tracked in the Deferred Revenue subledger within 3 business days of receipt.
2) Contract terms that include advance payments or retainers must be reviewed by Legal for clause alignment and by Finance for accounting impact prior to signature.
3) Procurement of vendor prepayments > USD 25,000 requires VP Finance approval and Security sign-off when the vendor will handle customer data.
4) Refund, netting, and escrow language standards must be used for advances > USD 100,000.

Approval matrix (summary):

- Up to USD 25,000: Product Manager + Procurement Lead signoff.
- USD 25,001 to USD 100,000: Head of Procurement + Finance Manager + Legal review.
- > USD 100,000: VP Finance + GC (General Counsel) + CRO (if customer impact).

(See sample approval table below for required artifacts.)

Procurement & Contract intake flow (required steps):

1. Business submits PR/Deal Intake with: SOW, proposed payment schedule, legal redlines, vendor security questionnaire (if vendor), and forecasted revenue recognition impact (Finance template).
2. Procurement validates vendor onboarding, tax/VAT questions, and completes supplier risk assessment.
3. Legal performs advance-payment clause review and inserts standard language (section below).
4. Finance performs recognition assessment (ASC 606 analysis), determines GL coding and deferred revenue schedule, and uploads prelim journal entries to NetSuite.
5. Approvals per matrix obtained.
6. PO/Customer Order and Payment Instructions issued. Cash recorded by Treasury; accounting entry created within 3 business days.

Required artifacts for approval (checklist):

- Fully executed contract or redline summary.
- Statement of Work or scope with acceptance criteria.
- Payment schedule and bank instructions.
- Finance revenue allocation worksheet (template in attachments).
- Vendor security questionnaire and remediation plan (if applicable).

Standard contract language (recommended clauses):

1) Advance Payment / Retainer Clause (example):

  "Customer shall pay an initial retainer equal to X% of the estimated fees upon execution. Such retainer will be held as a prepayment and applied to invoices as Services are performed. Refunds of unused retainer amounts will be made within 30 days of contract termination unless otherwise stated."

2) Escrow / Custodial Holders (for > USD 100,000):

  "If an advance exceeds USD 100,000, the parties shall place funds in a mutually agreeable escrow account or provide a bank guarantee. Escrow release terms will be tied to milestone acceptance."

3) Netting / Setoff Rights:

  "Redwood reserves the right to set off amounts owed to Customer against any outstanding unpaid obligations, subject to notice and applicable law."

4) Data & Security Addendum (if vendor holds customer data):

  "Vendor shall: comply with Redwood’s Data Processing Addendum, encrypt customer data at rest and in transit, and provide SOC2 Type II evidence within 30 days of request."

Accounting treatment (principles):

- Follow ASC 606 / IFRS 15 principles: identify the contract, separate performance obligations, determine the transaction price, allocate to performance obligations, and recognize when/ as obligations are satisfied.
- Typical treatments:
  - Annual support prepayment: Recognize ratably over support term (monthly amortization).
  - Retainer for on-call engineering: Recognize as services are delivered (transfer of control) — use usage-backed recognition if measurable.
  - Prepaid implementation milestone schedule: Recognize at the point of milestone acceptance if distinct.

Sample journal entries (simplified):

1) Receipt of advance payment from customer (cash receipt):

  Dr Cash (Bank)             USD 120,000
  Cr Deferred Revenue        USD 120,000

2) Recognize monthly revenue for annual support (12 months):

  Dr Deferred Revenue        USD 10,000
  Cr Revenue — Support       USD 10,000

3) Refund of unused portion of retainer (if customer terminates early):

  Dr Deferred Revenue        USD 6,000
  Cr Cash (Bank)             USD 6,000

4) Vendor prepayment for a specialized integration (expensed over useful life):

  Dr Prepaid Expense — Vendor USD 50,000
  Cr Cash (Bank)             USD 50,000

  Amortize monthly to Expense:
  Dr Integration Expense     USD 5,000
  Cr Prepaid Expense         USD 5,000

GL codes (recommended mapping examples):

- 2100 – Deferred Revenue — Customer Prepayments
- 2101 – Deferred Revenue — Retainers
- 1300 – Prepaid Expenses — Vendor Prepayments
- 4000 – Revenue — Support & Maintenance
- 4010 – Revenue — Professional Services

Revenue recognition templates & artifacts:

- Use the Finance "RevRec Assessment" spreadsheet for any deal including advance payments. The template captures performance obligations, allocation, and a recognition schedule. Link: /finance/revrec/templates/revrec-assessment-2025.xlsx
- Attach completed template to deal folder in NetSuite/DealRoom before routing for signature.

Billing & Invoicing requirements (customer-facing):

Required invoice fields when billing prepayments or applying retainer credits:

- Customer name and billing address
- Contract/PO number and SOW reference
- Invoice date and due date
- Line-level description showing: base fee, retainer applied, remaining retainer balance
- Amounts allocated to deferred revenue and amounts recognized as revenue this period
- GL mapping line (internal use)

Sample invoice narrative:

  "Invoice for Professional Services — Retainer application: Initial retainer USD 120,000 applied as credit for January 2026 services; remaining retainer balance USD 110,000."

Controls, monitoring, and KPIs:

- Monthly subledger reconciliation: Revenue Ops performs a deferred revenue subledger reconciliation by the 10th business day of each month.
- Aging report: Any deferred balance older than 90 days without a matching performance obligation or milestone triggers an investigation.
- Exception SLA: Investigation started within 3 business days; remediation completed within 15 business days, or escalate to VP Finance.
- Quarterly internal audit: select 10% of advance payment deals for audit each quarter (min 8 deals).

Escalation & exceptions procedure:

1) Discovery: Finance flags item via monthly reconciliation and adds to the "RevRec Exceptions" tracker.
2) Initial owner outreach: Revenue Ops pings deal owner (Sales or Customer Success) to provide SOW or evidence of performance.
3) If no resolution in 10 business days, Finance + Legal triage and propose remediation: either recognize on acceptance, refund, or contract amendment.
4) >30 days unresolved: Escalate to VP Finance and Legal for decision on reserve or write-off.

Operational examples & edge cases:

- Multi-year prepayment with annual renewals: allocate contract price across each year based on standalone selling price methodology and update allocation on material contract changes.
- Customer-credit note application: apply credit to deferred revenue balance first, then to outstanding AR. Document application in ticketing system.
- Currency & FX: advances received in foreign currency are recorded at receipt FX rate; translation of deferred amounts for reporting per the accounting policy (see FX policy).

IT/system requirements & recommended configuration:

- NetSuite: enable deferred revenue subledger and recognition schedules tied to contract IDs. All advance payments must reference the contract ID.
- Deal Room / CLM: tag contracts that include prepayments with metadata: payment_type=advance, bucket=deferred, escrow_required=(yes/no).
- Treasury: provide daily cash posting feed to Finance to minimize recording delay.

Responsibilities & owners:

- Revenue Operations (owner): maintain deferred revenue subledger and monthly reconciliations.
- Procurement: vendor onboarding, PO issuance for vendor prepayments.
- Legal: contract clause standardization and redline approval.
- Sales / CS: provide SOWs, acceptance evidence, and operational coordination for performance obligations.
- Treasury: cash receipt posting and banking controls.

Training & rollout:

- All Sales, Revenue Ops, Legal, Procurement, and Finance staff must complete the "RevRec & Advance Payments" training (learning module ID: FIN-ADV-2026) within 60 days of publication.
- Playbooks and quick-reference cards will be published in the Finance team wiki and linked from the deal intake form.

Appendix A — Quick checklist for deal desk (short):

1. Does deal include advance/retainer? Yes/No.
2. Forecasted advance amount and currency.
3. Completed RevRec Assessment attached.
4. Approval per matrix obtained.
5. Payment instructions and escrow (if required) documented.
6. GL codes and recognition schedule confirmed.

Appendix B — Example contract snippet (copy-paste safe):

"Payment and Retainer: Customer will pay an initial retainer equal to 20% of the estimated fees upon execution. Redwood will record receipt as a prepayment and apply amounts to invoices as Services are performed. Refunds of unused prepayments will be made in accordance with the Refund Schedule in Schedule B, unless the parties agree otherwise in writing"

Contact & escalation list:

- Revenue Ops Lead: Daniel Kim (revenue-ops@redwood.ai)
- Head of Procurement: Priya Shah (procurement@redwood.ai)
- Senior Counsel: Lukas Werner (legal@redwood.ai)
- VP Finance: Marta Liu (vpfinance@redwood.ai)

Revision history:

- 2025-11-07: Created by Amina Patel — initial draft.
- 2026-01-20: Updated approval thresholds and added escrow guidance after Legal review.
- 2026-02-15: Published; added reconciliation SLA and training rollout details.

Notes & references:

- Accounting policy: see /finance/policies/asc606-revrec-notes-2024.pdf
- Procurement policy: see /finance/procurement/procurement-authorization-framework-2024.pdf
- For unusual structures (vendor financing, letters of credit, or materially escrowed arrangements), engage VP Finance and Legal at the term-sheet stage.

End of document.

[Commitment Approval Queue and Legal Handshake — Cross-functional SOP]
Overview:
This document defines the operational flow, responsibilities, SLAs, and handoff artifacts for purchase commitments that require legal contract review and create revenue recognition/billing implications. It is intended for Finance, Legal, Procurement, Sales/Account Management, and Engineering teams who originate or manage commercial commitments.

Scope:
- Covers commitments that create a contractual obligation (subscription, reserved/dedicated capacity, multi-year commitments, SOWs, and enterprise support contracts).
- Excludes purely internal purchase orders (hardware/software purchases with no customer contract).

Goals:
- Ensure commitments are approved and recorded in forecasts within defined timelines.
- Standardize the legal handoff so contract language does not delay billing or revrec.
- Define a clear queue/triage and escalation path for approvals and exceptions.

Key Definitions:
- Commitment: Any customer or partner agreement creating a multi-period obligation or payment schedule (subscription, reserved capacity, committed spend).
- Revenue Trigger: The point at which Finance is authorized to record deferred revenue and/or issue invoices.
- Legal Handoff: The formal transfer of contract artifacts (redlines, signature pages, SOWs) from Legal to Finance/Revenue Ops and Procurement.

Approval Matrix (thresholds and approvers):
| Commitment Value (ARR equivalent) | Required Approvals | Primary Approver SLA | Notes |
|----------------------------------|--------------------|---------------------|-------|
| <= $50,000                       | Deal Owner + Finance | 3 business days     | Standard billing terms template OK |
| $50,001 - $250,000               | Deal Owner + Finance + Legal | 5 business days | Legal review required for non-standard clauses |
| $250,001 - $1,000,000            | Deal Owner + Finance + Legal + Sales Director | 7 business days | May require procurement/PO coordination for customers with procurement constraints |
| > $1,000,000                     | Deal Owner + CFO + GC + Sales VP | 10 business days | Executive notification; procurement may require additional KYC/credit checks |

Required Artifacts for Legal Handoff (attach to the approval ticket):
- Fully executed contract or final redline PDF (signed pages if available)
- Statement of Work (SOW) or Order Form with line-item billing cadence
- Pricing worksheets and discount approvals (signed pricing attestation)
- Customer billing/legal contact and invoicing address (including billing email and PO requirements)
- Implementation acceptance criteria (if recognized on delivery/milestones)
- Any compliance or data residency attachments (if applicable)

Operational Workflow (numbered procedure):
1. Origin: Sales/Account Manager creates an approval ticket in the procurement/commitments queue (JIRA ticket type: COMMITMENT-REQ) using the template below.
2. Finance Triage (within 2 business days): Finance validates that the commitment is reflected in the latest forecast bucket and assigns a forecast owner. If the commitment is material to forecast variance (>5% of ARR bucket), Finance flags for Forecast Committee review.
3. Legal Review (standard SLA: 5 business days): Legal triages for non-standard clauses (IP, indemnity caps, data residency, escrow, KMS). Legal provides either: approved contract, commentary with required edits, or escalates to GC for >$1M deals.
4. Procurement/PO Coordination (if customer requires PO): Procurement issues internal PO or confirms external PO flow to Accounts Receivable.
5. Signature & Artifact Collection: Once signed, Sales uploads the executed contract and the signature page into the ticket and moves the ticket to the "Handoff to Revenue Ops" status.
6. Revenue Ops/Billing (within 3 business days of handoff): Revenue Ops validates recognition model (subscription vs. milestone), assigns revenue recognition code, and creates the billing schedule in the billing system (NetSuite/Stripe/Zuora integration).
7. Forecast Update & Recognition Trigger: Finance updates MRR/ARR forecasts and, if recognition criteria are met, records a deferred revenue schedule. Any exceptions (e.g., acceptance criteria not met) are noted and posted to the contract record.
8. Post-Mortem: For any deal that misses SLAs or causes >10% forecast variance, the cross-functional team runs a 10-day incident review.

JIRA Ticket Template (COMMITMENT-REQ):
- Summary: [Customer] - [Product/Capacity] - [Currency Amount] - [Contract Type]
- Fields: Customer legal name; Sales Owner; Deal Value (ARR/EAC); Renewal/Start/End Date; Billing cadence; Required PO? Y/N; Attachments: draft contract, pricing sheet, SOW.
- Workflow statuses: New -> Finance Triage -> Legal Review -> Procurement (if PO) -> Handoff to Revenue Ops -> Billing Scheduled -> Closed

Legal Review Prioritization Rules:
- Expedited (48 hours): Security incident remediation agreements, legal holds, and customers requiring urgent cutoff dates.
- Standard (5 business days): Most SaaS/reserved capacity agreements using approved templates.
- Extended (10 business days): Complex multi-party agreements, export controls, or material IP transfers.

Escalation Path:
1. If Legal review exceeds SLA, Legal lead notifies Sales leader and Finance lead within 24 hours after SLA breach.
2. If procurement PO is delayed >7 business days, Procurement lead notifies Sales Ops and the customer procurement contact.
3. For high-value deals (> $1M) in active exception, the GC + CFO schedule a 1:1 review within 48 hours of escalation.

Revenue Recognition Checklist for Revenue Ops (required for RevRec posting):
- Contract type confirmed: Subscription / Usage / Milestone / One-time.
- Billing cadence: Monthly / Quarterly / Annual / Milestone-based.
- Start date for recognition: Signed date / Service start / Acceptance sign-off.
- Performance obligations explicitly listed in contract and mapped to revenue schedule.
- External customer PO or billing requirements documented.
- Any customer acceptance criteria or holdbacks captured with expected dates.
- GL codes and deferred revenue accounts assigned.

Sample Approval Matrix Table (CSV-friendly):
threshold,approvers,legal_sla,finance_sla,notes
50000,Sales Owner;Finance,3bd,2bd,standard template ok
250000,Sales Owner;Finance;Legal,5bd,2bd,legal review required
1000000,Sales Owner;CFO;GC;Sales VP,10bd,3bd,exec review

Common Exceptions and How to Handle Them:
- Customer requires campus/department-specific PO: Procurement to create a PO template and confirm split-invoicing if required.
- Data residency clauses or KMS requirements: Flag to Security & Compliance and Legal; include expected 10 business day review window.
- Discounting beyond approved threshold: Sales must attach Pricing Exception Approval signed by Revenue Operations + Finance.

Operational Metrics and Reporting:
- KPI 1: % of commitments processed within SLA (target: 95%).
- KPI 2: Average Legal review time (target: <= 4 business days for standard deals).
- KPI 3: Time from signature to first invoice (target: <= 5 business days).
- KPI 4: Number of forecast adjustments attributable to post-signature changes (target: < 3% monthly).

Roles & Responsibilities (short list):
- Sales/Deal Owner: Initiate ticket, attach artifacts, drive customer signature.
- Legal: Provide contract review, flag non-standard terms, sign-off on final language.
- Finance: Triage commitments, update forecasts, own revrec treatment.
- Procurement: Ensure PO flow, vendor/customer procurement onboarding if required.
- Revenue Ops/Billing: Create billing schedules, issue invoices, maintain recognition schedules.

Backout / Remediation Steps (if a signed contract cannot be recognized immediately):
1. Tag contract as "Pending Acceptance" in the system with reason code (e.g., implementation dependency).
2. Finance records a note and defers recognition; Revenue Ops schedules first invoice to be blocked until acceptance.
3. Account Manager to provide weekly status updates until acceptance criteria are met.
4. If outstanding beyond 90 days, escalate to Sales Director and Finance for resolution; consider credit memo or amendment.

Appendix A — Example Clause Language to Avoid (Legal Notes):
- Open-ended indemnities or unlimited liability without caps.
- Ambiguous acceptance criteria that delay start date determination.
- Auto-renewal terms without clear notice periods (Finance needs clear renewal triggers for forecasting).

Appendix B — Quick Contact Roster:
- Finance Triage: finance-triage@redwood.ai
- Revenue Ops: revenue-ops@redwood.ai
- Legal Intake: legal-intake@redwood.ai
- Procurement: procurement@redwood.ai

Change Log:
- 2026-01-12: Document created by Daniela Martinez.
- 2026-03-18: Added expedited legal SLA rules and JIRA template fields (review: Marcus Lee).
- 2026-09-02: Updated approval thresholds and post-signature SLA targets; clarified RevRec checklist (review: Priya Raman, Olivia Chen).

Related Documents:
- procurement/supplier-onboarding-and-invoice-routing-2026.json
- revrec-and-billing/chargeback-and-internal-billing-guidelines-2026.json

Notes for implementers:
- Use the COMMITMENT-REQ ticket exactly; missing attachments are the leading cause of SLA misses.
- Maintain an automated dashboard (Looker/Metabase) showing ticket age by stage; Finance and Legal leads must review weekly.


[enterprise-commit-and-billing-controls-framework-2026]
Purpose
-------
This playbook defines Redwood Inference’s Enterprise Commit and Billing Controls Framework: end-to-end rules for how we accept customer financial commitments, how we manage contract amendments, how procurement and vendor billing interact with revenue recognition, and the operational controls that prevent revenue leakage or accounting exceptions. It targets Finance, Legal, Sales Ops, Revenue Ops, and Engineering teams that integrate with billing and contract workflows.

Scope and audience
------------------
Applies to: customer contracts (hosted API, Dedicated reservations, Private deployments), vendor procurement, and internal purchase commitments exceeding $25k ARR or $50k CAPEX equivalent. Not a substitute for Legal review: all contract template changes must be routed to Legal per the Contract Change Procedure.

Key principles
--------------
- Single source of truth: customer commercial terms live in the CLM (Contract Lifecycle Management) system and the billing system (Stripe/Zuora mirror).
- Separation of duties: Sales negotiates commercial terms; Legal approves non-standard terms; Finance approves revenue treatment and AMs (amendments) > $100k ARR; Billing implements configuration and invoices.
- Revenue SRO (Single Responsible Owner): finance-legal team owns revenue recognition decisions and deferred revenue schedules.
- Minimal manual adjustments: changes to invoicing/deferral should be automated; manual journals must have RCA and approval.

Controls matrix (high-level)
---------------------------
| Control area | Owner | Threshold | Evidence required | Frequency |
|--------------|-------|-----------|-------------------|-----------|
| Contract approval (standard templates) | Legal | any | Signed contract in CLM | Per contract |
| Contract approval (non-standard terms) | Legal + Finance | Any non-template clause or > $100k ARR | Redlined contract + approval record | Per contract |
| Revenue recognition treatment signoff | Finance | > $50k ARR | Revenue memo + schedule | Per deal |
| Billing configuration change | Billing ops | Any | Config change ticket ID + test invoice | Per change |
| Procurement vendor onboarding | Procurement | > $25k/year | Vendor W-9, SSF, security attestation | Per vendor |
| Invoice dispute > $10k | Revenue ops | > $10k | Dispute case + remediation plan | As needed |

(Represented above as a table — the source of truth is the Controls spreadsheet in Finance Drive.)

Budgeting, Forecasting, and Commit Treatment
-------------------------------------------
1) Budget windows and cutoffs
   - Quarterly operating budget windows: Q1-Q4 planning opens 8 weeks prior to quarter start.
   - Booking cutoff for revenue forecast inclusion: deals signed and in CLM by the final business day of the quarter are eligible for recognition in that quarter subject to delivery/acceptance terms.

2) Forecast categories and flags
   - Committed: Signed, countersigned, invoiceable (CLM + billing config completed).
   - Provisionally Committed: Signed but pending billing config or KYC/security checks. Flagged as PENDING_BILLING.
   - Pipeline: Term sheet or verbal commitment only — not recognizeable.

3) Treatment rules for dedicated capacity and prepayments
   - Upfront prepayments are recorded as deferred revenue and amortized over the contracted service period. Example: $120k upfront for 12 months -> $10k recognized monthly.
   - Overprovision credits (e.g., reserved capacity discounts) are recorded as contra-revenue and applied pro rata unless the agreement specifies otherwise.

Contract Amendments and Change Management
-----------------------------------------
Procedure (step-by-step):
1. Sales submits Amendment Request in CLM and tags Legal + Finance.
2. Legal reviews redlines; if non-standard customer language is required, Legal documents the risk and assigns an approver.
3. Finance evaluates impact on revenue recognition (cash vs accrual, deferral windows) and approves proposed accounting treatment on the amendment.
4. Contract is countersigned and CLM status set to AMENDED.
5. Billing ops executes billing configuration changes (new payment terms, discounts, invoice dates) in billing system and marks change ticket with CLM amendment ID.
6. Revenue ops runs a pre-production invoice to a shadow customer account for any new billing cadence or price changes; results attached to the amendment record.
7. If accounting treatment changes materially (see Materiality thresholds), a revenue memo is archived and a journal entry created at period close.

Materiality thresholds
- Financial impact > $50k in a quarter OR changes ARR recognition > 2% of last 12 months revenue for the customer -> requires Finance Director signoff and memo.
- Any change that introduces multi-element arrangements requires Revenue Ops + Finance to map deliverables and recognition patterns.

Procurement interaction and vendor billing policies
--------------------------------------------------
- Procurement must route all vendor contracts > $25k through the supplier onboarding flow, capturing security attestation and pricing schedules.
- Capitalizable hardware/infrastructure purchases: Procurement tags POs as CAPEX; Finance-Procurement monthly review determines capitalization.
- Invoice review: AP team matches 3-way (PO, receipt, invoice) where applicable. Exceptions must be documented and escalated to Procurement Manager.

Billing operations and invoice lifecycle
-------------------------------------
Invoice cadence and types
- Monthly usage invoices (hosted API usage): emailed by the 7th business day following month close; thresholded auto-invoice enabled for customers with payment method on file.
- Advance/renewal invoices: generated 30 days before subscription renewal for annual/commit contracts.
- One-time invoices: generated when deliverables (onboarding, professional services) are accepted.

Dispute and remediation process
1. Customer raises a billing dispute (Support or Sales ticket).
2. Revenue Ops triages within 48 hours and acknowledges receipt.
3. If validation confirms a billing error, Revenue Ops issues a credit memo and adjusts deferred revenue schedules if needed.
4. If the dispute requires contract interpretation, Legal engages and delivers an opinion within 10 business days.
5. Record of dispute and resolution is attached to the CLM and the customer account.

Revenue recognition policy highlights
----------------------------------
- Revenue is recognized in accordance with ASC 606 principles (or equivalent IFRS 15): identify contract, identify performance obligations, determine transaction price, allocate price, recognize when (or as) performance obligations satisfied.
- Standalone selling prices: use observable list prices where available; otherwise use an internal SSP matrix maintained by Finance (SSP matrix file path referenced in related pages).
- Multi-element arrangements: allocate on a relative standalone selling price basis and recognize over the period when control of each deliverable transfers.
- Deferred revenue schedule: generated per contract in the close process and reconciled weekly.

Monitoring, KPIs and Reporting
----------------------------
Primary KPIs (monitored weekly/monthly):
- Forecast accuracy (Bookings vs Recognized Revenue) — target: <= 5% variance quarter-over-quarter.
- Time from contract signing to billing activation — target: <= 7 business days.
- Number of billing disputes > $5k per month — target: 0.
- Deferred revenue reconciliation exceptions — target: 0 exceptions unresolved > 2 business days.

Operational runbooks and escalation paths
---------------------------------------
- Billing activation runbook: step-by-step checklist (CLM ID, payment method verification, tax determination, invoice preview, test invoice). Owner: Billing Ops.
- Revenue memo template: includes background, impact analysis, deferred schedule, and GL impact lines. Owner: Finance Accounting.
- Escalation: any unresolvable billing issue after 3 business days escalates to Head of Revenue Ops; material accounting disputes escalate to CFO and General Counsel.

Templates and examples (appendix)
--------------------------------
1) Example deferred schedule (ascii table):
| Period | Amount recognized | Deferred balance |
|-------:|------------------:|-----------------:|
| 2026-03 | $10,000 | $110,000 |
| 2026-04 | $10,000 | $100,000 |
| ... | ... | ... |

2) Example amendment ticket checklist:
- CLM amendment ID
- Redline + summary of change
- Finance accounting impact statement
- Billing test invoice ID
- Legal approval stamp

Glossary of key terms
---------------------
- CLM: Contract Lifecycle Management system (source of truth for signed agreements).
- PENDING_BILLING: Flag used in CRM for deals awaiting billing configuration.
- Deferred revenue: cash received in advance of service delivery recorded as liability.
- SSP: Standalone Selling Price.

Next steps and open actions

[Quantization Profiles (Public Docs) — Customer Documentation Plan]
## Summary
This page defines the plan for customer-facing documentation for the Quantization Profile Library (opt-in). The goal is to help customers safely enable quantization profiles per route, understand limitations and compatibility, run appropriate evaluations, interpret observability signals, and roll back quickly if needed.

This is an internal planning doc for Redwood Docs + DevEx and will be used as the source of truth for docs IA, required examples, and cross-team review gates.

## Audience and use cases
**Primary audiences**
- Software engineers and ML engineers integrating Redwood routes who want to reduce cost/token.
- Platform teams managing production change control (audit logs, RBAC, rollbacks).

**Customer use cases we need to support in docs**
1. Enable an approved quantization profile for a single route (hosted API).
2. Enable profile for a route with region/tier constraints (Dedicated + multi-region hosted).
3. Validate quality and latency before expanding traffic.
4. Diagnose output changes, elevated fallback rate, or latency regressions.
5. Roll back (route-level disable; global kill-switch is internal-only but mention its existence at a high level).

## Goals (docs)
- Make it clear this is **opt-in** and **route-scoped** (v1), with baseline behavior unchanged when disabled.
- Provide a simple “happy path” enablement flow with copy-pastable examples (Console + API/SDK).
- Set expectations on **compatibility constraints** and **fallback behavior** (deterministic, baseline precision fallback).
- Provide a lightweight but concrete evaluation best-practices section that customers can follow without needing Redwood internal harnesses.
- Provide troubleshooting steps tied to the actual product signals customers will see (Console warnings/errors, request metadata, audit history, and dashboard panels).

## Non-goals (docs)
- Do not position this as automatic tuning/recommendations (out of scope for v1).
- Do not publish internal-only implementation details (artifact signing specifics, internal service names, kill-switch runbooks).
- Do not promise universal profile coverage across all models/GPU SKUs.

## Product language and terminology
We need consistent, customer-friendly wording:
- **Quantization profile**: A versioned, Redwood-validated configuration for running a specific model variant using a specific quantization method/precision combination.
- **Profile library**: The set of published profiles per model variant. Customers choose a profile for a route.
- **Route-level enablement**: Profiles are enabled per route, not globally for all tenant traffic (v1).
- **Fallback**: If a request is incompatible (hardware/sequence length constraints) or profile application fails safe checks, Redwood serves using baseline precision for that request (or route) while emitting an event.

Avoid ambiguous language:
- Avoid saying “Redwood automatically picks the best profile.”
- Avoid “lossless” claims. Use “aims to preserve quality” and emphasize eval/monitoring.

## Information architecture (public docs)
We will publish a small cluster of pages under: **Optimize → Quantization Profiles**.

### Page 1: Overview (concept + safety model)
**Proposed title:** “Quantization Profiles (Preview/Beta)” (or “Quantization Profiles” once GA)

**Outline**
- What quantization profiles are and why they reduce cost.
- Opt-in and route-scoped behavior.
- High-level lifecycle: published profiles, versioning, deprecations.
- Safety model summary:
  - Compatibility checks before enablement.
  - Deterministic selection.
  - Fallback to baseline.
  - Auditability and change history.

**Callouts**
- “Start with a canary route; expand after evals.”
- “Not all models/regions support all profiles.”

### Page 2: Enablement guide (Console + API/SDK)
**Proposed title:** “Enable a quantization profile for a route”

**Required elements**
- Console walkthrough (with screenshots once UX is final):
  1) Navigate to Route → Performance/Optimize → Quantization
  2) Choose model variant + eligible profiles
  3) Read compatibility warnings
  4) Confirm change (modal) and review expected impact
  5) Verify enablement and view change history

- API example (REST) for updating route config
  - Show setting `quantization_profile_ref` to a specific profile ID/version.
  - Show how to reset to `default` / disable.

- SDK examples
  - Python and TypeScript: configure route setting; retrieve route state; handle incompatibility errors.

**Verification steps**
- Confirm in Console that route shows “Enabled” and which profile is selected.
- Show how to verify in request metadata (e.g., response headers or trace attributes) that a profile was applied vs fallback.
- Show where to find fallback/latency/cost deltas in dashboards.

### Page 3: Compatibility + limitations
**Proposed title:** “Compatibility, constraints, and fallback behavior”

**Include**
- What compatibility depends on:
  - Model ID + model variant
  - Deployment mode (Hosted/Dedicated/Private as applicable)
  - GPU class/SKU (expressed as customer-friendly names)
  - Max context / sequence length limits
  - Region constraints (if/when supported in route policy)

- Customer-facing compatibility matrix
  - If we can’t maintain a full matrix, we must at least publish:
    - “Supported GPUs by profile type” (e.g., INT8 supported on X, FP8 on Y)
    - “Max supported context per profile” for popular models
  - Decide format: table in docs + downloadable CSV updated weekly (recommended).

- Fallback semantics
  - Define what happens when incompatible:
    - If enablement time: block with clear error and remediation.
    - If request time: safe fallback to baseline; emit a signal; no infinite retry loops.

- Limitations / known caveats
  - Output differences are possible.
  - Some profiles may be labeled “Experimental” with narrower guardrails.
  - If customers pin to a profile version, it won’t change unless they update.
  - If we ever add “recommended” aliases, document that aliases may move and how we prevent silent changes (see Open Questions).

### Page 4: Evaluation best practices
**Proposed title:** “How to evaluate quality and latency before rollout”

**Customer-friendly guidance**
- Suggested evaluation approach:
  - Identify representative prompts (production samples + edge cases).
  - Run baseline vs profile-enabled comparisons.
  - Use A/B sampling (e.g., 1–5% traffic) with a rollback threshold.

- What to measure
  - Quality: task-specific metrics (pass@k, exact match, ranking metrics) + human review where appropriate.
  - Latency: p50/p95 decode latency and time-to-first-token.
  - Cost: cost/token and throughput.

- Rollout strategy
  1) Enable in staging on a non-critical route
  2) Canary in production (small % traffic)
  3) Expand gradually with monitoring

- Provide explicit “stop conditions”
  - Elevated fallback rate
  - Increased error rate
  - Statistically meaningful quality regression on a defined slice

**Note:** We cannot publish Redwood’s internal thresholds verbatim if they are considered sensitive, but we can publish recommended guardrails (e.g., “predefine acceptable deltas and require sign-off”). We will align with Selene Huang (quality guardrails) on what’s safe to disclose.

### Page 5: Troubleshooting + rollback
**Proposed title:** “Troubleshooting quantization profiles”

**Structure: symptom → likely cause → how to confirm → resolution**

Required symptoms:
- Console says profile is incompatible
  - Common causes: wrong model variant, unsupported GPU class, context length exceeds profile limit.
  - Resolution: choose another profile; reduce max tokens/context; use baseline.

- Output quality changed unexpectedly
  - Confirm: compare baseline vs profile, check whether fallback occurred (mixed behavior can look inconsistent).
  - Resolution: disable profile; run eval; contact support with request IDs.

- p95 latency increased
  - Confirm: look at per-route latency panels; check TTFT vs decode; check batching/caching changes.
  - Resolution: disable profile; adjust route concurrency/batching; consult Redwood support.

- Elevated fallback rate
  - Confirm: dashboard panel + route events.
  - Likely causes: requests exceed profile constraints; region/GPU mismatch; deployment drift.
  - Resolution: tighten route constraints; pick compatible profile; disable.

- 5xx errors after enabling
  - Confirm: error class; check if errors correlate with specific profile version.
  - Resolution: disable; provide audit event ID and request IDs to support.

Rollback instructions (customer-actionable)
- Disable at route level (Console + API snippet).
- Verify disablement and that requests are using baseline.

We should also include:
- “What information to include in a support ticket” checklist:
  - Org/tenant ID
  - Route name/ID
  - Model + variant
  - Profile ID/version
  - Region/deployment mode
  - Approx timeframe
  - Request IDs/traces
  - Observed metrics (fallback rate, p95 latency)

[PRD: Quantization Profile Library (Opt-in, Route-level Enablement)]
h1. Summary
Redwood Inference will launch an *opt-in Quantization Profile Library* that publishes *per-model, versioned quantization profiles* and enables customers to turn them on *per route* (and optionally scoped by region and/or deployment tier) to reduce inference cost while preserving quality and meeting latency SLOs.

This PRD defines user stories, product scope, API + Console requirements, rollout plan, and success metrics for v1.

h1. Goals (v1)
*G1. Stable, versioned profile schema per model variant*
* Profiles are stored in the model registry with validation and compatibility metadata.
* Profiles are versioned and immutable once published.

*G2. Safe route-level enablement controls*
* Customers can enable/disable a specific profile per route.
* Optional scoping by *region* and/or *deployment tier* (Hosted, Dedicated, Private) where supported.
* Changes are auditable and reversible.

*G3. Deterministic runtime selection and safe fallback*
* Runtime applies an approved profile deterministically when enabled and compatible.
* If incompatible or unavailable, system safely falls back to baseline (default precision) and emits clear signals.

*G4. Quality guardrails and rollout safety*
* Offline eval harness gates profile publication.
* Canary enablement + telemetry to detect regressions quickly.
* Rapid rollback (route-level disable + global kill-switch).

*G5. Documentation and support readiness*
* Clear customer docs for enablement, limitations, and troubleshooting.
* Support playbook and internal runbooks are ready before Beta.

h1. Non-goals (out of scope for v1)
* Fully automated per-customer profile recommendations or “auto-enable.”
* Online auto-tuning in production.
* Making quantization default-on across all routes/models.
* Guaranteeing bit-identical outputs between baseline and quantized modes.

h1. Background / Problem
Customers increasingly ask for concrete levers to reduce cost/token while maintaining production latency and quality. Quantization is a high-leverage technique, but in production it introduces risk:
* model/hardware incompatibilities,
* quality regressions on specific tasks,
* tail-latency changes due to kernel selection or memory/KV-cache behavior,
* operational complexity when rolling changes across fleets.

The Quantization Profile Library provides an approved and observable path to enable quantization in production safely, with deterministic behavior and strong rollback.

h1. Users and Personas
h2. Primary personas
1) *ML Engineer / Applied ML (customer-side)*
* Wants lower cost while maintaining eval scores.
* Needs ability to A/B compare baseline vs profile on a subset of traffic.

2) *Platform / Infra Engineer (customer-side)*
* Owns route configuration, latency SLOs, and incident response.
* Needs guardrails, compatibility warnings, audit logs, and quick rollback.

3) *Redwood internal operators*
* Applied ML: generate and publish profiles.
* Runtime + Platform: ensure deterministic apply/fallback and stable ops.
* SRE/Release: safe rollout and monitoring.

h1. User Stories
h2. Customer stories
*US-1 (Enablement):* As a platform engineer, I can enable a specific quantization profile on a route, so that only traffic to that route uses quantization.

*US-2 (Safety/Validation):* As a platform engineer, I receive a compatibility validation result (model + hardware + max context constraints) before enabling, so that I do not accidentally break production.

*US-3 (Auditability):* As a platform engineer at an enterprise, I can see who changed quantization settings, when, and what changed, for change-control and compliance.

*US-4 (Rollback):* As an oncall engineer, I can quickly disable the profile for a route and confirm the runtime has reverted to baseline.

*US-5 (Scoped rollout):* As an ML engineer, I can enable a profile for a specific region and/or tier first, so that I can canary in a low-risk environment before expanding.

*US-6 (Observability):* As a platform engineer, I can see applied vs fallback rates and cost/latency deltas for the route, so I can verify savings and detect regressions.

h2. Redwood internal stories
*US-7 (Publishing lifecycle):* As Applied ML, I can publish a new profile version after it passes the required eval suites and perf checks.

*US-8 (Kill-switch):* As SRE, I can globally disable quantization profiles during an incident and verify resolution.

h1. Definitions / Terminology
* *Quantization profile:* A versioned configuration + artifacts describing a quantized execution mode for a specific model variant, including constraints and known caveats.
* *Baseline:* Default serving precision for a route/model when no profile is enabled.
* *Profile ref:* The identifier stored in route config referencing a specific published profile version. (v1 requires explicit, versioned IDs.)
* *Compatibility:* Deterministic evaluation that the profile can be applied for the current request context (model variant, GPU class/SKU family, deployment tier, max context, etc.).
* *Fallback:* When enabled but incompatible/unavailable, system uses baseline and emits signals.

h1. Requirements
h2. Product requirements (functional)
1) *Profile library visibility*
* Customers can list available profiles for a given model/variant.
* Profiles include:
  * profile_id (versioned), quantization method, supported hardware classes, max context/sequence constraints, and status (published/deprecated).
  * “known caveats” and “recommended use cases” text.

2) *Route-level config*
* Route config supports an optional field:
  * quantization_profile_ref: "default" | <profile_id>
* Default behavior remains unchanged when unset or "default".
* Support optional per-region/per-tier overrides:
  * If implemented in v1: route-level base setting + override blocks by region/tier.
  * If not implemented for a specific deployment mode, API returns a clear error and Console hides/locks the control.

3) *Deterministic selection*
* For a given request context, the resolved outcome must be deterministic:
  * applied(profile_id) OR fallback(baseline) OR disabled.
* No “silent” changes: v1 does *not* auto-advance to newer profile versions.

4) *Compatibility guardrails*
* Control plane must validate at write-time:
  * route model_id/variant is compatible with the profile’s model_id/variant
  * deployment tier compatibility
  * GPU class/SKU family compatibility where known
  * max context constraints and any “blocked” contexts
* Runtime must validate at apply-time as a second line of defense and safely fallback.

5) *Audit logs and RBAC*
* Enabling/disabling/changing profile ref must produce an audit event containing:
  * actor identity, route identifier, before/after diff, timestamp, and effective scope (global/region/tier)
* RBAC: only users with appropriate permissions can modify quantization settings.

6) *Emergency controls*
* Global kill-switch to disable profile application platform-wide.
* Optional per-tenant “disable all profiles” override (if approved for v1; otherwise tracked as follow-up).

h2. API requirements
Note: endpoint names are representative; exact paths owned by Platform Control Plane (Ethan Park / Benji Okafor).

*Read APIs*
1) List available profiles for a model variant
* GET /v1/models/{model_id}/variants/{variant}/quantization-profiles
* Response includes profile_id, status, quant_method, precisions, constraints summary, and “known caveats”.

2) Get resolved quantization setting for a route
* GET /v1/routes/{route_id}/quantization-settings
* Returns stored configuration and effective resolved setting per scope (default + overrides).

3) Validate compatibility (preflight)
* POST /v1/routes/{route_id}/quantization-settings:validate
* Input: profile_id + optional region/tier scope
* Output: compatible=true/false, reasons[], and suggested remediation.

*Write APIs*
4) Update quantization setting
* PATCH /v1/routes/{route_id}/quantization-settings
* Supports:
  * set quantization_profile_ref to "default" or <profile_id>
  * optional region/tier override blocks (if in v1)
* Must be idempotent and write an audit log event.

*Error and safety semantics*
* Incompatible enablement returns 4xx with structured error codes (e.g., QUANT_PROFILE_INCOMPATIBLE, QUANT_PROFILE_NOT_FOUND, QUANT_PROFILE_DEPRECATED).
* “Write-time validation” failures must be explicit; do not accept config and rely on fallback.

*Caching and resilience*
* Profile metadata fetches must be cached and rate-limited to protect the model registry under high QPS.

h2. Console UX requirements
Owned by Console & Tooling (Dylan Brooks / Chloe Martin / Tessa Morgan).

1) *Placement and discoverability*
* Route detail page includes a “Quantization” section under Performance/Cost controls.

2) *Enablement flow*
* Dropdown/select to choose a profile version (profile_id) or Default.
* Compatibility preflight runs before allowing save.
* Confirmation modal includes:
  * Selected profile_id
  * Model variant and scope (route, region, tier)
  * Warning that outputs may change
  * Link to docs and recommended eval playbook

3) *Warnings and guardrails*
* Surface compatibility warnings with clear reasons:
  * hardware unsupported
  * max context exceeded
  * profile deprecated/blocked
* If the global kill-switch is active, show a banner and disable the toggle.

4) *Change history*
* Route shows a “Change History” panel with:
  * timestamp, actor, change diff, and links to audit event ID.

5) *Observability affordances*
* After enabling, Console presents quick links to dashboards filtered by route/model/region:
  * applied vs fallback rate
  * p95 latency
  * cost/token deltas
  * error rates

6) *Canary support*
* v1 requirement: Console supports staged enablement by scope (region/tier) as the primary canary mechanism.
* (Optional follow-up) Traffic-percentage splitting is out of scope unless already supported by existing route canary primitives.

h2. Documentation requirements (customer-facing)
Owned by DevEx (Alex Martinez / Elliot Price).
* Explain:
  * what a quantization profile is
  * how to enable per route (API + Console)
  * how to run A/B evals and monitor quality
  * troubleshooting: how to confirm applied vs fallback; common incompatibilities
  * rollback steps and kill-switch behavior (high level)

h1. Quality and Safety Guardrails
h2. Publication gates (before a profile is “published”)
Owned by Applied ML & Evals (Arjun Desai / Jonas Weber / Selene Huang).
* Required eval suites per quantization-regression-thresholds policy.
* Statistical testing and acceptable deltas by task family.
* Perf benchmark suite across key GPU SKUs for cost/token and tail latency.
* Explicit “blocked contexts” recorded in profile constraints (e.g., max context).

h2. Runtime apply/fallback rules
Owned by Serving Runtime (Noah Patel / Hiro Tanaka / Omar El-Sayed).
* Must annotate traces/logs with:
  * quant_profile_id
  * resolution outcome: applied | fallback | disabled
  * fallback reason (enum)
* Must not enter fallback loops; fallback is single-step to baseline.

h2. Rollback triggers
Owned by SRE/Release (Connor O'Brien) + Telemetry (Paula Mendes).
* Automated alerts (examples; final thresholds set in SRE dashboards):
  * fallback_rate > 1% sustained over 10 min on an enabled route
  * p95 decode latency regression > 10% vs baseline for 15 min
  * 5xx error rate increase > 0.2% absolute vs baseline
  * quality guardrail alert fired (per eval harness or online proxy metrics where available)

h1. Success Metrics
h2. Primary (must-hit)
* *Cost reduction:* Demonstrated cost/token reduction on targeted models with enabled profiles (goal: meaningful savings; tracked per model/profile, not a single global number).
* *Quality:* No statistically significant quality regression beyond agreed thresholds on Redwood prompt sets/eval suites for published profiles.
* *Latency:* Stable p95 latency for enabled routes within SLO and within acceptable regression bounds.
* *Operational overhead:* Rollback within minutes via route disable; clear diagnostics for applied vs fallback.

h2. Secondary
* Adoption: number of customers/routes enabling profiles during Beta and within 30/60 days post-GA.
* Support: low ticket volume per enabled route; time-to-resolution < 1 business day for common issues.
* Internal velocity: cadence for publishing new profiles (weekly or biweekly target during initial expansion).

h1. Rollout Plan
h2. Phase 0 — Discovery & Design (Complete/In progress)
Deliverables:
* ADR confirming route-level enablement strategy.
* Schema v1 finalized and validated.
* Threat model and safety analysis (quality regressions, incompatibility, metadata fetch amplification).

h2. Phase 1 — Implementation (Engineering)
Deliverables:
* Model registry storage, signing/integrity checks, versioning.
* Control plane APIs and policy evaluation with compatibility checks.
* Runtime load/apply + deterministic signals.
* Console UI and backend wiring.
* Audit events + RBAC.
* Kill-switch.

h2. Phase 2 — Validation (Internal)
Deliverables:
* Offline eval harness and perf suite run for initial set of models.
* perf-canary scenarios and automated regression checks.
* Game-day rollback drill (route disable + kill-switch).

h2. Phase 3 — Beta (2–3 design partners)
Target: Hosted + Dedicated, allowlisted tenants.
* Explicit opt-in per route with published profile versions.
* Close monitoring dashboards and weekly check-ins.
* Rollback criteria defined per partner.

h2. Phase 4 — GA
* Expand availability to self-serve customers with appropriate RBAC.
* Publish docs and support playbook.
* Ongoing profile publishing cadence and deprecation policy.

h1. Dependencies
* Model Registry (Quentin Harris): schema + storage + caching.
* Control Plane + Routing (Ethan Park, Mina Haddad, Ravi Menon): route config field + policy evaluation.
* Runtime (Noah Patel, Hiro Tanaka): kernel selection guardrails, KV-cache interactions.
* Observability (Logan Wright, Nadia Rahman): metrics and dashboard panels.
* Security (Marcus Lin, Naomi Feldman): RBAC/audit requirements.
* DevEx (Alex Martinez): docs + SDK examples.

h1. Risks and Mitigations
1) *Quality regressions on narrow prompt sets*
* Mitigation: strict eval gates; label profiles experimental; block publication if borderline.

2) *Incompatibility leading to silent performance changes*
* Mitigation: write-time validation + runtime validation; explicit fallback signals; no silent version advances.

3) *Metadata fetch spikes causing registry load*
* Mitigation: caching/rate-limiting in control plane and runtime; prefetch on rollout.

4) *Operational confusion (is it applied? why fallback?) *
* Mitigation: consistent error codes, Console warnings, trace/log annotations, dashboard panels.

h1. Open Questions
1) Should we support a “recommended” alias in v1?
* Current v1 stance: *No* (avoid silent changes). Re-evaluate after GA with explicit customer opt-in for alias semantics.

2) Do we ship per-tenant global disable override in v1?
* Proposed: include if low engineering risk and requested by enterprise security reviews; otherwise track as v1.1.

3) What is the minimal set of regions/tiers for scoped rollout in v1?
* Proposed: region scope first (Hosted), tier scope for Dedicated where routing primitives exist.

h1. Launch Criteria (Beta → GA)
* At least 2 design partners have successfully enabled profiles on production-like traffic with measured savings and no unresolved regressions.
* Console enable/disable works with audit logging and RBAC.
* Dashboards and alerts are live.
* Kill-switch tested in a rollback drill.
* Docs published with troubleshooting and rollback guidance.

[Marketplace Feature Composition Playbook]
Overview

This playbook defines the product strategy, implementation requirements, rollout plan, pricing guidance, and release checklist for the "Feature Composition" capability in Redwood's Marketplace. Feature Composition allows customers to assemble multiple serving features (e.g., reranking, embeddings, caching, quantization profiles, and A/B fidelity routes) into composable bundles that behave as single consumable units in the Redwood Console and API. The goal is to accelerate customer time-to-value for common consumption patterns while preserving unit economics and observability.

Goals and success metrics

- Primary goal: Deliver a composable marketplace unit that reduces integration time for customers by 40% and increases bundle adoption rate to 20% of active tenants within 6 months.
- Business metrics: bundle revenue share (% of hosting revenue), avg tokens/sec per bundle, churn delta for customers using bundles, and incremental ARPU.
- Product metrics: time-to-first-bundle (console + API), failure rate for composite executions (<0.5%), average per-token latency delta vs baseline (<10ms).

Key concepts and scope

1) Composition unit: a named, versioned artifact that references one or more Redwood services and configuration profiles (model variant, quantization profile, cache TTLs, routing policy).
2) Execution graph: ordered stages (e.g., preprocessor -> model-A -> reranker -> cache-write) with per-stage SLOs and fallbacks.
3) Consumption contract: public interface (API surface + Console UX) plus pricing model that maps internal resource usage to billable units.
4) Compatibility guarantees: each bundle must include a compatibility matrix that lists supported runtime variants (hosted, dedicated, private) and minimal hardware footprint.

Non-goals

- Not intended to replace low-level SDK primitives. Developers will still be able to call individual services directly.
- No cross-tenant data mixing. Composed bundles adhere to tenant isolation rules and existing KMS/HSM integrations.

High-level product requirements (PRD style)

- PR-1: Bundle lifecycle: create / version / deprecate bundles. Bundles must be immutable once published; patch releases allowed (minor metadata only).
- PR-2: Declarative definition: support YAML/JSON bundle manifest with fields: id, name, description, stages (with service, model_ref, variant, resources), pricing_hint, telemetry_tags. Provide schema and sample manifests.
- PR-3: Execution guarantees: transactions across stages must support partial rollback semantics for idempotent stages; non-idempotent side effects must surface compensating actions in logs and alerts.
- PR-4: Observability: dashboards per-bundle with token-level cost breakdown, per-stage latency heatmaps, and error-trace waterfall.
- PR-5: Console UX: bundle composer with drag/drop stages, validation rules, preflight simulation using synthetic workload.
- PR-6: API: stable REST + SDK endpoints for listing, instantiating, and invoking bundles. Invocation should support streaming responses and function-calling where applicable.
- PR-7: Pricing: define a credit model (see Pricing Guidance section). Price preview in the composer and per-invocation estimate in the API.

Design constraints and decisions

- Decision D-1: Bundles will be first-class entities in the metadata service (service: catalog-api). Bundle manifests are stored versioned in the Config Store (service: cfg-store).
- Decision D-2: Execution will reuse existing runtime components; each stage resolves to an internal route token (route-svc) and executes with tenant-scoped quotas.
- Decision D-3: Bundles must declare a deterministic fallback policy: local-model fallback, variant fallback, regional failover, or degrade-to-sampled-response. The runtime will enforce the first compatible fallback.
- Decision D-4: For Private deployments, customers can opt-in to allow vendor-managed composition or run the composer locally via a CLI that emits a validated manifest.

Compatibility matrix (table-like summary)

- Supported modes: hosted (yes), dedicated (yes), private (opt-in, feature parity v1.1).
- Minimal footprints per composition complexity: small (1 model, no rerank) = 4 vCPU / 16GB GPU memory equivalent; medium (2–3 stages incl reranker) = 8 vCPU / 32GB GPU mem; large (multi-model + embeddings + cache) = 16+ vCPU / multi-GPU.

Runtime orchestration and telemetry

1. Resolution: catalog-api resolves manifest -> stage route tokens -> runtime graph.
2. Execution: running under an execution context that tracks request id, tenant id, trace id, and billing tags.
3. Telemetry: span per-stage with attributes: model_ref, variant, tokens_in/tokens_out, cost_estimate, compute_ms, fallback_triggered.
4. Sampling: include 100% sampling for bundle errors; 1% sampling for success traces (configurable per-tenant).

Pricing guidance and credit model

- Pricing primitive: charge per composite token-equivalent. Each stage contributes a token-weight multiplier based on model size and quantization profile (e.g., small model x1, reranker x0.6 per token, large model x2).
- Bundle-level surcharge: marketplace bundles carry a configurable partner surcharge (0–20%) and optional markup for managed bundles.
- Preview tool: composer shows a 30-day estimate (tokens, compute-hours, estimated credits) based on customer observed traffic patterns or synthetic defaults.

Operational runbook (high-level)

1) On-call flow: bundle execution failures that exceed 0.5% error rate for 10 minutes raise P1 to Runtime and Catalog owners.
2) Quick mitigation steps: toggle bundle to degraded mode (console action: disable external side-effects), route all traffic to variant with highest fidelity fallback.
3) Incident playbook: capture request ids, simulate failing manifest with known-good inputs via the preflight runner, and escalate if rollback not effective within 30 minutes.

Rollout timeline and milestones (quarterly phased)

- Phase 0 (Q4 2028): Internal alpha. Deliver catalog-api schema, composer wireframes, runtime graph prototype, and simple charging calculator.
- Phase 1 (Q1 2029): Private beta with 5 customers; console composer, execution telemetry, pricing-preview.
- Phase 2 (Q2 2029): General availability for hosted and dedicated; partner marketplace onboarding flow.
- Phase 3 (Q3 2029): Marketplace partner launch, revenue tracking, and A/B pricing experiments.

Owner and stakeholders

- Product lead: Leah Nakamura (this doc).
- Engineering owners: Runtime (Riley Chen), Catalog & Config (Marco Reyes), Console/UX (Priya Singh).
- Go-to-market owner: Anya Patel.
- Security/compliance reviewer: Edmund Briggs.

APIs and sample manifests

Sample bundle manifest (YAML) — composer will generate and validate this schema:

```

id: com.redwood.marketplace.compose.simple-summary-v1
name: "Summary-and-Rerank Bundle"
description: "Generates long-form summary then reranks candidate paragraphs for final selection"
stages:
  - name: summarize
    service: model-svc
    model_ref: open-llama-13b-v2
    variant: quantized-8bit
    resources:
      max_seq: 1024
      batch: auto
  - name: rerank
    service: rerank-svc
    model_ref: reranker-bert-large
    variant: standard
    resources:
      max_candidates: 8
pricing_hint:
  token_multiplier: 1.6
  partner_markup_pct: 10
telemetry_tags:
  - marketplace:feature-composition
  - vertical:knowledge
```

Release checklist (pre-GA)

- [ ] Schema stable and documented in cfg-store.
- [ ] Composer UX: synthetic-preflight and cost-preview integrated.
- [ ] Runtime: per-stage SLO instrumentation and fallback enforcement implemented.
- [ ] Billing: credit calculation validated against 3 traffic profiles.
- [ ] Security: threat model review and data residency checks for Private.
- [ ] Docs: developer guide, sample manifests, SDK examples, and migration notes.

Open questions and risks

- Q1: How to price cross-stage cache benefits (cache reduces compute downstream) without double-counting?
- Q2: Partner revenue share models—should we support revenue splits at invocation time or settlement time?
- Risk: Complexity of composed debugging for customers; mitigation: strong preflight simulator and 1-click trace collection.

Appendix: validation tests and KPIs for GA

- Functional tests: manifest validation, end-to-end execution for 8 canonical manifests, preflight fidelity simulation.
- Performance tests: 95th percentile per-bundle latency under 500 RPS with mixed short/long inputs.
- Billing tests: synthetic load that exercises token multipliers; reconciliation within 0.5% vs expected.
- Customer pilots: onboard 5 customers across e-commerce, knowledge, and support verticals; measure integration time and adoption rates.
