investigation:
Hypothesis: The identity provider rotation changed the subject namespace for service accounts (prefix change). Control-plane subject-prefix policy rejects requests when id_token.sub doesn't match the expected tenant-scoped namespace. Evidence: identity-proxy logs show alternating subject prefixes for the same client_id during rotation window. Trace links: https://observability.redwood.prod/traces?trace=req-20260310-87a. Metrics: token-exchange 403 spike correlated to 2026-03-02 AD rotation event. Reproduction steps executed in staging with replay tokens replicated the 403 behavior. Root cause: strict enforcement of exact subject-prefix mapping without accounting for rotation windows and multi-prefix allowlist per tenant.

resolution:
Workaround applied 2026-03-12: tenant-scoped temporary allowlist added to control-plane for BrightBank to accept both old and new subject prefixes. Observed immediate reduction in failures (<0.1%).

Permanent fix plan:
- Deploy tolerant subject-prefix matching logic that supports a short-lived rotation window per tenant and logs rotation diagnostics (ENG-2012). PR created: https://github.com/redwood/inference-auth/pull/298.
- Add console signal and alerting when subject-prefix variance exceeds threshold (OPS-894).
- Post-deploy: perform coordinated tenant rotation test with BrightBank to validate.

Follow-ups:

- Customer communication: notify BrightBank when permanent fix is deployed and recommend schedule for future rotations.

Ticket outcome: mitigation in place; awaiting deployment of PR and QA.

[Identity propagation delay prevents dashboard session token refresh for internal analytics console]
description:
Issue summary:
Users intermittently see a 401/403 from the internal analytics dashboard (console) immediately after an Okta profile change or a forced session refresh. The auth flow fails during the token refresh step: the auth-proxy exchanges the refresh token but the returned ID token appears to contain stale group/role claims, which the console then rejects due to tightened RBAC checks deployed last week.

Impact:
- ~12 engineers reported inability to load analytics dashboards since 2026-03-10 09:00 UTC.
- Affects internal dashboards and tooling only (not customer-facing APIs).
- Productivity hit for dashboard users and oncall when trying to verify incidents.

Environment:
- prod - us-east cluster serving internal-console routes.
- Okta as IdP, auth-proxy (v1.8.3) sits between console and Okta.

Steps to reproduce:
1) Log into console with a session established earlier (long-lived).
2) From Okta admin, update user's group membership (add/remove from analytics-admin).
3) Trigger console session refresh (browser refresh or wait for automatic refresh).
4) Observe 403 with "insufficient_role_claims" or 401 with "token_mismatch" in logs.

Expected behavior:
- After Okta claim change, the next refresh should either pick up new claims or gracefully fall back to previous session until the user reauths.

Actual behavior:
- Race condition: auth-proxy serves an ID token which appears to be from an older claim snapshot while backend RBAC service has the updated state, resulting in immediate denial.

Logs / evidence:
- auth-proxy logs (excerpt): "INFO exchange_refresh_token: returned id_token issued_at=1616161616 claims_version=42; cache_version=41"
- console logs: "ERROR access_check: claim_version_mismatch user=priya.shah@redwood.ai required=42 provided=41"
- Okta system log shows successful group update at 2026-03-10T09:02:14Z for affected users.

Business impact:
- Internal only, but P1 because it impedes oncall incident verification and slows engineering work.

Workarounds observed:
- Manual sign-out + full reauth resolves the issue for users.
- A temporary mitigation is to revert the strict claim_version enforcement in RBAC service (risky; requires rollback and careful rollout).

investigation_notes:
Initial hypothesis: identity cache/claim snapshot used by auth-proxy is behind Okta event processing or the token exchange pipeline; caching layer (claim-cache) may be serving stale claim bundles during refresh windows.

What we checked so far:
- Verified Okta event shows groups updated before auth-proxy token exchange.
- Replayed token exchange in staging: auth-proxy returns id_token with claims_version from local claim-cache, which is updated asynchronously by a background worker.
- Background worker shows occasional processing lag when claim updates are frequent (observed timestamps gap of up to 90s under burst).

Hypothesis: claim-cache update is eventual and not coordinated with token issuance; when RBAC service enforces claim_version strictly, short windows cause 403s.

Next steps:
- Add a short TTL invalidation on claim-cache on Okta webhooks (owner: auth-proxy team).
- Add defensive logic in RBAC service to accept id_token if issued_at is within 2m of claim update OR prompt reauth rather than 403.
- Add metrics and an alert for claim_version_mismatch rate > 1/min.
- Schedule a patch release for auth-proxy (v1.8.4) to synchronously refresh claims on token-exchange when webhook events are present.

Owners assigned: auth-proxy (Liam), RBAC (Sofia Martinez), SRE (Carlos Vega).

[Session linkage token mismatch blocks cross-account impersonation for support tooling]
description:
Issue summary: Since 2026-03-12 09:10 UTC, support tooling (impersonation flows used by oncall engineers via the internal console and CLI) intermittently fail with a 'session token mismatch' error when initiating cross-account impersonation. Impact: Oncall engineers cannot assume customer-facing service accounts for 5-30% of impersonation attempts, blocking urgent runbook actions and escalations. Environment: production us-east, identity-proxy v3.4.1, okta-device-trust enabled for privileged flows.

Steps to reproduce:
1) Login to console as admin (device trust approved)
2) Open 'Switch account / Impersonate' dialog and select external-tenant service-account
3) Click 'Assume role', or run 'rwd auth impersonate --account <tenant-id>' via CLI
4) Observe immediate failure in UI or CLI with error code 403/SESSION_LINK_MISMATCH and short correlation id in logs

Observed behavior: The identity-proxy returns 403 with message 'session_linkage_token invalid for target session'. The console shows a transient toast 'Unable to start impersonation — session verification failed'. CLI returns non-zero exit and logs: 'auth: session_linkage: verification failed: token not in session map'.

Expected behavior: Token exchange should validate and produce a scoped session for the target account or fall back to a clear diagnostic flow requesting reauthorization.

Investigation notes:
- Correlation IDs collected from affected attempts: rwd-imp-3f9b, rwd-imp-3fa0, rwd-cli-4b12. Logs attached to ticket in the support bucket (s3://redwood-support/logs/impersonation/2026-03-12/).
- Identity-proxy logs show the incoming assertion includes a linkage_token header (base64 string). The session-store (redis cluster auth-sessions-prod) lookup for the linkage token intermittently returns a 5xx from the replica nodes leading to token not found. The failure window aligns with a 2-minute rolling restart of redis-read replicas (maintenance job kicked off at 09:09 UTC by infra auto-heal).
- Reproduced locally by toggling a TTL skew: if session-store read misses then the verification fails immediately with the same error.
- No Okta assertion failures observed; device-trust asserts ok.
- Related code paths: identity-proxy handler verifySessionLinkage(), session-cache middleware, rwd-auth-cli token exchange.

Temporary mitigation:
- Oncall instructed to retry impersonation (most retries succeed). A short-term runbook added to the support-confluence page.
- Infra team paused the rolling restart and warmed read replicas; observed reduction in failures.

Next steps / Proposed fix:
1) Add a robust retry layer to session-store reads in identity-proxy (backoff + failover to primary) — PR proposed: https://github.com/redwood-inference/identity-proxy/pull/1872
2) Improve observability: emit metrics for session-linkage cache misses and 5xx on redis replicas. Dashboard ticket created under MON-impersonation-calls.
3) Add defensive behavior: if linkage token not found but assertion from Okta valid, present clear UI guidance to reauthorize rather than generic 403.

References: Slack thread #support-impersonation (https://slack.redwoodinference/support-impersonation/p12345), PR above, redis maintenance logs (infra ticket INT-931200).

[Org-wide Okta deprovisioning race causes token revocation blocking CLI/service-runner logins]
description:
Issue summary: During an org-wide deprovisioning job (safety cleanup for inactive contractors) we observed a race between Okta session revocation and our token re-issuance path. This caused a subset of ephemeral CLI tokens and long-running service-runner sessions to be rejected, preventing internal tooling authentication for affected users and automated jobs.

Impact: ~120 developer CLI sessions errored with 401/403 in us-east and eu-west; several nightly model-eval runners failed to start. No customer-facing inference endpoints were affected.

Business impact: internal dev velocity degraded, delayed nightly evaluations and blocked a small on-call escalation workflow.


steps_to_reproduce:
1) Ensure user has an active long-lived CLI session (issued >12h ago) and a service-runner job with token refresh configured.
2) Trigger the scheduled Okta deprovisioning job that revokes sessions for users marked inactive in LDAP (internal cron: identity-sync/deprovision/weekly).
3) Immediately attempt an API call with the existing CLI token or perform token refresh for the service-runner.
4) Observe auth failures (401 / 403) even though user shows as active in our local cache for a short window prior to sync completion.

observed_behavior:
Tokens that were issued prior to Okta deprovisioning are intermittently rejected during the deprovisioning window. Identity-proxy logs show a short window where our cache still returns the old user state but Okta responds 'revoked' to introspection calls, leading to a race and final rejection. Some retries succeed after ~30s when caches reconcile.

expected_behavior:
Either a graceful transitional state where existing sessions remain valid until rotated OR near-immediate propagation with consistent revocation across our token introspection and session caches so clients receive deterministic responses.

logs:
2026-03-10T02:04:12Z identity-proxy[auth-introspect] INFO token_introspect user=svc-runner-27 token_id=abc123 status=active
2026-03-10T02:04:13Z okta-sync INFO deprovision: start batch=contractors-20260310 count=187
2026-03-10T02:04:13Z okta API DEBUG introspect token=abc123 response=status=revoked code=401
2026-03-10T02:04:13Z identity-proxy WARN reconcile mismatch token=abc123 cache_state=active okta_state=revoked
2026-03-10T02:04:13Z cli-client ERROR api_request user=bob@example.com error=401 Unauthorized
2026-03-10T02:04:45Z identity-proxy INFO cache-refresh token=abc123 reconciled_state=revoked

investigation_notes:
Initial triage (Aisha): correlated spike of 401s with scheduled deprovision job at 02:04 UTC.
Hypothesis: identity-sync performs bulk Okta revoke then emits user status events; our identity-proxy uses a short-lived in-memory cache that can respond before the event stream processes the deprovision message, creating a TOCTOU (time-of-check time-of-use) window.
Observed that token introspection calls to Okta return 'revoked' while our local cache still marks session active for ~20-40s.
Reproducible locally by running deprovision job against staging Okta and issuing concurrent token introspection + cache read.

mitigation:
Applied an emergency server-side check: identity-proxy now performs an Okta-introspect call when cache indicates active but the token age is >6h OR when a bulk deprovision event is in progress. This reduces false-positives for invalid active-state responses. Deployed hotfix to prod at 2026-03-11T18:10Z.

resolution:
Ongoing. Hotfix reduces rate of failures by ~95% in short term. A durable fix (see follow-up tasks) will change event ordering and add a coordinated revocation phase to avoid races. Change to be implemented in identity-sync and identity-proxy coordination layer.

follow_up_tasks:
1) Implement coordinated revocation handshake in identity-sync so Okta revokes are gated until identity-proxy acknowledges event sequencing. Owner: Miguel. ETA: 2026-03-19
2) Add canary/deferred-revocation mode to weekly deprovision job to reduce blast radius. Owner: SRE team. ETA: 2026-03-24
3) Improve observability: add metric for 'introspect_mismatch' with labels (region, job_id). Owner: Observability. ETA: 2026-03-14
4) Postmortem and runbook update: document fallback policy and emergency mitigation steps. Owner: Support. ETA: 2026-03-16

2026-03-10T05:22:40Z - Miguel Ortega (SRE): Reproduced in staging. Confirmed TOCTOU race between Okta introspect and local cache. Will assemble quick mitigation.

[Cohort Comparator & Trace Linker for Deployment Health]
description:
Build a combined Cohort Comparator and Request Trace Linker inside the Console to make canary/A-B/shadow rollouts diagnosable end-to-end. The feature surfaces per-route metric diffs between cohorts, links anomalous metric deltas to sampled request traces, and exposes suggested rollback signals (automated and manual) backed by thresholded telemetry. This is intended to reduce MTTI for rollout regressions and make auto-rollback decisions transparent to product and platform teams.

acceptance_criteria:
Comparator UI shows side-by-side cohort-level charts for latency (p50/p95), error rate, token cost, and request throughput for a selected time window
Diff view highlights statistically significant deltas and annotates percentage change with confidence intervals
User can click a diff to see sampled traces from both cohorts with request-level metadata (route, model version, routing policy, input hash)
Trace Linker pins causal spans and shows top 3 signal contributors (e.g., model variant, batch size, region) derived from instrumentation
Auto-rollback triggers are visible per-rollout and can be toggled; Console records the reason and suggested fallback model
All telemetry queries are reproducible (copyable query) and dashboards exportable as PNG/CSV
Feature is behind a Console feature flag and gated to Dedicated/Hosted customers in beta

tasks:
Product: finalize comparator UX flows and error states (mockups)
Design: high-fidelity mockups for comparator panel, trace overlay, and diff heatmap
Engineering: instrument cohort labels in request pipeline and add trace sampling hook for cohort comparison
Engineering: build backend telemetry aggregator service to compute per-route deltas and significance tests
Engineering: expose API endpoints for cohort queries and trace joins
SRE: validate query performance and set retention defaults for cohort metrics
QA: e2e tests for trace linking across canary/A-B/shadow traffic scenarios
Docs: write Console help guide and rollout observability playbook

rollout_plan:
Alpha: enable feature flag for internal Redwood tenants only (1 week)
Beta: open to selected customers on Dedicated and Hosted with opt-in (4 weeks)
GA: enabled by default for all Console users with feature rollout controls (post-beta)

risks:
High cardinality of route/model/version labels could make diff computations slow
Trace sampling bias between cohorts may create false-positive causes
Auto-rollback without clear human-readable rationale could erode trust
Data retention costs if coarse-grained sampling is insufficient for forensic analysis

tradeoffs:
Aggressive trace sampling increases root-cause fidelity but raises cost — start with adaptive sampling tied to metric deltas
Pre-computing cohort diffs reduces UI latency but increases storage/compute; prefer on-demand with short cache window initially
Expose simple auto-rollback toggles first; defer fully automated ML-driven rollback recommendations to later cycle

[Rollout Convergence Inspector & Shadow Telemetry]
description:
Build a Console feature called 'Convergence Inspector' that gives engineers a compact, time-aware view for comparing cohorts during canary/A-B/shadow rollouts. The feature should surface per-route metric deltas (latency p50/p90/p99, token cost, error-rate), a divergence score over time, and linked traces/playback for outlier requests. Shadow traffic telemetry will be integrated to show continuous divergence even when traffic is mirrored, and automatic rollback suggestion signals will be emitted when sustained divergence exceeds thresholds.

acceptance_criteria:
A: Console shows side-by-side cohort overview for any two cohorts with selectable time windows
B: Per-route deltas include latency p50/p90/p99, token usage delta, success/error rate, and throughput change
C: Divergence score computed and plotted as time series; hover reveals contributing metrics
D: Trace links are available from the Inspector to the Trace Viewer for top-N anomalous requests
E: Shadow telemetry panel shows mirrored traffic divergence and a summary signal that can be used by auto-rollback rules
F: Product tests validate that the auto-rollback suggestion triggers when configured thresholds are exceeded for >= 5 mins
G: UX and copy reviewed and approved by Design and PM; Figma prototype linked

engineering_notes:
Backend: new rollout-inspector API that queries per-route time-bucketed stats from telemetry store (rollup by 1m/5m) and computes divergence score
Divergence score: weighted aggregate of z-scored p99 latency, error rate uplift, and token-cost drift. Prototype uses Holt-Winters for baseline smoothing; plan to benchmark against quantile-diff approach
Trace linking: include sample request IDs and route->trace_id mapping emitted by the runtime. ENG-23145 will add sample headers in shadow requests
Performance: inspector queries limited to 3 routes per view initially to prevent heavy aggregation joins; will iterate after benching
Security: ensure trace links honor project RBAC and PII redaction policies

test_plan:
Unit tests for divergence score computation (edge cases: low-volume routes, zero-traffic cohorts)
Integration test: end-to-end rollouts using synthetic traffic generator to produce controlled divergence patterns
E2E: QA run with internal canary to validate UX and trace linking before beta release
Load: backend aggregator tested with synthetic 10k reqs/min across 50 routes to validate 30s UI load target

rollout_impact:
Will enable platform engineers to detect silent regressions earlier during canary and A/B tests
Auto-rollback suggestion reduces time-to-mitigation for high-impact regressions (estimated 40% reduction in mean time to rollback during pilot)
Initial release limited to hosted customers and Redwood Dedicated tenants with telemetry enabled

decisions:
Show p50/p90/p99 by default; users can expand to custom percentiles
Divergence score will be visible as ordinal (low/medium/high) and a continuous metric to power automation rules
Shadow telemetry will sample 1% of mirrored traces by default to control storage costs (configurable per workspace)
Auto-rollback suggestion only surfaces (not automatic action) in v1; later iteration will add opt-in automatic rollback

Risk: Storage and cost growth from trace capture -> Mitigation: sample rate default 1%, allow workspace overrides, and compress traces for mirror traffic
Risk: Users misinterpret suggestion as auto-rollback -> Mitigation: clear UI copy and require an explicit enable flag for automation

[Rollout Cohort Diff Explorer and Trace-linked Auto-rollback Signals]
description:
Build a Rollout Cohort Diff Explorer inside Console that enables product and SRE teams to compare canary/A-B cohorts side-by-side across: per-route latency P50/P95/P99, token-level cost, error rate by error class, semantic quality signals (evaluation prompts pass/fail), and request trace samples. The Explorer should support: 1) instant diff views for recent rollouts (last 24h, 7d), 2) drill-through to representative traces and model outputs, 3) significance testing (bootstrap p-values) for metric deltas, 4) configurable auto-rollback triggers (threshold + trend), and 5) a shadow-traffic validation tab that overlays shadow vs production behavior without impacting traffic. Goal: reduce time-to-detect regressions during canary/A-B rollouts from hours to minutes and enable safe automatic rollback when regressions exceed configured tolerances.

acceptance_criteria:
Console has a new 'Cohort Diff Explorer' page that lists active rollouts and historical rollouts with start/end times.
Users can select two cohorts (control and treatment) and view per-route metric panels: latency P50/P95/P99, errors per 1k requests broken down by class, token cost per request, and a quality score derived from eval prompt pass rates.
Diff panels show absolute and relative deltas with statistical significance indicators (p < 0.05, trend arrows).
Clicking a metric tile opens a trace-linked sample list: each sample shows request metadata, model version, full prompt, model output, and trace link to distributed spans.
Auto-rollback configuration UI allows teams to define policy: metric, comparator (>, <), threshold, sustained window (minutes), and minimum sample size. Policy can be applied per-route or global to the rollout.
Shadow tab shows side-by-side distribution plots for production vs shadow traffic and highlights any behavioral divergence above a configurable JS divergence threshold.
Backend supports query latencies under 2s for a 7-day window for cohorts with up to 10M requests using pre-aggregated rollup tables and an index for (route, model_version, time_bucket).
Unit and integration tests for significance engine, auto-rollback webhook flow, and RBAC checks for viewing rollout data are present and passing.
Documentation and runbook for interpreting diff signals and manual rollback steps are published in Confluence (link included in comments).

implementation_notes:
Backend: add 'rollout_event_store' rollups keyed by (route, model_version, cohort_id, time_bucket) with precomputed: count, errors_by_class, token_cost_sum, quantile_sketch(latency).
Significance engine: bootstrap resampling on aggregated samples with configurable iterations (default 1000) and early-stopping when p-value stabilizes.
Trace linking: store exemplar trace_ids per time_bucket + error_class + route for O(1) drill-through retrieval.
Auto-rollback: webhook payload must include checksum of rollout config to prevent out-of-band actions; controller to record audit entry to immutable store.
Query perf: use TTL-based materialized views for 1m/5m rollups and background job to backfill when cohort definitions change.
RBAC: new permission 'rollout.view_sensitive' gating raw prompt/output access; masking default for orgs without approval.

[Shadow Replay & Divergence Explorer for Rollouts]
description:
Build an exploration UI and backend hooks in Console that helps operators compare live production traffic against shadowed or replayed responses during canary/A-B rollouts. The feature surfaces divergence hotspots (metric deltas by route and cohort), links from cohort diffs into traces and request samples, and a guided set of checks to decide on auto-rollback. It must support shadow traffic (mirror), live replay from stored requests, and side-by-side metric timelines for selected endpoints.

acceptance_criteria:

[Private Deploy Live-tail & Debugging Runbook]
Purpose:
This runbook documents the standard operator procedures for live-tailing, real-time debugging, and safe mitigation of incidents in Private (VPC / on-prem) Redwood deployments. It is written for on-call SREs and field operators who need to quickly triage runtime issues, capture evidence, and perform controlled mitigations or rollbacks without breaching customer isolation guarantees.

Scope:
- Applies to all Private (VPC and on-prem) tenants running the Redwood runtime (services: ri-runtime, ri-operator, ri-control-plane)
- Covers user-visible latency/regressions, quota saturation, model swap failures, KV-cache regressions, GPU / node degradation, and telemetry gaps
- Does NOT cover long-term capacity planning or procurement activities (see tenant-capacity docs)

Owner & Escalation:
- Primary owner: Private Deployments Ops (oncall: private-deploy-sre)
- Secondary: Runtime Engineering
- Escalation path: oncall -> private-deploy-team lead -> service-owner (runtime@redwood.ai)

SLOs and Detects (Reference thresholds):
- Generation p95 latency (end-to-end): target < 350ms; alert if p95 > 700ms for 5m
- Token throughput drop: alert if aggregate tokens/s drops > 60% vs baseline for 3m
- KV cache hit ratio: target >= 0.65; alert if < 0.4 for 10m
- Request error rate: alert if 5xx rate > 1% for 5m or 4xx surge indicating broken client integration
- Telemetry heartbeat: control-plane heartbeat missing for > 3m -> page oncall

Quick Triage Checklist (first 10 minutes):
1) Validate page details & scope: tenant, region, time, customer impact (latency vs errors).
2) Confirm incident on observability: check Prometheus, Grafana dashboards (Tenant / Model / Node breakdown).
3) Live-tail runtime logs (ri-runtime) and operator logs (ri-operator) for the tenant.
4) Check resource health: GPU (nvidia-smi), node disk, memory, and network queue depth.
5) If issue is a model swap or deploy, verify artifact availability and model-serving logs (model-loader).
6) If degradation persists after 15 min, escalate and open an incident channel; gather evidence (traces, tail logs, config snapshot).

Primary Observability Sources (locations & metrics):
- Prometheus metrics: ri_runtime_request_latency_seconds_bucket, ri_runtime_request_errors_total, ri_kvcache_hits_total / ri_kvcache_misses_total, ri_token_throughput_total, node_gpu_utilization_percent
- Dashboards: Grafana -> "Private Deploy - Tenant Overview", "Runtime - Model Latency", "KV Cache - Health"
- Tracing: Jaeger UI at https://jaeger.internal.redwood.ai (service: ri-runtime, operations: Generate/Stream/LoadModel)
- Logs:
  - Operator logs: /var/log/ri/ri-operator.log (or systemd journal: systemctl status ri-operator)
  - Runtime logs: /var/log/ri/ri-runtime.log
  - Model loader: /var/log/ri/model-loader.log
- Field CLI: rictl (used to query tenant state, toggle safemode, fetch runtime snapshots)

Common Commands (examples):
- Tail runtime logs for tenant "tenant-acme":
  sudo journalctl -u ri-runtime | grep tenant-acme -A 200 -n

- Query Prometheus for current p95 for tenant (example):
  curl -s 'https://prometheus.internal/api/v1/query?query=histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(ri_runtime_request_latency_seconds_bucket{tenant="tenant-acme"}[5m])) by (le))' | jq

- Check KV cache hit ratio:
  curl -s 'https://prometheus.internal/api/v1/query?query=(sum(rate(ri_kvcache_hits_total{tenant="tenant-acme"}[5m])) / sum(rate(ri_kvcache_misses_total{tenant="tenant-acme"}[5m])) )' | jq

- Get operator-managed deployment status: rictl tenant status tenant-acme --output json
- Trigger safemode (see Safemode section): rictl tenant safemode enable tenant-acme --reason "oncall-latency-spike" --actor $USER

Evidence Collection (required for any mitigation):
- Capture 5m traces around incident start from Jaeger, include request ids.
- Prometheus snapshot of relevant metrics (p95, errors, throughput, KV hit ratio, node GPU util).
- Tail of the three logs above (operator/runtime/model-loader) covering -5m to +5m of incident window.
- rictl tenant snapshot tenant-acme > snapshot-<timestamp>.json

Detailed Playbook (by symptom):
A) High latency (p95 > 700ms) with low error rate
1) Check runtime CPU/GPU saturation: top / nvidia-smi on affected nodes. If GPU saturating (>95% utilization sustained), check for model inference loops or runaway requests.
2) Inspect batching backlog: rictl tenant backlog tenant-acme --nodes. If backlog grows and latency increases, consider temporary increase of worker concurrency (rictl tenant scaling adjust --workers +1) or enable burst pool if configured.
3) If KV cache hit ratio is low, check kvcached logs and warm by replaying hot prompts (see kvcache warmup below).
4) If no resource issues, collect traces and escalate to runtime engineers for slow-path kernel debugging.

B) Error spike (5xx)
1) Identify error class in logs (OOM, model-mismatch, runtime panics).
2) If OOM on GPU process: capture core dump (if enabled), reduce concurrency and trigger safemode to route to backup model variant.
3) If model artifact load error: validate artifact integrity (sha256) on runtime: ls -l /srv/ri/models/<model-id> and compare against control-plane metadata. If mismatch, mark model unhealthy and initiate model rollback.
4) If 5xx caused by model evaluation regressions, consult product/ML for golden prompt set regression test before model rollforward.

C) Telemetry missing / heartbeat gap
1) Check ri-operator connectivity to telemetry-bridge: sudo systemctl status ri-operator; check /var/log/ri/telemetry-bridge.log
2) Validate network connectivity to control-plane endpoints (curl https://cp.internal.redwood.ai/health).
3) If telemetry is down globally for tenant, enable local collection: rictl tenant local-telemetry enable tenant-acme --ttl 24h; this stores buffered metrics for later upload and prevents immediate alert storms.

KV-cache warmup recipe (when cold-cache causes latency spikes):
1) Fetch top 50 heavy prompt prefixes from recent traces: rictl tenant hot-prefixes tenant-acme --since 24h --top 50 > hot-prefixes.txt
2) Replay prefixes against model-loader in read-only mode with low concurrency to populate prefix/KV: rictl kvcache warmup --tenant tenant-acme --file hot-prefixes.txt --concurrency 4

Safemode (controlled mitigation)
- Purpose: minimize customer-visible impact while preserving operational safety. Safemode disables non-essential features (autoscaling, aggressive batching changes, model swap) and optionally routes traffic to a fallback model variant.
- Activation: only by oncall SRE or with authorization from private-deploy-team lead.
- Command: rictl tenant safemode enable tenant-acme --reason "<brief-reason>" --actor $USER
- Recommended safemode actions:
  - Route to fallback: rictl routing set tenant-acme --model model-id:stable-quantized
  - Disable autoscale: rictl tenant autoscale disable tenant-acme
  - Reduce worker concurrency: rictl tenant scaling adjust tenant-acme --workers -2
- Deactivation: rictl tenant safemode disable tenant-acme --actor $USER --note "recovered"

Controlled Rollback Procedure (for runtime or model changes)
1) Confirm rollback criteria met: recent deploy timestamp within 60 minutes and correlated error/latency spike.
2) Gather artifacts to preserve: rictl tenant snapshot tenant-acme > rollback-evidence-<ts>.json; capture Prometheus snapshot.
3) Rollback runtime image (example): rictl deployment rollback ri-runtime --tenant tenant-acme --image ri-runtime:v1.29.2 --wait 900s
   - Monitor readiness: rictl deployment status --watch --deployment ri-runtime --tenant tenant-acme
4) For model rollback: rictl model set tenant-acme --model-id model-123-stable --version v2026-05-04 --wait
5) Verify post-rollback health for at least 15 minutes: p95 back within SLO, error rate normalized, KV cache stable.

Emergency node evacuation (severe hardware / noisy neighbor):
1) Mark node unschedulable: rictl node cordon <node-id> --reason "evacuation"
2) Initiate tenant relocation for affected tenants: rictl node evacuate <node-id> --tenants tenant-acme --grace 300s
3) Watch for safe handoff in operator logs. If evacuation stalls, contact field operator to power-cycle or attach serial console.

Post-incident: Evidence preservation & review - Preserve all snapshots and logs in incident storage: /incidents/<incident-id>/ (runbook step: rictl incident create --id <incident-id> --source oncall)
- File an incident review within 72 hours using the Incident Review Template (link below). Include root cause hypothesis, corrective actions (short and long term), and owners with timelines.

Safety checks & guardrails (do NOT run unless authorized):
- Do not manually delete model artifacts from /srv/ri/models unless instructed by runtime engineering.
- Avoid simultaneous scaling and safemode toggles across multiple tenants unless coordinated.
- For any rollback that touches customer data paths, notify security and legal (customer-impact evidence retention required).

Playbook appendices:
- Appendix A: Common rictl commands (cheat sheet)
- Appendix B: Trace and query examples (PromQL snippets for p95, KV ratio)
- Appendix C: Postmortem checklist and blameless review template

Appendix A (cheat sheet):
- rictl tenant status <tenant>
- rictl tenant snapshot <tenant> > snapshot.json
- rictl tenant safemode enable <tenant> --reason "..."
- rictl deployment rollback <service> --image <image-tag> --wait 900s
- rictl node cordon <node-id>
- rictl kvcache warmup --tenant <tenant> --file hot-prefixes.txt --concurrency 4

Appendix B (PromQL snippets):
- p95 latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(ri_runtime_request_latency_seconds_bucket{tenant="tenant-acme"}[5m])) by (le))
- kv cache hit ratio: sum(rate(ri_kvcache_hits_total{tenant="tenant-acme"}[5m])) / (sum(rate(ri_kvcache_hits_total{tenant="tenant-acme"}[5m])) + sum(rate(ri_kvcache_misses_total{tenant="tenant-acme"}[5m])))

Appendix C (postmortem template):
- Incident ID, Date
- Summary (1-2 lines)
- Timeline (Timestamps, actions)
- Root cause hypothesis
- Short-term mitigations completed
- Long-term corrective actions (with owners & ETA)
- Lessons learned

Related pages and links:
- Tenant onboarding and failover runbook: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/deployment-guides/private-deploy-onboarding-and-failover-runbook-2026.json
- Cold-start mitigation playbook: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/day-2-ops/cold-start-latency-mitigation-for-private-deploys-2026.json

Contact list (for escalation):
- private-deploy oncall: private-deploy-sre@redwood.ai (pager)
- runtime engineers: runtime@redwood.ai
- product/ML contact for model regressions: mlops@redwood.ai

This runbook is reviewed quarterly or after any major incident. For suggested edits, propose changes on the doc and notify the reviewers list.


[Tenant Exfiltration Detection and Quarantine Playbook for Private Deployments]
Purpose
-------
This document defines detection signals, automated response, and operator procedures for suspected data exfiltration originating from tenant workloads in Private (VPC / on‑prem) Redwood deployments. The playbook balances fast containment with evidence preservation so we can safely escalate to legal/compliance and to the customer when required.

Scope
-----
- Applies to Redwood Private control plane integrations and on‑prem tenant runtime instances.
- Covers detection signals, automated isolation (quarantine), evidence preservation, customer communication templates, and post‑incident remediation steps.
- Excludes application‑layer incidents inside customer managed containers where the customer has sole responsibility to remediate unless a Redwood agent detects infrastructure‑level data flows that violate telemetry contracts.

Assumptions and Principles
--------------------------
1. Minimize data loss and lateral spread while preserving logs and snapshots for forensic review.
2. Actions must be reversible and documented; irreversible actions (delete/erase) require explicit approval from security leadership and legal.
3. Maintain an evidence chain (timestamped artifacts, signatures) for regulated customers.
4. Playbook must work offline for air‑gapped customers: quarantine actions operate via local operator tooling and signed runbook artifacts.

Key Roles and Contacts
----------------------
- Detection Owner: Security Detection Engineering (oncall: sec-detection@redwood)
- Incident Commander: SRE oncall for Private Deployments (oncall: sre-private@redwood)
- Forensics Lead: Security IR Team (ir@redwood)
- Customer Success Lead: Assigned per customer (lookup: customer-mapping-service)

High‑Level Flow (summary)
------------------------
1. Signal triggered (automated alert from telemetry pipeline).
2. Triage: confirm anomaly, classify as probable exfil vs benign spike.
3. Automated provisional quarantine (network isolate / throttle) + evidence snapshot.
4. Human review within 30 minutes: escalate or rollback provisional quarantine.
5. If confirmed: full quarantine, preserve artifacts, engage legal and customer success.
6. Remediation and recovery plan, follow‑up report and POA.

Detection Signals and Thresholds
-------------------------------
The detection system correlates multiple signals. An alert is considered high confidence when 2 or more of the following are present within a 5‑minute window: 
- Unusual egress volume by a tenant (sustained > 3x baseline for 5 minutes).
- Large number of distinct remote destinations for small volumes (scanning pattern).
- Sudden spike in object storage PUTs combined with higher than normal key distribution entropy.
- New service account / API key used from an unexpected subnet and immediately performing bulk reads.
- Unusual KV cache dump or model artifact access from low‑privilege service account.

Suggested numeric thresholds (tunable per customer):
| Signal | Default Threshold | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| Tenant egress (5m rolling) | 1 GB | For latency sensitive customers set lower |
| Distinct remote IPs (1m) | 50 | High for low‑throughput tenants |
| Storage object writes (1m) | 200 objects | Consider object size weighting |
| New key usage | 1 key | Trigger if from unknown origin |

Detection pipeline components (examples)
--------------------------------------
- Network telemetry: local eBPF collectors -> aggregated to telemetry proxy -> Prometheus / Honeycomb metrics.
- Audit logs: model artifacts / storage access forwarded to secure log buffer with HMACed blocks.
- Flow analysis: enrichment service that resolves IPs, ASN, geolocation and computes destination entropy.
- Alerting: Prometheus alertmanager + on‑prem rules document stored in repo (see Appendix).

Automated Provisional Quarantine (safety‑first automation)
--------------------------------------------------------
When a high‑confidence alert fires, the system executes a provisional containment sequence (automated) that is reversible and short‑lived (default 30 minutes):
1. Apply tenant egress throttle policy to 10% of normal bandwidth.
2. Add tenant to network ACL denylist for external destinations flagged as suspect, allow control plane connectivity.
3. Capture immediate artifacts:
   - Signed snapshot of runtime state (list of running pods / processes and KV cache checksums).
   - Copy of last 60 minutes of flow logs, storage access logs, and audit events to a WORM evidence container.
4. Create an incident ticket (auto) with attached artifacts and assign to oncall.

The provisional quarantine must always preserve the control plane connectivity channel so operators can access the site and to allow customer‑facing APIs to check status.

Operator Triage Checklist (first 30 minutes)
-------------------------------------------
1. Validate alert provenance: review metric dashboards and raw flow logs.
2. Confirm anomalous destinations (ASN / geo / known bad lists).
3. Check for false positives: known backup windows, scheduled bulk transfers, vendor syncs.
4. If benign, rollback provisional quarantine with automated rollback command (see commands).
5. If malicious or uncertain, escalate to Incident Commander and move to Full Quarantine.

Full Quarantine Procedure (human approved)
-----------------------------------------
1. Err on the side of containment. The Incident Commander issues the Full Quarantine order.
2. Actions to perform (ordered):
   a. Isolate tenant network: sever outbound internet egress for tenant VLAN(s) while preserving inbound control plane ports to 443/8443 and operator SSH only from approved operator IPs.
   b. Throttling of inter‑tenant east‑west traffic where applicable.
   c. Suspend non‑essential jobs and scheduled backups originating from the tenant.
   d. Snapshot persistent volumes and model stores (preserve checksums).
   e. Preserve and export logs into a signed evidence bundle (include HMAC signatures).
3. Generate a read‑only access bridge for the customer success rep and legal for controlled investigation requests.
4. Notify customer per the communication template.

Evidence Preservation and Forensics
----------------------------------
- All artifacts must be stored immutably (WORM) for the retention window required by the customer or by legal hold.
- Tag artifacts with incident_id, tenant_id, timestamp, and cryptographic signature of the operator who initiated the snapshot.
- Maintain a manifest (JSON) that lists every artifact and the hash; example manifest line:
  {
    "incident_id": "INC-20260304-042",
    "tenant_id": "tenant-42",
    "artifact": "flows-2026-03-04T04-00-00.gz",
    "sha256": "<hash>"
  }
- For air‑gapped customers, place manifest and artifacts on signed USB tokens or a customer‑managed evidence vault and log the handoff.

Customer Communication Templates (short form)
-------------------------------------------
- Initial notification (provisional containment):
  Subject: Redwood: Temporary network containment for your deployment (tenant-42)
  Body: We detected anomalous outbound activity from your tenant environment on 2026‑03‑04 04:12 UTC. As a precaution we applied a temporary bandwidth throttle and initiated evidence collection while our team triages. No production data was deleted. Your assigned CSM (Jane Doe) will reach out with next steps.

- Confirmed incident notification (after human review):
  Subject: Redwood: Confirmed exfiltration investigation and containment actions for tenant-42
  Body: Our team has confirmed indicators consistent with data exfiltration. We have isolated outbound internet access and preserved forensic artifacts. We are engaging our legal team and will coordinate the next steps with you within 4 business hours.

Forensics and Legal Handoff
---------------------------
1. Prepare a forensics bundle: manifest, signed snapshots, timeline of events, operator notes.
2. For regulated customers (PCI / HIPAA / SOC2): run the additional evidence extraction checklist and request legal hold if needed.
3. Coordinate with the customer to agree on joint forensic activities and acceptable data sharing boundaries.

Rollback and Recovery
---------------------
- Rollback is only permitted when the Incident Commander and Forensics Lead confirm no ongoing exfiltration risk.
- Steps to rollback (numbered):
  1. Revoke denylist entries and restore tenant egress policy to baseline gradually (10% increments every 5 minutes while monitoring telemetry).
  2. Restart suspended jobs under supervision in a staging window.
  3. Reconcile and verify checksums for model artifacts and persistent volumes.
  4. Run a post‑incident audit report and present to the customer.

Operational Controls and Telemetry Requirements (customer requirements table)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Private deployment must provide the following telemetry to support detection. These are minimum requirements to onboard a customer to exfiltration monitoring.
| Requirement | Minimum | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Flow logs (per VPC/tenant) | 1s aggregation, 30d retention | Detect egress spikes and destination entropy |
| Storage access audit | object-level with timestamp, user, IP | Identify bulk reads / writes |
| Model artifact audit | artifact id, user, checksum, operation | Detect unauthorized downloads / dumps |
| Runtime state snapshot API | API to request current pod/process list | Rapid evidence capture |

Appendix: Example Alert Rules and Queries
----------------------------------------
Prometheus rule (egress spike):
  - alert: TenantEgressSpike
    expr: increase(tenant_network_egress_bytes_total[5m]) > 1073741824
    for: 2m
    labels:
      severity: high
    annotations:
      summary: "Tenant {{ $labels.tenant }} egress >1GB in 5m"

Splunk example search (object writes):
  index=tenant_audit source=storage_access tenant_id=tenant-42 action=PUT | stats count AS put_count by tenant_id | where put_count > 200

Kubernetes operator commands (local runbook):
- Rollback provisional quarantine:
  redwoodctl private tenant unquarantine --tenant tenant-42 --reason "false_positive_verified" --operator $OPERATOR
- Trigger full quarantine (manual):
  redwoodctl private tenant quarantine --tenant tenant-42 --preserve-evidence --incident-id INC-20260304-042

Post‑Incident Actions and Reporting
----------------------------------
1. 72‑hour incident summary (to internal stakeholders).
2. Customer incident report (timeline, impact, evidence summary, POA).
3. Retrospective and detection tuning: update thresholds, add signatures to IP denylist if confirmed.
4. Update runbook and training for oncall.

Related pages
-------------
- Hybrid control plane reference architecture (internal link: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/reference-architectures/hybrid-control-plane-reference-architecture-2026)
- Private deploy telemetry sampling and privacy playbook (internal link: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/onprem-packaging/onprem-telemetry-sampling-privacy-cost-playbook-2025)

Ownership and SLAs
------------------
- Detection engineering maintains the alert rules and evidence pipeline.
- SRE Private owns execution of quarantine actions and operator tooling.
- Security IR owns forensics and legal coordination.
- Target time to provisional containment: <= 5 minutes from a high‑confidence alert.
- Time to human review: <= 30 minutes.

Change log
----------
- 2026‑02‑20: Initial draft by Priya Raman.
- 2026‑03‑04: Published changes: tightened thresholds and added HMAC evidence manifest requirements.



[Operator resilience fabric and offline fallback reference]
Summary:\nThis reference describes the Operator Resilience Fabric (ORF): a lightweight control-plane and runtime pattern designed to keep customer-facing private deployments (VPC and on-prem) available when upstream control-plane connectivity is degraded or unavailable. The doc covers the architecture, failure modes, operator procedures for offline fallback, packaging and artifact requirements, day-2 operational checks, upgrade/rollback implications, and minimal customer readiness requirements.\n\nGoals and non-goals:\n- Goals:\n  - Maintain tenant-serving availability (read/write inference requests) for defined SLO windows when the Redwood control plane or regional telemetry gateways are unreachable.\n  - Provide deterministic fallback policies for model variants, KV cache warming, and admission control that preserve safety and cost bounds.\n  - Ensure operator-run recoverability: clear escape hatches, rollforward and roll back steps, and forensic evidence preservation.\n- Non-goals:\n  - Full feature parity with hosted operational tooling while offline.\n  - Arbitrary long-term autonomous operation without eventual reconciliation.\n\nHigh-level architecture:\n- Components (logical):\n  - Local operator agent (operatord): lightweight process responsible for orchestration of fallback workflows, local policy enforcement, and artifact validation.\n  - Runtime fabric (runtime-fabric): set of sidecar/daemon processes that manage model artifacts, KV cache, and inference runtime lifecycle on each node.\n  - Local control-plane replica (lcpr): minimal control-plane cache containing routing policies, model manifests, and safety gates; canonical only while online, fallbacks use cached manifests with attestation.\n  - Telemetry gateway (tg): local aggregator for sampling and buffering telemetry until upstream recovered.\n- Data flows and invariants:\n  - On connectivity loss: operatord consults lcpr and runtime-fabric to switch to fallback model variants and admission policies.\n  - Safety invariant: no automatic escalation to higher-cost model variants beyond configured budget percentages without operator approval.\n\nTopology patterns and reference diagrams (text):\n- Local single-region resilient topology:\n  - control-plane egress -> (proxy) -> operatord -> runtime-fabric -> GPU pool -> inference pods\n  - When upstream broken, operatord sets runtime-fabric to local-only routing and engages read-through KV cache.\n- Multi-AZ airgapped topology:\n  - Each AZ runs an lcpr instance with quorum-based checks. operatord uses cross-AZ heartbeats to decide forced evacuation or model eviction.\n\nSLOs and thresholds (recommended):\n- Tenant-serving availability during upstream blackout: 99.5% over a 1-hour window for requests below max_seq_len 1024.\n- Token latency increase cap: no more than 2x median baseline for degraded model variants; prefer queue-based admission to stay under 500ms p50 for short requests.\n- Cost guardrail: local fallback must not increase per-token spend by > 40% for the first 30 minutes without explicit operator approval.\n\nOperator playbook: offline fallback activation\n1) Detection and initial validation:\n   - Alert triggers: control-plane-e2e-heartbeat absent for > 45s or telemetry gateway unresponsive > 60s.\n   - Validation steps:\n     a) Confirm network disruption: curl -sSf https://control-plane.example.internal/health || true\n     b) Check operator agent status: kubectl -n redwood get pods -l app=operatord -o wide\n2) Safe-mode entry (automated by operatord):\n   - operatord writes a stamped event to lcpr and switches to 'fallback-pending' state.\n   - Runtime-fabric changes (atomic): pause automated model refresh, freeze KV eviction for 60s, enable admission queue with configured thresholds.\n3) Fallback candidate selection (automated with operator oversight):\n   - Selection rules (in priority): local quantized variants with known throughput profiles; [Progressive Degradation and Tenant Throttling Playbook]
Summary:\nThis playbook describes the recommended patterns, operator procedures, and automated controls for progressive degradation and tenant-level throttling in private (VPC/on‑prem) Redwood deployments. It provides a step-by-step runbook for safely limiting tenant resource consumption while maintaining the best possible service for remaining traffic. The goal is to keep high-priority requests healthy, preserve KV/LLM cache integrity where possible, and provide clear operator actions and rollback paths.\n\nScope and intent:\n- Applies to private deployments (VPC and on‑prem control planes) running multi‑tenant inference nodes or shared service planes.\n- Focus on non-destructive throttling (rate limits, concurrency caps, queueing and shed patterns) and progressive feature degradation (smaller model fallbacks, quantized execution, disabled non-critical features).\n- Designed for both reactive incident response and pre-emptive autoscale-driven protective behaviors.\n\nKey definitions:\n- Tenant: customer namespace, logical tenant on the control plane.\n- Progressive degradation: ordered, reversible reduction of functionality (e.g., disable long-context mode, reduce max_tokens) to reduce resource pressure.\n- Throttling: controls limiting request rate, concurrency, token throughput.\n- SLOs referenced: 99th percentile tail latency (p99), request success rate, and model correctness (measured by quality guards).\n\nHigh-level strategy:\n1) Detect: use telemetry to identify high-usage tenants or runaway traffic patterns.\n2) Contain: apply per-tenant soft limits and backpressure to stop immediate pressure on shared resources.\n3) Degrade progressively: move the tenant through an ordered set of fallbacks that trade capabilities for resource savings.\n4) Observe: confirm reduction in pressure and validate critical customer flows remain functional.\n5) Restore: rollback degradations in controlled stages after pressure normalizes.\n\nSignals and thresholds (operator-visible):\n- Metrics: tenant_request_rate, tenant_concurrent_sessions, tenant_tokens_per_minute, node_gpu_utilization_5m, kv_cache_hit_rate, p99_response_ms, error_rate_5m.\n- Primary thresholds (tunable per deployment):\n  - tenant_tokens_per_minute > 150k for 3 minutes => WARNING\n  - tenant_concurrent_sessions > 250 for 2 minutes => WARNING\n  - node_gpu_utilization_5m > 92% for 2 minutes => CRITICAL\n  - p99_response_ms > 1200ms and error_rate_5m > 0.5% => CRITICAL\n\nEscalation policy summary:\n- WARNING: auto-notify tenant owner via configured contact; place tenant into soft-throttle mode (see automated controls).\n- CRITICAL: escalate to oncall SRE (level-1) and apply controlled progressive degradation. Notify account team and CS.\n\nAutomated controls (order of operations):\n1) Soft Throttle (non-terminating): impose 20% rate reduction via token-bucket enforcement at the edge.\n2) Queueing with Priority: shift tenant to a priority queue with a 5s admission timeout; priority score based on SLA tier.\n3) Feature Reduction Stage 1: disable optional tooling (e.g., embedding rerank, long-context KV-prefetch).\n4) Feature Reduction Stage 2: cap max_tokens to 512 and reduce streaming chunk size.\n5) Model Fallback Stage: route requests to a smaller, cheaper quantized variant (e.g., redwood-llama-quant-1) with explicit response header X-RD-Model-Fallback.\n6) Burst-only Mode: allow short bursts but enforce a slow steady-state baseline (e.g., 10 requests/min).\n7) Tenant Quarantine (last resort): soft-eviction (reject new sessions with 409 + JSON body linking to support) — only after manual approval.\n\nOperator runbook: Immediate manual steps (for CRITICAL events)\n1) Confirm alert context and affected tenants. Review dashboards: tenant_request_rate, tokens_per_minute, node_gpu_utilization (links in the incident header).\n2) If node_gpu_utilization_5m > 92% and multiple tenants are impacted: trigger cluster-level autoscale (if allowed) or initiate tenant-level throttles.\n3) For single high-usage tenant: set \"soft_throttle\" attribute on tenant in control plane. CLI example:\n\n# Example CLI (Control Plane)\nredwoodctl tenant update --tenant my-tenant-id --set soft_throttle=true --throttle-rate 0.8\n\n4) After soft_throttle, monitor for 2 minutes. If no improvement, move to Feature Reduction Stage 1 using the control-plane flag set: reduce_prefetch=true.\n\n# Example API call (internal control plane API)\nPATCH /internal/tenants/my-tenant-id/degrade\nContent-Type: application/json\n{\n  \"stage\": \"feature_reduction_1\",\n  \"reason\": \"high_gpu_utilization_critical_2026-06-10\"\n}\n\n5) Continue through the stages as needed. Record each stage as an event in the tenant audit log with start_time, operator, and rationale.\n\nRollback and restore procedure:\n- Preconditions: node_gpu_utilization_5m < 70% for 10 minutes and p99_response_ms within SLO for 15 minutes.\n- Steps: reverse degradation stages in reverse order with 5–10 minute observation windows per step.\n  1) Remove Tenant Quarantine flag. 2) Re-enable Model Fallback to primary model. 3) Incrementally increase max_tokens back to configured value. 4) Re-enable optional tooling (rerank/long-context). 5) Clear soft_throttle.\n\nSafety and data integrity notes:\n- Never perform state-destructive operations during degradation (no KV state truncation or forced cache evictions).\n- When switching model variants, preserve model signature headers and surface a brief policy note to the tenant via X-RD-Degradation-Note so downstream integrators can detect fallback behavior.\n- Audit logs must include operator id and change request id for compliance evidence.\n\nSLO and acceptance criteria for degradation behavior:\n- Under progressive degradation, p95 latency should remain <= 1.5x baseline and errors <= 2x baseline for the degraded tenant.\n- Shared tenants should maintain 99% of baseline success rate.\n- Observability: every degradation stage change must emit an event with tags {tenant_id, stage, operator}.\n\nTesting and validation checklist (pre-production):\n1) Synthetic workload: generate 3x normal tokens/minute from a single tenant for 15 minutes.\n2) Verify soft throttle triggers and that edge rejects beyond configured rate.\n3) Validate that model fallback route returns compatible schema and that downstream QA tests pass.\n4) Run chaos test: induce node GPU saturation and confirm system moves tenants through degradation stages without state loss.\n\nConfiguration examples and snippets:\n- Rate limit policy (example YAML for Envoy/edge):\n\npolicies:\n  tenant_rate_limit:\n    type: token_bucket\n    params:\n      capacity: 1000\n      refill_tokens_per_sec: 5\n      tenant_key: \"%REQUEST_HEADER(tenant-id)%\"\n      soft_fraction: 0.8\n\n- Control-plane degradation policy (example JSON flag set):\n\n{\n  \"degradation_policy_v1\": {\n    \"stages\": [\n      {\"id\": \"soft_throttle\", \"actions\": [\"rate_reduce_0.8\"]},\n      {\"id\": \"queue_priority\", \"actions\": [\"shift_to_queue(priority=low,timeout=5s)\"]},\n      {\"id\": \"feature_reduction_1\", \"actions\": [\"disable_prefetch\",\"disable_rerank\"]},\n      {\"id\": \"feature_reduction_2\", \"actions\": [\"cap_max_tokens_512\"]},\n      {\"id\": \"model_fallback\", \"actions\": [\"route_to:redwood-llama-quant-1\"]}\n    ]\n  }\n}\n\n(Administrators: load the JSON as a policy with redwoodctl policy apply --file degradation_policy.json)\n\nOperator checklist for drill and runbook validation:\n- Ownership: oncall SRE (first responder) -> runtime team -> customer success for customer comms.\n- Communication template: short incident message stating that tenant experienced temporary degraded performance due to resource pressure, include expected restore window and a link to the support ticket.\n\nCommunication escalation template (example):\n- [Subject] Temporary Service Degradation for Tenant <tenant_name>\n- [Body] We detected sustained GPU utilization and token throughput originating from your tenant. We put you into a temporary degraded mode (rounded list of actions) to protect overall cluster health. We will restore full service after utilization stabilizes. Contact support@example.redwood.com or your account rep for questions.\n\nAudit and post-incident analysis:\n- For every degradation incident, open an incident review doc and populate: root_cause, timeline (events and stage transitions), metrics pre/post, owner decision logs, and remediation actions.\n- Required artifacts: tenant audit events export (.csv), relevant node telemetry window (1h), control-plane event log trace (trace-id).\n\nAppendix A — Example sanity table for operator thresholds:\n| Signal | Severity | Trigger | Immediate operator action | Auto-step | Notes |\n|---|---:|---|---|---|---|\n| node_gpu_utilization_5m | CRITICAL | >92% x2 minutes | Check cluster, consider autoscale | Feature reduction 1 | If whole cluster saturated, prioritize golden tenants |\n| tenant_tokens_per_minute | WARNING | >150k x3 minutes | Notify tenant owner, apply soft throttle | Soft Throttle | Tune per-customer in onboarding |\n| p99_response_ms | CRITICAL | >1200ms & error_rate_5m>0.5% | Escalate to SRE, start degrade stages | Queueing | Correlate with node metrics |\n\nAppendix B — Example observability query (Prometheus):\n- High-usage tenant candidate:\n  sum by (tenant_id) (rate(redwood_tenant_tokens_total[1m])) > 2500\n- Node saturation window:\n  max_over_time(node_gpu_utilization{job=\"runtime\"}[3m]) > 0.92\n\nAppendix C — Ownership and contacts:\n- Primary oncall: runtime-sre rotation (see roster)\n- Tier-1 support: customer-success-engagers@redwood.internal\n- Runtime team lead: Priya Kothari\n\nRevision history:\n- 2026-03-01: Created by Aisha Moreno\n- 2026-04-12: Added automated control order and CLI examples (reviewer: Tomás Reed)\n- 2026-06-10: Tuned thresholds and added rollback preconditions (reviewer: Leah Park)\n\nEnd of document.

[Tenant Key Rotation and Ephemeral Session Proxy Playbook]
Summary
This playbook describes the recommended architecture, operator procedures, and validation checks for tenant key rotation in private (VPC / on-prem) deployments using Redwood's Ephemeral Session Proxy (ESP). The goal is to provide a low-friction, auditable process that: (1) rotates tenant encryption keys and wrapping keys with minimal impact to traffic, (2) issues short-lived session credentials for runtime components, and (3) preserves forensic evidence for compliance reviews.

Scope
- Applies to private deployments (VPC and on-prem) using customer-managed KMS or HSM integrations.
- Covers rotation for: tenant-data encryption-at-rest keys, model-blob encryption keys, and service-to-service wrapping keys used by runtime proxies.
- Does NOT replace customer-specific key custody policies (customers may require additional approvals).

When to run this playbook
- Scheduled rotation cadence (recommended): every 90 days for wrapping keys, every 180 days for tenant data keys.
- Forced rotation: after key compromise, suspicious access detected, or regulatory requirement.

Owner and Roles
- Security (owner): maintains playbook, approves rotation windows, reviews audit evidence.
- Customer Success / Field Engineering: coordinates customer notifications and assist during run.
- Runtime / Operator team: executes the on-host commands, monitors latency and error rates.
- Customer (if customer-managed KMS): approves key actions in their KMS/HSM.

High-level Architecture
- Ephemeral Session Proxy (ESP): issues short-lived tokens (TTL <= 15m) to runtime components to access model blobs and tenant data stores.
- Key hierarchy: Customer Master Key (CMK) in KMS/HSM -> Wrapping Keys (rotatable by Redwood) -> Data Keys (DEKs) used to encrypt models and snapshots.
- Rotation path: CMK (if customer rotates) -> rotate wrapping key -> rewrap DEKs -> re-encrypt any cached artifacts if required.

Text diagram (logical flow)
Customer KMS/HSM (CMK) --sign/unwrap--> Redwood Key Service --wrap/rotate--> Wrapping Key vN --used to encrypt--> DEK (model, tenant DB snapshot) --cached in--> Runtime KV / Artifact store

Prerequisites
- Operator has access to the deployment control plane and the operator CLI (redwoodctl).
- KMS/HSM integration validated: key ARN/ID, IAM principals, and allowlist for Redwood service account.
- Nightly snapshot and one successful restore in the last 30 days.
- Monitoring baseline established: token issuance rate, per-request latency, 5xx error rate, and KV cache hit ratio.

Safety windows and SLOs
- Rotation should be scheduled during the agreed maintenance window (customer SLA dependent).
- Target: no more than 1.5x baseline p95 latency and <0.5% new 5xx errors attributable to rotation. If either threshold is exceeded, abort and roll back.

Key Rotation Procedure (operator runbook)
Pre-rotation validation (run in staging or canary tenant first)
1. Verify latest backups: confirm snapshot timestamp and checksum (operator CLI):
   redwoodctl snapshot list --tenant <TENANT_ID> --last 3
2. Validate KMS access and policy by performing a test encrypt/decrypt with current credentials:
   aws kms encrypt --key-id <CMK> --plaintext test-string | aws kms decrypt --ciphertext-blob fileb://-
3. Ensure all runtime nodes report healthy in the runtime dashboard and token-issuing rate within 10% of baseline.

Create a rotation plan and ticket
1. Open rotation ticket with the following fields: tenant, rotation type (wrapping|data|full), maintenance window, rollback criteria, and contact list.
2. Notify customer contacts (if applicable) and oncall with an expected timeline.

Rotation steps (safe path)
1. Create new wrapping key (WrKey vN+1) in the KMS/HSM or request Redwood-managed wrap key. Record new key id (WR_KEY_ID).
2. In a canary tenant: rewrap DEKs using WrKey vN+1 (non-destructive):
   - For each DEK: fetch encrypted_DEK_vN -> call KMS rewrap operation -> store encrypted_DEK_vN+1 as pending.
   Example (pseudocode):
   for dek in list_deks(tenant):
     dek_plain = kms.unwrap(encrypted_dek_vN, WRAP_KEY_ID=vN)
     encrypted_dek_vNplus1 = kms.wrap(dek_plain, WR_KEY_ID=vNplus1)
     store_pending_rewrap(dek_id, encrypted_dek_vNplus1)
3. Update ESP to read pending rewrapped DEKs (ESP supports atomic dual-key read mode).
4. Promote pending DEKs to active one-by-one and validate service operations:
   - Warm caches and run synthetic inference/embedding traffic at 10% of normal load.
   - Observe latency/error SLOs for 15 minutes.
5. If canary is successful, roll forward to remaining tenants in parallel groups of N (N depends on operator capacity).

Full rotation (when DEK re-encryption required)
- For very sensitive key changes or algorithm changes requiring full re-encryption: stage data re-encryption to an offline node or a rolling background job that re-encrypts blobs while leaving read path intact using dual-key strategy. See "Re-encryption background job" section below.

Re-encryption background job (recommendations)
- Job runs at low priority and honors the runtime backpressure API.
- Maintain a checkpoint table: blob_id -> last_reencrypted_at -> status.
- Throttle concurrent re-encryption workers to keep p95 latency < 1.5x baseline.

Rollback plan
- Abort promotion and revert ESP to read WrKey vN only.
- Re-point runtime processes to encrypted_DEK_vN copies (prior active).
- If datastore corruption is suspected, restore the most recent validated snapshot and reapply the key state.

Validation checks and evidence to collect
- Key operations log (KMS audit): create, rewrap, decrypt/unwrap calls during rotation window.
- ESP issuance events: token_id, issued_at, ttl, subject (service/host).
- Runtime error traces filtered by operation type that occurred within rotation window.
- Snapshot of DEK metadata (hashes) pre and post rotation for tamper evidence.

Operational telemetry (what to monitor)
- Token issuance rate and failure rate (metric: esp.token.issue_count, esp.token.fail_count)
- KMS error rate (kms.api.errors) and latency (kms.api.p95)
- Runtime 5xxs and p95 latency per tenant
- Re-encryption worker throughput and backlog length

Commands and examples
- Create a new wrapping key (example for AWS KMS):
  aws kms create-key --description "Redwood tenant wrapping key" --tags TagKey=tenant,TagValue=<TENANT_ID>
  aws kms create-alias --target-key-id <KEY_ID> --alias-name alias/redwood/wrap/<TENANT_ID>/v2

- Sample rewrap (pseudocode using redwoodctl):
  redwoodctl keys rewrap --tenant <TENANT_ID> --from-key alias/redwood/wrap/<TENANT_ID>/v1 --to-key alias/redwood/wrap/<TENANT_ID>/v2 --dry-run

Post-rotation verification (15–60 minutes after promotion)
1. Run synthetic traffic against primary tenant endpoints and validate correct responses with golden prompt set.
2. Confirm no increase in token-related failures: esp.token.fail_count delta < 0.25% absolute.
3. Confirm KMS 5xxs returned to baseline and that total KMS calls are within expected inflation factor (<=1.1x).
4. Archive rotation evidence: KMS logs, ESP token issuance snapshot, operator runbook steps in ticketing system.

Ephemeral Session Proxy (ESP) details
- ESP issues short-lived JWTs signed with an internal service key and includes key-version metadata (wrap_ver) so the runtime can request the correct DEK variant.
- Token TTL default: 900s (15m), maximum 1800s if customer approves.
- ESP supports a dual-key read mode where it returns both DEK variants under a single fetch API (used during atomic promotion).

Security considerations and hardening
- Ensure ESP service account has least privilege in KMS: only ReEncrypt/Decrypt/Wrap operations for the allowed keys.
- Use HSM-backed CMKs for customers with FIPS/PCI requirements.
- Rotate internal signing keys for ESP on a separate cadence (recommended 180 days).
- Enforce operator two-person approval for production wrap key creation when tenant sensitivity level is "high".

Audit & compliance artifacts
- Rotation ticket with timestamps and operator signatures.
- Exported KMS audit logs for the rotation window.
- Checksum manifest of DEK metadata before and after rotation.

Edge cases and troubleshooting
- If rewrap calls start failing with throttling (ThrottlingException): backoff and retry with jitter, and reduce parallelism.
- If runtime nodes begin failing to fetch DEKs after promotion: revert ESP to vN-only reads and escalate to oncall.
- If partial promotion leaves mixed key states across replicas: run recovery script to re-sync DEK pointer map from the authoritative metadata store.

Dry-run and canary recommendations
- Always run --dry-run for the rewrap operation to collect the list of affected DEKs and approximate runtime impact.
- Canary plan: select a low-traffic tenant with similar artifact volume and run full rotation. Document differences in performance.

Operator checklists (short)
- Pre-check: backups verified, KMS test pass, monitoring baseline captured.
- Canary: rewrap pending -> enable dual-key reads -> promote -> validate.
- Bulk: group rollouts, promote, validate, archive evidence.

Related runbooks and links
- Third-party KMS/HSM integration requirements (internal): /confluence/eng-private-deployments/customer-requirements-library/thirdparty-kms-hsm-integration-requirements-2026
- Airgapped KMS rotation playbook: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/onprem-packaging/airgapped-kms-hsm-offline-rotation-and-cert-renewal-playbook-2026

Appendix A — JSON example: pending rewrap manifest
{ "tenant_id": "tenant-123", "deks": [ {"id": "dek-01", "active_wrap": "v1", "pending_wrap": "v2", "blob_count": "42"}, {"id": "dek-02", "active_wrap": "v1", "pending_wrap": "v2", "blob_count": "7"} ], "created_at": "2026-02-20T01:23:45Z", "operator": "aisha.mensah@redwood.ai" }

Appendix B — Safe automation knobs (operators should expose these flags)
- --max-parallel-rewrap=N (default 4)
- --worker-backoff-ms=2000
- --dry-run (no writes, produce manifest)
- --throttle-to-restore-baseline (true|false)

[Burst-aware rolling batcher with KV snapshotting and memory reclamation]
description:
Problem statement: Mixed prompt/response workloads produce bursts of short, chatty turns interleaved with long generation requests. Existing continuous batcher strategies either keep KV residency aggressively (causing GPU memory pressure) or evict too eagerly (causing expensive KV rebuilds during bursts). This ticket implements a burst-aware rolling batching layer that coordinates: 1) short-window burst detection, 2) incremental KV snapshotting to enable fast rehydration of recently used KV slices, and 3) opportunistic memory reclamation (GPU slab compaction + async eviction) to reduce tail memory fragmentation during steady-state long generations. Goals: reduce out-of-memory incidents on 80GB GPUs under mixed traffic, lower p95 latency for bursty short-turns, and limit extra token-cost from rebuilding KV caches. Deliverables: code changes in continuous-batcher, a KV snapshot/restore library, bench harness, perf dashboards, and rollback/feature-flag gating for runtime rollout.

acceptance_criteria:
New rolling-batcher component is feature-flagged behind runtime flag 'burst_rolling_v1'
Under combined synthetic workload (50% short-turns <16 tokens, 50% long-gen average 1024 tokens) p95 latency of short-turns improves by >= 15% vs baseline with same token throughput
GPU memory fragmentation metric (per-GPU free-slab ratio) improves by >= 20% during mixed workloads compared to baseline
KV rehydration time measured from snapshot is < 12ms for 90% of hot slices
No increase in token-cost per request > 3% on average across bench suite
Automated e2e perf job added to CI (bench: mixed-dialogue-burst) that fails if p99 latency regresses > 10%
Design doc and migration guide published, and early canary rollout executed in 2 clusters with rollback plan validated

[Probabilistic admission controller and token-density KV compaction for mixed-turn continuous batching]
description:
Problem: Mixed prompt/response workloads (short prompts followed by long generated responses, or vice versa) cause inefficient slot utilization in the continuous batcher and lead to KV cache pressure and GPU memory fragmentation. This ticket experiments with a probabilistic admission controller that accepts or delays incoming requests based on a lightweight token-density estimate and a length-population model, combined with a token-density-driven KV compaction policy that aggressively compacts low-utility KV entries to reclaim GPU slab space without hurting hit-rate for hot prefixes. Goal: reduce tail latency for short critical requests, improve overall throughput for long responses, and decrease out-of-memory incidents on medium-sized V100/A100 nodes.

success_criteria:
10-20% reduction in 99th percentile latency for short-turn requests under mixed traffic
5-10% improvement in average token throughput on 8xA100 workers during long-response steady-state
reduction in KV-induced OOM events to zero in canary cluster

approach:
Admission controller: probabilistic admission with tunable base delay. For each incoming request we compute a token-density score = expected_output_tokens / (expected_context_tokens + 1). Use a short moving window of observed paired request-response lengths to estimate distribution per route.
If token-density > high_threshold, admit immediately to favor high-throughput long responses. If token-density < low_threshold and current slot occupancy > soft_target, probabilistically delay admission by sampling from an exponential backoff distribution scaled to slot pressure.
Soft quotas: assign soft KV reservation budgets per slot cohort (short, medium, long) rather than hard static reservations to prevent long requests starving short-turn throughput.
KV compaction: maintain per-key utility score (recency * response-length-weighted-hit-rate). Periodically compact keys below a dynamic utility percentile. Compaction is token-density-aware: more aggressive compaction during high token-density phases.
GPU memory management: perform defragmentation during low-util windows via coordinated slab repacking triggered when free contiguous memory falls below watermark. Ensure repacking is interruptible and has an abort path if latency SLOs tighten.
Simulation: run discrete-event simulation using recorded traffic traces from 'multi-turn-mix-2026-q1' to validate tuning knobs before canary.
Gradual rollout: feature flag behind rollout with canary on 5% of traffic -> 20% -> 50% -> full, with automated rollback if tail latency regresses >5% or OOMs occur.

experiments_and_results:
2026-02-25: Microbench on 4xA100 emulated mixed traffic (40% short prompts producing short responses, 60% short prompts with long responses). Baseline: 99p short latency=210ms. After admission controller: 99p short latency=175ms (-17%). Throughput unchanged within noise.
2026-03-01: KV compaction stress test on 8xV100 nodes with synthetic churn. Baseline kv-residency=78% of slab. After compaction policy: kv-residency=61%, observed small drop in cache-hit for very long prefixes (2.3% absolute), but end-to-end token cost decreased 8%.
2026-03-05: Combined canary on prod-west-canary (5%). Observed 12% reduction in short-request tail latency, 6% throughput increase for long-response flows, zero OOMs during 72h test. One regression: route /agent-stream-verbose saw 3% increase in median latency due to compaction causing KV-prefetch misses; mitigated by raising utility floor for that route.
Notes: simulation correlated with prod canary on short-tail improvements but underestimated compaction impact on low-frequency long prefixes.

tradeoffs_and_risks:
Probabilistic delays can increase perceived latency for some short requests if thresholds mis-calibrated — mitigate with strict SLO guardrails for high-priority routes.
Aggressive KV compaction reduces memory pressure but risks increased recomputation when rare prefixes are requested; mitigated via per-route utility floors and detection of low-frequency heavy hitters.
GPU repacking is intrusive and may transiently increase latency; schedule during low-load windows and ensure abort semantics.
Feature complexity increases operational surface; require additional observability (per-cohort admission rates, compaction churn, slab fragmentation metrics).

implementation_notes:
Admission controller implemented as lightweight pre-batcher hook; target CPU overhead < 0.5% of request path.
Token-density estimation uses exponential moving average with 30s half-life per route to adapt quickly to diurnal shifts.
Utility scoring stored as compact 32-bit floats in host-side metadata to avoid additional GPU allocations.
Compaction runs as background bounded tasks with backpressure to avoid saturating PCIe during repack.
Added metric labels: batcher_cohort, admission_action {admit, delay, reject}, kv_compaction_pass_id, slab_fragmentation_pct.
