[Block coalescing checkpointing and fine-grained GPU OOB eviction]
description:
Goal: Implement a paged/blocked KV cache implementation that reduces GPU OOMs and tail latency by (1) coalescing small KV fragments into block-aligned checkpointable units, (2) enabling low-latency out-of-band (OOB) evictions under memory pressure, and (3) integrating with continuous batching so batch reservation and residency behave predictably.

proposal_summary:
Introduce a block descriptor layer that maps variable-length KV entries onto fixed-size slab blocks (default 256KB). Maintain a compact residency bitmap and a host-backed checkpoint store for evicted blocks. Add an asynchronous OOB eviction path that runs at <1ms decision latency when free memory falls below a hysteresis threshold. Coordinate block-level locks with the serving runtime to avoid stalls during batch hot-paths.

implementation_details:
Data structures: BlockDescriptor[] with fields (block_id, slot_count, last_access_epoch, bucket_fingerprint) stored in a contiguous host/GPU-resident metadata buffer. ResidencyBitmap is a compact bitset replicated between host and device; GPU can query a small device-local cache of hot bitmaps. Checkpointing: Evicted blocks are serialized into a host pinned checkpoint ring that supports batched async DMA uploads/downloads. Eviction policy: watermarks (80%/65%) with per-model resident budgets and token-affinity scoring. OOB eviction path: fast heuristic that selects victim blocks based on stale epochs and low token-affinity, attempts to write back to host checkpoint ring using pre-allocated pinned buffers, then marks device pages free. Integration with continuous batching: batches allocate a soft reservation from model budget; blocks that are under active reservation are exempt from OOB eviction for the life of the batch. On mem pressure, continuous batching controller can reduce batch size or fallback to compatible smaller quantized model variant. Telemetry: track block hit-rate, eviction latency, checkpoint roundtrip time, OOM occurrences, and the number of batches throttled due to memory. APIs: expose per-model resident_budget and eviction_mode (eager|lazy|oob-only), and a /debug endpoint to snapshot residency and checkpoint ring state.

safety_and_consistency:
Atomicity: Block eviction marks go through a 2-phase commit: (1) mark 'evicting' in metadata, (2) flush KV payload to host checkpoint ring, (3) commit 'evicted' and free device pages. Crash recovery replays pending checkpoint entries at startup. Fallback: If checkpoint ring is saturated, eviction backs off and triggers runtime-level degradation (batch size reduction and model fallback). Rollback: On failed checkpoint writes, the block remains pinned and we raise a soft OOM alarm for operator intervention.

tests_and_validation:
Microbenchmarks: synthetic hotset with variable fragment sizes to verify coalescing improves GPU-residency efficiency. End-to-end: run continuous-batching workload traces (prod-sampled) with and without OOB eviction, measure 99th latency, per-token cost, and OOM rate. Chaos: force DMA stalls and verify eviction backoff triggers safe fallback. Load tests: per-model stress to validate residency budgets and cross-model isolation.

rollout_plan:
Feature-gated rollout. Stage 1: internal canary on staging with low-traffic models. Stage 2: opt-in on dedicated clusters for customers testing private deployment. Stage 3: default enabled for runtime-1.21 with telemetry gating and an on-call runbook. Provide 'eviction=off' knob for immediate opt-out.

success_metrics:
Reduce device-side OOMs by >=90% on long-tail workloads, improve resident block utilization by 20% (fewer small fragment overheads), keep 99th-percentile generation latency increase <5% compared to baseline, and reduce per-token device memory cost by >10% for oversubscribed clusters.

risks_and_mitigation:
Risk: Checkpoint ring saturation leading to stalls. Mitigation: dynamic ring sizing and immediate fallback to smaller batch / model variant; operator alerts. Risk: Incorrect block coalescing causing increased read amplification. Mitigation: hybrid strategy that limits coalescing depth for high-turnover keys and adds sampling-based heuristics. Risk: GPU metadata sync overhead. Mitigation: device-local hot-bitmap caching and asynchronous diff propagation.

[KV cache healing via generational reservoirs and GPU-aware scavenger]
description:
Background: Continuous batching and long-lived chat sessions create highly variable KV cache object size distributions. Small frequent updates (token-level KV writes) intermix with large prefix caches, producing fragmentation in GPU-backed allocations. Existing slab and chunked allocators handle steady-state well but show slow drift in free space patterns, causing out-of-memory tail events and elevated eviction churn.

problem_statement:
Design and implement an allocation and background reclamation strategy that reduces KV cache fragmentation without blocking hot inference paths and without degrading continuous-batching latency SLOs. The solution must be GPU-memory-aware, coordinate with batching/fence semantics, and be safe for live rollouts on Dedicated clusters.

goals:
Decrease fragmentation-driven OOMs by >= 40% in mixed short/long sequence workloads
Ensure background healing work never adds >1ms median per-request latency during normal traffic
Preserve throughput with <3% throughput regression under 95th percentile load profiles
Integrate with batching fences so reclaim only proceeds when KV references are safe

non_goals:
Full rewrite of allocator strategies (keep existing slab/chunk infrastructure)
Moving KV entries between GPUs — cross-device migration is out of scope

acceptance_criteria:
Load test: mixed chat + long-context benchmark shows fragmentation metric drop >=40% vs baseline (metric: free-range-count / total-free-memory)
Continuous-batching 95th percentile latency during healing <= baseline + 1ms
No correctness regressions on unit/e2e KV stress tests (coverage for read-after-write and concurrent eviction)
Feature gated behind runtime flag and rolloutable via canary

design_summary:
Introduce a generational reservoir model: new allocations are taken from a 'young' micro-pool with tight packing for small objects; objects surviving X compact cycles are promoted to a 'stable' pool optimized for larger allocations. A GPU-aware scavenger thread asynchronously compacts micro-gaps within a single GPU memory region by relocating only short-lived objects within that region using a two-phase fence and pointer-swap protocol to avoid global stops. We use per-region allocation bitmaps and hole-lists to guide compaction targets and a lightweight reservation API for continuous batching (fence-based reservations prevent reclamation of KV entries referenced by in-flight batches).

implementation_notes:
Add per-GPU region metadata: age_counters, hole_bitmap, occupancy_histogram (low-dim) stored in host pinned memory for cheap readouts
Young reservoir: fixed-size micro-blocks (32B/64B/128B pools) to reduce internal fragmentation for token-level KVs
Promotion policy: sampled survivor count; default promote after 3 scavenger passes; tunable via runtime flags
Scavenger operation: runs on a dedicated CPU core per GPU, estimates cost budget per second and only compacts if budget available; uses CUDA memcpy async to relocate within same device
Fence/reservation API: batching layer registers KV references at request start; scavenger checks reservation epoch before relocating; pointer-swap uses atomic CAS on 64-bit descriptor to avoid-lock moves
Avoid expensive full object moves for large values: large KV entries are left in stable pool and reclaimed via existing eviction paths
Telemetry: expose fragmentation_ratio, promoted_bytes, compaction_operations, reservation_conflicts via /metrics and Console dashboards

testing_plan:
Unit tests for reservation API and CAS-based pointer swap
Simulator test that injects mixed object lifespan distributions and validates no stale reads post-compaction
Load tests on dev-cluster with continuous-batching enabled and 8x A100 profile: baseline vs healed allocator
Safety tests: induce failures in mid-copy (GPU memcpy aborted) and verify roll-back path is safe and observable

migration_plan:
Implement feature behind runtime flag runtime.kv.healing.enabled=false by default
Roll out to canary fleet (5%) with aggressive telemetry, enable automatic rollback on error budget breaches
Gradually increase to 25%, 50%, 100% with 24h observation windows and custom dashboards

rollout_steps:
Design review + perf targets locked (done)
Merge gated feature branch + integration tests (PR link below)
Deploy canary, monitor frag/latency/oom signals
Tweak promotion thresholds and scavenger budget based on telemetry
Full rollout and deprecation of hotfix workaround code

fragmentation_ratio (free-range-count / total-free-memory)
compaction_ops_per_minute
median request latency with healing on/off
OOM incidents per-week
reservation_conflict_count

risks_and_mitigation:
Risk: scavenger steals CPU and degrades latency — mitigate by strict CPU budget and backoff when latency signals increase
Risk: mid-copy GPU memcpy failure could corrupt KV pointers — mitigate with two-phase commit and verification CRC; fall back to mark-and-evict pattern
Risk: promotion mis-tuning causes thrash — add conservative defaults and auto-rate-limiter for promotions

[Dynamic pressure scaler and GPU slot reclamation for sustained high-QPS]
description:
Reduce P95 latency regressions and out-of-memory incidents during sustained high QPS by introducing a Dynamic Pressure Scaler (DPS) and a GPU slot reclamation mechanism. This ticket designs and implements admission controls, probabilistic micro-batch shedding, NVMe spill for cold KV pages, and safe GPU slab compaction to keep latency SLOs while maximizing throughput and utilization.

background:
We've observed recurring P95 spikes and occasional OOMs when sustained QPS exceeds the inferred capacity for certain model-VM combinations. Existing micro-batch admission is static and reacts too late; KV cache eviction is LRU-only and moves cold data straight to host memory causing sudden GPU page faults; slab allocator can't compact safely during steady-state. This work is intended to act before tail-latency worsens and avoid hard capacity failures.

goals:
Maintain p95 latency <= 350ms at target sustained QPS (per model profile)
Avoid GPU OOMs during 30-minute sustained load tests at 1.5x expected bursting traffic
Keep throughput reduction below 7% compared to baseline under normal load
Provide observable metrics and knobs to tune DPS for customer-specific SLAs

acceptance_criteria:
DPS runs in runtime with config flags and exposes headroom and admission rates
Evidence from perfbench: p95 <= 350ms and no OOMs for 30-minute 1.5x sustained QPS test
KV cold pages spill to NVMe with bounded spill latency; end-to-end token latency impact < 10% for affected requests
Canary rollout plan documented and automated via console rollout config
Unit + integration tests and chaos test scenarios added to CI

decisions:
Use a hybrid headroom estimator: EWMA of free_gpu_memory_fraction + weighted p95 latency margin to compute available microbatch slots
Admission controller will use probabilistic shedding (token-aware random drop) rather than pure max-queue-length to avoid bias against long requests
KV cache eviction will tier: GPU -> host hot-cache -> NVMe spill. NVMe page metadata kept lightweight to avoid controller lock contention.
GPU slab compaction will be asynchronous and scheduled during detected low-utilization windows; a pre-compaction guard prevents compaction if active_headroom < 1.2x target

tradeoffs:
Probabilistic shedding may increase variance for a small fraction of requests but reduces global tail risk compared to heavy-handed queue trimming
NVMe spill adds read latency for cold requests; we accept a small hit for cold paths to preserve hot-path latency and avoid OOMs
Async slab compaction complicates memory accounting and requires conservative thresholds to avoid interfering with hot path. This increases implementation complexity but reduces forced evictions.

progress_updates:
2026-03-01: Ticket created after postmortem for incident #INC-2026-02-17. Assigned to Owen.
2026-03-03: Prototype DPS estimator implemented in a feature branch; initial headroom signal derived from 10s EWMA of free_memory_fraction.
2026-03-05: Integration test added for probabilistic admission with synthetic token-length distribution; observed 4% throughput drop with 60% reduction in long-tail latency.
2026-03-07: NVMe spill shim merged behind feature flag; measured 18ms median spill read plus 80ms tail on cold reads — acceptable for cold paths with cache warming strategy.
2026-03-09: First canary harness (5% traffic) run; no OOMs observed, p95 improved from 520ms -> 320ms for the targeted model at peak load. Some flaky failures around compaction task scheduling remain.

test_plan:
Unit tests for headroom estimator edge cases (division by zero, rapid free_memory changes)
Simulated workload: mixed short(<=8 tokens) / long(>256 tokens) requests with realistic inter-arrival times; run 30m at 1.5x expected QPS
Chaos test: kill one GPU worker node while canary is active to validate fallback and KV spill recovery
A/B perfbench against baseline with metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, OOM count, GPU memory fragmentation
Regression test in CI that runs lightweight DPS smoke scenario on PRs

rollout_plan:
Feature behind runtime flag and console toggle
Canary 1: 2% traffic for 24h with enhanced logging
Canary 2: 10% traffic for 48h if no regressions
Canary 3: 50% for 72h, monitor p95, OOMs, KV spill rates
Full ramp to 100% after two green canaries and post-rollout review

notes:
Follow-up ticket will explore dynamic quantization triggers paired with DPS to reclaim memory during extreme load
Coordinate with Dedicated infra for autoscaler interplay; autoscaler may report capacity that conflicts with DPS heuristics — add a sync hook in a follow-up
Design doc contains an appendix with command-line debugging utilities to inspect headroom signals in production

[09:42] Priya: We're also interested in how Redwood handles retraining/feedback loops. If our agents use model-assisted labeling, is that data retained?

[10:10] Sarah: A technical edge case — we do cross-border umbrella entities, where a EU subsidiary's logs are ingested by a central SIEM in the US for analytics. That is a no for some customers. Can Redwood route logs separately per tenant?

[10:42] Priya: I heard about model-variant fallbacks — if primary model is temporarily unavailable and you fallback to a cheaper or external model, does data route change? This is a risk for residency.
[10:53] Mateo: We have routing policies. You can configure strict no-fallback outside region; fallback is an opt-in policy that can be region-aware. We'll make sure rollback/fallback policies are explicit in the rollout config.

[11:10] Daniel: Anything else from our side before we go deeper?
[11:15] Priya: Just that whatever you send, we need artifact-level evidence for the security review. SOC2 plus deployment diagrams plus PII redaction acceptance tests.
[11:24] Lena: Understood. We'll send the pack and propose dates for the SE deep dive. Mateo, can you run the draft keystore and log routing deck?
[11:31] Mateo: Yup, I'll prepare that and include latency bench numbers for KMS unwrap, plus a sample retention config.

[Keystore residency & ops probe with Hollis Financial (data residency discovery)]
summary:
Discovery focused on keystore residency, HSM options, logging restrictions and legal hold for a financial-services deployment. Customer evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private; primary concerns are key control, audit evidence, cross-border replication, and minimizing log surface for regulated PII.

transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2026-10-21 | Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 47m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE); Liam Ortiz (Redwood SE); Sanjay Patel (Head Cloud Ops - Hollis); Erin McClellan (CISO - Hollis); Diego Ramos (Product); Priya Singh (Compliance)

Summary: Quick onboarding discovery to understand Hollis constraints around encryption keys, keystore residency, and what logging evidence Redwood can provide for auditors. Customer is a regulated fintech; they want to know whether Redwood Hosted can meet their keystore residency needs or if Dedicated/Private is required.

Shared artifacts: https://redwood.example.com/security-evidence (soc2/iso/keystore-overview), pricing sheet (link: https://redwood.example.com/pricing/hyperscale), private deployment diagram (to be shared).

Action items (recap in call): see metadata.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, and with me is Liam, our solutions engineer. Quick round intro?
[00:10] Sanjay: Sanjay here, head of cloud ops at Hollis, thanks for making time.
[00:14] Erin: Erin, CISO. We're primarily here to understand key control and what kind of audit evidence we can get out of Redwood.
[00:18] Diego: Diego, product - I'll be running the POC if we get there.
[00:22] Liam: Great - hi all. To frame the call: we want to map your requirements to the three hosting modes - Hosted API, Dedicated, and Private - and call out keystore and logging implications.
[00:30] Priya: Quick thing: Hollis needs to make sure KMS keys never leave EU control and audit logs must not include full PII. Also legal hold for investigations - retention across regions is a must.
[00:42] Maya: Understood. Maybe start with keystore - are you thinking customer-managed keys in an HSM, or is a cloud-KMS OK if we can restrict locations?
[00:50] Erin: Preference is customer-managed HSM. We need proof of key residency and separation - auditors want to see key control and no Redwood access.
[00:58] Liam: Right - so for Redwood Hosted we offer envelope encryption where customer KMS can be used in certain regions, but there are limits: some model operations (cache encryption/kv cache) may still store ephemeral state on Redwood-managed instances. For true key isolation and no Redwood control over keys, Dedicated or Private is usually the path.
[01:16] Sanjay: When you say "ephemeral state," do you mean anything persistent that could contain PII?
[01:20] Liam: Good question. The runtime writes token metadata and KV cache shards; persistent logs are configurable. We can redact or avoid writing user inputs to logs, but KV cache for performance can include prefixes derived from prompts - that's where we need to discuss minimization.
[01:01] Maya: (laughs) sorry, timestamp drift. To continue: on Hosted we can configure logging minimization and pseudonymization, but auditor comfort varies.
[01:40] Priya: Are you able to run with a customer HSM in our VPC? That's what our legal and risk teams ask for.
[01:47] Liam: For Private deployments yes, you can run an HSM in your network and Redwood's control plane only manages orchestration - keys never leave. For Dedicated, we can do a bring-your-key (BYOK) model where the key is in a cloud KMS with restricted access and we support HSM-backed keys in some regions. There are tradeoffs on autoscaling and maintenance windows.
[02:06] Erin: We need to know: if we go Dedicated and you support HSM-backed keys in the cloud provider, do auditors see evidence that Redwood doesn't have private key material?
[02:16] Liam: We can provide key access logs, KMS audit trails, and a cryptographic boundary description. For Private + customer-managed HSM the material never lands on Redwood controllers. For cloud-KMS we can show KMS CMEK logs showing who invoked Decrypt APIs, timestamps, and principal ids.
[02:30] Sanjay: What about cross-border replication? We operate in both EU and US, but regulated data must remain EU-only for some products.
[02:38] Maya: We support region pinning and model routing. For Hosted we have region options but some model variants are only in certain regions; for strict EU residency we often recommend Dedicated in an EU-only account or Private.
[02:52] Diego: Is there an on-prem pattern where we keep inference inside our data center and Redwood provides orchestration?
[02:58] Liam: Yes - Private includes an on-prem package with a customer-side control plane option. That lets you keep inference and all logs on-prem. The control plane still needs connectivity for updates unless you choose the fully air-gapped package.
[03:14] Priya: Logging: our auditors require that full request payloads are not stored in long-term logs. Can Redwood redact request bodies and only keep metrics?
[03:23] Liam: We have log redaction and sampling. You can configure: no request payloads stored, token-only metrics, and structured telemetry that omits user text. But note: certain debugging modes will capture clipped inputs — those are opt-in.
[03:36] Erin: We also need legal hold; if regulators ask for historical data, how does Redwood handle preservation for a given tenant without exposing other tenants?
[03:45] Maya: For Dedicated/Private we can isolate tenant logs and provide export mechanisms per-tenant. For Hosted we have logical separation and access controls but the underlying storage is multi-tenant; we can provide per-tenant exports and scoped audit logs as evidence.
[03:59] Sanjay: How about redaction quality? We tried a vendor who failed to remove account numbers reliably and that caused a big problem.
[04:07] Liam: Understandable. Our recommended approach is defense-in-depth: client-side masking for PII, plus server-side redaction, and schema-based constraints. For PII that needs to be absolutely never seen by Redwood, encrypt/pseudonymize before calling the model, or run Private on-prem.
[04:25] Diego: Does Redwood support tokenization libraries we can use pre-call?
[04:29] Maya: We have a reference library and patterns in our docs; we'll share the repo link. Also Redwood Optimize can suggest caching/quantization settings that reduce the need to send raw data in many flows.
[04:40] Priya: On auditors: they want to see SOC2 and ISO evidence, and detailed subprocessors list. Can you share that now?
[04:46] Maya: Yes - link in the shared artifacts; we'll also attach a subprocessors CSV in the follow-up.
[04:52] Erin: Another question - model fallbacks and graceful degradation: will logs or traces include prompts when you fallback to a smaller model?
[04:58] Liam: Fallback events are logged. We can redact prompt text and only log model ids, error codes, and token counts. If you prefer no prompt text at all, that's configurable but reduces debug surface.
[05:12] Sanjay: For the POC we'd like to measure KV cache lookup latency and the cost hit of using an HSM vs KMS. Can you run a benchmark with our sample dataset?
[05:20] Liam: Yes, we'll scope a POC. Typical plan: 1) we run KV-cache latency tests on your sample, 2) measure end-to-end RTT using your network egress profile, 3) compare KEK (key-encryption-key) flow added latency for HSM calls. We'll need a target SLA from you to size Dedicated pools if that's the route.
[05:40] Diego: Our target is 150ms p95 for API calls for our credit-check workflow.
[05:45] Liam: Noted. For that SLA we often recommend Dedicated capacity with optimized GPU types and continuous batching; Hosted can get close depending on region and workload. Private/on-prem gives most control but requires ops overhead.
[05:58] Erin: A compliance nuance: we have a subset of data that must be onshore and excluded from backups that replicate to third-country regions. How granular can retention rules be?
[06:07] Maya: We support per-tenant retention policies and route-by-policy. In Dedicated/Private you can set storage locations and disable cross-region replication for specific datasets. Hosted supports route tags and dataset-scoped residency but some low-level backups may still cross regions unless you choose an EU-only Dedicated offering.
[06:25] Priya: Can you produce a diagram showing the keystore flow with calls to KMS/HSM, what is encrypted at rest, and where the ephemeral caches live? Auditors ask for that.
[06:34] Liam: Absolutely — Liam: I'll produce a detailed diagram showing call flows, crypto boundaries, and log redaction points. We'll also annotate which artifacts we can provide as auditor evidence (KMS audit trails, application logs, retention policies).
[06:49] Sanjay: Any third-party subprocessors involved in your runtime? For Hosted we need to map that out for regulators.
[06:55] Maya: We have a subprocessors list; common ones are cloud infra providers, telemetry vendors for SaaS metrics, and our CDN. We'll include versions and contract scopes.
[07:06] Erin: One more - SSO and RBAC: we need SCIM and SAML for provisioning and fine-grained roles so only our security team can request exports.
[07:14] Maya: We support SAML, SCIM, and RBAC with auditing. For Dedicated/Private we can integrate with your IdP directly and sync groups to cluster roles.
[07:24] Diego: If we decide on Private, what is the rough timeline for on-prem provisioning?
[07:29] Liam: For on-prem Private it's typically 6-10 weeks depending on air-gap needs and HSM installation. Dedicated in a single region can be done in 3-4 weeks once contracts are signed. Hosted is immediate.
[07:44] Priya: Cost tradeoffs - HSM is expensive per-op. How do you recommend minimizing HSM calls?
[07:50] Liam: Use hybrid: wrap long-lived DEKs (data encryption keys) with HSM-backed KEKs and cache DEKs in memory with limited TTL. That way runtime does fewer HSM unwraps. We'll show concrete TTL parameters during the POC benchmarking.
[08:06] Sanjay: What about legal hold exports - can we export per-tenant logs without a full backup restore?
[08:11] Maya: Yes; Dedicated/Private support tenant-scoped exports. For Hosted we have APIs to request scoped exports; the process includes verification steps. We can produce attestations of exported datasets for auditors.
[08:25] Erin: Any gotchas with data subject requests (DSR) and deletion? If a user requests deletion, how do you guarantee removal from caches and backups?
[08:34] Liam: We document deletion paths: 1) remove live records, 2) schedule purge of caches (we provide TTL and explicit purge API), 3) backups are on retention cycles but we can perform targeted logical deletes and document the remediation steps. For immutable backups there may be retention windows; we include that in retention policies and can provide a legal justification log.
[08:58] Diego: We're also comparing a competitor who does per-call client-side encryption; how would that affect model features like streaming and tool-calling?
[09:06] Liam: Client-side encryption preserves strong confidentiality but limits model features because the model can't access raw content for tool calls or structured extraction. For streaming you can still stream tokens, but you'd need to decrypt in your environment for post-processing. It's a tradeoff.
[09:22] Maya: To wrap up, we recommend first steps: share your data flow and regulatory list (customer), Redwood will share security evidence and a Private/Dedicated diagram (Redwood), then we'll scope a POC to run KV-cache latency and HSM impact.
[09:36] Priya: Sounds good. Any questions from our side?
[09:39] Sanjay: Not at the moment.
[09:41] Erin: No. Please include an FAQ about what will appear in logs when running in Dedicated vs Hosted.
[09:48] Maya: Will do - we'll include a log-surface FAQ.
[09:52] Diego: Thanks everyone.
[09:54] Maya: Thanks folks — next steps in the calendar invite.

Call end.

Recap (emailed): 1) Redwood to share SOC2/ISO evidence and subprocessors CSV; 2) Redwood SE to deliver keystore flow diagram and POC plan; 3) Customer to send data flow and regulated entity list.


[Security review: logging + retention (Redwood Private)]
summary:
NorthBridge Financial reviewed Redwood Private logging behavior, retention defaults, and the split between audit logs and operational logs. Customer requirements emphasized: no prompt/response logging by default, deterministic redaction, export to Splunk HEC in VPC and in an on-prem/air-gapped environment via a forward proxy, and customer-owned retention controls. Redwood clarified: structured operational logs are emitted from control plane + data plane; payload logging is disabled by default; tenant identifiers are hashed; audit logs are separate from operational logs and intended for security-relevant events (auth, config changes, admin actions). Export options discussed included Splunk HEC and Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, with OTLP as an optional path depending on customer tooling. Next steps included sharing a field-level log schema and a retention/redaction guidance doc, plus confirming whether NorthBridge requires immutable audit log storage and minimum retention targets.

topics:
Operational logs vs audit logs (purpose, content, separation)
Default retention and customer-controlled retention settings
Redaction / PII handling and payload logging defaults
Log export targets: Splunk HEC, Elastic/OpenSearch, Loki, OTLP
Export controls (TLS, proxies, endpoint allowlists, air-gapped constraints)
Support access boundaries and incident troubleshooting expectations

questions:
Do Redwood components ever log prompts/responses or headers by default, and can customers enforce that at policy level?
What identifiers appear in logs (tenant, user, request_id) and are they pseudonymized?
Can audit logs be made immutable / WORM and exported separately from operational logs?

transcript:
Meeting: Security review: logging + retention (Redwood Private)
Date: 2025-07-02
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 55 min
Attendees:
- Redwood Inference: Markus Klein, Colin O'Donnell, Naomi Feldman, Marcus Lin, Kevin Osei, Diego Santos
- NorthBridge Financial: Alyssa Chen, Brian Holt, Priya Desai, Miguel Arroyo, Speaker 1

Auto-summary (Fireflies):
NorthBridge asked Redwood to clarify what is logged by the Private control plane and runtime, how long logs are retained, and how audit logs differ from operational logs. Redwood confirmed payload logging is disabled by default, logs are structured, tenant identifiers can be hashed, and export is supported to Splunk HEC and Elastic/OpenSearch. Customer requested stronger guarantees around redaction and retention controls, plus proxy-friendly egress options.

Topics:
1) What gets logged (and what does not)
2) Audit logging vs operational logging
3) Retention defaults and configuration
4) Export controls and supported sinks
5) Air-gapped/on-prem considerations

00:00 Markus Klein: Alright, thanks everyone. This is Markus from Redwood. Goal today is security review specifically on logging, retention, and exports for Redwood Private. We’ve got Colin and Marcus and Kevin from our security side, and Diego from Private deployments. Alyssa, you want to kick us off with what you need to get comfortable?

00:23 Alyssa Chen: Yeah thanks. We’re close on the Private architecture, but logging is the big hold. We need to be sure prompts and responses are not ending up in logs, we need to separate audit logs from like… operational debug logs, and retention needs to be customer-controlled. Also we have Splunk, and for on-prem we have like no direct outbound internet.

00:44 Brian Holt: And we’ve been burned before by “structured logs” that still include headers and tokens and stuff. So we want a field-level answer.

00:53 Markus Klein: Yep, makes sense. Colin, do you want to start with the high level and then we can go deep?

00:59 Colin O'Donnell: Sure. For Private, think of two buckets: operational logs and audit logs. Operational logs are for running the system—health, errors, request lifecycle, queue depth events, things like that. Audit logs are security-relevant actions—auth events, admin actions, policy changes, model registry actions, role changes, that kind of thing.

01:22 Priya Desai: When you say audit logs, do you mean like a separate stream with an integrity requirement? Or just “we log admin events”?

01:30 Kevin Osei: Good question. Today it’s a separate log category and separate sink configuration. Integrity/WORM depends on where you ship them—like if you export audit logs to your Splunk or an immutable bucket, that’s where you enforce immutability. We don’t, like, build a WORM store into the product in the minimum pack.

01:51 Miguel Arroyo: We would likely want audit logs to go to Splunk with longer retention and tighter access controls. Operational logs can be shorter.

02:00 Naomi Feldman: That’s consistent with what we recommend. Operational logs are primarily for SRE and support troubleshooting, so shorter retention is typical. Audit logs often require 90 days, 1 year, whatever your policy says.

02:14 Alyssa Chen: OK. Then the core question: do you log request payloads? Prompts, completions, embeddings text, any of that.

02:24 Marcus Lin: By default, no. The system emits structured fields like request_id, timestamp, component, severity, status code, latency, and a limited set of routing identifiers. We do not log prompt text or model outputs by default in Private.

02:40 Brian Holt: You say “by default”. So it’s possible to turn on?

02:44 Diego Santos: There are debug toggles, yes, but they’re not intended to be on in production. It’s more like “if you need to debug a specific failure in a lab.” For Private we ship with payload logging disabled, and we document it as not supported for production because of data leakage risk.

03:05 Alyssa Chen: We need a way to enforce that. Like, even if an engineer flips a flag, we want guardrails.

03:11 Marcus Lin: Understood. In the Private Helm values we can lock certain settings with admission policy on your side as well—OPA/Gatekeeper or Kyverno to prevent enabling debug payload logging. On our side we also try to make it “hard” to enable accidentally. But yeah, it’s configuration-driven.

03:30 Priya Desai: I also want clarity around headers. Do you log Authorization headers, cookies, client cert info, anything like that.

03:39 Colin O'Donnell: We do not log auth secrets. We log the auth mechanism in a coarse way—like “auth_type=oidc” or “mTLS” if applicable, and whether the request was allowed/denied. But not the token, not the certificate, not session cookies.

03:57 Brian Holt: And what about tenant and user identifiers?

04:00 Colin O'Donnell: Tenant id is logged as a hash in the operational log path. In audit logs it can be either a stable ID or hashed depending on your config. The intent is to support correlation without exposing direct identifiers.

04:16 Miguel Arroyo: Hashing is good but we need to know the hashing scheme. Is it salted? If it’s just SHA of tenant ID that’s reversible via dictionary.

04:25 Marcus Lin: It’s salted. We use a per-install secret salt, so you can correlate within your environment but it’s not useful outside. We can share the exact approach in the follow-up.

04:38 Alyssa Chen: Great. Another detail: do you log model name? Because model name can sometimes be sensitive for us. Like it implies what use case.

04:47 Diego Santos: We do log model identifier in some runtime logs and metrics, but for Private we’ve been reducing cardinality and we can also map to an internal alias. There’s a “model_group” concept for dashboards so you’re not exploding labels.

05:04 Brian Holt: Sorry, you said metrics too—are we just focusing on logs today?

05:07 Markus Klein: Primarily logs/retention, but metrics touches it. We can keep it on logs.

05:13 Alyssa Chen: Let’s stay on logs. Retention: what’s the default? And where is it stored?

05:20 Diego Santos: In the minimum pack, logs are collected from Kubernetes workloads, forwarded to a default sink—often Loki in the reference stack, or you can send to your existing ELK/Splunk. The default retention is short—like 7 days—because storage in customer clusters varies.

05:41 Priya Desai: Seven days is fine for ops logs. For audit, we need at least 180 days.

05:47 Kevin Osei: That would typically be configured by exporting audit logs to Splunk (or your long-retention system) and setting your Splunk retention. In cluster, we still recommend short retention for anything local.

06:02 Miguel Arroyo: Are audit logs a separate file/stream? Because for Splunk we want different sourcetypes and indexes.

06:09 Colin O'Donnell: Yes. In the collector config we tag and route them separately. You’ll see different labels, for example “log_category=audit” vs “log_category=operational”, and we can map to Splunk sourcetype/index.

06:23 Brian Holt: What log collector are you using? Fluent bit? Vector? Something else.

06:28 Diego Santos: In our current Private packaging we’re using Vector as the default collector because it’s easier to manage pipelines and backpressure. But we’re trying to keep it flexible. Some customers already standardize on Fluent Bit.

06:43 Alyssa Chen: Vector is fine. We just need to know config control and upgrade safety. Like, do your upgrades overwrite our collector config.

06:53 Diego Santos: Good call. We ship default values, but the chart allows customer overrides. Upgrades should be merge-safe—meaning your overrides persist. We’ve also been adding migration notes when we change fields.

07:10 Naomi Feldman: Also, we separate “supported defaults” from “you can do it but we can’t support it.” If you heavily customize, we’ll likely ask you to replicate an issue with baseline settings.

07:22 Speaker 1: Sorry, quick question on export controls. Does exporting logs mean egress from our network to Redwood?

07:29 Markus Klein: No. In Private, you own where logs go. Redwood does not receive your logs unless you explicitly configure an outbound export to us, which is not part of the minimum pack.

07:41 Alyssa Chen: Wait. Redwood Support—how do you troubleshoot without logs? Do you require us to send logs to you?

07:48 Markus Klein: Not required. The standard model is you keep logs in your system, and share snippets during an incident. For some customers we set up a secure support bundle process.

07:59 Marcus Lin: And to be clear, any support bundle is customer-initiated. It can redact and it can omit payloads. We don’t want raw data either.

08:11 Miguel Arroyo: OK. Export targets: we’re Splunk heavy. For VPC, Splunk HEC is easy. For on-prem, we have Splunk too but outbound is blocked; we can allow to internal Splunk only.

08:24 Colin O'Donnell: Splunk HEC is supported. Auth is token-based, TLS, and we can support mTLS if your HEC endpoint is behind an envoy/proxy that terminates mTLS. We also support Elasticsearch/OpenSearch as an alternative.

08:42 Brian Holt: What about OTLP? We’re standardizing on OpenTelemetry collector.

08:46 Colin O'Donnell: OTLP is on the roadmap. In some installs, customers run a sidecar that converts, but we don’t want to oversell. For v1 of the minimum pack, we’re prioritizing Splunk HEC and Elastic/OpenSearch because those are the most common in private environments.

09:07 Alyssa Chen: Understood. If OTLP isn’t officially supported, we’ll stick with HEC.

09:12 Priya Desai: Encryption: are logs encrypted at rest? In-transit? Especially if they land in Loki.

09:20 Marcus Lin: In-transit, yes—TLS when exporting. At rest depends on your storage class. In Kubernetes, if Loki uses a PVC, encryption at rest is your underlying storage encryption. We document that you should use encrypted volumes.

09:38 Kevin Osei: For audit logs specifically, we recommend shipping them to your centralized system where encryption and access controls are already in place.

09:47 Miguel Arroyo: Access controls: can we restrict who can query logs in your bundled Grafana?

09:54 Diego Santos: The bundled dashboards are for metrics mostly; log viewing depends on what you deploy. If you deploy Grafana with Loki, you can integrate SSO/SAML with your IdP, and apply RBAC so only certain teams can access logs.

10:11 Brian Holt: What about redaction? You said you don’t log payloads, but errors might include parts of requests. Like if the model server returns “invalid JSON” and includes the snippet.

10:22 Marcus Lin: Right, that’s the tricky part. We have explicit redaction filters to prevent common leak paths: request headers, auth tokens, and known JSON fields that might carry prompt text. We also try to ensure errors don’t include raw payload echoes. But there are edge cases, so we recommend a validation step—run a canary workload with known “marker strings” and verify they never show up in logs.

10:48 Alyssa Chen: That’s good. We will do that test.

10:52 Priya Desai: Can you provide a written statement: “Prompts and completions are not logged by default” and list any exceptions.

11:00 Naomi Feldman: Yes, we can provide that in the security packet, along with the configuration flags that control debug logging.

11:11 Miguel Arroyo: Audit logs content—what events are included? We need at minimum: login success/failure, role changes, policy changes, model deployment/rollback, and access to key material.

11:26 Kevin Osei: We cover auth events (success/failure), RBAC changes, policy changes, config changes, installer/upgrade actions, and administrative actions in the control plane. We do not log “access to key material” as in KMS decrypt calls, because those are in your KMS audit trail. But we can log “attempted to use KMS key alias X” without secrets.

11:50 Brian Holt: Model registry: if we pull from our internal registry, do you log image names or model artifact paths?

11:58 Diego Santos: We log success/failure of pulls and the referenced model ID. We avoid logging full URLs with credentials. If the URL contains credentials, we redact.

12:14 Alyssa Chen: Another concern: multi-tenant. We’re not truly multi-tenant but we’ll have internal business units. Can we avoid user-specific identifiers in operational logs.

12:25 Colin O'Donnell: Yes. Operational logs don’t need user identity; we focus on request_id and service-level. Audit logs can include acting principal if you want, but you can configure to pseudonymize.

12:41 Brian Holt: Request IDs: are they end-to-end across gateway, router, runtime?

12:46 Diego Santos: Yes, we propagate request_id. There are cases where it’s missing if a client doesn’t pass it and the gateway generates it. But we carry it across components.

12:58 Alyssa Chen: Retention configuration: is it per category? Like 7 days ops, 180 days audit.

13:04 Diego Santos: In our packaging, yes you can route categories differently. Retention is mostly a property of the backend. For example, Loki retention is global or per-tenant depending on setup; Splunk is per index. So we give you the routing; you apply retention in the backend.

13:26 Priya Desai: We want to ensure upgrades don’t change log schema without notice.

13:32 Naomi Feldman: We try to keep backward-compatible fields, and when we add fields we don’t break dashboards. For changes, we publish release notes and migration notes. For Private minimum pack specifically, we’re standardizing field names and trying to keep them stable.

13:51 Miguel Arroyo: What about verbosity. If we have an incident, we might want to increase logging. How do we do that safely.

13:59 Marcus Lin: Log levels per component can be increased (INFO to DEBUG) via config, but again, payload logging is separate and should remain off. We can provide a “safe debug mode” that increases component logs without recording sensitive content.

14:20 Brian Holt: Please, yes. We don’t want a scenario where turning on debug accidentally logs prompts.

14:25 Colin O'Donnell: Agreed.

14:28 Markus Klein: I’m going to jump to export controls because that’s usually the other gating item. Alyssa, you mentioned restricted egress.

14:36 Alyssa Chen: Right. For on-prem, we can only talk to internal endpoints. For VPC, we can allowlist outbound to our Splunk cloud, but we require mTLS and a proxy sometimes.

14:49 Colin O'Donnell: For Splunk HEC, standard is HTTPS with token auth. If you need mTLS, typically you put an internal proxy (Envoy/Nginx) in front of HEC that enforces mTLS from the collector. Vector supports mTLS. We can provide config examples.

15:12 Brian Holt: We also require an explicit allowlist in NetworkPolicies. Do you publish the endpoints your collector needs.

15:20 Diego Santos: Yes. In Private, the collector only needs to reach your chosen sink. There’s no default external endpoint.

15:31 Miguel Arroyo: Backpressure and dropping: what happens if Splunk is down. We’ve had agents drop logs silently.

15:39 Diego Santos: Vector supports disk buffers; you can configure memory vs disk. Default is bounded buffer so it doesn’t OOM the cluster. If the sink is down long enough, eventually you either drop or block. We default to bounded buffering and we surface metrics so you can alert on drops.

16:01 Alyssa Chen: For audit logs, we’d prefer “don’t drop”.

16:05 Diego Santos: You can configure audit logs with higher durability settings and separate buffer. But there’s always a tradeoff with disk usage.

16:18 Priya Desai: That’s acceptable if it’s documented.

16:21 Speaker 1: Is this included in the standard package or is it premium.

16:26 Markus Klein: The “minimum pack” includes baseline log collection and export configuration examples for Splunk/Elastic. Advanced long retention and multi-cluster federation is more premium, but durability tuning is part of normal operation.

16:42 Alyssa Chen: OK. Let’s talk about what we need in writing. We need a list of log fields for operational and audit. We need your default retention recommendations. We need a statement on payload logging and redaction.

16:56 Naomi Feldman: We can send that. We already have a doc that describes operational vs audit interaction and retention guidance, we’ll tailor it for Private.

17:06 Brian Holt: Also: do you have any “support access” where your engineers can access our cluster.

17:11 Marcus Lin: No implicit access. Any access is customer-granted. For on-prem, usually none. For VPC, some customers allow a bastion with time-bound credentials; that’s entirely under your control.

17:25 Miguel Arroyo: Good.

17:27 Alyssa Chen: One more item: you mentioned tenant_id hash. We’d like to also avoid logging IP addresses if possible.

17:35 Colin O'Donnell: IPs appear at the gateway layer for security events (like rate limiting) but can be configured to truncate or omit in operational logs. For audit logs, if you want source IP for login events, that’s usually required. But we can discuss what your policy allows.

17:56 Priya Desai: For us, source IP for admin login is required. For inference requests, not required.

18:04 Diego Santos: We can align to that.

18:08 Markus Klein: Time check, we’ve got about 35 minutes left. Maybe we go through a concrete example: a single inference request—what’s logged where.

18:17 Diego Santos: Yeah. So request comes in at API gateway. Gateway logs: request_id, route name (like /v1/chat/completions), response status, duration. It does not log body. Router/policy engine logs: request_id, selected backend, model alias, any policy decision (allowed/denied). Runtime logs: batch size info, queue time, GPU memory pressure events, errors if any. Again, no prompt text.

18:45 Brian Holt: The runtime logs “model alias” not model path.

18:49 Diego Santos: Correct, that’s the idea. Model registry mapping can be internal.

18:54 Miguel Arroyo: Audit log example: admin changes routing policy.

18:59 Kevin Osei: Audit entry: timestamp, actor principal, action=policy.update, object_id, result=success/failure, and optionally a diff summary that avoids embedding secrets. We do not include raw secrets, like credentials.

19:20 Alyssa Chen: Do you log the policy content. Because policy might contain customer IDs.

19:26 Kevin Osei: We log metadata and a safe diff. Full policy content is not in audit logs by default. If you need full content for change management, that’s usually in your GitOps or config management system.

19:43 Priya Desai: That is good.

19:46 Brian Holt: On retention again: do you have any defaults hard-coded? Like if we forget to configure, does it keep forever.

19:54 Diego Santos: No, we avoid “keep forever” defaults. The reference stack defaults to short retention. If you export to Splunk, Splunk controls it. If you keep local-only, then it’s your Loki/ELK retention config.

20:13 Alyssa Chen: OK.

20:15 Miguel Arroyo: Do you provide any detection for sensitive strings in logs? Like a scan.

20:21 Marcus Lin: Not built-in scanning today. We recommend you run DLP scanning in your log pipeline if needed. We can provide a “known marker test” approach for validation.

20:35 Brian Holt: That’s fine. We already have Splunk rules.

20:39 Alyssa Chen: What about rate limiting logs. Sometimes these include user IDs.

20:44 Colin O'Donnell: We log rate limit events with request_id and a key identifier. For Private, we can ensure that identifier is not raw user ID; it can be a hashed key.

20:58 Priya Desai: Great.

21:00 Markus Klein: I’m seeing some chat about OTEL. Brian, you said you standardize on OTEL collector.

21:06 Brian Holt: Yeah, if you can output OTLP, that’d be clean. But we can deal with HEC.

21:12 Colin O'Donnell: Understood. For the minimum supported pack, we’d rather be explicit: Splunk HEC and Elastic are tested. OTLP we can discuss as “best effort” but not guaranteed. We don’t want you to be the first.

21:30 Alyssa Chen: We appreciate the honesty.

21:33 Miguel Arroyo: One more “gotcha”: sometimes vendors log token usage, like “prompt tokens” and “completion tokens”. That’s fine. But sometimes they log the prompt length and the prompt itself. Can you confirm it’s just counts.

21:46 Diego Santos: It’s counts. You’ll see numeric metrics and log fields like token_in, token_out, latency_ms. Not the text.

21:55 Brian Holt: OK.

22:00 Alyssa Chen: Can you share a sample log line? Like a redacted example.

22:05 Colin O'Donnell: Yes, we can provide a couple sample JSON lines for each category.

22:10 Naomi Feldman: We’ll make sure the sample is aligned with what ships, not a “marketing” sample.

22:15 Priya Desai: And please include a list of redaction patterns.

22:20 Marcus Lin: We can share the categories, yes. Some specifics are implementation details, but we can explain what we redact: Authorization headers, cookies, common secret key names, and any fields labeled as payload.

22:35 Alyssa Chen: That should work.

22:38 Markus Klein: Let’s hit air-gapped quickly. On-prem with no internet. Does anything in your logging pipeline require pulling images or reaching out.

22:48 Diego Santos: No. We provide an offline bundle for the observability components as container images and configs. Log export in airgap means you export to an internal endpoint (internal Splunk or internal Elastic). There’s no “phone home.”

23:06 Brian Holt: And updates—how do we update the collector. Is it part of the Redwood installer upgrade.

23:12 Diego Santos: Yes, if you install our packaged collector. If you use your own collector, we integrate via standard outputs.

23:21 Miguel Arroyo: OK.

23:23 Alyssa Chen: We should also clarify audit logs vs application logs. Like, do you consider model outputs “application data” and never log it. Good.

23:33 Marcus Lin: Correct.

23:35 Priya Desai: I’m going to ask a compliance-y thing: do you have a default recommendation for log retention. Like what do you tell customers.

23:43 Kevin Osei: Typical: operational logs 7-14 days local, exported as needed; audit logs 90-180 days minimum, often 1 year depending on policy. We don’t enforce it; we recommend.

23:58 Priya Desai: OK.

24:01 Markus Klein: Maybe we can spend the rest on any specific policy statements you need for your vendor review.

24:07 Alyssa Chen: We need: (1) data in logs—no prompts/outputs by default, (2) redaction of secrets, (3) customer-controlled export and retention, (4) separation of audit logs and operational logs, and (5) support access is customer controlled.

24:23 Naomi Feldman: We can cover all five in writing.

24:27 Brian Holt: One more: can Redwood employees ever see logs in the console, like a hosted console.

24:33 Markus Klein: In Private, the console is deployed in your environment. We don’t have access unless you give it.

24:41 Brian Holt: OK.

24:44 Miguel Arroyo: For incident response, we sometimes need to know if logs were dropped. Do you have a metric for drop count.

24:52 Diego Santos: Yes, collector exposes metrics on buffer usage, retries, drops. Those can alert.

25:02 Alyssa Chen: Great.

25:04 Priya Desai: Also can you provide evidence of security review on your side. Like have you done a PII log review.

25:11 Marcus Lin: Yes, we do internal reviews and we have SOC2 controls around logging. For the Private minimum pack specifically, we’ve done a redaction review and we can share the summary in the security packet.

25:26 Alyssa Chen: OK.

25:29 Markus Klein: I think we’ve got the main items. Let’s do a quick round: anything else from NorthBridge.

25:36 Speaker 1: Just confirming, none of this changes pricing, right.

25:40 Markus Klein: Correct, this is part of Private delivery; export to Splunk uses your Splunk.

25:47 Alyssa Chen: I’m good. Brian?

25:50 Brian Holt: Just want the field catalog and sample logs.

25:54 Miguel Arroyo: And the durability/backpressure config, especially for audit logs.

25:59 Priya Desai: And the written statements.

26:02 Markus Klein: Perfect.

26:05 Colin O'Donnell: We’ll send: Splunk HEC config example, routing config for audit vs operational, and sample JSON log lines.

26:13 Kevin Osei: I’ll send the retention separation guidance and recommendations.

26:17 Marcus Lin: I’ll send redaction policy summary and the marker-string validation procedure.

26:24 Markus Klein: Cool. We’ll schedule a follow-up for the Splunk export in restricted egress, 30 minutes. Alyssa, we’ll coordinate times.

26:35 Alyssa Chen: Sounds good.

[Compact workspace chips + contextual micro-rail: progressive IA and routing prototype for Console]
description:
Design a compact, high-density workspace switcher and a contextual micro-rail to surface route-level controls (dashboards, rollouts, cost views) without overwhelming the left rail. Prototype interaction patterns for keyboard-first flows, progressive disclosure, and clear routing semantics for deep links and shared links.

background:
Current Console left rail is large and uses full workspace tiles which causes vertical churn for teams with many workspaces. Teams frequently need to pivot between dashboards, rollout controls, and per-model cost views; those pivots are buried in nested nav or require a separate search flow. Previous sidebar explorations favored a full-width reframe; this ticket explores a compact chip-based switcher paired with a lightweight contextual rail (micro-rail) that appears inline when a route has tool-level controls.

goals:
Reduce vertical space used by workspace switcher by at least 40% on typical 1080p screens
Provide single-click access to route-level tooling: dashboards, rollouts, cost breakdowns
Preserve deep-link stability: shareable URLs must open to the same route and micro-rail state where applicable
Support keyboard navigation and screen-reader semantics for accessibility
Surface quick cost pivots (last-24h / last-30d) without leaving current route

constraints:
Must use existing left-rail width constraints for 3 responsive breakpoints
Micro-rail must not require a full page reload; should be client-side rendered and route-aware
No changes to existing backend routing schema — only client-side routing and query params allowed
Design must account for both hosted and dedicated tenants where workspace names can be long

decisions:
Adopt a compact workspace chip (avatar + truncated name + chevron) with overflow menu for full list
Introduce contextual micro-rail: a second-level horizontal rail that slides out from under the primary nav when route metadata indicates available tooling
Encode micro-rail state in URL query param `?micro=tool:rollout` to maintain shareability
Keyboard nav: Tab focuses chips, Enter opens chip; pressing 'M' toggles micro-rail for focused route
Progressive disclosure: show only the most-used route tools by default, with a 'More' menu exposing full toolset

acceptance_criteria:
Prototype demonstrates workspace chip layout and overflow behavior (desktop + tablet)
Micro-rail opens and closes without full route reload; query param persists across refresh
Accessibility: micro-rail items have ARIA roles and keyboard focus order validated in prototype
Usability test (5 participants) shows <10s median time to switch workspace + open rollout control
Design handed off to ENG with component spec and responsive tokens, plus example GH ticket for implementation

stakeholder_feedback:
PM (Diego Morales): prefers query-param approach to preserve GA tracking for rollouts
Eng lead (Maya Sullivan): requests micro-rail initial render to be lazy-loaded to avoid bundle bloat
Security (Jon Park): flagged that micro-rail must not expose controls if the user lacks permission; needs server-side guard
Product Ops (Ravi Patel): likes the cost quick-pivots but asked for a lightweight sparkline in the chip hover state

next_steps:
Run 5 moderated usability tests with platform engineers and PMs (scheduled week of 2026-03-15)
Incorporate feedback and produce Handoff package (components, tokens, interaction spec)
Draft GH implementation epic and break into engineering tickets: responsive, routing, RBAC
Schedule a design review with Security and Accessibility to finalize ARIA patterns

[Orbital Pivot: Console navigation decomposition and compact workspace switcher prototype]
description:
Goal: Replace the current top-heavy workspace/navigation patterns with a compact, persistent left pivot that supports fast workspace switching, per-route cost lenses, and rollout state awareness without adding cognitive load. This ticket contains the primary prototype and the decomposition of the navigation into three independent layers: 1) global workspace selector and identity surface; 2) route cluster rail (primary product areas like Models, Deployments, Dashboards, Billing); 3) contextual micro-rail for per-route actions (rollouts, traces, cost breakdowns). The prototype explores a compressed collapsed state (icon-only), focused state (expanded icons + micro-labels), and a transient overlay for quick workspace switching with fuzzy search. Key constraints: preserve token-level cost visibility in Dashboards route, support canary/cascade rollout indicators in the rail, maintain 60px touch targets for mobile breakpoints, and ensure route persistence across private/dedicated/hosted account modes.

design_notes:
Decoupled routing: treat route cluster as idempotent router that maps to model/version+view. This enables pinning a model version at route-level without changing workspace context.
Cost lens integration: per-route pill shows delta vs baseline and links to expanded cost panel. Inline token-rate microcopy appears for routes that serve generation-heavy traffic.
Rollout affordances: three-state indicator (Stable / Canary / Failing) with hover summary and click-to-open rollout timeline in the contextual rail.
Compactness tradeoffs: reduced label density balanced by progressive disclosure and affordance shadows to communicate hierarchy.
Accessibility: ensured keyboard focus order maps to visual stacking; aria-expanded and aria-pressed added to toggle states; color contrast tested for rollout badges and cost deltas.
Responsive: mobile collapses to top nav with workspace chip; tablet uses collapsible left pivot; desktop uses persistent expanded pivot by default with user preference saved in account settings.
Telemetry hooks: interaction events for workspace switch, collapse/expand, and rollout CTA clicks are included for iteration and AB analysis.

review_feedback:
2025-02-14 - Priya Kapur (PM): Likes the compact switcher; requested an explicit fallback when private-mode network latency prevents fuzzy search results. Action: add local MRU list and offline cache UX.
2025-02-18 - Samir Gómez (Engineering): Concern about the rollout timeline overlay re-render cost at high QPS. Decision: defer heavy timeline rendering; use summarized precomputed snapshots and fetch details on demand.
2025-02-20 - Ana Rivera (Security): Asked for audit-log hooks when workspaces are switched in dedicated/private. Action: add event emitters and map to existing audit pipeline. Marked for enterprise checklist.
2025-02-24 - UX Review panel: Recommended stronger affordance for current-route cost lens and suggested micro-illustrations for empty dashboard states. Action: update illustrations and test with 5 customers.
2025-02-27 - Accessibility review by Tom Li: Keyboard flows good; requested larger hit area for collapsed icons at 44px minimum on touch devices. Action: adjust collapsed touch target and retest.

decisions:
Adopt left pivot as canonical nav for desktop and tablet, maintain top-chip fallback on phones.
Implement MRU (most-recently-used) local cache for workspace quick-switch to address offline and high-latency Private deployments.
Rollouts will show three-state badges; detailed timeline fetched lazily to reduce client CPU.
Cost lens will appear as an inline pill with click-to-expand panel; expanded panel reuses Dashboard components for continuity.
Preference persisted per-user in account settings and exposed via Console > Preferences.
Telemetry events standardized under 'nav.orbital.*' for product analytics and AB experimentation.

next_steps:
Finalize high-fidelity screens and handoff tokens (colors, spacing, microcopy) — due 2025-03-05.
Create a component PR for collapsed pivot + workspace MRU UX (Engineering pairing) — assign ENG-48221.
Run 5 moderated usability sessions focused on cost-lens discoverability and rollout comprehension — scheduled 2025-03-06 to 2025-03-10.
Update Console docs and release notes draft for console-2025.03 describing nav migration path and migration toggle.
Coordinate with Security to include audit-log tests in Dedicated/Private acceptance matrix.

notes_for_engineering:
Prefer precomputed rollout summaries in the reactions API to avoid client-side aggregation on large traces.
Expose a lightweight endpoint for MRU workspace suggestions that falls back to local cache when network is slow.
Style tokens for collapsed pivot: width 56px, expanded 232px, icon center 24px with 44px min hit target for touch.

[Console cardinal navigation grid: reduce surface friction for dashboards & workspace switching]
description:
Objective: Rework the Console information architecture to make key flows—dashboards, rollouts, and cost views—discoverable within two clicks while preserving low-latency access to workspace context. Proposal: a cardinal navigation grid that groups primary surfaces into four cardinal zones (Overview, Workspaces, Models, Operations) with a lightweight contextual micro-rail for in-place workspace switching. This ticket covers high-fidelity prototypes, heuristic reviews, and a handoff package for engineering to implement the grid and micro-rail transitions.

acceptance_criteria:
Primary surfaces reachable within two interactions from any Console entry point
Workspace switch completes in <150ms perceived transition (prototype target) and preserves route-scoped filters
Cost and rollout panels surface top-line metrics in the Overview quadrant with direct deep-links to per-route breakdowns
Design handoff includes responsive states for collapsed/expanded rails and accessible keyboard navigation (tab order documented)
Stakeholder sign-off from PM, Eng (runtime), and Accessibility review recorded in comments

decisions:
Adopt quadrant-first layout rather than a single monolithic left rail to surface cross-cutting metrics
Keep workspace switcher as context-sensitive micro-rail (flyout on hover/click) instead of full-screen modal to preserve continuity
Expose route-level deep-links in the Overview quadrant to enable direct sharing of rollout and cost views
Defer multi-tenant workspace bulk-actions to a follow-up ticket (scope limit for MVP)

tradeoffs:
Quadrant grid improves discoverability but uses more horizontal space; mitigated with a compact collapse and adaptive layout
Micro-rail preserves context but adds surface complexity for edge cases (nested workspaces); additional QA required
Surface-first focus may require runtime changes for route resolution—ENG dependency and temporary client-side redirects included in scope

2026-02-20 - Dev review by Priya Shah (ENG): Raised routing concerns for legacy /projects/:id routes; suggested route aliasing instead of rewriting server routes.

[Console navigation reorg: streamlined sidebar, route semantics, and workspace switcher UX]
summary:
Console IA refresh ticket to redesign the main navigation and workspace switching experience. Prototypes exist; team aligned on compact sidebar + modal workspace switcher. Remaining work: accessibility fixes, router and backend support, and canary rollout planning.

description:
High-level redesign of Redwood Console information architecture focusing on: 1) a condensed, role-aware left sidebar; 2) clearer top-level routing and deep-links for dashboards, rollouts, and cost views; and 3) a discoverable workspace switcher pattern that supports cross-workspace user flows and SSO guests. This ticket captures prototypes, review feedback, acceptance criteria, and next steps toward shipping the new nav in console-2026.04.

motivation:
Users struggle to find per-model dashboards and rollout controls when teams have multiple workspaces. The current sidebar is cluttered and makes routing unpredictable for deep links and browser history. We aim to reduce navigation noise, improve task completion for engineers and PMs, and enable stable deep-links for observability and incident workflows.

acceptance_criteria:
Left sidebar shows a maximum of 7 primary entries with ability to expand secondary items
Workspace switcher available from header and sidebar with quick-search; switching preserves last-used route in target workspace where permissible
Deep-linkable routes for: /workspaces/:id/dashboards, /workspaces/:id/rollouts/:id, /workspaces/:id/costs and stable query params for filters
Keyboard shortcut (cmd+k) opens global quick navigation with fuzzy search across routes and resources
ARIA-compliant sidebar interactions (role=navigation, proper focus management, visible focus ring, screen-reader labels)
Performance: no added JS bundle > 40KB for nav logic; lazy-load heavy components like cost analytics
Analytics: nav_click, workspace_switch, deep_link_open events instrumented with route and workspace_id

design_decisions:
Adopt compact vertical sidebar with icon+label; allow collapse to icon-only with tooltip on hover
Group secondary pages (billing, settings, API keys) into an expandable 'Admin' node to reduce top-level noise
Implement workspace switcher as a modalable overlay anchored to header avatar with inline search; also expose compact selector in sidebar for quick switching
Preserve last active sub-route per workspace in local storage and as parameter in the workspace switcher to support back-and-forth flows
Use route-first approach: navigation drives URL changes; components read route params for context rather than relying on global state
Introduce `router.suggestedFallback` mapping for older deep-links to redirect to new canonical routes (with 301-equivalent client behavior)
Prioritize keyboard navigation and screen-reader announcements during expand/collapse actions

InVision demo: https://invision.redwood.internal/console-nav-proto

Add feature flag `console_ia_v2` to gate release and enable A/B rollout; include telemetry toggles

[Portal Window: Workspace Gateway & Micro-rail Navigation System]
description:
Design and prototype a new compact workspace gateway that sits in the left rail and acts as a lightweight ‘portal window’ into another workspace. Primary goals: reduce context-switch friction, surface per-workspace cost and latency lenses, and simplify keyboard-first switching for power users. Deliverables: high-fidelity prototype, accessible interaction spec, annotated handoff to frontend, and experiment plan for incremental rollout.

design_decisions:
Persistent micro-rail over transient tooltip: supports quick comparisons between two workspaces without repeated clicks.
Use cached snapshot with infrequent refresh for preview content to avoid high backend load; provide manual refresh action in preview header.
Show per-workspace cost chips (24h spend + sparkline) as primary signal inside switcher to help triage cost regressions quickly.
Compact layout prioritizes left-rail real estate: avatar-sized workspace token, short title, cost chip, last activity time, overflow menu for workspace actions.
Keyboard-first access: prefix hotkey (Cmd/Ctrl+K) to open switcher, arrow navigation, Enter to open workspace, Space to expand portal preview.
Accessibility: preview must be reachable via keyboard, expose title and role to screen readers, color contrast and motion reduced mode supported.
Deferred items for MVP: drag-and-drop reordering, inline rollout controls, and interactive charts inside preview (phase 2).

accept_criteria:
Design assets and tokens committed to the design system (icons, chip styles, micro-rail spacing).
High-fidelity prototype with desktop and keyboard interactions documented.
Annotated behavior spec covering focus management, refresh cadence, and failure states.
Accessibility checklist met (ARIA roles, contrast, keyboard traps documented).
Handoff package in Confluence with engineering tasks broken out and dependencies called out (ENG-2218, ENG-2280).

usability_findings:
Internal round 1 (n=6): Users preferred persistent preview for comparison tasks; initial confusion about what data is live vs snapshot — resolved by explicit 'snapshot' label and refresh button.
Participants asked for cost signal granularity — aggregated 24h spend plus sparkline was adequate for initial discovery workflows.
Power users requested keyboard shortcuts and quick-open behavior; added to acceptance criteria.
Some participants worried about leaking sensitive info in previews across workspaces; added permission gating and filtering to scope previews to metadata-only view for non-admins.

rollout_plan:
Phase 0: Internal beta (10% of employees) — gather qualitative feedback and bug reports.
Phase 1: Canary (5% of customers, non-critical accounts) — monitor switch success rate and latency for 72 hours.
Phase 2: Gradual ramp (25% -> 50% -> 100%) over 2 weeks with automated rollback on defined SLO breaches.
Experimentation: A/B test with control (current switcher) vs variant (portal window) on task completion time for cross-workspace comparisons.
Telemetry: ensure ENG-2280 captures switch latency, preview refresh rate, user toggles, and cost-lens engagement.

metrics:
Workspace switch time (ms) — median and 95th percentile.
Preview open rate (percent of switches that expand preview).
Cost-lens engagement (clicks on cost chip -> cost dashboard).
Time-to-task for cross-workspace comparison tasks (measured via A/B test).
