[Tenant Observability & Evidence Contract for Regulated VPC Deploys]
Summary:
This document defines the observability, telemetry, and evidence requirements Redwood expects for regulated customers deploying the Private (VPC) product. It is an operational contract that outlines the metrics, traces, logs, retention, and artifacts required for customer acceptance, ongoing compliance, and post-incident audits.

Purpose and scope:
- Purpose: Provide a concrete, testable checklist that field engineers, SREs, and customer infra teams can use during private VPC deployments to satisfy regulatory evidence requests (PCI/ISO/SOC-style) and internal Redwood SLAs.
- Scope: Applies to all Private VPC deployments for customers with regulated workloads (PHI, PCI, PII-sensitive). This covers control-plane connectivity, runtime agents, telemetry pipelines, and secure artifact handoff.

Key objectives:
1) Ensure visibility to support 99.95% tenant-facing availability SLO and latency SLOs (see SLOs section).
2) Collect and preserve evidence for security and compliance audits with tamper-evident retention controls.
3) Standardize acceptance tests and artifacts to reduce delivery time and avoid rework.

SLOs and performance thresholds (tenant-facing):
- Availability: 99.95% monthly for tenant inference endpoint (measurement: synthetic probes from customer region + control-plane logs).
- Latency: p95 < 120ms for 256-token synchronous calls; p95 < 250ms for 1024-token calls (measured at ingress for successful 2xx responses).
- Error budget: 0.05% of requests may return 5xx or timeouts; any breach requires incident runbook and customer notification within 1 hour.

Observability categories and minimums:
1) Metrics (Prometheus-format):
   - Required metrics exported by runtime-agent and control-plane: redwood.runtime.requests_total, redwood.runtime.requests_failures_total, redwood.runtime.latency_seconds_bucket (histogram), redwood.runtime.kv_cache_hit_ratio, redwood.controlplane.sync_latency_seconds, redwood.controlplane.config_version{tenant}, redwood.controlplane.fallback_count.
   - Scrape frequency: 15s for runtime-agent critical metrics, 60s for control-plane aggregated metrics.
   - Retention: raw metrics retained in customer-visible TSDB for 90 days; aggregated rollups (1h) for 2 years.

2) Traces (OpenTelemetry):
   - Required spans: request ingress, runtime decode/encode, model kernel exec, kv-cache lookup, control-plane routing decision.
   - Sampling: adaptive sampling with minimum 5% global sample and 100% sampling for any request flagged as failed (>5xx) or taking >p99 latency.
   - Retention: traces retained for 90 days in a tamper-evident store (customer-managed or agreed third-party like Tempo+S3 with signed manifests).

3) Logs (structured JSON):
   - Required logs: access logs (per-request), runtime-agent system logs, control-plane audit logs, key rotations, and storage access attempts.
   - Format: JSON with at minimum {timestamp, tenant_id, request_id, route, model, status_code, latency_ms, node_id}.
   - Retention: 365 days for audit logs; 90 days for operational logs unless regulatory requirement dictates more.

4) Telemetry integrity and chain-of-custody:
   - All telemetry bundles delivered for audits must include salted hashes (SHA256) and a signed manifest from the control-plane operator.
   - For air-gapped customers, manifests must be exportable via signed tarball and verified with customer-provided key.

Evidence artifacts (deliverables for acceptance and compliance):
- Live SLO dashboard link (Grafana) scoped to tenant with view-only credentials.
- A 30-day extract of: metrics (Prometheus export), traces (OTLP export), and logs (JSON NDJSON) for the agreed window.
- Signed telemetry manifest and hash list (SHA256) with timestamped signatures.
- Configuration snapshot: control-plane config_version, model versions, container images with image digests, and quantization/precision profile.
- Access & audit log slice showing KMS/HSM key uses during install and initial 7 days.

Acceptance tests and checklist (field delivery):
1) Pre-install (customer infra):
   - Validate VPC CIDR and routing per network readiness checklist.
   - Confirm KMS/HSM integration and that customer can accept signed manifests.
2) Installation validation (engineer run):
   - Synthetic probe checklist: 5 probes from each customer region to runtime SNI endpoint. All probes must return 200 within latency SLO for initial acceptance.
   - Metrics ingestion validation: Verify runtime-agent metrics scraped at 15s and visible in Grafana panels.
   - Traces: Generate 100 synthetic requests with varied sizes; confirm 5% sampled traces + all failures sampled; spans contain model and kv-cache annotations.
   - Logs: Export last 24 hours of structured logs and validate JSON schema and presence of required fields.
3) Compliance artifact handoff:
   - Produce the signed telemetry manifest and initial 30-day artifact bundle (or since-boot) and deliver via agreed channel (secure S3, signed USB for air-gap).

Example telemetry ingestion config (YAML snippet for runtime-agent):
telemetry:
  metrics_scrape_interval: 15s
  otlp_endpoint: https://collector.customer-vpc.example:4317
  trace_sampling:
    default_rate: 0.05
    spike_capture_threshold_ms: 1500
  log_format: json
  log_shipper: fluent-bit

Evidence export command examples:
- Metrics (Prometheus TSDB block export): curl -u readonly:token "https://prom.customer-vpc.example/api/v1/export?range=30d" -o metrics-30d.tar.gz
- Traces (OTLP export): otelcli export --endpoint https://collector.customer-vpc.example:4317 --from=2025-09-01 --to=2025-10-01 --out traces-30d.ndjson

Operational runbook pointers (post-acceptance):
- Alerting: Must configure the following alerts at customer and Redwood side: runtime_errors_rate > 0.5% for 5m; p95_latency > 140ms for 10m; telemetry_pipeline_lag > 2m for 5m.
- Incident evidence protocol: When an incident is created for a regulated tenant, the on-call engineer must capture: 1) A zipped telemetry bundle (metrics + traces + logs) covering incident window +/- 60 minutes. 2) Signed manifest and chain-of-custody note stored in customer evidence bucket. 3) Post-incident RCA attached with references to artifact hashes.

Upgrade & rollback evidence expectations:
- For any runtime upgrade affecting model execution (kernel/quantization changes), the delivery packet must include: pre-upgrade baseline metrics/traces (7 days), smoke test results, and canary traffic plan; post-upgrade artifact bundle (first 24 hours) and a signed rollback-ready image digest list.
- Rollback procedure must preserve telemetry artifacts from the failed upgrade window and mark them immutable for the duration of the investigation.

Acceptance signoff template (required fields):
- Tenant ID: 
- Deployment ID: 
- Control-plane config_version: 
- SLO verification: pass/fail with measured values
- Evidence artifacts delivered: list of file paths and manifest hash
- Signatures: Field engineer / Customer security lead / Redwood delivery lead (email + timestamp)

Ownership and escalation:
- Primary owner: Private Deployments Delivery - delivery-oncall@redwood.ai
- Observability owner: Eng Platform Metrics team - metrics@redwood.ai
- Escalation matrix: see /confluence/eng-oncall/incident-process (must be mirrored into customer handoff docs).

Security and privacy notes:
- Telemetry exports MUST be filtered for tenant PII unless customer explicitly requests full payload capture and provides documented legal approval.
- KMS keys used to sign manifests must be rotated per customer policy; Redwood will provide rotation proof (signed key rotation log) as part of audit artifacts.

FAQ (short):
Q: What if a customer cannot host a Prometheus/OTLP endpoint?
A: Redwood can host a collector in a dedicated ingress VPC peered to the customer per the hybrid-control-plane model; in that case additional network ACLs and data residency controls are required and documented in the network appendix.

References and related docs:
- Private deploy acceptance and smoke validation (linked), post-install telemetry checklist (linked), and control-plane manifest format specification (internal doc).

Appendix A - Minimal evidence table (human readable):
Artifact | Minimum window | Format | Retention | Delivery method
Metrics export | 30 days | Prometheus TSDB / csv | 90 days raw, 2y rollups | secure S3 / scp
Traces | 30 days | OTLP -> ndjson | 90 days | signed tarball / s3
Audit logs (KMS/Install) | 365 days | JSON NDJSON | 365 days | s3 w/ bucket policy

Appendix B - Contact matrix and escalation SLA:
- Tier 1 response: Delivery engineer within 1 hour
- Tier 2 escalation: Platform SRE within 4 hours
- Tier 3 legal/compliance engagement: within 24 hours

- 2025-10-15: initial draft (Aisha Patel)
- 2026-02-20: expanded trace sampling policy and added signed manifest requirements (Lena Fischer)


[midmarket-deal-signal-cheat-sheet-and-competitive-angles-2026]
Overview

Purpose: A compact, actionable sales enablement reference for mid-market deals (ARR $100k–$1M). Use this in SDR <> AE handoffs, pre-call prep, and deal reviews. The doc collates positioning, qualifying signals, practical competitive rebuttals, sample pricing scenarios, a pitch-deck skeleton, and a short security FAQ tailored to procurement questions.

Quick summary (use verbally in 1–2 minutes):
- Redwood Inference: production-first inference platform that reduces unit cost and operational risk for teams that outgrow single-node demonstrations. Offers hosted API for quick launch, reserved Dedicated pools for scale predictability, and Private (VPC / on-prem) for regulated customers.

Target buyer profile (mid-market persona):
- Titles: Head of ML / Director of AI, Platform Engineering Lead, Product Manager (AI features), CTO for vertical SaaS
- Typical needs: predictable monthly spend, lower per-token costs at scale, SLOs for latency & availability, simplified rollout / model versioning, basic compliance for customer data
- Buying triggers: first revenue-generating AI feature, multi-model experimentation, unpredictable token spend, a production incident with slow inference or high cloud bill

Core messaging pillars (pick 2–3 for each call depending on prospect):
1) Predictable economics: reserved capacity + intelligent batching reduces per-token spend by up to 5–10x vs naive endpoint usage. Sell unit economics, not just features.
2) Production reliability: SLAs, automatic fallback routing, KV/prefix caching and rollout controls mean fewer outages and more graceful degradation.
3) Developer-first experience: same API and tooling across hosted, dedicated, and private — reduces integration effort and long-term lock-in.
4) Compliance-ready: VPC/private control plane options, KMS integrations, audit logs and configurable retention for regulated industries.

Qualifying checklist (fast-screen):
- Do you have >20k monthly active users or >1M tokens/month? (Yes -> qualify for dedicated sizing conversation)
- Are response latency or tail-percentiles business-critical (e.g., under 500 ms target)?
- Do you have data residency or encryption-at-rest requirements?
- Is there an expected growth trajectory (x3 ARR) in next 12 months?
- Do you run multimodal or many long-context workloads?

Deal signals and playbook (how to react):
- Signal: Prospect says ‘our inference bill spiked unexpectedly’ -> Play: lead with cost decomposition + quick audit offer (ask for top 2 endpoints and avg seq len). Offer a differentiated Dedicated estimate and caching strategy.
- Signal: Prospect needs corporate SLA and audit logs -> Play: emphasize Dedicated/Private options, list compliance integrations, propose a pilot with basic retention settings.
- Signal: Prospect worried about vendor lock-in -> Play: stress API compatibility and rollout tooling; offer migration checklist and proof of concept concurrently.

Competitive angles (one-page brief):
- Key competitors to call out: general cloud vendor endpoints (AWS/Azure/GCP), managed LLM APIs (OpenAI/Anthropic), and inference infra vendors/self-hosted stacks.

Comparative snapshot (use in pitch / RFP rebuttal):
| Capability | Redwood Inference | Major cloud endpoints | OpenAI / Anthropic | Self-hosted inference vendors |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Deployment modes | Hosted / Dedicated / Private (VPC & on-prem) | Primarily cloud endpoints | Hosted only (some enterprise options) | On-prem only or customer-managed cloud |
| Latency SLOs | SLO-backed for Dedicated, routing for low tail latency | Depends on instance and config | No SLA for public API; enterprise deals vary | Depends on customer ops maturity |
| Cost model | Usage + reserved capacity (committed discounts), cost controls | Instance + request pricing; can be higher per-token | Per-token public API; volume tiers | CapEx + ops costs; unpredictable infra TCO |
| Dev ergonomics | Unified API, rollout, observability, token-level attribution | Standard SDKs; less inference-specific tooling | Simple API but limited control over inference profile | Highly variable; requires custom infra work |
| Compliance & private deployments | Built-in private control plane, KMS, audit logs | Cloud-native compliance (region-limited) | Limited enterprise offerings | Can be compliant but customer responsibility |

How to use the table: call out Redwood differentiation quickly — predictable spend, deployment flexibility, and operational visibility. If prospect values single-call simplicity, acknowledge competitor strengths and propose a quick POC to show cost/latency delta.

Objection handling (scripts):
- Objection: ‘Your pricing is higher than raw cloud GPU.’
  - Response: ‘Raw GPU looks cheaper initially, but total cost includes batching efficiency, KV/cache savings, maintenance, and the engineering time to operate. For example, customers moving from unmanaged endpoints reduced token costs by 3–7x after enabling our batching + cache + reserved capacity.’
- Objection: ‘We’re worried about lock-in.’
  - Response: ‘We provide model version pinning, documented export/migration paths, and identical APIs across modes. Many teams prototype on hosted and then port to Dedicated/Private with minimal code changes.’
- Objection: ‘We can use OpenAI’s public API for lower friction.’
  - Response: ‘OpenAI is great for early experimentation. For production with SLOs, predictable pricing at scale, or data residency needs, our Dedicated/Private options provide stronger guarantees and controls while keeping developer ergonomics.’

Pricing guidance (mid-market play):
- Offer constructs: Hosted monthly usage + optional Dedicated reservation (GPU-equivalent units) + Professional services for pilot and onboarding.
- Common negotiation levers: commit duration (12 vs 36 months), upfront vs monthly billing, pilot-to-commit conversion credits, and observability add-ons.

Sample scenarios (talk tracks — real numbers to cite in calls):
- Small mid-market pilot (3-month POC): $15k total cap -> includes 6k–10k USD credits for hosted usage, 40 hours onboarding engineering support, a single workload cost analysis. Goal is to demonstrate 30–40% unit-cost improvement on core endpoint and identify caching opportunities.
- Typical midmarket reserved commit: $120k/year -> maps to a Dedicated pool sized for sustained throughput; includes 10% discount on incremental hosted usage and priority onboarding. Typical ROI pitch: recouped within 3–6 months from unit-cost savings and reduced incidents.
- High-growth midmarket (multi-environment): $360k/year -> multi-region Dedicated with private control plane, extended SSO/KMS integration, and 24x7 support. Offer staged discounts for 24–36 month commit.

Pricing negotiation playbook:
1) Establish baseline usage (ask for last 3 months token volumes, avg seq length, percent streaming).
2) Show modeled cost delta: (current cost) vs (Redwood hosted w/o reserve) vs (Redwood Dedicated includes batching+cache).
3) Offer a pilot with clear success criteria (X% cost reduction OR <Y ms p95 latency OR successful private deployment).
4) Move to reservation conversation only after pilot demonstrates delta; lock price with term and commit.

Pilot-to-commit conversion: 10 weeks.

  - A: For Hosted customers, data is stored in regional clusters; we support data residency by region. For Dedicated/Private, control plane and inference nodes are customer-isolated per contract.

[Customer onboarding: service-account, KMS boundary, and telemetry evidence playbook]
Summary

Purpose: This playbook standardizes how Redwood and customers agree on service account models, KMS boundary decisions, and the telemetry evidence package required for private/VPC deployments. The goal is to accelerate onboarding while preserving compliance and clear operational handoffs.

Scope

- Applies to all Private deployments (VPC and on-prem) where customer-managed keys or isolated service principals are requested.
- Intended audience: Solutions Engineering (pre-sales), Field Ops (installation), Security & Compliance reviewers, and the customer’s infrastructure/security teams.

Prerequisites

1) Signed NDA and Master Services Agreement covering evidence sharing.
2) Customer network diagram and control plane endpoints.
3) Inventory of customer KMS/HSM provider and service-account management process.

Decision matrix: service-account vs. token-based auth

- Service-account (recommended when):
  - Customer requires per-tenant auditability, RBAC scoping within their identity provider, or rotating principals tied to payroll systems.
  - They can provision OIDC or short-lived credentials.

- Token-based ephemeral credentials (recommended when):
  - The customer wants minimal identity footprint on their side and agrees to the Redwood-managed token rotation contract.

Service account model: recommended patterns

1) Customer-managed OIDC federation (Preferred)

- Summary: Customer creates an OIDC trust between their identity provider (IdP) and the Redwood operator role. Requests from Redwood to the customer environment are scoped to a service account with narrowly defined claims.
- Ownership: Customer owns IdP configuration; Redwood owns the short-lived provider role and mapping table.
- Advantages: No long-lived secrets, strong audition metadata, straightforward rotation.

2) Scoped long-lived service key in KMS (Alternate)

- Summary: Customer provision a symmetric key in their KMS/HSM and grants Redwood a key-encrypting capability scoped to a service account. This is useful for air-gapped or restricted environments where OIDC is not available.
- Constraints: Key usage limited to encrypt/decrypt operations for model weights metadata and artifacts; auditing must be exported to the customer’s SIEM.

Onboarding checklist (sequence)

1. Kickoff call and scope confirmation (SRE + Customer infra)
2. Agree on identity model: OIDC vs KMS-wrapped key
3. Exchange evidence requirements and scheduling for telemetry sampling
4. Create/validate service account and least-privilege IAM policy
5. Smoke deploy to staging control plane
6. Validate telemetry ingest and evidence bundle collection
7. Sign-off and schedule production cutover

Service account configuration examples

- Example minimal IAM policy (pseudo-JSON):

{
  "Principal": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/redwood-operator",
  "Action": ["kms:Encrypt", "kms:Decrypt"],
  "Resource": "arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:123456789012:key/abcd-ef01"
}

- OIDC claim mapping (example)

claims:
  - sub: "service/redwood-operator"
  - aud: "redwood-private-deploy"
  - scope: "inference.read inference.write telemetry.push"

KMS boundary options and guidance

- Option A: Customer-managed KMS (recommended for regulated customers)\  - Customer retains key material in their KMS/HSM. Redwood receives a signed access grant restricted by time and operations.
  - Evidence requirements: KMS audit trail extract for the onboarding window and ongoing monthly snapshots.

- Option B: Redwood-managed key (only for low-risk, fast pilots)
  - Redwood operates keys and provides proof of controls, but customer cannot cryptographically assert exclusive control.

KMS evidence template (required fields)

- Key ID, alias, and creation time
- Grant ID and grant lifetime
- List of principals granted (ARNs or service-account names)
- Audit log excerpts showing: grant issuance, key usage, key rotation events during the onboarding window

Telemetry contract (what Redwood will provide)

1) Default sampling and retention for onboarding:
  - Request traces: 100% for the first 72 hours post-cutover, 10% after stabilization (configurable)\  - Token-level cost logs: sampled at 100% for the first 7 days, aggregated hourly afterwards\  - Host and GPU telemetry: 5s resolution metrics for first 24 hours, 30s after stabilization

2) Evidence bundle delivered to customer on request:
  - Structured JSON package including trace IDs, corresponding SLO violations, and associated model/version hashes for a selected period\  - CSV audit of service account operations against the KMS for the onboarding window

Recommended telemetry sampling YAML (example)

sampling:
  traces:
    initial_window: 72h
    initial_rate: 1.0
    sustained_rate: 0.10
  token_logs:
    initial_window: 168h
    initial_sample: 1.0
    sustained_aggregate: hourly
  host_metrics:
    initial_resolution: 5s
    sustained_resolution: 30s

SLA negotiation checklist (field checklist for SE/Sales)

- Latency SLOs (p50/p95/p99) by model family 
- Throughput targets (tokens/sec) per tenant
- Failover and fallback model budgets (how much degraded capacity is acceptable)
- Evidence-sharing cadence and retention windows
- Escalation path and on-call contact for both sides

Evidence delivery and packaging (operational steps)

1) Define evidence window and retention scope with customer (typically onboarding window + 30 days)\2) Redwood ops run automated evidence collector:
  - Collect: KMS audit exports, OIDC token exchange logs, telemetry traces, error traces, host metrics\  - Normalize into the Evidence Bundle format (see schema below)
3) Secure transfer: S3 pre-signed URL (customer-owned bucket) or direct SFTP to customer security appliance
4) Walkthrough session: Ops + customer security review the bundle and confirm conclusions

Evidence bundle schema (tabular view)

- file: metadata.json -- fields: customer_id, evidenceset_id, start_time, end_time, collector_version\- file: kms_audit.csv -- columns: timestamp, key_id, operation, principal, request_id\- file: traces.ndjson -- each line: {trace_id, span_list, timestamps, model_hash, route}

Rollback and emergency keys

- Pre-agreed rollback anchors: identify the timestamped artifact (model hash) and the routing config version to revert to in case of evidence-based rollback.
- Emergency key revocation: Customer must provide a documented emergency revocation procedure. Redwood validates revocation effects in a staging run before production enforcement.

Operational playbook snippets (commands)

- Validate OIDC assertion (example):
  curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "https://redwood-internal.example.com/oidc/validate" | jq .

- Export KMS audit (AWS CLI example):
  aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=ResourceName,AttributeValue=<key-arn> --start-time "2025-01-01T00:00:00Z" --end-time "2025-01-07T00:00:00Z" > kms_audit.json

Risk matrix and mitigations

- Risk: Mis-scoped service account grants
  - Likelihood: Medium
  - Impact: High\  - Mitigation: Automated least-privilege validator and manual peer review before production grant approval

- Risk: Telemetry PII leakage
  - Likelihood: Low
  - Impact: Critical\  - Mitigation: Default telemetry scrubbing and customer-provided redaction rules; evidence bundle redaction step before handoff

Appendices

A) Glossary of terms
  - Evidence Bundle: Structured package containing logs and artifacts for an onboarding window\  - Grant: A time-scoped permission in KMS that allows a principal to use a key

B) Contact matrix

- Redwood Solutions Engineer: se-team@redwood.example.com
- On-call Field Ops (weekdays): field-oncall@redwood.example.com
- Security owner: security-ops@redwood.example.com

C) Templates

- Service-account least-privilege checklist (copy into customer ticket):
  1. Principal identity (ARN/email)
  2. Allowed API actions (list)
  3. Allowed resource scope (key IDs, bucket ARNs)
  4. Rotation cadence and proof-of-rotation artifacts

- Evidence handoff email template (brief):
  Subject: Redwood onboarding evidence bundle for <customer> (window: YYYY-MM-DD to YYYY-MM-DD)
  Body: Attached is the evidence bundle requested. We are available to review the package on a recorded call.

Approval and sign-off

- Sign-off requires:
  1) SE confirmation of service account configuration (screenshot of IAM policy or IdP trust)
 2) Security confirmation of KMS/HSM evidence bundle review
 3) Customer signature on the production cutover checklist

Revision history

- 2024-05-15: Created by Maya Chen (initial draft)
- 2024-11-02: Added sampling recommendations and initial evidence schema (reviewed by Daniel Park)
- 2025-02-10: Clarified KMS grant templates and telemetry retention windows (reviewed by Priya Kapoor)

Related documents

- See also: customer-onboarding-deployment-readiness-and-risk-checklist-2026 (acceptance criteria and smoke tests)
- See also: private-deploy-operational-hardening-and-safe-migration-playbook-2026 (day-2 ops guidance)

End of playbook


[Private Deployments: Compliance Addendum + Packaging & Pricing Notes (Regulated Customers)]
## Purpose
These notes capture Redwood Inference’s current (internal) commercial constructs for **Redwood Dedicated** and **Redwood Private (VPC / on-prem)** when selling into regulated environments (financial services, healthcare/PHI-adjacent, insurance, etc.).

This page is intended for Sales, Deal Desk, Product, and Security partners supporting regulated opportunities. It is **not customer-facing**.

**Key goals:**
- Keep packaging consistent across deals while preserving flexibility for compliance-driven requirements.
- Provide clear guidance on when to involve **Legal** and/or **Security**.
- Prevent over-commitment on compliance claims and non-standard contract language.

---

## Definitions (internal)
- **Dedicated**: Redwood-managed dedicated GPU pools (single-tenant compute) with SLA-backed availability/latency targets; customer uses Redwood control plane and standard API surface.
- **Private (VPC)**: Private deployment into a customer-controlled VPC with customer-managed networking boundaries; control plane components may be isolated based on the offering.
- **Private (on-prem / air-gapped)**: Deployment into customer-controlled data center; higher implementation effort and strict change-control.
- **Compliance addendum**: Contract attachment covering security & compliance obligations beyond the standard MSA/DPA (e.g., audit logging expectations, retention configuration responsibilities, support response requirements, evidence sharing process).

---

## Recommended default packaging by regulated need
Use this table to anchor the first proposal. Deviations should be documented in the deal record and escalated per the **Approvals** section.

| Buyer requirement (common) | Best-fit offer | Notes / positioning |
|---|---|---|
| Data isolation + predictable throughput; minimal deployment complexity | Dedicated | Emphasize predictable throughput, operational tooling, and SLA. Data isolation is compute-level; data handling is per DPA + product controls. |
| Network boundary (VPC), strict access controls, auditability | Private (VPC) | Use when they require VPC egress controls, private endpoints, strict integration with customer IAM/KMS, and/or internal security review demands. |
| Air-gapped / no internet, on-prem data residency controls | Private (on-prem) | High-friction; require SE scoping + Legal/Security early. Confirm support model and upgrade cadence up front. |
| “Prove it” requirement before procurement | Dedicated or Private pilot | Use a time-boxed pilot with explicit success criteria and guardrails (credits, limited scope, defined evidence pack items). |

---

## Commercial components (what we sell)
### 1) Base commercial constructs
**Dedicated** (typical structure):
- **Reserved capacity commitment** (monthly/annual) tied to a defined GPU pool size and region.
- **SLA**: availability + support response commitments (see Support tiers).
- **Burst / overage**: optional, pre-approved ceilings (strongly preferred vs unbounded “best effort”).

**Private (VPC / on-prem)** (typical structure):
- **Platform fee** (annual) for Private deployment rights + control plane components.
- **Capacity commitment** (where applicable) for managed compute, or **customer-provided compute** for on-prem models.
- **Implementation / onboarding**: one-time fee may apply for complex networking, custom deployment topology, or on-prem installs.
- **Support tier requirement**: Private generally requires Enhanced or Enterprise support (see below).

### 2) Support tiers (packaging guidance)
Support is a primary lever for regulated deals; default to the lowest tier that satisfies buyer requirements, but do not under-sell support for Private.

| Tier (internal) | Typical fit | Standard commitments (guidance) |
|---|---|---|
| Standard | Dedicated (mid-market), lower-risk workloads | Business-hours support, best-effort guidance on questionnaires. Not recommended for on-prem. |
| Enhanced | Dedicated (regulated) and Private (VPC) | Faster response SLAs, escalation path, structured security questionnaire support, and coordination for evidence pack requests. |
| Enterprise | Private (VPC/on-prem), strict compliance programs | 24x7 coverage (where offered), named escalation path, incident comms coordination, and planned change windows for upgrades (esp. on-prem). |

**Notes:**
- Regulated buyers frequently interpret “support” as part of their compliance posture (incident response, breach notification coordination, audit evidence turnaround). Ensure the support tier aligns with contract language.
- If the prospect requests named resources (TAM/SA), treat as **Enterprise** (or add a paid add-on).

---

## Compliance add-ons (what we can package)
Use add-ons to align pricing to compliance-driven scope. Do not promise “included” work that creates ongoing obligations without commercial coverage.

### A) Compliance & evidence handling add-on
Use when buyers require repeatable, fast-turnaround responses and controlled evidence sharing.

Typically covers:
- Defined turnaround target for **security questionnaires** (e.g., initial response within X business days for standard sets).
- Access to the **evidence pack** via controlled distribution (NDA required; Security owns release).
- Support coordination for follow-up questions and audit artifacts.

**Important:** Evidence pack items are what exists today; do not commit to producing net-new audit artifacts without Security approval.

### B) Audit log export & retention controls add-on
Use when the buyer requires:
- Formal commitment to **audit log export** availability/format, or
- Enhanced retention configuration support beyond defaults.

Packaging notes:
- The product supports audit logs and export patterns; however, long-term retention is often shared responsibility (customer storage + Redwood services). Keep responsibilities explicit.
- If a customer requests a specific schema or SIEM integration as a deliverable, treat as paid professional services (or a scoped SOW).

### C) Key management integration add-on (KMS/HSM)
Use when a buyer requires:
- Customer-managed keys (CMK) integration beyond standard encryption controls,
- HSM-backed workflows, or
- Specific key rotation attestations.

Packaging notes:
- Confirm whether request is policy-level (documentation/attestation) vs engineering work.
- Any statement implying “customer exclusively controls keys such that Redwood cannot decrypt” must be reviewed by Security and Legal for accuracy.

### D) Data residency & regional isolation add-on
Use when the buyer requires:
- Region pinning, geo-fenced failover constraints, or
- Contractual commitments around where data is processed.

Packaging notes:
- Ensure the SLA/fallback narrative aligns with residency constraints (e.g., “no cross-region failover” may reduce availability options).
- Any hard residency commitment must be mirrored in the order form and the operational runbook.

---

## Retention controls: how to sell it without over-committing
Retention is frequently where regulated deals go sideways. Use the language below as internal guidance.

### What we can generally support (directionally)
- Configurable retention windows for certain logs/telemetry (product-dependent) and export to customer-controlled storage.
- Customer-controlled retention in their systems once exported.
- Clear policy documentation describing default retention and options.

### What requires escalation
Escalate to Security + Product if the customer requests:
- “Zero retention” guarantees (especially across all systems) or immediate deletion requirements.
- Custom retention by tenant sub-group, by field, or by request type.
- Contractual commitments that conflict with operational needs (incident investigations, abuse prevention, billing reconciliation).

### Shared responsibility (must be explicit)
For Private and regulated Dedicated, retention typically includes:
- **Redwood responsibilities:** product controls, configuration guidance, and documented defaults.
- **Customer responsibilities:** configuring export destinations, retaining exported data per policy, and setting internal access controls.

---

## Discounts, credits, and pilot guardrails (regulated ABM defaults)
Regulated pilots can consume disproportionate SE/Security/Legal bandwidth. Use guardrails:

- Prefer **time-boxed credits** tied to a defined success plan (workload + KPI + decision date).
- Require a **mutual action plan** before granting non-trivial credits.
- Avoid “free compliance” (evidence, custom contract terms, bespoke retention) without a clear path to paid production.

**Escalate for approval** when:
- Credits exceed the standard pilot range for the segment,
- The customer requests a discounted platform fee for Private,
- The buyer ties credits to security questionnaire turnaround SLAs.

---

## Contracting notes (what typically shows up in redlines)
Common regulated redlines and how to route them:

1) **DPA + data processing scope**
- Usually handled by Legal; Security may review technical accuracy.
- Confirm what data types are in scope (e.g., PHI-adjacent vs PHI) and ensure we do not accept unsupported commitments.

2) **Audit rights / onsite audits**
- Default to evidence pack + third-party reports.
- Onsite audits or bespoke audits require Legal + Security approval and commercial coverage.

3) **Incident response timelines and notification**
- Ensure incident notification language aligns with our operational process.
- Do not accept aggressive timelines without Security review.

4) **Subprocessors and infrastructure disclosures**
- Legal owns; Security supports with accurate lists and evidence pack references.

5) **SLA + service credits**
- Ensure SLA terms align to the selected deployment model (Dedicated vs Private VPC vs on-prem).
- On-prem often needs different language due to shared operational control.

---

## When to involve Legal / Security (routing rules)
### Engage Legal (Michael Grant / Sofia Mendes) when:
- Any non-standard MSA/DPA language is requested.
- Customer asks for liability changes, indemnities, audit rights, or bespoke confidentiality clauses.
- Data residency becomes a contractual commitment.
- The order form includes custom support obligations, response SLAs, or guaranteed evidence delivery dates.

### Engage Security (Dr. Aisha Rahman / Naomi Feldman / Olga Petrov) when:
- A customer asks for SOC2/ISO reports or any restricted evidence artifacts (Security controls distribution).
- There are detailed requirements around encryption/KMS/HSM, audit logging schemas, or retention guarantees.
- The customer requests completion of a security questionnaire with contractual attachment.
- Any marketing/sales claim risks over-stating posture (e.g., “HIPAA-ready” phrasing).

### Engage Product (Vivek Kulkarni / Lauren Bishop) when:
- Requests imply product gaps or roadmap commitments (e.g., new export formats, novel retention policies, SAML/SCIM edge cases).
- The deal requires a formal exception to standard packaging (e.g., Private without Enhanced support).

---

## Approvals and deal hygiene (required)
For regulated opportunities (Dedicated or Private), the following must be recorded in the CRM deal notes before final quote:
- Deployment model (Dedicated / Private VPC / on-prem)
- Data types in scope (e.g., “PHI-adjacent,” “PII,” “PCI-related metadata”)
- Required compliance artifacts (evidence pack items requested)
- Retention/residency constraints and whether they are contractual
- Support tier selected and why
- Any promised timelines for questionnaires/evidence

**Approval minimums (internal):**
- Any compliance add-on or non-standard retention commitment: Security + Legal sign-off.
- Any Private/on-prem deal: SE scoping + Product alignment + Legal review before the first redline cycle.

---

## Internal talk track (how to position packaging)
Use consistent framing:
- “Redwood is optimized for production inference economics with deployment flexibility (Hosted, Dedicated, Private). For regulated workloads, we align commercial packaging to the operational and compliance scope you need—support, evidence handling, and deployment boundaries—so commitments are clear and durable.”

Avoid:
- “We are certified for your specific regulation” (unless explicitly verified and approved).
- Absolute statements about “no data retention anywhere” or “we never have access to decrypted data” without Security-approved language.

---

- 2025-06-06: Added routing guidance for residency commitments and retention escalation; clarified add-on structure for evidence handling.
- 2025-05-10: Updated support tier guidance for Private VPC and on-prem.
- 2025-04-18: Initial publication for regulated ABM readiness.


[Tenant Service Discovery and Connection Contract for Private Deployments]
Overview:\n\nThis document defines the service discovery and connection contract that Redwood operators and customers must follow for Private deployments (VPC and on-prem). It establishes the canonical DNS patterns, connection semantics, security expectations (TLS/mTLS, ephemeral credentials, KMS boundaries), operational SLOs for connectivity, and automated acceptance tests used during onboarding and upgrades. The contract is intentionally prescriptive to ensure cross-team compatibility (runtime, control-plane, operator) and to make day‑2 operations deterministic.\n\nScope:\n- Applies to all Private deployment modes: VPC-hosted customers, dedicated on-prem appliances, and hybrid edge bridges managed by Redwood.\n- Covers control-plane endpoints, model-serving frontends, telemetry collectors, KV-cache replication endpoints, and operator-admin interfaces.\n- Does not cover customer internal-only services that are outside Redwood’s ingress/egress surface.\n\nDefinitions:\n- tenant-runtime: the per-tenant serving process (GPU-backed) that accepts API requests.\n- control-proxy: the control plane’s egress/ingress proxy used for model management and metrics.\n- mgmt-endpoint: operator-facing administrative endpoints (bastion/SSH, agent control).\n- service-fqdn: the fully-qualified domain name assigned to a Redwood service for a tenant.\n\nDesign principles:\n1) Explicit naming: every tenant-visible endpoint uses a stable service-fqdn. Names are immutable during a major release to avoid TTL/rotation issues.\n2) Small, well-defined port surface: minimize open ports to reduce attack surface and simplify firewall rules.\n3) Defense-in-depth: TLS mandatory, mTLS for operator/control channels, and ephemeral credentials for tenant APIs.\n4) Observable health: every service must expose a /healthz and a header-aware readiness endpoint.\n\nService FQDN and Port Matrix (required):\n| Logical service name | FQDN pattern (customer-visible) | Port | Protocol | SLO (connectivity) | Notes |\n| -------------------- | ------------------------------- | ---- | -------- | ------------------ | ----- |\n| tenant-api | tenant.<customer>.private.redwood.net | 443 | HTTPS (HTTP/2 allowed) | 99.95% p95 connect within 150ms | TLS1.3 required, ALPN h2 or http/1.1 |\n| control-proxy | control.<customer>.private.redwood.net | 8443 | mTLS (HTTP/2 preferred) | 99.99% p99 connect within 100ms | Client certs rotated monthly |\n| kv-replica | kv.<customer>.private.redwood.net | 7000 | TLS-wrapped TCP | 99.9% p95 connect within 200ms | One-way allowlist + port ACLs |\n| telemetry-ingest | telem-<customer>.collector.internal | 6514 | TLS (syslog/HTTPS) | 99.9% p95 connect within 250ms | Support sampling and backpressure headers |\n| operator-mgmt | mgmt-admin.<region>.redwoodops.internal | 22/8444 | SSH / HTTPS | 99.99% availability for operators | Access limited by operator VPN and RBAC |\n\nDNS and TTL rules:\n- Registered names must be CNAMEs to regional endpoints when possible to allow safe operator failover.\n- Default TTL: 60s for production tenant endpoints. Lower TTLs (30s) require explicit operator approval.\n- When rotating endpoints during deploy/upgrade, maintain old IPs for at least 2x max DNS TTL + 60s to ensure outstanding connections drain gracefully.\n\nFirewall and Network ACL expectations (customer + operator):\n1) Customer must permit outbound connections to required service FQDNs and ports listed above.\n2) Operator-provided peering or Transit must implement least-privilege ACLs: allow only listed source CIDRs and ports.\n3) For on-prem air-gapped sites using edge bridge, a one-way egress tunnel over TLS to telemetry-ingest is required; inbound connections are proxied via control-proxy.\n\nConnection semantics and timeouts:\n- Idle connection timeout (load-balancer): 300s for tenant-api; 60s for control-proxy.\n- Backend keepalive: runtime must support HTTP keepalive and connection reuse for serialized requests. Documented keepalive: 90s.\n- Client should implement exponential backoff with jitter for connection failures: base 200ms, cap 30s, max retries 3 for idempotent calls.\n- Health check expectations: 2 consecutive successful probes to mark healthy; 3 failed probes to mark unhealthy. Probe interval: 10s, timeout: 3s.\n\nSecurity and cryptography:\n- TLS minimum: TLS 1.3. Weak ciphers disabled.\n- mTLS required for control-proxy and operator-mgmt channels. Client certificates are issued by Redwood CA and rotated monthly.\n- Tenant API authentication: short-lived bearer tokens (recommended JWT with 15m lifetime) or ephemeral API keys issued by the control plane. Long-lived keys require explicit approval and key-scoped ACLs.\n- KMS boundary: all tenant secrets used to authenticate with model artifacts and S3-like stores must be secured by customer-managed KMS in Private deployments where requested. Provide KMS attestation URL in onboarding metadata.\n- HSM/KMS integration: for regulated customers requiring HSM, use dedicated KMS endpoints and the HSM workflow in the operator handoff checklist.\n\nAcceptance test suite (automated) — executed during onboarding and every major upgrade:\n1) DNS resolution test: resolve service-fqdn to at least one IP within 100ms from each configured customer region.\n2) TLS handshake test: establish TLS1.3 handshake and verify CA chain and certificate CN matches expected pattern.\n3) mTLS test: for control-proxy, present operator client cert and validate mutual handshake.\n4) Throughput smoke: send 100 concurrent small requests to tenant-api, verify 95% success within p95 latency threshold.\n5) KV replication spot-check: write/read pair to kv-replica and validate consistency at T+5s.\n6) Telemetry ingestion: send 1k events; assert no more than 0.5% lost and that ingest latency p95 < 1s for sampled events.\n\nOperator onboarding checklist (field copy for customer handoff):\n- Pre-installation:\n  1) Confirm CIDR lists and peering details with customer (attach signed connectivity matrix).\n  2) Validate KMS/HSM endpoints and token-scope policies.\n  3) Exchange root-of-trust thumbprints for CA (operator and customer).\n- Install/commission:\n  1) Provision CNAMEs and validate DNS TTL.\n  2) Install operator client certs and verify mTLS channel with control-proxy.\n  3) Run acceptance test suite and resolve any failures before cutover.\n- Post-cutover verification:\n  1) Monitor p95 connect latency and dropped-connections for 1h.\n  2) Verify telemetry sampling and cost-attribution headers are present.\n  3) Record evidence bundle (acceptance logs, DNS snapshot, cert chain) and attach to customer record.\n\nUpgrade and rollback implications for the contract:\n- Backwards compatibility: ensure new runtime or control-plane versions are compatible with existing service-fqdn and TLS expectations. Breaking changes to port/protocol require 60-day customer notice and a staged migration.\n- Rolling upgrade pattern: use CNAME shadowing and traffic-shifting so that a subset of tenants point to the new endpoint. Validate acceptance tests on shadowed tenants before broad roll.\n- Emergency rollback: operator must restore previous CNAME targets and reintroduce previous certificates into the trust store. Verify certificate validity and health checks before marking rollback complete.\n\nOperational SLOs and alerting thresholds (connectivity-focused):\n- Tenant API connectivity: availability 99.95% monthly; alert when per-tenant p95 connect latency exceeds 200ms for >5 minutes.\n- Control-proxy connectability: 99.99% monthly; page on p99 failures > 1 minute.\n- KV replication: replication lag < 500ms p95; page on sustained lag > 2s for > 10 minutes.\n\nTroubleshooting playbook (quick steps):\n1) DNS: confirm A/CNAME records and TTL; use dig +trace and validate from customer region.\n2) TLS: openssl s_client -connect <host>:443 -servername <host> -alpn h2 to check handshake details.\n3) mTLS: check cert chain and OCSP stapling; if cert mismatch, pull operator CA thumbprint from stored evidence.\n4) Network path: run traceroute, check peering ACLs and Transit logs for blocked ports.\n5) Observe agent logs in operator-mgmt and control-proxy for TLS alerting (e.g., SNI mismatch).\n\nSample terraform snippet (customer outbound security group):\n```hcl\nresource "aws_security_group_rule" "allow_redwood_tenant_api" {\n  type              = "egress"\n  from_port         = 443\n  to_port           = 443\n  protocol          = "tcp"\n  cidr_blocks       = ["10.0.0.0/8"]\n  description       = "Allow outbound HTTPS to tenant API (replace with Redwood FQDN IPs)"\n}\n```\n\nSample client connection YAML (runtime SDK configuration):\n```yaml\nruntime:\n  endpoint: "https://tenant.acme.private.redwood.net"\n  tls:\n    min_version: "TLS1.3"\n    alpn: ["h2","http/1.1"]\n  auth:\n    method: "ephemeral"\n    token_ttl: 900\n  timeouts:\n    connect_ms: 150\n    read_ms: 30000\n```\n\nEvidence and audit requirements:\n- Store acceptance test results, DNS snapshots, cert chains, and signed connectivity matrices for a minimum of 2 years for regulated customers.\n- For customers using customer-managed KMS, include KMS attestation URL in the evidence bundle.\n\nOwnership and contacts:\n- Author (design owner): Aisha Navarro (serving-runtime networkations).\n- Primary engineering contact: Miguel Santos (eng-private-deployments).\n- Oncall escalation: eng-sre rotation via PagerDuty (see internal rota page).\n\nAppendix — Common failure modes and mitigations:\n- Symptom: TLS handshake fails for some clients. Possible causes: SNI mismatch, missing ALPN, incomplete CA chain. Mitigation: validate cert CN/SAN, check ALPN values, reissue certs with proper SANs.\n- Symptom: Intermittent DNS resolution failures. Possible causes: TTL too low, recursive resolver caching misconfiguration. Mitigation: increase TTL to 60s, add secondary authoritative nameserver, monitor resolver error rates.\n- Symptom: KV replication lag on failover. Possible causes: network partition, CPU saturation on replicas. Mitigation: promote healthy replica, throttle warm writes, schedule replication catch-up window.\n\nReferences:\n- Deployment: private-deploy-operator-commissioning-cookbook (internal)\n- Reference architecture: edge-gateway-and-airgapped-bridge-architecture-2026\n- Security: onprem-runtime-protection-and-rollback-checklist-2026\n\nChange log:\n- 2025-03-12: Created initial draft.\n- 2025-11-02: Added telemetry and KV replication tests.\n- 2026-02-15: Hardened TLS/mTLS requirements and updated operator onboarding checklist.\n

[Emission Stability and Tool-Orchestration: Soft-Fail & Streaming Acceptance]
description:
PRD-style acceptance and behavioral specification for: (A) deterministic structured output envelopes during streaming, (B) robust tool/function-orchestration semantics when downstream tool calls fail or time out (soft-fail modes), and (C) observable signal set for debugging degraded emissions. This ticket captures requirements, tradeoffs, and concrete acceptance tests for engineering to implement and QA to validate.

background:
Teams integrating function-calls and streaming structured output have encountered brittle failure modes: partial JSON emissions, stuck streams when a tool times out, and unclear signals in telemetry for root-cause. Previous specs focused on schema handshakes but did not fully specify soft-fail policies (when to continue vs abort), how to surface partial-but-valid objects, or required observability for production troubleshooting.

goals:
1) Define deterministic envelope semantics so consumers can parse incrementally and resume/reconcile partial objects. 2) Specify soft-fail modes for tool invocation: best-effort, fallback-only, and abort. 3) Establish acceptance tests for streaming + tool failures that exercise backpressure, resumability, and idempotent retries. 4) Define telemetry and SLI/alert thresholds to detect degraded emission reliability.

scope:
- Streaming text and structured frames emitted from Redwood API. - Function/tool invocation lifecycle (invoke, success, failure, retry). - Soft-fail policies and configuration. - Acceptance criteria and end-to-end test matrix (simulated tool latencies/failures).

out_of_scope:
- Changes to client SDKs beyond minimal parsing guidance. - New RPC transport protocols. - Billing/quotas changes related to retries (handled by a separate billing review).

tradeoffs:
- Strict abort-on-tool-failure yields highest data correctness but reduces availability; soft-fail increases availability at the cost of accuracy. We recommend defaulting to best-effort-with-degraded-indicators for hosted API and offering strict-abort configuration for enterprise Dedicated/Private deployments. - Emitting placeholder fields vs removing the field: placeholder maintains schema shape for parsers but may surface misleading data. We prefer placeholder objects with explicit 'soft_fail' enum and provenance metadata.

acceptance_criteria:
AC-1: Incremental Envelope Parsing: Streaming responses are emitted as ordered 'frames' where each frame is a top-level JSON object stringified and newline-delimited. Consumers can reconstruct the final object by concatenating frames and applying frame-level 'commit' markers. In tests, a slow client that disconnects and reconnects using resume token can re-sync and reconstruct a consistent object state.
AC-2: Soft-Fail Modes: System exposes three modes: 'abort' (default for strict endpoints), 'best_effort' (continue emitting remaining structured fields, include 'soft_fail' markers), and 'degraded_fallback' (switch to cheaper model or cached result then emit). Implementation must allow per-route configuration. Acceptance tests must validate each mode against simulated downstream tool failures.
AC-3: Partial-Object Validity: When a tool call fails and mode is 'best_effort', the emitted structured object must remain JSON-parseable at frame boundaries and include an explicit 'provenance' map with keys: source_variant, tool_status, tool_error_code, soft_fail=true. Test harness validates JSON validity after each frame and final reconciliation produces a documented 'incomplete' state.
AC-4: Function-Invocation Idempotency & Retry Signals: Tool gateway must return idempotency token on initial invocation. Retries (automatic or client-initiated) must attach token to avoid duplicate side-effects. Acceptance tests include simulated at-least-once delivery and assert idempotent behavior for a provided sample tool (mock webhook that records invocations).
AC-5: Timeouts & Backpressure Behavior: When a tool exceeds configured timeout: - in 'abort' mode, the stream emits an error envelope and closes (status=closed, code=TOOL_TIMEOUT). - in 'best_effort', emit soft-fail metadata and continue. System must not indefinitely block other concurrent streams; load tests will simulate N=500 concurrent streams with 10% slow tool responses and verify 99th percentile latency SLOs remain within target with degraded outputs accounted for.
AC-6: Observability Signals: For every streaming emission that includes a soft-fail, the following telemetry events must be emitted: tool_invocation.start, tool_invocation.end (status), stream.frame.commit, stream.soft_fail.marker, stream.resume.attempt (if consumer reconnects). Each event includes trace_id and frame_offset. Acceptance: Kibana dashboards show these events for a 1-hour test run and an alert rule triggers when soft_fail_rate > 0.5% over 5 minutes for production routes.
AC-7: Compatibility with Existing Schema Negotiation: Handshake must include 'preferred_envelope' and 'resume_token' semantics. Acceptance tests exercise older clients by verifying graceful degradation: if preferred_envelope is unsupported, server falls back to newline-delimited JSON frames and includes a compatibility header explaining the downgrade.
AC-8: Test Harness & E2E Test Cases: Provide automated tests that simulate network partitions, tool errors (500, 429, 504), tool latency spikes, and partial stream consumption. Tests must assert that consumers receive either a valid final object or a documented incomplete object with soft_fail metadata in all tested modes.
AC-9: Docs & Examples: Console docs must include examples for parsing frames, handling soft_fail metadata, configuring per-route mode, and troubleshooting guide with representative log queries. Acceptance: docs reviewed and approved by Developer Experience and Design reviewers and linked in PR.
AC-10: Security & Compliance: When soft-fail includes tool error payloads, sensitive fields must be redacted per PII policy. Acceptance: static analysis and a sample audit record confirm PII redaction for tool error messages containing email/SSN-like patterns.

test_cases:
TC-1: Best-effort tool timeout: Start streaming generation that triggers a tool lookup that sleeps for 8s (config timeout 2s). Mode=best_effort. Expect frames including 'tool_status':'timeout' and 'soft_fail':"true"; final object parseable. Verify telemetry events emitted.
TC-2: Abort mode on rate-limit: Simulate tool returning 429. Mode=abort. Expect error envelope and stream close with code TOOL_RATE_LIMIT. Verify client-observed close code and server-side logs reference idempotency token.
TC-3: Resume after disconnect: Consumer reads first N frames then disconnects. Server persists resume_token. Consumer reconnects with token and receives frames from last commit point through final. Assert final object equivalent to continuous stream.
TC-4: Fallback variant switch: Mode=degraded_fallback. Downstream model returns non-responsive. Server emits warning frame, switches to cached summary variant, emits final object with 'source_variant':'cached-summary' and 'tool_error_code' annotated. Verify SLO accounting attributes.
TC-5: Idempotent webhook verification: Mock tool endpoint records invocations. Trigger multiple retries with the same idempotency token. Verify single recorded invocation and correct response to client of 'duplicate-suppressed' marker.

monitoring_and_telemetry:
Minimum telemetry must include trace_id, route, model_variant, frame_offset, resume_token, tool_invocation.id, tool_status, tool_error_code, latency_ms. Dashboards: streaming-frame-latency, soft-fail-rate, tool-timeout-trend. Alerts: soft_fail_rate>0.5% over 5m, resume_failure_rate>0.1% over 15m.

notes:
Implementation must include a clear config surface (route-level parameter 'tool_failure_policy' with enum values) and safe defaults for public API. Provide migration notes for existing routes currently using legacy streaming format.

[Constraint Synchronizer: decode sentinels & oscillation regression tests]
description:
Add a focused regression test suite that verifies recovery and deterministic behavior when the decoder oscillates between schema-compliant and non-compliant outputs in streaming + tool-calling scenarios. This ticket builds a harness that injects failures and tool-call interleavings, asserts telemetry events (sentinel triggers, decode backoffs), and validates downstream structured-output consumers (function callers, SDK parsers) see either a valid JSON payload or a clearly signaled graceful-degradation path.

background:
We have sporadic customer reports and internal CI flakiness where a streamed response begins emitting a valid JSON payload, then an in-flight tool call or a partial token error causes the model to emit additional tokens that break the schema. Existing suites cover many constrained-decoder paths but don't capture the specific 'oscillation' where the model flips compliance state mid-stream and then recovers or falls back. This causes downstream function-call handlers to either crash or silently drop important fields. The goal is to make these behaviors deterministic and observable in CI.

test_plan:
1) Implement a deterministic stream replayer that can inject: token drops, duplicate tokens, delayed tool-call sentinel chunks, and kernel-level backpressure events. 2) Create scenario matrix combining: short/long sequences, nested JSON objects, required vs optional fields, and function/tool call boundaries. 3) For each scenario assert: a) final output is schema-compliant OR b) a well-formed fallback marker is emitted ("__REDWOOD_JSON_FALLBACK") and partial structured data saved to a stable telemetry path. 4) Add flaky-tolerance thresholds: CI must fail only if >3% of runs deviate from expected recovery behavior across 50 runs. 5) Wire events to console rollup dashboard and alert rules for regressions.

acceptance_criteria:

[Cross-SDK conformance linter and invocation adapter with progressive stream recovery]
description:
Goal: ship a multi-language SDK feature set that (1) statically and at-runtime validates function/tool schemas against a lightweight conformance linter, (2) provides a small runtime invocation adapter that enforces safe coercions and idempotency tokens, and (3) improves streaming ergonomics by enabling progressive recovery and partial-result fallbacks when downstream tool calls fail. This ticket covers design, implementation, tests and rollout across Python/TypeScript/Go SDKs.

acceptance_criteria:
A conformance-linter CLI runs as a dev dependency and flags schema mismatches and unsupported types with clear error codes
SDK runtime adapters perform pre-invocation validation and emit structured telemetry for every validation and retry decision
Streaming call paths can resume from the last emitted checkpoint for partial tool responses and continue token streaming without full restart
End-to-end examples included in each SDK repo demonstrating: schema linting, safe coercion, idempotent retries, and progressive stream recovery
Performance: validation + lightweight adapter adds < 2ms median overhead to a cold function call in each SDK on our benchmark harness
Docs and migration guide published; migration tests for existing users pass in CI

implementation_notes:
Conformance linter: small TypeScript core that parses JSON Schema-like function specs and enforces a restricted subset (primitives, enums, arrays-of-primitives, structured objects up to 3 levels). Linter emits machine-readable diagnostics and suggested coercions
Runtime adapter: language-specific thin layer (Python/TS/Go) that accepts a function spec and incoming args, runs the linter in fast-mode, applies safe coercions (string->number, allow empty->null) when configured, and attaches an idempotency token header for retries
Streaming recovery: introduce a compact checkpoint framing inside streamed responses (checkpoint metadata + KV of last-processed-call), adapter keeps last-complete-checkpoint and can replay only missing segments to resume stream
Retry policy: progressive retries with three tiers: fast jittered short-backoff, durable backoff for transient infra, and fallback to model-only response when tool is unavailable. Each retry emits telemetry with outcome labels: recovered|degraded|failed
Telemetry: new event types: sdk.validation.error, sdk.validation.suggested_fix, sdk.invocation.retry, sdk.stream.checkpoint, sdk.invocation.fallback. Include token counts and timing buckets
Examples: produce 3 canonical examples per SDK repo: (a) statically lint + fix, (b) runtime coercion + idempotent retry after 409, (c) streaming tool that fails mid-stream and recovers from checkpoint
Interop: ensure TypeScript core can be consumed by Go/Python via prebuilt JSON diagnostics and a tiny language shim for runtime checks to avoid shipping full TypeScript runtime

testing_plan:
Unit tests for linter rules (positive/negative fixtures across languages)
Fuzz tests: random malformed schemas and argument payloads to verify linter stability
Integration tests: end-to-end calls against a local test tool service that can simulate partial failures, dropped connections, 5xxs and delayed responses
Load test: benchmark median overhead and p95 with and without adapters on our standard invocation harness
Chaos scenarios: network partition between SDK and tool; ensure checkpoint resume within 30s for streaming workloads
Compatibility tests: verify existing customers' schema files still pass with 'strict:false' mode enabled

rollout_steps:
Merge conformance linter to monorepo and publish npm package (internal alpha)
Publish language shims for Python and Go that call linter outputs and include runtime adapter
Publish Python/TS/Go SDK releases behind a feature flag: allow opt-in via SDK config
Run opt-in dogfood with 3 internal product teams for 2 weeks, gather telemetry and fix edgecases
Flip default to enabled in minor release after internal validation and docs complete
Announce migration guide and sample PRs in SDK repo READMEs

description:
Background: We need a safe, observable path to enforce typed/JSON contracts in streaming responses (JSON mode) without breaking SDK users or tool-calling workflows. This ticket defines a canary + telemetry gating plan for the "typed_contract_enforcer_v2" component that performs constrained decoding and schema validation at the serving layer. The goal is to enable strict mode for eligible traffic incrementally and gather robust signals to drive a full enforcement decision.

Out-of-scope for this ticket: model-level decoding changes (handled in a follow-up), long-lived audit log retention increase (separate infra ticket).

[Tool proxy contract and observable fallback criteria]
description:
Problem: downstream applications depend on deterministic structured responses and reliable tool/function invocation. When a model emits partial or malformed frames during streaming or when a tool bridge is slow/fails, caller services need a clear, observable, and testable fallback path. Goal: define an immutable contract for a tool-proxy layer + observable fallback behaviors so SDKs, Console, and Runtime can all react consistently (retry, degrade, surface error type, or route to fallback model variant).

background:
We already have multiple PM specs dealing with streamed schemas and tool handoffs; this work focuses on the middle layer (tool proxy/gateway) responsibilities: conformance checks, canonical error classification, telemetry events, and safe fallbacks without leaking internal state. Recent customer incidents highlighted three gaps: 1) inconsistent error coding across SDKs, 2) missing telemetry for partial-frame reconciliation, 3) ad-hoc fallback logic in applications. This PRD aims to centralize the contract and acceptance criteria so engineering can implement a single, testable behavior across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.

scope:
Define the tool-proxy API surface (request/response envelope) with fields for schema-version, trace-id, and confidence metadata
Specify streaming invariants and a minimal framing for partial/continuation objects that the proxy will validate
Enumerate canonical error classes (validation_failure, tool_timeout, tool_error, transient_network, incompat_schema) and the proxy's default actions
Define telemetry & tracing events emitted by the proxy (names, payload shapes, sampling rules) and Console dashboard KPIs
Acceptance tests: unit, integration (mock tool), end-to-end with SDKs and curl, and chaos tests for transient failures
Rollout plan including feature flag gating, canary percentage, and automatic fallback thresholds

out_of_scope:
Model-level generative corrections for malformed schema (e.g., model re-generation heuristics)
Custom per-customer tool adapters (these will be separate connectors)
Large-scale re-architecture of the retry subsystem unrelated to tool-proxy behavior

acceptance_criteria:
Contract: The tool-proxy accepts a normalized envelope with fields: request_id, schema_version, trace_id, client_hint, and tool_mapping. Any request missing request_id or schema_version is rejected with validation_failure (400) and emits telemetry event 'tool.proxy.request.invalid'
Streaming: Partial frames must be wrapped with 'frame_type' in { 'partial', 'checkpoint', 'final' }. The proxy will buffer partial frames up to 4KB/stream and emit 'structured.emit.partial' for each checkpoint. If 'final' isn't received within configured window (default 2s) the proxy classifies the stream as 'incomplete_stream' and follows fallback rules
Fallback default behavior: on tool_timeout the proxy returns a structured error object shaped to the requested schema with 'fallback': true and 'reason': 'tool_timeout' and emits 'tool.proxy.fallback' telemetry. For high-confidence, low-latency routes the proxy will optionally route to a model-variant fallback specified in routing policy
Idempotency: Retries initiated by the proxy must be idempotent. Proxy will attach an 'idempotency_key' to retried tool requests and record 'tool.proxy.retry' with retry_count in telemetry. Acceptance tests assert no duplicated side-effects in mock tool adapter
Error classification: Each failure must be mappable to one of the canonical classes. SDKs and Console will display the mapped class and suggested remediation. Acceptance verifies UI shows the correct class for injected failures
Observability: Proxy emits the following core events: 'tool.proxy.request.start', 'tool.proxy.request.end', 'tool.proxy.retry', 'tool.proxy.fallback', 'structured.emit.partial', 'structured.emit.final', 'structured.emit.reconcile'. Each event includes timestamp, request_id, trace_id, latency_ms, and error_class when applicable
Backpressure & flow control: When downstream tool processing is saturated, proxy responds with HTTP 429 and emits 'tool.proxy.backpressure'. Configurable queue_depth and backpressure thresholds must be honored in Dedicated and Private modes
SDK behavior: SDKs will interpret the structured error fallback and surface a deterministic object to developers (fields: error_class, fallback, suggested_action). Unit tests across Python/Node clients must pass
E2E regression: Create a CI job that runs synthetic workloads simulating partial frames, tool timeouts, and transient TCP drops. Regression must pass with no uncaught exceptions and correct telemetry emitted
Security: For Private deployments proxy must respect KMS-provided keys for signing request envelopes. Acceptance requires a basic KMS integration smoke test

success_metrics:
Reduction in customer-reported schema-mismatch incidents by >= 60% within two releases
>95% of failed tool calls are classified under a canonical error class and surfaced with a fallback object
Telemetry coverage: at least 90% of proxied requests emit both start and end events
Mean time to detect (MTTD) for incomplete streams decreases from current baseline by 50%

dependencies:
ENG-5022 (runtime: streaming frames buffer implementation)
ENG-5110 (observability: event ingestion schema changes)
ENG-5245 (SDK: structured error surface in Python/Node)
SEC-301 (KMS integration for Private deployments)

risks:
Mismatch between proxy-surface and various SDK versions could cause developer confusion — mitigation: compatibility tests and clear semver guarantees
Introducing buffering increases memory pressure on the proxy during high-concurrency bursts — mitigation: conservative defaults and queue_depth limits
Fallback to model variants may change output semantics leading to customer confusion — mitigation: label fallbacks clearly in telemetry and UI

rollout_plan:
Phase 1 (internal canary): deploy feature-flagged proxy to 5% of traffic in staging and run synthetic script for 48 hours
Phase 2 (customer canary): enable for 10 beta customers, monitor Console dashboard for errors and KPIs for one week
Phase 3 (gradual ramp): 20% -> 50% -> 100% over three weeks if KPI thresholds are met
Rollback: instant feature-flag removal and automatic route to prior behavior. Postmortem required if fallback rate > 5% after ramp

test_plan:
Unit tests for envelope validation and error-class mapping
Integration tests with mock tool adapter injecting timeouts, partial frames, and malformed frames
E2E with SDKs verifying deterministic structured fallback objects and no uncaught exceptions
Chaos test: simulate 10% packet loss and assert proxy remains within memory/latency SLOs
Observability test: validate event pipeline contains required fields and Console charts render sample data

notes:
Design has been discussed with Runtime and Observability on 2025-02-20; see meeting notes in Drive
Prefer a pragmatic initial schema_version 'v1' that can be extended; avoid complicated handshake for phase 1
PM request: keep fallback object minimal to avoid leaking internal tool error messages to customers

2025-03-03: Observability agreed on event names and minimal fields. Luc will publish event schema to ENG repo by 2025-03-07

[Unexpected 502/503 surge caused by ephemeral keepalive FD exhaustion during mixed embed+chat burst]
description:
Issue summary:
Customer (Acme AI, dedicated) reported a sudden increase in 502/503s on their chat+embedding mixed route between 13:12-13:40 UTC. Symptoms: short-lived streaming sessions intermittently fail with 502; concurrent embedding bulk uploads receive 503s and large tail latencies.

Impact:
- ~12% error rate spike (502/503) observed for tenant traffic for ~25 minutes.
- Affected production customers using mixed streaming + embedding workflows; high user-visible error rate for chat features.

Environment:
- prod us-east-1, dedicated pool for Acme AI.
- Ingress via api-gateway -> ephemeral-proxy -> serving-runtime (tenant-shared).

Steps to reproduce (approximate):
1) Start a steady stream of long-lived streaming connections (1s keepalive interval) from many clients (~200 concurrent).
2) Trigger a large embedding bulk upload (~8k vectors, multiplexed into a few large requests) simultaneously.
3) Observe apigw accept-queue growth, ephemeral-proxy FD counts rising, followed by upstream runtime resets and 502/503 propagation.

Logs / Observations at time of spike:
- api-gateway metrics: accept_queue_depth > 800, connection_accept_latency p95 increased from 4ms -> 220ms.
- ephemeral-proxy process (proxy-ephemeral-12) reported file descriptor count ~62k (soft limit 65k) and transient EMFILE errors in logs.
- kernel dmesg showed repeated "too many open files" on ephemeral proxy host during peak.
- serving-runtime logs show watchog-triggered restart messages and "upstream connection reset by peer" prior to 502s.
- netstat/lsof snapshots captured large number of CLOSE_WAIT and LONG_ESTABLISHED websockets tied to a small set of client IPs.

Immediate customer-visible impact: 502/503s and increased first-byte latency for mixed-route calls.


investigation_notes:
2026-03-13 13:20 UTC - Support: Customer reported elevated 502s on mixed-route; collected request IDs and sample timestamps.
2026-03-13 13:22 UTC - SRE: Pulled apigw accept-queue, proxy fd usage, and runtime restart counts. Accept queue overflow correlated with FD saturation on ephemeral proxy node 'proxy-ephemeral-12'.
2026-03-13 13:25 UTC - Observation: Large embedding worker triggered high outbound connections to runtimes while streaming connections kept many fds open (keepalive misconfiguration).
2026-03-13 13:27 UTC - Hypothesis A: Ephemeral proxy reached OS soft FD limit resulting in EMFILE and failing accept() calls -> api-gateway returned 502s.
2026-03-13 13:28 UTC - Hypothesis B: Serving runtime watchdog restarted GPUs due to increased NVME IO from embedding checkpointing, compounding upstream restarts.
2026-03-13 13:31 UTC - Evidence: dmesg and proxy logs show EMFILE; runtime restarts coincident but error traces point at connection drops rather than OOM in runtime. More likely proxy accept failures first.
Tools/commands used: ss -s, lsof -p <proxy_pid> | wc -l, /proc/<pid>/limits, kubectl logs proxy-ephemeral-12, apigw metrics dashboard (AcceptQueue, p95_accept_latency).
Metric snapshots: ephemeral-proxy fd_usage 96% at 13:24 UTC, accept_queue_depth spike between 13:20-13:30 UTC, serving-runtime restart_count +6 within 10 minutes.

actions_taken:
2026-03-13 13:26 UTC: Scaled ephemeral-proxy replicas +3 in us-east to relieve accept queue. Immediate partial reduction in accept queue depth.
2026-03-13 13:30 UTC: Applied temporary connection culling rule to drop idle streaming connections > 350s for Acme tenant to free FDs.
2026-03-13 13:33 UTC: Increased OS soft ulimit (nofile) on affected ephemeral proxy hosts from 65536 -> 131072 as emergency mitigation.
2026-03-13 13:40 UTC: Applied backpressure to embedding ingestion (rate limit client-side via edge) to reduce burst concurrency. Error rate fell back to baseline over ~8 minutes.
Customer communication: Sent interim update and workaround steps at 13:36 UTC; customer acknowledged and applied client-side rate limiting for bulk upload.

comments:
Maya Patel (Support) - 2026-03-13 13:18 UTC: Customer reported sudden chat failures and embedding timeouts. Collecting logs and request IDs.
Liam O'Connor (SRE) - 2026-03-13 13:24 UTC: Seeing high fd usage on proxy-ephemeral-12 and EMFILE in proxy logs. Scaling proxies now.
Diego Morales (Platform Eng) - 2026-03-13 13:29 UTC: Noted runtime restarts but stack traces indicate connection resets. Prioritizing proxy remediation and ulimit bump.
