resolution:
Mitigated (temporary): scaled proxy replicas, increased per-host nofile soft limit, and applied tenant connection cull and client-side rate limiting. Error rate returned to baseline by 13:48 UTC. Root cause appears to be ephemeral-proxy file descriptor exhaustion driven by long-lived streaming connections combined with high-concurrency embedding bursts. Upstream runtime restarts were secondary, caused by connection churn.

follow_up_actions:
Create infra ticket to add heuristics for automatic culling of stale streaming connections when FD usage exceeds threshold (INT-xxxxxx).
Permanent change: Raise default ephemeral-proxy nofile limits via bootstrap and add alert when fd_usage > 75% (owner: infra).
Add admission control for large embedding bulk uploads that detect concurrent long-lived streaming sessions and automatically stagger or queue requests (owner: serving-runtime).
Runbook update: Document mixed-workload acceptance criteria and emergency mitigation steps in Confluence runbook.
Postmortem: Draft and link a short postmortem summarizing timeline, root cause, and permanent remediation, target completion 2026-03-20.

notes:
This incident surfaced an operational gap where long-lived websocket/streaming sessions together with DoS-ish embedding bursts can exhaust FD capacity on proxy nodes. Consider prioritizing work that adds headroom and smarter shedding for mixed routes.

[Intermittent 502/503 errors during large embedding uploads due to chunked body aborts at API gateway]
description:
Issue summary:
Customer LexiconSoft reports elevated 502/503 errors and failed embedding upload jobs when sending large batched embedding payloads (~50–200MB) using our REST API over HTTP/2 with chunked transfer encoding. Errors began 2026-03-12 09:10 UTC after a gradual traffic increase.

Impact:
- Several customer embedding jobs failed (25% failure rate on a 40-job run).
- Increased API error-rate across their tenant (~P50->P95 error increase).
- Affects production P95 latency and caused retry storms from client side.

Environment:
- prod cluster in us-east-1; customer on enterprise plan with Dedicated routing to high-priority pool.
- Requests use HTTP/2 with chunked transfer-encoding and per-request streaming.
- Model: text-embedding-3-large pinned for this customer.

Observed behavior and tentative root cause hypothesis:
- API gateway logs show upstream proxy closing the request stream with 502 when the client finishes chunked body. Runtime logs show the runtime process logging: "ClientRequest aborted while reading request body" immediately followed by a worker restart in a subset of pods.
- Hypothesis: a mismatch in keepalive/read-timeout handling between apigw and runtime-proxy for large chunked uploads leads to the runtime aborting body read, causing the gateway to surface a 502. The abort path is triggering an upstream crash or worker restart under memory pressure when multiple concurrent large uploads coincide.

Steps to reproduce (internal):
1) Use a test client to POST 10 embedding batches of 1000 items each, chunked over HTTP/2 with ~10MB chunk sizes.
2) Target the LexiconSoft tenant route and run at concurrency 8 from 3 clients to simulate their sustained upload.
3) Observe apigw responses and runtime stderr. Reproduce reliably in ~4/10 runs in our staging cluster when configured with low keepalive (10s) and request read timeout of 30s.

Logs and metrics (samples):
- apigw: request_id=apigw-04b2c, upstream_status=502, upstream_message="upstream read aborted" (2026-03-12T09:17:32Z)
- runtime: [worker-7] ERROR: ClientRequest aborted during request body read (stack trace attached in ticket artifacts).
- k8s: OOM kill count on runtime pod remained 0, but rss spiked to 78% of memory before restart.
- traces: span shows request body finish event occurs after runtime has flagged EOF read timeout.

Temporary workaround provided to customer:
- Advise LexiconSoft to reduce chunk sizes to <2MB and use lower concurrency for bulk uploads. This reduces observed failures while we investigate. Customer accepted and confirmed temporary workaround on 2026-03-12 18:00 UTC.

Investigation notes:
- SRE reproduced the abort locally when apigw keepalive timeout set to 8–12s and runtime request-read timeout at 30s; extending the runtime read timeout to 120s eliminated the abort in repro.
- The runtime code path for chunked body parsing does not gracefully handle mid-stream connection resets and triggers an assert followed by an emergency worker restart in a race condition.
- The issue is amplified when multiple large uploads hit the same worker and memory footprint increases; while not OOM, the worker restarts during memory compaction cycles.
- No evidence of keystore/tls rotation involvement in initial repro.

Proposed immediate fixes:
- Backport hotfix to runtime-proxy to tolerate early client-side resets and return a 499-style response to apigw instead of triggering a worker restart. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/apigw/pull/2248 (in review).
- Adjust default request-read timeout in apigw->runtime route to 120s for large-upload routes and add a per-tenant override for enterprise customers.
- Add guardrails in runtime to avoid restart on client-abort during body read; convert assert to soft-fail with controlled resource cleanup.

Longer-term actions:
- Add end-to-end load test scenario for chunked/streamed large payloads and include in canary gating.
- Improve memory accounting for streaming workers and add an alert when rss > 70% sustained during large-upload windows.

Expected next steps and owners:
- SRE (Miguel Ortega): finish runtime hotfix review and deploy to canary by 2026-03-15.
- Runtime eng (Priya Ramesh): change assert-to-soft-fail, prepare postmortem draft.
- Support (Ava Chen): coordinate with LexiconSoft for gradual rollout and confirm fix impact.

Artifacts attached: stack traces (logs/stacktrace-221111.txt), apigw traces (traces/apigw-04b2c.json), reproduction script (scripts/repro_chunked_upload.sh).

[Intermittent 5xxs caused by API gateway thin-pool backlog and runtime eviction spikes]
description:
Issue summary: Customers (NovaAssist) observed intermittent 502/503 responses for generation and streaming endpoints across multiple tenants. The errors started during a midday traffic shift and clustered around a short period of sustained prefetch-heavy traffic.

Impact: Multiple requests returned 5xx (~2-4% error rate over a 30m window) resulting in degraded product experience for NovaAssist customers on dedicated capacity. Latency also increased for some long-poll streaming sessions.

Timeline: 2026-03-13 11:34 UTC - first reports from NovaAssist via support token. 11:40 - monitoring alert: apigw 5xx rate > 1.5%. 11:44 - SRE paged. 11:52 - temporary mitigation (rate-limits + scale) applied.

Environment: prod/us-east dedicated fleet for NovaAssist. Affected routes include /v1/generate and /v1/stream.

Steps to reproduce: 1) Reproduce traffic pattern: sustained prefetch + N concurrent long-lived streaming sessions (keepalive every 15s). 2) Observe apigw accept queue and thin-pool metrics rising. 3) Hit generation endpoint with medium-size prompts (avg 600 tokens).

Observed behavior: Apigw accept backlog increases to the configured thin-pool limit, new connections experience 502; serving-runtime shows GPU eviction spikes and several runtimes exited with SIGSEGV around the same window. Prefetch workers reported persistent thread exhaustion and high memory growth in heap profiles.

Expected behavior: Requests should be queued gracefully or retried without amplifying to runtime restarts. Runtime should avoid GPU eviction cycles under this load pattern.

Relevant logs/metrics: apigw.accept_queue.length spiked to 1200 (configured soft limit 1024); apigw.5xx_rate peaked at 3.9%. runtime.gpu.evictions spiked with correlating OOM logs and SIGSEGV stack dumps at 0x7fffa3. Heap profiles from prefetcher show sustained growth over 20 minutes.


investigation:
Initial hypothesis: combination of prefetch worker leak + connection backlog causing apigw thin-pool saturation which amplifies retries and forces the serving runtime into memory pressure and GPU eviction.

What we checked:
- Correlated apigw metrics with runtime restarts (trace id map).
- Collected heap profiles from prefetcher and runtime core dumps from the two affected containers. Heap profiles show unbounded list growth in prefetcher request context objects.
- Kernel logs show repeated NVidia driver notifications about memory pressure prior to evictions.
- Tracing indicates a high rate of prefix prefetch requests for NovaAssist tenant between 11:20-11:50 UTC.

Partial findings:
- Prefetcher threadpool saturated: live threads == max threads and queue length in worker pool trending to max backlog.
- Prefetcher memory retention appears to be caused by a not-cleared metadata cache (pat: prefetchCache.entries not trimmed under high-concurrency).
- Apigw thin-pool accept backlog fill resulted in 502 responses instead of graceful backpressure due to a short-circuit path in the proxy when backlog >= hard_limit.
- Runtime crash (SIGSEGV) likely secondary to GPU eviction under memory pressure; core dump suggests an invalid pointer in kv-cache eviction path (stack trace attached to INT-482).

Next investigative steps: enable verbose prefetcher GC logging for the pool, collect further heap profiles at 1m intervals, and reproduce in staging with a synthetic traffic script to validate the backlog->eviction path.

12:02 UTC - Scaled prefetcher worker pool for NovaAssist to 3x (temporary) to drain backlog

12:25 UTC - Adjusted apigw accept queue soft_limit to 2048 while we triage (temporary)
12:40 UTC - Opened PR https://github.com/redwood/serving-runtime/pull/658 to fix prefetchCache trimming and add defensive checks in kv-cache eviction

[Rapid 5xx spike after scheduler backoff + ephemeral proxy thundering during large embedding fanout]
description:
Issue summary: BrightWrite reports a sudden, sustained increase in 5xx responses (502/503) from their dedicated tenant beginning ~2026-03-13 09:22 UTC. The spike coincides with a large embedding upload + mixed small chat traffic. Impact: Customer-facing upload jobs failing, automated ingestion retries, and visible latency spikes for downstream queries. Environment: Dedicated tenant on prod - us-east with reserved capacity. Steps to reproduce: 1) Upload a large embeddings batch (~120k vectors) via embeddings endpoint 2) Simultaneously send small chat requests to the same tenant 3) Observe API gateway 502/503 errors and runtime restarts/logged backoffs. Recent changes: no customer model pin changes; autoscaler applied a scheduler backoff tweak earlier today. Logs: see attached SRE logs and proxy traces referenced in investigation notes. 

investigation_notes:
Correlation: 09:22 UTC aligns with scheduler config sweep (auto-rollout) that changed backoff reset window for prewarm probes in us-east cluster.
api-gateway metrics: accept_queue_length increased 8x; 502s originate from upstream connection resets and proxy workers reporting 'watchdog: worker exited (signal 9)'.
"nvml logs" show transient GPU memory fragmentation and a sequence of quick model prefetches from embeddings shard coordinator which coincided with high ephemeral-proxy CPU. (see github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/issue/987)
ephemeral-proxy behavior: high concurrency embedding uploads created many concurrent long-lived connections; scheduler backoff oscillation attempted rapid prewarm then backed off, resulting in connection pile-up and thundering-herd of ephemeral proxies trying to recover.
Heap/oom: Several runtime proxy workers exhibited OOM-like exit traces; container restarts caused upstream to drop connections, amplifying 502s at API gateway.
Hypothesis A: Scheduler backoff parameter change reduced the damping on prewarm probes, amplifying concurrent prefetches and causing ephemeral-proxy CPU/memory thrash leading to worker exits.
Hypothesis B: Embedding bulk upload pattern interacts poorly with streaming chat traffic (mix of long-lived and short-lived connections) causing accept-queue head-of-line blocking and upstream resets.
Short-term mitigations executed: tenant ingress rate cap applied; advised customer to reduce embedding upload concurrency; cleared prefetched KV cache entries for affected shard to reduce spike load.
Monitoring: set alerting on accept_queue growth (>200) and proxy worker exit rate (>5/min).

[Sustained 5xx elevation from asymmetric upstream restart and HTTP/2 stream-slot starvation during mixed embed/chat burst]
description:
Issue summary: Customers started seeing a sustained elevation in 5xx responses for streaming and short-chat requests beginning 2026-03-12 10:50 UTC. Errors primarily reported as 502/503 from the API gateway with 'upstream reset' and 'stream slot unavailable' symptoms.

Impact: NovaDocs (dedicated tenant) observed 30-45% error rate on streaming chat routes for ~2 hours, causing real user failures and increased retry traffic. Other tenants on the same pool experienced degraded tail latency.

Environment: prod/us-east, Dedicated GPU pool (reserved), hybrid streaming+embedding workload (mix ratio ~60/40).

Steps to reproduce:
1) Start a burst of concurrent streaming chat sessions (50-80 concurrent streams) mixed with medium-size embedding uploads (batch size ~128).
2) Observe API gateway returning intermittent 502/503 and aborts within 30s.
3) Checking runtime shows frequent short-lived restarts on a subset of replicas and many HTTP/2 streams stuck in HALF-CLOSED_LOCAL state.

Observed logs/snippets:
- apigw: "upstream reset before response completed" / "502 upstream connection reset"
- runtime: "runtime: panic at kv_prefetch.go:482" followed by fast restart and subsequent "http2: stream slot unavailable" warnings
- autoscaler: flurry of scale-up/scale-down events within 10m window (oscillation)

Customer notes: NovaDocs reported that failures aligned with a product campaign spike and asked for priority remediation and mitigation while we investigate.

Urgency: Customer-facing impact for a paying dedicated tenant during business hours. Escalated to SRE oncall.

comments:
2026-03-12 11:05 - NovaDocs (CS contact): 'We're seeing 50% of chat requests fail with 502s since ~10:50 UTC. Can you route us to another pool? This is blocking our customers.'
2026-03-12 11:12 - Support (Aisha Khan): Acknowledged. We're investigating and will provide mitigation steps within 15 minutes. Asked for tenant id and example request IDs.
2026-03-12 11:28 - SRE (Jonah Park): Early telemetry shows a localized restart pattern on 3/12 runtime replicas and HTTP/2 stream slot exhaustion. Temporarily routed NovaDocs to a warmed fallback pool and disabled hedged retries for their tenant. Error rate dropped to ~8% after routing change.
2026-03-12 12:10 - Support (Aisha Khan): Customer confirmed partial recovery after routing. They still see intermittent 503s on long-lived streams.
2026-03-12 13:40 - SRE (Jonah Park): Collected core dumps and runtime logs from affected replicas. Uploaded artifacts to internal S3: s3://redwood-incident/SUP-277338/ and created trace links. Hypothesis added to investigation notes.
2026-03-13 09:15 - Engineering (Priya Desai): Reproduced stream-slot leak locally with a mixed workload harness. Found a race in prefetch cancellation that prevented HTTP/2 stream closure on restart. Draft patch PR opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/2314
2026-03-14 08:30 - SRE (Jonah Park): Patch approved for canary rollout. Plan: deploy patch to 10% of pool, monitor stream slot metrics and 5xx rate for 30m before wider rollout.

investigation_notes:
Timeline of actions and findings:
- 10:50 UTC: Error elevation begins correlated with NovaDocs campaign spike.
- 11:00 UTC: API gateway shows high upstream reset rates and increased connection re-establishments.
- 11:12 UTC: SRE observed three runtime replicas restarting repeatedly; their restart cadence aligned with prefetch worker failures in logs.
- 11:30 UTC: Evidence of HTTP/2 stream slot saturation: large number of HALF-CLOSED_LOCAL streams around affected replicas, preventing new stream allocation.
- 11:40 UTC: Autoscaler reacted to perceived capacity shortage then backfilled; rapid scale events amplified the issue via transient cold starts.
Hypotheses considered:
H1: Runtime prefetch cancellation race causes panic and restart, leaving half-closed streams -> downstream apigw 502s (most likely).
H2: Autoscaler cooldown misconfiguration causing oscillation that amplifies transient restarts (contributor).
H3: Client retry amplification (hedged retries) increased concurrent open streams (contributor).
Evidence: core dumps show prefetch goroutine stack consistent with known race. Canary reproduction confirms leak under mixed streaming+embed load.
Temporary mitigations applied:
- Rerouted NovaDocs to warmed fallback pool which significantly reduced 5xx rate.
- Disabled hedged retries at the tenant-level for NovaDocs.
- Increased HTTP/2 max-concurrent-streams soft limit on the gateway for the pool to reduce immediate rejections.
Next steps: roll out runtime patch to fix prefetch cancellation, adjust autoscaler cooldowns to prevent oscillation, update hedged retry defaults and add tenant-level backoffs.
Monitoring: dashboards updated (grafana link: https://grafana.redwood/s/incident/SUP-277338), alert thresholds lowered for stream-slot utilization.

resolution:
Workaround implemented: NovaDocs routed to fallback pool and hedged retries disabled for the tenant; HTTP/2 soft limit temporarily increased.
Permanent fix: merged runtime patch to properly cancel prefetch and ensure stream closure (PR merged 2026-03-13). Canary rollout completed 2026-03-14 09:10 UTC with success (5xx down to baseline).
Follow-up actions assigned:
- Adjust autoscaler cooldown and add jitter to reduce oscillation (owner: infra-autoscale team).
- Add automated acceptance test in the mixed-workload harness to detect stream-slot leaks (owner: runtime QA).
- Update runbook with steps for tenant routing during asymmetric restarts and document hedged retry opt-outs for large embedding/chat mixes.
Customer communication: NovaDocs informed of mitigation and planned fixes. They requested postmortem and we agreed to provide within 3 business days.

Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-03
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Mercer (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Carlos Vega (Redwood Product), Samir Patel (NimbusApps CTO), Jordan Lee (NimbusApps Lead Eng), Maya Chen (NimbusApps Security), Terry Huang (NimbusApps PM)

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: alright hi everyone, thanks for taking time, this is Alex from Redwood Inference, I'm an AE, with me is Priya our SE and Carlos product, uh hi team
[00:08] Samir: hey thanks Alex, Samir here, quick note we have about 40 minutes, we'd like to see a live sandbox run and understand retry behavior, and also want to confirm we can meet our data residency needs
[00:18] Alex: yep perfect, we'll start with a quick orientation to the hosted API and console, then Priya will run a live sandbox demo showing streaming and parameter tweaks, and we'll finish with security stuff and next steps
[00:29] Jordan: cool, high level our use case is an in-app assistant with short back-and-forth conversations, sub 300ms median latency ideal, but we care about cost — we might favor smaller models if quality is good enough
[00:40] Priya: sounds good, thanks Jordan. quick housekeeping, the sandbox we'll use is rate-limited but mirrors prod behavior for streaming and retries. i'll open the playground now — one sec
[00:52] Speaker 1: (typing sounds)
[01:04] Priya: okay loading, i pasted an example chat payload. first thing — streaming: you'll see tokens arrive incrementally over a single SSE stream, that's what we call streaming; it reduces perceived latency since the client sees tokens earlier even if final generation takes longer
[01:18] Terry: question, does streaming hold any extra state on our side? like session cookies or KV cache?
[01:24] Priya: good question, streaming is just the output transport. the runtime still manages the KV cache per conversation if you enable it; that cache lives on the server side (redwood-managed for hosted) unless you run private. you can pin cache ttl or disable prefix caching if you need strict data controls
[01:39] Maya: when you say cache lives on server side — is it encrypted and is it surfaced in logs?
[01:45] Carlos: short answer: cache is encrypted at rest with KMS, and we do not persist raw user PII in audit logs; you can configure retention windows and we have an option to disable certain debugging logs. we'll follow up with the security docs
[01:58] Jordan: nice. back to streaming — can we do chunking instead? we have a websocket-based client that prefers discrete messages
[02:05] Priya: yes, you can consume via websockets or SSE and you can buffer into logical chunks client-side. the responses are the same, it's just transport. we also support callback webhooks if you want server-to-server delivery for completed outputs
[02:18] Samir: ok demo time if that's cool
[02:20] Priya: yep starting with a simple prompt: "You are an assistant that summarizes user messages in one sentence." i'll set temperature to 0.2 and max_tokens to 60. watch the stream
[02:34] [02:34] Priya: (sends request)
[02:38] [02:38] STREAM OUTPUT BEGIN
[02:38] Priya: "User asks for concise summary of meeting notes — assistant provides one-line recap with action items."
[02:44] [02:44] STREAM OUTPUT END
[02:45] Jordan: that was immediate, was it actually streaming or just small output?
[02:50] Priya: small output but still streaming. for longer outputs you'll see partial sentences come through every, say, 50-150 tokens depending on model and batch timing. the runtime tries to flush tokens frequently to reduce tail latency
[03:03] Terry: curious — how do you tune for cost? is temperature tied to cost?
[03:09] Priya: temperature affects randomness not cost. cost is primarily tokens (input + output) and the model choice/size. we recommend smaller quantized variants for high-volume assistant tasks. also prefix caching and batching help amortize cost across similar requests
[03:22] Alex: quick interjection, for your use case — if you have short back-and-forths, enabling conversation-level KV cache and a compact model often gives a good cost/latency tradeoff
[03:33] Samir: what's your recommended retry/backoff pattern if we see transient 503 or timeouts? we want to avoid duplicate messages in the app
[03:40] Priya: typical pattern: idempotency key per user-turn, exponential backoff with jitter, and use the request status endpoints to reconcile if you need strong exactly-once semantics. Redwood returns partial tokens on timeouts if the runtime was able to produce them; we document best-effort semantics — for critical flows we recommend server-side dedupe and using model-side stop tokens to mark completeness
[03:59] Jordan: can you show an example of a retry where the first attempt times out and we resume without double-processing?
[04:06] Priya: sure — i'll simulate a transient by throttling the sandbox to cause a timeout. i'll include an idempotency key in the header and then re-call. watch the IDs
[04:18] [04:18] Priya: (runs simulated request — network hiccup)
[04:28] Priya: first call returned 504 after 10s (sandbox threshold). our client then waited 1s + jitter and retried, the second call found a cached KV snapshot and continued, returning the missing tail tokens — you can avoid showing the duplicate prefix by reconciling using the last received token id or sequence number
[04:46] Samir: that makes sense. what about streaming partials — if a client disconnects mid-stream, do you keep the generation alive server-side?
[04:54] Priya: for hosted with default settings the generation continues for a short grace window and if the client reconnects with the same idempotency key you can resume; otherwise it may be GC'd. in private deployments customers can tune grace windows and longer-term retention policies
[05:10] Maya: from a security lens we need to make sure session data isn't kept longer than 24 hours — is that configurable?
[05:16] Carlos: yes retention is configurable per account and we can set a 24-hour TTL for KV and logs in the pilot. we'll include the configuration snippet in the security docs we share
[05:28] Terry: can you show the Console briefly — how we inspect per-route latency and cost?
[05:33] Alex: sure i'll switch to the console, give me a sec
[05:38] [05:38] Speaker 2: (screen share)
[05:44] Alex: here is the requests dashboard, you can filter by model, route, and time. per-route breakdown shows median/95p latency, token counts, and cost per 1k tokens. there's also a trace we can pull for a single request to see kernel selection and batching behavior
[05:58] Jordan: kernel selection? like GPU kernel?
[06:01] Carlos: yeah, that's an internal detail — the runtime picks optimized kernels based on sequence length and model profile, and you can see a label saying quant_fast or long-seq optimized. it's mostly for our internal tuning but helpful during perf debugging
[06:16] Samir: any hard guarantees on latency for hosted? we may need a 200ms p95 for short queries
[06:22] Priya: hosted has best-effort SLAs; for firm latency SLOs we recommend Dedicated with reserved capacity and pinned model variants. hosted usually hits low latency for small models but can't guarantee a fixed 200ms p95 under heavy bursty traffic
[06:36] Jordan: what about regional routing? can we force traffic to eu-west?
[06:40] Alex: yes you can set routing policy per API key to prefer a region; we also have fallback to nearest region if capacity is full. for strict data residency we offer Private (VPC) deployments
[06:50] Maya: does hosted support customer-managed KMS?
[06:53] Carlos: hosted supports customer-managed KMS integrations for encrypting customer keys, and you can bring your own key in Dedicated or Private as well
[07:02] Terry: any competitors we should know about? we evaluated OtherCloudAI; they had simpler pricing but not the same KV features
[07:09] Alex: yep OtherCloudAI was mentioned earlier, and OpenHost; our differentiator is the production-first controls and observability for inference economics
[07:18] Samir: let's return to parameters — show me how to tune for more deterministic replies, e.g., for legal-sounding copy
[07:24] Priya: set temperature to ~0, top_p can be left at 1.0 or reduced to 0.7 for tighter sampling. also control length with max_tokens and use stop sequences to prevent run-ons. i'll demonstrate with an example: prompt: "Draft a one-paragraph legal-style summary" temp 0.0, top_p 0.7
[07:42] [07:42] Priya: (sends request)
[07:46] [07:46] STREAM OUTPUT BEGIN
[07:46] Priya: "Pursuant to the agreement, the party shall..."
[07:52] [07:52] STREAM OUTPUT END
[07:53] Jordan: looks good — do you have built-in safety filters for hallucinations or PII redaction?
[07:59] Priya: we have content safety checks and optional PII detectors that can redact or flag outputs. for high-sensitivity workloads you can enable stricter filters and human-in-the-loop review hooks
[08:11] Maya: what's in the audit logs? do they include token-level content?
[08:15] Carlos: audit logs include metadata and request hashes by default; you can choose to enable full payload logging for debugging, but it's off by default and auditable. retention configurable
[08:25] Samir: any example of how retries affect cost? if we retry often won't we pay double tokens?
[08:31] Priya: yes retries can increase tokens if the model re-generates the same output; that's why idempotency keys and partial-token reconciliation help. we also recommend short client-side timeouts and backoff so retries occur only when truly necessary
[08:46] Terry: on the SDK side, how do we do streaming in our React native app? we use websockets already
[08:52] Priya: we'll share example snippets; basically open a websocket to /v1/streams with the api key, send the chat messages and read incremental events. SDKs have helper abstractions for reconciling streaming fragments and deduping duplicates
[09:05] [09:05] Speaker 1: (crosstalk)
[09:10] Alex: quick recap before we dive into a short benchmark — agreed next steps are: send sandbox creds, share security docs, run perf test and meet again; any other asks?
[09:20] Samir: can you include cost estimates for 5M tokens/month with a compact model vs large one?
[09:26] Alex: yes we'll include a cost comparison sheet and a recommended profile for your workload
[09:31] Jordan: ok let's run the perf — Priya can you run a 1-min 50-concurrency chat generator against the compact model so we can see latency and error rate?

[10:05] Priya: results: median latency 230ms, p95 420ms, error rate 2.5% (mostly induced by sandbox throttle). tokens per response avg 34. i'll capture the full CSV and upload to your CRM note

[10:51] Carlos: yes console supports canary rollouts per route with percentage traffic splits and automatic fallback rules if error > threshold. we'll include a short doc on rollouts

05:18 Diego: Two immediate knobs: increase background warm-up (keeps KV cache hot) and tune continuous batching window to bias for latency at the cost of some throughput. We can also enable prefix caching for sessionized flows which cuts tail.
05:32 Rajiv: Let's try warm-up and prefix cache first.

[00:00] Avery (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. I'm Avery, I'm the AE on this account, and with me is Devon, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?

[01:34] Devon: (typing) curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -d '{"stream":true,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Summarize this patient intake note"}]}'
[01:55] Speaker 1: And you get pieces back, so UI can render progressively.
[02:02] Carlos: How often are chunks flushed? Is that per token or per buffer?
[02:07] Devon: Good question. Our runtime flushes in micro-batches — typically every 50-250ms depending on model throughput and sequence length. We chunk on token groups rather than single tokens to avoid a flood of tiny events. So UX feels snappier but not janky.
[02:30] Maya: So if we need very low-latency single token streams for typing indicators, is that supported?
[02:36] Devon: You can tune that a bit by selecting a model variant and enabling low-latency mode, but you'll trade cost/throughput. For most apps we recommend batching slightly and using progressive partials. We also support pushing smaller chunk intervals at the SDK layer.
[02:53] Priya: When you say model variants, do you mean quantized variants on faster hardware? Will data leave our VPC?
[03:00] Devon: For hosted, data flows through Redwood's control plane in managed regions. We log minimal metadata unless you opt-in; payloads are encrypted in transit and at rest with customer-managed KMS options available for dedicated/private deployments. If you require full VPC-on-prem, that's our Private option.
[03:20] Maya: Ok that helps. Let's run the demo.

[04:45] Avery: On retries — for idempotency we recommend an idempotency key attached to the request. If a client times out, you can retry with the same key to avoid double charging or duplicate stateful outputs.

[05:02] Devon: Yes, idempotency is tracked at the request layer, not per model. If we fallback, the same idempotency key ensures you don't get two different completions counted as separate attempts.
[05:15] Maya: What about exponential backoff recommendations? Our infra team does 3 retries with jitter.

[05:35] Priya: Can you keep logs for audit? We need to show access logs for SOC 2.
[05:40] Avery: Yes, our Console has per-request logs with headers, token counts, redaction options, and audit trails. For SOC 2 we can provide attestation docs and configure long-term retention as an add-on.

[06:12] Carlos: On cost — how do streaming partials affect billing? Are partial tokens billed early?

[06:34] Maya: Can we see the console now?

[07:20] Maya: The per-token cost graph is handy. Does that reflect batching optimizations?

[07:38] Carlos: Tell me more about prefix caching. How is it invalidated?
[07:43] Devon: Prefix or KV caching stores repeated KV cache entries across requests for a specific model/version. It's invalidated on model rollout or if you explicitly purge. There are TTL controls too. We recommend careful prompt design to maximize cache hits.
[07:58] Maya: Does the customer need to change prompts to benefit?
[08:01] Devon: Often small changes help — moving static context to system messages, using placeholders for variables, that kind of thing.
[08:10] Priya: For PHI, we need to ensure we don't persist patient data. How does Redwood handle PII scrubbing?
[08:16] Avery: We offer redaction hooks and the ability to prevent payloads from being stored in logs. For hosted, you can opt-out of request body retention; for Dedicated/Private we can configure no retention at the request layer.
[08:30] Priya: Would that affect troubleshooting?

[08:39] Carlos: On a POC, we'd like to run a small benchmark across 1k sample prompts. How would you suggest we set that up?
[08:46] Devon: We'll provide a small script that runs async streaming calls and collects latency percentiles, token counts, and error rates. We'll tune concurrency and batch windows to match your expected workload.
[09:00] Maya: Great. Can you show retry failures?
[09:04] Devon: Simulating a timeout, client can retry with idempotency key. On the Console you'll see a single request record with attempt metadata. If it's a true server failure, the SDK surfaces an error code and you can retry per backoff policy.

[10:11] Devon: Typically the call payload comes at the end of the generation; the streaming layer streams tokens until it emits the function call event. The SDK surfaces that as a structured event.

[10:28] Devon: Use a guarded parser: buffer until final event or look for a clear delimiter/JSON fence. If your app needs early partials for UX, have a reconciliation pass when final token arrives.

[11:27] Devon: On a well-optimized variant, think 120-250ms per chunk and end-to-end about 400-800ms for 256 tokens depending on concurrency and hardware. For faster low-latency optimized variants, you might see ~200-400ms. These are rough; we'll provide bench scripts.

[12:13] Devon: Mobile has jitter and may break longer-lived connections; use reconnection tokens and idempotency to resume gracefully. Also prefer batched partials to reduce many tiny messages over flaky networks.

[03:18] Samir: So start with lower max_tokens and server-side stop sequences. Temperature/top_p mostly affect randomness not latency. [08:16] Samir: Hosted can scale horizontally but p95 300ms for complex models is challenging on large contexts. You have options: 1) dedicated pool sized for that SLO, 2) quantized/faster model variants, 3) prefix caching and batch warmers. For a 300ms p95 you'd likely want a dedicated plan or aggressive quantization plus warm workers. We'll run a benchmark with your prompts.

The goal is to converge on a deployable configuration, measure key SLOs, and produce a prioritized action list for a 30-day pilot. This is not a product training — it's a lightweight engineering lab to make deployment decisions.\n\nWhen to use this runbook:\n- Customer has completed initial discovery and shared sample traffic and data\n- Customer is evaluating Redwood Dedicated or Private for a constrained workload\n- The expected outcome is a signed pilot statement of work within 30 days or a clear next-step plan\n\nOutcomes dedicated-balanced, private-secure (slide snapshots)\n- Discuss trade-offs: latency, cost, operations, SLA\n\n01:00–01:40 — Live validation: smoke test and small-load run (40m)\n- Run 100–200 requests through chosen candidate; capture p50/p95, token counts, error rates\n- If Private/Dedicated is chosen, confirm container images, model artifacts, and KV cache settings\n\n01:40–02:10 — Breakout: / objective slide (Facilitator: one-line objective and acceptance criteria)\n2) Customer context & sample workload (Show dataset characteristics: avg tokens, 95th token length)\n3) Constraints & success metrics (Compliance, latency, budget)\n4) Candidate deployment configurations (Three succinct bullets per option; include a small pros/cons table)\n5) Instrumentation & measurement plan (Which metrics to capture and where: Console traces, token-level cost breakdown)\n6) Live test plan (What we'll run during the lab, duration, and expected observations)\n7) Tuning levers (Batch size, cache TTL, quantization level, beam width)\n8) Guardrails & security checks (KMS, network, data retention, model sandboxing)\n9) Pilot acceptance criteria & rollback policy (Concrete pass/fail tests)\n10) Action register and timeline (Owners, due dates, follow-ups)\n\nFacilitation checklist (for the SE lead):\n- Confirm all stakeholders are present and their roles are clear\n- Validate sample dataset has been uploaded and is accessible\n- Ensure the load generator and test harness are pre-configured (locally or cloud)\n- Provision a short-lived pilot environment (if required) with expected model artifact path\n- Create a shared doc link and start the action register early\n- Timebox each activity; call for a decision at 02:40 even if some items are open\n\nLive validation: quick run recipe (technical steps):\n1) Prepare 200 requests extracted from the provided dataset (preserve real token lengths)\n2) Warm-up: send 10 small requests to populate KV cache\n3) Run main trial at low concurrency (qps ~ expected avg) for 2 minutes; collect traces\n4) Run short burst trial at expected burst qps for 60s\n5) Collect logs, errors, and tail latency samples; snapshot model config (quantization, batch size)\n6) Run an AKS/terraform quick teardown if using ephemeral infra\n\nTuning exercise examples (for breakout groups):\n- Experiment A: increase batching from 8 -> 32; observe change in p95 and cost per token\n- Experiment B: enable prefix/KV cache TTL 30s -> 5m and observe downstream token savings\n- Experiment C: switch model variant (fp16 -> int8) and measure quality delta on 50 golden prompts\n\nQuality checks and A/B prompts (sample golden prompts):\n- Prompt 1 (clarity): \"Given this support transcript, suggest the top 3 next steps for the agent to resolve the issue\"\n- Prompt 2 (safety): Provide a phrase that contains PII and confirm the model redaction response\n- Prompt 3 (consistency): Re-run the same prompt twice to confirm deterministic behavior for cached prefixes\n\nAcceptance tests (pass/fail style):\n- Latency: p95 <= agreed threshold (e.g., 600ms) across representative traffic\n- Cost: estimated monthly token cost <= budget cap [POC Stakeholder Roleplay Runbook + Slide Skeleton]
summary:
A compact runbook and slide skeleton to run a 3-hour customer POC workshop focused on validating integration points, SLA expectations, and operational handoffs. Emphasis on stakeholder roleplay to flush out acceptance criteria, security concerns, and rollout constraints.

objectives:
Validate end-to-end call flow from product UI -> Redwood Hosted API -> backend
Surface non-functional requirements (latency, throughput, isolation) from customer stakeholders
Agree on success criteria and initial rollout plan (canary size, fallback)

agenda:
0:00 - Welcome, objectives, logistics (10m)
0:10 - Customer context walk-through (business goals, KPIs) (20m)
0:30 - Architecture walkthrough and integration assumptions (20m)
0:50 - Live roleplay: Product Manager (customer) vs Platform Engineer (redwood) scenario A (30m)
1:20 - Coffee break (10m)
1:30 - Breakout labs: teams prototype API calls and prompts (40m)
2:10 - Consolidation: present breakout outputs and failing cases (25m)
2:35 - Runbook and rollout agreement (15m)
2:50 - Next steps, owners, wrap-up (10m)

slide_outline:
Title + goals + logistics
Customer context snapshot (metrics, GDPR/PII notes)
Target architecture diagram (UI, proxy, Redwood routing, KMS)
Latency & throughput expectations table
Roleplay scenarios & scripts (2 slides)
Breakout lab instructions and success checklist
Risk matrix and mitigation playbook
Proposed rollout plan and measurement plan
Action owners and timeline

facilitation_notes:
Keep facilitation tight — roleplay scripts are lightweight prompts, not monologues. Before the roleplay, assign roles explicitly and give 3 minutes to skim scripts. If the roleplay stalls, prompt with escalation triggers: 'customer sees 600ms tail latency spike' or 'unexpected hallucination example' and force decisions (fallback to smaller model, enable reranking). Use the whiteboard to capture decisions with headings: Assumption, Decision, Owner. When technical questions arise that require follow-up (infra quotas, IAM policies, KMS), capture as Jira action immediately with a tentative SLA for response. Encourage customers to call out regulatory constraints early — treat PII/data residency as show-stoppers until validated. For breakouts, pair one customer engineer with one redwood SE — rotate at 20m if multiple teams. End each breakout with a one-slide summary sent to facilitator via Google Slides comment. Note: test demo endpoints before the session and have a static fallback demo (recorded) in case live infra flaps.

prework:
Customer: share sample payloads and expected output formats 48h prior
Redwood: provision demo key with restricted scope and send usage instructions 24h prior
All: fill quick context form (link in linked_artifacts) with contact list and escalation phone

success_criteria:
Customer can send a sample request and receive expected structured response within SLA window (p95 latency < 350ms)
Agreement on rollout guardrails (canary % and fallback triggers)
List of top 3 unresolved risks with owners and target remediation dates

materials_and_assets:
Roleplay script deck (speaker notes included)
Architecture diagram editable slide
Live demo API key (scoped)
Breakout lab notebook with example curl requests and prompts
Prebuilt error scenarios (handy for roleplay)
Recording consent form template

logistics:
Meeting room with projector + whiteboard. Virtual attendees: Zoom link provided in meeting invite. Reserve breakout rooms in Zoom for two concurrent labs. Catering: light snacks at 1:15pm. Bring a laptop with VPN access if on private deployment demos. Facilitator owns recording consent; record only parts agreed to by customer and mark sensitive slides as 'do not share' in deck comments.

risks_and_mitigations:
Live infra instability -> mitigation: switch to recorded demo and run the scripted failures for discussion
Data residency concerns -> mitigation: show private deployment options and KMS flow; mark as escalation for security team
Misaligned success criteria -> mitigation: run quick vote at 2:45 and convert top items into measurable Jira tickets

follow_up_actions:
Create Jira epic for POC with tech tasks and owners (due +3 days)
Security review kickoff if PII is involved (owner: Samir Gupta)
Provision dedicated demo capacity if throughput tests required (owner: Diego Alvarez)
Send slide deck and one-slide breakout summaries to attendees within 24h

notes_to_self:
Try the new 'small-batch demo' script that exercises prefix caching — it surfaced two sticky edge cases in internal dry run. Keep the roleplay prompts assertive so customers reveal constraints (e.g., "we must operate within 100ms for search box suggestions"). If time gets tight, drop architecture deep-dive and prioritize roleplay + breakout outcomes. Remember to ask legal for NDA template if customer requests recordings.

[Deployment decision canvas + facilitator notes for customer POC]
summary:
Working facilitator guide and slide outline to run a 3-hour customer workshop focused on finalizing model selection, routing/fallback policies, and acceptance criteria for a production POC. Emphasis on decisions that unblock engineering and SRE work for Dedicated or Private deployment.

agenda:
1) 0:00 - 0:15 Introductions & objectives: quick round, confirm outcomes
2) 0:15 - 0:40 Current state walkthrough (customer leads): data volume, latency needs, privacy constraints
3) 0:40 - 1:10 Model capabilities and tradeoffs: open models vs. quantized variants (team demo)
4) 1:10 - 1:30 Decision canvas activity: constraints, SLOs, cost targets (breakout)
5) 1:30 - 1:50 Break & capture parking lot
6) 1:50 - 2:30 Routing and fallback design: region routing, dedicated vs hosted, canary plan
7) 2:30 - 2:50 Acceptance criteria & metrics: test prompts, regressions, latency windows
8) 2:50 - 3:00 Next steps and action owners

slide_outline:
Slide 1: Workshop goals and success measures
Slide 2: Current architecture snapshot (customer-provided) - ask for missing pieces
Slide 3: Workload profile summary (QPS, token distribution, peak patterns)
Slide 4: Candidate models and perf summary (accuracy proxies, latency, cost/unit)
Slide 5: Decision canvas template - constraints, SLOs, risk tolerance, preferred topology
Slide 6: Routing strategy options with visuals (single-region, multi-region, hybrid)
Slide 7: Fallback & graceful degradation patterns (model downgraded variant, cached responses)
Slide 8: Canary testing plan - traffic percentages, duration, rollback triggers
Slide 9: Acceptance test rubric (exact-match, semantic similarity thresholds, latency p95)
Slide 10: Implementation checklist and owners
Slide 11: Parking lot and unanswered questions
Slide 12: Next steps and agreed milestones

facilitation_notes:
Start by validating objectives aloud. Use a 2-minute lightning round so everyone states one success metric. For the decision canvas activity: split into two breakout groups - product+customer-success in one, eng+SRE in the other. Give 12 minutes, then 6 minutes reporting back. Watch for micro-concerns around data residency - if raised, surface private deployment options and call out additional compliance tasks. For routing discussion: provide concrete examples (route 80% to dedicated pool, 20% to hosted fallback). Emphasize measurable rollback triggers: p95 latency > target by 20% for 5m, or error rate > 2% sustained 10m. Encourage writing acceptance prompts now; capture 6 canonical prompts that exercise edge-cases. Keep tempo: if debates run long, park details and decide owners to draft configs post-workshop. Note to facilitator: have access to cost calculator sheet, model perf table, and a whiteboard link. Keep end-time strict and assign action owners in the last 5 minutes.

materials_and_prep:
Pre-reads to send 48h before: 1) workload profile template (sheet), 2) short model perf matrix, 3) proposed decision canvas PDF. Bring laptop for live demo of 1 model variant. SRE should pre-populate current infra diagram. Bring the cost calc export (csv) and latest p99/p95 latency from observability console. Ask customer to identify 2 subject-matter SMEs and 1 network contact for private/VPC questions.

success_criteria:
- Agreement on 1 primary model variant for initial POC and 1 fallback variant
- Written acceptance test set (min 6 prompts) committed to the POC repo
- Owner assigned for routing policy, canary plan, and rollback triggers
- Draft deployment timeline with milestone dates (canary start, full rollout)
- Identified compliance blockers for Private deployment (if any)

open_questions:
- Does the customer require FIPS or specific KMS integration for the POC?
- What is the realistic monthly token budget they are willing to commit to for Dedicated capacity?
- Are there external latency constraints from downstream systems (e.g., synchronous user flows)?
- Is dataset for acceptance tests available and scrubbed for PII?

risks_and_mitigations:
Risk: Model quality regression after quantization. Mitigation: Hold a short eval sweep comparing full fp16 vs quantized on 300-case prompt set; require no more than X% drop in semantic similarity.
Risk: Network egress constraints for Private deployments. Mitigation: Engage infra/network early and provision VPC endpoints; allow hosted fallback for initial tests.
Risk: Cost overrun during canary. Mitigation: Cap traffic and use token budget alerts; scheduled automatic rollback if budget threshold hit.

next_steps:
1) Within 48h: facilitator to post workshop notes and raw decision canvases to Confluence and tag owners
2) Within 5 business days: engineering to produce deployment config draft for canary
3) Customer: share acceptance prompt set and scrubbed sample data
4) Schedule 30-min follow-up to finalize timeline and sign-off

notes_to_self:
Keep phrasing neutral when discussing model failures; avoid promising SLA-level latency during POC. If customer asks for benchmarks vs competitor X, offer to run a focused microbenchmark after the POC scope is agreed. Capture any specific phrasing the customer wants surfaced in user-facing docs.

[Anchored Scope & Readiness Lab — Customer Workshop Facilitation Guide]
Purpose:
This working guide is for a 3-hour customer-facing ‘Anchored Scope & Readiness Lab’ to accelerate alignment on production constraints, acceptance criteria, and the minimal POC that demonstrates deployment feasibility. Focus is on making trade-offs explicit (latency vs. cost vs. accuracy) and producing a concrete, timeboxed next-step plan that both engineering and product stakeholders can sign off on.

Audience:
- Customer engineering leads (2–4)
- Product/PM (1–2)
- Customer security/compliance rep (optional)
- Redwood SEs: facilitator + 1 technical lead + 1 solutions engineer

Pre-Work (sent 72h before):
- Intake form responses (system architecture diagram, expected QPS, SLOs, data sensitivity class). Link in linked_artifacts.
- Short sample payload (50–200 examples) and 3–5 hard success/failure cases.
- Customer to confirm which cloud/VPC/private deployment category they expect (hosted, dedicated, private).
- Redwood to prepare: model variant options (2), estimated baseline latency and cost table for those options, and a proposed fallback flow.

Agenda (3 hours) — timeboxed with outcomes:
0:00–0:15 — Welcome & Anchoring
- Quick intros, roles, constraints.
- Read out intake highlights (owner: Maya) and confirm missing assumptions.
Outcome: Shared list of unknowns to resolve during session.

0:15–0:45 — Business outcome & acceptance criteria workshop
- Round-robin: customer articulates success metrics (e.g., 95p latency, accuracy threshold, error tolerance).
- Capture primary/secondary KPIs and non-functional constraints (data residency, encryption, audit logs).
Outcome: Draft acceptance criteria (1–3 bullet KPIs).

0:45–1:15 — Technical surface mapping (whiteboard)
- Walk through customer architecture diagram. Identify ingress points, throughput expectations, request size distributions, and sensitive data flow.
- Annotate zones where Redwood components would sit (API gateway, routing policy, cache, KV store, models).
Outcome: Deployment topology sketch and integration checklist.

1:15–1:30 — Break

1:30–2:00 — Model and runtime tradeoff rapid teardown
- Present 2 model candidates (e.g., open Llama-variant quantized 4-bit vs. a slightly larger 8-bit variant) + a small hosted fallback. Include expected median p95 latencies and token cost estimates.
- Discuss impact of batching, caching, and KV reuse on latency/cost.
Facilitator note: show a simple table with 3 scenarios: low-latency, cost-optimized, mixed.
Outcome: Agreed primary runtime configuration for the POC plus fallback policy.

2:00–2:30 — Simulated request flow and failure modes
- Walk through 3 user stories with sample requests from pre-work. For each, simulate normal, high-load, and degraded network cases.
- Decide on graceful degradation policy (fallback model, regional reroute, capacity burst).
Outcome: Failure-mode playbook and guardrails for POC.

2:30–2:50 — Hands-on breakout: integration checklist & quick runbook
- Split into two breakout groups (customer infra + SEs). Produce a prioritized task list for the first 2-week POC sprint: infra hooks, secrets/KMS, sample data ingestion, telemetry hooks, success eval harness.
Outcome: Draft 10-item POC sprint backlog with owners and 2-week milestone.

2:50–3:00 — Close & Next Steps
- Confirm owners, quick wins, and date for POC kick-off. Capture any follow-ups and blockers.
Outcome: Signed-off POC charter and kick-off calendar invite.

Slide outline (6–8 slides) — presentable as a short deck
- Slide 1: Title + Objective + Attendees + Timebox
- Slide 2: Synthesis of intake (architecture, QPS, data sensitivity)
- Slide 3: Success metrics & acceptance criteria (visual KPIs)
- Slide 4: Candidate models/runtime options & quick tradeoff table (latency/cost/quality)
- Slide 5: Deployment topology sketch (where Redwood components live)
- Slide 6: Failure-mode playbook (3 scenarios + response)
- Slide 7: 2-week POC sprint backlog (prioritized tasks + owners)
- Slide 8: Sign-offs & next milestones

Facilitation notes & dos/don’ts:
- DO keep the group anchored to acceptance criteria; redirect tangents back to what will move the POC forward.
- DO surface assumptions explicitly and mark them ‘action item to validate’ if unresolved.
- DON’T design final security architecture in the session — capture constraints and schedule a follow-up with security SME.
- DO use timeboxes strictly for breakout exercises; assign a reporter to present outcomes.
- DO call out preferred endpoints for telemetry (e.g., Console route + Prometheus metric names) and confirm agreement to share test metrics during POC.
- DO keep language simple when discussing quantization/bit-width — customers often care about effects, not terminology.

Prep checklist for Redwood SEs (before session):
- Confirm intake diagram read and annotate questions.
- Build two concise model-option summaries with estimated latency/cost numbers.
- Prepare slide with 3-scenario cost/latency table.
- Template POC backlog (Jira ticket seed) and a short eval harness (script skeleton) for quality checks.
- Create a telemetry sample dashboard link and demo data to show during session.

Artifacts produced during session (expected):
- Signed POC charter (one-paragraph objective + 3 acceptance criteria)
- 2-week POC backlog exported to Jira/Linear (10 items)
- Topology sketch image (png) and a short failure-mode playbook doc
- Owner list and scheduled kick-off meeting invite

Common risks & mitigations:
- Risk: Customer cannot share realistic sample data (Mitigation: use synthetic-but-structured payloads and flag evaluation caveats).
- Risk: Security/compliance blockers surface late (Mitigation: identify early and escalate to security SME; offer a dedicated private-deploy discovery session).
- Risk: Expectation mismatch on what POC proves (Mitigation: make acceptance criteria explicit in charter and get signatures).

Follow-ups & success criteria for REDWOOD internal tracking:
- POC kickoff occurred within 7 days of workshop.
- First smoke test (end-to-end request) within 10 days.
- Telemetry streaming with baseline metrics within 14 days.
- Customer verifies at least one acceptance KPI by end of POC sprint.

Appendix: Sample prompts / test cases (from customer pre-work)
- Prompt A (support chat): "Customer: I can't see my billing invoice for March. Assistant: Provide the path and ask for verification details." Expected: Structured response with invoice path + next steps.
- Prompt B (summary): "Summarize the attached policy doc to an executive in 3 bullets." Expected: High-level summary; accuracy checks against 3 anchor sentences.
- Prompt C (classification): "Given user message, return category: billing|technical|other." Expected: >95% agreement with human labels.

Notes about uniqueness of POC deliverable:
- Emphasize that the deliverable is not a full production integration but a validated path with a reproducible smoke-test, telemetry, and a measurable acceptance rubric.
- Keep the POC narrow: instrument one route end-to-end and validate one or two KPIs rather than attempting a complete migration.

Contact & escalation:
- Primary SE: Maya Chen (maya@redwood.ai)
- Technical lead: Evan Malik (evan@redwood.ai)
- Solutions lead for deployment: Priya Singh (priya@redwood.ai)

End of working guide.

summary:
Working playbook for a 3-hour customer-facing workshop focused on evaluating embedding quality, latency/cost tradeoffs, and designing fallback strategies for production POCs. Includes agenda, slide skeleton, facilitator prompts, risk checklist, and next-step acceptance criteria.

agenda:
0:00-0:10 — Welcome, objectives, success criteria (host + customer expectations)
0:10-0:25 — Current architecture & dataset overview (customer presents quick snapshot)
0:25-0:60 — Embedding quality primer: metrics and failure modes (short lecture + Q&A)
0:60-1:25 — Hands-on eval: sample queries vs candidate embedding configs (paired exercise)
1:25-1:40 — Break / quick sync
1:40-2:05 — Latency/cost tradeoff lab: quantization, batch sizing, and retrieval caching
2:05-2:35 — Fallback design session: policy sketch (region/model/approximate retrieval fallbacks)
2:35-2:50 — Runbook & monitoring quick-draft (what to alert on, SLOs, signal dashboards)
2:50-3:00 — Close: decisions, owners, immediate next steps, and success criteria for POC go/no-go

slide_outline:
Title: Embedding Eval & Graceful Fallbacks — Workshop
Slide 1: Goals & success metrics (Precision@k, R@k, latency p95, cost per 1M queries)
Slide 2: Customer data snapshot (corpora size, average doc length, typical query patterns)
Slide 3: Embedding options we’ll test (open models, quantized variants, dimensionality)
Slide 4: Retrieval stack diagram (ingest -> vector DB -> candidate rerank -> app), where Redwood fits
Slide 5: Failure modes and observable signals (stale vectors, hallucinations, P99 latency spikes)
Slide 6: Hands-on exercise instructions & expected outputs
Slide 7: Latency vs cost lever map (batching, async vs sync, caching, smaller models)

Slide 9: Monitoring & alerting checklist (example metrics and threshold guidance)
Slide 10: POC acceptance criteria and next steps

facilitator_notes:
Before the session: request 3 representative user queries + 200 sample docs from the customer (anonymized). Precompute a baseline embedding snapshot so the hands-on flows start fast.
Kickoff: be explicit about what we can and cannot prove in a single session. Align on what 'success' looks like (e.g., >0.7 P@10 on key user queries, p95 retrieval < 120ms).
During hands-on: split attendees into two teams — one focuses on quality (different embedder configs), other on infra (latency/cost).
Keep a running living doc of observed failure cases (copy rows: query, expected doc, retrieved doc, notes). This becomes the initial eval prompt set.
If vector DB access is slow, switch to local approximate ANN (FAISS) fallback demo — show how recall changes but latency improves.
For the fallback session: use a simple decision tree template (region/availability model) rather than trying to engineer a full state machine in-session.
Timebox every activity. If exercises slip, skip deeper parameter sweeps and capture configs to test post-workshop.
End with concrete owners and a 2-week checklist: ingest pipeline, index refresh policy, monitoring dashboard, and a smoke-test harness for canary releases.

prep_actions:
Ask customer for dataset + sample queries 5 business days prior
Precompute baseline embeddings (3 model variants) and a performance snapshot
Provision a small vector DB instance with chosen index types and preload samples
Prepare a short demo notebook (Colab or internal notebook) that reproduces top-3 flows
Create workshop slide deck from skeleton and share with customer 48 hours before
Confirm attendees and roles (POC owner, data owner, infra owner, two engineers for hands-on)

breakout_tasks:
Quality team: run P@5 and MRR on 20 golden queries across three embedding configs
Infra team: measure p50/p95 retrieval with different index params and batch sizes
Policy team: sketch a simple fallback decision tree and list required signals for routing
SEs: capture 5 reproducible failure examples to add to regression test set
Product: draft provisional acceptance criteria and rollout gating conditions

runbook_checklist:
POC owner assigned (customer + Redwood SE contact)
Baseline evaluation dataset and golden queries stored in repo/drive
Vector DB config exported (index type, ef/search params, distance metric)
Embedding model versions pinned and artifacts stored (with quantization metadata)
Cache policy documented (prefix caching, TTLs, cache warm strategy)
Fallback policies defined and sanity-tested (ANN -> smaller model -> cached answer)
SLOs defined for retrieval latency, overall end-to-end p95, and quality metrics to track
Alerting knobs configured (e.g., recall drop > X% over 1h, retrieval latency > 2x baseline)
Smoke test harness: automated queries with expected top-3 IDs and tolerance thresholds
Security review checklist (PII in docs, key management for embeddings if customer requires)
Stakeholder cadence defined (weekly sync + a 30-day review)

risk_mitigation:
Data availability: if sample data is delayed, use synthetic but realistic corpora and mark results as provisional
Latency surprises: prepare a cached-demo fallback for the demo path so UX does not break during session

Security concerns: always offer a private-run option or redaction script if customer refuses to upload raw docs

Latency: End-to-end median retrieval for common queries < target (customer-specific; default 80ms), p95 < 300ms
Cost: Estimate for steady-state < agreed budget band or a documented plan to optimize
Observability: Dashboard with recall/latency/cost visible and alerts wired
Fallbacks: At least one tested fallback path with documented behavior and owner

[Kernel Snapshot Observability Contract and Diagnostic Playbook]
Summary:
This page defines the Kernel Snapshot Observability Contract used by the serving runtime to capture lightweight, deterministic kernel-level state for fast post-hoc diagnostics, profiling correlation, and benchmark reproducibility. The contract describes snapshot contents, TTL/retention semantics, collection cadence, storage indexing, query semantics, and the recommended operational playbook for using snapshots during incidents and regressions.

Why we need a formal contract:
- Reduce triage time: snapshots provide a small, self-contained view of kernel scheduling state across shards without requiring full traces.
- Reproducible regression hunts: standardized fields make automated delta comparison (hashes/digests) possible across releases and benchmarks.
- Safe production capture: contract enforces size and cost limits to keep collection cheap and non-disruptive.

Scope and goals:
- Scope: GPU-scheduling kernels, kernel selector hints, active batch queue heads, kvcache hot entries metadata, and per-request token-progress markers. Not intended to replace full GPU traces or perf counters.
- Goals: <= 2KB compressed per snapshot per shard typical, capture latency < 5ms end-to-end, snapshot ingestion availability 99.9%.

Contract: snapshot manifest fields (string names and semantic description)
- manifest_type: "kernel-snapshot-v1" (identifies schema version).
- timestamp_utc: RFC3339 string (origin of capture).
- host_id: runtime host identifier (short hash).
- shard_id: logical shard name/id.
- kernel_hint: canonical kernel name in scheduler (e.g. "attn_sharded_kv_v2").
- active_requests: comma-separated list of up to 8 request_ids with short metadata (see Active Request Encoding below).
- batch_head_shape: concurrency/sequence-length tuple (e.g. "concurrency=12;avg_seq=128").
- kv_hot_prefix_digest: 64-bit hex digest of most-frequent KV prefixes (comma-separated up to 4).
- queue_depth: integer (number of queued kernel tasks).
- slot_usage_pct: integer 0-100 (measured GPU slot occupancy estimate).
- mem_watermark_mb: integer (resident MB attributed to shard at capture).
- fallback_flags: short tokenized list of active degradation flags (e.g. "quantized-fallback,eviction-throttle").
- capture_id: uuid string (unique id for this snapshot).
- sample_hash: sha1 hex of the canonicalized manifest (for fast equality checks).

Active Request Encoding (embedded): up to 8 items, each encoded as colon-separated tokens: request_id|model:ver|priority|est_remaining_tokens
Example: "r1234|redwood/7b:2026-03-01|p2|est32"

Size and performance constraints:
- Uncompressed manifest must be <= 8KB. Producers MUST gzip the payload before upload.
- Capture must be non-blocking for request latency: producers should sample at scheduling safe points (e.g. pre-dispatch / post-eviction) and limit synchronous work to timestamping and copying small metadata.
- Max capture cadence per shard: 1 snapshot / 5s by default; bursts up to 1/second allowed during active debugging windows.

Capture lifecycle and TTL semantics:
- Local ephemeral cache: snapshots are kept in-memory for 30s to enable immediate correlation with live traces.
- Short-term storage: snapshots forwarded to an indexed store with 7-day retention for operational triage.
- Long-term archive: on-demand (by capture_id or sample_hash) snapshots older than 7 days may be kept in cold archive for 90 days if pinned by a runbook or regression alert.
- Automatic eviction: snapshots exceeding store quotas are evicted by oldest-first per-host.

Storage & indexing conventions:
- Index keys: sample_hash, capture_id, host_id, shard_id, kernel_hint, timestamp_utc.
- Tags: release_tag (e.g. "canary-2026-03-10"), experiment_id (if collection was triggered by an experiment), incident_id (if captured during an incident).
- Searchable fields must be text-tokenized and exact-match filterable for sample_hash and kernel_hint.

Producer responsibilities and API contract:
1) Capture API (local agent): POST /v1/internal/kernel-snapshot 
   - Headers: X-Host-ID, X-Shard-ID, X-Capture-Src (auto|manual|diag).
   - Body: gzip'd manifest (UTF-8).
   - Response: 202 Accepted with JSON {"capture_id":"...","sample_hash":"...","ingest_ts":"..."}.
2) Backoff: if remote ingestion errors with 5xx more than 3 consecutive times, agent falls back to local retention only and emits metric runtime.snapshot.ingest.failures.
3) Priority: manual-triggered captures (via runbook) should include X-Capture-Priority: high and are exempt from per-shard cadence limits for a 60s window.

Query and diagnosis workflow (runbook):
1) Triage start: on a latency SLO violation or kernel regression alert, runbook owner initiates "snapshot-hunt".
2) Retrieve matching snapshots by filter: sample_hash, kernel_hint, timeframe, release_tag.
3) Run a delta comparison on sample_hash across canary vs baseline to find divergence.
4) If sample_hash matches but incident persists, escalate to full trace capture: enable continuous tracing for affected shards (see profiling-playbook integration below).

Integration with profiling playbooks and benchmarking suite:
- Profiling correlation: snapshots are lightweight keys to join streaming traces and microbenchmarks. Include capture_id in trace span attribute: runtime.kernel_snapshot.capture_id.
- Benchmark gating: nightly benchmarks must capture a deterministic snapshot for each workload and store sample_hash in benchmark results CSV. Regression rule: any benchmark run where the sample_hash distribution differs from baseline for > 20% of shards triggers a quality alert.
- Kernel scheduler experiments: when rolling out kernel changes, collect snapshot cohorts (baseline/canary) and run a pairwise hash-difference analysis as part of the release checklist.

Release gating checklist (minimum):
- Collect cohort snapshots for baseline and canary for 24 hours with at least 1000 snapshots per cohort.
- Run automated sample_hash cluster analysis and ensure no new kernel_hint set appears in >5% of canary shards unless intentionally rolled out.
- Verify average slot_usage_pct and queue_depth remain within +/- 10% of baseline.
- Sign-off required by runtime-scheduling and profiling owners.

Alerting and SLOs:
- Metric: runtime.snapshot.ingest.latency_p50 < 30ms, p95 < 100ms.
- Metric: runtime.snapshot.size_bytes_p95 < 4096 bytes compressed.
- Alert: snapshot-ingest-error-rate > 0.5% sustained for 5m -> paging to infra-oncall.
- Alert: sample_hash-drift-score > 0.2 across canary vs baseline -> notify runtime-release-team.

Known limitations and mitigations:
- Not a full trace: snapshots are intentionally small and do not include per-kernel GPU counters. Use them to triage and then escalate to detailed tracing.
- Digest collisions: sample_hash uses sha1 of a canonicalized manifest; collisions are possible but extremely unlikely. If collision suspected, attach raw manifest comparison.
- Cost: high-frequency snapshots across all shards increase storage costs; default cadence and burst limits are enforced by agents.

Operational playbook: incident example (step-by-step)
1) Pager fires for high tail latency on model X.
2) Oncall: run "snapshot-query --kernel attn_sharded_kv_v2 --since 5m --format table" across implicated shards.
3) If sample_hash variance high between recently-deployed canary and baseline: run pairwise-diff tool and note differing fields.
4) If mem_watermark_mb spike correlates with queue_depth rise -> trigger immediate spillover rollback (see runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook).
5) Capture extended traces for 10 minutes and mark capture_ids of interest.

CLI examples and snippets:
- Query tool (example):

  snapshot-query --kernel "attn_sharded_kv_v2" --since "2026-05-01T12:00:00Z" --limit 200 --output json

- Minimal producer example (bash curl):
