[forensic-telemetry-snapshotting-and-slo-evidence-retention-policy-2023]
Overview
========

Purpose: Define a reproducible, cost-aware process for capturing forensic telemetry snapshots that provide SLO-related evidence for incident review, post-incident analysis, and regulatory audit. This policy aligns retention windows for metrics, traces, logs, and request-level artifacts with incident severity, SLO class, and cost budget.

Scope: Applies to all services that carry an explicit SLO in the model-serving and routing stack (platform services, model inference, request-queueing, caching layers). This does not replace long-term archival for compliance; it prescribes a short-to-medium-term snapshot strategy that supports fast forensics and hypothesis-driven RCA.

Background and motivation
-------------------------
- SRE investigations require coherent cross-signal evidence (metrics + traces + logs + token-level samples) covering pre-incident, incident, and recovery windows.
- Keeping high-fidelity telemetry for all services indefinitely is cost-prohibitive; careless retention causes escalated cloud billing and slows tooling.
- A snapshot-first approach captures high-value data around SLO-impacting events while keeping the default retention conservative.

Key concepts
------------
- Snapshot: A logically consistent bundle of telemetry for a service over a time-window (start_ts, end_ts) stored as a named artifact (e.g., snapshot: inference-service/us-west-2/2023-09-15T14:04Z).
- Evidence tier: Classification of snapshot fidelity and retention based on severity and SLO tier. Evidence tiers: minimal, standard, full, archival-request.
- SLO class: Each service is mapped to an SLO class (gold, silver, bronze) that defines acceptable latency/availability thresholds and default evidence tier.

Evidence tiers and retention (table)
-----------------------------------
| Evidence tier  | Contents included                                                            | Retention (from capture) |
| -------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| minimal        | aggregated metrics (1s resolution for critical metrics), sparse traces (sampled 0.1%), error counts | 7 days                  |
| standard       | metrics (1s), full traces for top N error traces (N=500), request logs (indexed), sampling of token outputs (1%) | 30 days                 |
| full           | metrics (1s), all traces for affected trace IDs, raw request bodies (redacted), token-level output archives (per-tenant), debug profile dumps, heap/malloc snapshots if requested | 90 days                 |
| archival-request | Anything in full tier plus export to cold archive (GCS/Azure blob w/ 7-year retention) | per compliance request  |

Service SLO class mapping (example table)
-----------------------------------------
| Service pattern                | Default SLO class | Default evidence tier |
| ------------------------------ | ----------------- | --------------------- |
| public hosted text-generation  | gold              | full                  |
| internal routing/orchestration | silver            | standard              |
| low-traffic experimental model | bronze            | minimal               |

Trigger conditions for snapshot capture
---------------------------------------
1. Automatic triggers (system):
   - SLO burn-rate > 3x sustained for 10 minutes for a gold service.
   - Error-rate spike crossing configured SLI thresholds (5xx, model-inference-errors) exceeding 3σ relative to baseline.
   - Tail-latency (p99.9) exceeds threshold by >2x for >5 minutes.
2. Manual triggers (oncall):
   - Pager duty escalation for incidents where SLOs are impacted (any severity).
   - Postmortem author requests extended snapshot for targeted investigation.
3. Scheduled triggers:
   - Canary rollouts: capture 60 minutes before and 60 minutes after canary start for any rollout touching production models.

Snapshot composition and schema
-------------------------------
Each snapshot artifact must include a small manifest (manifest.json) with the following fields (stored as top-level keys in the bundle):
- snapshot_id, service_name, cluster, region, start_ts, end_ts, trigger_reason, evidence_tier, initiated_by, size_bytes, object_list (array of file names).

Storage locations and naming conventions
---------------------------------------
- Primary ephemeral store: object://sre-telemetry-snapshots/{region}/{service}/{yyyy}/{mm}/{dd}/{snapshot_id}.tar.gz
- Long-term export (archival-request): gs://sre-archive/evidence/{service}/{snapshot_id}/ (cold storage)
- Naming: {service}/{region}/{YYYYMMDD}T{HHMMSS}-{trigger}-{tier}

Cost control and quotas
-----------------------
- Each team has a monthly snapshot budget measured in GB. Default: 100 GB/month for teams owning silver/gold services; experimental teams start at 10 GB/month.
- Snapshot capture that would exceed the monthly quota must be reviewed by SRE lead and product owner; automated throttling will switch the evidence tier down one level during quota exhaustion.
- Compression: snapshots should use zstd -19 by default; token archives may be compressed with delta encoding for size reduction.

Operational runbook: capturing a snapshot (automated path)
---------------------------------------------------------
1. Detection: Monitoring system raises an 'slo-burn' alarm and posts a notification to #sre-alerts with alarm metadata.
2. Snapshot manager service (sre-snapshotter) reads the alarm, computes the affected time-window (T0-5m to now +5m), and schedules snapshot jobs across instrumentation backends.
3. Backends collect: metrics export (OpenMetrics), traces (Jaeger/OTLP), logs (indexed request logs), request bodies (if configured and redaction policies permit), and sampling of token outputs for inference requests.
4. Snapshot bundling: collected files are validated (manifest checksum), compressed, and uploaded to the ephemeral store. A notification containing snapshot_id and location is emitted to the incident channel and attached to the alert.

Manual capture (oncall)
-----------------------
1. Oncall run: /usr/local/bin/sre-snapshot-cli create --service inference-service --window "-10m:+10m" --tier full --reason "oncall_manual_capture"
2. CLI prompts for justification (free text) and optional add-on flags: --include-heap-dump, --include-token-archive.
3. Snapshot uploaded; CLI prints snapshot_id and short-link, and adds an entry to the incident evidence index.

Evidence handoff and post-incident process
------------------------------------------
1. During incident: attach snapshot link to the incident timeline. Oncall must add short justification and the list of hypothesis owners.
2. Post-incident: the incident reviewer will select snapshots for inclusion in the postmortem package. Evidence that remains required for regulatory reasons is forwarded to archival-request and exported to cold storage.
3. Evidence deletion: unless moved to archival, snapshots older than their retention period are auto-deleted by the snapshot manager. Deletions are logged and reversible only via a formal SRE change request within 30 days.

Access and redaction rules
-------------------------
- Principle of least privilege: access to snapshot artifacts requires an Evidence ACL. Default access: SRE oncall and service owners. Additional access granted via ticket and documented justification.
- PII and customer data: snapshots must run automatic redaction pipelines for request bodies and token outputs. Redaction rules are maintained in /infra/configs/snapshot-redaction.yaml.
- Token-level outputs: default sampling rate 1% unless evidence tier is full where sampling is 100% for affected keys/trace IDs. Token archives are stored encrypted with KMS keys scoped to the owning team.

Verification and quality gates
-----------------------------
- Every automated snapshot must pass a manifest checksum and schema validation before being considered evidence-grade.
- Nightly job validates that snapshots referenced by open incidents exist and are accessible; missing artifacts raise an operational ticket.

Runbook: retrieving a snapshot for analysis
------------------------------------------
1. Use the snapshot browser: https://console.internal/sre/snapshots and filter by service/incident id/date.
2. For CLI access: sre-snapshot-cli fetch --id {snapshot_id} --output /tmp/{snapshot_id}.tar.gz
3. Local inspection: tar -I "zstd -d" -xvf /tmp/{snapshot_id}.tar.gz && less {snapshot_root}/manifest.json
4. Common queries:
   - top error traces: jq '.traces | sort_by(.error_count) | reverse | .[:50]' manifest.json
   - metric deltas: prometheus diff queries with provided metrics CSV

Governance and review cadence
----------------------------
- SRE cadence: Monthly snapshot usage review with finance to adjust budgets and quotas.
- Audits: Quarterly evidence-sampling audit to ensure redaction rules are effective and access logs are complete.
- Postmortem requirements: Any Sev 2+ incident that used a snapshot must document the snapshot_id list and retention decisions in the postmortem.

Implementation notes for engineering
----------------------------------
- The snapshot manager will expose a REST endpoint: POST /v1/snapshots with JSON payload (flat fields only): {service, start_ts, end_ts, tier, initiated_by, reason}. Responses include snapshot_id and presigned upload locations for collectors.
- Collectors must stream data to presigned locations and mark completion via POST /v1/snapshots/{snapshot_id}/complete.
- Use protobuf for manifest serialization for performance; provide a human-readable manifest.json alongside a manifest.pb for tooling.

Logging and observability for snapshot pipeline
--------------------------------------------
- Instrumentation: success_rate, median_capture_time, size_bytes_histogram, failed_uploads.
- SLO for snapshot pipeline: 95% of automated snapshot captures complete and are available within 6 minutes of trigger; 99% within 15 minutes.

Appendix: example CLI snippets
-----------------------------
- Create automated capture (example):
  sre-snapshot-cli create --service routing-proxy --tier standard --window "-5m:+10m" --reason "slo_burn_detected"

- Fetch and inspect manifest:
  sre-snapshot-cli fetch --id snapshot-20231102-az1-12345 --output /tmp/snapshot.tar.gz
  tar -I "zstd -d" -xvf /tmp/snapshot.tar.gz
  jq . /tmp/snapshot/manifest.json

Change log
----------
- 2023-09-15: Initial draft and roll-out to SRE teams.
- 2024-03-12: Added quota throttling rules and compression defaults.
- 2024-11-02: Formalized evidence ACL and archival-request workflow; updated retention windows.

-------------------
- Document owner: Asha Patel (SRE Reliability)
- Snapshot manager owner: Marcus Li (Infra Services)
- Compliance contact: Sofia Ramirez (Security & Compliance)

Related artifacts and config references
-------------------------------------

- https://console.internal/sre/snapshots (snapshot browser)
- /runbooks/sre-oncall-playbook (oncall procedures)

[Customer data archival, snapshot, and restore requirements for private deployments]
Summary

This document captures the minimum customer-facing requirements and acceptance criteria for data archival, snapshotting, and restore workflows for Redwood private deployments (VPC and on-prem). It is intended to be used during procurement, onboarding, and operational handoffs so that engineering, SRE, and customer-success agree on retention windows, encryption, verification cadence, and automated restore proof points.

Goals
- Define required archival targets and snapshot frequency for control-plane and runtime state.
- Specify security, integrity, and compliance constraints for snapshot storage.
- Provide clear acceptance tests and runbook steps for restore verification during on-boarding and periodic audits.
- Provide example automation patterns and API/CLI snippets customers can run in acceptance tests.

Scope
- Applies to private deployment artifacts managed by Redwood: model artifacts (serving bundles), KV cache checkpoints (sharded), runtime metadata (tenant routing tables), and control-plane configuration (policies, secrets metadata).
- Excludes customer application data stored outside Redwood runtime (e.g., user DBs).
- Covers both VPC-hosted and fully air-gapped on-prem installations where network egress may be restricted.

Definitions
- Snapshot: point-in-time copy of runtime state sufficient to restore service to an operational state without re-running lengthy rebuilds (e.g., model weights are separate immutable blobs, snapshot captures pointers and runtime caches).
- Archive: long-term retention store for compliance/e-discovery where data is kept for regulatory reasons and may not be immediately accessible for restore without rehydration.
- Restore window: the expected end-to-end time to bring a tenant or control-plane service back to operational readiness from a snapshot.

High-level requirements
1) Retention and frequency
   - Control-plane configuration snapshots: full snapshot every 24 hours, incremental every 4 hours. Retention: 180 days standard; configurable up to 7 years.
   - Runtime KV cache checkpoints: snapshot every 6 hours; retention 30 days.
   - Model-serving metadata (version pins, rollout state): snapshot every 1 hour; retention 90 days.
   - Audit and telemetry indices required for incident investigation: archival weekly, retention per customer contract (default 365 days).

2) Encryption and integrity
   - All snapshots and archived objects MUST be encrypted at rest using customer-managed keys (CMK) where customer requests; otherwise default to FIPS-140-2 compliant KMS.
   - Snapshots must include a signed manifest with SHA-256 checksums for each object. Redwood tooling will verify checksum on write and periodic verification.

3) Access controls and separation
   - Snapshot read and restore operations require an RBAC role distinct from routine operator roles (e.g., snapshot-reader, snapshot-restorer).
   - Restore operations that access customer PII must trigger an approval workflow logged to the audit trail and require at least two approvers when confidentiality is high.

4) Storage targets and placement
   - Supported sinks: S3-compatible object stores (MinIO, AWS S3, GCS via interop layer), NFS for air-gapped environments (with manifests stored separately), and removable offline archives on encrypted volumes for extreme airgap workflows.
   - Snapshots SHOULD be stored in at least two availability zones or two independent physical vaults for on-prem airgapped sites (e.g., onsite + encrypted tape or offline vault).

5) Restore SLAs and verification
   - For control-plane snapshots: restore window <= 60 minutes for full control-plane to basic operational state (excluding model weight rehydration).
   - For tenant-level runtime restore (stateless model serving plus KV caches): warm restore <= 30 minutes (KV rehydration may be best-effort background process).
   - Every restore must include integrity validation: manifest checksum comparisons, post-restore smoke tests (token-level generation against sample prompts), and a routing sanity check.

Acceptance test matrix (table)
| Component | Snapshot cadence | Retention | Restore window (target) | Validation steps |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Control-plane config | 24h full / 4h incremental | 180d | <=60m | manifest verification, reconcile policies, API health checks |
| Runtime KV cache (per-tenant) | 6h | 30d | <=30m | checksum, sample inference requests, cache hit-rate sanity |
| Model-serving metadata | 1h | 90d | <=30m | version pin assertions, canary route verification |
| Telemetry indices | weekly archive | 365d | N/A (rehydration may be slow) | sample query, index integrity check |

Operational runbook: snapshot creation
1. Pre-checks:
   - Verify target storage is reachable and has >= 20% free space or cold-archive capacity.
   - Ensure KMS key policy grants Redwood snapshot service encrypt/decrypt for CMK operation.
2. Execute snapshot job:
   - CLI (example):
     redwoodctl snapshot create --scope control-plane --type full --target s3://customer-snapshots/tenant-123/$(date +%F)
   - Job outputs a signed manifest and a job id: SR-<timestamp>. Log the job id to customer handoff.
3. Post-checks:
   - Wait for checksum verification step to complete (redwoodctl snapshot verify --job SR-12345).
   - Send webhook notification to customer-specified URL on success or failure.

Operational runbook: restore (high-level)
1. Authorization:
   - Open a change request with snapshot id, reason, approvers, and expected impact window.
   - Get approval per customer policy; document approvers and timestamp.
2. Dry-run verify:
   - redwoodctl snapshot inspect --id SR-12345 --verify-manifest-only
   - If manifest verification fails, escalate to SRE.
3. Restore execution:
   - redwoodctl snapshot restore --id SR-12345 --scope tenant:tenant-123 --mode warm --target-cluster cluster-a
   - Monitor restore progress via /internal/restore/jobs/<job-id> and watch metrics restore.progress and restore.errors.
4. Post-restore validation:
   - API health checks (expected endpoints): /health, /v1/generate sample prompt, KV hit rate > baseline threshold.
   - Run a 5-minute canary traffic stream (configured in the runbook) to validate latency and correctness.

Automation examples
- Periodic verification job (YAML for orchestrator):
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: CronJob
  metadata:
    name: redwood-snapshot-verifier
  spec:
    schedule: "0 */6 * * *"  # every 6 hours
    jobTemplate:
      spec:
        template:
          spec:
            containers:
            - name: verifier
              image: redwood/ops-tools:stable
              args: ["snapshot", "verify", "--recent=48h"]
            restartPolicy: OnFailure

- Sample S3 lifecycle policy (JSON) for warm-to-cold tiering:
  {
    "Rules": [
      {
        "ID": "move-to-cold-after-30d",
        "Filter": {"Prefix": "tenant-123/"},
        "Status": "Enabled",
        "Transitions": [{"Days": 30, "StorageClass": "GLACIER"}],
        "Expiration": {"Days": 3650}
      }
    ]
  }

Monitoring and alerting
- Alerts to configure in customer/operator alerting stack:
  - SnapshotFailureRate > 1% over 1 hour -> page SRE (P1).
  - VerifyJobChecksumMismatch -> page SRE (P2) and alert customer ops channel.
  - StorageAvailable < 15% -> warn customer ops and create automatic retention review ticket.

Validation checklist for customer sign-off
- Snapshot schedule configured and created in writable storage accessible to customer and Redwood.
- CMK or equivalent KMS integration tested and decrypts snapshots in staging restore.
- Run at least two successful restores in a staging region or airgapped test environment: one control-plane and one tenant-level.
- Post-restore smoke tests pass (endpoints respond, sample generation within expected latency band).
- Audit entries recorded for each snapshot/restore operation and exported to customer audit sink for retention.

Roles and responsibilities
- Customer-success: coordinate acceptance tests, record approvals, and confirm policy choices for retention and KMS.
- SRE/Field-ops: execute snapshot/restore, run verification jobs, and troubleshoot checksum or storage failures.
- Security & Compliance: approve any retention longer than 3 years and validate archived data classification controls.
- Customer: provide target storage credentials, outbound webhook endpoints, and approved approvers for restores.

Edge cases and special considerations
- Airgapped sites: snapshots may be written to local encrypted volumes with manifest transfer out-of-band. Acceptance tests must include a manifest-only remote verification step and an offline restore drill.
- Large model rehydration: model weights are typically gigabytes; acceptance criteria should allow model rehydration to be asynchronous with snapshot restore if model blobs are stored in a separate immutable registry.
- Legal holds: when legal hold applies, retention policies must override automatic deletion; implement a ‘hold’ flag on snapshot objects.

Appendix A — Example acceptance test script (bash)
#!/usr/bin/env bash
SNAP_ID=$(redwoodctl snapshot create --scope control-plane --type full --target s3://customer-snapshots/test/$(date +%s) | jq -r .jobId)
redwoodctl snapshot verify --job $SNAP_ID || { echo "Snapshot verification failed"; exit 2; }
RESTORE_JOB=$(redwoodctl snapshot restore --id $SNAP_ID --scope tenant:test-tenant --mode warm --target-cluster test-cluster | jq -r .jobId)
# Wait loop (simple)
for i in {1..60}; do
  STATUS=$(redwoodctl restore status --job $RESTORE_JOB | jq -r .status)
  if [[ "$STATUS" == "completed" ]]; then
    echo "Restore completed"; break
  fi
  sleep 30
done
# Run smoke test
curl -s -X POST https://test-cluster.redwood/api/v1/generate -d '{"prompt":"health check"}' | jq -r .choices[0].text

Appendix B — Common failure modes and remediation
- Manifest checksum mismatch: run incremental verification, if persistent, mark snapshot as corrupted and use previous snapshot; escalate for forensics.
- KMS permission denied: validate key policy, ensure Redwood service principal is included, and replay the successful snapshot in staging.
- Slow restore due to network saturation: throttle parallel restore workers or move restore target to a local registry and rehydrate models separately.

Revision history and notes
- 2026-02-15 (Maya Chen) — initial published draft capturing canonical retention and restore SLAs.
- 2026-03-10 (Maya Chen) — added airgapped-specific acceptance steps and automation examples.

Contacts
- Primary author: Maya Chen (maya@redwood.ai)
- SRE lead (restore program): Arjun Patel (arjun@redwood.ai)
- Customer success (onboarding): Sofia Müller (sofia@redwood.ai)

[Ephemeral Data: Legal Hold, Retention Exceptions, and Evidence Collection Process]
Overview:

This document defines the standardized process for placing ephemeral system data under legal hold, requesting retention exceptions for short‑lived data stores, and collecting compliance evidence for investigations and regulatory requirements. Ephemeral data includes in‑memory caches, Kubernetes pod logs with short retention, session stores, temporary KV stores (e.g. Redis with TTL), preprocessed request buffers, and short‑lived diagnostics artifacts.

Goals:
- Ensure defensible, auditable evidence collection across ephemeral systems within SLA windows.
- Minimize blast radius and retain data only as necessary under legal/regulatory obligations.
- Provide clear roles, timelines, and technical steps for engineering, security, and legal teams.

Scope:
- Applies to all Redwood-managed environments (hosted, dedicated, private) and includes cloud regions where Redwood operates.
- Data types in scope: ephemeral caches (Redis/Memcached), in‑pod memory dumps, short‑lived diagnostics artifacts, container stdout/stderr with <14 day retention, ephemeral message queues, temporary S3 prefixes, preprocessed inference buffers, and KV stores with TTL < 30 days.
- Excludes long‑term persisted storage (primary databases, long‑term buckets) which follow standard data retention policies.

Definitions:
- Legal Hold: An instruction from Legal or Security to suspend normal retention/deletion for specific data subjects or artifacts.
- Retention Exception: A temporary authorization to extend retention beyond default policy for a defined timebox.
- Evidence Package: A verifiable bundle containing data extracts, a manifest, chain‑of‑custody notes, and audit logs.

Roles and Responsibilities:
- Legal: Issues formal legal hold notices; defines scope, custodian list, and hold duration.
- Security (Owner: Security Incident Response): Coordinates technical execution, preserves audit trails, and performs evidence packaging.
- Eng Platform / Infra: Implements retention changes for services under hold, runs extraction commands, and validates completeness.
- Service Owners: Confirm impacted services and execute in‑service steps (e.g., increase Redis TTL, snapshot pod state).
- Compliance / Evidence Reviewer: Validates evidence package and signs off for chain‑of‑custody.

Trigger Conditions (when to place a hold):
1) Formal legal or regulatory notice.
2) Internal investigation with potential legal exposure (escalated by Security).
3) Incident response where ephemeral artifacts are likely to contain key evidence (P1/P0 incidents).

High‑Level Process (summary):
1) Legal issues a hold request via the Legal Hold Intake form (Jira ticket template: SECURITY-LEGAL-HOLD). Include scope, custodian IDs, artifacts, and required retention end date.
2) Security reviews, clarifies scope with Service Owners, and assigns an Incident Evidence Lead.
3) Platform engineers apply technical retention controls and run immediate captures.
4) Security collects evidence, produces Evidence Package, and stores package in restricted evidence bucket.
5) Compliance reviews and records the final evidence manifest; Legal notifies release conditions.

Detailed Technical Steps:
A) Initial Triage (Security / Platform — within 4 hours of request)
- Confirm ticket and scope.
- Map artifact locations (service, region, bucket, cluster).
- Estimate risk of data loss given current TTLs and SLOs.

B) Immediate Preservation Actions (within 12 hours)
- Short‑lived caches: persist snapshot to restricted bucket and increment metric. Example Redis snapshot:

# Create RDB snapshot and copy to evidence bucket
redis-cli -h redis-main cluster save
aws s3 cp /var/lib/redis/dump.rdb s3://redwood-evidence/holds/LEGAL-12345/dump.rdb --acl private --server-side-encryption AES256

- Kubernetes pods with ephemeral logs: increase log retention in logging pipeline and export pod logs to evidence prefix. Example:

kubectl logs <pod> --since=72h > /tmp/pod-logs-<pod>.log
aws s3 cp /tmp/pod-logs-<pod>.log s3://redwood-evidence/holds/LEGAL-12345/

- In‑memory diagnostics: request live memory dump where supported; gather stack traces and attach metadata (PID, node, timestamp).

C) Configure Temporary Retention (within 24 hours)
- For services using TTLs: apply temporary override via feature flags or platform config:

# Example feature flag change (Platform CLI)
redwood-cli service update-ttl --service=session-store --ttl-days=90 --annotation "legal-hold:LEGAL-12345"

- For logging pipelines (Fluentd/Logstash): add hold rule for specific selectors to index into long‑retention index.

D) Evidence Collection and Manifest (within 72 hours)

[Multi‑Tenant Replay Oracle and Scheduler Debug Playbook]
Overview

This playbook describes a deterministic replay and investigation workflow (the "Replay Oracle") for diagnosing multi‑tenant scheduler and kernel interactions that cause SLO violations or throughput regressions. It unifies capture, deterministic reconstruction, scheduler decision replay, and hypothesis-driven kernel perturbation to root cause hard‑to‑reproduce latency and fidelity issues.

Audience

- Oncall SREs and runtime engineers performing post‑incident forensics.
- Runtime scheduler and kernel maintainers executing regressions or perf experiments.
- Applied ML/evals engineers validating quality regressions caused by scheduling/economic changes.

Scope and when to use this playbook

Use the Replay Oracle when any of the following are true:
1) Tail latency spikes (> p99.9) recur without a clear origin in ingress or model change.
2) Multi‑tenant interference suspected (queueing patterns match but treatment varies by cohort).
3) Kernel or preemption regressions are suspected and local instrumentation is insufficient to reproduce.

Signal model (what we capture)

We capture a minimal, reconstructable set of signals that allow deterministic replay across layers:

- Ingress event envelope: request id, route, client token, timestamp, raw prompt hash.
- Scheduler trace: policy decisions, priority, admission slot id, kernel assignment hint, preemption markers.
- Kernel execution trace: kernel id, launch parameters, input lengths, occupancy estimate, GPU memory deltas.
- KV cache delta log: keys read/written, cache hit/miss per request.
- System telemetry: GPU utilization, NVLink errors, host NIC drops, and node thermal events.

Capture format and storage contract

- Capture format: newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON) with one top-level envelope per request. Schema example: 

```
{ "request_id": "abc123", "route": "/v1/generate", "timestamp": "2026-02-02T15:22:11Z", "scheduler": { "decision_id": "d-99", "priority": "interactive", "assigned_kernel": "kv-sharded-v2" }, "kernel_trace": [ { "phase": "forward", "launch_ms": 123, "occupancy_pct": 78 } ], "kvcache_deltas": ["k1","k2"], "sys": { "gpu_util": 56, "nvlink_err": 0 } }
```

- Retention: store captures for 90 days in the incident archive S3 bucket. For high‑severity incidents, persist a 365‑day snapshot.
- Access controls: captures are confidential; set confidentiality: restricted for customer‑sensitive incidents.

Quick triage checklist (first 10 minutes)

1. Confirm incident scope: which routes/tenants are affected, timeframe, and SLO signal.
2. Check whether a capture already exists for sample request_ids; if not, trigger capture on the active nodes using the "ephemeral-replay-capture" flag.
3. Retrieve host/system telemetry (GPU thermal, NIC, CPU steal) for the timeframe.
4. Run a fast differential: compare scheduler decision distributions (priority mix, admission latency) between healthy and unhealthy windows.

Detailed investigation procedure (ordered)

1) Capture co‑located and cross‑tenant samples

- Use the capture coordinator CLI to atomically snapshot N requests across all affected pods. Example: 

```
redwood-capture --time-window="2026-02-02T15:20:00Z/2026-02-02T15:25:00Z" --routes="/v1/generate" --output=/tmp/capture.ndjson
```

2) Reconstruct scheduler decisions locally

- Replay the scheduler decision stream against a sandboxed scheduler that uses the same policy version and kernel mapper. The sandbox should be configured with deterministic pseudo‑random seeds and identical token accounting quotas.
- Tooling: scheduler-replay (see example below).

3) Deterministic kernel replay and micro‑perturbations

- Use the kernel‑replayer to feed kernel launches in the original launch order into an isolated node (or simulator) to observe per‑kernel timing and preemption behavior.
- Run perturbation experiments: add controlled delays at preemption points, adjust kernel preemption granularity, and toggle small occupancy caps.

4) KV cache reconstruction and warmup assessment

- Rebuild per‑request KV cache state using the delta log and re‑execute to measure delta hit/miss timings. Poor warmup sequences often manifest as long tails when many requests require sequential KV loads.

5) Hypothesis-driven kernel variation

- If the replay shows repeated long tail during kernel phase X, try the following:
  a) Swap to a fallback kernel with lower occupancy but better preemption responsiveness.
  b) Introduce batch slicing at the scheduler shim to reduce single‑kernel execution times.
  c) Temporarily mark the tenant for priority isolation and compare outcomes.

Instrumentation and sampling guidance

- Sampling rates: default capture sampling is 0.1% of requests; incidents should increase to 5–20% for the affected routes.
- Recommended additional spans to enable for incidents:
  - scheduler.decision_id (tag)
  - kernel.launch_id and kernel.phase
  - kvcache.key_hints (truncated)
  - host.gpu_thermal_trip

- Cost guidance: enable high‑fidelity capture only on a small set of nodes to limit telemetry volumes. Use the capture coordinator to shard samples across host pools.

Config and required knobs (table)

- The following table lists the runtime config keys, recommended incident defaults, and owner.

| config_key | default | incident default | owner |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| capture.sampling_pct | "0.1" | "10.0" | "runtime-observability" |
| scheduler.replay_mode | "off" | "on" | "scheduler-team" |
| kernel.preempt_granularity_ms | "8" | "4" | "kernel-team" |
| kvcache.replay_consistency | "best_effort" | "strict" | "runtime-team" |

(When pasting this table into Confluence, use the table insert UI for nicer rendering.)

Common findings and remediations (examples)

- Symptom: p99.99 increase during medium‑length prompts. Finding: kernel preemption windows too coarse; long-running kernel monopolizes GPU. Remediation: reduce preempt_granularity to 4ms, enable cooperative preemption patches.
- Symptom: intermittent tail localized to a single node. Finding: NVLink parity errors causing occasional kernel slowdowns. Remediation: cordon node, collect NVLink counters, schedule maintenance.
- Symptom: spike when a new model variant rolled out. Finding: differing kernel codepaths caused occupancy cliffs. Remediation: rollback model variant to previous model and trigger a controlled canary.

Escalation and ownership matrix

- Level 1 (oncall runtime): apply capture and run fast diff, attempt local replay.
- Level 2 (scheduler/kernel oncall): run deterministic kernel replay, run micro‑perturbation experiments.
- Level 3 (hardware/platform): collect detailed GPU FW logs, run NVLink diagnostics, and coordinate rack maintenance.

Escalation contacts (oncall rota names)

- runtime-oncall: anne-wong (pager)
- scheduler-oncall: marco-santini (pager)
- kernel-oncall: jamal-cooper (pager)
- infra-hardware: ops-hardware (pager)

Runbook: reproduce locally (step‑by‑step)

1. Identify a representative request_id from the incident window.
2. Start a replay sandbox with the exact scheduler and kernel versions: 

```
sandboxctl start --policy-version=2026-01-15 --kernel-image=kv-sharded-v2 --deterministic-seed=42
```

3. Ingest the NDJSON capture file into the sandbox: 

```
kernel-replayer --input=/tmp/capture.ndjson --sandbox=http://localhost:8080 --dry-run=false
```

4. Observe kernel timing and compare observed vs recorded launch_ms; log divergences > 15%.
5. Run a perturbation experiment (e.g., 4ms preempt granularity) and compare p95/p99 latency distributions.

Safety, privacy, and compliance notes

- Captures may contain hashed customer prompts. Do not export raw prompt text outside the incident team without an approved business reason and a redaction pass.
- Mark incident captures as "restricted" if customers have requested data export holds.

Post‑mortem checklist and measurable outcomes

- Required artifacts for postmortem: capture NDJSON snapshot, scheduler-replay logs, kernel-replayer logs, and perturbation experiment configs.
- Measurable outcome examples: 
  - p99.9 reduced to pre‑incident baseline for the route within 24 hours.
  - Kernel preemption granularity patch validated in a canary with no regression for 72 hours.

Appendix: useful CLI reference (short)

- redwood-capture (capture coordinator)
  - --time-window, --routes, --output
- scheduler-replay
  - --policy-version, --seed, --dump-decisions
- kernel-replayer
  - --input, --sandbox, --perturbation-profile

Acknowledgements and ownership

- Playbook author: Aditi Raman (runtime observability)
- Primary owners: runtime-observability, scheduler-team, kernel-team
- Reviewers: Marco Santini, Lina Ortega, Jamal Cooper

Related reading and links

- See runbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-incident-orchestration-and-capacity-decision-matrix-2026
- See profiling playbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/causal-latency-attribution-and-signal-enrichment-playbook-2027

Change log

- 2025-11-12 (A. Raman): initial draft and internal trial.
- 2026-02-03 (A. Raman): added kernel perturbation experiments and escalation contacts.

[00:18] Samir: Got it, yeah. Can you run through the stack and what you have today?
[00:21] Markus: Sure. We run a microservices platform on k8s across two primary regions, us-west-2 and eu-west-1. Frontend traffic comes into a traffic proxy, then we call a model service that currently talks to a self-hosted transformer via GPUs in EC2. [00:51] Lina: Right. That's the exact space Redwood tries to cover with three deployment options: hosted API for fastest onboarding, Dedicated for reserved capacity, and Private for VPC/on-prem. We typically recommend running a canary on hosted then move to Dedicated or Private for isolation.

[01:26] Markus: SLA tiers—what are we talking numerically? We need something we can put into contract language.
[01:30] Samir: Our standard hosted SLA is 99.9% for the configured endpoint for paid tiers, with options to buy higher. Dedicated comes with a commit-backed SLA that we negotiate—99.95 or 99.99 depending on reserved capacity and runbooks. We also offer credits for sustained breaches.

[02:06] Priya: Ok nice. Another big thing: graceful degradation. If the model backend is overloaded, we can't just drop requests. We need a deterministic fallback plan and a way to quantify quality loss. What are common patterns?
[02:16] Lina: There are a few patterns customers use: 1) model variant fallbacks—route to a smaller, lower-latency quantized model; 2) partial responses with condensed output or stable rerankers; 3) circuit breaker with queuing and client-side retry windows; 4) cached prefix responses for high-frequency prompts. We also support prefix/KV caching to massively reduce token cost and latency for repetitive prompts.
[02:35] Ethan: For model variants, does Redwood maintain those variants or do we need to host them?
[02:39] Lina: We can host both the primary and fallback variants for hosted and Dedicated. For Private, you can supply the fallback weights or we can help onboard variants. The routing policy is pluggable—you can say prefer latency, prefer cost, or strict SLO-first.
[02:51] Markus: How do you model the risk of cascading failures? Like if we switch traffic to another region, that region might get overloaded too.
[02:58] Samir: That's why we do progressive routing and capacity hedging. We can implement circuit-breaker thresholds and then fan out to a lower-cost fallback. [03:14] Priya: Do you support sticky sessions or session-aware routing? We have context windows and key-value cache locality matters for latency.
[03:20] Lina: Yes, session affinity is supported. We've seen customers pin users to a hot-standby cluster to keep a warm KV cache for shorter contexts. For longer contexts, prefix caching across regions is possible but has eventual consistency tradeoffs.

[03:50] Julia: For auditability, can you provide immutable request logs and a tamper-evident trail?
[03:55] Lina: We provide audit logs with append-only storage options and integrate with your SIEM. For Private we can configure WORM storage and HSM-backed signing of logs if that's required.

[04:41] Ethan: What's the expected latency delta when falling back to a quantized smaller model?
[04:46] Lina: It depends on model and quantization; we've seen 30-60% reduction in latency with smaller quantized models but expect quality drop. We pair fallbacks with a quality monitoring test-suite so customers can set regression thresholds.
[04:58] Markus: On contracts—if we sign Dedicated across two regions, are you able to guarantee cross-region performance or is that on us?

[05:36] Julia: Can you provide the security docs up front? We need SOC 2 type II report, encryption at rest/transit details, and a penetration test summary.

[00:00] Avery Johnson: Alright, cool. I think we’re on. Nina, Marcus, Jen, Tom—thanks for joining. We’ve got Markus and Fatima on from our side. Today’s goal is basically show you the Console, talk through the VPC/private options, and then leave time for the audit logging and region isolation questions you had in email.

[00:21] Nina Patel: Sounds good.

[00:23] Markus Klein: Yep, hi everyone.

[00:25] Fatima Noor: Hey folks.

[00:27] Avery Johnson: Quick agenda: two minutes on what’s in scope, then Markus will do product demo—Console, routing, fallback. Then we’ll do Dedicated versus Private, and we’ll reserve like 15 minutes for Q&A. If we don’t get through all the security stuff, we can do a separate security review.

[00:45] Marcus Reed: We’ll probably want that anyway. But yes, go ahead.

[00:49] Jen Alvarez: I mainly want to see, like, what operators on my team would see. Like dashboards, latency, failure reasons, that sort of thing.

[00:56] Markus Klein: Great, I’ll focus on that.

[01:00] Avery Johnson: Also just a reminder, we’re recording on our side via Fireflies.

[01:05] Nina Patel: OK.

[01:07] Markus Klein: Let me share my screen.

[01:10] (screen share starts)

[01:12] Markus Klein: So this is Redwood Console. I’m in a sandbox org. Left nav is Routes, Models, Deployments, Observability—stuff like that. Most teams start in Routes because it maps to your app endpoints.

[01:28] Jen Alvarez: Routes is like, API endpoints?

[01:30] Markus Klein: Exactly. Like /fraud-summary, /support-assist, or however you want to define. You can bind a route to a model and a policy. The important part is you get per-route latency, token usage, and error breakdown.

[01:46] Markus Klein: If I click Observability… you’ll see a time series for P50/P95 latency, tokens in/out, and then cost. Cost is basically token-based, but we break it down by prompt vs completion so you can see when prompts are ballooning.

[02:03] Jen Alvarez: So for my use case it’s like, some requests are huge because we shove in transaction history.

[02:08] Markus Klein: Exactly. And you can add truncation or summarization upstream, but at least you can see it. We also show streaming vs non-streaming latencies separately because people get confused by that.

[02:21] Nina Patel: Is this pulling from logs or is it like, agent-based?

[02:25] Markus Klein: It’s coming from the request path itself. For hosted it’s obviously in our control plane. For Dedicated and Private, the data path is in your environment; metrics get exported to the Console via a control plane connection you can restrict. We can talk about that more when we hit Private.

[02:44] Marcus Reed: That’s one of the questions. Like, do you need inbound access to our VPC or is it outbound only.

[02:51] Fatima Noor: Typically outbound only, but we’ll cover it in deployment section. We can support very locked down setups.

[02:57] Markus Klein: Staying in Console for a sec—here’s a Trace view. If I click an individual request, you can see the request ID, route, model version, and then breakdown like: queue time, prefill, decode.

[03:11] Jen Alvarez: Prefill and decode… sorry, what’s that?

[03:14] Markus Klein: Prefill is processing the prompt, decode is token generation. In fraud ops you might have long prompts, so prefill dominates; in chatbots decode dominates.

[03:26] Markus Klein: We also surface cache hit rate if prefix caching is enabled. That’s more relevant when you have repeated system prompts or repeated policy text.

[03:38] Nina Patel: You said model version—do we pin a model version? Because we can’t have it change underneath.

[03:43] Markus Klein: Yeah, you can pin a specific version. And then rollouts are explicit. We do canaries, A/B, and you can auto-fallback if error rate or latency crosses threshold.

[03:55] Avery Johnson: And for regulated folks, we’re very careful about “silent upgrades.” So you choose when to update.

[04:02] Marcus Reed: Okay.

[04:04] Markus Klein: Let me jump to Policies. So a policy can be: primary model is, say, Llama-3.1-70B-instruct quantized, fallback is Llama-3.1-8B or maybe a different provider—depending on deployment mode.

[04:19] Nina Patel: Different provider meaning like… OpenAI?

[04:22] Markus Klein: Potentially. But in Private deployments you typically don’t want egress to external APIs. So fallback would be within your cluster or within your allowed region. For hosted, some customers choose multi-provider fallback; for regulated it’s usually “same vendor, same environment” fallback.

[04:41] Marcus Reed: We need “same environment.” Like no external calls.

[04:44] Markus Klein: Got it.

[04:46] Markus Klein: Here’s what fallback looks like. You can do “fallback on capacity,” “fallback on latency,” and “fallback on error types.” For example, if the primary is saturated, route to a smaller model. If the smaller model fails, you can return a graceful error. You can also cap max tokens to protect yourself.

[05:08] Jen Alvarez: Does fallback mean we get inconsistent answers? That’s a big concern.

[05:12] Markus Klein: Yeah, it’s a tradeoff. Most teams set fallback for non-critical routes or they use it to keep the system up with a known lower quality. Some do it only when the system is unhealthy, not as a normal path. And we recommend measuring it with evals.

[05:30] Avery Johnson: The other pattern is: no fallback, but reserve dedicated capacity so you don’t need it. That’s where Dedicated comes in.

[05:37] Nina Patel: Can you talk Dedicated vs Private now? Because we have constraints.

[05:41] Avery Johnson: Yep, let’s do it.

[05:43] Markus Klein: Switching tabs.

[05:46] Markus Klein: So think of three modes: Hosted API (fastest), Dedicated (we host it but you get isolated GPU pool), Private (you deploy in your VPC or on-prem). For you, we’re mostly discussing Dedicated or Private because of your data boundary.

[06:03] Nina Patel: Right. We have a rule that anything with customer PII needs to stay in our AWS account. That’s the default.

[06:10] Markus Klein: That points to Private VPC. Dedicated can still meet some customers’ requirements if they allow vendor hosting with isolation and contractual controls, but if policy is “must be in our account,” then Private is usually the answer.

[06:23] Tom Kline: Dedicated is still a contract with you though, right? Like monthly commit.

[06:27] Avery Johnson: Yeah. Dedicated is reserved capacity—monthly or annual commits. Private is more of an enterprise license plus support, and then you run infra costs. We’ll keep it high level today; we can loop in commercial later.

[06:41] Fatima Noor: From a security lens, Private also gives you the strongest controls around network boundaries, key management, logging destinations, and residency—because it’s literally your environment.

[06:53] Marcus Reed: That’s what I need to understand: what logs exist, and where do they go.

[06:58] Markus Klein: Perfect, let’s talk about logs.

[07:00] Markus Klein: In Private, there’s (1) application logs from the inference gateway and runtime, (2) audit logs—events about access and config changes, and (3) metrics/traces.

[07:14] Marcus Reed: Define audit logs. Like who accessed what, when.

[07:18] Fatima Noor: Exactly. Think: user login events (if SSO is enabled), API key creation/rotation, policy changes, route changes, deployment changes, role changes, and administrative actions.

[07:31] Marcus Reed: Do you log prompt content?

[07:33] Fatima Noor: By default we do not recommend logging prompts or completions in audit logs. Audit logs are event metadata, not payload content. For request logging, you can configure sampling and redaction. In regulated deployments, most customers either disable content logging or do strict redaction.

[07:49] Nina Patel: We’d want content off. We can do our own app-level logging if needed.

[07:54] Markus Klein: That’s common.

[07:56] Marcus Reed: What fields are in the audit log event? Like source IP, actor, time, region.

[08:02] Fatima Noor: Typical fields: timestamp, actor (user/service principal), action type, resource type and ID (route ID, policy ID), result (success/failure), and context like IP address and user agent when relevant. For Private, you also know the cluster/namespace because it’s in your environment.

[08:22] Marcus Reed: Export format? We ingest into Splunk.

[08:25] Markus Klein: We can export as JSON lines. Some customers forward via Fluent Bit / Fluentd to Splunk or CloudWatch. If you want a direct Splunk HEC, we’ve seen folks do that too. We can provide an example config.

[08:41] Marcus Reed: Is that available now or is it “roadmap.”

[08:44] Fatima Noor: JSON export is available. The “pretty” turnkey templates vary depending on your environment, but the log stream is there. We’ll follow up with what’s productized vs reference examples.

[08:57] Jen Alvarez: Sorry, in our world “audit log” also means like, every time an agent uses the model, we need a record for compliance.

[09:05] Fatima Noor: Good question. That’s usually “inference request logs” not “admin audit logs.” We support request IDs and metadata. Many customers log request metadata (timestamp, route, model version, token counts, latency, success/failure) without prompt content. That gives you an audit trail without storing PHI/PII.

[09:24] Nina Patel: Can we make request logs mandatory and immutable? Like retention.

[09:28] Markus Klein: Retention is typically handled in your logging backend. We can configure how long the service retains local logs (short), and you forward them to your system for long-term retention.

[09:42] Marcus Reed: We also need to know if logs can cross regions. We have “no cross-region” rules.

[09:48] Avery Johnson: Let’s talk regional isolation specifically.

[09:51] Markus Klein: In Private, if you deploy in us-east-1, everything stays there unless you configure otherwise. There’s no hidden cross-region replication because it’s your AWS account. For Dedicated/Hosted, you pick a region and we keep your traffic in-region; cross-region failover is optional and would be something you opt into.

[10:12] Marcus Reed: So if you’re saying “optional,” I want to be clear: is there any automatic failover that would push data to another region if the region is down?

[10:20] Markus Klein: Not without explicit configuration. Default is same-region only. If you want multi-region, we’d set it up intentionally and document it.

[10:30] Fatima Noor: And we can put it in the architecture diagram and the contract exhibit. So there’s no ambiguity for auditors.

[10:38] Tom Kline: That’s helpful.

[10:40] Jen Alvarez: What happens if the region is down then? Like do we just get errors.

[10:44] Markus Klein: In single-region, yes—your service is down with that region. Some customers prefer that because it’s compliant. Others do warm standby in another region but still keep data controls. But that’s your policy decision.

[10:58] Nina Patel: For us it’s not just compliance, it’s also “we don’t want unknown data copies.” So single-region is fine for pilot.

[11:07] Markus Klein: Got it.

[11:09] Avery Johnson: Marcus, you also asked about KMS/HSM.

[11:12] Marcus Reed: Yeah. We use AWS KMS with customer-managed keys. In some cases we have CloudHSM, but KMS is baseline.

[11:20] Fatima Noor: For Private, encryption at rest is using your storage services—EBS/EFS/S3—so it’s your KMS keys by default. For app-level secrets, we integrate with your secrets manager patterns. For in-transit, it’s TLS.

[11:35] Marcus Reed: Any part of the runtime that uses its own keys?

[11:38] Fatima Noor: Not in Private. In Hosted/Dedicated we manage encryption keys, with options for customer-managed keys depending on tier. But if your requirement is “all keys are ours,” Private is the cleanest.

[11:53] Nina Patel: And control plane—does it need to phone home? That’s the thing.

[11:57] Markus Klein: There are two variants. One is “connected Private,” where the control plane can reach Redwood for updates and telemetry. The other is more isolated, where we minimize or remove external connectivity and you manage upgrades via packages. The second is more common for on-prem or stricter regulated customers.

[12:17] Marcus Reed: We can allow outbound to a fixed endpoint, but we prefer not. We can discuss.

[12:22] Avery Johnson: That’s exactly what the security review is for.

[12:25] Markus Klein: Let me show routing in a Private-ish context. The routing policy engine is the same—you define primary and fallback. In Private, the fallbacks are typically other deployments in the same cluster.

[12:40] Jen Alvarez: For fraud ops, latency matters but not like chat-level. We do batch too.

[12:45] Markus Klein: Great. Batch workloads often benefit from continuous batching and larger batch sizes. In Dedicated/Private we can tune those.

[12:55] Nina Patel: What about throughput predictability? That’s why we looked at Dedicated.

[13:00] Markus Klein: In Private, predictability is determined by what GPU you allocate and your autoscaling config. Dedicated gives you “we guarantee a pool.” Private gives you “you guarantee a pool” because it’s yours.

[13:14] Avery Johnson: But we still provide recommended sizing and we can do a benchmark with your sequence length distribution.

[13:20] Nina Patel: Okay.

[13:22] Markus Klein: Back to Console: rollouts. If you want to test a new quantization profile or a new model version, you can do a canary at 5% traffic, monitor latency and error rate, then ramp.

[13:36] Jen Alvarez: If we do a smaller model for fallback, can we restrict it to certain customers? Like, premium gets big model.

[13:44] Markus Klein: Yes, you can route by request attributes. Like account tier, route, or region. You can also use headers for that. We’d define it in policy.

[13:57] Marcus Reed: Headers can be spoofed though.

[13:59] Markus Klein: Right, you’d do it behind your gateway or sign it. We can talk about best practices.

[14:06] Fatima Noor: Typically the customer’s API gateway enforces the identity, then Redwood sees a trusted claim.

[14:14] Nina Patel: That makes sense.

[14:16] Avery Johnson: Markus, can you show what happens during an incident? Like what you see.

[14:20] Markus Klein: Yep. There’s an Errors view. It groups errors by type: timeouts, rate limits, upstream issues. In Private, you get runtime-level metrics, plus we can integrate with your PagerDuty.

[14:35] Jen Alvarez: Do you do automated rollback?

[14:37] Markus Klein: You can configure automatic fallback/rollback if a canary degrades. Like, if P95 latency > X for 5 minutes, revert. But again, you define it.

[14:50] Nina Patel: Okay.

[14:51] Marcus Reed: Back to audit logs—does it include reads? Like when someone views a prompt or views traces.

[14:58] Fatima Noor: In the Console, yes we can log access events for admin-level actions and certain views, but it depends on what UI features are enabled. For Private, if the UI is in your environment, you can log those events locally. We should confirm your exact requirement: is it “all admin actions,” or also “every read of metadata.”

[15:22] Marcus Reed: For us it’s admin actions at minimum. Reads would be nice.

[15:27] Fatima Noor: Great, we’ll capture that.

[15:30] Tom Kline: Also, do you support SSO? Sorry, tangential.

[15:33] Fatima Noor: Yes—SSO/SAML, plus RBAC. SCIM depends on setup. We can go deeper in security review.

[15:42] Marcus Reed: SCIM is one of the checkboxes.

[15:44] Avery Johnson: We’ve had a few SCIM edge cases but generally yes. We’ll validate for your IdP.

[15:50] Markus Klein: I’ll pause and ask: what are the top two workloads you’re thinking for the pilot, just so we keep the demo relevant.

[15:57] Jen Alvarez: For fraud ops: summarizing case notes, and maybe generating a next-best-action suggestion for analysts. Second is customer support—agent assist. We want to reduce handle time.

[16:12] Nina Patel: And from platform side, we want it to live in our VPC. We can give you a staging account.

[16:19] Markus Klein: Perfect.

[16:21] Avery Johnson: And just to confirm, you mentioned latency targets previously. Was it like 1-2 seconds for support?

[16:27] Jen Alvarez: Yeah, like under two seconds for the first token would be good. But fraud is more like, under 10 seconds is okay if it’s accurate.

[16:36] Markus Klein: That’s helpful.

[16:38] Marcus Reed: And compliance: no data outside us-east. Prefer no cross-region. Logs to Splunk. Encryption with our KMS.

[16:48] Fatima Noor: Noted.

[16:50] Markus Klein: Let’s do a quick Q&A section now.

[16:53] Avery Johnson: Yeah, go for it.

[16:55] Marcus Reed: In Private, who has access to the cluster? Do Redwood engineers get access.

[17:02] Fatima Noor: By default, no standing access. Support access is customer-controlled, time-bound, and auditable. Many customers require a break-glass process. We can support that. If you want fully air-gapped support, that’s also possible, just slower.

[17:21] Marcus Reed: Okay. And do you have SOC 2.

[17:24] Avery Johnson: Yes, we can share the report under NDA via the evidence pack process.

[17:28] Tom Kline: We’ll need that for procurement.

[Chain of Exemplars Curation Lab]
Purpose:
Quick personal lab notes for exploring rotating chains of exemplars (few-shot sequences where exemplars are sampled/rotated across calls) to reduce brittle overfitting to a fixed shotset and to measure stability regressions across versions.

Context / motivation:
- Fixed few-shot sets can cause the model to latch on to spurious surface patterns. Rotating exemplars might improve generalization and reduce single-shot catastrophic drift.
- Want an inexpensive client-side strategy for apps that can't or won't run expensive evals for each model version.
- Investigate operational patterns: rotation frequency, selection heuristics, weighting, caching tradeoffs.

Open hypotheses:
1) Rotating exemplars reduces variance in model outputs measured across prompt restarts for the same user query.
2) Including deliberately adversarial exemplars (edge cases) at low frequency acts as a regression sentinel.
3) Rotation combined with exemplar clustering (semantic diversity) will beat random sampling.

Experiment matrix (rough):
- Variables:
  * rotation_strategy: fixed-sequence | round-robin | weighted-sampling | cluster-sampling
  * exemplar_pool_size: 8 | 16 | 32
  * shots_per_prompt: 2 | 4 | 8
  * adversarial-injection-rate: 0% | 5% | 15%
  * cache_ttl: none | short(5s) | medium(30s)
- Metrics:
  * surface-stability: token-level edit distance across N runs (N=10)
  * semantic-consistency: embedding cosine variance (use redwood embeddings)
  * utility: task-specific accuracy/F1 if labeled dataset available
  * cost: average tokens / request (account for exemplar tokens)
  * latency impact: median p50/p90

Quick sampling heuristics to try:
- diversity-first: pick exemplars by max pairwise embedding distance until shots_per_prompt reached
- recency-bias: prefer exemplars from latest user interactions with decay lambda=0.7
- sentinel-seeding: always include 1 sentinel exemplar from a curated edge-case set when model version changes

Prototype client pseudocode (notes):
- maintain exemplar_pool metadata: {id, embedding, last_used_ts, tags, label(if any), difficulty_score}
- on request: build prompt by sampling according to strategy, assemble in order: seeds -> exemplars -> user_query -> instruction footer
- include meta-token to mark exemplar provenance for downstream evals (e.g., "[EXEMPLAR: id=xx src=curated]")

Observed fragilities so far (small ad-hoc runs):
- Naive random rotation increased surface variance but sometimes reduced semantic accuracy on small high-precision tasks (classification).
- Cluster-sampling + sentinel worked best for regression detection (small n experiments).
- Weighting by difficulty_score seems helpful to maintain performance but can reintroduce bias toward a few exemplars (need exponential backoff).

Representative few-shot templates (samples to test):
- Classification (intent):
  Prompt start: "You are an intent classifier. Use the examples to learn the label patterns. Respond ONLY with the label."
  Example formatting (shot): "EX: Query: "Schedule meeting next week" -> Intent: schedule"
  Shots: sample according to strategy; at end: "Query: "{user_query}" -> Intent:"

- Rewrite (style transfer):
  "Rewrite the sentence to be concise and formal. Examples: 
  Ex1: "Can we meet?" -> "Are you available for a meeting?"
  ...
  Input: "{user_query}"
  Output:"

Failure cases to track (logging keys):
- hallucinated_metadata: model invents entity attributes not present in exemplars or query
- exemplar-binding: model copies irrelevant exemplar-specific tokens into response (we see names/ids leaking)
- label-drift: classification label distribution shifts after exemplar rotation (monitor class-level precision/recall)

[Fewshot attenuation heuristics — lab notes]
Purpose
Quick personal scratchpad capturing experiments and heuristics for reducing exemplar overdominance in few-shot prompt sets (what I call 'attenuation') — aim: keep exemplar signal useful but avoid literal copying, brittle token-level overfit, and instruction hijacking.

Background / rationale
- Problem: when small numbers of exemplars are highly similar or strongly formatted, model tends to: copy exact phrasing, overfit label tokens, or treat examples as hard rules instead of cues. This shows up as hallucinated metadata, hallucinated reasoning steps, or brittle failures on paraphrase inputs.
- Goal: heuristics that are cheap to test in hosted/Dedicated flows; prefer prompt-side fixes (no fine-tuning) that interact well with Redwood runtime features: prefix caching, batching, and token-budget SLOs.

Experiment log (chronological)
1) baseline 3-shot (A)
- Template: \"Instructions: Paraphrase to plain English. Example 1 -> Q: \"What is the meaning of life?\" A: \"Life means...\"\" (simple exact format)
- Observed: 36% verbatim reuse for unique phrases, 18% hallucinated numeric claims.

2) example-noise (B) — tiny perturbations
- Apply light paraphrase to exemplars (tense swap, synonym replace). Keep labels same.
- Observed: small reduction in verbatim copying (~22%) but occasional polarity flips (because paraphrase introduced negation in two examples).

3) anchor-token dilution (C)
- Insert neutral anchor sentence before each example: \"(Example for style only; ignore facts.)\"
- Observed: Large drop in factual hallucination (13%), but model ignored label formatting more frequently -> answer brevity decreased.

4) exemplar-weighting via explicit meta cues (D)
- Prefix: \"Examples are guides, not rules. Provide your own phrasing.\" and add \"EXAMPLE_START\" tokens between examples (unique sequence).
- Observed: Better paraphrase diversity; lower exact-match. Slight latency + token usage increase (anchor tokens counted).

5) negative-exemplar (E)
- Include 1 negative example showing what *not* to do.
- Observed: helped on structure errors but introduced confusion when negative example had contradictory label tokens.

Quick takeaway: combination of paraphrase augmentation + explicit \"guidance\" prefix seems promising. Anchors reduce hallucination but cost tokens.

Prototype heuristics (to test systematically)
- ShotRotation: rotate order of exemplars per request to avoid position bias (cheap, interacts badly with caching — needs route-aware cache bypass).
- SoftParaphrasePool: maintain pool of 5 paraphrase variants per exemplar; sample 1–2 per prompt. Reduces verbatim reuse.
- AnchorLite: single short anchor token phrase (\"Style guide: be original.\") vs full sentence; measure delta/loss ratio.
- ExampleContrast: for categorical tasks, include 1 borderline example to widen model boundary; for generative tasks include 1 counterexample to show failure modes.
- TokenBudget-aware truncation: if request close to budget, automatically switch to AnchorLite + 1-shot.

Failure modes observed / notes
- Instruction hijacking: too many meta-cues cause model to treat prompt like a multi-step instruction list and follow the wrong step. Keep meta-language short.
- Contradictory anchors: negative examples that contradict label vocabulary can flip final labels. Use neutral phrasing for negatives (show format, not content).
- Caching/cold-start interaction: rotating exemplars defeats prefix caching; for high-QPS routes, prefer static exemplar unless you have hot cache invalidation.

Sample prompt prototypes (short)
1) SoftParaphrase 3-shot (compact)
\"GUIDE: Use your own words. \nExample 1:\nQ: How to reset my router?\nA: Turn it off, wait 30s, turn on.\n--\nExample 2:\nQ: Steps to cancel subscription?\nA: Sign in, go to billing, click cancel.\n--\nNow answer:\nQ: {{user_q}}\n\"

2) AnchorLite + negative (compact)
\"Style: concise, do not echo examples exactly.\nBAD EXAMPLE:\nQ: What is pi?\nA: 3.14159 EXACT (do not mirror)\nGOOD EXAMPLES:\n... (2 positive paraphrased examples)\nAnswer: {{user_q}}\n\"

Measurement plan (automated)
- Metrics: exact-token overlap rate, n-gram reuse, paraphrase-similarity (embedding cosine to exemplars), faithfulness score (task-specific), token cost delta, 95th pct latency.
- Dataset: 400 eval queries per template; include paraphrase + adversarial variants.
- Compare across: baseline static-3shot, SoftParaphrase, AnchorLite, Rotation-once-per-1000, Negative-example. Use Redwood Dedicated for consistent latency measurement.

Open questions / TODOs
- Q1: How much does exemplar diversity interact with model size/quantization? run small-medium-large (ggml/FP16/8-bit) matrix.
- Q2: Should we expose attenuation knobs in the SDK (e.g., sample_paraphrase_count, anchor_level)? sketch API surface.
- Q3: Best practice doc: one-pager for Solutions team summarizing heuristics + when to prefer server-side cache bypass. Draft outline needed.

[Exemplar Pruning — Gambit Lab Notes]
Purpose:
- Quick personal lab for systematically pruning few-shot exemplars to reduce token cost while preserving response quality on our customer support and summarization tasks.
- Try lightweight heuristics (semantic redundancy, label diversity, influence proxies) before heavier retraining/selection pipelines.

Notes on motivation:
- Many client prompts use 6–8 exemplars by default; unit token cost is high and latency increases because of context size.
- Some exemplars are noisy/contradictory and actually degrade answers (observed in INF-433 evals).
- Goal: get to a 2–3 exemplar “core” for each intent cluster with minimal quality drop.

Experiment ideas (quick list):
1) Redundancy filter (fast)
   - Embed all exemplars with embed-v2, cluster at cosine > 0.92, keep 1 representative per cluster.
   - Pros: cheap, stable. Cons: may drop edge-case coverage.

2) Label diversity score
   - For tasks with categorical labels (intent, tone), score sets by label coverage + inverse frequency weighting.
   - Prefer sets that maximize rare-label representation.

3) Influence proxy via leave-one-out prompting (slow):
   - For each exemplar e_i, measure delta in metric (accuracy/ROUGE/QA F1) when removing e_i from set of N.
   - Rank exemplars by positive delta and prune negatives.

4) Mix-and-match annealing (stochastic):
   - Randomly sample candidate subsets (k=2..4), evaluate on 50 held examples, keep Pareto sets.

5) Heuristic rules for position sensitivity:
   - Keep exemplars that perform well both when shown first and last (some models overweight first exemplars).

Quick protocol for runs:
- Dataset: 2k validation samples from support-triage and 1k for summarization test.
- Model: rwi-llm-small (quantized prod variant) and rwi-llm-medium (for stability check).
- Metrics: intent accuracy, slot-F1 (where applicable), and human-eval precision for 200 samples (binary: acceptable / not acceptable).
- Budget: aim for total context tokens <= 1.2k in trimmed prompts.

Preliminary observations (hand-run, noisy):
- Redundancy filter reduced exemplars from 6->3 with ~1.8% drop in intent accuracy but 0.4s median latency reduction.
- Leave-one-out showed 2 exemplars with negative or zero marginal value; one exemplar was contradictory (older policy example).
- Annealing found a 3-exemplar set that matched baseline on intent but beat it for a rare sub-intent (billing-dispute).

Failure cases and gotchas:
- Semantic-embedding clustering sometimes groups together exemplars with opposite labels if wording is similar ("refund approved" vs "refund requested"). Need label-aware distance.
- Removing exemplars that contain edge-case phrasing hurts robustness on customer support transcripts with ASR noise.
- Position/order matters more than I expected for rwi-llm-small; medium is more stable.

Actionable next steps (short):
- Implement label-aware redundancy: weighted distance where same label halves distance penalty.
- Run a 10x annealing sweep across 5 intent clusters (validation size 500 each) and save top-5 subsets.
- Create a small human-eval rubric for acceptability w/ 3 annotators on 200 examples.
- Add a quick automated check that flags exemplars with contradictory label tokens (simple regex heuristics).

- TODO: PR to prompt-bank to add metadata field "created_by" + "policy_version" for exemplar provenance.
- Note: check example ordering experiments in /shared_drives/engineering/developer-experience/prompt-ordering-experiments (might overlap).

- Candidate core (3):

Notes: candidate core removes ambiguous historical example that suggested "store credit" which conflicts with current policy.

[Shot Torque Architectures: quick lab notes]
Purpose:
Quick exploratory notes on a concept I've been calling 'shot torque' — the way few-shot exemplar ordering, exemplar semantic drift, and instruction rotation interact to create non-linear changes in model outputs (tone, factuality, hallucination). Operating assumptions: transformer LM with streaming, 8k context. Experiment focus = low-token-budget regimes where token efficiency and brittleness trade off.

High-level observations (informal):
- Small reorderings of exemplars (swap 2-3rd example) sometimes flip the guidance polarity (e.g., from ‘concise’ -> ‘verbose’) even when instruction header stays identical.
- Mixing exemplars that vary on a latent axis (style vs. rationale) creates a torque effect — model oscillates between copying style and producing reasoning steps depending on which exemplar is closer in embedding space to the query prefix.
- Short, high-salience exemplars (bolded keywords) disproportionately influence output when context budget is tight — suggests effective attention mass is concentrated on token-level hooks.

Experimental matrix (quick):
- Variables: exemplar order, exemplar brevity (short/med/long), exemplar label consistency (same label phrasing vs heterogeneous), instruction anchor phrasing (neutral vs directive), presence of negative examples.
- Metrics: token length, brevity score (heuristic: percentage of sentences < 12 tokens), hallucination markers (binary), instruction-adherence score (0-1, manual), latched style score (manual).

Prototype experiments (notes + seed prompts):
1) Rotation test (5-exemplar set):
  - Base instruction: "Rewrite the following customer message into a concise, professional summary in 1–2 sentences."
  - Exemplars: 5 customer->summary pairs, intentionally include 2 exemplars that are verbose but labeled 'concise'.
  - Rotation: rotate exemplar positions 1,2,3 while keeping 4,5 fixed.
  - Observed: rotation to put a verbose exemplar at position 2 caused outputs to be 30–40% longer on average and include extra reasoning phrases ("because..."), even though instruction was identical.
  - Hypothesis: torque arises when exemplar at early position contains high-attention tokens (dates, amounts).

2) Torque with negative exemplars:
  - Add 1 negative exemplar showing a bad output and annotate 'DO NOT EMULATE'.
  - Observed: negative exemplar sometimes backfires, model repeats the bad pattern in an explanatory way (e.g., describes what the bad output did), occasionally generating similar errors.
  - Quick rescue: append an explicit final line before query: "Ignore the example labelled BAD; follow only good examples." Mixed results.

3) Synthetic contrast pairs to stabilize polarity:
  - Provide pairwise contrast for top-2 exemplars: one labeled verbose, one labeled concise.
  - Observed: improves adherence by ~15% but at cost of small hallucination increase.

Failure cases catalog (examples):
- Failure A: style flip — instruction says 'concise' but output adds extra polite hedges.
- Failure B: label drift — exemplars use different label terms ("summary" vs "TL;DR") and model picks one arbitrarily, causing inconsistent length.
- Failure C: negative exemplar mimicry — when negative example demonstrates an error explicitly, LM sometimes reproduces the error as a paraphrase.

Diagnostics we've run (quick list):
- Token-level saliency probe (approx via ablation): removed high-salience tokens from exemplar, torque reduced.
- Embedding distance heatmap: queries closer to exemplar B's embedding correlates with style B appearing.
- Incremental prefixing: add clarifying sentence after exemplars (e.g., "All gold examples are concise.") and test drift. Helps in 60% of cases.

Quick heuristics/rescue strategies (working):
- Shot dampening: shorten high-salience exemplars and move them later in order.
- Anchor reinforcement: append short explicit anchor phrase ("CONCISE = 1-2 sentences") and repeat it twice with slight paraphrase.
- Contrastive microshots: insert a micro negative that is explicitly corrected ("Bad: long answer; Good: 1-sentence summary") — seems to give the model a comparative signal.
- Red-team exemplars: pre-generate adversarial queries that exploit one exemplar and include a correction pair.

Sample minimal few-shot set (5 exemplars) — DO NOT run as-is in prod (for debugging only):
EX1: Customer: "My account was charged twice for March subscription, can you fix?"
      Summary: "We were charged twice for March; please refund one charge."
EX2: Customer: "I can't log in since yesterday; resets say token invalid."
      Summary: "Account lockout after login failure; needs password reset."
EX3 (verbose): Customer: "I've tried resetting, cleared cookies, still can't access invoices, urgent pls."
      Summary: "I've tried resets and clearing cookies; still blocked from invoices. Need help ASAP."
EX4: Customer: "How to change billing email?"
      Summary: "Request to update billing email—provide steps or update on their behalf."
EX5: Customer: "Refund for annual plan cancelled within trial."
      Summary: "Request refund for cancelled annual plan during trial period."
INSTRUCTION: "Summarize concisely in 1-2 sentences for support agent handoff."

Observed: if EX3 placed earlier, generated summary adds 'urgent' and a mini-reason chain; if EX3 placed last, output is cleaner.

Open hypotheses (to test):
- H1: Early-position exemplars act as a 'style prior' weighted by token salience, not by label.
- H2: Negative exemplars require paired corrections (not isolated negatives) to avoid mimicry.
- H3: Repeating anchor instructions across exemplars enforces stronger adherence than a single instruction header.

Quick experiment plan (next 2 days):
- Run automated rotation sweep across 100 queries: positions 1..5 permuted, measure brevity score and hallucination markers. Use batch size 8, model variant 'x-small' and 'x-medium' to check size sensitivity. (JIRA: JIRA-ML-1289)
- Implement a lightweight prefix saliency ablation script to strip potential hooks and re-run top 20 torque-inducing exemplars.
- Try one prompt template with 2-line anchor repeated in different paraphrases to see diminishing returns.

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Log reproducible seed sets in repo PR (see linked PR).
- Check whether dedicated KV-cache warmup differences (on Redwood Dedicated) change torque magnitude — hypothesis: longer-lived KV cache may amplify exemplar effects for similar queries over time. Need SRE help to instrument.
- Try the same set on private deployment (on-prem) to rule out any hosting-specific tokenization mismatch.

References / related tickets quicklinks:
- Confluence page (theory notes): CONFLUENCE-6642
- Sweep tracking: JIRA-ML-1289
- Implementation skeleton: github.com/redwood-inference/prompt-experiments/pull/47

Bottom line / intuition (one-liner):
Shot torque = exemplar order + exemplar salience creating a lever effect on style/patterns; small mechanical tweaks (shorten, reorder, reinforce anchor) often buy stability but sometimes increase hallucination, so tune with evals.

If Samir or Riley read this: can you sanity-check the proposed rotation sweep parameters? I want to start with 100 queries (diverse) and both x-small and x-medium variants to look for model-size dependence.

Random fringe idea: compute pairwise exemplar saliency matrix and then run a small combinatorial optimizer to pick exemplar subset that minimizes torque potential (score = variance across rotations). Could be neat as a small Optimize feature idea.
