[Add structured per-token metrics exporter and OTEL log enrichment for traces]
description:
Summary: Adds a new opt-in structured per-token metrics exporter and OTEL log enrichment to attach token-level fields to traces and logs. Motivation: token-level visibility is necessary to diagnose long-tail latency/cost regressions (esp. when batching and KV cache interactions differ by request priority). Existing token cost/latency buckets cover aggregated cases but do not preserve per-token attributes (model, priority_tier, cache_hit, prompt_hash). This PR provides a low-overhead, sampled event stream and a Prometheus bridge for aggregated consumption.

What changed (high level): 1) telemetry.proto: new TokenEvent proto describing timestamp, model, token_index, token_type (prompt/response), priority_tier, cache_hit, sequence_len, approximate_cost_micros, hashed_prompt_id, and sample_reason. 2) token_exporter: an exporter that accepts TokenEvent and can push to OTLP collector or aggregate counters/gauges via a Prometheus bridge. Exporter supports sampling policies (always, head-only, uniform n/sample, priority-weighted) configured in config/flags. 3) runtime instrumentation: generation emits TokenEvent at token finalization; emission path is non-blocking and uses a ring buffer + background flusher to avoid adding tail latency. 4) OTEL log enrichment: log_enricher attaches token-related attributes to the existing request-scoped OTEL logs and spans when sampling is enabled. To avoid PII risks we only include hashed_prompt_id; raw prompt text is never emitted. 5) Dashboards & alerts: new Grafana panels and an alert bundle that surface per-model token latency histograms, stream of sample reasons, and cardinality metrics. 6) Tests & docs: unit/integration tests added; docs describe feature flag, retention guidance, and cost implications.

Backward/compatibility notes: feature is behind the config flag telemetry.token_events.enabled=false by default. Exporter uses OTLP protocol; when disabled the codepath is no-op. No breaking API changes. Migration: operators who enable the exporter should size their telemetry collector for event rate; we include example sampling configs in docs.

Checklist: - [x] proto and exporter implementation - [x] runtime emit + non-blocking flusher - [x] OTEL log enrichment (opt-in) - [x] dashboards and example alert rules - [x] unit and integration tests - [x] docs and config entries - [x] performance validation: microbenchmark on p99 tail showed <0.25ms median additional latency in sampled mode

Commit summary: see commits list. Files changed: see files_changed list above. Small snippets: - telemetry.proto adds TokenEvent message and TokenSampleReason enum. - emitter writes events to telemetry/token_exporter.go via EmitTokenEvent(ctx, event).

Testing performed: unit tests for exporter serialization and prom-bridge aggregation; integration test that spins up a mock OTLP collector and asserts receipt for sampled events; CI e2e telemetry job that ran against a small serve binary and validated enriched OTEL logs and metrics; load microbenchmark (scripts/telemetry/load_test) at 10k rps with 1% sampling to validate CPU and memory overhead.

Security & privacy: raw prompt text is explicitly excluded; only hashed_prompt_id (HMAC-SHA256 with instance key) is emitted. The feature will appear in the privacy review checklist (ENG-8791). Operator docs include guidance for rotating keys and retention limits.

Open follow-ups: - Add adaptive sampling policy based on queue depth (ENG-8820) - Integrate exporter with billing pipeline to derive token-level cost telemetry (follow-up PR) - Add per-tenant rolloff in Dedicated deployments to avoid noisy tenants

[A/B Rebalancing Runbook and Ownership Lattice (WIP)]
Purpose:
This is a working runbook for cross-functional A/B and canary rebalancing. Primary goal: provide a compact operations playbook that clarifies ownership during traffic shifts, defines the rebalancing lattice (who adjusts what and when), and prescribes teardown criteria. This doc is experimental — intended to be used during pilot rollouts and to collect field notes for a later formal playbook.

Scope and motivations:
- Target audience: product owners, release engineers, solutions eng, SRE oncall, data scientists monitoring evals.
- Why this exists: we repeatedly see mid-rollout manual rebalances that cause oscillation, cost overruns, and unclear incident ownership. The lattice formalizes responsibilities and step-ordering to reduce coordination friction.

Key concepts (terms we use)
- Ownership lattice: a small matrix mapping teams to control levers (traffic, model variant, quality gates, cost throttle) and escalation path.
- Rebalancing window: the time segment where traffic weights are allowed to change (default 30m).
- Variance budget: pre-allocated tolerance for primary metrics (latency, cost per token, negative-sentiment delta) to permit small fluctuation without manual rollback.
- Payoff matrix: quick decision table for when to expand, pause, or roll back based on signal and cost tradeoff.

Runbook quick flow (90s skim)
1) Observe: telemetry triggers (alert or steward request) -> notify steward channel #rollouts.
2) Triage: steward + oncall SRE decide if signal is noise (within variance budget). If noise, note and monitor (document in JIRA).
3) Contain: if outside budget, apply containment action in order of lattice: (a) disable feature-level sampling bake, (b) route to fallback variant, (c) reduce experiment weight by configured step.
4) Investigate: solutions eng and data scientist run rapid evals on sample logs and golden prompts.
5) Remediate: apply targeted fix or rollback; record decision and metric deltas.
6) Teardown: run postmortem checklist, reclaim traffic, and update payoff matrix with observed outcomes.

Ownership lattice (compact)
- Product/PM: hypothesis, acceptance criteria, release window, stakeholder comms.
- Solutions Eng: shepherds experiment runbook, runbook templates, operator handoffs, QA prompts set.
- Release Eng / SRE: executes traffic changes, applies surge/containment knobs, maintains routing infra.
- Data Science / Eval: signal definition, metric calculation, A/B statistical check, drift detection.
- Cost Ops / Finance (optional): approves burst cost limits and monitors spend alarms.

Rebalancing knobs (ordered by recommended use)
1) Micro-step weight shifts: 1–5% per rebalancing window. Use for marginal signal.
2) Cohort isolation: move affected cohorts (geos/accounts) out of experiment.
3) Model variant swap: promote stable variant as fallback.
4) Traffic siphon to canary pool: route a fixed small set to isolated infra for deeper inspection.
5) Full-step rollback: revert to control. Only under confirmed regression.

Playoff/payoff matrix (example)
- Signal: latency increase 10% over baseline, no quality drop, cost +5% -> Action: reduce weight by 10% and monitor 2 windows.
- Signal: quality metric drop (QA prompts > 3 points), latency unchanged -> Action: cohort isolation + model variant swap.
- Signal: cost spike (unexpected >25%) with no clear quality regression -> Action: enable cost-throttle, notify finance, pause expansion.

Signal handling recipes
- Burn-in probe: when enabling a new slice, run a 10min synthetic traffic probe with golden prompts; compare token-per-response distribution.
- Signal enrichment: attach sample payloads to telemetry alert (redact PII) and pin to incident thread.
- Confidence ramp: require 3 consecutive windows in the desired direction before promoting weights.

Teardown checklist (post-run)
- Reclaim weights: roll weights back to baseline allocation or next planned step.
- Snapshot artifacts: save model version, route config, traces, evaluation runs to linkedasses (JIRA).
- Cost reconciliation: capture delta vs expected cost, annotate deviations.
- Update payoff matrix and lattice decisions: what changed? Who acted? Time stamp.
- Lessons & next steps: list 1–3 action items and assign owners.

Operational templates
- Slack headline (steward): [ROLLOUT] {experiment} — observed {signal}. Actions taken: {containment}. Owner: {name}. Next update in 30m.
- Jira quick label: rollout-triage, experiment-{id}, severity-{low|medium|high}.
- Release task checklist: preflight (golden prompts), infra capacity check, variance budget set, rollback playbook attached.

Guardrails and heuristics (field rules)
- Never change routing + model variant in the same window unless in emergency.
- If cost > 50% of reserved committed capacity, pause experiment and escalate to finance lead.
- For cross-region rollouts, prefer region-by-region incrementalization (not global) to reduce blast radius.

Data / telemetry primitives we expect
- Experiment_state: {weight, variant, start_ts, steward} (recorded as a line in release logs).
- Key metrics: p50/p95 latency, cost-per-token, negative-feedback-rate, autoreject-rate, hallucination-regression (score).
- Comparison window: 3x rebalancing windows by default (90m) for stable readouts.

Open questions / things to iterate on
- How to automate variance budget adjustments per experiment class? (low-risk UI vs high-risk safety experiments).
- Should we expose a 'traffic reclaim' API for product teams to reclaim unused slices? Ownership and billing implications.
- Better tooling for sample redaction before attaching to telemetry.

Field notes (live)
- 2025-02-18: small experiment on reranker saw p95 latency bump after third traffic step; manual micro-step rollback avoided rollback — good case for micro-step defaults.
- 2025-02-26: cohort isolation saved a major customer from exposure; need a checklist for customer-owned cohorts.

Next actions (this doc)
- Convert lattice into compact YAML for use in release UI (owner: Sofia Kim, due 2025-03-10).
- Prototype 'variance budget' UI with cost knobs (owner: Jamal Rivera, due 2025-03-17).
- Run a dry-run rehearsal with SRE and Solutions Eng next sprint (owner: Priya Nambiar).

Appendix: quick decision heuristics (for oncall)
- If metric falls within +/- variance budget -> monitor only.
- If metric outside variance budget and impacts >1 cohort -> contain (isolate cohorts) then escalate.
- If cost spike without quality impact -> apply cost-throttle before rollback.

References and links:
- Confluence: rollout-ops playbook (see linked artifact CONFLUENCE-ROLL-789)
- JIRA: incident and experiment tracking prefix JIRA-RST-2145
- Repo: rollout-scripts PR 423 for traffic-siphon helper

[Regional utility balancer sketch: latency vs cost vs reliability]
Purpose
This is a working sketch for a compact control-plane component I’m calling the Regional Utility Balancer (RUB). The goal: pick where to route an inference request across model variants and regions by explicitly trading latency, cost, and reliability using a single interpretable utility score and a small decision lattice.

Why a new sketch?
Existing notes in the folder explore many routing heuristics (priority matrices, fallback graphs, probabilistic fallback). This doc tries to converge on a single lightweight runtime-friendly scoring model and an operational decision flow that SREs and product can reason about quickly during incidents and can be audited for fairness between customers. Emphasis on: clarity, simulation-friendly inputs, graceful degradation, canary-safe rollout.

High-level idea
- Normalize key signals into comparable scales: latency percentile (p50/p95), per-token cost, and recent success rate (or SLO compliance).
- Compute a weighted utility score for each candidate (region+model_variant).
- Apply constraints/guards (capacity, data-residency, policy exclusions).
- Select highest utility candidate.
- If candidate fails (timeout / error), apply fast fallback logic that prefers routes with lower regret (expected utility delta) rather than always lowest latency.

Signals we ingest (examples)
- latency_histogram_region_model: p50 and p95 in ms (window: last 1m, 5m, 1h)
- cost_per_token_region_model: USD per token (amortized, includes infra + license)
- reliability: success_rate = (successful responses / total) in last 5m and 1h
- capacity: available_concurrency (slots), queue_depth, and estimated headroom
- cold_start_risk: binary or scalar (recent container churn)
- customer_priority: tier flag (free/dev/standard/enterprise) - used for ties and budgeted routing rules

Normalization approach
- Convert p95 latency to latency_score in [0,1] by clipping to [baseline_ms, max_reasonable_ms]. Lower latency -> higher score. Example baseline_ms=20ms -> score 1, max_reasonable_ms=2000ms -> score 0.
- Convert cost_per_token to cost_score in [0,1], higher is better (i.e., cheaper->higher). Use log-scale to compress wide ranges.
- Convert reliability to reliability_score in [0,1], straightforward mapping with a small penalty window for 97%-99.9% ranges.

Utility function (simple, interpretable)
- Utility = w_lat * latency_score + w_cost * cost_score + w_rel * reliability_score
- Weights are policy knobs. Default starting weights: w_lat=0.45, w_rel=0.35, w_cost=0.20 (favours latency and reliability). All weights sum to 1.
- We also compute an uncertainty_term = alpha * sigma_estimate (sigma derived from signal variance over selected window) to penalize volatile candidates.
- Final utility = Utility - uncertainty_term

Example normalization formulas (toy):
- latency_score = clamp(1 - (p95_ms - baseline_ms) / (max_ms - baseline_ms), 0, 1)
- cost_score = clamp(1 - (log(cost_per_token) - log(cost_min)) / (log(cost_max) - log(cost_min)), 0, 1)
- reliability_score = clamp((success_rate - 0.9) / (1 - 0.9), 0, 1)  // maps >90% to 0..1

Decision lattice (operational flow)
1) Filter candidates by policy (legal/region constraints, model compatibility, customer pinning).
2) Filter out candidates with available_concurrency <= soft_capacity_threshold.
3) For each remaining candidate compute final_utility.
4) Sort by final_utility desc. Select top candidate if final_utility >= accept_threshold.
5) If top candidate < accept_threshold, enter conservative-mode: widen acceptable models (lower quantized variants), possibly route to a cold standby hot-path (longer latency but higher reliability SLA).
6) On failure paths (error/timeout), choose fallback by expected_regret = (utility_top - utility_candidate). Pick fallback with minimal regret among healthy candidates and with nonzero capacity.

ASCII decision tree sketch (simplified)

START
  |-- Policy filters (region/pin) --> candidates
  |-- Capacity check --> if none: use emergency-fallback (multi-region replicate)
  |-- Score each candidate --> rank
  |-- if top.utility >= accept_threshold --> route
  |-- else --> conservative widening --> rerank --> route or emergency-fallback

Operational knobs and guardrails
- accept_threshold: default 0.4 (tunable per workload)
- soft_capacity_threshold: requires at least 10% headroom for non-enterprise accounts
- emergency-fallback: route to a dedicated high-SLA pool (more expensive) when < 2 candidates pass soft capacity
- hysteresis windows: require two consecutive scoring intervals below threshold before triggering a global failover
- canary sampling: route X% of traffic to new policy weights before global switch

Fallback selection rationale
- Minimize regret > minimize latency: Example when top is slightly faster but brittle, fallback should prefer a slightly slower but higher reliability node.
- Maintain cost ceilings for non-enterprise customers: do not fallback to an expensive Dedicated pool for free tier unless no other healthy routes.

Control-plane integration notes
- RUB should expose a small API: evaluate(candidates, customer_context) -> ranked_list + debug_trace
- The control plane must log input signals, weight vector, and intermediate normalized scores with trace ids for postmortem.
- Push policy changes with feature flags: weight vectors and thresholds per customer segment saved in Git (policy-as-code) and rolled out via canary.
- Telemetry: for every route decision emit metrics: chosen_candidate, utility_top, chosen_utility, expected_regret, fallbacks_used, decision_latency.

Testing and simulation plan
- Offline: replay production traffic (sampled) through RUB with multiple weight sets to create Pareto front visualizations (latency vs cost vs reliability). Produce CSV outputs for plotting.
- Chaos test: spike p95 in one region, ensure RUB migrates traffic in expected order and respects hysteresis.
- Load test: saturate capacity in a region and verify emergency-fallback activates and that per-customer cost limits are respected.
- Canary: start with 1% of real traffic for 24h, compare SLOs and cost delta. If regressions < threshold, increase.

Edge cases and open questions (TODOs)
- How to factor warm vs cold KV-cache benefits for streaming chat sessions? Cache hit probability impacts perceived latency; need a way to bias for models with warm KV-caches for same conversation.
- Should utility include fairness penalty if the same customer gets routed disproportionately to slower regions due to cost-saving? Need product input.
- How to model spot/GPU preemption risk into uncertainty_term more explicitly? Propose a preemption_risk score from infra layer.
- Policy override APIs for Customer Success to temporarily pin routes during support incidents. Need RBAC and audit trail.

Notes for follow-ups
- Marco: can you add a simulation harness PR (PLAT-2345) that takes historic p95 and cost columns and outputs the utility ranking?
- Lin: propose a compact protobuf for the evaluation API (evaluate request/response) and include trace fields.
- Priya: draft a short runbook for oncall that explains RUB decisions during regional degradation (keep it 1 pager).

References and inspiration
- Pareto routing sketches from prior folder notes (this doc intentionally uses a single-utility approach to make ops simpler).
- Related tickets: PLAT-1872 (regional capacity model), PLAT-2019 (cold-start mitigation).

Summary
RUB is intended to be a concise, auditable policy layer that chooses routing targets by scoring latency, cost, and reliability into a single utility value, applying clear filters and guardrails, and failing over based on regret-minimization. This draft leans conservative: prefer reliability and explainability over opaque probabilistic mixes. Feedback welcome; next step is a lightweight sim and a tiny eval API proto.

[resume-download-hang-notes]
Context:
- Intermittent model load failures in staging: large checkpoint ( ~210 GB tar) will start downloading fine but stalls during resume/seek and never completes. Affects resume logic in blobstream -> tar stream -> shard reader path.
- Repro rate ~3/20 downloads in staging (k8s). Prod unaffected so far but worried about edge-case on poor networks.

Symptoms observed (from agent + proxy logs):
- Client issues GET with Range header to GCS signed URL. Typically requests range starting at byte N where N is resume offset.
- Server returns: HTTP/1.1 200 OK (not 206) for range request in ~30% of failing cases -> client code treats as fallback but then confusion in Content-Length vs expected remaining bytes.
- When 200 is returned we see Content-Length ~= full object and streaming attempt does chunked transfer; our BlobStream expects Content-Range/206 and does a single ranged read.
- Often the connection hangs after ~50-200MB transferred; stack shows blocked on read() in python requests (urllib3) with an open socket. Kernel stats show TCP retransmits and then connection reset.

Logs (sanitized):
[2026-02-16T03:14:12Z] blobstream: starting range request url="<signed-url>" range="bytes=137438953472-"
[2026-02-16T03:14:12Z] http-client DEBUG: > GET /... HTTP/1.1
[2026-02-16T03:14:12Z] http-client DEBUG: < HTTP/1.1 200 OK
[2026-02-16T03:14:12Z] http-client DEBUG: < Content-Length: 2251799813685248
[2026-02-16T03:16:03Z] blobstream: read stalled after 123MB transferred; last byte=137562383616
[2026-02-16T03:17:44Z] k8s: pod restart backoff due to readiness probe fail

Reproduction steps I used locally (quick):
1) Create signed URL for object (gsutil signurl)
2) curl with Range header to simulate resume: 
   curl -v -H "Range: bytes=137438953472-" "<signed-url>" -o /tmp/chunk.part
Observations: sometimes curl returns 200 + huge content-length and streams; sometimes returns 206 and only the requested range. The failing case tends to be the 200 response.

Quick experiments (commands tried):
- gsutil -D cp gs://redwood-checkpoints/llama-13b/ckpt-2025-11.tar ./  (works or stalls depending on run)
- curl -v -H "Range: bytes=0-1048575" "<signed-url>"  -> 206 expected, usually OK
- curl -v -H "Range: bytes=137438953472-" "<signed-url>"  -> sometimes 200; when 200: response header Content-Length==object_size (not remaining)
- python requests stream test:
    import requests
    r = requests.get(url, headers={"Range": "bytes=137438953472-"}, stream=True, timeout=(5,120))
    for chunk in r.iter_content(65536):
        process(chunk)
  -> chunk iteration blocks indefinitely after some MB
- tcpdump on node during hang: repeated retransmit (SYN/ACK?) and eventually FIN; remote resets.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Signed URL generation + caching on CDN side: signed URL sometimes routes to a backend that doesn't support range/206 properly (edge case in GCS/Cloud CDN), returning 200 and then inconsistent streaming behaviour.
2) Large resume offset + HTTP/2: interaction between our client (urllib3 over httpx?) and server: http/2 stream flow-control where server advertises large content-length, then stalls if client window not updated.
3) Middleboxes (sidecar/proxy) in k8s (istio/Envoy) rewrites Range headers or mishandles 206 responses for large offsets, causing proxy to buffer and then fail.
4) Tar reader/backpressure bug: our TarStream tries to seek/rewind on a stream that doesn't support random access and we get into a read-then-seek deadlock.

Notes on 206 vs 200 behavior:
- RFC: servers MUST reply 206 for Range if satisfiable. If 200 returned, client must assume server ignored Range. Our code currently treats 200 as 'fallback to full download' but still uses expected remaining bytes to set a read deadline -> mismatch. Need robust handling: if 200, compare Content-Length to expected remaining; if Content-Length > remaining then assume full object and restart with full download or abort.

Data points from telemetry: (last 48h)
- 37 total checkpoints downloaded by staging nodes
- 9 downloads logged partial-range requests (resume)
- 3 downloads stalled for >2 minutes and triggered pod eviction
- Failure cohort: all from nodes in us-central1-c, via node pool with custom sidecar version v1.8.2

Quick patches attempted (on staging):
- Patch blobstream: if response.status_code == 200 and content-length > remaining_bytes: close connection and retry without Range (full download). Reduced hang frequency but increased egress bandwidth (bad).
- Switch http client to requests.adapters.HTTPAdapter(pool_connections=100, pool_maxsize=100) to avoid connection reuse oddities; no measurable change.
- Added retry on socket timeout with exponential backoff (max 3). Brought success on 2/3 prior failing runs.

Stack trace (before retry patch) when hung (python):
  File "/app/blobstream.py", line 212, in _stream_range
    for chunk in resp.iter_content(chunk_size=65536):
  File "/opt/python/lib/python3.10/site-packages/requests/models.py", line 753, in iter_content
    for chunk in self.raw.stream(chunk_size, decode_content=True):
  File "/opt/python/lib/python3.10/site-packages/urllib3/response.py", line 818, in stream
    data = self.read(amt=amt, decode_content=decode_content)
  File "/opt/python/lib/python3.10/site-packages/urllib3/response.py", line 624, in read
    data = self._fp.read(amt)
  File "/usr/lib/python3.10/http/client.py", line 458, in read
    s = self.sock.recv(left)
# blocked here until socket closes

Ideas to probe next (short checklist):
- [ ] Collect server-side GCS logs for signed URL accesses around timestamps: 2026-02-16T03:10-03:20Z (ask infra for logs). Need to check if 206 or 200 was returned upstream.
- [ ] Reproduce with direct GCS XML API (no signed URL) to rule out CDN/signed-url layer.
- [ ] Try curl --http1.1 to force HTTP/1.1 vs default http2 to test flow-control hypothesis.
- [ ] Run test with no sidecar (bypass istio) on a few nodes to check proxy influence.
- [ ] Add more aggressive detection in blobstream: if read stalls for >15s and bytes_transferred < min_rate then abort and retry. Record metrics (bytes/sec) for postmortem.
- [ ] Validate tar reader path: make sure we do not attempt to seek on streaming response; convert to read-and-write-to-tempfile when resume not supported.

Notes-to-self:
- Edge case may be combination of server returning 200 + client expecting partial content and then holding on to socket for long time. Fixing to treat 200 as a hard mismatch and immediately restart full download or abort seems the safest short-term fix.
- Long-term: support resumable downloads via GCS compose / chunked upload pattern or use objectRange RPCs that are guaranteed to return 206.

Open questions:
- Why would GCS signed URL sometimes route to a node that returns 200 for a Range request? Is there a backend version skew?
- Are there load-balancers in front of GCS that rewrite Range?
- Is our signed URL malformed when resume offset > 2^32? (unlikely but check)

Useful links / refs:
- GCS signed URL docs (range requests): https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signed-urls
- RFC7233 Range Requests: https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7233
- GitHub issue: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/issues/612 (related: tar streaming/backpressure)

Next actions (short term):
1) Push blobstream quick fix: detect 200-on-range -> abort and retry without range (or switch to tempfile), add metric -> rollout to staging canary.
2) Run controlled reproduce forcing http1.1 vs http2 and sidecar on/off.
3) File ENGINF follow-up to collect GCS edge logs and ask Cloud support if signed URL behavior is expected.

[Lazy-fetch TTL / partial GCS fetch — scratchpad]
Goal: capture breadcrumbs for the intermittent model-load failures where the lazy-fetcher stalls or returns truncated shards when fetching weights from GCS signed URLs.

Symptoms observed:
- In-host logs: repeated failures during model init while streaming shards.
  - Loader prints: "EOFError: Ran out of bytes while reading tensor" or "tar: Unexpected EOF"
  - HTTP fetch logs show intermittent HTTP 503 or connection reset after about ~30–90s of a long-running ranged GET.
  - Example message: "fetcher: download aborted (status=503) url=gs://models-prod/abc/shard-0004.data range=0-1048575"
- Client-level: retry logic sometimes gets a partial file stored to cache, subsequent attempts reuse partial file and fail checksum.
- Repro rate: ~1.2% of loads over last 30d; spikes during heavy rollout windows.

Commands / quick repro attempts tried locally:
1) Basic gsutil fetchs (single threaded)
- gsutil cp gs://models-prod/abc/shard-0004.data ./shard-0004.data 
  -> usually succeeds, hash matches, suggests underlying object valid on GCS.

2) Simulate ranged streaming (emulate lazy-fetch behavior)
- curl -f -H "Range: bytes=0-1048575" -o part.bin "$(signed-url)"
  -> sometimes returns 206 partial content; sometimes HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable mid-transfer.

3) Using wget/aria2 to see resumable behavior:
- aria2c -x 4 -s 4 -c "$(signed-url)" -o shard-0004.data
  -> aria2 resumes ok on most failures; reproduces issue only when multiple parallel requests hit the same underlying object (points to GCS loadbalancer / signed URL TTL?).

4) Compare metadata & checksum via gsutil:
- gsutil stat gs://models-prod/abc/shard-0004.data
  - md5/hcrc/size all consistent between objects that fail and those that don't.

5) Validate manifest vs on-disk objects:
- cat weights_manifest.json (v2 style) contains byte ranges and offsets. Verified that manifest offsets are sane and sum to total file size.

Observed error snippets copied from logs:
- "ERROR loader: safetensors.InvalidHeaderError: unexpected magic bytes"
- "ERROR fetcher: http error 503 for url=... shard-0006.data range=52428800-62914559 attempt=2"
- "WARN model-init: checksum mismatch expected=2b7e... got=3f1a... file=/tmp/cache/shard-0006.data.partial"
- "Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/app/loader.py", line 248, in _map_shard
    tensor = torch.load(streamed_file)
  File "torch/serialization.py", line 783, in load
    raise EOFError('EOF while reading file')
EOFError: EOF while reading file"

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Signed URL TTL / GCS backend transient 503s trigger partial downloads which our fetcher treats as complete (race between close + rename).
   - We saw partial files with .partial suffix being atomically renamed into cache when last chunk came back, but if last chunk is missing the rename still happened in our older code path.
2) Multithreaded parallel Range requests against the same object get rebalanced to different GCS servers; one server returns truncated/timeout responses for long ranges.
3) Manifest vs object format mismatch: some older bundles uploaded with "weights_manifest_v1" (different offset ordering) are being interpreted by the v2 loader leading to bad range requests.
4) Disk pressure + mmap fallback: when ephemeral disk fills we fall back to streaming, but the fallback path has weaker retry semantics.

What we've tried and results:
- Change: make fetcher write to unique temp file (uuid) and validate size+sha256 before rename.
  - Result: reduced incidents but not eliminated. We still saw a case where the final size matched but content was corrupt (implies truncation followed by zero-padding? or server returned erroneous content-length).

- Change: force single-threaded ranged fetch for shards > 1GB (no parallel ranges)
  - Result: lowered repro rate during rollouts, but still occasional 503 mid-range.

- Change: enable resumable downloads using Google resumable upload/download protocol (python google-cloud-storage Transport).
  - Result: more resilient to connection drops, but doesn't change server-side 503 for long-lived ranges.

- Add extra verification step after download: compute gsutil hash locally and compare to manifest-stored checksum. Faulty ones flagged and retried from scratch (delete partial + retry).
  - Result: prevented bad file from being used; increased cold-start latency by ~0.2s on average.

- Temporary workaround: when loader detects EOF/InvalidHeader, attempt full object re-download via gsutil cp and then re-run. This unblocked some incidents quickly in prod.

Notes from correlating logs with rollout schedule:
- Incidents align with two events: (a) >3 parallel model loads for same bundle from multiple hosts and (b) large Cloud Build activity that modifies object ACLs (not sure if related).

Ideas to investigate / next steps:
1) Reproduce deterministically: create a small local MinIO cluster and a proxy that randomly aborts mid-range to emulate GCS 503; run our lazy-fetcher against it and observe rename vs validation logic.
2) Add server-side metrics: log content-length headers and last-byte-range-received from HTTP responses. Add a debug flag that keeps the .partial file (don't rename) and dump first/last 256 bytes to S3 for offline inspection.
3) Harden fetcher: require full-hash validation before rename. If hash matches manifest, atomically rename. If content-length reported by server != bytes received, fail and retry.
4) Investigate signed URL generation: ensure TTL covers expected long downloads (especially for ranged downloads that may need multiple attempts). Potentially extend TTL for large shard downloads.
5) Ask infra/cloud to check GCS SLA/incidents during spike windows and verify load balancer behavior for large ranged GETs.
6) Update manifest & uploader: standardize on weights_manifest_v2 format and add uploader-side test that verifies the object can be fully ranged-read by a simple script immediately after upload.
7) Add a small e2e test in PRs that uploads a test shard and runs 100 parallel ranged reads to catch LB-related truncation.

Short-term runbook (for on-call):
- If model load fails with EOF/InvalidHeader:

  2) Run: gsutil stat gs://<bundle>/shard-XXXX.data && gsutil hash -m gs://<bundle>/shard-XXXX.data
  3) If gsutil reports object intact, run: gsutil cp gs://... /tmp/shard && compute sha256; compare to manifest. Replace cache with gsutil-copied file.

[Shard recovery playbook (scratch)]
Context / tl;dr:
- Intermittent model load failures observed on Dedicated pool nodes: 2/50 requests fail during weights fetch -> model fails to initialize. Other requests succeed.
- Failure mode: one or more shard downloads return HTTP 403 or truncated content. In some cases torch/safetensors raises size/shape mismatch at load time.
- Goal: capture ad-hoc commands/screenshots and a reproducible checklist to triage next time.

Timeline notes (local testing):
- 2026-02-25 09:12: first alert from canary: node-a3 failed to instantiate model "redwood-14b-v2" (dedicated-pool-01).
- 2026-02-25 09:15 manual retry on same node: success.
- 2026-02-25 10:02 observed two more failures on different nodes, same model version.

Observed symptoms (logs):
- Download step log (wrapped):
  INFO: fetching index.json from s3://models/redwood-14b-v2/index.json
  INFO: beginning shard downloads: 8 shards expected
  WARN: shard model-00004-of-00008.bin failed: HTTP 403 (presigned URL expired?)
  ERROR: model init failed: safetensors.SafetensorError: buffer too small for expected bytes for tensor 'transformer.h.10.mlp.fc2.weight' (expected 7340032, got 3276800)

Commands I ran (local VM, reproducer):
- list remote index and check ETag/size:
  aws s3api head-object --bucket models --key redwood-14b-v2/index.json --region us-west-2

- attempt download of a single shard (presigned URL case):
  curl -v "<presigned-url>" -o model-00004-of-00008.bin  # sometimes returns 200, sometimes 403

- inspect partial download: (when curl returned 200 but file looks small)
  ls -lh model-00004-of-00008.bin
  sha256sum model-00004-of-00008.bin
  xxd -l 64 model-00004-of-00008.bin | sed -n '1,20p'

- attempted concatenation to emulate full checkpoint (not expected to work for sharded safetensors but tried):
  cat model-0000*-of-00008.bin > combined.bin
  # torch.load(combined.bin) -> fails with header mismatch

- tried robust downloader (aria2c) with retries and range requests:
  aria2c -x16 -s16 -k1M -o model-00004-of-00008.bin "<presigned-url>"
  # when underlying issue was 403, aria2c unsurprisingly fails. When the problem was truncation aria2 did better (resumed)

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) presigned URL expiration / clock skew on service that issues URLs -> intermittent 403s. Evidence: 403s in logs; some curl tries immediately after still 403, other times 200.
2) partial upload or multipart upload not completed on the artifact storage side -> content-length smaller than expected, leading to safetensors buffer errors. Evidence: sha256/size mismatch and truncated file sizes in failing cases.
3) CDN/edge caching serving stale/invalid byte ranges for some shards -> unexplained mismatch with ETag vs head-object.
4) client-side aggressive parallel downloader bug that corrupts files when multiple processes race on same target path (race during tmp file -> final rename). Evidence: we saw a racey tmp-file pattern in node logs once. Low probability.
5) mismatched checkpoint format (older index.json pointing to .bin shards produced by old serialization). Could cause shape mismatch if model code expects different config, but logs point to byte-size mismatch rather than incompatible layout.

Quick checks to run if this happens again (ordered):
- Step A: get the node logs + full stack trace asap, preserve node disk.
- Step B: run head-object for index.json and for the failing shard key (if using s3-stored shards) and record ETag, Content-Length, LastModified.
  aws s3api head-object --bucket models --key <key> --region us-west-2 | jq -r '.ETag, .ContentLength, .LastModified' > /tmp/shard-head.txt
- Step C: download shard with --retry and verify checksum, record HTTP response headers (curl -I) and full verbose output.
  curl -v -w "HTTP_CODE:%{http_code}
SIZE:%{size_download}
" -o /tmp/shard.bin "<url>" 2>&1 | tee /tmp/curl.log
- Step D: verify sha256 and file size, compare with metadata in index.json (if sha256 or size included).
  sha256sum /tmp/shard.bin ; stat -c '%s' /tmp/shard.bin
- Step E: if truncated, try range-retrievals to confirm server supports range requests (curl -r 0-1023). If range succeeds but full download truncates, strong sign of server-side incomplete object.

Useful one-liners I left in my shell history: (paste-ready)
- get index keys and sizes (bash):
  jq -r '.shards[] | "key=\(.key) size=\(.size) sha256=\(.sha256 // "")"' index.json | sort
- head-object for each shard in index (parallel):
  cat index.json | jq -r '.shards[].key' | xargs -n1 -P6 -I% aws s3api head-object --bucket models --key % --region us-west-2 | jq -r '.Key,.ContentLength,.ETag' > /tmp/heads.txt

Edge cases I stumbled on:
- Presigned URL TTLs: our presigned generator (artifact-service v1) used a default TTL=300s. On heavily loaded nodes that attempt to fetch after a brief queuing delay, the signed URL can already be invalid. Solution: extend TTL to 1800s for shard downloads or move to short-lived signed URLs per node pre-warm step.
- Multipart upload incomplete: an earlier failed deployment left some shards uploaded as 'parts' but not completed; s3 head-object returned ContentLength matching combined parts only after complete. We think some artifacts were published with incomplete completion and then re-uploaded; nodes sometimes hit the incomplete object during replication window.
- safetensors vs .bin: If index.json points to .safetensors but node tries to use a torch loader path, load fails with header mismatch rather than truncation. Check the index format and loader selection codepath.

Temporary mitigation (short term):
- Add client-side verification: after download, verify content-length against head-object and start-of-file magic bytes for safetensors or torch header; if mismatch -> retry with exponential backoff and jitter.
- Fail-fast and escalate to model-publish team if repeated retries hit the same missing shard.
- Add pre-warm step when instantiating large models on Dedicated: call artifact-service to mint and validate presigned URLs and TTL.

Longer term fixes / TODOs:
- artifact-service: emit per-shard sha256 and content-length in index.json at publish time. Add a post-publish verification job that HEADs each shard and ensures final visibility before marking model version "published".
- serving-runtime: when using parallel downloads, download into unique tmp paths (include pid+uuid) and atomic rename. Also ensure downloader handles HTTP 403 specially (do not treat as transient) and surfaces the signed-url expiration reason back to control-plane.
- infra: audit S3 replication metrics and multipart upload logs for the time window of the known incident (2026-02-25).
- add e2e test that simulates truncated shard (server returns 200 with short body) to make sure loader fails early with clear error and automatic retry.

- Confirm whether CDN (CloudFront) was configured with stale-while-revalidate or range caching. If so, edge nodes could serve partial cached responses while origin corrects.
- Should we standardize on safetensors-only releases to simplify header checks? Pros/cons: faster validation vs backwards compatibility for some older models.

Observed symptoms:
- Crash during torch.load or safetensors load when model is sharded (8 shards). Usually after the download completes but sometime while streaming.
- Errors: RuntimeError: unexpected EOF while reading bytes; EOFError: Ran out of input; safetensors.errors.InvalidFileError: magic header not found; AssertionError: expected 65536 bytes got 4096
- When failure occurs, size of local shard file is smaller than expected (truncated). Sometimes manifest/index.json lists correct sizes but actual bytes are short.

Commands / repro steps I tried:
1) HF snapshot download (repro with and without caching):
   huggingface-cli snapshot-download customerX/modelY --revision=main --cache-dir ./hf_cache_test
   -> sometimes snapshot-download exits successfully but one of the bin shards is truncated (smaller filesize).

2) raw HTTP download with curl and range to simulate streaming problem:
   curl -L -o pth-00001-of-00008.bin "https://huggingface.co/customerX/modelY/resolve/main/pytorch_model-00001-of-00008.bin" \
     --write-out "%{http_code} %{size_download}\n" --fail --retry 3 --max-time 120

   -> sometimes aws reports full size but sha256 differs from the hf-hosted copy.

Error snippets captured:
- RuntimeError: unexpected EOF while reading bytes (expected 8192 more bytes)
- EOFError: Ran out of input

2) Client-side streaming logic: huggingface-cli / requests library may not be checking Content-Length consistently for chunked responses; partial file written and rename completed too early.
3) Artifact replication mismatch: customer pushed two slightly different versions to different backends (S3 vs HF) and index points to different blob.
4) safetensors vs pytorch binary confusion: Some shards are published as safetensors but named .bin; loader mismatch causes magic header errors on attempt to load with torch.load.

- Added explicit content-length verification after download: compare header Content-Length vs downloaded bytes; keep retry if mismatch. Script:

- For Dedicated nodes, changed downloader to use ranged GET + reassemble (download in 8MB chunks, verify each chunk). This reduces occurrence in local tests.

[Runner service account token exfiltration alert: rotate tokens and validate CI access paths]
description:
Issue summary:
Security monitoring flagged potential exfiltration of a long-lived service token tied to a fleet of ephemeral CI runners. Alert originated from log anomaly: identical token used from two distinct datacenter IP ranges within a 5 minute window. Impact: potential unauthorized access to private repositories and deployments; immediate mitigation required for release pipelines scheduled tonight.

Impact:
- Nightly release pipelines (release-nightly) and a handful of ad-hoc build jobs are at risk of unauthorized usage.
- No confirmed production changes yet, but token reuse pattern suggests credential may be leaked to an external CI job runner.

Environment:
- prod control plane, primary runner pool in us-east-1, ephemeral runners launched via autoscaler with service-account tokens minted by internal token-service.

Steps to reproduce / observed sequence:
1) 2026-03-13T18:02Z: Security alert (Evidently: auth-anomaly-20260313-17) flagged token XXXXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX used from IP A and B.
2) Investigated runner logs: token XXXXXX appears in runner bootstrap logs for runner-id r-3487 and r-3491.
3) Token issuance log shows token minted by token-service for service-account ci-ephemeral-deployer at 2026-03-13T17:58Z with TTL 24h.
4) Access patterns include git fetch and artifact upload attempts to s3-bucket "ci-artifacts-prod".

Immediate requests:
- Rotate all active tokens for service-account ci-ephemeral-deployer and issue short-lived replacements (1h TTL) for any upcoming scheduled jobs.
- Block any outstanding runner sessions that present the old token.
- Audit artifact uploads and git pushes between 2026-03-13T17:50Z and 2026-03-13T18:20Z.


investigation:
Timeline and hypotheses:
- 2026-03-13T17:58Z token minted by token-service (log id ts-98231).
- 2026-03-13T18:02Z security alert for token reuse from multiple geo-ip blocks.
- Hypothesis A: token printed into a job log or artifact and then scraped by a scanning service or malicious actor.
- Hypothesis B: compromised runner bootstrap image contained a hardcoded token (unlikely, but check image digest).
- Hypothesis C: token-service issued a duplicate due to race and same token reused on two runners (race condition in token-service code).
Findings so far:
- Runner bootstrap scripts do not print tokens intentionally; however, one community script in customer templates folder was discovered in an older job that echoed env on error (CI job id 77312).
- Image digests for r-3487 and r-3491 match the current official ephemeral-runner image: sha256:fdc9..., no unauthorized modifications.
- Token-service code review shows a retry path that can return the same token if request ID deduplication occurs; engineering hypothesis plausible.
Logs & evidence locations:
- token-service logs: /var/logs/token-service/ts-2026-03-13.log (search ts-98231)
- runner audit: gs://redwood-ci-logs/runner/audit/2026/03/13/
- security alert: SIEM event auth-anomaly-20260313-17 (Slack #sec-alert archived thread)

comments:
Ava Martinez (reporter) 2026-03-13: Raised after SOC flagged token reuse; requesting immediate token rotation and kill of affected runners.
Samuel Cheng (assignee) 2026-03-13: Acknowledged. Initiating emergency rotation for ci-ephemeral-deployer; will create short TTL tokens for scheduled jobs. Requesting SRE to isolate runner pool.
Lena Ortiz (SRE) 2026-03-13: Isolating runner subnet and revoking existing tokens at the gateway level. Patching autoscaler to stop spawning new ephemeral runners from that SA until rotation completes.
Morgan Patel (Security) 2026-03-14: Found one suspicious artifact upload attempt; quarantine copy saved to secure bucket for forensic analysis. Suggest scanning artifacts for leaked secrets and checking access logs for third-party IPs.
Samuel Cheng 2026-03-14: Short-lived tokens issued (1h TTL) and deployed to release-nightly job definitions. Documented mitigation in runbook and linked a follow-up engineering ticket to fix token-service dedupe retry path.


resolution:
Mitigation steps executed 2026-03-14:
1) Revoked all active tokens for service-account ci-ephemeral-deployer in Vault and invalidated tokens at the gateway layer.
2) Issued new short-lived tokens (1h) and patched CI job definitions for release-nightly and related pipelines.
3) Quarantined suspicious artifact and initiated forensic scan.
4) SRE temporarily drained and reprovisioned the affected runner pool with fresh images.
5) Created follow-up engineering ticket INT-738211 to implement token-service fix (prevent duplicate token issuance under retry) and another task INT-738212 to add automated token-leak detection on artifact uploads.
Post-mortem/next steps:
- Engineering to harden token-service by 2026-03-20 and add extra logging for request IDs.
- CI config update to set default TTL for ephemeral tokens to 1h.
- Add a pre-flight check to runner bootstrap to redact env prints and fail if dangerous debug flags are present.
- Security to run backward scan for other service-accounts to ensure no further exposures.
Status: mitigations completed; further engineering work scheduled.

[MFA push approval attack followed by ephemeral CI token creation detected]
description:
Issue summary:
A member of the engineering org reported unexpected MFA push approvals on their corporate SSO during a short window (03/13 09:12–09:20 UTC). Shortly after, we observed a CI pipeline create an ephemeral token via the internal Developer Console service (dev-console) that was used to access repositories and trigger a build.

Impact:
- Potential unauthorized access to non-prod repos and CI artifacts for a limited window.
- Several builds triggered by an ephemeral token; no obvious data exfil attempts found so far.
- A subset of services experienced increased CI runs and elevated API call volume.

Environment:
- prod us-east tenants for identity and dev-console.
- Affected accounts belong to the engineering org (org-id: redwood-eng; internal only).

Steps to reproduce / timeline of observable events:
1) 2026-03-13T09:11:58Z: External push notification deliveries spike to multiple employees (observed in auth push logs).
2) 2026-03-13T09:12:20Z: User A (reporter) receives push prompt and taps 'Approve' (claims accidental).
3) 2026-03-13T09:13:05Z: SSO shows new privileged session for User A from 185.239.1.22 (ASN linked to foreign VPN provider).
4) 2026-03-13T09:14:10Z: dev-console API creates an ephemeral CI token (token id eph-9b3f) using User A's session.
5) 2026-03-13T09:14–09:18Z: Token used to trigger 3 pipeline runs across two repos (repo-alpha, repo-infra).
6) 2026-03-13T09:20:00Z: Anomaly detection flagged unusual CI token creation pattern and rate-limited dev-console API.

Logs / evidence links:
- Auth push deliveries: https://grafana.redwood.company/d/alerts/auth-push-spike (internal link)
- SSO session events (filtered): https://logs.redwood.company/sso?q=UserA+185.239.1.22
- Dev-console audit: https://audit.redwood.company/entries?token=eph-9b3f
- CI build traces: https://ci.redwood.company/builds?token=eph-9b3f

Initial hypothesis:
- This appears to be a push-approval social engineering attack (push fatigue or deliberate prompt) where an attacker originated push notifications from an external service and induced approvals. Once an MFA approval occurred, the attacker used the session to call dev-console APIs to create ephemeral CI tokens and run builds. The goal may be to plant a CI job that later exfiltrates secrets or extends access.

Immediate business questions:
- Were any secrets or artifacts uploaded to external endpoints during the build runs?
- Can we confirm whether the ephemeral token was scoped beyond build triggering (push rights or repo write)?
- Do additional users show similar push approval activity from the same IP range?

comments:
2026-03-13 09:30 - Rahul Mehta (SRE oncall): Triage started. Rate-limited dev-console and rotated active ephemeral tokens. Notifying Security Ops. Action: block IP range 185.239.0.0/16 at edge until further review.
2026-03-13 09:45 - Maya Liu (Security): Confirmed three builds triggered by eph-9b3f. No outbound HTTP to unfamiliar domains observed in network egress logs for those builds. Pulling full build logs for artifact checks.
2026-03-13 10:05 - Sofia Hernandez (Reporter): User A reports they clicked an unexpected notification after receiving a 'verification' SMS. Provided device timestamp and list of recent notifications. We requested device screenshot and blocked session.
2026-03-13 11:00 - Dev Console Team (engineer): Temporarily disabled token-creation API for non-admin sessions and pushed a config change to require reauth for API keys created via console. Will open PR with feature flag rollback if needed. Link: https://github.com/redwood/dev-console/pull/4876
2026-03-13 12:20 - Rahul Mehta (SRE): Detected two additional users with push prompts from the same foreign ASN. Requiring org-wide forced reauth for SSO sessions created between 09:00–10:00 UTC today.

investigation_notes:
Auth logs show push notifications originated from the org's push provider but were initiated via the provider API using a low-reputation API key (provider-key-zzx).
Provider API key activity traced to a rotation event last week; the key appears to have been used by a third-party integration. Working with vendor to identify requester IPs.
Ephemeral token eph-9b3f had limited scope: build.trigger, repo.read. It did not request write or secret:read scopes (based on token introspection).
No elevated GitHub PATs or service account keys were created in the window. However, one pipeline executed a script that attempted to curl to http://34.85.11.12/api/collect (blocked by egress rules).
We found a CI job step that downloads a community action from marketplace with version pin 'v1.2.3' — investigating supply chain risk and verifying checksum.

mitigation_steps:
Rotated dev-console service tokens and disabled ephemeral-token creation for sessions without step-up MFA.
Blocked ASN 185.239.0.0/16 at network edge and added to WAF denylist pending vendor coordination.
Forced SSO reauth for all org sessions created between 2026-03-13T09:00Z and 2026-03-13T10:30Z.
Scoped CI runners to deny outbound to non-allowlisted external endpoints and quarantined artifacts from the three suspicious builds.
Raised vendor incident with push provider; requested logs and API key usage audit for provider-key-zzx.
Notified legal and compliance; preparing internal communication for impacted employees asking for device review and MFA posture check.

resolution:
Ongoing. Immediate mitigations implemented; vendor coordination in progress. Security will update once vendor provides provider-key usage logs and CI artifact verification completes. Post-incident action items to follow for hardening dev-console token creation flow.

follow_up_actions:
Add MFA step-up requirement for token creation APIs (owner: Dev Console)
Vendor audit for push provider API keys (owner: Security)
Add CI runner egress allowlist and artifact verification pipeline (owner: CI Infra)

[CI runner proxy JWT TTL skew during vault rewrap evicting canary artifact cache]
description:
Issue summary: During an automated KMS/Vault rewrap of the proxy service token, CI runners started failing authentication to the internal HTTP proxy. This led to repeated runner reconnects and eviction of local artifact caches during a canary release window. Impact: several canary jobs were retried and lost cached artifacts, increasing runtime by ~10x and causing a canary rollback.

Impact: - 12 canary release jobs failed or were retried between 02:10–02:47 UTC. - Increased load on artifact store and degraded release pipeline throughput. - Customers on the canary window experienced delayed deployments (release rollback triggered).

Environment: production (us-east) runners behind internal proxy (runner-proxy-v2), vault transit rewrap job ran at 02:05 UTC.

steps_to_reproduce:
Schedule a Vault transit key rewrap that rotates the proxy service token (simulate with staging cert).
Trigger a canary release with CI runners pinned to the proxy pool in us-east and with artifact cache enabled.
Observe runner logs for repeated 401/403 from proxy followed by runner reconnect and cache eviction messages.
Observe canary jobs being retried and artifact pull rates spiking on the artifact store.

observed_behavior:
Runners received 401/403 for proxy requests starting ~02:10 UTC after rewrap completed.
Runner process performed TLS/connection re-establishment and then logged 'artifact cache invalidated: auth-mismatch'.
Canary orchestrator marked multiple jobs as unstable and initiated rollback at ~02:50 UTC.

expected_behavior:
Proxy token rotation should be transparent to active runners (grace period or token exchange).
Runner artifact cache should survive token refresh or have a graceful handoff path.

logs:
[runner-14321] 2026-03-02T02:12:07Z ERROR proxy_auth: 401 Unauthorized (token not found)
[runner-14321] 2026-03-02T02:12:09Z WARN cache: eviction triggered due to auth validation failure
[proxy-v2] 2026-03-02T02:05:02Z INFO rewrap: transit rewrap completed, new_token_id=tok-7b1f
[proxy-v2] 2026-03-02T02:05:05Z INFO token-publish: broadcast token epoch=97 ttl=300s

investigation_notes:
Initial hypothesis: token TTL published by Vault rewrap (300s) was shorter than runner re-auth window, causing mismatch.
Checked proxy token cache — observed a race where proxy accepted old token for ~10s, then started rejecting until runners picked up a new exchange endpoint.
Runner code expects token refresh via STS endpoint but proxy rewrap changed token id; no fallback to exchange endpoint was attempted by older runner version (v1.14.2).
Artifact cache is bound to a proxy-auth context; eviction is triggered when auth_digest changes.

root_cause:
Race between Vault transit rewrap publishing a token id change and older runner versions (v1.14.2) lacking the automatic exchange fallback. The proxy enforces token id binding for artifact cache; when tokens changed mid-session, cache was invalidated.

mitigation_steps:
1) Reverted to previous token epoch within 8 minutes to restore connectivity for outstanding runners.
2) Temporarily paused further vault rewrap jobs and scheduled a coordinated token-rotation rollout with a rolling grace window for runners.
3) Rolled forward runner fleet to v1.15.0 on a subset (canary) which contains exchange fallback logic.
4) Increased token grace TTL during rotation from 300s -> 600s for next scheduled rewrap to avoid immediate eviction.

comments:
Marisol Vega (reporter) 2026-03-02: Observed spike in artifact store egress and canary rollback triggered automatically by orchestrator. Raising urgency due to potential customer impact.
Evan Patel (assignee) 2026-03-02: Reverted token epoch and paused rotations. Gathering runner logs for versions; initial look points at v1.14.x fleet.
SRE on-call (Priya Kumar) 2026-03-03: Confirmed proxy accepted old token for ~12s then invalidated; added temporary metric for proxy-token-age and token-id-delta.
Release Eng (Luis Ortega) 2026-03-04: Will queue a controlled canary run once runner fleet patched and token grace TTL increased. Need postmortem to adjust rotation playbook.
Evan Patel 2026-03-05: Pushed v1.15.0 to 60% of runners in us-east; monitoring artifact hit-rate and authentication error rate.

resolution_notes:
Deployed runner v1.15.0 which implements token-exchange fallback; verified canary jobs completed without cache eviction on 2026-03-05 08:12 UTC.
Updated Vault rotation playbook to include: pre-notify runner fleet, set temporary grace TTL, and stagger rotations by region.
Added a proxy metric and alert for token-id churn and token-reject-rate > 1% per minute.
Follow-up action: author a runbook change and schedule retro with Release and Security teams (owner: Luis Ortega, due 2026-03-12).

followup_actions:
Create runbook PR to Confluence: 'Token Rotation for Runner Proxy' (owner: Luis Ortega).
Backfill canary tests to include token-rotation simulation as part of pre-merge suite (owner: QA team).
Plan a coordinated multi-region rotation drill 2026-03-18.

[Locked runner service account access due to Conditional Access policy during nightly gated release]
description:
Issue summary: During the 2026-03-12 nightly gated release, several CI jobs using the 'release-runner-us-east' service account failed to start. The pipeline stalled at 'Acquire runner' with 403/401-style authorization failures from the cloud IAM token exchange. Impact: Nightly release blocked for ~3.5 hours, manual rollback required for one canary. Environment: Production CI (self-hosted runners) in us-east region; release window 02:00-06:00 UTC. Affected components: ci-runner, auth, vault, gcp-iam. Steps to reproduce: 1) Trigger gated release pipeline targeting canary group. 2) Observe runner registration step hang and repeated auth errors in runner logs. 3) Attempt manual token refresh via ci-admin account fails with 'conditional access denied' response. Logs & observed errors: - Runner: "401: AccessDenied - ConditionalAccessPolicyRestrictsSignIn" - Token-service: "403 Forbidden: token exchange blocked by CA policy (require compliant device)" - Vault: "wrapped token unwrap succeeded" (no obvious Vault error) Notes: This appears related to a Conditional Access (CA) policy change that started enforcing device compliance for service principals earlier today. The release-runner service account uses short-lived OIDC tokens minted by the CI control plane; the policy may be evaluating the identity as a user session rather than a machine identity. No previous incidents observed for this runner pool.

comments:
2026-03-12 03:05 - Sophia Li (on-call SRE): Initial triage - runners failed to register; auth service returning CA-deny. Escalating to IAM team.
2026-03-12 03:18 - Ravi Patel (Release Eng): Confirmed pipeline blocked. We temporarily moved canary to earlier stable image to avoid user exposure. Need root cause before re-enabling nightlies.
2026-03-12 03:42 - Marcus Chen (IAM): Observed Conditional Access policy modification at 01:58 UTC that included a new 'require device_compliance' rule for service principals. Policy change came from SecOps request: 'tighten access for interactive sessions'.
2026-03-12 04:10 - Elena Gomez (Reporter): Note - release-runner identities authenticate via OIDC with audience claim 'ci-runner'. They do not surface a device_compliance signal. Suggest bypassing CA for this SP temporarily.
2026-03-12 05:05 - Marcus Chen (IAM): Applied temporary CA exclusion for service principal 'release-runner-sp' to restore flow. Nightly pipeline resumed. Need follow-up to define permanent fix.
2026-03-13 10:23 - Ravi Patel (Assignee): Investigation in progress - mapping where OIDC tokens are evaluated as user sessions. Drafting changes to token exchange to set 'auth_context' hint for machine identity.

investigation_notes:
Hypothesis A: Conditional Access policy treats any token exchange originating from the CI control plane as interactive because the exchange path includes a user-agent header from the webhook proxy.
Hypothesis B: New SecOps rule was applied broadly to service principals; vault-wrapped tokens lack the expected claim ('client_type':'machine') used by the CA gating logic.
Observed: Vault unwrap and local token caching succeeded; failure occurs on cloud IAM token mint step returning CA deny. 
Correlation: Policy change timestamp aligns with start of failures. No code deploys to CI control plane during window. 
Temporary mitigation: IAM applied an exclusion that restored runner auth but is not acceptable long-term. Need documented JIT exclusion and automation guardrails.
Next steps: 1) Define durable signal in OIDC token (e.g., add 'auth_method':'pod_identity' or 'client_type':'service') and coordinate with SecOps to map condition. 2) Harden CI token exchange to use dedicated mTLS channel for machine identities. 3) Add synthetic checks to detect CA policy regression before release windows.

resolution:
Temporary workaround applied: SecOps added a scoped Conditional Access exclusion for the 'release-runner-sp' service principal and the nightly pipeline was resumed. Root cause: SecOps rollout of a device_compliance requirement inadvertently matched the CI token exchange path because tokens lacked a machine signal. Permanent fix plan: 1) Implement token claim augmentation in the CI token-minting service to include 'client_type':'machine' and 'auth_method':'oidc:ci' (PRs opened: infra#2418, ci#1192). 2) Coordinate with SecOps to map a CA condition that evaluates the new claim instead of blanket device_compliance. 3) Add pre-release synthetic gating that validates runner registration under current CA rules (task assigned to Release Eng). Follow-ups: update runbooks and add an automated rollback if CA changes block runner auth. Target completion: 2026-03-24.

workaround_steps:
1) SecOps: Add Conditional Access exclusion for 'release-runner-sp' (scoped to CI token exchange endpoints) to restore pipeline. (Already applied) 
2) Release Eng: Avoid scheduling high-risk gated nightlies until claim augmentation is deployed. 
3) SRE: Monitor runner registration metrics and alert on CA-deny spikes with a 1-minute window.

[Unusual spike in IdP-signed JWT usage across multiple internal accounts]
description:
Issue summary:
We observed an anomalous spike in authentication events where IdP-issued JWTs (SAML->OIDC pipeline) were used to exchange for short-lived service tokens. These exchanges originated from a small set of IPs that are not common for our workforce and targeted multiple internal service and user accounts.

Impact:
- Potential credential or token re-use affecting 3 internal accounts and multiple service tokens issued to CI/CD runners.
- No evidence yet of data exfiltration, but some high-privilege service tokens were minted and used to call internal admin APIs.
- Could affect deployment pipelines and onboarding workflows if tokens are revoked without a coordinated mitigation.

Environment:
- Production SSO (IdP: corporate Okta) federated to Redwood SSO proxy in us-east-1.
- Time window: 2026-03-12 03:12:00 UTC -> 2026-03-12 03:45:00 UTC.

Observed indicators / logs:
- Auth audit logs show ~180 token exchanges with IdP-signed JWTs in the 33-minute window.
- Source IPs: 34.120.12.87, 34.120.13.192 (ASN / cloud provider observed).
- User agents: headless-bot/1.2, python-requests/2.31.0 (some variance).
- Several exchanges returned service tokens with admin-scoped claims for infra-ops account.
- No immediate 5xx or runtime errors observed on admin APIs; however, token usage patterns were unusual (burst requests to /v1/admin/keys).

Steps to reproduce (for validation):
1) Query auth audit index: query by event_type:token_exchange AND source_ip in [34.120.12.87,34.120.13.192] AND timestamp between 2026-03-12T03:00:00Z and 2026-03-12T04:00:00Z.
2) Correlate returned token IDs with internal token-usage logs in service-audit index.
3) Verify Okta org logs for suspicious OAuth/OIDC grant activity for the same time window.

Initial mitigation actions taken:
- Rotated affected service keys for svc-data-ingest and infra-ops.
- Forced SSO session revocations for implicated human accounts (alice@redwood.com).
- Throttled token exchange endpoint for non-corp IP ranges and added temporary WAF rule to block the two IPs.
- Opened an incident bridge and notified Legal and Product Security.
- Created this internal-support ticket to capture investigation and follow-up remediation tasks.


investigation_notes:
03/12 03:20 UTC - Alert from auth-monitoring: token_exchange_rate > 25/min for SSO proxy; triggered oncall.
03/12 03:25 UTC - Confirmed 180 exchanges from two external IPs; fetched raw auth logs and correlated to service-audit.
03/12 03:28 UTC - Hypothesis A: credentials/token capture from phishing or compromised CI/CD runner. Hypothesis B: misconfigured third-party integration replaying JWTs.
03/12 03:34 UTC - Checked Okta sign-in logs: no interactive human sign-in from these IPs, but several token-grant events via service app client. Opened ticket with Okta support for additional metadata.
03/12 03:40 UTC - Identified a CI runner artifact that had environment variable containing long-lived client assertion; rotated that credential and invalidated prior tokens.
03/13 09:00 UTC - SRE ran forensics on the two IPs: both map to ephemeral cloud VMs; abuse reports filed with provider.
03/14 10:30 UTC - Security team requested expanded audit retention for token_exchange logs and started payload-level parsing to extract JWT ids for replay detection.

comments:
Aisha Patel (Reporter) 2026-03-12: Initial detection and mitigation steps listed. On-call will coordinate rotations.
Diego Morales (Assignee) 2026-03-12: Applied WAF block for observed IPs and forced session revocations for implicated users. Continuing log correlation.
Priya Shah (Product Security) 2026-03-12: Requesting Okta export of app-level grant logs and list of affected app client IDs; also advise rotating any CI client assertions.
Samir Gupta (SRE) 2026-03-13: Found a Jenkins runner in project 'release-automation' with a stale service assertion. Rotated and removed hard-coded token from job config. Investigating whether token was exfiltrated via job artifacts.
Legal 2026-03-13: Please collect timeline for any external communications; we'll prepare a notice template if customer-facing impact is discovered.
Diego Morales 2026-03-14: Filing for a post-incident review once we confirm no further exchange spikes. Recommend making token-exchange rate limit permanent for non-corp ranges.

next_steps:
Complete full token lineage mapping for all exchanged tokens during window and mark any sessions/tokens for permanent revocation where appropriate.
Coordinate with Identity team and Okta support to determine the exact grant flow used and whether the client application was configured with overly-broad scopes.
Implement a permanent rule in API gateway to restrict token_exchange endpoint to corp IP ranges and known CI egress ranges, with an allowlist for validated third-party integrators.

No customer data confirmed accessed at time of last update.

[Refactor press transitions and theming fallback for chained buttons]
description:
This ticket refactors how we compute and apply press/hover/focus transitions for sequences of adjacent buttons (eg. compound actions, icon+primary, pill groups) and establishes a deterministic theming fallback when token aliases are missing or partially overridden. Recent regressions caused inconsistent elevation and color pops when disabled or loading states occur in chained button groups; this effort aims to unify the interaction model and provide a migration path for deprecated tokens.

context:
- Multiple regressions reported in console and product: hover glow flicker when adjacent icon button switches to loading; focus ring clipping when ghost button sits next to a primary pill; disabled opacity mismatch across themes.
- Root cause: token aliasing changes during last token migration introduced conditional fallbacks that resolve differently depending on DOM order and CSS specificity. Additionally, some CSS transition stacks are not isolation-safe which allows sibling state changes to trigger repaints.
- Goal: produce a resilient, theme-agnostic contract for chained buttons so interaction states are predictable and accessible across themes and sizes.

proposed_solution:
1) Introduce a tiny, explicitly-namespaced 'interaction-surface' token set that decouples pressed/hover/focus elevation and overlay color from per-variant color tokens. 2) Implement a defensive resolution layer in the component which: prefers explicit token -> falls back to theme anchored alias -> falls back to neutral interaction token. 3) Replace sibling-dependent CSS transitions with an isolation layer (transform + will-change + pointer-events adjustments) and a micro-state debounce so rapid sibling updates don't produce visible jitter. 4) Add a short migration guide and codemod to surface deprecated tokens during dev build.

engineering_notes:
Work with ENG runtime and frontend infra: ENG will expose kernel for micro-animation control (prefers transform over opacity where feasible). Need a Unit test harness for rendering focus ring clipping and snapshot tests for theming permutations. Plan to ship a small runtime flag to enable defensive resolution during rollout.

acceptance_criteria:
Chained buttons show no visual flicker when adjacent sibling enters loading state (manual QA + 3 theme snapshots)
Disabled state opacity across all variants matches token contract within 2% contrast delta (automated color assertions)
Focus ring is not clipped in compound groups at small sizes (a11y keyboard test pass)
Token fallback resolution order documented in DS guide and implemented in component codepath

tasks:
Design: final visual spec and edge-case sheets (María)
Engineering: implementation PR with theming fallback (ENG-48921)
QA: create regression suite and run across light/dark/low-contrast themes
Docs: migration guide and codemod example in Confluence

progress_updates:
2026-03-03: Initial spike completed — prototype using 'interaction-surface' token shows reduced repaint on Chrome 110.
2026-03-06: Found two token alias collisions when theme overrides define '--button-hover' at component scope; added defensive prefixing to spec.
2026-03-10: Engineering PR opened from ENG-48921; initial visual diff snapshots included.
2026-03-12: Accessibility review: focus ring contrast is borderline on high-contrast theme; adjusted ring width and updated spec.
2026-03-14: Design review meeting — reviewers approved visual direction; requested quantized transition durations for reduced-motion users.

decision_log:
Adopt 'interaction-surface' namespace rather than extending existing variant tokens (decision rationale: isolates interaction logic from color tokens and simplifies migration)
Use transform-based micro animations as default; opacity permitted only for overlay fades (decision rationale: avoids layout repaints and sibling repaint cascades)

[Migrate interaction tokens to theme variable layer and resolve hover glow regression]
description:
Summary: Migrate all interactive state colors and elevation effects (hover, focus, active, disabled, pressed, and loading overlays) from component-local tokens into the new theme variable layer so they resolve consistently across light/dark/high-contrast themes. While doing this migration, fix a visible hover 'glow' regression that appears on icon-only and compact buttons when motion is reduced and when both inner and outer shadows are applied.

Background: During the tokens consolidation in Q4 we introduced per-component state tokens for buttons to support rapid experiments. Those tokens diverged from the theme layer and produced inconsistent hover/active treatments in some combinations: dark theme + high-contrast + reduced-motion. A recent customer bug report surfaced a flicker/glow where stacked shadows briefly show as double outlines on icon-only buttons when moving the pointer or programmatically toggling loading state.

Goal: Ensure all button interactive states are sourced from theme variables (not component-level overrides), eliminate the stacking shadow/glow regression, and add automated visual/interaction tests to catch regressions across themes and motion preferences. Deliverables: token migration PR, Figma token update, updated component docs, automated Cypress+Percy snapshots, accessibility signoff.

Out of scope: Rewriting button anatomy or changing visual language beyond aligning existing tokens to the theme; any JS runtime batching of hover events (handled by runtime team).

Hover glow regression reproduced in a test harness before the fix and verified resolved after changes in light/dark/high-contrast
Reduced-motion preference preserves semantics (no new motion introduced) and no double-shadow artifacts
Figma token set updated and cross-checked with the new theme variables; figma link added to PR
Unit/visual tests added: component-level storyshots and e2e visual snapshots across themes and reduced-motion

[Smooth hover suppression and icon-cluster hitbox alignment]
description:
Problem: Several product teams have reported subtle regressions where icon-only buttons in dense toolbars have inconsistent hover flicker, misaligned hitboxes between visual outlines and pointer targets, and opaque hover suppression when rapid cursor movements cross adjacent controls. These issues are pronounced in high-contrast themes and when token overrides (density / spacing tokens) are applied at the app layer. This ticket scopes a design-led remediation that standardizes token mapping, introduces a smooth hover-suppression interaction pattern (debounced fade + kinetic micro-gesture), and defines a hitbox alignment contract for icon clusters to avoid accidental activations and restore keyboard/focus parity.

design_notes:
We observed three classes of failures: visual offset between SVG icon bounds and CSS interactive padding; immediate hover-on/hover-off flicker when moving between tightly spaced icons; and focus ring clipping in high-contrast themes where ring thickness exceeds token-provided padding.
Proposed interaction: apply a small pointer "safe area" of 6px around icon visuals as the canonical hitbox, independent from visual padding. Implement hover suppression by ignoring enter/leave events shorter than hover-debounce token (60ms). Use opacity transitions for hover surfaces to avoid layout jank.
Accessibility: ensure focus-visible always shows after keyboard tab regardless of hover suppression. For users with reduced-motion preference, reduce fade to an instant state transition and skip debounce when assistive tech is detected.

proposed_solution:
Token additions: --button-hitbox-offset (6px), --button-hover-debounce (60ms), --button-hover-fade (120ms), --button-focus-ring-padding (4px).
Component change: make hitbox computed from token; visuals (background, shadow) remain inside existing padding. Update CSS logical properties so RTL works naturally.
Transition plan: roll out tokens as a nonbreaking opt-in in designlib 2026.03, provide migration guide for applications that previously relied on custom padding overrides. Add a temporary compatibility flag (prefers-legacy-hitbox) for early adopters.

acceptance_criteria:
Icon-only buttons across desktop toolbar, compact lists, and card controls have consistent pointer hitboxes that match the defined interactive area in visual specs (no more than 6px misalignment on any axis).
Hover state uses a 60ms suppression debounce then a 120ms fade-in for hover affordance; rapid cursor passes (<60ms) should not trigger visible hover flicker.
High-contrast and dark themes map spacing/touch tokens correctly so hover overlays and focus rings do not overflow neighboring controls.
Keyboard navigation exposes the same focus visuals as pointer hover (focus-visible parity), and focus restoration after a pointer-initiated press-cancel returns to logical focus.
Design tokens required (spacing, hitbox-offset, hover-debounce, hover-fade-duration) are documented in the token catalog and example token overrides are provided.
Cross-team regression tests (visual snapshot + a11y keyboard flow) added to the component suite and passing in the designlib playground.

visual_specs:
Canonical hitbox: icon visual bounds + --button-hitbox-offset on all sides; visual background remains 8px inset from hitbox in default density.
Hover surface: semi-transparent overlay with 0.06 alpha in light theme, 0.12 in dark theme; subject to hover-fade token.
Focus ring: uses --button-focus-ring-padding and matches accessible color tokens for each theme variant.

qa_checklist:

Confirm hover suppression prevents visual flicker for <60ms passes and still triggers for steady hover >60ms.
Keyboard tab focus shows focus-visible same as hover overlay and returns correctly after press/cancel.
Reduced-motion preference disables fade but keeps suppression semantics.
Visual snapshots match approved Figma comps for default and high-contrast themes.
