[Demo tenant hitting 429 throttling during live customer demo (Northstar Payments)]
description:
Issue summary
- During a live SE-led demo for Northstar Payments, the Redwood demo tenant began returning HTTP 429 responses mid-flow (streaming chat + tool call step). This caused the demo to stall and required switching to backup screenshots for the Console section.

Customer impact
- Live demo interruption (~6–8 minutes). Customer saw repeated 429s and intermittent retries.
- Risk: undermines reliability story and raises concern about quota predictability/noisy-neighbor.

When / where
- Date/time: 2025-11-12 ~19:10–19:25 UTC
- Environment: prod / us-east
- Tenant: Redwood internal demo org ("demo tenant")

Observed behavior
- Chat/completions requests started returning:
  - 429 Too Many Requests
  - Response headers included rate-limit remaining=0 (per-minute)
- Retries from demo app increased request volume, exacerbating throttling.

Expected behavior
- Demo tenant should be sized for at least 2 parallel demos, with headroom for retries/streaming and synthetic traffic seeding.

Steps to reproduce (as seen during call)
1) Start demo app scenario runner (streaming chat)
2) Execute tool-calling step (adds 1–2 additional calls)
3) Open Console in parallel (refreshes usage/cost panels)
4) Within ~2 minutes, observe 429s

Initial hypotheses
- Demo API key configured with self-serve default RPM/TPM limits.
- Synthetic traffic generator + live demo sharing same project/key.
- Parallel demos earlier in the hour consumed burst capacity; rate-limit window not reset.

Investigation notes
- Checked gateway logs for the demo org/project: throttles triggered on request-rate limit (RPM), not GPU capacity.
- No elevated 5xx in serving runtime; this was an API gateway quota/rate-limit enforcement event.
- Console page refreshes were not the root cause but contributed to request count and distracted during recovery.

Mitigation applied (during incident)
- Temporary quota uplift applied to demo org/project in us-east:
  - Increased RPM cap + burst allowance
  - Increased TPM cap to reduce retry amplification for streaming
- Confirmed new limits took effect within ~60 seconds; 429s stopped.

Root cause
- Demo tenant was provisioned with quota defaults intended for standard self-serve tenants, and our automation did not reliably apply the higher demo profile. Additionally, synthetic traffic seeding was configured to use the same project/key as live demos, consuming part of the minute-based request budget.

Resolution
- Short-term: raise demo tenant quotas and move synthetic traffic generator to a dedicated "seed" project/key to isolate from live demo activity.
- Long-term: update demo tenant provisioning automation defaults to always apply demo quota profile + create separate scoped keys (live-demo vs seed-traffic), and add a demo healthcheck gate that verifies quota/rate-limit settings before SEs start a call.

Customer-facing notes (what SE said)
- Framed as: "We hit our safety rate limit in the demo environment; production customers set limits appropriate to their workloads, and Dedicated capacity has separate controls. We’ll adjust the demo tenant so it never happens again."

Follow-ups / action items
- [DONE] Document immediate workaround in demo runbook: if 429s occur, switch to backup mode and run healthcheck.
- [DONE] Add healthcheck validation for quota/rate limits and surface clear pass/fail output (linked PR).
- [DONE] Provisioning automation: ensure demo profile quotas applied idempotently; prevent seed job from sharing live-demo key.
- [TODO] Add alerting on demo-tenant approaching RPM/TPM caps (warning threshold) routed to demo on-call alias.

Workarounds (SE playbook)
- Run demo tenant healthcheck endpoint; if quotas not applied, page #support and switch to backup screenshots.
- If throttling persists, pause synthetic traffic generator for the live window and retry after 60s rate-limit window reset.

Notes on data/security
- All traffic is synthetic/demo; no customer data involved.

References
- Slack: #support and #sales thread (internal) around live demo throttling
- Confluence: Demo capacity/quotas runbook + demo tenant reset runbook
- Related: SUP-4189 (Console dashboards empty; seed traffic generator separation work overlaps)


comments:
2025-11-12 19:22 UTC — Markus Klein (Reporter): Hit repeated 429s in the demo tenant mid-call with Northstar. Demo app was streaming + tool-calling. We had to switch to screenshots. Can someone check rate-limits/quota on demo org? This should be sized for parallel demos.
2025-11-12 19:31 UTC — Sean Gallagher (Assignee): Looking. Please share request IDs or approximate timestamps; I’ll pull gateway throttling logs. Initial guess: RPM cap too low on the demo key and retries are amplifying.
2025-11-12 19:44 UTC — Allison Grant: Confirmed in gateway metrics: throttling is on RPM (not capacity). Spikes line up with demo app retries + Console refreshes. No serving-runtime errors.

2025-11-12 20:07 UTC — Markus Klein: Confirmed. Reran the tool-call step and streaming stayed clean. Thanks. We still need this fixed in provisioning so it’s not a manual knob every time.

resolution:
Resolved by increasing demo tenant RPM/TPM quotas, isolating synthetic traffic to a dedicated seed project/key, and adding a demo healthcheck to validate quota/rate-limit settings before demos. Provisioning automation updated to apply demo quota profile idempotently; subsequent demos confirmed stable.

[Adaptive sparkline density and column compression mode (prototype)]
description:

Goal is to reduce vertical space for high-cardinality datasets while preserving key signals (trend sparklines, sort/filter affordances, and accessible keyboard navigation). This ticket covers design exploration, prototype Figma frames, developer handoff tokens, and a lightweight usability test with 6 internal reviewers.

Accessibility checklist passed: tab order preserved, aria-labels for compressed cells, contrast for sparkline strokes
Developer-ready component spec including prop surface for: density, sparkline-on/off, compression-threshold, accessible-label-fn
Lightweight usability feedback notes captured and follow-up tickets created for prioritized engineering work

[Gesture-driven column stacking and incremental virtualization for large tables]
description:
Problem: Our current virtualized table handles high row counts well but struggles with very wide tables (many columns) on narrow viewports. Users frequently need to scan groups of related columns and then collapse them to preserve space. Existing solutions (column pinning, responsive collapse) are either too static or require multiple clicks. We need a design that enables rapid, discoverable column compression/stacking driven by natural gestures and incremental rendering to keep memory/paint cost low.

Goals:
- Provide a gesture-driven way to compress groups of less-important columns into stacked summaries without losing scannability.
- Make transitions cheap by coupling UI gestures with incremental virtualization (render only visible column groups + their stacked summaries).
- Preserve keyboard and screen-reader accessibility; gestures must have equivalents (keyboard shortcuts and toolbar controls).
- Surface quick cell-level summaries (mini-aggregates) for stacked groups so users can still compare values at-a-glance.
- Capture telemetry around reflow/resize/stack events to inform heuristics for auto-compress.

Proposed approach:
1) Column stacking concept: allow the user to select a contiguous column range and invoke a stacking action via a two-finger horizontal swipe (touch/trackpad) or a sustained drag on the column gutter. The selected range collapses into a compact stacked cell that shows the top 3 values and an overflow indicator. Stacked state is reversible with the opposite gesture or via a small inline chip control.

2) Incremental virtualization: when columns are stacked, the renderer will treat the grouped columns as a single virtual column for layout/paint purposes. Only the visible rows' stacked summaries are rendered initially; detailed cells are lazily hydrated on hover or expand. This keeps memory and paint costs proportional to viewport complexity rather than total column count.

3) Gesture-based density switcher: incorporate a pinch-zoom gesture (trackpad/touch) over the table header to cycle density modes (comfortable / compact / dense). Each mode tweaks font-size, row-padding, and the threshold for when columns become eligible for auto-stacking. Provide a keyboard shortcut (Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + =/-) and a persistent toolbar density menu for discoverability.

4) Mini-aggregates and summaries: stacked cells include one-line summaries (mean/median/count as configured by user), sparklines for numeric columns (optional), and a tooltip with the top N values. For mixed-type columns, a concise textual summary (e.g., "2 labels, 1 date") is shown.

5) Accessibility and keyboard flow: gestures have explicit equivalents: select columns via Shift+click or keyboard range selection, then press S to stack/unstack. Screen readers announce stacked groups as "collapsed group: columns A–D (3 visible rows summarized)" and expose an action to expand. Focus must move predictably into stacked cell controls.

6) Telemetry and heuristics: collect opt-in telemetry (user-configurable) about stacking frequency, auto-stack suggestions accepted/rejected, density changes, and latency/paint measurements during stack/unstack. Use this data to refine automatic suggestions for column stacking on similar datasets.

Trade-offs and constraints:
- Complexity: gestures add discovery burden; we mitigate with initial onboarding overlay and explicit toolbar controls.
- Performance: incremental virtualization reduces paint cost but introduces complexity in hydration. We'll prototype a minimal hydration API so engineering can reuse existing cell renderers.
- Backwards compatibility: existing table APIs should remain functional; stacking will be an opt-in feature behind a feature flag.

Acceptance criteria:
- Users can stack and unstack column ranges using both gesture and keyboard/toolbar controls (end-to-end flow).
- Stacked groups render summaries for visible rows only; expanding a single row hydrates detailed cells without re-rendering the entire table.
- Density pinch gesture switches density reliably on supported devices and falls back to toolbar/keyboard on desktop.
- Screen readers correctly announce stacked groups and expose expand/collapse controls.
- Telemetry events emitted for stack/unstack and density changes and visible in Product analytics dashboard (basic event schema documented).

Deliverables:
- High-fidelity prototype (Figma) showing gestures, stacked cell visual states, and density transitions.
- Interaction spec complete with keyboard equivalents, ARIA notes, and animation durations.
- Engineering API proposal for incremental hydration and virtual column grouping.
- Small lab usability test (n=6) with participants from Support and Solutions to validate discoverability.

Rollout plan:
- Week 1: complete prototype and interaction spec.
- Week 2: engineering spike to validate hydration approach and perf benchmark.
- Week 3: iterate design based on spike and run small usability sessions.
- Week 4: soft launch behind feature flag to internal users with telemetry enabled.

Links to artifacts: Figma: https://redwood.design/figma/table-stacking-proto (placeholder), Spike doc: https://drive.redwood.com/docs/eng/table-stacking-spike (placeholder), GitHub RFC: https://github.com/redwood-inference/rfcs/pull/182 (placeholder).

[Refine table affordances: sticky guides, clip-over previews, and smooth density transitions]
description:
Deliver a cohesive set of UX patterns and production-ready assets for the table component to improve discoverability and control of column resizing, sorting/filtering, and density changes. Focus areas: 1) sticky column guide lines and snap hints to make resizing precise on high-density tables; 2) clip-over hover previews that reveal clipped cell content without breaking virtualization performance; 3) smooth density transitions (a 'density glide') so users can move between compact/comfortable modes without layout jank. Work includes interaction specs, accessibility requirements, and handoff-ready Figma components and tokens.

acceptance_criteria:
Design specs for sticky column guide lines with snap magnetism documented and approved by Eng and PM
Clip-over hover preview behaviour defined, with keyboard-accessible alternative and a performance budget (no >10ms additional per-row cost in our perf test harness)
Density glide prototypes demonstrating smooth interpolation across at least three density presets (compact, standard, comfortable) and clear token mapping for spacing/line-height
Figma components and tokens delivered, variant-ready, with clear naming and token usage notes
Accessibility checklist completed: focus order, keyboard resize handle, aria descriptions for clipped content previews, contrast checks for guide lines
Engineering acceptance: small demo PR integrating design tokens and the hover preview stub (link in 'links')
Design review approved and a rollout plan added to the Console roadmap (release tag)

design_decisions:
Use a thin, high-contrast sticky guide line that appears on column hover/drag rather than persistent grid lines to reduce visual noise
Adopt 'magnetic snapping' to common column widths with an optional modifier key to temporarily disable snapping for fine-grained control
Implement clip-over hover previews as a portal that layers above the virtualized viewport to avoid reflow; provide keyboard invocation via 'Enter' on focused cell
Implement density glide by interpolating spacing tokens rather than hard-swapping classes to minimize layout shifts and reflows
Keep default behaviour conservative on mobile (no hover previews) and provide an explicit preview action in the row context menu

tradeoffs:
Clip-over previews require a layering solution that sits outside the virtualization window. Pros: no rerender of virtual window and instant reveal. Cons: additional complexity in z-order management and potential accessibility edge cases.
Magnetic snapping simplifies resizing for most users but can be frustrating for power users; we propose a modifier key (Ctrl/Cmd) to disable snapping rather than a global setting to minimize UI surface.
Interpolating tokens for density reduces visual jank but increases the complexity of token mapping and may require engineering work to support fractional pixel spacing on some browsers.
Adding keyboard preview flow improves accessibility but needs careful UX to avoid accidental activation; chosen pattern ties preview activation to focus+Enter rather than simple focus to reduce false positives.

[Introduce dynamic column compression and tactile resize rails for large virtualized tables]
description:
Goal: Design an interaction pattern and visual affordance that allows users to resize columns in extremely wide virtualized tables with minimal layout thrash, predictable snapping, and an optional compression mode that reduces adjacent column widths to preserve table width without forcing horizontal scroll. This includes a new tactile resize rail (a persistent visual rail that surfaces on hover/focus) and a 'dynamic compression' behavior that isolates content overflow to lower-priority columns.

Background: Current column-resize behavior in the component library causes janky layout shifts for large result sets (especially with virtualization). Teams want both fine-grained control for power users and a compacting behavior for dense screens (dashboards, logs). Existing tickets focus on resizing, density tokens, and virtualization separately; this ticket unifies them into a single UX that is resilient to virtualization and accessible for keyboard/screen reader users.

Scope and deliverables:
- Interaction spec for tactile resize rails (hover/focus affordance, persistent rail mode, drag handles).
- Compression algorithm spec (priority-based shrink, min-width enforcement, snap thresholds, Overflow indicator).
- Accessibility: keyboard resize via arrow keys + modifier, live region messages for SRs, focus states.
- Visual tokens: new token set for rail thickness, hover color, compression overlay opacity, and snap micro-animation.
- Prototype: lightweight React prototype demonstrating behavior on large virtualized list with 10k rows.
- Engineering handoff doc with performance constraints and recommended implementation hooks (transform-based column offsets, measurement cache, requestAnimationFrame batching).

Acceptance criteria:
1) UX flows documented with annotated Figma file and click-through prototype.
2) Prototype demonstrates resize without layout jank at 10k rows on a mid-range laptop.
3) Compression algorithm preserves min-width tokens and exposes a per-column 'priority' attribute for shrink ordering.
4) Keyboard and screen reader interactions are documented and tested with simple a11y checklist.
5) Design review sign-off from PM and two engineers; follow-up engineering tickets created for runtime APIs.

Constraints and trade-offs:
- We avoid forcing engineers to rework the serving runtime; prefer adding hooks that sidestep per-row reflow (e.g., use column transform offsets and clip masks).
- Compression must be deterministic across browsers; this requires a well-defined tie-breaker for equal-priority columns.
- Visual density tokens must remain backward-compatible; introduce new tokens as opt-in so existing tables are unaffected.

[Docs: explain batching SLO tiers (fast/standard/cost-efficient), defaults, overrides, and troubleshooting]
body:
Summary: This PR updates public documentation to introduce Redwood’s workload-aware batching defaults and the three customer-facing latency SLO tiers: fast, standard, and cost-efficient. It explains what each tier optimizes for, how Redwood selects a profile, how to choose a tier per route/use case, and how to override defaults (Hosted API request-level, route-level policy, Dedicated tenant/cluster override). It also adds a troubleshooting checklist focused on common post-migration issues (tail latency spikes, streaming jitter, throughput vs latency trade-offs, and override precedence confusion). Motivation: We’re rolling out tiered batching defaults in runtime 1.22; customers need a clear mental model and concrete examples so they can adopt defaults safely without accidentally degrading streaming UX or overpaying for throughput. Scope of docs changes: Adds a new conceptual page “Batching tiers (SLO defaults)” under Performance → Inference tuning; Updates API reference to document `batching_tier` parameter and the corresponding request header; Updates Python/TypeScript examples to show tier selection for chat (streaming) vs batch summarization; Adds “How defaults are chosen” section with high-level signals (prompt length distribution, streaming vs non-streaming, concurrency) and an explicit note that Redwood does not do per-tenant real-time autotuning in this release; Adds FAQ: what happens if you don’t pick a tier (answer: standard by default, unless your route policy pins a tier); Adds Dedicated-specific notes on override precedence and where to view the effective tier in Console; Adds troubleshooting checklist and a short decision tree for latency vs cost issues. Key guidance included: Tier definitions (customer-facing): fast: prioritizes tail latency protection for interactive experiences and streaming; standard: balanced defaults for mixed workloads; cost-efficient: prioritizes throughput/$ per token with higher batching aggressiveness while maintaining published targets under typical loads. How to choose: fast for streaming chat endpoints, agent loops, user-facing autocomplete; standard for most APIs and mixed usage; cost-efficient for offline/batch jobs (summarization pipelines, embeddings at scale, rerank batches) and non-interactive endpoints. Overrides: Hosted API: per request via SDK parameter `batching_tier="fast"|"standard"|"cost_efficient"` (and header `X-Redwood-Batching-Tier` for raw REST callers); Route-level: policy config in Console/route configuration (documented as recommended for consistency and auditability); Dedicated: tenant/cluster override (documented precedence: customer override > route policy > platform default). Troubleshooting: If p99 increases after switching to fast: verify endpoint is actually set to fast (effective tier), check concurrent requests per route, ensure streaming is enabled for UI, and consider reducing concurrent tool calls or switching heavy routes to standard. If streaming feels “bursty”: confirm you’re using streaming responses end-to-end, and understand that tier selection affects queuing/batching but not token content; if UI jitter persists, fast tier is recommended and you may need to lower client-side chunk aggregation. If cost-efficient causes queueing: move interactive routes back to standard/fast, or apply cost-efficient only to batch routes; if you need both, split routes or create two policies pointing at the same model with different tiers. If overrides don’t seem to apply: check precedence (Dedicated override vs route policy), and confirm you’re not mixing request-level tier with a pinned route policy (docs now call out the behavior explicitly). Notes/limitations called out: Tiers are SLO defaults, not a guarantee for all workloads; workloads with extreme prompt lengths or highly bursty concurrency may still need route-level tuning or capacity adjustments; Tier selection does not change logging/retention or data handling; it only affects runtime scheduling/batching behavior; In overload, Redwood may apply backpressure and/or degrade gracefully; docs reference standard retry/timeout guidance rather than exposing internal modes. Rollout coordination: Copy aligns with Hosted API messaging and runtime rollout. Console screenshots are intentionally minimal in this PR (design is still landing), but we added textual pointers to where users can view ‘effective tier’ and ‘why this profile’. Related work: Runtime tiered defaults (runtime 1.22) and SDK parameter support are being shipped in parallel; this PR links to the example snippets that match the upcoming SDK releases. Testing: `docs:build` and `docs:linkcheck` passing; ran `npm test` for docs site; verified code samples compile (TypeScript) and run (Python) against current SDK APIs on main.

[Coalescing Invoker: grace-period batching, deterministic injection, and structured-output streaming compatibility]
description:
Context: Multi-tool call patterns at scale expose a tradeoff between per-request latency and downstream execution overhead when we naively fan out tool invocations. Customers reported jitter in streaming handshakes when several tool results were injected concurrently (see ENG-8921). Motivation: Smooth out spikes from parallel tool warmups and avoid duplicate retries while preserving deterministic injection order (for structured output consumers and OpenAI tool-calling compatibility). This PR implements a lightweight coalescing invoker that introduces a configurable grace period (default 10ms) to allow closely timed tool calls from the same top-level request to batch their execution, plus deterministic merge points for tool-result injection and a coordinated retry protocol that reduces duplicate tool executions. Key changes and design: 1) Grace-window coalescer (api/invoker/coalescer.py): collects tool call intents for a single request context for up to grace_period_ms before dispatching a prioritized execution set. Grace window is short (default 10ms) to keep tail latency bounded; tunable via request-level config. 2) Deterministic mergepoints (runtime/invoker/mergepoint.go): tool results are assigned stable sequence slots at dispatch time so downstream structured output assembly is order-deterministic even if tools finish out-of-order. This preserves existing structured-output expectations and OpenAI function-call ordering semantics. 3) Coordinated retry token (protocol/invoker_retry.proto + runtime): introduces a small idempotency token coupled with a coordinator lease to avoid concurrent retries launching duplicate side effects when multiple workers observe timeouts. Token acquisition is optimistic; fallback retry uses backoff and escalates to a single-quorum retry owner. 4) Streaming handshake stabilizations (api/gateways/openai_compat_stream.go): when streaming a response that will include tool-result injections, the gateway now waits for mergepoint assignment and streams slot-wrapped fragments to clients. We added a lightweight client-side marker in TS SDK so OpenAI-compat clients can present partial structured frames while preserving tool-call streaming expectations. 5) SDK ergonomic surface updates (redwood-sdk-typescript/src/tool-coalesce.ts): a new helper wraps parallel tool calls in a coalesce() helper so application code can opt into the grace-window behavior explicitly (default opt-out). 6) Tests and telemetry: integration tests added for high-concurrency tool scenarios, unit tests for mergepoint sequencing, and new metrics (invoker.coalesce.window_ms, invoker.mergepoint.latency, invoker.retry.quorum_falls) for Console dashboards. Backwards compatibility: default behavior is opt-out via the coalesce helper; internal routing will enable coalescing for customer-tiered policies where cost/perf tradeoffs favor batching (Dedicated plans). For users relying on immediate dispatch, new request flag coalesce=false bypasses the grace window. Rollout plan: feature gated behind runtime flag 'invoker_coalesce_v1'. Start with internal dogfood and canary on perf-canary cluster for 48 hours, then staged enablement on 10% of hosted traffic. Monitoring and observability: dashboards added to the 'invoker' tab in Redwood Console to track coalesce rate, average delay introduced, and any observed regression in percentiles for end-to-end token latency. Risks and mitigations: - Small added latency due to the grace window; mitigated by short default and per-request override. - Complex retry semantics could hide transient failures; mitigated by alerts for quorum_falls and automatic disabling if threshold crossed. Test plan: - unit tests for coalescer (edge cases: zero grace, long tail arrivals) - integration tests simulating 200 concurrent tool calls per request - streaming handshake tests with OpenAI-compat client simulation - load test comparing cost/requests before/after merge. Documentation: docs/api/tool-coalescing.md and an SDK example added in redwood-quickstarts/tool-coalescing-example. Related: builds on earlier tooling around deterministic injection and complements ENG-9047 (structured output regressions), ENG-8921 (streaming jitter incident).

review_thread:
Ravi Patel: Nice direction. A few questions about the retry quorum---can we avoid a blocker where the quorum holder dies before finishing and leaves a duplicate side-effect?
Ava Martinez: We added a short-lived lease with automatic failover; the coordinator will escalate to a quorum-based owner after lease expiry. Added tests to simulate owner crash (see test_invoker_coalesce.py).
Lin Chen: For OpenAI streaming compatibility, are clients expected to upgrade SDK? What's the plan if they don't?
Ava Martinez: Streaming format remains backward compatible. The SDK helper gives better ergonomic surface but gateway emits slot-wrapped fragments that degrade gracefully: older clients will receive plain text stream with injected payloads; new clients get structured frames. Documented in docs/api/tool-coalescing.md.
Marta Kowalska: Performance numbers? I want to make sure P99 doesn't regress for chat workloads.
Ava Martinez: Added perf-canary results in the PR: median increased by 2ms, P95 by 6ms, P99 unchanged within noise. Included flags to disable per-request. See telemetry/dashboards/invoker_coalesce.json.
Ravi Patel: Suggest tightening default grace window to 5ms for hosted tier to be conservative.
Ava Martinez: Reduced default to 10ms for Dedicated and 5ms for Hosted in subsequent commit and added runtime policy to override.

release_notes:
Introduces an opt-in coalescing invoker that batches closely timed tool calls using a short grace window to reduce duplicate warmups and stabilize streaming handshakes. Adds deterministic mergepoints for ordered tool-result injection and a coordinated retry token to minimize duplicate side-effects. Opt-in via SDK helper or request flag; gated rollout.

[runtime/scheduler: add queue time, batch assembly, and batch size distribution metrics]
body:
Title: runtime/scheduler: add queue time, batch assembly, and batch size distribution metrics

Context
Perf baseline & representative workload suite work (Q1 2026) needs better attribution for TTFT/TPOT regressions: we can currently see end-to-end latency and some GPU-level counters, but we don’t have enough scheduler-level detail to answer: is p99 worse because requests wait longer in the queue, because batch formation takes longer, or because we’re forming suboptimal batches?

This PR adds low-overhead scheduler instrumentation for:
- Queue wait time (enqueue -> dequeued into a batch)
- Batch assembly time (start building batch -> submit to execution)
- Batch size distributions and “why” counters (e.g. flush reason)

These metrics are used by benchmark-lab/perf-suite runs and will be consumed by baseline dashboards + perf-canary gating. In production, the default configuration is conservative (sampling + coarse histograms + no per-request labels).

What’s included
1) New metrics (runtime)
All metrics are emitted from the scheduler loop on the server side. Definitions:
- redwood_scheduler_queue_wait_ms (histogram)
  - Measures time a request spent waiting in the scheduler’s pending queue before being admitted into a batch.
  - Scope: per request, measured at scheduler boundary (server-side only).
- redwood_scheduler_batch_assembly_ms (histogram)
  - Measures wall time spent assembling a batch (collecting requests, checking constraints, building the submission payload).
  - Scope: per batch.
- redwood_scheduler_batch_size (histogram)
  - Number of requests per submitted batch.
- redwood_scheduler_batch_tokens_prefill (histogram)
  - Total prefill tokens in the batch at submit time.
- redwood_scheduler_batch_tokens_decode (histogram)
  - Total decode tokens “budget” at submit time (best-effort estimate; see notes below).
- redwood_scheduler_flush_reason_total (counter)
  - Reasons: max_batch_size, max_tokens, max_queue_delay, no_capacity, fairness_yield, model_mismatch.
- redwood_scheduler_overload_dropped_total (counter)
  - Incremented when scheduler load-sheds due to overload/backpressure thresholds (existing behavior; this makes it visible).

Tagging (cardinality guardrails)
- Required tags (always on): model_family, deployment_mode (hosted|dedicated|private), region, gpu_sku
- Optional tags (off by default; on for perf-suite runs): bench_run_id, workload_name
- Explicitly NOT tagging by: request_id, tenant/customer_id, route, prompt_length_bin (those are handled elsewhere, or in benchmark harness results)

2) Feature flags / guardrails
- Default: only batch-level metrics on; request-level queue-wait metrics sampled.
- New config:
  - scheduler.metrics.enabled (default true)
  - scheduler.metrics.request_sample_rate (default 0.01 in prod, 1.0 in benchmark mode)
  - scheduler.metrics.enable_bench_tags (default false)
  - scheduler.metrics.histogram_mode (coarse|fine; default coarse)
- In benchmark mode (env REDWOOD_BENCHMARK_MODE=1), the server:
  - sets request_sample_rate=1.0
  - enables bench tags
  - switches histograms to “fine” bucket set

3) Minimal codepath overhead
- No allocations in the hot loop for the common case (coarse histograms + no extra tags).
- Queue-wait timing uses an integer timestamp stored on the Request object at enqueue time; sampled emission avoids per-request histogram updates at 100% QPS.
- Batch assembly timer uses a single timer per batch.

Notes / measurement boundaries
- Queue wait starts at scheduler enqueue and ends at admission into a batch. It does not include network receive, request parsing, auth, or model execution.
- Batch assembly time includes time spent in scheduler checks and building the batch payload, but not time waiting for GPU execution.
- Decode tokens at batch submit time are an estimate derived from request max_tokens and current phase; it is intended for distribution/trend analysis (not accounting).

Illustrative snippet (for reviewers)
- Request enqueue timestamp:
  - request->scheduler_enqueued_at_ns = clock::now_ns();
- Sampled queue wait:
  - if (rng.sample(request_sample_rate)) histogram.observe(now - request->scheduler_enqueued_at_ns)
- Batch assembly:
  - auto t0 = clock::now_ns();
  - ... assemble ...
  - batch_assembly.observe(clock::now_ns() - t0)

Files / areas changed (high level)
- runtime/scheduler/
  - added enqueue timestamp plumbing
  - batch assembly timer + flush reason counters
- runtime/metrics/
  - new metric definitions and bucket sets
- runtime/config/
  - scheduler.metrics.* config surface + benchmark-mode defaults
- docs/internal/
  - metric definitions + dashboard query examples

Testing
- Unit tests:
  - SchedulerMetricsTest.QueueWaitSamplingDoesNotEmitWhenDisabled
  - SchedulerMetricsTest.FlushReasonCounters
  - ConfigTest.BenchmarkModeOverrides
- Load test (local): verified CPU overhead within noise at 50k rps with request_sample_rate=0.01.
- Benchmark harness: ran representative chat streaming workload; metrics visible and correlate with observed TTFT changes when forcing max_queue_delay.

Rollout plan
- Merge behind conservative defaults.
- Enable bench tags only in benchmark fleet via REDWOOD_BENCHMARK_MODE.
- After dashboards land, SRE can choose to temporarily increase sampling for incident triage with a time-bounded config override.

Review conversation (abridged)
- Sean Gallagher (SRE): “Please ensure we’re not exploding cardinality in prod. bench_run_id/workload_name must be opt-in.”
  - Sofia: Updated config to default bench tags OFF; benchmark mode is explicit.
- Allison Grant (Observability): “Histogram buckets need to match our standards; avoid high-resolution buckets in prod.”
  - Sofia: Added histogram_mode (coarse|fine) and made coarse default.
- Noah Patel: “Queue-wait measurement boundary should be documented; otherwise people will misinterpret it as end-to-end latency.”
  - Sofia: Added ‘Notes / measurement boundaries’ section and inline comments in code.
- Marcus Reed: “Can we emit a batch size distribution split by prefill vs decode phase?”

[Introduce tiered CI lanes with opt-in longtests and dependency coalescer]
description:
Motivation: As our monorepo grows, pull requests get slow feedback because all checks run for every change. We observed increased CI cost and developer wait time for low-risk changes. This PR introduces a tiered CI model and a small dependency coalescer tool to reduce churn from frequent patch-level dependency updates.\n\nSummary of changes: 1) Introduce three CI lanes: \n- fast-feedback: runs on every push and PR changed files (lint, unit tests, lightweight smoke). Designed to give <5m feedback for common edits.\n- extended: opt-in by adding /run-extended (or adding label 'run-extended'). Runs integration tests and longer but important suites. Opt-in avoids blocking fast iteration for simple changes.\n- nightly-longtests: scheduled nightly job that runs the full longtest matrix and regression prompt-evals.\n\n2) Add dependency-coalescer: a small script (go) and GitHub Action that aggregates minor/patch-level dependency updates across the repo and opens a single coalesced PR weekly. The goal is to reduce PR noise and minimize CI runs for mechanical upgrades. Coalescer supports package manifests: package.json (node), go.mod, and pyproject.toml and respects allowlists.\n\n3) Quarantine strategy for flakies: introduces a test tagging convention and a quarantine registry. Tests annotated with @flaky in pytest or // flaky in Bazel are skipped in fast-feedback and run in extended/nightly with extra retries so they don't block developers. A small opt-out policy allows critical PRs to force-run quarantined tests.\n\nWhat I changed (high level):\n- .github/workflows/ci-fast-feedback.yml: new workflow that uses path filters and change-aware test selection; adds cache warm-up and faster containers.\n- .github/workflows/ci-extended.yml: new workflow that is label/command triggered and executes integration suites.\n- .github/workflows/nightly-longtests.yml: scheduled nightly pipeline with longer timeouts and higher resource pools.\n- tools/dep_coalescer/: new Go command and action wrapper + manifest processors (3 files).\n- infra/scripts/selective-test-runner.py: improvement to detect affected test subsets (used by fast-feedback).\n- tests/quarantine-registry.md: docs for annotating and triaging flaky tests.\n- ci/README.md: doc updates explaining lanes, labels, and how to opt-in/out.\n\nCommits (summary):\n- 2a9f7b8: bootstrap dep coalescer (initial parser for package.json + pyproject)\n- 7b3c1d4: add fast-feedback workflow and selective-test-runner integration\n- 4f2a0e1: add extended workflow, label trigger and example configs\n- 9c6a5d2: nightly-longtests schedule and runner resource tuning\n- 0b3d9e5: quarantine registry docs and pytest marker support\n- 1f8e6c0: tests and small fixes after reviewer feedback\n\nFiles changed (high-level snippets):\n- .github/workflows/ci-fast-feedback.yml: reduced matrix, path filter rules, integration with selective-test-runner. Example: \"runs-on: ubuntu-latest; steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v3; - uses: actions/cache@v3 ...\"\n- .github/workflows/ci-extended.yml: label-triggered workflow; uses larger runner pool and sets CONTEXT=integration.\n- tools/dep_coalescer/main.go: parses manifests, groups upgrades, emits a single PR body with grouped changelogs.\n- infra/scripts/selective-test-runner.py: adds changed file -> test mapping.\n\nTests and CI: initial run failed due to an uncovered Bazel cache invalidation in the extended matrix. I pushed a follow-up commit (1f8e6c0) that ensures bazel-remote is warmed before heavy integration runs. CI timeline: first run 2026-02-25: fast-feedback passed, extended failed (flake in integration/db-setup). Second run after fix 2026-02-27: all checks passed. Nightly pipeline run scheduled 2026-03-01 executed successfully.\n\nReview conversation (highlights, chronological):\n- Aisha Raman (review): \"Love the tiered approach. Two asks: please ensure we have an easy override to run quarantined tests and make the coalesced PR include a manifest of bump details.\"\n- Logan (author): \"Added an override label /run-quarantined and included a per-package bump manifest in the PR body. See commit 1f8e6c0.\"\n- Ethan Cole (review): \"Concerned about accidental opt-out — can we make the label explicit and document the UX for release managers? Also please add integration smoke to fast-feedback for infra changes.\"\n- Logan: \"Added docs update in ci/README.md and a small rule: if files under infra/ change, fast-feedback will run the infra-smoke job.\"\n- Marisol Vega (review): \"Dep coalescer looks useful; add an allowlist and ensure we don't combine major bumps. Also request: add a Carbon copy to release managers for coalesced PRs.\"\n- Logan: \"Allowlist added (tools/dep_coalescer/allowlist.yaml) and coalescer will skip major semver bumps; PRs now ping the release-managers team automatically.\"\n- Aisha: \"Approved after docs and override added.\"\n\nAccessibility and rollout plan: Gradual rollout over two weeks. Day 1: enable fast-feedback for all PRs. Day 3: enable infra-smoke detection. Day 7: enable opt-in extended lanes and run coalescer in dry-run mode (no PR) for one week to validate behaviour. Day 14: enable weekly coalesced PRs. A follow-up task (ENG-2460) was created to monitor developer velocity and noise metrics.\n\nObservability: Added lightweight metrics emitted by the selective-test-runner and dep_coalescer: ci.lane.duration, ci.samples.per-pr, deps.coalesced.count. They appear in the console under CI / Pipelines -> Metrics.\n\nFallbacks and safety: If the coalescer produces a PR that fails tests, it will open a draft PR and add the label 'needs-attention'. Coalescer will not merge automatically. The quarantined tests are tracked in tests/quarantine-registry.md with owner pointers.\n\nRelease/merge: After approvals and green CI, merged via squash on 2026-03-04. Rollout tracked in ENG-2460.\n\nNotes/Follow-ups:\n- ENG-2460: monitor CI cost and PR latency after rollout.\n- ENG-2475: add support to coalesce Dependabot PRs into the weekly bundle.\n- Tech debt: consider migrating selective-test-runner mapping into a centralized test-index service.\n\nIf you want to preview the coalescer run locally: tools/dep_coalescer/README.md contains quickstart and sample outputs. For questions about labels/opt-in, see ci/README.md or ping @Logan.

[Introduce wait-score slab redispatch and probabilistic starvation mitigation in continuous batcher]
description:
Motivation: Continuous batcher has edge cases where long-lived KV-pinned requests or heavy single-user tails can monopolize dispatch scheduling and cause starvation for short requests. Previous fixes (deadline windows, aging) reduced cases but we still see slippery fairness regressions under mixed workloads. This PR introduces a wait-score 'slab' bucketing approach plus an inexpensive redispatch slab to reduce tail-driven starvation while keeping scheduling overhead minimal.

What this PR changes (single-string description): - Add wait-score slab histogram: requests are scored by effective wait-time + penalty terms and placed into O(8) slabs instead of a full priority queue; slabs reduce contention and make redispatch cheaper. - Introduce a redispatch slab that holds recently-evicted or delayed requests and probabilistically re-injects them with jittered backoff to avoid synchronized storms. - Probabilistic starvation mitigation: a per-request decay token that increases chance of promotion for requests observed behind repeated dispatches; deterministic promotion path retained for strict deadlines. - KV pin detection hook: lightweight probe that marks requests touching long-term KV pins and biases them to the redispatch slab to avoid long-duration holds on hot lanes. - Timeout jitter window: jittered soft-timeouts to avoid thundering retransmit toward the scheduler at bucket boundaries. - Kernel hint plumbing: pipeline API accepts an optional hint (latency_sensitive|throughput_favored) used by the batcher to prefer compact batches with small latency-sensitive tokens; no model kernel changes here but this paves the way for per-batch kernel selection. - Observability: new metrics batcher.wait_score_slab_counts, scheduler.redispatch_injections, kv.pin_starvation_incidents and a dashboard template. - Config knobs: continuous.batch.wait_score_slab_count, continuous.batch.redispatch_fraction, continuous.batch.starvation_decay_ms, continuous.batch.timeout_jitter_ms. Defaults chosen conservatively to match current production tail numbers.

Checklist: - [x] Design doc referenced in Linear ENG-4512 - [x] Unit tests for slab placement and promotion - [x] Microbenchmarks for scheduling overhead - [x] E2E replay test showing improved 99th/99.9th percentiles on mixed workloads - [x] Observability dashboard PR (linked) - [x] Docs/CHANGELOG entry

Risk and rollout plan: Defaults are conservative (slab_count=8, redispatch_fraction=0.02). We will rollout as a progressive feature flag: 1) small internal canary (10% traffic), 2) cohort expand to 50% while watching scheduler.redispatch_injections and kv.pin_starvation_incidents, 3) full rollout if regressions are absent. Hot fallback: feature flag off reverts to previous queueing.

Notes: I intentionally avoided moving to a fully preemptive scheduler to keep the runtime lock-free paths and batching costs low. This change aims for <=1% CPU overhead at 8k qps while improving 99.9p by 15-35% in skewed KV workloads.

Asha: We use per-worker slab lanes with eventual global merges; hot path does two relaxed atomics to increment slab counters. Microbenchmarks show ~0.25% overhead at 8k qps.
Riley Morgan: Please ensure the jitter distribution doesn't hide real SLO violations (i.e. don't push latency beyond client timeouts).
Asha: jitter window is soft and bounded by continuous.batch.timeout_jitter_ms (default 10ms), we added tests to prove no observable client timeout regressions in replay.

[Soft failover & surge redispatch protocol (draft)]
Purpose:
This is a working draft for a soft failover / surge redispatch protocol to handle partial or full degradation of a region while minimizing user impact and preserving state when possible. The goal is to provide a safe, reversible sequence of actions that SRE on-call can follow to shift traffic away from a degraded region, pre-warm caches and KV state on target capacity, and restore service with minimal rollback friction.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to region-level degradations that impact latency or error-rate but do not require an immediate hard-cut DNS switch (e.g., elevated p99 latency, distributed 5xx increase, partial GPU node pool saturation).
- Assumes hot and warm standby pools exist in one or more secondary regions and that routing supports weighted traffic steering both at the edge (CDN/edge LBs) and at the API routing layer.
- Assumes we have low-ttl DNS entries for emergency weighted failover (TTL <= 30s) and tooling for programmatic DNS updates (Route53 / Cloud DNS change-batch automation).
- This is NOT the hard failover playbook for catastrophic region outage (see regional-failover-oncall-playbook). Use those steps if control plane is inaccessible.

Detection signals (examples):
- p99 latency > 2x baseline for 5 minutes across >=3 availability zones
- 5xx rate > 2% of traffic for API tier or > 5% for edge tier for 3 minutes
- Host-level load: GPU queue length > 80% sustained for 10 minutes
- Autoscaler unable to provision capacity (repeated provisioning errors)
- Telemetry: circuit-breakers tripping on >= 20% of active routes

Decision matrix (quick guide):
- Green: transient blips (<3m), monitor.
- Amber: sustained degradation (>=5m) but control plane and routing healthy -> proceed with soft failover.
- Red: control plane or cross-region network fabric compromised -> escalate to hard failover.

Prerequisites (verify before executing):
- Incident channel created: #sre-ops-incidents with incident ID in topic.
- Pager/contact list available (on-call, infra owners, routing owner, product).
- Warm standby health checks pass (API health, KV connectivity, model processes) in target region.
- Pre-warm scripts available and access to run them (privileged account + ssh/exec rights).
- Route change automation tool (routing-cli) accessible from on-call workstation.

High-level plan (order of preferred actions):
1) Shift a controlled fraction of traffic (10-30%) away from degraded region to warm standby using internal routing weights.
2) Monitor error/latency signals closely for 10 minutes. If target region shows errors increase, stop and rollback weights.
3) If steady, incrementally increase traffic to 50% while running KV pre-seed and cache-warming passes in target region.
4) Once target region shows stable latency and error rates below thresholds, proceed to DNS weight adjustments (edge/Route53) to reduce dependency on degraded region.
5) Continue incremental shifts until degraded region <10% traffic then apply throttles and/or graceful drain to 0% if necessary.

Detailed steps (operator commands and checks):
A. Initial controlled internal shift (preferred):
- Run: routing-cli set-weight --route api-redwood --from-region us-west-2 --to-region eu-west-1 --weight 20
- Verify: routing-cli status --route api-redwood | grep weights
- Check: p50/p95/p99 dashboards for both source and target regions (allow 10m warm window).
- Monitor: redis/memcache miss rates, KV cache hit ratio, and model latency histograms.

B. Pre-warm KV cache and model caches on target region:
- Run prewarm job: ./scripts/prewarm-prefixes.sh --prefix-list top-100-app-prefixes --target eu-west-1
  - This issues non-user traffic to populate prefix/KV caches. Rate-limit to avoid spike.
- Start small: 50 concurrent prewarm workers, observe KV write throughput and network egress.
- Typical time: 3-7 minutes for top-100 prefixes; larger workloads may need longer.

C. DNS weighted adjustment (if edge routing weight insufficient):
- Prepare Route53 change-batch JSON with small weight shift (10-25%). TTL should be 30s or lower for emergency records.
- Example (operator): aws route53 change-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id Z12345 --change-batch file://shift-weights.json
- Verify: dig +short @8.8.8.8 api.redwood.ai -> check returned IPs/weights through edge provider APIs.

D. Sticky sessions and affinity considerations:
- If clients use long-lived sessions, ensure target region supports session affinity or apply sticky cookie forwarding. Expect uneven immediate errors for long-lived open sessions.
- Consider injecting a 302 redirect for session rehydration to force new connections when appropriate.

E. KV cache state and consistency:
- For prefix-based KV caches, prefer read-through + background pre-seed. Avoid synchronous shard replication during surge unless tested.
- If KV consistency issues detected, reduce traffic shift and run a targeted reconciliation job for hot keys.

Rollback policy and cooldowns:
- After any weight change, wait at least 10 minutes of stable metrics before additional shifts.
- If error rate rises > 50% relative to baseline in target region after shift, revert to previous snapshot and call a second opinion from routing owner.
- Cooldown window after rollback: 30 minutes before retrying changes. Document both action and timestamp in incident channel.

Communication templates (paste into Slack):

[Cross-region rollout phasing and standby capacity (Q4 2025)]
Goal: Define a phased, low-risk GPU driver upgrade and maintenance window plan across four primary regions (us-west1, us-east1, eu-west1, ap-southeast1) that preserves SLOs and leaves standby capacity for emergency failover. This sheet captures per-region time windows, targeted drain percentages, canary steps, rollback criteria, and communication templates for product and sales teams.

Summary of approach:
- Stagger windows by 48–72 hours between regions to allow measurement and rollback.
- Keep a minimum of 15–25% of regional GPU capacity on warm standby (not drained) during each window for immediate failover.
- Use a 3-phase canary inside each region: micro-canary (1 host), mini-canary (5–10% capacity), bulk drain (to target).
- Pre-warm cross-region routing and validate fallback playbook before draining.
- Automated health checks + manual signoff at each phase transition.

Per-region schedule and capacity plan (UTC):
- us-west1:
  * Window: 2025-11-05 02:00–06:00 UTC (primary maintenance)
  * Target drain: 38% of total GPU slots (125 of 330 GPUs)
  * Standby reserve: 20% (~66 GPUs) kept warm, not drained
  * Canary steps: micro-canary at 02:00 (single host), mini-canary at 02:20 (10% capacity), decision point 02:50 for bulk drain
  * Fallback region: us-east1 (pre-warmed routing capacity + KV cache warmup)

- us-east1:
  * Window: 2025-11-07 04:00–09:00 UTC
  * Target drain: 33% (110 of 335 GPUs)
  * Standby reserve: 18% (~60 GPUs)
  * Canary steps: micro-canary 04:00, mini-canary 04:30, bulk decision 05:00
  * Fallback region: eu-west1 for cross-continental overflow (limited to read-only eval traffic during peak)

- eu-west1:
  * Window: 2025-11-10 01:00–06:00 UTC
  * Target drain: 40% (140 of 350 GPUs)
  * Standby reserve: 25% (~88 GPUs) because of predicted higher steady traffic
  * Canary steps: micro-canary 01:00, mini-canary 01:30, bulk drain 02:15
  * Fallback region: us-east1 (latency > threshold gating)

- ap-southeast1:
  * Window: 2025-11-13 03:00–09:00 UTC
  * Target drain: 30% (90 of 300 GPUs)
  * Standby reserve: 15% (~45 GPUs)
  * Canary steps: micro-canary 03:00, mini-canary 03:40, bulk drain 04:30
  * Fallback region: eu-west1 (capacity constrained during daytime local hours)

Operational playbook (step-by-step):
1) Pre-window (T-72h):
   - Announce maintenance to product, sales, and external status page (draft message in 'communications' section below).
   - Verify: driver package signed, rolling image salted and in registry, kernel compatibility matrix validated for all instance types.
   - Run capacity simulation: synthetic traffic replay to check cold-switch routing and cache warmup times.
   - Confirm on-call roster for SRE, infra, and product liaison.

2) Pre-drain (T-2h):
   - Snapshot metrics baseline (p50/p95 latency, error rate, GPU utilization, queue depth).
   - Create per-region incident channel and runbook pinned.
   - Tag warm standby hosts and mark them as non-drainable in autoscaler config.

3) Micro-canary (start):
   - Evacuate single host, upgrade driver, run smoke generations and eval set (10 prompts).
   - Pass criteria: no increase >2x in error rate and p95 latency delta < 25% vs baseline for 15m.

4) Mini-canary (scale):
   - Drain 5–10% capacity, upgrade, and run throughput tests plus end-to-end app path.
   - Pass criteria: sustained error rate <0.5% and 95th percentile latency within agreed SLO tolerance for 30m.
   - If failure: rollback to previous driver on canary hosts and abort bulk drain.

5) Bulk drain and upgrade:
   - Proceed in 10–15% increments until target drain reached. Manual signoff at each increment.
   - Monitor real-time dashboards (token-level latency, model timeouts, kernel OOM alerts).

6) Post-upgrade validation (T+30m after bulk complete):
   - Run regression set: 200 prompts across high-frequency customers and open-models.
   - Validate routing failover by simulating a cold host failure and ensuring warm standby picks up <60s.

Rollback criteria and thresholds (immediate rollback triggers):
- Sustained p95 latency increase >50% across two consecutive 10m windows.
- Error rate spike to >2% sustained for 10m (customer-visible 5xxs or model timeouts).
- Kernel-level OOMs or CUDA driver crashes on >3% of upgraded hosts.
- Canary-specific instability (flaky initialization) observed during micro- or mini-canary.

Fallback routing plan and capacity math:
- Maintain advertised standby for each region in routing config; ensure cross-region egress limits are increased ahead of maintenance.
- Example: us-west1 standby 20% = 66 GPUs. If bulk drain requires additional 60 GPUs, route 30–40% of excess traffic to us-east1 queue while keeping token-level timeouts increased for affected customers (notify).
- Pre-warm KV cache on fallback hosts for top-50 customers to avoid cold-start quality regressions.

Communication templates (status snippets):
- Pre-window announcement: "Planned maintenance: GPU driver upgrade in us-west1 on 2025-11-05 02:00–06:00 UTC. We expect up to 38% capacity to be drained; standby capacity will remain. No API key changes required. Contact infra-oncall@redwood.ai for urgent questions."
- Incident start: "Maintenance window started for us-west1. Canary underway (1 host). Monitoring for regressions. Status channel: #infra-maintenance-us-west1."
- Recovery/complete: "Maintenance completed for us-west1. All upgraded drivers are healthy. No customer-facing incidents detected. Post-mortem to follow at CONFLUENCE-12345."

Testing and validation matrices to run during each phase:
- Functional: sample prompts + deterministic checks for top 20 models.
- Performance: p50/p95 latencies, tokens/sec, tail latency heatmap across GPUs.
- Reliability: GPU process restarts, driver panics, kernel OOMs.
- Quality: output regression tests against golden prompt set (token diffs threshold per model).

Runbook links and artifacts (quick list):
- Driver packaging checklist: CONFLUENCE-12345
- Automated canary job: github.com/redwood-inference/ops-scripts/actions/upgrade-canary
- Capacity simulation harness: JIRA-INFRA-8702

Owners and on-call assignments:
- Region owner (us-west1): Andre Kim (primary), Priya Rao (backup)
- Region owner (us-east1): Liam O'Sullivan (primary), Maya Chen (backup)
- SRE lead (coord): Sofia Martinez
- Product liaison: Elena Novak

Open risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Cross-region network egress limits might throttle fallback traffic. Mitigation: Pre-request quota increases and schedule bulk drain off business hours for regions with fragile egress.
- Risk: Unexpected model-level regressions after driver change. Mitigation: Hold 10% of capacity un-upgraded for 48h as a quick rollback pool for high-value customers.
- Risk: On-call fatigue during multi-region run. Mitigation: Keep stagger >=48h and cap work windows to 6h per region; use 3-person critical rotation.

Next steps / action items (owners):
- [Maya Chen] Finalize driver package and sign-off checklist by 2025-10-31.
- [Andre Kim] Run top-50 customer cache pre-warm script on fallback hosts by 2025-11-03.
- [SRE] Add automated rollback trigger to deployment pipeline and smoke-run integration by 2025-11-01.
- [Product] Draft customer-facing post-maintenance note and pre-announce to enterprise accounts by 2025-11-02.

Notes and historical context:
- This plan differs from earlier mass-drain approaches by emphasizing small-step canaries, explicit standby percentages, and pre-warmed cross-region fallbacks. Past upgrades where we skipped mini-canary led to localized latency spikes (see postmortem JIRA-INFRA-7401).

Appendix: quick checklist (T-24h, T-2h, T+1h)
- T-24h: Confirm clear communication, ensure backup images, check monitoring alerts baseline.
- T-2h: Lock autoscaler policies, mark standby hosts, pin routing configs.
- T+1h: Confirm metrics stable, unpin standby hosts after 4h stable, schedule post-mortem.

Document history:
- Created: 2025-10-28 by Maya Chen
- Reviewers: Andre Kim, Priya Rao, Liam O'Sullivan
- Last modified: 2026-02-18 (added more conservative rollback thresholds and ap-southeast1 window adjustments)

[Ops shift rotation debrief — GPU on-call week 2026-09-23 to 2026-09-30]
Summary:
This note captures the on-call handoffs, incidents, and operational observations from the GPU fleet on-call rotation covering 2026-09-23 to 2026-09-30. Focus areas: cross-region surge during APAC morning peak, two short NVMe node degradations in eu-west, and a recurring QoS throttling pattern tied to a background snapshot job.

Timeline (high level):
- 2026-09-24 02:10 UTC — APAC burst: unexpected spike in hosted API small-chat endpoints bumped queue depth in ap-southeast-1. Smart-routing handed off 12% of traffic to dedicated pool; latency climbed from 120ms -> 340ms for 6 minutes. No data loss.
- 2026-09-25 11:40 UTC — eu-west NVMe: degraded disks on 3 nodes in cluster gpu-eu-3, pods evicted and rescheduled across remainder of cluster. Evictions lasted ~18 minutes, autoscaler filled 2 of 3 slots with preemptible instances.
- 2026-09-27 23:00 UTC — Snapshot job overlap: quarterly snapshot job for dedicated customers overlapped with inference cache warm-up, causing repeated KV cache evictions and steady token throughput drop for ~40 minutes.
- Handovers completed each day between 08:00 UTC and 09:00 UTC with short notes pushed to the #gpu-ops channel.

Metrics snapshot (observed during incidents):
- 99th percentile token latency: baseline 210ms -> spike 420ms during APAC burst
- Eviction count (eu-west event): 31 pod evictions across 3 hosts
- Autoscaling fill time: average 9.2 minutes to steady-state after preemptible boots
- Snapshot overlap CPU pressure: dedicated-control plane CPU saturation observed at 78% (spike to 92%)

What went well:
- Smart-routing fallback worked as designed: the policy rerouted excess requests to dedicated capacity and degraded gracefully instead of erroring. Post-mortem shows the policy threshold caught traffic at ~85% saturation and applied the route rule within 20s.
- Eviction automation: evicted pods were rescheduled successfully; persistent volumes reattached without manual intervention. Recovery within SLA.
- On-call communication: handoffs consistently posted summarized bullet points to channel and updated status page. Engineers were reachable and escalation chain used correctly.

What could be improved / Root causes & notes:
- APAC spike origin unclear: initial traffic source looks like a customer A/B test (INFRA-2781) that rolled out in ap-southeast region with an aggressive fan-out. Need confirmation from CS/product before we finalize mitigation rules.
- Snapshot scheduling mismatch: quarterly snapshot job is still running on the same low-traffic windows we use for cache priming. The job is non-latency-sensitive and should be moved to a different maintenance window or rate-limited.
- NVMe health telemetry: disk SMART thresholds are conservative; nodes reported I/O latency but not explicit SMART failure until after partial degradation. Recommend adding earlier I/O anomaly alerts to avoid mass evictions.
- Autoscaler cold-fill time: cold start for preemptible instances remains a tail risk (9m median). For dedicated-critical pools we should look into burst-capacity warmers (small reserved pool) to reduce 9m to <3m.

Action items (owners and ETA):
- AI-1: Ask product/CS to pause INFRA-2781 test in ap-southeast-1 and provide traffic pattern. Owner: Evan Liu. ETA: 2026-10-01.
- AI-2: Move quarterly snapshot job to secondary maintenance window and add token bucket limiter to snapshot worker. Owner: Samira Khan. ETA: 2026-10-07.
- AI-3: Add NVMe I/O latency anomaly alert: new alert when sustained 95th I/O latency > 15ms for 10 minutes. Owner: Miguel Ortega. ETA: 2026-10-05.
- AI-4: Prototype a 10-node warm pool in ap-southeast-1 for rapid burst absorption (opt-in config per customer tier). Owner: Noah Patel. ETA: 2026-10-20 (design), 2026-11-03 (trial).
- AI-5: Update shift handoff template to include quick-run metrics snapshot (top-3 clusters by tail latency) and any running maintenance jobs. Owner: Priya Desai. ETA: 2026-10-02.

Small operational notes / quick wins: 
- Add a small note to the runbook reminding on-call to check scheduled snapshot jobs before high-risk releases.
- Temporary mitigation: set lower concurrency cap for small-chat hosted route in ap-southeast-1 until the A/B test completes (config toggle exists in the console).
- Replace an ambiguous page in the status dashboard that aggregated both autoscaler and preemptible fill metrics; separated views will help on-call spot fill lag sooner.

Open questions / follow-ups for next rotation:
- Was the INFRA-2781 rollout intentionally global? (Product confirmation required)
- Can we standardize a ‘staggered start’ for maintenance snapshots across regions to avoid cache warm-up collisions?
- What SLO delta do we accept for a 5–10 minute autoscaler cold start for low-tier customers vs. enterprise-tier customers?

Post-rotation notes for managers:
- Suggested trial of warm pool in one region (ap-southeast-1) to validate warm-start economics vs. cost of occasional latency spikes. If successful, expand to eu-west.
- Consider a quarterly review of background jobs (snapshot/backup/benchmarks) that may interfere with cache behavior; propose to include infra in the release cadence calendar for these jobs.

Appendix: Relevant links and logs
- APAC spike trace (internal link): traces/2026-09-24/apac-spike-02-10
- NVMe degraded node logs: logs/gpu-eu-3/2026-09-25/*
- Snapshot job run details (task id): JOB-SNAP-20260927-11
- Pager history: incident/INC-2026-09-24-A

Notes to self & friction points observed during handoffs (informal):
- Handoff notes often miss the quick metric snapshot; adding a short CLI command in the template to capture top-3 tail latencies would be handy.
- The on-call rota has repeated adjacent shifts for a few engineers next month; recommend rebalancing to avoid burnout.

If there's anything missing from this debrief that folks want added before publishing to Confluence, ping me and I'll fold it in.

-- Priya

[11:53] Alex Marino: Quick sync on ownership: who on Vellum will be primary on-call during the rehearsals and go-window?
[12:05] Jordan Lee: Priyanka will be primary SRE; Marcus will be AI lead for quality issues; Elena is product owner for go/no-go. I'll make that formal in the runbook.
[12:25] Elena Park: I'll add escalation contacts and calendar windows to the doc after this meeting.
[12:40] Priyanka Rao: One operational request: can Redwood emit a short-lived runbook URL that we can hand to the on-call during the canary? A single page with steps, rollback, and PD links.
[12:55] Priya Desai: Yes — we can produce a one-page runbook link and an abbreviated checklist. I'll send both and a PDF copy.
[13:12] Jordan Lee: Regarding monitoring telemetry - what exact metrics should we include in the required sightlines?
[13:25] Priya Desai: Required: p50/p95/p99 latency, request/sec, tokens/sec, error rate, KV cache hit rate, model-variant distribution, token-cost-per-request. Optional: quality eval score and user-visible success rate.
[13:52] Marcus Nguyen: Can Redwood stream those metrics to our existing Prometheus? We prefer centralized alerting.
[14:05] Priya Desai: Yes — metrics can be exported to Prometheus or via Datadog. For Prometheus, we'll provide a scrape endpoint in the private deployment or an agent for hosted.
[14:28] Jordan Lee: Great. Let's talk about the rehearsal schedule — we propose two rehearsals: one dry run of the runbook, one load-rehearsal with synthetic traffic. Can we do them next week?
[14:45] Alex Marino: Redwood is available Tuesday and Thursday morning PT. Which works for you?
[14:55] Jordan Lee: Thursday morning works better for our SREs. Let's tentatively pick 2026-02-26 09:00 PT for the load-rehearsal and 2026-02-24 11:00 PT for the dry run.
[15:18] Elena Park: We also need a post-rehearsal retro — 30 minutes to capture lessons, ops notes, and tweak thresholds.
[15:31] Priya Desai: We'll add a retro agenda to the calendar invites.
[15:45] Marcus Nguyen: One last technical note: we observed minor tokenization differences between the two model variants; can Redwood ensure identical tokenizer config?
[15:59] Priya Desai: We can pin tokenizer and vocabulary at model versioning; Redwood's model catalog includes tokenizer metadata. I'll confirm the exact tokenizer hash used in your test model and share it.
[16:20] Jordan Lee: Docs and artifacts — what will be shared after this call?
[16:31] Alex Marino: I'll share SOC2 + KMS doc, Priya will share dashboard template, canary thresholds in a spreadsheet, and a one-page runbook. Links will be in the follow-up email.
[16:48] Elena Park: For the acceptance criteria for go-decision, let's be explicit: 48hr synthetic run with p95 within threshold, zero critical errors, and quality delta within 5%.
[17:05] Priya Desai: That aligns with Redwood's recommended acceptance criteria. We'll add a checklist item to the runbook and mark responsible owners.
[17:26] Jordan Lee: Anything we missed?
[17:32] Alex Marino: We covered main items. I'll recap next steps now then open for any final clarifications.
[17:45] Alex Marino: Recap — Redwood to send SOC2/KMS doc, dashboard template, canary thresholds, and one-page runbook by Monday 2026-02-22. Vellum to provision test networking and run the 48hr synthetic window by 2026-02-26. Schedule rehearsals for 2026-02-24 (dry run) and 2026-02-26 (load rehearsal).
[18:12] Jordan Lee: Sounds good. Priyanka, Marcus, any last comments?
[18:20] Priyanka Rao: Nothing else from SRE, just please make the runbook concise and call out warm-up suppression to prevent alert noise.

The group aligned on a staging test plan: subscribe with a test buyer account, validate entitlement lookup, provision/link a Redwood org, generate an API key, send test inference traffic, confirm metering events appear with the expected dimensions, and verify cancellation/plan change behavior. Redwood will send a proposed dimension list and sample metering payloads for review.

GCP Marketplace SKU dimensions and Cloud Commerce metering
