transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-01-16
Time: 10:03 AM PT
Duration: 54 min
Title: GCP Marketplace onboarding + billing review (Redwood Inference)
Attendees:
- Redwood Inference: Stephanie Nguyen, Chris Osei, Cole Summers, Nadia Rahman, Ben Carter
- Google Cloud Marketplace: Priya Shah, Anika Desai, Miguel Alvarez

[00:00] Stephanie Nguyen: Cool, thanks everyone for making time. This is Stephanie from Redwood, I run a lot of the enterprise motion, and we’ve got Cole and Nadia on billing and metering, Ben on onboarding funnel. We wanted to do a sanity pass on the GCP marketplace requirements, specifically billing dimensions and the onboarding UX expectations before we submit.

[00:18] Priya Shah: Sounds good. Thanks Stephanie. Priya here, partner dev manager. Anika and Miguel are the experts on the technical billing side. We saw your email about new SKUs, so today is basically make sure it’s compatible with Cloud Marketplace and Cloud Commerce.

[00:33] Chris Osei: Yep, and I’m Chris, program lead on our side for the marketplace refresh. I’ll keep us on agenda and capture action items.

[00:41] Anika Desai: Hi all. Anika, partner engineering. I can talk through entitlement, procurement IDs, and the typical “gotchas” we see when SaaS vendors wire up the onboarding.

[00:50] Miguel Alvarez: Miguel here. Cloud Commerce metering / billing integrations. Happy to go deep on dimensions, aggregation, rounding, and what reviewers will look for.

[01:01] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. Quick context: we’re replacing legacy listings. We now have Hosted API usage-based, Dedicated capacity, and Private deployment. We want the marketplace SKUs to map cleanly to our internal billing meters. The primary issues we want to avoid are dimension mismatches and the buyer gets invoiced for something weird.

[01:20] Miguel Alvarez: Yeah. The big thing is consistency. Dimension names and IDs in the offer need to match what you’re sending in metering events. And be careful if you’re changing them later—customers don’t like it and it can break reporting.

[01:35] Cole Summers: That’s exactly what we’re trying to nail. Let me outline what we were thinking and you can tell us what’s realistic. For Hosted, we meter “tokens generated” and “input tokens” internally, but we can expose it as “tokens” total if that’s simpler. We also have embeddings measured as “embedding units” (basically per 1K tokens equivalent). For Dedicated, we have reserved GPU capacity, which internally is monthly commit + overage. Private is more of a platform fee plus support tier.

[02:05] Miguel Alvarez: Okay. So in Cloud Marketplace, you can do usage-based dimensions and you can do subscription pricing models, and you can also do committed-use style constructs depending on the product type. Most SaaS partners keep it simple: one or a small number of usage dimensions, like “1K tokens” or “1M tokens”, and then for a base subscription you do a seat or a flat monthly fee.

[02:29] Nadia Rahman: Quick question on granularity. If we do “1K tokens” as the unit, do you see partners reporting fractional quantities? Like 123.456 units? Or is it recommended to round?

[02:41] Miguel Alvarez: You can send decimal quantities, but you should document how you compute it and be consistent. The most common pattern is you aggregate per hour or per day and send integer quantities. But for token meters, lots of folks send decimals, just be explicit. Rounding differences between your UI and the invoice is where support tickets come from.

[03:02] Ben Carter: On the onboarding side, we have this subscription -> entitlement -> Redwood org provisioning. One issue we see on AWS is entitlements sometimes take a few minutes to show up. Is that also a thing on GCP?

[03:14] Anika Desai: Yep. It’s not usually super long, but there can be propagation delay. The UX expectation is you handle “pending” gracefully. Like, don’t show a scary error that says “you are not entitled.” Instead say “we’re still syncing your subscription, retry in a few minutes” and maybe a refresh button.

[03:32] Stephanie Nguyen: That’s helpful. We’ve got an entitlement verification endpoint and a sync job; we can make sure the UI does the “pending” messaging.

[03:41] Priya Shah: Also important: the marketplace reviewers will click through the onboarding. If they hit a dead end, that’s friction during review. Provide a support link and clear instructions.

[03:53] Chris Osei: Got it. Maybe we jump into identifiers. Anika, can you talk about what we should store and what we can expect to receive? We’ve seen “consumer ID” in docs but there are like multiple names for it.

[04:07] Anika Desai: Yeah. So, you’ll have a procurement account / buyer account. When a customer subscribes, there’s an entitlement created. Depending on your integration, you’ll get a consumerId and entitlement name or resource. Your system should treat that as the source of truth for “is this customer subscribed” and also for mapping metering events to the right buyer.

[04:30] Cole Summers: For metering, we need a stable key to associate usage to the marketplace customer. We also have our internal “org_id”. So our thought was: marketplace entitlement maps to Redwood org, and then that org has one or more projects / API keys. Usage is aggregated at org level and then billed.

[04:49] Miguel Alvarez: That’s typical. Just ensure you don’t mix multiple entitlements into a single org without clear logic. If a customer buys two subscriptions, you need to decide whether that’s two entitlements attached to one org or two orgs. Reviewers will look for correct allocation.

[05:06] Ben Carter: We have an edge case: existing Redwood customers may subscribe later through marketplace for procurement reasons. So they want to link the marketplace subscription to an already-existing org.

[05:17] Anika Desai: That’s also common. UX expectation: you allow linking to an existing account. But ensure authentication is done. And avoid a scenario where someone can claim an entitlement that isn’t theirs.

[05:31] Stephanie Nguyen: Right. We require sign-in, then they paste an entitlement or we detect via login? We were thinking detect via a “claim token” page in our console.

[05:42] Anika Desai: Either works. Most partners do a redirect back with parameters, or they ask the user to input the entitlement ID. Redirect flows are nicer but more work. For review, either is acceptable as long as it’s documented.

[06:00] Chris Osei: For this phase we’re doing a marketplace-specific entrypoint in our console. It will prompt for “GCP marketplace subscription” and then run entitlement verification.

[06:10] Miguel Alvarez: That’s fine. On billing: I want to zoom in on the dimension list. Can you share what you propose?

[06:18] Cole Summers: We don’t have final IDs yet, but draft is something like:
- Hosted: “hosted_tokens_1k” and “hosted_embeddings_1k”
- Rerank: “rerank_requests_1k” (maybe)
- Dedicated: “dedicated_gpu_hour” or “dedicated_capacity_unit”
- Private: “private_platform_month”
- Add-ons: “compliance_pack_month”, “extended_audit_log_retention_month”
The big question is whether “Dedicated” should be a usage dimension or a subscription SKU.

[06:55] Miguel Alvarez: Dedicated capacity tends to fit better as subscription / contract. Usage metering for “gpu hours” works, but you need to align it with what you’re actually providing. If it’s truly reserved, then a monthly subscription fee is clearer. If there’s burst/overage, you can meter overage separately.

[07:16] Nadia Rahman: We can do either. Internally we track reserved pool size and then tokens anyway, but the contract is the key. If you recommend subscription for reserved, then our metering is mostly for overage.

[07:29] Priya Shah: From a procurement standpoint, enterprise buyers usually prefer a predictable subscription line item. Then usage-based Hosted is more PLG.

[07:41] Stephanie Nguyen: That matches what we’re seeing. One thing we’re worried about: we want three clear “paths” in the listing—Hosted, Dedicated, Private. But under the hood GCP constructs are not always “three products.” It’s one listing with plans, right?

[07:57] Priya Shah: Exactly. You typically have one product listing and multiple plans. You can describe the three modes in the copy, but technically it’s one product with pricing plans.

[08:12] Ben Carter: On the onboarding, would you expect different landing pages for different plans? Like, if someone buys Private, they shouldn’t be dropped into “create API key and call the hosted endpoint” because their next step is networking and deployment.

[08:26] Anika Desai: That’s a good point. Ideally yes: after entitlement, route them to the appropriate next steps. But you can also have a general landing page that asks “what did you purchase?” or reads the plan from the entitlement.

[08:43] Cole Summers: Reading the plan from entitlement is doable if the entitlement includes plan name. We just need to be careful with plan rename.

[08:52] Miguel Alvarez: Plan rename is okay if you keep the underlying plan ID stable. Don’t key logic off display name.

[09:01] Chris Osei: Noted. We’ll key off ID.

[09:05] Stephanie Nguyen: Let’s talk about reviewer expectations on the metering payload. Miguel, can you share what they check?

[09:14] Miguel Alvarez: Sure. They’ll check: (1) you’re using the correct API endpoints, (2) the consumerId or entitlement is valid, (3) the dimension is a valid one configured in your offer, (4) the quantity is non-negative and within reason, (5) timestamps are sane (not future by a day), (6) idempotency—you don’t double bill on retry.

[09:40] Nadia Rahman: On idempotency: we have an internal “usage_event_id” and we can keep a ledger. If we retry, we send the same event id. Is that a pattern you like to see?

[09:52] Miguel Alvarez: Yes. Exactly. Store the request ID and mark it as sent. Most of the “billing mismatch” issues are duplicate sends during outages.

[10:05] Ben Carter: Do you have any advice on how to validate end-to-end that metering is going to show up for the customer? Like, in AWS we can see it in the buyer account pretty quickly.

[10:15] Miguel Alvarez: On GCP, you can see metering records in the partner console and via reports, but it’s not always instant. For testing, you want to confirm your API calls succeed and then use the console to verify the usage events are recorded. Anika can share the checklist.

[10:33] Anika Desai: Yeah, I can send a link. There’s a “test buyer” flow too. You procure with a test account, then you validate that entitlement is created and your backend can resolve it.

[10:47] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. Another question: dimension naming constraints. We saw some limitations around character length and allowed characters.

[10:56] Miguel Alvarez: Keep it short, alphanumeric plus underscore usually. Avoid spaces. If you have to include a version, don’t. Better to keep the same dimension and change the price model rather than changing the dimension name.

[11:13] Cole Summers: That’s helpful. We were going to do “hosted_tokens_1k” rather than “hosted_input_tokens_1k” and “hosted_output_tokens_1k” to keep it one dimension. We can still show the breakdown in our console for observability, but bill as total tokens.

[11:32] Miguel Alvarez: That’s a good compromise.

[11:35] Stephanie Nguyen: And embeddings we can keep separate.

[11:38] Miguel Alvarez: Yes.

[11:40] Chris Osei: I want to make sure we cover onboarding UX expectations. Ben, can you describe what we’re building and get GCP feedback?

[11:49] Ben Carter: Sure. So in our console, when you click “Get started”, there will be a “Purchased via marketplace?” path. If they choose GCP marketplace, we ask them to sign in. Then we try to auto-detect entitlements tied to that user, and if we can’t, we allow them to paste an entitlement ID. If entitlement is found, we show “link to existing org” or “create new org.” After that, we prompt them to create first API key for Hosted, or if the plan is Dedicated/Private, we route to request provisioning steps.

[12:24] Anika Desai: That’s pretty aligned with what we like to see. Two things: (1) make it very clear what to do if they’re not the person who purchased. Sometimes procurement buys and engineering uses. So include instructions like “ask the billing admin to invite you” or “forward this entitlement ID.” (2) include a retry experience for pending entitlements.

[12:50] Ben Carter: Yep. We have an error state “Entitlement not found” that currently suggests contacting support. We can change that to “may take a few minutes” and include refresh.

[13:02] Priya Shah: Also include support SLA information and the right support channel for marketplace customers. It doesn’t have to be complex, but the listing should say how to get help.

[13:12] Stephanie Nguyen: We’ll incorporate that into listing FAQs. On testing: we need a clear test plan. Chris, we have some draft steps; can we align with GCP?

[13:22] Chris Osei: Yeah. Proposed test checklist:
1) Subscribe to plan in GCP Marketplace using test buyer
2) Verify entitlement exists (via API/console)
3) In Redwood console, run entitlement verification and link/create org
4) Generate an API key
5) Send a small set of inference requests (chat/text and embeddings)
6) Verify metering calls succeed and appear under correct dimension
7) Cancel subscription and verify access behavior (grace period?)
8) Re-subscribe / plan change and verify entitlements update
9) Negative tests: wrong entitlement, cross-org linking, delayed propagation

[14:03] Miguel Alvarez: That’s good. On cancellation: define your policy. Some partners cut off immediately, some allow a grace period. But it needs to match your listing terms and how you interpret the entitlement state.

[14:18] Cole Summers: Our default is to stop accepting billable traffic if entitlement is inactive, but we may allow a short grace if the cancellation is accidental. For marketplace we probably keep it strict.

[14:31] Anika Desai: During review, they’ll test cancel and see if your UI reflects it. If there’s a grace, document it.

[14:40] Nadia Rahman: On entitlement state changes, how quickly do we see “active -> cancelled”? That’s a potential race.

[14:49] Anika Desai: It’s usually quick, but again, you should poll or have a scheduled sync. Don’t assume immediate.

[15:00] Ben Carter: We have a sync job that runs every few minutes and on-demand verification. We can tighten it during onboarding.

[15:08] Miguel Alvarez: Just be careful with rate limits. If you have everyone spamming “verify entitlement” you might hit quotas. But for normal scale it’s okay.

[15:19] Stephanie Nguyen: One more thing: our SKUs include compliance add-ons (like extended audit log retention, compliance pack). Is it common to have add-ons as separate dimensions or separate plans?

[15:34] Priya Shah: It depends. If it’s truly an add-on, separate plan can be complicated. Some do “bundle plans” (base + add-on). Others handle add-ons off-marketplace. If you want it procured via marketplace, bundling plans is usually easiest.

[15:54] Miguel Alvarez: If you do it as a usage dimension, that’s weird for a monthly compliance pack. Better as subscription line item. But you can create a plan called “Hosted + Compliance” and so on.

[16:09] Cole Summers: That increases plan combinatorics. We were trying to keep it minimal.

[16:14] Stephanie Nguyen: For enterprise procurement, it might be okay. We can do a small number: Hosted, Hosted+Compliance, Dedicated, Dedicated+Compliance, Private. Something like that.

[16:26] Priya Shah: Exactly. Keep it manageable.

[16:29] Chris Osei: Let’s capture that as an open decision: add-ons as bundles vs separate plans.

[16:35] Ben Carter: If it’s bundled, onboarding can still read plan ID and show the right “features enabled” banner.

[16:42] Anika Desai: Yep.

[16:44] Miguel Alvarez: For dimensions, fewer is better. If you have too many, it’s harder to validate.

[16:52] Nadia Rahman: Another metering nuance: we do streaming responses. Tokens get generated over time. We aggregate at end of request. That means we may emit one usage record per request or per batch. Is that okay?

[17:07] Miguel Alvarez: That’s okay. The marketplace doesn’t care if you batch, as long as it’s accurate and you can explain your aggregation. Many partners aggregate per hour to reduce volume.

[17:19] Cole Summers: We can aggregate per hour per org per dimension. That’s probably a good default.

[17:26] Miguel Alvarez: Yes.

[17:28] Stephanie Nguyen: Any pitfalls with multi-region? Our hosted API runs in multiple regions. If a GCP marketplace buyer uses us in EU, does billing care?

[17:39] Priya Shah: Billing doesn’t care, but listing and security docs might. If you claim data residency, make sure it’s accurate. The marketplace reviewers may look at your data handling statements.

[17:52] Chris Osei: We’re preparing a security packet; we’ll align wording.

[17:57] Anika Desai: From onboarding side, if you route them to a region selection, ensure it’s clear. Some customers think marketplace implies region-specific. It doesn’t necessarily.

[18:10] Ben Carter: We plan to ask region at org creation and default to the closest region, but allow override.

[18:18] Stephanie Nguyen: Great.

[18:20] (brief crosstalk)

[18:22] Stephanie Nguyen: Miguel, can we ask about “dimension mismatch” issues you’ve seen? We had one on AWS where our internal meter name didn’t match the marketplace dimension and we billed wrong. We’re trying to prevent it.

[18:37] Miguel Alvarez: Yeah, common. It’s usually one of: using display name instead of dimension ID, or typos, or changing the offer and not updating code. The best practice: keep a single source config file for mapping, version it, and add automated tests that validate the dimension list against what’s configured in marketplace.

[18:57] Cole Summers: We have a billing catalog config in code. We can add a test that asserts “these dimensions are the only allowed ones.” But we can’t programmatically query the marketplace config easily.

[19:10] Miguel Alvarez: You can still do a manual gate before launch: export the dimension list and compare. And once stable, don’t change often.

[19:21] Nadia Rahman: We also emit telemetry events in our pipeline. We can alert on unknown dimension errors.

[19:28] Miguel Alvarez: Perfect. Set alerts on 4xx responses from metering API.

[19:35] Chris Osei: Okay. Let’s do a quick pass on what GCP needs for submission beyond billing: screenshots, support, security docs, etc. Priya?

[19:46] Priya Shah: You’ll need: final listing copy, pricing plans configured, support contact info, a privacy policy link, and security documentation depending on the category. For enterprise oriented products, we often see SOC 2 statements, encryption, retention, audit logging. You don’t need to paste the whole report, but your claims must be accurate.

[20:10] Stephanie Nguyen: Understood. We’ll provide a marketplace security overview and pointers to evidence under NDA.

[20:18] Anika Desai: Reviewers like diagrams. Even a simple data flow diagram helps.

[20:23] Ben Carter: We have a diagram showing subscription -> entitlement -> Redwood control plane -> inference runtime. We’ll use it.

[20:31] Chris Osei: Back to testing. Anika, you mentioned a test buyer flow. Can you outline quickly? Just so we know if we need special accounts.

[20:40] Anika Desai: Typically you’ll have a partner test project and a test buyer project. You procure your own product as a test buyer. Then you verify that your integration receives the entitlement. If you’re using the Cloud Commerce Partner API, you can query entitlements. If you’re using webhooks, ensure those are wired. Since you’re doing a console-based claim flow, you can also validate by retrieving entitlement status from your backend.

[21:08] Cole Summers: We’re using the partner API and a sync job, plus on-demand verify endpoint. Webhook we considered but didn’t want to rely solely on it.

[21:19] Miguel Alvarez: That’s fine. Webhook can be flaky if not retried. Polling plus retry is okay, just mind quotas.

[21:30] Nadia Rahman: For quotas, do you have ballpark? Like requests per minute? We’re not huge but we want to be safe.

[21:38] Miguel Alvarez: It depends on the project and API. I’ll send the doc. But generally, if you do a sync every 5 minutes and on-demand for onboarding, you’re fine.

[21:53] Stephanie Nguyen: Great.

[21:55] (pause)

[21:56] Ben Carter: A small UX question: when entitlement is not found, do you recommend we show “wait 10 minutes” or “wait 2 minutes”? We don’t want to over-promise.

[22:06] Anika Desai: I’d say “a few minutes” and allow retry. And show a timestamp “last checked at” to reassure them you’re doing something.

[22:18] Ben Carter: Nice idea.

[22:20] Chris Osei: Another edge case: procurement might buy in a different Google identity than the engineer uses (like billing@company.com). That means auto-detect entitlements won’t work.

[22:31] Anika Desai: Exactly. That’s why inputting entitlement ID is helpful, or a separate “admin invites user” workflow.

[22:41] Stephanie Nguyen: We’ll make sure docs call that out.

[22:45] Miguel Alvarez: On billing, one more thing: if you’re doing token usage, define what “token” means. Different models count differently. You should base it on what you count internally, but documentation should say it’s per model tokenizer.

[23:01] Cole Summers: Good point. Our API already reports token usage per request in the response metadata. We can use that as source of truth.

[23:10] Nadia Rahman: And we can expose daily usage summaries in console to match marketplace billing.

[23:15] Miguel Alvarez: That’s helpful for customer trust.

[23:19] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay. Let’s talk about dimension naming and plan structure. It sounds like recommended is:
- Hosted plan with usage dimensions (tokens, embeddings)
- Dedicated plan as subscription, possibly with an overage usage dimension
- Private plan as subscription
- Compliance add-on as bundle plans (Hosted+Compliance etc)
Is that fair?

[23:44] Priya Shah: Yes.

[23:46] Miguel Alvarez: Yes, that would be a clean structure.

[23:49] Cole Summers: For Dedicated overage, would we meter tokens or something else? Because customers might still care about tokens, not GPU hours.

[23:59] Miguel Alvarez: If the overage is “extra usage beyond included”, tokens is okay. If it’s “extra capacity”, maybe hours. But tokens is more straightforward given your product.

[24:12] Cole Summers: Great. We’ll think through included vs overage.

[24:16] Chris Osei: I want to make sure we leave with concrete outputs. Cole will send a proposed mapping table and example payloads. Anika and Miguel will send docs and constraints. Ben will share screenshots/wireframes.

[24:31] Stephanie Nguyen: One question: in GCP marketplace, do customers expect to get credits / trial? We offer free credits on our website; does marketplace support that?

[24:41] Priya Shah: Marketplace trials exist in some contexts but not universally. Many partners handle trials outside marketplace or do a low-cost starter plan. If you want a trial, we can discuss, but it may complicate approval.

[24:56] Stephanie Nguyen: We’ll keep it simple for now.

[24:59] Ben Carter: Another thing: we have a dedicated onboarding docs page. Is it okay to link external docs from the listing?

[25:07] Priya Shah: Yes, you can link to documentation. Just make sure it’s stable URLs.

[25:12] Chris Osei: We’re finalizing vanity redirects for marketplace. Okay.

[25:16] (minor audio glitch)

[25:18] Nadia Rahman: Can we ask about time window for metering submissions? Like can we send usage events delayed by a day?

[SilverMantle Marketplace: LLM Gateway + Helm Operator + KMS Check-in]
summary:
30min technical deep-dive focused on integrating Redwood's LLM Gateway into SilverMantle's marketplace offering. Covered Helm operator deployment patterns, KMS/HSM key exchange, audit/logging integration, and fallback routing for dedicated vs hosted models. Decided on a short pilot: Helm operator install into staging, KMS policy review, and a runbook dry-run with SREs.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-08
Time: 15:00 - 15:48 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Alyssa Chen (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Lena Park (Redwood Solutions), Dana Ortiz (SilverMantle Platform), Samir Patel (SilverMantle SRE), Priya Nair (SilverMantle Security), Jonas (DevOps)

[00:00:00] Alyssa Chen: okay everyone good afternoon, um thanks for joining. quick agenda - helm operator packaging, k r m s key flow, marketplace listing constraints, and next steps. Marco will lead the operator bit.
[00:00:23] Marco Ruiz: hey all, yeah i'll start. so we, we built a lightweight helm operator that installs the LLM gateway as a k8s operator. it exposes a CRD called llmgateway.svc.redwood.dev, and you can define modelRoutes, routingPolicy, and kmsConfig. note: CRD name in the repo atm has a typo in some samples - llmgatewy - sorry we'll fix that.
[00:01:05] Dana Ortiz: oh okay that's the sort of thing we run into, ty. question: does the operator require cluster-admin? we can't give that in staging.
[00:01:23] Marco Ruiz: good call. no cluster-admin needed for the chart if you use the namespaced install. there is an optional nodeAffinity webhook that requires additional privileges; we can disable that in values.yaml. default permissions are limited to the namespace and create/watch on the CRD resources.
[00:01:50] Priya Nair: and from a security perspective we need to ensure the operator never logs plaintext keys. where do tokens live?
[00:02:04] Marco Ruiz: tokens are stored in k8s secrets by default. we support sealed-secrets and external KMS integrations where you can provide a kmsConfig referencing an external keyArn. we also have a sidecar that will rotate attach tokens on a schedule. small note: the sidecar rotation code path uses a short-lived service token (60s) - that's something we need to document better.
[00:02:36] Samir Patel: rotation sounds good. how about metrics? we need per-route latency percentiles and per-model cost tags for billing.
[00:02:50] Lena Park: yes, our telemetry exports prometheus metrics and we can emit token-level cost tags as labels on the request span. we also support pushing traces to jaeger or honeycomb. but tag cardinality is a concern, so we usually recommend sampling for high-cardinality user_id labels.
[00:03:20] Jonas: quick interruption — which KMS are we talking? AWS? we have a hybrid environment, some keys on cloudhsm.
[00:03:31] Priya Nair: yeah we use AWS KMS + internal HSM for PII workflows. the marketplace listing requires that private keys never leave customer boundary per our governance.
[00:03:48] Marco Ruiz: understood. we support both AWS KMS and PKCS11 HSM integrations. for onprem HSM we have a connector that uses the kmsConfig with type: pkcs11 and you mount socket to the operator. the operator itself doesn't export key material, it only sends signing requests to the HSM. note: the PKCS11 path is relatively new and the docs are a bit sparse.
[00:04:22] [00:04:24] Dana Ortiz: can we see an example policy for the KMS key so our compliance folks can sign off?
[00:04:30] Alyssa Chen: yes, marco will share a minimal policy snippet after the call. (inaudible) i'll add that to next steps.
[00:04:45] Marco Ruiz: i'll dump the example — it's basically kms:Encrypt,Decrypt for the operator role plus kms:GenerateDataKey when using envelope encryption. we'll include a least-privilege sample.
[00:05:05] Samir Patel: another operational question - what happens if the gateway can't reach hosted Redwood model endpoints? we need graceful fallback to a cheaper quantized local model to preserve availability.
[00:05:21] Marco Ruiz: good question. there are two strategies we recommend: 1) route policy with failover: primary route to hosted redwood api, secondary to a local quantized variant running in the same cluster, 2) local inference sidecar that keeps a tiny LLM cache (prefix cache) for high-frequency prompts. both require you to add a modelVariant config in the CRD. the fallback is synchronous and respects SLOs but adds some latency — we measured +70–180ms depending on the quantized runtime.
[00:06:02] Dana Ortiz: latency delta is acceptable, but we need to quantify cost. any estimate for token cost difference?
[00:06:10] Lena Park: hosted calls are metered per-token, local quantized model is mostly infra cost. rough ballpark: hosted ~ $0.0008 per token for our curated model profile, local infra depends on GPU utilization; for small quantized models on CPU it's maybe $0.00005 per token equivalent, but that's very workload dependent. we'll share a cost worksheet.
[00:06:38] [00:06:45] Priya Nair: for marketplace listing, we also need audit logs that show the request path and key usage without exposing prompt content. is there an obfuscation or hashing feature?
[00:06:57] Marco Ruiz: yes we have a redact middleware you can enable that hashes PII fields or replaces text with tokens before logs are emitted. it runs as part of the gateway filter chain. caveat: if you redact too aggressively you may hamper quality monitoring.
[00:07:20] Jonas: how are we publishing billing meter tags to the marketplace? we need to attach partner and customer ids so the marketplace can attribute usage.
[00:07:30] Alyssa Chen: the gateway emits billing headers and usage tags as HTTP headers and Bookkeeping metrics. we can configure partner_id in the CRD values and the operator will ensure all spawned pods have the env var for meter tagging. note: we added a recent change so tags are also included in the prometheus exporter.
[00:07:55] Samir Patel: we saw a prior note in the repo about prefix cache and memory leaks in k8s 1.24. are you patched for that?
[00:08:05] Marco Ruiz: yes we tracked a leak pattern in the prefetcher; fixed in v0.9.2 of the operator. recommend upgrading to >=0.9.2. the helm chart in the repo will default to that. we'll call out the k8s compatibility matrix in the README.
[00:08:30] [00:08:34] Dana Ortiz: good, we run 1.24 in staging. next: marketplace listing constraints — we have to limit runtime container images to scanned SBOMs and restrict network egress. how does the operator help with that?
[00:08:49] Marco Ruiz: operator can enforce image policies via an admission webhook (optional) and we support supply-chain attestation fields in the Chart metadata. for egress we provide a per-model egressPolicy that you can set to internal-only or allowlist endpoints. the egressPolicy will be enforced by the operator's sidecar network proxy.
[00:09:20] Priya Nair: for the allowlist, we need a pattern that doesn't hardcode endpoints because our infra sits behind a private NAT. can we do CIDR ranges instead?
[00:09:30] Marco Ruiz: yes the egressPolicy accepts CIDR ranges and service names; we also support a service mesh compatibility mode where we rely on the mesh egress rules.
[00:09:44] [00:09:50] Lena Park: on quantization tradeoffs, i want to call out that 4-bit quant gives smaller memory but may slightly degrade hallucination rates on longer contexts. for the marketplace we recommend evaluating with your eval-set and we'll provide a quant profile suggestion table.
[00:10:10] Dana Ortiz: speaking of evals, can we wire our pre-existing prompt suite into Redwood's eval harness?
[00:10:19] Marco Ruiz: yes there's an adapter. send us the prompt pack (a csv or jsonl) and we can run a quick sweep comparing hosted vs quantized local. expect results in 48–72 hours for a starter set.
[00:10:40] Jonas: small ops question — what's the rollout story for new model versions? we need canary plus auto rollback on latency regressions.
[00:10:51] Marco Ruiz: built-in rollout supports canary percent and automated rollback if latency or error budget thresholds are breached. we integrate with your existing alerting (pagerduty slack) and you can configure SLOs in the CRD.
[00:11:10] [00:11:30] Samir Patel: network secrets - do you recommend vault or k8s native? we are heavy on HashiCorp Vault.
[00:11:40] Marco Ruiz: both supported. operator has a Vault provider that will sync secrets into k8s as projected volumes; you can choose short-lived tokens. for compliance we often recommend vault with dynamic creds.
[00:11:59] Priya Nair: wanna call out an audit ask — can we get an event stream with KMS key usage events in near-real time so our auditors can reconcile?
[00:12:12] Lena Park: yes we provide a usage export that can push to an S3 bucket or to your SIEM via Kinesis. it includes key operation stamped events but we can filter prompt content.
[00:12:30] [00:12:46] Dana Ortiz: thanks. i'd like to walk through a proposed minimal staging install. Marco?
[00:12:53] Marco Ruiz: sure - step 1: helm repo add redwood; step 2: values.yaml minimal: namespace: sm-staging, enableWebhook: false, kmsConfig: { type: "aws_kms", keyArn: "<placeholder>" }, modelRoutes: [ { name: "default", model: "redwood/fast-13b", route: "hosted" } ] — note: the transcript sample here includes braces — in the shared notes we'll provide a full values file.
[00:13:30] Jonas: will that deploy a sidecar or a daemonset?
[00:13:35] Marco Ruiz: it's a deployment per gateway instance; sidecars are injected as part of the pod template. for cache-heavy workloads we recommend a small statefulset for the cache component.
[00:13:50] [00:13:57] Alyssa Chen: i'll pause for a sec — any blockers for you to proceed with staging?
[00:14:03] Dana Ortiz: two blockers: 1) need the KMS policy example, 2) need SBOM and image scan evidence for the container.
[00:14:11] Alyssa Chen: we can provide both. Marco will send KMS policy; Lena will attach the SBOM and the recent scan report.
[00:14:22] Lena Park: i'll upload SBOM and a short explanation of our CI scan in the shared drive. note: some of the images are based on distroless slices and buildinfo may be noisy.
[00:14:37] [00:14:45] Samir Patel: curious about latency SLOs — do you have sample dashboards we can import?
[00:14:52] Marco Ruiz: yes, Grafana dashboard json is in the repo /dashboards/llm_gateway.json. it includes per-route p50/p95/p99 and token counts. we'll share a preconfigured dashboard link.
[00:15:12] Dana Ortiz: perfect. quick question about marketplace listing governance — our legal needs an exportable audit report showing which customer used which model and when, without revealing prompts. is that feasible?
[00:15:25] Priya Nair: also need to be able to revoke access to a specific partner ID quickly.
[00:15:32] Marco Ruiz: both doable. audit export includes model_id, partner_id, request_hash, and timestamps; request_hash lets you correlate without storing content. partner revocation is a simple CRD update to remove partner_id or mark partner_id as suspended; operator will reconcile and remove env vars from pods; for immediate cut we can implement a network policy pivot.
[00:15:58] [00:16:05] Jonas: are there any known performance regressions when running under CRI-O vs containerd?
[00:16:14] Marco Ruiz: minimal differences; our testing matrix covers both. CRI-O had one sporadic pod restart in older k8s versions due to log driver assumptions but that's fixed in recent images. we'll note compatibility in the README.
[00:16:40] [00:17:00] Alyssa Chen: ok we're mid-call — i'm going to cover the pilot scope and success criteria quickly. pilot: staged helm operator install, kms policy validation, run a 24h synthetic workload with 10 qps, measure p95 latency and cost baseline. success = p95 < 250ms (hosted) and fallback effective < 400ms and audit exports validate.
[00:17:30] Dana Ortiz: those success criteria seem reasonable. what about data residency — some requests must never leave eu-west region.
[00:17:42] Marco Ruiz: routingPolicy supports regionAffinity; you can pin routes to endpoints in eu-west and failover to eu-west quantized variant. for marketplace listing we recommend adding region metadata to the modelRoute CRD and the operator will enforce region locality.
[00:18:05] [00:18:20] Priya Nair: small nit — the CRD example we saw earlier had a camelCase mix; our linting wants snake_case. can you provide both?
[00:18:31] Marco Ruiz: yeah we actually provide both in examples; the parser accepts either but README will standardize to snake_case. thanks for the callout.
[00:18:45] [00:19:00] Lena Park: another thought on cost: when evaluating quantized variants we recommend tracking hallucination metrics (F1-style on your evals) in addition to token cost - sometimes the lower-cost model increases manual review overhead.
[00:19:20] Dana Ortiz: okay — good reminder. next, around the marketplace onboarding checklist — what items should we expect from Redwood?
[00:19:31] Alyssa Chen: we'll provide: helm chart + values.yaml, SBOM and scan report, KMS policy snippet, Grafana dashboard json, pilot SOW template, and a short runbook for cutover.
[00:19:45] Samir Patel: and from us: staging namespace access, KMS key ARN or HSM contact, existing prompt test suite, and a compliance contact for signoff.
[00:19:58] [00:20:10] Jonas: how about integration tests — do you have a CI harness we can run that validates install and smoke tests?
[00:20:18] Marco Ruiz: yes, we have a GH Action that runs chart install in KinD and a smoke curl test. it's in .github/workflows/helm-smoke.yml. it doesn't exercise production scale but it catches install regressions.
[00:20:35] [00:20:48] Dana Ortiz: can we get the action to run against our chart repo mirror?
[00:20:54] Lena Park: you can fork the repo and enable the actions, or we can add a repo_dispatch to trigger from your pipeline — both options possible.
[00:21:10] [00:21:20] Alyssa Chen: ok we're coming up on the second half — any deep technical blockers left?
[00:21:26] Priya Nair: KMS policy + SBOM scan are the primary blockers for compliance sign-off. after those we can proceed to install.
[00:21:36] Marco Ruiz: i'll attach the policy and the helm values. quick note: the helm chart includes a toggle for attestation and supply-chain metadata.
[00:21:49] Dana Ortiz: for the pilot workload, what sample size do you recommend for evals? 1k prompts?
[00:21:57] Lena Park: start with 1k diverse prompts. we'll run both hosted and local and produce a delta table showing accuracy, latency, and cost per prompt bucket.
[00:22:10] [00:22:30] Samir Patel: can we also test a canary with sticky sessions? some of our flows rely on maintaining KV cache across chat turns.
[00:22:38] Marco Ruiz: yes the gateway supports sticky-session affinity via a session cookie or header. you can configure KV cache TTL per-route. we'll include a sample canary config.
[00:22:55] Dana Ortiz: what about secrets rotation cadence? we prefer automatic rotation every 7 days.
[00:23:02] Marco Ruiz: sidecar rotation supports configurable cadence; default is 7 days in the operator values.
[00:23:15] [00:23:30] Alyssa Chen: i'm going to summarize the concrete next steps we agreed on — Marco to share helm chart + values + dashboard + KMS policy by 2026-09-10; Lena to share SBOM + scan report in shared drive by 2026-09-10; SilverMantle (Priya/Dana) to share KMS ARN and compliance contacts by 2026-09-14; schedule runbook dry-run week of 2026-09-21. does that capture?
[00:23:57] Dana Ortiz: yes, capture that. Also please include the eval adapter instructions so we can upload the prompt set.
[00:24:05] Alyssa Chen: will do.
[00:24:12] [00:24:20] Lena Park: small follow up — i'll add quantization profile suggestions for your eval set in the shared notes.
[00:24:30] Jonas: one last ops question — if we want to pin to a specific model version, can we do automated migration with traffic splitting?
[00:24:39] Marco Ruiz: yes, the route CRD supports traffic weights. you can do 90/10 split and progressively shift; rollback is automatic if SLOs break.
[00:24:55] [00:25:10] Alyssa Chen: great — looks like we're aligned. any other questions from SilverMantle?
[00:25:16] Priya Nair: just one procedural — we need a short statement of data residency and encryption-at-rest for the marketplace listing doc.
[00:25:26] Alyssa Chen: we'll include that in the SOW. Marco, Lena - can we add that?
[00:25:33] Marco Ruiz: yes we'll add a one-paragraph statement about region affinity and default encryption using KMS/HSM.
[00:25:44] [00:26:00] Dana Ortiz: thanks team. we'll aim to run the smoke install next week once we have the helm chart.
[00:26:08] Alyssa Chen: perfect. last note — pricing: there was a question earlier about Dedicated vs Hosted cost delta. i'll follow up with a short matrix after this call.
[00:26:22] Samir Patel: okay thanks.
[00:26:28] [00:26:35] Alyssa Chen: all right if nothing else we'll wrap. thanks everyone for the time.
[00:26:40] Marco Ruiz: thanks all.
[00:26:45] Dana Ortiz: thank you.

[Private Console: Network Path Storyboard & Upgrade Rehearsal (prototype)]
description:
Design and prototype an interactive ‘Network Path Storyboard’ for the Private/VPC Console that helps tenants rehearse cluster upgrades and connectivity changes before they are applied. The storyboard surface should let operators: 1) narrate a connectivity scenario across logical layers (tenant app -> VPC route -> cluster node -> egress), 2) step through simulated events (maintenance window, node drain, route failover) with visualized latency and cost delta annotations, 3) surface automated risk flags derived from recent health metrics and policy guardrails, and 4) emit a shareable checklist and rollout plan (canary steps + rollback). Goal: reduce upgrade fear and on-call churn by making network impacts explicit and actionable for SREs and tenant owners. Prototype scope for this ticket covers the storyboard interaction patterns, a compact risk summary card, and a cost-annotation overlay tied to the batching/throughput estimate model. Does not include backend simulation engine integration (separate ENG ticket).

[Private VPC: Topology Editor & Cluster Status Hub (console UX prototype)]
description:
Objective: Design a focused console surface for Private/VPC customers that combines an interactive network topology editor with a lightweight cluster status hub. This surface should make it fast for platform engineers to: visualize cluster layout, inspect private networking (subnets, peering, NAT/GW), surface upgrade/rollout state, and see cost/latency signals for each cluster.

Scope: Topology canvas (drag-to-arrange nodes), cluster card list with health and current release, status timeline for recent events, quick upgrade controls (canary/rollout/fallback), and a compact cost & latency breakdown per cluster. Include contextual help for RBAC and KMS requirements. Prototype must be responsive to console widths and support keyboard nav for accessibility.

Constraints & assumptions: Work within existing console theming and components; reuse cluster-card, toast/notification, and rollout modal components where possible. Backend endpoints for topology persistence provided by ENG-2456; rollout API surface depends on ENG-2499. Avoid introducing new backend fields unless essential. Prototype should not assume cross-account topology edits — initial iteration is single-tenant only.

Key screens/components:
- Topology Canvas: canvas grid, add/remove nodes, link creation (peerings, route tables), node details panel (metrics snapshot, IP ranges, security groups).
- Cluster Status Hub: sortable list of clusters with inline health microcharts, latest event badge, upgrade status pill, and cost-per-hour estimate.
- Upgrade/Rollout Panel: canary slider, target subset selector, preflight checklist, rollback button.
- Cost & Performance Insights: small sparkline for token-ms latency, estimated monthly cost, suggestions (e.g., "enable KV cache" or "lower batching for low-latency routes").
- Incident banner & timeline: full-width banner for active incidents and a per-cluster timeline of recent health events.
- Onboarding flow: short modal to guide first-time users through topology basics and security reminders.

[Private Deployment: Ops Command Center — compact status, escalation & cost context]
description:
Design a condensed Operations Command Center view for Private/VPC deployments that combines cluster health, network reachability, active rollouts, and cost exposure into a single surface for SREs and platform owners. This ticket covers prototype, interaction spec, and review artifacts for the console panel that sits alongside the existing Cluster Overview.

background:
Customers running Redwood Private asked for a single-pane operational surface that reduces context switching during incidents. Existing cluster pages are too modal and require jumping between Network, Upgrade, and Billing tabs. This design aims to summarize critical signals with quick escalation paths and lightweight drill-ins.

goals:
Create a compact, scannable status strip for each tenant/cluster showing health, connectivity, recent upgrades, and cost anomaly flags
Provide instant escalation actions (create incident, page on-call, rollback rollout) from the same surface
Surface estimated per-hour cost pressure and the dominant driver (eg. burst GPU, long seq lengths, >X requests/min)
Design for responsive layouts so the command center works at desktop widths and tablet-sized operator consoles

acceptance_criteria:
High-fidelity Figma prototype with desktop and tablet variants linked from this ticket
Interaction spec for drill-in (click-through to Network, Upgrades, Rollouts, Billing) with keyboard shortcuts documented
Engineering feasibility review completed and trade-offs captured (render cost, telemetry requirements)
PM sign-off on escalation wording and recommended default actions
Usability notes from 3 SRE/Platform interviews included

design_notes:
Primary row items: cluster name, health pill (ok/warning/critical), network reachability icon, active rollout badge, cost delta % badge
Health pill aggregates: node availability, 95p latency, recent errors — hover expands to small sparkline and top error class
Network icon shows last successful inter-region ping and active VPC peering status; clicking opens a connection health modal
Cost delta uses 24h baseline and highlights the top cost contributor with a tooltip showing estimated token-level vs infra-level split
Rollout badge expands to a tiny timeline with canary size and time-to-complete; offer quick rollback CTA when >1 canary step failed
Escalation menu (three-dot) includes: Create Incident (links to PagerDuty/Gen AI assistant), Page On-Call, Open Runbook, Start Safe-Rollback
Compact mode collapses secondary badges into an overflow menu while keeping health and cost visible

[Deferred Failover Runbook Designer — Private Console flow]
description:
Problem: Private/VPC customers need a predictable, auditable way to define and rehearse multi-cluster failover and maintenance runbooks that respect tenant SLA, cost constraints, and network topology. Current console pages show cluster status and connectivity graphs but lack an interactive authoring surface to compose sequences, delays, dependencies and safe rollback steps for zero-downtime upgrades or emergency failovers.

What this ticket builds: a Failover Runbook Designer embedded in the Private Console that lets operators: author step-by-step playbooks (eg. drain node group A, cut traffic to region B, promote backup cluster C), schedule deferred windows, attach prechecks/postchecks, and simulate the runbook against live topology and synthetic traffic. The designer surfaces SLO impact, estimated token-cost delta (eg. additional cross-region egress), and a confidence score driven by historical telemetry.

Key UX features to prototype: timeline lane editor with drag-to-reorder steps; conditional branches (eg. if precheck fails -> abort and alert); network-path risk overlay (heatmap per step); canary step generator with parameter presets; a "what-if" slider to simulate latency/cost trade-offs; compact audit trail panel with required approvers and links to associated PRs/Playbooks.

Design constraints and trade-offs: keep primary authoring flow simplified for small ops teams while exposing advanced conditional logic behind an "expert mode" toggle. Prefer visual primitives over textual scripts to reduce errors, but provide an exportable JSON/YAML runbook for infra automation (hand-off to ENG). Tight coupling with telemetry and rollout systems raises security review requirements (privileged actions). We will gate execution behind RBAC and two-step approvals.

Deliverables for this ticket: high-fidelity flow in Figma for the designer surface (desktop), an interactive prototype demonstrating a 3-step failover with simulation controls, copy for inline help and approver modal, and an accessibility pass for keyboard-first editing. Include a short PRD summary for Eng handoff listing API contracts and telemetry queries needed for confidence scoring.

acceptance_criteria:
Figma screens for timeline editor, step inspector, simulation panel, and approval modal reviewed and approved by PM and Eng
Prototype demonstrates creating, scheduling, and simulating a 3-step runbook against a sample private cluster topology
Audit trail UI shows approver list, timestamps, and links to related PRs/dashboards
Design spec includes required telemetry queries and RBAC states for Eng implementation
Accessibility checklist completed: keyboard-only reorder, ARIA labels for timeline lanes, color contrast checks passed

The badge summarizes readiness (green/yellow/red) across network connectivity, capacity headroom, KV cache validity, and pending security prerequisites. The action strip provides one-click runbooks, preflight checks, canary enable toggles, and a quick rollback trigger. The prototype should work in both single-cluster and multi-cluster views and scale to 50+ clusters without visual overload.

[v1-chat: mitigate param-echo and stabilize fncall streaming frame recovery]
description:
Summary: This PR addresses two related classes of v1/chat compatibility issues surfaced in production and by customers: (1) 'param-echo' where the streaming path could emit fragments that duplicated system/instruction text into the final assembled completion, and (2) fragile fncall/structured-output streaming frames that could leave the client with partial JSON or missing function-call metadata after transient network disconnects.
Motivation: Customers migrating to the v1/chat compatibility layer observed occasional duplicated instructions in the final completion and incorrect fncall objects after reconnects; both reduce reliability for production apps (especially tool-calling and structured-output use cases). This change reduces duplication and makes streaming frame reassembly deterministic on reconnect and partial replays.
What changed (high level):
- Introduced a streaming "echo filter" at the param-negotiation boundary that identifies tokens/segments highly-correlated with pinned system/instruction parameters and suppresses them from the final merge unless there is model-confirmed divergence. The filter uses a lightweight prefix-match heuristic and confidence threshold derived from the runtime token scorer to avoid false positives.
- Reworked fncall streaming framing: fragments now include a 2-byte frame header (version + frag-index) and an end-sentinel marker. A heartbeat/ack sequence allows servers to mark frames as committed; clients reconnecting in the middle of a stream can request the last-committed index.
- Added final-payload reconciler that aggregates streaming logprobs and stop hints with the non-streamed completion generation step. This prevents the streaming path from overwriting canonical stop/logprob state.
- Tests and observability: added deterministic unit tests for param-echo heuristic, integration tests that simulate reconnect/failure during fncall streaming, and new metrics: streaming.frame_reassembly_failures, streaming.echo_suppressed_count.
Commits (summary):
- 1a3f2e9: add param-echo filter and unit tests
- 2b9e4c1: implement fncall frame header + sentinel, add frame commit/ack handshake
- 7c5d113: reconcile streaming logprob aggregation with final payload
- 9ae5b2f: integration tests for reconnect / partial frame replay
- c4d8f07: docs: console notes on heartbeat/compat
- f5b1a22: fix linting and race in frame ack path
Changed files (illustrative):
- server/streaming/echo_filter.go (new) — implements prefix similarity heuristic and integration with token scorer
- server/streaming/frame_protocol.go (modified) — adds headers, frag-index, and ack handling
- server/streaming/handler_test.go (modified/added) — tests for reconnect scenarios and fncall reassembly
- sdk/python/redwood/v1/chat_stream.py (modified) — client-side support for reconnect and committed-index request
- sdk/typescript/stream-client.ts (modified) — small compat helpers for browsers
- docs/compat/v1-chat-streaming.md (modified) — added section about heartbeat and canary rollout notes
Small snippet (illustrative) included in server/streaming/frame_protocol.go: "// frame header: version(1) | fragIndex(1) - allows deterministic reassembly across reconnects"
Tests:
- Unit: echo_filter_test.go covers prefix-collision cases, threshold tuning and false positive regression.
- Integration: simulated 3 reconnect scenarios with random drops; fncall object reassembled successfully in 98/100 runs locally; CI runs are deterministic via mocked runtime.
CI:
- Pre-merge pipeline: lint, unit, integration, e2e-candidate.
- Current run: all checks passed (lint warnings auto-fixed), integration harness passed 28/28 scenarios.
- Flaky tests noticed initially (integration: reconnect-flaky) were stabilized by increasing frame timeout from 100ms->250ms.
Review thread (highlights):
- Owen Patel (reviewer): "Please ensure we don't silently drop legitimate repeated text when model actually re-states an instruction intentionally (e.g., role-reflection). The heuristic needs an escape hatch." Maya: "Added an escape: if final-generation logprob mass on the prefix exceeds 0.6 we bypass suppression and mark as explicit-repeat in telemetry."
- Priya Singh: "Add e2e that runs a small tool-calling example through the python and TS clients to validate fncall JSON shape end-to-end." Maya: "Added python/ts e2e callers and wired them into the integration job; added OP-level assertion on fncall.name and args."
- Luis Fernandez: "Risk: consumers of the streaming format may not be able to handle the 2-byte header. Need a compatibility flag." Maya: "Default frame version is backward compatible: legacy clients ignore the header and server emits a compat fallback for older agent-headers. Documented in compat notes."
- Owen (approve after fixes): "LGTM — tests look good, metrics added. Please watch canary closely."
Release notes (in PR body): "Fixes param-echo duplication in v1/chat streaming path and improves fncall frame recovery on reconnects; no API change for callers, minor client-side updates available in SDKs for better reconnect handling."
Deployment plan and canary:
- Canary rollout to 10% of hosted v1-chat traffic for 48 hours; streaming.frame_reassembly_failures and streaming.echo_suppressed_count monitored with alert thresholds.
- If any regression >0.5% error rate in fncall shape, automatic rollback will be triggered.
Backwards compatibility:
- Server emits header but will continue to stream compat frames when client advertises legacy agent via User-Agent/Handshake.
- SDK updates (python/ts) are optional but recommended for deterministic reconnect behavior.
Follow-ups:
- ENG-2071: telemetry dashboards for echo suppression across customers.
- ENG-2104: explore ML-based prefix de-duplication using scoring model (longer-term).
Merge: Squash-merged into main on 2026-02-03 after approvals from Priya and Owen. Canary started immediately; initial canary metrics show reduced duplication events (telemetry drop ~78% on sample customers).
Known limitations:
- Very adversarial prompts that intentionally echo instruction tokens may still appear in final output when model logprob supports it (we preserve these via escape hatch).
- There is a small increase in server-side CPU for the echo heuristic (~1.8% at 95th), measured and included in the release notes for capacity planning.
If you want to test locally:
- Run `make integration` under server/streaming with MOCK_RUNTIME=1
- Python example: examples/streaming_fncall.py (calls new client reconnect helper)

release_notes:
Fix streaming duplication where system/instruction content could be echoed in final completions; improved fncall streaming frame reassembly and heartbeat recovery to reduce client-visible truncation and malformed structured outputs.

[v1 chat: unify stop propagation and robust tool-call handshake for streamed responses]
description:
Motivation: customers using the /v1/chat.completions compatibility layer reported inconsistent stop handling and truncated toolcall exchanges when streaming responses and falling back across model variants. This PR unifies parameter normalization for stop arrays/sentinels, ensures logprobs and stop signals are propagated deterministically through streaming envelopes, and introduces a resilient tool-call handshake/resume protocol to avoid lost tool outputs in intermediate reconnections.

What this changes (single continuous description): canonicalize v1 chat params: introduce a single param-normalizer that accepts legacy stop formats (string, array, special tokens) and produces an internal stop-set representation used by both batch and streaming paths; coerce role aliases and preserve role metadata when mapping between adapter layers; implement stop-propagation: stops are now evaluated at token-generation and stream-framing layers with consistent precedence (explicit stop list > stop weight heuristics > model-inferred EOS) so clients see matching stop points between sync and streaming responses; logprobs envelope: add compact logprob delta messages emitted on the stream with clear token indices and an explicit final logprob frame for non-streamed fallback; tool-call handshake/resume: new two-way preflight step in the stream (TOOL_HANDSHAKE / TOOL_ACK) plus a resume token so downstream tool runners can rehydrate partial tool outputs after connection blips; streaming stability: introduce heartbeat sentinel frames and backoff-aware fragment coalescing to reduce duplicate fragments and improve reassembly across proxies.

Files changed (high level): api/compat/v1/param_normalizer.py (new) — canonicalization and migration shims; serving/streaming/framer.go — stop evaluation and heartbeat frames; runtime/tooling/handshake.go — tool handshake and resume token state machine; tests/compat/test_chat_stops.py — coverage for stop formats and streaming parity; tests/streaming/test_resume_reassembly.js — fuzz tests simulating partial reconnects; docs/openapi/v1_chat_compat.md — updated compatibility notes and migration guidance.

Commits (summary):
- 4f92d5d: add param normalizer and adapter glue;
- 9c1b3a7: implement streaming stop evaluation + heartbeat frames;
- a6e4b2f: tool handshake/resume protocol and runtime state;
- 2b7f113: tests, docs and CI flakiness fixes.

Backward compatibility and migration notes: existing clients should continue to work unchanged. Edge cases fixed: stop arrays passed as comma-separated single strings (legacy client bug) are normalized; stop handling differences between non-streamed and streamed codepaths are eliminated. Tool runners that rely on implicit stream termination should adopt the new handshake ACK semantics to avoid missing final fragments — see docs/openapi/v1_chat_compat.md for example pseudocode. No breaking API changes were made; developers wanting to opt into stricter stop-prioritization can set the new parameter "stop_mode=strict" (opt-in).

Tests and CI: added unit and integration tests that exercise mixed-mode streaming and reconnects; included a small synthetic latencies harness that revealed an off-by-one stop fence which was fixed. CI: build/test/lint all pass on main matrix except a transient macOS flake that required a rerun. Final CI status: pass.

Review thread (condensed): Reviewer Liam asked for clearer separation between param-normalizer side effects and request telemetry; I split the telemetry emission into a separate tracing hook as requested. Sofia requested an additional fuzz test for tool reassembly under packet reorder; added test case in tests/streaming/test_resume_reassembly.js. Eliot flagged a potential race in the resume token garbage collection; I added a bounded TTL and unit test. After two rounds of changes reviewers approved and marked ready.

Deployment notes: staged to canary and exercised against dedicated workloads; observed 0.4% p99 latency increase under large stop lists but 18% reduction in duplicate stream fragments. No rollout blockers.

Related work: references ENG-9384 (streaming parity effort) and ENG-9422 (tool-runner reliability). Links: internal design doc at /docs/design/chatv1-stop-tool-handshake.md and migration examples in docs/openapi/v1_chat_compat.md.

Release notes: "Improve v1 chat compatibility: consistent stop handling for streamed and sync responses; robust tool-call handshake with resume support to avoid lost tool outputs during reconnects; streaming stability improvements (heartbeat, fragment coalescing) and logprob envelope frames for clearer token-level diagnostics."

review_comments:
Liam Chen: clarify telemetry side-effects -> moved telemetry to tracing hook; Sofia Rodriguez: add fuzz case for packet reorder -> added; Eliot Brooks: race on resume GC -> added TTL and tests; approvals after changes (LGTM x3).

release_notes:
Improve v1 chat compatibility: deterministic stop propagation across streaming and sync paths; resilient tool-call handshake with resume tokens; streaming stability fixes and compact logprob frames.

[openai-v1-chat: param-smoother and tool-output reconciliation to stabilize streaming and logprob alignment]
description:
Motivation: customers using the OpenAI /v1/chat.completions compatibility layer reported two classes of failures during heavy streaming workloads: 1) fragmented chunking under transient backpressure caused stop tokens and logprob patches to be emitted inconsistently across fragments, producing malformed structured outputs; 2) partial tool/function-call outputs (large JSON blobs emitted over multiple deltas) could be interleaved with text deltas and result in invalid JSON or lost function-call metadata. This PR implements a lightweight "param smoother" and an output reconciliation layer that reduces visible fragmentation to clients while preserving low latency for short responses.\n\nWhat I changed (summary): consolidated three coordinated changes into one PR to keep the compatibility surface cohesive: 1) stream fragment coalescer: a small in-memory horizon buffer that merges micro-deltas shorter than a tunable threshold (config: chat.streaming.coalesce_ms default 40ms). This reduces the probability of split stop tokens/logprob envelopes without adding noticeable tail latency; 2) tool-output reconciliation state machine: tracks active tool/function-call envelopes per-stream, rehydrates partial JSON output until it reaches a syntactic boundary before emitting a completed tool response event; partial tool events are now annotated with "partial": true but are not forwarded to structured-output consumers until reconciled; 3) logprob/stop normalizer: when logprobs or stop signals arrive across fragment boundaries we run a reconciliation pass that deduplicates overlapping tokens and marks the authoritative stop position based on sequence ids and fragment offsets.\n\nFiles touched (high-level): \n- runtime/streaming/coalescer.go - new coalescing buffer and timer logic\n- runtime/streaming/coalescer_test.go - unit tests for micro-delta merging\n- api/openai/compat/stream_adaptor.go - integration with v1/chat adapter to leverage coalescer and reconciliation state\n- api/openai/compat/tool_reconciler.go - new state machine for partial tool outputs and finalization rules\n- api/openai/compat/logprob_normalizer.go - logic to align logprob envelopes across fragments\n- docs/openai/compatibility.md - compatibility notes and config knobs\n- tests/e2e/chat_stream_tool_canary.yaml - a canary scenario run in CI\n\nImplementation notes: the coalescer is purposely conservative: it only coalesces when upstream fragments are below the threshold and when the downstream SLO headroom is positive. We expose two experimental knobs (coalesce_ms and coalesce_size_bytes) so SRE can tune in canary deployments. The tool reconciler keeps up to 64KB of in-flight partial tool output per stream; large tool outputs are supported via backpressure signals to the client (we already had a soft cap but this makes behavior deterministic). Logprob normalization uses fragment sequence metadata added by prior instrumentation (sequence_id + fragment_offset).\n\nTesting and validation: added unit tests covering boundary cases for stop token crossing, overlapping logprob patches, and partial tool output finishing on mid-fragment boundaries. Ran an expanded e2e canary with 1k concurrent short-chat sessions and 200 concurrent tool-heavy sessions; observed a 94% reduction in malformed JSON events and a 30% decrease in re-streamed aborts. CI initially flaked on a canary harness timing test — increased timer blur in test harness and reran; all checks passed.\n\nBackward compatibility / migration: default settings preserve previous behavior for long-running responses; coalescing only affects micro-fragments and is opt-out via chat.streaming.coalesce_ms=0. Tool reconciler only changes what gets forwarded to structured-output consumers: partial deltas still exist (for observability) but consumers relying on the older behavior will continue to see raw deltas if they opt into experimental.raw_stream=true. We documented the knobs in docs/openai/compatibility.md.\n\nRollout plan: staged canary -> internal tenant alpha -> 2-week public canary for hosted customers -> enable by default for dedicated/private with patch release notes. We coordinated with SRE for alerting on malformed-structured-output rate to rollback quickly if needed.\n\nRelated: Linear ENG-1321 implements the coalescer research spike; SUP-784 captured customer reports used to craft failing test cases.\n\nChecklist: [x] unit tests added, [x] integration tests added, [x] docs updated, [x] SRE alerted and canary plan created, [x] feature knobs exposed for tuning.

release_notes:
Stabilize /v1/chat streaming under bursty backpressure by smoothing small fragments into coherent frames
Normalize logprob outputs and stop-token reconciliation across fragmented streaming segments
Improve tool/function-call envelope reconciliation so partial tool output does not corrupt structured output JSON

[v1/chat.completions: preserve role metadata & introduce framed tool-output envelope for parity]
description:
Context: Customers integrating Redwood through the OpenAI /v1/chat.completions compatibility layer reported two recurring issues: (1) role and custom metadata on assistant/tool messages getting lost during streaming/framing round trips, and (2) tooling/function outputs arriving as raw text blobs which made downstream structured parsing brittle, especially when stop token heuristics and logprobs are in play. Motivation: to improve parity with OpenAI semantics while keeping our streaming framing efficient and robust for function/tool calls. What this PR does: - Introduces a compact, backwards-compatible framed envelope for tool/function outputs (structured_output_v2) that carries: role, name, json_schema_hint (optional), and a base64-encoded payload when needed. This keeps streaming boundaries stable and keeps downstream parsers unambiguous. - Adds a preserve_role parameter mapping in the /v1/chat.completions adapter so role and any role-level metadata survive adapter translation and streaming framing. Default behavior remains backward-compatible. - Tightens stop token heuristics when framed envelopes are present: stop sequences are matched both at byte and token boundaries to reduce accidental truncation of structured payloads; we also avoid injecting artificial end tokens into the envelope body. - Ensures logprobs are attached to the correct top-level message tokens even when streaming emits intermediate frame boundaries; added a small KV-tagging scheme to re-associate token logprobs with message spans. - SDK surface: small TS and Python typing changes so that clients can opt into receiving structured tool envelopes instead of free-text tool outputs. - E2E regression tests and docs updates describing the new envelope and migration notes. Backwards compatibility and rollout strategy: the envelope is opt-in via a new adapter flag openai_compat.structured_output="v2" and a request-level param preserve_role=true. Default behavior preserves existing wire format (no frame envelope) so existing customers see no change. We will promote v2 by default in a minor release after a short canary. Related Linear: ENG-4132 (compat parity), PM-227 (docs/migration). Checklist: - [x] add envelope encoder/decoder (runtime) - [x] map preserve_role param in adapter - [x] update TypeScript/Python SDK types - [x] add e2e tests and flaky guardrails - [x] update docs/openai-compat.md - [x] add telemetry counters for envelope usage Commits: see commit_summaries.

[v1-chat-compat-param-normalizer-role-coercion-and-structured-toolcall-stability]
description:
Context: Customers using the OpenAI /v1/chat.completions compatibility layer hit a few edge-cases when mixing older client payloads with newer structured tool/function calling. In particular: 1) numeric/boolean stop values emitted by upstream proxies were being passed through and causing unexpected behavior; 2) role aliases (assistant/system/user) were not consistently normalized which hurt our role-based delta compression and safety heuristics; 3) streaming toolcall fragments occasionally produced invalid JSON fragments when interleaved with plain text deltas.

Motivation: Provide a conservative, backwards-compatible layer that coerces and normalizes incoming /v1/chat parameters to our canonical v2 internal shape, while fixing a handful of regressions observed in customer telemetry and SRE incident reports (ENG-3742). This reduces operator confusion and prevents toolcall stream deserialization errors without changing surface-level API semantics for well-formed clients.

What this PR does (summary):
- Adds a param coercion module for /v1/chat that:
  - coerces non-string stop entries (numbers/booleans) into their string equivalents and wraps single stops into arrays
  - canonicalizes role names and role-aliases (e.g. 'system_message' -> 'system') and dedupes contiguous role tokens
  - preserves original raw param metadata on the request context for telemetry/debugging
- Improves streaming framer to support atomic toolcall envelopes when tool outputs are emitted interleaved with plain text, reducing malformed JSON fragments in the stream
- Normalizes logprob packaging under /v1 compatibility so clients get stable shape regardless of model variant
- Adds extensive unit and integration tests, and small SDK compatibility shim in the Python SDK to demonstrate safe coercion behavior

[Failsafe SLO stabilizer and eviction oscillation dampener]
description:
Motivation: We observed repeated short-lived tenant evictions during regional transients where the SLO enforcer and eviction controller raced to drain resources, causing oscillation and throughput loss for other tenants. This change introduces a lightweight stabilizer layer between the SLO budget allocator and the eviction orchestrator to prevent oscillatory evictions and to provide an emergency 'quiet window' for KV cache syncs during regional reconvergence.

Design summary: Single-process stabilizer that tracks short-term SLO credit delta and applies a dampening multiplier to eviction scores for tenants that have been evicted and re-requested within a short time window. Key features: 1) tenant-weighted exponential decay on penalty scores to avoid deterministic flip-flops; 2) regional slack propagation that allows neighboring healthy zones to advertise spare capacity for short-lived bursts; 3) emergency KV quiet window to suspend aggressive KV drain during region flaps to avoid repeated cache warmups; 4) fast rollback flag and opt-out for customers on Dedicated.

What changed (high level): Added stabilizer service and controller glue, integrated dampener with existing eviction prioritizer, added feature flag (slo.stabilizer.enabled) and an emergency quiet-window (slo.kv_quiet_window_ms) that defaults to 1500ms during detected regional instability. The feature is gated behind a runtime flag for controlled rollout and metrics are exposed under redwood.runtime.stabilizer.*.

Checklist: - [x] Design doc reviewed (SRE and Runtime) - [x] Unit tests for decay math and prioritizer integration - [x] Integration tests exercising back-to-back evictions under simulated regional packet loss - [x] Load test on perf-canary with tenant-weighted mix - [x] Feature flagged rollout and telemetry verified - [x] Post-merge monitoring runbook added

Testing notes: Local unit tests cover decay curves and boundary conditions (0-60s). Integration harness simulates regional heartbeat loss using the perf-canary network fault injector; observed reduction in eviction churn from median 3 flips/min to 0.2 flips/min in targeted scenario. Canary showed negligible impact on median P95 latency for non-evicted tenants and a 3% improvement in overall successful request rate during the storm window.

Commits summary: (squashed for merge) - Implement stabilizer service and dampener algorithm - Integrate stabilizer with eviction prioritizer and SLO budget allocator - Add feature flag, config defaults, and runtime metrics - Tests: unit, integration, and canary harness adjustments - Docs: rollout runbook and troubleshooting notes

Files changed (high level): - runtime/stabilizer/controller.go (new) - runtime/eviction/prioritizer.go (modified) - infra/config/flags.go (added slo.stabilizer.enabled and slo.kv_quiet_window_ms) - telemetry/metrics_registry.yaml (new metrics) - tests/integration/eviction_stability_test.go (new) - docs/runbooks/slo_stabilizer_rollout.md (new)

Risk and rollback: The stabilizer can be disabled immediately via the slo.stabilizer.enabled flag. If unintended side effects are seen, we will revert the flag and perform a targeted rollback for affected regions. We also added a fast-fail-safe that disables the quiet window if KV drain times exceed a configured threshold to avoid long-lived cache inconsistencies.

Related work: This complements the regional slack propagation work but differs by acting as a short-term dampener rather than a long-lived priority adjustment. Addresses SUP-3421 (customer reported repeated evictions during regional jitter).

[Granular slot defragmenter and stable spill handoff for KV cache]
description:
Motivation: reduce long-tail latency and memory fragmentation observed on multi-tenant KV cache under mixed sequence-length workloads. This change introduces a lightweight granular slot defragmenter that compacts small free slots within hot segments without global stop-the-world passes and a stable spill handoff mechanism to reduce jitter when multiple tenants trigger spill simultaneously. The defragmenter runs opportunistically during low CPU utilization windows and is placement-aware so it avoids interrupting active continuous batching kernels. The spill handoff guarantees an ordered, per-tenant spill queue that prevents oscillation between eviction and rehydration under bursty workloads. Changes: 1) new slot_defragmenter module that tracks slot usage at ~64B granularity and performs local compaction when free-slot fragmentation exceeds a threshold; 2) soft-quota-aware eviction path that prefers reclaiming subsegment holes before evicting whole entries; 3) stable_spill coordinator that serializes spill initiation per-tenant and provides a backpressure token to the scheduler; 4) small scheduler hook in batch_router so continuous batching kernels can opt-out of compaction windows when latency SLOs are tight; 5) observability additions: metrics for fragmentation_ratio, compaction_cycles, spill_handoff_rate and tenant_spill_latency histogram; 6) integration tests and microbenchmarks comparing end-to-end tail latency and token cost. Commits summary: [a1b2c3d] introduce slot_defragmenter scaffolding and unit tests; [b2c3d4e] implement compaction algorithm and integration with cache allocator; [c3d4e5f] add stable_spill coordinator and per-tenant queues; [d4e5f6a] scheduler hook and continuous-batching opt-out path; [e5f6a7b] docs, metrics, and benchmarks. Files changed (high level): internal/kv/cache/slot_defragmenter.rs - new module with compaction loop and heuristics; internal/kv/allocator/soft_quota_reclaimer.cc - changes to prefer slot coalescing; internal/kv/evictor/stable_spill.go - new coordinator and tests; internal/scheduler/batch_router.cpp - opt-out hook and minor APIs; docs/kv/defrag.md - design notes and operator guidance; tests/kv/defrag_integration_test.go - multi-tenant scenarios; benchmarks/kv/slot_vacancy_bench.yaml - benchmark harness; tools/observability/kv_metrics_exports.yaml - prometheus metric exports. Testing and CI: initial CI run had a flaky integration test related to timing of compaction and continuous batching; flaky test was quarantined and fixed by introducing a deterministic wait in tests and replacing time.Now()-based assertions with logical event markers. All unit, integration, and benchmark CI jobs passed on the final run. Benchmarks: 95th percentile request latency improved by 18% on mixed short/long sequence workloads vs baseline, median cost-per-token reduced by 6% under steady-state due to fewer full-entry evictions. Rollout plan: feature gated behind kv.defrag.enabled false by default. We will rollout to canary tenants for one week with fragmentation_ratio and tenant_spill_latency dashboarding and automatic rollback if tenant_spill_latency increases by >15% for more than 10 minutes. Related work: complements prior slab-based reclaimer work and the soft-spill backpressure PRs; references ENG-6421 and ENG-6590 for backlog context. Changelog: add entry about defragmenter and stable spill coordinator. Merge: squash and merge to main.
