release_notes:
Added a granular slot defragmenter and a stable spill handoff coordinator for the KV cache. This reduces fragmentation-induced evictions and stabilizes spill behavior during tenant bursts resulting in improved tail latency and lower cost-per-token. Feature is gated and disabled by default. See docs/kv/defrag.md for enablement and operational guidance.

[sre: adaptive load-shedding + regional failover hardening and circuit-breaker fix]
description:
Motivation: We observed a sequence of cross-region latency spikes that caused one region to exhaust available worker slots and then trigger aggressive failover to a neighboring region. That region then experienced transient saturation and entered a degraded state, producing a cascading degradation loop. This change introduces an adaptive per-region load-shedding policy tied to short-window SLO signals, hardens the circuit-breaker state transitions to avoid stuck OPEN states after partial capacity loss, and adds a conservative regional fallback backoff to prevent oscillation. The change is gated behind a feature flag (ops.feature_flags.regional_adaptive_shed) and is rolled out as a canary followed by a full rollout. Checklist: 1) Implement adaptive load-shedding controller that computes shed probability from recent error rate and P99 latency SLO windows; 2) Add token-based pre-queue throttle to protect control plane and auth services; 3) Fix circuit-breaker state machine bug where HALF_OPEN transitions could be skipped when a subset of shards returned inconsistent health; 4) Add metrics (region_load_shed_percent, region_cb_state, region_fallback_backoff_seconds) and tracing hooks for incident investigation; 5) Add integration test that simulates partial region outage and asserts no failover oscillation; 6) Docs and ops runbook updates; 7) Hotfix: fix a race that could keep fallback backoff at zero on rapid repeated failovers. Why this matters: reduces user-facing error spikes during regional disturbances, preserves global availability by limiting blast radius and preventing cascading failovers. Rollout plan: enable feature flag in canary region (eu-west-1) for 48h, monitor region_load_shed_percent and request latency/error SLOs, then enable globally if no regressions. If regressions occur, toggle feature flag off and rollback via the existing deployment pipeline. Related: SUP-412 was opened during the incident window and contains patient repro steps for the CI smoke failures we observed.

Priya Nair: The shed probability is sampled per-request at the admission point. We use a deterministic hash+probability when request has a stable id to avoid flapping for retries; otherwise we sample per-call. Added notes in load_shedding.rs comments.
Sasha McDermott: Can the circuit-breaker fix be toggled independently? If it stays merged we want the ability to revert only the adaptive shedding if we see new patterns.
Priya Nair: Yes, circuit-breaker state machine change is controlled by ops.flags.cb_state_harden and defaults to true because it fixes a correctness bug; adaptive shedding is behind regional_adaptive_shed and defaults to false. Documented in deploy/feature_flags.yaml.
Liam O'Connell: Integration test looks good but flaked on first run in CI due to timing; please make timeouts slightly looser and add a deterministic seed.
Priya Nair: Adjusted test timeouts and added seeded RNG to the test harness to make result reproducible. Reran locally and in CI.
Ethan Park: LGTM after CI pass
Sasha McDermott: Approved

release_notes:
Added adaptive regional load-shedding with an ops feature flag, hardened the circuit-breaker state machine to avoid stuck OPEN states during partial regional loss, and added telemetry for region_load_shed_percent and circuit-breaker state. Default behavior unchanged until feature flag enabled.

notes_for_oncall:
If enabled and you observe sudden increase in region_load_shed_percent without corresponding CPU/GPU saturation, toggle ops.feature_flags.regional_adaptive_shed off to restore prior behavior and open SUP-412 for follow-up. Use region_cb_state metric to determine per-region circuit breaker health.

testing_notes:
Canary tested in eu-west-1 for 48h with synthetic traffic that injected a 30% worker availability loss; no oscillations observed. Integration test simulates shard inconsistency and asserts circuit-breaker recovers to CLOSED only after controlled HALF_OPEN probe. See tests/integration/regional_failover_test.go for scenarios.

deploy_instructions:
1) Merge to main, 2) Toggle ops.feature_flags.regional_adaptive_shed=true for canary region via ops console, 3) Monitor metrics for 48h, 4) If stable, enable globally in stages by region. Rollback: toggle flag false and redeploy if necessary.

[introduce-tenant-surge-dribble-and-epochal-handoff-protector]
release_notes:
Adds a staged tenant surrender mechanism and ephemeral egress fuse to make regional failovers less noisy and reduce SLO oscillations. Exposes two new telemetry counters and a small config knob for surge-dribble window length.

description:
Motivation: During regional overload and coordinated failovers we've observed cascading evictions where tenants are fully discharged then aggressively re-admitted causing SLO oscillations and KV cache churn. This change introduces a 'surge dribble' admission path and an epochal handoff protector that preserves short-term reservation credits and prevents immediate aggressive rejoin. Design: 1) Staged tenant surrender: when a node decides to shed tenant traffic it first enters a dribble phase where admission is throttled to a low steady rate while KV cache is preserved for a configurable window. 2) Epochal handoff protector: the node attaches an epoch token to surrendered tenants; downstream nodes defer hard-eviction for the token TTL and apply an exponentially decaying reservation credit to prioritize graceful rejoin. 3) Ephemeral egress fuse: a configurable per-region egress cap that will soft-deny new allocations when the region-wide egress budget is saturated; the fuse emits detailed telemetry that feeds the Console to explain soft-denies. Backwards compatibility: tokens are opt-in per deployment via runtime flags for Dedicated/Private. Metrics: tenant.surge.dribble_rate, tenant.surge.reservation_tokens_issued, tenant.surge.epoch_rejoins. Checklist: - [x] Design doc referenced in ENG-3145 - [x] Unit tests for reservation decay - [x] Integration test for dribble window - [x] Telemetry wired to Console dashboards - [x] Feature-flag gating for Private/Dedicated rollout Implementation summary: commits: see commits list. Files changed: high-level changes include new package pkg/slo/dribble.go that implements the dribble admission controller, runtime/egress/fuse.go to implement the ephemeral fuse and region coordinator hooks, pkg/slo/epoch_token.go for token lifecycle, telemetry/metrics.yaml to declare metrics, console/dashboards/surge-dribble.json to add a dashboard, integration/tests/regional_drain_test.go to exercise the flow, and small wiring changes in deploy/helm to expose flags. Why this is different: most prior solutions aggressively evict and rely on rebalancing; this PR creates a small, observable window that trades minimal additional latency for large reductions in repeated evictions and SLO churn. Rollout plan: feature-flag on main for 2 weeks in canary region, then staged ramp to 25%, 50%, global. Monitoring and alerting: added SLO regressions alert for 5xx increase during dribble window and an ops dashboard to inspect token churn.

[Adaptive slice suballocator with tiered spill hysteresis and compact-on-evict]
description:
Context: The KV cache has increasingly suffered from micro-fragmentation under mixed-length workloads (short response KV entries interleaved with large context blobs). This causes premature spills and paging which degrades tail latency. Motivation: introduce a lightweight, adaptive suballocator that reduces internal fragmentation, coordinate compaction with eviction to avoid double-copy churn, and add a tiered spill hysteresis to dampen oscillatory spill/reload cycles. Summary of changes: 1) New adaptive slice suballocator (pkg/kv/suballocator.go) that splits large slabs into variable 'slices' sized by observed allocation-size histogram and runtime fragmentation score. The suballocator supports fast-path allocation for hot-size buckets and a fallback coalescing slow-path for large sparse allocations. 2) Compact-on-evict policy: when an eviction candidate is selected, the allocator attempts an in-place compact if the tenant's fragmentation score is above a configured threshold; this reduces downstream spill volume. 3) Tiered spill hysteresis: spill thresholds now use a three-level hysteresis (soft/warm/hard) per-tenant and are backed by a moving-average resident-set and OS page-fault signal to prevent oscillation during bursty traffic. 4) OS-paging-aware backpressure: runtime signals (page-fault rate and swap utilization) feed into the spill controller to throttle batching aggressiveness and avoid cascading IO. 5) Background compactor: asynchronous compaction runs with an IO budget aware rate limiter that cooperates with the scheduler to yield during high-batching windows. 6) Telemetry and runtime knobs: new metrics (kv.slice_size_distribution, kv.fragmentation_score, kv.compaction_cycles, kv.spill_hysteresis_state) and configuration flags (kv.slice_min, kv.slice_max, kv.compact_eviction_threshold, kv.spill_warm_ratio). Checklists: - [x] Implement adaptive slice suballocator - [x] Add compact-on-evict path and unit tests - [x] Implement tiered spill hysteresis and OS signal integration - [x] Add telemetry and knobs - [x] Benchmarks and microbench harness added - [x] E2E perf validation against stress harness (bench/kv/sim_bench.go) Perf summary: Microbench on p4d and internal GPU clusters shows 18-26% reduction in mean eviction-induced spill bytes and a 12% improvement in 95th percentile tail TTFB for mixed small/large workloads. Under sustained large-blob workloads the soft-warm tiers reduce unnecessary full spills by ~40%, lowering datastore IO. Risk: Compaction can add CPU overhead; the compact-on-evict path is gated behind per-tenant thresholds and an adaptive sampling rate. Related: builds on earlier KV residency and eviction work; coordinates with scheduler changes in runtime/evictor to ensure compaction doesn't collide with token-critical batches. Links: Linear ENG-2345 design doc internal link (design/redwood/kv/adaptive-slice-suballoc), incident SUP-4211 notes for previous paging spike.

[Role resolution fails after Okta group id type change; ModelObservability API returns 403 for newly provisioned users]
description:
Summary: Since 2026-03-09 ~03:00 UTC a subset of newly provisioned users are getting 403 when calling the ModelObservability API. Initial triage shows users exist in OKTA and have expected groups, but the RBAC role lookup in auth-service fails because group identifiers in the incoming auth claim are integers instead of strings after a recent Okta mapping change. Impact: Affected SREs and ML engineers cannot access model observability dashboards or runbook actions; blocking incident response in us-east for customer-impacting alerts.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Create or modify an Okta user with group assignment via provisioning (SCIM).
2) Wait for scim-sync job to run (0-5m).
3) Login to console and call /v1/model-observability/metrics (or open dashboard).
4) Observe 403 and no role in auth-service logs for the user.
Expected: role lookup succeeds and 200 returned. Actual: 403 denied due to missing role mapping.

logs:
auth-service warning: role-lookup: claim.groups value types: [123456, 234567] (type: integer)
expected mapping key types: "123456"

example token claim (decoded): {
  "sub": "00u1abcXyZ",
  "email": "eng+test@redwood.ai",
  "groups": [123456, 234567],
  "iss": "https://okta.redwood.ai"
}

auth-service debug: mappedRoles=[] for user 00u1abcXyZ at 2026-03-10T03:12:07Z
model-observability-api access denied: headers: { x-rw-user: 00u1abcXyZ } response: 403 {
  "error": "unauthorized",
  "reason": "no-matching-role-for-groups"
}

investigation_notes:
Timeline: change window 2026-03-08 22:00 UTC when Okta admin updated group import mapping to emit numeric IDs (Okta API update). Hypothesis: identity-proxy and scim-sync historically normalized group ids to strings; the new mapping produced integers and our role index uses string keys -> lookup misses.
Findings:
- scim-sync stored groups in DB as strings when coming from canonical SCIM paths, but identity-proxy forwards token claims verbatim.
- auth-service role lookup code compares claim group IDs with role-index map (string keys). No type coercion.
- Reproduced locally by forging token with numeric group values; role lookup returns empty.
- Not all users affected: only those provisioned after Okta mapping change (group ids numeric). Older tokens remain as strings and continue to work.
Evidence: logs above and successful reproduction in staging by creating token with numeric groups.
Mitigation attempted: temporary canary: identity-proxy will coerce numeric claim.groups to strings on ingress; deployed to canary cluster (canary-2) 2026-03-11 18:30 UTC.

comments:
2026-03-10 04:05 - Priya Kapoor (Support): Reported initial customer-facing impact after SRE oncall noted missing access for 3 engineers. Attached sample decoded token and stack trace.

description:
Issue summary: A recently hired PM cannot access the internal DataViz console after completing SSO and SCIM provisioning. The user record appears in Okta and SCIM logs, but the console returns 403 with a message 'no roles assigned'. Impact: New hire onboarding blocked (cannot run dashboards or join pairing session). The console auth middleware logs: "role_lookup: 0 roles for subject=okta|12345-abcd". Hypothesis: crosswalk mapping between Okta group displayName and internal role key is failing due to a legacy transform that strips punctuation and lowercases; some groups created by IT include a trailing non-ASCII hyphen which is not normalized and therefore fails match in the role catalog.

Assign user to that Okta group

root_cause:

Permanent fix deployed: PR #1724 normalizes incoming group displayName by applying unicode NFKD normalization, mapping common dash-like characters (U+2013, U+2014, U+2212) to ASCII hyphen, then lowercasing and collapsing whitespace before performing role lookup. The fix was rolled out to identity-proxy and provisioner v2.2.3 on 2026-03-12 in us-west with canary at 10% then 100% after 30 minutes. [Stream warmup + credential-lease adapter: unify ergonomic iterators across SDKs]
description:
Context: Users reported stream cold-start variance and awkward reauth race conditions across SDKs when long-lived streaming sessions are resumed behind resumable tokens. This PR introduces a lightweight credential-lease adapter plus a small ergonomic surface for 'stream warmup' hints so SDKs can coordinate an early KV-cache priming request and avoid repeated auth handoffs.
Motivation: reduce token-swap races, unify retry/backoff defaults for streaming, and provide a minimal cross-language adapter that keeps idiomatic iterators in each SDK.
Summary of changes: - Introduce a credential lease abstraction (lease Adapter) in sdk/common that exposes RenewableLease interface and a small HTTP handshake for short-lived session leases. - Python: add redwood.session.lease.LeaseClient, a small context manager used by the async stream iterator to pin token leases for the duration of a resumed stream; add stream_warmup hint to StreamingClient.start_stream. - TypeScript: add compact StreamWarmupHint and a thin LeaseProvider shim that conforms to existing token provider types; add tests covering abort semantics. - Go: add adapter.go implementing the LeaseProvider for go-sdk, update stream iterator to accept WarmupHint and lease token context. - Backoff: add a 'streaming-warmup' preset in sdk/common/backoff with conservative initial window and jitter tuned for streaming heartbeats. - Docs: new markdown guide docs/sdk/stream-warmup.md and example in examples/stream-warmup. - Tests: end-to-end integration tests for streaming warmup in python/ts and unit tests for lease renewal edge cases.
Commits (high level): - 1a2b3c4: implement common lease contract and basic shim - 2b3c4d5: python LeaseClient + iterator integration + unit tests - 3c4d5e6: typescript lease provider + stream warmup hint - 4d5e6f7: go adapter + iterator changes + go tests - 5e6f7g8: docs, examples, and changelogs - 6f7g8h9: fix CI flake, adjust backoff timing
Motivation and rollout plan: This change is backwards compatible for all current token providers. The LeaseAdapter is optional: if no lease provider is supplied, SDKs fall back to existing token-refresh behavior. We will ship with an opt-in flag in the console for a small set of internal customers for two weeks, monitor stream error rates and auth exchange traces, and then flip the default.
Review conversation (abridged): - Miguel: "Nice overall shape. Two asks: please add a changelog entry per SDK and shrink the LeaseClient constructor surface for Python." - Asha: "Added changelog entries and tightened constructor; also added an example in examples/stream-warmup to show the minimal pattern." - Lena: "Can you add a test that simulates a failing renewal and ensures the iterator surfaces a RetryableStreamError?" - Asha: "Added test (tests/python/test_stream_warmup.py) and returned a RetryableStreamError with clear message; updated TS test accordingly." - Ravi (approval): "Verified E2E with dedicated infra - warmup reduced first-response latency variance by ~18% in our synthetic trace."
CI notes: Initial CI run: lint passed; python unit matrix had a flaky test (test_stream_backpressure) failing intermittently due to a timing assumption; addressed by replacing time.sleep with event-driven synchronization. Re-run CI: all checks passed (lint, unit, integration, e2e-smoke).
Files of interest (high level): - sdk/common/credentials/lease_adapter.go: core lease contract and a small HTTP handshake client. - sdk/python/redwood/session/lease.py: LeaseClient implementation and context manager used by async iterator. - sdk/typescript/src/stream/iterator.ts: new optional warmupHint param on startStream and LeaseProvider shim. - sdk/go/stream/adapter.go: Go lease adapter and small helper to thread context.Context for lease lifecycle.
Backward compatibility and breaking changes: none; all new surfaces are optional and fall back to existing behavior when unused.
Semantic version bumps: python SDK -> 2.1.0 (minor), typescript SDK -> 1.8.0 (minor), go SDK -> v0.12.3 (minor).
Release notes: "Introduce optional streaming warmup and credential-lease adapter to reduce stream cold-start variance and make cross-SDK streaming auth more robust. Opt-in for two weeks before flipping default for GA."
Merge outcome: merged via squash-and-merge after approvals from reviewers.
Follow-ups planned: - ENG-7310: rollout monitor and alert on stream auth error rate - ENG-7321: telemetry: add metric for lease-renew failures and warmup-success ratio - cleanup: consider collapsing token provider interfaces after broader adoption
Risk/mitigation: The only notable risk is over-reliance on the lease handshake adding a small constant (<5ms) to stream establishment; mitigated by the warmup hint which allows a parallel priming request that overlaps with existing connection setup. Internal testing showed net latency variance improvements for bursty workloads.

release_notes:
Introduce optional streaming warmup and credential-lease adapter. Adds LeaseClient (Python), LeaseProvider (TS), and adapter for Go. Minor SDK bumps: py 2.1.0, ts 1.8.0, go v0.12.3. Opt-in rollout, monitor auth metrics.

[Unify stream cursor abstraction, auth handshake, and backoff across Python/TS/Go SDKs; cross-sdk version bumps]
description:
Motivation: We have multiple inconsistent streaming iterator semantics, token-refresh handshakes, and backoff defaults across the Python, TypeScript and Go SDKs. This has caused developer confusion and subtle production bugs (lost partial messages on reconnect, token race during refresh) across customer integrations. This PR unifies the behaviour by introducing a common "StreamCursor"/iterator abstraction and standardizing the auth handshake lifecycle and retry/backoff defaults across the three SDKs.

What this PR does (high level): - Adds a StreamCursor abstraction in each SDK that provides: next()/has_next() style iteration, resume tokens for safe reconnects, and deterministic finalization to drain KV caches. - Implements a two-step auth handshake: (1) token pinning at stream open to avoid mid-stream rotation races, (2) transparent refresh callback with optimistic retry on auth failure. - Replaces per-language ad-hoc backoff constants with a shared policy: jittered exponential backoff starting at 200ms, max 8s, max retries 6 for transient stream errors. - Surfaces ergonomic helpers for common patterns: stream.to_async_iterator() in Python, stream.asyncIterable() in TS, and StreamCursor.Iter() in Go. - Updates examples, tests, and bump package versions in each SDK.

Files changed (high level): see changed_files for exact paths.

Migration notes: - Existing streaming loops that relied on the old per-chunk callback shape should switch to the StreamCursor API. Migration helpers are provided and are backwards-compatible wrappers for the most common patterns. - If you have custom token rotation, review the new refresh callback hook; handlers that mutate tokens should be idempotent and accept a context param in Go / cancellation token in TS / timeout in Python. - The default backoff is more aggressive than some client-customized configs; customers can override via the SDK config object (see examples).

Testing and QA: - Added cross-language unit and integration tests that validate partial message resume across disconnects and token rotation scenarios. - Ran full e2e matrix on linux/arm and linux/x86, and verified memory profiles for long-running streams. - Security scan: no new secrets; auth handshake code reviewed by security.

Checklist: - [x] Python implementation + tests + docs - [x] TypeScript implementation + tests + docs - [x] Go implementation + tests + docs - [x] Migration guides updated - [x] Bumped package versions and changelogs - [x] CI green (see ci_checks)

Related: ENG-3412 (stream reliability), ENG-3571 (sdk ergonomics), SUP-9182 (customer incident tied to token rotation).

release_notes:
Unified stream cursor API across Python/TS/Go, consistent auth handshake and exponential backoff defaults; ergonomics improvements for streaming loops; bumped SDK versions: python 2.8.0, typescript 1.12.0, go 0.9.0. No runtime-breaking changes expected; minor API surface tweaks documented in migration notes.

[polyglot SDK: smoothing token handshake, unified retry backoff, and stream iterator ergonomic updates]
description:
Motivation: Multiple customer reports + internal benchmarks (ENG-2891) showed two recurring issues across SDKs: 1) streaming reconnects during token rotation could drop or duplicate streamed events, and 2) SDKs exposed inconsistent retry/backoff surfaces which made cross-service configs error-prone. This PR implements a cross-language pattern (polyglot RetryPolicy + StreamCursor ergonomics) to make behavior consistent and reduce operational surprises.

Scope and approach: - Introduces a lightweight RetryPolicy contract (language-specific types) with sensible defaults tuned for typical inference latency distributions (initial: 100ms, factor: 1.8, max: 8s, jitter: full). Defaults are chosen to avoid tight retry loops on auth failures while preserving fast transient recovery. - Streaming: adds a StreamCursor abstraction in Python (iterator that yields ResumeToken + Event tuples) and standardizes async-iterable behavior in TypeScript to match it. Go exposes a context-aware Consumer that returns a channel of events and a ResumeToken; all three maintain the same semantics for token handshake on reconnect. - Auth/token rotation: handshake sequence updated so SDKs validate server-ack of new tokens before dropping existing KV cache offsets. This prevents resumed streams from jumping backward when a reconnect race happens during token refresh. - Backwards compatibility: All new surfaces are opt-in defaults that preserve existing simple usage patterns. Where signatures changed, overloads or adapter helpers were added so existing callers compile without edits.

Checklist: - [x] Design doc + perf notes posted in ENG-2891 - [x] Unit tests for Python/TS/Go stream reconnect scenarios - [x] E2E cross-language test in benchlab harness - [x] Docs/migration guide added

Motivation notes: This is intended to reduce reported incidents where live features (chat streaming, tool-calls) observed duplicated tokens or missing final events after token rotation or short network blips.

Summary of changes (high level file list): - sdks/python/redwood/stream.py: StreamCursor, token_handshake(), unit tests in tests/stream_test.py - sdks/typescript/src/stream/async_iterable.ts: normalize async-iterable consumer, add reconnect handling - sdks/go/stream/consumer.go: context cancel-friendly consumer + resume token semantics - sdks/common/retry_policy.md: language-agnostic backing doc describing defaults and knobs - docs/sdk-migration.md: migration steps and examples - tests/e2e/bench_inference/reconnect_auth_rotation: harness + scripts

Notable design decisions: - Single RetryPolicy surface: reduced config duplication across SDKs to a small set of knobs (initial_delay, multiplier, max_delay, jitter). SDKs expose language-idiomatic wrappers but share the same defaults. - Token handshake verify-on-ack: on reconnect the SDK attempts to re-establish the stream at the last known offset, sends the rotated token in the handshake, and waits for an explicit server ACK containing the resume cursor. Only then does the client drop the cached offset. This avoids a window where the client assumes resume succeeded but the server has no matching cursor. - Streaming ergonomics: Python exposes a generator-based StreamCursor that yields (resume_token, event) so callers can persist cursors easily. TypeScript returns an AsyncIterable of { resumeToken?, event } objects to match. Go uses channels to match idiomatic Go patterns.

Tests and CI: - Unit tests added per SDK (python/ts/go) covering reconnect, token swap races, and backoff behavior. - One flaky TS integration test on Windows CI triggered an intermittent timing assertion; we stabilized it by making the test resilient to timing fuzz and reran. CI outcome: all checks green after rerun.

Review conversation (summary): - Owen: "The token handshake ACK makes sense but is there an observable perf regression on steady-state streaming?" -> Maya: "No measurable regression in our benchlab; handshake adds one minimal RTT only on reconnect paths which are already rare; added bench numbers to ENG-2891." - Rae: "Backoff defaults look conservative; can we halve initial_delay for low-latency customers?" -> Maya: "Made initial_delay configurable; added a sample config for low-latency deployments in docs." - Diego: "Can we avoid changing public method signatures in Go?" -> Maya: "Added an adapter that keeps previous signature and delegates to the new consumer internally." - Rae (approval): "LGTM after minor doc clarifications"

Merge: squash and merge by Rae Thompson on 2026-02-20.

Post-merge actions: - Backported a small fix to the release/1.8 branch for a hotfix (pr-65235) addressing a test-only race discovered during backport. - Announced change in #sdk-updates and posted migration guide link.

Example usage snippets (from docs): Python: "for resume, evt in StreamCursor(client.stream(...)): process(evt); save_cursor(resume)" TypeScript: "for await (const item of client.stream(...)) { /* item.resumeToken, item.event */ }" Go: "events, token := client.Stream(ctx, req); for e := range events { /* ... */ }"

Impact: This PR reduces duplicated-events incidents seen in recent customer reports, standardizes retry behavior across SDKs, and improves cross-language portability for streaming consumers.

Follow-ups: - Add a telemetry event for handshake failures to SLO dashboards (ENG-2950) - Evaluate lowering default multiplier for mobile customers (ENG-2961)

[converge-slim-retries-and-explicit-stream-close-across-py-ts-go]
description:
Context: We have three SDKs (Python/TypeScript/Go) drifting in ergonomics for retry presets and streaming lifecycle: consumers have inconsistent default backoff windows, token refresh races subtly leak stale bearer tokens during resume, and stream consumers have no canonical close/handoff semantics which makes deterministic cleanup tricky for upstream frameworks. Motivation: small, cross-language ergonomics wins reduce support burden and make tri-sdk examples portable. This PR introduces a compact, documented 'slim' retry presets bundle, a lightweight explicit stream-close API surfaced consistently across languages, and a defensive auth handshake change to avoid a token-swap race during stream resume. Summary of changes: 1) Add retry_presets.slim (spec) and implement bindings for py/ts/go. The presets provide three profiles (fast, balanced, conservative) with deterministic jitter math consistent across runtimes. 2) Introduce StreamHandle.close()/asyncClose() and CloseStream(ctx) to ensure the SDK flushes KV cache cursors and emits a final telemetry event; this is exposed as a simple sync/async method in each SDK. 3) Fix token-swap race: introduce a short-lived token window (50ms) while resuming streams and ensure outgoing requests observe the latest token via atomic swap. 4) Make small public API surface changes: add retry_policy=RetryPresets.SLIM on client constructors and a StreamOptions.auto_close boolean defaulting to false to avoid behavioral change for current users. 5) Add end-to-end tests for resume + token refresh, stream close idempotency, and cross-language parity asserts in the monorepo harness. 6) Bump versions: python -> 1.12.0, typescript -> 1.8.0, go -> 1.5.2. Migration notes: existing users are unaffected by default; to opt into the new presets pass retry_policy=RetryPresets.SLIM (or equivalent). If you rely on implicit stream finalization via GC, opt-in to StreamOptions.auto_close=true to enable explicit close hooks. Checklist: - [x] API design review with SDK leads - [x] Unit tests for each SDK - [x] E2E parity tests in harness - [x] Documentation snippets for migration - [x] Telemetry event added for stream.close - [x] Version bumps and changelogs updated Files of note changed: see changed_files list below. CI: first run failed due to a flaky ts test (race in mock timer), fixed by introducing deterministic fake timers in ts harness. All checks green on final run. Merge: squash-merged to main with canonical commit message below. Related: ENG-2048 (retry profile consolidation), ENG-2101 (stream lifecycle hygiene).

Introduced explicit StreamHandle.close()/asyncClose() across SDKs and an opt-in StreamOptions.auto_close flag. Fixed token-swap race on stream resume with a configurable resume_token_window (default 50ms). Added e2e parity tests and bumped SDK versions: python 1.12.0, typescript 1.8.0, go 1.5.2.

description:

Current trace inspector prototypes show a single-pane waterfall; teams frequently asked for quick span-to-span comparison, cost-per-token context, and the ability to keep a focused correlation panel pinned while navigating other traces. This ticket proposes a correlation-focused sidebar plus a temporary 'Span Comparison Mode' that surfaces aligned timelines, side-by-side metadata and token-cost deltas for selected spans.

acceptance_criteria:
Correlation Sidebar can be toggled from any trace drilldown and pins to the right side of the UI without losing scroll position in the main waterfall.
Span Comparison Mode supports selecting up to 3 spans (from same correlation ID across requests) and displays them in aligned mini-waterfalls for visual diffing.
Metadata comparison table shows attributes (service, host, GPU type, model variant, sequence length, tokens, cost estimate) with clear deltas and inline links to logs and request payloads.
Interactions: keyboard shortcut (C) to open sidebar, shift-click to multi-select spans, and Escape to exit compare mode.
Prototype reviewed by frontend lead and PM and usability-tested with 5 engineers; feedback items tracked and addressed.
Performance: sidebar virtualization strategy keeps initial render < 120ms for traces up to 5k spans.
Design spec contains redlines, focus states, color accessibility checks, and animation specs for timeline alignment.
Handoff artefacts: Figma file, interaction spec doc, and component tokens included in the handoff bundle.

design_notes:
Sidebar is context-aware: when opened from a span it auto-selects related spans with same correlation ID and shows a compact histogram of request arrival times.
Span Comparison Mode aligns spans by request timestamp and displays a shared time ruler to surface skew and latency hotspots.
Introduce a lightweight cost estimator column that computes a normalized token-cost per-span using model and quantization metadata surfaced from the trace envelope.
Use a muted palette for non-selected spans and a high-contrast accent for active comparisons; ensure WCAG AA for 3:1 where possible.
Mobile behavior: sidebar collapses into a bottom-sheet with summary cards; full comparison reserved for desktop (secondary requirement).
Edge-case: for traces with >1000 spans we surface a summary view and require user to 'Zoom into segment' before enabling compare mode to avoid memory spikes.
We decided against full dual-canvas rendering (two independent waterfall canvases) because it doubled memory; instead we implement modular aligned mini-waterfalls per-span.
Include quick actions in each row: Open logs, Copy correlation ID, Open request in new tab, Pin pair for longer comparisons.
Suggested micro-interactions: gentle crossfade when adding/removing spans; nudge animation for new correlation matches discovered while sidebar is open.
Telemetry events to track: sidebar_opened, compare_mode_entered, span_selected_for_compare, compare_export_csv.
Accessibility: spans are keyboard-focusable; comparison table supports screen-reader summaries (short verbal diff).

Limit compare selection to 3 spans to keep UI legible and to avoid overwhelming the metadata table.
Introduce an estimated 'cost delta' metric in the metadata table but label it as heuristic and link to billing details in the Console.
Virtualize long lists in the sidebar rather than paginate to keep interactions fluid for power users.

[Validate and temporarily pause aggressive per-tenant batching/cache/quant profiles; provide traffic-split mitigation and safe restore]
description:
Issue summary: Customer BrightHealth AI reports recurring 95p latency spikes after we applied an aggressive per-tenant optimization bundle (large batch size + KV prefetch + int8-like quant profile). Impact: High - production traffic sees repeated 95th/99th percentile tail latency > 1.2s causing downstream request timeouts and a customer SLA alert. They want a low-risk way to pause the tenant's optimization set, shift a small percentage of traffic to a stable profile, and then validate behavior before a full restore.

We need support-run commands and an ordered playbook that avoids mass restart or global config changes. Customer prefers zero downtime for most users; willing to accept a small controlled traffic split.


steps_to_reproduce:
1) Tenant BrightHealth AI configured optimizer profile: batching.max_tokens=1024, batching.preferred_batch_size=64, kv_prefetch=true, quant_profile=fast-approx-v2
2) Synthetic load: 120 concurrent users, median request length ~ 120 tokens, intermittent long-context sessions (up to 1024),
   observe tail latency over 95th percentile on production route redwood-api/v1/generate
3) Monitor: console -> routes -> redwood-api/v1/generate -> 95p/99p latency spikes correlated with increased batch construction time and elevated GPU busy-waits

[Tenant credit-based region routing with variant shadowing and graceful hosted backfill]
description:
Summary:
Design and implement a tenant credit allocator that influences region & tier selection for dedicated capacity while enabling controlled hosted spillback. The allocator issues soft "credits" (soft reservations) based on pre-commit, historical consumption, and SLA tier. Credits drive probabilistic routing decisions: prefer dedicated when credits >= cost_estimate, gradually bleed to hosted when credits are low.

Goals:
- Reduce unexpected hosted spillovers for customers with reserved capacity while allowing controlled, observable backfill to hosted for short bursts.
- Maintain latency SLOs for P0/P1 tenants and keep unit cost predictable for reserved customers.
- Provide a transparent, debuggable fallback mechanism to hosted and to lower-cost model variants.

Design highlights:
1) Credit allocator
- Each tenant has a credit balance updated continuously: credits += reserved_rate * time_window - actual_consumption_cost. Credits are bounded and never drop below a soft negative floor.
- Credit tiers: GREEN (>75%), AMBER (25%-75%), RED (<25%). Routing preference score = base_affinity * f(credit_tier) * tenant_priority_scale.

2) Probabilistic routing with hysteresis
- For each request compute P(dedicated) = sigmoid((score - threshold)/temperature). Add request jitter and short-term moving-average smoothing to avoid flapping.
- Hysteresis windows vary by tier: GREEN (30s), AMBER (2m), RED (10m).

3) Variant shadowing and demotion
- If hosted or lower-cost variant is selected, send a shadow copy to a demoted variant for quality monitoring (no charge to tenant). Shadowing includes: prompt/response hashing, deterministic knob to redact sensitive fields, and TTL for cache.
- Maintain per-variant quality deltas; if demoted variant drops below quality delta threshold for >N requests, automatically escalate to human-in-the-loop review and revert demotion if necessary.

4) Graceful hosted backfill policy
- Backfill is allowed for short bursts if predicted dedicated wait time > backfill_threshold and tenant in RED/AMBER. Backfill must carry metadata (origin:dedicated-backfill, credit_balance, fallback_decision_id) for observability and billing reconciliation.
- Introduce a backfill budget per-tenant per-day to limit cost exposure from hosted spillover.

5) Preemption & recovery
- Dedicated slots are preemptible by a request to reclaim credits: reclaiming triggers a soft-fence preventing re-routing to hosted for a brief cooldown, and emits an event to the tenant alerting them to degraded capacity.
- Recovery path replenishes credits based on committed onboarding schedule and usage smoothing.

Telemetry & observability:
- Emit these metrics at request-level and aggregated: routing_decision(reason), credit_balance_gauge, time_in_tier, backfill_event_count, variant_quality_delta, failed_shadow_rate, cost_delta_per_hour.
- Dashboards: tenant-level SLO heatmap, backfill budget burn-rate, variant-regression alerts.

[Soft handoff protocol for dedicated-to-hosted tiering]
description:
Problem: When dedicated capacity becomes saturated or a node drain occurs, we need a deterministic, tenant-safe way to spill traffic to hosted while avoiding sudden latency/cost spikes and preserving tenant SLAs. Current hard-cutover approaches cause request amplifications, cache churn, and noisy telemetry which makes incident triage slow.

Goal: Implement a soft handoff protocol that gradually migrates sessions from dedicated pools to hosted backstops using probabilistic sampling, credit-based reservations, and progressive variant demotion so we achieve graceful degradation, predictable unit cost changes, and observable safety signals. This ticket covers design, config surface, implementation hooks in the routing adjudicator, and rollout plan.

Scope:
- New per-tenant soft-handoff config (thresholds, window, sample_rate, credit_budget) surfaced in the routing adjudicator.
- Integration with the capacity allocator to expose ephemeral reservation tokens that can be borrowed during a handoff window.
- Probability-based spillover: requests are diverted progressively rather than all-or-nothing.
- Model variant demotion policy that prefers cheaper quantized variants on hosted as load increases.
- Telemetry and SLOs: new metrics for handoff_rate, eviction_rate, observed_latency_delta, and cost_delta_by_tenant.
- Runbook and rollback steps for rapid remediation.

Out of scope: billing UI changes and long-term autoscaling policy tuning (handled in separate RFC).

Metrics appear in the Console (hand_off_rate, dedicated_to_hosted_count, handoff_latency_delta) and alert triggers for unexpected error spikes
Playbook verified in staging with synthetic tenant burst test and chaos node drain scenario

design_decisions:
Use credit-based ephemeral reservations instead of immediate preemption to reduce thrash when dedicated capacity flaps
Probabilistic sampling (incremental ramp) preferred to deterministic eviction to maintain tail latency stability
Model variant demotion happens on the hosted side only to avoid modifying dedicated pool behavior
Expose conservative default configs per tier (enterprise vs dev) and allow overrides at tenant-level
Make the handoff mechanism reversible within the window: if capacity recovers, routing weight decays back to dedicated with hysteresis

[Priority buckets + credit-slicing with regional spillover for tiered traffic]
description:
Design and implement a tier-aware routing layer that enforces per-tenant/plan credit buckets (free/paid/enterprise), slices burst credits, and enables controlled regional spillover and model-variant fallbacks when capacity or credits are constrained.

background:
We currently route requests by simple tier mapping with a blunt quota enforcement that returns 429s when exceeded. Customers with mixed plans (free -> paid) experience poor UX during regional outages and burst usage. Product requests a softer degradation path that preserves enterprise SLAs while offering best-effort processing for paid and free users with graceful fallbacks to cheaper model variants or alternate regions.

proposal:
Introduce three coordinated mechanisms: (1) priority buckets per tenant plan (enterprise > paid > free) with token-credit accounting and burst reservoirs; (2) credit-slicing engine that lets paid tiers borrow soft credits from short-lived burst pool based on historical cadence and fairness; (3) regional spillover policy and a model-variant degradation ladder (full-pro, quantized-pro, small-proxy) that routing can select automatically when local capacity or credits are low.

design_decisions:
- Use per-tenant credit ledger stored in Redis with atomic Lua ops for debit/peek to avoid race conditions.
- Implement soft-decrement semantics: when soft credits exhausted, route to lower-cost variant; when hard credits exhausted, return 429 for free tier but enqueue low-priority paid requests to a deferred queue instead of immediate failure.
- Regional spillover is enabled only for paid+enterprise tiers and gated by geographic latency thresholds (max added tail 80th <= 150ms).
- Model-variant compatibility matrix declared in catalog metadata; runtime performs compatibility check before automatic fallback.
- Metrics emitted include credit_balance, credit_burn_rate, fallback_rate_by_tier, regional_spill_count, avg_added_latency_by_spill.

tradeoffs:
- Pros: better customer experience, fewer hard failures, controllable cost.
- Cons: additional operational complexity and state (credit ledger), potential for unexpected cross-region egress cost, subtle fairness issues if burst pools are abused.
- Mitigations: rate-limited borrow, per-tenant daily borrow budget, autoscaling cost alerting and budget caps for spillover.

acceptance_criteria:
- Credit ledger updates are atomic and pass concurrency fuzz tests.
- For synthetic load tests, free tier sees graceful 429 behavior after soft fallback attempts.
- Paid tier can borrow from burst pool under controlled conditions; borrow rate adheres to configured per-tenant caps.
- Regional spillover triggers under simulated region-constrained tests and falls back to alternate region with <200ms added tail latency to enterprise traffic.
- Telemetry surfaces fallback reasons and per-tier SLA adherence.
- End-to-end integration test in staging with realistic workload passes without data loss.

1) Feature flag behind routing.priority_buckets and routing.spillover, off by default.
2) Canary: enable for 2 internal tenants with low traffic and telemetry only.
3) Beta: enable for a subset of paid customers with monitoring and on-call runbook.
4) Gradual: expand to all paid then enterprise tenants after 2 weeks stability.
5) GA: enable for free tier with conservative defaults.

[Token reservoir & latency-hysteresis routing playbook for dedicated→hosted overflow]
description:
Problem: During regional traffic spikes we often see oscillation between Dedicated capacity (tenant-owned GPU pools) and Hosted backfill when short bursts exceed committed throughput. Existing guardrails either (a) immediately spill to hosted which raises cost and potential QoS differences, or (b) hard-reserve tokens which underutilizes Dedicated.

This ticket proposes a playbook and implementation sketch for a token-reservoir based routing policy combined with latency-hysteresis to: (1) allow short, predictable bursts on Dedicated without immediate spill to Hosted, (2) prevent oscillatory thrashing between Dedicated and Hosted, and (3) provide clear telemetry/headers for downstream services to make cost/quality tradeoffs.

Core idea: allocate a replenishing per-tenant "token reservoir" on Dedicated. Each request consumes tokens proportional to expected cost (tokens ~= estimated compute/time/window). When reservoir is depleted, requests are routed to Hosted. A latency-hysteresis controller monitors p50/p95 latency and prevents reservoirs from being refilled aggressively if Dedicated latency degrades, thereby implementing graceful demotion. The system emits explicit signals (X-Reservoir-State, X-Reservoir-TTL, routing_decision_reason) so Console and SDKs can expose why a request hit Hosted.

acceptance_criteria:
Define token accounting schema (token cost per model variant + multiplier for sequence length) documented in Confluence
Prototype router implements per-tenant reservoir with replenish-rate and max-capacity configs
Latency-hysteresis controller observes p50/p95 and enforces refill backoff when p95 > configured SLO margin
System emits routing signals in headers and telemetry; Console shows per-tenant reservoir burn and refill rates
End-to-end tests: synthetic burst traffic causes short drain+refill without immediate spill, and sustained overload drains reservoir and falls back to Hosted
Runbook updated with playbook for manual interventions and rollback steps

design_notes:
Token accounting: base tokens = model_cost_table[model_variant] * (seq_len / 512). Reservoir config: {capacity_tokens, replenish_tokens_per_sec, min_reservoir_fraction}. Refill backoff: linear decay with exponential factor if p95 remains above SLO for >30s.

Routing decision order (fast path): 1) Check soft reservations for tenant (hard reservations still respected) 2) If reservoir.tokens >= request.token_cost -> route to Dedicated and decrement 3) Else consult fallback policy: use Hosted if allowed by tenant tier OR try queued short-delay (50-200ms) to wait for replenish 4) Emit routing_decision_reason: [DEDICATED_OK | DEDICATED_DEPLETED | HYSTERESIS_BLOCK | QUEUED_RETRY]

implementation_tasks:
Add reservoir metadata to tenant config and admin API (console + infra) (ENG backend + config-schema)
Implement in edge router: in-memory token cache + consistent hashing for reservoir ownership
Integrate latency-hysteresis controller tied to existing SLO metrics (p50/p95) in metrics pipeline
Add SDK/REST header propagation (X-Reservoir-State, X-Reservoir-Remaining, routing_decision_reason)
Telemetry: new Grafana panels and Console widgets for reservoir burn, refill_rate, triggered_hysteresis_events
E2E tests: load generator scenarios (burst 10x for 30s, sustained 3x) and validate routing outcomes
Create a canary rollout plan: start with low-risk tenants (internal staging customers)

tradeoffs_and_decisions:
Tradeoffs: a reservoir increases Dedicated utilization and behavioral predictability at the cost of implementation complexity and slightly delayed fallback when necessary. To reduce cost risk, reservoirs will be smaller for non-enterprise tiers and will include tenant-configurable caps.

Quality vs cost: some requests will run on Hosted during sustained overload which may have different quantization/latency. We will surface explicit reasons and token costs so product teams can choose model variants or degrade gracefully.

Decision: Prefer soft reservoirs + hysteresis over aggressive immediate spill to Hosted to avoid stateful thrash and to preserve SLOs for non-burst traffic. If p95 latency degrades >15% vs baseline for >30s, we enter HYSTERESIS mode which prevents refills until stable for 2x the degradation window.

runbook_notes:
If Dedicated latency p95 crosses Service SLO and hysteresis engaged, Console shows 'Reservoir: HYSTERESIS' and auto-routes to Hosted after queued retries fail
Manual override: admin API to force-drain or freeze reservoirs for tenant (useful during incidents)
Rollback: disable reservoir feature flag and revert router config; flush in-memory counters and restart shards
Incident indicators: reservoir_burn_rate >> replenish_rate for >2 minutes; rising queued_retries and increased hosted_fallback_rate

examples:
Scenario A (short burst): tenant with capacity_capacity=100rps and reservoir_capacity_tokens=50k receives 200rps for 20s. Router consumes reservoir tokens and maintains Dedicated routing with small latency impact; reservoir refills over next 5 minutes.
Scenario B (sustained overload): same tenant receives 200rps for 10min. Reservoir depletes in ~1min; hysteresis observes p95 > SLO at 80s and blocks refills; remaining requests route to Hosted until baseline returns. Post-incident, replenish backoff prevents immediate thrash.

risks_and_mitigations:
Risk: Token misaccounting due to clock skew -> Mitigation: short-lease decrement + periodic reconciliation and counters persisted to RocksDB for shard restarts
Risk: Complexity increases debugging surface -> Mitigation: Clear headers + Console displays + linkable trace IDs for reservoir events
Risk: Cost leak if reservoirs too permissive -> Mitigation: per-tenant caps, tier-based defaults, and monthly cost alerts

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-14 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Priya Patel (Redwood AE), Evan Chen (Redwood SE), Marta Ruiz (Redwood Infra), Samir Gupta (Monarch Analytics), Tess Huang (Monarch ML Eng), Diego Alvarez (Monarch SRE), Anya K. (Monarch DS)
Links referenced: https://redwood.app/quant-guide (shared), s3://monarch-qa/quant_runs/latest.zip, https://redwood.app/bench-script

[00:00:00] Priya: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. quick intro, i'm priya, AE on the account, and evan from the SE team is gonna lead the tech part. do you want to quick run through the symptom?

[00:00:15] Samir: yeah thanks, priya. real quick context — we converted our 13B summarization model using a mix of g p t q and int8, and after deployment onprem we've started seeing a subtle drop in ROUGE and some hallucination on long-context prompts. it's small but visible on our regression tests.

[00:00:33] Evan: okay, thanks. when you say mix — can you share the exact conversion path? g p t q for most layers and int8 for attention?

[00:00:40] Tess: we used GPTQ on FFN and AWQ on attention for speed. config is in the s3 link — we did per-channel int8 on a couple of early layers.

[00:00:52] Evan: got it. one immediate question: are you keeping the KV cache in fp16, or did you quantize it too?

[00:00:58] Samir: we kept the kv in fp16, should be fp16. but the runtime here is an onprem triton-ish stack with a custom kernel set; i'm not 100% sure about the memcpy paths.

[00:01:12] Diego: yeah on the nodes we saw some memcpy spikes when prefix length is > 1024. p95 latency jumps. could be prefetching behavior.

[00:01:25] Evan: ok that suggests two vectors: one is model numeric sensitivity from the quantization, second is runtime I/O and batching interaction. both can make behaviors look like an accuracy regression.

[00:01:39] Anya: our failing tests are mostly long-document summarization and some QA pairs with reasoning chains — seems like attention patterns break.

[00:01:47] Evan: attention is notoriously sensitive. AWQ does great perf but can change outlier behavior for attention weights. GPTQ on FFN usually safe, but mixing can expose cross-layer dynamics.

[00:02:01] Priya: maybe let's list quick hypotheses so we can triage.

[00:02:06] Tess: hypothesis A: AWQ affected attention heads in middle layers causing mis-aligned attention and thus downstream hallucination.

[00:02:15] Samir: B: runtime kernel differences — our triton build might use a slightly different fused attention kernel that behaves differently with int8 paths.

[00:02:23] Marta: C: batching and KV cache eviction timings — with our batching strategy and prefix caching we are seeing KV reorder or stale cache reads on heavy concurrent workloads.

[00:02:36] Evan: good list. for A, we can run a per-layer sensitivity test — quantize one block at a time and measure delta on your eval set. we have a notebook that automates this.

[00:02:48] Priya: i'll share that notebook and an example AWQ config after the call.

[00:02:54] [00:03:00] Samir: when you say per-layer, do you mean freeze everything in fp16 and only quant the target block? that's what you suggest?

[00:03:08] Evan: exactly. blockwise bisect: quantize block index i and keep rest fp16. run evaluation, collect metrics. that isolates which layers drive regressions.

[00:03:20] Tess: is there a recommended default for attention versus ffn? like int8 for ffn, awq for attention? we've seen both recommended.

[00:03:29] Evan: common pattern: FFN -> GPTQ (int8/gptq) tends to preserve quality; attention -> AWQ or mixed 4/8 sometimes better. but it depends — heads with large outliers may need per-channel scaling. AWQ can be tuned with per-head outlier thresholds.

[00:03:45] Diego: any runtime knobs we should be aware of? batch sizes and kv cache op ordering?

[00:03:52] Marta: on our infra, we have continuous batching that coalesces requests, and KV cache writes happen post-token. if a request's prefix shares keys, memcopy contention shows up. maybe we've got a lock contention.

[00:04:05] Evan: yes, and that can manifest as latency increases which triggers client timeouts and partial responses — clients retry and that looks like a functional regression. so must separate pure numeric errors from timing-induced errors.

[00:04:18] Anya: we did isolate a couple examples where the model actually produced a wrong fact, not just timeout errors — those are the concerning ones.

[00:04:26] Evan: ok for that we'll focus on numeric bisect. please run the per-layer test and attach a sample of inputs that reproduce the wrong fact. we'll run it with reference fp16 and with your mixed quant.

[00:04:38] Priya: there's also the possibility that calibration data used during quantization didn't match your production distribution — that causes off-by-some errors in activations. what cal dataset did you use?

[00:04:47] Tess: we used a mix of internal docs and public web scraped news, ~10k tokens.

[00:04:52] Evan: 10k might be okay but needs to match token length distribution. AWQ and GPTQ are both sensitive to long-tail sequences; include longer contexts in calibration.

[00:04:59] Samir: good point. we will include longer docs and re-run cal.

[00:05:05] [00:05:30] Evan: another diagnostic: run a layer norm output comparison in L2 error between fp16 and quantized variants. often a single outlier layer shows 10x higher delta.

[00:05:42] Tess: how do we capture kv cache interaction? is there a way to dump the kv under different quant states?

[00:05:48] Evan: yes, dump the keys/values for a few tokens in fp16 vs quant-run and diff them. if the kv values diverge early, it's a numeric issue; if they match and downstream diverges later, could be runtime or accumulation error.

[00:06:02] Diego: on our side, i can enable extra tracing for memcopy and lock times on the nodes. we'll capture traces during the bench runs.

[00:06:09] Marta: note: our triton build is custom; we had to patch a kernel for low-latency attention. could be regression there. we'll include git sha.

[00:06:18] Priya: perfect, add that to the action items.

[00:06:22] [00:06:40] Samir: one more thing — p99 latency went up only during peak, p50 stable. that suggests batching effects.

[00:06:48] Evan: right. Batching improves throughput but increases tail latency when combined with variable prefix lengths. We recommend adaptive batching window heuristics where short prefixes get micro-batched and long prefixes go on a low-latency path. Redwood runtime supports per-route batching policies.

[00:07:02] Priya: we can propose a temporary mitigation: serve long-context traffic to a fp16-only model pool while we triage quantization. that reduces risk to production.

[00:07:11] Tess: can we do a hybrid pool? like mix per-route pins? we'd like to avoid a full rollback.

[00:07:17] Priya: yes, you can route long-doc traffic to a dedicated pool (fp16) and short responses to quantized pool. it's a routing rule in console. i can send config.

[00:07:26] Evan: also runtime fallback: for requests that exceed an accuracy threshold we can fall back to fp16 at inference time for specific prompt templates (if flagged). that's more heavy-handed but available.

[00:07:36] Anya: about AWQ config — what specific knobs should we tune?

[00:07:41] Evan: key ones: per-head outlier clipping, group size for quantization, and per-channel scaling. AWQ also supports block-wise mixed bits, e.g., 4-bit for non-critical channels and 8-bit for high-sensitivity channels. experiment with larger group sizes first.

[00:07:56] Tess: can GPTQ and AWQ be combined deterministically? our pipeline ran GPTQ for FFN then an AWQ pass for attention. maybe ordering matters.

[00:08:04] Evan: ordering can matter because GPTQ changes the distribution the AWQ pass sees. typical approach: calibrate on fp16 distribution, run GPTQ on FFN blocks, then run AWQ on attention with a fresh calibration pass. also try an interleaved approach if needed.

[00:08:17] [00:08:40] Priya: let's talk about metrics to collect in the bench runs so we can correlate numeric vs infra issues.

[00:08:45] Evan: collect per-layer L2/Linf deltas, per-head attention cosine similarity, token-level perplexity delta, p50/p95/p99 latency with prefix lengths buckets (0-128,129-512,512-2048), KV cache hit/miss stats, memory copy times, and GPU occupancy.

[00:09:05] Diego: i'll add memcopy and lock contention traces. we'll also capture kernel launch times and cuda stream stalls.

[00:09:12] Tess: do you have a script for running these with our onprem runtime?

[00:09:16] Evan: yes, the bench script link we shared — redwood.app/bench-script — has templates for onprem triton stacks. we will fork one for your env and send the command lines.

[00:09:27] Priya: do you want us to spin up a dedicated pool so we don't interfere with prod?

[00:09:31] Samir: yes please, we prefer a dedicated capacity node. we'll schedule a maintenance window for the heavy runs.

[00:09:37] Evan: ok, for ded pooling you'll need to share vpn creds and we'll help configure. Priya will send the infra checklist.

[00:09:44] [00:10:00] Anya: small note — some of the regression examples are reproducible locally with a single prompt. we'll include those in the issue.

[00:10:07] Evan: perfect, that speeds bisecting.

[00:10:12] Tess: on the point of calibration, we should probably try both offline calibrate and online dynamic calibrate runs and compare. any runtime cost for online calibrate?

[00:10:21] Evan: online calibration increases startup time but can adapt to distribution shift. for inference-heavy production it's safer to do offline calibrate with a representative long-tail dataset. but try both for triage.

[00:10:34] [00:10:50] Samir: Curious: any known bugs with AWQ when used with certain fused-attention kernels?

[00:10:55] Marta: briefly — we had a bug in a patched kernel where quantized matmul used an incorrect reorder on 8-bit lanes; that was fixed earlier this year but if you have a custom build it may differ.

[00:11:08] Evan: that's why we asked for kernel SHA. some micro differences cause divergence at long contexts.

[00:11:14] Priya: quick administrative: we'll preserve the meeting recording and the call notes in the deal thread. next meeting in 7 days? does that work?

[00:11:21] Samir: yes next week works.

[00:11:25] [00:11:40] -- fast forward, deeper technical discussion --

[00:11:40] Evan: diving into specifics: for your model the biggest p99 regressors were layers 8-10 and 22-24 per initial diff. that pattern suggests mid-range attention heads. try quantizing only FFN then only attention in separate runs.

[00:12:00] Anya: the delta table you mentioned earlier — what threshold should we consider alarming?

[00:12:06] Evan: heuristic: if layer-wise L2 grows > 3x from baseline or attention cosine < 0.95 for a head, mark as high sensitivity. use those to target per-layer 8-bit fallback.

[00:12:19] Tess: per-layer fallback at runtime — can we configure that in redwood?

[00:12:23] Evan: yes, model config supports overrides per-layer to enforce fp16 for specific blocks during runtime. that requires a model variant but can be automated via rollout.

[00:12:33] Samir: does that add latency overhead?

[00:12:35] Evan: small overhead on model size and cold start but during steady-state tokens it's per-op cost; overall it's preferable to full rollback.

[00:12:42] Diego: regarding batching: we observed p99 spikes correlate with high variance in prefix length. maybe we should segregate request classes by prefix length.

[00:12:50] Evan: yes, segment by prefix length buckets and set max batch windows per bucket. short prefixes get aggressive batching, long prefixes get lower batching and prefetch for KV.

[00:12:59] Marta: also note our CUDA version is 12.1 and we had some deprecation warnings on a fused kernel; might want to check with the kernel vendor.

[00:13:07] Evan: we will map kernel shas to supported CUDA builds. add that to the action list.

[00:13:14] [00:13:30] Tess: question on eval: should we run with sampling temperature 0 or full sampling to capture hallucinations?

[00:13:36] Anya: we run both — deterministic and stochastic. hallucination shows up in both but more frequent with sampling. include both in the bench.

[00:13:44] Evan: good. also capture token-level confidence and logprob shifts. quantization often nudges logits subtly which can make beam searches prefer different tokens.

[00:13:55] Priya: i'll follow up with recommended metric list and the redwood config snippet for routing.

[00:14:02] [00:14:30] -- mid-call side discussion about regression example --

[00:14:30] Samir: here's an example from our failing tests — prompt id 9832 — fp16 output includes the correct company name, quantized run replaces it with a similar name.

[00:14:40] Evan: thanks, we will reproduce. can you also attach the token-level logits for both runs?

[00:14:46] Samir: yes will attach.

[00:14:52] Tess: are there any quick toggles that can reduce risk without a full bisect?

[00:14:57] Evan: quick toggles: increase group size in AWQ, use per-channel scaling on attention, disable quantization for top-k most sensitive heads (we can identify them via the sensitivity notebook).

[00:15:08] Priya: also consider a staged rollout: 5% traffic to quant pool, monitor regression metrics, then scale if safe.

[00:15:17] Diego: question about KV: you recommended keeping KV in fp16 — any reason to try int8 for kv to save memory?

[00:15:24] Evan: kv in int8 can reduce memory but introduces accumulation error over long contexts; we generally avoid quantizing the KV cache for long-context summarization workloads. short chat workloads sometimes can tolerate it.

[00:15:36] Anya: what about fp8 — is that worth trying?

[00:15:39] Evan: fp8 is promising on newer HW — much less quantization noise compared to 4-bit int and good memory saving. but runtime kernel support is still spotty on custom triton builds. if you have HW that supports FP8 (A10X/A100 gen variants), test it, but prioritize INT8/GPTQ/AWQ first because they are more mature in our toolchain.

[00:15:57] [00:16:20] Marta: summarize: we'll collect kernels/sha, cuda versions, triton build, run per-layer bisect, and run bench script with memcopy traces. correct?

[00:16:27] Priya: yes, and redwood will help analyze the per-layer deltas and propose a per-layer fallback config if needed.

[00:16:35] [00:16:50] -- later, walkthrough of proposed bisect notebook --

[00:16:50] Evan: the notebook automates: 1) create N variants each quantizing a single block 2) run eval set 3) compute layerwise metrics 4) output top-k sensitive layers. we'll add a step to capture attention head cosines.

[00:17:05] Tess: will that run on our onprem nodes or do you want to run on a redwood dedicated instance?

[00:17:11] Priya: we prefer you run it on your environment for fidelity; redwood can also run the same notebook in our dedicated pool for a parity check.

[00:17:19] Samir: we'll do both and compare results.

[00:17:24] [00:17:40] -- wrap up: decisions and mitigations --

[00:17:40] Evan: recap of technical plan: 1) per-layer bisect and sensitivity table, 2) calibration dataset expansion to include long-form contexts, 3) run bench script with kernel and memcopy traces, 4) try per-layer fp16 fallback for top sensitive layers, 5) route long-context traffic to fp16 pool during triage.

[00:17:58] Priya: next steps: we'll share the AWQ/GPTQ best-practices doc and the config snippets.

[00:18:04] Tess: ok. thanks — can we get a concrete deadline on the first artifact?

[00:18:09] Evan: i'll upload the per-layer diff script and an example output by friday (2025-10-17).

[00:18:16] Samir: we'll start the bench runs Monday and post results by the 20th.

[00:18:22] Priya: great. anything else from the team?

[00:18:26] Diego: no, we'll get the traces.

[00:18:30] Anya: no other asks.

[00:18:33] Priya: all right thanks everyone — we'll reconvene next week.

[00:18:38] [00:54:00] End of recording

We also added a manual override for product owners.
[00:04:49] [00:04:49] Diego: we need to ensure the trace IDs and KV correlation keys are visible to SREs in the first five minutes — make debugging faster.

[01:47] Dana: timeline please, we need the full log set + cause attribution.

[02:05] Sofia: to dig into the root cause — the sequence was: a traffic pattern change yielded many longer sequences in a short timespan, batching window and merge algorithm created oversized batches, memory accounting in the batching queue didn't trigger early shedding, so transient memory pressure grew. because of prefix cache misses — K V cache misses — the runtime had to recompute more keys and allocate more memory, amplifying the issue.
[02:30] Liam: and to clarify, the autoscaler thresholds were tuned for CPU and throughput, not this particular mem spike. the HPA didn't react fast enough because memory metrics are sampled at a lower cadence, so the scale out lagged.

[02:55] Dana: correct. and importantly, our app retries were exponential and that increased load as well.
[03:05] Sofia: yep retry storms are classic — we need better client-side guidance and maybe a token bucket server-side limit for burst protection.

[04:44] Liam: that's alarming — we should get those alert changes ASAP.

[05:00] Sofia: for mitigations, we pushed: 1) batching memory accounting patch; 2) reduced max_batch_size from 64 to 32 temporarily; 3) temporary tenant rate-limits and token-bucket enforcement; 4) tuning autoscaler to sample memory every 15s instead of 60s and scale faster.

[08:20] Tom: if we accept the mitigation plan, what's the timeline to be back to pre-incident risk levels?
[08:26] Sofia: short term (week): deploy permanent memory accounting patch across clusters, adjust autoscaler cadence, create runbook. medium term (4-8 weeks): circuit breaker + token-bucket + dashboard pack and chaos test. long term (3 months): expanded canary testing, refine model routing checks, automated failover.

[08:45] Dana: okay that sounds reasonable. please also document the customer-facing change log so our product teams can align.
[08:52] Rajiv: we'll publish a changelog and a timeline for expected rollouts.

[09:00] Ethan: i want to call out an operational note — we found a race inside the batching code where the accounting counter could briefly undercount during concurrent merges; fix is in the patch. it's subtle and not immediately obvious in the raw logs.

summary:

transcript_body:
Meeting header:

Duration: ~57 minutes

[01:12] Maya Chen: Understood. Two high-level directions: short-term cost wins (batching, prefix/KV cache, shorter-seq models or quantization) and medium-term capacity (dedicated or reserved pools). Liam, can you walk tuning options we can implement quickly?
[01:28] Liam O'Neill: Yep. For immediate wins: enable continuous batching on the product desc job — it's high QPS and tolerant to a few hundred ms. Use prefix caching for repeated templates, that saves tokens and compute. Also recommend using a 8-bit quantized variant for background generation jobs; that'll reduce GPU time by 30–40% in our tests. Note: quantization might slightly change outputs — need evals.
[01:54] Carlos Medina: Quick question: how bad will quality drift be with 8-bit for our few-shot templates? We have strict merchandising phrasing.

We'll supply a config snippet. Small caveat: if you fallback to a smaller model, outputs may differ — we'll include guardrails.
[04:30] Asha Patel: Sounds good. For security/compliance: we need an audit trail for any changes and confirmation that dedicated pool can be tied to our KMS. Also retention for logs for 90 days.
[04:41] Maya Chen: Redwood supports KMS integrations and audit logs. We'll attach SOC2 docs and a short how-to on linking KMS for your private cluster.

[05:20] Carlos Medina: On the verification plan: we can provide 3 canonical prompts from our recommendation pipeline and the checkout prompt to run microbenchmarks. We'll want p50/p95/p99 and token counts.

[Org-level promo credit reallocated across subaccounts after hybrid (dedicated+hosted) reconciliation]
description:
Issue summary:
Customer BrightPath Health reports their monthly invoice shows a net increase despite an org-level promotional credit being listed on the account. The promotional credit appears on the parent org invoice but the subsequent allocation pass during reconciliation split the credit across subaccounts incorrectly, producing higher net charges for the paying entity.

Impact:
- Customer-facing: finance at BrightPath cannot reconcile month-end ledger; they report a perceived overcharge of $12,450 on invoice INV-2026-03-08-BP.
- Functional: billing export for the account shows a negative line item at the parent level and positive reallocation entries to 7 child subaccounts.

Environment:
- Prod (us-east primary) with dedicated capacity (dedicated-gpu-pool-bp) and hosted API overflow for batch embeddings.
- Billing reconciliation job: billing-reconcile-2026-03-01-run-45

Steps to reproduce (recommended triage):
1) Pull raw metering logs for org_id=org_7842 for 2026-03-01 to 2026-03-07.
2) Run billing-reconcile job locally with --dry-run and compare allocation table outputs to production run-45.
3) Inspect allocation records where allocation_owner_id is null or differs from parent_owner_id.
4) Cross-check invoice lines for INV-2026-03-08-BP in the invoice ledger export.

Observed behavior:
- Org-level promo credit is present in the parent invoice but allocation items show the credit split and applied as positive charges against child subaccounts.

Expected behavior:
- Promo credit applied at org-level should reduce amount owed by the invoice owner (paying_account) and only be redistributed if customer explicitly configured allocation rules.

Additional context provided by customer:
- They added a usage-based promo in February (promo code: BRIGHT-Q1-2026) scoped to org_7842.
- They use reserved Dedicated capacity for production traffic and hosted endpoints for ad-hoc embedding batches.

Attachments from customer: invoice PDF (INV-2026-03-08-BP.pdf) and billing-export CSV (billing_export_2026-03-08.csv).

investigation_notes:
Hypothesis: allocation service failed to propagate owner_id for hosted-overflow events when the reconcile pipeline merged streaming and batch inputs; when allocation pass ran it treated credit as distributable, creating reallocation lines instead of applying to paying_account.
Evidence: produced a short list (20 events) where allocation_key == null and resource_tag 'via_hosted-overflow' present. Trace log shows event merger step 'merge_stream_batch' returned owner_id empty for events processed between 03:02:11 - 03:06:40 UTC.

Hotfix deployed to prod-us-east 2026-03-13 18:30 UTC. A backfill job has been scheduled to re-run billing-reconcile for run-45 producing corrected allocation rows; finance will re-issue the amended invoice INV-2026-03-08-BP-amended after backfill completes. Customer confirmed provisional credit acceptance and will verify once amended invoice is available. Post-deploy smoke tests for repro case passed. Follow-up: monitor next three reconciliation runs for owner_id propagation and add a check in CI to detect empty owner_id in merged input streams.

[Ambiguous microbatch rate applied to multi-model microbatch job causing invoice overcharge]
description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports what appears to be an overcharge on invoice INV-2026-03-09-4842 for a scheduled microbatch job that routed mixed-model requests in a single job. Customer believes the billing engine applied a single (higher) per-token rate to the entire microbatch instead of computing a weighted cost across model variants, leading to an overcharge of approximately $1,250.

Impact:
- Invoice INV-2026-03-09-4842 shows a single line for 'microbatch-processing' for job_id cb-job-19f8 with 10,234,000 tokens billed at $0.00012/token.
- Customer claims the job included 6.7M tokens for redwood-13b-v2 (rate $0.00006/token) and 3.534M tokens for open-llama-7b-q4 (rate $0.00012/token). If billed correctly, expected charge is $6.7M * 0.00006 + 3.534M * 0.00012 = $402 + $424 = $826 (approx), but invoice shows $1,228 (approx), delta ~$402.

Request:
- Immediate provisional credit to cover the delta while we investigate.
- Adjustment to final invoice if bug confirmed.

Customer contact: alice.chen@cognifylabs.ai (CC: finance@cognifylabs.ai)

steps_to_reproduce:
Customer runs scheduled microbatch job (cb-job-19f8) that contains mixed requests routed to two models in one job window.
Serving runtime batches requests across models when possible for throughput optimization.
Metering postback aggregates batch-level token counts and looks up per-model rates to produce invoice lines.
Observed behavior: postback created a single invoice line using a single per-token rate of $0.00012 for the entire aggregate instead of splitting by model or computing weighted average.

impact:
Customer-facing invoice discrepancy (charged ~49% more than expected for the microbatch job). Potential financial impact for Cognify Labs and reputational risk for Redwood. Customer requests provisional credit and corrective invoice adjustments.

[Customer reports unexpected billing delta after API key tag rename affecting usage attribution]
description:
Issue summary: Customer reports a ~27% negative billing delta on their Feb 28 provisional invoice after renaming API key tags across multiple service accounts. The charges were attributed to a legacy org ID instead of their primary org, causing a provisional overcharge and missing reserve/burst credits on the final invoice.

Impact: LexaHealth is seeing an unexpected invoice variance (~$4,300) and missing application of scheduled reserved-burst credits for several 3-hour windows during Feb 25-27. This affects reconciliation for month-end close and blocks autopay. Customer is on an enterprise contract and requires an itemized explanation and corrective credit.

Environment: Production (us-east). Affected model traffic: mixture of hosted chat (redwood/gptx-8k) and batch embeddings (open/embedding-128). Activity timeframe: 2026-02-25 03:00 - 2026-02-27 12:00 UTC.

Steps to reproduce / observed sequence:
1) Customer renamed API key tags via Console API on 2026-02-24 at ~22:10 UTC (bulk tag rename from "production-team" to "lexa-prod").
2) We observed postback delivery succeeding but a subset of postbacks contained the old tag metadata in the payload (postback.source.tag = "production-team").
3) Billing attribution pipeline mapped tag to org/ledger and routed usage to legacy org ID 10124 instead of customer org 90211 for the outlier postbacks.
4) Invoice generation aggregated those lines under legacy org, leading to missing credits and an apparent overage on the customer's provisional invoice.

Expected behavior: Tag rename should atomically update the metadata mapping used by the postback pipeline; postbacks after rename should be attributed to customer org 90211 with reserved/burst credits applied.

Actual behavior: 8.3k postbacks (~2.6M tokens) were misattributed. Some postbacks were tagged correctly; others retained the old tag because of a race in the key metadata cache during the rename rollout.

Logs/attachments: Customer provided provisional invoice and screenshots; attached server-side postback logs and sample hashed request_ids.

Customer request: Detailed explanation of what caused the misattribution, an itemized reconciliation, and immediate provisional credit while engineering completes root-cause and rebackfill.
