[Proactive Headroom Controller with Fallback Throttles and Per-Model Guarantees]
description:
Problem: Customers on Dedicated expect both per-tenant throughput guarantees and stable latency. Our current autoscaler reacts too slowly to short spikes and is too aggressive during oscillatory workloads, resulting in missed SLAs or large cost swings.

Proposal summary: Implement a two-layer autoscaling policy engine that combines: (1) a predictive headroom allocator that forecasts short-term demand per tenant and per model (60s horizon) and allocates conservative headroom credits, and (2) a reactive fallback throttler that enforces safety limits and graceful degradation when capacity or routing fails. The system will surface per-model guarantees (tokens/sec or requests/sec) and support configurable burst credits, slew-rate limits, and discrete scale steps.

Key features: predictive EWMA+seasonality forecasting, model-aware KV-cache penalties, discrete ramp steps (10% increments), per-tenant minimum floor to preserve baseline SLA, emergency throttles with staged response (reject -> queue -> degrade model variant), and a rollback-safe canary rollout mechanism. Emphasis on observability (token-level accounting, P50/P90/P99 latency, cost delta) and operator controls (pause autoscale, force headroom, manual override).

acceptance_criteria:
Predictive allocator produces headroom recommendations every 10s with <=5% repro error in synthetic load tests
Autoscaler can enact discrete scale steps and honour per-tenant floor/ceiling in integration test clusters
Fallback throttler triggers within 5s when node count falls below threshold and transitions through staged responses without data loss
End-to-end e2e test shows P99 latency under guaranteed load within 10% of baseline while cost delta <= +8% in steady-state
Monitoring dashboards created and alerting configured for: missed guarantees, oscillation detection, rollback events, and cost anomalies

tasks:
Design doc and API: finalize Confluence design and public autoscale policy schema
Implement forecasting service: lightweight EWMA+seasonal component with per-model tuning
Implement allocator: converts forecasts to headroom credits and recommends scale deltas
Implement reactive throttler: staged degrade paths and emergency quota enforcement
Integrate with existing scaler control loops and deployment orchestration
Add instrumentation: token accounting, burst-credit ledger, and model-variant routing traces
Create e2e test harness and synthetic workload profiles
Canary rollout: 5% -> 25% -> 100% with automated rollback gates

[Introduce "safelock" fast-path gating + precision toggle and KV-eviction safety for runtime]
body:
Context and motivation:\nThis PR addresses a recurring class of incidents where aggressive fast-path kernel selection and lower-precision execution (fp16 / int8) produced rare but hard-to-detect correctness deviations for edge prompts. At the same time, customers expect throughput and lower cost. We need a runtime mechanism that lets us enable high-performance paths without risking silent correctness regressions in production.\n\nWhat this PR does (summary):\n- Adds a 'safelock' gating layer in the kernel selection path. The safelock prevents switching to a fast path unless a set of runtime validators pass (numerical consistency, kv-cache integrity checks, and recent success window).\n- Introduces a precision toggle API (per-model, per-deployment) with three modes: strict (fp32 only), balanced (fp16 with strict validators), aggressive (fp16/int8 allowed once warmed).\n- Adds a lightweight runtime validator harness: stochastic correctness probes run as background requests against canary inputs to compute divergence metrics (token-level mismatch rate, logit-delta distribution). Validators are cheap and attach metadata to requests that triggered path selection failures.\n- Changes KV cache eviction policy to be conservative when cache-warmness is below threshold; combined with safelock it avoids invalidating cached KV frames that fast kernels rely on.\n- Integrates safelock signals with the continuous-batching scheduler: until a deployment's validators reach a success threshold, scheduler prefers conservative batching and disables cross-model micro-batching that can expose interleaving bugs.\n- Adds observability hooks: metrics (safelock.blocked_count, validator.mismatch_rate, precision.switch_count, kv.eviction_suppressed) and a dashboard stub.\n- Adds a feature flag runtime.enable_safelock (default true for new deploys) and model config fields precision_mode and validator_policy.\n\nDesign notes and rationale:\n- The safelock is intentionally conservative: it is designed to minimize customer-visible regressions at the cost of initial throughput until a model warms. We prefer false negatives (staying on slow path) over false positives (silent incorrect outputs).\n- Validators are probabilistic and run only on a small fraction of traffic (configurable). We do not rely on end-user prompts alone; the system feeds a small canary corpus that includes known edge cases and adversarial tokens used in previous incidents.\n- KV-cache eviction suppression is implemented as an additional guard in the eviction worker: if cache_warmness < 0.7 and safelock.enabled, eviction respects a soft TTL and only evicts when memory pressure exceeds a higher threshold. This prevents state churn that invalidates prefix caching assumptions used by some kernels.\n\nCommits (high-level):\n- feat(runtime): add safelock kernel gating and validator harness (A. Kumar)\n- feat(config): model precision_mode and validator_policy proto + defaulting (A. Kumar)\n- fix(kv): conservative eviction path and warmness estimator (R. Patel)\n- perf(scheduler): integrate safelock signal into batching decisioning (L. O'Connor)\n- test: end-to-end validator integration tests and canary job (E. Tan)\n- docs: runtime safelock/precision-mode doc, migration notes (doc team)\n\nFiles touched (high-level):\n- runtime/kernel_selector.cpp/h (safelock implementation, gating checks)\n- runtime/precision_policy.proto (new model-level config)\n- runtime/validator/ (background probe harness, small canary corpus)\n- serving/scheduler/continuous_batcher.cpp (respect safelock signals)\n- serving/kvcache/eviction_worker.cpp (suppressed eviction path)\n- metrics/registry (new metrics added)\n- tests/e2e/validators_integration_test.cc (new suite)\n- docs/runtime/safelock.md (operator-facing guide and flags)\n\nSmall illustrative snippet included in the patch (non-executable):\n\"\"\"\nif (safelock.enabled() && !validators.passed_recently(dep)) {\n  // force fallback to conservative kernel + fp32 path\n  selectKernel = KernelSelector::conservative(model, seq_len);\n} else {\n  selectKernel = KernelSelector::fastpath(model, seq_len, precision_mode);\n}\n\"\"\"\n\nBenchmarks / numbers:\n- Baseline (main, before PR) on rtx-a100-80gb, long-tail tests: median latency 48ms, p99 180ms, throughput 2200 tok/s.\n- With safelock enabled (default config) immediately after deploy: median latency +6% (51ms), throughput -8% (2024 tok/s) while validators warm.\n- After 30m of live traffic and validator success: median latency +1% (48.5ms), throughput -2% (2160 tok/s).\n- Aggressive mode (opt-in, warm): throughput +12% over baseline; we see a measurable cost win.\n- We ran a correctness sweep against our regression corpus (n=1200 prompts) showing token-level mismatch reduced to <0.02% for balanced mode; in aggressive mode mismatch rises to ~0.6% on the corpus (expected, opt-in).\n\nTesting and CI:\n- Added unit + integration tests for validator harness and eviction behavior.\n- Added synthetic stochastic tests that simulate rare floating-point edgecases.\n- CI: initial pipeline had one flaky test (eviction_worker race) failing on Linux-asan; fixed in second commit. Final CI: all checks passed (build, unit, integration, perf-smoke).\n\nReview discussion (highlights):\n- Marco: \"I like the safelock abstraction; can we ensure the validator corpus is editable by SREs without code changes?\"\n- Aisha: \"Yes — validators read a canary file from /etc/redwood/validators/corpus.json and we added operator docs. SRE can update via configmap for k8s deploys.\"\n- Eve: \"Concerned about metric cardinality when we annotate every request with validator metadata.\"\n- Aisha: \"We emit aggregated counters and histograms; only a small sampling logs request-level debug traces behind a flag.\"\n- Liam: \"Scheduler changes look sane. Need additional canary rollout plan for enterprise customers with strict SLAs.\"\n- Aisha: \"Added rollout doc and an opt-out label on deployment config; default for existing deployments is unchanged (safe-mode learned).\"\n\nEdge cases / known tradeoffs:\n- There is an initial throughput hit until validators warm. We mitigate by sampling only a small portion of traffic for validators and allowing manual warm-up (canary traffic injection).\n- Aggressive precision_mode is opt-in; customers should enable only after verifying on internal test prompts. We include a CLI tool for running the validator corpus locally against a deployment.\n- The KV eviction suppression increases memory use under some failure modes; we documented emergency knobs and introduced an automatic disable threshold if memory pressure remains high for 10s.\n\nMigration / operator guidance:\n- New deploys: safelock enabled by default. Operators can set runtime.enable_safelock=false to revert (not recommended).\n- To opt into aggressive precision: update model config: precision_mode=aggressive and monitor validator.mismatch_rate.\n- Dashboards: added a starter Grafana dashboard (docs link) and alerts for validator.mismatch_rate > 0.1% and safelock.blocked_count being unexpectedly high.\n\nBackward compatibility:\n- All config fields default to conservative behavior; no breaking changes. Models without precision_mode set continue to use fp32 until they pass validators.\n\nPost-merge actions / follow-ups (linear):\n- ENG-4983: add automated warmup job to inject synthetic canary traffic during deploy windows (follow-up).\n- ENG-5122: add per-customer precision analytics and billing impact report.\n\nMerge outcome:\n- Final status: merged via squash. Branch merged to main after approvals from Marco, Eve, and Liam. CI green at merge.\n\nIf you want to test locally: run tools/runtime_cli --run-validators --config test/configs/precision_local.yaml against a dev deployment; run scripts/kv_warmup.sh to pre-fill the kvcache with the canary prefix set.\n\nThanks to Rohan Patel for eviction work, and the QA team for extended regression runs.\n\nPatch size: moderate; favors safety and observability over aggressive micro-optimizations up front.\n

release_notes:
Added a runtime 'safelock' gating mechanism to avoid correctness regressions when enabling fast-path kernels and lower-precision execution. New precision toggle with runtime validators. KV-cache eviction made conservative under uncertain cache-warmness. Backwards-compatible; opt-in via config.

[low-precision-path-allocator-and-kernel-hookups]
description:
Motivation: Continued work to reduce per-token cost and tail latency for low-precision inference. Prior PRs added isolated INT8/FP8 kernels and dequant fusion primitives; this change weaves those pieces into the serving runtime with a small, deterministic allocator and dispatch layer that routes requests to the best low-precision execution path based on model variant, sequence-length distribution, KV-cache state, and batching profile. The goal is pragmatic: improve throughput and p99 latency for production workloads while preserving correctness and fast fallback to FP16/FP32 when numerical risk is detected.

Summary of changes (single-shot): adds a LowPrecisionPathAllocator that makes per-request routing decisions, wires kernel dispatch tables for INT8 and FP8 fused-dequant paths, introduces lightweight per-worker hints to the continuous-batching scheduler to avoid head-of-line blocking when long sequences and small batches mix, and optimizes KV cache hot-path bookkeeping to reduce CPU overhead on cache-miss heavy workloads. Also includes microbench harness changes and canary rollout config for safe production enablement.

Why this is different: previous PRs provided kernels and fusion infra in isolation; this PR focuses on connecting those kernels into runtime scheduling and KV-cache-aware routing so that benefits are realized in end-to-end serving. It emphasizes deterministic allocation (no global locks), low-overhead decision logic, and explicit fallback rules when stability checks fail.

Behavioral details and invariants: allocator decisions are per-request at enqueue time and are stable for the request lifetime; dequant fusion is only selected when the model variant metadata marks weights as stable for fusion and dynamic range checks pass for the first token; KV cache uses an additional small per-request bitmap to avoid expensive lookups for fully warmed prefixes. Fallback to FP16 is immediate and logged when a numerical anomaly (NaN/Inf or outlier token likelihood shift exceeding a threshold) is detected.

Benchmark highlights (internal perf harness, 8xA100 p4d-like profile, mixed sequence lengths): INT8 fused-dequant path: +12% throughput, p99 latency -18% on chat-like traffic compared to baseline FP16 runtime; FP8 path: +8% throughput, p99 -10% for short-sequence-only workloads; KV cache bookkeeping optimization reduces CPU-side cache-miss accounting overhead by ~25% in high-concurrency tests. End-to-end cost projection (model-dependent) shows unit token cost reduction up to 20% in aggressive INT8 mode under production batching distributions. Full benchmark run artifacts attached to the PR.

Compatibility and safety: feature gated behind runtime flag low_precision.path_enabled and staged via canary config (release/ops/rollouts). No model format changes required. Contains extensive checks that prevent low-precision selection for models listed in a denylist or when model metadata lacks quant-stability hints.

Testing: unit tests for allocator heuristics, kernel routing, and fallback; integration tests with the continuous-batching scheduler and KV cache; regression tests exercising numerical stability thresholds. CI includes microbench regression checks on the perf lab.

How to exercise locally: run tools/perf/harness --profile=canary-int8 --model=gpt-medium --seq-distribution=chat-mix; the harness supports toggling low_precision.path_enabled. See docs/perf/low_precision_readme.md for experiment configuration and metrics artifacts.

References: related Linear ticket ENG-2145, earlier kernel PRs that added fused-dequant primitives and FP8 kernels.

Release strategy: deploy to a 5% canary for 48h with end-to-end latency/cost monitors and automatic rollback if p99 regresses beyond the configured SLO delta.

Checklist:
- [x] runtime allocator and dispatch implemented
- [x] kernel hookups and fused-dequant path enabled behind flag
- [x] KV cache bookkeeping optimization implemented
- [x] unit and integration tests added
- [x] perf harness runs and artifacts committed

Notes: this PR intentionally avoids aggressive auto-quant decisions; quant selection remains model-owner controlled until we have more confidence from cross-customer benchmarks.

review_comments:
Priya Menon: Can you add a short experiment that shows when the allocator would prefer FP16 despite INT8 availability? Reason: we need a clear example to justify operator overrides.
Luca Ortega: Added a test case that simulates a model with unstable dynamic ranges and verified the allocator chooses FP16; expanded the readme with an operator override note.
Sara Kim: The continuous-batching hint looks good; are there pathological cases where this increases tail latency? Suggest a stress test with interleaved very long sequences.
Luca Ortega: Added a stress bench in tools/perf and updated scheduler comments. Stress tests show minimal regression when long sequences are rare; if long sequences dominate, we fallback to a conservative scheduling mode.
Daniel Park: KV cache bitmap is elegant — can you confirm memory overhead per worker?
Luca Ortega: Bitmap is 64 bytes per request slot by default (configurable); added comment and a unit test asserting memory bounds.
Priya Menon: Approved after perf data added.

release_notes:
Introduces a runtime-low-precision allocator that routes requests to INT8/FP8 fused-dequant kernels when safe, reduces p99 latency and improves throughput for many production batching patterns; gated behind feature flag and staged via canary rollout. See docs/perf/low_precision_readme.md for usage.

[runtime: hybrid kernel fallback with KV-consistency gating and safe-mode thresholds]
description:
Motivation: intermittent correctness regressions and rare kernel assertion OOMs during long-sequence continuous-batching workloads were being handled by an all-or-nothing safe-mode that fell back to FP32 CPU execution. That approach eliminated correctness incidents but caused large tail latency and cost spikes. This PR implements a hybrid fallback that trades small latency regressions for correctness while keeping most requests on the fast GPU path.

What this change does (single-line summary): Adds a gate that triggers a controlled fallback to compatible kernels (FP32 or CPU) when a set of runtime signals indicate likely correctness risk: KV cache checksum mismatch, kernel assert counter > threshold, or per-request token-level divergence above configured tolerance. The gate is conservative by default and behind a feature flag `hybrid_kernel_fallback` set to off in main; rollout configuration and safe defaults are included.

Key components in the diff (high-level):
- runtime/fallback/hybrid_gate.cc/h: new gate logic that aggregates signals, applies hysteresis and cooldown windows.
- runtime/kernels/kernel_selector.cc: exposes compatibility metadata and fallback candidates per model artifact.
- runtime/kv/consistency_checker.cc: lightweight KV prefix checksum hooks and sample counters.
- scheduler/continuous_batching_manager.cc: emits per-batch KV stability stats and integrates cooldown decisions.
- observability/metrics.yaml: new metrics: fallback_rate, kv_inconsistency_count, fallback_cooldown_seconds, fallback_latency_penalty.
- integration tests: tests/runtime/hybrid_fallback_integration_test.py: e2e scenarios with long sequences and simulated kernel asserts.
- docs/operational/fallbacks.md: rollout and runbook updates.

Commits (summary):
- 1/6 Add gate primitives and API for aggregated signals
- 2/6 Implement KV checksum sampler and lightweight counter
- 3/6 Hook gate into continuous batching manager and kernel selector
- 4/6 Add metrics and dashboards for visibility
- 5/6 E2E tests and deterministic replay harness
- 6/6 Docs and feature-flagging + rollout config

Testing and CI: Unit tests for gate logic and KV sampler were added. E2E integration tests were flaky at first due to nondeterministic replaying of kernel asserts; added deterministic random seeds and a 'test-only' bypass for timing. CI pipeline initially failed 2 runs on integration tests; failures traced to timing races in the test harness and fixed in commit 5. Final CI status: pass (build + unit + integration + lint).

Perf and correctness numbers from canary (10% traffic in staging for 48h):
- Correctness incident rate: down 93% (from 15 incidents to 1)
- Overall median latency: +0.8% (insignificant)
- 95th percentile latency: +8% (due to fallback tail) — mitigations: cooldown and batching-aware fallback reduce this in subsequent rollouts
- Token-level divergence (regression tests): eliminated for sampled workloads
- Unit-cost impact: +4% at 10% traffic; expected to be neutral at scale with further tuning of thresholds

Rollout plan: feature-flag off in main. Canary -> 10% for 48h (done) -> 50% for 72h (monitor fallback_rate and fallback_latency_penalty) -> 100% if no regression. Alert thresholds added: fallback_rate > 0.5% sustained triggers on-call, fallback_latency_penalty > 15% triggers rollback.

Back-and-forth in review (high level):
- Miguel Alvarez: requested stronger telemetry (per-model fallback_rate) and a new metric for 'fallback_reason' tag. Author: added per-model tags and expanded runbook.
- Sofia Chen: flagged potential double-accounting of KV checks when multiple batches mutate same KV; requested a cooldown hysteresis change from 30s->60s. Author: implemented 60s default but left param configurable.
- Derek Wong: requested an e2e test that simulates rapid switchback scenarios; author added an additional integration test and a 'no switchback' policy toggle.

Author notes and rationale: We prefer a conservative hybrid approach that preserves correctness without wholesale safe-mode fallbacks. The gate aggregates cheap signals that are already collected or cost <1% of request time. The tuning parameters (checksum sample rate, hysteresis windows, divergence tolerance) are exposed and documented. The default behavior offline is to be conservative; operators can enable a more aggressive mode for lower cost at their own risk.

Files changed count: 12. Notable small snippets included in runtime/kernels/kernel_selector.cc to avoid breaking ABI; kernel metadata additions are backward compatible. Integration tests added are deterministic and run in CI with fixed seeds.

Merge and deploy: Approved by reviewers after two rounds of changes. Merged via squash on 2026-02-22. Feature flagged off by default; ops aware via runbook and dashboard. Follow-ups: a follow-up PR will add automatic threshold tuning based on workload profiles (ENG-5410).

[selective-fallback-policy-and-dynamic-precision-for-latency-sensitive-paths]
Summary: Implement a selective fallback policy plus a dynamic precision toggle and scheduler heuristics that route only high-risk requests to conservative kernels while keeping the fast kernels for the common case. This reduces 99th percentile latency for interactive routes without broadly sacrificing throughput or eviction correctness.

Motivation: The existing fallback-on-every-error approach is too conservative for many interactive workloads. We observed that a small fraction of sequences trigger correctness guards and force slow kernels for all concurrent work on the same worker, causing tail latency amplification. This PR introduces heuristics that: 1) identify high-risk requests at admission time, 2) apply safe-mode kernels only to those requests, and 3) allow other requests to continue on fast paths with a dynamic precision toggle that can temporarily relax precision for short-lived tokens. The goal is to balance correctness guarantees for vulnerable inputs with overall latency and throughput improvements.

Design: - admission classifier: lightweight checks based on sequence length, token-entropy hints from tokenizer, and presence of structured output constraints. Tunable thresholds are stored in configs/fallback_policy.yaml. - request tagging: requests that fail conservative checks are tagged as safe_mode=true and routed to conservative kernels. Others are allowed to take fast kernels; if a downstream kernel returns an invalidation, only that request is elevated and its KV entries are quarantined to avoid polluting shared caches. - dynamic precision toggle: the kernel_selector can change precision (fp32->fp16/quantized) for non-critical tokens for a bounded prefix window; toggles are logged and decay after N tokens. - KV cache isolation: kv_cache_manager adds lightweight per-request quarantine buckets and probabilistic re-insertion after validation. - scheduler changes: admission is integrated into the continuous batcher so that mixed batches are split gracefully rather than forcing entire batch to safe-mode.

Implementation notes: commits touch runtime and rust components: - src/runtime/scheduler.cc: split batch paths and gating hooks added. - src/runtime/kernel_selector.cc: new precision_toggle API and telemetry. - services/kv/kv_cache_manager.rs: quarantine and reinsertion logic with eviction-safe guards. - configs/fallback_policy.yaml: default thresholds and tuning knobs. - tests/perf/fallback_latency_test.py: benchmark harness that runs synthetic and real prompts. - docs/design/fallback_isolation.md: design doc describing correctness properties and rollout guidance.

[Introduce precision-aware fast-path gating and safe-mode fallbacks for runtime kernels]
Motivation and summary: We observed rare correctness regressions in production when the runtime selected aggressive high-throughput kernels (mixed-precision, fused attention variants) under tail-case sequence patterns. These regressions correlate with two factors: (1) precision toggles (bfloat16/int8 paths) where numerical drift can cross threshold checks, and (2) scheduling-induced KV cache aliases when continuous batching mixes sequences with different policy hints. This PR implements a multi-pronged runtime mitigation: (A) fast-path gating that evaluates a cheap oracle before selecting an aggressive kernel, (B) per-request precision policy toggles with fallback coherence, and (C) a global 'safe-mode' that enforces conservative kernel selection for deployments that prioritize determinism over peak throughput. The changes are designed to be conservative by default and configurable per-deployment.

What this PR changes (high-level): - fast-path gating: a lightweight verification that runs at kernel-selection time; checks include sequence-length alignment, head-dim divisibility, kv-cache layout compatibility, and a floating-point stability heuristic. Gate returns ALLOW or DENY for fast kernels. When denied, runtime picks a conservative compatibility kernel. - precision toggles: requests may specify a preferred precision (fp32, bf16, int8) in the runtime flags. When an aggressive precision is selected, we attach a precision-stamp to the request and ensure that batched operations only group compatible stamps or demote to a conservative execution path. - safe-mode: a deployment/runtime flag that forces deterministic kernels (no fused/approximated kernels), disables some heuristics that risk nondeterminism (e.g. async kernel chaining), and enables stricter KV cache verification. Intended for regulated customers or incident mitigation. - KV cache invariants: added explicit verification hooks when moving KV shards between devices or reusing cached prefixes; these checks are lightweight by default but can be promoted to strict checks in safe-mode. - scheduling changes: continuous-batching scheduler now respects precision-stamps and fast-path gate outcomes when forming batches; the scheduler will split or reorder to preserve correctness rather than blindly maximizing batch size. - tests and benchmarks: added unit tests reproducing prior regression patterns and a micro-benchmark to measure fast-path gate overhead.

Description/notes for reviewers (single-line style): This is a behavioral change to kernel selection — default experience should be unchanged unless a customer enables precision overrides or safe-mode. The fast-path gate is intentionally cheap (single-digit microseconds for common inputs) and caches decisions per model/sequence-profile. The PR contains both the gate logic and the policy integration points (runtime flags, scheduler hooks). Please focus review on correctness of the KV cache invariants, scheduler batch-paths, and the interaction between precision-stamps and continuous batching.

[BYOK tenant key lifecycle, rotation playbook, and SIEM mapping]
Purpose:
This is a working playbook for onboarding tenant BYOK (bring-your-own-key) flows, defining the tenant key lifecycle, deterministic safe rotation procedures, and the canonical SIEM/audit export schema for key events and evidence bundles. It ties together KMS/HSM import patterns, envelope encryption design for encryption-at-rest, RBAC v2 integration points, and automated evidence generation for audits.

Scope and intent:
- Applies to Redwood-hosted data stores (object, block, caches) and managed runtime that use tenant-supplied keys or Redwood-managed keys when BYOK is not opted in.
- Covers HSM import patterns (PKCS#11 / vendor import), cloud KMS wrapping, and procedures for on-prem customer HSM onboarding.
- Defines the minimum SIEM audit schema for key lifecycle and encryption operations required to satisfy SOC2 / ISO27001 evidence requests.

Glossary (short):
- KEK: Key Encryption Key (master key stored in KMS/HSM).
- DEK: Data Encryption Key (used to encrypt individual objects/volumes).
- BYOK: Bring Your Own Key (customer supplies KEK material or HSM-protected key).
- HSM: Hardware Security Module.
- Wrap/Unwrap: Operations where KEK encrypts/decrypts DEKs.
- Tenant-key-id: Redwood-assigned stable identifier for a tenant-provided key.

High-level design decisions (summary):
1) Envelope encryption is mandatory for all tenant data at rest. KEKs are used only to wrap/unwrap short-lived DEKs.
2) All KEKs that hold customer key material must be HSM-backed or imported into an HSM-equivalent service with attestation.
3) Redwood stores only wrapped DEKs and key metadata. Plaintext DEKs are held only transiently in memory and are zeroed after use.
4) Rotation must be transparent to tenant workloads where possible: dual-write/dual-wrap patterns + graceful switch-over.
5) Comprehensive audit events for key lifecycle and DEK operations are exported to SIEM with a minimal canonical schema (below).

Tenant BYOK onboarding flow (step-by-step):
- Step 0: Pre-onboarding checklist (legal & contract signature, agreed regions, rotation cadence, allowed algorithms).
- Step 1: Create tenant record in platform (tenant_id). Assign tenant-key-id placeholder.
- Step 2: Customer provides key material via one of: HSM import token + attestation report OR KMS external-key wrapping (customer uploads wrapped KEK).
- Step 3: Security validates attestation (HSM vendor report) and approves import. (Ticket: JIRA-SEC-4312)
- Step 4: Platform imports key into HSM/KMS with a generated tenant-key-id and records metadata (algorithm, origin, import-time, expiry/rotation-policy).
- Step 5: Run initial audit snapshot (evidence bundle) and push to evidence store.
- Step 6: Enable tenant service routing to use KEK for envelope operations.

Key lifecycle states and allowed transitions (operational):
- states: created -> active -> scheduled_rotation -> rotating -> retired -> archived/deleted
- transitions must be atomic with clear audit events emitted.
- created: key metadata exists but not in-service. created->active occurs when import validated and attestation complete.
- active: normal operating state. DEKs are wrapped with this KEK for new objects.
- scheduled_rotation: admin or policy scheduled rotation at timestamp T; SIEM event KEY_ROTATION_SCHEDULED emitted.
- rotating: dual-wrap window where new DEKs are wrapped by new key version while existing data remains readable by old key. After successful validation, promote and emit KEY_ROTATED.
- retired: key removed from active use and only used to unwrap legacy DEKs for rewrap operations; access tightly controlled.
- archived/deleted: after retention window and legal approvals, key material and metadata removed per retention policy.

Rotation patterns (recommended):
- Recommended default cadence: 12 months for KEK material; minimum 90 days for high-risk customers (contractually defined).
- Rotation method A (zero-downtime rolling): create new key version (k_v2), begin dual-wrap: new writes use k_v2, reads attempt unwrap with k_v2 then fall back to k_v1. Once rewrap sweep completes for objects older than policy threshold, deprecate k_v1.
- Rotation method B (bulk rewrap): schedule maintenance window to rewrap all DEKs with new KEK material. Only for tenants that accept downtime for faster full rekey.
- Safe-guards: automated pre-checks (can k_v2 unwrap a sample list?), canary rewrap of 1% objects, circuit-breaker on unwrap error rates > 0.1% per minute to auto-pause and alert SRE.

Rekey / re-encryption procedure (high level):
- Phase 1: Prepare new KEK and validate unwrap/wrap functions in staging.
- Phase 2: Enable dual-wrap for new writes.
- Phase 3: Background rewrap worker: pick object, unwrap with old key, wrap DEK with new key, write new wrapped_DEK meta and emit audit.
- Phase 4: Monitor error rates; on sustained errors rollback to previous version for reads only; open runbook.
- Phase 5: After 100% successful rewrap and aging window, retire old KEK.

RBAC v2 integration notes (where to check):
- Principle of least privilege: separate roles for Key Admin, Key Import, Key Usage (unwrap/wrap), and Key Auditor.
- Minimum roles: key_admin (create/import/retire), key_operator (initiate rotation), key_warper (wrap/unwrap at runtime), key_auditor (read-only metadata for audits).
- IAM conditions: restrict key use to specific compute roles and IP ranges, and to tenant-bound resources.
- Example policy fragment (string example for engineers):
  "allow": ["kms:Wrap", "kms:Unwrap"], "resource": "tenant_{tenant_id}:key/{tenant-key-id}", "condition": {"source=" : "service:runtime.redwood"}

SIEM / audit export schema (canonical minimal fields):
- event_type (string): e.g., KEY_CREATE, KEY_IMPORT, KEY_ROTATION_SCHEDULED, KEY_ROTATED, KEY_RETIRE, KEY_DELETE, DEK_WRAP, DEK_UNWRAP, ACCESS_DENIED
- timestamp (ISO8601)
- tenant_id
- tenant_key_id
- key_version (if applicable)
- actor (user/service principal id)
- action_source (string): e.g., api, hsm-import, admin-console, scheduled-job
- outcome (string): success | partial_success | failure
- correlation_id (trace id for operation)
- request_id (platform request ID)
- request_ip
- user_agent
- error_code (optional)
- message (text blurb)
- evidence_id (if an evidence bundle created)

Sample exported log (single-line JSON string -- this is the canonical format we send to SIEM):
{"event_type":"KEY_ROTATED","timestamp":"2026-02-28T18:14:05Z","tenant_id":"t-82a9","tenant_key_id":"tk-0c12","key_version":"v2","actor":"svc-key-orchestrator","action_source":"rotation-job","outcome":"success","correlation_id":"trace-1a2b3c","request_id":"req-9f8e","request_ip":"13.45.22.88","user_agent":"rotator/1.3","message":"Rotation completed; 1.0M objects rewrapped","evidence_id":"evid-20260228-0c12"} 

Mapping to popular SIEM vendors (notes):
- Splunk: index=sec_kms sourcetype=redwood:kms | parse JSON fields directly; use tenant_id for multi-tenant dashboards.
- Elastic: ECS mapping: map event_type->event.action, tenant_id->agent.ephemeral_id or event.dataset depending on dashboarding needs, correlation_id->trace.id.
- Datadog: use tags:tenant_id: , tenant_key_id: ; put event_type in title and add structured fields on the event object.

Evidence automation and audit bundles:
- Evidence bundle contents: key metadata snapshot (no plaintext key material), import attestation artifacts, rotation schedule records, SIEM export slice for the requested period, RBAC audit for principals with key permissions, sample wrapped_DEK hashes and a digest manifest.
- Bundle format: gzipped tar with a manifest.json that lists files and SHA256 checksums. Bundle named: evid-{tenant_id}-{tenant_key_id}-{YYYYMMDD}.tar.gz
- Auto-generation triggers: on import, on rotation completion, quarterly snapshot, and on-demand with ticket (JIRA-SEC-xxxx).
- Retention: keep evidence bundles for audit retention period (default 7 years) unless legal instructs otherwise.

Operational playbook snippets (commands and checks):
- Pre-import validation checklist: confirm attestation, confirm allowed algorithm (AES-GCM-256 for DEK wrapping), confirm tenant signed contract, confirm regions allowed.
- Quick health checks: run unwrap test on sample wrapped_DEK set; check HSM connectivity; validate SIEM sink health; verify RBAC mappings.
- Circuit breaker: if unwrap error rate > 0.1% for 5 minutes, rotate to degraded mode (stop background rewrap, disable new writes to encrypted store for that tenant if policy strict), notify on-call SRE + security.

Data protection specifics and encryption-at-rest design details:
- DEK algorithm: AES-256-GCM preferred for object/record encryption. Use per-object DEKs when feasible.
- KEK wrapping: use RSA-OAEP-256 or AES-KWP depending on KMS/HSM capability. Keep algorithm in key metadata.
- Key versioning: every import produces a new key id + version id. Versioned keys must be referenced explicitly in audit logs.
- Cache behavior: DEKs cached in memory (per runtime) with TTL of 60s by default; caches must be flushed on key retire/rotate events.
- Disk-level encryption: LUKS full-disk can use platform-managed DEKs that are themselves wrapped by tenant KEK if required.
- S3/object-store: prefer server-side encryption with customer-provided keys for BYOK objects where applicable; otherwise use envelope encryption + object metadata with wrapped_DEK.

Security controls and reviews:
- Periodic attestation checks: annually re-validate HSM attestation for imported keys.
- Emergency rotation: policy and runbook for suspected key compromise; immediate scheduled rotation + full rewrap sweep with high priority.
- Access logging: capture every wrap/unwrap and key admin action with detailed fields and export to SIEM in near real-time (<= 1 min).

[Attested Key Rotation Runbook — Terraform interop for air-gapped VPCs (v0.1 draft)]
Purpose
This runbook describes the end-to-end process for performing an attested key rotation for customer-managed KMS backed by HSMs inside air-gapped VPCs or on-prem clusters. It focuses on Terraform module interoperability, preflight checks, orchestration steps, audit log capture, and a safe rollback path.

Scope and assumptions
- Applies to Redwood Private deployments where customer controls the HSM (Cloud HSM or on-prem HSM appliance) and the Redwood control-plane integrates via a constrained bridge.
- Target scenario: rotate the master wrapping key (KEK) and re-encrypt envelope-wrapped secrets stored in the secrets backplane.
- Assumes existing Terraform modules for kms-hsm-connector and sealed-secrets-operator are in use.
- Assumes an attestation system (attestd) is deployed to each on-prem node to produce hardware-backed attestations.

Non-goals
- This doc does not prescribe hardware vendor commands (vendor-specific HSM CLI). It describes the orchestration and Terraform-level changes.

High-level design overview
- Attestation: each HSM node produces a signed attestation (measurement + public key) that is recorded in the attestation registry.
- New KEK derivation: the HSM generates a new KEK; public material is published to the attestation registry and transparent log.
- Envelope rewrap: secrets stored in the secrets backplane are re-wrapped using the new KEK via a controlled rolling process.
- Audit chain: every step emits structured events to the local audit pipeline (syslog -> audit-forwarder -> central ELK/Tempo) with tamper-evident checkpoints.

Key terminology
- KEK: Key Encrypting Key (wraps DEKs).
- DEK: Data Encryption Key used to encrypt individual secrets.
- Attestation registry: signed store of attestation blobs (immutable append-only).
- Rewrap worker: a short-lived job that re-encrypts secrets with a new KEK.

Preflight checks (must pass before proceeding)
- Terraform plan success for both kms-hsm-connector and sealed-secrets modules in a staging workspace.
- Attestation registry reachable from orchestration host and contains valid attestations for all HSM nodes (check: attest-cli verify --registry <url>).
- Backup: encrypted snapshot of the secrets backplane and current KEK metadata stored off-cluster and checksum-verified.
- Audit forwarding test: generate test-event and verify it appears in central audit index within expected SLA.
- Operator availability: at least 2 on-call SREs and HSM operator available during the maintenance window.

Terraform module notes and change checklist
- New module inputs (suggested):
  - hsm_attestation_blob_url (string) – url to attestation registry blob for new key
  - kek_rotation_id (string) – opaque id used to index the rotation in the state
  - rewrap_batch_size (number) – for the rewrap worker control
  - audit_checkpoint_bucket (string) – where checkpoint manifests are stored
- Outputs to read after apply:
  - kek_public_key_pem
  - rotation_manifest_url
- State handling recommendations:
  - Use a separate Terraform workspace for rotation operations to keep rotation artifacts isolated.
  - If remote state is in an airgapped object store, ensure the connector has a consistent snapshot mechanism (avoid in-place state rewriting during rewrap).
- Upgrade compatibility: the kms-hsm-connector module must be backward compatible to accept both old and new KEK public material for a 7-day overlap window.

Step-by-step rotation procedure (orchestration)
1) Schedule maintenance window and notify customer and internal stakeholders.
2) Create rotation workspace: terraform workspace new rotation-<date>-<id>.
3) Upload attestation artifact for new HSM-generated KEK to registry and record the URL.
4) Terraform change: update kms-hsm-connector module input hsm_attestation_blob_url and set kek_rotation_id. Run terraform plan and apply.
   - Expected effect: connector provisions the new KEK reference and publishes rotation_manifest_url.
5) Verify connector health and that both old and new KEK materials are available to the sealing service.
   - Health checks: /health, /wrap-test (wrap/unwrap a test payload), attestation verify.
6) Start rewrap worker in controlled batches: set rewrap_batch_size to 500 (configurable). Monitor throughput and error rate.
   - Each worker run should post a checkpoint to audit_checkpoint_bucket with: rotation_id, batch_id, start_ts, end_ts, success_count, failure_count, batch_checksum.
7) For any failed items, run a retry worker (idempotent rewrap). Maintain a quarantine list.
8) Once all secrets rewrapped and checkpoints show zero outstanding failures, run finalization: mark rotation manifest as ACTIVE in attestation registry.
9) After a 24–72 hour observation window (business case dependent), remove support for old KEK from sealing service via terraform apply that flips the compatibility flag.
10) Archive rotation artifacts and push a signed rotation summary to the audit index.

Rollback plan (if rewrap causes data loss or unacceptable failures)
- Immediately pause rewrap workers (operator command: rewrapctl pause --rotation <id>).
- Re-enable old KEK in connector if removed prematurely (terraform workspace rotation-<id> apply with compatibility=true).
- Restore secrets backplane from pre-rotation encrypted snapshot into a quarantine namespace and run validation.
- Open an incident (jira:PD-1248) and follow SRE incident runbook.

Audit and observability
- Mandatory event types emitted:
  - rotation.requested (rotation_id, initiator, attestation_blob_url)
  - rotation.kek_generated (hsm_id, public_key_fingerprint, manifest_url)
  - rewrap.batch_completed (batch_id, counts, checksum, worker_id)
  - rotation.finalized (rotation_id, manifest_url, signer)
- Events must be signed with the orchestration key before forwarding to central audit. Use the audit-forwarder agent to attach provider stamps.
- Transparent log: every rotation manifest should be appended to a transparent log (tlog) that supports offline verification.

Attestation verification checklist
- verify attestation signature chain (vendor CA -> HSM attestation cert).
- validate measurements against known-good baseline (firmware hash).
- confirm HSM has not been tampered (physical checks by operator if required).

Operational knobs and timeouts
- rewrap_batch_size: default 500, max 2000 for high-throughput clusters.
- rewrap_worker_timeout: default 15m.
- checkpoint_interval: default 5m.
- compatibility_window_days: default 7 (must be configurable via module input).

Example Terraform pseudo-snippet (conceptual; put in module rotation.tf)

# module "kms_hsm_rotation" {
#   source = "git::https://github.com/redwood-inference/private-terraform-modules.git//kms-hsm-rotation"
#   hsm_attestation_blob_url = var.hsm_attestation_blob_url
#   kek_rotation_id = var.kek_rotation_id
#   rewrap_batch_size = var.rewrap_batch_size
#   audit_checkpoint_bucket = var.audit_checkpoint_bucket
#}

Operational run commands (examples)
- attest-cli upload --file new-kek-attestation.json --registry https://attest-registry.internal/rotations
- terraform workspace select rotation-2026-02-25-01 && terraform apply -var="hsm_attestation_blob_url=..."
- rewrapctl start --rotation rotation-2026-02-25-01 --batch-size 500
- rewrapctl status --rotation rotation-2026-02-25-01

Testing and canary strategy
- Canary 1: run rewrap worker against non-critical namespace (config: rewrap_batch_size=50). Validate application behavior for 2 hours.
- Canary 2: progressively increase to critical namespaces with monitoring thresholds: error_rate < 0.1%, latency < 200ms for wrap/unwrap calls.

Security considerations
- Minimal privileges: Terraform service principal used for rotation must have least privilege (apply-only to rotation workspace and read against attestation registry).
- Secrets in transit: ensure mTLS between rewrap workers and KMS connector; enforce TLS 1.3 and mutual auth.
- HSM operator authentication must be multi-factor for any key ceremony operation.

Open issues (next steps)
- Add explicit support for threshold HSM (Shamir/K-of-N) in the module (PD-1332).
- Improve attestation registry indexing for faster verification (contrib: attestation-indexer).
- Create a small automated verifier that replays a rotation on a local staging cluster and produces a signed readiness report.

Post-rotation checklist (to be completed and signed off)
- [ ] All rewrap checkpoints show zero outstanding failures.
- [ ] Audit log contains rotation.finalized with signer and manifest URL.
- [ ] Customer notified and acceptance confirmed.
- [ ] Rotation artifacts archived to retention bucket and checksums recorded.
- [ ] Terraform rotation workspace destroyed after 30 days (or retained per customer policy).

Appendix: quick trouble-shooting notes
- wrap-test fails with "invalid-unwrap": check HSM policy binding for the new KEK and ensure public_key PEM matches manifest.
- rewrap worker stuck on item: inspect item metadata in secrets-backplane; try idempotent retry with rewrapctl retry --item <id>.
- attestation verification fails: fetch vendor firmware manifest and compare; if mismatch, escalate to hardware ops.

Owner and on-call
- Owner: Sana Iqbal (eng-private-deployments).
- Primary on-call SRE: Marco Rivera.
- HSM operator: Priya Deshmukh.

Notes and provenance
- Drafted from recent purple-team exercise (Dec 2025) and internal tabletop (Jan 2026).
- Related tickets and PRs listed above. This is a living document — update as modules evolve.

[Encryption Governance: Operator SOP and SIEM Export Mapping]
Purpose:
This operator-facing playbook consolidates runbook steps, RBAC v2 role mappings, the canonical audit log schema we emit for key operations, and SIEM export mapping for ingestion in Splunk/Elastic/Datadog. It is intended for on-call operators, security reviewers, and automation engineers who implement evidence automation for compliance audits (SOC2/ISO/PCI).

Scope and intent:
- Covers tenant & platform key lifecycle for hosted and dedicated deployments (BYOK onboarding, HSM-backed root keys, envelope key rotations, data-key refresh).
- Describes RBAC v2 roles, least privilege operations, and suggested policy expressions.
- Provides the canonical audit schema (fields + examples) and mappings to common SIEM fields.
- Contains an operator SOP for scheduled and emergency rotations and a checklist for evidence exports.

High-level key hierarchy (operator summary):
- Platform Root (HSM) — hardware-protected root used only for wrapping/unwrapping tenant root keys and signing evidence manifests.
- Tenant Root / Customer Master Key (CMK) — customer-assigned or Redwood-managed; used to wrap intermediate keys.
- Service/envelope keys — short-lived keys used by runtime for token hashing, caching, and transport encryption.
- Data keys — per-blob/per-file keys managed by the keystore and rotated frequently.

RBAC v2 roles and minimum allowed actions (operator cheat-sheet):
- role:crypto-operator (team:security-ops)
  - purpose: run rotations, view audit evidence, trigger rewraps
  - allowed_actions: ["kms:RotateKey","kms:ScheduleRotation","kms:CreateRewrapJob","evidence:Export","logs:ViewAudit"]
  - denied_actions: ["kms:ExportRawKey","kms:BypassHSM"]
- role:key-admin (team:platform-crypto)
  - purpose: full lifecycle management for platform-generated keys
  - allowed_actions: ["kms:CreateKey","kms:DeleteKey","kms:UpdateKeyPolicy","kms:GrantAccess"]
  - constraints: require 2-step approval for tenant-visible key deletion
- role:key-approver (team:legal, compliance)
  - purpose: approve BYOK onboarding / key escrow requests
  - allowed_actions: ["requests:ApproveBYOK","evidence:SignAcceptance"]
- role:svc-kms-broker (machine identity)
  - purpose: perform wrap/unwrap during runtime path
  - allowed_actions: ["kms:WrapKey","kms:UnwrapKey","kms:GenerateDataKey"]
  - token_constraints: short TTL, pinned to instance or connection fingerprint
- role:auditor (team:security-audit)
  - purpose: read-only audit access for compliance
  - allowed_actions: ["logs:QueryAudit","evidence:DownloadArtifacts"]

Policy notes for operators:
- All sensitive actions (RotateKey, ExportWrappedKey, GrantAccess) must include an authorization context: correlation_id, ticket_id, approver_id.
- Enforce attribute-based conditions where possible: source_ip_range, agent_fingerprint, mfa_verified.
- Any action that results in key material export must create an evidence manifest signed by the HSM key.

BYOK onboarding flow (operator steps):
1) Customer request received (ticket created) — assign ticket and attach BYOK metadata template.
2) Validate public key blob: ensure key format (PKCS#8/PEM), verify size & algorithm.
3) Policy sanity checks: allowed algorithms, expiration, and rotation policy.
4) Create temporary onboarding job: create tenant placeholder key in keystore with state=PROVISIONING.
5) Customer/partner performs key prove-of-possession challenge (signed nonce).
6) Operator approves in UI (requires key-approver approval) -> state=ACTIVE.
7) Emit evidence: onboarding-manifest.json signed by HSM. Store manifest and signed certificate in evidence-bucket and index into SIEM.

HSM fallback and dual-control pattern:
- Primary: HSM cluster in region (FIPS-validated).
- Fallback: remote HSM cluster in separate availability zone with automated quorum check.
- Dual-control for unwrapping platform roots: require two operator roles or operator + service principal.
- Emergency unseal: documented, time-limited breakout windows logged with high-fidelity evidence and privileged approval.

Rotation policy (recommended defaults):
- Data keys: rotate every 7–30 days (depending on data sensitivity).
- Envelope keys: rotate every 90 days or after N rewraps (N configurable).
- Tenant root (BYOK): customer-configurable; default policy recommends 1 year with automated non-disruptive rewrap.
- HSM root: rotate per vendor guidance (firmware/slot rotation) and on firmware upgrade, with full test vector validation.

Operator SOP: scheduled rotation (non-disruptive):
- Step 0: Prechecks
  - Verify system health: serving runtime > 99.9% last 6h, request queue < threshold.
  - Ensure evidence-bucket has >48h redundancy and SIEM pipeline healthy.
- Step 1: Create rotation job
  - Create job with correlation_id and ticket reference, set rollout window and canary subset.
- Step 2: Canary rewrap
  - Rewrap 1% of traffic (canary tenants) and run smoke tests against canary. Validate integrity of KV caches.
- Step 3: Gradual rollout
  - Expand to 10%, 50%, 100% with 30–60 minute observation windows. Abort on errors or high error_rate delta.
- Step 4: Validation
  - Verify metrics: unwrap latency, cache hit ratio, request error rate, and audit log entries for all rewrap operations.
- Step 5: Evidence export
  - Generate rotation-manifest.json (signed by HSM), store artifacts and index to SIEM with ticket and correlation_id.

Operator SOP: emergency rotation (compromise suspected):
- Immediate actions: freeze new key grants, move impacted keys to state=QUARANTINED, notify security & account teams.
- Create emergency rotation job with high priority and dual approval.
- Run full-backfill to re-encrypt affected ciphertext using new keys.
- Evidence: collect raw audit streams, HSM log snapshots, rewrap job deltas and sign them.

Audit log schema (canonical) — required fields (emit for every key operation):
- timestamp: ISO8601 string (e.g. 2026-01-18T15:43:21Z)
- event_id: UUID
- correlation_id: string (operator ticket or automation id)
- request_id: string (API gateway request id)
- principal_id: string (user:alice or svc:svc-kms-broker)
- principal_type: enum [user, service, system]
- actor_role: RBAC role name performing action
- action: enum [CreateKey, RotateKey, Rewrap, Wrap, Unwrap, GenerateDataKey, DeleteKey, GrantAccess, RevokeAccess, ExportEvidence]
- resource_type: enum [HSMSlot, TenantKey, EnvelopeKey, DataKey]
- resource_id: opaque id
- key_version: semantic version or epoch (e.g. v2026-01-09-3)
- key_state: enum [PROVISIONING, ACTIVE, ROTATING, QUARANTINED, DECOMMISSIONED]
- outcome: enum [success, failure]
- outcome_code: short string (e.g. KMS-ERR-1023)
- duration_ms: integer
- hsm_slot: optional string
- hsm_firmware: optional string
- evidence_artifact_id: id pointing to signed artifact in evidence-bucket
- request_payload_hash: sha256 hex
- response_signature: base64 (when operation signed by HSM)
- request_source_ip: ip
- request_user_agent: string
- approver_ids: list of principal ids (if approval required)
- notes: free text

Example audit log event (as emitted):

  "timestamp": "2026-01-18T15:43:21Z",
  "event_id": "7d6b3e7a-fb3d-4b9a-9c12-5aee1f2c6a2b",
  "correlation_id": "ROT-20260118-9987",

  "hsm_slot": "hsm-cluster-1/slot-02",
  "evidence_artifact_id": "ev-20260118-rot-9987",
  "request_payload_hash": "a3f5c1d7...",
  "response_signature": "MEUCIQDJ...",
  "approver_ids": ["ravi.shah@redwood.com"],
  "notes": "Canary rotation; all checks green"
}

SIEM export mapping (recommended):
- Canonical -> Splunk (KV ingest)
  - _time = timestamp
  - event_id = event_id
  - host = hsm_slot OR resource_id host portion
  - user = principal_id
  - action = action
  - resource = resource_id
  - result = outcome
  - evidence_id = evidence_artifact_id
  - duration_ms = duration_ms
- Canonical -> Elastic Common Schema (ECS)
  - @timestamp = timestamp
  - event.id = event_id
  - event.action = action
  - event.outcome = outcome
  - user.name = principal_id
  - service.name = "redwood-kms"
  - service.type = "kms"
  - cloud.instance.id = hsm_slot (if HSM-hosted)
- Canonical -> Datadog
  - timestamp -> dd.timestamp
  - host -> tags:host
  - event.action -> title
  - evidence_artifact_id -> body or extra_tags

Operator checklist for evidence automation (to produce audit package for auditors):
- Collect: rotation-manifest.json (signed), job logs (rotation job id), full audit stream slice (event_id list), HSM debug snapshot (if available), rewrap deltas.
- Hash & sign: compute sha256 of artifacts and sign with HSM signing key (response_signature).
- Store: upload artifacts to evidence-bucket under path: /evidence/<tenant>/<ticket>/<correlation_id>/ and set retention tags.
- Index: emit index event to SIEM with evidence_artifact_id, ticket_id, approvers list, and signed manifest.
- Export: produce zipped export for auditors with README.md (includes verification commands and sample verification keys).

Retention and encryption-at-rest design notes (operator guidance):
- Evidence artifacts: retain 7 years for enterprise customers who require extended retention; default 1 year for standard. Mark artifacts with retention-policies and immutable flags on object storage.
- At rest: all artifacts and keys are stored encrypted with tenant-root-wrapping keys. Evidence manifests are additionally signed by HSM signing key.
- Database encryption: use envelope encryption for PII columns in the metadata DB. Keys rotated on the same cadence as service envelope keys.

Incident runbook (suspected key compromise):
1) Triage: gather audit slice for last 72h, freeze key grants, escalate to incident-commander.
2) Contain: put impacted keys in QUARANTINED state and disable unwrap endpoints for them.
3) Rotate: generate new keys, re-encrypt affected ciphertext, and deploy new wrapping.
4) Evidence: snapshot HSM logs, collect all export artifacts, lock down evidence-bucket (read-only) and sign manifest.
5) Postmortem: run cryptographic proof checks, produce a signed report, and schedule customer communications per contract.

Operator troubleshooting quick tips:
- Missing audit entries: check log forwarder health, verify local buffer retention in keystore (usually 1h) and inspect backlog consumer.
- Rewrap failures: common causes: stale KV cache, incompatible key policy (policy version mismatch), HSM overload (observe hsm_queue).
- Performance regressions after rotation: verify chosen kernel/quantization profile for model-serving if relying on runtime caches — rotation should not change runtime kernels but may affect cache hit ratios.

Appendix — sample SIEM queries:
- Splunk: find failed rotates in last 24h
  index=kms_audit action=RotateKey outcome=failure | stats count by resource_id, outcome_code
- Elastic (KQL): high-latency rotations
  event.action: "RotateKey" and duration_ms:>10000 | sort by duration_ms desc
- Datadog (Log query): evidence exports last 7 days by tenant tag
  logs("service:kms AND evidence_artifact_id:*", from:now-7d).group_by(["@tenant_id"])

Appendix — verification commands for auditors (examples):
- Verify signed manifest (local):

[Dynamic credential cooldown orchestration — runbook draft]
Context:
This is a working runbook for handling incidents where a subset of API keys or tenants produce sudden high-rate traffic consistent with credential leakage or automated scraping. The goal is to provide a graduated response that: (1) contains the abusive traffic quickly, (2) minimizes collateral impact to adjacent tenants, and (3) creates a reproducible automation path so oncall can act quickly without manual key rotation for every incident.

Why this is different: current fast-path playbooks are either global throttles or full key revocation. Both extremes either cause excessive app-level disruption or require heavy manual ops. This draft proposes a coordinated cooldown window, progressive circuit-breaker thresholds, and automated temporary token suspension with safe fallback routing.

Detection signals (composite):
- sudden per-key request rate > 10x historical median for that key over 15m AND
- token new-IP entropy: > 30% of requests from IPs not seen for that token in last 7d OR rapid geo fanout (>3 regions in 10 minutes) AND
- error profile skew: high 4xx (401/403) or repetitive identical prompt payloads (indicator scanning)
- telemetry spike on application-side: late-stage LLM rejection/failure loops (increased retry count)

Initial triage (first 10 minutes):
1) Confirm with dashboards: per-key rate chart, IP distribution, linked customer contact. Link to quick-query: QUERY_KEY_TRAFFIC(<key>) -> returns 1m/5m/15m rates and top 10 IPs.
2) Correlate with recent deploys or infra changes (check release-engineering slack and CI tags). If deploys present within last 30m, tag incident as "deploy-related" and follow deploy rollback checklist.
3) If signal meets composite threshold, start the "credential-cooldown" incident in PagerDuty and notify product-security.

Immediate actions (manual, low-friction):
- Step A: Apply soft cooldown (recommended default) -> limit token to 2x baseline throughput but keep route open. Use the API: POST /admin/tokens/<key>/limits {"rate": "soft-2x", "window": "15m", "reason": "cooldown-suspected-leak"}.
- Step B: Enable temporary IP allowlist/denylist on WAF for the top 3 abusive IPs pending forensic review. Do NOT global-block until confirm.
- Step C: Turn on request sampling for that token at 100% and increase log retention for 24 hours to collect full payloads (for legal/product review).

Automated escalation (what to trigger if cooldown doesn't reduce abuse):
- After 10 minutes of soft-cooldown, if request rate > 5x historical median OR new IPs continue arriving, transition to progressive circuit-breaker: incrementally reduce rate to 1x -> 0.5x -> 0.1x on 5m intervals.
- If circuit-breaker reaches 0.1x and abuse persists, trigger temporary token suspension with auto-rotation: call automation: POST /ops/rotate-token {"token_id": "<key>", "mode": "temporary-suspend-and-rotate", "notify": ["owner","eng-sre"]}. Automation will: create replacement token, mark old token as suspended, provision replacement to customer owner via secure channel, and attach a rollback TTL of 24h.

Fallback routing:
- For customers using Hosted API with failover to Dedicated or alternate regional endpoints, if token suspension occurs, the system will apply a per-tenant fallback policy to route authenticated requests to read-only embedding endpoints where possible (non-generation paths). This preserves customer visibility while preventing abuse-driven generation costs.

WAF interplay guidance:
- Prefer targeted WAF rules keyed by IP ranges + UA fingerprint, not broad-based rules that affect entire region.
- When adding WAF exceptions, annotate rule with incident id and the reason. Example WAF note: "INC-2026-0041: temporary block 18.205.93.0/24 - matched repeated token spray patterns".
- Keep a rolling list of "safelist test IPs" to ensure WAF rules are tested before enforcement.

Customer communication and security handoff:
- If token rotation or suspension happens, CS must send templated notification: short explanation, mitigation actions taken, instructions to rotate keys on their side (if applicable), and offer 24h support window. Template link: Confluence/DynamicTokenTemplates.
- If evidence of data exfiltration or PII access is suspected, immediately escalate to security@redwood and follow the formal incident response checklist (forensics imaging, preserve logs).

Forensics checklist (post-containment):
- Export top 1k request logs for the token, preserving original timestamps and IPs.
- Capture runtime metrics for model invocations during the attack window: token latency, GPU utilization, KV-cache hit ratio.
- Collect sample prompts and deduplicate. Flag those that look like credential-stuffing, scraping, or injection attempts.
- Run IP reputation lookup and add to evidence bundle.

Testing and exercises (SRE-run):
- Quarterly tabletop: simulate a leaked-token scenario using a non-prod token and ramp traffic using internal loadgen. Verify the cooldown automation transitions through soft->circuit->suspend without impacting other tenants.
- Chaos test: randomly inject NAT IPs from 5 source regions to confirm geo-detection heuristics.
- Smoke test: run the full rotation automation in staging and verify notification flow to CS and that rollback TTL correctly re-enables token when requested.

Runbook CLI snippets (for oncall):
- Quick view top IPs for token: 
  curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $SRE_API_KEY" 
    "https://telemetry.internal/api/token-traffic?token=<key>&window=15m" | jq .top_ips
- Apply soft cooldown: 
  curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $SRE_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" 
    -d '{"rate":"soft-2x","window":"15m","reason":"cooldown-suspected-leak"}' 
    https://admin.internal/api/tokens/<key>/limits
- Trigger rotation automation (manual override): 
  curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $SRE_API_KEY" -d '{"token_id":"<key>","mode":"temporary-suspend-and-rotate","notify":["owner","eng-sre"]}' https://ops.internal/api/rotate-token

Manual escalation criteria (when to ring human):
- Evidence of cross-tenant lateral movement (same IPs hitting multiple unrelated tokens)
- Sustained cost delta > $1k per hour attributable to the token after 30 minutes of automated controls
- Legal or regulatory signal (customer says they are seeing user data in requests or suspected PII).

Post-incident follow-ups (action items):
- Short-term (assigned within 48h): run a telemetry correctness audit for signal thresholds, tune geo-fanout and IP-entropy thresholds. Owner: Liam O'Connor.
- Medium-term (2 weeks): build synthetic canary to validate soft->suspend transitions in CI. Owner: Chen Wei.
- Long-term (quarter): evaluate offering an opt-in forensic mode for customers with high-risk data that provides stronger per-request provenance and easier rotation UX. Owner: Product-Security.

Metrics to capture for continuous improvement:
- Mean time to containment (MTC) in minutes from detection to soft-cooldown and to full suspension.
- False positive rate (customer-impactful suspensions / total suspensions).
- Cost saved per incident (estimate avoided generation tokens billed to infra).

Open questions / TODOs in this draft:
- Exact numeric thresholds for soft vs hard cooldown need A/B testing in production (suggest starting conservative to avoid customer disruption).
- How to best surface rotation actions to customers using Managed Dedicated with their own key store? Need product input.
- Legal constraints on storing sampled request payloads for 24h (confirm with compliance).

Notes to self / oncall hints: keep change windows small, annotate every temporary WAF and token action with incident id, and prefer short-lived automated rotations rather than blanket revocations. This runbook should live next to the fast-path automations but separate enough to emphasize credential-specific heuristics.

[Crypto hierarchy, rotation, and SIEM export — runbook]
Purpose and scope:
This runbook captures the operational design and step-by-step procedures for key lifecycle management (cloud KMS, HSM-backed keys, and customer BYOK), rotation patterns, and formatted audit export to the SIEM. It is intended for security engineers, platform engineers (private/dedicated), and on-call SREs who will perform rotations, evidence collection, and incident responses related to encryption-at-rest.

Non-goals:
- Specifying vendor-specific API docs (those are linked in the artifacts section).
- Replacing the Verified KMS onboarding checklist — this complements it with operational playbook material.

Overview of crypto hierarchy (recommended model):
- Root/Signer (offline or HSM-protected root key): only used to sign intermediate keys and for bootstrapping. Extremely high entropy, stored in FIPS-validated HSM or offline guard.
- Master Key (MK): KMS-managed single-purpose key used to encrypt/unwrap key-encryption-keys (KEKs). Rotated infrequently; stored in cloud KMS or HSM with strict RBAC.
- Key-Encryption Keys (KEKs): Per- tenancy (customer or environment) keys used to wrap Data Encryption Keys (DEKs). KEKs live in KMS/HSM and are subject to rotation policies independent of DEKs.
- Data Encryption Keys (DEKs): Short-lived keys used for envelope encryption of object data (S3, blockstore, DB column encryption). DEKs are generated by the service, encrypted with KEK, and stored alongside ciphertext.

Why envelope encryption: improved rotation and small blast radius — DEKs are cheap to rotate and do not require re-encrypting blobs when KEK rotates (only rewrap operation).

RBAC v2 for keys (mapping to roles):
- key-admin: create/delete/grant/revoke KEKs and manage key policy metadata. Should be restricted to Security Eng and Platform Admins. (Granting on a per-key resource basis.)
- key-operator: initiate rotate/rewrap operations, request key usage metrics, and run emergency revocations. Intended for SRE on-call + rotation automation service accounts.
- kms-viewer: read-only access to key metadata, audit entries, and rotation history; used by auditors and compliance reviewers.
- crypto-service (machine/account): service principal used by runtime to perform encrypt/decrypt operations — scoped to specific KEKs via least privilege.

Access controls and constraints:
- No human accounts with direct encrypt/decrypt rights on production KEKs unless explicitly approved and logged.
- All changes to key policy must require multi-approver workflow via ticket (JIRA-SEC or ServiceNow) with a signed justification field.

Rotation policy matrix (recommended default):
- Root/Signer: rotate only on explicit key compromise or re-keying cycle every 5+ years (with offline ceremony).
- Master Key (MK): 18–36 months, or immediately on suspected compromise.
- KEK (per-tenant): 6–12 months; automated rewrap of DEKs recommended during low-traffic windows.
- DEK: TTL 24 hours to 90 days based on workload sensitivity; for high-volume object stores, prefer short TTL (7–30 days) and frequent rewraps.

Rotation step-by-step (KEK rotation, automated):
1) Pre-checks:
   - Confirm current KEK metadata and last_rotation in KMS.
   - Verify successful snapshot/backup of key metadata snapshot (S3 location: s3://redwood-sec-key-metadata/yyyymmdd).
   - Check outstanding re-wrap tasks and in-flight writes; consult per-route write-latency dashboard.
   - Ensure automation runbook is in a healthy state (CI job green).
2) Create new KEK version in KMS/HSM using secure API. Tag version with rotation-correlation-id and timestamp.
3) Update service principal grants for the new key version (if using explicit version grants).
4) Enqueue rewrap job that will read ciphertext metadata, call KMS unwrap with old KEK -> DEK, then wrap DEK with new KEK, and write back wrapped value. Jobs are sharded and rate-limited to preserve latency SLOs.
5) Monitor rewrap progress, look for rewrap-failure counts and backoffs. Failures trigger automatic re-try with exponential backoff and eventual pager escalation to on-call.
6) After >= 95% rewrap completion, update key policy primary-version pointer to new KEK version. Keep old version alive for 30–90 days for rollback and emergency decrypt.
7) Post-ops: generate evidence bundle (audit logs, job run IDs, manifest of rewrapped object IDs) and export to secure evidence store.

Manual emergency rotation (compromise suspected):
- Immediate steps: set KEK to disabled state for new wraps (maintain unwrap to allow decrypts if needed), create incident ticket, notify CS/Legal if customer keys involved. For BYOK, escalate to customer contact according to contract.

BYOK specific flows and customer-supplied HSMs:
- Onboarding requires: customer intent form, key rollover policy acceptance, and KMS import key ceremony recorded in Confluence page.
- BYOK keys are treated as external-key IDs — Redwood stores only wrapped DEKs. Key operations with external HSM require dedicated connector host in customer VPC or HSM proxy with mutual-auth TLS.
- Rotation for BYOK: coordinate schedule with customer; do not perform unilateral rotation of a customer-supplied root. Documented SLA window must be observed.

Audit log schema (key events) — canonical fields (JSON log entry):
- timestamp: ISO8601 string
- event_type: one of [KEY_CREATE, KEY_ROTATE, KEY_VERSION_CREATE, KEY_DISABLE, KEY_ENABLE, KEY_DELETE, KEY_UNWRAP, KEY_WRAP, KEY_POLICY_CHANGE]
- resource_id: kms://<region>/<key-id>
- actor: <principal-id or service-account>
- actor_type: human|service|external-customer
- action_id: UUID (correlation across services)
- request_id: cloud-kms-request-id (if available)
- outcome: success|failure|partial
- reason: free text (failure reason / policy change note)
- correlation_tags: list of tags (rotation-correlation-id, ticket-id)
- old_version: version-id (if rotation)
- new_version: version-id (if rotation)
- rewrap_manifest_loc: s3://... or null
- sampled_trace: diagnostic trace id or null
- raw_event: raw provider event (if available)

Example log (single-line JSON):
{
  "timestamp": "2024-11-05T22:14:31Z",
  "event_type": "KEY_ROTATE",
  "resource_id": "kms://us-east1/ke-abc123",
  "actor": "svc-key-rotation@redwood-infra",
  "actor_type": "service",
  "action_id": "b3a85d6f-4c2b-4a9d-8e1c-3d9f7a9d2fbb",
  "request_id": "cloudreq-9922",
  "outcome": "success",
  "reason": "scheduled-rotation",
  "correlation_tags": ["rotation-20241105", "JIRA-SEC-1290"],
  "old_version": "v1",
  "new_version": "v2",
  "rewrap_manifest_loc": "s3://redwood-sec-key-manifests/rewrap-20241105.json",
  "sampled_trace": "trace-7a9e",
  "raw_event": null
}

SIEM export mapping guidance:
- Ingest each canonical audit log into the SIEM as a single event with the following mapped fields: time, src_principal (actor), event_type, resource, correlation_id (action_id), outcome, tags, message.
- Enrich events with identity attributes from IAM (team, manager, risk_score) and with customer ids for tenant-scoped keys.
- Create SIEM detection rules for abnormal activity patterns:
  - Multiple KEY_UNWRAP calls from different service principals for the same resource within a short window.
  - New key-version creation without a preceding JIRA ticket tag.
  - KEK rotates outside maintenance window.
  - Unexpected external-customer key access from internal VMs.

Evidence automation (post-rotation evidence bundle):
- Components to collect automatically after a rotation or emergency action:
  - Audit log slice covering action_id and +/- 24 hours.
  - Rewrap manifest (list of objects rewrapped and shard ids).
  - KMS provider raw response payloads and request IDs.
  - CI/CD job run ids and artifacts (automation run logs).
  - Signed PDF of rotation approvers (if manual approvals present).
- Automation job will package the above into a signed tarball, compute a SHA256, upload to s3://redwood-sec-evidence/<action_id>/evidence.tar.gz and emit an evidence-created audit event.

Testing, validation and rollback:
- Canary run: pick a low-traffic tenant and perform a KEK rotate + rewrap. Validate decrypt success on sampled objects for 48 hours. Use automated smoke tests (github.com/redwood-infra/tests/key-rotate-canary).
- Rollback: if rewrap fails en masse, revert primary-version pointer to previous version and abort further wrap jobs. Keep failure manifest for investigation.

Monitoring and observability:
- Key metrics to publish: rewrap_progress_percent, rewrap_error_rate, key_usage_per_minute, key_latency_p50/p90/p99 for wrap/unwrap calls, key_policy_change_count.
- Dashboards: per-region key counters, tenant-impact view, and a security incidents dashboard that surfaces any disabled keys or rapid version churn.

Operational playbook checklist (pre-rotation):
- [ ] Confirm maintenance window and customer notifications (if tenant scoped).
- [ ] Snapshot key metadata.
- [ ] Ensure rewrap jobs have capacity and throttles configured.
- [ ] Backup evidence store writable.

Post-rotation checklist:
- [ ] Rewrap >= 95% completed or documented exception list.
- [ ] Evidence tarball produced and verified.
- [ ] Post-rotation smoke tests green.
- [ ] Update key inventory and rotation calendar.

Compromise handling (short runbook):
1) Immediately mark key as disabled for new wraps and log action.
2) Create incident ticket with correlation_id and contact list.
3) If customer key (BYOK), notify customer per contract and follow agreed escalation.
4) Start forensic capture: full audit slice, host traces, and rewrap manifest.
5) If necessary, perform emergency rewrap to new KEK and reject old version; expedite evidence export for compliance.

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Do we require HSM for all MKs by default or only high-sensitivity tenants? (propose: high-sensitivity and enterprise with SLA >$Xk/month)
- Retention policy for old key versions beyond rollback window (30/90/365 days?)
- Integration point for RBAC v2 authorization checks in the KMS proxy — pre-check or delegated to provider?
