[Discovery hub routing policy & telemetry workspace]
Purpose:
This is a working workspace for a lightweight "Discovery Hub" concept: a federated control-plane component that centralizes service discovery decisions and node capability indexing across regions. Aim is to simplify routing policy enforcement, surface GPU compatibility, and provide a compact health signal index that downstream routers can query quickly.

Background / motivation:
- We currently have multiple discovery layers: local kube service registry, per-region inventory caches, and ad-hoc routing logic in the edge proxy. This duplication leads to stale capability info and makes multi-region failover brittle.
- Many routing failures trace back to subtle GPU incompatibilities (driver mismatch, cuda patch level) or transient degraded nodes that are still 'Ready' but failing fast-path kernels.
- A small, consistent aggregated view (fingerprint + capability + health score) per node will let routing policies make better choices without expensive real-time probes.

Goals:
1) Define a compact per-node index (fingerprint) that captures immutable attributes + dynamic capability tags.
2) Provide a protocol for pushing health signals and scheduled heartbeat reconciliation.
3) Allow routing policy authors to express multi-criteria rules: region affinity, GPU feature filter, health threshold, cost tiering, drift tolerance.
4) Keep the Discovery Hub lightweight and eventually shoppable as a library for Private deployments.

Design sketch - Discovery Hub responsibilities:
- Ingest: node heartbeats, GPU profiler outputs, node metadata, and patch-level telemetry from the agent.
- Normalize: map raw GPU identifiers to canonical types and feature sets (e.g., quantization-friendly, bf16, fp16, sparse-support).
- Score: compute a rolling health score (0-100) combining heartbeat latency, recent kernel failures, eviction counts, and temperature throttling alerts.
- Expose: a small HTTP/gRPC index API for selectors and a push subscription model for routers to receive delta updates.
- Audit/log: append-only stream (compact) for reconciliation and drift detection.

Node identity and label model (proposal):
- fingerprint_id: sha1(node_uuid + region + gpu_serial) - stable until hardware swap.
- immutable_labels (set once at registration): region, zone, cpu_arch, machine_type, base_image, node_pool
- capability_tags (updated by agent): gpu_family (e.g., a100, h100), cuda_version, cudnn_version, quant_support=[int8,int4,bf16], fp16_fast_path, sparse_kernels
- runtime_tolerations: workloads can declare tolerations (e.g., tolerate-high-latency-cache, tolerate-throttling)

GPU taxonomy mapping (why we need it):
- Agents will report vendor strings and driver IDs. The Hub maintains a small mapping table -> canonical GPU features. This lets routing policies avoid brittle string compares and reason in capability predicates.
- Example canonical tags: "A100-80GB.PCIe", "H100-SXM.80GB", "A10G.24GB". Feature flags attached: [bf16, fp16-opt, int8-sparse, nvlink-topo].

Health signals and scoring (proposal):
- Signals consumed: heartbeat_ms, kernel_error_rate_5m, p95_token_latency_delta, thermal_throttle_events_1h, eviction_count_24h, disk_pressure_5m
- Scoring: weighted score: 40% kernel_error, 25% heartbeat freshness, 15% thermal, 10% eviction_history, 10% other. Scores normalized to 0-100 and stored as a short history (last 6 buckets).
- States derived: healthy (>85), degraded (60-85), warning (35-60), critical (<35).

Routing policy DSL (examples):
- Basic selection: region=="us-west1" AND gpu_family=="H100" AND health_state=="healthy"
- Cost-aware fallback: prefer region==primary THEN region==secondary with health_state>=60; allow quantized model route if gpu_supports.int8==true
- Canary routing: route 10% to new kernel-enabled pool where kernel_error_rate_5m < 0.02 and score >=90

Control-plane interactions and data paths:
- Agents push to regional Hub ingress (gRPC unary with TTL). Regional Hubs do local normalization and persist in the region's compact store (RocksDB-like).
- Global Hub shards subscribe to regional delta streams to synthesize cross-region views for cross-region routing (on-demand materialization).
- Routers query local Hub for fast selector evaluation; if not found or stale, router may call global view with fallback policy.

Multi-region considerations:
- Consistency model: eventually consistent with vector clocks per-node; we must accept slight staleness for routing to prioritize availability. Heartbeat TTLs are region-aware (shorter for intra-region failover).
- Regional affinity: default policy favors local region where latency matters; explicit cross-region routing requires health thresholds + cost delta check.
- Data residency: private deployments can opt-out of global replication; Discovery Hub supports local-only mode with same schemas.

Telemetry schema (compact):
- node_id, ts_iso, fingerprint_id, health_score, health_state, top_errors (list of strings), gpu_tags (list), heartbeat_ms
- Telemetry payloads are intentionally narrow to keep delta sizes small (prefer lists of codes over verbose messages).

Operational runbooks (initial):
- On rising kernel_error_rate_5m: mark node degraded, evict new long-running requests, schedule kernel re-probing in 5m.
- On score<35: mark node as drain candidate, notify SRE team, trigger automatic cordon if eviction_count>3 in 24h.
- Reconciliation job: daily pass to compute fingerprint drift and reconcile any nodes with changing immutable labels (flag for manual review).

Storage / capacity notes:
- Compact store per region: expect ~10k nodes in peak -> each node's record ~1KB (fingerprint, tags, last 6 scores) => ~10MB per region + overhead. Small and cheap.
- Delta streaming: protobuf with compact ints; typical update rate ~1-5s per node under load (check sampling options).

Open questions / TODOs:
- Exact fingerprint algorithm (sha1 vs murmur). Security notes: avoid exposing hardware serials in public endpoints.
- We need a canonical GPU feature catalog. Who owns it? Suggest applied-ml + platform to co-maintain.
- Policy DSL surface: integrate with existing rollout DSL or create a small standalone matcher? (Linked JIRA-INF-482)
- Backpressure behavior: how do agents retry when Hub is down? Backoff policy needed.

[Pinning legacy retirement and customer migration playbook]
Purpose:
This is a working playbook for retiring the legacy region-pinning mechanism (legacyPinToken) and migrating customers to the new territory-binding flow (pin-v2 / tenancy-anchor). The doc focuses on operational steps, customer impact analysis, telemetry, and rollback criteria. This is intentionally pragmatic — expect follow-ups (tickets linked above).

Summary of motivation:
- LegacyPinToken has incompatibilities with private deployments (edge anchors + VPC routing) and blocks multi-region failover logic.
- Pin-v2 adds audit metadata, stronger geo-constraints, and a clear entitlement field that the router and policy engine can consume.
- We must retire legacyPinToken to simplify routing code, reduce special-case fallbacks, and remove a source of inconsistent residency evidence.

High-level migration strategy:
1) Launch pin-v2 as opt-in for new tenants (already done: API stable).
2) Run a 90-day co-existence window where both tokens are honored but legacyPinToken is logged with higher severity to telemetry (flag: legacy_pin_warning=true).
3) Begin targeted opt-in nudges for tenants (month 0-2).
4) Start graduated enforcement: for low-risk tenants (internal, dev/qa) disable legacy acceptance after 90d; for high-risk/enterprise customers, negotiate migration SLAs and extended windows.
5) Full enforcement (reject legacy tokens) after customer migration: target 9 months from kickoff but adjustable based on customer commitments.

Stakeholders and RACI (short):
- Eng (API + routing): Responsible for rollout gates, feature flags, and telemetry events. (Owner: Liam Chen)
- SRE: Responsible for observability, capacity impact checks, and canarying. (Owner: Priya Nair)
- Solutions/CS: Customer outreach, migration assistance, and contract exceptions. (Owner: Diego Martinez)
- Product Legal: Approve any contract change or SLA modifications.
- Support: Runbooks and escalation paths.

Telemetry & success metrics (must be instrumented before enforcement):
- % of calls using legacyPinToken (by tenant, region, and account tier) — baseline and weekly trend.
- Error rate uplift when we disable legacy acceptance in a canary pool.
- Number of migration support tickets opened per week and mean time to close.
- Number of tenants with automated migration using the SDK script.
- False positive enforcement rate (calls rejected incorrectly) < 0.1% for production enforcement.

Operator checklist (pre-canary):
- [ ] Add legacy_pin_seen and legacy_pin_blocked telemetry events (schema versioned).
- [ ] Create dashboard with tenant breakout and top 50 tenants by legacy usage.
- [ ] Add feature flag: routing.accept_legacy_pin (global + per-tenant override).
- [ ] Smoke test: ensure pin-v2 tokens accepted across hosted/dedicated/private flows.
- [ ] Prepare emergency rollback: ability to re-enable legacy acceptance globally in <15m.

Canary plan (staged):
Stage A (internal):
- Target: internal accounts + sandbox tenants (~5% of traffic).
- Action: turn off legacy acceptance for this cohort; monitor for 72 hours.
- Rollback criteria: >0.5% production-wide latency increase or >0.2% increase in 5xxs attributable to pin errors.

Stage B (low-risk customers):
- Target: small non-SLA customers that opted-in to early migration.
- Action: disable legacy acceptance; support on slack + dedicated migration runbook.
- Monitor ticket volume and per-tenant error spikes for 7 days.

Stage C (enterprise customers):
- Target: tenants with contracts and region-SLA dependencies.
- Action: coordinate Migrations AB with Solutions Eng and legal; apply per-tenant feature flags when ready.

Customer communication (templates & cadence):
- Phase 0 (announcement): "We're introducing a safer, auditable region pin that enables better failover and compliance. Legacy pins will be retired — here's the timeline and migration options." (send 60 days before first enforcement)
- Phase 1 (reminder + migration offer): 30 days before: include migration SDK, one-click console migration, and invite to migration office hours.
- Phase 2 (pre-enforcement warning): 7 days before disabling legacy for their cohort, send explicit warning and migration links.
- Emergency/Exception request: CS can request a 30-day extension via ENG-1503 ticket and must provide migration plan.

Migration tools & automation:
- SDK helper: pin-migrate (python + node) that exchanges legacyPinToken for pin-v2, preserves audit fields, and reloads tenant bindings. (PR linked above — needs docs and tests).
- Console migration flow: quick toggle that issues pin-v2 from existing session when admin verifies region preference.
- Bulk CSV import: for customers with many sub-tenants. Support script checks for collisions and creates migration-change audit events.

Risk matrix (high-level):
- Risk: silent failures for embedded clients using very old SDKs. Mitigation: add user-agent telemetry, target those tenants in migration outreach, and provide embedded SDK patches.
- Risk: customer perceived data-movement when we re-anchor region metadata. Mitigation: include clear language that pin-v2 does not move stored data, only routing metadata.
- Risk: legal/regulatory objections for some sovereign customers. Mitigation: escalate to Product-Legal and offer extended timelines or on-prem migration assistance.

Rollback & emergency runbook:
- If enforcement causes >1% global error surge attributable to pin failures: enable routing.accept_legacy_pin globally and notify SRE oncall.
- If single large tenant (top 5) is impacted: re-enable per-tenant flag and open a dedicated migration incident with CS and Eng.

Open questions and TODOs (work-in-progress):
- Q: Do we want legacyPinToken to continue emitting residency evidence in audit logs post-retirement? Pros: historical trace. Cons: keeps old codepaths in critical flows. (Action: product to decide by 2025-01-20)
- Q: Billing/contract impact if region pin change triggers different pricing (rare). Need legal guidance.
- TODO: add templates for in-console banners and migration office hours sign-up page.
- TODO: schedule cross-functional cutover rehearsal with SRE and Solutions Eng (target week of 2025-02-05).

Customer migration priority heuristics (suggested):
1) Tenants with >50% legacy usage and no dedicated private deployment — high priority (easy fix).
2) Tenants on Private with bespoke routing (requires Solutions Eng) — high touch.
3) Tenants in regulated regions with contractual residency clauses — coordinate legal and offer extended timelines.

Estimated effort (rough):
- Eng infra work + telemetry: 3.5 engineer-months (split across routing, API, feature flags).
- SDK console + docs: 1.0 engineer-month.
- CS enablement + migrations: 0.8 PM-month + 1.0 SE-month over runway.

Appendix: sample escalation snippet for Support engineers:
- If a customer reports a sudden 403/422 during migration window: check tenant feature flags -> check legacy_pin_seen events -> escalate to Eng oncall with correlation_id and sample request headers.

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc purposely mixes tactical runbook items with product/contract considerations — please flag anything that should be split into separate artifacts.
- Looking for approval/comments on: enforcement timeline (9 months default), rollback thresholds, and the customer communication cadence.

End of playbook (working draft).

[Edge scheduler preemption spike investigation notes]
Summary:\nWe observed a cluster-wide spike in scheduler preemptions and pod churn in the edge (us-west1-edge) cluster between 2025-02-11T23:42:00Z and 2025-02-12T00:30:00Z. Visible symptoms: sudden increase in pod evictions, ~30% of pods in edge pool restarted at least once, and a correlated increase in etcd write latency and API-server 5xx errors for ~40 minutes. Impact: customer-facing low-latency endpoints experienced tail latency > 2s and a small fraction (~0.6%) of requests dropped due to backend 500s. No data loss or long-term outages, but degraded SLAs for the window.\n\nInitial hypothesis (v1):\n- A wave of spot/discount node reclaims (cloud provider preemption) triggered aggressive cluster-autoscaler (CA) reactions.\n- CA scaled up on-demand pool but did so with short delay, causing scheduler to reorder work and preempt lower-priority pods to make room for high-priority ones; combined with many small preemptions this caused scheduling thrash and increased API-server load.\n- PodPriority values and PodDisruptionBudgets (PDBs) were not aligned for the most-churned workloads, allowing many preemptions simultaneously.\n\nWhat we saw (data points):\n- Eviction rate: baseline ~0.2 evictions/min -> peaked ~26 evictions/min at 2025-02-11T23:48Z.\n- Scheduler scheduling latency p95: baseline 120ms -> peaked 1.8s.\n- etcd apply latency p95: baseline 7ms -> peaked 120ms.\n- API server 500 rate: 0.03% -> peaked 1.2% of requests.\n- Cloud provider event logs: multiple spot termination notices for nodes in edge-spot-pool around 23:40-23:46Z (IDs: gke-edge-s-*-usw1).\n\nKey timeline (collected from monitoring + oncall notes):\n- 23:37 UTC: First spot termination notice in provider logs.\n- 23:40 UTC: CA sees capacity reduction; starts scale-up attempts into on-demand pool. CA log: "scale-up: need 18 nodes, finding best nodegroup".\n- 23:44 UTC: Evictions start climbing; kube-scheduler preemption events recorded in system logs.\n- 23:48 UTC: Eviction spike peak. Several controllers (ingress, sidecars) create new pods; scheduler attempts to satisfy priorities, preempting multiple low-priority pods across nodes.\n- 23:50 UTC: API server 5xx rate climbs as controllers and nodes flood etcd with updates.\n- 00:02 UTC: Mitigation: oncall ran emergency action: increased on-demand pool min nodes from 8 -> 12 (manual override), cordoned 3 most unstable nodes to reduce churn.\n- 00:15 UTC: Evictions rate drops; scheduler latency returns toward baseline by 00:28 UTC.\n- 00:30 UTC: System stable; follow-ups started.\n\nEvidence snippets (selected):\n- Example scheduler event: "Preempting pod frontend-low-1234 to make room for backend-high-9876 (priority 1000 > 500)"\n- kubectl get pods --field-selector=status.phase!=Running --namespace=prod-edge (snippet during peak):\n  frontend-low-1234  Evicted   23:47:12  Node gke-edge-s-23\n  metrics-agent-5x   Evicted   23:47:20  Node gke-edge-s-12\n- CA log excerpt: "will not scale up: limited by quota in zone us-west1-a" (this delayed >30s for some requests)\n\nImmediate mitigations applied: (actions we took during the incident)\n- Manually increased on-demand pool to absorb incoming pods (oncall: cordon->drain not used broadly to avoid extra evictions). Owner: Miguel.\n- Temporarily relaxed CA scale-down aggressiveness (to avoid removing on-demand nodes quickly).\n- Applied a short-term override to PDB enforcement for low-priority batch jobs (migrated via kubeclient to reduce simultaneous eviction targets).\n- Raised alert threshold for preemption rate so SRE gets earlier signal next time.\n\nRoot-cause analysis (working):\n1) Primary driver: Spot node reclaim wave in edge-spot-pool. Provider returned many preemption notices in a short window.\n2) Secondary driver: CA configuration and node pool quotas caused delayed and batched scale-up decisions (CA had to evaluate quota/limits leading to retries). This made pressure last longer and increased eviction churn.\n3) Contributing factors: a) PodPriority distribution: a number of mid-priority stateful controllers exist that are easily preemptible; b) PDBs did not cover enough of critical services so multiple critical-replaceable pods were evicted simultaneously; c) Some nodes were eligible for preemption and for draining by daemonset controllers causing extra churn; d) Cluster lacked a throttling mechanism for preemption-induced API churn (i.e., many controllers reconciling at once).\n\nWhy this is different from a normal node-pressure event:\n- Node-pressure / OOM events usually show resource exhaustion on nodes that is slower and limited to specific nodes. This event was driven externally (provider reclaim) and caused many small, fast evictions across many nodes, which interacts badly with CA heuristics and scheduler preemption logic.\n\nRunbook gaps we identified:\n- No documented escalation path for "spot reclaim wave" as a first-class event. Runbooks have OOM/pressure and CNI, but not preemption surge guidance.\n- CA configs lack explicit guardrails for sudden multi-node spot loss (e.g., conservative minimum on-demand buffer size per zone).\n- No automation to temporarily throttle controller reconcilers or pace PDB updates during spikes.\n\nProposed follow-ups & action items (owners + ETA):\n- SRE-1422: Add a preemption-surge play to SRE runbook (doc) with exactly these mitigations: temporarily increase on-demand min pool, cordon candidates, and adjust CA flags (owner: Aisha, ETA: 2025-02-21).\n- infra-ops-67: Change CA config: ensure per-zone on-demand buffer of 2 nodes for edge clusters by default (owner: Miguel, ETA: 2025-03-01).\n- sched-65: Review PodPriority tiers and reclassify middle-priority batch jobs as lower priority where acceptable; create stable priority for latency-sensitive services (owner: Priya, ETA: 2025-02-28).\n- pdb-31: Audit existing PDBs for critical services in edge clusters; ensure we don't allow simultaneous eviction of more than 20% of replicas (owner: Noah, ETA: 2025-02-25).\n- metrics-90: Add a new metric and alert: preemption_rate (evictions initiated by preemption) > 5/min for 5m -> page SRE on-call (owner: monitoring, ETA: 2025-02-18).\n- autoscaler-ops-12: Add a CA health-check that detects quota-limited scale-up loops and surfaces an alert to owners instead of silently retrying (owner: infra, ETA: 2025-03-10).\n\nRunbook draft (short) — to be added to ops playbooks: (this is a working checklist for preemption surge)\n- Step 0: Detect: preemption_rate > 5/min OR spot-termination webhook shows > 10 nodes flagged within 5m.\n- Step 1: Assess scope: list affected nodegroups (gcloud/az/eks). tag affected zone.\n- Step 2: Quick mitigation: if on-demand buffer < threshold, manually increase on-demand pool min by +N (N = max(2, floor(spot-lost/3))).\n- Step 3: Cordons: cordon the most unstable nodes (by termination age) but avoid mass drains to prevent cascading evictions.\n- Step 4: CA tuning: disable aggressive scale-down and check quota failures; if CA logs show quota errors, open infra incident with cloudops.\n- Step 5: Stabilize: reduce controller concurrency where safe (helm/patch deployment replicas-> 0? Not generally advised; prefer throttling via annotations if controllers support it).\n- Step 6: Postmortem: capture full CA logs + provider termination notices; reopen for root cause follow-up.\n\nQuick checks & commands used during the incident (notes to self):\n- kubectl get nodes -o wide --selector=pool=edge-spot\n- kubectl get events --all-namespaces --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -n 200 | grep Preempt\n- gcloud compute instances describe <node-id> --zone=us-west1-a | grep termination\n- kubectl -n kube-system logs deployment/cluster-autoscaler | sed -n '1,200p'\n- kubectl get pdb --all-namespaces -o wide | grep edge\n\nOpen questions / unresolved items:\n- Why did CA choose to request such a large number of nodes at once? (suspicion: CA saw pending pods with high resource requests; need to inspect pod resource requests and CA scale-up algorithm logs).\n- Could we have reduced API-server write amplification by queuing certificate/controller writes differently? (need deeper analysis into controller reconcile storms).\n\nNotes to reviewers:\n- This doc is intentionally informal; preserve the timeline and raw snippets. When we convert to the full postmortem, we should add graphs (evictions/min, scheduler latency, etcd latency) and attach CA logs and provider termination list.\n- We should also consider a short-term policy: avoid >40% of edge capacity being spot-backed for business-critical clusters until CA per-zone buffer is implemented.\n\nMisc/learning:\n- Preemption spikes are a distinct failure mode from simple node pressure — they create a cascade by forcing scheduler to mediate resource conflicts quickly across the control plane. Planning and automation should treat 'reclaim wave' as an explicit threat model.\n\nTODO (assigned):\n- Aisha: Draft runbook entry and notify kube-scheduling working group (ETA 2025-02-21).\n- Miguel: Push CA min buffer change to staging, run load test (ETA 2025-02-25).\n- Priya: Audit priorities for edge namespaces and propose remappings (ETA 2025-02-28).\n- Noah: PDB audit and quick fixes for critical services (ETA 2025-02-25).\n\nEnd of notes.\n\n-- raw oncall snippets below (keep for trace) --\n- oncall@redwood: "23:48:12 - seeing mass eviction across edge-spot nodes, API 500s spike"\n- "23:50:33 - miguel: manual on-demand bump applied (min 8->12), cordoned nodes: gke-edge-s-12,gke-edge-s-23,gke-edge-s-30"\n- "00:05:02 - system cooling; evictions down to 3/min"\n\n(If anything here is unclear ping me directly)

[Competitor behavior probe cases and signal harvester]
description:
Background: As open-model availability and vendor feature sets accelerate, we need a lightweight, repeatable way to collect structured competitor behavior signals (latency profiles, quantization variants, API contract deviations, pricing micro-deltas) across regions and workload archetypes. Existing model-landscape docs are high-level; this ticket produces a reproducible 'signal harvester' toolkit and a prioritized set of probe cases that PM, Eng, and Solutions can run with minimal setup.

Goal: Deliver a small, instrumented playbook + artifact set that captures normalized signals across 6 competitor endpoints and 4 synthetic workload archetypes. Output is a CSV/BigQuery-ready schema and a short ops runbook so field teams can re-run probes monthly or on-demand after vendor changes.

Scope (what we'll deliver):
- Probe case catalog (24 cases): regional latency, 1-shot vs streaming, embeddings throughput, quantization-downsampled accuracy, tokenization edge-cases, structured-output stability.
- A lightweight harvester script (Python, `harvester.py`) that runs each probe, collects latency histograms, token counts, error types, and response similarity scores.
- Standardized schema & README for storage (example BigQuery table schema + mapping).
- Rapid runbook for Solutions/SEs and a one-page exec summary for GTM.
- Short dashboard spec (Console view) for top-line signals (latency P50/P95, error rate, compat drift) to feed into weekly model-watch sync.

Out of scope: Deep model-quality evaluations (e.g., adversarial NLG scoring) and long-running synthetic workloads. We will hand off to Research for deeper experiments.

Acceptance criteria:
1) Harvester runs end-to-end in < 45m for the full 24-case matrix under a CI job and uploads results to the canonical storage path.
2) Probe outputs conform to the supplied schema and include required tags (region, model-id, quantization-flag, run-timestamp).
3) Two field tests run by Solutions with different accounts (one NA, one EU) and documented results.
4) Short Console dashboard mock attached and product review approved.

Metrics for success:
- Reproducibility: 95% of probe runs succeed without manual fixes.
- Signal density: At least 8 actionalizable signals per vendor (latency, error spike, API diff, tokenization mismatch).
- Time-to-run: Full matrix completes within target window in >= 90% of CI runs.

Implementation plan (high level):
- Week 1 (PM + Eng): finalize probe matrix, schema, and runbook draft.
- Week 2: Eng builds harvester, basic telemetry, and upload path.
- Week 3: Run field tests (NA/EU), iterate on flaky cases.
- Week 4: Product review, dashboard mock, and publish runbook to Confluence.

Links & artifacts:
- Draft probe matrix (Confluence): https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/MKT/pages/Competitor+Harvester+Draft
- Harvester repo (WIP): https://github.com/redwood-inference/market-harvester/pull/12
- Example payloads and schema: https://drive.redwood.com/drive/folders/market-harvester/samples

Stakeholders:
- PM: Priya Desai (owner)
- Eng: Liam O'Connor (lead), Ana Cortez (runtime advisor)
- Solutions/SE: Carlos Mendes (field runs)
- Research: Elena Fischer (quality handoff)

Risks & trade-offs:
- Running probes against commercial endpoints runs the risk of rate-limiting; we will throttle test concurrency and add retry backoff.
- Vendor TOS may restrict certain automated probes; Solutions will validate account-level permissions before running.
- Harvester aims for speed over depth; for deep model regressions we'll flag and pass to Research.

Next steps: finalize matrix with Eng by 2026-02-02, land initial harvester PR by 2026-02-16, and schedule Solutions field runs for week 2026-02-23.

[Clarify provisional license reclaim window and equipment-return grace period for immediate offboarding]
description:
Issue summary:
HR received reports from Finance and IT that when an employee is placed on Immediate Termination (ITerm) in Workday, the seat/license in third-party SaaS (notably the design/legal tool vendor) remains billable for up to 14 days and the assigned corporate laptop sometimes remains tagged as 'active' in our asset management inventory. This ticket seeks clarification of the intended policy (grace windows) and the operational mechanics (which systems enforce the reclaim/return windows).

Impact:
- Potential short-term double-billing for SaaS seats when seats are quickly re-assigned.
- Delays in device recovery leading to inventory inaccuracies and security exposure for high-risk departures.
- Confusion between HR, IT, and Finance on expected timelines and required manual steps.

Environment:
- Identity sync: Okta -> SCIM -> downstream SaaS (prod)
- Asset tracking: FleetOps (prod) with inventory sync to ITSM
- HR system: Workday (prod)

Observed behavior / Steps to reproduce:
1) Create an employee termination in Workday with 'Immediate' flag at 09:00 UTC.
2) Workday emits termination event, HR webhook updates Okta.
3) Okta SCIM provisioning sends deactivation to SaaS vendor; we observe the user status change but vendor maintains seat as billable for a 14-day grace window (vendor policy).
4) FleetOps does not mark the laptop as 'awaiting pickup' until an asset-handback task is created manually by IT; automatic tagging is not triggered by the termination event.
5) Finance reports a new invoice line for an additional seat 3 days later after license reassign because the old seat was not reclaimed yet.

Logs / evidence: 
- Okta SCIM audit (okta-audit-2026-03-09.log) shows deactivation event at 09:02 UTC and response 200 from vendor with response body: {"status":"deprovision-scheduled","grace_days":14}.
- FleetOps event stream shows no asset lifecycle change tied to the Workday termination event (fleetops-events-2026-03-09.ndjson).
- Finance ticket FIN-1189 referencing unexpected seat charge for week of 2026-03-02.

Question / Requested clarification:
- What are the company-wide defaults for SaaS license reclaim windows and how many days are considered 'standard' vs 'exception' requiring manual immediate reclaim?
- For Immediate Terminations, do we have an established exception/accelerated flow that forces vendor-side seat revocation and device pickup tagging?
- Which teams are expected to take manual actions vs which actions should be automated by identity/asset tooling?

Desired outcome:
- A concise policy statement HR/IT/Finance can rely on for immediate-term offboards, including: default reclaim window, criteria for accelerating reclaim, and the single authoritative runbook link for immediate offboards.

comments:
2026-03-10 11:10 — Marco Ruiz (IT): Noted. In our logs the SCIM response includes vendor-side grace window. We don't currently override vendor windows. IT can manually request offboarding escalation with vendor support but that requires a ticket and often 24–48h processing.
2026-03-10 12:02 — Priya Shah (HR): Can we make 'Immediate' terminations trigger a one-click 'accelerate reclaim' in the HR portal? That would reduce churn between teams.
2026-03-11 09:47 — Ethan Park (Identity): Hypothesis: Okta sets user to 'suspended' and vendor interprets that as soft-deactivate and applies a vendor-side grace window. We can attempt to send a 'hard-delete' SCIM call for critical departures but need legal approval and vendor API support confirmation.
2026-03-11 13:15 — Jana Müller (Finance): Current invoices show an average of 2.3 days of overlap per reassign. Shortening reclaim window will materially affect monthly spend forecasts. Please include Finance in policy decisions.
2026-03-12 08:03 — Support Bot (automated): Linked CONFLUENCE: License Reclaim Policy draft updated (v0.4) — https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/HR/pages/License+Reclaim+Policy

investigation_notes:
Okta->SCIM behavior: The connector implementation uses PATCH to set 'active' to false. Vendor accepts this and sets an internal grace policy (14 days) rather than immediate seat relinquish.
FleetOps integration: Asset lifecycle changes are only triggered by ITSM ticket creation at present; there is no webhook or SCIM-driven asset tagging for device pickup. This is a gap for immediate offboards.
Workday mapping: 'Immediate' termination is mapped to Okta attribute 'terminationType=immediate' but that attribute is not propagated to downstream SCIM calls currently; therefore downstream vendors cannot differentiate Immediate vs standard terminations.
Hypothesis: If Okta emitted a 'terminationType' custom attribute or we used a 'hard-delete' SCIM call on certain vendors, seats could be reclaimed faster, but vendor policies and contracts may prohibit forced immediate deletion (data retention concerns).

resolution_notes:
Tentative operational plan agreed on 2026-03-12:
1) Policy clarification: Default reclaim window remains vendor-determined; for 'Immediate' terminations, HR + IT will follow an accelerated flow.
2) Automation tasks: Identity team to add terminationType flag propagation to SCIM (Ethan Park) and to implement a 'hard-delete' option gated behind a documented approval step.
3) Asset tagging: FleetOps to listen for Workday/Okta terminationType events and auto-tag devices as 'awaiting-security-pickup' (IT will still approve pickup).
4) Finance: will be looped into the vendor contract review to identify vendors that support immediate seat removal vs those with mandatory grace windows.
5) Runbook: Create a concise 'Immediate Offboard' runbook in Confluence with decision tree and contact channel (#it-offboarding).
Follow-ups (action items): [INT-821408] implement SCIM terminationType propagation; [INT-821409] FleetOps webhook for immediate offboard tagging; legal to review vendor TOS for forced seat deletion.
Notes: Until automation is in place, manual vendor escalation is the workaround for high-risk departures. This ticket should remain open until the SCIM flag propagation PR (INT-821408) is merged and FleetOps webhook (INT-821409) is live.

[Okta group expiry policy blocks temporary access to Feature Flags console for contractors]
description:
Issue summary: Several contractors reported immediate 403 / Access Denied when opening the Feature Flags console after receiving a temporary access approval. Impact: Contractors who were previously in ff-admin-like groups were removed by Okta due to an applied group expiry policy (Okta Lifecycle), causing RBAC lookups to deny access. This affects runbooks and time-sensitive release toggles.

Observed behavior: After approval flow completes, the user lands on the console sign-in but receives 403 and no RBAC roles are returned. Okta System Log shows a GroupMembership.deactivate event for the contractor groups around the same timestamp as the approval. SCIM provisioner logs show a subsequent "ignored" deprovision event attributable to an attribute mapping mismatch (expiredUntil != expirationDate).

Expected behavior: Temporary access approvals should result in users being in a valid group/role for the requested TTL and SCIM + RBAC should remain consistent for the life of that approval. Group expiry policy changes in Okta should not silently drop active temporary approvals without a re-provision attempt or alert.

Business impact: Blocks contractors from completing feature flag reviews and emergency toggles; could delay production fixes.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Provision contractor user and add to 'contractor-ff-admins' with Okta expiry set to 7 days
2) Trigger self-service temporary approval (internal feature-flags console) and complete SSO sign-in
3) Observe immediate 403 on console even though approval flow completed
4) Check Okta System Log for GroupMembership.deactivate and SCIM provisioner logs for a rejected deprovision mapping

logs:
Okta System Log: 2026-03-10T14:02:03Z GroupMembership.deactivate userId=00u9abcD reason=expiry policy
SCIM Provisioner: 2026-03-10T14:02:04Z WARN - incoming group change: user=evan.contributor@acme.com mapping mismatch: expiredUntil vs expirationDate -> action=ignored
RBAC Service: 2026-03-10T14:02:05Z INFO - lookup roles for userId=00u9abcD returned empty set (cache miss)

comments:
Evan Morales (Reporter) 2026-03-10: Customer-facing contractor reported 403 after approval completed; raising as P1 since it blocks releases.
Oncall (SRE) 2026-03-10: Initial triage - looks like Okta group expiry events are arriving during approval flow. Suspect lifecycle policy change push last night.
Priya Nair (Assignee) 2026-03-10: Assigned. Reproduced locally with test contractor account. Will instrument SCIM mapping and propose workaround.
Identity Eng (Aisha Patel) 2026-03-11: Confirmed Okta org has a new Group Expiry Rule applied to groups with name pattern 'contractor-*' rolled out 2026-03-09. SCIM mapping expects 'expirationDate' while Okta uses 'expiredUntil' TTL attribute in this rule.

investigation_notes:
2026-03-10 14:30 UTC - Reproduced with test account; auth flow completes but RBAC returns empty due to missing group membership row.
2026-03-10 15:10 UTC - Reviewed Okta System Logs: batch of GroupMembership.deactivate events coincide with approval timestamps. No explicit re-provision attempt observed.
2026-03-10 16:00 UTC - SCIM Provisioner (provisioner-3) code path ignores group change when attribute key != configured mapping; attribute key mismatch 'expiredUntil' vs 'expirationDate' prevents deactivation handling path from reconciling state.
2026-03-11 09:00 UTC - Session behavior: existing active sessions continue until cookie expiry; new logins fail because group membership already removed in Okta and not present in RBAC DB.
Hypothesis: Recent Okta Lifecycle rule introduced a TTL attribute key name incompatible with our SCIM mapping. SCIM treats deprovision events as 'ignored', leaving RBAC in inconsistent state (no re-add).

resolution:
Workaround applied 2026-03-11: Identity Eng rolled back the Okta Group Expiry Rule for 'contractor-*' groups to prevent further deactivations. Manually reconciled 14 affected contractor accounts by re-provisioning group memberships and running the RBAC sync job.

Permanent fix: Update SCIM provisioner mapping to accept both 'expiredUntil' and 'expirationDate' attributes, and add an alert rule for sudden group membership delta (>5% change in 5 minutes) for monitored groups. Created follow-up INT task to ship the mapping change and tests.

Follow-ups: identity team to schedule a postmortem and update the approval flow to validate group membership post-Okta events before presenting final success to the user.

[Delegated access approval links expire immediately for some SSO sessions]
description:
Issue summary:
Users attempting to use delegated access approval links (used by Support/SRE to grant temporary console access) see an immediate 'link expired' error even when they open the link within minutes of generation. This affects a subset of internal users and appears correlated with sessions created via our legacy SSO route (Okta session created by older IdP cookie path).

Impact:
- Prevents on-call engineers from granting temporary elevated access via the normal approval flow.
- Blocks urgent troubleshooting workflows for production dashboards and runbooks.
- Affects ~8-12% of approval links generated in the past 48 hours for prod-us-east.

Timeline and initial detection:
- 2026-03-09 22:10 UTC: First customer-facing report from Support noticing multiple failed approvals during an incident triage.
- 2026-03-10 08:05 UTC: Ticket opened by Maya after reproducing with a test account.
- 2026-03-11 02:30 UTC: SRE confirmed pattern spans multiple Okta issuers; not all sessions affected.

Steps to reproduce:
1) From console, request delegated access for user alice@example.com using the Support->Request A Grant flow.
2) Approval service generates a one-time approval link and emails Slack notification.
3) Click the approval link using a browser session that already has an Okta SSO session (created via legacy-idp redirect).
4) Observe page shows: 'Approval link expired' even though the link timestamp is within 2 minutes of generation.

Expected behavior:
Approval link validates the one-time token against the approval-service store and Okta session, then displays an approve/deny UI. Token TTL is 10 minutes.

Actual behavior:
Approval service returns 401/400 flow with message 'token validation failed: session mismatch' and UI surface shows 'Approval link expired'.

Relevant logs / errors (samples):
- approval-service (2026-03-10T08:06:12Z): WARN token_validation: tid=8f3b, user=alice, reason=okta_session_cookie_missing, issuer=okta-legacy-1
- identity-proxy (2026-03-10T08:06:12Z): DEBUG auth: inbound-cookie: OktaSession=; path=/; secure=true; samesite=None
- console-ui (2026-03-10T08:06:12Z): ERROR approval-ui: display_token_error: token=8f3b, user-facing='Approval link expired'

Additional context:
- A/B testing shows the same flow works when the approval link is opened in a fresh browser session (no existing Okta cookie).
- Suspected the identity-proxy is reading the Okta cookie but returning an empty value for legacy-session paths (cookie path mismatch + recent cookie path normalization rollout).
- This manifests as approval-service requiring an Okta session (for identity binding) but receiving none so it rejects token.

Notes on frequency and scope:
- Observed ~150 failures in last 24 hours (prod-us-east) out of ~1.5k generated links.
- Affected users primarily have desktop browsers with older cookie jars or have been SSO-redirected by legacy-idp shortcuts.

[openai-compat: responses-v3 deterministic-seed routing + metadata passthrough and streaming reassembly]
description:
Motivation: the OpenAI Responses API v3 introduces a seed/determinism flag and richer per-response metadata fields. Customers expecting parity through our OpenAI compatibility layer were hitting two classes of issues: 1) requests with deterministic seeds sometimes routed to fallback model variants causing non-deterministic behavior, and 2) streaming reassembly and function/tool-calling events lost user-supplied metadata (e.g., trace ids) on intermediate fragments. This PR: - Propagates the new 'seed' and 'determinism' fields from OpenAI-style Requests through our compatibility translation layer so upstream callers can control RNG determinism when we map to compatible model variants. - Adds per-request metadata passthrough: preserves and forwards top-level metadata and nested response-level metadata (user supplied) through streaming frames and the final assembled Response object. - Stabilizes streaming reassembly for mixed partials (text chunks, tool call fragments, structured JSON outputs) by introducing a sequence/frame id and last-frame markers in the compat layer; this avoids interleaving when a single call fan-outs to auxiliary model variants. - Ensures function/tool-calling events are emitted with the original 'metadata' and 'seed' fields intact so SDKs relying on tool traceability continue to work. - Adds exhaustive integration tests against the Responses v3 contract and extends streaming unit tests to emulate packet reorder and intermittent delivery. Implementation notes: - New compatibility translator: redwood/openai_compat/responses_v3_translator.py maps OpenAI fields to internal inference request flags (seed->rng_seed, determinism->sampling_profile). Translator is intentionally minimal: we preserve unknown fields in a passthrough map under compat_metadata for future extensions. - Streaming layer changes: redwood/api/streaming.py: implement frame_sequence_id and final_fragment bool. Reassembly uses (request_id, frame_sequence_id) ordering plus a small re-sequencing buffer gated by latency_slo to avoid head-of-line blocking. - Routing: routing/policy.py updated to prefer exact-architecture variants when determinism is requested; fallback still allowed if pinned variant unavailable. - Tests: tests/integration/test_responses_v3_compat.py includes deterministic-seed repeatability checks, metadata round-trip assertions, and simulated packet reordering scenarios. - Docs: docs/openai_compat.md updated with Responses v3 mapping and guidance for determinism semantics. Backwards compatibility: default behavior unchanged if seed/determinism not provided. We intentionally do not make determinism true by default because it impacts throughput. Checklist: - [x] Translator for seed/determinism fields - [x] Metadata passthrough in streaming frames - [x] Stable reassembly and ordering buffer - [x] Routing preference when determinism requested - [x] Integration + unit tests - [x] Docs update - [x] CI passing on rerun Rollout/rollback notes: feature gated behind a compatibility flag (OPENAI_COMPAT_V3=true) and an experiment toggle for routing. If customer issues are observed around tail latency with deterministic requests, the routing policy can be relaxed to fallback earlier while preserving seed values in logs for replay/diagnosis.

[Responses v3 compatibility shim: resilient stream stitching, function-call fidelity, and deterministic-seed propagation]
description:
Introduces a compatibility shim and runtime fixes to support an evolving Responses v3 streaming envelope used by OpenAI-compatible clients. This PR addresses three user-visible classes of issues observed under load: (1) fragmented streaming frames that split UTF-8 token boundaries or split function_call tool frames which caused out-of-order assembly, (2) loss or mutation of function_call intent during gateway->router->worker handoffs and cross-region fallbacks, and (3) client-specified seed/determinism flags and arbitrary response-level metadata not being forwarded into the serving pipeline or audit rows. The implementation normalizes incoming v3 envelopes into a compact internal event model, provides a deterministic reassembly algorithm that stitches partial byte sequences and tool frames, serializes function_call intent into the routing context to survive asynchronous queuing and fallbacks, and attaches client seed and metadata to the request context and audit enrichment. The feature is behind a runtime flag openai_responses_v3_compat and gated by an explicit client-version header so that older traffic is unaffected. Rollout plan: dark-launch 10% traffic, staging dogfood with end-to-end tracing, canary ramp to 50% then promote after 48 hours of stability. Includes unit/fuzz tests for reassembly invariants, an integration fallback scenario to validate header preservation, SDK adapters in TypeScript/Python, CI pipeline additions, and docs for SDK consumers and operator flags.

[OpenAI-bridge v4: seed propagation and metadata forwarding for Responses]
description:
Context: Customers are starting to adopt the OpenAI Responses v4 style endpoint and expect parity with existing v3/v2 behavior for determinism controls and metadata propagation. Prior attempts preserved basic streaming compatibility but lost deterministic seed hints and user metadata when routed through the OpenAI compatibility layer. This caused flaky repros for customers relying on 'client_seed' and made audit logs incomplete.

This PR implements three coordinated changes to the compat bridge and runtime: 1) deterministic seed propagation: accept an optional client_seed|seed_hint field on the mapped Responses v4 request and reliably propagate it through the bridge into the internal InferenceRequest seed field (used by deterministic sampling kernels). Seed is stored on the canonical ResponseRecord so downstream logs/keys include it. 2) metadata forwarding: user-supplied metadata blob (freeform JSON) is attached to the ResponseRecord and surfaced in internal telemetry and audit exporters, with size-limits and sanitization. The compat shim no longer strips top-level user_metadata fields. 3) streaming stability + reassembly: streaming packets are now annotated with a stream_chunk_index and seed_affinity flag to ensure reassembly logic groups tokens emitted under the same seed context, preventing cross-chunk reseeding that caused non-deterministic outputs during stream reconnects. 

Checklist: 
- [x] API mapping and translation layer implementation (pkg/bridge)
- [x] Kernel/runtime plumbing to accept propagated seed (internal/runtime)
- [x] Streaming reassembly changes and tests
- [x] SDK helpers in python/ts to expose seed and metadata on client side
- [x] E2E tests and CI matrix updates
- [x] Docs (api-mapping/responses-v4.md)

Compatibility notes: This change preserves the existing default behavior when no seed/client_seed is provided. When a seed is supplied, it acts as a deterministic hint for sampling kernels; we do NOT guarantee bit-exact outputs across hardware variants. The seed is honored deterministically within a single runtime configuration. For customers using Dedicated or Private deployments, the seed propagation is a no-op unless the underlying runtime is configured to enable deterministic sampling.

Security and privacy: forwarded user_metadata is rate- and size-limited (4KB) and scrubbed of known sensitive keys (password, ssn, credit_card) with a best-effort redaction. Audit-exporter tests updated to include user_metadata.

Migration: No breaking changes to public Redwood API. OpenAI-compat clients can start attaching 'client_seed' and 'user_metadata' in Requests v4 body; SDK helpers added to python/ts to make this ergonomic.

Related: ENG-1347 (compat), ENG-1412 (streaming-reassembly), SUP-9021 (customer case).

[openai-bridge-v5: preserve determinism hints and annotated metadata in Responses compatibility]
description:
Motivation: New OpenAI Responses variants expose two practical features we need to support in the compatibility bridge: (1) determinism hints that affect rerolling/seeded inference (not always a raw numeric seed), and (2) an annotated metadata envelope that clients expect to be passed through back to their application layer. Without preserving these we see mismatch between Redwood responses and customer expectations (reproducibility and attribution).\n\nWhat this PR does: Adds a compatibility layer in the OpenAI bridge that: 1) accepts the newer 'determinism_hint' top-level field (and the legacy 'seed' when present) and maps both into an internal safe representation (x-rdwd-determinism-hint) which is forwarded to the serving runtime and persisted with the response event. 2) accepts an 'annotations' / 'metadata' object from incoming Responses-style requests, validates it against a white-list (string keys, small scalar values) and forwards it as an opaque envelope into our response records and emitted events. 3) improves streaming reassembly by introducing "liveness anchors"—small sequence markers attached to partial events so the client can reconstitute ordered structured outputs even when chunks arrive out of order. 4) ensures tool/function calling headers (x-rdwd-toolcall-id, x-rdwd-toolcall-wrap) are carried through the bridge to the tool runtime and mapped back into the OpenAI-compatible "tool_call" frames so SDKs receive function call events as expected.\n\nCompatibility and fallbacks: The bridge recognizes multiple Response variants via a 'response_variant' flag (v1/v2/v5). For older requests we fall back to prior behavior. For determinism, if both 'seed' and 'determinism_hint' are provided we prefer the explicit 'determinism_hint' and log an inspector warning. Customers using Redwood Dedicated with strict determinism can pin a deterministic profile; the bridge now surfaces the upstream hint for audit and replay.\n\nDesign notes (high level): - Minimal surface: use header translation (x-rdwd-*) rather than changing core request schemas. This keeps the runtime agnostic and limits blast radius. - Validation: annotations are size-limited (max 2KB serialised), keys must match ^[a-z_][a-z0-9_]*$, values must be strings or numbers. Invalid annotations are dropped and a warning returned in the response 'warnings' array. - Streaming anchors: binary-safe 8-byte anchor appended to the metadata of each partial event. Receiver reassembly uses anchor order, then sequence index. Anchor collisions are rare and cause a compact re-fetch of the missing shard. - Toolcall mapping: toolcall headers are stable strings; we generate a synthetic 'tool_origin' attribute that ties the function invocation back to the original request's metadata envelope.\n\nTests and CI: Added unit tests in bridge tests covering mapping and validation, integration tests that spin up the openai-compat harness and verify function-call roundtrips, and an e2e streaming test that simulates chunk reordering and validates reassembly. Also added a small dedicated load test that measures latency impact of anchor embedding (negligible in our quick runs).\n\nCommits (summary): - Add compatibility translator for determinism_hint and seed -> bridge/header mapping - Validate and forward annotations envelope to events store - Implement liveness anchors for streaming reassembly and consumer helper - Propagate toolcall headers through bridge to tool runtime and back to OpenAI frames - Tests: unit + integration + streaming e2e harness - Docs: how-to and compatibility notes in docs/openai_compat.md\n\nFiles changed (high level): ["src/bridge/openai_compat.ts", "runtime/stream/anchor_reassembly.go", "api/handlers/toolcall_proxy.py", "docs/openai_compat.md", "tests/bridge/test_determinism.ts", "tests/integration/test_toolcall_roundtrip.py", "tests/e2e/test_stream_anchor_reassembly.sh", "pkg/events/annotations.go", "pkg/events/events_store_migration.sql", "ci/workflows/openai-compat.yml", "examples/openai/response-variant-samples.json", "README.md"]\n\nPatch snippet (illustrative, kept tiny):\nconst mapped = {\n  headers: {\n    ...incoming.headers,\n    'x-rdwd-determinism-hint': incoming.body.determinism_hint || incoming.body.seed || undefined\n  },\n  metadata: validatedAnnotations(incoming.body.annotations)\n};\n\nReview conversation (condensed):\n- Arjun Patel: "Nice focused change. Two asks: (1) can we avoid adding anchors to every single token event by coalescing them when streaming rate is > 200 RPS? (2) add stronger unit tests for malformed annotations."\n- Maya Singh (author): "Answer: we coalesce anchors when rate threshold hit (see runtime/stream/coalesce.go left-in). Added more tests for malformed keys and oversized payloads."\n- Sofia Reyes: "Please confirm metrics emitted for dropped annotations and the inspector warning shape. Also check security review for arbitrary metadata size/keys."\n- Maya Singh: "Metrics added: bridge.annotations.dropped and bridge.annotations.accepted. Security: white-list + size limit. I ran a short audit and added doc note."\n- Ben Kwan: "Integration passed locally but CI hit a flakey test on macos runner (socket timeout). Rerun fixed it."\n- Arjun Patel: "LGTM after semantics clarified on deterministic precedence. Approving now."\n\nCI status history: initial CI run: lint pass, unit tests pass, integration tests fail (timeout on test_toolcall_roundtrip.py), rerun integration -> pass, workflow green. Coverage delta: +0.6%.\n\nNotes for release: This change is non-breaking for the vast majority of users. Customers that depended on silently dropping unknown top-level fields should verify their clients if they rely on exact payload shapes. We added two documented headers (x-rdwd-determinism-hint, x-rdwd-toolcall-id) and the annotations envelope behavior to docs/openai_compat.md.\n\nRelated: ENG-1429 (compatibility with Responses v5), ENG-1587 (structured streaming reassembly).

[OpenAI-compat: Support Responses API variants + seed/determinism flags and metadata passthrough]
description:
Problem: The OpenAI Responses API introduced a set of semantics (responses vs completions, explicit seed/determinism controls, and response-level metadata passthrough) that our OpenAI-compatibility layer did not fully honor. This caused incorrect caching behavior, sporadic nondeterministic results in determinism test suites, and loss of user-supplied metadata when proxying requests.

This PR implements end-to-end support for the new Responses API variants in the compatibility shim, including: mapping `responses.mode` to appropriate model routing, plumbing `seed` and `deterministic` flags through to our runtime so user-requested determinism is honored, and preserving arbitrary `metadata` objects from request -> internal request -> response. It also includes several small streaming stability fixes uncovered while testing long-running streaming responses (fragment reassembly and backpressure on partial tool calls).

What changed (high level):
- Add a Responses-compatible request parser that accepts both completions and responses shapes and normalizes to our internal request model.
- Expose `seed` and `deterministic` parameters in the OpenAI-compat layer and ensure those are communicated to the runtime scheduling/kernel selection codepath so quantization/batching heuristics avoid interfering with deterministic runs.
- Preserve `metadata` keys on the proxied request and include them verbatim on the returned response envelope; add whitelist-based passthrough config for enterprise users wanting stronger controls.
- Streaming fixes: ensure partial tool/function call events include metadata and stream markers in the same envelope to avoid reassembly ambiguity for clients. Add idempotent reassembly on the client-side helper we publish in the SDKs.
- Tests: add unit and integration tests for parse/serialize roundtrips, deterministic seeds, and an end-to-end streaming canary that exercises large payload streaming + metadata passthrough.

Checklist:
- [x] Compatibility parsing and normalization
- [x] Runtime flags plumbing (seed/deterministic)
- [x] Metadata passthrough + enterprise whitelist config
- [x] Streaming reassembly fixes and unit tests
- [x] Integration canary and e2e tests in eval-harness
- [x] Documentation snippets and migration notes in redwood-docs

Design notes and rationale:
- Determinism is best-effort across lower-level optimizations. We mark requests with determinism metadata and ensure the scheduler selects single-worker, non-batched execution when deterministic=true or seed is set. This increases latency/cost for those requests; documentation and telemetry flag these requests separately so customers can understand tradeoffs.
- Metadata passthrough is implemented as a minimal-copy envelope change at the compatibility shim boundary; we deliberately avoid schema enforcement in the shim and provide an enterprise toggle to enforce a server-side whitelist for regulated customers.
- Streaming: inconsistent partial envelopes were the main cause of reassembly bugs — we now include sequence numbers and a final=true marker for tool call closures; SDK helpers were adjusted accordingly.

Backward compatibility and migration: The shim accepts both old completions-style requests and the newer responses payloads. Most customers require no change. For deterministic workloads, customers should set `deterministic: true` or provide `seed` to get reproducible outputs; documentation link: https://docs.redwood.ai/openai-compat#responses-determinism

Rollout plan:
- Feature behind compat flag `openai_responses_v2` on the tenancy and account level.
- Canary rollout to 2% of traffic for 48 hours with synthetic prompts exercising streaming and deterministic paths.
- Monitor token-latency, deterministic-error-rate, and metadata-loss metrics in console.

Related: Linear ENG-4821, PM-219. See also the eval-harness PR that adds the deterministic test vectors.

Jordan Park: Streaming reassembly looked flaky in initial run — fixed race by adding sequence numbers and final marker; reran streaming canary and all passes.

OpenAI-compat: Adds support for Responses API variants including seed/deterministic flags and metadata passthrough. Deterministic requests will select single-worker, non-batched execution — may increase latency/cost. Feature is behind `openai_responses_v2` flag; see docs for migration steps.

HMAC / KMS approach (one-way tokenization)
- Mechanism: compute HMAC(key=customer_kms_key, message=raw_trace_id || customer_id) and store the HMAC value as the token in logs.

- Mechanism: a small SDK or sidecar inspects outgoing requests and removes or replaces configured fields before they leave your network.

- Mechanism: run a mapping service in your VPC that returns short-lived opaque IDs. Redwood only sees these opaque IDs. TTL configurable (e.g., 6h–24h).
- Advantage: allow short-lived correlation without long-term risk.

[Unit cost investigation - Zephyrus Labs]
summary:
Intro discovery to map Zephyrus' usage patterns, target latency and strict monthly budget. Main discussion focused on per-token unit economics, batching and KV/prefix caching tradeoffs, hosted vs dedicated cost and private deployment compliance (VPC/KMS/SOC2). Agreed next steps: pilot scope and micro-benchmarks.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-25 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Ethan Cole (Zephyrus Head of ML), Lina Morales (Platform Eng), Rafael Hu (Finance), Amara Singh (CTO)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, Jordan from Redwood. Thanks for taking the time. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Ethan: Ethan here.
[00:10] Lina: Lina.
[00:12] Rafael: Rafael.
[00:14] Amara: Amara.
[00:16] Priya: Priya from the solutions eng side. Happy to dig into benchmarks.

[00:28] Jordan: High level agenda — understand Zephyrus workloads (qps, typical prompt/response lengths), budget constraints, latency SLOs, and tradeoffs between hosted, dedicated, and private. Then outline a pilot. Sound good?
[00:36] Amara: Yep that's perfect. We're specifically worried about token burn — our legal and finance team are nervous about runaway costs if we spike.

[01:05] Ethan: Quick context: we run an assistant that summarizes internal docs and generates code suggestions. Average request is 750 tokens input, 600 tokens output, peak qps around 8 but most of the day it's 1-2 qps. We want sub-400ms latency for short assistant flows but 1-2s is okay for longer generation. Budget ceiling per month for inference is $45k.

[01:47] Rafael: And just to be explicit — we need predictable unit economics. If we do hosted, how do we cap spend or get alerts? If dedicated, what's the break-even?

[02:12] Priya: Great, those are the right levers. A few concepts to set expectations: per-token pricing (hosted), reserved GPU cost for Dedicated (committed monthly), and private / VPC which adds a platform fee. Then there are runtime levers — batching, prefix/KV cache, and quantization which materially change cost per token.

[02:50] Lina: Can you quantify — like if we enable KV cache and batch to 8 requests, does cost drop 30%? 50%?

[03:12] Priya: It depends on request distribution. For a lot of small repeated queries, prefix/KV caching can be 40-70% savings on recurrent tokens. For our serving runtime with continuous batching, you typically see 20-45% effective token-cost reduction vs naive single-request inference when batching to sizes of 4-8 and keeping latency SLOs. But for long outputs (600 tokens) batching often helps amortize overhead so savings can be smaller per token but large in throughput terms. Those are rough numbers; we'll run a micro-benchmark on your prompt set.

[04:05] Ethan: When you say prefix cache — does that store user context in KV on GPUs? We're concerned about PII persistence and retention.

[04:22] Priya: Good point. We let customers configure cache policies. For hosted we can do ephemeral KV cache not logged to persistent storage; for Dedicated/Private you can point cache to your own managed store or disable it entirely. We also support TTLs and zero-retention modes. We'll include KMS details in the security pack.

[05:10] Rafael: From finance perspective — show us break-even for dedicated. If our peak qps is 8 but steady is 1-2, committed capacity might be wasteful unless autoscaling with burst works.

[05:32] Jordan: Exactly. Dedicated has a committed GPU pool and predictable throughput. We have automatic burst options and routing policies — fall back to hosted variants when reserved capacity is saturated. The break-even is driven by utilization: if you use >~65% of a reserved token throughput for the month, dedicated typically becomes cheaper. But again depends heavily on model size, quantization, and batching.

[06:10] Amara: Can you explain quantization here? We have some internal concerns about quality regressions.

[06:21] Priya: We offer QC profiles — 8-bit and mixed-precision quantization paths. For many of the open models we onboard, 8-bit gives near-parity for most generation tasks, but we'll run evaluations on your eval set to measure delta. Redwood Optimize will recommend quantization profiles per workload and flag regressions.

[07:00] Ethan: Ok so pilot looks like: run our representative small/medium/large prompts, measure latency, tokens, and quality under three modes: hosted (standard), dedicated reserved pool with autoscale/burst, and private VPC. Also measure with/without KV cache and batching.

[07:28] Priya: That's our usual micro-benchmark. We'll need sample prompts, sample traffic shape (qps histogram), and expected SLOs per route. Also any blocked tokens or redaction rules.

[08:00] Lina: On the private/VPC side — will Redwood manage the control plane or do we need to run anything on-prem?

[08:18] Jordan: For Private we offer a customer-managed data plane, optional on-prem pack, and a private control plane. You can choose the model — VPC peered control plane or fully air-gapped. KMS/HSM integrations are supported. We'll surface the architecture diagram in the security docs.

[08:45] Rafael: SOC2 and audit logs are non-negotiable. We need API-level audit for token lineage and RBAC.

[08:58] Priya: We have per-token tracing and token-level cost attribution in the Console. Audit logs and SSO/SAML with SCIM are supported; we'll attach our SOC2 report and the logging sample.

[09:22] Ethan: Competitor question — how do you compare to Anthropic/openai on pricing?

[09:30] Jordan: On raw hosted per-token, we're competitive on open models, and for dedicated we can beat managed endpoints when utilization is high due to GPU amortization and batching optimizations. Also our routing and fallback gives predictable latency during spikes. We'll include a competitor compsheet.

[10:02] Lina: About throttles and spend controls — can we enforce hard monthly caps or per-route budgets?

[10:12] Priya: Yes — we support per-route quotas, alerts, and hard limits. For hosted we can set quota thresholds and soft limits; for Dedicated we can add caps in the control plane and also route to lower-cost model variants when thresholds are hit.

[10:45] Amara: For our planning, can you give an example calculation? Say 1.5 qps steady, 45k budget, average total tokens per call 1350, what do we look at?

[11:00] Jordan: Quick back-of-envelope: steady 1.5 qps is ~129,600 requests/month (1.5 * 3600 * 24 * 30). At 1,350 tokens per request that's ~175M tokens/month. If hosted per-token = $0.00003 per token (example), that would be about $5.25k — but that per-token number varies by model and context — embedding vs gen different. If using larger model and higher per-token rates, it scales up. The key is batching, caching and model choice can drop effective cost per served token considerably. We'll produce scenarios with realistic per-token rates for the models you want.

[12:10] Rafael: That example number seems low — are you counting both input and output?

[12:18] Priya: Yes both. But remember per-token rates differ for input vs output on some pricing plans; we'll annotate that. Also for long outputs, batching helps less for tail latency so effective cost per user request might be higher; that's why we do the benchmark.

[13:00] Speaker 6 (mumble): question on caching architecture — how is cache invalidation handled?

[13:10] Priya: Cache invalidation is TTL-based and explicit API calls to clear prefix keys. For shared contexts we recommend a short TTL and user-scope keys. We'll document recommended policies.

[14:05] Ethan: On measurement — we want to be able to attribute cost to features and products internally. Can Redwood break down cost per route and per token type?

[14:18] Jordan: Yes the Console provides token-level cost breakdown, route-level dashboards, and traceable request IDs. You can export CSVs for cost allocation.

[15:00] Lina: Any limitations on model pinning across hosted and dedicated? We want consistent behavior when we roll from hosted to dedicated.

[15:12] Priya: You can pin model versions and rollout policies. The same model artifact can be used across hosted and dedicated; kernel selection and quantization may vary but we try to keep behavior consistent. We recommend a canary rollout to validate outputs.

[16:00] Rafael: Inventory question — what's the minimal committed term for Dedicated? Monthly? Annual?

[16:12] Jordan: We have monthly and annual reserved options. Monthly reserves give flexibility; annual reserves give pricing advantages. We'll include a few reserved capacity price points in the pilot materials.

[16:40] Ethan: Tuning question — will Redwood suggest batching configs automatically?

[16:48] Priya: Redwood Optimize recommends batch sizes and cache policies based on observed latency distribution and usage patterns. You can also set hard latency SLOs and it will suggest conservative batch sizes to meet them.

[17:20] Amara: Ok, quality. We need to run our eval set for rouge/bleu and also human spot checks. If quantization drops accuracy for our code suggestions, we need a rollback plan.

[17:33] Priya: Absolutely — we'll run model regression evals and tie alerts to quality thresholds. Rollback is supported and we suggest progressive rollouts.

[18:00] Jordan: Quick risks — unpredictable spikes, long-tail requests that blow up tokens, and data residency/compliance. How important is region residency?

[18:12] Amara: Strongly prefer EU residency for certain customers. We need logs and data at rest in EU for some cases.

[18:28] Jordan: We support region pinning and private deployments in selected regions. We'll note the regions available for Private.

[19:05] Rafael: Financial ask — show a 12-month spend plan for hosted vs dedicated with scenarios Low/Med/High usage.

[19:18] Jordan: We'll prepare a 12-month spreadsheet with break-even points and sensitivity to avg tokens, qps, and batch sizes.

[20:00] Ethan: For the pilot telemetry — what logs do you need from our side?

[20:08] Priya: Representative prompt set, qps histogram, target eval queries, and any per-request metadata you want to propogate like tenant-id so we can show cost attribution. Also a sample of blocked tokens/redaction rules.

[20:45] Lina: How long does a typical pilot take?

[20:52] Jordan: Micro-benchmarking can start in a week and results in 5-7 business days. A fuller pilot with regression evals and dedicated capacity tests is typically 3-4 weeks.

[21:20] Rafael: On procurement — any security questionnaires we can pre-fill?

[21:27] Jordan: We'll send an NDA/security packet, SOC2, and a standardized security questionnaire. We can also fill customer security questionnaires as part of the enterprise process.

[22:00] Ethan: Wanted to raise a potential blocker — our legal might force us to avoid sending PII to hosted endpoints. If so, private on-prem is likely. How much overhead for private?

[22:14] Priya: Private incurs an onboarding and platform fee and possibly on-prem infra. We can give a cost delta and implementation plan. For many customers we do a VPC/private control plane which reduces friction versus full on-prem.

[23:05] Amara: Any quick wins we should try first to reduce token-cost before changing architecture?

[23:12] Priya: Prompt engineering: truncation, instruction tuning to shorten outputs, caching repeated prefixes, and aggressive batching for non-latency-critical routes. Also using a smaller model variant for lower-cost routes.

[24:00] Lina: Are you able to run a quick sim for our 1.5 qps baseline during the pilot to validate queueing/latency under burst?

[24:12] Priya: Yes — we'll simulate steady and burst patterns, and show latency percentiles and cost.

[25:00] Ethan: On reporting — we want monthly alerts if any route goes > 20% above forecast.

[25:08] Jordan: That's doable. We'll configure cost monitors and Slack/webhook alerts.

[26:00] Rafael: Curious — for auditing token lineage, do you store raw tokens? How is redaction handled?

[26:12] Priya: By default we do not persist raw input tokens for hosted customers unless explicitly enabled for debugging. For Dedicated/Private you control persistence. Redaction hooks can filter PII before logs.

[27:20] Ethan: Ok final thing — show us a sample SLA for Dedicated latency targets.

[27:30] Jordan: Dedicated SLA typically commits to P99 latency targets for a class of requests and uptime. We'll send the SLA draft.

[28:00] Amara: Good. Let's summarize next steps so everyone is aligned.

[28:06] Jordan: Summary recap: 1) Jordan sends pilot scope including hosted/dedicated/private cost scenarios and 12-month spend model 2) Priya runs micro-benchmark on the sample prompts with/without KV cache and batching and shares results 3) Customer provides prompt set, qps histogram, and compliance contacts. Any additions?

[28:36] Ethan: Add security docs and SOC2.

[28:40] Rafael: And a finance-specific break-even table comparing monthly vs annual Dedicated reserves.

[28:50] Jordan: Got it. We'll aim to deliver pilot materials by next Tuesday.

[29:05] Amara: Timeline-wise, procurement review will take ~2-3 weeks once we have security pack.

[29:15] Jordan: Great — we'll be responsive. Any other blockers?

[29:22] Lina: One small one — we may need a short demo of Console cost breakdown during the next meeting.

[29:30] Jordan: We can do a 30-minute walkthrough of Console.

[29:40] Priya: I'll also include the micro-benchmark runbook and scripts so you can reproduce locally.

[30:00] Ethan: Thanks, this is productive.

[30:05] Jordan: Thanks all. We'll follow up with the documents and schedule the bench run.

[30:12] (end call)

Notes on transcript quality: Some speaker tags are generic or approximate, occasional words mis-transcribed (e.g., "K V cache" vs "KV cache", "quantize" vs "quantization"), filler words and overlaps present.

Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Sarah (Redwood AE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Maya (Bluehaven Head of ML), Liam (CTO), Evelyn (Security Lead)

[00:10] Maya: Hi, Maya here. Head of ML at Bluehaven. We run recommendations and an in-product assistant, both chaty and embed-style use cases.
