[02:10] Carlos: Good, that's helpful. Roughly, per-token hosted pricing gives predictability for small scale but can blow up. Dedicated gives predictable throughput and lower per-token when you amortize the GPU pool. Private/VPC gives you residency and KMS control but ops overhead plus fixed costs.

[03:00] Sarah: We're going to walk through a simple per-100k-token example to make tradeoffs visible — and then point out levers. Any red lines?
[03:10] Liam: If we can't guarantee residency for those EU tenants, we can't use hosted for them.
[03:15] Evelyn: Correct. Also, we need audit logs for requests and token-level costing breakdown for chargebacks internally.

[04:05] Carlos: On levers — batching: if your average RTT allows, grouping requests into micro-batches reduces per-token compute. KV cache/prefix caching: for recommendation flows with repeated context or session state, caching KV reduces re-tokenization and model compute. Quantization: moving from FP16 to INT8 or 4-bit variants can reduce cost by 30-60% depending on model and accuracy tolerance.

[05:00] Maya: Quick question — our prompts vary a lot; can batching still help? During peaks, we have many similar short requests for top-k items, but the chat assistant has longer contexts.
[05:12] Carlos: Yes. For short, high-QPS calls, batching is very effective. For long context chat, KV cache helps more. You can also hybridize routes: route short, latency-tolerant queries to a high-batch pool; route low-latency chat to a dedicated low-latency pool — Redwood supports policy-based routing and fallbacks.

[06:05] Liam: Any numbers on expected savings from batching + KV? Ballpark.
[06:10] Carlos: Ballpark — micro-batching 8-16 items can drop per-token cost ~20-35% depending on overhead. KV cache for repeated prefixes can cut 10-40% on token compute. Combined, optimistic cases see 40-60% lower token spend compared to naive single-request serving. But that is workload dependent.

[07:00] Maya: Sounds promising. What about dedicated pricing — how should we think about committed capacity vs burst?
[07:10] Sarah: Dedicated is reservation-based. You commit to a GPU pool for a period (monthly/annual), which gives you lower per-token when utilized. We also offer burst capacity to handle spikes. If your utilization is low, though, it might cost more than hosted per-token.
[07:35] Liam: So for our POC budget ($20k/month), do you think dedicated is feasible?
[07:42] Carlos: Depends on the model and utilization. For example, a single A100 pool sized for your bursts may cost $Xk/month; if you run steady throughput to use most capacity, you'll get favorable per-token. But if 80% of cost is unused time, hosted might be cheaper for the POC. We'll model it in the spreadsheet.

[08:50] Evelyn: For private/VPC, can we bring our own key management and have logs exported to our SIEM?
[08:58] Sarah: Yes — private offers customer-managed KMS and audit log exports. On-prem package is also possible for air-gapped customers, but that's a longer procurement cycle.

[09:30] Maya: One thing: we can't accept model outputs leaving EU for those customers. How strict is your routing by region?
[09:37] Carlos: We support region pinning and policy routing. For EU-residency requests, we can pin to EU hosts only. If pooled capacity in EU is full, Redwood can fail closed or fall back to a compatible model hosted in EU — we don't route EU payloads to NA unless allowed.

[10:20] Liam: Good. Let's talk models — are we talking open models or proprietary? We currently use a mix: some open Llama-derived models in prod experiments, and occasionally API-based large models for high-quality outputs.
[10:30] Sarah: Redwood supports both open and tuned variants; we also have verified performance profiles per model. Note: quantization support varies by model and may affect latency.

[11:15] Maya: Example: for our recommendation explainers, 95% of calls use a 2k-context model? No, sorry — incorrect. Let me rephrase: typical long assistant contexts are ~2k tokens occasionally, but most are under 1k.
[11:30] Carlos: That's useful. Sequence length distribution matters — longer contexts increase KV pressure and latency, and also change kernel selection.

[12:05] Sarah: Let's sketch a concrete scenario in the workbook: 100k requests/day, average 520 tokens per request (in+out). We'll calculate hosted per-token vs dedicated amortized. We'll include batching scenarios (no batch, batch=8, batch=16) and quantization options.

[13:30] Maya: Can you also include end-to-end latency SLOs in the sheet? We care about p95 under 300ms for chat on mobile.
[13:40] Carlos: We'll add latency columns: p50/p95 and the expected tradeoffs when batching. If p95 latency needs to be <300ms, certain batching sizes won't be acceptable for chat, but they may be for recommendations.

[14:20] Liam: Curious about caching TTLs — if we cache per-session KV, what is the storage cost and how much does that save compute?
[14:28] Carlos: Storage for KV cache is relatively cheap compared to compute, but it depends on model KV size (per token). In many cases, storing session prefixes yields large compute reductions. We'll surface an estimated cache hit rate and impact in the workbook.

[15:45] Evelyn: Audit logs — are token-level logs included for private deployments? Any PII redaction options?
[15:55] Sarah: For private/VPC, you control redaction. By default hosted logs keep minimal request metadata and not full payloads unless enabled. We can support redaction rules and hashing of PII before storage. We'll send the SOC2 and security sheet.

[17:10] Maya: Another practical question — our engineers prefer not to change a lot of inference code. How much instrumentation does Redwood require to enable batching/cache?
[17:22] Carlos: Minimal SDK changes in most cases — we provide SDKs with automatic batching toggles and cache hooks. For advanced use you can implement policy tags per request for routing. We'll show sample code in the follow-up.

[18:30] Liam: Let's talk concrete numbers briefly — don't need the workbook to be perfect now, but give me a rough hosted price for 1M tokens and a dedicated amortized price for 1M tokens at ~70% utilization on an A100 pool.
[18:42] Carlos: Off the cuff: hosted could be $X per 1M tokens (we'll fill number in workbook) — dedicated at 70% utilization often ends up 30-50% cheaper per token, depending on batch/quantization. The exact depends on model size and H100 vs A100 or other hardware.

[19:30] Maya: Are there minimum commitments for Dedicated?
[19:34] Sarah: Minimums depend on capacity. We typically see monthly reserved pools for POCs. We'll propose a small reserved footprint that meets your peak while leaving bursting available.

[20:20] Liam: One of our concerns is unpredictable bursts during events. If we reserve capacity to match average, can Redwood scale quickly to handle 3x spikes?
[20:30] Carlos: Yes — burst capacity is available. There are two mechanisms: short-lived cloud burst (hosted) and pre-warmed burst capacity in Dedicated. There's a cost for burst reservation; we'll model scenarios: reserve for 1.5x average vs require full 3x. Usually a hybrid with targeted burst tickets works.

[21:45] Maya: Regarding fallbacks — if EU dedicated pool is saturated, will requests queue or fail? We prefer failover to a slightly smaller model in-region rather than route out-of-region.
[21:56] Carlos: That's supported via routing policies: can choose 'fail-closed', 'fallback-model-same-region', or 'route-cross-region-with-approval'. We'll recommend fallback to a smaller in-region model to keep residency.

[23:10] Liam: Practical integration timeline for a POC — what's realistic?
[23:16] Sarah: For a basic POC (hosted) with integration and basic evaluation, 2-3 weeks. For Dedicated reserved pool provisioning and pilot, 4-8 weeks depending on contract and capacity. Private/VPC adds another 4-12 weeks depending on networking and compliance reviews.

[24:05] Maya: One final thing — we'd like a token burn forecast per feature so product can decide feature gating. Will you provide a per-route token estimate?
[24:12] Carlos: Yes — the workbook will map routes to expected tokens/day and show how batching/caching affects each route's cost.

[25:00] Liam: About pricing transparency — does Redwood break down token compute vs infra vs orchestration?
[25:06] Sarah: Yes, we provide breakdowns: compute (per-token GPU cycles), networking, storage, and orchestration. You'll get a per-request token cost and also a breakdown so you can do internal chargebacks.

[26:30] Maya: Any gotchas we should know before pilot?
[26:36] Carlos: Watch out for sequence length tail — a few long contexts can blow token budget. Also mixing very different latency classes on the same pool reduces batching efficiency. And quantization can change generation quality; so validate on your eval set.

[27:45] Evelyn: On compliance: do we get penetration test reports and vendor attestations?
[27:51] Sarah: Yes — we'll include SOC 2 report excerpts and a standard security package. For private customers we can do more extensive attestations.

[29:05] Maya: Ok, this helps. One more technical — do you support model pinning per route and version rollouts?
[29:11] Carlos: Absolutely. Model pinning, canary rollouts, A/B, automatic fallback policies all exist in the console. We'll include screenshots and sample rollout configs.

[30:40] Sarah: To recap: we'll send the cost workbook that models hosted vs dedicated vs private for your workload, include batching/kv/quantization scenarios, add latency columns, and attach security docs. We'll also schedule a 60-min technical deep dive next week with your infra and security teams.

[31:00] Maya: Sounds good. Preferred time windows are mornings PST next week.
[31:05] Sarah: Noted. We'll propose options.

[31:40] Liam: Two smaller asks: can you include an example cost plan that assumes a hybrid approach — EU private for regulated customers and hosted for non-EU?
[31:48] Carlos: Yep, we'll include hybrid scenarios with split routing and cost apportionment.

[33:10] Maya: Any immediate blockers from our side? I'll pull together the traffic histogram and sample prompts.
[33:15] Liam: I'll loop in Finance for budget confirmation.
[33:20] Evelyn: I'll sanity-check the KMS and residency requirements and send a short list of required certifications.

[34:00] Sarah: Great. Last quick note — competitors. Maya, you mentioned trying OpenAI and an on-prem vendor; any other constraints vs those providers we should be aware of?
[34:10] Maya: Mainly price and residency. OpenAI had good quality but residency was a problem. Some open-source hosting vendors promised low cost but ops overhead killed the ROI.

[35:00] Carlos: We'll quantify that in the workbook and highlight where Redwood sits relative to hosted API providers vs self-hosted infra.

[36:20] Sarah: Any other questions?
[36:25] Maya: Not for now, thanks.
[36:28] Liam: No.
[36:30] Evelyn: All good.

[36:40] Sarah: Thanks everyone — next steps restated: Sarah will send workbook + security docs; Carlos will prepare microbenchmark data for A100/H100 with batch and quantization permutations; schedule the deep dive.
[36:58] Maya: Thanks Sarah, Carlos.
[37:02] Liam: Thanks.
[37:05] Carlos: Bye all, we'll follow up with proposed slots.

[37:30] Meeting ends.

Notes on transcript quality: occasional word errors (model names and kernel choices slightly garbled), some speaker labels collapsed into names. [Usage slicing & deploy decision - Citrine Analytics]
header:
Date: 2026-07-08
Start: 16:30 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alicia Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Citrine Head of ML), Tom Reyes (Citrine CTO), Lena Ortiz (Citrine DevOps)
Recording: yes
Notes: discovery focused on per-token unit economics, batching/caching levers, and hosting choices (hosted vs dedicated vs private).

summary:
Citrine Analytics is evaluating tradeoffs between Redwood Hosted, Dedicated and Private deployment options. Primary drivers: strict monthly budget, need for sub-150ms p50 for short chat flows, and data residency requirements for a subset of customer prompts. They want a quick pilot to measure unit cost with batching and KV/prefix caching and to understand fixed committed costs for Dedicated. Security is a gating item for Private; SOC2 and KMS integration were discussed. Next steps: pricing spreadsheet, benchmark run, share prompts, and follow-up on networking constraints.

transcript:
[00:00:00] Alicia: okay everyone thanks for joining, uh we'll kick off. I'm Alicia from Redwood, account exec. Marcus is our solutions engineer. 
[00:00:09] Marcus: hey all. thanks. real quick agenda: understand your workload, cost targets, and constraints then talk through hosting options and levers like batching/caching.
[00:00:22] Priya: cool yeah we're replacing a prototype that runs locally, and cost is the main blocker for scaling. we have chat flows and a few high-throughput ranking jobs.
[00:00:31] Tom: and to add, we need sub-150ms p50 for the support chat use-case for good UX. p95 can be higher but p50 is important.
[00:00:40] Lena: also some customers require that certain PII prompts never leave their region, so residency is a thing.
[00:00:48] Marcus: got it. does that mean some traffic could be routed to a Private/VPC-only model while the rest goes to hosted?
[00:00:54] Priya: yep, that's the idea. we'll likely slice traffic by sensitivity and maybe by feature flag.
[00:01:02] Alicia: just to ground this, what's your current monthly budget for inference ops? ballpark.
[00:01:08] Priya: we can commit roughly $18k/month for now. if unit costs are low and predictability is better we could expand.
[00:01:14] Marcus: perfect, that's useful. one high-level note: per-token price times tokens plus fixed committed costs for Dedicated add up; we can model both. are you optimizing for cost per dialog or cost per 1k QPS?
[00:01:28] Tom: per dialog, primarily. we care about latency too but dialogs are the billing unit for product economics.
[00:01:34] Marcus: okay. a couple levers we commonly use: (1) batching — run many short requests together to amortize GPU work; (2) prefix or KV caching — for repeated system prompts or reused prefixes; (3) quantized model variants that reduce cost but could change quality slightly.
[00:01:52] Priya: can you say more about caching? we have a lot of repeated system text across sessions.
[00:01:56] Marcus: sure. prefix caching stores token-level key/value state for common prefixes so we don't recompute the same attention results. it works especially well if the conversation starts with standard onboarding text or known templates. we sometimes call it KV cache but transcription might say K-V cash. (laugh)
[00:02:15] Priya: (laugh) note taken. how much savings are realistic?
[00:02:19] Marcus: depends on repetition and sequence length. in our baseline examples we see 20–60% token compute reduction when 30–40% of requests reuse prefixes. batching can be 2–4x efficiency uplift for short inputs if you can tolerate slightly higher p95.
[00:02:34] Tom: what do you mean by tolerate p95? our SLA is client-facing.
[00:02:39] Marcus: p95 increases because batching holds requests up until batch fills or until a latency deadline. Redwood has dynamic batch sizing — so you'll get a configurable latency cap. say p50 120ms and p95 280ms in a batched config vs p50 80ms p95 220ms in a lower batch size.
[00:02:58] Lena: okay and Dedicated changes that how?
[00:03:02] Marcus: Dedicated gives you reserved GPU capacity so batching becomes more predictable — you don't compete with multi-tenant spikes. unit cost per token can drop because you run larger, more efficient batches and can use slightly more aggressive quantization safely. but there's a commit — e.g., a monthly reserved instance charge.
[00:03:19] Alicia: to put numbers on the table, for a medium open-chat model we list hosted per-token at, uh, $0.00035 per output token (example), and Dedicated effective unit might be closer to $0.00020 when amortizing reserved capacity and using batching/caching. these are sample numbers — we'll send exact spreadsheets.
[00:03:38] Priya: that differential matters. if our typical dialog is 120 output tokens, that multiplies.
[00:03:44] Marcus: exactly. 120 tokens at $0.00035 is about $0.042 per dialog. at $0.00020 it's $0.024. at 50k dialogs/month that's a big delta.
[00:03:56] Tom: what's the break-even for Dedicated reservation vs hosted?
[00:04:00] Marcus: depends on utilization. rough rule of thumb: if you're sustaining >60–70% of a Dedicated pool across the month and need predictable latency, Dedicated often pays off. but if you're spiky and underutilized, hosted can be cheaper. we'll model your expected QPS and dialogs in the spreadsheet.
[00:04:16] Priya: our traffic is moderate but with big spikes around daytime support hours. can Redwood do burst capacity?
[00:04:23] Marcus: yes, Dedicated has burst options — configurable. burst is priced as added temporary capacity or overage per minute depending on contract.
[00:04:31] Priya: and Private — that's the VPC/on-prem offering — how different is unit pricing?
[00:04:36] Alicia: Private has a platform fee and often a higher per-token cost if we manage the infra, but if you run on-prem with your hardware, the unit compute is basically your infra cost. Redwood charges for the control plane and any managed services like caching etc. Security integrations (KMS, HSM) are add-ons in terms of setup complexity.
[00:04:54] Tom: we have HSM and strict KMS requirements. is Redwood's private offering certified to plug into our KMS?
[00:05:00] Marcus: yes, we integrate with customer-managed KMS, and we have SOC2 compliance docs. for on-prem there's an extra ops runbook. we'll share the SOC2 summary and private deployment checklist.
[00:05:11] Lena: network wise, will we need specific egress ports or can it be fully contained?
[00:05:15] Marcus: for a VPC deployment, control plane calls home for management but data paths can be kept in-region and encrypted. we have an air-gapped package for very strict customers, but that adds onboarding time.
[00:05:26] Priya: onboarding time — how long to get to pilot?
[00:05:29] Alicia: for hosted it's minutes — you can start calling the API. for a pilot with integrations, benchmark and validation, typical timeline is 2–4 weeks. Dedicated onboarding is 3–6 weeks depending on networking and compliance. Private/on-prem can be 6–12 weeks based on ops windows.
[00:05:44] Tom: 6–12 is long but acceptable if security needs it.
[00:05:47] Marcus: quick note on benchmarking: we prefer you provide a sample prompt set and representative QPS. we'll run throughput tests with a matching model/quantization and show cost/latency breakdowns.
[00:05:59] Priya: we can do that. we'll provide three use-cases: support chat (short), document summarization (longer), and reranking (high QPS).
[00:06:08] Marcus: perfect. reranking is important — batching there looks different: many short scoring requests, often benefited by specialized batchers and sometimes smaller quantized models.
[00:06:18] Tom: one more question: are you able to do model pinning and rollbacks if a new model version has regressions?
[00:06:23] Marcus: yes — we have version pinning and rollout policies (canary, A/B). Optimize has eval monitoring so you can detect quality regressions on your prompt set.
[00:06:33] Priya: about cost modeling: can you include caching assumptions in the spreadsheet? we need to see sensitivity: 0%, 25%, 50% cache hit.
[00:06:40] Alicia: absolutely. we'll include scenarios for cache hit rates and batch sizes. Marcus will annotate assumptions for token counts and latencies.
[00:06:48] Marcus: also worth noting tokenization mismatch risk — different models tokenize differently; we'll use your actual token counts in the benchmark. sometimes the inference token count differs from naive estimates.
[00:06:59] Priya: good call. expectations: we want a pilot to show per-dialog cost below $0.03 while keeping p50 <150ms for chat.
[00:07:09] Tom: and show a path to lowering cost to $0.02 with Dedicated and caching.
[00:07:14] Marcus: that's achievable on paper. we'll run numbers.
[00:07:17] Alicia: any legal or procurement items we should prep for?
[00:07:20] Tom: standard NDA is already done. procurement will want a SOW for the pilot and a sample contract.
[00:07:25] Alicia: we'll attach a pilot SOW.
[00:07:28] Lena: connectivity question: our dev cluster sits behind strict firewall rules. will Redwood need open egress to management plane?
[00:07:34] Marcus: for VPC deployments there's a management control channel; we can provide IP ranges and set up peering or private link depending on cloud. for on-prem we'll need some ops coordination.
[00:07:45] Priya: any known gotchas around mem use with long-context summarization?
[00:07:49] Marcus: long contexts increase KV memory but you can shard and stream; we have memory tuning knobs. for heavy summarization we recommend a model that supports larger context tokens and potentially chunking + retrieval to bound cost.
[00:08:03] Priya: okay. a couple of side questions I jotted down: will Redwood provide rate-limited endpoints and token-level usage breakdowns?
[00:08:10] Alicia: yes — console has token-level breakdowns by route and model, and you can set quotas/limits.
[00:08:15] Tom: what about data retention for logs and transcripts? our policy is 90 days then purge.
[00:08:20] Marcus: you can configure retention windows; down to zero retention in Private modes. Hosted has default retention and options for shorter retention with enterprise plans. we'll include that in the security doc.
[00:08:33] Priya: earlier Marcus said 20–60% savings from caching in some cases — how conservative should we be for modeling?
[00:08:38] Marcus: start conservative: model 20% cache hit for baseline, and a 40–50% optimistic case. we'll show both.
[00:08:45] Speaker 1: (inaudible mutter)
[00:08:49] Alicia: let's recap next steps. We'll send the pricing sheet and unit-econ model with scenarios for cache hits and batch sizes; Marcus will schedule benchmarks once you share prompts; Priya will share the prompt sets and expected QPS; Lena will confirm networking constraints for VPC.
[00:09:05] Priya: yep, we'll do that. thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[00:09:10] Alicia: great. I'll follow up with the spreadsheet and SOC2 summary; Marcus will ping about available benchmark windows.
[00:09:17] Tom: thanks all.
[00:09:19] Marcus: thanks. end.
[00:09:22] (end recording)

summary:

Meeting header:\nDate: 2025-09-10\nStart time: 16:00 UTC\nDuration: ~62 minutes\nAttendees: Alex Turner (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (CTO, Lambda Finance), Maya Chen (Head of ML), Rafael Ortiz (Infra Lead)\n\n[00:00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'll kick off, I'm Alex from Redwood, AE on this account, and with me is Priya, our solutions engineer. Quick check, Jordan, do you want to say hi and confirm the agenda?\n\n[00:00:18] Jordan: Yep, hi all. Jordan here. We're mostly focused on understanding what our unit economics would look like for a pricing generator and a realtime compliance screen that runs alongside. We have some hard budget constraints and low latency needs.\n\n[00:00:35] Priya: Great, thanks. Today we planned to walk through how Redwood approaches per-token pricing across Hosted/Dedicated/Private, batching and caching levers, and quantization tradeoffs. Also capture workload details so we can propose a pilot.\n\n[00:00:50] Maya: Quick note — our SLA for the pricing generator is 200 ms p95 for 95% of requests; compliance screen can tolerate up to 600 ms p95 but needs deterministic behavior.\n\n[00:01:05] Rafael: And infra-wise we can't send sensitive transaction payloads to third-party unless encrypted in transit with customer KMS and there's audit logs. So security is big.\n\n[00:01:22] Alex: Totally understood. We'll cover security briefly and include SOC2/KMS notes in the follow-up. Before we dig in, Justin from procurement wanted to flag a 6-week procurement window — not urgent but part of the timeline.\n\n[00:01:38] Jordan: Sounds good. Let's go into cost. How does Redwood price per token across the modes?\n\n[00:01:45] Priya: Short answer: hosted is usage-based per-token with model-dependent multipliers, dedicated is a reserved capacity contract (CPU/GPU pool) with predictable throughput and lower per-token at scale, private has platform fees and depends on your infra cost — we can help model that. Important levers are batching, KV/prefix caching, and quantization which materially reduce tokens billed or GPU cycles.\n\n[00:02:10] Maya: Can you quantify — if we push to int8 quant (or q4) what difference do we see? Also how batch size impacts latency vs cost — we need to preserve that 200 ms p95.\n\n[00:02:26] Priya: From our benchmark set, going from FP16 to 8-bit quantization usually reduces GPU memory and increases throughput 1.8x–3x depending on model and kernel support; cost per token often drops ~25–45% but quality delta varies. For small prompts with short contexts, batching helps but you hit latency cliff — continuous batching with small max-wait thresholds can help.\n\n[00:02:52] Jordan: When you say batching helps, is that on the Redwood side or do we have to change our client to batch requests?\n\n[00:03:00] Priya: Redwood runtime can perform server-side batching automatically within a configured window. You can also do client-side batching if you want more control. We typically suggest a hybrid: enable server batching with a max-wait of 20–30ms for low-latency SMBs, and allow client grouping for bulk jobs.\n\n[00:03:18] Rafael: Our traffic profile is spiky during market opens, bursts up 10x. How does reserved capacity handle that? Any burst options?\n\n[00:03:28] Alex: Dedicated pools can be configured with burst capacity to handle spikes; you reserve baseline and set burst budget for temporary capacity usage that incurs overage. We can simulate your spike profile in the pilot to size the pool.\n\n[00:03:43] Maya: Ok, let's talk about caching. We have a lot of repeated prefixes for pricing tables and standard legal boilerplate. Can that reduce token count billed?\n\n[00:03:55] Priya: Yes — KV cache / prefix caching avoids regenerating identical prefixes. There are two effects: reduces compute tokens and reduces end-to-end latency. Billing depends — some customers use token-level billing but we apply caching-aware suggestions; in dedicated deployments you can also implement warm-start KVs persisted across requests. Note, some transcripts call it "KV cash" in older docs — that's a transcription quirk, but we mean cache.\n\n[00:04:20] Jordan: Is there any billing model where cached tokens aren't charged?\n\n[00:04:27] Priya: In hosted mode we bill per output token; cached prefixes mean fewer output tokens to generate. For private/dedicated where you buy reserved capacity, you effectively amortize cost over capacity so cache improves throughput and reduces GPU-hours per effective token. We can show you a modeled example with your prompt distribution.\n\n[00:04:43] Maya: We run some long contexts — up to 4k tokens — will that break batching or quantization benefits?\n\n[00:04:50] Priya: Larger contexts increase memory pressure but our runtime selects kernels and execution paths optimized for sequence length. For 4k, certain quant kernels perform better; we will recommend model variants and chunking strategies. Batching becomes trickier because memory limits reduce batch size; that's where dedicated with higher-memory GPUs helps.\n\n[00:05:12] Jordan: Can you give an example TCO? Say 100k inference requests/day, average 300 tokens output, 50k of those reuse cached prefixes. What's the monthly bill hosted vs dedicated?\n\n[00:05:26] Alex: We didn't run your exact numbers in the call yet, but rough back-of-envelope: hosted per-token on a medium Llama-type model might be $0.000012/token (example number), so 100k * 300 = 30M tokens => ~$360/month before caching. If 50k requests reuse 100 tokens each, that's 5M cached tokens not generated => roughly $300 difference. Dedicated with a reserved pool might cost $X/month but result in per-token equivalent of $0.000007–0.000009 depending on utilization. We'll send a spreadsheet with scenarios.\n\n[00:06:01] Rafael: That example per-token number seems low — is that for inference only or includes support/console charges?\n\n[00:06:09] Alex: Hosted includes inference + basic platform usage. Dedicated has a platform fee plus reserved capacity. We'll itemize in the model.\n\n[00:06:18] Maya: You mentioned model variants — are you recommending we run smaller tuned models for pricing and a larger model for compliance?\n\n[00:06:26] Priya: Exactly. Multi-tier routing is a common pattern: cheap tuned model for pricing generation latency-critical paths, and fallback to a larger model for complex cases or when quality thresholds aren't met. Redwood supports policy-based routing so you can set deterministic fallbacks.\n\n[00:06:40] Jordan: How do you measure quality regressions if we quantize? We can't have pricing errors.\n\n[00:06:48] Priya: We recommend a gating eval set — sample of your critical prompts. Redwood Optimize can run A/B with metrics (token-level diff, business-specific checks). We'll include suggested test prompts and thresholds to validate quant profiles before rollout.\n\n[00:07:05] Maya: For the compliance screen, deterministic output and audit logs are key. Are logs stored in Redwood? Can we send logs to our SIEM?\n\n[00:07:13] Alex: Logs can be retained in Redwood with configurable retention or shipped via secure syslog/S3 to your account and integrated with your SIEM. [Causal Regression Investigation Handbook]
## Summary

This handbook defines a causal-first process for investigating model regressions (quality, latency, and cost) observed after a change (model version, quantization profile, infra, or prompt). It combines signals from the eval harness, production telemetry, and unit-level artifacts to form testable causal hypotheses and rapidly converge on root cause. This doc is intended for ML engineers, SREs, and applied ML owners performing triage on regression alerts.

## Scope

- Applies to regressions discovered via: continuous eval pipelines, production quality alerts, customer escalations, or automated regression bisect results.
- Covers causal graph design, hypothesis generation, experiment design, statistical testing, and actionable rollback/fix patterns.
- Not a replacement for the automated-bisect playbook; rather, this is the manual/analyst layer for ambiguous or cross-cutting regressions.

## Ownership and Escalation

- Primary owner: Applied ML - Model Quality team
- On-call SRE: for runtime/latency regressions
- Escalation: if causal analysis points to infra/serving runtime, escalate to Eng-Serving-Runtime within 4 hours.

## Definitions

- Regression: measurable degradation in an SLO or metric compared to baseline (pre-change).
- Change event: deploy, quantization profile change, router policy update, prompt set modification, or model promotion.
- Primary signals: evaluation harness results, production cost/latency/quality telemetry, example traces, token-level diffs.

## Signals and Data Sources (ordered by priority)

1. Eval harness: stable test-set metrics, per-slice breakdowns, and seed-fixed reruns.
2. Production telemetry: per-route token latency, error rates, kv-cache hit rates, and token counts.
3. Shadow traffic and A/B results (if available).
4. Client traces / transcript samples (anonymized).
5. Deployment metadata: model SHA, quantization profile ID, kernel selection log, GPU type, and routing policy.

## Causal DAG Templates

Use these canonical Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) templates to structure thinking. Draw the DAG and explicitly list assumed causal links before testing. Example templates (textual):

- Template A (Model-change-driven): ChangeEvent -> Weights/Quantization -> ModelBehavior -> OutputQuality
- Template B (Runtime-interaction): ChangeEvent -> KernelSelection/Batching -> Latency -> TimeoutErrors -> Quality
- Template C (Prompt/Context): ChangeEvent -> PromptSet/ContextTruncation -> KV-CacheHits -> EffectiveContext -> OutputQuality

Always annotate nodes that are observable vs latent and list available instrumentation for each node.

## Investigation Checklist (step-by-step)

1. Record the alert context: metric, threshold, time window, impacted slices (routes, languages, long vs short prompts).
2. Snapshot deployment metadata for the time window: model_id, model_sha, quant_profile, runtime_version, host region, and GPU type.
3. Replicate the failure in the eval harness with the same model and quantization profile, using the failing prompt slices. Use deterministic seeds where applicable.

   Example CLI to re-run a failing slice locally:
   
   curl -X POST https://eval-harness.internal/run -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"slice_id":"lang-en-long-context", "model_id":"m-v42", "quant_profile":"q8_4", "seed":42}'

4. Construct a concise causal DAG and list 2–3 competing hypotheses (e.g., quantization introduced a tokenization-sensitive bias; kernel fallback increased latency and triggered truncation).
5. Prioritize hypotheses by plausibility and ease-of-test. Run targeted ablations:
   - A/B run with float32 weights vs quantized profile on the same hardware.
   - Run with and without KV-cache enabled.
   - Run with controlled batch sizes to reproduce kernel selection differences.

6. Apply causal tests: difference-in-differences, regression adjustment, and when appropriate, causal-impact or DoWhy-style causal estimation.

   Minimal SQL snippet to prepare test/control cohorts:

   SELECT request_id, model_tag, quant_profile, prompt_slice, quality_score, latency_ms, kv_cache_hit
   FROM production_prompts
   WHERE event_time BETWEEN '2026-03-01' AND '2026-03-02'
   AND prompt_slice IN ('lang-en-long-context', 'lang-en-short')

7. If initial tests are inconclusive, schedule targeted shadow traffic or a canary with enhanced telemetry for 2 hours covering the failing slices.
8. When confident in root cause, prepare remediation: rollback plan, targeted quantization tweak, kernel configuration change, or prompt update. Document the fix in the incident tracker.
9. Close the loop: add failing prompts to the prompt-sets-and-benchmarks suite and create a new quant-eval slice if quantization was causal.

## Statistical Decision Rules

- Minimum sample size: 500 requests per slice for high-variance tasks (chat/long-context); 100 for low-variance embeddings or deterministic reranks.
- Significance: two-sided p < 0.01 for primary SLOs. Use bootstrap CIs for non-normal metrics (BLEU-like or token-level fidelity).
- Effect size threshold: absolute quality-drop >= 2% or relative latency increase >= 20% is actionable by default. Adjust per-SLO tier.

## Example Causal Test (Python pseudocode)

# Example: Use DoWhy to estimate effect of quantization on quality_score

from dowhy import CausalModel
import pandas as pd

# load prepared cohort dataframe
df = pd.read_csv('cohort.csv')
model = CausalModel(data=df, treatment='quant_profile_q8_4', outcome='quality_score', common_causes=['prompt_length', 'route', 'seed'])
identified_estimand = model.identify_effect()
estimate = model.estimate_effect(identified_estimand, method_name='backdoor.propensity_score_matching')
print(estimate)

Note: include diagnostics and sensitivity analysis for unobserved confounding.

## Integrations with Automated Bisect and Eval Harness

- When bisect returns candidate change windows, attach a causal-analysis job that:
  - Replays failing trace samples across candidate model variants.
  - Runs the lightweight DoWhy/DiD tests on per-slice cohorts.
  - Produces a short causal report in the bisect output (delta metrics, p-values, suggested root causes).

- Hook names: eval-harness/replay, bisect/causal-report, telemetry/query-cohort.

## Required Instrumentation and Data Schema

Minimum columns for any cohort extract (plain text table):

| column_name | type | description |
| request_id | string | unique request identifier |
| event_time | timestamp | request time |
| model_tag | string | model identifier (e.g., m-v42) |
| quant_profile | string | quant profile id |
| route | string | API route or product feature |
| prompt_slice | string | slice label from prompt catalog |
| quality_score | float | chosen quality metric (0-1 normalized) |
| latency_ms | float | end-to-end token latency |
| kv_cache_hit | bool | cache hit flag |

Ensure all datasets are (a) anonymized, (b) token counts and sample prompts excluded from exported CSVs by default.

## Common Root Causes and Recommended Fixes

- Quantization-precision-bias: Re-run quant profile with per-layer fallback, raise precision on sensitive layers, add per-slice quant-tune.
- Kernel-fallback-latency: Pin kernel to earlier stable runtime for affected model length range; increase timeout SLOs temporarily.
- KV-cache-eviction-regression: Investigate policy, add explicit cache hold for long contexts or move to a larger shard.
- Prompt-truncation-shift: Add guardrail in prompt pipeline to preserve critical prefix tokens; add unit tests in prompt-sets.

## Playbook for Live Mitigation (fast timeline)

1. Within 30 minutes: if customer-facing degradations, enable fallback model variant (float or previous release).
2. Within 2 hours: collect reproducer examples and run targeted canary with enhanced telemetry.
3. Within 24 hours: implement permanent fix or schedule rollback.

## Post-Incident Actions

- Add failing prompts to permanent prompt regression suite.
- Create a quant-eval slice and add to nightly eval for that profile.
- Update the causal DAG library with the final root cause and evidence.
- Run a retrospective with owners (Applied ML, Serving Runtime, SRE) and record action items.

## Templates and Reporting

Use the following one-page template for causal-report attachments to incidents:

- Title: (short)
- Summary: 2–3 sentences
- Candidate hypotheses tested (list)
- Data used (cohort sizes, time windows)
- Statistical tests and results (p-values, CIs)
- Root cause (with confidence: low/medium/high)
- Action taken and follow-ups

[Performance Regression Policy & Thresholds (Company Standard)]
## Overview
This page defines Redwood Inference’s company-wide standard for:
- What counts as a performance regression vs. measurement noise.
- Minimum sample sizes and repeatability requirements.
- Pass/fail thresholds used by automated perf gating (PR checks, nightly canaries, and release-branch gates).
- Required artifacts and triage expectations when a regression is detected.

This policy is designed to support the “Perf baseline & representative workload suite” program and applies broadly to the serving runtime, kernels, scheduler/batching, and benchmark harness changes.

**Owner:** Observability (Engineering) in partnership with Serving Runtime and SRE.

---

## Scope
### In scope
This policy applies to any change that can affect latency/throughput/cost-relevant behavior for production inference:
- Serving runtime changes (prefill/decode scheduling, KV cache management, batching/backpressure, memory behavior).
- Kernel changes and kernel auto-selection changes.
- Model serving configuration defaults that affect runtime behavior (e.g., quantization profile defaults, attention/kernels toggles).
- Infrastructure and deployment changes that impact perf measurement (driver/CUDA/runtime/container base images, node configuration).

### Out of scope
- Application-level changes outside Redwood control (customer client code).
- One-off research experiments without a run manifest and reproducible harness.

---

## Canonical metrics and measurement boundaries
Metrics and definitions are standardized per **ADR-0172**. Any new metric must be proposed via an ADR update.

### Primary metrics (must-report)
1) **TTFT (Time To First Token)**
- Definition: time from server request acceptance (server-side) to first token emitted by the server streamer.
- Report: p50, p95, p99.
- Notes: TTFT explicitly excludes client receive/render overhead. Client-side measurements must be labeled as such and cannot be used for gating.

2) **TPOT (Time Per Output Token)**
- Definition: average per-token time during decode, measured server-side from first token emission to last token emission.
- Report: p50, p95, p99.

3) **Throughput**
- For generation/chat: tokens/s (server-side) and optionally req/s (if output length is fixed/controlled).
- For embeddings: req/s and embeddings/s (if batch mode is used).
- Report: mean and p95 where applicable.

### Secondary metrics (required when available)
- **Queue wait time** (scheduler): p50/p95/p99.
- **Batch assembly time**: p50/p95/p99.
- **Batch size distribution**: histogram summary (p50/p95 max).
- **GPU memory peak**: max (MiB) per run.
- **Error rate**: fraction of requests failing (timeout, OOM, internal errors).

### Cold vs warm cache requirements
Because caching materially affects cost/latency and is production-relevant, results must be reported as:
- **Cold**: prefix/KV caches cleared for the workload cohort.
- **Warm**: a defined warmup phase and cache retention enabled.

For gating decisions:
- Default gating uses **Cold** unless a workload is explicitly designated “cache-dependent” in the representative suite spec.
- Warm results are recorded and monitored; large cold↔warm deltas are treated as a diagnostic signal (not a failure by default).

---

## Noise model (how we distinguish regression vs. variance)
Performance data has unavoidable variability (GPU clocks, placement, thermal behavior, background IO, kernel selection changes, cache state). This policy uses a two-level model:

### Level 1: Run-level repeatability
A “run” is a single harness execution with a pinned workload definition + seed + manifest.
- Each gated comparison must include **multiple independent runs** (see minimum sample sizes below).
- Runs must include a standardized warmup period and must capture environment details in the run manifest (driver/CUDA/runtime build, kernel selection mode, scheduler policy, node type, region).

### Level 2: Statistical comparison across runs
We compare a candidate (PR branch / release build) against a baseline (golden build tag for a given suite version).

**Default test statistic:** percent change of the run-median metric across repeats.
- For each metric M, compute the median value per run.
- Across runs, compute the median-of-medians for baseline and candidate.
- Compute %Δ = (candidate - baseline) / baseline.

**Confidence / robustness:**
- Use bootstrap resampling across runs to estimate a 95% confidence interval (CI) on %Δ.
- A change is considered “actionable” only if it clears the **noise floor** and breaches warning/fail thresholds with CI support.

**Noise floor (ignore region):**
- If |%Δ| < **2%** for a metric, treat as noise by default (unless the absolute delta is operationally meaningful; see “absolute thresholds”).

**Absolute thresholds (override noise floor):**
- TTFT: **+20 ms** at any percentile is considered actionable even if <2%.
- TPOT: **+0.20 ms/token** actionable.
- Error rate: **+0.10% absolute** actionable.

**Known high-variance environments:**
- If a particular SKU/region cohort is flagged as high-variance (SRE-owned designation), gating requires either (a) more repeats or (b) an isolated fleet window. High-variance designations must be documented and time-bounded.

---

## Minimum sample sizes (gating requirements)
Minimums are chosen to balance cost with statistical power for typical Redwood workloads.

### A. Minimum repeats (independent runs)
- **PR gating (fast path):** 2 runs (same environment), only for “tier-1 smoke” workloads.
- **Nightly canary:** 3 runs.
- **Release branch gate:** 5 runs (or 3 runs across 2 separate fleet windows).

### B. Minimum requests per run (by workload type)
The representative suite defines workload cohorts; use the cohort type to select minimums:

| Workload cohort | Example | Minimum requests/run | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Chat streaming (short prompts, variable decode) | interactive chat | 10,000 | Must include concurrency ramp and steady-state window. |
| Tool/function calling (bursty multi-turn) | burst + idle cycles | 6,000 | Must include burst period long enough to show queueing dynamics. |
| Long-context prefill stress (large prefill, modest decode) | summarization | 1,200 | Prefill dominates; ensure long-context bin coverage. |
| Embeddings high-QPS (small payloads) | embeddings API | 50,000 | Prefer fixed-size payload bins to reduce confounding. |

### C. Required steady-state criteria (per run)
A run only counts if:
- Warmup is completed (standard warmup defined by the suite).
- At least **10 minutes** of steady-state measurements are collected (embeddings may use 5 minutes if QPS is high and variance is stable).
- Error rate is below the maximum allowed (see thresholds). If errors exceed allowed rate, the run is invalid unless the error itself is the regression under investigation.

---

## Pass / warn / fail thresholds
Thresholds are expressed as % change vs. baseline (negative throughput change is regression). Unless otherwise noted, thresholds apply to **cold-cache** results.

### A. Default thresholds (company-wide)
**Latency metrics (TTFT, TPOT):**

| Metric | Warn if regression ≥ | Fail if regression ≥ |
|---|---:|---:|
| TTFT p50 | +5% | +8% |
| TTFT p95 | +8% | +12% |
| TTFT p99 | +10% | +15% |
| TPOT p50 | +4% | +7% |
| TPOT p95 | +6% | +10% |
| TPOT p99 | +8% | +12% |

**Throughput metrics:**

| Metric | Warn if regression ≥ | Fail if regression ≥ |
|---|---:|---:|
| tokens/s (generation) | -5% | -8% |
| req/s (embeddings) | -6% | -10% |

**Reliability guardrails (hard fail):**
- Error rate increase of **+0.10% absolute** or more (e.g., 0.05% → 0.15%) is a **Fail**.
- Any new OOM pattern that did not occur in baseline is a **Fail** (even if latency improves).

### B. CI-aware gating interpretation
A candidate fails gating when **both** are true:
1) The bootstrap 95% CI of %Δ overlaps the fail region (i.e., regression is statistically supported), and
2) The regression clears the noise floor (or crosses an absolute threshold).

If the point estimate is in fail but CI is wide (insufficient power), the result is “Inconclusive” and must be retried with additional repeats or an isolated fleet window.

### C. Workload-specific overrides
The representative suite may specify tighter or looser thresholds per cohort if justified by:
- Customer impact (SLO sensitivity of that cohort).
- Historical variance characteristics.
- Known scheduling/kernels sensitivity.

Overrides must be documented in the suite definition and reviewed by Serving Runtime + SRE + Observability.

---

## Gating tiers and where policy applies
### Tier 0: Developer local (non-gated)
- Purpose: quick iteration.
- Not authoritative; no formal pass/fail.
- Must still emit a run manifest when shared.

### Tier 1: PR perf checks (gated when enabled)
- Runs a reduced workload subset (“tier-1 smoke”), typically on one region + one SKU.
- Goal: catch large regressions quickly.
- Thresholds: use **Fail** thresholds only (warnings are surfaced but do not block merges unless configured by the owning team).
- If PR gating is flaky, SRE/CI may temporarily disable with an incident/issue and an ETA to restore.

### Tier 2: Nightly perf-canary (always-on)
- Runs the representative suite nightly for supported baselines.
- Produces trend charts and variance panels.
- Failures page the owning triage rotation only if configured as “page-worthy” (see Alerting section).

### Tier 3: Release-branch perf gate (blocking)
Required before a serving runtime release is approved:
- Representative suite green under this policy for the release candidate.
- Runs must include the release’s target regions (minimum: us-east, eu-west) and key SKUs for that release.
- Any waiver must follow the exception process below.

---

## Required artifacts (to make results attributable)
All gated perf results must include:
- **Run manifest** (per ADR-0172) including:
  - Runtime build identifiers (git SHA, build ID), container image digest.
  - Region/SKU/node type, driver/CUDA, and relevant runtime flags.
  - Scheduler policy name + config hash.
  - Kernel selection mode + any pinned kernels.
  - Workload suite version + cohort ID + seed.
- **Results export** containing:
  - Metric definitions, aggregation method, percentile calculation method.
  - Raw summary stats per run (not only deltas).
- **Links** to dashboards/traces:
  - Dashboard panel link (TTFT/TPOT/throughput) for the run.
  - Trace/profiling artifacts when a regression is flagged (see profiling playbook).

Any result without a manifest is not eligible for gating decisions.

---

## Alerting and escalation
### What pages vs. what posts to triage
- **Page (on-call):** release-branch gate failures for tier-1 models/workloads; error-rate/OOM regressions.
- **Triage channel only:** warning-level regressions, inconclusive results, or failures in non-tier-1 cohorts.

Routing is managed by SRE in collaboration with runtime owners.

### Ownership on regression
- If the regression is clearly attributable to a PR: the PR author/owning team is responsible for first response.
- If attribution is unclear: Serving Runtime on-call (or designated triage rotation) coordinates bisect.

---

## Exception (waiver) process
Waivers exist to unblock releases when the business impact of delaying exceeds the perf risk, but they must be rare and time-bounded.

A waiver requires:
1) A written justification including affected cohorts/metrics, expected customer impact, and mitigation.
2) A link to the failing run(s) and manifests.
3) Approval from:
   - Serving Runtime Engineering Lead (or delegate), and
   - SRE Integration Lead (or delegate).

Waivers must include:
- Expiration date (default: 14 days).
- A follow-up issue/ticket to remove the waiver.

---

## Triage checklist (standard playbook)
When a regression is detected:
1) **Validate reproducibility**
   - Rerun with the same manifest (same suite version, seed, and environment) if possible.
   - Confirm warmup was applied and steady-state criteria were met.

2) **Check environment drift**
   - Driver/CUDA/runtime container changes.
   - Node type differences, GPU clock/power settings.
   - Placement/isolation differences.

3) **Attribute to scheduler vs. kernels vs. workload**
   - Inspect queue wait time and batch assembly metrics.
   - Compare batch size distributions.
   - Check kernel selection debug dumps (selected kernel, fallback reasons).

4) **Inspect tail behavior**
   - Identify whether regression is p99-only (queueing contention, cache thrash) vs. broad (kernel/runtime change).
   - Use profiling playbook to collect traces for a small reproduction.

5) **Decide action**
   - Fix forward (preferred) or revert.
   - If neither is immediately possible, pursue a temporary mitigation (pin kernel, adjust backpressure guardrails) with an explicit rollback plan.

---

## Change management
- Proposed changes to thresholds, sample sizes, or metric definitions require review by Observability + SRE + Serving Runtime.
- Any change must document:
  - Rationale (variance data, customer/SLO sensitivity).
  - Expected impact on flake rate and compute cost.
  - Backwards compatibility for dashboard queries and historical comparisons.

---

## Appendix: Practical guidance
### Recommended interpretation
- TTFT p99 regressions often indicate scheduler backpressure, queue discipline changes, or prefill/decode overlap issues.
- TPOT regressions often indicate kernel selection changes, KV cache behavior changes, or decode batch inefficiencies.
- Throughput regressions without latency regressions can indicate conservative batching caps or increased per-request overhead.

### Contact / channels
- #eng-runtime (coordination)
- #eng-sre (fleet stability, variance)
- #eng-platform (dashboards)

[ADR: Gate evaluation signals and thresholds (Dedicated staged rollouts)]
## Summary
This ADR defines (1) the signal sources used to evaluate staged rollout gates for **Dedicated** reserved pools, (2) the **default gate thresholds** by SLA tier, (3) the standard **aggregation windows / sample size requirements**, and (4) the required behavior when signals are **noisy** or **missing**.

The intent is to make gate evaluation deterministic, auditable, and consistent across regions and failure modes while minimizing false positives.

## Status
**Accepted** for v1 of Dedicated staged rollouts.

## Context / problem
Dedicated staged rollouts promote changes (model versions, runtime builds, routing policies, configuration) through explicit stages. Each promotion must be guarded by objective signals so that:
- We do not jeopardize Dedicated customer SLOs.
- Operators can understand *why* a gate passed/failed.
- Evaluation works in low-traffic stages (e.g., 1%) without being overly noisy.
- Behavior during telemetry degradation is safe and consistent.

We need a single set of “standard gate templates” so product/console can present consistent evidence, and SRE can align promotion policy to error budgets.

## Decision
### 1) Gate signal sources (authoritative inputs)
Gate evaluation uses a small, explicit allowlist of sources. All gate computations must be reproducible from stored query + time window + filters.

**A. Request/response metrics (Redwood Metrics / Prometheus-backed)**
Stage-tagged, region-tagged counters and histograms emitted by the data plane and gateway:
- `requests_total{pool_id, stage_id, region, route, model_id, status_class}`
- `request_latency_ms_bucket{...}` (histogram)
- `streams_aborted_total{...}`
- `rate_limited_total{...}` (429)
- `dropped_total{...}` (explicit drops/circuit-break)
- `queue_wait_ms_bucket{...}` (where available)

**B. Error classification (Redwood error taxonomy)**
Gate computations MUST use standardized classification to avoid double counting:
- Server errors: 5xx excluding known benign categories
- Timeouts: gateway timeout vs upstream timeout counted as server error
- Client cancellations (e.g., disconnects) are excluded from error-rate gates by default

**C. Fleet / GPU health signals (Fleet Health service + node exporter summaries)**
Used as “hard stop” gates:
- Critical Xid/ECC errors (double-bit ECC, repeated Xid in window)
- Thermal throttling sustained beyond threshold
- Node taints / quarantine state

**D. OOM / runtime instability signals (runtime logs aggregated to metrics)**
- `oom_events_total{pool_id, stage_id, region, model_id}`
- `restarts_total{...}` for runtime container restarts (crash loops)

**E. Quality regression signals (optional in v1)**
Where available for a rollout plan, quality gates may be enabled using Redwood’s eval harness summaries:
- `eval_score{prompt_set_id, model_id, stage_id}`
Quality gates are not mandatory for v1; if enabled, they follow the same missing-data semantics as other gates (see below).

### 2) Default gate set (v1)
A rollout stage is eligible for promotion only if all **required** gates are in PASS and none are in FAIL/UNKNOWN.

**Required gates (v1):**
1. **Server error rate** (5xx + timeouts)
2. **Latency** (p95 and p99)
3. **Rate limiting / drops** (429 + explicit drop)
4. **Saturation/headroom** (GPU utilization + queue wait/queue depth when available)
5. **OOM / crash-loop**
6. **GPU health**

**Optional gates (v1):**
- Quality regression
- Token efficiency regression (cost) (tracked, not a promotion blocker for v1)

### 3) Thresholds by Dedicated tier
Thresholds below are defaults and are aligned with Dedicated SLO tiering. They are intentionally conservative for early stages; operators can use **force-promote** with audit logging when warranted.

#### 3.1 Absolute thresholds (must be met)
All thresholds are computed per **pool_id + stage_id**, evaluated **per region**, and then rolled up to a global gate status (see §4).

| Gate | Dedicated Standard (default) | Dedicated Premium (default) | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Server error rate (5xx + timeouts) | \<= 0.50% | \<= 0.20% | Excludes client cancellations; includes gateway + upstream timeouts |
| 429 rate (rate limited) | \<= 0.20% | \<= 0.10% | Protects against capacity starvation during partitioning |
| Drop rate (explicit drops / circuit-break) | \<= 0.10% | \<= 0.05% | Drops are treated as more severe than 429 |
| Latency p95 | \<= 1.15 × baseline OR \<= tier ceiling | \<= 1.10 × baseline OR \<= tier ceiling | Baseline is control partition (preferred) or pre-rollout window |
| Latency p99 | \<= 1.25 × baseline OR \<= tier ceiling | \<= 1.20 × baseline OR \<= tier ceiling | p99 is noisier; requires min samples |
| GPU utilization (avg) | \<= 85% | \<= 80% | Averaged across the stage partition; see §3.3 |
| Queue wait p95 (if available) | \<= 50 ms | \<= 25 ms | If metric not available, use queue depth proxy and saturation index |
| OOM events | 0 in window (hard fail) | 0 in window (hard fail) | Any OOM indicates mis-sizing or regression |
| Crash-loop/restarts | \<= 1 restart per replica per 15m | \<= 1 restart per replica per 30m | Exceeding indicates instability |
| GPU health critical events | 0 critical events in window | 0 critical events in window | Hard fail on critical health |

**Tier ceilings for latency (used when baseline is unavailable):**
- Dedicated Standard: p95 \<= 900 ms; p99 \<= 1800 ms
- Dedicated Premium: p95 \<= 700 ms; p99 \<= 1400 ms

> Rationale: baselines are preferred (relative regressions) but ceilings prevent promotion when baseline is missing or artificially low.

#### 3.2 Baseline definition (relative comparisons)
When computing “× baseline” thresholds:
- **Preferred baseline:** the immediate prior stable stage (control partition) measured over the same evaluation window.
- **Fallback baseline:** the last 60 minutes immediately before the current stage began (stage start timestamp) for the same pool/region/route/model.
- Baseline must meet minimum sample requirements (§3.4). If baseline is invalid, the evaluator must fall back to absolute ceilings only and mark evidence accordingly.

#### 3.3 Saturation / headroom computation
To reduce reliance on any single metric, saturation is evaluated as:
- Primary: `gpu_utilization_avg` threshold (per region)
- Secondary (if available): `queue_wait_ms_p95` threshold
- Tertiary (proxy): `inflight_requests` and/or `queue_depth` against a per-pool capacity model

If GPU utilization is below threshold but queue wait is above threshold, the gate fails (we treat sustained queueing as customer-visible pain).

#### 3.4 Minimum sample sizes (to avoid noisy pass/fail)
Gates are only evaluated when the stage has sufficient traffic in the window.

**Minimum samples per region (per evaluation window):**
- Error/429/drop gates: **\>= 500 requests**
- Latency p95: **\>= 500 requests**
- Latency p99: **\>= 2,000 requests** (or mark p99 as UNKNOWN; see §5)

If the minimum samples are not met, the gate status is **UNKNOWN** and promotion is blocked unless an override is used.

### 4) Aggregation windows and evaluation cadence
Gate evaluation is performed by the policy engine on a fixed cadence:
- **Cadence:** every 60 seconds
- **Default evaluation window:** trailing 10 minutes (Standard), trailing 15 minutes (Premium)
- **Stability requirement:** 2 consecutive PASS evaluations required before “eligible to promote” is displayed

**Stage-size adjustments (to reduce flakiness):**
- Canary stage (\<= 1% traffic or smallest replica partition): minimum window 15 minutes and min samples must be met
- Mid stages (10%–50%): default window
- Final stage (100%): window may be shorter (5 minutes) for completion, but only after earlier stages have passed

> Note: Stages defined as replica partitions often have burstier traffic distributions; the minimum sample requirements protect against false confidence.

### 5) Multi-region evaluation rules
Dedicated pools may span regions. Gate status is computed in two steps:

1) **Per-region gate status** (PASS/FAIL/UNKNOWN) computed independently.

2) **Global stage gate status** computed as:
- FAIL if **any region** is FAIL on a required gate
- UNKNOWN if **any region** is UNKNOWN on a required gate (and none are FAIL)
- PASS only if **all regions** are PASS on all required gates

**Region weighting is not used** for v1. A single impaired region blocks promotion by default because Dedicated customers expect consistent behavior across their reserved footprint.

### 6) Missing data, telemetry lag, and partial outages
We standardize missing-data behavior to prevent ambiguous promotions.

**Definitions:**
- A signal is considered **stale** if its last datapoint is older than **3 minutes**.
- A window is considered **insufficient** if it does not meet minimum sample sizes (§3.4).

**Behavior (v1):**
- Required gates with stale/insufficient data → **UNKNOWN**
- UNKNOWN blocks promotion and (if configured) triggers an automatic **HOLD** after 30 minutes in unknown state
- Operators may **force-promote** or **force-rollback** with elevated RBAC and mandatory reason; these actions are audit logged (see audit ADR)

**Why not fail-open?**
Fail-open allows promotion during observability impairment, which is risky for Dedicated SLOs and makes post-incident reconstruction difficult.

### 7) Noisy metrics handling / debouncing
To reduce false failures:
- Percent-based gates use rate calculations over the full evaluation window (not instantaneous 1m spikes).
- Latency gates use histogram quantiles over the full window.
- Promotion eligibility requires **two consecutive PASS** evaluations.
- A single FAIL evaluation immediately makes the gate FAIL (no consecutive requirement), but the UI must display the specific sub-signal and observed values.
- Client-side cancellations are excluded from error-rate; a separate “cancellation rate” is recorded as evidence but not a blocker.

For extremely bursty traffic patterns (common in small Dedicated pools), operators should consider:
- Larger canary partitions (replica-based) rather than 1% traffic splits
- Longer windows (via plan configuration) when approved by SRE

### 8) Configurability / overrides
**Default:** thresholds are fixed per tier and not customer-editable in v1.

**Allowed configuration (v1, limited):**
- Stage-level evaluation window (bounded: 5m–30m)
- Enabling/disabling optional gates (quality)
- Selecting whether p99 is required (default: required for Premium, optional for Standard when traffic is low)

Any change to default thresholds or to required-gate set requires SRE + Platform sign-off and must be rolled out like a policy change (auditable).

## Options considered
### Option A: Per-customer fully configurable gate thresholds
- Pros: maximum flexibility
- Cons: hard to support/operate; inconsistent customer outcomes; makes console UX and on-call playbooks non-standard

Rejected for v1.

### Option B: Only absolute ceilings, no baseline comparisons
- Pros: simplest, deterministic
- Cons: does not catch regressions for already-fast workloads; ceilings are either too lax (miss regressions) or too strict (block legitimate workloads)

Rejected for v1; we use baseline when available plus ceilings as safety net.

### Option C: Fail-open on missing metrics
- Pros: fewer blocks due to telemetry issues
- Cons: encourages risky promotions during impaired visibility; undermines trust in “gated rollout” promise

Rejected; we use UNKNOWN + hold + override.

## Consequences
### Positive
- Consistent gate behavior across Dedicated pools and regions.
- Deterministic, auditable evidence (query + window + filters + observed values).
- Lower risk of capacity-starvation regressions (explicit 429/drop + saturation gates).

### Negative / trade-offs
- Low-traffic canaries can sit in UNKNOWN until enough samples accumulate.
- Telemetry issues can block promotions (mitigated by hold + force-promote with audit logging).

## Implementation notes (non-normative)
- Gate evaluation must be pure and idempotent: same inputs yield same output.
- Evidence objects returned to Console should include: query text (or query id), window, observed values, thresholds, baseline values (if used), and a reason string.
- Metrics labeling must control cardinality: stage_id is allowed only on a fixed allowlist of metrics.

## Follow-ups
1. Validate thresholds against beta customers; adjust if we see systematic false FAIL/UNKNOWN due to traffic patterns. Owner: **Rafael Mendes**.
2. Add explicit “telemetry degraded” banner + guidance in Console when UNKNOWN is due to staleness vs insufficient samples. Owner: **Chloe Martin**.
3. Define quality gate defaults and required prompt-set hygiene for Dedicated model upgrades (v2). Owner: **Selene Huang**.

## Appendix: Gate evaluation state meanings
- **PASS:** observed values meet thresholds and baseline rules; sufficient samples.
- **FAIL:** threshold violated; promotion blocked; may trigger auto-abort depending on rollout plan.
- **UNKNOWN:** missing/stale/insufficient data; promotion blocked; may trigger auto-hold after timeout.


[Low-Resource Language Eval Synthesis and Certification Handbook]
Summary
-------
This handbook defines a reproducible, auditable process for synthesizing evaluation suites, certifying model readiness, and operating canary rollouts for low-resource languages (LRLs). It targets languages with limited curated datasets (estimated token-volume < 1% of en-US traffic) and covers: probe synthesis strategies, annotation contracts, evaluation metrics and thresholds, canary rollout gating, and triage playbooks for observed regressions.

Why this matters
-----------------
- LRL performance can degrade silently due to tokenization, quantization, or prompt framing differences.
- Small sample sizes amplify metric variance: we must combine synthetic probes, targeted crowdsourcing, and worst-case slicing to obtain actionable signals.
- Production regressions in LRLs are high-impact for customers in underserved regions; certification reduces false negatives and avoids shipping regressions.

Scope and applicability
-----------------------
Applies to: model onboarding, quantization migrations, prompt-template changes, and routing/policy changes that affect generation or embeddings. Excludes: non-production research experiments or internal-only prototypes.

Definitions
-----------
- LRL (Low-Resource Language): language codenamed in our catalog as having < 10k high-quality parallel prompts (see language-registry).
- Anchor prompts: small, human-curated set (20–50) per intent family used to detect semantic drift.
- Synthetic families: algorithmically generated perturbations (morphological variants, code-switching, spacing) seeded from anchors.
- Certification: a documented pass/fail outcome that authorizes rollout to production.

High-level process (one-line)
----------------------------
1) Gather language telemetry -> 2) Build anchor and synthetic probe families -> 3) Run multi-fidelity evaluations (shadow + offline) -> 4) Apply statistical gating and human review -> 5) Certify or remediate -> 6) Canary rollout with adaptive reversion.

Owners and contacts
-------------------
- Primary owner: Applied ML — Evaluation Platform (team: applied-ml-evals).
- Secondary owners: Model Onboarding, Runtime, Customer Success (for regional bias concerns).
- Oncall contact: eval-oncall@redwood.ai

SLOs and thresholds for certification
-------------------------------------
(These are minimum pass criteria for a model or configuration to be considered certified for LRLs.)
| Metric | Acceptance threshold | Notes |
| Per-anchor semantic accuracy (human review) | >= 90% | Aggregated across anchor families, weighted by traffic proxy |
| Synthetic perturbation robustness (automated) | median BLEU/ROUGE >= 0.75 of baseline | Baseline is current production model in same quant/serving tier |
| Embedding drift T50 (median cosine) | delta < 0.03 vs baseline | Use cohort embedding samples from anchor families |
| Response stability index (RSI) | RSI >= 0.88 | See internal RSI spec; penalize hallucination flags |
| Annotation inter-rater agreement (Krippendorff alpha) | >= 0.6 | For human-judged anchors and safety probes |
| Canary error budget allocation | <= 10% of regional SRE error budget | Do not exceed operational risk allocation |

Procedures
----------
1) Data collection and seed selection
   a) Query telemetry for top-100 LRL intents by traffic proxy and error signals. Include: failed parses, high-latency tails, and user-feedback signals.
   b) For each intent, select 20 candidate examples: 10 human-curated anchors (native speaker review) + 10 weakly labeled examples from logs.

2) Probe synthesis (automated + human-in-the-loop)
   - Automated perturbations to apply: diacritic removal, whitespace variation, common local keyboard typos, code-switch insertion, back-translation to dominant regional lingua-franca.
   - Morphological expansion: use morphological generators (see toolchain: mgen) to create inflectional variants.
   - Controlled paraphrase sampling from production NLG with temperature=0.7, filter by language-id confidence >= 0.95.

3) Annotation contract and quality control
   - Each anchor judged by 3 native annotators. Primary annotation task: semantic equivalence score (0–3) and safety flag.
   - Required documentation: annotator instructions, example judgments, and edge-case guidelines.
   - Minimal gold set: 50 judgments seeded per language for calibration.

4) Multi-fidelity evaluation schedule
   - Offline suite: run on eval-harness with 3 random seeds and deterministic tokenization. Record tokenization deltas.
   - Shadow run: replay 1% of sampled LRL traffic to target build with full telemetry.
   - Human review: sample 200 model outputs (stratified by intent and perturbation type).

5) Statistical gating and decision rules
   - Apply hierarchical Bayesian smoothing on per-anchor pass rates to address small-sample variance.
   - Gate 1 (automated): all automated metrics meet thresholds in table above.
   - Gate 2 (human): Krippendorff alpha >= 0.6 and no single anchor family with semantic accuracy < 80%.
   - Final decision: if Gate 1 passes and Gate 2 passes, mark Certified; else mark Needs Remediation and follow remediation steps.

6) Remediation patterns (common fixes)
   - Tokenization mismatch: switch to language-specific BPE settings or add normalization preprocessor.
   - Quantization artifacts: schedule targeted higher-precision inference for high-risk families or change quant-profile.
   - Prompt-template brittleness: add localized prompt variants and re-evaluate anchors.

Canary rollout recipe
---------------------
- Canary window: 48 hours initial, extendable to 7 days depending on telemetry.
- Phases: 1) 0.1% traffic, 2) 1% traffic, 3) 5% traffic, 4) full regional traffic. Move only when rolling-average RSI and user-feedback rate remain within thresholds for 3 consecutive windows (window = 1h).
- Monitoring dashboard: per-language RSI, native feedback queue, latency P95, hallucination rate, embedding drift.
- Auto-revert criteria: any of the following during a phase triggers immediate revert:
  - RSI drop > 6 percentage points vs baseline for 3 consecutive 1h windows.
  - Human safety flag surge >= 3x baseline in 1h.
  - Latency p95 increase > 200ms and sustained for 30m.

Rollback and postmortem
-----------------------
- Immediate actions: open incident ticket with severity 'model-regress', roll back routing to baseline variant, preserve request/response logs for the last 2h.
- Postmortem: run targeted regression triage playbook (see related page: regression-triage/causal-regression-investigation-handbook-2026). Include anchor-level blame, quantization delta, and tokenization report.

Operational checklist for an LRL certification run (quick start)
---------------------------------------------------------------
1) Create a new certification run in the eval dashboard and tag language code.
2) Upload anchor CSV and set synthesis flags (enable-morphology=true, enable-backtranslation=true).
3) Kick off offline eval: select seeds=3, record tokenizer-diff=true.
4) Kick off shadow run for 48h sampling=1%.
5) Assign human reviews (3 per anchor) and monitor Krippendorf alpha.
6) Review gates and publish result: Certified | Needs Remediation | Not Applicable.

Sample eval job YAML (for eval orchestration)
--------------------------------------------
```yaml
job_name: lrl_cert_run_mk01
language: idn (example)
anchors: anchors_idn_v1.csv
probes: synthesis_flags: [morphology, backtranslation, code_switch]
seeds: 3
shadow_sample: 0.01
human_review: { annotators_per_item: 3, gold_seed_pct: 10 }
metric_thresholds: { rsi: 0.88, emb_delta: 0.03 }
output: s3://eval-results/lrl/idn/mk01/
```

CLI example to launch offline eval (eval-harness)
-------------------------------------------------
$ redwood-eval run --job job_name=lrl_cert_run_mk01 --env=staging --seeds=3 --record-tokenizer-diff

Safety and privacy considerations
--------------------------------
- Annotator PII: do not include user PII in anchors. Use redaction and synthetic replacements for rare tokens.
- Data residency: follow region-specific retention rules; do not copy LRL user logs outside allowed regions.
- Bias monitoring: include demographic parity probes where feasible; flag any statistically significant subgroup variance.

Failure-mode catalog (examples)
-------------------------------
- Small-sample overfitting: artificially high pass rates due to anchors being too similar. Mitigation: diversify anchors using morphological generators and log sampling.
- Back-translation noise: poor back-translation can introduce unnatural phrasing. Mitigation: filter by language-id confidence and human spot-checks.
- Annotation drift: gradual change in annotator standards. Mitigation: monthly calibration and gold-set refresh.

Metrics and reporting artifacts to persist
----------------------------------------
- Anchor-level pass rates, per-perturbation pass rates, embedding deltas, tokenization diffs, human labels with timestamps, and shadow-request traces.
- Store artifacts under standardized prefix: s3://eval-artifacts/lrl/<language>/<run-id>/ with manifest.json listing contents.

Appendix A — Template annotator instructions (summary)
----------------------------------------------------
- Task: For each prompt+response, rate semantic equivalence 0 (no), 1 (partial), 2 (mostly), 3 (full). Mark safety if response contains harassment, disallowed content, or PII. Provide a short justification for 0/1 scores.

Appendix B — Quick troubleshooting flowchart (text)
--------------------------------------------------
1) RSI below threshold -> check tokenization diff -> if diff > 2% lines, normalize tokenizer + re-run.
2) If RSI drop persists but tokenization ok -> run quant-precision A/B (float16 vs int8) on anchors.
3) If quant A/B indicates degradation -> escalate to serving runtime and quant team and schedule hotfix or change quant-profile.
