[Remediation SLA options + customer tier mapping (Hosted / Dedicated / Private) — working doc]
Doc purpose (Product Ops)
========================
We need a consistent set of internal remediation SLAs (time-to-mitigate / time-to-fix expectations) that:
- match what we can realistically execute across tiers (Hosted, Dedicated, Private)
- align with customer expectations and enterprise commitments (especially Dedicated/Private)
- can be implemented in tooling (ENG-4829 / SLA timers + breach alerts) without constant exceptions
- remains low-cardinality and understandable during live incidents

This is a working evaluation doc of options; final policy will live in Confluence in the Remediation SLA matrix.

Definitions
===========
- Remediation SLAs in this doc are internal operational targets and escalation triggers.
- We track two clocks:
  1) TTM (time-to-mitigate): time from incident declared (Sev assigned) to customer-impact mitigation in place (or credible workaround). Mitigation may include rollback, routing/fallback changes, traffic shaping, or isolating a bad region/model.
  2) TTF (time-to-fix): time from incident declared to a durable fix deployed OR a signed-off plan with committed ship date (depending on severity). For Sev0/Sev1, we typically expect a durable fix, not just a plan.

- “Tier” definitions:
  - Hosted: multi-tenant public API.
  - Dedicated: reserved capacity; stronger expectations for predictability and comms.
  - Private: VPC/on-prem control plane + data plane; sometimes customer-controlled networking and change windows.

- Severity (draft; matches on-call practice):
  - Sev0: broad outage / severe customer impact / safety risk / inability to serve core requests at scale.
  - Sev1: major degradation (e.g., high 5xx, severe latency) affecting meaningful customer set or a major enterprise customer; urgent.
  - Sev2: partial degradation; workarounds exist; limited scope.
  - Sev3: minor; limited impact; typically handled in normal on-call flow.

Decision principles
===================
1) Make the SLA actionable during incidents (what it forces us to do: staff, escalate, decide).
2) Keep differences by tier minimal, but acknowledge Dedicated/Private have different reality (capacity isolation, maintenance windows, customer networking).
3) Avoid a matrix so complex that incident-bot can’t enforce it.
4) “Pause/override” exists but must be auditable and rare.

Where tier differences are real (observations)
============================================
Hosted
- We control infra + routing + runtime deploys; can mitigate quickly via routing policies, throttles, or rollbacks.
- Customers accept “platform-wide” incidents but expect fast mitigation.

Dedicated
- Stronger expectations: named account pressure, high-touch comms, fewer acceptable repeated incidents.
- Mitigation sometimes means reallocating fleet capacity; can be constrained by GPU availability.
- Some mitigations require coordination with specific customer traffic patterns and agreed “degradation mode.”

Private
- Customer networking, DNS/TLS, firewalls, and change windows can dominate.
- “Mitigation” may require customer action; we can provide fix/instructions but can’t always execute.
- On-prem/air-gapped environments may block fast patching.

Key question: Do we set stricter SLAs for Dedicated/Private because customers pay more, or do we set realistic SLAs acknowledging dependencies and shift strictness into comms/escalation?

Option set
==========
Option A — Single SLA matrix (same targets across tiers) + comms escalation tiers
Pros: simple; consistent; easy to implement + dashboard.
Cons: risks being unrealistic for Private; breaches become noisy; forces frequent overrides.

Option B — Tier-adjusted TTF only (TTM consistent, TTF differs)
Pros: keeps the “stop the bleeding” behavior consistent; reflects reality that durable fixes take longer when customers control deploy windows.
Cons: still may be tight for certain Private classes; requires tier in SLA evaluator.

Option C — Tier-adjusted TTM and TTF (Dedicated stricter on TTM; Private looser on TTF)
Pros: matches customer expectation: Dedicated should be mitigated extremely fast; Private fixes can take longer.
Cons: more complex; risk of perceived unfairness (“why does private get longer?”).

Option D — Incident-type-aware SLA within severity (e.g., Private connectivity vs Control plane vs Runtime regression)
Pros: most accurate.
Cons: too complex for v1; high maintenance; taxonomy drift.

Recommendation (draft): Option B for v1
======================================
- Keep TTM targets consistent by severity across tiers (behavior we want in every incident: mitigate quickly).
- Allow tier-adjusted TTF targets (Private often needs customer maintenance window; Dedicated should still be fast but not necessarily faster than Hosted in all cases).
- In addition, define comms/escalation requirements by tier (Dedicated/Private proactive outreach thresholds), separate from remediation timers.

Proposed draft SLA targets (v1 candidate)
========================================
Notes:
- Times are proposed internal targets for breach alerting + leadership escalation.
- TTM measured to: restored SLO or reduced to acceptable degradation mode (documented).
- TTF measured to: fix deployed OR (Sev2/Sev3 only) fix scheduled with owner + date.

TTM (same across tiers)
-----------------------
Sev0: 30 minutes
Sev1: 2 hours
Sev2: 1 business day
Sev3: 5 business days (or next planned release train)

TTF (tier-adjusted)
-------------------
Hosted:
- Sev0: 24 hours
- Sev1: 3 business days
- Sev2: 10 business days
- Sev3: 30 business days

Dedicated:
- Sev0: 24 hours (same as Hosted; expectation is mitigation is faster, fix can be similar)
- Sev1: 5 business days (slightly longer than Hosted because some fixes involve fleet reshaping or customer-specific config review)
- Sev2: 15 business days
- Sev3: 30 business days

Private:
- Sev0: 48 hours (some fixes require customer coordination/change window; still want high urgency)
- Sev1: 10 business days
- Sev2: 20 business days
- Sev3: 45 business days

Rationale snapshots (to validate)
================================
- Private Sev0 TTF at 48h is the most controversial number. The intent is: if a Private incident is Sev0, we should be able to ship a fix quickly OR provide a validated workaround package quickly. But we may not be able to deploy it into the customer’s environment inside 48h. Proposed compromise: define “TTF = fix available” vs “TTF = deployed” for Private only.

Proposed adjustment for Private only:
- For Private tier: treat TTF as “fix available + customer delivery completed (artifact + instructions + support handoff)” rather than “fully deployed in customer environment.” Deployment tracking becomes a CS/Support deliverable.

This avoids constant SLA breaches from customer-controlled schedules, while still forcing Redwood to produce the fix quickly.

Edge cases + carve-outs (must be explicit)
=========================================
1) Cloud provider / upstream outage
- If root cause is confirmed upstream (AWS/GCP region/network, managed KMS outage, etc.):
  - TTM still applies (we should mitigate via failover/fallback where possible).
  - TTF may be waived or converted to “post-incident hardening actions” with due dates.
- Implementation requirement: incident-bot must allow “Upstream dependency” as a contributing factor and a “SLA exception reason” (audited).

2) Customer-caused or customer-controlled failures (mostly Private, occasionally Dedicated)
Examples:
- Customer rotated certs incorrectly; firewall blocks new endpoints; DNS misconfig; customer refuses recommended upgrade.
- TTM definition may be “workaround identified + communicated + support engaged.”
- TTF becomes a tracked action plan with customer owner and Redwood owner; SLA breach should not trigger paging.
- Implementation requirement: a controlled “Customer action required” exception reason.

3) Planned maintenance / change windows
- If incident is triggered by a planned change performed by Redwood:
  - SLAs still apply (we own it).
- If fix requires customer change window:
  - Private: allow “Fix available” measurement as above.

4) Multi-cause incidents
- Primary incident_type determines SLA class.
- Contributing systems recorded separately; do not create multiple SLA clocks.
- If reclassified, SLA clock should not reset (only severity changes reset behavior).

Comms and escalation requirements (separate from remediation timers)
===================================================================
We should not bake comms into remediation SLAs, but we do need consistent obligations by tier.

Draft comms rules (for CS alignment; see comms templates doc):
- Hosted
  - Sev0/Sev1: status page + initial update within 30 min; updates at least every 60 min until mitigated.
  - Sev2: case-by-case; internal update; status page optional.

- Dedicated
  - Sev0/Sev1: proactive outreach to affected accounts; initial customer-facing update within 30 min; updates every 60 min.
  - Sev2: proactive outreach within 1 business day if single account materially impacted.

- Private
  - Sev0/Sev1: proactive outreach; include “customer action required” assessment early.
  - Emphasize safe language: symptoms, mitigations, next update time.

Open issues / questions to resolve before signoff
=================================================
1) Private TTF definition: “available” vs “deployed”
- Need decision from SRE + Product Private (Vivek) + CS.

2) Dedicated Sev1 TTF: 3 vs 5 business days
- Dedicated product (Lauren) asked for realism: some changes require capacity rebalancing + canary.
- Counterpoint: enterprise expectation is faster. Maybe keep 3 BD but allow exceptions for capacity procurement work.

3) Severity-to-tier mapping clarity
- Can a Private incident be Sev0 if it affects only one customer? Yes, if it blocks core use case and is high urgency.
- Need crisp language in the incident process policy so on-call doesn’t under-severity enterprise incidents.

4) Implementation feasibility in tooling (ENG-4829)
- SLA evaluator needs tier + severity + type.
- Ensure we don’t create a combinatorial matrix. Proposed v1: severity x tier only, with optional overrides.

5) Reporting expectations
- Aisha to confirm dashboards will report:
  - SLA breach rate by tier, severity, incident_type
  - Exception counts by reason (upstream, customer-action, force majeure)

Data sanity check (informal)
============================
Based on last 2 quarters anecdotal review (see top-incidents analysis):
- Most Sev0/Sev1 mitigations happen within 15–90 minutes for Hosted when the mitigation is routing/rollback.
- Dedicated mitigations vary: quick when routing-only; slow when capacity constrained.
- Private “fix deployed” often exceeds 1–2 weeks due to customer windows; “fix available” is typically within a few days if we prioritize.

Action items (next steps)
=========================

- Rafael/SRE: confirm if “TTF = plan w/ ship date” is acceptable for Sev2/Sev3 (Hosted/Dedicated) (by 2026-02-10)
- Vivek + CS: propose Private TTF measurement definition language for Confluence (by 2026-02-10)
- Lauren: confirm Dedicated Sev1 TTF target (3 vs 5 BD) and list top constraints (capacity procurement, release trains) (by 2026-02-12)
- Aisha: verify dashboards can label tier correctly and track exceptions without high cardinality (by 2026-02-12)

Appendix: quick matrix (for copy/paste)
======================================
TTM (all tiers):
- Sev0: 30m
- Sev1: 2h
- Sev2: 1 BD
- Sev3: 5 BD

TTF:
- Hosted:   Sev0 24h | Sev1 3 BD | Sev2 10 BD | Sev3 30 BD
- Dedicated:Sev0 24h | Sev1 5 BD | Sev2 15 BD | Sev3 30 BD

===================================================

[PagerFlow: incident communication templates + response scripts (draft)]
Purpose and scope:
This doc is a lightweight, transferable kit for run-of-the-mill and high-severity incidents. It is intentionally concise so on-call responders can copy/paste, adapt, and publish quickly. Focus areas: status page snippets, customer-facing bulletins, internal command-center checklist, and short response scripts for initial triage.

How to use this file (quick):
- Immediately after paging: open this doc and pick the severity tier below.
- Publish a status stub within 10 minutes using 'Status page: initial' template.
- Post internal bulletin to #incidents and start the incident bridge (see checklist).
- Use customer template for external-facing accounts (segment by SLA tier).

Severity tiers (use first-match):
- P0 / Emergency: widespread outages, failed model serving, data loss exposure. Publish every 15m until mitigated.
- P1 / Degraded: higher latency or partial feature loss affecting many users. Publish every 30-60m.
- P2 / Performance/Minor: increased latency on non-critical paths, or single-region slowdowns. Publish initial + one follow-up.

Status page templates
1) Status page: initial (copy to status page dashboard)
- Title: Service disruption impacting model inference (region/tier)
- Time: {{ISO_TIMESTAMP}}
- Impact: Customers may experience failed requests or elevated latency for text generation/embeddings in <region>.
- Scope: We have detected increased error rates for some API endpoints; onboarded traffic may be redirected to healthy capacity.
- Current status: Investigating — we have engineers actively looking into the root cause.
- Next update: {{+15m}}
- Incident ID: {{INCIDENT_ID}}

2) Status page: mitigation in progress
- Title: Mitigation in progress — degraded performance reduced
- Time: {{ISO_TIMESTAMP}}
- Impact: Error rates are reduced but intermittent failures may occur for a subset of customers in <region>.
- What we're doing: Rolling back recent routing change / scaling extra worker pool / activating fallback model.
- ETA: ~{{ETA}} minutes for stabilization; next update: {{+30m}}

3) Status page: resolved
- Title: Service restored — monitoring
- Time: {{ISO_TIMESTAMP}}
- Impact: All services are operating normally; we will continue monitoring for the next 2 hours.
- Postmortem: A follow-up summary will be posted when available.

Customer-facing templates (pick tone by severity)
- High-severity (P0) external bulletin
Subject: Urgent: temporary outage affecting inference in <region>
Body: Hi <CustomerName>,
We’re reaching out because you may be seeing failed or slow API requests for Redwood Inference in <region>. Our on-call team detected this at {{ISO_TIMESTAMP}} and is actively investigating. We understand this impacts your production traffic and are prioritizing a mitigation.
What we know now: increased error rates originating from <component or cluster> — scope is being assessed.
What we’re doing: scaling extra capacity, enabling fallback routing, and a hotfix is being evaluated.
When we’ll update: next update in 15 minutes, or sooner if we have new information.
Contact: Your account rep is on the incident bridge and will notify you directly if your SLA requires. For urgent escalation reply to this message or contact support@redwood.ai.
Thanks for your patience — we’ll keep you updated.
- Low-tone (P1/P2) customer bulletin
Subject: Degraded performance noticed for inference in <region>
Body: Hi <CustomerName>,
We detected elevated latency for some requests in <region> beginning at {{ISO_TIMESTAMP}}. We don’t expect data loss; root cause is under investigation. We’ll share an update within 60 minutes.

Legal-safe phrasing (for Customer Success/Legal review)
- Avoid speculation: do not use root-cause language until confirmed.
- Commit to monitoring and follow-up: give a specific next-update time window.
- Offer contact path: include account rep or premium support escalation.

Internal command-center (incident bridge) checklist — rapid sequence
1) Kickoff (first 5 min)
- Assign INCIDENT_LEAD (owner for the bridge) and COMM_LEAD (owns status page & external messages).
- Set bridge link and Slack channel: create thread in #incidents and pin link to bridge.
- Post INITIAL internal bulletin (use 'internal bulletin' template below).
- Attach key telemetry: SLO dashboards, recent deploys, autoscaler logs, error spike graphs.

2) Triage (5–20 min)
- Quick hypothesis grid: network | model runtime | routing | recent deploys | infra autoscaling | storage.
- Check recent merges and deploys: run git log + last deploy IDs (Jenkins/GH Actions).
- Confirm if mitigation is needed: increase replicas, toggle fallback model, or roll back recent deploy.

3) Mitigation (20–60 min)
- Apply mitigation with a single commited actor (assignee) and verify metrics within 5–10 min.
- If mitigation works: update status page to 'mitigation in progress' and CRITICAL customers via direct message.
- If mitigation fails: escalate to SRE lead and consider failover to alternate region.

4) Stabilize & close (after service normal)
- Set status page to 'resolved' and prepare postmortem notes.
- Run blast radius review: list impacted customers and affected features.
- Start postmortem owner assignment and timeline for a full RCA within 72 hours.

Internal bulletin (copy into #incidents)
- Subject: [INCIDENT_ID] Investigating elevated errors — <service/component>
- Body: Timeline: first alarm at {{ISO_TIMESTAMP}}.
Short summary: Elevated 5xx/error-rate for <endpoint>.
Initial actions: scaling + rollback candidate identified + triage team assigned.
Bridge: {{BRIDGE_LINK}} | Comm lead: @<handle> | Incident lead: @<handle>

Response scripts (quick paste for engineers)
- When asked to check logs: 'Run: kubectl -n inference logs -l app=worker --since=10m | grep ERROR'
- To inspect replication: 'kubectl get hpa,pods -n inference -o wide'
- To trigger fallback routing: 'rlsctl route set inference --fallback=true --force' (OPS-only)
- Hot rollback (when authorized): 'deployctl rollback inference-deployment --to=previous --confirm'

Escalation triggers (suggested)
- Fail open: auto-retry > 20% of inbound requests for > 10 minutes -> escalate to P0.
- Latency: p95 > 2s for > 15 minutes for production tier -> escalate to P1.
- Data integrity: any sign of dropped or corrupted user data -> immediate P0 + legal & security on-call.

Post-incident checklist (first 72h)
- Capture full timeline and raw artifacts (logs, traces, deploy ids) and attach to Jira ticket.
- Run smoke tests against canary and prod after mitigation.
- Draft customer-facing root cause summary (with COMM_LEAD).
- Schedule RCA with relevant owners inside 48–72h; assign action items with due dates.

Open questions / TODOs (for this draft)
- Standardize exact SLA wording for Status page vs. direct customer messages.
- Add quick links to observability dashboards (Grafana/Tempo) for each service.
- Make checklist one-click in our incident tooling (nice-to-have).

Notes to on-call (short):
- Publish early, publish often. Even "we're still investigating" helps reduce duplicate pages.
- Keep copy simple and factual. Avoid root-cause claims until validated.
- Use templates and fill placeholders — speed beats prose in the first 30 minutes.

Example filled initial status (for quick copy/paste):
- Title: Service disruption impacting inference (us-west1)
- Time: 2025-07-12T14:03:00Z
- Impact: Some customers in us-west1 may experience 500 errors for text generation endpoints.
- Status: Investigating
- Incident ID: RF-2025-0712-01
- Next update: 2025-07-12T14:18:00Z

Revision history:
- 2024-11-03: initial draft by Aisha P.
- 2025-02-17: updated escalation triggers and response scripts (Miguel S.)
- 2025-08-12: added legal-safe phrasing and customer escalation notes (Rina K.)

End of draft — feedback welcome in thread.


[Rapid response message architectures and war-room checklist]
Purpose:
This is a compact, copy-first runbook for incident communications used by SREs and Oncall to get a war-room stood up, publish a clear public status, and send coordinated customer-facing updates. Focus: clarity, cadence, safety (no speculation), and minimal but informative public messages.

Scope and when to use this doc:
- Use for any incident impacting customer-facing inference APIs, console workflows, or telemetry that persists beyond a single automatic retry (severity P2/P1).
- For short flaps (<5 minutes) that recover automatically, use a brief internal note — no public status unless customer impact seen.

Roles (quick reference):
- Incident Lead (IL): owns triage, decisions, and next-update cadence.
- Communications Lead (CL): drafts public and customer messages, coordinates with CS and legal.
- SRE Triage: initial diagnostics, mitigation attempts, and runbook execution.
- Engineering Lead: deploy/blocker decisions, rollback ownership.
- Customer Support Lead: surfaces critical customer tickets; prepares targeted customer outreach.
- Legal/Compliance: engaged if PII/security exposure suspected.

War-room quick checklist (first 10 minutes):
1) Create incident channel: #war-{{INCIDENT_ID}} (private) and add IL, CL, SREs, Eng lead, CS lead.
2) Assign IL and CL explicitly in channel header.
3) Record initial timeline: detection time, first alert source, initial symptom.
4) Snapshot status page: record current public page state and any existing messages.
5) Set update cadence: default 15 minutes until degradation/mitigation then extend.
6) Start triage: identify impacted services, affected regions, topology (host vs infra vs model).
7) If customer-visible: post initial status page entry (see templates below).
8) Put a readout in #oncall-escalations: 1-line summary + link to war-room channel.
9) Create a ticket in JIRA with incident tag and link to war-room and status page.
10) Decide on targeted customer notifications (CS-led) for top-tier customers.

Status page templates (copy-first; edit variables in place):
- Status: Investigating (public short)
  Title: "Investigating service degradation affecting inference API"
  Impact: "Some requests may fail or experience increased latency in US and EU regions."
  What we know: "Beginning at {{DETECTED_AT}} we observed elevated 5xx/errors and increased tail latency for text generation endpoints."
  What we're doing: "SREs are actively investigating routing and model-serving nodes. We will post updates every 15 minutes or as significant milestones occur."
  ETA for next update: "{{NEXT_UPDATE_TIME}}"
  Affected services: "Inference API (completion/chat), streaming responses"
  Workaround: "Retrying requests with exponential backoff may succeed; we are not recommending model changes at this time."

- Status: Partial service restored (public short)
  Title: "Partial restoration: inference request success rates improving"
  Impact: "A portion of requests remain affected; a subset of traffic now routed to fallback instances."
  What we know: "Mitigation applied at {{MITIGATION_AT}}: traffic routing adjusted to fallback pool which reduced error rate by ~70%."
  What we're doing: "Monitoring to confirm stability and rolling out a permanent fix. Next update in 30 minutes."
  Workaround: "No action required from customers; continuing retries are honored."

- Status: Resolved (public short)
  Title: "Incident resolved: inference API back to expected levels"
  Impact: "All services restored to normal performance."
  What we know: "Root cause under investigation; mitigation fully restored traffic at {{RESOLVED_AT}}. A follow-up postmortem will be shared within 5 business days."
  What we're doing: "Collecting logs and KV cache states for RCA. If you continue to see problems, contact support with incident ID {{INCIDENT_ID}}."

Customer-facing message templates (email / support message):
- Initial customer alert (short):
  Subject: "Notice: Service disruption impacting Redwood inference API ({{INCIDENT_ID}})"
  Body: "Hello,

We're investigating an issue affecting inference requests that started at {{DETECTED_AT}} which may cause failed or delayed responses. Our engineers are working on a fix and we'll send updates by {{NEXT_UPDATE_TIME}}. We apologize for the disruption and will follow up with a full summary after resolution.

If you have a critical impact or active incident in your product, reply to this message and we'll prioritize a direct touch.

— Redwood SRE Team"

- Follow-up/update to affected customers (mid-incident):
  Subject: "Update: Ongoing investigation for {{INCIDENT_ID}} — next steps"
  Body: "Hello,

Quick update: Our mitigation reduced error rates by {{PERCENT}}%. We are continuing to monitor and apply a permanent fix. We expect the next status update at {{NEXT_UPDATE_TIME}}.

We will proactively notify you once your traffic is confirmed stable. Thanks for bearing with us.

— Redwood SRE"

- Resolution summary (short RCAs go to customers, full postmortem internal):
  Subject: "Resolved: Incident {{INCIDENT_ID}} — summary and next steps"
  Body: "Hello,

The incident that began at {{DETECTED_AT}} has been resolved as of {{RESOLVED_AT}}. Impact: failed or delayed inference requests for some customers in US/EU regions. Root cause: degraded routing state caused by a configuration drift in the autoscaling controller (high level). Mitigation: we rolled back the faulty config and restored traffic to healthy model-serving pools.

Actions taken: rollback at {{MITIGATION_AT}}, additional guardrail added to autoscaler, and alerting tuned to catch config drift earlier.

Next steps: we will publish a detailed postmortem in 3 business days with timeline and remediation items. If you observed persistent errors after resolution, please reply with your request IDs and region.

— Redwood SRE & Product"

Internal Slack/war-room announcement samples (concise):
- Initial ping (one-liner): "INCIDENT {{INCIDENT_ID}}: Investigating elevated 5xx on inference-api — war-room #war-{{INCIDENT_ID}}. IL=@Priya. Next update in 15m."
- Escalation ping to Director: "Escalation: Incident {{INCIDENT_ID}} impacting production inference for multiple customers; IL assigned, mitigation in progress. Joining war-room: @Director-Eng."
Do / Don't list for communications lead:
Do:
- Use the template language of 'what we know / what we're doing / next update'.
- Keep public messages under 4–6 bullet lines for clarity.
- Coordinate targeted customer outreach for top-10 accounts.
- Timestamp messages and include incident ID every time.
Don't:
- Don't speculate about root cause in public messages.
- Don't promise exact ETA unless confirmed.
- Don't include internal debugging output or stack traces in public notes.

Posting cadence and escalation rules:
- Start: updates every 15 minutes for the first hour.
- If stabilization occurs: move to every 30–60 minutes until fully resolved.
- If a mitigation is in place but a long-term fix is needed: hourly updates and an ETA for postmortem.
- If incident reaches SEV0/P1 and affects >30% of traffic: exec notification and dedicated comms to top customers.

Technical steps for status page update (reference):
1) Title: short, action-oriented.
2) Set impact correctly (degraded / partial outage / major outage).
3) Use the three-part structure in the public body (what we know / what we're doing / next update).
4) Add 'affected services' list and approximate scope (regions, endpoints).
5) Add a one-line workaround when available.
6) Publish and pin latest update; remove stale workarounds if replaced.

Post-incident checklist (after resolved):
- Lock timeline and collect logs. Owner: SRE Triage.
- Communications: publish resolution and planned RCA cadence. Owner: CL.
- Customer tickets: CS to follow-up with any flagged customers and offer credits if warranted.
- Postmortem: IL to schedule RCA within 3 business days; include impact metrics and remediation owners.
- Action items: convert remediation tasks to tracked JIRA issues and assign SLAs.

Templates for postmortem public summary (short):
- Headline: "Incident {{INCIDENT_ID}}: Summary — {{SHORT_DESCRIPTION}}"
- One-paragraph timeline, one-paragraph root cause (non-technical high-level), list of remediation actions and owners, and link to full internal postmortem.

Quick reference snippets (copy-paste ready):
- "We are investigating increased error rates for inference endpoints. Incident ID: {{INCIDENT_ID}}. Next update: {{NEXT_UPDATE_TIME}}."
- "Mitigation applied: traffic reroute to fallback pool reduced errors by ~{{PERCENT}}%. Monitoring closely. Incident ID: {{INCIDENT_ID}}."
- "Resolved: service restored. We will publish a detailed postmortem by {{PM_DUE_DATE}}. If you see residual issues, include request IDs and region in replies."

Notes and rationale:
- Keep customer messages short and action-oriented; customers prefer a reliable cadence vs verbose technical detail.
- Avoid premature diagnosis; internal channels can include detailed logs, public messages should not.
- Templates should be used as-is for speed; CL can add 1–2 customer-specific lines when necessary.

Open questions / TODOs for this doc:
- Add a ready-to-send SMS/phone script for top-10 customers.
- Define explicit crediting policy text for long outages.
- Add a step-by-step UI guide to update the status.redwood.ai page for new hires.

End of runbook draft.

[Implement composite SLO probes for VPC deployments (latency, errors, saturation, token throughput)]
description:
Create and deploy a set of robust, composite health probes for Private (VPC) deployments that combine latency percentiles, request error rates, node saturation, and token throughput into actionable SLOs. These probes should be surfaced in the Console, wired into alerting, and usable by Terraform IaC so operators can configure thresholds per-customer and per-cluster. The goal is earlier detection of regressions that affect tail latency and token-level throughput while avoiding noisy alerts for transient load patterns.

acceptance_criteria:
Composite SLO exporter implemented in runtime exposing Prometheus metrics for latency p50/p95/p99, 5xx rate, cpu/gpu/utilization, and tokens/sec per tenant
Terraform module exposes configuration for probe thresholds, evaluation windows, and alerting policies
Console dashboard shows composite SLO with breakdown by signal and provides drill-down to per-node and per-tenant traces
Canary rollout with synthetic traffic demonstrates probes trigger alerts and graceful rollback when thresholds exceeded
Documentation and runbook published (Confluence link) and ops trained on escalation steps

technical_notes:
Metrics sources: runtime Prometheus endpoint (tokens/sec), Envoy/nginx for request counts, node exporter for CPU/GPU saturation, and application logs for error codes
Composite SLO computation: weighted aggregator where default weights = {latency:0.4, errors:0.3, saturation:0.2, token_throughput:0.1}; allow per-tenant overrides via Terraform
Latency windows: evaluate p95 over 5m and p99 over 1m with adaptive suppression for ephemeral spikes
Error SLO: 5xx rate threshold at 0.5% over 5m for P1; degraded state at 1% triggers paging
Token throughput probe requires KV cache instrumentation to surface tokens/generated per second and per-tenant token backlog metric
Alerting integration: PagerDuty + Slack + Console in-product banners; use composite alert that fires only when two or more signals breach thresholds to reduce noise
Storage/retention: metrics kept at 1s resolution for 1d, 10s for 7d to support short-window SLOs; long-term aggregates to be sampled
Security: metrics endpoints will be behind mTLS and require RBAC mapping; Terraform module will reference customer KMS keys for any secrets

testing_plan:
Unit tests for composite aggregator logic with synthetic metric streams
Integration tests: deploy to staging and run load-sim with 3 traffic profiles (baseline, burst, long-tail)
Chaos tests: kill a node during steady-state to verify suppression and failover behavior
Performance test: measure exporter CPU overhead at 95th percentile traffic and ensure <2% additional CPU
Cardinality test: simulate 5k tenants to evaluate Prometheus scrape and query cost

rollout_plan:
Phase 0: feature gated in staging, collect baseline metrics for 48h
Phase 1: canary to 2 low-risk customer VPCs with passive alerting (no paging), collect feedback 72h
Phase 2: enable active alerting for SRE on canary clusters with tightened suppression rules
Phase 3: gradual rollout to remaining Private clusters with Terraform module versioned and documented
Rollback: Terraform variable slo_enabled=false and remove exporter sidecar; run quick rollback playbook from runbook doc

risks:
Overly-sensitive composite SLO may generate pager fatigue during autoscale events if suppression rules are insufficient
Token throughput instrumentation could add measurable overhead to runtime if sampling not tuned
Per-tenant metrics at high cardinality may increase Prometheus storage costs and query latency
Terraform API changes for per-customer thresholds must be backwards compatible to avoid upgrade headaches for existing Private customers

Add Terraform module wiring and validate with example customer stacks in infra/terraform/modules/vpc-slo (MR: https://git.company/infra/terraform/merge_requests/659)
Create Console dashboard panels and add unit tests for composite SLO calculations
Run canary in two low-risk customer clusters with synthetic and replay traffic for 72h

[Private/VPC bootstrap & egress flow: failure scenarios, test matrix, and acceptance contract]
description:
Scope: Define deterministic acceptance criteria for Private/VPC deployments focused on initial bootstrap (operator/controller startup), controlled egress flows for artifact sync and telemetry, and upgrade/fallback behavior in air-gapped or restricted-egress environments. This doc specifies failure scenarios, observable signals, automated test matrix, and operator playbook required before shipping the private deployment operator 1.0. Goals: (1) ensure zero-surprise bootstraps in customer VPCs with restrictive egress, (2) define minimal egress allowlist and mirror patterns, (3) codify rollback and offline upgrade acceptance criteria for customers running air-gapped clusters.

acceptance_criteria:
AC-1: Operator bootstrap succeeds end-to-end in a VPC with deterministic minimal egress: only HTTPS to allowed mirror endpoints and customer-provided image registry. Full bootstrap means all pods reach Ready and control-plane health checks pass within configured window (15m) without manual operator intervention.
AC-2: When external egress is blocked, operator reports clear, actionable diagnostic codes in /status and logs; each code maps to an automated remediation suggestion in the Console. Example codes: EG-REG-403 (registry auth), EG-DNS-FAIL (DNS resolution), EG-MIRROR-404 (mirror missing artifact).
AC-3: Offline upgrade flow: given a pre-staged image mirror and signed artifacts, the operator can perform a node-by-node upgrade without contacting public endpoints. Acceptance requires a scripted validation run that verifies version skew tolerance and CV health metrics post-upgrade.
AC-4: Controlled egress policy documented and validated: a single-page allowlist with ports/hosts/subnets for (a) artifact mirror, (b) time-limited telemetry relay (optional), (c) license/license-verification endpoints. Tests demonstrate graceful degradation when telemetry is disabled (no crashloops; metrics buffered and exported when connectivity resumes).
AC-5: Rollback contract: if a canary upgrade reduces available replicas below SLO or triggers pod crashloops across dependent services, the operator triggers an automated rollback and generates a postmortem template linking telemetry windows and resource snapshots.
AC-6: Auditability: every bootstrap and upgrade action emits an immutable event with timestamp, operator version, and checksums of pulled images; events are exportable to customer SIEM and visible in Console activity timeline.
AC-7: Test automation: each acceptance criterion is wired to an automated test harness that can run in both the Redwood staging environment and a minimal on-prem emulation (airgapped VM cluster).

test_plan:
TP-1: Network partition matrix: simulate blocked egress to registry, partial DNS failure, and intermittent packet loss; verify bootstrap progress and error codes within 15m window.
TP-2: Mirror-first offline install: validate operator install from local mirror with signed manifests; verify checksums and signature verification path.
TP-3: Upgrade smoke: canary subset upgraded while load generators run, monitor P99 latency and replica count; automated rollback if >10% of requests fail at P50 or two or more pods crashloop.
TP-4: Telemetry-disabled validation: run full install with telemetry disabled; ensure metrics are buffered locally and no control-plane features depend on telemetry availability.
TP-5: Deterministic timeout gating: ensure timeouts and retry windows are configurable by customer and defaults are conservative for low-bandwidth environments.
TP-6: Security gate: validate KMS/HSM integration for key rotation during upgrade and that images are validated against signed attestations in offline mode.

rollout_strategy:
Staged rollout across customers: 1) internal staging with synthetic VPCs (mirror + restricted egress), 2) opt-in early access customers (two pilot customers with non-production workloads), 3) gated general availability. Rollout toggle controlled by feature flag 'private.egress.validation' and release notes required for pilot customers.

risks:
R-1: Customer environments are highly variable; edge cases (proprietary proxies, custom MTU settings) may cause unpredictable bootstrap failures—mitigation: expand test harness with customer-supplied network profiles.
R-2: Mirror freshness and signing mismatch may block upgrades—mitigation: include artifact checksum reconciliation and clear operator UI for manual override with audit log.
R-3: Overly permissive allowlist reduces security posture—mitigation: recommend minimal defaults and provide validated mirror helper tools to seed mirrors securely.

decisions:
D-1: Operator will prefer mirror-first fetches with built-in retry/backoff; public endpoints used only as fallback and require explicit operator config.
D-2: Error codes will be standardized across controller components and documented in a single Console help article; each code has a RBAC-visible remediation link.
D-3: We will ship a standalone 'mirror-seeder' CLI to help customers bootstrap mirrors in disconnected environments; the CLI is out-of-band but required for offline acceptance tests.

[eng-runtime]
mina: Heads up — saw a reproducible decode jitter when we enable FP8 KV with the new dithered calibration on long-context runs (8k). Not a full regression but token-level probability wobble causing occasional token flips.

arjun: Can you paste a short repro and perf snapshot?

mina: Repro (quick):
```
# repro (local perf VM)
run_profile --model llama2-13b --kv-quant fp8-dither --calib-samples 2048 --batch 1 --seqlen 8192 --steps 50
```
Output summary (truncated):
```
config: fp8-dither, calib=2048
mem: peak_gpu=10.4GB (vs 25.8GB fp32)
latency: p50=24ms p95=48ms p99=120ms
decode-jitter-rate=0.8% (token flips on greedy vs. non-dithered baseline)
kv-cache-hit-rate ~99.7%
```

leah: Interesting — memory improvement looks great. 0.8% token flip feels small but could be visible for some chats. Did you check with deterministic seeds?

mina: Yes, deterministic seed reduces nondeterminism but the flip remains in a subset of prompts (mostly low-entropy prefix transitions). Hypothesis: quantization dither + kernel rounding during cache writes produces small probability perturbations that get amplified by softmax in next-step decoding.

sam: Any kernel switch logs around the jitter windows? We recently enabled opportunistic INT8->FP8 kernel switching for smaller batches.

mina: I attached a short log extract (copied):
```
[12:02:11.103] kernel_select: chosen=fp8_kv_smallseq (latency_est=19ms)
[12:02:11.104] kv_store: quantize=dithered_fp8, commit_bytes=12288
[12:02:11.125] kernel_switch: fallback=int8_kv (hysteresis not met)
[12:02:11.126] decode_step(42): token: "the" prob=0.121->0.117 (baseline 0.119)
```

arjun: Kernel flip during a single request is bad — that could explain mid-request changes. We should avoid switching kernels while a request is in-flight; there is already a per-request sticky flag but maybe it wasn't honored for the new fp8 path.

leah: Also calibration sample size might be insufficient. 2048 samples for some attention heads is borderline. Try 8192 or change sampling distribution (more long-seq examples).

sam: Quick A/B numbers from my side running 8192 calib samples + sticky per-request kernel:
```
8192 samples + sticky: p50=26ms p95=52ms p99=110ms, token flips=0.12%
512 samples: p50=22ms p95=46ms, token flips=1.7%
```
So calibration helps a lot but adds a few ms. Tradeoff: quality vs latency.

mina: Agreed. Another mitigation: add small hysteresis window for kernel switching (>3ms estimated delta) and prefer in-request stickiness. Also consider deterministic quant rounding (no dither) for low-entropy prefix routes while keeping dither for general traffic.

arjun: We should also profile KV write encoding variance. If the quant commit bytes vary across kernel implementations, that could change layout/padding and slightly alter numerical ops. Can someone run a byte-exact dump of KV writes across kernels?

[Adaptive Degradation Safety & Verification Manual]
Summary:\n\nThis manual defines the safety contracts, verification checks, benchmarking protocols, and operational runbooks we use to validate adaptive degradation and fallback behavior in the Redwood serving runtime. It is intended for runtime engineers, SREs, and release owners who gate runtime and scheduler changes. The document consolidates architecture contracts, test harnesses, profiling playbooks, measurable acceptance criteria, and incident response steps into a single reference.\n\nScope:\n- Covers adaptive degradation (fidelity staircases, model-variant fallback, burst shedding) and scheduler/kernel interactions.\n- Includes verification checks executed in CI, pre-release staging, and canary phases.\n- Prescribes profiling and benchmark procedures for SLO verification and performance regressions.\n- Provides runbooks for on-call and release owners for graceful rollback and mitigation.\n\nPrinciples and safety goals:\n1) Observable and measurable: every degradation path must have a minimal observable signal (metrics, traces, events) and a single source-of-truth trace ID for forensic replay.\n2) Fail open vs fail closed rationale: correctness-critical requests (enterprise-configured) should prefer fail-closed; non-critical/latency-sensitive requests can fail open to preserved throughput.\n3) Bounded fidelity loss: fidelity steps should degrade quality predictably (quantified by eval sets) and be reversible.\n4) Deterministic rollback: any automated fallback must expose a deterministic rollback path and human-confirmable guardrails.\n\nArchitecture contracts (high-level):\n- Degradation tiers: primary (full model), degraded-1 (quantized), degraded-2 (short-context variant), fallback (smaller model / cached-embeddings). Each tier has an SLO budget and cost profile.\n- Kernel scheduling contract: the scheduler must maintain per-request kernel affinity for the first N tokens and preserve KV cache affinity during tier transition windows (default N=16).\n- Eviction and warmup contract: when a session is evicted from KV cache, a warmup window of configurable length (default 60s) is reserved to rehydrate frequently-seen prompts without degrading SLOs.\n\nVerification matrix (summary table):\n| Check ID | Purpose | Where executed | Acceptance threshold | Action on fail | Owner |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| VD-01 | End-to-end tail latency under 95th percentile SLO | CI staging + canary | p95 < 1200ms for interactive path | block release, auto-rollback in canary | runtime-sre |\n| VD-02 | Kernel latency jitter for hot kernels | perf-lab | 95th/50th ratio < 3.0 | schedule throttling + revert kernel flags | runtime-kernel-team |\n| VD-03 | Fidelity regression on golden prompt set | automated evals | task-specific metric delta < 1.5% | fail gating | applied-ml |\n| VD-04 | KV cache hitrate during warmup | synthetic replay | hitrate > 70% after 120s | degrade to cached-response fallback | runtime-sre |\n| VD-05 | Correctness of fallback routing (no request loss) | chaos lab | 0 dropped requests during routing switch | incident | runtime-oncall |\n\nVerifiable artifacts for each check:\n- Synthetic replay corpus snapshot (sha256) used in CI.\n- Expected telemetry schemas (metric names, tags) and trace samples.\n- Baseline benchmark outputs (binary artifacts) for diff-based gating.\n\nCI and pre-release harnesses:\n1) CI unit stage: microbenchmarks for individual kernels (latency, occupancy, memory). Thresholds are enforced as fast-fail rules.\n2) Staging perf run: full-stack replay of production traffic sampled (1:1000) with degraded-tier injection. Output artifacts: histogram dumps, kernel traces, KV cache heatmaps.\n3) Canary: traffic ramp with A/B model variants and automated rollback on VD-* failures. Canary policy: 1% -> 5% -> 20% over 30m windows with automated health checks every 5m.\n\nBenchmarking protocol (detailed):\n- Workloads to run:\n  - Interactive short-chat (mean tokens=40, 90th=128) — target low-latency SLOs.\n  - Streaming long-output (mean tokens=800) — target throughput and memory stability.\n  - Embeddings burst (large batch sizes) — target batching efficiency and memory footprint.\n- Metrics collected:\n  - end_to_end_latency_ms (p50/p90/p95/p99), kernel_exec_time_ms per-kernel, gpu_mem_used_mb, kv_cache_hitrate_pct, tokens_per_second_per_gpu.\n- Tooling & commands (examples):\n  - Run synthetic replay: \n    ./perf-runner --profile=replay --corpus=sha256:abcd1234 --duration=15m --out=artifacts/replay-$(date +%s).tgz\n  - Microbenchmark kernel: \n    python tools/microbench.py --kernel matmul --batch 1 --seq 128 --out json --repeat 50\n  - Collect trace samples for a request: \n    curl -H \"Authorization: Bearer $CI_TOKEN\" https://staging.api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -d '{\"prompt\":\"<<golden>>\"}' -o /tmp/trace.json\n- Acceptance criteria pattern:\n  - No p95 regression > 8% vs baseline.\n  - Kernel jitter (95/50) <= 3.0.\n  - KV cache delta < 5% hitrate loss after warmup period.\n\nProfiling playbook snippets (how-to):\n1) Latency fingerprint collection (on perf-lab machine):\n  - Start full instrumentation: export PERF_SAMPLER=on; ./runtime --enable-tracing --trace-sample-rate=0.01\n  - Run workload for 10 minutes and collect traces: tar -czf traces.tgz /var/tmp/traces/*\n  - Post-process: python tools/trace-aggregate.py --input traces.tgz --output traces-summary.json\n2) Kernel causality mapping:\n  - Use kernel-hint exporter to annotate kernels with request-id and token-index. Example PromQL to find kernel hotpaths: sum(rate(kernel_exec_time_ms_bucket[5m])) by (kernel_name)\n3) Latency attribution checklist:\n  - Confirm p95 skew aligns with a specific kernel or queue time via trace waterfall.\n  - Check GPU utilization and eviction events within the window.\n  - Validate KV cache hit/miss correlation with session affinity changes.\n\nRunbook: Adaptive Degradation incident triage (short):\n1) Detection: Alert triggers if p95 or error-rate breaches gating thresholds (see Verification matrix).\n2) Initial triage (first 10 min):\n  - Owner: oncall-runtime.\n  - Query: run the baseline PromQL dashboards (listed below) and capture current vs baseline.\n  - Commands:\n    - promql: rate(request_latency_seconds_bucket[5m]) by (route)\n    - runtime CLI: runtimectl list-sessions --filter=evicted=true --since=10m\n3) Containment (10–30 min):\n  - If caused by kernel regression: flip kernel rollout gate to previous stable tag (runtimectl kernel-set active:stable-<tag>) and pause canaries.\n  - If caused by cache warmup regression: enable elevated pre-warm (config: prewarm_multiplier=2) and route new sessions to degraded-1 temporarily.\n4) Remediation (30–90 min):\n  - Roll back flagged config or kernel. Run perf-runner quick replay to validate.\n  - If degradation persists, scale dedicated pool capacity for 15 minutes to reduce pressure and collect artifacts.\n5) Post-incident verification: Ensure all VD-* checks pass in staging before re-enabling automated rollouts.\n\nRelease gating checklist (for runtime and scheduler changes):\n- Code owner review and ADR reference.\n- Automated CI checks: unit tests, lint, kernel microbenchmarks.\n- Perf artifacts present: replay corpus, baseline histograms, and guard thresholds.\n- Canary policy configured and health checks defined (list health checks and thresholds attached).\n- Rollback plan and human approvers designated in the release ticket.\n\nInstrumentation and metrics schema (quick reference):\n- metric names: runtime.request.latency_ms, runtime.kernel.exec_ms, runtime.kv.hits, runtime.fidelity.tier, runtime.eviction.count\n- required tags: service, model_name, model_variant, route, region, canary_id\n- recommended tracing fields: request_id, session_id, token_index, kernel_name, warmup_phase\n\nOwnership and escalation:\n- Runtime architecture owner: runtime-arch@redwood.ai (primary: Sanjay Rao).\n- Kernel scheduling owner: kernel-team@redwood.ai.\n- Oncall rota: runtime-sre (see internal roster).\n- Escalation path: oncall -> SRE lead -> runtime-arch -> Eng Director (timed escalation at 45m).\n\nAppendices:\nA) YAML example: adaptive degradation policy (example config to be applied via runtime fleet config)\n\n  degradation_policy:\n    tiers:\n      - name: degraded-2\n        model_variant: v2-shortctx\n        slos:\n          p95_latency_ms: 350\n    warmup:\n      kv_cache_warmup_seconds: 120\n      prewarm_multiplier: 1.5\n    fallback:\n      strategy: route-to-smaller-model\n      max_inflight_fallback: 250\n\nB) PromQL examples (quick):\n- p95 latency for route: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(runtime_request_latency_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, route))\n- kernel jitter index: (histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(kernel_exec_time_ms_bucket[5m])) by (le, kernel)))/(histogram_quantile(0.5, sum(rate(kernel_exec_time_ms_bucket[5m])) by (le, kernel)))\n\nC) Minimal reproduction recipe for regressions:\n1) Snapshot failing commit and baseline artifacts.\n2) Run perf-runner with the failing kernel flag enabled and the baseline corpus.\n3) Collect traces (traces.tgz) and microbench outputs.\n4) Upload artifacts to /artifacts/regressions/<ticket-id>.\n\nRelated reading and references:\n- See routing and fallback architecture ADR (link in related_pages).\n- Profiling playbooks and telemetry contract (links in related_pages).\n\nNotes and change log:\n- 2026-01-15: Initial draft and adoption of verification matrix (S. [PRD: Fidelity Chaos Experimentation and Rollback]
Overview

This PRD describes the Fidelity Chaos Experimentation and Rollback (FCER) product: a controlled test harness and operational playbook to exercise fidelity degradation paths (quantization fallbacks, lower-tier model variants, prefix truncation, KV cache eviction) in production-like environments and verify automated rollback behavior before broad rollouts.

Motivation

Redwood’s adaptive-fidelity features reduce cost by degrading output fidelity in controlled ways. Customers must not observe uncontrolled regressions. We need a repeatable product that: (1) safely injects fidelity degradations across deployment modes, (2) validates observability signals and quality metrics, (3) exercises rollback/mitigation automations, and (4) provides summary artifacts for stakeholders and customer communication.

Goals (measurable)

1. Provide a repeatable experiment runner that can execute 10 common fidelity-degradation scenarios against a tenant-configured workload within 1 hour.
2. Surface fidelity regressions on the platform dashboard within 2 minutes of divergence from baseline metrics (latency, token quality, token rejection rate).
3. Validate automated rollback policies (canary abort, model variant fallback, credit-safe fallback) succeed 95% of the time in controlled experiments.
4. Produce an experiment report (JSON + human-readable summary) for every run with deterministic artifacts for audit and legal.

Non-goals

- We will not implement new model quantization kernels. This product tests and validates existing runtime behaviors.
- We will not automate customer-visible price changes as part of an experiment.

Stakeholders and Owners

- Product (owner): Lena Ortiz (owner)
- Eng - Serving Runtime: Marcus Chen (technical lead)
- Eng - Observability: Priya Rao (telemetry & alerting)
- SRE / Reliability: Diego Alvarez (runbook & escalation)
- Legal & Compliance: Arjun Mehta (audit requirements)
- Customer Success: Mei Wallace (customer communication)

User Personas

- Internal QA engineers: run experiments and review artifacts.
- Platform engineers: validate rollout policies in staging and canary.
- Customer success / account teams: review experiment summaries for opt-in customers.

Functional Requirements

1. Experiment Definition API (REST + CLI): users must be able to define experiments with fields: name, description, target_tenants (list), degradation_type (enum), start_window (UTC), duration_minutes, traffic_shape (example: 5% ramp to 25% p50), baseline_reference (snapshot id), rollback_policy (enum), monitoring_tags (list).

2. Supported Degradation Types (initial):
   - quantization-profile-switch (e.g., q8 -> q4)
   - model-variant-lower-tier (e.g., rlx-3 => rlx-3-small)
   - kv-cache-eviction (evict prefix caches for specified session ids)
   - prefix-truncation (truncate input prompts above N tokens)
   - batching-constraint (force smaller batch sizes to emulate latency pressure)

3. Safe Execution Guards:

   - Experiments may only run against tenants that opted-in; system must prevent cross-tenant bleed.
   - A kill switch must allow immediate abort across all affected nodes.
   - Concurrency cap: max 3 parallel experiments per region.

4. Telemetry and Quality Signals:

   - Capture token-level loss delta, generation perplexity delta, latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99), token error rates, allocator OOM events, and downstream client error rates.
   - Emit a 1-minute aggregated metrics snapshot to the observability pipeline for the experiment window.

5. Automated Rollback Policies (must support):

   - Threshold-based rollback (if quality_loss > X% or latency increase > Yms for Z min).
   - Canary abort if canary cohort shows regression > threshold versus baseline.
   - Escalation policy: if automatic rollback fails, create a high-severity incident and notify SRE.

6. Reporting and Artifact Storage:

   - Each experiment must store: experiment.json (definition), metrics_diff.csv, sample_generation_diffs.jsonl (10k lines cap), and human_summary.md.
   - Retention default: 90 days; export to S3 for audits via manual export.

Non-functional Requirements

- Security: experiments run under tenant-scoped IAM; logs must redact PII.
- Performance: experiment orchestration must add <2% overhead to runtime latency outside the experiment window.
- Reliability: experiment runner SLA 99.9% for orchestration APIs.
- Compliance: audit trail (who launched, approvals, timestamps) must be immutable for 2 years for flagged customers.

Acceptance Criteria

- QA team successfully runs the provided starter suite (10 scenarios) in staging and can reproduce a rollback within 5 minutes when a threshold is met.
- Dashboard surfaces experiment status and key deltas as specified.
- Generated report includes example diffs and enough context for CS to craft customer comms.

UX and Operator Flows

1. Create experiment (UI + CLI):

   - UI shows: experiment name, target tenant(s), degradation type, ramp schedule editor (prebuilt templates), expected impact box (auto-calculated from baseline), approval workflow (optional).

2. Preflight checks (automated):

   - validate tenant opt-in, validate model compatibility matrix, validate rollback policy presence, validate monitoring hooks ready.

3. Run + Monitor:

   - Live dashboard: status, traffic shape, top 10 metric deltas, sample diffs (toggle redact), auto-suggested rollback triggers.

4. Post-run report and signoff:

   - Role-based signoff flow: QA signs off to promote policy to production. CS receives sanitized summary for customers.

Rollout Plan (phased)

- Phase 0 (Pilot - 6 weeks): internal-only in staging with synthetic workloads. Deliverables: API, CLI, baseline dashboard, report generator.
- Phase 1 (Canary - 8 weeks): limited beta with 5 engineering tenants and 2 opt-in customers; expose UI and automated rollback.
- Phase 2 (GA - 12 weeks): self-serve opt-in in Console, retention policies, export tools, documentation and runbooks.

Metrics and Success Criteria

- % of experiments that auto-rollback within policy window (target: >= 95%).
- Mean time from regression detection to rollback (target: <= 3 minutes).
- False-positive rollback rate in staging (target: < 2%).
- Customer-reported fidelity incidents post-rollout (target: none for opted-in customers; monitor and escalate).

Experiment Configuration Matrix (example table)

| Scenario ID | Degradation Type | Traffic Shape | Rollback Trigger | Expected Impact | Owner |
|-------------|------------------|---------------|------------------|-----------------|-------|
| S-QUANT-1   | quantization-profile-switch | 10% -> 50% over 10m | quality_loss > 4% p95 | small drop in BLEU-like metric | QA Team |
| S-VARIANT-2 | model-variant-lower-tier | steady 5% | latency p95 + 40ms | higher hallucination risk | Serving Runtime |
| S-KV-3      | kv-cache-eviction | burst 20% 2m | client_error_rate > 0.5% | transient latency spike | SRE |

Operational Runbook (summary)

1. Abort: click Abort on experiment console -> orchestration sends kill to agents -> system verifies rollback completion across nodes.
2. If rollback fails: open /incident/new with template: "FCER rollback failed: <experiment-id>", tag SRE and Observability.
3. Post-incident: capture sample diffs and attach to incident for analysis.

Security, Privacy, and Compliance Notes

- All sample outputs must be sanitized and PII redacted before persistent storage. The experiment API must log the identity of the person who started the test and any approvers.
- For regulated customers, experiments are only allowed with explicit contract addendum; enforce at API level.

Risks and Mitigations

- Risk: noisy telemetry leads to false rollbacks. Mitigation: require sustained threshold for Z minutes, apply statistical smoothing, and provide simulation mode.
- Risk: cross-tenant exposure. Mitigation: strict tenant scoping, synthetic traffic isolation, and preflight checks.

Appendix: Example CLI snippets

Acceptance signoff checklist

- [ ] API implemented and tested in staging
- [ ] UI experiment builder exists with templates
- [ ] Telemetry hook integrated with observability pipeline
- [ ] Rollback policies execute in 95% of test runs
- [ ] Documentation and runbook published

Open questions

1. What default thresholds should we ship for quality_loss vs latency to minimize customer impact? (Product & Serving Runtime to propose).
2. Should experiment exports be automatically pushed to customer-owned S3 for regulated customers?

[KV-prefetch audit and experiment guide]
Overview
This document is a pragmatic audit + experiment playbook for evaluating and iterating on KV-cache prefetch strategies in the Redwood serving runtime. It consolidates instrumentation, test-corpus design, hypothesis-driven experiments, safety gates, and clear remediation steps to validate that a prefetch change improves throughput or cost without regressing latency or output fidelity.

Intended audience
- Runtime engineers (kernel and scheduler owners)
- Performance and profiling teams
- SREs running capacity and incident drills
- Release engineers validating runtime rollouts

Goals
1) Provide a repeatable audit checklist to assess existing prefetch behaviour and its observability gaps.
2) Define experiment templates (canary, A/B, ramp) with required telemetry, sample sizes, and SLO-aligned success criteria.
3) Offer rollout and rollback runbook steps with specific threshold values and playbook actions.

Scope and non-goals
- Scope: KV prefetch heuristics, warmup policies, prefetch batch sizing, prefetch prioritisation across tenants/model variants, and their impact on kernel scheduling and KV cache hit/miss behavior.
- Non-goals: Changes to model serialization or offline model compile pipeline (handled elsewhere). This guide does not substitute for security or compliance sign-off for customer-sensitive telemetry.

Background and terminology
- KV prefetch: pro-active population of a model's key-value cache before predicted use (e.g., during warmstart or after canary shadowing).
- Warmstart: placement of a model variant onto a GPU with pre-warmed KV state for a target user session.
- Prefetch window: sequence-length- and token-count-derived horizon for which we request early KV population.
- Shadow traffic: mirrored request streams used for dry-run experiments.

Observability contract (what to collect)
Collect these signals for all experiments. Instrumentation must be enabled at service, runtime-shard, and kernel levels.
- Metrics (per-second or histogram as noted):
  - kvcache.prefetch.requests_total (counter)
  - kvcache.prefetch.success_ratio (gauge) = success / attempts per minute
  - kvcache.hit_ratio_by_prefix_length (histogram buckets by prefix tokens)
  - kvcache.prefetch_latency_p50/p95 (histogram ms)
  - kernel.queue_wait_ms (histogram) labeled by priority bucket
  - runtime.topology.eviction_rate (counter per shard)
  - gpu.memory.oversubscription_events (counter)
  - request.latency.p50/p95/p99 (end-to-end including network + kernel)
  - request.tail_slo_breaches (counter) where tail SLO := requests > configured target (e.g., 95th > 120ms)
  - cost.per_token.estimated (derived using token counts + kernel accounting)
- Traces: request span with children: prefetch.call, prefetch.cache_write, kernel.exec, kv_lookup; include tags: model_id, variant_tag, session_id, shard_id, kernel_id, tenant_id, prefetch_hint_id.
- Logs: structured event for prefetch decisions: {"decision":"prefetch|skip","reason":"prefix-match|heuristic|manual","estimated_tokens":N,"evicted":true|false,"latency_ms":N} as newline-delimited JSON to the observability pipeline.

Audit checklist (baseline assessment)
1) Baseline traffic capture
   - Capture at least 72 hours of representative production traffic or use a validated synthetic corpus (see Test corpus section).
   - Ensure sampling includes peak hour and low-hour slices.
2) Reproduceability of prefetch events
   - Verify prefetch events are traceable to requests in shadow logs. Correlate prefetch_hint_id across traces.
3) Telemetry completeness
   - Confirm all metrics and traces listed in Observability contract are present. If any are missing, add target instrumentation and replay a synthetic subset to validate.
4) Heatmaps and correlation checks
   - Build the following diagnostics:
     - heatmap: prefix_length -> prefetch_success_rate
     - scatter: per-request prefetch_latency vs request_latency
     - timeline: eviction_rate vs memory_pressure
5) Failure mode inventory
   - Enumerate cases found in logs (e.g., prefetch eviction within 2s, prefetch causing kernel queueing). Classify severity and likely root causes.

Test corpus recommendations
- Canonical corpora: use a mix of (a) production-scrubbed request traces, (b) replayable synthetic sessions (session bundles), and (c) jittered-edge sequences to exercise long prefixes.
- Session bundle format (JSONL, one session per line):
  {"session_id":"s-123","model":"vicuna-13b-q4","turns":["Hello","Summarize: ...","Followup: ..."],"timestamps":[...]}
- Size guidance: minimum 5000 sessions covering 10k prefix variations for a statistically meaningful p95 comparison in canary windows.

Experiment designs
All experiments must be hypothesis-driven and limited in blast radius. Follow the experiment checklist below.

A) Shadow (no impact) hypothesis test
- Goal: Validate prefetch hit-rate and false-positive eviction costs without affecting production latency.
- Method: Mirror 1:1 traffic to a shadow runtime with the new prefetch strategy. Do not route responses.
- Duration: 48–72 hours or until 10k prefetch decisions observed.
- Required metrics: kvcache.prefetch.success_ratio, eviction_rate, prefetch_latency.
- Success criteria: improvement in prefetch.success_ratio by >=5% or reduction in cold-start kernel execs by >=10% with no increase in eviction_rate > 2% over baseline.

B) Canary small ramp (impactful but controlled)
- Goal: Measure end-to-end latency and kernel queue impact under production conditions.
- Method: Route 1% of traffic to canary pool with the new prefetch strategy. Use canary tags and separate metrics.
- Observation windows: 1 minute, 15 minutes, 1 hour, 6 hours.
- Safety gates (auto-rollback triggers):
  - request.tail_slo_breaches increases by >20% relative to baseline in a 15-minute window -> immediate rollback.
  - kernel.queue_wait_ms.p95 increases by >30% sustained for 10 minutes -> immediate pause and manual review.
  - gpu.memory.oversubscription_events > 0 (new events) in canary -> pause.
- Success criteria: no SLO breach increase; p95 request latency change within +/- 5% and prefetch.success_ratio improved or neutral.

C) A/B experiment with fidelity measurement
- Goal: Measure fidelity / model output drift when prefetching influences KV state timing (rare but possible).
- Method: 50/50 split where identical prompts are sent to control (no change) and candidate (new prefetch). Collect deterministic evaluation prompts and human-eval random sample.
- Fidelity metrics: BLEU/ROUGE/embedding-similarity on deterministic prompts, plus small human quality cohort (n=200) to detect hallucination/regression.
- Success criteria: embedding cosine similarity > 0.995 on deterministic prompts and no statistically significant decrease in human-score (alpha=0.05).

Telemetry and sample size calculations
- Latency experiments: to detect a 5% p95 change with 90% power typically needs O(20k) p95 samples per group; for canaries prefer longer duration instead of increasing blast radius.
- Hit-rate experiments: to detect a 5% absolute increase in hit rate with alpha=0.05/power=0.8, ~thousands of prefetch events are required depending on baseline rate; use exact binomial test calculator.

Experiment orchestration and dashboards
- Dashboards: create canary-specific dashboards with the prefixed label canary=kv-prefetch-vX. Panels: prefetch.success_ratio, request.p95, kernel.queue_wait_ms.p95, eviction_rate, memory_pressure, tail_slo_breaches; include shaded baseline band.
- Alerts: temporary canary alerts that auto-resolve after ramp is complete.

Rollout and rollback runbook (step-by-step)
1) Preflight (1–3 days before canary)
   - Verify instrumentation and dashboards are green.
   - Run shadow test and ensure metrics are recorded.
   - Prepare rollback image and clear owner contact list.
2) Canary 1% (0–2 hours)
   - Deploy config to canary pool. Monitor 1m and 15m windows.
   - If any auto-rollback trigger fires, execute rollback playbook (step 5).
3) Ramp to 5% (2–12 hours)
   - After 6 hours of stable signals, increment to 5%. Continue monitoring 1m/15m/1h/6h windows.
4) Ramp to 20% (12–48 hours)
   - Confirm A/B fidelity checks pass on deterministic prompts.
5) Full roll (48–72 hours)
   - Only after 72 hours with no gate violations and cost analysis favorable, schedule full rollout.
6) Rollback procedure (when triggered)
   - Step A: Pause canary routing (set weight=0).
   - Step B: Revert runtime config to previous prefetch policy image.
   - Step C: Collect postmortem trace dump, capture 2-hour window around trigger for RCA.
   - Step D: Open incident with severity classification and tag owners.

Common failure modes and mitigations
- Failure: Increased kernel queueing due to premature prefetch floods.
  - Mitigation: Add rate limiter on prefetch.requests per shard per second; add backpressure signal from kernel.queue_wait_ms.
- Failure: Prefetch evicts hot state for other tenants.
  - Mitigation: Implement tenant-aware prefetch budgeting and soft reservations.
- Failure: Memory oversubscription from prefetch writes.
  - Mitigation: Pre-allocate lightweight shadow stores and throttle writes when memory_pressure > 70%.

Debugging checklist (fast triage)
1) Correlate prefetch decision trace with kernel.exec and eviction events (trace id).
2) If prefetch_latency_p95 > 100ms, inspect network path and serialization overhead.
3) If eviction_rate spikes after prefetch, check memory per shard, recent model swaps, and estimate of prefetch window size.
4) Re-run small synthetic session set in debug pool with verbose logging on canary image.

Example config snippets
- Prefetch policy YAML (example):
```yaml
prefetch_policy: 
  name: horizon-predictor-v2
  enabled: true
  max_concurrent_per_shard: 8
  token_horizon: 64
  priority: low
  tenant_budget_percent: 5
  eviction_backoff_seconds: 30
  metrics_emit_interval_s: 10
```
- CLI commands (examples)
  - Capture shadow stream (devbox):
    rdxctl kvcapture --model vicuna-13b-q4 --window 72h --out /tmp/vicuna-shadow.jsonl
  - Deploy canary config:
    rdxctl deploy-config --pool canary-kv-prefetch-v2 --config ./prefetch-policy.yaml --tag kv-prefetch-v2
  - Pause canary routing:
    rdxctl set-weight --pool canary-kv-prefetch-v2 --weight 0

Post-experiment analysis and documentation checklist
- Produce a short experiment report that includes: hypothesis, traffic windows used, sample sizes, raw metrics time-series, heatmaps, global and per-tenant impact, cost delta estimate, and recommended next action (rollback, tweak, full rollout).
- Archive experiment artifacts: traces, dashboards, config version, and sample sessions used for reproducibility.
- If fidelity regressions observed, escalate to model onboarding and research for root-cause and mitigation.

Ownership and escalation
- Primary owner: Runtime performance team (runtime-perf@redwood.com).
- Secondary owner: SRE (sre-runtime@redwood.com).
- Pager: oncall-runtime (pager duty) for canary auto-rollback events.

- Row 2: Kernel impact: kernel.queue_wait_ms.p95 (compare canary/control), kernel.exec_count_per_min
