Run discovery job across S3/DB to enumerate v1 configs and generate migration plan
Execute idempotent migration in dry-run mode and publish report to migration-bucket
Perform controlled migration on a small set of non-critical Dedicated clusters
Flip runtime to reject v1 payloads only after all persisted configs migrated
Remove v1 reader code and compat-proxy from runtime in the final release

rollout_plan:
Phase 0: Nightly dry-runs for 3 days and manual review of reports
Phase 1 Canary: Migrate 1-2 canary clusters (approx 3% traffic) for 6 hours
Phase 2 Staged: Expand to 20% traffic over 24h if canary stable
Phase 3 Ramp: 60% for 24h with automated health checks and human-on-call
Phase 4 Full: 100% with deprecation notice and archive of v1 artifacts

testing_plan:
Unit tests for config parser and migration utilities covering edge cases
Integration tests simulating old-client requests against migrated configs
Contract tests for public API to ensure no behavioural deltas after migration
Load tests at 2x expected peak with traffic shapes that previously hit compat-proxy
Chaos test: kill compat-proxy in staging to validate graceful degradation path

risks:
Dedicated customers using custom config loaders may experience failures if not coordinated
Silent behavioural regressions for rare request shapes due to flag-key renames
Alert noise from duplicated metrics during partial rollout could mask true regressions

[Remove legacy route shims and compress versioned configuration surface]
description:
Summary:
We will remove a set of legacy route shims and collapse multiple versioned configuration entrypoints into a single normalized surface. The goal is to eliminate historical admin/compat endpoints and flag-driven code paths that complicate rollout routing and runtime kernel selection. This reduces maintenance surface area and prevents regressions when changing rollout logic.

Scope of work:
1) Inventory: assemble full list of legacy endpoints (admin v0/v1), compatibility middlewares, and feature flags that alter routing behavior.
2) Mappings & translation layer: implement a one-time migration mapping that normalizes incoming requests to the new config schema. This lives behind a transient compatibility middleware that can be removed after the migration and can run in shadow mode.
3) Config version collapse: migrate persisted rollout configs and toggle metadata from multi-version records to a single canonical config version (add migration script and backup).
4) Flag removal: stage the deletion of deprecated flags in three phases (shadow, soft-delete, hard-delete).
5) Validation & monitoring: add smoke tests, integration tests (router + runtime), and dashboards to monitor 5xxs, tail latency, and routing mismatch rate during rollout.
6) Rollout plan: canary 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% per region, with 24h observation windows and automatic rollback triggers on SLO regressions.
7) Cleanup: after 100% and 48h stable, fully remove middleware and delete DB compatibility columns; archive migration artifacts.

Why this matters:
- Removes fragile conditional logic in the router that causes subtle tokenization/cache mismatches.
- Simplifies kernel selection paths and enables further batching improvements.
- Lowers operational cognitive load for on-call and future feature rollouts.

Risks & mitigations:
- Risk: transient routing mismatches causing latency spikes. Mitigation: shadow traffic + canary + rollback thresholds.
- Risk: migration script failing leaving partial configs. Mitigation: snapshot configs, reversible migration, run in dry-run first.
- Risk: unexpected external integrations hitting old endpoints. Mitigation: telemetry for hits to legacy endpoints; extend compat window for partners if needed.

- All configs are stored in canonical versioned schema and DB migration completed with zero data loss.
- After 72h post-100% rollout, middleware and flag artifacts are removed and relevant dashboards show no regressions.

[Retire dual-write flag pipeline and canonicalize rollout timeline]
description:
Background: Over the last 3 years we introduced a dual-write pipeline that writes feature flag and rollout timeline changes to both the legacy 'compat' store (compat-rollouts) and the newer canonical rollout_store. The compat store exists to support legacy admin endpoints and older SDKs. Keeping both writers has increased operational complexity (double failure modes), caused divergent state during partial failures, and slowed migration of rollout history queries.

Goal: Stop dual-writing, migrate any missing historical timeline rows into rollout_store, remove the compat-adapter codepath, and decommission the compat-rollouts dataset. After completion, all reads should be served from rollout_store and the legacy endpoints should return 410 or proxy to new endpoints per the API migration plan.

Success criteria (high level):
- Backfill job migrated all historical timeline entries for 99.9% of organizations (with a manual audit for the remainder).
- No read traffic hits compat-rollouts for 14 consecutive days in canary region.
- Compat adapter binary removed from repo and no feature flags reference the legacy store.
- Admin UI and SDKs switched to canonical endpoints and tests updated.
- Monitoring dashboards show no increase in rollout-query latency; error budget impact <= 0.5% during migration window.

Risks & mitigations:
- Large timeline objects: discovered some orgs have >2GB aggregated timeline blobs. Mitigation: chunking in the backfill job and incremental reassembly in the migration verification.
- Race conditions during cutover: plan a two-phase switch (reads-only proxy -> read-from-canonical -> disable dual-write). Canary traffic and a supervised ramp help detect regressions.
- Audit/legal retention: ensure admin audit logs are snapshotted and preserved in S3 before deleting compat dataset.

Rollout plan (summary):
1) Read-only proxy: route reads from compat endpoint to rollout_store while keeping legacy endpoint available behind a compatibility shim.
2) Backfill: run throttled backfill job that copies missing timeline rows and compacts duplicates into canonical schema. Job writes progress checkpoints and supports resume.
3) Canary: enable read-from-canonical for 5% of orgs for 48 hours, monitor errors/latency.
4) Switch: flip routing for all reads to canonical store and disable dual-write.
5) Cleanup: deprecate compat endpoints, remove adapter code, delete compat dataset after snapshot.

Operational notes: Backfill job should use per-org rate limits and exponential backoff. Avoid scanning entire compat dataset in a single pass. Use a cursor-based approach keyed by org_id and last_seq. Include hooks to surface problematic orgs to the oncall team for manual remediation.

Implement backfill job with chunking + checkpointing (in progress)

Canary routing config and observability dashboards (pending)
Switch dual-write off in staged regions and monitor (planned)
Remove compat adapter and deprecated endpoint handlers (post-cutover)

[Unify route manifests and decommission legacy flag transport]
description:
Summary:
We will collapse multiple versioned routing/config surfaces (route-manifests v0/v1 legacy variants, legacy flag transport endpoints, and the old rollout redirect paths) into a single canonical manifest that the runtime and Console will read. This ticket removes the legacy flag transport pipeline (the /api/v0/flags push and the DB-backed compat layer that rewrote routing keys), migrates active rollouts to the canonical manifest format, and retires the compatibility HTTP endpoints and redirect logic.

Motivation:
- Legacy transport and multiple manifest versions add runtime branching, increase CPU/alloc costs, and complicate kernel selection and caching.
- Consolidating into a single manifest simplifies rollouts, reduces on-path checks, and eliminates a thin-but-wide class of bugs observed in long-tail rollouts.

Scope & Goals:
1) Implement a canonical route manifest schema and a migration tool to convert active manifests from v0/v1 -> canonical.
2) Stop writing to legacy flag transport endpoints and migrate producers to the new publish API.
3) Remove the compat HTTP endpoints (/api/v0/flags, /rollout-compat/*) and the path-based redirect middleware.
4) Update runtime routing to depend only on canonical manifests and delete the runtime branching code paths.
5) Run a safe rollout with feature gates, canarying, and automated rollback on errors.

Non-goals:
- This ticket does not change rollout semantics or evaluation logic; it only consolidates config surfaces.

High-level Plan:
A) Analysis & discovery (done): inventory of active manifests and clients that post to legacy endpoints. Produced a list of 142 distinct clients and 28 active rollouts still using compat transport.
B) Migration tooling (in progress): build a one-shot converter utility that reads legacy manifests and outputs canonical manifests, with validation and a dry-run mode.
C) Producer migration: update internal services (flag-service, rollout-service, infra-provisioner) to publish canonical manifests. Provide a short compatibility shim package for internal clients.
D) Runtime guarded switch: add a config flag runtime.use_canonical_manifests (default: false) and a rollout window to move traffic to the canonical path per-region.
E) Deprecation & removal: after 2 weeks of canaries and no regression, flip the flag global, remove compat code, and close the legacy endpoints.
F) Cleanup & audits: delete schema v0/v1 parsers, remove docs, and archive manifest migration logs.

Migration details:
- Data migration will be performed in-place with idempotent converters; every converted manifest will be written to the new manifests table and annotated with a migration checksum.
- A verification job will compare runtime resolution results between legacy and canonical parsing for a 48-hour dry-run window.
- For any rollout with active traffic > 5 RPS we will run manual P0 review and schedule a plateaued canary phase.

Tests & Validation:
- Unit tests for converter and schema validation (target 100% coverage on schema mapping).
- Integration tests with runtime in a staging cluster that replays a 72-hour snapshot of production routing traffic.
- Synthetic traffic tests to exercise cold-start, caching, and KV behavior under canonical manifests.

Monitoring & Rollback:
- Dashboards: manifest-coverage, parse-errors, routing-delta, latency-by-route. Links: https://dash.redwood.internal/d/manifest-coverage
- Alerting: page on > 1% parse-errors over 10m or routing-delta > 2% for a critical route.
- Rollback: re-enable legacy compat flag and redeploy runtime build that contains the compat code. We will maintain the compat branch for 30 days after the flip.

Risks & Mitigations:
- Risk: Some internal clients can't be migrated quickly. Mitigation: provide shim library (compat-client) and run short-term proxy while owners migrate.
- Risk: Unexpected routing deltas. Mitigation: staged canaries with automated traffic comparison and manual P0 path.

Deliverables:
- converter tool with dry-run and migration reports (artifact: s3://redwood-artifacts/manifest-converter/ENG-62345)
- updated producer SDKs and internal compat-client package
- runtime change behind runtime.use_canonical_manifests feature flag
- decommission plan and post-mortem template

Next steps (short term):
- Complete the converter unit and integration tests (owner: Lena Park, ETA: 2025-10-22).
- Begin producer migrations with two low-traffic services (flag-service and infra-provisioner) as first canaries (owner: Diego Morales).
- Schedule a canary window for eu-west-1 cluster for 2025-10-30.

[Convert opaque flag payloads to typed flag contracts and compact rollout history]
description:
Problem: The current feature-flag surface stores semi-structured JSON blobs and string-encoded contract payloads (version tags embedded in arbitrary strings). This makes runtime parsing expensive, causes a proliferation of ad-hoc version checks in the serving runtime, and bloats rollout history with repeated legacy versions. It also complicates audits and automated policy checks.

Goal: Migrate flag storage and runtime handling from opaque string/JSON blobs to a small set of typed, versioned flag contracts with canonical serialization. Compact historical rollout traces into a canonical manifest format and remove stale opcode handling in the runtime after a safe deprecation window. The effort should preserve compatibility for two release cycles while reducing runtime parsing overhead and rollout-history storage by at least 40%.

tasks:
Design typed flag contract schemas (YAML + JSON Schema) for the 8 most-used flag types and review with PM/Design/SEC
Implement a compatibility shim in the runtime that accepts both opaque blobs and typed contracts (feature-flag-parser v2)
Write an offline migration tool that scans flags table, validates payloads, translates to typed format, and produces a compact manifest per rollout
Add DB migration to store typed payloads in new columns while leaving legacy_column as read-only for rollback window
Create an admin UI change to show typed contract fields and a migration progress view
Add e2e and unit tests covering parsing, fallback to legacy, and schema validation failures
Run a staged canary: internal service -> small customer cohort -> wide rollout; monitor errors and latency impact
Compact rollout-history: implement background job to collapse repetitive historical entries into canonical manifest and mark older entries as archived
Schedule removal of legacy parsing code two releases after migration completion and add a changelog entry
Document migration steps in Confluence and update runbooks for rollback and incident recovery

acceptance_criteria:
Runtime handles typed contracts natively and falls back to legacy blobs without errors for at least 2 release cycles
DB contains new typed_payload column populated for 95% of active flags after migration job runs on staging
End-to-end latency for flag resolution does not regress by more than 5% in p95 compared to baseline
Rollout-history storage for migrated flags is reduced by >=40% after compaction job completes
Admin UI surfaces typed fields and migration progress; product sign-off received
All new unit/e2e tests pass in CI and new integration tests land in nightly runs

risks:
Migration may encounter malformed legacy payloads requiring manual remediation (we will capture those in a quarantine list)
Edge-case flags with ad-hoc fields could cause policy mismatches in rollout semantics
Customer workloads depending on opaque encoding for downstream automation might break if we remove legacy support too soon
Large table migration could increase DB write IO and affect peak traffic; plan for rate-limited background migration

rollout_plan:
Week 1: Schema design + RFC + security review signoff
Week 2: Implement runtime compatibility shim + unit tests
Week 3: Build migration tool and dry-run on staging snapshot; collect quarantine list
Week 4: Run migration in a controlled internal canary and validate admin UI
Week 5: Open beta for 10% of customers (controlled via routing policy)
Week 6: Full migration for active flags, start rollout-history compaction job
Monitoring: watch flag-resolution errors, p95 latency, admin UI errors, and migration progress dashboard
Post-migration: keep legacy_column readable-only for 2 cycles, then remove parsing code and drop column

qa_checklist:
Unit tests for each new schema + negative cases
Integration test using staging snapshot with both legacy and typed payloads
Regression smoke for admin UI and flag edit flows
Load test the migration worker at production-like scale in staging
Verify compaction job produces canonical manifest and archived entries are immutable

notes:
This ticket bundles schema + migration + runtime compatibility. Aim to keep public API and SDK behavior unchanged during migration. Coordinate closely with SRE for on-call windows during DB migration. If customer automation relies on opaque payloads, notify via announcement and provide migration compatibility guide.

Hi Anika — thanks for the questions, answered inline below. I've attached a brief CSV (answers-table.csv) with the same items for your questionnaire.

> Is prompt input stored by default in hosted mode? If so, for how long and is that configurable per-API key/route?
Short answer: For Redwood hosted API, prompt inputs and generated outputs may be persisted by default for debugging/quality for up to 30 days. Retention is configurable at the customer level for enterprise accounts — we can set per-route retention policies (e.g., 0 / 7 / 30 / 90 days). For Dedicated/Private deployments, customers can choose zero retention (ephemeral) for prompts and outputs.

> Do you keep a copy of generated outputs? Our compliance team treats outputs that may include PHI the same as inputs.
Yes — generated outputs are treated equivalently to inputs in our retention model. Defaults match the input retention above. We recommend setting TTL=0 for any route that may contain PHI unless you require auditability for a window.

> For debugging, do you keep token-level logs or full request bodies?
We capture request metadata (timestamps, model, route, token count) by default. Full request/response bodies are captured only when the customer enables "tracing/debug" for a route or if a support ticket requires trace capture; those captures are limited and timeboxed. Token-level logs are available as an opt-in for debugging; we can disable token-level capture for Clearsight.

> We require US-only storage for both data at rest and for backups/snapshots. Can you commit to that for a production environment?
Yes — hosted environment can be scoped to US regions only via account-level controls; backups and snapshots for those accounts are stored in US-only regions. For stricter isolation we recommend Dedicated (reserved GPU pools in a US region) or Private (customer-managed VPC) which provide stronger residency guarantees.

> Key control: we prefer customer-managed KMS in production. Is that available with Dedicated or Private only?
Correct: customer-managed KMS/HSM is available for Dedicated and Private deployments. Hosted accounts use Redwood-managed keys by default, but enterprise customers with specific requirements can work with our security team and account engineering to arrange a dedicated keying arrangement or deploy Private.

> Deletion SLA: we need a documented delete API and confirmation that deletions are honored across backups within 48 hours.
We provide a programmatic delete endpoint for persisted prompt/output artifacts. For Hosted accounts, deletion is usually reflected in primary storage within 24 hours and backup/snapshot propagation within 48–72 hours depending on snapshot cadence; we can commit to a 48-hour window for enterprise contracts (documented in the DPA/SLA). Dedicated/Private deployments have configurable snapshot cadence to meet stricter windows.

Notes on access controls and audit logs:
- Encryption: AES-256 for data at rest and TLS 1.2+ in transit.
- RBAC: role-based access controls with minimum-privilege for support engineers; access to request/response captures requires an approved support ticket and is logged.
- Audit logs: request metadata and admin actions kept for 365 days by default for enterprise; logs can be exported to customer S3, CloudWatch, or SIEM via streaming.

[Priority-weight transition lag results in background-flushes consuming burst credits and causing early 429s for interactive routes]
description:
Issue summary:
SkylineChat reports repeated early 429s affecting low-latency chat routes after their account was promoted to an enterprise plan with higher burst credits. The tenant experiences normal throughput for bulk/background flush jobs but interactive SSE/chat endpoints begin receiving 429s within minutes of the promotion.

Impact:
- Intermittent 429s on interactive chat routes (SSE & websocket) causing degraded real-time UX for SkylineChat customers.
- Bulk ingestion (background flushers) shows increased token consumption and appears to be draining burst credits during the transition window.
- Customer reports business impact: chat sessions dropping for end-users during peak business hours.

Environment:
- Tenant: SkylineChat (enterprise)
- Region: prod-us-west primary, spillover to eu-west reported
- Models: redwood-2-large for chat, redwood-1-quantized for background encode
- Config: priority-split enabled with separate lanes for interactive (high) and background (low) traffic; recently changed weight thresholds as part of onboarding.

Steps to reproduce / observed sequence:
1) Promote tenant plan to enterprise (increase burst credits + priority weights)
2) System kicks off background flushes to catch up (many short-lived parallel workers)
3) Within ~3-7 minutes interactive connections begin seeing 429 responses
4) Token accounting shows large sink from background workers attributed to the same tenant during the transition window

Observed behavior (logs/metrics):
- Ingress rate-limiter traces show priority_ladder transition event at 2026-03-08T14:02:11Z then a burst of low-priority background-worker calls between 14:02:12Z-14:09:00Z.
- Example token-accounting line (edge logs):
  [2026-03-08T14:04:37Z] tenant=skylinechat route=/v1/generate tokens=23872 worker=flush-coordinator-22 priority=LOW counted=true
  [2026-03-08T14:04:38Z] tenant=skylinechat route=/v1/chat tokens=12 session=abc123 priority=HIGH result=429 reason=quota_exhausted
- Rate-limiter debug shows window refill event delayed by ~45s after promotion due to epoch swap on rate-controller nodes.
- Prometheus metrics: rate_limit_token_pool_available{tenant="skylinechat"} dropped from ~120k to <4k in the transition window; background_worker_token_rate spiked x8.

Expected behavior:
- Priority promotions should not allow background flushers to siphon newly-allocated burst credits before interactive lanes get rebalanced; interactive sessions should be prioritized during and immediately after plan change.

Temporary mitigations attempted by Support/Customer:
- Customer paused background flushers (reduced worker parallelism) which restored interactive success within ~30s.
- Support toggled a temporary soft-isolate flag that pins interactive routes to a protected burst pool; prevented further 429s for the duration.

Investigation notes and hypotheses:
- Hypothesis A: Rate-controller epoch exchange during tier update causes a short window where refill assignments are not synchronized across origin and edge, allowing background workers to claim new credits first.
- Hypothesis B: Priority weight recalculation happens asynchronously; background lane retains older token slice until the weight update completes, resulting in effective over-allocation to background workers.
- Hypothesis C: Orchestrator warms up many parallel short-lived flush workers after promotion; our per-route token attribution (edge-side) misattributes some of those against interactive route token pools when path normalization occurs (signed-url/callbacks).

Next steps / action items:
- Engineering (rate-limiter team) to reproduce epoch-swap refill lag in staging using the plan-promotion script; create a deterministic integration test reproducing the race. (assigned: Diego)
- Add short-term guard: when a tenant plan changes, apply a 120s protected window that favors interactive lanes for refill allocation. (owner: rate-limiter)
- Add logging around refill assignment decisions and add metric: refill_lag_seconds per-tenant. (owner: telemetry)
- Consolidate runbook steps for customers performing plan upgrades to reduce parallelism of background workers during the first 5 minutes. (owner: customer-success)

Workaround provided to customer:
- Recommended action: pause background flush worker pool and resume gradually with concurrency capped at 2 for the first 5 minutes post promotion.
- Support applied a temporary route-protect flag while engineering works on the long-term fix.

Attachments / evidence:
- rate-limiter traces: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/rate-limiter/tenant-skylinechat/trace-2026-03-08
- support convo: https://slack.redwood.ai/archives/C0123ABCDE/p1678643200

Resolution notes: (in progress)
- Short-term protective guard implemented as tenant flag (rollout candidate) and tested in staging.
- Root-cause reproduction pending; target for patch and global rollout: 2026-03-20.

[Request: Align rate-plan refill semantics for mixed webhook callback + embedding bulk orchestration to avoid post-upgrade 429 waves]
description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports recurring 429 throttles immediately after a billing/tier upgrade and an orchestrator migration. Traffic mix: long-lived SSE sessions for real-time UI updates + high-throughput background workers that bulk-upload embeddings (multipart). Both flows use the same API key prefix but different routes.

Impact:
- NovaLens engineers see 10-20% of requests return 429s for 10-30 minutes after upgrade/migration windows.
- Real-time UI sessions are affected (SSE disconnects) causing poor UX; background embedding pipeline stalls and retries, increasing cost.

Environment / context:
- Private tenant on dedicated capacity (enterprise).
- Orchestrator migrated from a single long-lived API key per pod to ephemeral subkeys for per-worker identity last week.
- Tier upgraded from dedicated-standard -> enterprise-plus earlier today.
- Edge proxies in us-west cache refill counters for rate windows for up to ~90s.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Start bulk embedding backfill (500 concurrent chunk uploads across 20 workers).
2) Open 200 SSE connections from UI clients multiplexed through an ingress layer.
3) Trigger billing tier update in Console (simulate upgrade).
4) Observe 429 waves on SSE endpoints and chunk upload endpoints immediately after upgrade and for ~15-25 minutes.

Observed behavior:
- Throttles occur at both route and tenant layers.
- Throttle headers sometimes show different windows depending on which edge served the client.
- Console shows quota refreshed, but edge metrics show stale refill counters and sudden token depletion events.

Expected behavior:
- Tier upgrade should refresh refill rates consistently across edge and origin within a short reconciliation window without producing opaque 429 waves for mixed traffic patterns.

Attachments:
- Customer's packet capture snippets and sampled throttle headers (provided in ticket attachments).
- App logs showing SSE reconnects and embedding worker retry backoff traces.

[Unexpected spike in 429s after upgrading SDK (quota mismatch vs rate-limit headers)]
description:
Customer reports a noticeable increase in HTTP 429 responses immediately after upgrading Redwood SDK (Python -> latest minor). Customer believes they are under their purchased quota and that prior to upgrade they did not see sustained throttling.

Issue Summary
- Symptom: Increased 429s ("Too Many Requests") with inconsistent/misleading rate limit headers across endpoints.
- Trigger: SDK upgrade + switching more traffic to streaming + increased concurrency.
- Suspected: Edge-case in quota enforcement / header classification (429 returned with headers that do not reflect actual enforcement window), plus SDK retry behavior amplifying bursts.

Impact
- Customer-facing impact: Elevated request failures; customer implemented aggressive retries, causing additional burst traffic and more 429s.
- Scope: Primarily hosted API traffic; reported across us-east and eu-west.
- Business impact: Customer escalated due to downstream search latency and perceived platform instability.

Customer Environment
- Tier: self_serve (high-usage hosted account)
- SDK: Redwood Python SDK (upgraded within last 24 hours). Customer also has a TS service calling embeddings.
- Workload pattern: mixture of chat completions (streaming) + embeddings batch jobs.
- Concurrency: increased by customer during rollout.

What we need from customer (requested)
- Approx time range (UTC) for the spike
- Request IDs for sample 429s (5-10)
- Endpoint breakdown (chat vs embeddings)
- SDK version + language, and whether retries/backoff are enabled

Observed / Provided Examples
- Sample response indicated 429 with headers suggesting remaining=0 while dashboard usage looked below hourly quota.
- Some 429s appear to be rate-limit (burst) while others appear to be quota enforcement, but both surface as 429 and sometimes share the same error message.

Initial Hypotheses
1) Quota enforcement edge-case incorrectly classifies (or caches) limit state, leading to 429s even when token/quota counters look below the contracted limit.
2) Rate-limit headers inconsistent across endpoints and/or under fallback routing, confusing customer-side logic that keys on headers.
3) SDK upgrade changed default retry semantics or timeouts, causing higher effective RPS bursts (especially with streaming reconnect patterns).

Immediate Mitigation Guidance (Support)
- Reduce concurrency temporarily (cap worker pool)
- Implement exponential backoff with jitter for retries; do not retry immediately on 429
- If using streaming, avoid reconnect loops without a backoff; log request IDs per attempt
- Use server-provided Retry-After (if present) over custom fixed delays

Engineering Follow-up
- Linked ENG-4825 to address rate-limit/quota mismatch and header consistency; request confirmation on whether fallback can affect header calculation.
- Track for known-issues sprint article: workaround-429-quota-mismatch-and-rate-limit-headers (draft already in progress).

Environment: prod us-east-1, mixed websocket and HTTP/2 clients.

Observed behavior:
- Customer upgraded plan at 2026-03-10T12:05:00Z via billing API.
- Console quota reflected new limits at 12:06:30Z.
- Error spike begins 12:08Z: rate-limit 429s with X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0 and X-RateLimit-Reset: ~12:08:30Z on some edge-nodes, while origin shows non-exhausted token counts.
- Spike subsided ~12:48Z after interventions (see resolution).

Why this is different from prior tickets: quota refresh is visible in control plane but refill/refill-window alignment across edge nodes appears delayed, causing a ‘soft’ 429 pattern (not global exhaustion). Customer-facing symptoms look like sustained throttling even though tenant credit balance is sufficient.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Have an active tenant on dedicated plan with sustained background workers (~300 concurrent requests).
2) Trigger a billing tier change (upgrade) using the billing API during a high-concurrency window, record the time.
3) Observe console shows quota/top-up success immediately.
4) Send steady traffic through a subset of edge nodes (simulate ~200 short-lived websocket sessions and 100 HTTP/2 multiplexed calls).
5) Watch for edge-level 429s while origin rate limiter reports available tokens.

investigation_notes:
Edge nodes maintain a local token-window and rely on control-plane broadcasts to reset refill_epoch after billing changes. When the billing service wrote the new balance, the broadcast to edge sub-clusters sometimes lagged behind due to an intermittent NATS partition (~30s).
Edge logs showed consistent local refill_epoch values that did not match the origin's refill_epoch for ~20-40s, causing local remaining counters to report 0 despite global balance being updated.
Hypothesis confirmed by reproducer in staging: paused broadcast for 45s while applying top-up produced identical soft-429 pattern on subset of nodes.
Root cause: lack of idempotent, versioned broadcast with acknowledgement from edges. Control-plane assumed eventual consistency; under high-concurrency window this surface caused customer impact.
Risk: Transient but customer-visible throttling during billing operations or manual quota adjustments if the broadcast path experiences partitioning.

resolution_notes:
Applied emergency hotfix: force-sync endpoint added to edge agent that accepts a refill_epoch and force-recomputes local token windows; invoked for the single tenant on affected edge subset at 2026-03-10T12:48Z.
Rolled a small control-plane change (PR github.com/redwood/inference/PR/4318) to publish top-up as a versioned message and require an ACK from edge sub-clusters; retried broadcasts until ACKs received. Deployed to canary 2026-03-11 02:00Z and to prod 2026-03-11 03:30Z.
Validated success: no recurrence after broadcast path reinforced; edges now report matching refill_epoch within <5s in normal conditions.

workarounds_provided:
1) For immediate relief, support can run edge force-sync for affected tenant (internal runbook: Confluence -> Rate Limiter -> Force Sync).
2) Recommend scheduling billing-tier changes during low-concurrency windows to minimize blast radius until broadcast ACKs roll out to all regions.
3) As a short-term client-side mitigation, throttle client concurrency (max parallel requests) during upgrade window or implement exponential backoff on 429s with jitter.

2) Product to update billing upgrade playbook to recommend background refill sync and show a progress indicator in Console (assigned: Ava Lin, ETA: 2026-03-25).
3) Dev to harden message publish retries and mark top-up events as strongly-consistent for enterprise tier (PR merged: github.com/redwood/inference/PR/4318).
4) Support to prepare KB article for customers explaining safe upgrade patterns and how to request immediate edge-sync (target publish: 2026-03-20).

[Orchestrating Multi-Model Pipelines for Cost-Latency Tradeoffs (PRD)]
Summary:
This PRD defines a product initiative to add first-class orchestration for multi-model pipelines in Redwood Inference. The goal is to let customers declare multi-step pipelines (e.g., embed -> rerank -> generate) composed of different model variants and to automatically optimize routing and instance selection for cost and latency tradeoffs while preserving per-pipeline SLOs.

Background and motivation:
- Customers commonly chain multiple model calls in a single feature (e.g., cheap encoder for retrieval, higher-cost reranker or generator).
- Current Redwood surface treats calls independently; customers must implement orchestration client-side or in application backends, leading to duplicated logic and missed opportunities for cross-request batching, KV cache reuse, and cost-aware routing.
- Providing a managed pipeline orchestration layer improves unit economics (lower cost per end-to-end request), reduces latency via coordinated batching and cache reuse, and centralizes rollout and variant management for pipeline steps.

Goals (what success looks like):
1) API surface for declaring pipelines composed of named steps, model selectors, and SLO targets.
2) Runtime orchestration that optimizes placement/routing to meet user-specified end-to-end latency SLO while minimizing expected cost.
3) Automatic cross-step batching and KV/prefix cache reuse when steps involve the same serving runtime and model family.
4) Integrated metrics and traces surfaced in Redwood Console per-pipeline: end-to-end latency, per-step latency, cost breakdown, and failure rates.
5) Migration path for existing single-call customers to adopt pipelines with minimal code changes.

Non-goals:
- This initiative does not implement an end-to-end workflow engine with arbitrary conditionals and long-running orchestration (we focus on synchronous pipelines for inference requests).
- We will not initially support third-party execution (external webhooks) as a pipeline step.

User personas and primary use cases:
- Product/ML Engineer integrating a multi-step search+generate feature who wants a single SLO and visibility into bottlenecks.
- Platform team creating cost-windowed routing policies for enterprise tenants to stay within budget while meeting latency SLOs.
- Solutions engineer building a reference template for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) that customers can adopt.

High-level design overview:
- Pipeline Descriptor: declarative JSON schema that describes steps (name, model selector, input mapping, resource hints), SLOs (p95 latency target, availability), and cost preference (aggressive-cost | balanced | aggressive-latency).
- Planner: Service that converts a descriptor into a per-request plan: assigns candidate model variants for each step, decides whether to colocate steps on the same instance/pool for cache reuse, and estimates cost/latency distributions.
- Execution Fabric: Extends existing serving runtime to accept multi-step request envelopes, enabling intra-request batching, KV cache rehydration, and shared IO handling.
- Adaptive Runtime Policies: Uses feedback (observed latencies, queueing) to swap in cheaper variants or add burst capacity when SLO violations are observed.

Key product requirements:
1) Pipeline Descriptor API (v1):
   - POST /pipelines (create), GET /pipelines/{id}, PUT /pipelines/{id}, DELETE /pipelines/{id}
   - Minimal example payload (JSON):

   {
     "name": "rag-search-generate",
     "steps": [
       {"id": "encode", "model_selector": "small-embed:dynamic", "timeout_ms": 50},
       {"id": "retrieve", "type": "internal_retrieval", "timeout_ms": 100},
       {"id": "rerank", "model_selector": "medium-ranker:latest", "timeout_ms": 120},
       {"id": "generate", "model_selector": "large-gen:quantized", "timeout_ms": 300}
     ],
     "slo": {"p95_ms": 600, "availability": 0.999},
     "cost_preference": "balanced"
   }

2) Planner constraints and outputs:
   - Inputs: pipeline descriptor, tenant plan (Dedicated/Hosted/Private), runtime capacity snapshot, historical step latencies, and cost models.
   - Outputs: chosen variant per step, placement hint (same-pool | separate-pool), batching window suggestion (ms), and estimated end-to-end latency and cost.

3) Runtime behaviors:
   - When steps are colocated and cache-compatible, share KV caches and avoid repeated tokenization where possible.
   - Allow cross-step continuous batching when customer SLO and step timeouts permit (configurable batch window 1-50ms).
   - Fall back to independent execution paths on incompatibilities (model family mismatch, security restrictions for private deployments).

4) Observability requirements (exposed in Console):
   - End-to-end p50/p95/p99 latency, per-step latency histogram, per-request cost breakdown (tokens + model-hours), batch size distribution, and SLO breach traces.

5) Security and privacy:
   - Respect tenant isolation: pipelines for Private deployments must be executed within tenant-only pools.
   - Audit logs for pipeline creation and plan changes.

SLOs and acceptance thresholds (product-level):
- Default target: p95 end-to-end latency within declared SLO 95% of calls in a week.
- Cost delta: for balanced preference, expected end-to-end replication must reduce or not increase total customer spend compared to naive client orchestration in 75% of customer workloads (measured in alpha).
- Availability: pipeline endpoints inherit tenant availability SLAs (Hosted: 99.9%, Dedicated: 99.95).

Compatibility matrix (important constraints):
- Hosted: full feature set for supported model families (Redwood-verified).
- Dedicated: supports co-located pooling and private capacity policies; customers can opt-out of cross-tenant batching.
- Private (VPC/on-prem): supports orchestration but requires enabling shared KV cache option in config and may not support automated burst region fallback.

Example configuration table (text-table):
- Fields: name, type, required, example
- name: string, required, "rag-search-generate"
- steps: list, required, see example above
- slo.p95_ms: integer, required, 600
- cost_preference: enum, optional, "balanced"

API and CLI examples:
- Create pipeline (curl):
  curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/pipelines -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' -d @pipeline.json

- Run pipeline synchronously (client call):
  POST /v1/pipelines/{id}/invoke { "input": {"query": "how to reduce token cost"} }

Rollout plan and milestones:
1) Alpha (Q1): API-only pipeline descriptors stored in control plane; planner returns static plans but execution runs as sequential calls (no runtime improvements). Target: 5 internal customers and 2 reference templates.
2) Beta (Q2): Execution fabric accepts envelope requests; add cross-step batching and KV reuse for verified model combinations. Add Console insights.
3) GA (Q3): Add adaptive runtime policies, cost/preference knobs, and enterprise controls for Dedicated/Private. Provide migration tooling.

Success metrics (measurable):
- Adoption: 20+ customers converting at least one feature to a pipeline within 3 months of GA.
- Cost improvement: median end-to-end cost reduction >= 12% on RAG pipelines measured across early adopters.
- SLO stability: fewer than 3% of pipeline calls with p95 > declared SLO in steady state.

Operational considerations and runbook snippets:
- Alerting: Create alert when pipeline SLO error budget burn > 40% in 24h or rolling p95 exceeds target by 20% for 30m.
- Runbook (SLO breach):
   1) Identify offending pipeline and step via Console traces.
   2) Check planner recent decisions; if a cheaper variant was selected recently, roll forward a canary with a higher-latency-but-higher-throughput variant.
   3) If systemic, throttle new pipeline creations and open paging incident.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Planner makes suboptimal choices leading to repeated rollbacks. Mitigation: allow operator override and safe default to "balanced" or tenant-specified pinned variants.
- Risk: Cross-step batching increases tail latency for some workloads. Mitigation: conservative default batch-window and per-pipeline tuning.

Open questions (for product and eng discussion):
- Should pipeline descriptors allow conditional branches (if-else) for v2?
- How to represent non-ML steps (retrieval or DB lookups) formally in the descriptor?
- What is the economic model for charging per-pipeline orchestration? per-step tokens only, or small orchestration surcharge?

Owner and contacts:
- Product lead: Aisha Kaur (product).
- Eng leads: Daniel Meyer (serving runtime), Priya Raman (planner & optimization).
- SRE/Oncall: Jorge Alvarez.

Appendix: example planner output (JSON, simplified):
{
  "pipeline_id": "rag-search-generate",
  "chosen_variants": {"encode": "small-embed-v2-quant", "rerank": "medium-ranker-v3", "generate": "large-gen-q8"},
  "placement_hint": "colocate-steps-0-2",
  "estimated_p95_ms": 520,
  "estimated_cost_usd": 0.0092
}

Notes on measurement approach:
- Run A/B experiments on staged traffic to compare "client orchestration" vs Redwood orchestration using identical inputs and measure cost + latency distributions.
- Use workload classes (short prompt, medium prompt, long prompt) to stratify evaluation.

Next steps:
- Kickoff design review (week of 2026-03-08).
- Implementation spike for planner cost/latency models (2 sprints).
- Internal alpha with two reference templates: RAG and retrieval + summarization.

References:
- See Console observability spec for metrics instrumentation guidance.
- See runtime-architecture docs for current KV cache capabilities.



[Quality-Aware Quantization Rollout PRD]
Summary:

This PRD defines a product-led rollout for model quantization profiles that reduces per-token inference cost while enforcing measurable quality guardrails across Redwood’s Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployment surfaces. The goal is a staged release that enables customers to opt-in to quantized variants (4-bit/8-bit) with predictable latency, throughput, and worst-case quality bounds, and packaging and pricing options that reflect the economics and risk profile.

Why this matters:
- Quantization is the single highest-impact operational lever to reduce GPU memory footprint and per-token cost for many open models.
- Uncontrolled quantization introduces quality regressions that manifest differently per workload and prompt distribution.
- Customers (especially enterprise/Dedicated/Private) need predictable, measurable guarantees and a simple opt-in/rollback experience.

Scope and non-goals:
- In scope: definition of quantization profile taxonomy, acceptance metrics, rollout strategy (canary → staged → general), packaging/pricing options, telemetry & alerting requirements, owner and runbook for rollback.
- Out of scope: model training changes, new quantization algorithm R&D (research can be referenced but not implemented as part of this rollout), deep kernel-level optimization beyond selected runtime knobs (handled by eng-serving-runtime ongoing work).

Product overview and definitions:
- Quantization profile: a named bundle of model artifact + runtime flags + config that produce a deterministic inference variant (e.g., q4_legacy, q4_higher_bias, q8_dynamic).
- Quality guardrail: a set of automated checks (metric thresholds and delta budgets) that must be met before a variant advances stages. Examples: Perplexity delta vs baseline, BLEU/ROUGE regressions on prompt-sets, hallucination rate on safety prompts, human accept rate on sample prompts.
- Packaging tier types: 1) Hosted opt-in (per-account toggle + usage reporting), 2) Dedicated default (tenant-level policy selectable with SLA caveats), 3) Private reference package (deployment artifacts + guidance, no managed fallback).

Requirements (customer-facing):
1) Opt-in experience: customers can enable quantized variants for a specific model version via API flag and Console toggle. Change must be reversible for individual keys.
2) Transparency: list the quantization profile, estimated per-token cost delta, expected latency changes, and known failure modes in the Console and API metadata.
3) Safety/Quality SLO: no more than 2% customer-visible quality regressions (measured by configured evals) vs baseline for Hosted opt-in; Dedicated customers can select a tighter 1% SLA in their contract.
4) Fallback behavior: automatic fallback to a compatible non-quantized variant on an exceeded error or latency threshold.
5) Billing: quantization-driven unit pricing reflected in invoices and quotas with clear conversion rates.

Product requirements (internal):
- PR-1: Profile Registry: central store (service: model-registry) of quantization profiles, metadata, and compatibility matrix. Fields: profile_name, model_arch, quant_bits, expected_memory, validated_on_prompt_set_ids.
- PR-2: Telemetry hooks: add telemetry events for profile selection, per-request profile_id, quality-check outcomes, and fallback triggers.
- PR-3: Eval suite integration: every profile must be validated against a standard prompt-set (quality-guardrails collection) with automated daily replays and statistical drift alerts.
- PR-4: Rollout control plane: support staged flags per-customer and global canary cohorts with percent rollouts and time windows.
- PR-5: Billing mapping: define pricing multiplier table and ensure metering emits tokens_consumed_{profile_name} dimension.

Acceptance criteria and metrics (quantitative):
- Quality: For each profile, measured automated eval delta (primary metric = normalized utility score) must be <=1.5% for Hosted canary to move to general availability; dedicated SLA target configurable to 1%.
- Latency: P50 token generation latency must not increase by more than 20% vs baseline for small-sequence workloads; p99 must remain under configured tenant SLO (default 2s).
- Cost: Expected per-token cost reduction >= 20% for q4 profiles vs baseline; billing accuracy <0.5% error on metering.
- Reliability: Fallback success rate > 99.95% when triggered; no cascading failures across tenants.

Design overview (high level):
1) Profile registry + metadata surfaced in model-catalog UI.
2) Evaluation pipeline: nightly replay job that runs new commits and profiles against canonical prompt-sets and pushes metrics to Optimize dashboards.
3) Runtime tagging: inference requests carry profile_id; the serving runtime selects corresponding kernels and memory layouts.
4) Canary orchestration: use rollout service to target 1% external traffic cohort, monitor real-time metrics and automated quality checks.
5) Billing plumbing: augment metering job to annotate tokens by profile and include in per-key usage exports.

Detailed rollout plan (phases):
Phase 0 - Preparation (2–4 weeks):
- Implement Profile Registry and Console UI mockups.
- Create canonical prompt-sets (safety, hallucination, domain-specific) and register them.
- Define billing multipliers and update billing schema.
- Owners: Product (Maya Chen), Runtime (Rafael Ortega), Billing (Priya Desai).

Phase 1 - Internal Canary (2 weeks):
- Enable profiles for internal teams and Redwood QA. Run daily automated evals; collect human raters for 500 sample prompts.
- Stop criteria: any automated metric exceeding threshold or >0.5% human regression.

Phase 2 - External Controlled Canary (4 weeks):
- Target 1% of traffic for hosted public accounts and a small cohort of Dedicated customers (opt-in). Monitor daily: utility score, latency, fallback rate, metering.
- Accept criteria: quality <=1.5% delta, latency p50 within 20%, billing annotations validated.

Phase 3 - Staged Expansion (6–8 weeks):
- Expand to 10% → 50% cohorts with progressive checks. For Dedicated customers signed to tighter SLAs, require explicit contract flag before expansion.

Phase 4 - GA and Packaging (2 weeks):
- Mark profiles as GA in Catalog. Publish pricing multipliers and Console toggles. Update docs and release notes.

Rollback and mitigation playbook (short):
1) Automatic rollback: if automated quality checks breach thresholds for more than 3 consecutive windows, the control plane will revert affected requests to baseline model and notify SRE/PD.
2) Manual rollback: product or runtime can instantly flip tenant toggles; billing records preserved.
3) Post-incident triage: collect saved generations, telemetry, and prompt-set failures for regression triage.

Telemetry and alerting requirements:
- Dashboards: per-profile KPI dashboards (quality delta, p50/p90/p99 latency, fallback rate, billing delta).
- Alerts: threshold alerts for quality delta > configured (default 1.5%), fallback rate spikes >0.5% absolute, metering mismatch >0.5% daily.
- Logging: sample-level logging for failed checks with redaction rules; store sample artifacts to a secure bucket for triage.

Packaging and pricing considerations:
- Hosted: default opt-in with a visible per-token discount; usage shows both baseline and quantized token counts.
- Dedicated: offer two tiers: Conservative (default: quantization off) and Optimized (profile enabled with 1% quality SLA; pricing reflects committed usage).
- Private: provide artifacts and validated profiles; charge a packaging fee + support for updates.
- Discount framing: present estimated savings and a recommended profile per-model to customers based on their historical sequence length distribution.

Open risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Edge-case quality regressions for niche prompt patterns. Mitigation: enlarge canonical prompt-sets and require human review for domain-critical tenants before Dedicated expansion.
- Risk: Billing disputes due to per-profile metering. Mitigation: expose per-profile metering exports and reconciliation reports.
- Risk: Runtime incompatibilities across older hardware. Mitigation: compatibility matrix in Profile Registry and automatic routing to base variant when no compatible kernels exist.

Timeline and milestones (quarter-level):
- Week 0–4: Profile Registry + Prompt-set authoring + Billing schema changes.
- Week 5–6: Internal canary + human rater batch.
- Week 7–10: External controlled canary.
- Week 11–16: Staged expansion and Dedicated customer onboarding.
- Week 17–18: GA, docs, and billing live.

Ownership and contacts:
- Product lead: Maya Chen (product)
- Runtime owner: Rafael Ortega (eng-serving-runtime)
- Eval / E2E metrics: Priya Desai (applied-ml-and-evals)
- Billing & packaging: Aisha Kumar (finance-legal)
- SRE alerting and rollback: Liam O'Connor (eng-sre)

Appendices:
A) Example billing multiplier table:
| profile_name | quant_bits | estimated_token_cost_multiplier | notes |
| q4_small | 4 | 0.70 | Best for short sequences, slight bias observed on numeric tasks |
| q8_dynamic | 8 | 0.85 | Low risk, moderate savings |
| q4_tf_robust | 4 | 0.65 | Requires special kernel; higher memory savings |

B) Example automated eval config (YAML):
--
prompt_set_ids: ["safety_v1", "hallucination_basic_v2", "finance_smoke_v1"]
metrics:
  - name: normalized_utility
    threshold: 0.985   # allow 1.5% drop
  - name: hallucination_rate
    threshold: 0.02
retries: 3
backfill_days: 7
--

C) Rollout decision checklist (to move from canary to staged):
1) Automated metrics pass for 14 consecutive days.
2) Human rater sample error <= target.
3) No billing inconsistencies in reconciliation report.
4) No more than one unrelated SRE incident correlated to profile.

Next steps (action items):
- Product: finalize profile taxonomy and UI copy (owner: Maya) — due 2026-11-22.
- Runtime: implement profile_id tagging and fallback plumbing (owner: Rafael) — due 2026-11-29.
- Evals: curate initial prompt-sets and schedule human rater batch (owner: Priya) — due 2026-11-26.
- Billing: update metering schema and export (owner: Aisha) — due 2026-11-30.

- 2026-11-22: Profile taxonomy v1 added.

[Optimize Lite - Launch Kit, PRD and Roadmap]
Overview:

This document consolidates the product brief, minimal viable PRD, light design constraints, phased roadmap, pricing guidance, and the initial release notes for a compact optimization add-on named "Optimize Lite". Optimize Lite targets small engineering teams and early-stage customers who want measurable inference cost savings with minimal operations overhead.

Purpose:
- Single source of truth to align product, engineering, solutions, and GTM for the first release.
- Keep scope small and safe: automated, explainable suggestions; conservative canaries and shadowing; billing tied to auto-apply usage.

Audience:
- Product managers, engineering leads (Optimize & Runtime), Applied ML, SEs, Sales, Customer Success.

Executive summary (one paragraph):
Optimize Lite provides per-tenant, per-route optimization suggestions (batching, prefix caching, curated quant profiles) surfaced in the Redwood Console and via a small Suggestions API. Customers can evaluate suggestions in shadow mode, then opt to canary and auto-apply changes. The goal is a low-friction cost-reduction product with built-in safety and clear commercial packaging.

Top-level goals (measurable):
1) Deliver three suggestion classes with console and API access within GA.
2) Demonstrate >=22% token-cost reduction for transactional benchmarks during pilot.
3) Ensure auto-applies do not increase 99p latency by >5% (automated rollback).
4) Convert 40% of beta customers to paid within 90 days of GA.

Out-of-scope:
- Full Optimize Conductor orchestration (no multi-model switching).
- Automated private/on-prem packaging in v1 (Phase 2 adds manual import/export).

MVE feature list:
- Console: per-route "Optimization Suggestions" panel showing ranked recommendations, estimated savings, risk level, and actions: "Evaluate (shadow)", "Apply (canary)", "Rollback".
- API: suggestions retrieval and apply endpoints (tenant-scoped).
- Suggestion types: batching (adjust batch window and thresholds), prefix/KV caching recommendations, curated quantization profiles (validated list).
- Safety: shadow evaluation, staged canaries, automated rollback triggers, audit trail.

High-level PRD (requirements):
- RQ-01 Suggestion API:
  - Tenant and route scoping required.
  - Response fields: suggestion_id, tenant_id, route, type, friendly_description, estimated_tokens_saved_per_1M, estimated_latency_delta_ms, confidence_score, risk_level.
- RQ-02 Console UX:
  - Suggestions appear on route page. Each suggestion shows an explanation, expected savings, and confidence. Buttons: "Shadow Evaluate", "Canary Apply" (with canary size/duration UI), "Rollback".
- RQ-03 Safety and SLOs:
  - Canary default: 1% traffic for 30m. Monitors: shadow-evaluator delta (default threshold 2%), 99p latency (>5% trigger), error rate increase (>0.5% absolute). On trigger, auto-rollback within 5 minutes and page owner.
- RQ-04 Billing & Quotas:
  - Track suggestions evaluated and suggestions auto-applied. Billing meter charged only for auto-applies and a low monthly add-on fee.
- RQ-05 Metrics & observability:
  - Emit metrics for suggestions_generated, suggestions_evaluated, suggestions_applied, canary_regressions, estimated_tokens_saved. Console shows time-series for these per-tenant.

Design notes and constraints:
- Reuse telemetry ingestion and sampling components from Optimize Conductor where feasible to reduce implementation scope.
- Suggestion ranking uses deterministic heuristics plus an offline-trained lightweight ranker updated weekly; no heavy online retrain in v1.
- All apply operations must be idempotent and accept a dry_run flag.
- Applies translate to runtime policy updates via an internal runtime policy API; the runtime owner must provide a backwards-compatible apply contract.

Data flow (textual):
1) Sampling agent collects request metadata -> profiler constructs distributions (seq_len, latency, prefix entropy).
2) Suggestion engine (rules + ranker) writes candidate suggestions to suggestions-store.
3) Console/API reads store; user triggers shadow/canary workflows which call evaluation service and runtime policy apply API.

Runtime apply contract (summary):
- Endpoint: POST /internal/runtime/policy/apply
- Required fields: tenant_id, route, apply_token, suggestion_id, dry_run (bool).
- Must respond with apply_id, status, and be idempotent for the same apply_token.

Example Suggestion (JSON as text for docs):
{
  "suggestion_id": "sug-20260601-042",
  "tenant_id": "t-01xWz",
  "route": "/v1/chat/completions",
  "type": "prefix_cache",
  "friendly_description": "Enable prefix cache for common 1-3 token prefixes and TTL 30s for requests with seq_len <= 128.",
  "estimated_tokens_saved_per_1M": "18,400",
  "estimated_latency_delta_ms": "-0.5",
  "confidence_score": "0.78",
  "risk_level": "low"
}

CLI example (apply canary):
redwood optimize-lite apply --tenant t-01xWz --suggestion sug-20260601-042 --canary-pct 1 --duration 30m --dry-run=false

Safety, monitoring, and alerts:
- Primary automated triggers for rollback: shadow loss delta > 2%, 99p latency increase >5%, error-rate delta >0.5% absolute.
- Alerts to create: P0 when any canary triggers; P1 when an apply occurs with no audit entry.
- Required dashboards: per-tenant suggestion health, canary outcomes, cumulative estimated tokens saved.

Acceptance criteria for GA:
- Suggestions API P95 latency < 200ms under expected load.
- E2E pilot shows >=20% token-cost reduction on target transactional benchmark with no >5% 99p latency regression during canary.
- Security review completed for suggestion-store access and apply workflow (KMS/SSO integration validated).

Roadmap and rollout plan (phased):
- Phase Alpha (4 weeks): internal pilot with 3 internal tenants. Deliver profiler, suggestion engine, suggestions-store, basic console view (read-only).
- Phase Beta (6 weeks): public beta for hosted tenants. Shadow-evaluation enabled; onboarding templates for SEs. Target: 25 external beta customers.
- Phase GA (6-8 weeks): enable canary auto-apply and billing integration. Launch Starter and Scale SKUs.
- Phase Dedicated Support (Q3 post-GA): add manual import/export of suggestion policies for Dedicated and on-prem customers; plan for automated on-prem runner in a future release.

Pricing & packaging guidance (proposal):
- Pricing objectives: low entry cost, transparent ROI, predictable unit billing.
- Proposed SKUs:
  - Free (shadow-only): 0-3 evaluations/month per tenant.
  - Starter: $99/month + 0.2% of monthly inference spend; up to 50 evaluations and 100 auto-applies/month.
  - Scale: $799/month + 0.1% of monthly inference spend; higher quotas and SLA options.
  - Enterprise: negotiated with Dedicated support and professional services for policy transfer.
- Billing meters to implement: suggestions_evaluated (count), suggestions_autopplied (count), estimated_tokens_saved (tokens).

GTM / Sales enablement notes:
- Core pitch: "Reduce inference spend safely with explainable, one-click optimizations".
- Key objections & suggested responses:
  1) "We fear quality regressions" -> emphasize shadow-eval, small canaries, automatic rollback, and SE review.
  2) "We already tune batching in-house" -> highlight easy operationalization, continuous suggestions as traffic patterns change, and quantization recommendations validated by Applied ML.
  3) "How are we billed?" -> clear quota-based monthly subscriptions plus per-auto-apply meter; free shadow-only tier.

SE onboarding checklist (for first deploy):
1) Capture 48-72 hours of representative traffic via profiler.
2) Produce and review first suggestion set with customer; agree risk appetite and observability signals.
3) Enable shadow evaluation for 72 hours and inspect loss and latency deltas.
4) If acceptable, enable canary apply at 1% for 30 minutes and review results.

Support & incident playbook (short):
- If canary triggers rollback automatically, notify customer and SE owner; create incident and collect request/response traces and shadow evaluation artifacts.
- If auto-rollback fails, manual rollback CLI: redwood optimize-lite rollback --tenant <id> --apply_id <id>.
- Escalation: Applied ML for quality investigations; Runtime oncall for performance/latency regressions.

GA Release Notes (v1.0) Summary:
- Release date: 2026-05-10
- Status: GA (hosted)

[Adaptive Cost Gatekeeper - launch kit and PRD]
Overview

Summary: The Adaptive Cost Gatekeeper (ACG) is a product initiative to provide per-request, policy-driven gating of model variant choice and runtime fidelity to meet customer SLOs while minimizing unit cost. This doc bundles the product overview, PRD, high-level design, rollout roadmap, pricing/packaging guidance, and v1.0 release notes into a single launch kit for cross-functional teams.

Problem statement

Teams building LLM features often trade latency and quality for cost manually: maintaining multiple model variants and bespoke routing logic. Customers need a thin, centrally managed service that automatically chooses an acceptable model/fidelity per request based on explicit policies (latency, cost budget, regulatory guardrails). Without this capability customers either overprovision (pay too much) or under-deliver (miss SLOs).

Goals and success metrics (product-level)

- Primary goal: Reduce billed per-token cost for typical conversational workloads by 15–30% for customers that opt in to ACG within 90 days of GA.
- Shield customer application-level SLOs: 99.95% availability, p99 latency degradation of route <= +50ms relative to pinned baseline for small (<= 128 tokens) responses.
- Fallback correctness: fallback-to-safe-variant rate <= 0.5% under normal operation.
- Cost regressions: detect and alert if per-tenant cost delta > 20% vs baseline within 24 hours.

User personas

- ML/Platform engineer (primary): integrates Gatekeeper into routing, configures policies, reviews telemetry.
- Product engineer: sets per-route cost budgets and fidelity constraints.
- Customer success / Solutions (CS/SE): uses playbooks to advise customers on policy selection and commercial options.

Must-have requirements (MUST)

1) Runtime decisioning: ACG must accept an HTTP/GRPC evaluation API that returns a routing decision (variant id, fidelity profile, estimated cost delta) in <= 10ms median.
2) Policy engine: support declarative policies: latency_budget_ms, cost_budget_usd_per_1000_tokens, safety_labels (e.g. pii_prohibited), regional_affinity.
3) Observability: emit per-decision telemetry with labels: tenant_id, route, decision_reason, estimated_cost, chosen_variant, p99_est_latency. Must integrate into Console dashboards and billing reconciliation.
4) Fallbacks: automatic safe fallback policies that prefer compatibility (API contract) and safety over cost savings.
5) Auditing & SSO: decisions must be auditable for 90 days and visible in tenant audit logs.

Should-have (SHOULD)

- Local simulator: customer-facing simulation CLI to run synthetic traffic through policies and produce cost/latency impact projections.
- Canary rollout hooks and feature flags per-tenant.
- Suggestion engine: using Optimize signals to recommend policies based on historic traffic.

Design overview (high level)

Components (service names):
- cost-gatekeeper-api: evaluation endpoint (HTTP/gRPC).
- policy-store: durable rules DB with versioning and rollouts.
- cost-sim: simulation engine (offline and CLI).
- variant-selector: real-time selector that queries pricing and runtime profiles.
- routing-orchestrator: issues actual routing decisions to serving runtime via routing policy service.
- telemetry-ingest: structured decision telemetry; feeds Console and billing pipelines.

Data flow (summary):
1) Request arrives at routing tier.
2) routing-tier calls cost-gatekeeper-api with attributes: route, tenant, input_size, user_fidelity_hint, session_state.
3) cost-gatekeeper evaluates policies (policy-store) and runtime profiles (variant-selector) and returns decision object.
4) routing-tier implements decision (route to model variant / apply fidelity knobs) and records telemetry.

Decision latency SLAs and thresholds (configurable):
- Decision median <= 10ms; p95 <= 40ms.
- For session-affine fast paths (session pinned) decision median <= 4ms.

Policy examples (text table):
- Row format (policy_name | constraints):
  - default-cost-guard | latency_budget_ms:200, cost_budget_usd_per_1000_tokens:0.30, safety: allow_all
  - regulatory-eu-strict | latency_budget_ms:250, cost_budget:0.45, region_affinity: eu-west-1, safety: pii_prohibited

API surface (example)

Request (pseudo-JSON in one line):
{ "tenant_id": "acme-inc", "route": "/chat/gen", "input_tokens": 42, "session_id": "s-1234", "hints": {"max_accept_delay_ms":150} }

Response (pseudo-JSON):
{ "decision": "use_variant:v3-q4", "fidelity_profile": "pruned-encoder:low-attn", "estimated_cost_usd": "0.00027", "decision_reason": "meets_latency_and_cost" }

Billing and telemetry hooks

- Every decision emits telemetry keys: tenant_id, route, decision_id (uuid), estimated_cost_usd, chosen_variant, policy_applied, timestamp.
- Billing pipeline must consume estimated_cost_usd tags to attribute pre-billing estimates for feature-level cost visibility. Final billing still reconciled from token meters.

Operational controls and safety

- Emergency kill-switch per-tenant: immediate bypass to pinned variant (owner: eng-sre).
- Safety precedence: policies marked safety:strict override cost budgets.
- Quota enforcement: ACG integrates with rate-limiter to ensure cost policies do not cause quota escalation.

Roadmap and rollout plan (Q4 2026 -> Q2 2027)

Phase 0 (spec & prototypes) Q4 2026 (owner: product + eng-platform)
1) Finalize policy language and config schema.
2) Build minimal cost-sim prototype and CLI.
3) Integrate prototype into internal developer sandbox for experiments.

Phase 1 (experimental alpha) Q1 2027 (owner: eng-serving-runtime)
1) Implement cost-gatekeeper-api with in-memory policy-store.
2) Expose CLI simulator to 10 internal teams.
3) First telemetry dashboard iteration in Console.

Phase 2 (private beta) Q2 2027 (owner: product + eng-sre)
1) Persistent policy-store, versioned rollouts, canary scheduler.
2) Billing integration for estimated_cost signals.
3) Beta customers (3 tenants) with SLA experiments.

Phase 3 (GA) Q3 2027 (owner: go-to-market)
1) GA SDKs and docs, SLA contract addendum, pricing bundles.
2) Expand CS playbook and migration assistance.

Pricing and packaging notes (initial guidance)

Pricing objectives: make ACG accessible to developers while capturing commercial value for enterprise tenants needing SLA-backed guarantees.

Suggested packaging: 
- Developer tier (free/low-cost): access to cost-sim and soft decisions (no SLA).
- Team tier (metered): metered per-decision charge + small percentage of cost-savings captured as "optimization fee" (e.g. 5% of measured monthly savings compared to baseline).
- Enterprise tier (reserved + SLA): monthly seat + guaranteed decision latency SLOs + optional revenue-share escalation for delivered savings exceeding threshold. Includes audit log retention and prioritized support.

Billing model notes: estimated_cost_usd is used for visibility only; final billed tokens still come from token meters. For Team/Enterprise tiers we instrument a reconciliation window (7 days) to account for differences between estimated and actual.

Commercial guardrails and discounts:
- Beta program: waive metered fees for first 3 months; apply professional services credits for migration.
- Enterprise discounts for multi-tenant reserved capacity commitments.

Release notes - v0.1 (alpha)

Released components:
