2026-02-20 - Design kickoff: reviewed envelope schema and shoplifted HEC batch format; agreed on at-least-once with idempotency tokens. Attendees: Priya, Marco, Sanjay (SRE), Elena (Security).
2026-02-25 - Spike complete: validated Kafka consumer group pattern and durable per-destination staging queue. Performance sketch: 2000 eps per worker with batching. Spike notes in Confluence: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/AUDIT/spike-delivery-kafka-results.
2026-03-02 - PR opened for DeliveryState persistence and worker skeleton: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/342. Initial integration tests added for Splunk HEC happy path.

2026-03-12 - Working on observability hooks: Prometheus metrics + Console API to surface per-destination delivery rate. Next: wire metrics to Console dashboard and add replay button.

[Private tenant assertion gatekeeper & role-reconciliation urgent remediation]
description:
Summary: Multiple enterprise Private customers reported short windows where newly-joined service requests were authorized with an overly permissive RBAC binding and corresponding audit events were not present in the control-plane logs. Impact affects tenant onboarding and SAML-based SSO flows on Private clusters that also use on-prem KMS envelopes.

Observed behavior: During tenant onboarding the SAML assertion processing pipeline sometimes proceeds before the tenant key rewrap/unwrap handshake completes, causing a fallback code path that attaches a transient permissive role-binding for continuity. Simultaneously, the local audit-uploader batcher experienced a transient 503 from the control-plane ingest endpoint and dropped a small buffer of recent events (buffer not yet flushed to durable store). Combined, this produced: brief window of over-permissive access (seconds) + missing audit trail for those requests.

Root cause (summary): 1) race between assertion-to-role mapping and KMS envelope availability when tenant key metadata is being rehydrated; 2) non-idempotent audit buffer drop on transient ingest failure (uploader did not persist failed batch to durable staging and retry idempotently).

Impact: Several customers escalated (support cases #C-9342, #C-9411) citing compliance violation risk. No evidence of data exfiltration; observed accesses were limited to ephemeral metadata reads. Still classified as security-sensitive and regulatory-impacting.

Acceptance criteria / definition of done: - Prevent assertion processing from attaching permissive fallback role during KMS rewrap window. - Ensure audit events are durably queued and retried; implement backfill path to reconstruct missing events for affected time windows. - Ship emergency patch with a canary rollout to Private space and an automated post-deploy reconciliation job. - Provide customer-facing incident notes and reconciliation artifacts for affected tenants.

updates:
2026-03-10: Pager: Oncall received multiple escalations from Enterprise customers in EU region during tenant onboarding. Triage: blocked reproduction in staging; reproduced in a Private dev cluster using simulated delayed KMS unwrap. Initial mitigation: applied temporary rate-limit to the assertion conveyor to slow processing (manual throttle).
2026-03-11: Root cause analysis completed: identified assertion pipeline does not check 'tenant_key_state==READY' before applying role bindings. Audit-uploader dropped buffered batch on 503 without writing to disk. Created design doc for gating and durable buffer (Confluence: https://confluence.redwood.internal/display/PCS/ENG-315208).
2026-03-12: Patch designed: (a) gate SAML/assertion processing on explicit 'key_ready' signal emitted by key-rewrap handler, with a short optimistic backoff to avoid adding high-latency path; (b) make audit-uploader write pending batches to local encrypted staging (S3 for hosted, local FS for Private) and idempotent-retry with deterministic batch IDs; (c) reconciliation worker to reconstruct missing events from staging buffers and tenant-proxy logs and push to audit store. Draft PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/controlplane/pull/1219
2026-03-13: Security review: asked SEC team for expedited review of gating logic and staging storage encryption. SEC feedback: require HSM-wrapped metadata pointer in staging and a short TTL for staged batches (encrypt with tenant KMS). Implemented encryption wrapper and TTL enforcement.
2026-03-14: Canary rollout plan approved by SRE and PM. Canary targets: two Private customers with low-risk staging clusters, 15-minute observation window with strict SLO guardrails. Reconciliation script prepared to backfill last 2 hours of events for affected tenants. Customer comms draft posted to support drive: https://drive.redwood.internal/incident/ENG-315208/notes
Next steps: Merge PR, deploy canary to Private cluster region eu-west-1, monitor for role-binding regressions and audit ingest success. If stable after canary, promote to all Private clusters and run reconciliation job for impacted tenants. Update customers with signed-off backfill artifacts.

[Retirement playbook for legacy multiplexed transport and offline-replay adapter]
description:
Background: The legacy multiplexed transport (multiplex-v1) and its offline-replay adapter were introduced as an experimental low-latency transport to multiplex multiple logical channels over a single persistent connection and to allow clients to replay missed events from device-local buffers. Over the last 24 months this path has accrued operational complexity, subtle ordering bugs, and an outsized maintenance burden on infra and security teams. The new unified streaming API (sse/v2 + event-archive) and the client-side durable queue in SDKs provide the same guarantees with simpler semantics and stronger observability. Goal: Orchestrate a low-risk, well-communicated retirement of multiplex-v1 and offline-replay adapter, provide first-class migration tooling and a short-lived compatibility shim for laggard clients, and ensure zero unplanned customer-impact for high-value customers.

background:
Multiplex-v1 exhibits three recurring incidents: message reordering with larger fanout, head-of-line blocking under network flaps, and subtle auth token scoping gaps. Offline-replay adapter bypassed server-side audit checks in some failure modes. Both features increase the attack surface and block SLO improvements (we cannot safely guarantee ordering SLA). The new architecture centralizes routing, supports deterministic per-channel ordering, and archives events for server-side replay that integrates with KMS-backed audit logs.

out_of_scope:
Removing multiplexed protocol support from third-party OSS SDKs (we will offer adapters but not auto-remove OSS docs in this project). Rewriting customer application logic; we will provide migration guides and tools but not execute migrations for customers except for enterprise support engagements.

goals:
Provide a documented, tested migration path that covers 99% of active customers within 90 days of announcement
Ship an open-source compat adapter (client-side) and a server-side short-lived shim to reduce immediate breakage
Ensure observability and regressions detection: define metrics and alerting for migration progress and critical failures
Remove multiplex-v1 and offline-replay adapter from hosted runtime after a 180-day transition window, unless blocked by enterprise exceptions

acceptance_criteria:

Compat adapter released (npm/pypi/github) and used by at least 50% of remaining clients within first 30 days
Customer impact SAG (support action group) created and staffed for 120 days with runbook
Telemetry: synthesis shows <0.1% error-rate attributable to transport incompatibility after canary rollout
SLA and audit tests updated (ordering, replay, auth) and included in CI for runtime-1.28
Executive sign-off from PM, Eng Director, and Security on final shutdown date

migration_steps:
Technical announcement + timeline (D+0): publish deprecation notice, FAQ, and migration guide in docs and email active API keys
SDK updates (D+7): land SDK changes that default to unified streaming and expose compatibility shim opt-in
Compat adapter release (D+14): publish OSS adapter that translates multiplex-v1 semantics to unified streaming for clients that cannot update immediately
Canary runtime shim (D+21): deploy server-side shim in limited region to translate incoming multiplex-v1 traffic to internal routing with enhanced logging
Telemetry gating (D+28): enable migration dashboards and alerts; begin weekly migration review with support/engineering
Customer outreach (D+30 - D+60): targeted emails/SE outreach for top 50 customers still on multiplex-v1, offer migration assistance
Gradual throttling (D+90): begin soft throttling for new multiplex-v1 connections and show clear client-side error codes to prompt upgrades
Final shutdown (D+180): retire compat shims and fully remove multiplex-v1 and offline-replay adapter from hosted runtime unless exception approved

[Structured batch proxy for OTLP HTTP -> Tempo with atomic ack semantics]
description:
Implement a lightweight HTTP proxy that accepts OTLP/HTTP span batches from SDKs and downstream services and forwards them to Tempo with structured batching and atomic acknowledgment semantics. The proxy must: 1) accept OTLP/HTTP JSON and protobuf envelopes and normalize to internal canonical batch format, 2) persist batches to a local write-ahead buffer (durable filesystem queue) to survive short node restarts, 3) forward batches to Tempo using existing /api/traces endpoint with configurable max batch size and concurrency, 4) expose an ACK to the upstream only after the batch is durably accepted by either Tempo or the durable queue (atomic ack), 5) surface per-tenant backpressure metrics (queue_depth, inflight_batches, dropped_batches) and a health endpoint for graceful shedding, 6) degrade gracefully to a lightweight sampling-only mode under sustained overload, and 7) include compatibility transforms for Jaeger/Zipkin envelope fields (trace_id padding, span.tags mapping). Deliverables: design doc, unit+integration tests with Tempo mock, load benchmark results, Grafana dashboards for the new metrics, migration plan for customers switching from direct OTLP ingestion to the proxy.

[Rank-and-Recall decision path + hosting evaluation]
summary:
Discovery focused on whether QuantaHealth should run a recall-first then rerank pipeline or an integrated rerank-first approach, plus which hosting mode to pick. Key constraints: 2k QPS burst target, P99 tail latency target of ~120ms for search responses (rerank included), strict PHI-like data residency concerns, and platform team's preference for VPC-managed private control plane. Redwood proposed a Dedicated pool with model fallbacks and a 48-hour throughput benchmark. Agreed next steps around sample data, cost comparison, and benchmark plan.

topics:
current architecture: recall index + external re-ranker
throughput targets and tail latency
embedding dimensionality tradeoffs (256 vs 512 vs 1024)
vector DB sharding and hybrid search
hosting choices: Hosted API vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC/on-prem)
security/compliance: SOC2, KMS, audit logs, SSO
benchmarking plan and PoC scope

transcript:
[00:00] Avery Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Avery from Redwood, AE, and with me is Diego, our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Maya Patel: Good, thanks. Running a bit late but all set.
[00:09] Diego Martinez: Hi Maya, Omar, Lena. Quick note on format - we'll ask a few discovery questions then walk through options and trade-offs.
[00:15] Omar Rahman: Sounds good. We're mostly interested in a decision for our search stack: whether to keep recall-first with a light reranker or move to a heavy rerank after recall. Also, where to host — we have PHI-adjacent data so VPC/private is on the table.
[00:26] Lena Gomez: And throughput. Our internal SLAs are aggressive, we have sustained ~500 QPS with 2k burst. We need P95 ~50ms and P99 ideally <120ms end-to-end.
[00:35] Avery Chen: Great — that's the crux. Quick question: what's your current recall index and re-ranker?
[00:40] Maya Patel: We use OpenSearch for dense + sparse hybrid retrieval. For re-ranking we run a small BERT-based ranker (approx 60M params) in-house. It does batch reranking but it's getting expensive at scale.
[00:51] Diego Martinez: Okay so recall-first today with an in-house reranker. Are embeddings generated at ingestion or on-the-fly?
[00:56] Omar Rahman: At ingestion. We precompute 512-d embeddings using a proprietary embedder. Index size is roughly 40M vectors, ~2.1GB after compression per shard — actually, we have multiple shards.
[01:07] Avery Chen: That's helpful. Two axes to think about: embedding dimensionality and where reranking runs. Lower dims (e.g., 256) reduce VDB footprint and improve fanout, but may cost recall quality; higher dims (1024) improve relevance but cost more compute and memory.
[01:21] Lena Gomez: We're evaluating 512 vs 768 for a balance. Also, we are interested in Redwood's Quantized embeddings suggestions — you mentioned compact embeddings?
[01:29] Diego Martinez: Yeah, Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization profiles by workload. For a recall-first pipeline, compact embeddings plus approximate nearest neighbor reduces IOPS and network overhead for the DB. But the reranker model size and placement will dominate tail latency.
[01:40] Maya Patel: For reranking, we can't have slow tails. If we keep rerank in path, that's an extra hop. Are customers doing the rerank in-hosted vs in Dedicated GPUs?
[01:49] Avery Chen: Both. Typical patterns: Hosted API for easier setup and fast iteration — good for dev and small prod. Dedicated pools for predictable throughput and lower per-token costs at scale. Private (VPC/on-prem) if regulatory constraints require a customer-managed network. Many customers run recall in their VDB and call Redwood for a small high-quality reranker hosted on Dedicated GPUs, sometimes colocated in the same region for minimal network latency.
[02:07] Omar Rahman: Latency is our big worry. If reranking is in the cloud and our recall is in our VPC OpenSearch, adding egress and cross-VPC hops could add 30-60ms. Any ways to mitigate?
[02:16] Diego Martinez: Yes — Redwood supports private endpoints and VPC peering options for Dedicated and Private deployments. With Private (customer-managed control plane) you can keep traffic within your VPC and use our inference nodes in the same subnet. That removes public egress and keeps latency down. There's also a hybrid hosting: you can keep recall on your VDB and run rerank on a Dedicated Redwood pool inside your cloud account (we've done this with AWS PrivateLink and VPC endpoints).
[02:35] Maya Patel: Costs — Dedicated looks pricey but predictable. How do we think about per-query econ if we push a 175M reranker vs a 1.3B reranker?
[02:44] Avery Chen: Good question. Rough heuristics: smaller rerankers reduce latency and cost per query; larger models improve MRR/precision. Redwood Optimize can simulate expected token counts and suggest batching and KV cache policies. Also, fallbacks are common: route high-confidence queries to a smaller reranker and only call the large model for edge cases or low-confidence scores. That reduces unit cost significantly.
[02:59] Lena Gomez: What's the tradeoff of doing rerank-first (i.e., run a small ranker over a broader candidate set early) vs recall-first?
[03:06] Diego Martinez: There's nuance. Recall-first keeps retrieval efficient and relies on the reranker to reorder top candidates. Rerank-first (or cascade) can prune earlier with a cheap ranker applied to a larger candidate set to improve quality downstream — this saves on heavy reranker calls but increases initial compute and can complicate latency curves. For high QPS, recall-first with a cascade rerank works well: compact ANN for recall, then a mid-sized ranker, then occasional large model.
[03:28] Omar Rahman: Ok, we like cascade attempts if it reduces calls to big models. But we also need clear SLOs and fallbacks when the big model is slow or unavailable. How does Redwood handle graceful degradation?
[03:38] Avery Chen: Redwood has smart routing and automatic fallback to smaller model variants or regional fallbacks. For Dedicated, you can define canary rollouts and A/B and set automatic fallback policies to a compatible model when latency or capacity thresholds are hit. Also caching of reranker outputs for repeated queries helps reduce calls.
[03:51] Maya Patel: About vector DB — we're on OpenSearch but exploring moving to a specialized VDB like Pinecone. If we switch, how does Redwood integrate?
[03:59] Diego Martinez: Redwood integrates with major VDBs via standard protocols (ANN query over gRPC/HTTP). We also provide connectors and best-practice configs for sharding/fanout. Important things: ensure shard fanout doesn't blow up QPS and watch for cold-start IO. Redwood Optimize will flag shard sizes and suggest embedding dims that match your index layout.
[04:16] Lena Gomez: Can you expand on sharding and fanout? We have 6 shards across regions and current fanout for a query is all shards — that drives latency.
[04:23] Diego Martinez: Right — full fanout increases recall but also increases latency. Strategies: route queries to subset shards using routing keys, prefiltering, or use a two-level index (category-level recall then shard-level). We also recommend topology-aware query routing and edge caching for very hot records. For some customers, a hybrid approach with a lightweight initial filter (sparse + compact embed) reduces fanout by 60% and keeps recall acceptable.
[04:42] Omar Rahman: Security checklist: we need SOC2 Type II, SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit logs, KMS support, and ideally an option for on-prem. Do you have those?
[04:52] Avery Chen: Yes. Redwood provides SOC2 attestations, SSO via SAML/OIDC, RBAC in the Console, audit logs (configurable retention), and KMS/HSM integrations for Private deployments. On-prem is available as a Private deployment package for regulated customers. We'll share the whitepaper and SOC2 report.
[05:05] Maya Patel: Great. For the benchmark, what does Redwood need from us?
[05:09] Diego Martinez: Sample corpus (2GB preferred), representative query log (with QPS profile and peak patterns), and target SLOs. We'll run a 48-hour throughput benchmark against both Hosted and Dedicated configs: measure median, P95/P99, token/unit costs, and failure modes. We'll also test fallback behavior under load.
[05:24] Lena Gomez: Re: embeddings dimensionality — if we move to 256 dims and quantize, how big a drop in recall should we expect?
[05:31] Diego Martinez: It depends on your data. For many corpora, going from 512->256 with a good quantization profile yields minor recall degradation (1-3% recall lift loss) but huge savings in storage and throughput. But for fine-grained medical semantics, sometimes 512 or 768 is safer. We recommend running an offline eval with your query set to measure the exact impact — Redwood can help run those evals.
[05:49] Omar Rahman: Do you support sparse + dense hybrid queries (we sometimes run keyword boosting and dense similarity simultaneously)?
[05:55] Avery Chen: Yes — Redwood's routing supports hybrid search patterns. You can run a weighted combination of sparse + dense signals and then rerank the merged candidate list. We have customers that use BM25 prefilter + ANN recall + tiny reranker to get high precision with lower cost.
[06:06] Maya Patel: One operational question — we're concerned about model drift and quality regressions after updates. How do you monitor quality?
[06:12] Diego Martinez: Redwood Optimize provides eval hooks: tie quality monitoring to prompt/query sets, surface regression alerts, and integrate with your CI for model rollouts. For rerankers, we track ranking metrics over time, alert on drops, and can automate rollbacks.
[06:24] Lena Gomez: For SLA — can Dedicated guarantee tail latency?
[06:28] Avery Chen: Dedicated gives predictable throughput and is SLA-backed for uptime and baseline latency targets, but exact P99 guarantees depend on workload and model choices. We supply expected performance profiles for model variants — if you need hard P99 guarantees we can scope a performance SLA in the contract with runbook and performance testing clauses.
[06:43] Omar Rahman: Let's go back to costs. If we run a cascade: compact recall (Host local) -> mid-size rerank on Dedicated -> large model fallback, what ballpark savings should we expect vs calling large reranker for all queries?
[06:55] Diego Martinez: It varies, but customers often see 4-6x reduction in per-query cost on average because the large model is invoked only on 10-20% of queries. [07:19] Avery Chen: Redwood Console shows token-level cost, per-route and per-model breakdowns, and you can export reports. For Dedicated, we also provide reserved capacity accounting and per-customer allocation.

[07:34] Diego Martinez: We support KV cache policies that persist across requests for the same session and cache warmed prefixes. For rerank pipelines, we often cache intermediate embeddings and partial reranker outputs for a short TTL to avoid repeated work for similar queries. Cache semantics are configurable in Dedicated and Private deployments.
[07:48] Maya Patel: Ok, let's talk timeline. We want a pilot in Q2. What should the PoC look like?

[08:31] Avery Chen: Yes — several healthcare and finance customers run Dedicated in their cloud accounts with VPC peering/private endpoints; a few run Private on-prem for higher assurance. We'll share anonymized case studies.
[08:40] Lena Gomez: Errors and fallback testing — what happens during model OOM or node failures?
[08:44] Diego Martinez: Redwood runtime has automatic fallback routing, cross-region failover, and can route to a smaller, compatible model on capacity issues. We also do graceful degradation where we return last-known-good ranking if needed. For Dedicated, redundancy and autoscaling policies help mitigate OOM.

[09:04] Avery Chen: Absolutely. You can pin model versions and control rollouts. Redwood Console supports canary deploys and rollbacks.

[09:26] Maya Patel: Great. So recapping — you will send the cost comparison, benchmark plan, security docs, and we will send sample data. Anything else?
[09:33] Avery Chen: We'll also propose a recommended pilot architecture (cascade pattern + Dedicated reranker in VPC), and a config for the benchmark that mirrors your traffic shape.

[09:46] Diego Martinez: Yes, Redwood Optimize can schedule evaluators and send regression alerts; we can integrate with PagerDuty or Slack.

[GPU entropy + headroom export (slice & queue attribution) 2026-06-09]
Executive summary:\n\nThis export captures a novel lens — 'entropy' — to quantify short-timescale variability across GPU slot occupancy by cluster/pool and by logical queue. The goal is to highlight where headroom is brittle (low sustained free capacity but high churn) versus where there is truly steady free capacity we can reassign. Entropy here is a heuristic measure (see definition below) that helps prioritize where to place reserved capacity or throttle burstable workloads.\n\nKey takeaways (high level):\n- APAC-eu1-pool-A shows low avg utilization (47%) but high entropy (0.72) indicating frequent slot churn due to ephemeral developer jobs; headroom is unreliable during 9:00–13:00 UTC.\n- na-west-cluster-3 has consistently high p95 (>92%) and low entropy (0.18) — saturated and stable, needs either scale-up or stronger routing to dedicated capacity.\n- Pools with entropy >0.6 tend to have short-lived queue spikes that inflate p95 but leave temporary windows of free slots; consider opportunistic batch placement (+cache) instead of reserved commitments.\n\nEntropy metric (operational definition):\n- For each slot we consider occupancy time-series over 1-minute bins for the export window (7 days). Convert to a binary occupied/unoccupied per bin. Entropy per slot = -p*log2(p)-(1-p)*log2(1-p) where p = fraction of bins occupied. Cluster/pool entropy = mean(slot_entropy) normalized by max entropy (1.0).\n- Interpretation: 0 => perfectly stable (always busy or always idle), higher values => more unpredictable churn. We care about high entropy when avg_util > 40% (means churn reduces reliability of headroom).\n\nData snapshot (CSV excerpt, fields: cluster,pool,logical_queue,avg_util,p95_util,entropy_norm,estimated_headroom_hours_at_peak,notes):\n\ncluster-01,core-pool-1,default,0.47,0.83,0.72,3.2,\"dev ephemeral jobs causing short spikes 08-14UTC\"\nna-west-cluster-3,compute-pool-x,ml-train,0.94,0.98,0.18,0.0,\"steady saturation; many inference lanes pinned\"\napac-eu1-2,burst-pool-b,experiments,0.61,0.89,0.65,1.1,\"high p95 but available short windows, consider slot-level preemption\"\neu-central-5,reservoir-1,highprio,0.36,0.57,0.12,8.5,\"clean headroom for reservation; low churn\"\nna-east-cluster-2,spillover-A,background,0.55,0.88,0.69,0.9,\"large entropy and short headroom; throttle candidate\"\n\nNotes on numbers:\n- avg_util and p95_util are token-weighted occupancy (slot-time weighted by GPU core percentage).\n- estimated_headroom_hours_at_peak = (free_slots_during_global_peak / slots_consumed_per_hour_by_typical_request) converted to hours; rough estimator used for quick ops decisions.\n\nQueries & extraction notes (working):\n- Slot occupancy collected from fleet telemetry (shipper v2) with 1-minute resolution; missing samples forward-filled up to 10m then considered unknown.\n- SQL-ish pseudocode used to compute entropy: SELECT cluster, pool, slot_id, SUM(occupied_bins)/count(bins) as p FROM slot_timebins WHERE ts BETWEEN $start AND $end GROUP BY 1,2,3; then compute per-slot entropy and aggregate.\n- PromQL used to cross-check p95 util: max_over_time(avg_over_time(gpu_utilization[1m])[7d:1m]) and p95() on the resulting series for the cluster scope.\n\nObserved anomalies and hypotheses (work-in-progress):\n1) cluster-01 dev spikes line up with scheduled CI window in the APAC morning — hypothesis: CI runners are not being routed to dedicated background pools after 2026-05-25 config change. Action: check PR #3417 (runner routing) and re-route CI to spillover pools.\n2) na-west-cluster-3 sustained saturation appears correlated with rollout of model-x v2 (in hosted inference); peak usage coincides with new customer on-boarding on 2026-06-03. Action: engage solutions-eng for throttle policy and consider bumping dedicated capacity for that tenant.\n3) burst-pool-b has high entropy but short headroom windows that are inconsistent with our batching heuristic — suspect short TTL jobs from experiments service with aggressive backoffs. Task: instrument job durations in experiments to confirm.\n\nOperational recommendations (short term):\n- For pools with entropy > 0.6 and avg_util between 40-70%: enable opportunistic eviction + batch placement and add a 10% conservative buffer to routing headroom estimates.\n- For clusters with p95 > 90% and entropy < 0.25: prioritize capacity growth (either add nodes or shift production routes to dedicated capacity) — these are stable hot spots.\n- Add a daily alert for \"entropy drift\": if entropy increases by >0.15 over a rolling 3-day window for a cluster that has avg_util > 45%, create an ops ticket.\n\nDashboard links used for export: /d/fleet/gpu-entropy-heatmap, /d/fleet/cluster-headroom, /d/fleet/queue-attribution-sankey (internal).\n\nAction items & owners:\n- Maya: add entropy to the weekly infra report and push a lightweight Grafana panel for quick glance (due 2026-06-11).\n- Arjun: check CI runner routing PR and propose a rollback or reroute for APAC jobs (JIRA-OPS-934) (due 2026-06-12).\n- Sofia: instrument experiments service job TTLs and post a follow-up with duration distribution (due 2026-06-16).\n\nOpen questions / discussion points:\n- Sensitivity: is 1-minute binning the right fidelity for entropy detection or should we move to 30s for low-latency churn? Tradeoff: telemetry cost vs signal quality.\n- Policy: what is the acceptable entropy threshold for committing reserved capacity? - This sheet groups clusters by region and flags sustained high-band runs (>12 hours in high band per day average).

Sheet: Orphaned GPU sockets and idle pockets by cluster/pool (investigation)

Purpose:
Quick triage sheet to identify pools and clusters with unexpectedly low active allocation but non-zero kernel-level GPU socket activity — i.e., GPUs present on hosts but not attached to active inference instances (suspected orphaned sockets from crash/reboot sequences or daemon mismanagement). Use this as input for capacity reclamation and remediation runbook.

Notes to self:
- This is an exploratory export mixed from cluster metrics and host-level GPU socket counters (nvidia-smi sockets and runtime-agent heartbeat).
- Values are sampled daily at 02:00 UTC to catch off-peak anomalies.
- ‚Orphaned sockets‘ = total_gpus - active_vms - reserved_for_preserved (where reserved_for_preserved is from reservation tags) minus expected idle buffer.
- Flag threshold: orphaned_sockets >= 2 AND avg_util_pct < 5% for 3 consecutive samples.

Table (recent 7-day snapshot):

High-level observations:
- Spot pools (us-west-2-cluster-C) show the largest correlated orphaned pockets. Hypothesis: rapid VM termination/eviction leaves GPU device mappings in a state where runtime-agent doesn't reattach and host drivers still report socket availability but K8sCRI hasn't reclaimed properly.
- eu-west preemptible pool also showing persistent small pockets across multiple days — likely agent crash or version skew around 2025-11-13 (see linked infra-ops#431).
- Dedicated pools maintain expected low orphan counts; suggests problem is eviction/termination related rather than hardware.

Quick remediation suggestions (prioritized):
1) Patch runtime-agent to add a watchdog at agent startup that forces GPU device re-scan and clears stale /dev/nvidia* references. Short-term rollout to spot/ preemptible pools only. (PR: runtime#762).
2) Add a Kubernetes finalizer/cleanup job that runs on node Terminating state to ensure CUDA socket teardown. Schedule as a DaemonSet with low burst.
3) Capacity reclamation script: nightly job to identify hosts with orphaned_sockets >= 4 for >24h and cordon + drain + reboot, with automated alert to on-call. Use a soft-drain first to avoid user impact.
4) Instrumentation: add a metric orphaned_socket_count exported via node-exporter and create a Grafana alert (threshold: 5 sockets for 6h) and an email + PagerDuty escalation path for infra.

- exact mapping between 'idle_gpus' and 'orphaned_sockets' differs by driver version — need to include driver version in future exports.
- how many callbacks from kubelet during termination are lost? correlate with kubelet logs (ticket GHD-1284)

[GPU utilization anomaly investigation - na clusters - march 2026]
GPU Utilization anomaly - North America clusters (investigation notes)

Summary:
- Between 2026-03-19 22:00 and 2026-03-20 03:30 UTC we observed sustained elevated GPU utilization across three NA clusters (na-cluster-7, na-cluster-11, na-cluster-14) with sudden drops in headroom on pool:dedicated-a and pool:ephemeral-ml-b. Peak per-cluster GPU utilization reached 87% (3h moving average) on na-cluster-11 at 2026-03-20 01:12 UTC.
- This doc is an export of dashboard panels, ad-hoc queries, hypotheses, and short-term mitigation proposals for capacity planning and follow-ups.

Key metrics / snapshots (derived from Grafana panels and Prometheus queries):
- na-cluster-11: 3h avg util = 87%, 95th pct instantaneous = 94%, free-gpu-sockets = 6 (down from baseline 42)
- na-cluster-7: 3h avg util = 72%, sustained at ~70% for 5 hours
- na-cluster-14: 3h avg util = 64%, spike coincident with scheduled batch job window (00:45-02:00 UTC)
- pool:dedicated-a (multi-tenant reserved): cluster-weighted util = 83%, variance across nodes high (stdev 12pp)
- pool:ephemeral-ml-b (spot style / burst): observed eviction churn + queue backlog growth (queued requests +120% vs baseline)
- overall NA region headroom dropped from 28% -> 9% (24h baseline comparison)

Timeline of notable events:
- 2026-03-19 20:30 UTC: Routine overnight batch rollout started (deploy batch-model-v3 across infra projects) — recorded in deploy log (linked in JIRA-OPS-1248).
- 2026-03-19 21:05 UTC: Autoscaler config for pool:ephemeral-ml-b was changed (scale_down_grace_seconds lowered from 300 to 60) — PR #872.
- 2026-03-19 22:05 UTC: Monitoring alerted: region_gpu_headroom < 12% — alert routed to #infra-alerts.
- 2026-03-20 00:50 UTC: na-cluster-11 shows memory pressure events coincident with long-running KV-cache misses (observed via runtime tracing).
- 2026-03-20 02:00 UTC: Temporary mitigation (scale up + provision 8 gpus to na-cluster-11) applied; headroom restored to ~23% by 02:45 UTC.

Ad-hoc queries used (Prometheus / BigQuery style):
- prom: sum(rate(gpu_utilization_seconds_total[5m])) by (cluster) / count(node_gpu_sockets_total{cluster})
- prom: topk(10, sum(gpu_utilization_seconds_total) by (pool, cluster))
- bq: SELECT cluster, pool, AVG(util_pct) FROM gpu_daily_metrics WHERE date BETWEEN '2026-03-15' AND '2026-03-20' GROUP BY cluster, pool
- grafana panel link: https://grafana.redwood.company/d/cluster-utilization/na-gpu-overview?panelId=7

Per-cluster observations and hypotheses:
- na-cluster-11:
  - Observation: Highest sustained util, high variance, multiple long-running sessions pinned to few GPUs (a small number of jobs consuming >40% of a GPU for hours).
  - Hypotheses: 1) A rollout caused old long-tail batch jobs to re-run without queue sharding; 2) KV cache misses forced model contexts to regen, increasing token compute; 3) Noise from a single tenant running aggressive eval tests.
  - Evidence: Traces show repeated model reloads (runtime logs) and one job id (job-8893) shows repeated restarts.

- na-cluster-7:
  - Observation: Elevated baseline but no extreme variance; distribution suggests many smaller sessions rather than a single offender.
  - Hypotheses: Traffic shift (small customers) + autoscaler thresholds too conservative for short bursts.

- na-cluster-14:
  - Observation: Spike window aligned to scheduled nightly batch (00:45-02:00 UTC). Pool eviction queue grew 30% during that window.
  - Hypotheses: Nightly batch sizing too large relative to pool capacity; batch jobs not using local cache warming; scheduled concurrently with canary experiments.

Pool-level notes (dedicated-a, ephemeral-ml-b, shared-inference):
- dedicated-a: high utilization with hot nodes — imbalance likely due to placement affinity (customer pinning) and insufficient redistribution logic. Suggest: run a rebalance job to shuffle low-priority workloads to clusters with spare capacity.
- ephemeral-ml-b: autoscaler config change on 2026-03-19 likely reduced effective headroom by shortening scale-down; coupled with eviction churn this amplified queuing. Suggest: revert scale_down_grace_seconds to 300 for this pool and monitor.
- shared-inference: unaffected, baseline steady at 21% util. Good candidate to borrow one node temporarily if needed.

Immediate actions taken (short-term mitigations):
- +8 GPUs added to na-cluster-11 (manual provisioning) at 2026-03-20 01:58 UTC — reduced immediate pressure. Owner: Ethan Park.
- Rolled back autoscaler change for ephemeral-ml-b at 2026-03-20 03:05 UTC (PR #879). Owner: Ava Chen.
- Added temporary alert rule to flag pool imbalance when node-level stdev(util) > 10pp for >15m.

Recommended follow-ups (capacity planning & longer term):
1) Capacity rebalancing runbook: schedule an automated rebalance to redistribute pinned workloads from dedicated-a hotspots to na-cluster-14 and shared-inference. Estimated impact: recover 6-10% headroom in dedicated-a. Owner: Priya Nambiar. ETA: 2026-03-25.

3) Batch scheduling window evaluation: move non-critical nightly batches to staggered windows; add prewarm steps to avoid cold KV-cache penalties. Owner: Platform Scheduling. ETA: 2026-04-05.
4) Invest in per-tenant fairness throttles: protect reserved pools from noisy evaluations that can spike utilization. Product ticket: PRD-398 (link pending).
5) Add a daily capacity digest (dashboard panel) showing predicted 7-day headroom using job calendar and recent trend to inform Dedicated capacity commits. Owner: eng-infra analytics.

Notes for capacity planning models:
- Use median 95th-utilization baseline rather than mean to avoid being skewed by short spikes when planning reserved capacity.
- Model an 'eviction amplification factor' for ephemeral pools when average eviction rate > 5/hr — historical factor ~1.4x extra GPU time used because of retries.

[variance-aware-autoscaler-and-intermittent-surge-fairness]
release_notes:
Add variance-aware autoscaler controller and per-tenant variance telemetry; improves stability under intermittent surge workloads and increases fairness of burst allocation.

description:
Summary: Introduces a new variance-aware autoscaler that factors request-rate variance and burstiness into scale decisions and burst token allocation. This is targeted at intermittent-surge workloads (spiky, short-lived bursts from many tenants) where standard utilization-based autoscaling either overreacts or under-allocates burst capacity. Motivation: We observed several support incidents where tenants with highly variable arrival patterns caused oscillation in node counts and unfair consumption of burst tokens, degrading tail latency for other tenants. This change aims to reduce oscillation, make burst distribution fairer across tenants, and provide observability to tune policies. Key components: 1) controller/autoscaler/variance_controller.go: new controller that computes per-tenant mean and variance over a sliding window, derives an "effective demand" metric combining 95th percentile rate and variance penalty, and exposes decisions to the scaling plane; 2) pkg/scheduler/fair_burst_allocator.go: integrates variance metric into burst token allocation algorithm, preferring tenants with consistently high short-term variance to receive temporary soft credits while enforcing tenant-level fairness caps; 3) pkg/telemetry/metrics_exporter.go: new Prometheus metrics and Grafana dashboard templates for per-tenant request variance, effective_demand, burst_credit_usage, and burst_credit_hitrate; 4) cmd/controller-manager/main.go: wires the new controller behind a feature flag (--enable-variance-autoscaler); 5) helm/charts/autoscaler/templates/: adds config options for sliding window length, variance weight, and maximum soft burst per-tenant. Design notes: - Effective demand = alpha * p95_rate + beta * sqrt(variance), where alpha and beta are tunable. Default alpha=1.0, beta=0.5. - Hysteresis and cooldown: dynamic cooldown scales with variance to avoid thrash: cooldown = base_cooldown + gamma * normalized_variance. - Burst fairness uses a time-decayed ledger so transient spikes don't permanently drain credits. Tests and CI: unit tests added for variance estimator, allocator fairness invariants, and edge cases (zero-traffic, constant traffic, synthetic heavy-tail spikes). Integration test added in perf-canary suite simulating 1k tenants with exponentially distributed spike arrivals to validate stability and tail latency. CI: all checks passed after two iterations (lint, unit, integration perf-lite). Rollout plan: gated behind --enable-variance-autoscaler and feature gate variance_autoscaler_v1. Step 1: deploy to canary clusters with default beta=0.5 and monitor metrics for 48h. Step 2: if tail latency improves and no regressions, enable in staging clusters. Step 3: gradual rollout to Dedicated fleet with telemetry-backed rollback triggers (burst_credit_hitrate drop or node oscillation rate > threshold). Backwards compatibility: default behavior unchanged when feature flag disabled. Migration: none. Observability and dashboards: new Grafana panels added (per-tenant variance heatmap, effective_demand distribution, burst_credit_consumption by tenant percentile). Performance impact: controller runs O(N) over active tenants; optimized with shard workers and sampling for large clusters. Implementation notes and tradeoffs: - We intentionally use sqrt(variance) to keep units closer to rate while still reflecting variability. - To limit overhead, high-cardinality tenant metrics are aggregated into percentiles by default; full per-tenant metrics are optional via config. - There is a small potential for temporary unfairness during burst draining windows; the time-decayed ledger mitigates this. Links: Related Linear tasks ENG-3492 (variance estimator), ENG-3620 (fair allocator integration). Related PRs: none.

Diego Morales (requested changes): The allocator loop has a potential O(M*N) path when reconciling many tenants; please add sharding and a cap. Author reply: Reworked allocator to use sharded workers and bounded queue, updated tests and added benchmark results to PR description.

[Introduce steadyband autoscaler and throttle-reconciliation loop to reduce oscillation and preserve throughput SLAs]
description:
Problem / motivation: we have observed repeated scale-down + throttle loops for medium-tenancy workloads where brief drops in incoming concurrency cause the autoscaler to shrink capacity, then a quick surge triggers throttles and a costly scale-up. This leads to transient SLA gaps and increased tail latency. Goal: add a minimal steadyband that preserves a small, continuously allocated throughput floor per pool and introduce a reconciliation loop that aligns the autoscaler's decisions with the gateway throttler/token pools to avoid conflicting signals.

What this PR does (single-string body): Adds a new 'steadyband' concept to the Dedicated autoscaler: steadyband is a per-pool, tunable throughput reservation (in rps-equivalent) that persists even during aggressive scale-downs. Implements an EWMA-based steadyband estimator that consumes recent sustained usage (90s window by default) and clamps to configured min/max fractions to limit oversize. The autoscaler now exposes steadyband as a separate topology weight used when computing desired replicas and headroom. Introduces a throttle-reconciliation controller that watches gateway token pool levels and autoscaler headroom decisions; when token pools are dropping while the autoscaler is concurrently scaling down, the reconciliation controller delays scale-downs and optionally triggers soft-burst allocations from the warm pool.

Key design notes: - Steadyband is opt-in per fleet via FleetSpec.steadyband.enabled + FleetSpec.steadyband.min_rps + FleetSpec.steadyband.max_fraction. Default off for backwards compatibility. - The EWMA smoothing alpha and observation window are configurable; defaults chosen to trade reactivity for stability. - Reconciliation loop runs periodically and implements hysteresis: it requires two consecutive conflicting-signal ticks to inhibit a scale-down to avoid needless dithering. - Soft-burst path leverages existing warmlet prewarming; we add a short-lived lease that can be charged back to fleet reservations. - Telemetry: new metrics (fleet_steadyband_target_rps, fleet_steadyband_effective_fraction, throttle_reconcile_block_count) and an alert rule template included in observability package. - Tests: unit tests for the estimator and reconciliation logic, integration test that simulates a sawtooth load (drop -> surge) to assert no SLA gap for 95th percentile latency, and a benchmark harness run showing median cost delta < 1.2% with improved 99th latency on representative workloads.

Checklist: - [x] Feature flag gated and off by default - [x] Unit tests added - [x] Integration scenario reproducer + assertion - [x] Documentation snippet for FleetSpec + examples - [x] Telemetry and alerting snippets - [x] Backwards compatibility checks

Risks and mitigation: risk of over-reserving capacity when operators misconfigure min_rps; mitigated by conservative defaults (disabled by default, min_rps=0, max_fraction=0.15) and clear console warnings. The reconciliation controller is isolated and will only delay scale-downs (never force scale-ups), minimizing blast radius.

Related tickets/PRs: ENG-8765 (steadyband design doc), ENG-8810 (throttle-reconciliation spike investigation), and internal spike pr-511202 which prototyped the estimator.

[Harmonic Autoscale Controller and Burst Fidelity Reporter]
description:
Context: Customers running Dedicated fleets observed oscillatory scale behaviour during intermittent multi-tenant microbursts and poor observability into burst fidelity (how closely a burst payload matched a capacity reservation). Motivation: Reduce oscillation while preserving rapid burst acceptance for short-lived spikes and provide actionable telemetry so SRE and capacity-planning teams can tune reserve and burst policies. What this PR does: 1) Introduces a new harmonic autoscale controller that uses a harmonic-mean based estimator over multiple utilization windows to bias scaling decisions toward preventing under-provisioning during bursts while damping noisy high-percentile samples. The controller exposes knobs: burst_window (seconds), smoothing_alpha (0..1), min_commit_reserve_pct, and scale_step_ceiling. 2) Adds a Burst Fidelity Reporter that aggregates per-tenant burst events and reports fidelity metrics: peak_to_average, burst_duration_ms, headroom_violation_count, accepted_vs_rejected_burst_ratio, and a histogram of instantaneous utilization during bursts. The reporter emits Prometheus-compatible metrics and an export for longer-term S3-backed rollups. 3) Adds a safety policy layer that prevents aggressive downscales for a configurable cooldown after any detected burst acceptance and ties decays to harmonic estimates rather than raw instantaneous utilization. Design notes: The harmonic estimator is deliberately conservative for tail events (H = n / sum(1/x_i)) — it reduces the influence of extreme high samples compared to arithmetic mean but still responds quickly when many samples are elevated. We combine multiple windows (short, medium, long) with weights to enable both quick reaction and stability. The Burst Fidelity Reporter uses lightweight sampling (1% by default) and event-aggregation to avoid adding CPU overhead to the serving path. Rollout plan: staged canary (5% of Dedicated pools) -> 25% -> 75% -> all, with a contingency to revert to arithmetic-based controller if tail latency regressions exceed 3x baseline for two consecutive 5-minute windows. Backwards compatibility: Controller honours existing per-tenant reservation and burst-credit configs; defaults keep behaviour unchanged until operators opt-in. Migration: includes a feature flag (harmonic_autoscale_enabled) and a Helm values toggle. Testing and validation: unit tests for estimator math and controller state transitions; integration tests running synthetic burst traces against a local cluster; k8s e2e manifest for controller and reporter. Observability and alerts: new SLO alarms for sustained headroom_violation_count > 5/min and a dashboard that surfaces accepted/rejected burst ratio per-tenant. Related: follows ENG-2419 (autoscaler stability initiative) and ENG-2543 (dedicated burst observability).

- Added Burst Fidelity Reporter: per-tenant burst metrics and histograms for capacity planning and SLO analysis.

[introduce-bellcurve-autoscaler-and-utilization-exposure]
description:
Motivation: Dedicated fleets have two recurring failure modes: noisy spikes cause overprovisioning and oscillatory scale-downs hurt long-tail cost. This PR implements a new 'bellcurve autoscaler' algorithm and an exposure-style utilization telemetry signal to make scaling decisions robust to transient outliers while preserving fast upscales for real demand. The bellcurve autoscaler computes a Gaussian-weighted window over recent utilization samples, producing a smoothed utilization estimate that discounts single-sample spikes but still respects sustained increases. We combine that with a stepwise scale policy: small, deterministic up-steps for latency-critical pools and conservative tiered down-steps with a configurable micro-epoch to reduce oscillation. Additionally, the PR introduces a burst-safety limiter that caps ephemeral burst grants relative to the fleet's recent p95 sustained throughput to avoid starving committed tenants. Key config knobs: scale_step_ms (how frequently to allow step changes), decay_sigma_ms (Gaussian sigma for weighting), safety_tail_buffer_pct (percent headroom retained when capping bursts), and micro_epoch_ms (minimum time between scale-downs). Work completed: 1) autoscaler core: pkg/autoscaler/bellcurve_controller.go with public interface compatible with existing ScaleDecider; 2) config and defaults: pkg/autoscaler/config.go and defaults for Dedicated fleets; 3) safety limiter: pkg/autoscaler/burst_safety_limiter.go that audits historical pXX sketches and enforces a soft cap with exponential backoff if bursts exceed threshold; 4) telemetry: telemetry/collectors/util_exposure_collector.go and metrics_registry.go registering new metrics redwood.util.exposure.p50|p95|p99 and redwood.util.exposure.delta; 5) docs and runbook: docs/autoscaling/bellcurve.md describing behavior, tuning guide, and rollback steps; 6) integration and perf: examples/perf-canary/bellcurve_loadgen.yaml and perf-canary harness patch to exercise micro-epochs; 7) tests: unit tests and deterministic e2e in pkg/autoscaler/controller_test.go. Testing and rollout: unit tests cover corner cases (all-zero traffic, sustained ramp, synthetic microbursts). Perf-canary runs showed 12% lower scale cost over a 48h noisy trace with identical p95 latency. Gradual rollout plan: enable feature flag autoscaler.bellcurve.enabled=false by default, stage to a 5% fleet cohort for next release, then 25% and full rollout after 2 rolling windows. Docs and changelog updated. No customer-facing API changes. Related work: follows design proposal in ENG-4782 and integrates feedback from ENG-5124.

[Thresholded throughput certifier and smoothing autoscaler]
Context: As Dedicated customers require predictable throughput guarantees while avoiding excessive overprovisioning, we need a controller that issues soft throughput certificates per-tenant and uses a damped autoscaling loop to smooth provisioning during transient spikes. This PR introduces a Thresholded Throughput Certifier (TTC) and a Smoothing Autoscaler that consume utilization and token-bucket style signals to certify short-term throughput guarantees and drive scale decisions. Motivation: Prior reactive autoscalers caused sharp up/down churn and noisy billing for tenants with bursty but bounded traffic. TTC establishes an explicit, decaying 'certified throughput' envelope based on recent high-percentile delivery and a configurable safety margin. The Smoothing Autoscaler uses the envelope to prefer gradual upscales, limited fast ramps for confirmed certificate breaches, and conservative downscales with a deploy-time hysteresis. Summary of changes: 1) telemetry/throughput_certifier.go: new certifier that computes sliding-window p95/p99 throughput, applies configurable thresholds, issues TTL-bound certificates, and emits metrics: ttc_cert_issued, ttc_cert_expired, ttc_cert_utilization_ratio. 2) autoscaler/smoother_controller.go: new controller that ingests certificates, utilization histograms, and queue-length signals; implements damped rate-of-change limiting, emergency ramp path (for sustained 30s breaches), and soft-fallback to lower-cost model variants when cold-starts risk SLOs. 3) api/throughput_cert_crd.yaml: CRD schema for ThroughputCertificate objects (versioned v1alpha1). 4) docs/operations/throughput-certifier.md: operator playbook for tuning margin, TTL, and emergency ramps. 5) tests/smoother_unit_test.go and e2e/scale_scenarios.yaml: unit and end-to-end scenarios covering synthetic microbursts, steady increases, and noise robustness. 6) examples/private/tenant-cert-example.yaml: example tenant config showing certificate goals and conservative-downscale flags. Commits: "init: add throughput certifier prototype and CRD","autoscaler: integrate smoother controller and emergency ramp path","telemetry: wire metrics and unit tests","docs: add operator playbook and examples","tests: add e2e scenarios and CI gating" Files changed (high level): - pkg/autoscaler/smoother_controller.go: core logic (~420 LOC) with comments and exported tuning knobs - pkg/telemetry/throughput_certifier.go: calculation and metrics (~180 LOC) - api/throughput_cert_crd.yaml: CRD and validation schema - docs/operations/throughput-certifier.md: ops playbook and tuning guide - tests/smoother_unit_test.go: 9 unit tests - e2e/scale_scenarios.yaml: three workload profiles Highlights and rationale: - Certificate model: compute sliding-window 5m p95 and 1m p99 delivery rates, then apply a margin multiplier (default 0.85) and an exponential decay with configurable half-life to produce a TTL-bound certificate. Certificates are advisory but surfaced to autoscaler and Console. - Autoscaler behavior: default is conservative smoothing (max 10% scale-up per minute, max 5% scale-down per minute). If certificate breaches are sustained beyond emergencyWindow (30s by default), an emergency ramp can increase capacity up to a configured fastRampPct. - Cost controls: when emergency ramp triggers, system prefers cheaper model variants (quantized) for newly provisioned capacity; this is opt-in per-tenant. - Observability: added tracing spans for cert issuance and scale decisions; Console dashboard tiles baked into docs. Backwards compatibility: the CRD is opt-in; default behavior when TTC is not present remains unchanged. Tests: unit tests verify certificate math, TTL decay, and controller damping. [Smoother autoscaler signal and gateway backpressure for dedicated pools]
Summary: Introduces a smoothing layer in the Dedicated Autoscaler and a lightweight backpressure signal propagated from the gateway to fleet controllers. This reduces autoscaler thrash on spiky traffic and gives gateways a controlled way to shed load gracefully against per-pool soft capacity and throughput guarantees.

Motivation: Customers on Dedicated have reported oscillations when short bursts cross autoscaler thresholds and then recede; this leads to unnecessary GPU spin-ups and billing variance, as well as transient error spikes. The gateway currently responds with 429s or fallback heuristics; we need a first-class, observable mechanism that cooperates with autoscaling and preserves headroom for SLA-critical requests.

Changes in this PR:
- Autoscaler: add Exponential Moving Average (EMA) smoothing of utilization and request rate with configurable half-life per-pool. New config fields: smoothing_window_ms, smoothing_alpha (derived).
- Soft capacity & grace tokens: each pool now tracks a small ephemeral token bucket (grace_tokens) to allow short bursts without triggering scale-up, decaying over time and replenished by underutilization.
- Gateway backpressure: add a new X-Redwood-Backpressure header and a compact gRPC/backchannel (gateway->controller) event to advertise desired ingress rate reductions per-route when pool smoothed_utilization > threshold.
- Controller/gateway handshake: gateway subscribes to per-pool backpressure_quota updates; controllers include backpressure_rate in scheduling decisions and expose metrics.
- Telemetry: new metrics smoothed_utilization, grace_tokens_available, backpressure_rate, backpressure_rejections. Add Prometheus labels for pool_id, model_id, and region.
- API schema: extend dedicated pool spec with smoothing and backpressure knobs; added validation and defaults.
- Console/docs: admin UI now surfaces smoothing window and current backpressure state with guidance.
- Tests: unit tests for smoothing math, integration e2e that injects burst traffic and asserts reduced scale-up churn and controlled 429 behavior.

Checklist:
- [x] Design review with SRE and Runtime teams (ENG-2147)
- [x] Unit tests for smoothing and token bucket
- [x] Integration e2e simulating bursty traffic
- [x] Telemetry dashboards updated

- [x] Backwards-compatible API schema changes (defaults safe)

Implementation notes:
- EMA parameters chosen to have ~30s half-life by default; pools serving low-latency workloads can set shorter windows.
- Grace tokens default to 2 tokens per pool; a token represents ~1s worth of headroom at pool's nominal throughput.
- Backpressure is advisory: scheduler will attempt to respect backpressure_rate before rejecting; only when backpressure persists will the gateway return 429s.
- To avoid unsafe throttling loops, backpressure updates include a monotonic seq and TTL.

Breaking changes: none expected; all new fields are optional with safe defaults.

Rollout plan: staged rollout: 1) feature gated off by default; 2) enable on Canary Dedicated clusters for 48h; 3) enable for opt-in customers with console toggle; 4) enable by default after 2 weeks of stable metrics.

Migration: API customers can ignore new fields; operators upgrading on-prem should ensure controllers and gateway are updated together.

- Load test harness reproduces 1-2 minute burst profiles and asserts scale-up events reduced by >=50% while 95th-p99 latency impact <5% in our baseline.

[Phased Elasticity Rollout and Sampled Utilization Harness]
description:
Background: fleet autoscaling at high churn leads to noisy utilization signals and unstable burst behavior for Dedicated pools. Motivation: ship a low-risk rollout path for a new phased elasticity controller that smooths burst windows and uses sampled utilization telemetry to avoid noisy triggers. This PR introduces a phased rollout controller (elasticity.rollout_phase) and a sampled-utilization-harness that emits lightweight sampled telemetry to the provisioner to make incremental scaling decisions. Changes: 1) controller: add PhasedElasticController with three phases (observe-only, conservative-actuate, adaptive-actuate) and a configurable phase duration and success criteria. 2) metrics: add sampled_util_percentiles (p50,p90) and util_sma_1m/5m to the telemetry fanout with a small memory footprint. 3) policy: introduce elasticity.policy v2 which supports soft_reservation_windows, burst_smoothing_alpha and min_window_ms to cap oscillations. 4) rollout: implement canary targets metadata so the controller can target pools by tag and ramp phases deterministically. 5) safety: introduce an emergency-decay-backstop that enforces conservative scale-down when tail latency or error rates cross thresholds. 6) observability: dashboards and alerts for phase transition success rates, sampled-util drift, and burst_smoothing impact. Migration: new controller is opt-in via cluster config: "elasticity.rollout_phase": "observe-only", and can be promoted to conservative/adaptive after CanarySuccess metrics are met. Performance: sampled telemetry reduces cardinality by 12x for large fleets compared to full-emit while retaining actionable signals for p90-based burst decisions. Testing: unit, integration, and simulated-fleet acceptance tests included. Rollout plan: 1) deploy observe-only to 2 Canary pools for 24h, verify no actuations and that sampled-util correlates with full metrics (correlation >0.95 on p50/p90). 2) promote to conservative-actuate on 10% of pools for 48h, monitor tail latency and canary success gates. 3) if gates pass, enable adaptive-actuate on staggered groups (25% -> 50% -> 100%) with 6h stabilization windows and automatic rollback on RegressionAlert. Impact: improves utilization stability during microbursts and reduces unnecessary scale churn, while preserving throughput guarantees via soft reservations. See Linear ENG-3124 for experiment dashboards and thresholds. Breaking changes: none by default; new policy is backward-compatible and behind feature flag. [adaptive-provisioning-pacer-for-steady-degradation-and-burst-smoothing]
description:
Introduce an adaptive provisioning pacer that smooths autoscaler decisions across dedicated fleets by applying a gamma-weighted pacing window to reservation and burst allocations. Motivation: recent incidents showed repeated oscillation when tens of tenants simultaneously ramp causing flapping autoscaler decisions and transient SLA slippage. This PR implements a pacing layer between the decision engine and provisioner so that scale up/down intents are rate-limited with stateful momentum, tenant-level dampening, and configurable burst forgiveness. The change touches three areas: 1) decision smoothing: a new Pacer module that consumes scale intents and emits paced deltas using a configurable half-life and gamma decay parameter; 2) budget and burst integration: pacer respects per-tenant guaranteed throughput envelopes and optional ephemeral burst credits; it can defer non-critical adjustments to preserve headroom; 3) instrumentation and alerting: adds metrics for pacer_active, pacer_output_delta, pacer_rejections, and tenant_pacer_latency plus dashboards and an alert when pacing causes more than 3 consecutive deferred scale operations. Includes unit tests for edge-cases, an integration test that replays historical incident traces, and a canary job for dedicated clusters. Backwards compatible: pacer is off by default and enabled through the autoscaler.policy.pacer config. See linked Linear items for rollout plan and experiment gating.

additional_context:

[Thresholded throughput certifier and smoothing autoscaler]
Context: As Dedicated customers require predictable throughput guarantees while avoiding excessive overprovisioning, we need a controller that issues soft throughput certificates per-tenant and uses a damped autoscaling loop to smooth provisioning during transient spikes. This PR introduces a Thresholded Throughput Certifier (TTC) and a Smoothing Autoscaler that consume utilization and token-bucket style signals to certify short-term throughput guarantees and drive scale decisions. Motivation: Prior reactive autoscalers caused sharp up/down churn and noisy billing for tenants with bursty but bounded traffic. TTC establishes an explicit, decaying 'certified throughput' envelope based on recent high-percentile delivery and a configurable safety margin. The Smoothing Autoscaler uses the envelope to prefer gradual upscales, limited fast ramps for confirmed certificate breaches, and conservative downscales with a deploy-time hysteresis. Summary of changes: 1) telemetry/throughput_certifier.go: new certifier that computes sliding-window p95/p99 throughput, applies configurable thresholds, issues TTL-bound certificates, and emits metrics: ttc_cert_issued, ttc_cert_expired, ttc_cert_utilization_ratio. 2) autoscaler/smoother_controller.go: new controller that ingests certificates, utilization histograms, and queue-length signals; implements damped rate-of-change limiting, emergency ramp path (for sustained 30s breaches), and soft-fallback to lower-cost model variants when cold-starts risk SLOs. 3) api/throughput_cert_crd.yaml: CRD schema for ThroughputCertificate objects (versioned v1alpha1). 4) docs/operations/throughput-certifier.md: operator playbook for tuning margin, TTL, and emergency ramps. 5) tests/smoother_unit_test.go and e2e/scale_scenarios.yaml: unit and end-to-end scenarios covering synthetic microbursts, steady increases, and noise robustness. 6) examples/private/tenant-cert-example.yaml: example tenant config showing certificate goals and conservative-downscale flags. Commits: "init: add throughput certifier prototype and CRD","autoscaler: integrate smoother controller and emergency ramp path","telemetry: wire metrics and unit tests","docs: add operator playbook and examples","tests: add e2e scenarios and CI gating" Files changed (high level): - pkg/autoscaler/smoother_controller.go: core logic (~420 LOC) with comments and exported tuning knobs - pkg/telemetry/throughput_certifier.go: calculation and metrics (~180 LOC) - api/throughput_cert_crd.yaml: CRD and validation schema - docs/operations/throughput-certifier.md: ops playbook and tuning guide - tests/smoother_unit_test.go: 9 unit tests - e2e/scale_scenarios.yaml: three workload profiles Highlights and rationale: - Certificate model: compute sliding-window 5m p95 and 1m p99 delivery rates, then apply a margin multiplier (default 0.85) and an exponential decay with configurable half-life to produce a TTL-bound certificate. Certificates are advisory but surfaced to autoscaler and Console. - Autoscaler behavior: default is conservative smoothing (max 10% scale-up per minute, max 5% scale-down per minute). If certificate breaches are sustained beyond emergencyWindow (30s by default), an emergency ramp can increase capacity up to a configured fastRampPct. - Cost controls: when emergency ramp triggers, system prefers cheaper model variants (quantized) for newly provisioned capacity; this is opt-in per-tenant. - Observability: added tracing spans for cert issuance and scale decisions; Console dashboard tiles baked into docs. Backwards compatibility: the CRD is opt-in; default behavior when TTC is not present remains unchanged. Tests: unit tests verify certificate math, TTL decay, and controller damping. E2E scenarios run against local canary cluster and assert bounded churn and sustained SLOs for synthetic tenants. Review summary and conversation: "Arjun Patel requested more fine-grained metrics and explicit labels on certificate objects for tenant-scoped aggregation; noted potential race between CRD reconciliation and autoscaler informer cache." "Author (Maya Chen) replied: added ttc_cert_tenant and ttc_request_scope labels, and increased informer resync in controller; added comment and test to demonstrate reconciliation order resilience." "Leila Gomez asked for hard limits to prevent runaway emergency ramps; author responded by adding a global emergencyBudget and test coverage for budget exhaustion behavior." "Tomás requested clearer operator guidance on margin selection; docs updated with sample SLI-to-margin mapping and a tuning checklist." CI and validation: initial CI run had a flaky e2e failure in scale_scenarios (test flaked under 1% variance); reran with e2e test stabilization patch and all checks passed. CI checks: unit tests (pass), linters (pass), build (pass), e2e (pass). Security review: quick pass for CRD validation schema and RBAC rules; no privileged access added. Merge notes: squashed and merged to main after approvals from Arjun and Leila. Merge method: squash. Merge commit: "squash! Thresholded throughput certifier and smoothing autoscaler (Maya Chen)" Rollout plan and ops notes: - Begin as opt-in per-tenant by applying ThroughputCertificate objects. - Monitor metrics: ttc_cert_issued, ttc_cert_utilization_ratio, autoscaler_smooth_scale_events. - Start with conservative margin (0.7-0.85) and longer TTL (default 10m) for first 2 weeks. - Track billing deltas and adjust emergencyBudget to cap rapid cost spikes. Release notes: "Introduce Thresholded Throughput Certifier (TTC) and Smoothing Autoscaler to provide advisory short-term throughput guarantees and reduce autoscaling churn. TTC is opt-in via CRD. Adds new metrics and operator guidance for tuning." Breaking change: false

[Dedicated: document autoscaling bounds + predictive mode (config, semantics, troubleshooting)]
description:
Summary This PR updates customer-facing documentation for Dedicated autoscaling policy bounds and Predictive Mode. It is written to support pilot->GA rollout and reduce support load by clarifying semantics (what is enforced, what is advisory), recommended starting ranges, and what to do when customers hit max bounds or experience queueing during ramps. The new docs cover: configuring min/max replicas (and GPU equivalent guidance), cooldown behavior, Predictive Mode basics, signal arbitration (reactive overrides predictions), and troubleshooting steps with references to the new dashboard panels/metrics. Motivation Recent Dedicated escalations (SUP-28411/SUP-28437) and pilot feedback indicated confusion around (1) whether max is a hard ceiling, (2) why scale-up may stop while queue grows, (3) how Predictive Mode interacts with reactive signals and cooldowns, and (4) what customers should do during region capacity shortages where min cannot be met. This PR consolidates answers into a single doc set and aligns wording with the ADR semantics (hard invariants: never exceed max, never drop below min; deterministic clamping; emit bounded-state signals). Scope / What changed - Added docs page: "Dedicated autoscaling policy" (min/max, cooldowns, predictive toggle, examples for common workloads) - Added section: "Predictive Mode" (what it is, required history, confidence, staleness, fallback to reactive) - Added "Recommended starting points" including baseline min for SLA protection and max as spend guardrail; includes guidance to iterate based on observed queue depth and bound-hit rate - Added troubleshooting playbook: "Max-bound saturation", "Oscillation/jitter", "Forecast stale/unavailable", "Min not met due to capacity shortage" with suggested mitigations and when to contact support - Updated API/Console configuration snippets and terminology to match implementation (field names and UI labels) - Added small FAQ (e.g., "Does Predictive Mode scale to zero?", "Can I exceed max during incidents?" -> no; use contract/CS process) Not in scope - No product behavior changes; this is documentation only - No full runbook content (SRE runbook lives in internal Confluence); we link to customer-facing troubleshooting steps and support contact points Testing - Docs site build + link check - Verified code snippets against Console API endpoint shapes referenced in ENG-22141 (as of 2025-08-21) Rollout notes - Docs are written to be feature-flag aware: clearly marked "Available by request during pilot" and "GA" sections. Where behavior differs between pilot builds and GA target (e.g., confidence indicator display), language is guarded to avoid overpromising. Screenshots are intentionally minimal; we rely on text that matches UX labels in DES-981 to avoid churn during final UI polish. Links - Linear: PM-1842, ENG-22149 - Support references: SUP-28501 (how to set bounds), SUP-28437 (daily ramp), SUP-28479 (oscillation) - Internal semantics: ADR "Autoscaling bounds precedence and safety invariants" (referenced but not linked in public docs) - Observability: references the public-facing metric names that appear in the Dedicated dashboard (bound hit rate, desired vs bounded replicas, queue depth) Changed areas/files (high-level) - docs/dedicated/autoscaling-policy.md (new) - docs/dedicated/predictive-mode.md (new) - docs/dedicated/troubleshooting/autoscaling.md (new) - docs/reference/api/dedicated-scaling-policy.md (updated) - docs/console/dedicated-scaling-policy-ui.md (updated) - docs/shared/glossary.md (updated terms: bound, desired, bounded desired, cooldown) - redirects + nav sidebar updates Example snippet added (from docs) JSON example: { "autoscaling_policy": { "min_replicas": 4, "max_replicas": 24, "cooldown_seconds": 180, "predictive_mode": "ENABLED" } } Notes: - The system will clamp requested desired replicas into [min_replicas, max_replicas]. - If predictive signal is stale/unavailable, the autoscaler falls back to reactive scaling (still respecting bounds).
