Liam Chen (SRE): Reproduced in staging with proxy handoff simulation. Adding edge proxy in-path logs and session handoff markers to traces. Tentative root cause: affinity flip during stream flush.
Riley Patel (Platform Eng): We need to check the edge's connection drain policy — current setting aggressively closes old upstreams after 250ms. Propose increasing drain window for streaming routes.
Customer (Slateware): We can tolerate a short drain window change if it avoids broken streams. Please keep us informed about any config changes and rollback plan.
Liam Chen: Filed INT-1851 to track change to edge drain timeout configuration and rollout gating for streaming customers.
Support: Temporary mitigation applied for Slateware: pinned their routing to a more stable edge pool (no handoffs) and asked them to resume traffic; reporting zero failures in 6 hours.

resolution:
Workaround: Pin affected customer to a stable edge pool and increase drain timeout for streaming routes to 2s while we implement durable framing changes.
Planned fix: Update serving runtime to emit an explicit resume token and make finalizer framing tolerant to chunk boundary merges. Also coordinate with edge team to modify drain behavior for streaming endpoints.
Rollout notes: Incremental rollout of drain timeout change behind feature flag; integration tests to simulate handoff-induced half-close. Target ETA for server-side framing changes: 2026-04-05.

[Windowed Flow-Control Canary with Dependency Safeguards and Amortized Ramp]
description:
Summary: Adds a new windowed flow-control canary controller that ramps traffic only during configured release windows, amortizes increases across multiple windows, and performs dependency-aware prechecks and automated rollback. Motivation: We still see regressions when simple timeouts or sudden ramp-ups coincide with downstream cold starts or dependent service incidents. This controller reduces blast radius by only increasing cohorts during low-risk windows and by validating downstream dependencies (KV cache warm, schema checks, healthy upstreams) before advancing.

What this PR changes: single controller and operator flow, new release window CRD extension, a lightweight dependency health probe framework, telemetry hooks (per-window SLO snapshots), and a small e2e job for the amortized ramp behavior. The controller implements a composite rollback policy that combines service-level indicators (p95 latency, 5xx rate), user-facing quality metrics (eval set regression delta), and dependency health gates.

Design and behavior (high level): - Release windows: operator config accepts a list of windows (day-of-week, start/end UTC, optional timezone override). Ramps are only advanced if the current time falls within an allowed window. - Amortized ramp: instead of doubling traffic in one window, the controller spreads increases across N windows (configurable, default N=3) to smooth capacity needs and observe drifting signals. - Dependency safeguards: before each ramp step the controller runs dependency prechecks (kv_warm: bool, upstream_schema_ok: bool, feature_flag_consistency: bool). If any precheck fails, the canary enters 'quarantine' where traffic is held and periodic rechecks are scheduled. - Composite rollback: triggers when any of the following are true within a window: p95 latency increases > 40% vs baseline, 5xx error rate > 1.5%, eval set regression > 2% absolute, or a dependent service health check flips to unhealthy. Rollbacks are immediate and include a short cool-down lock to avoid flapping. - A/B support: the controller understands cohort mappings and will pause other A/B arms while an amortized ramp is in flight if configured.

Commits (summary): - feat(canary): add window parsing, ramp scheduler, and state machine (Maya Chen) - feat(health): add dependency health probe library with adapter hooks for KV and upstream APIs (Maya Chen) - test(e2e): add amortized ramp e2e harness and CI job (Maya Chen)

Files changed (high level): - pkg/controller/canary/windowed_controller.go (core controller state machine and scheduler) - api/v1alpha/releasewindow_types.go (CRD fields for windows and amortization) - internal/health/probes/kv_probe.go (KV warm probe adapter) - internal/health/probes/upstream_probe.go (upstream schema/health checks) - docs/rollouts/windowed_canary.md (operator docs + examples) - test/e2e/windowed_amortized_ramp_test.go (harness) - charts/redwood/templates/canary-controller.yaml (helm values for windows)

Small config snippet (example release window in YAML):

kind: ReleaseWindow
metadata:
  name: low-traffic-evening
spec:
  windows:
    - day: "Mon-Fri"
      start: "22:00"
      end: "03:00"
      timezone: "UTC"
  amortizeAcrossWindows: 3
  dependencyGuards:
    - kv_warm
    - upstream_schema_ok

Two asks: make the 40%/1.5%/2% thresholds config-driven (not hardcoded) and add telemetry labels to indicate which window caused the rollback so SRE can filter incident noise." - Maya Chen (author): "Thanks Samir — thresholds and telemetry labels are now configurable via the CRD and emitted as canary.window_id in metrics. Updated in commit 2." - Evelyn Ross: "Can we add unit tests that simulate a failing dependency probe and ensure quarantine behavior doesn't accidentally block other independent canaries?" - Maya Chen: "Added a focused test in test/e2e/windowed_amortized_ramp_test.go and a small mock harness to validate quarantine scoping. See commit 3." - Lars Berg: "CI flaky test noted earlier — once green I'm fine with merging." - Lars Berg (approve): "LGTM"

Rollout should be tested first in staging with amortizeAcrossWindows=1 then gradually increase. Rollback: operator supports immediate revert and a 15-minute cooldown lock to prevent thrash.

[Introduce Batch-Cache Policy Synthesizer for automated batching, cache TTLs, and quant profiles]
description:
Motivation: Production teams increasingly ask for safe, explainable defaults for batching, cache TTLs, and quantization profiles tuned to their unit-econ targets. Manual tuning is slow and error-prone; naive defaults either leave money on the table or cause latency regressions. This PR introduces the 'Batch-Cache Policy Synthesizer' — a small service and integration that synthesizes conservative, runbook-driven defaults and optional suggestions for aggressive cost-saving profiles, backed by workload traces and unit-econ objectives.

What this changes:
- New service: internal/optimizer/policy_synthesizer that consumes sampled request traces, cost/latency SLO goals, and historical model perf profiles to output a ranked set of policy candidates (batching window, max batch size, prefix cache TTL, kv-cache-hotlist-size, quantization profile id).
- CLI: tools/cost-synthesizer/bin/rcs (runbook-config-synth) for operators to generate profiles locally from a trace file and preview expected token-cost and p50/p95 latency deltas.
- API: /v1/internal/policy_synthesizer/generate (protected) to request on-demand policy suggestions for a customer or model route.
- Redwood Console integration: Add a lightweight Recommendations drawer that surfaces the top-3 candidates along with estimated saving, expected latency impact, and confidence score.
- Safeguards: Every suggestion includes a conservative fallback policy and an automatic canary rollout plan (10% traffic -> 50% -> 100%) with automatic rollback on latency or quality regressions.
- Tests: unit tests for candidate scoring, integration tests for the CLI path, and e2e smoke that runs a small synthetic trace through the service and validates metrics emitted to metrics.redwood (new metric: optimizer.synthesized_policy.{applied,rolled_back}).

Design notes (short):
- Scoring model: multi-objective heuristic that combines estimated per-token cost delta, expected p95 latency delta (from per-op instrumentation), and an uncertainty penalty derived from sample size. Operators can pick a unit-econ target multiplier (e.g., 0.8x cost target) and the synthesizer returns candidates that meet the target while keeping p95 within a user-configured latency window.
- Quant profiles: the synthesizer references the model-registry quant profiles and recommends the lightest quant that has a validated quality delta < configured threshold (default 1% BLEU/ROUGE-style surrogate). If no profile passes, quant recommendations are omitted.
- Safety floor: all policies include a required minimal TTL and max_batch safeguards to avoid excessive batching for latency-sensitive routes.

Files changed (high level):
- internal/optimizer/policy_synthesizer/service.go (core synthesizer)
- internal/optimizer/policy_synthesizer/score.go (scoring heuristics + unit-econ logic)
- tools/cost-synthesizer/cli.go (trace -> suggestion path)
- api/internal_routes.go (new internal endpoint + auth guard)
- console/src/components/RecommendationsDrawer.tsx (UI surface)
- docs/operator/runbooks/policy-synthesizer.md (runbook + rollout playbook)
- tests/integration/synth_cli_test.go
- tests/e2e/synth_smoke_test.yaml

Short commit summary:

- feat(cli): rcs tool and local trace parsing
- feat(api): internal endpoint and auth scope
- feat(console): recommendations drawer and telemetry hooks
- test: integration + e2e smoke coverage and CI job
- docs: runbook and operator guidance

Backwards compatibility: The synthesizer produces policy JSON that is fully compatible with the existing /configs/policy schema. There are no default changes to runtime behavior unless an operator explicitly applies a synthesized policy or accepts a Console recommendation.

Rollout plan: Merge to main -> feature flag guarded release for 48h to internal canary orgs -> open beta for customers with opt-in flag in Console -> enable for customer accounts with automated guardrails after 30 days if telemetry shows safe behavior.

Notes on CI: Initial CI run showed a flaky timing-dependent test in synth_cli_test.go (race with metrics exporter). I added a deterministic fake exporter and re-ran. The final CI run passed: all unit, integration, and e2e smoke checks green.

[Introduce continuous phase batcher and realtime tail sampler]
description:
Summary: Adds a continuous-phase batcher to the benchmark-lab harness and a lightweight realtime tail sampler that tags and exports extreme token-latency events for the reporting pipeline. Motivation: existing bursty-mix runners create large variance when short and long sequences are indiscriminately co-batched. The continuous-phase batcher groups requests by a phase metric (sequence-length percentile + warmup state) to produce batches with tighter intra-batch length distribution while allowing controlled backpressure ramping to avoid cold-start spikes. The tail sampler runs in-process during benchmark runs to capture per-token latency traces and emits compact protobuf records to the heartbeats reporter for downstream analysis (no persistent DB dependency). Implementation notes: - New scheduler module: bench/schedulers/continuous_phase.go. Implements a sliding-window histogram of recent seq lengths and computes a phase_id for each request. Batches are formed by phase-aware binning with a max-skew threshold and optional latency SLO guard. - Backpressure ramp: a per-pool gradient limiter that increases offered concurrency when observed p50 latency is below target, decreases when p95 exceeds threshold. This uses exponential smoothing and a cooldown timer to avoid oscillation. - Realtime tail sampler: bench/samplers/realtime_tail_sampler.go; samples hard-tail events (token latency > dynamic threshold) and attaches context (model, seq_len, kernel_hint) before publishing to reporter via an existing /reporter/collector API. Records are size-limited and include a short stack of scheduler decisions. - Test harness: new unit tests and an e2e scenario in bench/testdata/mix-phase-run.yaml that reproduces a bimodal sequence mix and asserts reduced p99 variance. - Reporter wiring: updates reporter/ingest to accept compact tail records and a new reporter/transform/tail-annotator that enriches traces with kernel and batch composition metadata. - Opt-in flag: continuous phase batching is feature-gated behind BENCH_PHASE_BATCHER=true to avoid affecting other repos until rollout. Checklist: - [x] Design doc reviewed (ENG-5241) - [x] Unit tests for scheduler and sampler - [x] E2E regression scenario added - [x] Backpressure safety limits / cooldown implemented - [x] Telemetry formats documented in reporter README - [x] Feature flag added for controlled rollout Commits: - 5c3b8f2: initial continuous phase batcher implementation and scheduler tests - a23d7b1: realtime tail sampler and exporter wiring - 4f9e118: e2e mix-phase-run scenario and baseline traces - 90b2e0d: reporter ingest + transform plumbing and lightweight schema - d12a77c: feature flag, docs, and minor flake fixes Changed files (high level): - bench/schedulers/continuous_phase.go - bench/samplers/realtime_tail_sampler.go - bench/schedulers/continuous_phase_test.go - bench/testdata/mix-phase-run.yaml - reporter/collector/ingest.go (small change: added TailRecord path) - reporter/transform/tail_annotator.go - docs/bench/phase-batcher.md - ci/bench-e2e.yaml (added new scenario) - BUILD.bazel (new deps) Small illustrative diffs: - continuous_phase.go: core batching loop (simplified) "for req := range q { phase := phaseHistogram.Bucket(req.SeqLen); scheduler.AssignToBin(phase, req) }" - realtime_tail_sampler.go: emission logic "if tokenLatency > sampler.DynamicThreshold() { collector.Publish(TailRecord{...}) }" Review conversation (condensed into single-threaded summary): - Samir Rao (reviewer) 2026-02-20: "Nice approach — two questions: 1) do we risk starving very short sequences when binning with long ones? 2) can the sampler add measurable CPU overhead under extreme load?" - Aisha (author) 2026-02-21: "Addressed both: bins have a short-request priority quota and the backpressure ramp avoids unbounded queue growth; sampler uses a cheap moving-threshold and samples at most 1/1000 tokens by default, CPU overhead measured <1% in local run — numbers added to design doc." - Elena Garcia (reviewer) 2026-02-24: "Please add clearer schema versioning for tail records so we can evolve the annotator without breaking downstream parsers." - Aisha 2026-02-25: "Added schema_version field and a tiny compatibility shim in reporter/collector; updated docs." - Tom Briggs (approver) 2026-03-01: "Perf numbers look good in staging; LGTM." CI summary: - bazel/test:bench-unit — pass - bench/e2e (ci/bench-e2e.yaml) — pass (staging run measured p99 variance down ~22% versus baseline) - lint/gofmt — pass - security/snyk — pass - perf/regression-check — pass (no regression) There was one transient failure on bench/e2e on the first run due to a flaky timing assertion; rerun passed. Merge outcome: merged via squash on 2026-03-03 by Tom Briggs, commit message summarizes the feature and links ENG-5241. Notes on rollout and follow-ups: - Feature will be enabled behind BENCH_PHASE_BATCHER in canary runs for 2 weeks before wider staging. - Follow-up work: add an adaptive phase-compression heuristic (ENG-5350) and integrate with the kernel selection telemetry so the annotator can surface which kernels are implicated in tail events. - Ops: reporter retention for tail records is limited to 7d by default; a pipeline job will downsample and keep pinned exemplars for 90d for long-term analysis. Compatibility/impact: no changes to public APIs; opt-in flag prevents accidental changes to other teams. If issues surface, revert via toggling BENCH_PHASE_BATCHER=false or reverting the single squash commit. [Cohort-aware Progressive Swap Controller for Model Version Lifecycle]
description:
Context and motivation: Rolling model versions safely at scale requires more than traffic splitting — it requires cohort-based swaps that respect downstream dependencies, per-cohort evaluation windows, and automated rollback when service-level guards fail. This PR introduces the Cohort-aware Progressive Swap Controller (CPSC), a controller in the rollout orchestration layer that performs swap-style rollouts by progressing model versions cohort-by-cohort rather than sample-level splits.

Goals: reduce exposure of regressions, preserve cold-start isolation, enable dependency-aware health checks (datastore schema, adapter compatibility), and provide deterministic swap semantics for auditability.

High-level design:
- Cohorts are lightweight tagged slices of users (by tenant, georegion, or feature flag).
- Swap phases: prepare (warm KV caches, prefetch embeddings), probe (low volume sanity queries), verify (metrics evaluation), promote (full cohort swap), and finalize (rotate canaries out).
- Safety gates: latency p99, error_rate, model-output-divergence against baseline (approx-match), and dependency liveness.
- Rollback: automated hysteresis back-off + dependency trust graph to determine rollback scope (single cohort vs global).
- Integrations: Redwood Model Registry (version pinning), Console UI hooks for cohort rollout visualization, and Linear/Jira links.

[Rewire lint cartography, introduce staged toolchain lease, and add lightweight release safeguard]
description:
Motivation: Our presubmit lanes and release hooks have grown ad-hoc around various lint rule sets and developer toolchain versions which leads to spurious failures and slow feedback. This PR reorganizes lint rule ownership (lint cartography), adds a lightweight staged toolchain lease to reduce presubmit image churn, and introduces a minimal release safeguard that verifies provenance metadata before signing/releasing artifacts. What this PR does: 1) Introduces a lint cartography manifest that maps lint rules and rule-sets to repo subtrees and owners; the mapping is used by presubmit to run targeted lint shards rather than the full monorepo lint when changes touch small areas. 2) Adds a toolchain lease service (ci/toolchain/lease.go, runtime shim and GH Action wrapper) that grants ephemeral toolchain leases for presubmit runners so cached microimages are reused across related PRs. 3) Implements a release-safeguard check in our release workflow that validates artifact provenance headers and KMS signing eligibility; it fails releases that don't have the expected provenance but logs a clear remediation path. 4) Adds a gradual dev-dependency rotation helper that automates staged updates of devDeps via a small presubmit-friendly bot; dev-dep updates are batched by package-owner group as defined in the lint cartography manifest. Rollout plan: feature gated behind ci.flags.lint_cartography and ci.flags.toolchain_lease. Step 1 (canary): enable lint_cartography for the redwood/* packages for 2 weeks and observe presubmit runtime and false-positive rate. Step 2: enable toolchain_lease in the presubmit runners for at-most-10 concurrent leases and measure cache hit rate. Step 3: enable release_safeguard in pre-release environments for non-prod releases for 1 month, then flip for production. Testing: unit tests added for lease logic and cartography parser; presubmit smoke job added to validate targeted lint shards; e2e on a pinned small repo subset. Backwards compatibility: all changes are opt-in via flags and default to existing behavior. Checklist: - [x] lint cartography manifest + parser - [x] presubmit integration to shard lint by affected areas - [x] toolchain lease service + GH Action wrapper - [x] release-safeguard added to release workflow with clear remediation logs - [x] unit and integration tests - [x] documentation in docs/ci/tooling.md Links: Linear ENG-2271 (lint cartography), ENG-2309 (toolchain lease). Notes: This is intentionally lightweight; it is not a full replacement of our CI orchestration. The goal is to reduce noise and speed up the common small-change feedback path. If you are a package owner and see your rules remapped, please file ENG-2309 with examples of false positives.

[Warp-banked KV streaming and launch coalescing notes]
Summary:

This note collects notes and microbench results from exploring a warp-banked approach for streaming paged KV entries into inference kernels and a coarse launch-coalescing heuristic to amortize CUDA launch overhead for tiny requests. The goal: reduce end-to-end token latency tail for low-concurrency workloads (PLG warm-starts) while preserving throughput for high-concurrency bursts.

Motivation / problem statement:
- In hosted inference we often see a bimodal distribution: many requests produce very short decode steps (1-8 tokens) and a minority produce long sequences.
- Per-token kernel launch + small memcpy overhead dominates latency for short sequences, especially when KV pages are cold or sharded across device memory regions.
- Existing prefetch strategies pull whole pages synchronously or rely on global prefetch queues; that either increases memory pressure or adds latency spikes.

Hypothesis: warp-banked streaming + double-buffering + launch coalescing will reduce tail latency by:
1) overlapping async device page stage with compute using a dedicated set of CUDA streams (one stream per warp-bank).
2) compressing KV on the fly (lightweight 4-bit -> 16-bit expansions in-register) to reduce memory footprint and DMA time.
3) grouping tiny token-advance launches into a single kernel when they target contiguous or same page KV ranges (coalescer in runtime scheduler).

Design sketch:
- Warp-banked streamer: split the block grid into B 'warp-banks'. Each warp-bank owns a CUDA stream and a small ring-buffer region in device memory (page staging area). Kernels that will consume KV page X check a per-page owner hint; if owner != current warp-bank then runtime issues async copy to that bank's staging region on its dedicated stream.

- Double-buffered consumption: consumer kernel reads from staging buffer A while page streamer may be copying into B. Switch pointers via atomic flag and small handshake (cudaEvent / atomic int). This keeps consumer kernels lightweight (no per-element conditionals).

- Launch coalescer: runtime inspects microbatch queue (requests in same millisecond) and coalesces up to N tiny launches into one composite kernel when their KV page sets are disjoint OR fully overlap (fast-path). If they overlap partially, we fallback to separate launches to avoid complex synchronizations. Coalescing is best-effort and disabled if a request is latency-sensitive (explicit flag).

Kernel interface (recommended):
- __global__ void consume_kv_warpbank(float* staging_ptrs[], int page_meta[], int page_count, ConsumerArgs args)
  - staging_ptrs: array of B pointers (one per warp-bank), small and passed as kernel parameter.
  - page_meta: compact metadata per page (page_id, quant_format, length, block_stride).
  - ConsumerArgs: fused params (attention mask, seq_len, writeback pointer). Keep this small.

Implementation notes / CUDA specifics:
- Use cudaMemcpyAsync + cudaMemPrefetchAsync where supported (managed pinned) to move pages into device staging. Prefer pinned host -> device if host side fetch is required.
- Assign one persistent cudaStream_t per warp-bank to avoid stream creation overhead. Reuse streams across requests.
- Use cudaEventRecord to handshake buffer switches. Avoid blocking cudaStreamSynchronize inside hot path.
- For on-the-fly dequant: implement a tiny warp-level expansion that reads 4-bit packed values and writes FP16 into staging area using __shfl_sync based unpacking for coalesced reads. This keeps the DMA payload small and moves the decompression cost to the GPU where cycles are cheap compared to PCIe.
- For NVLink/peer copies in multi-gpu private deployments, consider cudaMemcpyPeerAsync into the same warp-bank staging region (performant vs remote page mapping).

Microbench experiments (summary):
- Setup: A100-40GB, single model layer (1 head, hidden 4096), synthetic inputs mimicking length=1 tokens at 100 qps. Baseline: naive per-token kernel launch + synchronous page copy.
- Results (median / p95 latency for a single-token advance):
  - Baseline (sync copy + launch): median 6.2ms, p95 18.9ms
  - Double-buffered warp-banked streamer (no coalesce): median 3.9ms, p95 8.7ms
  - Streamer + light-weight 4->16-bit expand in-flight: median 3.5ms, p95 7.8ms
  - Streamer + launch-coalescer (coalesce window 2-4 requests): median 2.6ms, p95 4.9ms
- Observations: the biggest wins are from avoiding synchronous host-device stalls and amortizing launch overhead when coalescing 2-4 tiny requests. Dequant on-device gave modest wins for PCIe-bound tests (~10-12% latency improvement) but is neutral on NVLink setups.

Heuristics for runtime integration:
- Coalescing policy: enable when (avg_seq_len <= 4) AND (concurrency < 16) AND (coalesce_window_ms <= 5). We measured diminishing returns beyond 4 requests.
- Page-owner heuristics: prefer affinity mapping based on last-consumer GPU stream to minimize cross-bank copies. If a page is hot (access count > threshold) pin it to its owning warp-bank for T seconds.
- Fall-back: if coalesced kernel would exceed shared-memory or register budgets, fall back to individual launches. Report telemetry for any fallback.

Telemetry to add (low cost):
- per-request: coalesced_flag (true/false), coalesced_group_size (int), page_copy_ms, kernel_launch_ms, total_token_advance_ms
- per-page: last_access_ts, owner_bank, hotness_score, size_bytes, quant_format
- kernel-level counters: buffer_switch_count, stream_waits, dequant_cycles_est (approx)

Edge cases and caveats:
- Partial overlap across pages: coalescing must ensure writeback lanes don't conflict. This requires a cheap intersection test at coalesce time; avoid doing expensive set-unions.
- Multi-tenant GPUs: warp-bank dedicated streams assume some fairness; in heavy noisy co-tenancy this can starve other work. Mitigate by making B configurable and auto-reducing when scheduler detects host contention.
- Kernel complexity: fused kernels that also do FlashAttention may increase register pressure. If register usage grows beyond occupancy sweet spot, throughput can regress; implement a build-time autotuner that emits two kernel variants (low-reg and high-reg) and pick at runtime via occupancy model.

Open questions / next experiments:
- Try microbench with T4 and V100 to see behavior with older PCIe stacks. Early small runs suggest more benefit on PCIe machines.
- Evaluate effect on token-quality: ensure that coalescing doesn't change scheduling/timing for timeout-sensitive callbacks or streaming responses.
- Experiment with adaptive coalescing window that uses moving-average of arrival gaps rather than fixed ms window.

Next steps / action items:
- Prototype consumer kernel with staging pointer array and double-buffer handshake (owner: Ethan). Target PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serve/pull/4823 (WIP).
- Add coalescer to runtime request queue as opt-in flag behind feature gate (Liam to add config + telemetry).
- Add small microbench harness to measure page copy vs on-device dequant (Sofia). Collect results for T4/V100 as above.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is exploratory. The aim is to reduce p95 for short-token requests without destabilizing throughput. Keep an eye on memory footprint of staging (tradeoff between B and ring size).
- Suggested review focus: correctness of buffer handshake and potential races, coherence with existing KV eviction (evict should not free an in-use staging buffer), and telemetry coverage.

References / context:
- Related tickets: JIRA-ENG-987 (paged-KV hot/cold experiments), CONFLUENCE-ENG-2345 (prefetch strategy doc), github PR referenced above.
- Slack thread: #serving-runtime "warp-bank streamer" (internal notes and early profiling graphs attached there)

TODO:
- [ ] Add unit test for buffer switch racing (simulate delayed stream)
- [ ] Add autotuner to pick coalescing window per deployment profile
- [ ] Validate with full model inference pipeline (not synthetic) and run load tests on dedicated cluster

End of note.

[Kernel eval sweep: flash-attention + paged-KV + continuous-batching]
Purpose:
This note captures the results of the kernel/runtime change sweep that landed flash-attention v2, paged-KV (8k page size), and continuous-batching heuristics on the staging inference fleet. Goal was to detect regressions in model onboarding evals (chat, summarization, retrieval-qa) and to surface any quality vs. performance tradeoffs introduced by the new kernels.

Top-level summary:
- Perf: Overall token throughput improved 18–42% depending on sequence length/CPU host. Median generation latency (p50) improved ~12% on medium sequences (512 tokens). p95 latency improved in most cases but worsened for very short requests (<32 tokens) when dynamic batching delayed small requests.
- Quality: Most prompt sets show no statistically significant quality delta. Notable exception: long-context summarization promptset (summ- long-ctx-50) shows a soft regression in ROUGE-L (~-2.6 points) and increased hallucination incidence on 5/50 transcripts.
- Regressions correlated with two conditions: (1) paged-KV boundary behavior for sequences that straddle page edges (observed in summarization prompts that include many repeated system tokens), and (2) continuous-batching when max_wait_ms was set high (40ms) causing cross-request KV reuse patterns to produce stale past-kv interactions for some attention kernels.

Experiment design / reproducibility:
- Baseline runtime: runtime@main (kernel: attn-v1, KV: linear, batching: legacy)
- Test runtime: runtime@feature/flash-paged-contbatch (FlashAttn v2, PagedKV page_size=8192, ContinuousBatching max_batch_tokens=2048, max_wait_ms=40, dynamic_batching=true)
- Model: onboarding/redwood-1.3b-fp16 (same model binary for baseline/test)
- Hardware: p4d-like nodes, single-GPU per request runner, CUDA 12.1, cuBLAS/cuDNN matched
- Prompt sets used (seeded runs):
  - chat-onboard-100: 100 multi-turn chat samples (open-domain), eval metrics: helpfulness_score (0–1), safety-flag rate
  - summ-long-ctx-50: 50 long-document summarization prompts (context lengths 6k–10k tokens), metrics: ROUGE-1/2/L, hallucination_count
  - retr-qa-200: 200 retrieval QA prompts with gold answers, metrics: F1, EM
  - code-assist-120: 120 code generation prompts (average 200 tokens), metrics: compile_rate, exact_match_snip
- Each run repeated 6 seeds; run order randomized; logs aggregated with seed and trace_id

Key quantitative diffs (aggregated means, baseline -> test):
- chat-onboard-100:
  - helpfulness_score: 0.78 -> 0.77 (delta -0.01, p=0.12)
  - safety-flag rate: 2.4% -> 2.4% (no change)
  - latency p50 (ms): 210 -> 185 (improve 11.9%)
  - latency p95 (ms): 620 -> 540 (improve 12.9%)

- summ-long-ctx-50:
  - ROUGE-1: 44.1 -> 41.8 (delta -2.3)
  - ROUGE-2: 20.5 -> 18.7 (delta -1.8)
  - ROUGE-L: 38.9 -> 36.3 (delta -2.6)
  - hallucination_count: 3 -> 8 (raw count across 50 samples)
  - latency p50 (ms): 1120 -> 900 (improve 19.6%)
  - notes: regressions concentrated on docs where repeated policy tokens appear near page boundaries (examples listed below)

- retr-qa-200:
  - F1: 78.2 -> 78.6 (delta +0.4)
  - EM: 61.1 -> 61.0 (no sig change)
  - latency p50 (ms): 340 -> 300 (improve 11.8%)

- code-assist-120:
  - compile_rate: 86% -> 86% (no change)
  - exact_match_snip: 32.4 -> 32.1 (delta -0.3)
  - latency p50 (ms): 410 -> 360 (improve 12.2%)

Qualitative failure analysis (summ-long-ctx):
1) Example A (trace_id: abc-20260102-11): source doc contains repeated header block tokenized as long run of the same system prompt. Paged-KV boundary happened mid-header; when FlashAttn v2 fused attention windows across the page boundary the absolute attention weights for the header tokens decreased, and the model skipped an important context sentence when generating the summary. This produced omission + subtle factual drift.
2) Example B (trace_id: abc-20260103-07): continuous-batching pooled two near-simultaneous summarization requests, and background request ordering created a stale KV re-use scenario where a cached page included tokens from the other request; though we expected strict per-request isolation, a micro-bug in page invalidation (paging table TTL) caused ephemeral leakage of context for ~120ms. Result: hallucinated sentence referencing unrelated doc content.

Root-cause hypothesis and supporting evidence:
- Paged-KV page-alignment: our page-aligned KV writes are correct, but read-time offsets for tokens at page edges rely on a rounding heuristic that interacts poorly with FlashAttn's block fusion optimization. When fusion combines two adjacent blocks spanning a page boundary, the effective attention receptive field shifts by a small token offset (1–3 tokens) in some implementations; for dense summarization prompts this moves anchor sentences out of peak attention. Reproduced in unit test with deterministic seed (see linked PR).
- Continuous-batching: default max_wait_ms=40 was too high for low-latency workloads; it increased probability of multi-request batches in edge ordering sequences and exposed a TTL/invalidation gap in the paging metadata. Lowering max_wait_ms reduces the relevant window and eliminated the leak in canary runs.

Mitigations tested (short-term):
- Rollback option: deploy fallback to attn-v1 for summarization workloads via routing policy (product tag: summarization-long-ctx) — proven to remove the ROUGE regressions at cost of 15–20% increased latency for that route.
- Config change: lower continuous-batching max_wait_ms from 40 -> 8 for latency-sensitive routes; dynamic_batching keep enabled. This reduced multi-request batch incidence from ~4.6% -> 0.7% and removed most observed hallucination cases in canary.
- Patch: small fix to page read offset rounding in paged-KV (PR linked). Unit tests added to assert identical attention alignment across page boundaries for synthetic repeated-token sequences.

Longer-term actions:
- Add an onboarding eval check: for any kernel change, run a targeted long-context summarization suite (n=200) with an attention-alignment assertion that compares token-level attention mass on anchor sentences. Fail change if attention mass drop > 12% compared to baseline. (JIRA-INF-7901)
- Improve batching heuristics: implement adaptive max_wait_ms that lowers wait when request-size distribution indicates many short requests. Add a sampling trace that records batch composition and KV page ownership for offline diagnosis. (GH issue #4612)
- Expand promptsets: add more duplicated-prefix tests and system-token-run prompts to the standard onboarding suite; these triggered the paged-KV edge cases.

Immediate recommendations (for product/infra owners):
- Hold feature rollout for production until page-read offset fix lands and continuous-batching default max_wait_ms lowered for hosted-grade routes.
- Ship diagnostic canary with flooding of summarization-long-ctx requests and monitor hallucination_count and attention-mass metric.
- Re-run the full onboarding suite (chat, retr-qa, code, long-summ) after fixes and produce a block-diff report for decision meeting.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Is the attention shift purely an implementation artifact of FlashAttn v2 fusion, or also affected by kernel numeric precision differences on edge tokens? (investigate by running fusion flag off)
- Should we implement a per-route page_size tuning knob for Paged-KV? Some routes benefit from smaller pages when document structures have many repeated small blocks.
- Do we need per-request KV isolation telemetry at the trace level (adds overhead) vs. the rolling TTL approach?

Appendix: short reproduction recipe for the failing long-summ example:
- Checkout runtime PR branch and run example script: tools/repro/run_long_summ_repro.sh --seed 111 --page_size 8192 --flash_fusion on
- Input doc saved in /experiments/summ_repro/doc-abc.txt (attached in the ticket)
- Deterministic seed produces the misaligned attention pattern; inspect attention dump: /tmp/trace-abc-attn.json

Linked artifacts and references:
- runtime PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4523 (paged-KV rounding fix committed)
- telemetry dashboard (canary): https://grafana.redwood.local/d/abcd/onboarding-kernel-sweeps
- JIRA: INF-7892 (kernel sweep), INF-7901 (attention-mass gating)

Notes to reviewers:
- Focus first on the long-context summarization failures — they are the only high-confidence quality regression. Other deltas are within noise.
- The perf wins are real and material; we should avoid blanket rollback if targeted mitigations are quick to deploy.
- I can run the next canary with adaptive max_wait_ms knob if infra wants a dataset to watch.

-- Avery

[Probe Prioritization Sprint Canvas for Prefetch Warmth]
Purpose:
This canvas captures a compact experiment plan to prioritize instrumentation and dashboard probes that improve visibility into prefetch / KV-cache warm paths. The goal for the sprint is to reduce investigation time for cold-cache latency spikes by 50% and provide a low-cost signal set suitable for multi-tenant rollouts.

Sprint goal (2 weeks):
- Ship 4 prioritized probes + 1 dashboard microkit.
- Validate probe fidelity on two canary tenants and measure query cost.
- Create a short runbook for cold-cache investigation.

Decision matrix (how we score probes):
- Criteria (weight):
  - Customer impact (weight 30) = reasoned by feature surface affected (latency-sensitive routes).
  - Signal fidelity (weight 25) = % of incidents where probe sheds light (historical / pilot).
  - Query cost (weight 15) = approximate monthly query expense at 10k qps normalized.
  - Implementation effort (weight 20) = engineer-days to instrument + deploy + test.
  - Investigation payoff (weight 10) = expected reduction in triage time (minutes).

Scoring example (0-5 per criterion, multiply by weight, sum -> priority score):
- Prefetch-hit-rate (lightweight event): 5*30 + 4*25 + 5*15 + 5*20 + 4*10 = 150 + 100 + 75 + 100 + 40 = 465
- Per-tenant-kv-eviction-rate (sampled): 4*30 + 3*25 + 2*15 + 3*20 + 3*10 = 120 + 75 + 30 + 60 + 30 = 315
- Cold-path-trace-anchor (trace spans): 5*30 + 5*25 + 1*15 + 2*20 + 5*10 = 150 + 125 + 15 + 40 + 50 = 380

Prioritized probes for the sprint (finalized):
1) Prefetch-hit-rate probe (global lightweight metric) — implement as counter & 1m rollup. Owner: Priya.
2) Cold-path-trace-anchor (request-scoped trace with prefetch span) — implement sampling policy for tail traces. Owner: Alex.
3) Per-route-first-token-time (quantile) — add 50/95/99 to dashboard. Owner: Liam.
4) Synthetic-prefetch-check (scheduled probe) — HTTP probe that simulates canonical prompt/payload to exercise cache. Owner: Maya.

Metric definitions (compact, copyable):
- metric: prefetch.hit.count
  - type: counter
  - description: increments when a request hits a prefetched KV entry (prefetch logic observed during routing).
  - calc: raw count aggregated per-minute, per-tenant, per-route
  - unit: requests
  - alert guide: sustained drop of >60% vs 7d baseline and p95 latency rising by >30% -> create P1 investigation.

- metric: prefetch.attempt.count
  - type: counter
  - description: attempts to prefetch (successful + queued).
  - calc: ratio prefetch.hit.count / prefetch.attempt.count = prefetch success rate
  - unit: ratio
  - owners: eng-serving-runtime, obs

- metric: route.first_token_ms
  - type: histogram (buckets + quantiles)
  - description: time from request arrival to first streaming token emitted by model runtime (includes routing + prefetch cost).
  - calc: 50/95/99 quantiles over 1m windows; label by route, tier, tenant
  - alert guide: p99 > 800ms for >5min on high-tier routes

- metric: kv.eviction.count
  - type: counter (sampled at 1/10 for low-cost tenants)
  - description: number of eviction events per-GPU-pool; used to infer cache churn
  - calc: normalized per-tenant per-hour
  - unit: evictions/hour

Tracing guidance (how we instrument spans and annotations):
- Important spans: inbound.http -> router.evaluate -> prefetch.enqueue -> prefetch.fetch -> runtime.kv.access -> runtime.generate
- Naming convention: service.operation[.sub] e.g., prefetch.fetch, runtime.kv.get, router.policy.eval
- Span tags to attach: tenant_id, route_id, request_id, prefetch_hint, kv_pool, node_id, sequence_len
- Trace sampling: tail-sampling at error/severity weight + probabilistic 0.2% for cold-cache route candidates. For prefetch probes prefer higher sampling (5%) during the experiment window.
- Trace anchor: mark the earliest runtime.kv.access for a request as "prefetch_anchor" tag so dashboards can link traces to probe metrics.

Dashboard microkit (layout and drill paths):
- Page: Prefetch Health (single page microdash)
  - Top row: 3 KPI cards: Prefetch success rate (1m), Route p95 first_token_ms, Synthetic probe success
  - Middle: Heatmap of prefetch.hit/count ratio by route vs hour of day (interactive time range)
  - Bottom left: Top-10 routes by delta p95 vs baseline (sparkline) with quick link to trace search for route_id
  - Bottom right: Eviction churn panel (per-pool stacked bars) + link to recent deployment tags
  - Drill links: Card -> trace explorer with filter "prefetch_anchor:true and route_id:<selected>"

Dashboard UX notes:
- Keep query windows small by default (1h) with quick presets (6h, 24h, 7d).
- Avoid high-cardinality grouping on default panels; surface per-tenant only behind a dropdown.
- Use derived metric panels (ratios computed server-side) to reduce live query cost.

Synthetic probe plan:
- Script: small canonical prompt that exercises a warm path and a forced cold path variant (unique prompt id forces miss).
- Frequency: 1 per 30s / region for canary tenants; 1 per 5m for global non-canary.
- Measurement: success boolean, first_token_ms, full-response-size, route chosen. Store as metric series and attach latest run ID to trace when present.

Investigation playbook (cold-cache latency spike):
1) Check Prefetch success rate KPI -> if dropping: go to heatmap by route/time.
2) Open top-affected route -> look at per-route first_token_ms p95 and synthetic probe results.
3) If synthetic indicates miss -> search traces filtered by prefetach_anchor:true and route_id.
4) From traces, check for long prefetch.fetch spans or high queue times (prefetch.enqueue).
5) If kv.eviction.count high -> inspect recent scaling or deployment activity; correlate with infra events (K8s node churn).
6) If no eviction evidence, sample full request payloads (obeying PI policy) and validate prefetch hint propagation.

Cost & query budget notes:
- Target probe rolling cost < $250/month for baseline rollout (across all tenants).
- Use aggregated 1m rollups and server-side derived ratios to keep Grafana/BI query volume low.
- Sample trace collection for detailed spans; prefer trace anchors with links rather than full-trace ingestion for every request.

Metrics rollout checklist (for each probe):
- [ ] Schema registered in metric catalog (name, owner, unit, retention)
- [ ] Instrumentation PR + integration tests
- [ ] Dashboard widgets implemented in microkit
- [ ] Canary validation on 2 tenants with pre/post comparison
- [ ] Runbook short doc + owner oncall handoff

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Can we add a lightweight per-tenant kv-warmth index without exploding cardinailty? (Priya to prototype sampled index)
- Determine whether synthetic probe should be able to toggle forced-miss at runtime for deeper experiments. (Maya)
- Agree on retention tiers for prefetch.* metrics (30d vs 90d) to balance trend detection vs cost.

Notes to implementers (quick tips):
- Add metric labels sparingly: route_id, tenant_tier, region are usually sufficient. Avoid tagging by model_version at high-cardinality.
- For trace spans, capture sequence_len only on samples to limit size.
- Write small unit tests that assert prefetch_hit increments when prefetch.fetch returns cached:true.

[Queue-pressure simulator and fairness probebook]
Purpose:
This note captures the design, runs, and preliminary analysis for a simulator-driven stress test that emulates queue-pressure conditions at the request-routing layer. Goal is to compare fairness strategies under adversarial and long-tail input shapes and to surface kernel-level hotspots that amplify tail latency during sustained pressure.

Background / motivation:
- Many previous experiments focused on batch formation heuristics in production traces. Those were indispensable, but they under-sample rare sustained pressure patterns (5–30s windows) that cause persistent p99 spikes and recovery hysteresis.
- We built a lightweight, parameterized queue-pressure simulator to generate repeatable, tunable stress windows (burst amplitude, sustained pressure duration, fraction of long-context requests, urgency skew). This allows controlled comparisons across fairness policies without noisy upstream traffic variability.

High-level hypotheses:
1) Under sustained queue pressure, "age-boost" policies maintain lower p99 latency for long-lived requests vs strict size-based coalescing but cost throughput slightly.
2) Proportional-share fairness (weighting by service-class) limits starvation but can increase average latency under high ctx-length variance.
3) Kernel overheads (small-kernel launches, CPU memcpy-to-GPU) become dominant contributor to p99 during high batch churn — not just batch size.

Simulator design (short):
- Request model: poisson base arrival + configurable burst injection. Each request has: token_count (short: 16–128, medium: 256–1024, long: 2048+), urgency (0..1), and a simple priority tag (service, background).
- Pressure window: parameters {burst_rps, sustained_seconds, decay_tau}. We sweep burst_rps from 2x baseline to 10x.
- Outcome metrics emitted per run: throughput (req/s), tokens/s, p50/p95/p99/p999 latencies, batch size distribution, preemption events, queue depth over time, fairness index (Jain's index over per-class latency), and kernel-level counters (CUDA launch count, memcpy ms, CPU scheduling stalls).
- Implementation: simulator integrates with local dev runtime harness so we can toggle real serving runtime vs mocked execution (fast-mode). Tracing uses the runtime's trace id and logs to perf-collector.

Policies compared:
- size-first: flush when batch reaches token-cap or timeout (baseline)
- age-boost: requests accrue urgency with queue time; urgency can upweight selection into batches
- proportional-share: per-service weight that enforces ratios at formation time
- capped-antique: prioritizes oldest requests but enforces a cap to prevent huge latency regressions for small requests

Runbook (how to reproduce locally):
1) checkout serving-runtime branch: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime branch queue-press-sim
2) run: ./dev/harness --simulator --policy=age-boost --burst=600 --sustain=20 --long_frac=0.1 --out=./out/ageboost-run1
3) collect traces: ./tools/collect-trace.sh ./out/ageboost-run1
4) upload with: python tools/upload_perf.py ./out/ageboost-run1 --dst perf-dash/probebook
Note: these flags map to the simulator spec in tools/simulator/README.md (see linked Confluence).

Key experimental settings used (summary table in text):
- Baseline arrival: 200 rps steady
- Burst amplitude: 600 rps (3x), 1200 rps (6x), 2000 rps (10x)
- Sustain durations: 8s, 20s, 60s
- Long request fraction: 0.02, 0.10, 0.25
- Token-cap per GPU batch: 48k tokens
- Flush timeout sweep: 5ms, 12ms, 25ms, 50ms

Representative run notes (selected interesting runs):
Run A (age-boost, burst=3x, sustain=20s, long_frac=0.10):
- p50: 7ms, p95: 28ms, p99: 84ms, p999: 230ms
- Average batch size: 18 requests (900 tokens avg)
- Fairness index: 0.86 (improved versus size-first 0.71)
- Kernel profile: memcpy host->device spikes correlate with p99 spikes (avg memcpy per batch increased by 3.4x during window). CUDA launch count increased 1.6x relative to steady-state (more small batches).
- Observation: age-boost prevented starvation of long requests; tail still high due to increased batch churn and memcpy overhead, not queueing alone.

Run B (proportional-share, burst=6x, sustain=20s, long_frac=0.25):
- p50: 9ms, p95: 48ms, p99: 220ms, p999: 880ms (very bad)
- Average batch size: 10 requests (1800 tokens avg) but high variance
- Fairness index: 0.93 (per-class latencies balanced)
- Kernel profile: kernel busy time high but dominated by long-context compute; small-batch launch overheads plus repeated preempt/resume created jitter.
- Observation: although per-class fairness metrics look good, aggregated p99 exploded because long requests serialize GPU compute and prevent batching efficiency; proportional-share allowed too many long requests to start early, reducing coalescing for short ones.

Run C (size-first with aggressive timeout = 5ms, burst=3x, sustain=8s):
- p50: 6ms, p95: 33ms, p99: 190ms
- Average batch size: 24 requests but many small batches during spike
- Kernel hotspots: CPU scheduling stalls increase during bursts — threads blocked waiting on IO for small copies.
- Observation: aggressive timeout reduces average latency but increases kernel launch overhead; tail suffers.

Profiling notes (how we gathered kernel-level data):
- We instrumented these layers: request-router (timestamps), batch-assembler (batch formation events), host->device memcpy timings (via CUPTI/metric API), kernel start/finish times (CUDA events), CPU thread scheduling latencies (schedtrace), and runtime internal queue lock hold times.
- The majority of observed p99 increases during pressure windows traced to three correlated phenomena: more frequent host->device memcpy calls due to smaller batches; higher kernel launch rate; increased contention for batch-assembly locks causing latency spikelets that cascade into p99.

Diagnostics and root-cause pointers:
- Memory copy inefficiency: when batches are smaller, the amortized memcpy per token is higher (higher driver overhead). We see this as longer memcpy_ms per batch even for identical token counts split across more batches.
- Kernel launch overhead: small batches cause more kernels to be launched overall; driver overhead and CUDA stream scheduling amplifies tail.
- Lock contention: batch-assembler holds a global lock briefly to splice request descriptors into a batch. Under pressure this critical section becomes a bottleneck; threads waiting for the lock show up as CPU scheduling stalls.

Quick mitigations tested in-situ:
- coalescing window slack: increase the flush timeout slightly during detected pressure windows (auto-scale timeout) — reduced p99 by ~25% in age-boost runs at cost of small increase to avg latency.
- batch-assembly lock sharding: split assembly locks by hash of request id to reduce contention (prototype): reduced CPU stall time by ~40% and p99 by ~15% in several runs.
- memcpy aggregation: use contiguous pinned staging buffer to aggregate small copies in fast-mode path — improved memcpy_ms by ~30% for small batches in the lab harness.

Open questions / follow-ups:
1) Can we implement an adaptive heuristic that trades off short-request latency vs amortized memcpy cost when long-request fraction spikes? Preliminary idea: detect long_request_fraction over sliding window and temporarily bias batch formation toward size (increase token limit) to keep memcpy amortization good.
2) How do preemption and kernel-level multi-tenant isolation interact with these policies on Dedicated hardware (multi-process GPU)? Need to run on a dedicated GPU machine with actual multi-tenant interference to validate lab improvements.
3) Is the fairness index (Jain) the right single-number summary? It hides the fact that proportional-share looked great on fairness but terrible for p999. Consider reporting a fairness-latency curve (latency per quantile per class).

Action items (next sprint):
- Implement lock sharding in batch-assembler (Diego) — target: prototype by 2025-03-07.
- Add adaptive timeout trigger (Sana) to the age-boost policy: heuristic based on sustained queue depth and observed memcpy_ms.
- Run Dedicated-machine validation (Markus) with mixed tenant load — schedule for 2025-03-10 test window.
- Add p999 telemetry per-class to perf dashboard and a 'pressure window' alarm for production to trigger simulations.

Appendix: useful commands/logs collected during experiments:
- dev harness cmd: ./dev/harness --simulator --policy=%POLICY% --burst=600 --sustain=20 --long_frac=0.1 --trace-collect
- perf trace collector: ./tools/collect-trace.sh ./out/%RUN%
- quick profile summary: scripts/quick_profile.sh ./out/%RUN% > ./out/%RUN%_summary.txt
- dashboard links: perf-dash/probebook (internal), traces/rt/2025-02-14/queue-sim-A
Notes to self (informal):
- The simulator is intentionally aggressive on long_frac to expose pathological cases. Real traffic rarely hits 25% long requests but when it does (e.g., document-summarize bursts) we saw dramatic impact.
- Keep experiment IDs in filenames; makes trace correlation much easier.
- When sharing with SRE/infra, include the kernel flame graphs; those made it obvious that driver calls were the hidden culprit.

End of probebook.

(If anything here looks like a duplicate of recent run notes, apologies — this is the canonical writeup consolidating lab runs A/B/C and action items.)

[Platform Brief: SaaS GTM — Inference Value Metrics & Battlecards]
Overview

Purpose: This brief consolidates product positioning, high-impact value metrics, competitive battlecards, pricing guidance, a compact case study, and a prospect-facing security FAQ tailored for SaaS platform buyers evaluating LLM inference solutions. Audience: AEs, SEs, solutions engineers, and product marketing running discovery and technical evaluation calls with mid-market and enterprise SaaS buyers.

Executive positioning (one-liner)

Redwood Inference: Predictable, production-grade LLM inference that maximizes performance and minimizes unit cost across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments — giving platform teams a single API and operational surface to ship reliable AI features without rebuilding inference infrastructure.

Top 3 buyer outcomes we lead with

- Reduce per-inference cost while keeping sub-100ms tail latency for common interactive flows.
- Move from prototype to SLA-backed production without re-architecting (same API for hosted, reserved, and private).
- De-risk compliance through private deployment and audit-friendly telemetry.

Key value metrics and how to frame them in discovery

- Latency (P95/P99): Typical hosted P95 for chat flows: 80–180ms (short prompts, <256 tokens). P99 target for Dedicated: <250ms. Discuss tail-latency SLOs and fallback routing to smaller quantized models for spikes.
- Throughput: Batch-aware throughput gains: 2–6x cost savings for high-concurrency embedding jobs with batching & caching. Ask about queries/sec (QPS) and average request size.
- Cost per 1k prompt tokens: Provide customer-specific model/quantization comps. Example framing: "Switching from single-instance self-host to Redwood Dedicated saved AcornCRM ~48% per-token on standard 8K-chat workload."
- Availability / SLA: Hosted: 99.9% regional uptime; Dedicated: 99.95% backed by contract. Use these to quantify expected downtime impact on revenue ops.
- Time-to-production: Typical onboarding (hosted) = 1–3 days; Dedicated proof-of-concept = 2–4 weeks (infra & capacity provisioning).

Battlecard: Primary competitors and how to position

- Cloud-managed endpoints (Hyperscaler-managed LLM endpoints)
  - Strengths: deep cloud integration, single-provider billing.
  - Redwood advantage: Superior latency predictability, multi-model catalog (open models + tuned variants), and lower unit cost via continuous batching, quantization profiles, and model routing policies.
  - Messaging: "Like managed endpoints, but tuned for inference economics and predictable tail latency for production apps."

- LLM API providers (simple hosted APIs)
  - Strengths: easy dev experience, low time-to-value.
  - Redwood advantage: Matches dev ergonomics but adds Dedicated / Private lanes and enterprise controls (VPC, KMS, audit logs) so customers don’t have to replatform as they scale.
  - Messaging: "From prototype to SLA-backed production without rewriting your integration."

- Self-hosted inference stacks (open-source runtime + infra)
  - Strengths: maximum control, on-prem fit for regulated data.
  - Redwood advantage: We provide a hardened runtime, autoscaling, cost controls, and rollout tooling—plus optional on-prem packaging and a customer-managed control plane for compliance. Lower TCO for teams that value operational simplicity and performance tuning.
  - Messaging: "Get the benefits of a maintained, optimized inference runtime without hiring a deep infra team."

Pricing guidance (rules of thumb for AEs to use in discovery)

- Pricing levers to highlight: model family, instance type (Dedicated SKU), quantization tier, reserved commit vs burst, embedding vs generative unit pricing.
- Proposal archetypes:
  - Self-serve hosted starter: no commit, pay-as-you-go per-token and per-embedding. Ideal for product/feature proofs.
  - Dedicated entry: 3–6 month reserved capacity (monthly commit), includes capacity reservation, 24/7 priority support, and model access. Typical for midmarket customers expecting consistent QPS.
  - Private Deployment: fixed platform fee + per-node license + premium support and compliance bundle. For regulated customers or those requiring air-gapped environments.

- Example customer scenario (SaaS search & assistant) — ballpark illustration to use during commercial conversations:
  - Baseline: 3M tokens / month, predominantly generation (average 500 tokens/session), 2M embeddings / month.
  - Hosted cost estimate (pay-as-you-go): $6,000–$9,000 / month depending on model family and streaming usage.
  - Dedicated cost estimate (reserved): $3,200–$5,500 / month equivalent (with 12-month commit) — includes better latency SLAs and lower per-token unit economics.
  - Use these numbers as conversation starters and include precise model-match quotes from pricing desk for final proposals.

Pitch deck outline (6 slides, one-line purpose each)

1. Problem: Rising inference costs, tail latency, and operational debt when scaling LLM features.
2. Vision & Value: Unified inference runtime with predictable economics and deployment flexibility.
3. Product: Redwood product map (Hosted API, Dedicated, Private, Console, Optimize).
4. Proof points: Performance benchmarks (P95/P99 numbers), cost comparisons vs self-host & hyperscalers, and a short case study.
5. Security & compliance: VPC, KMS integrations, SOC2 / ISO posture, audit logs, and private deployment options.
6. Commercials & next steps: Pricing archetypes, pilot offer, success criteria and timeline.

Compact case study: AcornCRM (SaaS CRM) — 8-week engagement

- Situation: AcornCRM needed a contextual assistant for sales reps with sub-200ms P95 latency and tight data residency constraints for EU customers. Their prototype used a mix of self-hosted models and occasional hyperscaler endpoints.
- Action: Redwood onboarded AcornCRM to Hosted API for an initial pilot (2 weeks), instrumented prompt caching and prefix KV caching, then migrated them to a Dedicated pool with quantized model variants for EU traffic. Provided rollout plan with canary and automatic fallback policies.
- Results: 
  - Latency: P95 from ~420ms to 160ms after Dedicated + batching optimizations.
  - Cost: Estimated per-token unit cost reduced 48% vs their previous single-instance hosting baseline.
  - Reliability: Achieved 99.96% uptime for critical inference routes over 90 days.
- Quote (paraphrased): "We launched our assistant into production faster than expected and kept response times consistent across our EU and US customers — the cost reduction was material to our unit economics." — Head of Platform, AcornCRM

Security FAQ for prospects (short and direct)

Q: Can Redwood run in my VPC / on-prem?
A: Yes. We offer Private deployment (customer-managed control plane) and an on-prem package for air-gapped environments. Contact sales for deployment checklist and lead time (typically 4–8 weeks depending on network & hardware).

Q: How is customer data protected in Hosted?
A: Data is encrypted in-transit (TLS 1.2+) and at-rest (AES-256). Optional per-customer keying via KMS (bring-your-own-key supported on Dedicated & Private). We retain only transient inference artifacts by default; retention is configurable.

Q: Do you have third-party attestations?
A: Redwood maintains SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 evidence; customers with enterprise contracts can request evidence under NDA.

Q: How are audit logs surfaced?
A: Redwood Console exposes request-level telemetry, per-token cost breakdowns, model version, and an audit trail for administrative actions. Logs can also be forwarded to your SIEM via secure forwarding.

Q: What controls exist to prevent data leakage in model updates?
A: Model onboarding and updates are gated by the model-onboarding team. We sign model-change notices and provide canary/eval runs tied to your evaluation suites. Private deployments allow complete model binaries under customer control.

Q: How do you handle incident response and notifications?
A: We maintain a documented incident process with dedicated SRE on-call rotation. Customers with Dedicated or Private get a designated technical account lead (TAL) and a post-incident report within 72 hours for Sev1 incidents.

Objection handling snippets (short scripts for SEs/AEs)

- "We can build this ourselves": Ask about the cost of hiring/retaining ops talent, time-to-first-SLA, and the ongoing tuning effort. Offer a TCO comparison and pilot to prove the economics.
- "We need data to stay on-prem": Lead with Private deployment and provide the deployment checklist + typical timelines.

Success criteria and pilot checklist (what we want to validate in a POC)

- Business/technical success criteria (mutually agreed): target P95 latency, acceptable per-token cost delta vs prototype, error rate threshold (<0.5% request errors), and integration completion (SDK + tracing).
- Technical deliverables: sample prompt set, representative traffic replay (1–3 days), evaluation prompts for quality checks, production routing plan, and SLO definition.

  - Week 1–2: Hosted pilot, instrumentation, perf tuning.
  - Week 3–4: Dedicated provisioning (if applicable), canary rollout.
  - Week 4–8: Stabilization, cost tuning, and handoff to platform/ops.

[Warm Capacity Subscriptions — Product Brief & Pricing]
Summary:

This product brief describes Warm Capacity Subscriptions (a.k.a. Warm Pools), a new add-on for Dedicated and Private customers that guarantees a configurable pool of pre-warmed model-serving slots to reduce cold-start latency and provide predictable tail latency for bursty traffic patterns. The doc covers the product rationale, target personas, technical design constraints, pricing model, SLO/SLA impacts, launch plan, and required implementation deliverables.

Problem statement:

Many enterprise customers integrating LLM inference experience high tail latency or transient errors when traffic spikes or when infrequently used model variants are rotated onto GPUs. The existing Dedicated reserved capacity reduces this risk, but small or variable workloads still face cold-starts caused by model loading, compilation, or quantized kernel warm-up. Customers building interactive experiences (chat, code-assist, search) require >95th-percentile latency stability and explicit cost controls for standing warm capacity.

Goals (Success criteria):

- Reduce 95th/99th percentile cold-start latency for targeted routes by at least 60% versus baseline without warm capacity.
- Provide a predictable pricing model customers can purchase monthly/annual for standing warm capacity.
- Integrate with existing Dedicated autoscaling and Private on-prem packaging without requiring service interruption.
- Provide telemetry, usage reporting, and cost attribution per-tenant and per-route.

Target users / buyer personas:

- Platform engineers at SaaS companies deploying interactive LLM features (chat, autocomplete, code gen).
- Enterprise procurement/staff who prefer predictable monthly committed spend for critical latency guarantees.
- Solutions engineers who onboard customers with compliance or audit requirements and must prove latency stability.

Product overview (How it works):

- Warm Pool: a named subscription of N warm slots (N GPUs or vCPU-backed serving slots depending on deployment) that are continuously kept ready for fast assignment. Each slot is associated with a set of allowed model families and sequence-length templates.
- Assignment & Routing: Smart routing reserves a warm slot for a matching route when request rate or a scheduled reservation occurs. If no matching warm slot is available, the normal serving path applies and the request may experience cold-start semantics (but with fallback policies available).
- Pre-warm actions: model binary resident in GPU memory, warmed CUDA kernels compiled, KV cache primed for most-common prefixes where applicable, and lightweight model-validation warm runs executed to avoid JIT stalls.
- Integration: warm-pool management surfaces as an optional flag on Dedicated purchase and as an add-on to Redwood Private via the control plane agent. Warm pools honor tenant isolation and RBAC rules.

Technical constraints & compatibility table:

| Feature | Hosted API | Dedicated | Private (VPC/on-prem) | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| GPU-backed warm slots | Yes (hosted reservations) | Yes | Yes | Hardware must support pinned pages and device residency policies |
| Quantized-only variants | Partial | Yes | Depends on platform | Some quantization pipelines require extra warm steps |
| Multi-model on single GPU | No | Yes | Configurable | Requires shard-aware warm placement |
| Edge / lightweight runtime | No | No | Limited | Not recommended for <GPU edge targets> |

Pricing model (high-level):

Pricing must balance predictable revenue and clear ROI for customers. Proposed tiers:

- Warm Unit: unit of 1 warm slot for 1 model family (monthly commitment). Warm Unit price varies by hardware class (A100, H100, or vCPU pool). Example list price (US dollars):
  1. A100-class slot: $7,500 / month (per slot)
  2. H100-class slot: $11,500 / month
  3. vCPU warm slot (for small LMs): $1,200 / month

- Minimum commitment: 2 Warm Units for monthly plans, discounts for annual commitment (20% off).
- Burst credits: each subscription includes 200 burst assignments per slot per month; additional bursts billed at per-request microcredits.
- Metering: metered by configured slot-count, active assignments, and burst overage. Billing report exposes: reserved slots, active-hours consumed, bursts consumed, and model-family tags.

Pricing examples (illustrative):

- Small SaaS: 2 A100 warm slots monthly = $15,000 / month (expected to reduce customer tail latency and replace expensive overprovisioning by ~40%).
- Mid-market: 5 vCPU warm slots (for quantized LMs) annual = 5 * $1,200 * 12 * 0.8 = $57,600 effective yearly.

SLA and SLO impact:

- Warm-capacity subscription includes an SLO for warm-assignment availability: 99.9% of warm assignment attempts must return within 100 ms for matching routes. This is scoped to the control plane and routing logic; model runtime and hardware failures are covered by existing Dedicated SLAs.
- Error budget accounting: warm-availability SLOs are tracked independently; warm subscription refunds (credits) are applied when monthly warm-availability < 99.9% following the standard credits playbook.

Telemetry and observability:

Required telemetry signals (exposed in Redwood Console):
- warm_slots_reserved (gauge per-tenant)
- warm_assignment_latency_ms (p95, p99)
- warm_burst_consumed (counter)
- warm_slot_efficiency (active-assignment-hours / reserved-hours)
- cold_start_rate_on_matching_routes (rate)

Reports to surface in Console:
- Warm capacity utilization heatmap (by hour, by model family)
- Cost-saving estimation: baseline cold-start penalty vs. warm-subscription cost per month
- Per-route tail-latency improvement attribution

Operational Playbook (on-call and failure scenarios):

1) Warm assignment fails (no slot): controller retries up to 3 times with exponential backoff, then falls back to normal serving with a tagged cold-start event. Alert: SRE warm-assignment-failure-rate > 0.5% sustained for 15 minutes.
2) Slot becomes unhealthy: drain slot, kick off replacement pre-warm, mark slot as degraded. Ownership: serving-runtime team.
3) Over-subscription detected: if warm-slot-efficiency < 20% for >7 days, trigger notification to customer success and propose downscale.

Launch plan and go-to-market playbook (90 days):

- Phase 0 (30 days): Beta with 6 strategic customers. Deliverables: console UI mock, billing schema, beta contract addendum, SLO measurement dashboards.
- Phase 1 (30 days): Public launch to Dedicated customers with self-serve purchase for monthly plans. SaaS docs, solutions playbook, SDK flags for warm preference.
- Phase 2 (30 days): Private deployment support, annual pricing, and field enablement with sales kits and ROI calculator.

Rollout checklist (operational & engineering):

1. Control plane: warm-pool subscription CRUD APIs and RBAC scoping.
2. Runtime: slot reservation protocol, pre-warm steps, and health-check instrumentation.
3. Billing: new invoice line item, usage exporter, and burst overage meter.
4. Console: dashboard tiles, utilization charts, and purchase workflow.
5. Legal: template addendum, terms for refunds/credits, and SLA text.
6. Customer Success: onboarding runbook, playbook for sizing recommendations, and escalation matrix.

Implementation requirements (developer-facing):

- API contract example (JSON payload):

  {
    "subscription_name": "team-x-warmpool-1",
    "slots": 3,
    "model_tags": ["llama-2-70b", "redwood-verified-gpt-compat"],
    "hardware_class": "A100",
    "burst_credit_policy": { "included_bursts_per_slot_month": 200 }
  }

- Config flags: enable_warm_pool_routes=true, warm_assignment_timeout_ms=100, warm_health_probe_interval_s=30
- Backward compatibility: warm pools must not change default routing for customers who do not opt in.

Open questions & decisions required:

- Pricing elasticity: should burst overage be metered in microcredits or token-based units? Decision impacts billing plumbing.
- Slot accounting granularity: per-VM vs per-GPU shard for multi-model placements.
- Support for ephemeral warm reservations tied to scheduled events (e.g., daily demos): immediate vs delayed billing adjustments.

Risks and mitigations:

- Risk: Customers overbuy warm slots and underutilize, leading to churn. Mitigation: offer 14-day trial and utilization-based recommendations in Console.

1) One‑paragraph positioning (lead with what engineers care about)
Redwood Inference is a production-first LLM inference platform that gives platform and ML engineers consistent latency, predictable unit cost, and deployment flexibility (hosted, dedicated, private) without rebuilding the serving stack. We pair a GPU-optimized runtime (continuous batching, KV cache control, quantization profiles) with a unified control plane for routing, rollouts, and observability so teams hit latency, cost, and reliability targets faster.

2) Quick value bullets for technical audiences (elevator bullets)
- Predictable tail latency at p95/p99 via smart routing and autoscaling policies.
- 20–60% token-cost reductions on typical chat workloads by combining prefix caching and quantization profiles (customer-observed range).
- Single API and rollout model across hosted, dedicated, and private (reduces engineering maintenance).
- First-class observability: token-level cost breakdowns, per-model latency heatmaps, and prompt-set regression alerts.

3) Conversation scripts (engineer → engineer)
- Opening (discovery-focused): "Walk me through the end-to-end path from user request to model output in your app — where do you see the most variability in latency or the highest token cost today?"
- Value framing: "If you need predictable p99 latency under load and want to avoid building batching/eviction/caching logic, Redwood gives you the runtime primitives and control plane so your team can focus on product logic, not serving plumbing."
- Cost objection: "Instead of comparing MSRP, let’s model a real workload. Give me your avg tokens per request and expected qps and I’ll show a 3-way comparison (open self-host, other managed provider, Redwood Dedicated) with real unit economics."
- Vendor lock-in concern: "We expose standard model versions, can pin to specific weights, and our routing policies support seamless fallback to compatible model variants. For Private deployments, the control plane can be customer-hosted to reduce control-plane lock-in concerns."

4) Technical demo narrative (5–7 minute walkthrough)
1. Show a quick sample: REST request to Redwood API returning a streaming response.
2. Open Console: highlight per-route latency breakdown and token charge visualization.
3. Explain a rollout: canary 1% traffic -> metrics check -> auto-increment with rollback window.
4. Toggle quantization profile and show simulated cost/latency delta.
5. Show fallbacks: primary model OOMs -> auto-fallback to quantized variant with preserved output schema.

5) Competitive brief (one-paragraph takes + short table)
- MajorCloudAI: Strong on ecosystem integrations and data services; weaker in continuous-batching optimizations and observability granularity. Good fit for customers prioritizing managed MLOps beyond inference.
- ModelServeCo: Focused on self-hosted runtimes; flexible but requires substantial engineering to hit production economics at scale.
- EdgeOps: Excellent at ultra-low-latency on-device inference; less strong for centralized multi-tenant cost optimizations and rollout tooling.

Guiding principles:

- Assumptions: 1M transactions/month, require VPC + KMS + audit logs and 99.9% uptime SLA.

Customer: LexiBank (regional bank) — scenario: chatbot + document ingestion for fraud detection triage.

8) Security & compliance FAQ (designed for prospect security reviewers)
Q: What certifications and audits does Redwood maintain?
A: Redwood maintains SOC 2 Type II and is in the process of ISO 27001 certification for the control plane. For Private deployments, customers can supply their own evidence packages and we support third-party attestation reviews.

Q: How is customer data protected in transit and at rest?
A: All data in transit is TLS 1.2+; at rest data is AES-256 encrypted. For Redwood Hosted, we use provider-managed KMS with the option for customer-managed KMS (bring-your-own key). Private deployments can be configured with HSM-backed key stores.

Q: Where is customer data stored (data residency)?
A: Hosted customer data can be region-pinned to AWS/GCP regions we operate. Dedicated and Private allow explicit region control and on-prem options. We provide data retention and deletion controls per contract.

Q: What controls exist to prevent model drift and regression?

Q: Do you support customer-managed audit logs?
A: Yes — we expose detailed audit logs (API keys used, route, token counts, model versions, timestamps). For Private customers we offer a streaming audit log integration to SIEMs.

Q: What is your incident response posture?
A: We have documented IR runbooks, an on-call rotation for SRE, and an SLA-based incident escalation path for Dedicated/Private customers. We provide post-incident RCA and mitigation plans.
