[Heterogeneous Deployment Sales Brief for Technical Buyers]
Summary:
This brief equips sales and solutions engineers with a concise, deployment-focused narrative for technical buyers considering a mixed deployment strategy: combining Redwood Hosted, Redwood Dedicated (reserved capacity), and Redwood Private (VPC/on‑prem). It explains when to recommend each option, how to quantify latency and cost tradeoffs, competitive positioning vs cloud-managed endpoints, and an objection-handling playbook for compliance, reliability, and TCO concerns.

Audience:
- Platform engineers evaluating production constraints
- Security/compliance stakeholders assessing data residency and auditability
- Architects designing multi-region, mixed-capacity inference topologies

1) One-line value proposition for technical buyers:
Redwood enables predictable, low-latency LLM inference at the unit economics and operational maturity required for production — and lets you mix hosted, reserved, and private capacity at route level so your app meets SLAs without rebuilding your stack.

2) When to recommend each deployment mode (quick checklist):
- Hosted API: rapid onboarding, experimental workloads, or low-SLA features where TTV matters. Recommend when: team wants SDK-level speed-to-product (<1 day), no strict data residency, expected steady monthly usage < 200M tokens.
- Dedicated: long-running, high-throughput endpoints with predictable demand and strong isolation. Recommend when: 95th percentile latency targets are strict, predictable sustained traffic > 1M tokens/day, or contract-level SLAs required.
- Private (VPC/on-prem): highly regulated or air-gapped workloads with strict control over keys, audit trails, and network egress. Recommend when: data residency, E2E auditability, or internal governance policies forbid cloud-stored PII.

3) Concrete SLO/operational examples to use in conversations:
- Typical Hosted baseline: median latency for a 512-token generation on a Redwood-curated Llama-variant: 55–80 ms median, 95th percentile 140–220 ms (depending on region & model).
- Dedicated baseline (reserved GPU pool): 95th percentile 60–90 ms for the same workload when steady-state batching and pinned kernels are enabled.
- Private (on-prem with optimized inference stack): achievable 95th percentile 50–80 ms when matching equivalent GPU class and using Redwood’s runtime.
- Availability SLOs: Dedicated customers often purchase 99.9% SLA with automatic failover policies; Hosted is covered by best-effort SLOs and visibility dashboards.

4) Pricing stanzas and example scenarios (talking points; use formal quote for commitments):
- Hosted: list-style per-token pricing (example anchor): $0.012 per 1k prompt tokens + $0.015 per 1k generation tokens for LLM-x family. Example: 1M prompt + 2M gen tokens/month -> ~$45/month.
- Dedicated: base reservation + usage multiplier. Example: 8-GPU reserved cluster $18k/month + usage add-on $0.006 per 1k tokens beyond baseline. For predictable high-volume customers, Dedicated typically reduces per-token unit cost by 40–70% vs Hosted.
- Private: platform licensing + installation and support (one-time setup + annual maintenance). Example: 1x rack on-prem bundle $120k initial + $35k/year support; per-token costs modeled on GPU utilization and ops.
- Hybrid recommendations: show blended TCO for migration phases (pilot on Hosted, steady-state on Dedicated, controlled PII routes on Private). Use a 12-month model: estimate 6 months Hosted pilot then 6 months Dedicated ramp.

5) Competitive brief (neutral language) — common competitors and positioning points:
- Competitor A (large cloud vendor managed endpoints):
  - Strengths: deep cloud integration, single-bill simplicity.
  - Redwood counter: our runtime and routing policies reduce per-token cost under bursty traffic by 20–50% via batching and KV caching; we provide a unified API across deployment modes so migration and governance are simpler.
- Competitor B (self-hosted inference vendors):
  - Strengths: tight on-prem control, appeal to infra teams.
  - Redwood counter: we combine on-prem packages with a managed control plane option, reducing ops burden while preserving audit/logging and KMS integrations.
- Competitor C (LLM API providers focused on simplicity):
  - Strengths: easy developer UX and fast iteration.
  - Redwood counter: we match developer ergonomics while adding route-level policies, cost controls, and performance predictability required for production.

6) Objection handling (scenarios and short scripts):
- "We can just use the cloud provider's model endpoints."
  - Response: "Cloud endpoints are convenient, but for production economics and predictable latency under bursty load, Redwood’s runtime and routing reduce per-token costs and guardrails (batching, prefix cache, kernel tuning) that cloud endpoints do not expose. We’ll run a 2-week pilot and show per-token delta and 95th latency graphs."
- "We need absolute data residency and no control plane exposure."
  - Response: "Redwood Private supports a customer-controlled control plane in a VPC or fully air-gapped on-prem package with KMS/HSM integrations and local audit logging. We will map the data flows, provide architecture diagrams, and run a compliance checklist with your security team."
- "We don’t want vendor lock-in for model formats."
  - Response: "Redwood serves common open checkpoints and supports model version pinning and exports of model artifacts and KV cache snapshots. Migration paths are part of the Dedicated contract and private deployment runbook."

7) Pitch deck outline (single-slide bullets for rapid customization):
- Slide 1: Customer challenge — inconsistent latency, unpredictable token spend, compliance constraints.
- Slide 2: Redwood approach — unified runtime + routing + mixed deployments.

  - A: By default, minimal telemetry is stored for billing and analytics. Customers can opt-out of retention or move sensitive routes to Dedicated/Private where logs are retained per customer policy.

[introduce KV freelist defragmenter and selective hot-prefix pinning]
description:
Motivation: under high-concurrency, the paged KV cache freelist would fragment after repeated allocations/frees of mixed-size blocks, increasing allocation latency and causing more frequent slow-path compaction. This PR adds an opportunistic freelist defragmenter that compacts adjacent free pages on free-paths and a lightweight hot-prefix selective pinning policy so frequently-accessed key prefixes avoid costly eviction. Goals: reduce p99 allocation latency, lower background compaction pressure, and improve tail latency for workloads with hot prefixes (chat sessions, long contexts).

Summary of changes:
- Opportunistic freelist defragmenter run inline on frees when a small threshold of contiguous free segments is observed (configurable).
- Compact-on-free path that coalesces adjacent free pages into larger blocks to improve reuse for larger token sequences.
- Adaptive reuse scoring: tracks short-term reuse frequency per page bucket and prefers reuse of high-score pages.
- Hot-prefix selective pinning: a small resident pin set for top-N hot key prefixes with LRU eviction; pins are persisted across ephemeral reconnects to stabilize performance.
- Scheduler hint: allocator exposes a gentle backpressure hint to the request scheduler when fragmentation crosses configured thresholds so the scheduler can delay batch growth and avoid thrashing.
- Tests and microbenchmarks: new unit tests for defragmenter invariants and a throughput/latency benchmark demonstrating behavior across workload mixes.

Compatibility: fully opt-in via runtime config flags (defaults are conservative).

Checklist:
- [x] Design doc linked in PR
- [x] Unit tests
- [x] Microbenchmark
- [x] CI green after flake fix
- [x] Perf measurements attached

Related tickets: Linear ENG-4823 (KV fragmentation), ENG-4781 (hot-prefix regressions).

[temporal-affinity-refill-and-scavenger-for-paged-kv]
description:
Summary: Introduces a temporal-affinity driven refill strategy and a light-weight scavenger for the paged KV cache to reduce tail latency in continuous-batching workloads. The change combines a small per-block temporal score, a refill iterator that biases reuse toward recently accessed neighborhoods, and a background scavenger that reclaims cold blocks in low-contention phases.

Motivation: production traces showed frequent cold-evictions followed by immediate re-loads in chat-heavy workloads (p95 token latency spikes during bursty sessions). Existing LRU-like eviction was brittle under small working sets per shard; this PR aims to reduce re-fetch churn and improve p95 latency while keeping allocation fast and allocator lock contention low.

Design:
- Temporal affinity score: each block maintains a u8 score incremented on reuse and decayed on periodic ticks. Score affects refill priority but is cheap to read/write (atomic u8 ops).
- Refill iterator: when a request misses, the allocator first probes the local page neighborhoods ordered by temporal score to prefer reuse of recently-warmed blocks (improves KV cache hit-locality for streaming sessions).
- Scavenger thread: a low-priority background worker scans age-buckets and coalesces contiguous cold blocks for efficient reclamation. It only runs when heap pressure is below a configurable threshold to avoid interfering with latency-sensitive fast-paths.
- Fast-path admit/evict: a non-blocking admit path reserves a hot-slot for short windows to avoid ABA churn when multiple fibers are refilling the same keys. Contention fallback uses a short spin-and-yield policy.

Compatibility: no changes to on-disk layout or RPCs; config knobs exposed via runtime flags for decay interval and scavenger thresholds.

Checklist:
- [x] Design doc (ENG-1987) and bench plan (ENG-2045)
- [x] Unit tests for refill iterator determinism
- [x] Stress test under continuous-batching harness
- [x] Benchmarks added and stable
- [x] Docs notes describing knobs and migration considerations

Testing and results:
- Unit and integration tests: all passing locally and in CI.
- Benchmarks (kv_batch_bench): p95 generation latency reduced by 18% on a 4-GPU dedicated worker under synthetic chat sessions with 60s bursts. Tail behavior improved: p99 reduced by ~12%.
- Memory churn: observed working set re-loads reduced by ~22% in flamegraphs; CPU overhead of scavenger measured at <1% on average.

Risks and mitigations:
- Increased metadata (per-block score): limited to +1 byte per block; accounted for in allocator sizing.
- Scavenger interfering with latency: runs only when allocator free-pages > threshold and its work budget is capped per tick.
- Contention on fast-path: fallback path in allocator uses adaptive backoff.

Commits: see commit list above.

Changed areas (high-level):
- src/kv/paged_cache.rs: adds temporal score field, refill iterator, and a small API for score bump/decay.
- src/kv/allocator.rs: fast-path admit/evict reservation logic and contention fallback.
- src/kv/scavenger.rs: new lightweight background worker and config.
- bench/kv_batch_bench.rs: synthetic harness to reproduce bursty chat sessions and measure p95/p99.
- tests/kv_refill_test.rs: deterministic scenarios for refill and eviction ordering.
- docs/notes/kv-refill.md: operational guidance and recommended knob values.

- Ethan Park: "How does this interact with cross-shard routing?" Author: "Refill iterator is per-shard and doesn't change routing semantics; added a test for cross-shard misses."

[Dynamic slot reclaimer and smooth evictor adapter for fragmentation mitigation]
description:
Motivation: Production clusters observed increased KV cache fragmentation under mixed-length sessions, causing frequent small-page spills and uneven memory pressure between tenants. This PR introduces a runtime-side fragmentation sensor and a graded (smooth) eviction adapter that cooperates with the scheduler and continuous-batching layer to reduce tail latency and spill frequency.

What changed (high level): added a low-cost fragmentation sensor that tracks free-slot distribution and local occupancy variance per arena; implemented a dynamic slot reclaimer that opportunistically coalesces adjacent free slots without global stops-the-world compactions; introduced a graded eviction adapter that smooths eviction aggressiveness based on sensor signals and tenant pressure; added anticipatory paging hints so the kernel-selection layer can prefer compact-friendly layouts during hot sequences; exposed metrics and tracing to the console for visibility.

Checklist: [x] unit tests for sensor heuristics, [x] e2e perf harness against perf-canary workload, [x] migration path for existing allocator configs, [x] docs draft for console and ops runbook, [x] feature-flag gating for staged rollout.

Commit summary (single-string list below):
- Add fragmentation sensor (runtime/kv/frag_sensor.rs) and related metrics
- Implement DynamicSlotReclaimer with gentle coalescing pass (runtime/kv/reclaimer.go)
- GradedEvictorAdapter: translate sensor signals to eviction windows (runtime/kv/evictor_adapter.cc)
- Hook anticipatory paging hints into kernel selector (runtime/compilation/kernels.go)
- Integrate with continuous-batching to avoid batch amplification during reclaim passes (runtime/batching/controller.py)
- Tests, benchmarks, documentation and feature-flag gating

Files/areas changed (high level): runtime/kv/{frag_sensor.rs,reclaimer.go,evictor_adapter.cc}, runtime/compilation/kernels.go, runtime/batching/controller.py, observability/metrics/kv_frag_metrics.yaml, docs/ops/kv-reclamation.md, tests/perf/cluster_fragmentation_test.sh. No API surface changes to user-facing inference API.

Benchmarks: On the perf-canary mixed-length session trace (p99 tokens per second workload) we saw: 12% reduction in p99 latency for generation endpoints, 18% fewer spill-to-disk events under sustained 85% resident memory, and a 7% improvement in end-to-end token throughput due to reduced fragmentation-induced requeuing. Microbenchmarks show the sensor adds <0.8% CPU at steady state.

Rollout plan: gated behind feature flag kv.gradedEvictor. Canary rollout to two Dedicated regions for 3 days, monitor kv_frag_score, spill_rate, batch_latency. If regressions discovered, auto-fallback to previous evictor policy (built into adapter).

Related work: follows up on ENG-2145 (observation telemetry) and complements ENG-2210 (batching-scheduler co-op).

[Granular slot defragmenter and stable spill handoff for KV cache]
description:
Motivation: reduce long-tail latency and memory fragmentation observed on multi-tenant KV cache under mixed sequence-length workloads. This change introduces a lightweight granular slot defragmenter that compacts small free slots within hot segments without global stop-the-world passes and a stable spill handoff mechanism to reduce jitter when multiple tenants trigger spill simultaneously. The defragmenter runs opportunistically during low CPU utilization windows and is placement-aware so it avoids interrupting active continuous batching kernels. The spill handoff guarantees an ordered, per-tenant spill queue that prevents oscillation between eviction and rehydration under bursty workloads. Changes: 1) new slot_defragmenter module that tracks slot usage at ~64B granularity and performs local compaction when free-slot fragmentation exceeds a threshold; 2) soft-quota-aware eviction path that prefers reclaiming subsegment holes before evicting whole entries; 3) stable_spill coordinator that serializes spill initiation per-tenant and provides a backpressure token to the scheduler; 4) small scheduler hook in batch_router so continuous batching kernels can opt-out of compaction windows when latency SLOs are tight; 5) observability additions: metrics for fragmentation_ratio, compaction_cycles, spill_handoff_rate and tenant_spill_latency histogram; 6) integration tests and microbenchmarks comparing end-to-end tail latency and token cost. Commits summary: [a1b2c3d] introduce slot_defragmenter scaffolding and unit tests; [b2c3d4e] implement compaction algorithm and integration with cache allocator; [c3d4e5f] add stable_spill coordinator and per-tenant queues; [d4e5f6a] scheduler hook and continuous-batching opt-out path; [e5f6a7b] docs, metrics, and benchmarks. Files changed (high level): internal/kv/cache/slot_defragmenter.rs - new module with compaction loop and heuristics; internal/kv/allocator/soft_quota_reclaimer.cc - changes to prefer slot coalescing; internal/kv/evictor/stable_spill.go - new coordinator and tests; internal/scheduler/batch_router.cpp - opt-out hook and minor APIs; docs/kv/defrag.md - design notes and operator guidance; tests/kv/defrag_integration_test.go - multi-tenant scenarios; benchmarks/kv/slot_vacancy_bench.yaml - benchmark harness; tools/observability/kv_metrics_exports.yaml - prometheus metric exports. [KV: fragmentation-aware reclamation and prioritized spill policy]
description:
Motivation: In long-running nodes we observed slow memory growth and suboptimal eviction choices caused by fragmentation and size-skewed items. This PR implements a fragmentation-aware reclamation strategy plus a prioritized spill policy to reduce tail latency when the KV cache needs to free pages. [model-catalog: add filters, compatibility flags, and pricing/limits fields to /models API]
description:
Summary: Adds richer filtering and capability metadata to the public model catalog endpoints. This PR introduces query filters for capability-based discovery and model attributes, plus explicit compatibility flags and first-class pricing/limits fields on model descriptors. Motivation: customers have asked for a machine-readable way to pick models by capability (e.g., tool-calling, structured output, streaming-stable) and to programmatically surface cost/limit information for routing and billing. The current /models response is sparse and requires ad-hoc parsing of descriptions in downstream services. What this changes: 1) API surface: GET /v1/models now accepts new query params: 'capability' (comma-separated values: chat, completion, embedding, tool_calling, structured_output, streaming), 'openai_compat' (true|false), 'pricing_tier' (free|standard|premium), and 'min_max_tokens' (min,max). Example: GET /v1/models?capability=tool_calling,structured_output&openai_compat=true 2) Response schema additions: each model object gains optional fields: 'capabilities' (string[]), 'compatibility_flags' (string[]; e.g. "openai_chat", "openai_completion", "openai_embeddings"), 'pricing' (object with flat_rate, per_token_input_usd, per_token_output_usd, currency), and 'limits' (object: max_tokens, max_requests_per_minute, concurrent_requests). These are optional to preserve backwards compatibility; existing clients will continue to work if they ignore new fields. 3) OpenAI compatibility adapter: adapter maps compatibility_flags to legacy OpenAI-style fields for the OpenAI compatibility layer. Added translation layer so openai_compat=true returns aliases expected by older clients. 4) Server-side indexing: index added for capability tags to keep catalog query latency within SLOs (see perf notes below). 5) Docs & SDK: OpenAPI spec updated, python/ts SDKs surface the new fields and query helpers. Compatibility/migration notes: fields are additive and optional; no required fields were changed. The only risk is downstream code that relies on the previous string parsing of model descriptions — we've added an integration test and a migration note in docs. Rollout plan: staged rollout with feature flag 'model_catalog_caps_v1'; default enabled for beta accounts and disabled for strict compat customers. Monitoring: new metrics added: model_catalog.filter_latency_ms, model_catalog.cache_hit_rate, and pricing_field_populated_ratio. Related: Linear ENG-1729 (catalog filter work), PM-404 (pricing requirements). Checklist: - [x] API schema and OpenAPI docs updated - [x] Server implementation of filters and response enrichment - [x] OpenAI compatibility adapter translation layer - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] SDK updates (python + ts) - [x] Perf benchmark added to benchmark-lab - [x] Docs + release notes Notes: see inline snippets below for example response and query. Example response snippet (illustrative): {"id":"rw-mini-1","name":"rw-mini","capabilities":["chat","embedding"],"compatibility_flags":["openai_chat","openai_embeddings"],"pricing":{"per_token_input_usd":"0.00001","per_token_output_usd":"0.00002","currency":"USD"},"limits":{"max_tokens":"4096","max_requests_per_minute":"600","concurrent_requests":"10"}}

[Deprecate legacy capability schema; add runtime hint headers, function-call credits, and streaming degradation policy]
description:
Motivation: We have multiple downstream needs that couldn't be satisfied by the legacy model capability schema: (1) lightweight, per-request runtime hints that the routing layer and serving runtime can use without deserializing the full model profile; (2) a transparent metering knob for tool/function calling (customers asked for per-invocation crediting separate from token billing); and (3) richer guidance for streaming fallbacks so clients can degrade more gracefully when a model variant switches to a lower-throughput tier. This PR introduces three related surfaces: capability_headers, function_call_credit, and streaming_degradation_policy, alongside an OpenAI-compatible shim that surfaces structured-output hints in /v1/models list responses.

Summary of changes (high level):
- API: Add optional capability_headers map to /v1/models and /v1/models/:id responses. These are short key/value runtime hints intended for fast routing decisions (examples: "supports_prefix_cache": "true", "max_prefetch_tokens": "256").
- Catalog schema: Deprecate legacy capability_schema.v1 (kept as legacy_capabilities for migration) and introduce capability_schema.v2 that references compact headers + full capability document. Migration docs added.
- Billing: Introduce function_call_credit as a first-class optional numeric field on model profiles and endpoints. This allows the billing system to attribute cost for tool/function call ops independently; SDKs and console will display credits usage.
- Streaming: Add streaming_degradation_policy on model profiles to expose a list of ordered fallbacks and suggested partial-output tokens thresholds (helps clients decide when to switch to a summarized streaming path). Also include preferred_prefetch_hint to suggest prefix caching window.
- OpenAI compat: Update the /v1/models listing returned by the OpenAI-compat shim to include capability_headers and structured_output_hints under the "capabilities" umbrella so downstream OpenAI-compatible clients can discover behavior without touching Redwood-specific endpoints.
- Docs & SDK: Docs page describing migration, examples for reading capability_headers and consuming streaming_degradation_policy; Python and TypeScript SDK surfaces to parse new fields.

Commits (summary):
- commit 1: api: extend model list + get handlers to populate capability_headers and streaming_degradation_policy (handlers and serializers)
- commit 2: catalog: add models_v2 schema, migration script to copy legacy_capabilities into full_profile and generate default headers
- commit 3: billing: record function_call_credit into usage events and expose in billing UI (console changes)
- commit 4: sdk/docs: parse helpers and docs for migration and examples

Files changed (representative):
- src/api/handlers/models_list.go (updated serializer and OpenAI-compat shim)
- src/catalog/schemas/models_v2.json (new compact schema)
- tools/migrations/migrate_capabilities_v1_to_v2.go (migration script)
- services/billing/credits.go (add function_call_credit aggregation)
- console/src/components/model/ModelDetails.tsx (show capability headers and credits)
- sdk/python/redwood/models.py (new fields + helper parser)
- docs/migrations/capability_headers_migration.md (migration and rollback guide)

Testing and validation:
- Unit tests: added for serializer and parser behavior (capability_headers omitted vs present), billing aggregation tests for function_call_credit.
- Integration: end-to-end test in perf-canary that validates streaming_degradation_policy is honored by the router under simulated capacity pressure; canary shows no increase in 95p latency on main model variants.
- Backwards compatibility: /v1/models still returns legacy_capabilities field for consumers that haven't migrated; the OpenAI-compat shim prefers capability_headers but will fall back to legacy_capabilities when capability_headers is absent.

Migration strategy & rollout:
- Stage 1 (canary): populate capability_headers from existing full capabilities via migration script; run canary for 2 days to ensure no regression in routing or billing.
- Stage 2 (gradual): expose new headers to 20% of API responses; monitor routing decisions and SDK parsing errors.
- Stage 3 (opt-in enforcement): allow customers to opt-in to strict schema validation via a console toggle (default off).
- Final: Deprecate legacy schema via announcement; grace period until 2026-06-01, after which legacy_capabilities may be removed for new write operations.

Review conversation (condensed):
- Owen Park: "Large change — please ensure migration script is idempotent and add a safety flag so we can revert on dataset problems." — Author: "Migration is idempotent; added --dry-run and --cutover flags in migrate_capabilities_v1_to_v2.go; documented in migration md."
- Lina Gomez: "Need to ensure function_call_credit can't be negative and that default is 0 where absent; also clarify how it interacts with token billing." — Author: "Validation added; billing pipeline will emit both tokens and function_call_credit events. Release notes updated to clarify pricing semantics."
- Harriet Zhao: "Does the streaming_degradation_policy open us up to oscillation if multiple routers act on hints?" — Author: "Router change includes a small randomized jitter and a dead-time to prevent oscillation; added comment in routing code and unit test."
- QA (Slack): reported one flaky test in console snapshot related to ModelDetails layout — fixed by stabilizing test data ordering in the SDK.

CI summary: initial run had lint warnings (long line in models_list.go) and one flaky integration test; both addressed in follow-up commits. Final status: all checks passed (unit, lint, integration, e2e canary). Performance canary showed stable tail latency; billing integration tests validated function_call_credit emitted for simulated tool calls.

Rollout notes for operators:
- The migration tool writes a migration_log to S3; if any migration errors occur, the --rollback flag will reverse schema updates made to the catalog DB.
- Feature gate: runtime.capability_headers (default: enabled for all API nodes in next release). If issues appear, ops can disable gate per region to return legacy behavior immediately.

Decision rationale and follow-ups:
- We intentionally kept capability_headers compact and stringly-typed to avoid heavyweight schema churn; full capabilities remain available for deep inspection and compatibility with existing tooling.
- Follow-ups: ENG-2639 to add UI visualization for streaming_degradation_policy, ENG-2670 to instrument per-function-call credit telemetry in the billing dashboard, and ENG-2692 to add a half-life cache invalidation for capability_headers to support fast rollbacks.

Merge outcome: Squash merge by Lina Gomez on 2026-02-19 after approvals from all reviewers and green CI. Release note entry drafted and scheduled for the 2026-02 minor release.

release_notes:
Add new capability header fields (capability_headers) and introduce function_call_credit metric for per-call accounting; deprecate legacy capability schema v1 with migration path; add streaming degradation policy and prefetch hint support. Non-breaking for read-only clients; write-migration recommended before 2026-06-01.

[Model catalog: add interoperability flags, streaming resilience hints, and function-call shaping]
description:
Context: Customers frequently need to discover models by how they interoperate with OpenAI-style clients (function/tool calling, strict structured output, streaming backpressure characteristics) and by practical limits (per-request tokens, tool concurrency). Motivation: expose lightweight interoperability flags and numeric hints in the model catalog so client-side shims and the openai-compat layer can make better routing/formatting decisions without a heavyweight schema migration. This PR adds: 1) new capability flags on the catalog API (tool_support, structured_output: [strict|lenient], openai_compat_level) 2) numeric hints (max_tools_concurrent, max_tokens_per_request, baseline_cost_1k_tokens, streaming_reliability_score) intended as advisory fields only 3) streaming resilience hints to suggest preferred chunking/batch sizes and fallback policies for slow consumers 4) function-call shaping metadata to help the OpenAI-compat shim choose whether to synthesize tool manifests or fallback to text-only outputs 5) query filters for listing by these capabilities (e.g., ?tool_support=true&structured_output=strict&min_streaming_reliability=0.8) Checklist: - [x] API schema additions (catalog schema + openapi docs) - [x] Listing filters and query parsing - [x] Backward-compatible behavior when flags are absent - [x] Unit tests for filtering logic and JSON schema validation - [x] Integration tests exercising openai-compat shim routing - [x] API docs + examples for SDKs - [x] Release notes Draft/Notes: This is intentionally advisory: fields are not enforced by runtime; they are hints for routing and SDK behavior. The streaming_reliability_score is a 0.0-1.0 heuristic combining observed tail-latency, chunk-drop rate, and historical reconnects; it will be refined in follow-ups. Related: RFC: internal rfc/catalog-interop-2024 (link: https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-5412/catalog-interoperability-flags), depends on ENG-5231 (streaming-slo-metrics). Migration: old clients continue to work unchanged. New query parameters are additive.

SDKs updated to surface optional fields. These fields are advisory; clients should treat them as hints, not guarantees. See docs/api/model-catalog.md for examples and migration notes.

[schema negotiation: bidirectional response_format + OpenAI-compat error mapping]
description:
Motivation: Customers building strict structured-output pipelines need predictable behavior when models stream partial tokens, when clients ask for OpenAI-compatible error codes, and when function-calling instruments interact with response_format negotiation. This PR implements bidirectional schema negotiation (client-specified response_format + runtime-augmented hints), a compact error-code mapping layer for OpenAI-compat consumers, and stream-recovery signals so callers can decide whether to retry or fallback.

What this changes at a high level: 1) ResponseFormatNegotiator: a small runtime component that takes the user-supplied response_format (json_schema, text, openai_compat) and the model capability profile and selects a streaming/strictness strategy. 2) StrictMode Opt-in Flag: new request parameter response_format.strict (opt-in) that enables hard schema validation on complete and streaming mode; violations are surfaced as structured errors rather than free-text warnings. 3) Stream Recovery Header: during streaming, when an invalid JSON chunk or schema violation is detected, the runtime emits a small control event (EVENT: schema_error) with a canonical error code and a short token cursor so clients can choose to rewind/skip or fallback to a non-strict route. 4) OpenAI-compat error mapping: new compact mapper that translates internal schema error classes to OpenAI-compatible error categories (e.g., invalid_request_error -> invalid_response_format, resource_exhausted -> model_capacity) and preserves guidance text. 5) Function-calling interplay: the negotiator now marks function call envelopes as tolerant by default unless response_format.strict=true. This avoids hard failures in common function-calling workflows while allowing strict validation for verification flows.

Changes included (summary): commits: add negotiator, add strict flag parsing in API surface, stream event plumbing, error mapper and tests, docs update, TS SDK typing for response_format, Python SDK acceptance tests, small perf tweak to streaming parser to keep latency within SLO.

Compatibility notes: - Default behavior unchanged for existing clients (strict=false by default). - OpenAI-compat explicit mode maps legacy error shapes; behavior only activates if client requests openai_compat or sets compatibility headers. - Private/Dedicated customers can pin default strictness via account config (follow-up PR in dedicated config).

Testing and rollout: unit + integration coverage added for negotiation permutations (json_schema streaming/non-streaming, text, openai_compat). End-to-end canary on perf-canary for 24h with rollback flag. Feature gated behind runtime flag `negotiator_v2` and released via canary->gradual->global rollout.

Follow-ups: - Dedicated: expose account-level default strictness and an importable policy bundle. - Observability: surfaced metric redwood.response_format.violation.count and histogram of recovery latency. - SDK ergonomics: add high-level helper to auto-handle schema_error events.

Related Linear/Jira: ENG-2024, ENG-2121, SUP-891.

Adds a negotiated response_format layer with an opt-in strict mode for JSON-schema validation during streaming; introduces schema_error streaming control events and OpenAI-compatible error mapping. Default behavior unchanged. Feature is behind a runtime flag and rolled out via canary.

[unified-capability-endpoint-and-openai-compat-shim]
description:
Motivation: Product teams need a single, queryable surface to discover model capabilities, pricing tiers, and OpenAI-compatibility hints for routing and SDK fallbacks. Current model-listing endpoints scatter hints across several fields and duplicate logic in SDK shims. This PR introduces a unified /v1/models/capabilities endpoint (and corresponding openai-compat shim enhancements) to centralize capability flags (streaming, function_calling, structured_output), pricing/limits info, regional availability, and compatibility metadata.

Summary of changes: - New API: GET /v1/models/capabilities with query filters (capabilities, region, min_qps, openai_compatible=true|false, price_tier). Responses include a standardized capability set and price/limit objects. - Backwards compatibility: existing /v1/models and /v1/models/:id behavior unchanged; clients can opt-in to the new endpoint. The OpenAI-compat layer now consults the capabilities endpoint when resolving model choice for streaming and function-calling fallbacks. - Capability flags expanded: streaming_support (bool), streaming_latency_hint ("low"|"medium"|"best-effort"), function_calling (bool), structured_output_schema (optional JSON-schema URL string), kv_cache_supported (bool). - Pricing and limits: each model listing includes price_per_1k_tokens (float string in USD), max_tokens_supported (int string), recommended_batch_size (int string), and soft_qps_limit (int string). These are advisory and used by Redwood Optimize and routing decisions. - Query filters server-side: filter_by_capabilities (comma-separated), min_price_tier, region, and openai_compatible. Filtering is implemented efficiently using the existing catalog index and a new capability inverted index populated at model onboarding time.

Checklist:
- [x] API contract defined and documented in API spec.
- [x] Server implementation with pagination and filter validation.
- [x] OpenAI-compat shim updates to prefer models that advertise matching capabilities.
- [x] Unit tests for capability parsing, filter combinators, and price/limit format validation.
- [x] Integration tests covering streaming fallback and function-calling route selection.
- [x] Docs and SDK examples updated (Python and TS quickstarts).

Backward compatibility and rollout: This change is additive. Existing clients keep current behavior. The new endpoint is gated behind a feature flag (default on in staging, opt-in in prod for first 48h) and will be rolled to all regions after monitoring. The openai-compat shim will prefer models with matching flags but will fall back to previous selection logic if no capability match is found.

API contract (excerpt): GET /v1/models/capabilities?q=filter_by_capabilities=function_calling,streaming&region=us-west-2&openai_compatible=true&page_size=50
Response shape (fields): id, name, capabilities (csv flags), streaming_support, streaming_latency_hint, function_calling, structured_output_schema, price_per_1k_tokens_usd, max_tokens_supported, recommended_batch_size, soft_qps_limit, regions (list), openai_compatible_hint. All numeric values are returned as strings for stable parsing across SDKs.

Tests and CI: Initial CI run failed lint in api/specs (minor formatting); fixed in second commit. Unit test coverage added for catalog filter combinations and migration logic. Integration tests simulate a streaming-enabled model and validate that the openai shim reroutes requests to streaming-optimized endpoints when streaming_support=true and latency_hint=low.

Documentation and SDKs: API spec markdown added under docs/api/models-capabilities.md. Python and Typescript SDKs get a small helper (get_models_by_capabilities) that calls the new endpoint and normalizes returned fields into sdk-friendly types. Quickstart example demonstrates selecting a model capable of tool/function calling and streaming simultaneously.

Security and cost notes: Pricing fields are advisory; routing decisions should always respect tenant quotas. No sensitive data added to the catalog. All catalog writes are authenticated via existing model registry ACLs.

Related tickets: ENG-1289 (catalog capability indexing), PM-452 (product requirements for model discoverability), SUP-341 (support request for clearer streaming guarantees).

Rolling to production: staged feature flag, 48h telemetry window focusing on: 1) error rate for the new endpoint, 2) percent of requests using capability-driven routing, 3) latency P95 for streaming-handshake when routed via shim.

If merged: release notes will mention the new endpoint and the SDK helper. Migration: customers using custom model-selection logic should evaluate adopting the endpoint to simplify routing and to get advisory pricing/limits in a single call.

[Compact retry adapter, typed stream iterators and SDK version pin]
description:
Motivation: multiple SDKs had divergent retry logic for ephemeral streaming requests which led to inconsistent user experiences and repeated ad-hoc fixes. This PR introduces a compact RetryAdapter library (golang + shared interface used by each SDK), exposes lightweight typed stream iterators in Python/TypeScript/Go to reduce boilerplate when consuming server-sent events, and pins the SDK packages to v1.6.0-alpha for a controlled rollout. Summary of changes (single-string description): add internal/retry adapter with configurable policy (max_attempts, base_backoff_ms, jitter, idempotency header support) and a small circuit-breaker for repeated 429/503; python: add redwood.sdk.streams.TextStream and StreamEvent typing, expose .events() async iterator and convenience .read_text() for single-message flows; typescript: add StreamEvent<T> and createStreamIterator() helper returning AsyncIterable<StreamEvent<T>>; go: add stream.IterEvent typed channel helper and NewRetryAdapter constructor used by client.StreamStart; common: update proto/stream.proto to add optional start_idempotency_key (backwards compatible), bump docs and examples; test: add unit and e2e checks covering idempotent restart, jitter distribution, and typed iterator ergonomics. Testing and rollout: CI initially failed on a flaky python streaming test, rerun fixed; canary rollout of pinned SDKs to internal prod team for 48h before wide release. Backwards compatibility: streaming start adds an optional header/field; SDK helpers are additive and do not require callers to change. Checklist: [x] unit tests added for retry adapter and iterators; [x] integration test for transient 503->recover; [x] docs updated; [x] linear tickets referenced (ENG-4127, ENG-4139).

release_notes:
Introduce compact RetryAdapter to centralize idempotent retry/backoff behavior across SDKs
Expose typed async/iterable stream helpers for safer streaming consumption in Python/TypeScript/Go
Pin SDK packages to v1.6.0-alpha to avoid transient dependency breakage during rollout
Add Idempotency-Key support on streaming-start requests to enable safe retries
No breaking API surface changes; ergonomic improvements only

[Compact reauth helpers and typed stream adapters to align ergonomics across Python/TypeScript/Go]
description:
Motivation: SDK users reported repeated friction when reauthorizing long-lived streaming sessions and when migrating examples across languages. This PR introduces a compact set of reauth helpers and small typed stream adapter layers for Python, TypeScript, and Go to achieve API ergonomics parity and reduce boilerplate. Goals: 1) Provide a minimal "credential refresher" helper that can be composed into existing stream connectors; 2) Add lightweight typed stream adapters that expose a consistent async-iterator/pull-stream surface across languages; 3) Reduce duplication in examples and make cross-language migration straightforward; 4) Bump TypeScript and Go SDK patch versions to include the adapter and helper packages. High level changes: - Py: package redwood_sdk.streaming.reauth with CredentialLease and refresh callback shim; new examples in examples/streaming/reauth_demo.py. - TS: introduce @redwood/sdk-helpers/reauth and stream-adapter async generator wrapper; update ts-sdk readme examples. - Go: add compact cred.Refresher interface and stream/adapter package with typed channel-backed iterator; small concurrency guard to avoid double-refresh. - Cross-lang: harmonize env var names and docs snippets (REDWOOD_TOKEN_TTL_HINT). Compatibility: default behavior is backward compatible; helpers are opt-in. We added a low-overhead heartbeat/lease check that will attempt reauth only when TTL drops below threshold. This PR intentionally avoids a global credential cache to keep surface area small and deterministic for Dedicated/Private deployments.

Small to medium: add helper modules in each SDK, a couple of example files, docs page, and version bumps. No changes to runtime or server-side code. Tests: new unit tests for reauth logic (py/ts/go), integration smoke test updated to exercise a credential lease refresh path.

[Unify push/pull streaming APIs across Python/TS/Go and introduce retry-shim]
description:
Motivation: multiple downstream teams reported divergent streaming semantics across SDKs (push vs pull, ownership of connection lifecycle, and subtle reauth edge cases when token rotation happens mid-stream). This PR harmonizes the observable API shape and introduces a small builtin retry-shim that standardizes reauth+backoff behavior for streaming consumers across Python, TypeScript, and Go.

Summary of changes (single continuous description): Consolidated streaming surface by defining a 'PushPullStream' conceptual model: consumers can opt-in to a push-style callback model or a pull-style iterator/async-iterator; underlying transport is shared. Added a lightweight retry-shim in each SDK that intercepts transient transport errors (401/429/5xx) and performs coordinated token refresh + exponential backoff with jitter. Python: added RedwoodStream context manager (supports with/async with) and Stream.close() for deterministic shutdown; introduced an iterator->async iterator adapter for parity. TypeScript: normalized stream consumer to return an AsyncIterable by default and provided a small pushCallback overload for compatibility; improved TypeScript generics to preserve typed events. Go: introduced PullStream interface (Next(ctx) (Event, error)) alongside an adapter to channel-based push consumers; added connection pool safety checks.

Commits summary: - 7 commits, high-level messages: unify: define push/pull stream interface across SDKs; python: add context manager and retry-shim; ts: default async iterable + push overload; go: PullStream adapter + pool fixes; ci: add cross-sdk e2e for streaming reauth; docs: add quickstart and migration notes.

Files changed (high level): src/python/redwood/stream.py, tests/python/test_stream_retry.py, src/ts/stream/index.ts, src/ts/types/stream.d.ts, src/go/stream/pullstream.go, src/go/stream/adapter.go, docs/sdks/streaming.md, examples/streaming-retry/*.md, ci/workflows/stream-e2e.yml, package.json (ts version bump), setup.cfg (python version bump), go.mod (version bump).

Implementation notes and tradeoffs: - The retry-shim is intentionally conservative: max 3 retries, base backoff 150ms, jittered, max backoff 2s. For dedicated deployments where clients manage tokens, the shim is opt-out via a client config flag. - We avoided surface breaking changes by adding small overloads and adapter helpers rather than swapping existing return types; where return types changed (TS defaulting to AsyncIterable) we provided a compatibility overload. - To minimize bundle size in the TS SDK, the shim code is tree-shakeable and split behind a small helper exported only from the streaming entrypoint.

Testing: added unit tests for reauth scenarios in all three SDKs and a cross-language e2e that runs a short-lived local test server to simulate 401 mid-stream and verifies that the shim refreshes tokens and resumes without dropping user events. CI run failed initially on flaky TS test related to backpressure simulation; I reworked the test (deterministic tick-based driver) and reran full matrix.

Merge: squash merge to main after approvals and green CI. Migration guidance is included in docs/sdks/streaming.md and examples/streaming-retry/ migration notes.

[Unify stream cursor abstraction, auth handshake, and backoff across Python/TS/Go SDKs; cross-sdk version bumps]
description:
Motivation: We have multiple inconsistent streaming iterator semantics, token-refresh handshakes, and backoff defaults across the Python, TypeScript and Go SDKs. This has caused developer confusion and subtle production bugs (lost partial messages on reconnect, token race during refresh) across customer integrations. This PR unifies the behaviour by introducing a common "StreamCursor"/iterator abstraction and standardizing the auth handshake lifecycle and retry/backoff defaults across the three SDKs.

What this PR does (high level): - Adds a StreamCursor abstraction in each SDK that provides: next()/has_next() style iteration, resume tokens for safe reconnects, and deterministic finalization to drain KV caches. - Implements a two-step auth handshake: (1) token pinning at stream open to avoid mid-stream rotation races, (2) transparent refresh callback with optimistic retry on auth failure. - Replaces per-language ad-hoc backoff constants with a shared policy: jittered exponential backoff starting at 200ms, max 8s, max retries 6 for transient stream errors. - Surfaces ergonomic helpers for common patterns: stream.to_async_iterator() in Python, stream.asyncIterable() in TS, and StreamCursor.Iter() in Go. - Updates examples, tests, and bump package versions in each SDK.

Files changed (high level): see changed_files for exact paths.

Migration notes: - Existing streaming loops that relied on the old per-chunk callback shape should switch to the StreamCursor API. Migration helpers are provided and are backwards-compatible wrappers for the most common patterns. - If you have custom token rotation, review the new refresh callback hook; handlers that mutate tokens should be idempotent and accept a context param in Go / cancellation token in TS / timeout in Python. - The default backoff is more aggressive than some client-customized configs; customers can override via the SDK config object (see examples).

Testing and QA: - Added cross-language unit and integration tests that validate partial message resume across disconnects and token rotation scenarios. - Ran full e2e matrix on linux/arm and linux/x86, and verified memory profiles for long-running streams. - Security scan: no new secrets; auth handshake code reviewed by security.

Checklist: - [x] Python implementation + tests + docs - [x] TypeScript implementation + tests + docs - [x] Go implementation + tests + docs - [x] Migration guides updated - [x] Bumped package versions and changelogs - [x] CI green (see ci_checks)

Related: ENG-3412 (stream reliability), ENG-3571 (sdk ergonomics), SUP-9182 (customer incident tied to token rotation).

release_notes:
Unified stream cursor API across Python/TS/Go, consistent auth handshake and exponential backoff defaults; ergonomics improvements for streaming loops; bumped SDK versions: python 2.8.0, typescript 1.12.0, go 0.9.0. No runtime-breaking changes expected; minor API surface tweaks documented in migration notes.

[SDK Error UX and API-to-SDK Mapping Guide]
Summary:
This page codifies Redwood's recommended error taxonomy, message surface, and example mappings from HTTP API errors to SDK-level exceptions and developer-facing messages. It is a single-source reference for SDK authors, docs writers, and the docs-site team so that error behavior is consistent across official SDKs, examples, and quickstarts.

Goals:
- Provide a small, pragmatic taxonomy developers can rely on when building integrations.
- Ensure SDK surface areas map to actionable, localized error strings and structured fields for programmatic handling.
- Describe rollout steps for changing error shapes and for adding new codes.

Scope and audience:
- Applies to all Redwood public REST/JSON endpoints and official SDKs maintained in the monorepo (python, node, go).
- Audience: SDK engineers, docs authors, developer experience (DX) maintainers, and support engineers.

Principles (high level):
1) Keep error surface minimal: stable numeric code, stable machine-readable field, human-friendly message.
2) Separate transient vs permanent failures: SDKs should expose retry hints and idempotency markers.
3) Preserve raw payload in logs for support; present sanitized message to users.
4) Do not rely on free-text parsing: prefer enumerated codes and structured metadata.

Error taxonomy (canonical list):
- INVALID_REQUEST (400) — client payload issues (missing param, invalid schema).
- AUTH_FAILED (401|403) — auth/permission problems.
- RATE_LIMIT (429) — quota exceeded or burst throttling.
- MODEL_UNAVAILABLE (503) — requested model variant not available on this region/capacity tier.
- TIMEOUT (504) — gateway or inference timeout.
- PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE (413) — input exceeds configured limits.
- INTERNAL_ERROR (500) — non-deterministic server-side errors.
- DEPENDENCY_ERROR (502) — third-party or infra dependency failure.

Recommended API error JSON shape (stable contract):
{
  "error": {
    "code": "RATE_LIMIT",
    "message": "Rate limit exceeded: seen 120 requests/min for key",
    "details": { "retry_after": 30, "namespace": "generation", "request_id": "rwd_abcdef123" },
    "hint": "backoff_exponential"
  }
}
Notes on fields:
- code (string): enumerated value, machine-consumable.
- message (string): short, actionable, safe for display.
- details (object): optional key/value map; SDKs should expose whitelisted detail keys.
- hint (string): optional retry/behavior hint: none | backoff_exponential | no_retry | try_alternate_model

SDK mapping guidance (examples):
- Python SDK exception model (recommended):
  class RedwoodError(Exception):
      code: str
      message: str
      retry_after: Optional[int]
      request_id: Optional[str]

  # Usage examples (pseudocode)
  try:
      client.generate(...)
  except RateLimitError as e:
      # e.retry_after is present when API provides 'retry_after'
      sleep(e.retry_after or default_backoff)
  except InvalidRequestError as e:
      # Surface the validation errors in-line in UI forms
      raise UserVisibleError(e.message)

- JavaScript/TypeScript SDK pattern (recommended):
  type RedwoodError = { code: string; message: string; details?: Record<string, any>; }
  class ApiError extends Error { constructor(public payload: RedwoodError) { super(payload.message); } }

Canonical mappings (table):
- API code => SDK exception class => Default SDK behavior => DX message guidance
- INVALID_REQUEST => InvalidRequestError => throw; no automatic retry => "Check request fields or schema; see validation hints."
- AUTH_FAILED => AuthError => throw; attach auth diagnostics (token expiry) => "Authentication failed. Check API key/scopes."
- RATE_LIMIT => RateLimitError => expose retry_after; SDK default: exponential backoff with jitter => "Rate limit hit: retry in Xs or reduce concurrency."
- MODEL_UNAVAILABLE => ModelUnavailableError => surface fallback options (if configured) => "Model unavailable in this region; try an alternative model or region."

Docs site UX guidance (for error messages shown in examples and quickstarts):
- Always show the SDK high-level phrase plus the code in monospace: e.g., Error: RateLimitError (RATE_LIMIT)
- Never paste raw full server stack traces into public docs. Use sanitized request_id for support lookups.
- Provide copy-pasteable troubleshooting steps below each example snippet.

Telemetry and observability knobs (what SDKs should emit):
- emit_event('sdk.error', { code, retry_after, request_id, model, region, http_status })
- attach sample request hash for sampling (do not emit full prompt content unless user consent/PII scrubbed)
- tag events with "sdk_version" and "platform" (python/node/go)

Testing and QA checklist for changes to error shapes or codes (must be executed before doc-site updates):
1) API contract test in integration pipeline: assert error JSON contains code and message for each failing scenario.
2) SDK unit tests: verify exception class, error fields mapping, and retry behavior.
3) Docs examples smoke tests: the quickstart snippets should demonstrate both success and one canonical failure with sanitized output.
4) Observability: confirm telemetry event emitted for failure.
5) Support runbook update: add sample search queries for request_id.

Rollout procedure for adding or renaming an error code (step-by-step):
1) Create ADR in eng-developer-experience/decision-records with motivation and backward-compatibility plan.
2) Add new code to API schema and include in integration contract tests (feature flagged).
3) Implement SDK mapping in all official SDKs behind minor version bump.
4) Publish docs-site draft showing new error and sample handling.
5) Run coordinated canary: enable feature flag for 5% of traffic for 48 hours and monitor error telemetry and support noise.
6) Remove feature flag and roll to general availability after signoff.

Canonical fixes and support playbook (top patterns):
- Symptom: 429/RateLimit for bursty traffic. Fix: add concurrency limiter + client-side queue + exponential backoff; surfacing retry_after makes automated retry safer.
- Symptom: 401/403 after token rotation. Fix: ensure token refresh pipeline updates SDK credentials atomically; validate token scopes in integration tests.
- Symptom: 503/ModelUnavailable in prod region. Fix: configure route policy to fallback to compatible model variant and notify oncall via pager.
- Symptom: 413 Payload too large in batch jobs. Fix: implement client-side chunking with size heuristic and expose per-request token usage in UI.

- API contract and runtime owner: eng-serving-runtime (lead: Jasmine Li)

[SDK Templates, API Examples, and Support Playbook for Developer Experience]
Purpose:
Provide a single, practical reference for SDK quickstarts, canonical API examples, docs-site operating procedures, and the top support issue patterns with reproducible fixes. This doc is aimed at DX engineers, SDK maintainers, support engineers, and on-call SREs who triage developer-facing problems.

Scope:
- Minimal production-ready quickstart templates (Node and Python)
- SDK authoring and versioning guidelines for consistent developer expectations
- Example API usage patterns (batching, streaming, embeddings, fallback routing) with curl and pseudo-SDK snippets
- Docs site operating runbook: preview, CI, content linting, and emergency rollback
- Top 10 support issue patterns and canonical fixes with commands and observability checks

Audience:
- Developer experience engineers
- SDK maintainers and technical writers
- Support and SRE engineers who escalate developer-facing issues

1) Quickstart templates (production-focused)
A. Node (TypeScript) - minimal server pattern with retry and batching
Steps to get started:
1. Install: npm install @redwood/inference-sdk axios
2. Create an express proxy that forwards requests, enforces per-user rate limits, and batches short sequences for cost savings.

Example index.ts:
```ts
import express from 'express'
import Redwood from '@redwood/inference-sdk'
const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY })
const app = express()
app.use(express.json())
app.post('/gen', async (req, res) => {
  const { prompts } = req.body // expect array of short prompts
  // Batching: group by model and max_tokens to reduce overhead
  const resp = await client.generateBatch({ model: 'redwood-1.4', prompts, max_tokens: 64, timeout_ms: 5000 })
  res.json(resp)
})
app.listen(3000)
```
Operational notes:
- Set timeout_ms to 3x the 95th-percentile token latency observed in dashboards.
- Use generateBatch when prompts.length >= 2 to reduce per-token unit cost.
- Add a circuit-breaker metric that trips after 5 timeouts/minute per route.

B. Python - lightweight CLI helper and streaming consumer
Install: pip install redwood-inference-sdk
Example stream_consumer.py:
```py
from redwood import RedwoodClient
client = RedwoodClient(api_key="${REDWOOD_API_KEY}")
with client.stream_generate(model='redwood-1.4', prompt='Summarize: ...') as stream:
    for chunk in stream:
        # write to websocket or SSE to browser
        print(chunk, end='')
```
Operational notes:
- Prefer streaming for UX-sensitive endpoints (chat) to reduce perceived latency.
- Implement idempotency tokens for retries on non-streaming endpoints.

2) SDK authoring & versioning guidelines
- Semver for SDKs: follow MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Breaking API surface changes increment MAJOR only.
- Release cadence: patch releases for bugfixes within 72 hours of merge; minor releases for new features every 2–4 weeks; major releases planned (RFC + migration guide).
- Compatibility matrix (example):
  - redwood-1.x runtime: SDK v1.x supported (no guaranteed wire compatibility with SDK v2.x)
  - redwood-2.x runtime: requires SDK v2.x or compatibility shim
- Test matrix must include: Node 16/18, Python 3.9/3.11, major Linux distributions used by customers.
- QA: include an end-to-end smoke test that calls the hosted sandbox model with a deterministic prompt and checks embedding length/hash to detect regressions.

3) API examples and patterns
A. Batching example (REST curl):
```bash
curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate/batch \n  -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" \n  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \n  -d '{"model":"redwood-1.4","prompts":["Explain DNS","List best practices for caching"],"max_tokens":80}'
```
B. Streaming example (curl with SSE):
```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" -N \n  "https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate/stream?model=redwood-1.4&prompt=Generate%20a%20summary"
```
C. Embeddings usage (pseudo-Python):
```py
emb = client.embeddings.create(input=['a','b','c'], model='embed-small')
# Use cosine similarity indexing; store vectors in vector DB with metadata: model, sha256(prompt_template), created_at
```
D. Fallback routing policy example (config snippet):
```
route: /generate
policies:
  - name: low-latency
    order: 1
    match: { priority: latency }
    actions:
      - try_model: redwood-lowlatency-quant
      - fallback: redwood-standard
```

4) Docs site operating procedures (docs-site ops runbook)
A. Content pipeline overview:
- Authors push markdown or Confluence-flavored content to docs repo under /content.
- CI: run content-lint -> accessibility checks -> link-checker -> build preview site with Gatsby/Next.
- Preview URLs: PR previews are generated and posted to the PR with a 7-day retention.
- Merging to main triggers canonical build and a staged rollout to the public docs CDN.

B. CI commands (example):
- Local preview: npm run docs:dev
- Run lint + accessibility: npm run docs:lint && npm run docs:a11y
- Force rebuild (if caches stuck): npm run docs:clean && npm run docs:build

C. Emergency rollback:
1. If a release contains a critical regression (broken code examples, 500s for API examples), open the docs rollback PR template.
2. Revert the offending merge commit and trigger docs CI.
3. If CDN still serving stale broken content, purge CDN cache with the admin tool (ops/docsite/purge) and notify comms.

D. Localization notes:
- Keep the canonical English source in /content/en. Localized branches should reference the English doc id and include a translator metadata header.

5) Top support issues & canonical fixes (ranked by frequency)
Each issue below includes: symptom, likely root cause, immediate mitigation, permanent fix, dashboard signals to monitor, and sample commands.

Issue 1 — API key permission error (401)\- Symptom: SDK calls return 401 for all endpoints for a user\- Root cause: API key scoped to embeddings-only or expired rotation policy\- Immediate mitigation: Ask customer to generate a new key via Console or rotate key in secret store\- Permanent fix: Update onboarding flow to validate token scopes at creation and add an integration test that exercises text generation endpoints\- Observability: 401 spike in auth.errors (per-minute)\- Commands: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" https://api.redwood.ai/v1/models to validate scopes

Issue 2 — Large-batch latency spikes and OOMs\- Symptom: Dedicated pools see OOMs or >99th latency spikes when customers send large single-request token counts\- Root cause: Unbounded max_tokens + uncoordinated client-side batching\- Mitigation: Implement server-side request size limit and per-request token cap of 4096 with informative 413 response\- Permanent: Update SDKs to auto-split oversized prompts and provide a guidance doc for prompt chunking\- Observability: GPU memory pressure and OOM count metric on serving nodes

Issue 3 — Streaming truncated mid-response (client disconnect)\- Symptom: UX shows responses cut off after a short chunk\- Root cause: Client-side HTTP timeout or intermediary proxy (NGINX) idle timeout\- Mitigation: Instruct clients to set keepalive and socket timeouts to >60s for chat streams\- Permanent: Add header X-Request-Streaming: true and advertise recommended proxy configs in SDKs

Issue 4 — Mismatched embeddings across SDK versions\- Symptom: Customer complains that vector search results changed after SDK upgrade\- Root cause: Default preprocessing/tokenization changed in minor SDK release\- Mitigation: Provide a compatibility endpoint that returns embedding metadata including preprocessing hash\- Permanent fix: Require an embeddings-compatibility test in the CI and add a changelog warning for preprocessing changes

Issue 5 — Docs examples stale (broken curl URLs)\- Symptom: New users copy curl from docs and receive 404/410\- Root cause: Mismatched example hostnames between staging and prod or missing redirect rule\- Mitigation: Hotfix docs examples to use canonical host variable ({{API_HOST}}) and regenerate previews\- Permanent fix: Enforce link-check CI gate that fails on absolute hostnames in examples

Issue 6 — SDK install fails on specific Linux distro (glibc mismatch)\- Symptom: pip wheel install fails with manylinux tag error\- Root cause: Binary wheels built for older glibc; no universal wheel provided\- Mitigation: Provide source wheel fallback with pip install --no-binary :all: redwood-inference-sdk\- Permanent: Rebuild wheels on the CI matrix including musl/manylinux variants and publish platform tags

Issue 7 — Rate-limiting misconfiguration (429s early in rollout)\- Symptom: Customers experience 429 for low QPS after migrating routes to new gateway\- Root cause: Gateway default rate-limit policy applied before client token tier mapping\- Mitigation: Temporarily lift gateway rate-limit for rollout cohort and monitor tokens_used per-minute\- Permanent: Add a canary policy that rejects only when token tier is resolved to avoid cascading 429s

Issue 8 — Incorrect content-type encoding in SDK-generated requests\- Symptom: API returns 415 or body parsing errors\- Root cause: SDK used application/json; charset=utf-8 inconsistent with server expectations for certain endpoints\- Mitigation: Patch SDK to explicitly set Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8 for endpoints expecting JSON\- Permanent: Add contract tests between SDK and mock server validating headers and content types

Issue 9 — Model alignment/regression alerts fired erroneously\- Symptom: quality-monitoring alerts flagged for minor punctuation differences\- Root cause: Evaluation prompt set too brittle; thresholds too tight\- Mitigation: Escalate to Eval team to add robust fuzzy-match rules and lower false-positive thresholds by 30%\- Permanent: Add semantic similarity checks (embedding-based) to verdict pipeline

Issue 10 — Local dev preview fails to render examples with private-assets\- Symptom: Authoring preview 500s when fetching private example images/snippets\- Root cause: CI preview runner not authenticated to internal assets bucket\- Mitigation: Make preview fall back to placeholder assets and warn authors in preview UI\- Permanent: Add short-lived preview credentials injected via GitHub Actions secrets scoped to PR builds

6) Troubleshooting playbook (triage flow)
- Step 0: Reproduce locally using latest SDK pinned to the version reported by customer. Capture request/response including headers and body size.
- Step 1: Check metrics: auth.errors, request.latency.p95, gpu.ooms, streaming.disconnects. Timebox 15 minutes.
- Step 2: If server-side, capture a trace id from customer request and use trace → span logs to find failing node.
- Step 3: If SDK-related, run compatibility smoke scripts in /infra/smoketests/sdk against sandbox.
- Step 4: If docs-related, check the PR preview URL and run link-checker locally.
- Step 5: Escalate to owner_team with summary: reproducible? steps? trace_id? recent deploys?

7) Ownership, SLAs, and escalation contacts
- DX SDK owner: @maya (Maya Lin) — primary for SDK/quickstart issues
- Docs site ops owner: @diego (Diego Morales) — preview infra, CDN, localization
- Oncall escalation: eng-sre oncall channel (#eng-sre-oncall) for production regressions
- Expected TTR for P1 developer-facing regression: 4 hours initial response, 24 hours resolver plan

8) Templates & checklists (use in PRs and runbooks)
- SDK release PR checklist: compatibility tests, e2e smoke, changelog entry, migration guide if breaking
- Docs PR checklist: preview link, link-checker green, code sample execution smoke (where possible), localization stub for translated docs

9) Change log (selected updates)
- 2025-11-03: initial consolidation of SDK quickstarts and playbook (created)
- 2026-02-14: added top-10 support issues, docs CI rollback steps, and streaming proxy recommendations (updated)

Appendix: Useful commands and debug shortcuts
- Verify model list & token scopes: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" https://api.redwood.ai/v1/models
- Rebuild docs preview locally: npm run docs:clean && npm run docs:dev
- Example to check embedding preprocessing metadata: curl https://api.redwood.ai/v1/embeddings/metadata?model=embed-small -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY"

If you have additions or new recurring issues, please file a ticket in the DX backlog and tag the doc for review.


[Developer Tooling SDK Onboarding Playbook]
Overview

This playbook provides a single, opinionated onboarding path for engineers integrating Redwood SDKs (Python/Node/Go) and the hosted API. It combines quickstart templates, a CI/CD checklist, docs-site operational notes, and canonical fixes for the most frequent support issues. The goal is to reduce time-to-first-success from hours to minutes and to surface deterministic troubleshooting steps for support.

Audience

- New SDK integrators (frontend/backend engineers)
- Solutions engineers doing customer demos
- Developer experience (DevX) on-call and docs maintainers

Prerequisites

1) Redwood account with API key and a default project.
2) Local development environment with Docker (optional) and language runtimes: Python 3.10+, Node 18+, Go 1.20+.
3) Access to the Docs Site repo (confluence/docs-site) for template edits.

Quickstart templates included

- Minimal Python generator (fast path)
- Chat sample in Node (streaming + function-calling demo)
- Embeddings pipeline (Go) with vector store examples
- CI smoke test YAML for GitHub Actions

Each template lives in the DX templates repo; use these commands to clone and run locally:

1) git clone git@github.com:redwood/devx-templates.git
2) cd devx-templates/sdk/onboarding/minimal-python
3) python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
4) pip install -r requirements.txt
5) export REDWOOD_API_KEY=your_key_here && python demo.py

SDK integration checklist (fast path)

Follow these steps when publishing a new integration or modifying SDK surface area:

1) Local dev: run template demo and unit tests.
   - Expected: demo returns non-empty text within 2s for a short prompt.
2) Linting & type checks: run mypy/tsc/gofmt.
3) CI smoke: add job that runs the demo against a sandbox key.
4) Docs: add a short how-to page on the docs site using the docs-site template (see Docs Site Operating Notes).
5) Telemetry: ensure SDK emits metrics for requests, errors, and token usage (see telemetry example below).
6) Release: create changelog entry and increment SDK version per semver.
7) Post-release: schedule a canary test in staging for 48 hours.

Canonical fixes for top support issues

Issue: SDK returns 401 / unauthorized
- Symptom: "401 Unauthorized" from the first API call.
- Quick triage steps:
  1) Confirm REDWOOD_API_KEY is set in environment (echo $REDWOOD_API_KEY).
  2) Verify key scope: `redwood keys inspect <key>` (console or ctrl plane).
  3) Check time skew if using signed short-lived tokens; confirm client time is within 2 minutes of NTP.
  4) If using Private deployment, verify the control-plane endpoint and routing (see eng-private-deployments/reference-architectures).
- Root cause and fix: Most often an expired key or misconfigured env var. Rotate key and restart process.

Issue: Long tail latency on small requests (p99 > 1s)
- Symptom: Short prompts experiencing p99 latency spikes.
- Quick triage steps:
  1) Confirm region and model selection: ensure client is routing to nearest region via REDWOOD_REGION or SDK config.
  2) Inspect SDK batching settings: if `auto_batch: true` and concurrency is low, disable batching for latency-sensitive routes.
  3) Run the runtime profiling endpoint (internal only): `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" https://runtime-internal/profiler?trace=short` and attach results to ticket.
- Root cause and fix: Incorrect default batching or cross-region routing. Adjust SDK runtime config and add a per-route override.

Issue: Streaming responses stop mid-stream / partial output
- Symptom: Client receives truncated events or the SSE/WS stream closes.
- Quick triage steps:
  1) Check client network stability and idle timeouts (client SDK has a 60s keepalive).
  2) Reproduce with curl to isolate SDK vs network: `curl -N -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" https://api.redwood.com/v1/stream`
  3) If reproduced, capture headers and response code; escalate to eng-serving-runtime with logs.
- Root cause and fix: Commonly due to intermediate proxies dropping connections or incorrect keepalive settings. Recommend enabling heartbeat frames and increasing proxy idle timeouts.

Docs Site Operating Notes (for DX maintainers)

- Canonical structure: each SDK guide must have: Quickstart (1 page), API reference (auto-generated), Troubleshooting (this playbook links), and Migration notes.
- Publishing workflow:
  1) Open a docs-site PR against `main`.
  2) CI runs docs lint and builds a preview at `https://docs-preview.redwood.com/<pr-number>`.
  3) Add reviewers from devx and the owning SDK team.
  4) After merge, schedule a backfill in the docs redirects table if you renamed routes.

Docs CI smoke test (example GitHub Actions job)

name: docs-smoke
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  smoke:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Build preview
        run: ./scripts/build-docs.sh
      - name: Run smoke curl
        env:
          DOCS_PREVIEW_URL: ${{ steps.build.outputs.preview_url }}
        run: curl -fsS "$DOCS_PREVIEW_URL/sdk/minimal-python"

Telemetry and alerts (DevX-owned metrics)

- Metric names (Prometheus-style):
  - devx_sdk_requests_total
  - devx_sdk_errors_total (label: error_type)
  - devx_sdk_ci_smoke_failures_total
- Alert thresholds (PagerDuty escalation):
  - devx_sdk_ci_smoke_failures_total > 5 in 1h -> page on-call
  - devx_sdk_errors_total{error_type="unmarshal"} > 20 in 10m -> create Jira to SDK team

Ownership and escalation

- Day-to-day ownership: Developer Experience (DevX) team.
- Escalation path: DevX on-call -> SDK owner -> Runtime on-call (if traces indicate server-side issues).
- Contact matrix: include Slack channels `#devx-oncall`, `#sdk-py`, `#sdk-node`.

Appendix: sample code snippets

Python minimal example (sync):

```python
from redwood import RedwoodClient
client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.environ["REDWOOD_API_KEY"])
resp = client.generate(prompt="Write a haiku about observability")
print(resp.text)
```

Node streaming example (client handles SSE):

```js
import Redwood from 'redwood-client';
const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY, region: 'us-west-2' });
const stream = await client.chat.stream({ model: 'redwood-chat-1', messages: [{ role: 'user', content: 'Summarize micropatching' }] });
for await (const chunk of stream) { process.stdout.write(chunk.delta); }
```

Appendix B: environment variables reference (table)

VAR | PURPOSE | SUGGESTED DEFAULT
-----|---------|----------------
REDWOOD_API_KEY | API key used by SDKs | none (required)
REDWOOD_REGION | Preferred region for routing | us-west-2
REDWOOD_ENV | Environment label for telemetry | dev/staging/prod
SDK_AUTO_BATCH | SDK-level batching (true/false) | true

Maintenance notes

- Review this playbook quarterly.
- When an SDK ships a breaking change, update the migration notes and add a compatibility test into the docs CI.

Attachments and references

- Templates repo: git@github.com:redwood/devx-templates.git
- Docs runbook: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/docs-site/docs-runbook
- Runtime profiler runbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook
