[00:00] Alex: Okay welcome everyone, thanks for joining our weekly POC sync, um we have about 50 minutes so we'll run through results, proposed pinning, and fallback playbook.
[00:12] Maria: Thanks Alex, we had a busy week on the eval side, saw some interesting latency spikes on the 13B runs but cost looked favorable, we'll share the raw logs.
[00:22] Priya: Quick note, the spikes you saw sound like batching mismatch—when sequence length distribution changed the autoscaler pulled in extra workers and that introduced queuing, so it looked like a model issue but it's infra-behavior.
[00:34] Tom: Yeah we observed queuing, and some of our endpoints have unpredictable token lengths because of long user messages.
[00:40] Alex: Right, so first agenda item: model selection. Our recommendation this week was to try pinning a 13B quantized variant for the primary route and keep 7B quantized as a cold fallback. The tradeoff is better quality at slightly higher median latency.
[00:55] Maria: Can you remind us of the quant profiles again, Priya? q2 vs q4? I'm mixing them up.
[01:02] Priya: Sure, we ran 7B with q2 and 13B with q4 int8-ish profile. The 13B q4 tends to give more coherent completions on long-context prompts, especially for multi-step extraction tasks. 7B q2 is cheaper and lower latency but occasionally fails hallucination checks.
[01:18] Maria: Okay that jibes with the evals. The quality delta matters for our NER cascades.
[01:24] Rafael: From security side we want to make any rollback path auditable — who changed the pin, when, and what triggered it.
[01:32] Alex: Absolutely, we can include audit-log entries for pin changes in the runbook. Our control plane records actor, timestamp, and reason but we'll add explicit runbook instructions for when to pin/unpin.
[01:45] Tom: On canary gates — what's the recommended traffic split? We want something conservative but actionable.
[01:50] Priya: Typical pattern we use: start with 1% traffic to the new pin for 30 minutes, monitor latency p50/p95, error rate, and model-quality evals against a prompt set. If metrics stable, increase to 10% for 2 hours, then 50% for the rest of the day before full roll. For POCs, you can shorten windows but keep the same thresholds.
[02:12] Maria: Do you support automatic fallback if error rate crosses threshold?
[02:15] Alex: Yes we have automated fallback policies — you can configure error-rate and latency triggers. We'll send you the standard policy but also include a 'soft' fallback that redirects to 7B and keeps the traffic on the same route but with lower cost.
[02:29] Rafael: Important: any automated fallback must emit an audit event and we need to retain that in our logs. Also KMS key usage for model telemetry needs to be documented.
[02:38] Priya: Noted, we'll include KMS access logs sample.
[02:42] Tom: Quick question on prefix caching / KV cache, is it preserved across fallback? Because we saw cold starts when we switched between variants.
[02:50] Priya: Good call — prefix cache isn't compatible across different model architectures or quantization profiles, so when you fallback between 13B and 7B you'll likely see KV cache misses; that explains the cold latency. We're working on transparent cache warmers but for now expect a short penalty on switch.
[03:10] Maria: So that suggests we should prefer soft-rollback where we route new requests to fallback but keep existing sessions on primary until they finish?
[03:16] Alex: Exactly — sticky sessions and drain behavior minimize user-visible regressions. We'll detail drain windows in the runbook.
[03:22] Tom: On the benchmark results — we got a CSV from you, but some columns look truncated; could you re-run with absolute token counts (input/output) and per-request walltime?
[03:30] Priya: Yep we'll reformat. Also we'll add percentiles and median and the cost per request based on your token mix.
[03:36] Maria: Regarding model pins, what's the recommended duration to hold a pin in pilot? If we pin for too long and then new model drops, how do we avoid tech debt?
[03:45] Alex: Good question. For pilots we recommend pin windows of 1-2 weeks with scheduled evaluation at 72-hour and 1-week marks. If a new model variant is released you can create a canary from it rather than flipping the pin immediately.
[03:58] Rafael: From compliance, we need a change freeze window before any production roll: a checklist and sign-off by SRE and Security. Can you provide a template?
[04:07] Alex: Yes we'll include a sign-off template in the runbook, with the required fields (owner, rollback plan, metrics checked).
[04:14] [crosstalk] Tom: (inaudible) — also want to check network egress if we move to dedicated.
[04:20] Priya: For Dedicated, egress stays in your VPC in Private deployments, and for Redwood Dedicated we can restrict egress via peering and firewall rules. We'll include network diagrams.
[04:30] Maria: On the latency spikes, is there a way to simulate sequence-length distribution that mimics live traffic for the benchmark?
[04:36] Priya: Yes we can replay a sampled set of 5k requests from your logs — that will give a more accurate p95 than synthetic uniform tests. Please send a sanitized sample and we'll run it.
[04:46] Maria: We'll anonymize and send.
[04:48] Alex: Next topic: degraded-paths naming. We call them fallback, soft-rollback, and emergency route. I'd like to confirm your preference because docs use inconsistent names.
[04:56] Maria: Let's standardize on fallback (planned), soft-rollback (automatic with warm switch), and emergency-redirect (manual hot switch).
[05:05] Alex: Noted. We'll align runbook.
[05:08] Priya: Also a small gotcha—if you use model variants with different vocab/tokenizer versions there can be subtle output differences; keep an eye on tokenization drift.
[05:17] Tom: Oof, tokenizer drift caused us some issues before. Good call.
[05:20] Rafael: Security quick question — where are logs stored for the pinned model change events? Retention policy?
[05:25] Alex: We store audit logs in your configured logging sink (Cloud Logging / SIEM), with retention configurable per account. Default is 90 days, but enterprise plans can extend.
[05:34] Rafael: We need 365 days for compliance.
[05:36] Alex: That's possible; we'll note that in the proposal.
[05:39] Maria: Can we get an example of the rollback condition syntax? Like a rule we can paste into our tooling?
[05:44] Priya: Yes — an example: if route.p95_latency > 1500ms for 10m OR error_rate > 2% over 5m then trigger soft-rollback; we'll send the JSON/YAML snippet but in this call quick example is that.
[05:58] Tom: We use Prometheus for metrics; will alerts integrate?
[06:02] Alex: We can emit metrics to Prometheus or cloud monitoring; integrations are supported.
[06:07] Maria: One more ask — during canary, how do we evaluate model quality? We need automated checks beyond basic metrics.
[06:13] Priya: We can run a prompt-based quality eval against a golden prompt set and surface drift metrics (F1/NER score, hallucination heuristics). For the POC we'll run the golden set every 30 mins during canary. That will be in the benchmark spreadsheet.
[06:28] Maria: Sounds good.
[06:30] Alex: Alright let's recap: Priya runs the 1k/5k replays with tokenized counts and writes up a cost/latency spreadsheet; Alex will draft the runbook with canonical names and soft-rollback playbook; Maria will confirm success criteria/PM; Rafael will list compliance artifacts.
[06:47] Rafael: Also please include KMS key rotation policy notes if we're evaluating private.
[06:53] Priya: We'll add KMS rotation and HSM notes.

[07:10] Priya: Looking at the logs from last week one more note — the autoscaler scales on GPU utilization which sometimes overprovisions if you have bursty small requests; consider request-based concurrency limits per worker in addition to CPU/GPU thresholds.
[07:26] Tom: How does request concurrency interact with batching? We don't want small requests to starve large ones.
[07:31] Priya: We partition batches by priority and sequence-length buckets; smaller requests can be batched together but we also reserve a fraction of slots for long-sequence tasks. It's configurable in the route policy.
[07:45] Maria: That seems useful — maybe we start with a 20% reserved for long tasks.
[07:50] Alex: We'll include recommended defaults.
[07:53] [crosstalk — 2 people talking]
[08:00] Tom: On pins, is there an API? We prefer infra-as-code changes rather than manual console fiddling.
[08:05] Alex: Yes we have both — an API and CLI that support model pin creation, history, and rollbacks. Pins are auditable and you can script the canary windows.
[08:14] Maria: We'll want an example Terraform snippet.
[08:17] Alex: We'll provide one.
[08:19] Priya: One possible gotcha: if you pin and then later pin a model that gets updated in-place (same model name different binary) you might not get what you expected; we recommend pinning exact model-version hashes when you need determinism.
[08:34] Maria: Good to know.
[08:36] Alex: Closing questions?
[08:38] Maria: None from me. We'll send the sample logs by EOD tomorrow.

[08:46] Rafael: We'll confirm the compliance doc list by next week.

[00:00] Jordan: Alright everyone, thanks for being on time. We'll run through the results and then get into the pinning/rollback playbook. Priya and I will own the technical bits, Caleb on success metrics and next steps.
[00:27] Dr. Elena: sounds good, we only have 50 so keep tight please. We've looked at the high-level numbers you sent.
[00:38] Priya: Cool. Quick note — the sheet has three model candidates: rwd-3b-v1, rwd-7b-v2-q4, and community-8k-v1. We measured median p50/p95 latencies and a small quality sample. The KV cache was on for half the runs and off for the other half; I included both columns.
[01:05] Marcus: small comment, the p95 looked a bit... higher in eu-west, is that expected?
[01:12] Priya: yeah we routed some jobs to our test region which had slightly older infra, that's on the spreadsheet — eu-west nodes were 2.5x slower for rwd-7b-v2-q4 under peak.
[01:30] Jordan: I'll flag that in the email. But main callout: cost delta between rwd-3b and rwd-7b-q4 is ~1.8x token cost for the 7b at our pilot mix, but quality improvements on hallucination were noticeable on the clinical QA set.
[02:01] Dr. Elena: by "noticeable" do you mean clinically meaningful? We need to be explicit for risk.
[02:09] Priya: Good point. For the sample of 120 clinical prompts, rwd-7b-q4 reduced incorrect condition mapping by 12%, rwd-3b had higher brevity errors — that said the community-8k produced fewer false positives but struggled on long context.
[02:40] Tom: So tradeoff is latency/cost vs safety/accuracy. We have budget for a small cost uptick if the error rate is lower.
[02:53] Jordan: Right, which is why we proposed pin strategy of "major pin" to model family (e.g., rwd-7b) and "minor pin" to patch levels only after validation. If there's an emerging regression we want automatic fallback to rwd-3b or the quantized variant that passes our guardrails.
[03:20] Sonia: For security is there a difference in audit logs if we fallback across hosted <> private? We need guaranteed request-level audittrace retained for 90 days.
[03:33] Priya: Hosted preserves the full trace w/ request IDs and token-level cost breakdown. Private can be configured to ship the same fields to your KMS and SIEM but we need to enable extended retention — that's in the SOC2 appendix. I'll attach the doc.
[03:57] Marcus: Also, latency SLO — can the autoscaler do instant fallback? If we pin to rwd-7b and it becomes saturated will the system route to rwd-3b automatically?
[04:15] Priya: Yes, we have smart routing policies: capacity-based fallback that considers model compatibility (same tokenizer) and region preferences. There's a short-circuit for steady overload where we will route to a compatible quantized variant or smaller family. That's what we tested in the soak-run last week.
[04:38] Dr. Elena: How do you define "compatible"? Tokenizer differences are the biggest risk for prompt/response divergence.
[04:45] Priya: good call. Compatible = same tokenizer + same output shape for tool-calls. If tokenizer differs we do a strict translation layer but we flag the outputs and fall back to read-only mode until validated. That flagging shows up in the audit.
[05:10] Jordan: Real quick, another operational suggestion — we recommend pinning at the major level for 30 days and only minor patches after canyon testing. Sorry, car-ness, can we — canyon? (laughs) typo, can we limit auto-upgrades?
[05:28] Dr. Elena: Yes, we prefer explicit upgrades.
[05:32] Tom: If we pin MAJOR only, how do we get security patches? We can't delay critical CVE fixes.
[05:39] Priya: We support exceptions: critical security patches can be auto-rolled to minor if you enable the curated security channel. Otherwise we put them through a canary on 5% of traffic.
[05:54] Sonia: That works if canary logs are separate and auditable. We need a report for any auto-rolled patch.
[06:04] Priya: We'll add that to the rollout notes.
[06:12] [06:12] Caleb: quick recap of the numbers — rwd-7b-q4 p50 = 140ms local, p95 = 480ms, cost/unit = $0.018 per 1k tokens; rwd-3b p50 = 90ms, p95 = 260ms, cost/unit = $0.01 per 1k tokens. community-8k p50 = 220ms but lower hallucination on prompt set A.
[06:45] Dr. Elena: On the usability side, we need deterministic outputs for certain templates. Which model gave the narrowest variance?
[06:55] Priya: rwd-3b had the tightest entropy on templated prompts, interestingly. The 7b is better on open-ended reasoning but more variable length-wise.
[07:10] Marcus: For the pilot we'd like to pin to rwd-7b for the clinical scoring pipeline but fallback to rwd-3b for patient-facing chat where determinism matters.
[07:25] Jordan: That's exactly the route-based pin we can do: per-route enforcement. We'll add a per-route fallback priority list and a roll-forward/rollback hook.
[07:40] Dr. Elena: Can you show a quick mock of the config?
[07:45] Priya: Sure — I pulled the example from the docs: route: /clinical-score -> pinned: rwd-7b@major, fallbacks: [rwd-7b-q4, rwd-3b@major], rollout: canary 5% -> 25% -> 100% with health checks. I'll share the snippet after.
[08:10] Tom: Any gotchas around tokenization with the quantized variant? I worry about scoring drift.
[08:18] Priya: Quantization doesn't change the tokenizer, but aggressive quantization can affect logits and cause subtle answer changes. That's why we run regression tests on your prompt set during canary. We recommend a small golden set for deterministic checks.
[08:36] Dr. Elena: We have a golden set of ~200 prompts, is that enough?
[08:42] Priya: That should be fine for initial regression; we do stratified sampling across entities to catch edge cases.
[08:52] Jordan: Next up—rollback playbook. The idea: automatic detection -> mitigation via fallback -> alert + postmortem. Detection signals: error rates, hallucination score bump, latency SLO breach.
[09:10] Marcus: how do you measure hallucination score automatically? We use heuristics but need to avoid false positives.
[09:18] Priya: We compute a similarity-based check vs. reference answers + heuristics on negation and entity hallucination, it's not perfect but effective to trigger investigation rather than immediate rollback unless severity is high.
[09:32] Dr. Elena: Would we be able to set thresholds? i.e., 10% increase in hallucination triggers canary rollback?
[09:40] Priya: Yes thresholds are configurable per-route.
[09:43] [10:00] Jordan: Let's talk about timeline — LumenHealth wants a decision by next Monday. We proposed two options: 1) Pin to rwd-7b family for two-week evaluation then freeze; 2) Pin to rwd-3b for lower cost and keep 7b as optional on high-risk prompts. Which is leaning?
[10:20] Dr. Elena: The clinical team favors option 1 but security wants written guarantees on audit and rollback speed.
[10:28] Sonia: Specifically we need request-level logs, user ids redaction policy, and confirmation that fallback events are recorded with original model id.
[10:36] Priya: All recorded. Fallback events include original model, chosen fallback, reason code, and a trace id that maps across systems.
[10:46] Marcus: for throughput, if we fallback during peak what happens to in-flight KV cache states? do we lose context?
[10:55] Priya: We preserve KV cache per session; when migrating to a smaller model we rehydrate a compatible prefix. In some edge cases we drop non-critical cache entries and flag the session. We'll note that in the playbook.
[11:20] Dr. Elena: ok, show us the exact fields in the audit log.
[11:26] Jordan: I'll attach the SOC2 appendix but quick list: request_id, timestamp, model_id, model_version, fallback_flag, fallback_model, reason_code, route, token_count, cost_estimate, user_id (hashed), truncated_input, confidence_scores where available.
[11:55] Sonia: Need to see retention SLA and export hooks to our SIEM.
[12:02] Jordan: we'll provide retention options: 30/90/365 days exportable via S3 or pushed to your SIEM.
[12:12] [12:12] Caleb: circling back to the decision matrix — we propose scoring: 40% clinical accuracy, 25% latency, 20% cost, 15% operational risk. You can tweak weights.
[12:29] Dr. Elena: That seems fair. We'll take it to the clinical PM and rank models.
[12:36] Tom: on the automation side, we want a test harness to run the golden set nightly and alert on drift. Can Redwood run that against canary?
[12:45] Priya: Yes, Redwood Optimize can schedule and run nightly regression and we can surface drift alerts into slack or pagers. We'll set up a channel.
[12:58] Marcus: do you have an example of the slack alert payload?
[13:02] Priya: I'll add an example in the follow-up.
[13:10] Dr. Elena: Anything else on rollbacks? We want runbooks for the SREs.
[13:16] Jordan: We'll provide runbook + playbook: commands to pin/unpin, to trigger full rollback, to force-route, and the postmortem template.
[13:28] Sonia: one last compliance note — encryption at rest keys and KMS integration for Private. Need confirmation of HSM support.
[13:36] Priya: HSM via your KMS provider is supported in Private mode; hosted uses Redwood-managed keys but we offer customer-managed keys for enterprise.
[13:44] Dr. Elena: good.
[13:50] Jordan: Alright to wrap: decision timeline, docs to share, and action owners. Caleb will synthesize and send internal recap.
[14:00] Caleb: I'll send a short recap and include the config snippet, and I will link pilot_results.csv and latency traces.
[14:08] Jordan: Great — thanks everyone.

End of transcript.

[Degradation thresholds and SLA clauses discovery - Hypatia AI]
summary:
High-level discovery on reliability expectations: Hypatia cares about contractual SLA language and acceptable degradation modes. Evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private; primary concerns are partial-degradation behavior, MTTR guarantees, data residency, and penalty/credit mechanics for multi-minute outages. Hypatia requested example runbook snippets and a canary rollback policy. Action: Redwood to send pricing + SLA addendum and schedule technical deep-dive.

topics:
SLA wording and uptime measurement windows
Graceful degradation vs hard fail (partial responses, degraded models)
Multi-region routing and regional failover choreography
Canary rollouts, automatic rollback and circuit breakers
Dedicated vs Hosted cost/latency tradeoffs
Data residency, KMS/HSM and audit logs

transcript:
[00:00] Jamie (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Priya (Hypatia SRE): Priya here. Morning to you all.
[00:09] Miguel (Hypatia CTO): Miguel, hi.
[00:11] Elliot (Procurement): Elliot on the line.
[00:14] Omar (Redwood SE): Omar, Redwood SE.
[00:18] Jamie: Perfect. We set aside an hour to go over how you want reliability encoded into the contract and technical fallbacks. We'll cover behavior during partial degradation, multi-region failover, and what we can guarantee with Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private.
[00:35] Priya: Great. To set context: Hypatia runs inference for real-time assistant features, 99.5% of traffic is sub-200 token requests but we have bursts where sequences hit 2k tokens, and during those we saw latency spikes. Our legal team wants firm SLOs and a clear list of allowed degradation behaviors — like returning cached prefixes versus 502s.
[00:58] Jamie: Understood. Quick clarification — when you say "allowed degradation behaviors" do you mean what the application might see (e.g., truncated responses, lower-quality model variant, or explicit errors)?
[01:08] Priya: All of the above. We prefer graceful degradation — return shorter or partial completions rather than hard errors — but legal may require thresholds for when you'd switch to that behavior and when they'd qualify for credits.
[01:21] Omar: Yeah, our platform supports graded fallbacks: 1) prefix/K-V cache hits, 2) model variant fallback (quantized or smaller family), 3) region steering, 4) explicit circuit-breaker error. Those are policy-driven and plumbed into the routing layer.
[01:36] Hannah (Platform Eng): How deterministic is region steering? If a region fails, what's the expected warmup and cold cache penalty?
[01:44] Omar: Good question. For multi-region we keep per-region KV caches if you opt in; warmup depends on your workload shape. For short outages we prefer transparent failover with cached prefixes served while the KV fills. For longer outages, fallback to smaller model variants provides capacity but accuracy degrades. Warmup might cost you increased P95s for a few minutes.
[02:08] Miguel: From a contractual angle, our security/policy folks want MTTR targets and how credits are measured. Is MTTR measured from detection or customer-reported?
[02:18] Jamie: By default our SLA windows measure from when we detect a service-impacting incident in our monitoring and automatically open an incident ticket. But we're flexible in Enterprise agreements; we can add clauses for customer-reported incidents if you need symmetric treatment.
[02:33] Priya: We also wanted specific language about partial degradation. For example, if you return a truncated completion because of a degraded model, does that count as availability or partial availability?
[02:43] Omar: We define availability at the API surface: a non-2xx response counts as outage. Truncated/shortened but 200 responses are still considered available, but we can add a separate quality metric to track meaningful completion rate. Contracts can include a "quality SLI" in addition to availability SLI.
[03:02] Elliot: For procurement we need to see the proposed credit calculation. Flat percent-of-month credit or sliding scale per minute?
[03:10] Jamie: Typical Enterprise SLAs use a sliding credit tied to monthly uptime percentage. For Dedicated customers we can offer tighter SLOs and smaller credit windows; plus options for monetary credits or future bill offsets. We'll include sample language in the SLA addendum.
[03:24] Priya: Can we get example runbook snippets? We want to see the automatic fallback thresholds and the exact circuit-breaker timeouts.
[03:31] Omar: Absolutely. I'll pull a few runbook examples: a canary rollback policy (evaluates error rate and latency deltas), a circuit breaker config (threshold, cool-off, retry jitter), and a region-failover playbook.
[03:45] Miguel: On the hosted vs dedicated question: what's the difference in mean time to failover and support for private network egress?
[03:54] Jamie: Hosted gives fastest onboarding but fallbacks are controlled by Redwood's global routing — good for most use cases. Dedicated provides reserved capacity in your chosen region(s) with richer SLAs and support for private peering. Private (VPC/on-prem) puts the inference plane in your network so you control ND policies, but the initial setup is heavier. MTTR tends to be lower for Dedicated because you have reserved pools and closer support, but Private gives you ultimate control if you have strict residency requirements.
[04:25] Priya: For Dedicated, do we get N+1 across racks within the region? What about AZ failover?
[04:33] Omar: Dedicated is configurable. We can do N+1 in a cluster and distribute across AZs; our standard Dedicated config for enterprise does cross-AZ redundancy. In the SLA we clarify what counts as zonal vs regional outage.
[04:48] Hannah: If we go with Private, will Redwood still provide the control plane for updates and rollout policies or is that fully customer-managed?
[04:56] Jamie: For Private we run a control plane you can opt to host with us or to self-host. Many customers choose a hybrid: control plane in the customer VPC with Redwood-managed runtime images. We can add a clause about maintenance windows so you have predictability.
[05:14] Priya: Back to quality SLI — can you instrument the model family fallbacks and attribute quality loss to fallback events for credits?
[05:23] Omar: Yes, we emit telemetry per-request: which model variant served, whether cache hit, latency, and a quality tag when fallback occurred. We can bake a credit policy that only applies when fallback-induced quality loss exceeded a threshold. That will require mutually agreed telemetry fields and a litmus prompt set for automatic regression detection.
[05:46] Miguel: Our legal team will push for explicit examples where the vendor must use best efforts to route around a failure before crediting. How do you balance aggressive fallback vs trying to maintain higher quality?
[05:57] Jamie: That's where policy tiers come in — you can choose conservative (prefer quality, higher chance of error responses) or permissive (prefer availability, more aggressive fallbacks). We'll map those to pricing tiers.
[06:11] Priya: Can you walk us through a sample incident flow? Say a GPU host in one AZ spikes azure? sorry, spikes CPU causing token generation 10x P95.
[06:23] Omar: Sure. [high level flow]. Detect via p95 anomaly triggers -> traffic automatically routed off the impacted nodes -> traffic routed to healthy nodes in-region -> if region capacity insufficient, routing policy attempts other regions tagged as 'region-failover candidates' -> once cross-region is engaged, KV cache cold-start penalty applies -> after X minutes if error rate still elevated, we spin up fallback model variant. If error persists, circuit breaker trips and we return 503s.
[06:54] Priya: That cold-start penalty — is that typically 30s, a few minutes?
[06:59] Omar: Depends on your prefix hit rates. For typical chat workloads it's often a minute or two for meaningful cache rewarming, but if you have long tails of unique prompts it could be longer. We'll estimate based on your histograms.
[07:11] Miguel: Could we negotiate a clause that for cross-region failover Redwood must attempt warm-warm capacity first (i.e., keep a small buffer in each region) to avoid cold-starts?
[07:21] Jamie: Yes, that's achievable via reserved burst pools or reserved cross-region standby which is optional for Dedicated. It increases cost but reduces warmup pain. We'll put example numbers in the pricing sheet.
[07:34] Priya: On observability: we need token-level breakdown, per-route latency, and model-variant attribution in our logs.
[07:41] Omar: Redwood Console has token-level cost/latency where you can filter by route, model, and time; we can stream those logs into your SIEM and include audit logs for retrievability.
[07:52] Priya: KMS question — for Private, can we integrate with our HSM?
[07:56] Jamie: Yes. For Private we support customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations and bring-your-own-key. We'll provide the integration checklist.
[08:05] Elliot: Procurement side — what about termination for convenience clauses if SLA repeatedly missed? Will there be cure periods?
[08:13] Jamie: Standard practice is cure periods with remediation plans; termination for repeated SLA breaches is negotiable for enterprise deals. We'll include typical legal language and can escalate to legal for redlines.
[08:23] Miguel: We should talk about run rate impact. If we accept a permissive fallback policy that returns lower-quality outputs rather than fail, how will that affect our downstream metric and customer experience?
[08:35] Priya: Right, we don't want to silently degrade experience without telemetry gating.
[08:39] Omar: We recommend a staged approach: Canary in production with a small percent of traffic using the fallback policy and a set of litmus prompts to measure regressions; if quality delta within tolerated band, increase rollout.
[08:50] Jamie: That can be codified into the SLOs too — e.g., a quality SLI measured on the litmus set must remain above X during rollouts, or rollback triggers.
[08:59] Priya: Legal wants explicit time windows for SLA measurement (calendar month vs rolling 30-day). Which do you suggest?
[09:06] Jamie: Most customers pick calendar month for billing alignment, rolling 30-day for operational monitoring. We can propose calendar month for credits.
[09:15] Hannah: Are there constraints for on-prem Private in terms of patch windows? We run a regulated environment and need change freeze windows.
[09:23] Jamie: We can honor maintenance blackout windows and carve them into the contract; for security patches we usually require a narrow window, but can coordinate with your change management.
[09:33] Miguel: Competitors — quick note: we've talked to Vendor X (Anthropic) about model fallbacks and their approach was a single global failover and heavier error rates. Curious about Redwood's multi-tier approach.
[09:45] Omar: Our multi-tier approach provides more control at the routing policy level: you can tune preference for cache, variants, regions, or hard failures. That granularity is a differentiator.
[09:56] Priya: Let's get specific: what does your SLA credit table look like for Dedicated with cross-AZ redundancy?
[10:02] Jamie: Typical example: >=99.9% monthly uptime — no credit; 99.0%-99.9% — 10% credit; 95%-99% — 25% credit; <95% — 50% credit. We'll provide a proposed table and we're open to negotiation. For Private we can adapt language since operations are partly customer-run.
[10:22] Elliot: Are there blackout exclusions for large-scale cloud provider incidents?
[10:27] Jamie: Yes, force majeure and third-party cloud provider incidents are typically called out. We can discuss carving out public cloud provider wide outages vs Redwood-managed infra. For Dedicated with Reserved capacity we can negotiate narrower exclusions.
[10:41] Priya: We need to make sure our SLAs don't create perverse incentives to suppress detection to avoid credits. How do you ensure incident detection and transparency?
[10:52] Omar: We provide incident timelines and postmortems for all incidents affecting customer traffic; for Enterprise we offer direct Slack channels and incident bridge invites. The SLA includes definitions of detection sources and how timelines are recorded.
[11:05] Miguel: Can you support synthetic probing from our side that you will accept as a detection method?
[11:11] Jamie: Yes, we can accept mutually agreed synthetic probes as triggers for the incident timeline. We'll include the specifics: probe endpoints, rate limits, and authentication.
[11:20] Priya: For canary rollbacks, what's the typical criteria? 2x baseline error rate? Latency deltas at P95?
[11:27] Omar: Canary thresholds usually combine error rate delta and latency at P95 over a window. Example: if error rate increases by >1% absolute or P95 latency increases by >200ms vs baseline for 5 continuous minutes, trigger rollback. We can customize.
[11:43] Hannah: If we have a legal dispute on measurement, what is the source of truth?
[11:48] Jamie: We recommend using mutually agreed telemetry exports stored in both parties' systems as the source of truth. That's a common enterprise approach.
[11:57] Miguel: Talk to us about pricing impact of providing warm-standby cross-region capacity. Ballpark numbers?
[12:03] Jamie: We'll put some options: a small cross-region standby (e.g., 10% reserved capacity in a secondary region) typically adds X% to the committed spend. We'll include exact numbers in the pricing sheet.
[12:15] Priya: Is there a way to limit credits to incidents that violate both availability and quality SLIs? We don't want small, brief infra blips to trigger large credits.
[12:25] Omar: Absolutely — you can define a credit trigger that requires breach of both availability and quality SLIs for >Y contiguous minutes. We'll propose sensible defaults.
[12:35] Elliot: From procurement: what documentation do you need to start a PO?
[12:39] Jamie: We'll need your SOW details, estimated committed spend (if Dedicated), legal contact for redlines, and the technical contact for network setup. We'll send a checklist.
[12:50] Priya: One more technical: does Redwood support session affinity for chat flows so KV cache hit rates stay high during failovers?
[12:58] Omar: Yes, session affinity via sticky routing keys is supported; that helps preserve KV cache hits. If you need global affinity across regions, that's a bit trickier but can be approximated with consistent hashing and a small reserved warm pool.
[13:14] Miguel: Good. I think we have the inputs. For next steps, we'll review the SLA draft and reconvene after we review pricing.
[13:22] Jamie: Great. Omar, Lena, we'll prepare the SLA addendum, runbook snippets, and canary configs.
[13:29] Omar: I'll also include an example rollback graph and the actual JSON of the circuit breaker policy so your platform eng can ingest it.
[13:35] Priya: Thanks everyone.
[13:37] Elliot: Thanks.
[13:38] Jamie: Closing notes — we'll aim to send docs by Friday the 15th and book the technical deep-dive for the week of the 18th.
[13:45] Meeting ended.

Notes on transcription quality: occasional misheard acronyms ("K-V cache" sometimes transcribed as "K V cache"), filler words, and overlapping talk in a few places. Some proper nouns may be imperfect.

Date: 2026-10-11 14:00 UTC | Duration: 48 mins | Attendees: Lara Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Rivera (Redwood SE), Nina Patel (QuantaHealth Head of ML), Ethan Brooks (Platform Eng), Marta Ruiz (Data Privacy)

[00:00] Lara Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we were told QuantaHealth wanted a compact walkthrough of how we pick open models and how the compatibility heatmap helps you narrow candidates — I'm Lara AE, with Marcus SE.
[00:07] Nina Patel: Hi Lara, hi Marcus, thanks. We want to get through the catalog, then see how to interpret bench numbers for our summarization pipeline. Timebox 45-ish.
[00:12] Marcus Rivera: Great, I'll share my screen — pulling up Console > Models > Compatibility heatmap. Quick note, apologies if labels are fuzzy, the internal name mapping sometimes has minor mismatches in the view.
[00:22] Ethan Brooks: That's fine, just FYI we run on GKE with private subnets, and we have a 99th percentile latency SLO around 600ms for 512-token prompts.
[00:30] Marta Ruiz: And we need a KMS integration and audit logs for any PII processing. Also, SOC2 is a must for production.

[00:40] Marcus Rivera: Understood — we map those constraints to routing policies and dedicated profiles. Okay heatmap up: rows are models, columns are workload profiles — summarization/QA/embedding — colors indicate compatibility score (green = recommended, amber = borderline, red = poor). Note: the score is composite — latency estimate, token cost, eval score on a small calibration set.
[00:55] Nina Patel: That "composite" — can you unpack weights? Which factor dominates?
[01:03] Marcus Rivera: Sure, by default for Console Optimize the weights are latency 40%, quality 40%, cost 20%. You can adjust per-workspace — many customers bias quality up for clinical text. Also note kernel compatibility and quantization support influences the latency estimate — e.g., some 4-bit quantized variants can be faster but degrade certain safety tokens.
[01:22] Lara Chen: Also worth noting: the heatmap flags models that have partial feature mismatches, like missing function calling or output schema enforcement — those show as hatch marks.

[01:35] Nina Patel: We do need structured output (JSON summary + confidence) for downstream ingestion. How do you represent that capability?
[01:42] Marcus Rivera: There's a column for 'structured-output fidelity' — it's 0-100 based on evals with your prompt set, but for customers we recommend an explicit small eval because out-of-the-box numbers are noisy. We'll ask you to share a sample prompt set.
[01:55] Ethan Brooks: When you say 'evals are noisy' — is that tokenization mismatch? We use byte-level tokenization and sometimes Open-source forks have different tokenizers.
[02:04] Marcus Rivera: Exactly, tokenization and prompt length distribution affect both token cost and accuracy. That's why our bench script includes a tokenization step that normalizes to model's tokenizer. We'll provide a bench harness.

[02:18] Marta Ruiz: For private deployment, do we get the same heatmap? We can't send data to hosted service for the mapping.
[02:25] Lara Chen: Good question — for Private deployments we can run the same compatibility scanner inside your VPC, it requires a short agent that runs bench flows on your infra. We also offer sanitized synthetic data mode if you prefer.
[02:38] Nina Patel: What's the timeline to run a one-week pilot?
[02:43] Lara Chen: For a 1-week dedicated pilot, we typically provision a small Dedicated pool, run a 24-hour calibration bench, then deploy a canary for live traffic with routing rules. So prep + infra + bench is usually 3–5 business days.

[02:55] Marcus Rivera: Ok I'm pulling up an example heatmap we did for a finance customer — you'll notice the top row models are small Llama-derivatives — they look green for cost/latency but amber for summarization quality. The higher-quality models show as green for our clinical eval but cost more.
[03:15] Nina Patel: Is there a way to pin a model for production but have an automatic fallback to cheaper variant on heavy load?
[03:22] Marcus Rivera: Yes — routing policies support pinning plus fallbacks. There's also a 'graceful degrade' policy where for tail-latency spikes we route to a lower-cost variant that supports the same output schema. We preserve KV cache semantics when models are ABI-compatible, otherwise we rehydrate context which affects latency.
[03:40] Ethan Brooks: ABI-compatible — can you clarify?
[03:43] Marcus Rivera: ABI as in same tokenizer, same KV cache format. When you switch between models compiled to different kernels/quantization, cache can't be reused. We show compatibility in the heatmap and flag cache-retention score.
[03:55] Marta Ruiz: About encryption — will audit logs include per-token redaction markers? We need proof we didn't store PII.
[04:02] Lara Chen: Audit logs include request/response hashes and metadata, but not full plaintext unless you enable that. For PII we recommend client-side redaction before sending or sending to Private where logs can be controlled. We integrate with customer KMS for key rotation.

[04:20] Nina Patel: Can we see an example bench output? Small sample please.
[04:25] Marcus Rivera: I'll paste a snippet — "model: open-llama-30b-4bit, mean-latency: 220ms@256, p99: 610ms@512, quality: 0.81 (ROUGE-L-like), token-cost: $0.003/token-equivalent"
[04:46] Ethan Brooks: So that one p99 610ms is too high — could quantization or kernel choice improve p99?
[04:52] Marcus Rivera: Sometimes switching to a kernel that has better attention streaming reduces tail. Also batching parameters and prefilling KV cache for repeated context helps. For dedicated infra we can tune kernel selection per model variant to shave p99 by ~10-25% in many cases.
[05:08] Nina Patel: If we pick a higher-quality model but it costs 3x, can Optimize suggest a quantized variant that keeps quality within a delta?
[05:15] Marcus Rivera: Yes, Optimize suggests quantization profiles with estimated quality deltas — we show a tradeoff curve. For clinical summarization many customers accept a 1-2% quality drop for ~40-60% lower token cost.
[05:27] Lara Chen: I'm toggling the sidebar to show 'recommendations' — here Optimize suggests 'open-med-13b-quant-qlora' for your summarization sample, with fallback to 'open-med-7b-quant' during bursts.
[05:38] Nina Patel: "open-med" — are those models curated by Redwood or community-uploaded? We have legal constraints about model provenance.
[05:45] Lara Chen: We maintain a model catalog — some are community open models, some Redwood-curated variants with verification. For enterprise we provide provenance metadata (training license, weights URL, vetting notes). That's included in the model detail pane.
[05:59] Marta Ruiz: About licenses — do you provide a summary of license risk? Some Open weights are Apache, some are unclear.
[06:06] Marcus Rivera: We annotate license type; for ambiguous ones we flag them 'review required' and include notes. We can export a compliance report per selected model list.
[06:16] Nina Patel: If we run bench in our VPC, will Redwood see results?
[06:20] Lara Chen: No, for Private mode bench results stay in your control. For Hosted/Dedicated we can optionally collect anonymized telemetry if you opt in.
[06:29] Ethan Brooks: On the integration side: how do we route requests from our service to Redwood Dedicated? Do you provide SDK and proxy?
[06:34] Marcus Rivera: We have SDKs (Python/Go/JS) and a lightweight sidecar that can run in your cluster to manage routing and secrets. For VPC peering we have a private endpoint, and a sidecar handles auth and KMS.
[06:47] Nina Patel: Let's talk about benchmarks: what's in the bench harness? Are you running multi-turn?
[06:52] Marcus Rivera: Bench harness is configurable: single-turn, multi-turn, structured output checks, hallucination tests, and stress tests for concurrency. We also simulate tokenization differences and measure token cost.
[07:05] Lara Chen: Quick demo: I'm switching to the 'bench compare' view showing three candidates and a delta chart of quality vs cost. Notice the bubble sizes represent memory footprint.
[07:15] Nina Patel: I like the visualization. Can we export the data as CSV for our ML team to ingest?
[07:20] Marcus Rivera: Yes — 'export bench CSV' and an XLSX with per-sample breakdown. I'll add that to the action items.
[07:27] Marta Ruiz: For pilot, we need SOC2 and network diagrams before infra changes.
[07:31] Lara Chen: We'll send SOC2 docs and the Private deployment checklist (network diagram template) as part of the security packet.
[07:38] Ethan Brooks: On cost reporting — can Console provide token-level cost attribution by route/feature?
[07:43] Marcus Rivera: Yes — Console shows per-route cost breakdown and token-level charts, and you can query cost by model version and deployment mode.
[07:53] Nina Patel: Let's make this concrete — what's the minimal config to start a 1-week pilot?
[07:58] Lara Chen: Proposal: 1) Provision a 2-GPU Dedicated pool (NVIDIA H100 or equivalent) with autoscaling to 4 during bench; 2) Run 48h calibration bench with your prompt set and our harness; 3) Canary deploy one route with 5% traffic for 3 days then ramp. We'll provide a price estimate for that.
[08:18] Ethan Brooks: Do you support on-prem bare metal for H100? Our infra team might prefer that.
[08:22] Marcus Rivera: Yes — Private on-prem is supported but timeline is longer due to network and HSM setup. For short pilot Dedicated is fastest.
[08:30] Nina Patel: Okay sounds good. Could you also check that the recommended model supports JSON output with coarse confidence?
[08:36] Marcus Rivera: Will do — I'll run a targeted eval for structured-output fidelity and include examples.
[08:42] Lara Chen: Quick recap — we'll send the heatmap export + bench CSV, SOC2 and private deploy checklist, and Marcus will share bench harness and run a targeted eval once you provide sample prompts/data distribution. We'll schedule pilot kickoff next week if this looks good.
[08:58] Nina Patel: Thanks, this was helpful. One last question — competitor differences: Anthropic had good safety for hallucinations, any notes?
[09:05] Marcus Rivera: We annotate safety profiles and add safety evals; Redwood's runtime supports safety filters and function-based grounding to mitigate hallucinations in post-processing. We'll include a safety eval pass in the bench.
[09:17] Marta Ruiz: Please include a data retention policy doc.
[09:20] Lara Chen: Will do.
[09:23] Nina Patel: Great, look forward to the files. Thanks Lara, Marcus.
[09:26] Lara Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with the artifacts.

[END]

description:

The invoice has been finalized and posted to their accounting system, and the customer is requesting an explanation and corrective action.\n\nImpact: Finance at BrightPulse is unable to reconcile month-end expenses across cost centers. This affects internal chargebacks for two product teams and delays their internal audit. The amount is material for the customer's internal billing (>$10k).\n\nEnvironment: Dedicated account ID bp-9983 running reserved pool in us-west-2, using hybrid fallback to hosted for burst windows. Billing pipeline processed the invoice on 2026-03-07 with postbacks aggregated hourly.\n\nSteps to reproduce / observed sequence:\n1) Customer ran a cross-team batch embedding job on 2026-03-04 that spanned two cost center tags in their metadata (AD-ML and OPS).\n2) During a burst window (2026-03-04 22:00-22:30 UTC) the job triggered hosted fallback and microburst credits were generated.\n3) Billing postback handler received mixed postbacks; one subset had cost_center tag \"AD-ML\" and another subset had a legacy tag \"ops\" (lowercase) sent by the customer's orchestration layer.\n4) Final invoice lines show the credits consolidated under CostCenter:OPS (normalized uppercase mapping) while usage lines for the same job were split.\n\nLogs / evidence provided: Attached CSV of postbacks (postbacks_bp-9983_2026-03-04.csv), invoice PDF INV-2026-03-07.pdf, and a screenshot of customer's internal chargeback report.\n\nCustomer request: Explain root cause and provide remediation (adjust invoice lines or apply correcting credit), and confirm a fix so future postbacks are normalized consistently.

comments:
2026-03-13 - Initial customer comment (Sarah Wong, BrightPulse finance): 'We see a $12,450 credit on line 4 of INV-2026-03-07 that is labeled OPS. This credit should be applied to AD-ML. Please advise — this prevents our month-end close.'
2026-03-13 - Support (Maya Chen): 'Thanks Sarah — we have opened SUP-665432 and are triaging. Could you attach the postback export (raw JSON) if available and confirm the API keys used for the job? We'll prioritize this because the invoice is finalized.'

The reconciler normalizes via exact-match mapping table which currently contains "OPS" => CostCenter:OPS and "AD-ML" => CostCenter:AD-ML, but does not canonicalize case. Filing as root-cause candidate: case-sensitive tag mapping.'
2026-03-14 - Support to customer (Maya Chen): 'We have a provisional plan: apply a correcting credit of $12,450 to CostCenter:AD-ML in your next billing cycle and backfill an off-cycle credit if you need an immediate correction. Engineering will implement a reconciler fix to case-normalize cost_center tags. Documentation will be updated. We will confirm next steps after engineering triage.'

Queries run: SELECT count(*) FROM billing.postbacks WHERE account_id='bp-9983' AND DATE(event_time)='2026-03-04' GROUP BY lower(cost_center); Results show 1120 with lower(cost_center)='ops' and 2480 with lower(cost_center)='ad-ml'. Reconciler mapping uses exact string matching: mapping table lacked lowercasing step. Correlated invoice lines: credit line id CL-8891 aggregated credits using mapping resolution logic that selected OPS bucket for lowercase 'ops' values because of a legacy alias entry 'ops' => OPS but full-route consolidation collapsed mixed-case inputs into a single canonical bucket due to alias precedence rules.\n\nRelevant artifacts: attached postbacks CSV, invoice render, reconciler config (billing-reconciler v2.1.3).\n\nHypothesis: Inconsistent tag case from customer's worker fleet combined with alias precedence in the reconciliation algorithm caused credits to be grouped under OPS. This only affected credit aggregation path (not usage lines) because the credit aggregator uses a different alias resolution step for historical reasons.\n\nImmediate risk: Customer's accounting mismatch and potential duplicate corrective actions if not handled carefully. No platform-wide financial exposure identified beyond this account so far.

resolution_notes:
Status: Pending engineering fix and customer agreement on remediation. Work items and proposed timeline:\n1) Short-term remediation (executed 2026-03-14): Support applied a provisional off-cycle credit of $12,450 to CostCenter:AD-ML and issued a credit memo CM-2026-03-14-665432. Customer requested the off-cycle credit to expedite their reconciliation.\n2) Engineering change (target): Implement case-normalization in billing-reconciler mapping logic and add unit test coverage. Target PR: billing-reconciler#412 (in review). Expected deploy to staging 2026-03-17, to prod 2026-03-20 after validation.\n3) Post-deploy follow-up: Re-run invoice reprocessing tool for bp-9983 for the window 2026-03-01 -> 2026-03-07 with corrected mapping to verify no other misattributed lines. If discrepancies remain, issue formal invoice adjustment and notify customer billing contacts.\n4) Preventive: Add a monitoring alert for cost_center tag entropy (new metric: pct_unknown_alias > 0.5% over 1h) and update support KB about common customer tag normalization pitfalls.\n\nFollow-up actions assigned: Liam O'Connor (engineering) to land PR and run reprocess job; Maya Chen (support) to coordinate credit memo and confirm with BrightPulse finance once reprocessing completes. Estimated resolution: 2026-03-20.

Pending - provisional credit applied and engineering fix in progress

Vendor balance inaccurate; potential duplicate credit to wrong cost center when finance closes month-end. Affects one active vendor (HelioMetrics) and one past PO. Accounting needs a clean AP ledger before month-end close (3 business days).

4) Observe that the payment was allocated to PO-2024012 (status = Closed) rather than to vendor-credit account/suspense as expected

Refund/credit from vendor should land in vendor suspense account or create a credit memo, not be applied to closed PO lines. Allocation rules should ignore closed POs for auto-apply logic.

This compaction incorrectly converted previously-applied provisional credits into a reversal on the finalized invoice line.\n- Metering team observed tag-shadowing: temporary tag deduped into parent org tag due to a mismatch in namespace normalization rules introduced by PR 8b7c3a2.\n- Reproducer: replaying the exact postback subset in staging replicates the compaction behavior and produces a negative adjustment in the aggregator staging invoice.\n\nCustomer requested outcome:\n- Immediate hold on autopay until resolved.\n- A clear explanation of the cause and a correction entry on the next billing cycle (or immediate manual credit).\n- Confirmation that future dedicated failovers will not trigger the same reclassification behavior.\n\nNext steps planned:\n- Billing eng (Diego) to open hotfix to skip compaction for postbacks tagged with \"dedicated-fallback-*\" by 2026-03-11 EOD.\n- Metering to add a normalization test asserting namespace isolation between temporary fallback tags and reserved-hour tags.\n- Support to coordinate manual credit/adjustment for NexusAI pending engineering fix and to provide timeline to customer.\n\nRequested from customer (already provided):\n- Sample invoice (INV-2026-02-28-NA) and internal cost-center where the reversal was observed (provided).\n- Confirmation they paused autopay (provided).\n\nRemarks:\n- This ticket spans billing reconciliation, meter normalization, and dedicated routing logic. We should track as high-priority until corrected on ledger and applied as a manual adjustment or patch that prevents recurrence.

[Dedicated capacity: customer readiness rubric and scaled-routing playbook]
description:
Objective: produce a reproducible customer-readiness rubric and a scaled-routing playbook that lets Sales/CS/Onboarding quickly map a customer request to a reserved throughput SLA, GPU family recommendation, and an initial scaling policy. This is a non-bug, product triage effort to lift intake speed, reduce back-and-forth with customers, and standardize fallback behaviors across tiers.

Scope:
- Design a 12-question intake rubric (traffic profile, p50/p95 latency needs, data residency & compliance, expected concurrency, burst tolerance, model family & sequence length distribution, acceptable quantization) that yields a numeric readiness score and recommended SLA band.
- Define three default scaling policy templates (Conservative / Balanced / Aggressive) including autoscale thresholds, burst credit allowances, and preemption/fallback ladder.
- Map SLA bands to GPU family recommendations (e.g., A100x2 for high-throughput low-latency P0, H100/Avx-optimized variants for short sequences, T4/RTX for lower-cost throughput) with cost delta guidance.
- Create a 'scaled-routing playbook' that prescribes routing (region, capacity tier, model variant fallbacks) given capacity constraints and readiness score.
- Produce acceptance criteria, onboarding checklist, and a customer-facing one-pager for AE/CS teams.

Out-of-scope: detailed infra implementation of autoscaler algorithms (ENG will own), and SLA contract language (Legal/Finance will finalize).

Success criteria (measurable):
- Intake-to-recommendation time reduced from avg 4 business days to <24 hours for 80% of requests.
- 90% of incoming enterprise requests map to an SLA+GPU recommendation without follow-up questions.
- First 2 pilot customers onboarded using the rubric with no major SLA revision after 30 days.

acceptance_criteria:
Intake rubric published as a Google Doc and embedded into Customer Intake form (CS/AE).
Three scaling policy templates defined with concrete parameter values and playbook steps.
SLA-to-GPU mapping table with estimated monthly cost delta published to internal pricing playbook.
Routing playbook includes at least three fallback scenarios with clear triggers and owner handoffs.
Pilot onboarding runbook and AE one-pager created; 2 pilot customers agreed to try within 6 weeks.

[Capacity Command Center: granular throughput knobs, predictive autoscale, and audit stream]
description:
Goal: Ship a unified Console experience (Capacity Command Center) for Dedicated fleets that combines direct throughput controls (per-fleet and per-route), predictive autoscaling policies, and an immutable change history/audit stream. This ticket covers PM requirements, acceptance criteria, stakeholder sign-offs, and rollout plan for the UI + API surface needed to operate throughput guarantees and autoscale policies without deep infra knowledge.

background:
Customers running Dedicated capacity have asked for a single-pane operations view: a way to set hard throughput guarantees (tokens/sec), create workload-aware autoscale policies, preview cost impact, and see a chronological audit of changes with rollbacks. Current console panels are fragmented (preset toggles, separate autoscale editor, and an opaque activity log). This initiative targets platform parity across Hosted/Dedicated while preserving reserved commit constraints.

scope:
- New Capacity Command Center page under Fleet > Capacity
- Per-fleet throughput controls with explicit SLA target, burst allowance, and estimated cost delta
- Autoscaling policy builder: schedule, reactive rules (p50/p90 latency, queue depth, token burn rate), and cooldown windows
- Predictive scaling preview using last 7/30 day workload patterns (UI-only initially)
- Immutable change history stream with diff view and rollback link to previous policy version
- API endpoints for programmatic changes and audit retrieval (backwards compatible)

out_of_scope:
- Implementing backend predictive autoscaler (only UI preview in this phase)
- Deep billing integration for committed discounts (cost deltas are estimates)
- Private on-prem packaged installer changes (handled in follow-up)

acceptance_criteria:
Capacity Command Center accessible from Fleet nav and shows list of fleets with current throughput targets and health indicators
PM-set throughput target can be edited inline, saved as a new policy version, and pushed to runtime with confirmation modal
Autoscaling policy builder supports at least three rule types: scheduled (cron), reactive-latency (p90 > threshold), and reactive-throughput (queue depth) with cooldown and max/min bounds
Preview shows predicted scaling events for last 7-day workload and shows estimated token cost delta for a chosen policy
Change history stores every policy change with user, timestamp, diff, and an affordance to rollback to a previous version (audit only; rollback triggers existing API)
All actions are logged to the audit endpoint and visible in the Console -> Activity stream within 60s
E2E tests for editing throughput, creating autoscale policies, and viewing history are added to console e2e suite
Design and PM sign-off on copy, layout, and failure states (low-data, backend errors)

risks_and_mitigations:
Risk: Operators accidentally set throughput above committed capacity and cause billing disputes. Mitigation: add guardrail that shows committed capacity and requires a two-step confirmation with explicit cost delta when exceeding commit.
Risk: Predictive preview misleads customers. Mitigation: label previews as estimates and include confidence band; do not auto-apply predictive changes in this phase.
Risk: Large fleets cause UI performance issues. Mitigation: paginate fleet list, lazy-load charts, and surface sampling for long histories.
Risk: Audit log growth and storage cost. Mitigation: retention policy defaults (90 days) with export to S3/enterprise archive option.
Risk: Ambiguity about precedence between policy types (scheduled vs reactive). Mitigation: define precedence rules in UI help text and tooltips; schedule wins unless overridden by emergency override feature (future ticket).

dependencies:
ENG-9202
ENG-9450
PM-50321

implementation_notes:
Frontend: React + ChartJS for throughput timelines; reuse Fleet table component; new PolicyEditor modal component
Backend: Add policy-version resource and policy-applier proxy endpoint; events written to audit stream on write
API: POST /fleets/{id}/policies to create versioned policy, PATCH to update, GET /fleets/{id}/policies?version=latest
Telemetry: emit events capacity.policy.update, capacity.throughput.set, capacity.policy.rollback with metadata for cost estimate

qa_plan:

Automated e2e: create policy -> simulate metric breach -> ensure reactive rule would trigger (mock metrics)
Load test: UI list with 5k fleets to validate pagination and chart sampling
Security: verify audit export only accessible to org-admin role

rollout_plan:
Alpha: internal dogfood on staging with two engineering customers and internal SREs (2 weeks)
Beta: opt-in in production for customers with Dedicated capacity (feature flag)
GA: enable for all Dedicated customers with opt-out for enterprise customers requiring custom retention
Monitoring: SLOs for API latency (95th < 200ms) and UI load times (95th < 600ms)

[Provisioning Checklist and Interactive Canvas for Dedicated Capacity Onboarding]
description:
Design an illustrated provisioning checklist and an interactive canvas that walk customers through Dedicated capacity setup: select GPU pool size, configure autoscaling policies, set SLA targets, and validate networking/KMS prerequisites. Deliverables: hi-fi Figma mockups for desktop and tablet, annotated screenshot assets for the docs site, an interactive prototype for the Console team to embed, and a lightweight PDF runbook for account execs.

acceptance_criteria:
Figma file with annotated frames for each checklist step (Estimate capacity, Network & KMS, Autoscale policy, SLA selection, Review & Confirm)
Interactive canvas prototype (Figma prototype link + annotated handoff notes) demonstrating progressive disclosure and in-context help
Set of 6 export-ready screenshot assets (desktop + tablet variants) sized and named for docs and marketing use
A one-page PDF runbook summarizing checklist items with quick troubleshooting tips
Design tokens and microcopy approved by PM and Localization team

Start -> Quick capacity estimate (slider + sample workloads) -> Network & KMS check (pass/fail with remediation) -> Autoscale policy composer (min/max/scale-in/scale-out rules) -> SLA selector (latency/availability tiers + cost delta) -> Review & provision (summary card + CTA)

Use progressive disclosure: show minimal options first (quick estimate), reveal advanced options via 'Show advanced' toggles
Illustration metaphor: use a lightweight 'power gauge' to communicate provisioned throughput instead of raw GPU counts
Autoscale composer should default to conservative min/max based on common workloads; engineers will provide sampled defaults

[prepack-int8-weights-and-smoothquant-fuse-with-kernel-lane-allocator]
description:
Motivation: INT8 inference for large decoder models showed suboptimal memory layout overhead and extra dequant steps when combined with smoothquant-style per-channel scaling. This PR introduces a weight prepack path and a small kernel-lane allocator that lets the runtime fuse smoothquant dequantization into the kernel dispatch without materializing intermediate dequant tensors. Goals: 1) lower wall-clock latency for first-token and steady-state by removing memory-bound dequant copies, 2) reduce peak GPU memory for multi-tenant workloads by prepacking int8 weights in a compact layout and sharing lane metadata across batches, 3) keep compatibility with existing KV cache and continuous-batching pipelines. What changed (high-level): - New weight prepack module (src/runtime/kernel/int8_weight_prepack.cc/h) that produces a packed INT8 layout with per-channel scale/zero-point metadata optimized for our vectorized GEMM kernels. - Kernel adapter hooks (src/runtime/kernel/kernel_adapter.cc) to accept packed weights and apply smoothquant per-channel scaling on-the-fly inside the GEMM launcher when the model has smoothquant metadata. - Kernel lane allocator (src/runtime/scheduler/lane_allocator.cc/h) that assigns model weight lanes to worker threads/GPU streams so packed weights can be reused across microbatches without copying. - KV cache coordinator updates (src/runtime/scheduler/kv_cache_coordinator.cc) to pin KV cache blocks to the same lane affinity when the request uses pinned weights, avoiding cross-lane synchronization. - A shortfall fallback: when model uses dynamic shape patterns incompatible with lane reuse, runtime falls back to previous dequant-copy path automatically. Performance: microbenchmarks on a 32B decoder model (batch sizes 1..8, seq len 1..1024) show median token latency improvement of 9-16% at steady state and 18-28% for first-token latency on Ampere A100, with peak memory reduction of ~12% at high concurrency. Compatibility/risks: The change touches low-level kernel dispatch. We limited the surface by gating packed-weight paths behind a model feature flag and added runtime checks for per-channel metadata version. Rolling plan: staged canary rollout on Dedicated pools with a 2-hour canary window, monitor latency, token error-rate regressions, and memory counters. Checklist: - [x] Unit tests for weight prepack and kernel adapter - [x] Integration test exercising smoothquant models through hosted API - [x] Performance bench scripts added - [x] Migration doc and feature flag gating - [x] Observability: added counters for lane cache hits/misses, packed-weight size. Related: ENG-3421 (quant kernel latency), ENG-3498 (kv cache affinity).

Anika Rao: Added header docstrings and a diagram in prepack_smoothquant_notes.md per Marcus' request.
Diego Torres: The lane allocator is clever. Concern: potential starvation if many small requests contend for lanes. Suggest adding a fairness counter or aging policy.
Anika Rao: Added simple LRU aging policy and a unit test to simulate heavy small-request contention; PTAL.
Priya Nair (SRE): We need an observability signal for fallback-to-copy rate; ops will want to alert if it spikes after rollout.

[GEMM dequant fusion + prefetch KV-cache coordinator for hybrid INT8/FP8 paths]
description:
Motivation: hot GEMM kernels for quantized inference showed a recurring cost in per-token dequant/scale bookkeeping (scale table lookups and per-layer dequant ops). This PR introduces a fused dequant->GEMM kernel path plus a small KV-cache-coordinated prefetcher for per-layer scale metadata to reduce memory traffic and avoid branchy dequant fallbacks. The goal is to reduce tail latency for short to medium sequences and increase throughput for steady-state streaming workloads under continuous batching, without changing high-level APIs. Approach: 1) Add fused_dequant_gemm kernel implementations for INT8 and FP8 source tensors (runtime/kernels/fused_dequant_gemm.*). The fused kernel consumes quantized weights + precomputed scale factors and emits the GEMM output in the runtime's preferred dense format, eliminating a separate dequant pass. 2) Introduce a ScaleTableCache (runtime/kv_cache/scale_cache.{h,cc}) that stores per-layer quant scales and prefetches them into the local worker memory when a model is loaded or when a new attention key arrives. The cache coordinates with the existing KV cache lifecycle to warm scales ahead of the first token generation. 3) Modify the path allocator and scheduler weight heuristic (runtime/scheduler/path_allocator.cc) to prefer fused paths when sequence length and batch sizes indicate latency-sensitive mode. 4) Continuous batching integration: batching logic updated to mark fused-path-compatible batches and ensure that batching coalescing preserves scale-table locality (runtime/batching/continuous_batcher.cc). 5) Safety: full fallback to the legacy dequant+gemm path if kernel selection fails (hardware mismatch, missing scales, or precision mismatch). Includes feature gate runtime.config.enable_fused_dequant_gemm (default: true for internal clusters; disabled for some legacy GPU tiers until validated). Benchmarks: microbench harness (benchmark/microbench/quant_paths.py) and CI bench runs show median latency down ~18% and 90th percentile down ~25% for representative chat workloads on H100 (sequence length 64, batch=8), throughput increase ~22% on A100 for large batches due to reduced memory bandwidth pressure. Memory working set reduced ~28% when scale tables are hot. Tests & Validation: unit tests added for kernel correctness (tests/unit/fused_dequant_gemm_test.cc), integration quant smoke tests (tests/integration/quant_smoke.py), and correctness cross-precision validation against FP32 reference. CI: initial CI run exposed a numerical mismatch on an early FP8 schedule; fixed by delaying reorder of scale-prefetch for particular kernel tiling (commit "fix: avoid scale reorder for fp8 tiled paths"). Rollout plan: behind feature flag; staged canary across dedicated pools: 1) internal perf canary (5% traffic) for 48h, 2) dedicated reserved clusters (20%) for 72h with regression alarms, 3) global rollout if no regressions found. Related work: ENG-4872 (perf sprint), ENG-4921 (kv-cache lifecycle), SUP-1124 (customer case for low-latency chat). Checklist: [x] Kernel implementation, [x] Scheduler ties, [x] KV-scale cache, [x] microbench harness, [x] unit + integration tests, [x] docs/release note. Security & compatibility: no API surface changes; backward compatible kernel fallback in place. Merge: squash.

feat(kv): implement ScaleTableCache + prefetch hooks onto KV lifecycle

[Optimize INT8 dequant-fusion kernel and smoothquant scheduling to reduce p99 and token cost]
description:
Motivation: For the quantized inference stack we've been shipping two main bottlenecks: (1) the dequantization+matmul fusion path for INT8 kernels introduces extra memory traffic and kernel launches at each attention and FFN block; (2) SmoothQuant scaling interacts poorly with our scheduler and continuous-batching heuristics, causing variable p99 regressions under mixed-sequence workloads. This PR introduces three coordinated changes: 1) a fused dequantize+gemm kernel that accepts packed INT8 weights and produces FP16 accumulation with optional requantization hooks; 2) a scheduling tweak that biases smoothquant scaling application to the slower stage of the pipeline and batches compatible sequence shapes together more aggressively; 3) a lightweight KV-cache-aware fast path that skips per-step dequant for cached KV blocks and reuses FP16 cached keys when the model quantization profile allows it.
High-level summary of changes: - Implement fused_int8_dequant_gemm CUDA kernel with vectorized loads, int8->fp16 accumulation, and single-kernel scale+bias application; exposed via runtime/kernel_registry. - Add quant_profile metadata to model descriptors to select the optimal kernel variant at load time (INT8_PACKED, FP8_DYNAMIC, FP16_FALLBACK). - Scheduler: introduce SequenceShapeAffinity rule to group similar-length requests for continuous batching; add SmoothQuantWindow heuristic to only apply per-layer scaling on first N tokens of a request when streaming is enabled. - KV cache: store an optional FP16 shadow of int8-packed KV blocks for reuse; add LRU soft cap and transparent eviction. - Telemetry: new perf counters (kernel_time_fused_int8, kv_shadow_hit, smoothquant_applied) and unit tests.
Performance numbers (microbench on T4 and A10G; averaged across 50k requests of mixed lengths 16/128/512): - Baseline (old INT8 path): p50 12.8ms p95 38.2ms p99 78.5ms throughput 22 toks/s - This PR (fused + scheduling + kv-shadow): p50 11.4ms p95 29.6ms p99 49.3ms throughput 28 toks/s - Relative: p99 reduced ~37%, throughput +27%, token GPU time reduced ~18%.
Safety and compatibility: default model load remains unchanged; INT8 packed models must declare quant_profile or fallback to old path. This avoids accidental perf regressions for older deployments.

[Per-token affine merge and KV-prefetch scheduler to reduce INT8/FP8 dequant stalls]
description:
Motivation: We observed tail latency spikes when mixing INT8 and FP8 model variants with dynamic KV-cache reuse. Root cause traced to microstalling during per-token dequantization when the kernel scheduler switched execution lanes and the KV window prefetcher tripped an extra serialization point. This PR introduces a lightweight per-token affine-merge pass in the kernel pipeline coupled with a windowed KV-prefetch scheduler to coalesce dequant work and remove serialization across microbatches.

What this changes: Adds a new kernel fusion step (affine_merge_pass) that merges the tiny affine rescale + requant (dequant-affine-requant common pattern for smoothquant) into a single vectorized microkernel for INT8/FP8 hybrid paths. The scheduler changes introduce a KV-prefetch window (default 8 tokens) that aligns prefetching with affinity windows from the batcher to avoid cross-lane cache thrash.

Goals: Reduce per-token latency jitter on mixed-precision workloads, improve throughput in small-microbatch scenarios (1-8 tokens), and keep steady-state token/sec at parity or better with prior fused paths.

Design summary: - New pass: affine_merge_pass applied after layout normalization and before attention kernel selection. - Kernel: socalled "affine_merge_v2" implements fused dequant (INT8->FP32), affine scale/bias, and optional requant to FP8 in a single loop with prefetch hints. - Scheduler: kv_window_prefetcher schedules KV reads in aligned windows and defers cross-lane prefetches until the window completes. - Batcher integration: microbatcher includes affinity hints (affinity_id) which scheduler uses to avoid prefetching KV for lanes that will be drained soon. - Configuration: runtime flags (env and per-deployment config) to tune window size and enable/disable fused kernel.

Performance results (internal e2e bench): - Testbed: A100x4, Llama-3-8B variants (fp32 baseline / int8-smoothquant / fp8-heuristic), synthetic chat trace of 12k tokens. - Median latency (1-token microbatch): - baseline: 23.4ms, with this PR: 17.6ms (-24.8%) - P95: baseline 61.0ms -> 38.2ms (-37.4%) - Throughput (tokens/sec steady): baseline 9.8k -> 10.9k (+11.2%) - Cost proxy (GPU utilization): +3% steady util, net decrease in wasted stalls measured by scheduler traces. Regression tests show no quality delta on output when requant path used; we added opt-in param to bypass requant for strict FP8 fidelity.

Backward/compatibility: No API changes to the public inference API. Runtime flags are opt-in; deployments can gate rollout. Default is enabled for dedicated and private clusters with GPU >= Ampere.

[Eager dequant merge with KV hotpath prefetch adapter and lane-aware clamps]
description:
Motivation: latency spikes and memory pressure observed when dequantization is performed late in the ATTENTION hotpath for mixed INT8/FP8 models. This PR implements an eager dequant merge that fuses dequant ops into the kernel entry where possible, introduces a small prefetch adapter on the KV cache hotpath to warm per-lane state, and adds lane-aware clamp heuristics to stabilize scale drift for FP8 emulation. The change reduces p99 and median latency, smooths variance under bursty traffic, and avoids extra transient allocations. Changes include a new eager merge pass in the kernel router, a lightweight prefetch adapter that attaches to KVCache::read, and safe fallbacks for models that require canonical per-token dequant. Checklist: - [x] Implement eager dequant merge and kernel hook - [x] Add KV hotpath prefetch adapter with bounded async prefetch window - [x] Add per-lane clamp heuristics + config flag runtime.quant.lane_clamp - [x] Extend continuous-batcher tests to cover fused paths - [x] Benchmarks and perf tests added - [x] Security review for prefetch adapter memory access - [x] Docs updated (runtime tuning guide) Compatibility notes: the eager merge only activates for verified model signatures (quantizable weights + contiguous weight layout). For models that violate assumptions we fall back to the previous dequant-on-demand path. Linear/Jira: ENG-2184 tracks prioritization and rollout, SUP-7412 captures support cases reported during canary. Rollout plan: staged canary on Dedicated pools -> gradual ramp to hosted API with feature flag off by default for older model versions.

[openai-compat: adaptive tool aliasing and choice-priority resolver]
description:
Context: We're seeing subtle differences in tool selection when downstream systems expect tool aliases (e.g., 'weather' vs 'weather_v2') and when model-produced tool_choice signals arrive as ranked lists or soft-probabilities. This PR introduces an adaptive aliasing layer plus a priority-resolver that normalizes tool_choice semantics across streaming and non-streaming paths.

summary:
Adds a canonical alias map, selection weighting resolver, and streaming-safe tool-choice handling to the OpenAI compatibility adapter. Preserves backwards compatibility while enabling deterministic fallbacks and tunable preference weights for enterprise tool routing.

motivation_and_rationale:
Operators previously had to maintain brittle 1:1 name mappings in the application layer. With multiple model variants and function name drift, misrouted tool invocations caused retries and incorrect outputs. This change centralizes alias resolution and introduces a priority resolver that consumes: 1) explicit tool_choice entries, 2) streaming partial tool hints, and 3) operator-provided preference weights to produce a single canonical tool invocation decision.

design_highlights:
- alias_map: YAML-backed mapping supporting exact, prefix, and regex aliases with optional deprecation metadata.
- priority_resolver: scoring pipeline that combines operator weight, model confidence (soft or hard), and recent invocation success metrics.
- streaming_adapter: incremental aggregation of partial tool_choice fragments to avoid premature invocations while maintaining low latency.
- compatibility_mode: feature flag to toggle strict legacy 1:1 resolution for customers that rely on old semantics.

api_changes:
- New optional parameter in /v1/compat/dispatch: 'alias_profile' (string) and 'choice_resolution' (enum: strict|adaptive|legacy).
- SDK: redwood-sdk-python adds DispatchOptions.alias_profile and .choice_resolution with docs and example.
- Admin: YAML schema for alias_map under /config/openai/aliases.yaml.
Note: Default remains legacy-compatible but uses adaptive resolution for new accounts.

rollout_plan:
1) feature gated behind 'openai_adaptive_aliasing' runtime flag; 2) start with internal canary (10% traffic) for 48h; 3) enable for PLG accounts opted-in; 4) full rollout after two weeks if no regressions.
Traffic routing includes automatic fallback to the previous resolver when invocation error rate increases above 2x baseline.

migration_notes:
Operators can supply an alias_profile to map existing tooling names. A migration tool (scripts/migrate_aliases.py) is included to convert customer-provided CSVs into the YAML alias_map format. Backwards compatibility tests included for customers with strict mappings.
