[v1 OpenAI chat: response sculpting, stop coalescing, and streaming logprob envelope]
description:
Motivation: Customers using the OpenAI /v1/chat.completions surface expect a few nuanced behaviors (stop semantics, role-preserving role mapping, streaming logprob envelopes, and deterministic function_call hints). Our compatibility layer has historically handled these piecemeal; this change bundles a deterministic, well-tested mapping layer plus a streaming envelope that reduces parser churn for downstream SDKs.

What this PR does (high level): 1) Introduces a response-sculpting adapter that normalizes incoming v1 parameters (temperature/top_p/stop arrays/stop strings) into Redwood runtime configs, coalescing stop tokens with deduplication and priority ordering (explicit stop > system-supplied stop). 2) Adds a streaming logprob envelope: each delta event includes a compact logprob map when requested (logprobs mode) and a stable "terminate_reason" token on final events to remove ambiguity for partial consumers. 3) Preserves role metadata and adds role_alias resolution so tools that pass custom roles still receive canonical role labels in responses. 4) Extends function_call handling to surface both suggested and forced calls: when the model suggests a call we emit a standardized tool-call event; when callers force a function_call we validate against registered schemas and return an immediate structured output. 5) Implements conservative backpressure hooks in the stream coalescer to improve stability under bursty clients.

Compatibility notes: The adapter keeps backward-compatible defaults; previous consumers that do not request logprobs or function schemas should see no change. New behavior is opt-in via the v1 parameter mapping and an additional header (X-OpenAI-Compat: true) for private deployments that want explicit parity checks.

Testing and validation: Unit tests added for stop coalescing, role aliasing, function schema validation and negative cases. End-to-end tests simulate streaming clients (chunk reordering, reconnect resume) and assert final assembled events for both SDKs. Benchmarked against a production-like workload: median p99 tail latency increased by ~1ms in the worst case; CPU overhead on the agent path is <2% for common workloads.

Rollout plan: Feature gated behind openai_v1_compat flag. Canary on dedicated region us-west-2 for 48 hours with traffic mirroring; if stable, promote to main with a one-week monitoring window (alert on increased stream reconnects or event schema validation failures).

Related: ENG-1842 (param mapping), SUP-5523 (customer incident that exposed stop token mismatch).

[Introduce OpenAI-compat tool hint encoder and fragment guard to stabilize tool selection across streams]
release_notes:
Adds OpenAI compatibility shim for deterministic tool selection during streaming and a structured-output normalizer; non-breaking, opt-in via config flag openai.compat.tool_hinting

description:
Summary: This PR adds a lightweight 'tool hint' encoder to the OpenAI compatibility adapter and a 'fragment guard' layer that prevents mid-stream tool_choice flips when the model emits fragmented function/tool call messages; Motivation: We observed nondeterministic tool selection when large responses were streamed in fragments; downstream invocation systems would receive partial evidence and flip the chosen tool mid-stream causing duplicate tool invocations or aborted handoffs; Goal is to stabilize tool_choice semantics without changing the OpenAI-compatible API surface; Changes: 1) tool hint encoder: encodes deterministic, order-preserving per-tool hints into the stream as opaque, short provenance tokens (header: x-rw-tool-hint) that the invoke layer uses to lock the selected tool for the lifetime of a response; 2) fragment guard: coalesces contiguous tool-invoke fragments and defers decision until fragment boundary or signature-confidence threshold; 3) schema normalizer: aligns tool parameter schemas from external registries to the OpenAI function schema (type coercions, required->optional mapping, canonical name aliases); 4) tie-break policy: deterministic score+id tiebreak to avoid nondeterminism when scores are near-equal; 5) telemetry: new metrics rw.compat.tool_choice.locked_count and rw.compat.fragment_coalesce_rate; 6) opt-in config: openai.compat.tool_hinting (default false for now) and rollout plan; 7) docs and SDK: TS + Python compat tests and example; 8) e2e test harness that simulates fragmented streams and validates at-most-once tool handoff; Backwards compatibility: no API schema changes; behavior is gated by config and flag rollout for Dedicated/Private; Risk: subtle differences when models already rely on token-level heuristics; mitigation: gradual rollout and A/B canary; Why unique: instead of changing model scoring we add a streaming-level coordination primitive that is transparent to most callers; Technical notes: the tool hint tokens are HMAC'd short strings carrying (tool_id, seq, partial_hash) and are stripped before user-facing output; they are applied only in internal streaming frames; The fragment guard uses a small state machine per-stream to coalesce fragments up to 512 tokens or until an explicit end_of_function marker is observed; This avoids re-parsing partial JSON fragments mid-stream; See commit list and file changes below for implementation detail and tests.

[Normalize OpenAI invocation envelope, clarify tool-selection signals, and add stream-resilient framing]
description:
Motivation: Several customers and internal evals showed inconsistent behavior when the OpenAI-compat layer returned tool selection signals (e.g. 'tool_choice' with ambiguous metadata) across streaming and non-streaming modes. This caused duplicate tool invocations, incorrect schema inference, and brittle downstream tool routers in Redwood Dedicated/Private deployments.

This PR introduces a deterministic normalization step for the OpenAI invocation envelope, plus stream-resilient framing for tool/message fragments. The goal is to: 1) make the compatibility layer emit a single canonical selection signal for every invocation, 2) map OpenAI tool schemas into a stable internal schema with minimal changes for existing customers, and 3) make streaming fragments idempotent and re-assemblable at the service edge.

What changed (high level):
- New package: pkg/openai/normalize_invocation.go — normalizer that transforms incoming OpenAI-style responses into Redwood's canonical InvocationEnvelope. It collapses multiple tool signals into one selected_tool hint and preserves tool confidence/metadata in a stable metadata map.
- Tool schema mapper: pkg/tooling/tool_schema_mapper.go — conservative mapping rules for OpenAI 'parameters' -> Redwood typed schema, including type coercion rules and a small whitelist for nested objects.
- Streaming: server/streaming/frame_parser.go updated to add fragment IDs and checksum headers for tool/message fragments. Parser now supports out-of-order fragments and dedup by fragment id+checksum.
- API layer: server/api/openai_adapter.go updated to call the normalizer before routing to tool routing pipeline; updates to response shape sent back to clients to maintain OpenAI wire-compatibility while ensuring a single 'selected_tool' semantic in the internal router.
- Docs: docs/openai-compatibility/invocation-normalization.md with migration notes and examples.

Compatibility notes:
- Outbound API responses remain OpenAI-compatible: we do not change the visible OpenAI fields returned to customers. Internally, however, the runtime will prefer the normalized 'selected_tool' hint to decide which tool to invoke. In the rare case of conflicting tool signals, the normalizer uses (in order): explicit_invocation field, highest-confidence tool_choice, then deterministic fallback to first available tool that matches schema.
- Customers who implemented custom tool routers based on raw tool_choice fragments should migrate to using the new normalized hint or consult the docs which show a 1-line change to switch to the normalized envelope.

Testing and rollout plan:
- Unit tests for mapping rules and type coercions included.
- Integration tests: simulated streaming sessions with fragmented tool metadata; verified idempotent assembler under network reorders.
- Canary rollout: staged to 10% of traffic for hosted API for 48 hours, then to Dedicated nodes behind a feature flag. Private installer includes an opt-in toggle for the first release cycle.

Migration steps for operators (short):
1) Review docs/openai-compatibility/invocation-normalization.md for the mapping table.
2) If you have custom routers, update to read the normalized 'selected_tool' header from the invocation payload.
3) Toggle feature flag if running Redwood Private/Dedicated during rollout.

Related work: links to internal Linear tasks ENG-7421 (tool-selection ambiguity), ENG-7553 (stream-fragment dedup).

Rationale for not changing public wire format: minimize breaking client changes while fixing internal flakiness in tool invocation semantics.

Release notes summary: Normalizes OpenAI invocation envelopes to ensure a single canonical tool-selection signal, improves streaming fragment resilience, and provides safe mapping rules for tool parameter schemas. Operators with custom routing should follow the migration guide in docs/openai-compatibility/invocation-normalization.md.

No public wire-format breaking changes. Operators with custom routers should read docs/openai-compatibility/invocation-normalization.md for migration steps.

[stabilize tool_choice weighting and add compact v2 invoke envelope for OpenAI compatibility]
description:
Motivation: Several customer integrations hit nondeterministic tool selection when multiple tools had near-equal scores and streaming fragments from tool invocations produced noisy, reparsed payloads. This PR introduces two coordinated changes: (1) a deterministic, weight-aware tie-breaker for tool_choice decisions that combines explicit tool weight, provenance, and a seeded stable-hash to remove flakiness across retries; (2) an opt-in v2 invoke envelope for OpenAI-compatible streams that reduces per-fragment overhead, carries compact schema hints, and improves reassembly resilience under high-concurrency streaming. Summary of changes: Added ToolChoiceResolver that normalizes incoming OpenAI-style function/tool scores into a single selection score using configurable weight_decay and provenance_priority. The resolver exposes deterministic behavior via a stable seed derived from the request-id to ensure repeatable outcomes for retries and hedges. Introduced invoke_envelope v2: compact fragment header fields (env_id, frag_index, last_frag, frag_schema_crc, prov_ref) and a small delta encoding for repeated keys to reduce payload size. Implemented a v1->v2 compatibility adapter in the streaming decoder so hosted customers keep working while new clients opt-in. Telemetry and observability: emit tool_choice.resolve events with fields (chosen_tool, score_components, seed_hash, resolve_latency_ms) and new histograms for invoke.envelope_v2.emit.size_bytes and invoke.envelope_v2.reassembly.latency_ms. Tests: unit tests around deterministic tie-break across seeded retries, fuzz tests for fragmented v2 reassembly, integration tests covering OpenAI-compat adapter and fallback to v1. Also added a small canary job to perf-canary that runs 1000 short-stream invokes to measure regression. Backwards compatibility: v2 is opt-in; when the client sets header X-OpenAI-Envelope: v2 the runtime emits v2 fragments. Default remains v1. Rollout plan: start behind a feature flag for 48h on canary fleet, collect telemetry, then enable for 10% traffic before global rollout. See linked linear tickets for follow-ups on runtime autoscaling tweaks for v2 envelope.

release_notes:
Stabilizes OpenAI-compatible tool_choice semantics by introducing deterministic weighted tie-break and introduces a compact v2 invoke envelope to reduce streaming fragmentation and improve schema-resilience. Includes telemetry for choice resolution and envelope emission. Backwards compatible with v1 envelopes.

[Conditional multitenant rate limiter priority skew causing transient under-enforcement]
description:
Intermittent cases where per-key priority overrides combined with per-org and per-route policies result in transient under-enforcement (requests allowed when they should be throttled). Observed as short windows of elevated usage for a small set of tenants after shard reassignment and policy hot-reload. This ticket captures investigation, repro, short-term mitigation, and a long-term fix plan.

impact:
Transient over-allow for small number of tenants leading to underbilling and potential customer perception issues; visible as short-lived bursts up to ~2x expected throughput for affected keys. Affects hosted and dedicated clusters during rolling updates or instance restarts.

reproduction_steps:
1) Create two tenants T1 and T2 sharing a shard (sticky-shard assignment enabled).
2) Configure per-org policy: default priority = low, per-route quota = 1000/min.
3) Configure per-key override for a service key K1 belonging to T1: priority = high, burst credits = +200.
4) Start a steady stream of requests from T1 at near-quota rate; verify enforcement hitting quota windows.
5) Trigger a shard reassignment for one edge node (simulate instance bounce or maintenance) while simultaneously applying a policy hot-reload that changes route fallback behavior.
6) Observe a ~10-30s window where requests for K1 are allowed beyond quota; metrics show credits attributed to the wrong in-memory bucket and enforcement checks returning allow from fast-path cache.
7) Collect tracer spans and edge logs for the window; reproduce locally using the shard-reassignment harness and time-accelerated policy reloads.

logs_snapshot:
edge: allow decision fastpath: key=K1 shard=sh-23 cache_hit=true priority=high quota_window_id=2026-03-12T10:04:00Z
shard-reassign: lease=renewal failover->sh-27 old_owner=sh-23 new_owner=sh-27
policy-hot-reload: version=v2026-03-12-1 route-fallback=enabled
meter-commit: credits_applied target_bucket=org:T2:key:Kx unexpected=true amount=200

hypothesis:
A race between sticky-shard mapping update and policy hot-reload causes fast-path cache entries (priority and credit pointers) to be re-keyed incorrectly. Per-key overrides store a pointer to a tenant-scoped credit bucket; during reassignment we are dereferencing a stale pointer and applying credits to the wrong tenant's bucket. Enforcement uses the fast-path decision if cache present, so the wrong credits cause an allow where a deny should occur.

experiment_results:
Replayed the sequence in staging using the shard-reassign harness. With no policy reload the issue did not occur. When timed policy reload coincided with reassignment, we reproduced the over-allow consistently. Enabling stronger pointer validation (temporary patch) eliminated the over-allows in the harness.

root_cause:
Sticky-shard pointer (in-memory bucket reference) is validated only by shard id but not by tenant id during fast-path credit application. Policy hot-reload mutates the route/priority indices while a shard transfer copies pointers; combined these can produce a transient pointer that points at an unrelated tenant's bucket. Enforcement fast-path accepts the cache without full tenant-level validation.

mitigations:
Short-term patch deployed to staging: on fast-path cache hit, perform tenant-id validation on the cached credit pointer before applying credits. Also increased grace period on shard handoff to reduce overlap. Rolled patch to canary edge fleet.

rollout_plan:
1) Canary for 2 hours on low-traffic region with added telemetry (done). 2) Gradual ramp to 30% of traffic with continued trace sampling for next 24 hours. 3) Full rollout after 48 hours if no regressions. 4) Follow with a database reconciliation backfill job to detect credits misapplied in last 7 days and create accounting fixes if needed.

long_term_fix:
Refactor in-memory credit pointer representation to be immutable and namespaced by tenant+shard+route. Replace pointer dereference fast-path with a lightweight validation token check (versioned binder). Add unit and property tests for concurrent shard handoff + policy reload scenarios.

regression_test_plan:
Add deterministic concurrency tests to runtime-policy-simulator: combinations of shard reassignment, policy hot-reload, per-key overrides, and burst credit application. Add e2e test in CI harness that exercises rolling updates with randomized interleavings. Add a smoke check after canary verifying no over-allow traces in last 10 minutes.

notes:
PM (Aisha Kapoor): prioritize mitigation; billing reconciliation may be needed if misapplied credits persist beyond 24h.
Security (Rajiv Patel): no PII involved in pointers but ensure tracing does not expose tenant ids in public dashboards.
Observation: reproduces more reliably when policy reload contains route fallback toggles rather than pure priority edits.

[Atomic usage debit lost during concurrent shard failover causing brief unthrottled window]
description:
Summary: We observed intermittent brief periods (1-3s) of unthrottled requests for a small subset of orgs during a cross-region shard failover. During these windows, the per-key debit that should have been atomically committed to the authoritative ledger appears to be lost, resulting in enforcement allowing more requests than the per-route quota. Billing reports later show undercounting for the same period (reconciler later compensates but only after delay).

Observed behavior:
- Traffic spike from a customer causes one edge shard to hit a lease revocation/failover path.
- In-flight requests targeting the old shard are retried/redirected to new shard instances.
- The old shard acknowledges requests to the client (200/streaming) before its async debit write to the durable aggregator succeeds or is replicated.
- New shard receives retried requests and, because the ledger didn't reflect previous debits, allows them.
- Billing tallies show a transient undercount; enforcement metrics show short-lived over-allow.

Expected behavior:
- Either the debit is made durable before we return a success to the client, or enforcement/redirect logic treats in-flight requests as tentatively debited so duplicate accepts are prevented. Billing should not undercount and enforcement should not briefly over-allow.

Steps to reproduce (unstable but reproducible under chaos):
1) Deploy canary with injected latency on aggregator commit path (~250-500ms).
2) Generate concurrent requests from a single API key with high concurrency (>=100) with a per-key small burst quota configured.
3) Trigger a shard lease revoke on the edge (simulate region failover / restart) during peak.
4) Observe short window where more than allowed tokens are served and billing ingestion lacks corresponding debits.

Logs / traces / metrics of note:
- log: rate-engine:shard[shard-17]: ack_sent request_id=... commit_status=pending ledger_tx=null
- trace: policy-adapter -> aggregator write latency spike 420ms -> ack path returned before commit
- metric: enforcement.overallow.count spikes coincident with aggregator.write.latency>200ms

Hypothesis / root cause (current):
- There is a race where the path that returns success to the client is not waiting for the durable debit to be acknowledged. The system optimistically acknowledges to keep latency SLOs, but on lease transitions/redirects the optimistic state isn't reconciled, so retried requests see stale state and double-spend the same burst window.
- Secondary factor: idempotency keys are not consistently propagated across the retry/redirect flow, so deduplication doesn't prevent the double-allow.

Immediate mitigation options considered:
- Make ack path wait for durable commit: fixes correctness but regresses p95 latency for hot keys (customer impact).
- Make redirect path attach tentative locks/leases so retried requests are forced to check pending-debits; this requires cross-shard coordination.
- Short term: add a fast-path reconcile at redirect target: check recent in-memory evidence and soft-block if uncertain.

Decision (03/11): Implement two-part approach: (1) short-term conservative guard that prevents accepts when target shard sees ambiguous commit state (saves correctness, minimal latency impact); (2) medium-term: flip ack path to await durable commit for quota-affected routes behind a feature flag and add idempotency propagation for retries.

Acceptance criteria (see field 'acceptance_criteria') required before Close.

[Rate limiter window edge-case causing attribution gaps during tenant migration]
description:
Summary: Several customers have reported that the Console per-model breakdown shows sudden drops for a small number of final-minute requests during tenant migrations between shard groups. Root cause hypothesis: an edge-case in the global rate-limiter window boundary combined with tenant migration logic causes last-second tokens to be dropped from the billing pipeline rather than queued and forwarded, resulting in undercounting in reconstructed usage charts when delayed/backfilled events are replayed.\n\nContext: We do frequent tenant reassignments across ingestion shards to rebalance load. When a migration happens close to a rate-limiter fixed-window boundary, the lease handoff logic can cause two behaviors: (1) transient acceptance of requests on the new shard while the old shard still holds short-lived window state, and (2) a path that treats excess requests as \"dropped\" (rate-limited) rather than buffered for retry. Downstream, our backfill replay job expects dropped tokens to be recorded in a \"rate-limit-retry\" stream; in this scenario those tokens are missing, leading to undercounts in per-model charts and quota reconciliations.\n\nImpact: Affected tenants see a small undercount concentrated at window edges (typically 5-20 tokens per migration event) but it accumulates for busy tenants and shows up in monthly per-model leaderboards and quota reconciliations. Customer-facing severity: medium for most but high for a few large dedicated customers that trigger frequent migrations during scale events.\n\nWhat we've done so far:\n- Reproduced locally by simulating shard handoff at a fixed-window boundary with synthetic traffic (repro script in repo: infra/tests/rate_limit_migration_sim).\n- Captured traces showing that requests that arrive within the last 200ms before the window boundary are sometimes flagged by handoff code path as \"drop\" instead of \"retryable\".\n- Confirmed missing events in the reconstructed ledger: no corresponding rate-limit-retry entries for those requests, and downstream aggregator marks them as \"unknown\" origin.\n\nHypothesis: The migration handoff short-circuits the normal failure path for requests that would otherwise be enqueued for a retry (token bucket backoff). This is a logic gap in the handoff handshake; it treats the request as a final rejection because the old shard does not complete window state exchange fast enough.\n\nProposed fix: Update the handoff protocol to always tag last-second rejections with a \"retryable:rate_limit\" flag and forward minimal provenance metadata to the intake buffer so the backfill/ledger can recover them during shard replay. Concretely: (1) modify handoff ACK path to return code 429 with header X-RateLimit-Retryable=true for requests impacted by migration; (2) ensure the ingress gateway translates that into a guaranteed record in the rate-limit-retry stream; (3) add a reconciliation check in the backfill job to detect missing provenance and mark them for synthetic reconstruction if within a small window.\n\nRollout plan:\n- Stage 1 (canary): Patch handoff code in staging and enable on 3 low-traffic tenants for 24h. Validate reconstructed usage against raw request logs.\n- Stage 2 (pilot): Enable on 10 customers in region-us-east for 48h. Monitor Console per-model deltas and quota ledgers.\n- Stage 3 (global): Default enable with feature flag, follow with sweep to reprocess any affected day ranges via a one-time backfill job.\n\nMonitoring and success criteria:\n- No net increase in 429s served to clients (we will prefer metadata tagging over client-visible changes).\n- Backfill job should accept the retryable-tagged events and restore per-model counts to within 0.1% of raw request logs for sampled tenants.\n- Console per-model heatmap should no longer show minute-edge dips during migrations for canary tenants.\n\nDocumentation and links:\n- Reproduction script: https://git.internal.redwood/infrastructure/rate_limit_migration_sim (internal repo)\n- Investigation notes and timeline: https://confluence.redwood.com/display/BILLING/Rate+Limiter+Migration+Edge+Case\n- Proposed PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/2789 (WIP)\n- Dashboard (canary metrics): https://grafana.redwood.com/d/usage-edgecases/rate-limit-migration\n\nNext steps: finish PR, run canary, log results, and schedule one-time backfill window if validated.\n\nLonger-term: evaluate moving to sliding-window rate-limiter or per-tenant rolling window with transfer-safe semantics to reduce boundary effects overall.

[Investigate per-key shadow-window overlap causing brief unmetered bursts]
description:
Summary: We are seeing short-duration bursts of unmetered usage for some orgs and API keys when the rate-engine transitions shards/epochs. Symptoms: transient spikes in allowed requests (seconds-long) that are not reflected in metering aggregates; observed at scale during planned shard reconciliation and some unplanned rebalances. Impact: customers observe token usage that does not increment billing records resulting in revenue undercount (est. $2k-10k/week depending on failover frequency) and product throttles not applied, which can cause noisy neighbor latency spikes and potential SLO violations.

reproduction_steps:
1) Use a load generator to drive steady single-key traffic at near-burst threshold (client: ~120 RPS, per-key burst=100 tokens/sec).
2) Trigger a shard rebalance by toggling shard assignment on staging (k8s label rotate or leader eviction).
3) Observe that for ~1-8s after handoff, throttle decisions allow >2x expected throughput and meter events are missing from the aggregator.
4) Trace shows policy evals on the new primary returning 'allow' due to gap in shadow-window stitching.
Observed artifacts: missing meter RPCs in shard-aggregator logs, KV cache TTL mismatches for per-key epoch tokens, trace IDs: trace=trace-20260307-9a3f, trace=trace-20260308-4b21.

initial_findings:
- Fastpath: policy pre-evaluation cached per-key windows are not being atomically advanced during shard lease transfer.
- Race: lease expiry handler applies a local 'grab' and recomputes window buckets; concurrent inflight requests use old window boundaries before aggregator has received the final debit events.
- Metering: aggregator dedupe logic drops debits that appear out-of-order when they arrive with an older epoch timestamp, causing net delta < actual.
- Partial mitigation observed when we increase write-through debounce (makes window stitching slower but reduces unmetered allowance).

hypothesis:
When a shard loses leadership, outstanding requests that were token-charged locally but whose debit message to the aggregator is delayed can be replayed/accepted on the new leader due to overlapping shadow windows. The aggregator's out-of-order handling currently discards debits with timestamp <= last-committed-epoch, which lets a small amount of usage escape billing and enforcement.

logs_and_traces:
Relevant logs stored in GCS: gs://redwood-logs/rate-engine/2026-03/rebalance/*.log. Example trace snippets: - trace-20260307-9a3f: shows request T1 allowed by new leader at t=164s; aggregator receives debit at t=170s but drops due to epoch <= committed_epoch. - pod: rate-engine-rl-7f5d (zone us-west2-a) shows lease-handoff logs 'lease: revoke -> grab' at 2026-03-07T14:03:12Z.
Attached dashboards: runtime->rate_engine->per_key_allow_overrun, billing->aggregator->late_debits (alerts firing).

metrics_impacted:
- per_key_allow_overrun: spike to +150% for affected keys
- aggregator_late_debits: 0.8% of total debits during incidents
- billing_diff_backfill: increasing backlog of unaccounted tokens
- SLO: p99 latency ripple for other tenants during unthrottled period

short_term_mitigation:
1) Enable a temporary conservative enforcement mode that reduces per-key burst window by 50% on new leaders for 30s post-lease. This is a config flip (feature-flag: conservative-post-handoff) that has been tested in staging.
2) Add metric-based alert: aggregator_late_debits > 0.5% for 5m -> pages on-call.
3) Backfill: run aggregator replay job to reconcile debits for windows with missing records (one-off job: billing/reconcile_v2).

long_term_plan:
1) Fix aggregator dedupe semantics: accept debits with older epoch if they carry a monotonic sequence number and apply them idempotently instead of dropping.
2) Implement atomic window advance during lease transfer: leader should publish a 'handoff marker' event with final pending-debits so new leader can reconcile before starting permissive windows.
3) Add end-to-end integration tests simulating shard handoffs with high concurrency, including timing fuzzing.
4) Add telemetry: per-key handoff_latency histogram, and end-to-end debit delivery latency SLA (target < 200ms).
5) Postmortem and billing correction policy: design an automatic backfill + charge notice flow for impacted customers.

current_blockers:
- Need consensus on sequence-number propagation format with storage team (affects wire compatibility).
- Perf concern: handoff marker introduces extra RPCs which must be benchmarked before runtime-1.21 GA.
- Billing team wants proof we can reconcile charges before auto-charging customers.

proposed_schedule:
Week 1: implement conservative flag + alerting + run backfill job in staging. Week 2: submit aggregator dedupe fix PR and handoff-marker prototype (code review). Week 3: integration tests + perf benchmarks. Week 4: canary rollout to 10% traffic, monitor metrics, then full rollout.

risks_and_tradeoffs:
- Conservative-post-handoff reduces burst capacity and may increase legitimate throttles (customer experience hit).
- Accepting out-of-order debits increases complexity in aggregator state machine and might require compacting historical seq numbers to bound memory.
- Handoff marker increases cross-node coordination latency for leader elections; need microbenchmarks to ensure it doesn't impact failover times beyond acceptable window.

runbook:
Playbook for on-call: 1) Toggle conservative-post-handoff flag. 2) Kick billing reconciliation job with job-id. 3) Monitor p99 latency and aggregator_late_debits for 30m. 4) If mitigation fails, roll back shard migration and open emergency incident.

[Route policy fanout amplification after route rename causing transient unmetered windows]
description:
Several customers reported brief periods where per-route quota usage dropped to zero despite sustained traffic. Investigation shows a policy fanout amplification that occurs when a route is renamed: the policy engine temporarily produces duplicated policy keys and the metering path misses debits for one of the duplicates, creating short unmetered windows for affected orgs/routes. This ticket captures the investigation, short-term mitigations, and the proposed permanent fix to prevent future occurrences.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Create route R with policy set P and generate steady traffic (synthetic client ~100 req/s).
2) Rename route R -> R_new via Console API while traffic continues.
3) Observe metering/tokens emitted to the billing pipeline and per-route aggregation dashboards.
4) Look for a transient drop to near-zero debits for R_new or duplicate debit keys in the runtime debug logs (metric: meter.key.duplicates).
5) Reproduce in a staging cluster with a subset of orgs to validate fix candidates.

observed_behavior:
During route rename there is a ~5-20s window where the policy engine emits two distinct fanout keys for the same logical route. The meter ingestion deduplicator treats them as separate buckets and, due to a race in the debit path, one bucket's debits are dropped. The result is a transient period of unmetered usage for affected route/org pairs, causing incorrect quota allowance and potential overage.

expected_behavior:
Route renames should be atomic from a policy/metering perspective: the engine should either consider the old or the new route key but not both, and all debits should be accounted to a single stable bucket. No transient unmetered windows should be possible as a result of metadata changes.

impact_summary:
Medium: affects a small fraction of route renames (customer-driven operation) but can cause short unmetered windows leading to inaccurate quotas and potential unexpected usage. We've observed this in 3 paying orgs during the last 30 days (support tickets opened). No charge-level billing losses identified yet but accounting drift makes reconciliations harder and may allow brief misuse.

investigation_notes:
2026-02-13 09:12 - Initial triage: alert spike for per-route usage gap; correlated with route rename events recorded in Console Audit Log.
2026-02-14 14:40 - Attached a staging reproducer that performs route rename under load; debugger shows two policy fanout keys: 'route:12345:name:v1' and 'route:12345:name:v2'.
2026-02-16 11:03 - Found the policy-transform step was using a route name string in the fanout fingerprint. The rename path creates a short window where both old and new fanout fingerprints are considered live until the policy cache TTL expires or an explicit reconcile runs.
2026-02-18 16:27 - Debit path race: when two fanout keys exist the meter-aggregator uses last-writer semantics and an async commit path can drop debits for the older fanout bucket if a shard leader rotates during the rename window.
2026-02-25 10:55 - Confirmed end-to-end that disabling the policy-transform name component prevents duplicate fanout keys and eliminates the unmetered window in staging.
2026-03-01 08:22 - SRE simulated leader rotations and confirmed the race surface is the async debit ack path + inconsistent fanout key set in the policy cache.

root_cause:
The fanout fingerprint used by the rate-limiter included mutable metadata (route name). A route rename creates two fingerprints that both map to the same logical quota, but the runtime treats them as distinct buckets. Combined with an async debit acknowledgement path and shard leader re-election, debits for one fingerprint can be lost, producing transient unmetered windows.

short_term_mitigation:
1) Disable route-name-in-fingerprint toggle on the policy transform (feature flag) in production to prevent generation of mutable fingerprints (rolled out 2026-02-26 to all regions).
2) Schedule an immediate reconcile job to collapse duplicate fanout keys for recently renamed routes (background job queued; targeted run executed 2026-02-27).
3) Add a guard to the metering pipeline that rejects a duplicate fanout key set if both keys map to the same stable route id and instead canonicalize debits to the stable id until the cache converges.
4) Temporarily advise Console to throttle route rename operations for high-throughput routes via admin guideline (PM note issued).

proposed_fix:
Permanent fix consists of three coordinated changes: (A) remove mutable route name from the fanout fingerprint and ensure fingerprints are derived only from immutable identifiers (route_id + org_id + route_version), (B) strengthen the debit ack path to be idempotent for duplicate fanout keys (introduce per-bucket causal tokens), and (C) add a fast reconcile path on rename to retire old fingerprints immediately. Implement change A first (low risk), then B, then C.

rollout_plan:

[Interleaved canary and operator review for batching and caching recommendations]
description:
Goal: Implement a staged, observable system to safely apply batching and KV-cache recommendations produced by the Optimize engine. The flow must combine short-lived canaries with an operator review step so we can auto-deploy low-risk changes while requiring human approval for higher-impact ones. This ticket scopes the control plane and runtime hooks needed to: 1) create ephemeral canary deployments that route a configurable percentage of traffic, 2) gather quality and cost signals, 3) evaluate automatic pass/fail thresholds, and 4) escalate to operator review when thresholds are uncertain or risk is high. The system must also support automatic rollback triggers and an OK-to-apply manual approval workflow with audit logging for Private/Dedicated customers.

acceptance_criteria:
Can create a canary rollout for a single Optimize recommendation with traffic routing percentages configurable per-release
Dashboard shows per-canary metrics: token-cost delta, median/95th latency, error rate, sample-quality delta (BLEU/ROUGE or embedding-similarity), and request-side regressions
Auto-pass policy exists: canary auto-promotes when cost savings >= 8% AND latency delta <= +5ms AND quality regression <= 0.5% over 10k requests
Operator-review gate: recommendations flagged as high-impact (cost saving > 15% OR any latency increase > 10%) require a manual approval action recorded in the audit log
Automatic rollback runs within 30s of triggered rollback condition and documented in runbook
Unit/integration tests that simulate canary metrics and validate promotion/rollback logic
Works for both hosted and Dedicated deployments; Private flows require operator approval by default unless customer opts-in

design_notes:
We will extend the rollout controller to understand two new recommendation metadata fields: estimated_cost_delta_pct and estimated_quality_risk_score. The controller spawns a short-lived canary cluster (same binary and model binary) using existing dedicated pool abstractions. Metric collection hooks attach to the per-route tracer and the Console ingestion pipeline. Evaluate quality using a small random sample + embedding-similarity baseline stored in Optimize's eval store. Decision engine is a simple ruleset today (configurable policies stored in the Console); long-term plan is to plug in a scoring ML policy. Audit events are emitted to the existing audit-log stream and surfaced in the Console UI. For Private deployments we add an RBAC check so only admin roles can perform the operator-approval action.

rollout_plan:
Phase 1 (dev): implement controller and local canary simulation with synthetic traffic. Phase 2 (staging): hook the metrics pipeline and run 50 internal canaries across diverse workloads. Phase 3 (beta-hosted): enable opt-in auto-promote for low-risk recommendations for 10 customers, gated by SLOs. Phase 4 (GA): default behavior for hosted; Dedicated retains opt-in; Private requires approval by default. Traffic percentages for canary: 1% -> 5% -> 20% over 24h, with automatic promotion checks at each step. Manual operator review pauses the pipeline and surfaces a checklist (slo, quality sample, PR link).

test_plan:
Unit tests for decision engine, e2e test that spins up a canary with a fake recommendation and synthetic traffic (latency/cost/quality knobs). Create chaos tests where the canary increases error rate to validate rollback. Add regression tests for audit event emission and RBAC enforcement. Add performance test to ensure controller scale: 200 concurrent canaries across Dedicated pools without control-plane OOM.

[HyperOnboard: Role Launch Snapshot and 30-90 Activation Template]
Purpose: quick, reusable working template to take a candidate through offer acceptance to contribution in 30/60/90 days. Combine a compact hiring plan, a measurable interview rubric, and a pragmatic onboarding checklist that managers and POs can copy-edit for specific roles.

Status and intent: working draft for FY26 hiring sprints (early trials with infra and platform-engineering hiring waves). This is intentionally opinionated about signals we care about (ramp speed, cross-team communication, test-driven ownership). Use as a baseline; annotate with role-specific tasks and replace TODOs.

Quick orientation (one-liner): HyperOnboard is a "launch packet"—a short, shareable checklist + rubric to align hiring, the hiring manager, mentor/buddy, and recruiting operations on acceptance -> day 90 outcomes.

Scope: ICs (IC2–IC5) across engineering, product, and SRE. Not a replacement for full People Ops handbook; intended to accelerate first-90 days and instrument early quality signals for hiring calibration.

Hiring plan snapshot (for manager + recruiter):
- Hiring signal: 2–3 concrete deliverables expected in first 90 days (choose 1 fast win in month 1, 1 impact work in month 2, 1 cross-team deliverable by month 3).
- Timeline: Week 0: offer & logistics; Week 1: shadow + infra access; Week 2–4: small shipable task; Month 2: feature/infra milestone; Month 3: cross-team rollout + owner handoff.
- Interview loop (baseline for eng roles): Recruit screen (30m) -> Hiring manager (45m) -> Two technical rounds (60m each: system design + code pairing) -> Collaboration/communication round (30–45m) -> Exec/skip-level if IC4+ (30m). Total on-site loop time 3.5–4.5 hours.
- Comms: recruiting to post-offer email should include role launch snapshot (this doc), buddy assignment, first-week calendar skeleton, and links to requisite access checklists.

Offer packet checklist (ops items to complete before start):
- Signed offer + I-9 (if applicable)
- Manager assigned, buddy assigned, and initial 1:1 scheduled for day 1
- Infra access requests issued (jira access + repo perms + cloud console)
- Workstation shipped or on-site booking confirmed
- Security & compliance onboarding assigned (if private deployment/regulatory customer)
- Prestart reading pack shared (team RFCs, relevant incidents, current PRs)

Interview rubric (single-page, numerical scale 1–5, with anchor examples). Use for calibration and debrief notes. Keep score fields in ATS but capture qualitative: examples, gaps, and evidence.
- Areas and anchors:
  - Technical correctness (1–5): Can the candidate implement correct, maintainable code during pairing and explain tradeoffs? Anchors: 5 = correct and robust solution with edge cases and tests; 3 = correct but brittle or missing edge cases; 1 = incorrect or major misconceptions.
  - System design (1–5): Ability to decompose requirements, propose measurable SLAs, identify bottlenecks, and consider operational costs. Anchors: 5 = clear architecture + failure modes + rollout plan; 2 = vague tradeoffs, misses core ops concerns.
  - Product sense & impact orientation (1–5): Prioritization, outcome-thinking, ability to tie technical choices to user/business impact. Anchors: 5 = identifies measurable metrics and tradeoffs; 1 = overly academic solutions with no product tie.
  - Collaboration & communication (1–5): Clarity of explanations, receptive to feedback, cross-functional mindset. Anchors: 5 = proactive clarifying, invites feedback; 2 = closed off or unclear.
  - Ownership & learning velocity (1–5): Evidence of shipping end-to-end, learning new domains quickly. Anchors: 5 = repeated examples of shipping and improving systems; 1 = no evidence of ownership.
  - Cultural/values fit (1–5): Evidence of glue work, candidate’s ability to operate in high-performance, ambiguous environments. Anchors: 5 = pragmatic, bias for action, clear examples; 1 = passive.
- Interview debrief template (copy into ATS notes): "Top strengths (2–3): ...
  Top risks (2–3): ...
  Required onboarding supports if hired: ...
  Recommended 30/60/90 milestones: ..."

Onboarding checklist (practical, manager-first):
- Pre-day-1 (recruiting + manager): welcome doc + first-week calendar sent; Slack invite; send buddy intro email; create required infra tickets; create first-ticket for fast-win task (estimate <3 days).
- Day 1: 1:1 with manager (30–60m) covering role context + 30/60/90 goals; team lunch (virtual/in-person); buddy walkthrough of repos and dev flow; confirm access to ticketing and CI.
- Day 2–5: environment setup validation (local dev, tests pass), complete required security trainings, pair on the fast-win task with buddy, first-week retrospective on Friday (30m).
- Week 2–4: ship fast-win (owner signs off), start second deliverable (mentor-guided), scheduled sync with adjacent team leads.
- Month 1 manager check (end of month): evidence review of fast-win, signal check on documentation contributions, feedback conversation and adjustments to 30/60/90.
- Month 2: take ownership of a mid-scale deliverable, lead a small design doc, participate in oncall rotation shadow if applicable.
- Month 3: lead cross-team rollout or ship major milestone; provide retrospective + proposal for ongoing ownership.

Manager checklist and risk mitigations:
- Before start: confirm buddy and first-ticket exist.
- Weekly 1:1 agenda template: 5m personal check-in, 10m blockers, 20m skill-building or project planning, 10m feedback loop.
- Escalation triggers (email to p-ops + hiring manager): not shipping a measurable artifact by day 30, ongoing access blockers >48h, repeated missing meetings.

Buddy playbook (short):
- First 2 weeks: pair 3x for 90–120m on dev flow and codebase.
- Provide curated list of 6–8 reading items (design docs, incidents, coding standards).
- Shadowing: 2 oncall tickets, 1 deploy cycle.

Evaluation signals (early):
- Technical: able to run test suite locally and fix one failing test in week 1.
- Product: articulates impact metric for a fast-win by end of week 1.
- Collaboration: schedules and leads at least one cross-team sync by week 4.
- Ownership: closes owner-assigned ticket with PR and reviewer responses in <2 weeks.

Template: 30/60/90 milestones (copyable):
- 30 days (learn & ship): complete environment, ship small bug/feature, present learnings to team.
- 60 days (own & expand): own a component or endpoint, reduce latency/bug rate or deliver feature scope, mentor newcomer pairing.
- 90 days (integrate & lead): lead a cross-team launch or own SLA for a subservice, propose roadmap items.

Recruiting playbook notes (ops & interviewer hints):
- Recruiter checklist: send role launch snapshot with offer email; collect candidate prestart constraints (visa, hardware needs); confirm buddy availability.
- Interviewers: focus on concrete examples. Ask for "past 2–3 months shipped work" and one code example. Rate on evidence, not potential.
- Calibration: every hiring round should include at least one calibrated interviewer (eng lead who has completed calibration exercise in last 6 months).

Open questions / TODOs (working):
- Define explicit ramp metrics per org (platform vs. product eng) — who owns this? action: Priya to draft baseline by 2026-02-12.
- Should we require a documented 90-day plan in the offer packet for IC4+? pros/cons noted (clarity vs. inflexibility).
- Add a short checklist for Private deployments hires (HSM/KMS onboarding).

Sample email snippets (copyable):
- Pre-start welcome: "Congrats and welcome — attached is a short launch snapshot with your first-week calendar, your assigned buddy (NAME), and a link to our quick-start repo. Please complete the short security training before day 3."
- Manager day-1 note: "Hi NAME — excited to have you. Today we'll cover role context and your first-week goals. Please bring questions about accounts/access. Expect a walking tour of current work and an intro to the fast-win ticket."

Notes-to-self / working artifacts:
- Keep this doc <2 pages for offer attachments. Expanded examples belong in Role Launch Library (linked_artifacts).

[Manager shadow slate rubric and boarding template]
Purpose:
This doc is a working template used by People Ops + Hiring Managers to: (1) run a manager shadow slate for cross-functional candidates, (2) capture structured interview scoring for paired interviews, and (3) surface a 30/60/90 onboarding template tailored for managers that will own IC teams. Aim is to reduce variability between hiring panels and speed up onboarding once offer is accepted.

Scope and when to use:
- Use for non-executive manager roles (IC+1 to mid-level managers) where cross-functional collaboration and operational delivery matter.
- Best paired with a calibrated hiring slate (3–5 candidates) where candidates are given a short shadow window with 2 teams.
- Not intended for director+ or deep individual contributor roles.

High-level flow (one-pager):
1) Prep (People Ops + Hiring Manager) — 3 days before slate: confirm rubric, shadow hosts, interviewers, and candidate brief.
2) Shadow session — 1/2 day per candidate: 60–90m observed time split across 2 teams + 30m debrief with HM.
3) Interview panels — same day or next: paired technical/business/people interviews using standardized scorecard.
4) Calibration sync — hiring manager + interview leads: same day. Decision window: 48 hours.

Shadow session structure (suggested):
- 10m candidate intro + expectations (People Ops host)
- 25–30m observational block with Team A: candidate observes team standup/code review/product planning; small task or critique prompt optional.
- 25–30m observational block with Team B: different lens (eng ops, product, or support).
- 15–20m private conversation with hiring manager focused on role-specific situational discussion.
- 20–30m panel debrief (interviewers only) — collect initial notes and scores.

Interview rubric (calibration primers):
Scoring scale: 1–5 (1 = no evidence, 3 = meets expectations, 5 = exceptional)
Core dimensions (each dimension should have 1–2 example evidence prompts):
- Team leadership & coaching (prompt: describe a time you developed a lower-level engineer)
- Execution & prioritization (prompt: how do you settle tradeoffs when roadmap slips)
- Technical judgment (prompt: system design for X, read code and suggest improvement)
- Cross-functional influence (prompt: give example of aligning product + infra)
- People ops partnership & bar-raising (prompt: hiring decisions, performance conversations)
- Role fit & mission alignment (prompt: why Redwood and what would you change in week 1)

Rubric guidance notes:
- Interviewers should capture 1–2 behavioral anchors for each score (e.g., "3 = ran consistent 1:1s with documented development plan; 4 = measurable promotion outcomes").
- Avoid grading on technical trivia; focus on pattern recognition and outcomes.
- For internal candidates, add a field for "context of previous team" to avoid bias.

Scorecard template (one-line per field to paste into interview form):
- Candidate name:
- Role:
- Interview date:
- Interviewer:
- Scores: leadership (1–5), execution (1–5), technical (1–5), cross-functional (1–5), ppl-ops-partner (1–5), fit (1–5)
- Written evidence: 6 short bullets capturing specific examples
- Red flags (Y/N + notes)
- Recommendation: Strong hire / Hire / Consider / No hire

Calibration checklist (for HM + interview lead):
- Are scores correlated across interviewers? If variance >2 points on core dims, convene quick follow-up interview or assign a tie-breaker reviewer.
- Confirm role must-haves vs. nice-to-haves before final decision.
- Document any compensation exceptions or relocation needs.

30/60/90 onboarding template (manager-tailored)
Notes: this is intentionally outcome-driven and oriented to first 90 days after offer accept. Share with candidate at offer stage to set expectations.
- Week 0 (pre-start): hardware, access, org chart, 1:1 schedule for first 30 days, intro emails drafted, stakeholder list, first-week reading list.
- Days 1–30 (Discover): attend core team rituals, 1:1s with direct reports (initial listening plan), meet cross-functional partners, review existing roadmaps/KPIs, quick wins (deliverable: run first project post-mortem).
- Days 31–60 (Align & Act): set team goals and ownership mapped to company objectives, establish 30–60 day success metrics for direct reports, begin active hiring or role reshapes if needed, lead first planning cycle end-to-end.
- Days 61–90 (Scale & Improve): start performance calibration, implement at least one process improvement (e.g., release cadence, onboarding checklist for new ICs), present working plan to VP.

Manager onboarding checklist (copyable):
- [ ] Offer letter signed and counter-signed
- [ ] Manager kickoff packet sent (org chart + 1:1 templates)
- [ ] Hardware provisioned and VPN/KMS access requested
- [ ] First 8 1:1s scheduled with direct reports
- [ ] People Ops scheduled 30/60/90 checkpoints on calendar
- [ ] Hiring queue and scorecard templates shared
- [ ] Access to Redis/Observability dashboards + billing view if applicable

Communication templates (short):
- Pre-start intro email to team: short script included in appendix
- 1:1 cadence template: 30m weekly for first 30 days, agenda items prioritized as: 1) concerns, 2) goals, 3) career development.

Common FAQ / edge cases:
- If a candidate misses a scheduled shadow day, allow one reschedule within 7 days; beyond that, withdraw from slate.
- For internal transfers, accelerate decision timeline to 72 hours, ensure skip-level manager signs off.
- If calibration shows strong disagreement, bring in a neutral senior interviewer (not previously involved) for tie-break.

Appendix: sample behavioral anchor table (copy-paste friendly)
- Leadership 5: repeatedly promoted direct reports; has documented mentoring curriculum and measurable team growth
- Leadership 3: runs regular 1:1s and has provided development plans; inconsistent promotion outcomes
- Execution 5: drove multi-quarter projects with clear impact metrics across org boundaries
- Execution 3: delivered projects on time most of the time; relied on direction for scoping

Next steps (People Ops owners):
- Run a 1-hour calibration workshop with all hiring leads to adopt this rubric (target: within 2 weeks).
- Pilot this template with the next manager hire in Q4 and gather interviewer feedback via a short survey.
- Iterate templates and push final copy to Confluence after 2 pilot hires.

[Contractor rapid onboard & knowledge-transfer playbook]

Include manager, sponsor, and people-ops.\n- Assign 1:1 buddy (not the sponsor) for first-week pairing.\n- Draft 7-day activation plan and share with contractor before day 1.\n\nDay 0 / Day 1 checklist (goal: move from zero to visible activity)\n- People Ops: e-sign docs, background verification (if applicable), contractor badge/access.\n- IT: laptop shipped (or provisioning window noted), VPN creds, SSO invite, MFA enrollment.\n- Security: confirm least-privilege IAM role requested. [Role ramp backstop and probation checklist playbook]
Purpose and scope:\nThis playbook is a pragmatic, manager-facing tool for two related problems we keep hitting: 1) ad-hoc role ramps that drift past expected timelines, and 2) lack of a clear backstop/escalation when probation signals are negative. It is intended for People Ops partners and hiring/managing managers for IC and manager hires across teams (eng, product, go-to-market).\n\nHigh-level goals:\n- Reduce variance in time-to-autonomy for new hires by codifying a 30/60/90 ramp plus backstop triggers.\n- Provide a short, repeatable escalation path when new hire outcomes don't match expectations.\n- Surface hiring/prioritization signals so hiring managers and recruiting agree on acceptance thresholds up front.\n\nQuick definitions (team shorthand):\n- Ramp signal: quantitative/qualitative evidence that someone is progressing (code reviews merged, feature ownership, stakeholder check-ins).\n- Backstop: an agreed set of interventions (mentoring shift, role narrowing, performance plan, or off-ramp) that are enacted when signals are negative.\n- Probation period: first 90 calendar days after start unless otherwise negotiated.\n\nPart A: Hiring priority triage (pre-offer)\n1) Role readiness checklist (completed at offer):\n   - Hiring manager checklist: must attach at offer: 1) three prioritized 90-day outcomes (must be measurable), 2) list of required stakeholders and owners for onboarding, 3) primary mentor assigned.\n   - Recruiter checklist: confirm candidate acceptance includes start date, timezone constraints, and required compliances (NDAs, vetting).\n2) Acceptance thresholds (minimums for offers):\n   - Strong hire: scored >= 8 on final rubric and has explicit examples for 2 of 3 priority outcomes.\n   - Conditional hire: scored 6–7 and hiring manager commits to a 15-day focused mentor plan (documented).\n   - Reject: score <=5 or critical skill gaps without feasible remediation.\n3) Priority signal tags (used in ATS): must tag new hire with at least one: \"fast-ramp\", \"needs-mentor\", \"high-uncertainty\". These bubble up to People Ops for resource planning.\n\nPart B: 30/60/90 ramp checklist (manager + People Ops joint)\nTemplate outcomes (manager fills): objective, measurable, and owner-aligned. Example: \"Ship data schema validation MVP and own production rollout checklist by day 60.\"\n\n30-day: foundation\n- Orientation completed: company systems, security training, payroll, and access to repos.\n- First-week 1:1 cadence with manager scheduled and documented in calendar.\n- Mentor onboarding: mentor has a 4-item shadow plan and first week pairing sessions scheduled.\n- Quick wins: new hire completes one documented, merged PR or customer-facing doc.\n- Manager notes: weekly short feedback posted in private onboarding doc.\n\n60-day: competence\n- Primary 90-day outcomes have initial progress evidence (PRs, design notes, stakeholder emails).\n- Ownership: candidate has at least one area with read/write permissions and a list of next steps they are responsible for.\n- Cross-team sync: introduced to key stakeholders and added to recurring meetings.\n- Feedback loop: formal 60-day check-in scheduled and invites include People Ops.\n\n90-day: autonomy check\n- Outcomes verification: compare filled outcomes against expected acceptance thresholds.\n- Transition plan: if continuing, assign long-term goals and next performance milestones.\n- Close-out: People Ops confirms completion of checklist and files final onboarding note to hire record.\n\nPart C: Backstop triggers and remediation options (what to do when signals are negative)\nSignals that trigger an escalation (any of these):\n- Misses 2+ core milestone deadlines (30/60/90 outcomes) without acceptable blocker documentation.\n- Persistent lack of engagement in paired-learning or asynchronous deliverables.\n- Repeated feedback from 2+ stakeholders citing quality or collaboration concerns.\n\nImmediate next steps (day 0–3 after trigger):\n- Manager documents specific examples in the private performance packet (date+links).\n- Rapid sync: People Ops, manager, and mentor meet within 3 business days to triage and decide intervention.\n\nIntervention tiers:\n- Tier 1: Mentor intensification (2-week focused pairing + explicit micro-goals). Manager documents daily pairing notes.\n- Tier 2: Role narrowing (reduce scope to 1–2 deliverables for 30 days) + weekly status reports to People Ops.\n- Tier 3: Formal performance plan (PIP-lite) for 30 days with clear exit criteria; legal/HR loop-in and optional coach assigned.\n- Tier 4: Off-ramp discussion (if other tiers fail and evidence supports). People Ops to run off-ramp checklist and closure comms.\n\nPart D: Manager guidance and templates\nManager 60-day check-in script (short bullets):\n- Start with strengths observed (2 mins).\n- Review 60-day progress against 3 outcomes (5 mins).\n- Identify blockers and agreement on 2 concrete next steps (5 mins).\n- Ask: \"What support would help you be more effective?\" (2 mins).\n- Close with follow-up: date+owner for next check-in and note saved to onboarding doc (1 min).\n\nManager note template (to paste in private doc):\n- Week X note: date, what went well (bullets), concerns (bullets), objective evidence (links), next steps (owner+date).\n\nOffer acceptance + start-day checklist (concise):\n- Confirm start date, timezone, laptop/hardware needs, security email set up, and 1st week meeting schedule sent.\n- Slack intro message template: \"Hi team — excited to join! I’m X, joining as Y. My focus first 30 days will be X. Please say hi and share any quick tips.\"\n\nPart E: Interview rubric addendum (use at final onsite/hiring loop)\nWe keep the main rubric in ATS. Addendum fields to capture ramp signals at hire:\n- Evidence of autonomous delivery under ambiguity (1–5).\n- Learning velocity (ability to pick up new stack) (1–5).\n- Cross-team communication and stakeholder management (1–5).\n- Manager’s ramp confidence (1–5, free text comment required).\nScoring guidance: treat combined score >=14 as strong hire, 11–13 conditional, <=10 not ready.\n\nPart F: Documentation and data capture (for people ops metrics)\nRequired artifacts to attach to the hire packet on day 0: offer letter, manager 90-day outcomes doc, mentor assignment, signed compliance docs.\nPeople Ops metrics to track per hire (minimum): time-to-first-merge, time-to-own-component, 30/60/90 qualitative score, escalation events (Y/N), final outcome (retained/transitioned/off-ramp) — these feed quarterly hiring retrospective.\n\nOpen questions / tensions (for discussion):\n- Should probation period be 120 days for some specialized roles? Suggested approach: manager flags in role-readiness brief and People Ops approves.\n- How do we budget mentor time across many conditional hires? Proposed experiment: central mentor pool with 0.2 FTE allocation for qualifying hires.\n\nAppendix: quick templates and links\n- 60-day check-in calendar invite subject: \"60-day sync: [New Hire] — progress & blockers\"\n- People Ops escalation Slack channel: #people-ops-escalations (tag @peopleops-oncall)\n- Confluence onboarding folder: /display/HR/Onboarding-Playbooks (please attach final packet here)\n\nNotes to self / TODOs (work-in-progress):\n- Create an ATS tag map to surface \"conditional hire\" + mentor assignment automatically (open ticket HIRE-412).\n- Draft an email template for off-ramp closure with legal and manager wording (assign to Marco).\n- Run a 6-week pilot with two eng teams to validate time-to-autonomy metrics and mentor pool demand.\n\nAcknowledgements: thanks to Sara & Marco for early drafts and Evan for pilot metric suggestions.\n\nEnd of document.\n

[Probation Success Bucket and Mentor Rotation Protocol]
Purpose:\nProvide a lightweight, reproducible protocol to (1) define a small set of \"success buckets\" that constitute passing probation for IC roles and (2) run an intentional mentor rotation to reduce single-person onboarding risk. This is a pragmatic playbook for people-ops + hiring managers to use when designing 30/60/90s and calibrating offers.\n\nContext and motivation:\n- Observed pain: uneven probation outcomes driven by inconsistent expectations and single-mentor bottlenecks.\n- Goal: standardize pass criteria across similar role families, make evidence explicit, and create a repeatable mentor-rotation handoff so new hires get a diversity of signals and feedback.\n- Scope: IC engineers (backend/frontend/infra), product managers, and solutions engineers. Leadership roles follow a separate calibration path.\n\nQuick summary (TL;DR):\n- Create 3–5 role-specific \"success buckets\" (technical delivery, collaboration + communication, operational ownership, learning velocity).\n- Each bucket has 2–4 observable signals (tickets shipped, PR quality, triage leadership, docs owned, bugs reduced).\n- Assign 2 mentors + a peer buddy. Rotate mentors every 2 weeks for the first 8 weeks. Handoff checklist must be filled at rotation.\n- Use an \"evidence ledger\" (shared doc) where mentors and the hire log 1–3 artifacts per week tied to buckets.\n\nSuccess buckets (example template) — keep short and measurable:\n1) Technical delivery (outcome, not hours)\n   - Signals: at least 1 small production change merged (owner-level), code review comments addressed within SLA, a deterministic test added for a regression class.\n2) Collaboration & communication\n   - Signals: runs a short async update in team channel, leads one pairing session, stakeholder sync scheduled + notes posted.\n3) Operational ownership\n   - Signals: owns one oncall rotation task or runbook update, reduces a recurring alert by a measurable amount, postmortem contributor.\n4) Learning velocity & feedback loop\n   - Signals: weekly learning goals recorded, evidence ledger contains progress artifacts, implements feedback from mentor within 1 cycle.\n\nRubric guidance (quick):\n- For each bucket, score on 1–5 scale. Passing threshold: majority of buckets >= 3 and no bucket <= 2 if that bucket is core to role.\n- Use comments to tie score to artifacts (link to PR, doc, ticket). Avoid vague language.\n\nMentor rotation protocol (operational):\n- Roles: Primary mentor (first 2 weeks), Secondary mentor (weeks 3–4), Cross-domain mentor (weeks 5–8), Peer buddy (ongoing).\n- Cadence: 30–45 min mentor sync twice weekly for first 4 weeks, then weekly through week 8. Peer buddy meets 2x/week for ramp tasks.\n- Rotation: switch primary mentor responsibility every 2 weeks for 8 weeks (so hire sees 3 distinct mentors total). Purpose is breadth of perspective and reduced single-point-of-failure.\n- Handoff checklist (required at rotation):\n   * List of open tickets owned by hire + status (Jira keys)\n   * Short notes on learning blockers (2 bullets max)\n   * Outstanding PRs and reviewers needed\n   * One suggested micro-scope for next 2 weeks (<= 3d work)\n   * Evidence ledger pointer (link) + one artifact to review\n- Handoff must be completed in writing before mentor change; incoming mentor schedules a 30m sync to align.\n\nEvidence ledger (how we record):\n- Single shared doc per hire (template attached in GITHUB link above). Headers: week, bucket, artifact type (PR/Doc/Ticket/Runbook), link, short note, mentor sign-off.\n- Minimum: 1 artifact/week for first 8 weeks; 2/week preferred for delivery roles.\n\nInterview/hire plan tie-ins (to reduce probation risk):\n- When hiring, capture 2+ signals that map to success buckets (e.g., take-home that exercises ownership, behavioral question about cross-team tradeoffs).\n- Interview rubric should include explicit items for \"mentorship dose\" (how the candidate learns from peers) and \"handoff mindset\" (can they document and handoff a task?).\n- For marginal hires, consider a structured 6-month ramp with checkpointed re-evaluation at 60 days (not just 90).\n\nOnboarding checklist (first 30/60/90 highlights) — actionable items to attach to evidence ledger:\n- Day 0–7: account accesses, dev env green, first pairing session scheduled, review of team's incident runbook.\n- Week 2: small production change deployed with mentor; first evidence ledger entry.\n- Week 4: owns a small triage or customer ask end-to-end.\n- Week 8: leads an internal demo or doc update; mentor rotation complete.\n- Week 12: cross-functional stakeholder feedback captured and added to ledger.\n\nManagers: calibration & check-ins\n- Weekly manager sync should review ledger artifacts (5–10 min). Formal manager checkpoint at day 30 and day 60 (15–30 min) and probation review at day 90.\n- If manager observes 2 consecutive weeks with no artifacts, escalate to people-ops to diagnose.\n\nEscalation triggers (examples)\n- Missed two rotation handoffs in a row without written notes.\n- Zero artifacts logged in ledger after week 3.\n- Clear safety/regulatory concern.\n\nTemplates & tooling (short)\n- Evidence ledger template: GITHUB:company/onboarding-templates/pull/58 (linked above).\n- JIRA labels: onboarding:<hire-name>, onboarding:artifact. Add label to any ticket that counts as evidence.\n- Confluence page: HR/Probation-Framework-2025 — canonical definitions and legal considerations.\n\nOpen questions / TODOs (work in progress)\n- How to scale mentor rotations for very small teams (1–2 engineers)? Proposal: cross-pod mentor pairings with neighboring team. Need budget signal.\n- Should manager have veto power to extend probation by 30 days automatically? Legal review required. (JIRA:HR-4123)\n- Add direct manager training for running written handoffs — short async module needed.\n\nNotes to self / pragmatics:\n- Keep buckets intentionally small to avoid "checkboxing" — we want narratives tied to artifacts.\n- Save a few anonymized case studies of successful rotations for an internal playbook page.\n- Align with Legal on language for extension and evidence retention.\n\nReferences and links:\n- Confluence: HR/Probation-Framework-2025 (policy + legal guidance)\n- JIRA: HR-4123 (policy questions thread)\n- GitHub: onboarding-templates PR with ledger template\n\nIf you're reviewing this: please add suggestions inline. [Rework BuildKit integration and add dependency-stability probes to CI]
description:
Motivation: our monorepo build and release pipeline has been brittle due to a mix of legacy shell builders, inconsistent BuildKit usage across workflows, and no automated signal for transient dependency drift. This PR centralizes BuildKit integration into a single reusable composite action, introduces a lightweight builder image used in tests, and adds a CI job (dep-stability-probe) that detects lockfile/registry instability and surfaces it to release gating. Summary: 1) Add actions/ci-buildkit-composite: a composite action that wraps docker buildx setup, canonical cache-keying, and layer-level cache priming. 2) Replace ad-hoc bash builders in .github/workflows/* with the composite action. 3) Introduce docker/test-builder: small pinned image (FROM busybox + buildkit client) for faster containerized test setup used by unit/integration smoke jobs. 4) Add .github/workflows/dep-stability-probe.yml which uses a lightweight matrix to fetch package registries (npm/pip/crates), verify checksums against lockfiles, and record transient download failures to a short-lived artifact and Prometheus pushgateway for short-term alerting. 5) Update workflow cache keys to include repository-tooling-version and buildkit-pipeline-hash to reduce corrupt cache reuses. 6) Remove legacy scripts infra/scripts/build_and_push.sh in favor of the composite action and add migration notes in CONTRIBUTING.md. Checklist: - [x] Implement composite action and document inputs/outputs - [x] Migrate two long-running workflows (release-build, quick-ci) to new composite - [x] Add dep-stability-probe workflow and lightweight builder image - [x] Update tests to run with containerized harness - [x] Verify caches and rerun flaky jobs in CI - [x] Add release notes and rollout plan Context: this was driven by repeated CI incidents in Jan-Feb where build cache corruption and upstream registry timeouts caused spurious release failures (see SUP-4121). The dep-stability probe is intentionally conservative: failures are informational by default and only flip the release-stage gate when a threshold of transient failures is observed in 3 consecutive runs. Testing: local integration verified buildx cache priming reduces cold build time ~28% for the monorepo base image. The dep-stability probe was tested against intentionally-mocked registry timeouts; the job correctly marks an artifact and creates a short artifact bundle for debugging. Rollout plan: merge to main with feature flag OFF for release pipelines. After 48 hours of green CI, flip the release-gate flag in infra/ci-config.yaml to opt-in. Monitor the pushgateway metrics and pause if we see >5% increases in observed transient failures. Related work: this complements ENG-8342 (ci cache consistency) and reuses some of the cache-keying ideas from ENG-8427. Notes for reviewers: focus on the composite action inputs/outputs, cache key formulation, and the dep-probe thresholds. I also included small helper scripts under infra/ci for local reproductions; they should be treated as testing-only and are not intended for production automation.

[Introduce fast-feedback lanes for trivial changes and a dependency safety gate]
description:
Motivation: CI cycle time has been steadily increasing as we add more integration and security checks. For small, low-risk changes (docs, single-file lint fixes, infra config tweaks) engineers should get feedback in under 5 minutes. At the same time we need an automated, conservative gate for dependency updates to catch transitive supply-chain regressions.

Summary: this PR introduces a small change detection tool and a staged CI workflow that routes PRs to a fast-feedback lane or a full-check lane based on change classification. It also adds a composite dependency-safety action that performs transitive dependency quarantine checks and configurable quarantine policies.

What changed: 1) .github/workflows/staged-ci.yml implements two lanes: fast-path (lint/units/docs + cached build) and full-path (integration, e2e, heavy flakiness-prone tests). 2) tools/change_detector: tiny Rust binary used in the CI to classify PRs by file globs and repo-scope rules. 3) .github/actions/dep-safety: composite action that runs our internal transitive-scan.sh, invokes Snyk for vulnerability context, and can attach a work item to Linear and block merging if policy thresholds are exceeded. 4) CI cache keying updates: finer-grained cache scopes keyed on workspace-subset to reduce invalidation blast radius. 5) docs/ci/fast-feedback.md describing developer experience, how to opt-out, and adding a quickci label to force fast-path or to bypass fast-path when requested.

Checklist: [x] change detector binary + unit tests, [x] staged-ci workflow, [x] dep-safety composite + integration test in CI, [x] docs and READMEs, [x] performance telemetry added to Console for CI latency.

Impact: default is conservative: most PRs still go to full path until the change-detector pool of rules grows. Fast-path is honored only for PRs that touch docs, shaders, README, comments, and single-package lint-only changes. Rolling rollout: feature flag via workflows/ci-config.yml to enable fast-path org-wide in phases.

Related: Linear ENG-15802 (ci-fast-feedback), ENG-16210 (dep-gate), and notes in #infra-ci slack for rollout planning.

How to validate locally: 1) cargo build --manifest-path=tools/change_detector/Cargo.toml 2) tools/change_detector --base main --head HEAD --rules-file .github/ci-rules.yaml 3) run actions locally via act or use GitHub UI to open a PR to a personal branch.

[Modernize CI by replacing legacy bash pipelines with composite actions and plugin hooks]
description:
Motivation: The monolithic bash pipelines under .github/workflows and scripts/legacy-ci.sh have become brittle and hard to iterate on across services. This PR modernizes the pipeline by introducing reusable GitHub composite actions, a plugin hook system for per-repo policy, and a small cross-platform ci-toolbox binary to compute robust cache keys and talk to the remote cache store. Scope: 1) Add .github/actions/checkout-composite, test-shard-composite, lint-runner-composite. 2) Replace repo-level shell orchestration with composite action calls and a dynamic matrix generator (tools/ci/matrix-gen.js). 3) Remove scripts/legacy-ci.sh and in-repo Docker-in-Docker usage; use buildah/kind where needed. 4) Add ci-toolbox (tools/ci-toolbox/main.go) used by composite actions for cache keying and fast retries. 5) Add .github/ci-config.yml with opt-in staged rollout flags for teams to adopt incrementally. Checklist: - [x] Add composite actions and document inputs/outputs - [x] Implement matrix generator and update matrix shapes - [x] Port lint/test usages to new composites - [x] Add ci-toolbox with basic cache key and remote fetch - [x] Add integration CI job that runs composites end-to-end on a canary subset - [x] Remove legacy script invocations and update README-ci.md Migration notes: The new composites are backward-compatible by default and live alongside legacy workflows during a 2-week canary. Owners can enable ci-config.yml flags to opt into new flows. Rollback is as simple as switching the workflow reference back to legacy scripts if an issue is detected. Risks and mitigations: Cache-key changes may cause cache misses on first runs; ci-toolbox includes a dry-run mode to preview keys. Matrix reshaping can increase pipeline concurrency; we added a default concurrency limit and a dynamic shard sizing heuristic. Future work: Add telemetry hooks to Redwood Console for per-route CI latency and cost, and introduce a GH App to enforce team opt-ins.
