[Telemetry Signal Calibration and Operator Fatigue Retrospective — Q1 2026]
Overview
--------
This retrospective reviews a three-week campaign (2026-01-15 to 2026-02-05) where noisy telemetry, duplicated alert signals, and an off-nominal sampling configuration caused repeated oncall interruptions and elevated operator fatigue across the Platform Operators team. The doc summarizes the incident timeline, root causes, operator impact, mitigation steps, and concrete corrective actions that were adopted and rolled out in February 2026.

Background
----------
What happened: During a region-wide config rollout to increase sampling granularity for prefix-cache misses, a misapplied rewrite caused certain low-entropy telemetry events to surface as high-severity SLO alerts. Alerts were fired on: token-latency-99p, kv-prefix-cache-miss-rate, and runtime-op-rate-limit-errors due to correlated instrumentation amplification.

Why this matters: Frequent, high-noise alerts erode trust in dashboards, increase mean time to repair (MTTR) for genuine incidents, and materially increased operator cognitive load during an otherwise low-impact performance experiment.

Timeline (abridged)
------------------
1. 2026-01-15 09:00 — Sampling roll-out begins targeting regional cache frontends.
2. 2026-01-15 11:45 — First burst of kv-prefix-cache-miss-rate alerts; paging threshold exceeded.
3. 2026-01-15 12:30 — Operators acknowledge alerts; multiple duplicate tickets created from separate alert rules.
4. 2026-01-16 — Short-term mitigation: escalation rule adjusted to suppress duplicate signals (adhoc).
5. 2026-01-20 — Investigation identifies a telemetry enrichment step that duplicated event counts for sharded prefix caches when sampling_rate > 0.75.
6. 2026-01-25 — Permanent fix deployed to enrichment pipeline.
7. 2026-02-01 — Post-fix dashboard tuning and new alert gating rules rolled out.
8. 2026-02-05 — Formal retrospective and operator survey initiated.

Measured Impact
---------------
- Total pages during incident window: 142 (normal baseline: ~18/week).
- Average time-to-acknowledge (TTA): 7m 12s (baseline: 3m 20s).
- Average time-to-resolve (TTR): 1h 42m (baseline: 35m).
- Oncall burnout signal (anonymous survey): 62% reported "high" cognitive load; 28% considered stepping down from rotation.

Root causes
-----------
- Telemetry configuration: Sampling granularity changed without a coordinated cross-team validation plan. The enrichment job inadvertently multiplied counts for sharded cache keys.
- Alert design: Overlapping alert rules lacked de-duplication and grouping semantics. Independent rules paged the same operator for the same underlying event.
- Dashboard ergonomics: No single-pane view combined token-cost and kv-cache signals with request attribution (tenant ID, model-version), making triage slower.
- Runbook gaps: Oncall playbooks did not include a rapid dedupe mechanism or CLI snippet to silence noise across multiple alert sources.

Immediate mitigations taken
-------------------------
1. Rolled back the high-sampling variant for the enrichment pipeline (2026-01-16 03:00).
2. Added a temporary alert suppression tier for cached noisy signals for 48 hours while debugging.
3. Consolidated three overlapping PagerDuty escalation policies into a single grouped policy for cache-related SLI alerts.
4. Added a short CLI helper to silence grouped alerts:

   # Silence grouped cache alerts for 30m
   pd-silence --policy "cache-grouped" --duration 30m --author maya.patel@redwood.com

Technical root-cause analysis (summary)
-------------------------------------
- The enrichment job took sampled events and applied a join to per-shard metadata. Because sampling was applied upstream but the join operated pre-aggregation, it produced duplicate rows for multi-shard keys. The downstream metric emitter did event_count++ for each row, thus amplifying counts by shard cardinality.
- An innocuous configuration flag `preserve_shard_rows=true` had a default change during the roll-out PR; testing missed the scenario where sampling_rate was high.

Corrective actions (accepted and prioritized)
-------------------------------------------
A. Telemetry pipeline hardening (owner: eng-platform/telemetry; owner: Jun Park) — Complete by 2026-03-01
   - Add unit + integration tests that validate emitted cardinality against a golden sample (target tolerance +-2%).
   - Introduce a canary gate: sampling config changes must run on 1% production traffic for 24h with automated sanity checks.
   - Add a lint rule in cfg-repo that prevents `preserve_shard_rows=true` from being set without explicit justification and a reviewer tag.

B. Alert consolidation and dedupe (owner: eng-platform/observability; owner: Liam O'Connor) — Complete by 2026-02-20
   - Replace three cache-related rules with a single rule that exports a `cache_incident_id` label for grouping.
   - Implement contact-wise dedupe in PagerDuty: one page per incident_id per escalation window.
   - Reduce severity of kv-prefix-cache-miss-rate from P1->P2 when 95p latency < SLO.

C. Dashboard and triage UX improvements (owner: Platform Dashboards; owner: Sofia Ramirez) — Complete by 2026-02-28
   - New "Cache Triage" dashboard combining: token-latency-99p, kv-prefix-cache-miss-rate, and per-tenant request traces.
   - Add a top-level header for ongoing experiments and their rollout windows.

D. Runbook and oncall policy updates (owner: eng-sre; owner: Maya Patel) — Complete by 2026-02-15
   - Add dedupe CLI snippet (see Immediate mitigations).
   - Add explicit steps for validating sampling rollouts and a checklist for experiment owners.
   - Adjust rotation policy: limit consecutive oncall weeks to 2 during active experiment windows; require a secondary operator for the first 72 hours of any telemetry change.

Updated SLI/alert configuration (published values)
-------------------------------------------------
| metric                               | old threshold           | new threshold / gating                            | severity |
|--------------------------------------|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------|----------|
| token-latency-99p (region)           | 200ms (alert @ 220ms)   | same, but gate by incident fingerprinting         | P1 -> P1 |
| kv-prefix-cache-miss-rate (global)   | 0.8% (alert)            | alert only if sustained for 5m and backed by error spikes | P1 -> P2 |
| runtime-op-rate-limit-errors         | 0.05%                  | require correlated latency or tenant error rate   | P1 -> P2 |

(Above table is a concise representation. Full prometheus rule files are in: git@infra:redwood/observability/alert-rules/tree/2026/sampling-safety)

Rollout plan for fixes
----------------------
1. Merge pipeline tests and lint rule (telemetry-team).
2. Run sampling canary for 24h on 1% traffic; automatic check must pass (metric cardinality within tolerance).
3. If canary passes, stage config to 10% traffic for 48h with operators on standby.
4. After 72h without anomalies, incrementally expand to 100% per normal change windows.

Owner matrix and dates
---------------------
- Jun Park (eng-platform/telemetry) — tests + canary gate — due 2026-03-01
- Liam O'Connor (eng-platform/observability) — alert dedupe changes — due 2026-02-20
- Sofia Ramirez (dashboards) — Cache Triage dashboard — due 2026-02-28
- Maya Patel (eng-sre) — runbook updates + rotation policy — due 2026-02-15

Acceptance criteria (how we will confirm closure)
------------------------------------------------
- Pages/week reduced to baseline ±10% for six consecutive weeks.
- Operator survey score "high cognitive load" reduced from 62% to <20% in next quarterly pulse.
- Canary cardinality checks integrated and in CI; PRs that change sampling require passing canary check.
- Dashboard has live links and owner; triage time (TTR) returns to baseline within 30 days of rollout.

Follow-ups (action items)
------------------------
- [ ] Run a 1-week simulated experiment with platform-operators as observers to validate dedupe behaviors (owner: Platform Operators).
- [ ] Add an incident tag to the status page for "telemetry calibration" experiments for increased visibility.
- [ ] Quarterly review of alert rules: maintain a short list of 10 high-noise candidates for potential suppression.

Appendix: diagnostic queries and CLI snippets
-------------------------------------------
1) Prometheus example: compare emitted cardinality by shard\n   sum by (shard) (increase(prefix_cache_event_count[10m]))
2) Golden sample test (py)test snippet (example):
   assert abs(emitted_cardinality - expected_cardinality) < expected_cardinality * 0.02
3) PagerDuty dedupe example:
   pd-rule create --name "cache-incident-grouping" --label incident_id --dedupe true

Links and references
--------------------
- Incident ticket: INF-2026-3067
- Observability repo: git@infra:redwood/observability
- Runbook: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/operator-safe-mode-and-manual-intervention-playbook-2026
- Dashboard template: /confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/cache-triage-template

Conclusion
----------
This retrospective surfaced a recurring risk pattern: changing telemetry sampling and enrichment without small-scale canaries and cardinality tests produces noisy, trust-eroding alerts and operational overhead. The prioritized corrective actions focus on adding automated guards in the pipeline, consolidating alert logic with grouping/labels, improving triage UX, and reducing operator load through policy changes.

If you own any action item above, update the ticket INF-2026-3067 with progress and expected blockers.


[Operator Scenario Marketplace and Mentorship Program]
Summary:

This page defines the Operator Scenario Marketplace (the marketplace) — an internal catalog and CI-validated registry of synthetic incident scenarios — and the paired Operator Mentorship Program designed to accelerate operator proficiency across the platform operator population. The goal is to make production-like incident practice repeatable, discoverable, and measurable, and to fold mentorship into regular operational training.

Why we need this:
- Operators encounter a wide range of inference-specific faults (prefix cache corruption, model-variant misrouting, cross-tenant token spikes, GPU thermal preemption). Ad-hoc drills leave knowledge gaps and are hard to audit.
- A centralized scenario registry + mentorship pairing increases reuse, shortens ramp time for new operators, and reduces mean time to acknowledge (MTTA) and mean time to recover (MTTR).

Goals and success criteria:
- Provide a catalog of >= 60 vetted scenarios covering: cache, routing, model-swap, thermal/spot preemption, neighbor-tenant noisy behavior, and telemetry drift by Q3 2025.
- Each scenario has an owner, test manifest, acceptance criteria, and postmortem template.
- Mentorship pairs 1 senior operator to 2 new/junior operators; after 3 months, juniors should show a 25% reduction in MTTA on synthetic incidents.
- Track scenario usage and learning outcomes in a dashboard (see "Metrics and dashboard" section).

Scope and non-goals:
- In-scope: operator-facing simulation manifests, runbook snippets, playbooks for safe execution in a sandbox, and mentorship curriculum.
- Out-of-scope: production-changing automation (chaos that runs directly against production without a gate), vendor-managed training, and external customer-facing exercises.

Definitions:
- Scenario: A reproducible, parameterized incident simulation manifest (YAML) that can be executed in a sandbox or synthetic tenant.
- Marketplace: The git-backed registry and UI listing scenarios with metadata, tags, and test results.
- Simulation Owner: Person who vets and maintains a scenario.
- Mentor: Senior operator assigned to paired learning sessions.

Operator Scenario Manifest (required fields)
(Example manifest used by the CI validator and scenario runner)

---
name: prefix-cache-shard-corruption-v2
owner: eng-platform/operators-team
impact_area: runtime-kv-cache
severity: medium
description: "Simulate stale/incorrect KV prefix cache entries causing hallucinations and elevated token latency for a synthetic tenant."
environment: sandbox
prereqs:
  - synthetic-tenant: tenant-sim-014
  - model: redwood-vicuna-13b-quantized
steps:
  - action: seed-kv-shard
    params:
      key-prefix: "/user/sim/"
      corrupt-rate: 0.08
  - action: launch-load
    params:
      rps: 12
      profile: long-tail-1024
acceptance_criteria:
  - alert: kv-cache-error-rate < 500 per hour generated by simulation runner
  - slo_check: 95th_token_latency_delta > 25% from baseline
rollback_steps:
  - action: flush-kv-shard
  - action: revert-tenant-routing
observability_links:
  - /dashboards/eng-platform/runtime-prefix-cache-health
  - /dashboards/eng-platform/simulated-tenant-latency-traces
---

Scenario tagging taxonomy (required tags):
- impact_area: runtime-kv-cache | scheduling | routing | model-swap | network | infra-thermal | telemetry
- mode: sandbox | blue-green | shadow
- severity: low | medium | high | critical

Marketplace process and governance:
1) Submit a scenario MR to the marketplace repo (repo: github.com/redwood/platform-simulations). Include the manifest YAML, description, owner, expected telemetry signals, and a short runbook snippet.
2) CI validation runs static checks: required fields, safe-environment flag, presence of rollback steps, and test harness smoke-run in a simulated environment.
3) Two reviewers must approve: a runtime SME and an operator mentor.
4) Merge creates an entry in the marketplace UI and schedules the scenario for the quarterly validation run.

Safe execution guidelines:
- All scenarios must run in a sandbox tenant or a dedicated simulation cohort; no scenario may target production without an explicit multi-party approval and a written runbook that includes backout windows.
- Simulation noise must be rate-limited. Example: rps <= 20 for synthetic tenants; model-swap tests must be throttled to < 0.5% of model-serving capacity per region.
- Observability hooks (spans, traces, synthetic user tokens) must be labeled with tags scenario_id and sim_owner to avoid confusion with real incidents.

Mentorship Program overview:
- Pairing model: 1:2 senior-to-junior for a minimum 12-week pairing window. New hires and rotated engineers are prioritized.
- Commitments per mentor pair: two 90-minute scenario walkthroughs per week for first 4 weeks, then one guided drill per week for the following 8 weeks.
- Curriculum: week-by-week checklist covering foundational telemetry, top 10 infra faults, incident comms, SLO triage, and postmortem writing.

Mentorship session template:
- Pre-read: scenario manifest and baseline dashboard links (10m)
- Walkthrough: mentor talks through likely root causes, detection signals, and runbook steps (30m)
- Live run: junior executes the scenario in sandbox while mentor observes (30–45m)
- Debrief: write a short post-exercise note in the scenario entry and update the runbook snippet if gaps found (15m)

Post-exercise obligations:
- The simulation owner files a two-paragraph postmortem in the scenario entry and assigns any runbook bugs to the runbook backlog.
- Mentor and junior complete a short learning survey (3 questions) which feeds the operator learning dashboard.

Metrics and dashboard (implementation notes):
- Fields to capture per-execution: scenario_id, owner, mentor, participants, start_time, end_time, MTTA_sim, MTTR_sim, alerts_fired, false_positives, SLO_delta, and survey_score.
- We will onboard a dedicated dashboard in Grafana: "Operator Learning & Scenario Usage" with panels for usage by team, scenario heatmap, average MTTR improvements week-over-week, and mentor engagement rate.
- Baseline targets: by month 3 of mentorship, average MTTA_sim <= 3 minutes, MTTR_sim <= 18 minutes for medium severity scenarios.

Quality gates and continuous improvement:
- Quarterly scenario review cycle: all scenarios older than 6 months are re-validated by the simulation owner and a runtime SME.
- Retired scenarios must include a reason and a migration plan if the underlying infra changes (e.g., quantization rollout or runtime kernel update).

Operator certification and badges:
- Completion of the mentorship program + passing a scenario capstone (execute a medium+ scenario solo with MTTR_sim <= target) results in a "Certified Platform Operator (Level 1)" badge recorded in the team wiki.
- Senior mentors can nominate juniors for Level 2 after demonstrated independent incident leadership across 5 distinct scenarios.

Roadmap (next 12 months):
- Q2 2025: Launch marketplace MVP with 20 scenarios, CI validator, and initial mentor cohort (10 mentors).
- Q3 2025: Integrate scenario execution telemetry into Grafana dashboard and add automated post-exercise survey.
- Q4 2025: Add scenario tagging by customer-impact footprint and enable cross-team scenario sharing.
- Q1 2026: Develop an automated scenario-scheduling service to seed weekly practice rotations for oncall teams.

Runbook and docs links (canonical references):
- Marketplace repo: github.com/redwood/platform-simulations (README: how to add a scenario)
- Scenario runner CLI: tools/sim-runner (usage: sim-runner --manifest path/to/manifest.yaml --dry-run)
- Postmortem template: /eng-platform/runbooks/postmortem-template-compact
- Operator handbook: /eng-platform/team-wiki/platform-operator-handbook-compact

Owners and contacts:
- Program steward: Asha Patel (ashap@redwood.ai) — overall program manager and release cadence owner.
- Simulation platform: Diego Alvarez (diegoa@redwood.ai) — CI validator and runner owner.
- Mentorship coordinator: Maya Chen (mayac@redwood.ai) — pairing and badge program.

How to propose a scenario (quick steps):
1) Fork platform-simulations -> add YAML manifest + runbook snippet + observability links.
2) Open MR and add the label "scenario-proposal".
3) Request reviewers: @runtime-sme and @mentor-coordinator.
4) After merge, schedule the scenario for the next quarterly validation run via the marketplace UI.

Appendix A — Scenario review checklist (CI + reviewers)
- Manifest schema validated (all required fields present)
- Safe environment flag is true and run environment is sandbox by default
- Rollback steps exist and restore points are defined
- Observability links included (dashboards, logs, traces)
- Acceptance criteria are measurable and tied to telemetry metrics
- Owner and mentor assigned

Appendix B — Quick example sim-runner commands
- Dry run: sim-runner --manifest scenarios/prefix-cache-shard-corruption-v2.yaml --dry-run
- Execute in sandbox: sim-runner --manifest scenarios/prefix-cache-shard-corruption-v2.yaml --env sandbox --approve

Appendix C — Post-exercise note template (copy into scenario entry)
- Summary: one-line summary of what happened
- Key signals observed: metrics/alerts that were most useful
- Action items: runbook updates or monitoring alerts to tune
- Learning: what the junior learned and what mentor recommends

FAQ
Q: Who can be a mentor?
A: Any operator with two+ years on the platform or a successful completion of the senior mentor course (listed in the learning catalog).

Q: Can scenarios run against a customer tenant?
A: No. Scenarios must use synthetic tenants or dedicated simulation cohorts; exceptions require documented approvals from Security and SRE and are extremely rare.

Q: How do we measure the program ROI?
A: Primary signals: reduction in MTTA/MTTR on synthetic incidents, mentor engagement rate, scenario reuse, and reduced frequency of repeated human errors on similar incident classes in production.

Contact and next steps:
- If you want to be a simulation owner or mentor, complete this short interest form: /forms/operator-simulation-interest (internal).
- To contribute a scenario now, see the contribution guide in the marketplace repo README.

[service-contract-change-signal-and-safe-fallback-playbook]
Overview

This playbook defines a cross-cutting standard for signaling intentional API contract changes and executing safe fallback behavior across the Redwood inference stack. It ties together API surface design, runtime coding patterns, infra controls, model-serving expectations, observability gates, and performance verification steps. The objective is to allow evolution of request/response contracts while guaranteeing predictable degradation behavior, traceability, and rapid rollback when quality or SLO regressions are detected.

Why this exists

- Contract changes are inevitable: model capabilities, streaming semantics, and cost-tiered payloads will evolve.
- Poorly signaled changes cause silent client failures, high-error rates, and costly rollbacks.
- Cross-layer coordination is required: routing, cache affinity, runtime kernels, and telemetry must cooperate during change windows.

Scope

Applies to: public and internal REST/gRPC/streaming endpoints that carry model invocation payloads, especially generation, chat, embeddings, and reranking APIs. Not intended for front-end-only UI changes.

Owners and Contacts

- Primary owner: API Platform (engineering) — contact: amina.duarte@redwood.ai
- Runtime fallback steward: Serving Runtime team — contact: marco.li@redwood.ai
- Observability owner: Eng Platform — contact: sofia.patel@redwood.ai

Key Principles

1) Explicit capability negotiation: clients must express a minimal capability header for optional features. Backends may return a compatible response and a summary of accepted capabilities.
2) Non-breaking defaults: server-side additions must preserve existing fields unless an explicit opt-in signal is present.
3) Fail-safe fallbacks: when a new field or variant is not understood by downstream components, the request must either (a) fall back to a conservative variant, or (b) return a clear 4xx/422 with guidance.
4) Observable contract transitions: every change window must emit structured telemetry: change_id, gating_metric, rollforward/rollback decisions.

Contract Signaling Specification

Headers and Metadata

- X-Redwood-Contract: semantic token representing contract version (e.g., contract.v2.render-hints)
- X-Redwood-Contract-Intent: comma-separated capabilities the client is requesting (e.g., structured-output,stream-multiplex)
- X-Redwood-Client-Approx: optional perf hint (fast|balanced|high-fidelity) used by routing and kernel selectors

Request Body Schema Rules

1. Additive-only for opt-in fields: new optional fields must be namespaced under 'opt' or 'features'.
2. Required fields may only be added after a staged rollout and with explicit deprecation windows.

Sample header example

curl -X POST \ \ 
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>' \
  -H 'X-Redwood-Contract: contract.v2.render-hints' \
  -H 'X-Redwood-Contract-Intent: structured-output,function-calls' \
  https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate

Fallback Patterns (ranked by recommendation)

1) Variant Downgrade (preferred): map the request to a previous model variant or quantization profile that maintains semantics.
2) Partial Response + Hints: return a partial structured response with a top-level 'incomplete: true' flag and diagnostic suggestion.
3) Reject-with-guidance: return 422 with a structured error pointing to required contract capabilities and a suggested client fix.

Implementation Checklist (developer-facing)

- API: validate X-Redwood-Contract and X-Redwood-Contract-Intent; log mismatches at info level with change_id.
- Runtime: expose a fast-path for variant downgrade that preserves tokenization and KV cache compatibility.
- Cache: ensure prefix cache keys include contract.version to avoid poisoning.
- Router: make traffic-splitting rules aware of contract token and use weighted fallbacks.
- SDKs: expose helper to query supported capabilities and to opt-in safely.

Observability and Telemetry Gates

Mandatory telemetry emitted for a contract transition window:

- contract.change_id (tag)
- contract.request_count (counter)
- contract.error_rate (p50/p95/p99) per route and per variant
- contract.latency_ms.p95
- contract.fidelity_regressions (derived from eval harness)
- contract.rollback_reason (event)

Alerting thresholds (default)

- Error rate > 2% absolute increase over baseline in first 30 minutes -> P1 alert to oncall.
- 95th latency increase > 50% vs baseline -> P1.
- Fidelity regression (eval set delta) > configured threshold -> block rollout.

Testing and Performance Verification

Before any staged rollout:

1) Unit + contract tests: validate new optional fields deserialize in both new and old code paths.
2) Integration: run canary traffic at 0.5% for 30 minutes with synthetic load.
3) Perf: run 5-minute stress with representative sequence length histogram; capture kernel selection variance.
4) Eval: run a small eval set (100 prompts) comparing outputs against quality gates; track semantic drift via automatic scoring.

Rollout Procedure (numbered)

1. Open a Change Window: register change_id and high-level plan in the rollout registry.
2. Run preflight: run CI checks, integration smoke, and perf profile.
3. Canary 0.5% for 30m: monitor contract metrics and fidelity evals.
4. Gradual expand: 0.5% -> 2% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% with 30–60 minute observation at each step.
5. Automatic halt: gate expansion on telemetry; halt if any P1 threshold triggers.
6. Rollback: if halted, execute variant-downgrade path and open incident ticket; capture diagnostics and run postmortem.

Coding and Infra Standards (practical rules)

- Backwards compatibility suites must be part of the pre-merge CI for any API surface change.
- Use feature flags for server-side opt-ins; flags must include owner, expiry date, and test coverage.
- Prefix cache key and KV layout with contract.version and variant.id.
- Runtime sidecar must support a /compat endpoint that returns current supported contract tokens and capability matrix.

Model-serving expectations

- Model artifacts must include a capability manifest (manifest.json) listing supported contract tokens, max_sequence, quantization profile, and deterministic_hash.
- When serving multiple variants, maintain a compatibility ledger that maps variant->compatible-seed-versions for KV cache reuse.

Decision Record (ADR) — summary of tradeoffs

Decision ID: ADR-2027-04-contract-signal
Date: 2026-11-14
Decision: Require explicit contract headers and conservative fallback by default.
Reasoning: Implicit changes were causing silent client breakages and made incident triage slow. Explicit headers improve observability and allow deterministic routing to compatible variants.
Consequences: Slightly larger request surface (extra headers), additional runtime checks, more complex cache keying. Long-term benefit: faster rollouts, fewer P1 incidents.

Appendix: Quick reference table

| Field | Purpose | Required during rollout? | Default behavior |
|-------|---------|--------------------------|------------------|
| X-Redwood-Contract | Contract token | Yes | When missing, server treats as contract.v1 (legacy) |
| X-Redwood-Contract-Intent | Opt-in capabilities | No | Missing intent => conservative processing |

[Inference Platform Sales Brief — Developer & Enterprise Messaging]
Purpose
Provide a single, sharable sales brief that the field can use for pre-sales conversations with engineering and platform stakeholders. The document bundles messaging, key competitive differentials, sample pricing guidance, a short customer case example, a pilot offer, objection-handling, and a concise security FAQ for prospects.

1) One-line positioning
Redwood Inference: a developer-first inference platform that delivers predictable latency, measurable unit economics, and a single operational surface across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

2) Core value pillars (talking points)
- Performance certainty: predictable p50/p95/p99 tail latency profiles and autoscaling that keeps production SLAs intact.
- Cost controls: batching, KV/prefix caching, and quantization profiles tuned for workload tradeoffs to reduce per-token costs.
- Deployment flexibility: same API/ops experience across Hosted API, Dedicated capacity, and Private (VPC/on‑prem) for regulated workloads.
- Reliability & fallbacks: automatic model-variant fallbacks, regional routing, and transparent degraded-mode behaviors.
- Observability: token-level cost and latency breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and prompt-regression alerts.

3) Elevator pitch (30–60s)
"If your team is building LLM features you care about predictable inference economics and disruption-free rollouts. Redwood gives you a single API and console to ship fast on hosted infrastructure, move to reserved Dedicated capacity for predictable throughput, or run privately behind your network controls — all while lowering per‑token cost through batching, caching, and quantization recommendations, and giving you SLOs and observability you can rely on."

4) Quick technical highlights (for engineering stakeholders)
- Serving runtime: GPU-optimized continuous batching, KV cache-aware execution and quantization-friendly kernels.
- Smart routing: policies for latency, cost, region and customer tier; automated fallback to compatible model variants.
- Observability: per-request token timeline, cost attribution (model, compute, I/O), and alerting for quality regressions tied to labeled prompt sets.
- Integrations: Kubernetes-based Dedicated runtime or OCI-compliant on‑prem package; KMS/HSM integrations for keys; SSO and fine-grained RBAC.

5) Competitive brief — concise battlecard
Competitors considered: OpenAI (hosted), Anthropic, AWS Bedrock, Self-hosted runtimes (KServe/Replicate), Hybrid vendors.
- Differentiators (what to emphasize):
  - Unified product surface across Hosted / Dedicated / Private (most competitors split these experiences).
  - Production-first telemetry: token-level cost + latency timelines and regression alerts (rare at this granularity).
  - Cost control levers exposed to customers: batching, caching, quantization recommendations and policy-based routing.
  - Enterprise-grade private deployment with optional air-gap and KMS/HSM integration.
- Weaknesses / concessions to acknowledge proactively:
  - We do not have the broadest model catalog compared to general model marketplaces; we focus on verified models and performance profiles.
  - For very small teams wanting a purely managed black-box API, OpenAI may be simpler — but lacks deterministic cost controls and private deployment options at scale.

6) Short battlecard table (talk-to bullets)

Hosted latency & SLOs | Predictable p95/p99 tail SLOs and circuit-breaker fallbacks | OpenAI: low friction but less transparent unit economics

- Commerce levers for negotiation: minimum commitment length (6/12/24 months), committed throughput (reserve QPS), feature packs (longer retention, advanced observability), professional services (onboarding, private deployment).
- Sample quick TCO framing (for buyer’s infra team):

[Falkon Systems: embedding index reconciliation mismatch & audit-log delivery gap during high ingest (billing exposure)]
description:
Issue summary:
During a peak ingest window on 2026-03-10 08:45–09:20 PST, Falkon Systems reported that semantic search results returned incorrect document ids for a subset of recently ingested vectors. Simultaneously, audit logs for ingestion latency and billing counters were missing for a 22-minute interval which prevented Falkon from reconciling billed usage.

Impact:
- Customer-facing search returned stale or mismatched results for ~3.2% of queries routed to the dense-index-service in us-west-2.
- Falkon reported a billing delta (observed vs expected) of ~12% for the ingestion window due to missing audit log events.
- Customer escalated to enterprise support; legal/finance looped in for potential credits.

Environment:
- Dedicated deployment (customer-managed VPC peering) in us-west-2 using embedding-encoder-v2 -> dense-index-service (quantized).
- Autoscale pool scaled up at 08:40 but indexer pod restarts were observed between 08:46 and 08:53.

Steps to reproduce (investigation checklist rather than deterministic repro):
1) Ingest high-throughput batch (approx 18k vectors/min) with mixed small and large payloads.
2) Observe indexer task restarts in the dense-index kube pool.
3) Run sample search for recently ingested document ids and compare to precomputed vector->id map.
4) Check audit-log stream for missing log sequence numbers in the 08:45–09:07 window.

Logs / telemetry pointers:
- Observability trace: https://observability.redwood.internal/traces/2026-03-10/idx-mismatch-08-47
- Grafana panel: embeddings-indexer pod restarts: https://grafana.redwood/internal/d/embeddings/indexer-pod-restarts?from=2026-03-10T08:30:00Z&to=2026-03-10T09:30:00Z
- Billing delta dashboard: https://console.redwood/internal/billing/deltas/falkon/2026-03-10

Temporary workaround provided to customer:
- Switched Falkon to a pinned read-route that bypasses the in-flight indexer shard (read-only replication) while we replayed the missing events into the index.
- Issued temporary billing credit to cover immediately visible delta pending reconciliation.

Customer impact and communication:
- Customer was updated on-call and received an interim timeline within 30 minutes. Finance requested formal reconciliation and credits; CS opened this ticket to coordinate post-incident follow-up and evidence delivery.

comments:
2026-03-10T09:05Z - Lydia Park (Customer Success): Customer on the line; reporting returned results pointing to wrong doc ids. They can reproduce against queries hitting us-west. Asked for immediate mitigation and credit hold. Escalating to SRE.
2026-03-10T09:12Z - Priya Nair (SRE): Observed 3 indexer pod restarts starting 08:46. Restarted due to OOM eviction on node gpu-12. Raising hypothesis: burst ingest + large batch led to memory pressure on indexer causing partial write batches to be lost before durable ack to audit log stream.
2026-03-10T09:30Z - Evan Chen (Engineer, Index Service): Found gaps in RSM (replicated state machine) commit log for shard-7 between 08:46:23 and 08:58:41. Some commit entries were retained in local ephemeral storage but not flushed to the audit-log producer before the process restart.
2026-03-10T10:10Z - Raul Mendez (Falkon DevOps): Confirmed behavior from our side: ~11% of recent ingest batch ids not present when we ran verification against our sidecar map. Appreciate the temp read-route fix. Need formal reconciliation file and proof of replay before we close billing request.
2026-03-11T14:22Z - Marco Ortega (Assignee): Replay completed and verified. Attached reconciliation CSV to customer Slack and Confluence. Initiated billing adjustment flow. Planning a postmortem and longer-term fix (persistent commit flush before ack).
2026-03-12T16:00Z - Aisha Kumari (Support): Customer accepted reconciliation and billing credit. Customer asked for a timeline for persistent fix and a test plan for future peak ingest scenarios. Added to post-incident action items.

investigation_notes:
Timeline and findings:
- 08:40: autoscaler increased indexer pool to handle surge; several indexer pods scheduled onto new GPU node types.
- 08:46: node gpu-12 experienced transient memory pressure; kernel OOM killed indexer process leading to abrupt restart.
- 08:46–08:59: RSM commit log had unflushed entries that were not propagated to the audit-log Kafka topic due to in-memory batching.
- 08:59–09:10: indexer recovered, but some vector->id mappings were written to ephemeral local store only; replication missed the durable ack.
Root cause hypothesis:
- Combination of aggressive in-memory batching in the dense-index-service and a recent change that increased batch size for latency optimization caused larger transient memory usage. When a pod was OOM-killed, in-memory batch in producer was lost before flush to audit log, creating both search inconsistency and missing billing events.
Contributing factors:
- Autoscaler packed pods onto a smaller set of nodes during the burst (bin-packing behavior).
- No enforced pre-ack flush semantics for commit batches on indexer restart.
Evidence:
- Commit log gaps in index shard-7 trace.
- Missing sequence ranges in audit-log topic for 08:46–09:07.
- Pod OOM event records on node gpu-12.
- Replayed entries successfully restored search parity and reduced billing delta to <0.2%.

resolution_notes:
Immediate remediation:
1) Executed controlled replay of missing commit ranges into indexer from durable write-ahead log stored in object storage.
2) Temporarily pinned Falkon read-route to read-only replica while replay completed.
3) Issued pro-rated billing credit covering the measured delta; finance notified and reconciliation file delivered.
Permanent fixes applied (short-term):
- Rolled out indexer v2.1.3 which reduces in-memory batch size under memory pressure and forces flush on SIGTERM.
- Autoscaler safety adjustment to avoid bin-packing sensitive pods onto a single node by setting podAntiAffinity hints in dense-index-service deploy.
- Added alert rule for audit-log sequence gaps and a check for commit-flush duration > 2s.
Follow-up verification:
- Post-deploy canary with synthetic high-throughput ingest (20k vectors/min) passed for 3 consecutive 30-minute windows with no commit gaps.
Customer communication:
- Shared reconciliation CSV, replay proof, and audit-log segment references. Finance accepted credit; customer closed the escalation after verification.

Create a durable flush-on-commit test and add to CI for indexer (owner: Evan Chen) - due 2026-03-20
Adjust autoscaler bin-packing policy for indexer class pods (owner: Priya Nair) - due 2026-03-18
Run a cross-team runbook review session with SRE, Indexing, and Billing to validate audit-log handoff semantics (owner: Marco Ortega) - due 2026-03-25
Provide Falkon with a monthly report for two months showing post-fix ingest parity and billing reconciliations (owner: Lydia Park) - deliver by 2026-04-10
Add an observability dashboard to surface audit-log sequence continuity per-customer and per-shard (owner: Observability Team) - due 2026-03-22

[Embedding padding/trim mismatch causing rerank order oscillation and autoscaling surge]
description:
Issue summary: AtlasDocs reports intermittent rerank quality regressions (top-k order flips) coincident with brief 500/timeout spikes and a burst of autoscaling activity. Impact: customer search relevance fluctuates for ~5-30s windows, end-users see wrong top results and increased latency. Observed primarily on dedicated pool in us-east. Hypothesis: mismatched embedding vector length from ingest vs reranker (padding vs trim) interacts with prefix caching and leads to CPU fallback and reordering.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Ingest documents with legacy client that sends variable-length embeddings (prefix-preserve ON).
2) Trigger rerank calls with batched requests that rely on cached prefix KVS (cache hit ratio ~70%).
3) Observe occasional top-k order flips and concurrent increase in 5xx/timeouts for rerank route.
4) Re-run with strict-length header enforced -> issue does not appear.
5) Toggle client to pad to fixed dim -> issue immediately reproduces in load test 38/50 runs.

logs_and_metrics:
- Spike window 2026-03-09T21:03Z: rerank 500s increased from 0.2% baseline to 6.8% for 18s
- CPU fallback events on serving replicas: +420% during spike (observed in dedicated pool metrics).
- Autoscale adds 3 nodes in 25s following increased CPU and queue depth; scale-down after 90s.
- Top-1 reorder rate: baseline 0.03% -> 2.7% during windows reported by AtlasDocs telemetry.
- Evidence: request payloads show embedding length header missing or set to 0 for ~14% of requests in affected interval.

investigation_notes:
2026-03-10: Triage - onboarded AtlasDocs support engineer on call. Retrieved request traces (trace IDs logged to slack #support-embed).
Hypothesis A: client-side trimming/padding parity mismatch - some clients trim trailing zeros and omit length header; reranker assumes fixed-length and interprets padded zeros as meaningful leading dims -> numerical ties.
Hypothesis B: caching layer stored 'compressed' prefix keys without embedding-length metadata; cache hits returned incompatible vectors causing soft ties and additional CPU normalization work.
Reproduction: Created synthetic load with mixed-length embeddings. Confirmed top-k oscillation when cache returns a vector with trimmed length while live encoder returns padded vector. Order stabilization when strict dimension header included.
Root cause narrow: cache key schema omitted embedding-dimension tag. When cached vectors with trimmed length were returned to reranker expecting padded vectors, internal normalization path triggered an alternate code path that is slower and occasionally produces near-equal scores, causing non-deterministic sort ties depending on batch ordering.
Secondary effect: heavier CPU normalization caused more requests to fall back from GPU path to CPU path in serving runtime, triggering autoscaler during brief bursts.

[Intermittent out-of-order rerank scores + timeouts after embedding normalization default change]
description:
Issue summary: Customer reports intermittent rerank responses where top-k ordering flips unpredictably and API requests to /v1/rerank occasionally time out (~10-15s) when request payloads exceed ~3000 candidate vectors. Impact: Relevance-sensitive search producing wrong results for production customers (VectorFind Inc.), causing perceived ranking regressions and elevated latency. Logs attached: excerpt of reranker logs show occasional fallback to cpu-rerank kernel and repeated "vector-compare: tie-break fallback" entries. Customer impact: Search results inconsistent for end users, several production queries failing intermittently.

2) Issue POST /v1/rerank in eu-west with same model as query embedding; set top_k=10
3) Repeat the exact payload 5x in a short window; observe ordering differences and occasional 5xx/timeouts
4) Re-run with explicit normalize=true on client-side — ordering stabilizes and latency reduces

[Clarify burst-credit accounting for transient signed-url multipart uploads mixed with priority-weighted streaming]
description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports recurring 429s and quota exhaustion during mixed workload: a fleet of short-lived pre-signed multipart upload workers (for vector ingestion) running concurrently with low-latency priority streaming (interactive sessions). They believe burst credits are being charged twice or applied in the wrong window.

Impact:
- Intermittent 429 responses on ingestion clients causing backfill stalls (throughput drop ~35%).
- Interactive users see elevated latency or request rejections during concurrent heavy multipart uploads.
- Customer on Dedicated pool; impacting production search indexing and user-facing queries.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool (LuminaSearch), region: us-east, prod
- Ingest workers use short-lived signed URLs to upload chunks to object store and then POST completion to /v1/embeddings/batch
- Concurrent low-latency streaming sessions (websocket) use priority routing with weight class = high

Steps to reproduce (as provided by customer):
1) Start 200 parallel pre-signed multipart upload workers (each worker opens ~4 parallel HTTP connections to upload chunks, then calls completion endpoint).
2) At t+30s, start 100 low-latency streaming sessions that open websockets and push small messages every 2s.
3) Observe 429 spikes on the /v1/embeddings/batch route and intermittent 429s for streams within same tenant.

Observed logs/snippets (customer supplied):
- "2026-03-11T14:22:43Z tenant=lumina request=/v1/embeddings/batch status=429 quota_window=60 burst_credits_before=12 burst_credits_after=7"
- "2026-03-11T14:22:44Z tenant=lumina request=/v1/streams/ws status=429 quota_window=10 burst_credits_before=3 burst_credits_after=0"
- Worker telemetry: "upload_conn=4 chunks=16 signed_url_ttl_sec=120"

Questions from customer:
1) Are pre-signed multipart upload completions and streaming websocket opens drawn from the same burst-credit pool and token window, or are they separated by route/class?
2) How are short-lived signed URLs accounted for—when is the token deduction applied (on URL mint, chunk upload, or completion POST)?
3) Why are burst_credits_before and burst_credits_after differing between routes leading to near-simultaneous exhaustion?
4) Recommended config changes or best practices to avoid these 429 spikes without sacrificing low-latency streaming SLA.

Investigation summary (support):
- Verified customer traces in ingress: both embeddings/batch and streams routes are attributed to the same tenant id and weight class mapping is present.
- Rate-limiter logs show per-route windowing but a shared tenant-level burst pool. During the reproduction window, a large fraction of the burst credits were consumed by many short-lived signed-url completions which charge at completion time.
- Observed small discrepancy: signed-url chunk uploads (direct to S3) do not hit our API, but the final completion POST to /embeddings/batch does full accounting. Several workers call completion in tight bursts, each completion counts as a token-heavy operation.
- Websocket session opens are charged against a smaller, lower-frequency window; however tenant-level burst exhaustion causes route fallback and 429s propagate to all routes.
- Found evidence of priority-weighting: streaming routes had higher weight but weighting does not isolate burst credit sources when tenant pool is depleted.

Hypothesis:
- Burst credits are tenant-scoped. Signed URL flow results in clustered completion POSTs that rapidly consume tenant burst credits. Priority-weighted streaming still requires tenant credits; when the tenant pool is drained by completions, weighted routes receive 429s despite higher priority. The customer expected route isolation for burst credits, but current dedicated pool config uses tenant-level burst budgets by default.

Immediate workaround provided to customer:
- Stagger completion POSTs (spread by jitter) to avoid synchronized drain.
- For signed-url flow, delay completion callbacks by small randomized backoff (10–60s) and enable client-side exponential backoff on 429.
- Temporarily raise tenant burst_credit_quota on the dedicated pool (we patched a non-prod test and confirmed reduction of 429s).

Recommended long-term actions:
- Option 1: Configure separate quota buckets per route class (enable per-route burst isolation) for high-ingest customers on Dedicated. Provide config snippet and rollout caveats.
- Option 2: Use a separate service account/api-key for bulk ingestion paths to have an independent quota from interactive streaming keys.
- Option 3: Apply smoothing policy at edge to spread completion POSTs over a sliding window and avoid epochal drains.

Follow-ups required:
- Engineering: small change to documentation clarifying when signed-url operations are accounted (mint vs completion).
- Product: expose a Console toggle for per-route burst isolation for Dedicated customers (feature request filed).
- Ops: evaluate default burst_credit_quota for new Dedicated tenants to reduce these collisions.

Resolution (so far):
- Temporary increase to tenant burst_credit_quota applied for LuminaSearch (rolled for 24h) — customer reports immediate improvement.
- Provided staggered backoff guidance and a short sample library (client-side) to help spread completions.
- Ticket left open for follow-up feature work and documentation update.

[Embedding distribution variance ('entropy surge') triggers ANN fallback and 99th-percentile rerank latency spikes]
description:
Issue summary: Beginning ~2026-03-10 02:14 UTC QuillSearch reported intermittent but sharp increases in 99th-percentile latency for the /rerank endpoint on their dedicated cluster. Impact: customer-facing search UI experienced slow 'load more' responses and occasional 503s for heavy queries. Hypothesis at intake: unusual embedding distribution (high variance in vector norms / 'entropy surge') caused the ANN routing layer to consider many shards as low-confidence resulting in fallback to exact scan or CPU-based path, increasing tail latency and causing queue buildup.

Environment: Dedicated cluster for QuillSearch (dedicated-gpu-pool-7), production, primary region us-east with cross-region reads to eu-west. Ingest pipeline: embed service rwd/embed-tilt-1.1 -> indexer -> ANN index (hnsw) served by rerank-fast-v2.

Expected behaviour: Stable rerank 99th <= 300ms for this workload; ANN index should return consistent candidate sets and avoid frequent CPU fallbacks.

Customer impact: QuillSearch reports degraded UX and increased error rate during peak indexing windows. They are on a dedicated capacity contract; SLA implications active.

[Adaptive request slicing and deferred affinity to reduce CPU path congestion]
description:
Motivation: production traffic showed persistent CPU-side tail latency spikes under mixed short/long sequence workloads. Investigation pointed to three correlated bottlenecks: coarse-grained request serialization that forces full-copy paths, eager thread affinity/pinning of worker threads leading to imbalance during garbage bursts, and KV cache prewarm thrash when large in-flight prefixes queue up. This PR introduces three coordinated runtime changes to address these: 1) adaptive request slicing: split long inferences into small CPU-affine micro-slices that can be interleaved by the scheduler to reduce lock hold times and make batching more opportunistic; slices are a runtime-visible unit, not a user-facing change. 2) deferred affinity: worker threads avoid hard pinning during non-critical phases and only escalate to CPU-affinity when the slice enters the kernel-critical path (kernel exec + KV lookup) — this minimizes expensive handoffs and syscall churn. 3) on-demand serialization + lightweight copy-on-write frames: we replace the old eager full-object serialization with a lazy/path-dependent serializer that performs zero-copy for read-only buffers and only materializes copies on mutation. Complementing these are: small KV prefetch windows to warm hot prefixes for the upcoming slice set and scheduler heuristics that bias interleaving to keep the GPU/tokenizer hot while limiting CPU lock contention. This change is implemented in the runtime scheduler, serializer, and KV components and is backward compatible with existing request semantics. Implementation notes: adaptive slicing sits inside src/runtime/scheduler/slicer.rs and introduces a Slice struct with lifecycle hooks. The serializer change is in src/runtime/serializer/on_demand.rs and a new CopyOnWriteFrame wrapper. Deferred affinity logic is gated behind a runtime flag runtime.scheduler.deferred_affinity=false by default for conservative rollout and can be enabled per-node via node config. Safety: added unit and integration tests cover slice reassembly, serializer edge cases, and race windows around deferred affinity. Benchmarks: microbench harness under mixed short(<=64)/long(>1024) workloads shows p95 latency reduction from 82ms to 67ms (-18%), aggregate throughput improvement +14% at tail-preserving load, CPU syscalls and context-switches dropped ~23%, and steady-state median latency change <2%. On internal end-to-end L7 workload the change reduced observed CPU queuing delay by 26% and brought down incident-prone bursts in 95th tail by 30%. Rollout plan: feature-gated on node level; staged canary to 5% of traffic for 48h with an automated rollback threshold of +10% token-cost or +15% p95 latency. Related work: follows background from ENG-2467 and complements work in ENG-2503 on KV cache eviction policies. Backwards compatibility: no breaking changes to API. Migration: none required.

Feature-gated and opt-in per-node.

[Microbatch interleaver and KV primer: conditional prefetch to reduce prefill stalls]
description:
Motivation: Prefill-heavy workloads still exhibit GPU stalls when large prefill windows block decode progress for shorter requests. Existing speculative approaches either overfetch KV state or serialize stages too conservatively, wasting throughput. This change introduces two coordinated mechanisms: (1) a microbatch interleaver scheduler that interleaves small prefill microbatches with decode work to reduce idle GPU time, and (2) a KV primer hint that conditionally prefetches KV entries only for sequences predicted to need them soon. The design balances latency and memory pressure and is configurable per-route.

What this PR does (single-line continuous description): Adds Scheduler::MicrobatchInterleaver, an interleaving policy that slices prefill windows into microbatches and opportunistically schedules decode kernels between slices; introduces kv_primer hint propagation from request admission through scheduling to the runtime kernel selector; implements a predictive prefetch heuristic (sequence-length + remaining budget) that gates KV priming; introduces guards to limit concurrent primer memory usage; updates runtime kernel selection to accept primer hints and avoid eager KV expansion for low-probability sequences.

Commits summary: [commit 1] introduce microbatch interleaver scheduler and unit tests; [commit 2] add kv_primer hint plumbing and API surface; [commit 3] predicitive prefetch heuristic and memory guard; [commit 4] runtime kernel changes to honor primer hints and avoid eager KV expansion; [commit 5] integration tests and perf canary config; [commit 6] address reviewer feedback and add stress test for memory regression.

Files/areas changed (high level): src/scheduler/microbatch_interleaver.cc/h, src/scheduler/policy_registry.cc, src/runtime/kernel_selector.cc, src/runtime/kv_primer.cc/h, src/serving/route_config.cc (new per-route config flags), integrations/perf/canaries/microbatch-interleaver.yaml, tests/scheduler/microbatch_interleaver_test.cc, tests/runtime/kv_primer_integration_test.cc. Small edits: docs/observability.md (added notes about new per-route metric microbatch.interleave.ratio) and examples/quickstarts/microbatch-config.yaml.

Backward compatibility and flags: Feature guarded behind runtime config microbatch_interleaver.enabled (default: false). KV primer is off by default and enabled via route-level config kv_primer.mode = "conditional". No changes to public API or client SDKs. Migration: operators can flip the flags and tune microbatch_interleaver.max_microbatch_tokens and kv_primer.memory_limit_mb.

Performance results: Internal perf canary on T4-like nodes with mixed workloads (60% short requests <= 32 tokens, 40% long prefill requests) showed: p50 generation latency -7%, p95 -12% on mixed traffic; effective throughput increased ~8% for the same GPU pool; small memory increase at peak when kv_primer enabled (+4% RSS) but within configured limits. Deterministic unit tests added and integration stress harness to detect KV memory regressions.

Testing: Unit tests for scheduler heuristics and priority inversion cases; integration tests simulating interleaved prefill/decode streams; added perf canary (microbatch-interleaver) which runs nightly and reports microbatch.interleave.ratio and kv_primer.hit_rate. CI: all checks green after rerun (one flaky test in mem-monitor was retried and passed).

[Interleaved activation checkpointing and buffer coalescing to cut peak GPU workspace]
description:
Motivation: In production we observed recurring OOMs and large transient workspace peaks for long-sequence (>=4k) generation and KV-heavy batched workloads. Previous work focused on per-layer checkpointing and arena sizing; this PR targets three complementary levers to reduce peak GPU footprint without changing numeric behavior: 1) interleaved activation checkpointing that staggers recompute windows to shrink concurrent activation sets, 2) scratch buffer coalescing that merges short-lived per-op scratch allocations into a reusable sub-arena, and 3) scheduler hints that adjust continuous-batching flush thresholds to avoid pathological peak overlaps with KV cache refill phases.

Summary of changes (commits):
- commit 1: implement interleaved checkpoint planner and unit tests (planner/ckpt_planner.{cpp,h}, tests/ckpt_planner_tests.cpp)
- commit 2: introduce coalesced scratch allocator and sub-arena lifecycle (runtime/scratch_coalesce.{cpp,h}, runtime/sub_arena.{cpp,h})
- commit 3: hook allocator into kernel queue; add allocator metrics and tracing points (runtime/kernel_queue.cpp, observability/metrics_registry.cpp)
- commit 4: scheduler hint API and continuous-batching adjustments (scheduler/flush_policy.{cpp,h}, api/scheduler_config.md)
- commit 5: perf harness & benchmarks (perf/bench_long_seq.py, perf/bench_report_24678.md)
- commit 6: address review comments, test flakiness fixes, additional microbenchmarks (various)

Files/areas changed (high level):
- runtime/*: new scratch coalescing allocator, sub-arena management, updated kernel queue to use sub-arena
- planner/*: new interleaved checkpoint planner for grouped layers
- scheduler/*: new flush threshold heuristics and opt-in scheduler_hint config
- tests/*: unit tests for planner and allocator, end-to-end perf harness
- perf/*: benchmark scripts and result artifacts
- docs/api: scheduler config doc and short rationale

Key implementation notes:
- Interleaved checkpointing preserves existing deterministic recompute semantics; it schedules which layers are recomputed together to minimize the live activation set. The planner uses a simple greedy grouping heuristic with a max-concurrent-activation target derived from a per-model profile.
- Scratch coalescing introduces a short-lived sub-arena that consolidates fast scratch allocations from kernels that previously carved many small temporary buffers. Sub-arena size is auto-sized from recent epoch allocation histograms and is reclaimed per-batch. The allocator implements a small freelist and uses 8- or 16-byte alignment to avoid fragmentation.
- Scheduler hints are opt-in via the scheduler_config and default to conservative values for existing deployments. When enabled, the scheduler slightly reduces continuous-batching accumulation when the planner predicts a high KV-cache refill overlap (important for chat/history workloads).

[Stripe-packed checkpoint layout + kernel-swap workspace scheduler]
description:
Motivation: Runtime peak GPU memory for long-context and multi-concurrent sessions is dominated by transient activation checkpoints and scratch buffers. Existing arena packing reduces fragmentation but still leaves worst-case peaks when large kernels and KV cache operations coincide. This PR introduces two complementary techniques: 1) a stripe-packed checkpoint layout that packs checkpointed activation fragments into tightly interleaved stripes to reduce per-kernel working set, and 2) a kernel-swap workspace scheduler that defers non-critical kernel workspace allocations and opportunistically swaps packed checkpoint stripes to a hotset buffer during safe epochs. The result is lower transient GPU footprint with negligible throughput impact for typical workloads.

Design summary: The changeset contains: - runtime/allocator/stripe_packer.{cpp,h}: new packing allocator that writes checkpoints as interleaved stripe pages and maintains a compact index. The layout is guided by per-layer size histograms so larger activations are split across stripes to avoid single large contiguous allocations. - runtime/scheduler/kernel_swap_scheduler.{cpp,h}: a lightweight scheduler that tracks upcoming kernel workspace needs (based on compiled kernel descriptors) and introduces micro-delays or pre-eviction of low-priority checkpoint stripes when a high-water mark is predicted. It integrates with existing continuous-batching signals to avoid affecting short-latency requests. - runtime/kv/cache_timing_adjuster.{cpp,h}: small heuristics that shift eager KV prefetchs slightly earlier or later (configurable window) to avoid simultaneous peaks with planned large kernel work. - runtime/config/runtime_flags.yaml: feature flag stripe_packed_ckpt + kernel_swap_mode with three modes (off, conservative, aggressive) to control rollout. - tests/benchmarks/stripe_packed_peak_mem.py: microbench harness used for the numbers below. - doc/ops/stripe_pack_notes.md: operator-facing notes and recommended knob settings.

Compatibility and safety: All new behavior is gated behind runtime flags and default to conservative mode in hosted. The stripe layout preserves on-disk and in-memory checkpoint semantics (index translates to original offsets) so no model changes are required. Kernel-swap scheduler only defers workspace allocations when allocation would otherwise fail the memory check; in conservative mode it only triggers for kernels > 32MB workspace.

Benchmarks and results: Measured on p4d.24xlarge with a long-context transformer (64k tokens synthetic) under mixed small/large batch traffic. Numbers are 95th percentile across runs: - peak GPU working-set: baseline 43.1GB -> stripe+swap 35.3GB (~18% reduction) - sustained throughput: baseline 112 seq/s -> stripe+swap 118 seq/s (+5%) due to reduced GC/evict churn in KV - 99p latency increase: +3ms in aggressive mode, <1ms in conservative mode - KV miss spikes reduced on concurrent load by ~40% (observed in trace samples)

Testing and QA: - Unit tests for stripe_packer allocation/compactness and index correctness. - Integration tests for kernel_swap_scheduler under synthetic batch traces. - End-to-end smoke runs against hosted canary with conservative flags enabled. - Load tests for KV timing behavior in the benchmark lab. CI includes unit + integration + e2e canary checks; initial CI run had a lint failure which was fixed in commit 3.

Rollout plan: 1) Merge to main behind flags. 2) Enable conservative mode in dedicated lab for 2 weeks and monitor peak memory and 95th latency. 3) Enable conservative for a small percentage of hosted traffic. 4) If metrics look good, enable aggressive mode in private clusters where customers opt-in.

Related work: follows on ideas from ENG-2170 (arena packing) but focuses on temporal co-location and ordering rather than raw fragmentation. Also complements KV windowed eviction work (see SUP-512) by smoothing timing interactions.

Checklist: - [x] Design doc reviewed - [x] Unit tests added - [x] Benchmarks present - [x] Feature flags added - [x] Docs for operators - [x] Security review N/A (no external surface change)

Notes: this PR intentionally keeps the stripe packer conservative in memory movement; a follow-up will add a compact-on-idle pass that further reduces fragmentation but requires pinned-memory staging to avoid host<->device thrash.

[Blockwise attention microkernel with in-place rotary + KV coalescing]
description:
Motivation: reduce per-token compute and memory pressure for mixed-length workloads by introducing a blockwise attention microkernel that applies rotary embeddings in-place and a coalesced KV slab layout to reduce eviction churn under continuous batching. This is targeted at production inference workloads where many short requests interleave with occasional long sequences, and where KV cache eviction/compaction hurts tail latency and throughput.

Design summary: single-string overview of the changes and rationale. The change introduces: 1) a blockwise attention microkernel (C++/CUDA) that operates on fixed tiles (configurable tile sizes per-device) and performs matmul, rotary application, and softmax reduction across tiles to improve register reuse and reduce intermediate memory traffic; 2) in-place rotary application baked into the microkernel so we avoid an extra QKV transform buffer and extra memcopies for rotary/rope, enabling a fused Q*K pass for short sequences; 3) a coalesced slab layout for KV cache where cache entries are allocated in device slabs grouped by model-shard and sequence-block to reduce fragmentation and avoid frequent small reallocations; 4) scheduler hints to prefer homogenous micro-batches (same tile shapes) and a lightweight placement heuristic that pins streams to slots with matching slab affinity; 5) an opt-in runtime flag redwood.runtime.attn.blockwise_enabled and a dynamic tunable redwood.runtime.attn.tile_size that defaults to 64 for A100/B100 families but is auto-tuned during warmup.

What changed (high level):
- Serving runtime: new kernel registration and selection path for blockwise_attn (kernel selector picks blockwise_attn when model architecture and sequence distribution fit heuristics).
- Kernels: new CUDA microkernel (src/serving/kernels/blockwise_attn.cu) and a small CPU fallback (src/serving/kernels/blockwise_attn_cpu.cc).
- KV cache: allocator and layout changes (src/serving/kv/coalesced_slab.h, .cc) plus eviction policy tweaks to prefer LRU within slab groups.
- Scheduler: runtime/router updates to emit tile-shaped batch groups (src/serving/scheduler/tile_grouping.{cc,h}) and added placement hints in request metadata.
- Config/flags: runtime config and console flags for tuning.

Benchmarks (perf-lab A100, end-to-end inference with standard chat workload and continuous-batching enabled):
- Seq=128, batch mix skewed to short: throughput +1.9x, median latency -22%, p95 latency -18%.
- Seq=512, mixed: throughput +1.4x, p95 -11%.
- Seq=4096 (long): p95 latency -12% due to reduced KV eviction stalls when long sequences interleave.
- Token/dollar improvement measured at 1.45x on our internal cost model for typical production mix.

Safety / compatibility: feature gated behind redwood.runtime.attn.blockwise_enabled=false by default for private/dedicated until validated per-customer. The API surface (generation/embeddings endpoints) is unchanged: kernel selection is internal. Backwards compatible with pinned model-versions and will not run when a model requires a kernel not supported by blockwise_attn (e.g., certain fused custom ops).

Testing and validation:
- Unit tests for slab allocator and eviction (tests/kv/coalesced_slab_test.cc).
- Microbench harness added under perf/bench/blockwise_attn_bench.cc with autotest runs on perf-canary.
- Integration smoke tests in CI: python-sdk functional tests and a reduced perf-smoke were run; perf smoke was flaky once but the rerun passed.
- End-to-end perf runs recorded in perf-lab and uploaded as artifacts (perf-lab job IDs in comments).

Checklist: [x] Kernel correctness tests [x] Bench harness added [x] Perf regression guard rails [x] Feature flag + config [x] Documentation: docs/ops/blockwise_attn.md added (usage, tradeoffs, tuning guidance) [x] Rollout plan: staged canary -> dedicated pool opt-in -> wider default.

Changed files (high level): list of key files modified and purpose. Small illustrative snippets included only where helpful.

Related tickets and context: Linear: ENG-4892 (continuous-batching KV eviction reduction), ENG-5031 (kernel selector improvements). Also follows up on earlier work on fused rotary/flash integration but purposely uses a simpler, narrower microkernel to increase robustness and support a broader range of models.

Merge: squash-merged after perf lab artifacts matched expectations and two approvals.

Notes for reviewers: pay special attention to memory ordering in coalesced_slab and the fallback slow path correctness. Tuning knobs are intentionally conservative; we expect incremental future improvements (auto-tiling, int8 kernels).

release_notes:
Introduces a blockwise attention microkernel with in-place rotary application and a coalesced KV slab cache layout. Provides up to ~1.9x throughput improvement on short-sequence heavy mixes and lower tail latency for mixed workloads. Feature is behind a runtime flag and opt-in for Dedicated/Private until fully validated.

[Service account impersonation scoping prevents delegated admin operations in private prod]
description:
Issue summary: Customer reports that new service account tokens cannot perform delegated admin ops (user management and billing read) after migrating to a private deployment token broker. Impact: Multiple automation jobs and SRE runbooks fail; customer-facing admin UI returns 403 when acting-as a service account. Environment: Private deployment (Aurora private VPC), prod - us-east, Redwood private control plane with identity-proxy v1.9.2 and token-broker v0.8.2. Observed start: 2026-03-09 18:20 UTC. Business impact: Blocks Aurora's automated onboarding and scheduled invoice exports; they are a HIPAA-regulated customer and cannot proceed with several tasks until impersonation works.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Create service account 'onboard-runner@aurora' in Aurora tenant. 2) Request token via Aurora's token-broker that exchanges internal long-lived key for a short-lived access token. 3) Call Admin API /v1/admin/users with X-Redwood-Impersonate header set to 'user:alice@aurora.com' and Authorization: Bearer <token>. 4) Observe 403 'insufficient_scope' returned. 5) Same call with the original human user's token succeeds.

logs_snippets:
identity-proxy (2026-03-09T18:21:12Z) WARN request_id=3fa2ed 'token scope mismatch: expected [admin:impersonate,admin:users] got [service:read,service:write]'; admin-api (2026-03-09T18:21:12Z) ERROR request_id=3fa2ed 'authorization failed for impersonation: missing permission admin:impersonate'; token-broker (2026-03-09T18:20:58Z) INFO 'issued token sub=svc:onboard-runner aud=redwood-api scope="service:read service:write" exp=2026-03-09T19:20:58Z'

investigation_notes:
Initial hypothesis: token-broker is attaching default service scopes rather than tenant-mapped impersonation scopes. Confirmed that tenant mapping rule set 'aurora-mappings' in token-broker was not applied after the private control-plane upgrade (v0.8.0->v0.8.2). Identity-proxy performs additional scope filtering: it strips any scope not in allowed_scope_table for service accounts. Allowed_scope_table for Aurora appears to be stale and only lists 'service:*' scopes. Replayed token exchange locally with debug flags: mapping step returned intended impersonation grant, but the token-broker's caching layer served an earlier cached token profile. Cache invalidation appears tied to last-deploy timestamp; deployment delta on 2026-03-08 likely left cache entries inconsistent. Cross-referenced with INT-4112 where SRE rolled out token-broker config but noted a missing cache-buster flag. Observed related PR that changed default scopes (see related_github_prs).

workaround:
Temporary workaround provided to customer: 1) Use a human admin token for critical admin calls. 2) As short-term automated fix, update identity-proxy config to whitelist the service account 'onboard-runner@aurora' with an explicit mapping to include admin:impersonate and admin:users. Provided steps and a patch snippet to Aurora engineering. Note this bypass is allowed only in their private VPC and will be removed after full fix.

resolution:
Investigating full fix: coordinated deploy sequence to invalidate token-broker cache and roll token-broker + identity-proxy together with a cache-buster flag. SRE to schedule an out-of-band config reload for Aurora's token-broker and then redeploy identity-proxy v1.9.3 which contains a protective check to reject stale cached scope profiles. After reload, verified token exchange returns token with scopes [admin:impersonate,admin:users] and admin API calls succeed. Resolution steps documented in confluence page and will be included in a postmortem. Customer notified and temporary whitelist removed. Planned follow-up: add integration test in CI to simulate config drift and prevent mapping cache staleness.

comments:
Support (Maya Chen) [2026-03-09T19:05Z]: Ticket created after Aurora CS reported 403 on impersonation endpoints. I requested logs and a live replay session. Assigned to Ethan from SRE.
SRE (Ethan Park) [2026-03-09T20:12Z]: Confirmed 403s in customer's request traces. Found token scope on exchanged tokens only has service:* scopes. Suspect token-broker mapping/caching. Pulling broker logs and cache state now.
Customer (Aurora - Priya Desai) [2026-03-10T01:33Z]: We saw this start right after you performed the private-control-plane upgrade last week. The automation jobs that create users are failing and we need a short-term bypass.
SRE (Ethan Park) [2026-03-10T03:00Z]: Provided a temporary whitelist patch and instructions to apply in their private VPC. We will not keep this as permanent; it's a stopgap. Planning coordinated cache invalidation and redeploy for 2026-03-12 02:00 UTC.
Support (Maya Chen) [2026-03-12T02:30Z]: Scheduled the deploy window and confirmed Aurora's approval for the maintenance window. Will notify when done.
SRE (Ethan Park) [2026-03-12T02:47Z]: Performed cache invalidation and rolled identity-proxy v1.9.3. Observed token-broker issuing tokens with admin scopes. Runbook verification: admin API calls now return 200 for impersonation tests.
