[Dependency Failure Containment and Customer Communication Cookbook]
Summary:
This cookbook describes standard procedures for containing, mitigating, and communicating incidents caused by external dependencies (third-party APIs, cloud managed services, vendor models, and shared infra components). It focuses on rapid containment patterns, safe degradations, and customer-facing communications. The goal is fast, predictable response with clear ownership and minimal customer surprise.

Scope:
- Applies to incidents where a Redwood customer-visible failure is caused primarily by a non-Redwood dependency (e.g., upstream model host, cloud DB region, vendor auth provider, CDN outage).
- Does NOT replace generic service outage runbooks; it augments them with dependency-specific checks, routing options, and communication templates.
- Intended audience: on-call SREs, service owners, incident commanders, and customer success leads.

TL;DR Playbook (one-page):
1) Detect: confirm alerts and customer signals (pager, dashboards, support queue). Note root-suspect dependency.
2) Contain: apply traffic routing & circuit breakers; switch to cached responses or degraded mode; disable non-critical feature paths.
3) Communicate: publish a short-status page message and notify customer success for high-impact customers. Use the "Partial degraded experience" template (see below).
4) Mitigate: apply vendor workarounds (retry policies, alternate endpoints), escalate to vendor/partner.
5) Restore: re-enable normal routing once metrics recover for min-stability window (see thresholds).
6) Post-incident: capture timeline, evidence (metrics/traces/logs), and owner action items; schedule a dependent-party RCA with vendor if needed.

Detection and Triage:
- Primary signals:
  - Service 5xx spike correlated with a single upstream hostname or SDK (tagged in traces).
  - P95/P99 latency jump on specific call site (example: /models/embeddings endpoint to vendor X).
  - Customer support tickets referencing new errors or timeouts.
- Quick triage checklist (first 10 minutes):
  1. Confirm alert and scope (regions, clusters, customer segments).
  2. Identify upstream hostnames/IPs and SDK version.
  3. Check circuit-breaker metrics and existing retry logs.
  4. Look for vendor status page updates or security advisories.
  5. If high-impact (SLO-blow or large customer swarm), declare an incident and assign IC.

Initial responder checklist (immediate actions):
- Mark affected services and set incident priority.
- Gather key artifacts: one representative failing request/trace, recent deploys, configuration changes.
- Flip read-only toggles if applicable.
- Rate-limit or disable background jobs making heavy upstream calls.
- Enable increased logging around dependency call sites (short-lived).

Containment patterns (choose based on topology):
1) Fail-fast/circuit-breaker: open the circuit for the dependency when error rate > 5% for 2 minutes. Return graceful fallback or cached response.
2) Regional re-routing: if only one cloud region affected, shift traffic to unaffected region (with capacity guardrails).
3) Graceful degradation: turn off non-essential features that rely on the dependency (e.g., re-ranking or non-critical embeddings).
4) Local cache fallback: serve from last-known-good embeddings/search index for up to 30 minutes.
5) Rate limiting & admission control: reduce per-user token budget for generation features to preserve throughput.
6) Alternate vendor endpoint: switch to known-compatible model variant or vendor endpoint if validated during runbook authoring.

Decision matrix (short):
- If >10% customers affected OR SLO breach: containment + status page + CSM notify + vendor escalation.
- If <10% and degraded only for non-critical ops: monitoring and vendor ticket; update customers if it persists >30m.

Customer-facing comms templates
- Status page short (initial):
  "Summary: We are investigating increased error rates for [service-name] that appear related to an external partner (vendorX). Impact: some API requests may return errors or experience increased latency. Mitigation: we've applied temporary traffic controls and fallback paths. Next update: in 15 minutes."
- Status page update (post-containment):
  "Update: We have implemented a failover and reduced feature surface to limit customer-facing errors. Error rate down from 18% to 3% in the last 10 minutes. We continue to monitor and are working with vendorX. ETA for full restoration: unknown; next update in 30 minutes or sooner."
- Customer success email (high-impact customers):
  Subject: Incident affecting [service-name] — current status
  Body: Hello [CustomerName], we are currently investigating an issue affecting [service-name] that may impact [exact features]. We have applied temporary mitigations (failover/degraded mode). Our engineering team is actively working with the upstream provider (vendorX). We will provide a technical timeline and postmortem after resolution. If you require a workaround or status call, reply to this thread and we'll prioritize.
- Internal incident Slack snippet (IC → #oncall):
  "INCIDENT: Dependency degradation on [service-name]. Vendor: vendorX. Impact: ~20% error rate for customers in us-east-1. Containment actions: opened circuit, enabled local cache, reduced model precision. IC: @<name>. Contact: @CSM-Team for VIP customers."

Internal comms and vendor escalation checklist:
1. Collect evidence: representative request IDs, trace IDs, timestamps, SDK versions, and full error payloads.
2. Open vendor ticket: include rate graphs, p95/p99 latency, sample traces, and a clear desired action (e.g., "please confirm whether your control plane reported quota throttles for our API key between T1 and T2").
3. Share incident channel link and SRE contact with vendor escalation engineer.
4. If vendor can't respond within SLA and customer impact is severe, trigger backup plan (alternate vendor or model variant).

SLO / Metrics to record in incident timeline:
- Error rate for affected RPC (1m/5m/15m).
- p95/p99 latency before and after containment.
- Fraction of requests served from cache/fallback.
- Customer seats affected and list of enterprise customers with errors.
- Duration from detection to containment and to full restore.

Restoration criteria and stability window:
- Restoration considered successful when:
  1. Error rate < SLO-threshold for 15 continuous minutes (default: error rate <= 1% for user-facing RPCs) AND
  2. Latency p95 within 20% of baseline for 15 continuous minutes.
- Post-restore steps: gradually remove rate-limits and feature toggles over 30–60 minutes while monitoring.

Post-incident responsibilities (30/60/90 day actions):
- 0–3 days: IC writes timeline and preliminary RCA draft; notify customer success for impacted accounts.
- 3–14 days: schedule vendor RCA call; collect vendor evidence and ticket closure.
- 14–30 days: implement mitigations (circuit-breaker tuning, cache TTL changes, model fallback path testing).
- 30–90 days: schedule a game day to rehearse the same failure mode and validate automation.

Postmortem template (starter fields):
- Title, date, IC and authors.
- Summary (one-paragraph impact).
- Timeline (minute-granular for first hour, 5–15 minute thereafter).
- Root cause hypothesis and evidence.
- Customer impact and severity classification.
- Corrective actions (owners + ETA).
- Preventive actions and verification plan.
- Vendor follow-up and SLA changes (if any).

On-call rotation and ownership notes:
- Primary on-call: owns rapid containment actions and status page updates.
- Secondary: vendor escalations and CSM handoffs.
- Engineering lead (post-incident): leads RCA and remediation prioritization.
- Rationale: keep action items close to the code owners; keep vendor comms centralized through a rotated escalation owner.

Game day scenarios (playbook exercises):
1) Vendor auth service returns 403 for 50% of requests for 30 minutes: practice failover to cached tokens and vendor ticket escalation.
2) Cloud region DB latency spikes causing model store timeouts: practice regional reroute and degraded-mode ranking.
3) Embedding vendor goes into degraded throughput: rehearse switch to low-cost local embedding quantization profile + customer notice cadence.

Example runbook snippets and commands:
- Toggle a circuit breaker (k8s annotation example):
  kubectl annotate deployment service-a rdb-circuit-breaker=open --overwrite
- Re-route traffic (Istio route weight example):
  kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
  apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1alpha3
  kind: VirtualService
  metadata:
    name: service-a-routing
  spec:
    hosts: ["service-a.internal"]
    http:
    - route:
      - destination:
          host: service-a-primary
          subset: v1
        weight: 0
      - destination:
          host: service-a-secondary
          subset: v1
        weight: 100
  EOF
- Sample status page JSON for short update:
  {
    "component": "Model Embeddings API",
    "status": "degraded_performance",
    "message": "We are investigating elevated error rates likely due to vendorX. Temporary mitigations are in place."
  }

Thresholds and configuration table (reference):
- Error-rate-open-circuit: 5% sustained for 2 minutes
- Cache-TTL-fallback: 30 minutes by default
- Min-stability-window-before-restore: 15 minutes continuous
- Customer-notify-threshold: >10% customers impacted OR >5 enterprise accounts affected

Ownership and contact matrix:
- Service owner: @service-a-team (oncall rotation link: https://pager/rosters/service-a)
- SRE escalation: @eng-sre-oncall (primary phone tree)
- CSM lead for VIPs: Customer Success team rotation (contact: csm-rotation@redwood.com)

Guidance for vendor contracts and SLAs:
- For critical dependencies, contractually require: 24/7 escalation path, dedicated escalation engineer for P1s, and uptime SLA with credit terms.
- Track vendor incident frequency and renegotiate if recurring incidents exceed N per quarter.

Appendix: sample escalation message to vendor
Subject: URGENT: Production errors from Redwood account [account-id] — request immediate escalation
Body:
We are experiencing production errors impacting multiple customers. Evidence attached: error logs, trace IDs, timestamps. Impact: 20% of API calls failing in us-east-1. Please escalate to your on-call escalation engineer and confirm whether this is caused by quota throttling, control plane issue, or a degradation in downstream service. Required: callback within 15 minutes and summary within 60 minutes.

Appendix: Game day checklist for exercise facilitators
- Pre-game: pick a target dependency and failure mode; create simulated vendor silence or degraded responses.
- During: measure detection time, containment actions, and status page latency.

[WebRTC fallback path causes SSE "trickle" connection to miss final epilogue after reconnect]
description:
Issue summary:
Customers using the browser SDK report that when the client falls back from SSE to a WebRTC datachannel (fast reconnect after a flaky mobile network), the server-side SSE stream appears to deliver all prefix tokens but the final epilogue (closing sentence/metadata block) never arrives. The client sees a successful reconnect and partial completion, but the last paragraph and the "choice: done" metadata are missing.

Impact:
- Affects BrightNote Labs (enterprise) production traffic in eu-west; intermittent (~2-3% of streaming sessions during mobile network handoffs)
- User-visible: trailing sentence or final JSON metadata block omitted, causing client to wait indefinitely for end marker or to treat the response as truncated

Environment:
- Browser SDK v1.12.2 (Chrome & Safari mobile)
- Server side: Hosted API behind streaming-proxy (edge-router -> api-gateway -> serving-runtime)
- Model: redwood-v2-large, long-form summarization workloads (avg 1.2k tokens)
- Observed primarily during WebRTC fallback path (client chooses WebRTC datachannel when long polling/SSE flake)

Steps to reproduce (observed):
1. On mobile (cellular) with intermittent connectivity, start a streaming SSE generation request via SDK with streaming:true.
2. Induce a short disconnect (toggle airplane mode or force network path migration).
3. Client falls back to creating a WebRTC datachannel and attempts to resume the session using our resume token protocol.
4. Server accepts resume and replays buffered prefix tokens. Client receives content up to the last few tokens, but never receives the final epilogue JSON (closing choice/metadata).

Observed logs / snippets (redacted):
- edge-router: INFO 2026-03-09T14:21:12Z session=bn-89ac resume accepted path=webrtc-fallback
- api-gateway: DEBUG 2026-03-09T14:21:12Z req=0x7f2ff reattach-session token=*** resume_offset=129876
- serving-runtime: WARN 2026-03-09T14:21:12Z session bn-89ac partial_flush final_chunk_written=true kv_flush_deferred=true
- serving-runtime: INFO 2026-03-09T14:21:12Z choice_stream_end_emitted=false
- client SDK console: warn: "stream resumed but no terminating metadata after 12s"

Notes:
- This appears different from simple chunk duplication or splitting. The prefix is reassembled correctly and tokens look consistent; only the terminal metadata and final punctuation are missing.
- Customers sometimes report the client eventually drops the session after a user-visible spinner timeout (5-15s).

Desired outcome:
- Ensure that when a resume occurs over WebRTC fallback, the server emits the terminal epilogue (final JSON event or end marker) reliably, or the SDK should surface a deterministic end-of-stream event after a bounded wait to avoid UX hang.

[SSE streaming session stalls after ~20s on long-context chat (dedicated)]
description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports that SSE-based streaming chat responses for long-context prompts regularly stall partway through generation. The HTTP request returns 200 and tokens stream for ~15-30s, then emission stops without final event or error; client remains connected but receives no data and eventually times out or reconnects. Sometimes clients see WebSocket 1006 (abnormal closure) instead of a clean finish. Impact: customer-facing chat sessions degrade; automated UI reconnections cause duplicated partial responses.

Impact:
- Affects multiple users at Acme Analytics on their production dedicated cluster in eu-west.
- Progressively started after last weekend's autoscaler and proxy config rollout.

Environment:
- Dedicated cluster (customer-dedicated pool) in eu-west.
- API endpoint via customer subdomain -> internal load-balancer -> Envoy streaming-proxy -> serving runtime.
- Models used: open-llama-13b-quant (primary), redwood-compat-7b (fallback).

Steps to reproduce:
1. Start a chat session with a ~6k token context and request stream=true over SSE.
2. Wait ~15-45 seconds: tokens appear normally for the first chunk(s).
3. Observe emission pause; client reports no further data.
4. Connection sometimes stays open (no trailing event) or closes with code 1006.
5. Retrying sometimes resumes generation but may produce duplicated content.

Observed logs / traces (snippets):
- Envoy proxy: no immediate 5xx, connection shows long-lived TCP but no bytes forwarded after pause.
- Serving runtime: generation process still active; last logged token emission at t0+22s, then no further Write() calls seen for that request id.
- Autoscaler: minor scale event on same minute as first reported stalls (scaled from 2 -> 3 pods).
- Kernel/runtime logs: periodic KV-cache eviction and a JIT recompile event logged within same timeframe.

Customer impact and frequency:
- ~30% of long-context streaming requests for this customer in eu-west during peak load.
- Mostly reproducible with their workload (long prompts + structured output).

Hypothesis: proxy-level backpressure + an idle timeout or keepalive issue causing intermittent stall; potential interaction with KV-cache eviction/JIT recompile delaying token production and leaving proxy buffers idle causing Envoy upstream to consider connection idle.
2026-03-11 08:22 - Support (Maya Patel): Customer provided browser devtools HAR showing 200 SSE followed by no more data. They also reported an uptick after Friday's infra change (autoscaler/proxy tweak).
2026-03-11 11:03 - Infra (R. Chen): Found matching spike in Envoy upstream 504/timeout counters and upstream flush backpressure metrics. Envoy configured with downstream_idle_timeout=60s and upstream_idle_timeout=60s in the recent rollout. Suggest change: send heartbeat SSE comment every 10s while generator is active, and increase upstream idle timeout in proxy config to 2m for dedicated pools handling long generations.

Alvarez): Created PR to streaming-proxy to add periodic heartbeat frames and adjust default Envoy timeouts for dedicated clusters (PR: github.com/redwood/streaming-proxy/pull/314). Also added defensive retry on transient EAGAIN in serving runtime write path (PR: github.com/redwood/serving-runtime/pull/1297).
2026-03-13 03:02 - SRE (Liam O'Connor): Deployed streaming-proxy patch to eu-west dedicated pool behind a feature flag and enabled heartbeat = 10s for Acme cluster. Monitoring shows successful reduction of stalled sessions. No regression observed in short-latency workloads.
2026-03-13 09:45 - Support (Maya Patel): Confirmed with customer that incidents dropped to ~2% of previous rate. Customer validated UX improvement and closed their immediate support request. Marking resolved; follow-ups tracked as tasks.

investigation_notes:
Reproduction in staging used same long prompt and SSE client; intermittent stall consistent with customer repro steps.
Key finding: serving runtime occasionally pauses token emission while internal maintenance (KV eviction or JIT recompile) occurs, producing a gap. If the proxy's idle timeout and buffer backpressure settings are tight, the upstream connection becomes effectively stalled rather than being woken by resumed writes.
Envoy metrics showed increase in upstream_expired_streams and downstream_flush_backpressure correlated with reported stalls.
Autoscaler scale events coincided with some incidents but were not the root cause; they exacerbated timing windows where buffer pressure and idle timeouts overlapped with generator pauses.
Risk assessment: short-term server-side heartbeat and timeout relaxation is low-risk for dedicated pools. Runtime write-path retry reduces chance of transient EAGAIN becoming client-visible stall. Long-term: consider prioritizing background maintenance off the hot token path or streaming-aware maintenance scheduling.

resolution:
Applied a two-part fix in eu-west dedicated clusters: 1) streaming-proxy now emits SSE comment heartbeats every 10s for active generator sessions and proxy upstream idle timeout increased to 120s for dedicated pools; 2) serving-runtime write path hardened to retry on EAGAIN with a short backoff and to yield less aggressively during KV-cache/JIT events. Changes deployed 2026-03-13 behind feature flag then rolled to full rollout after monitoring. Customer confirmed reduction in stalls and closed incident.

[SSE reconnect behind CDN Brotli compression strips trailing punctuation and drops final metadata block]
description:
Customer reports that when using server-sent events (text/event-stream) through their CDN (Cloudflare with Brotli enabled) the streamed response often arrives intact but when they perform a reconnect to resume a long-running response the last punctuation (periods, closing brackets) and the final metadata event are missing. The missing metadata causes the SDK to treat the session as incomplete and the client to display an abrupt truncation to end users.

impact:
Production customers of InkWell.ai see truncated sentences and missing final metadata for some user-facing chat responses. Multiple customers reported confusing partial paragraphs and occasional missing 'end-of-stream' metadata used by InkWell to reconcile message state. Affects dedicated customers in us-east. Business impact: user-facing glitches and degraded UX; workaround available but not ideal.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Configure Cloudflare with Brotli compression enabled for the domain.
2) From a browser or Node SDK, open an SSE stream to Redwood: GET /v1/generate with Accept: text/event-stream using the customer's API key.
3) Allow the stream to begin and observe intermediate chunks (choices/partial tokens).
4) Simulate a short network interruption (tab background + network toggling or firewall TCP reset) causing client reconnect using the API resume token.
5) On reconnect, observe the final portion: trailing punctuation (e.g., "." or "]") is missing and the final metadata event containing "final_offset" / "duration_ms" does not arrive.
6) Repeat with Cloudflare Brotli disabled — issue does not reproduce consistently.

logs_and_traces:
- Customer-provided SSE capture (sanitized): last successful event: 'data: {"delta":" ... closing sentence'}\n\n' then reconnect yields 'data: {"delta":"incomplete continuation'}\n' and no 'data: {"meta":...}' final event.
- Edge logs (us-east-lb-42) show connection 0x7f3a closed with RST_STREAM; server emitted a final chunk but Content-Encoding: br transform at CDN appears to alter final chunk boundaries.
- Server telemetry: last-byte-sent timestamps present, server reported a normal stream termination (200+event), no internal error.
- Packet capture from customer edge shows Cloudflare performing a final brotli flush that sometimes collapses the trailing event terminator sequence ('\n\n') into a single byte sequence that the resume logic misinterprets.

investigation_notes:
Initial triage (Support): reproduced in-house using Cloudflare Workers with Brotli enabled. When Brotli compresses streaming text/event-stream responses, the CDN's output flush semantics vary: some final event bytes are buffered until a compression block boundary and when a reconnection/resume occurs the resume offset calculation is off-by-few-bytes, causing the client to miss the terminal event and any trailing punctuation that was bundled with it.
SRE hypothesis: the resume protocol expects byte-accurate offsets relative to the raw (uncompressed) stream. CDN compression changes wire bytes, and the resume flow assumes identity encoding or consistent flushes. A race between the CDN chunk flush and the server's final write results in a shortened visible tail in some sessions.
Reproduced conditions: Brotli enabled, HTTP/2 between client and CDN, keepalive probe during background tab causes abrupt TCP close then new connection with resume header. Disabling Brotli at CDN eliminates the symptom consistently in our tests.

customer_communication:
2026-03-10 09:12 UTC - Customer (InkWell.ai): 'Seeing production users get truncated messages. Happens ~3-5% of sessions, mostly when mobile users background and foreground the app.'
2026-03-10 10:05 UTC - Support (Aisha): 'Thanks — can you confirm you have Brotli enabled at the CDN? Any middle proxies? Also could you capture the SSE stream and share the tail events?'
2026-03-10 11:30 UTC - Customer: 'Confirmed: Cloudflare with Brotli on, some page rules. Attached sanitized SSE capture.'
2026-03-11 14:00 UTC - Eng (Liam): 'We can reproduce. Workaround: disable Brotli for streaming endpoints or add Cache-Control: no-transform. Engineering will own a platform fix.'

temporary_workaround:
InkWell disabled Brotli for the streaming endpoint via a Cloudflare Page Rule targeting /v1/generate* (Disable Performance -> Brotli). Alternatively, they can set response header 'Cache-Control: no-transform' from their edge to hint CDN not to compress or transform. Both mitigated the symptom in acceptance tests.

root_cause:
Mismatch between CDN compression (Brotli) flush semantics and the resume-by-byte-offset logic used by the SSE resume protocol. The CDN's compression transform can coalesce or split trailing newline/event delimiters across compressed frames, so a resume that uses raw byte offsets ends up reattaching at an incorrect boundary and the client misses the final event and trailing punctuation.

resolution_and_next_steps:
Short term: document and recommend 'no-transform' or disable Brotli for streaming endpoints in Redwood support KB and advise customers to disable CDN compression for SSE endpoints. Customer applied the workaround and verified fix on 2026-03-11.
Medium term: engineering to implement platform-side mitigation: ensure streaming endpoints include 'Cache-Control: no-transform' and add explicit 'Content-Encoding: identity' for text/event-stream responses to avoid CDN compression. Follow-on engineering task created: INT-22109 to add header injection in API gateway and add integration tests with common CDNs (Cloudflare, Fastly) to confirm resume correctness.
Long term: consider adding resume semantics that are resilient to transform layers (e.g., logical sequence numbers independent of wire bytes) — tracked as roadmap research item.

follow_up_items:
- INT-22109: API gateway change to add Cache-Control: no-transform for SSE paths.
- ENG-12501: Add CDN integration tests and Cloudflare smoke suite.
- Update KB article: 'Streaming + CDNs: Recommended headers and page rules' and link from support template.

resolution_status:
Workaround applied by customer; engineering ticket opened for platform fix. Awaiting ENG prioritization. Support to follow up when INT-22109 is scheduled.

Marcus Rivera - Customer (InkWell.ai) (2026-03-12): 'Workaround effective for now, but requesting ETA for permanent fix as disabling Brotli increases bandwidth.'

[Missing final sentence after fast TLS session resume behind nginx HTTP/2 proxy]
description:
Issue summary: Customers on ScribeAI are reporting that long streaming responses occasionally finish with a missing final sentence when the client reconnects quickly using TLS session resumption while traffic is routed through an nginx HTTP/2 front proxy.

Impact: Final sentence (often the last punctuated sentence) is truncated or absent from the transcript. This affects end-user experience for ~3% of long streaming sessions (>60s) and is reproducible under specific network/proxy conditions.

Environment: Production (us-west-2), customer on Dedicated plan with private routing through customer-managed nginx gateway; backend Redwood nodes running serving-runtime v2.4.1. Browser clients primarily Chrome 114/115 and iOS app WebView.

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) Start a long streaming request that emits multiple SSE events over >60s (prompt with multi-paragraph answer).
2) Client backgrounded for ~1s and then foregrounded immediately (this forces a fast reconnect via TLS session resumption).
3) Client reconnects; nginx on customer side accepts session resumption and multiplexes the new HTTP/2 stream to a different upstream worker behind load-balancer.
4) The resumed stream delivers the remaining tokens but the final sentence punctuation and final event boundary are not delivered to the client; transcript ends abruptly.

Observed behavior: The last sentence is missing; stream appears to end cleanly from the server side (no 5xx), but the client never receives the terminal event marker. Server logs show the final token batch was emitted, but the SSE boundary/event delimiter appears to be coalesced/stripped in transit when HTTP/2 data frames are re-framed by nginx during session resumption.

Expected behavior: Client should receive the full final sentence and the terminal stream marker within the resumed session.

Initial hypotheses:
- nginx HTTP/2 re-framing + proxy_buffering settings can coalesce small frames and drop a trailing newline/event delimiter if the client reconnect and the upstream connection switches mid-stream.
- TLS session resumption + fast reconnect sometimes routes to a different worker with slight KV-cache alignment differences; the runtime assumes the downstream will preserve SSE chunk boundaries.

Immediate mitigation: Advise customer to set 'proxy_buffering off' and 'http2_max_field_size' defaults for testing. A temporary client-side workaround is to append explicit sentinel text at the end of each generation (e.g., "[[END_OF_ANSWER]]") until server-side fix is deployed.

Related links: Slack thread #support-scribeai (https://redwood.slack.com/archives/C01234567), customer nginx config snippet provided in attachment, lightweight capture of failing session (S3 link provided to support).

Notes: This ticket captures a production customer reproducible under their nginx+http2 configuration; we should prioritize because it affects user-visible completion integrity.

2026-03-11T14:08:24Z INFO nginx-proxy: http2 frame reframe: coalesced=3 frames, last_frame_len=0

2026-03-11 Ethan Cole (SRE): Acknowledged. Reproduced in staging by simulating TLS resumption + nginx http2. Added to our investigation. See slack thread #support-scribeai.

Creating a small integration test to demonstrate. Linked GH issue: gh/issues/4583.

Repro on staging: reproduce by background/foreground within 500ms while nginx has proxy_buffering on and http2 enabled; failure rate ~7% in synthetic test harness.

[SSE session cookie race after CDN TTL refresh splits final bulleted list and duplicates inline images]
description:
Issue summary:
Customers (AceroHealth) observe truncated streamed responses when reconnecting after an edge cache (CDN) TTL refresh. The final bulleted list in generated markdown is sometimes missing the last 1-2 bullets and inline images are duplicated earlier in the stream.

Impact:
- Enterprise customer workflows that rely on complete policy text are failing to render final bullets; downstream ingestion rejects truncated policy documents.
- Occurs ~3-5x/day for the customer, impacting ~12% of streaming sessions for a subset of longer responses (>2,000 tokens).

Environment:
- Production Redwood hosted API (us-east-1).
- Customer using SSE streaming from browser behind corporate CDN (edge configured to cache authorization cookie via a path-based rule).
- Models: redwood/rwkv-14b-instruct, fallback to open/gpt-neox-20b under load.

Steps to reproduce (reported by customer):
1) Start SSE streaming request for a long multi-section markdown document with embedded images and bulleted lists.
2) While stream is in progress, the CDN edge entry TTL for the session cookie expires and edge revalidates against origin (edge issues a conditional request).
3) The origin accepts the new cookie and starts a short revalidation sequence; the client sees a transient reconnect.
4) After reconnect, stream resumes but the final bulleted list is missing last bullets and one or two inline image references appear duplicated earlier in the output.

Expected behavior:
- Resume should stitch prefixes and suffixes without duplication or clipping; final bullets and image references should render exactly once.

Observed behavior / sample logs (redacted):
- SSE frames captured show: 
  * prefix frames prior to reconnect (choices.delta tokens ... )
  * an immediate EOF frame from origin around the same time the CDN signals revalidation complete: "event: eof\ndata: {\"type\":\"terminal\"}\n"
  * resume frames from a new connection that replay some earlier inline-image markdown and then continue but missing the last "- Implement audit log" bullet.
- Edge logs (CDN): conditional GET at 2026-03-12T14:03:21Z, 304->200 revalidation sequence, small window where cookie-binding changed.
- Client-side: browser console shows a short 502->200 rebind, then SSE stream connection opened with new session id.

Attachments:
- Redacted SSE capture provided by customer (attached to ticket).
- CDN conditional GET trace (edge-id, timestamps).

Workaround provided by customer:
- Short-term: request shorter responses (less than 1,000 tokens) or force client to re-run request on detect of missing trailing bullet. Both are poor UX for enterprise flows.

Notes:
- This reproduces reliably in customer's environment when we emulate the CDN behavior locally (inject TTL refresh mid-stream). It does not reproduce in simple direct client->origin setups without CDN.

[Predecode Adapter + Prefetch: design sketch for tokenizer/runtime boundary]
Context and motivation:

We routinely see tokenization as a non-trivial portion of per-request latency in production for short-text traffic and bursty concurrent workloads. The runtime currently treats tokenization as a synchronous CPU-bound step at the request ingress; this couples runtime scheduling, batching and cold-start behaviour with tokenizer cost variability (different models, vocab/merges, normalizers).

This doc sketches an alternative boundary: a lightweight predecode adapter + prefetch caching layer that moves common work off the critical path and exposes a small asynchronous contract between the serving runtime and tokenizer. Goal is reduced tail latency, better batching behavior, and pragmatic cacheability without demanding a full rework of model loaders or tokenizers.

High level idea:

- Predecode adapter: a thin service/bolt inside the runtime process or colocated helper that converts request text into a compact intermediate representation (IR) suitable for fast conversion into model token ids. The IR is intentionally smaller than full token ids and more cache-friendly (e.g., normalized text fingerprint, byte spans, token boundary candidates, and stable tokenizer-version tag).
- Prefetch + persistent key-value cache: cache IR and/or final token ids keyed by a stable key (hash of normalized text + tokenizer-version + model-config). Cache supports both in-memory LRU for hot keys and a backing persisted cache (rocksdb/redis) for cross-process reuse.
- Async handoff and fallback: runtime schedules tokenization work based on SLO/priority and can choose: (a) serve from cache, (b) schedule predecode work to return IR rapidly and continue decoding to tokens in background, (c) fallback to synchronous tokenizer if deadlines are tight.

Why use an IR rather than tokens?

- Token id sets vary by model and quantization; an IR that captures normalization + boundary candidates + tokenizer-version allows cheap conversion to final ids by model-specific fast path. This shrinks cached value sizes and increases cache hit-rate for minor model/merging differences.
- IRs can be merged or chunked for long inputs, enabling reuse of overlapping prefixes.

Proposed boundary contract (sketch):

API: TokenAdapter.request_predecode(request_id: string, text: string, hints: list[string]) -> {status: string, key: string, ir_ready: bool}
- status: ACCEPTED | REJECTED
- key: stable cache key for this text+tokenizer-version
- ir_ready: whether IR is in cache immediately or a background task was scheduled

API: TokenAdapter.get_tokens(key: string, timeout_ms: int) -> {tokens: list[int] | null, partial_ir: blob | null, reason: string}
- If tokens exist in cache return immediately; if not but IR exists return partial_ir (small blob) so runtime can begin constructing request routing/kv-cache checks and continue generation once tokens arrive; if neither, block up to timeout_ms before returning null and runtime must decide to fallback to sync tokenization.

Scheduler heuristics (runtime integration):

- Priority buckets: high-priority (interactive, p95 latency SLO tight), medium (background interactive), low (batch/async inference). High-priority requests prefer cache or sync tokenization to avoid queueing; medium will accept IR-first flow; low will be scheduled to background tokenizers.
- Microbatch-aware tokenization: batch tokenization jobs by first grouping predecode keys that share tokenizer-version + normalization pipeline. Use batching window configurable by priority: high 1–2ms, medium 5–10ms, low 20–50ms.
- Backpressure signals from model queue: if GPU queues are full, proactively predecode to smooth upcoming load.

Cache key and invalidation rules:

- Key schema: sha256(normalized_text) + ":" + tokenizer_version + ":" + model_tokenizer_profile_id
- Normalization pipeline must be deterministic and pinned; any change increments tokenizer_version causing cache misses (design tradeoff: re-tokenization vs correctness).
- Eviction: LRU with size cap + TTL for persisted backing; explicit invalidation when tokenizer_version bump or merge table changes.

IR format (compact, stable, few hundred bytes max):

- normalized_text_fingerprint: 64-bit or 128-bit
- boundary_spans: list of start/end byte offsets (prefer delta-encoded)
- unicode_normalization_tag: string
- tokenizer_version: string
- hints: bitflags (prefer_fast_unicode, preserve_whitespace, allow_split_on_punct)
IR should avoid embedding full token id arrays except when the conversion to token ids is expected to be identical across many model variants (rare).

Conversion fast-paths within runtime:

- IR -> token ids: each model loader should expose a tiny native fast-path that consumes IR and emits ids using table lookups; optimized for CPU vector ops and memory-local vocab.
- If model requires specialized tokenization (custom merges), those loaders register conversion hooks with TokenAdapter on start.

Key metrics to add (suggested names):

- tokenizer.predecode.requests_total
- tokenizer.predecode.cache_hit_ratio
- tokenizer.predecode.ir_return_ms_p50/p95/p99
- tokenizer.tokens_from_ir_ms_p50/p95/p99
- tokenizer.sync_fallback_rate
- tokenizer.batch_size_histogram (when batching predecode jobs)
- tokenizer.memory_cache_bytes

Experiment matrix (initial A/B plan):

- Canary cohort (5% traffic): IR-only path + in-memory cache, measure p95 and p99 latency, CPU utilization, cache hit ratio.
- Middle cohort (20%): enable persistent backing store (local RocksDB) and microbatching window tuning for medium priority traffic.
- Aggressive cohort (50+%): enable predecode for low priority traffic only; measure tail latency changes and cost delta.
Rollout safety and fallback plan:

- Start with read-only mode: token adapter computes IR but runtime always falls back to existing sync tokenizer for actual tokens; compare latencies and IR usefulness offline.
- Next opt-in caching read path: serve tokens from cache only if hit and tokens validated against runtime model mapping.
- Full path enabled per priority bucket with auto-disable if p99 increases beyond threshold or error rates rise.

Open questions / risks:

- Token reuse across models: how often will IR->token conversion produce same ids across model variants? If low, benefits diminish. We mitigate by focusing on IR reuse for prefix-sharing and normalization fingerprinting rather than tokens.
- Cache storage cost vs hit rate: persistent cache sizing needs capacity planning. Consider sharding by tokenizer-version and hot-key replication constraints.

Action items (next steps):

- Prototype: build a minimal TokenAdapter that returns IR and supports a simple LRU in-memory cache. (Owner: Maya)
- Instrumentation: add metrics hooks in adapter and runtime to capture timings for IR generation, IR->tokens conversion and sync fallback. (Owner: Ethan)
- Offline evaluation: run dataset of 10k recent short requests to estimate compressibility and IR reuse rate across top-5 tokenizers. (Owner: Priya)
- Design doc PR: draft a runtime integration spec with exact API shapes and fallbacks for the serving scheduler (Owner: Jordan).

Notes to reviewers:

- This is intentionally a sketch. The aim is to surface the operational tradeoffs and a minimal-contract API that the rest of the runtime can use without a heavy refactor. Focus feedback on the chosen IR shape, cache invalidation semantics, and scheduling knobs.

Quick timeline suggestion:

- 2 weeks: prototype + basic metrics on small canary traffic
- 4–6 weeks: persistent cache & prioritized scheduling experiments
- 8–12 weeks: iterative rollout into more traffic with auto-disable thresholds

References and similar prior work:

- Related internal: microbatch-kv-cache-eviction-handoff-spec (see historical notes for eviction strategies).
- External idea similarity: upstream model-serving projects that split normalization and byte-level token span detection from full token id generation.


[KV + Prefix Cache Telemetry — metric draft notes (working)]
Context
- Sprint goal: make cache behavior observable + actionable with low overhead and safe cardinality.
- We need a consistent story across:
  (a) prefix cache (prompt/prefix reuse, more “string/prompt identity”)
  (b) KV cache reuse (token-level reuse in attention cache; impacted by batching + scheduling)
- We also need to support SRE/operator questions: “why did unit cost increase yesterday?” and “is this real or telemetry drop?”

Terminology (as used in runtime today)
- Prefill: compute for prompt tokens / initial context.
- Decode: iterative token generation.
- Prefix cache: mapping from (canonicalized prompt features) -> cached prefill artifacts (implementation detail varies).
- KV cache: attention key/value tensors resident on GPU that can be reused when next request shares prefix tokens.
- Reuse depth: number of tokens in request that were served from cache before we had to prefill.

High level: what we want to measure
1) Hit-rate (but defined carefully):
   - Token-weighted (how many tokens avoided compute) is more meaningful than request-weighted.
   - Must handle partial hits (e.g., 300 tokens reused out of 800).
2) Miss reasons:
   - If we can’t tell “policy off” vs “evicted” vs “hash mismatch” vs “version mismatch” then hit-rate by itself isn’t actionable.
3) Pressure / eviction signals:
   - Hit-rate dips can be due to memory pressure or workload shift; need pressure gauge + evictions.
4) Wasted prefill:
   - Prefill tokens computed that didn’t contribute to later reuse (regression signal; helps quantify cost of bad locality).

Draft metric candidates (names are placeholders; Nadia/Telemetry will enforce final naming)
A) Core counters (token-weighted)
- kv_cache_reused_tokens_total
  - Increment by count(reused prefix tokens) for each request.
  - This is the “numerator” for token-weighted KV reuse.
- kv_cache_requested_prefix_tokens_total
  - Increment by count(prefix tokens eligible for reuse) for each request.
  - Denominator depends on definition of “eligible” (see open questions).
- kv_cache_missed_tokens_total
  - Increment by count(prefix tokens not reused) when reuse_depth < eligible_prefix_tokens.
  - Might be derivable from requested - reused, but explicit helps avoid subtle drift.

B) Request-level counters (request-weighted)
- kv_cache_requests_total
  - Total requests processed (at the point we know reuse stats).
- kv_cache_requests_full_hit_total
  - Reuse depth == eligible_prefix_tokens.
- kv_cache_requests_partial_hit_total
  - 0 < reuse_depth < eligible_prefix_tokens.
- kv_cache_requests_miss_total
  - reuse_depth == 0 (or eligible_prefix_tokens==0 ? needs clarity).

C) Histograms / distributions
- kv_cache_reuse_depth_tokens_bucket
  - Histogram of reuse_depth tokens per request.
  - Useful for seeing shifts in reuse depth (many requests with 1-20 reused vs 500+ reused).
- prefix_cache_reused_tokens_bucket
  - Similar histogram but scoped to prefix cache layer (if distinct from KV layer).
- prompt_length_tokens_bucket
  - Probably already exists; we can tag other metrics by prompt bucket rather than emit a separate metric.

D) Miss reason taxonomy (counter)
- kv_cache_miss_events_total{reason=...}
  - Proposed reasons (early draft):
    - capacity (no cache space / allocation fail / memory pressure forced skip)
    - evicted (entry existed but was evicted before reuse)
    - ttl_expired (entry expired by TTL policy)
    - policy_disabled (route config disables caching, or request opted out)
    - hash_mismatch (prompt canonicalization mismatch, tokenization mismatch, or different prompt bytes)
    - version_mismatch (model version differs from cached entry)
    - schema_mismatch (rare: cache format/version mismatch across runtime versions)
    - unknown (fallback bucket)
  - Important: keep taxonomy stable; do not add per-week “new reasons” that break dashboards.

E) Eviction / pressure
- kv_cache_evictions_total{reason=...}
  - reasons: lru, ttl, memory_pressure, compaction, manual_clear (if supported)
- kv_cache_memory_bytes (gauge)
- kv_cache_memory_limit_bytes (gauge)
- kv_cache_memory_pressure_ratio (gauge)
  - pressure = memory_bytes / limit_bytes, clamped [0, 1.5] maybe.
- kv_cache_eviction_age_seconds_bucket
  - How long entries lived before eviction (if available cheaply).

F) Wasted prefill (draft; be careful)
- wasted_prefill_tokens_total
  - Definition attempt: tokens prefilled for a request that would have been eligible for reuse but were recomputed due to miss/eviction/etc.
  - Equivalent-ish to kv_cache_missed_tokens_total *when* those missed tokens actually incurred prefill compute (but under batching/continuous prefill, attribution gets tricky).
- wasted_prefill_requests_total
  - Count requests where wasted_prefill_tokens > 0.

Labels/tags (draft) — cardinality constraints noted
We need metrics sliceable by how Redwood operates:
- model_id (allowlisted short ID, not full path)
- model_version_id (maybe allowlisted; risk: high churn)
- route_id (strong need, but must be allowlisted / hashed stable mapping)
- deployment_mode (hosted|dedicated|private)
- region (e.g., us-east-1)
- tenant_tier (free|pro|enterprise?) possibly from gateway
- prompt_length_bucket (coarse, e.g., [0-128, 129-256, 257-512, 513-1k, 1k-2k, 2k+])
- request_type (chat|completion|embedding?) — for cache probably only chat/completion
- streaming (true|false)

Explicitly avoid (or gate behind sampling)
- tenant_id raw (cardinality explosion)
- exact route path string
- request_id/session_id
- user_id
- prompt hash as label

Metric computation notes / where to hook
- We only know reuse_depth once we attempt to attach to cache during prefill planning.
- For streaming: retries + reconnect can cause double counting if we emit at “request start” and then retry. Prefer emitting at a single “finalized reuse stats” point (or guard with idempotency key).
- For continuous batching: reuse depth might be computed per request, but prefill work is shared; wasted_prefill attribution per request is potentially misleading.

Open questions (capture from runtime chats)
1) What is the correct “eligible_prefix_tokens” definition?
   - Option A: eligible = prompt_tokens - system_tokens? (no, too product-specific)
   - Option B: eligible = tokens before first divergence in token IDs between request and cache key.
   - Option C: eligible = prompt_tokens up to a configured max_reuse_tokens cap.
   - Concern: if eligible includes tokens that we never intended to cache (e.g., over size limit), we’ll show a fake “miss”.

2) Token-weighted vs request-weighted: which is the primary hit-rate?
   - Proposal: publish both, but dashboards default to token-weighted.
   - Token-weighted tells cost impact; request-weighted tells user experience distribution.

3) Prefix cache vs KV cache: do we need separate hit-rates?
   - If prefix cache is just a policy layer feeding KV, then separate metrics may confuse.
   - But operators need to distinguish:
     - “we matched the prefix identity but KV allocation failed” (prefix hit, KV miss)
     - “we never matched identity” (prefix miss)

4) Multi-turn chat attribution
   - If request contains conversation history, reuse depth should treat the entire prompt as the unit.
   - If conversation includes timestamps / non-deterministic fields, canonicalization can help but must be privacy-safe.
   - Question: do we treat reused tokens from same session differently than cross-session reuse? (Probably not for v1; just measure reuse.)

5) Streaming retries / partial responses
   - If a stream is retried mid-flight, do we count it as a new request? If so, reuse stats likely differ.
   - Proposed: record a label retry=true and/or count retries separately, OR ensure metrics are emitted only once per “logical request” from gateway.
   - Need to align with gateway semantics (Ethan/Amara).

6) Batched prefill correctness
   - We can compute “reused tokens” per request, but “wasted prefill tokens” could be inflated/deflated if prefill is shared.
   - Potential approach: treat wasted_prefill as “missed eligible tokens” rather than literal extra GPU work. But naming must reflect that.

7) Where does eviction reason come from?
   - Runtime currently knows “evicted due to pressure” vs “ttl” vs “lru”.
   - But a miss may not know if it missed due to eviction unless we can detect “would-have-hit key existed recently”. Might require an optional debug map (too expensive?).
   - Pragmatic approach: miss reasons separate from eviction reasons; only attribute eviction when you can be certain.

Sampling / overhead (draft)
- Counters are cheap; high-frequency per-token events are not.
- Emit per-request aggregated numbers (reused_tokens, eligible_tokens, miss reason) instead of per-token events.
- For histograms, keep bucket count low; avoid p99-level buckets.
- Consider sampling for:
  - detailed miss reason breakdowns
  - reuse_depth histogram (if too heavy)
- Default in prod: 1.0 for core counters, <1.0 for histograms if needed. Marcus to confirm with perf.

Cardinality guardrails (runtime-side ideas)
- Route/model labels should use short stable IDs from gateway allowlist, not arbitrary strings.
- If label value not recognized: set to "other" or "unknown".
- If route_id missing: set "unattributed".
- Potentially emit two metric families:
  - high-level (no route_id)
  - per-route (sampled, allowlisted)

Proposed initial acceptance tests (for ENG-4821/4822)
- Repeated identical prompt => reuse_depth increases to ~prompt_len (after warmup), reused_tokens_total increments, miss reasons drop.
- Different prompt => reuse_depth=0, miss reason hash_mismatch (or "no_match").
- Same prompt, different model_version => miss reason version_mismatch.
- Cache disabled at route => miss reason policy_disabled; eligible tokens should be 0 or excluded (TBD).
- Force eviction via tiny cache => evictions_total increments; hit-rate drops; pressure ratio ~1.
- Streaming retry simulated => counters not double counted (or explicitly counted in retry bucket).

Notes from brainstorming (raw)
- “Hit-rate” should not be a single number; we need a bundle: hit-rate + miss reasons + pressure.
- Keep metrics names stable; dashboards depend on it; do naming once after ADR.
- Don’t emit prompt hash label. If we need to debug prompt canonicalization, do it via traces (span annotations) not metrics.
- Wasted prefill might be the most valuable operator metric, but also most likely to be wrong. Prefer shipping it behind a flag until validated.

Next steps (as of Mar 12)
- Omar/Samir: align on eligible_prefix_tokens definition and where to compute it in request lifecycle.
- Nadia/Logan: confirm metric naming + required labels + bucket scheme.
- Ethan/Amara: finalize route_id/model_version_id propagation to runtime context.
- Marcus: perf canary runs at sampling=1.0 core counters, evaluate histograms cost.
- Schedule a 30m review with SRE (Sean/Allison) on which 3-5 panels must be correct on day 1.

Appendix: example derived metrics (for dashboards)
- kv_token_hit_rate = sum(kv_cache_reused_tokens_total) / sum(kv_cache_requested_prefix_tokens_total)
- kv_request_hit_rate = sum(kv_cache_requests_full_hit_total) / sum(kv_cache_requests_total)
- partial_hit_share = sum(kv_cache_requests_partial_hit_total) / sum(kv_cache_requests_total)
- miss_reason_share(reason) = sum(kv_cache_miss_events_total{reason}) / sum(kv_cache_requests_total)
- wasted_prefill_ratio = sum(wasted_prefill_tokens_total) / sum(prompt_tokens_total)  (prompt_tokens_total may come from existing request token counters)


[kernel-coalescing-and-memory-bank-conflict-diagnostics-may-2026]
Purpose and context:
Quick investigation notes on a regression observed in the 8-bit quantized attention kernel (attn_fwd_q8) where GPU throughput dropped ~20% on long-history chat loads. Suspect memory access pattern changes in a recent refactor (tensor layout -> blocked-by-16) introduced non-coalesced loads and increased shared memory bank conflicts in the reduction step. This doc collects Nsight traces, microbench ideas, hypotheses and immediate mitigations.

Summary of findings (short):
- End-to-end latency increase concentrated in a single kernel: attn_fwd_q8 (forward pass).
- Warp execution efficiency fell from ~91% -> ~67% for problematic inputs.
- Measured achieved occupancy for the kernel is ~0.45 on A100 (theoretical max with current block size ~0.937), suggesting SM underutilization despite many active warps.
- L2 transactions and serialize stalls increased (L2_TEX and EXEC_DEPENDENCY visible in Nsight timeline).
- Memory access trace shows strided accesses with 64B misaligned starts; likely caused by blocked-by-16 layout + embedding dim not multiple of 16.

Environment and commands run:
- Hardware: NVIDIA A100-SXM, CUDA 11.8 driver stack, nvml v470, nsight systems 2025.3.1.
- App build: serving-runtime @ commit 0b3e4f, attn quant branch attn-refactor-16block.
- Capture commands used (representative):
  - nsys profile -o traces/coalesce-run-2026-05-12 --trace=cuda,nvtx --capture-range=cudaProfilerApi --sample=none --env="NSYS_MON_TRACE=1" --target-processes=all ./bin/serve_local --config tests/long_history.json
  - nvprof deprecated but used an older microbench: nvprof --metrics warp_execution_efficiency,inst_executed,branch_efficiency ./build/microbench/attn_memcheck
  - cuda-memcheck for invalid accesses in earlier iteration.

Key timeline observations (from Nsight .nsys-rep):
- Two hotspots around the same timestamp: attn_fwd_q8 kernel (duration ~12.2 ms) and a following kernel attn_softmax (duration ~2.1 ms). The long attn_fwd_q8 segment includes repeated memory copy bursts (async P2P) observed as memcpy nodes.
- Kernel internals: long gaps between warps launching; trace shows sequential micro-batches being serialized rather than overlapped. Stream use appears correct but kernel launch pacing varies.
- Stall reasons flagged: L2_TEX (elevated), EXEC_DEPENDENCY on some threadblocks, and MEMORY_THROUGHPUT_LIMIT.

Low-level metrics (sampled):
- attn_fwd_q8:
  - warp_execution_efficiency: 67%
  - sm_efficiency (approx): 48%
  - achieved_occupancy: 0.45
  - gld_transactions_per_request: 3.6 (expected ~1.0 for coalesced loads)
  - shared_load_bank_conflicts: high (per-block reduction shows 5+ conflicts on hot warps)

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Layout change -> misaligned base pointers + blocking-by-16 causes per-warp strided loads that hit multiple cache lines => higher L2 traffic and uncoalesced requests.
2) Reduction code uses 32-bit indexing into shared memory but kernel was recompiled with 64-thread tiles; bank conflict pattern changed because bank mapping is different for 32-bit words vs 64-bit views.
3) Kernel launch configuration (blockDim.x) shifted during autotuning pass; for some sequence lengths the kernel uses block sizes that under-utilize SM resources, which combined with serial launches reduces occupancy.
4) cudaMemcpyAsync ordering: host->device prefetch stage sometimes stalls due to single stream device-side dependency; should use multiple streams / cudaMemcpyPeerAsync for P2P copies.

Repro steps and checks to isolate cause:
- Reproduce microbench with controlled tile sizes: build microbench that loads same memory pattern with varying alignment offsets 0..127 bytes, measure gld_transactions and warp_efficiency.
- Run nvprof/ncu on microbench with metrics: dram_read_transactions, l2_read_transactions, warp_execution_efficiency, shared_load_bank_conflicts.
- Add NVTX markers around memory layout conversion routines to ensure we can see when conversion happens relative to kernel dispatch.
- Run kernel with different blockDim.x (32,64,128,256) to observe achieved_occupancy and latency tradeoffs.
- Create small repro that toggles embedding_dim%16==0 vs !=0 to confirm coalescing sensitivity.

Quick mitigations tried (results):
- Restored old layout (pre-refactor) locally: latency returned to baseline. Conclusion: layout change is primary suspect.
- Forced __restrict__ pointers + aligned attribute (align(128)) on some buffers: improved gld_transaction count from 3.6 -> 1.4 and warp_efficiency up to ~82% in microbench, but full app still shows serialization likely due to leftover bank conflict in reduction.
- Slightly increased blockDim.x from 128 -> 256 lowered per-kernel latency but increased register pressure; achieved occupancy improved to ~0.6 but performance for short sequences degraded. So there’s a sequence-length-dependent sweet spot.

Open experiments and next steps:
- (A) Microbench matrix: for offsets in [0,16,32,48,64,80,96,112], run gld transaction measurement and bank conflict counters. Owner: Miguel. Target date: 2026-05-20.
- (B) Shared memory view alternative: test both 32-bit and 64-bit reductions (pack/unpack) to measure bank conflict delta. Owner: Hannah. Target date: 2026-05-22.
- (C) Autotuner sweep: include alignment-aware penalty term to avoid layouts that create heavy uncoalesced access. Owner: Ethan. Target date: 2026-05-28.
- (D) Short-term patch: revert layout change for production builds for sequence lengths > 1024 until we have robust quantized kernel. Owner: Aisha. Target date: 2026-05-19 (hotfix).

Longer term ideas:
- Introduce a lightweight runtime check that computes embedding_dim % warp_size and falls back to an alignment-correcting path at runtime (cheap and avoids recompile).
- Add a small instrumentation mode in release builds that emits per-kernel gld/l2 metrics to CloudMetrics for automatic regression detection (use sampling to limit overhead).
- Consider revisiting quantized kernel tiling to use vectorized loads (uint4/uint2) when alignment permits; add allocator hint API to satisfy 128B alignment for hot tensors.

Notes on measurement fidelity and cautions:
- Nsight can reorder reported events slightly vs on-device behavior (timestamps relative to host). Use device-side timers (clock64) inside microbench to confirm absolute times if uncertain.
- nvprof and ncu sometimes disagree on conflict counters; treat trends as signal rather than absolute ground truth.
- When increasing blockDim.x we saw register spill warnings; always watch max registers per thread to avoid spilling into local memory which will confound results.

[Elmwood Health – integration brain dump]
Context / quick summary:
- Elmwood Health (regional hospital chain, 6 hospitals + telehealth) exploring an on-prem / VPC Private deployment for triage assistant + discharge-summary generation. Primary drivers: PHI residency, auditability, and deterministic latency for clinician workflows.
- Initial ask: prototype that ingests EHR progress notes (HL7/FHIR), extracts problem list + medication changes, and drafts a one-paragraph discharge summary suitable for clinician edit.
- Risk/constraints called out repeatedly by Elmwood: strict PHI handling, hospital infosec requires no tokens leave VPC, Syslog-compatible audit trails, and KMS/HSM for key management.

Who was on the call:
- Elmwood: Dr. Karen Liu (CMIO), Marcus D'Souza (SRE), Priya Rao (Clinical informatics)
- Redwood: Sofia Patel (SE), Diego Ramos (solutions eng), Nina Park (security partner)

Notes from convo / highlights:
- Data flow they want: EHR -> middleware (internal) -> Redwood Private inference (inside their VPC) -> result returns to middleware -> EHR UI. Emphasized minimal hops and synchronous < 1.2s median to preserve clinician flow for short notes.
- They have a batch use-case too (overnight summaries) where throughput matters more than latency; willing to accept lower-cost quantized models for batch.
- PHI classification: everything in progress notes flagged PHI. They require redact+audit if anything leaves customer boundaries. This rules out hosted API. Private only.
- Auditing: retention 365 days, immutable append-only logs exported to their SIEM. Must support per-request metadata (user id, patient MRN hashed, route).
- Model explainability: clinicians want a traceable token-to-output mapping for some high-risk fields (diagnoses change). Not expecting full token-level provenance but want attribution-ish notes (which prompt lines influenced summary).
- Regulatory: possible state-level constraints around mental health notes; need redaction options and a policy to exclude certain note types from automatic summarization.

Technical constraints / architecture considerations:
- Preferred infra: Elmwood runs on AWS GovCloud-like isolation in a VPC; they are open to a Redwood Private control plane with customer-managed networking.
- Hardware: their infra team prefers 2x A100-class or equivalent for early prototype (they already have a small GPU pool). For production would want Dedicated-like reserved capacity but on-prem.
- Model choices: customer leans toward a smaller fine-tuned open-source model (instruction-tuned, medically-aligned) to keep costs down and reduce hallucination risk. We suggested comparing 7B/13B quantized variants + our curated med model if available.
- Tokenization/costs: large notes (progress notes ~2k tokens) — need prefix/KV caching per patient visit to avoid re-encoding shared context for multi-step edits. Suggest session affinity routing.
- Streaming: for the UI edit flow, streaming partial summary tokens could improve perceived latency; we need to validate integration with their middleware that expects chunked HTTP/WS.
- Security: KMS integration required (customer-managed keys, HSM preferred). Need to support FIPS endpoints.
- Networking: allowlist IPs and mutual TLS between their middleware and Redwood runtime endpoints inside the VPC.

Gotchas called out / potential pitfalls:
- Data residency vs. control plane: they will accept a Redwood control plane outside their VPC only if metadata and model artifacts are non-PII and they can sign an agreement — strongly prefer fully private control plane.
- EHR attachments and images: Elmwood wants future OCR for scanned docs; we must call that out as out-of-scope for MVP. If they push, estimate +4–6 weeks and need GPU memory planning.
- Persistence of KV cache: if we use per-visit cache, eviction policies must be explicit (e.g., evict after discharge). Otherwise cache could leak PHI across patients in mistakes.
- Fine-tuning vs. prompt engineering: their compliance team will prefer prompt engineering + guardrails (redaction, classifier pre-check) over storing new weights unless we provide an auditable fine-tuning pipeline.
- Logging volume: audit logs per request + token counts will be large; recommend separate pipeline to S3 -> SIEM; budget for log egress within their infra.

Open questions (need answers from Elmwood):
- Q1: Which EHR vendor + version? (Dr. Liu said 'Cerner-ish cluster' — get exact). Ticket created: JIRA EH-1023 to confirm.
- Q2: Exact latency SLO— they said 1.2s median for interactive flow; confirm 95th percentile SLO allowed.
- Q3: Are their clinicians ok with partial streaming or do they require final complete text before presenting? UI UX decision.
- Q4: Does their legal team require the control plane to be in-customer account (yes/no)?
- Q5: Is there an internal patient-consent policy affecting automated summarization of psych/behavioral notes?

Immediate next steps / owners (week-of actions):
- Sofia: create two prototype architecture sketches — (A) fully private control plane + runtime in customer VPC, (B) customer-runtime + Redwood-managed control plane with metadata-only tokens. Due: 2026-03-15. Linked: confluence:EH-integration-playbook.

- Create a short demo plan (30m) focusing on: single-note summarization (interactive), batch overnight run, and audit log review. Tentative demo week: 2026-03-22.

Prototype acceptance criteria (MVP):
- Summaries produced inside Elmwood VPC, no tokens leave customer boundaries.
- Median latency for interactive summarization <= 1.2s on provided sample notes (measured on their infra).
- Audit logs emitted per request to customer's SIEM, retained 365d.
- Redaction step present: any note type flagged as "sensitive" excluded from auto-summarize and routed to manual queue.
- Clinician editing flow: ability to accept/modify generated summary and write-back partial metadata to EHR.

[Standardize ephemeral workspace creation and autosweeper for feature pods]
description:
Issue summary:
We need a standardized, auditable automation that provisions ephemeral Slack channels, Confluence draft spaces/pages, and temporary Jira groups when a feature pod requests a sandbox workspace. The automation should attach an owner, enforce RBAC, and schedule an automatic review/archival (autosweeper) after a configurable TTL (default 30 days).

Background / why: 
Feature teams frequently create ad-hoc channels and Confluence pages for short-lived experiments. Lack of standardization causes orphaned channels, inconsistent permissions, and audit gaps. Security and Platform would like a predictable lifecycle that reduces noise and improves cost/retention hygiene.

Impact: 
- Cross-pod clutter in Slack and Confluence; difficulty finding active workspaces.
- Manual cleanup burden on Platform and SRE.
- Potential permission drift and audit holes (unknown owners).

Request: 
1) Implement a lightweight self-serve flow (Slack slash command + Jira form) that creates: a named ephemeral Slack channel (private by default), a Confluence draft space or page created from a template, and a Jira group with scoped view permissions.
2) On creation, require an explicit owner (email) and set metadata tags: pod, feature, ttl-days.
3) Autosweeper: after TTL expires, automated job posts a 7-day warning in the channel, then archives Slack channel and sets Confluence space/page to read-only and not searchable. Create a small audit artifact (confluence note / jira task) capturing the action.
4) RBAC/Compliance: integrate with existing role-sync; owners must belong to an org group; deny creation if owner is not in an allowed list for private workspaces.
5) Provide a Confluence runbook and a short onboarding doc for product leads.

Scope and constraints: 
- Must reuse existing Slack-bots infra; do not introduce new long-lived credentials.
- The automation must emit an event to our audit topic (kafka/audit-events) for every create/modify/archive action.
- Default TTL = 30 days; allow override per-request up to 90 days (enterprise exceptions handled via manual process).

Acceptance notes: see acceptance_criteria field.

Operational handover expectations:
- Include a runbook with playbook steps to reverse archive, reassign owner, and override TTL for enterprise requests.
- Provide a migration/cleanup plan for 60-day backlog of orphaned pods (separate follow-up ticket).

acceptance_criteria:
Provisioning flow: ability to create workspace via Slack slash command and Jira form with owner, pod, and ttl metadata recorded.
RBAC enforcement: creation blocked if owner is not in allowed identity group for private workspaces.
Audit events: every create/modify/archive emits a record to kafka/audit-events with workspace id and actor.
Autosweeper behavior: 7-day warning -> archive Slack channel + set Confluence to read-only -> create audit note. Verified in a staging test with ttl=2 days.
Runbook and docs: public runbook created and reviewed by Security and Internal Tools; 1 pager for product leads published in Confluence.
Graceful override: Platform staff can extend TTL via admin Jira action; extension events are audited.

[Launch-Signal automation: scaffold ephemeral experiment pods (Slack channel + Confluence space + Jira sandbox) with RBAC and audit export]
description:
Issue summary:
We need a new automated 'launch-signal' flow that scaffolds a short-lived experiment pod when a Product/Research lead requests a new experiment. The flow should create a Slack channel, a Confluence space + templated pages, and a Jira sandbox project with pre-seeded issue templates. The automation must enforce RBAC groups, timebound retention, and produce an audit export for compliance.

Impact:
Currently pod creation is manual and inconsistent: delays onboarding by days, misconfigured permissions leak sensitive data, and cleanup is ad-hoc. This automation will reduce lead time for experiments, enforce guardrails, and provide an auditable lifecycle.

Requirements (must-have):
- Trigger: a single form submission in Confluence/Shortcut (we prefer Confluence Create page or a small Jira intake ticket).
- Slack: create #pod-<shortname>-<team> channel, default topic, purpose, and pinned onboarding message. Channel should be private when requested. Add members from an input list and map team roles to Slack user groups.
- Confluence: create space with key POD<YYMM><id>, generate three pages from templates (Overview, Runbook, Data Access Matrix), and set space permissions: view/edit restricted to specified groups.
- Jira: create project with key POD-<shortid>, create issue templates (Experiment Plan, Data Access Request, Safety Review), and set project role mappings.
- RBAC: map requestor -> space admin, map product/eng reviewers -> space editors, create or assign ephemeral groups (ttl-bound) rather than adding individual org-wide groups.
- Timebound retention: default lifecycle 90 days; automation must include optional TTL extension workflow and automatic archival (unpublish + archive space, archive Jira project, set Slack channel to read-only and then archive).
- Audit export: create a JSON summary of actions (who triggered, resource ids, timestamps, members added/removed) and store in a central S3 bucket and Confluence audit page.
- Approvals: if data classification >= Sensitive or experiment includes private model data, require Approver group (Data Privacy / Security) to approve before provisioning.
- Notifications: notify #platform-ops and the requestor at each lifecycle stage.

Nice-to-have:
- Terraform-style declarative manifest saved in a repo (PR created automatically) representing the pod resources.
- Single-click 'teardown early' from Confluence page which triggers archive.
- Metrics emitted to observability for onboarding times and retention compliance.

Acceptance criteria:
- A PoC automation exists for a subset of teams (example: Research-UX).
- Provisioned Slack, Confluence, and Jira resources follow naming conventions and permission templates.
- TTL process runs and archives resources automatically after 90 days in a staging run.
- Audit export generated and verifiable in S3 and attached to the Confluence runbook page.
- Approval gating triggers for sensitive-data requests and blocks provisioning until approved.

Implementation notes / constraints:
- Use existing org Slack app bot; avoid creating new bot tokens. Leverage SCIM/group sync where possible.
- Confluence automation should use the Confluence Cloud REST API and page templates; avoid using server-side scripts.
- Jira provisioning must use our existing project-create automation to ensure project role mappings and permission scheme consistency.
- Keep default TTL conservative (90 days) but allow requestor to choose shorter.
- Ensure encryption and least-privilege when writing audit exports to S3.

Edge cases to handle:
- Requestor provides an email outside org: return validation error and require an org member or add-as-guest flow.
- Slack channel name collision: append numeric suffix and surface change in response to requestor.
- Approval timeouts: if approver doesn't respond within X days (configurable), escalate to Security on-call.
- Partial failures: if Slack succeeds but Confluence creation fails, automation must roll back Slack channel (or deprovision) and create a ticket in #platform-ops.

Testing plan:
- End-to-end test will run in a staging org where TTL is 1 day to validate archival, and approvals use test approver group.
- Unit tests for each API interaction and a chaos test to simulate partial failures.
- Security review of permission mappings before pilot.

Rollout plan:
1) Build PoC for Research-UX and run 10 pilot pods.
2) Collect feedback; fix permission edge cases.
3) Expand to growth/product teams behind feature flag.
4) Full rollout and document in Platform runbooks.

Owner / next steps:
- Requestor: Maya Chen (Research Platform)
- Suggested implementation owner: Platform Automation team (owner: Priya Nair)
- Next step: schedule 30m sync with Platform Automation and Security to align on approval gating and audit schema.


acceptance_criteria:
PoC automation created for Research-UX; Slack/Confluence/Jira resources provision with naming and permission templates; TTL archival runs in staging; audit export appears in S3 and Confluence; approval gating blocks sensitive requests.

implementation_plan:

[Enable conditional Confluence space cloning with ownership handshake and RBAC snapshot for ephemeral project spaces]
description:
Background: Rapid experiment teams frequently request cloned Confluence spaces spun up from a canonical template. Current manual cloning loses a reliable snapshot of page restrictions and group membership, and onboarding owners is manual. This increases audit overhead and causes surprises when access needs to be reverted after a project ends.

Request: Implement an automated, conditional Confluence space cloning flow that: 1) performs a template-based clone of a source space; 2) captures and stores an RBAC snapshot (groups, page restrictions, explicit user grants) for the cloned space; 3) triggers an ownership handshake workflow (invites nominated owner(s) to accept ownership within a configurable TTL, default 72 hours); 4) returns the space to a quarantine/archive state if ownership is not accepted; 5) optionally creates matching Jira project skeleton and Slack channel with linked lifecycle hooks.

Acceptance criteria (high level):
- A self-serve UI or slash-command triggers a clone with parameters (source template, owners list, ttl, create-jira, create-slack).
- RBAC snapshot is stored as an auditable artifact (read-only) and accessible to security/audit teams.
- Owners receive an email and Slack DM with an accept/reassign link; acceptance flips a 'live' flag and sets retention rules.
- If ownership not accepted within TTL, space is set to "archived-quarantine" and requestor + infra notified.
- Audit log entries created for clone and ownership events; Confluence page-level restrictions are preserved in the cloned space.
- Optional Jira project and Slack channel created when toggle enabled; each gets lifecycle hooks tied to the Confluence space state.

Why this matters: Reduces manual steps, prevents lingering access after short experiments, and provides an auditable RBAC snapshot for compliance reviews.

Proposed timeline: 3 sprints (discovery + design; automation prototype + RBAC export; owner handshake + lifecycle integration + rollout).

Contacts: Aisha Patel (Product, requester), Liam Chen (Platform eng, primary assignee), Priya Rao (Security reviewer)

acceptance_criteria:
Self-serve clone action with parameters exposed in Console and via a slash-command
RBAC snapshot (groups, page restrictions, explicit grants) persisted and queryable by security/audit
Owner handshake invites sent (email + Slack) and accept/reassign recorded in audit log
TTL-based auto-archive/quarantine if no acceptance within configured window
Optional Jira and Slack resources created and linked; lifecycle sync to Confluence state

steps_to_validate:
Trigger clone from Console using 'Clone with RBAC snapshot' option
Verify cloned space content matches template and page restrictions are present
Check audit artifact for RBAC snapshot containing groups and explicit grants
Confirm owner handshake message sent and acceptance flips space to live
Simulate TTL expiry and validate space moves to archived/quarantine state and notifications fire
If toggled, verify corresponding Jira skeleton and Slack channel exist and are linked

risk_and_mitigation:
Risk: Automated cloning could inadvertently grant broader access if RBAC snapshot applied incorrectly. Mitigation: Implement a dry-run mode that logs intended grants without applying them; require security approval for initial rollout to top-level spaces; limit self-serve to templates in a vetted namespace.

Slack provisioning: can create channels via admin API but workspace bot needs 'channels:write' and 'users:read' scopes; approval required

[Create on-demand team bootstrap gateway: scoped service accounts, expiring Slack bot roles, and archival hooks]
description:
Issue summary:
We need an automated 'team bootstrap gateway' that creates a new Jira project scaffold, Confluence space, Slack channel, and a minimal set of scoped service accounts/bot roles for short-lived experiments or external partner pods. The gateway must enforce timebound credentials (automatic expiry), include audit hooks that log who requested what, and wire in archival/retention policies for the created artifacts.

Background & why:
- Multiple pods request ad-hoc project sandboxes weekly; ops manually creates projects, channels, and service accounts which is error-prone and slow.
- Recent audits flagged gaps in ephemeral credential revocation and inconsistent Confluence space templates.
- We want a single, auditable flow that reduces toil while keeping security guardrails.

Request details & requirements:
1) Single webhook/API endpoint (AuthZ via Okta group) to trigger bootstrap. Input: team name, owner, duration (1d-90d), template choice (dev, experiment, partner).
2) Creates: Jira project (with standardized permission scheme), Confluence space (templated with onboarding checklist), Slack channel (#team-<name>-sandbox private), scoped service account(s) with least privilege and explicit TTL, and a Slack bot role scoped to the channel.
3) Automatic revocation job that runs at TTL expiry: removes service account keys, deactivates bot role, archives Slack channel, and sets Confluence space to read-only then archived after 30 days.
4) Audit logs forwarded to central logging (ELK) with requestor, timestamp, actions, and linked ticket key.
5) Admin UI in console to list active bootstraps, extend TTL once with approval, and force-terminate. Approvals should be implemented via a lightweight JIRA approval task to the owner's manager.
6) Tests & acceptance criteria (see below).

Security considerations:
- All service accounts created must use short-lived credentials (where possible exchange for federated tokens).
- No creation of high-privilege project roles in the bootstrap; only template-limited roles allowed.
- Record Okta actor, IP, and justification as part of the audit record.

Acceptance criteria/Test steps:
- Provision a sandbox for 'ml-eval-experiment' for 7 days: verify Jira project created with template, Confluence space present with checklist, Slack channel created and private, service account created with TTL set and token not reusable after expiry.
- Attempt to escalate permissions via Jira project admin UI should be blocked unless done through a separate org-level admin flow.
- After TTL expiry run: confirm service account tokens revoked, Slack channel archived, Confluence space set to read-only, and entry in ELK shows the lifecycle events.
- Admin UI shows the bootstrap and allows one extension after manager approval, otherwise shows queued archival.

Proposed rollout plan:
- Design & implementation (2 sprints): API + workflow + templates.
- Internal beta with one pod for 2 weeks.
- Audit and iterate based on beta.

Notes on dependencies:
- Okta group for requesters must exist (ops/grant-team-bootstrap).
- Slack bot provisioning API permissions (we may need an elevated bot for channel-scoped role assignment).
- Confluence template created and canonicalized (link above).

```json
  "pin_type": "canary",        // hard | soft | canary

  "fallback_model": "gpt-lower-latency-v1",

```
