03/10 15:05 - Eng (Marta): hypothesis: proxy connection pooling + buffering leads to artificial pause before final chunk is flushed. Also saw keepalive COALESCE behavior on proxy (github.com/proxy-vendor/issue/432).

Linked Slack thread: #support (thread SUP-128999) and #infra (messages: p01)

2026-03-10 09:22 - Asha Kumar (Support): Customer attached HAR and pcap. They say ~1 in 8 reconnects fail with last sentence missing. Requested SDK and server logs.

[WebSocket upgrade + early window reset causes missing trailing attachments and partial choices on reconnect]
description:
Issue summary:
Customer (NovaDocs) reports that long-running chat streams that go through their corporate transparent proxy and then upgrade to WebSocket intermittently drop trailing attachments (base64 images / rich-embeds) and final sentence fragments after a reconnect. The problem surfaces when the client's connection flows through a probe/rewrite-capable load balancer that briefly resets the TCP write window during an HTTP->WS upgrade.

Impact:
- Customer sees partial responses: final image links or base64 chunks missing, and last sentence of the assistant truncated or absent on reconnects.
- Affects ~5% of long-running streams from NovaDocs (dedicated account) in us-east; sporadic reports from eu-west.
- User-facing: end-users receive incomplete content; some chats appear to end abruptly.

Environment:
- Dedicated account on prod/us-east with private ingress via NovaDocs' transparent LB.
- Streaming over WebSocket with on-the-fly model fallback enabled.
- Observed with redwood-v1.3 and llama-2-13b-chat model endpoints.

Steps to reproduce (high-level):
1) Start a long streaming generation (~>6k tokens) over TLS using client behind a transparent proxy + LB that performs periodic health probes.
2) Trigger a connection path change (e.g., LB probe causes a short TCP window reset / TCP zero-window for <1s) during the HTTP->WebSocket upgrade or early in the WS session.
3) Client reconnects and attempts resume/continue.

Observed behavior:
- The resume completes but the final attachment/frame metadata is missing or partial (base64 truncated); the final assistant sentence is cut mid-token.
- Server logs show the original session's last frames were accepted, but the proxy inserted a tiny RST/rewrite that caused the edge to mark a partial frame as drained.

Expected behavior:
- Streaming resume should stitch the stream state and include final frames/attachments. Small kernel-level window adjustments at the LB should not cause loss of terminal frames or attached metadata.

Logs / traces (excerpt):
- Edge (envoy) trace: "stream-resume: session_id=abc123, last-offset=18923, accepted-by-worker=true, drain-detected=true"
- Proxy logs (from customer): "haproxy[3245]: probe-reset on socket 10.1.2.3: ephemeral window=0 -> 65535"
- Serving runtime: "kvcache-primed true, terminal-frame-received false (frame-truncated)"

Reproducer notes:
- We built a deterministic reproducer using websocat and tc/netem to simulate window-zero events during upgrade. Reproducer shows same truncated base64 chunk ~40% of runs when the zero-window occurs during upgrade handshake.

Additional context:
- Customer uses short-lived client tokens and performs an auth refresh during some reconnect paths. Token rotation appears orthogonal but increases observed frequency when combined with LB resets.


investigation_notes:
Initial hypothesis: proxy/LB zero-window or probe is causing an in-flight frame boundary to be lost or the edge to mark the stream drained early.

What we checked so far:
- Correlated customer haproxy logs with our edge traces; timestamps align with drain-detected flags.
- Verified that the serving runtime reports receiving the partial chunk but marks 'terminal-frame-received' false for those sessions (indicates corruption/truncation).
- Reproducer using tc/netem shows deterministic correlation with zero-window events during upgrade; if the zero-window occurs after full handshake then issue is rare.
- Confirmed this is not client SDK reassembly bug: reproducer using two different clients (websocat + browser-based) both show the same truncation signature when the network condition is injected.

Intermediate hypothesis: the proxy resets the socket write window, causing our edge to see a half-closed write state and to flush buffered frames prematurely without attaching terminal metadata. During resume, the system believes terminal frame wasn't delivered and the resume protocol omits re-sending partial attachments (edge thinks they were already sent).

Data points to collect/next steps:
- Request packet captures from NovaDocs for a sample truncated session (they have agreed to provide).
- Add extra debug logging around frame boundary detection in edge (temporary verbose mode).
- Run CI-level reproducer across multiple kernels (we saw some OS TCP stack variance).
- Evaluate changing resume logic to treat missing terminal-frame flag as 'must-retransmit attachments' for 30s post-resume.


resolution_summary:
Workaround applied: recommended customer enable sticky session affinity on their LB to avoid transient path changes during upgrades and to disable aggressive probe that sets zero-window briefly. Customer rolled out sticky sessions to a subset and reported drop rate fell to <0.5%.

Engineering fixes in progress:
- Patch PR created to make edge more conservative when detecting 'drain' during upgrade: do not mark terminal frames as delivered when an upgrade-related zero-window is detected (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/proxy/pull/329).
- Longer-term: change resume handshake to request explicit terminal-frame re-confirmation from the serving runtime; if missing, re-request attachments. PR opened: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/4582.

[Dashboard UX and micro-SLI design notes for inference]
Purpose:
This note captures pragmatic guidance for designing dashboards and micro-SLIs for Redwood inference services. Focus is on making dashboards that are readable at-a-glance, actionable for oncall, and structured so that product engineers can quickly map a symptom -> hypothesis -> remediation.

Scope and constraints:
- Applies to hosted API / dedicated / private inference endpoints (same UX principles, but different data availability).
- Goal is low-noise, high-signal dashboards for day-to-day ops and incident response. Not an exhaustive metrics catalog.
- Assumes metric ingestion with tags: request_id, customer_id (hashed), model_family, model_version, deployment_zone, routing_policy, batch_size, has_kv_cache, response_tokens.

Design principles (high level):
1) Surface the user-visible experience first: P95/P99 tail latency for end-to-end request (client-obs) + errors + success rate.
2) Decompose into independent micro-SLIs that map to probable root causes (runtime, routing, infra, model).
3) Keep the top panel small: 4–6 widgets with clear thresholds; everything else is drilldown.
4) Avoid alert fatigue: prefer compound conditions (e.g., sustained increase in end-to-end latency AND increased model compute latency).
5) Use consistent color/lexicon across dashboards (green/yellow/red bands, "degraded" vs "failed").
6) Include cost signals in drilldown so engineers can trade latency vs cost during triage.

Micro-SLI recommendations (names are intentionally concrete):
- consumer_e2e_latency_ms_p95: end-to-end latency as observed by API front door, p95 over 1m/5m windows.
- compute_step_latency_ms_p95: time spent in the serving runtime (kernel + decode) p95.
- kv_cache_hit_rate_1m: fraction of requests served with a valid KV/prefix cache hit.
- batch_formation_delay_ms_p95: time waiting for batch assembly before the first token is produced.
- request_queue_depth: current queued requests per worker shard.
- stubbed_fallback_rate: fraction of requests that fell back to cheaper model variant due to routing policy.
- token_generation_rps: tokens produced per second per model_family (useful for cost curves).
- successful_responses_ratio: 2xx/total requests, broken down by model_version.
- grpc_stream_resets_rate: number of stream resets or client disconnects per 1k requests.

Alerting guidance (rules and thresholds):
- Incident-level alert (P0): consumer_e2e_latency_ms_p99 > 3x baseline sustained for 3 minutes OR successful_responses_ratio < 95% for 2 minutes.
- P1 (investigate): compute_step_latency_ms_p95 increased >50% relative to rolling 7d baseline AND batch_formation_delay_ms_p95 < baseline (indicates compute hot-spot).
- P2 (inform): kv_cache_hit_rate_1m drops >20% absolute and sustained for 10 minutes.
- Avoid single-metric noisy alerts: require at least one corroborating signal (error spikes, queue depth, resource saturation).
- Create customer-impacted alert variants (annotate with customer_id top-n) for billing-sensitive customers.

Dashboard layout suggestions (top-down):
1) Top row: single-line summary widgets (heat map for latency by region/model_family, SLI sparklines for the past 1h) + traffic/cost overview.
2) Second row: consumer experience panel (e2e latency p50/p95/p99, success ratio, errors with HLL counts of customer_id).
3) Third row: serving runtime panel (compute_step_latency p50/p95, GPU utilization percentiles, batch size distribution, kv cache hit rate).
4) Fourth row: routing & fallback (routing decisions by policy, fallback rate, capacity-bumps/bursts).
5) Bottom row: supporting panels (trace waterfall sample, recent heavy traces list, token cost histogram).

Widget examples & queries (pseudo):
- E2E latency P95 by model: timeseries: redwood.requests.latency.p95_ms{env:prod} by model_family
- Compute vs wait split: stacked area: redwood.requests.stage_latency_ms{stage:compute} and {stage:queue} stacked to show proportion.
- Cache hit rate: ratio(redwood.kv.cache.hits, redwood.kv.cache.requests) rolling 1m.
- Heavy traces table: top-20 traces by compute_step_latency with columns [trace_id, model_version, batch_size, response_tokens, sample_link].

Tracing and explorer ergonomics:
- Sampling: preserve 100% traces for high-severity errors; for normal ops ~1% uniform sampling + targeted 100% for requests above p99 latency or above tokens threshold.
- Span design: keep spans coarse-grained and stable: front_door -> router -> batcher -> runtime_kernel -> decode. Each span should include tags: model_family, model_version, routing_policy, batch_size, kv_cache_hit (bool), customer_id_hash.
- Link traces to dashboard: heavy traces widget should include a direct link to the trace viewer with filter pre-applied.
- Session view for multi-step interactions: aggregate traces by conversation_id to see time spent per turn (useful for chat flows).

Instrumentation checklist (to implement before dashboard rollout):
- Ensure all requests emit request_id and trace_id and both are carried in logs, metrics, traces.
- Add model_version and routing_policy tags to request-level metrics.
- Emit latency broken down by logical stage with consistent units (ms).
- Emit batch_size and response_token_count as histograms (use exemplar linking to traces for heavy buckets).
- Emit a short-lived counter for "fallback_reason" counts (labelled by reason).

UX considerations for oncall vs product:
- Oncall dashboard should default to last 15m window; product/analytics default to 24h.
- Provide one-click filters to limit to a customer_id (hashed) for escalations.
- Use a single canonical dashboard per service; create minimal per-model variant views for experiments only.

Rollout checklist / quick win changes (next 3 sprints):
- Sprint 1: implement micro-SLI metrics + p95/p99 aggregation, create top-row summary widgets.
- Sprint 2: add heavy traces widget and exemplar linking from histogram buckets.
- Sprint 3: implement alert rules with compound conditions and test in staging.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- Sampling cost vs visibility: how many p99 traces do we store centrally? Can we offload detailed trace storage to S3 for ad-hoc retrieval?
- Customer privacy: hashed customer ids are OK, but what about traces that contain PII in prompts? Need automatic redaction before indexing.
- Micro-SLI proliferation: How many micro-SLIs do we allow before the top-level becomes noisy? Proposal: cap primary SLI panel to 6 signals.

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Put together a brief demo video showing triage flow from e2e alert -> drilldown -> trace. @Arjun to own demo recording.
- Lina: sketch final dashboard wireframe (Figma) with annotated drilldown paths.
- Ethan: spike on exemplar linking from histogram buckets to traces.

References and inspiration:
- internal: CONFLUENCE-OBS-UX-142 (dashboard style guide)
- external: "Practical Monitoring" book notes for SLI decomposition (informal)

End.

[Widget deprecation and attribution play slate]
Summary
Short working slate for how we retire, replace, and attribute dashboard widgets while keeping SLI continuity. Focus is on low-noise deprecation, operator handoff, and trace sampling adjustments for probes that detect user-visible regressions. Meant to be a lightweight playbook to run during a 2-week dashboard sprint.

Goals
- Avoid sudden blind spots when panels are removed.
- Maintain SLI continuity (no breaks in alerting or regression windows).
- Provide clear attribution for metrics so infra/rt/serving teams can act.
- Reduce query costs by consolidating and retiring redundant widgets.

When to deprecate a widget (quick checklist)
- Panel has < 5 manual opens/week (grafana opens) for 90 days OR
- Panels duplicate upstream tenant-level metrics already surfaced in a canonical dashboard OR
- Owner identifies high query cost without corresponding ops value.
- Product/CS confirms no downstream dependency (email or slack thread).

Pre-deprecation steps (1–2 week window)
- Owner adds a yellow banner in the panel and update panel description: "Marked for deprecation — feedback before YYYY-MM-DD".
- Announce in #observability and ping owners. Link: Confluence OBS-DRIVER-19.
- Add a feature-flag-like flag to dashboard metadata (dashboard annotation) indicating deprecation plan and date.
- Create a small synthetic probe (canary) that exercises the underlying query at a lower cadence (1/10th) so we keep data continuity if panel removed.
- Add metric-contract note to the metric doc (e.g., metric cols, cardinality hints).

Deprecation execution (day of removal)
- Replace panel with a single compact panel that points to canonical metric (owner, query snippet, and link to replacement). Keep it for 30 days as a redirect.
- Add alert mapping: ensure any alerts that referenced old panel/metric have a mapped replacement alert or a ticket created (Jira ENG-4321 style).
- Keep the synthetic probe for 30 days to ensure time series continuity and SLI checks continue working.

Post-deprecation (30–90 days)
- After 30 days, remove redirect panel and reduce probe cadence if not needed.
- If regressions observed tied to removed panel, reopen via rollback instructions (see below).
- Close the deprecation ticket and update metric ownership roster.

Attribution matrix (how to map who owns what)
- Host-level infra metrics (gpu-util, mem-used): infra.owners = infra-eng@redwood.com.
- Serving runtime (tokens/sec, kv-cache-hit-rate, batch-size-dist): serving-runtime team.
- API and routing (request-latency, 5xx-rate, region-fallback-rate): platform-api team.
- Quality signals (per-prompt hallucination-rate, rerank-loss): applied-ml/product-hosted-api (collab).
- Cost signals (token-cost-per-request, gpus-hours): finance + infra.
Note: maintain a single canonical metric doc per metric with owner and a fallback oncall alias.

Metric definition examples (suggested minimal contract)
- inference.request_latency_p50_ms: type=histogram / buckets; labels: model, deployment, region, route; owner: platform-api; intent: SLI for interactive P50.
- inference.kv_cache_hit_ratio: type=gauge; labels: model, tenant; owner: serving-runtime; intent: efficiency optimization for cost.
- inference.hallucination_flag_rate: type=counter (bool per-response); labels: model, eval_set; owner: applied-ml; intent: quality SLO.
Each metric definition must include: description, units, cardinality estimate, instrumentation pointer (file/line/GitHub PR).

Trace sampling play (balanced cost vs. fidelity)
Problems we see: full trace capture for every token request is prohibitively expensive and produces noisy spans. Need tiered sampling:
- High-fidelity sampling for SLI violations and anomalies (100% capture for requests that triggered an alert within 5m).
- Deterministic sampling for a small percentage (0.5%–1%) of traffic for baseline longitudinal analysis. Use hash(model, tenant, route) to ensure stable samples across time.
- Rate-limited ad-hoc sampling: operators can turn sampling to 100% for a specific tenant or deployment for live investigations via console toggle.
- Lightweight span-only traces: capture only high-level spans (no token-level span) for regular traffic to keep linkability but lower cardinality.

Heuristics and triggers
- If a request crosses token-cost threshold (e.g., > 5k tokens) OR latency > 95th percentile of model baseline -> increase sampling for that session.
- For multi-model fanout, capture the root request and per-model root spans but avoid token-level children unless flagged.
- For KV cache cold-starts, tag traces with kv_cold=true and sample at a higher rate.

Investigation runbook (operator-friendly)
1) Identify symptom: SLO alert or user complaint. Note time window + sample request ids.
2) Check synthetic probes & redirect panel. Is baseline probe failing?
3) Pull deterministic traces for the impacted window. Use query: "trace.service='inference' AND trace.tag.route='chat' AND duration>500ms"
4) If insufficient detail, flip ad-hoc sampling for tenant/route in console (create incident flag). Capture for 10 minutes.
5) Correlate with KV cache metrics, batch-size histograms, and model variant routing.
6) Open a triage ticket and assign to owner from attribution matrix.

Dashboard lifecycle cadence (recommendation)
- Quarterly dashboard audit: owners review panels, mark duplicates, and note cost-heavy queries.
- Weekly mini-sprint: rotate 2–3 low-traffic panels for consolidation.
- Monthly cost report: top 20 queries by data egress + compute time.

Notes to self / unresolved items
- Need a lightweight tagging scheme for dashboard panels so the console can list "deprecated_by" and "canonical_metric".
- How do we purge old synthetic probe data without breaking regression history? Maybe tiered retention.
- Should we add a "panel-cost" metric into Grafana for query-level cost attribution? (work with finance).

Action items (next 2 weeks)
- Create dashboard annotation schema RFC (Sofia). Link to GH PR telem/pull/212.
- Implement deterministic hash sampler prototype (Amir).
- Run a mini audit on "operator-quickcards" dashboard and propose 5 panel removals (Priya + Carlos).

Slack threads / references
- #observability: https://slack.redwood.com/archives/COBSERV123
- Confluence: OBS-DRIVER-19 (dashboard deprecation model)

If you want to test deprecation flow end-to-end, pick a non-critical dashboard and run through pre-deprecation steps this week. I'll draft the email template for owners.

[Trace annotator cheatsheet and widget prioritization]
Purpose
This is a compact, operator-friendly cheatsheet for annotating traces and prioritizing dashboard widgets during the upcoming rollout of the compact observability surface for inference. The doc is intentionally short — a single-page reference operators can paste into incident channels and a companion checklist for dashboard owners.

Scope and audience
- Audience: oncall operators, SREs, runtime engineers, and dashboard owners who need a fast mapping from symptom -> trace annotation -> dashboard action.
- Scope: inference request path (API gateway -> router -> runtime shard -> model exec -> cache layer -> response aggregator). Excludes offline batch jobs and embeddings ingestion pipelines (we'll link those separately).

High-level goals
1) Standardize span names and a minimal attribute set so sessions/requests can be reconstituted quickly.
2) Define a compact metric set and widget priority tiers so dashboards remain small and effective for paging.
3) Provide a small checklist for annotating rollouts / experiment traces to support postmortems and performance regressions.

Span naming conventions (recommended)
- api.request.received  -- first inbound HTTP entry for a user request (include request_id, route, tenant_id)
- api.request.auth     -- auth/quota check (outcome: allowed/denied)
- router.route.resolve -- routing decision (chosen_model, chosen_variant, fallback_reason)
- runtime.exec.start   -- runtime scheduling and queue wait start (queue_len, priority)
- runtime.exec.invoke  -- actual model invocation (model, seq_len, kv_cache_hit)
- runtime.exec.kvfetch  -- KV/prefix cache fetch (cache_key, hit)
- runtime.exec.kvstore  -- cache write path (evicted, ttl)
- runtime.exec.kernel   -- low-level kernel/quant path (kernel_name, dtype, device)
- runtime.exec.finish   -- total runtime exec end (tokens_generated)
- response.aggregate    -- aggregation/streaming assembly and postproc (streaming:true/false)
- api.response.sent     -- final response send (status_code, latency_ms)

Required span attributes (minimal set)
- request_id (string) -- unique per API request
- session_id (string) -- optional but strongly recommended for chat/multi-turn flows
- tenant_id (string) -- customer identifier for multi-tenant correlation
- route (string) -- route name or endpoint
- model (string) -- model identifier + quantization tag (eg: gpt-j-6b.q4_0)
- variant (string) -- fallback or canary tag (eg: production, canary-2024-11)
- shard (string) -- runtime shard/host id
- seq_len (int) -- prompt sequence length in tokens
- kv_cache_hit (bool) -- whether prefix KV cache was used for this request
- kernel (string) -- kernel name or path selected for exec
- queue_wait_ms (int) -- time spent in runtime queue
- exec_ms (int) -- time spent in actual model execution

Sampling and retention notes
- Default sampling: 0.5% full-trace sample across all tenants for regular traffic; increase to 100% for tenants in active incident windows or canary rollouts (feature-flagged).
- Severity-weighted sampling: always keep traces where exec_ms > P99_latency_threshold OR error status_code != 200 OR kv_cache_hit=false on warm-cache flows.
- Redaction: redact prompt text; keep prompt token counts and prompt hashes when safe. Use privacy tags for PHI-sensitive tenants.

Widget prioritization rubric (for compact dashboard lanes)
Tier 0 (must-have for paging):
- Per-tenant 95th/99th latency for api.request.received -> api.response.sent (latency_ms P95/P99)
- Request rate (rps) 1m/5m
- Error rate (4xx/5xx) by route and model
- Runtime queue length and queue_wait_ms distribution
- Token generation rate and cost-per-token estimate

Tier 1 (operational diagnosis):
- KV cache hit ratio (global & per-shard)
- Exec_ms distribution by model variant
- Inflight requests by shard and priority class
- Fallback rate (when router chooses fallback variant)

Tier 2 (investigation / forensics):
- Per-route span flamegraph sampler (hot spans for slow requests)
- Kernel selection cardinality over time (surfacing regressions after deployments)
- Request session-reconstruction quickcard (links to stored trace ids)

Widget sizing guidance
- Only one P99 panel per dashboard lane; prefer P95 for routine ops. Reserve P99 for incident dashboards.
- Use sparklines for long-term trends, heatmaps for latency slices, and small tables for top-k models by cost.

Trace annotation templates (copy-paste for rollout channels)
- Canary start: ANNOTATE request_id={{id}} tags=[canary,variant=canary-2024-11,experiment=kv-opt] note="canary start - watching queue and exec_ms"
- Canary failure: ANNOTATE request_id={{id}} tags=[canary,incident] note="canary observed >2x baseline P95 - escalate"
- Hotpath reproduction: ANNOTATE request_id={{id}} tags=[repro,hotpath] note="repro instructions: curl --header X-Req-Id={{id}} ..."

Rollout instrumentation checklist (pre-rollout)
- [ ] Add kernel and kv_cache attributes to spans in PR (GH: redwood/telemetry#482)
- [ ] Add lightweight synthetic probe that exercises canary model path
- [ ] Ensure dashboard Tier 0 panels exist and alerting thresholds are set for P95
- [ ] Configure increased trace sampling for canary tenant(s)
- [ ] Run smoke probe for 24h and validate metric drift < 5%

Quick operator drills (how to use this cheatsheet)
1) If latency alert fires: check Tier 0 P95 latency + queue length. If queue high, annotate run with "queue_backpressure" and escalate to runtime-scheduling.
2) If error spike: filter traces for status_code != 200, look for auth/route faults first (api.request.auth).
3) If model exec slow: examine kernel selection heatmap and exec_ms distribution by model. Tag traces and open OBS-311 with sample traces.

Open questions / tradeoffs
- How to surface kernel-level stalls without exploding trace cardinality? Proposal: aggregate per-minute kernel metrics (counts + 95th exec_ms) and only sample full traces when kernel-specific P95 jumps > 2x.
- Should we store prompt hashes centrally for easier repro? Privacy/legal wants stricter rules; need product/legal signoff for retention.

Next steps
- Iterate this cheatsheet into a single-pane Slack quicklink for oncall (owner: Dana Kim).
- Add small templated panels to dashboard starter kit and bump Tier 0 coverage for high-traffic tenants (owner: Aisha Patel).
- Review sampling and retention policy with privacy and legal (owner: Maya Singh).

Notes & references
- See linked Confluence page for full trace schema and attribute types.
- Related GH issue for kernel attributes: redwood/telemetry#482.
- Triage playbook references: OBS-311 (alerting thresholds and postmortem template).

Quick paste list (for runbooks)
- Key spans: api.request.received, runtime.exec.invoke, runtime.exec.finish, api.response.sent
- Key attrs: request_id, tenant_id, model, variant, shard, seq_len, kv_cache_hit, exec_ms

End of cheatsheet — keep this in incident runbook and sync with dashboard owners before each major runtime rollout.

[Investigate GPU pool starvation: queue buildup, KV-cache cold starts, and mitigations]
description:
Summary: On 2026-03-09 02:17 UTC a hosted API GPU pool experienced progressive queue buildup and eventual request rejections for ~75 minutes. Symptoms: queue depth grew in affected pools, large tail latencies for streaming generation, autoscaler did not add enough nodes fast enough, and multiple customers saw 503/429 errors. Immediate emergency mitigations included a temporary capacity bump, per-org emergency QPS caps, and rolling back a staging autoscaler change. This ticket collects the root cause analysis, short/medium/long term fixes, owners, and validation plan so we avoid repeat GPU starvation events.

timeline:
2026-03-09 02:17 UTC: first sustained queue growth in us-east-1-hosted-pool-3
2026-03-09 02:25 UTC: alert fired (queue_depth > 70% capacity) — oncall acknowledged
2026-03-09 02:35 UTC: throttling and global rate limits applied to reduce inflow
2026-03-09 02:42 UTC: temporary +12 GPUs provisioned from spare reserved pool
2026-03-09 03:10 UTC: rollback of autoscaler tuning patch (was reducing aggressiveness)
2026-03-09 03:50 UTC: queue returned to normal and incident declared mitigated at 03:58 UTC

root_cause:
Compound factors: (1) recent change to default batching window increased average per-request GPU occupancy for long-generation jobs leading to slower throughput, (2) a CPU-side regression in request routing deferred prefix/KV-cache warmup causing many cold KV-cache hits, and (3) an autoscaler change deployed the previous day which raised scale-in cooldown and lowered scale-out aggressiveness for a subset of pools.
A single large customer's automated rerun of long stream jobs magnified the effect by concentrating long-lived sessions on a small set of pools.
Monitoring gaps: we lacked an early queue-imbalance alert tied to per-pool KV-cache hit-rate and per-request GPU-occupancy which would have signaled the pattern earlier.

short_term_actions:
(Done) Emergency +12 GPU provision from reserved capacity for us-east-1-hosted-pool-3 (owner: infra-oncall).
(Done) Applied temporary per-org QPS caps for high-volume customers that matched historical 99p usage (owner: rate-limiting).
Adjust autoscaler defaults for all hosted pools: reduce scale-out cooldown to 30s and remove the overly-conservative backlog multiplier (owner: infra/autoscale).
Deploy a hotfix to ensure routing warms KV-cache for streaming start requests (owner: serving/runtime).
Add a short-lived queue-depth dashboard and alert that includes KV-cache hit rate as a correlated signal (owner: observability).

medium_term_actions:
Implement progressive request shaping: early reject or pause for oversized token requests above model-specific thresholds with configurable per-org policies (owner: api-team).
Build 'warm' standby workers per hot-model: pre-loaded KV cache and model weights on a fraction of nodes to drain cold-cache spikes faster (owner: serving/runtime).
Enhance autoscaler to use per-pool request-duration distribution (p50/p95/p99) instead of only queue length; include fast-burst short-lived nodes in the pool types (owner: infra/autoscale).
Run a load test scenario simulating 10x long-stream bursts for 3 customers to validate new shaping + warm pools (owner: sres)

long_term_actions:
Predictive capacity hints: feed historical usage + calendar signals into an ML model to pre-scale pools for known high-demand windows (owner: capacity-forecasting).
Introduce SLA-aware admission policy that reserves headroom for customers with reserved capacity and gracefully degrades lower-tier traffic (owner: product/infra).
Invest in kernel and sequence-aware batching that prioritizes finishing short requests to keep throughput high under mixed workloads (owner: serving/optimizer).
Formalize capacity playbooks and runbook automations for automatic emergency capacity grafting from other regions (owner: incident-response).

runbook_updates:
Add a 'GPU pool queue growth' section describing diagnosis steps (check queue depth, KV-cache hit-rate, per-request GPU-occupancy, recent deploys).
Document immediate mitigations and safe rollback steps for autoscaler changes.
Add exact Grafana queries and thresholds to the runbook for 3 alert tiers (warning 50%, action 70%, critical 90%).

testing_and_rollout_plan:
Feature branches for serving and autoscaler changes; end-to-end tests in staging with synthetic cold-cache and warm-cache scenarios.
Canary rollout of KV-cache warmup on 1 region and 1 customer cohort (1% traffic) for 72 hours; metrics to monitor: queue depth, tail latency, KV-cache hit-rate, GPU occupancy, and error rate.
If tail latency or error rate increases by >10% vs baseline during canary, abort and revert changes. Otherwise progressively increase to 25% then 100% over two weeks.
Run scheduled chaos test once per quarter that simulates concentrated long-lived sessions on single pool to validate warm pools and admission controls.

acceptance_criteria:
New alerts fire at the defined thresholds and are routed to oncall with runbook links.
Autoscaler updates consistently return queue depth to <= 50% within target time during synthetic bursts in staging.
KV-cache warmup reduces cache-miss tail latencies by at least 30% in canary traffic for affected models.
Progressive shaping correctly rejects >95% of known oversize requests before they hit GPU (avoids long-living sessions when overloaded).

monitoring_changes:
Add per-pool 'in-flight token count' metric and alert when > 60% of max tokens capacity for >30s.
Emit 'kv_cache_warm' flag per request to enable heatmap of warm vs cold requests per model/pool.
Correlation dashboard: queue_depth vs kv_cache_hit_rate vs avg_request_gpu_time (owner: observability).

notes_and_discussion:
2026-03-10: Postmortem review held with Eng, SRE, Product and Design. Agreed to prioritize warm pools and auto-scaler tuning as top two mitigations (Aisha P, Miguel R).
Design feedback: console should surface per-customer 'burst risk' indicator so sales and CS can proactively contact heavy customers (owner: design).
Product note: consider offering a paid option for 'guaranteed warm pool' for enterprise customers that need consistent tail latency.

2026-03-11 - Miguel Rivera: Started RFC draft for warm pools and progressive shaping. Link in 'links' above.
2026-03-12 - Aisha Patel: Infra approved temporary cooldown change; will be reverted if regressions seen in staging.

[Reset pager policy and burn-rate sensitivity after capacity regression]
description:
Follow-up from the 2026-02-16 capacity regression that produced multiple rapid SLO burn spikes and triggered noisy paging for tiered SLOs. This ticket consolidates action items to reduce alert noise while preserving fast detection for genuine capacity drops. Deliverables: updated paging rules, calibrated burn-rate windows per tier, canary rollout plan, and updated runbook guidance for oncall engineers.

postmortem_summary:
On 2026-02-16 a capacity regression in the autoscaler caused transient latency and error spikes across a subset of serving clusters. Existing burn-rate alerts fired quickly and paged SREs repeatedly while the system recovered via existing fallbacks. Noise obscured root-cause signals and increased MTTR for unrelated incidents. We will adjust burn-rate sensitivity, introduce a two-stage paging workflow (pager for sustained critical burn, slack for transient elevated burn), and improve dashboards and runbook steps to reduce noise while keeping detection latency low.

investigation_notes:
Initial incident: autoscaler regression increased queueing; 90th and 99th latency percentiles jumped for 12 minutes before autoscaler recovered (see dashboard link).
Burn-rate alert rules used a 3-minute window with a low tolerance for transient spikes; multiple alerts retriggered when background recovery retried pods.
Noise pattern: <50% of pages correlated with degradations that required manual intervention; remaining pages were informational while the system healed automatically.
Root cause: change in autoscaler cooldown introduced delayed scheduling during node churn (PR: github.com/redwood/autoscaler/pulls/1284).
Risk assessment: increasing burn window reduces pages but may delay human intervention for true regressions. We'll mitigate with a tiered policy and canary rollout.

action_items:
Adjust burn-rate alert windows: increase critical tier from 3m->6m, adjust high tier to 10m with higher thresholds (owner: Diego Martinez).
Introduce two-stage notification: slack-ops channel for first elevated burn (info) and pager only after sustained critical window (owner: Priya Singh).
Add aggregation by customer tier and route low-impact customers to non-pager channels (owner: Platform Routing).
Create a canary rollout plan to deploy alert changes to eu-west-1 clusters first with 72h observation (owner: SRE oncall group).
Update runbook: explicit steps for verifying autoscaler health, when to escalate to pager, and checklist for follow-ups (owner: Liam O'Connor).
Create a Grafana dashboard panel that shows correlated autoscaler events, burn-rate, and paging history for post-incident analysis (owner: Observability team).
Ship a small client-side debounce in the alerting aggregator to suppress refiring within 2m unless severity increases (owner: Alerts infra).

acceptance_criteria:
New alert config deployed to canary region and observed for 72h without missed critical regressions.
Pager volume for SLO burn alerts reduced by >=60% in non-actionable cases over a 7-day baseline window.
Runbook updated and reviewed by oncall rotation with acknowledgement from at least two engineers.
Dashboard shows clear mapping between autoscaler events and burn windows for 30 days of history.

comments:

[Tenant fractionalization and burst fallbacks proposal]
description:
Summary: After the March 2026 capacity incident (large eviction spike in dedicated-gpu pools) we observed correlated noisy-tenant behavior where several mid-size tenants consumed transient working sets that exceeded their reserved footprint and then burst tokens overwhelmed the soft-burst policy. Root cause hypothesis: a combination of under-provisioned fractional reservations for bursty inference patterns, lack of a short-window noisy-tenant detector, and an overly-permissive burst fallback that allowed a small group of tenants to amplify token allocation under steady-state load. Goal: implement lightweight tenant fractionalization (pro-rate reservation model for short-lived high-fanout requests), add an early noisy neighbor quarantine detector, and tighten burst fallback policies with graceful degradation and quota rebalancing to prevent cascade evictions.

acceptance_criteria:
Deploy noisy-tenant detector with false-positive rate < 2% on the validation cluster
New fractional reservation mode reduces eviction rate in synthetic burst tests by >= 60%
Burst fallback policy enforces per-tenant degrade path (latency-first) and prevents more than one downstream eviction per incident window
Telemetry dashboard shows tenant-level KV cache miss rate, short-window token burn, and synthetic-simulated mitigation results
Runbook updated with step-by-step quarantine and recovery flow; on-call can run automated mitigation in under 6 minutes

implementation_plan:
1) Prototype fractional reservations: implement pro-rata reservation layer that allocates a transient fractional credit pool (owner: Ravi) - RFC PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/proto/pull/876
2) Detector: integrate short-window noisy-tenant detector using 30s rolling token burn and KV miss rate (owner: Mei Chen) - feature branch: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/compare/noisy-detector
3) Burst fallback rewrite: change fallback path to favor per-request latency degradation over global burst assignment. Implement graded token throttling and fallback to smaller quantized model when necessary (owner: Carlos Dominguez)
4) Telemetry: add per-tenant panels and alerting for short-window token burn > X and eviction spike probability > Y (owner: DataInfra)
5) Canary: run in dedicated-lab with synthetic tenants at 3x baseline for 72h, iterate on thresholds, then staged rollout to 10% of clusters
6) Post-deploy: 48h runbook drill and follow-up incident review (owner: On-call)
Estimated work breakdown: 3 devs (2w), 1 SRE (1w), 1 data engineer (1w)

New metric: tenant.kv_cache_miss_rate_1m
Dashboard: Dedicated -> Tenant Stability -> Fractionalization Canary
Alert: P0 if eviction_rate_cluster > 0.5% AND top-5 tenants account for > 60% short_window_token_burn

runbook_changes:
Add step: 'Detect noisy tenant' with query and automated action to place tenant in quarantine-cgroup
Add step: 'Apply fractional reservation' for suspected tenants to prevent global burst exhaustion
Add step: 'Escalation' to capacity-engineering Slack channel and attach synthetic load artifacts
Recovery checklist: how to revert fractional mode and rollback fallback changes

risks:
False positives in detector could throttle legitimate traffic - mitigated by conservative initial thresholds and manual review flag
Fractional reservations may increase latency for legitimate large-batch jobs; we'll provide an opt-out path for enterprise tenants via reservation override
Complexity in burst fallback increases operator surface area - mitigate with end-to-end tests and observability

[Post-incident: Noise containment playbook and reservation sizing adjustments for Dedicated clusters]
description:
Summary:
During the March 2026 peak, one Dedicated cluster experienced a multi-hour degradation due to a combination of a single tenant generating unusually high concurrent streaming requests (noisy neighbor), a set of reservations that were undersized relative to observed traffic patterns, and an overly permissive burst policy that allowed transient demand to starve steady-state workloads. This ticket captures the post-incident analysis, proposed mitigations, and a phased rollout plan to reduce recurrence risk and improve customer SLOs.

Root causes identified:
1) Noisy tenant produced sustained concurrent sessions with long KV-cache lifetimes, causing eviction pressure and GPU memory churn.
2) Reservation sizing was based on historical average throughput; recent model changes increased per-request token processing and caused steady-state reservations to be insufficient.
3) Burst policy allowed unlimited short-term concurrency using cluster spare capacity; without a graceful backoff the burst consumption prevented reservation reclaim and delayed autoscaler response.

Impact observed:
- 3 production customers experienced elevated tail latency and token drop rates for 110 minutes.
- Increased evictions triggered fallback to smaller model variants for internal traffic routing for ~90 minutes.
- Pager awakenings and two customer incident escalations (one enterprise SLA breach narrowly avoided via manual routing).

mitigation_plan:
Short-term (<=2 weeks):
- Add tenant-level soft quota enforcement (rate cap + session cap) configurable by SRE.
- Adjust burst policy to use a token-bucket with decay and per-tenant share; enforce a hard cap on sustained burst consumption per reservation.
- Update runbook with immediate steps to throttle noisy tenants and escalate to on-call SRE.
Medium-term (2-8 weeks):
- Implement reservation autosizing heuristic: compute reservation target = max(historical 95th, incoming forecasted 75th * 1.3). Use replay harness to validate across recent model versions.
- Introduce a predictive eviction buffer: reserve 8-12% GPU memory headroom to reduce KV-cache churn during transient spikes.
- Expose per-reservation burst-credits metric in Console and add alert when a reservation consumes >40% of cluster burst for >5 minutes.
Long-term (8-16 weeks):
- Enhance scheduler to support tenant-weighted isolation: ensure minimum steady allocation for reservations even while allowing limited burst across shared pool.
- Add QoS tiers that let customers opt into guaranteed headroom at higher price points.
- Bake learnings into autoscaler: consider burst-aware scale-up decisions so autoscaler differentiates between transient bursts and steady load growth.

acceptance_criteria:
Automated replay shows no latency regression for steady tenants when a noisy tenant generates 3x historical peak for 30 minutes.
Soft-reserve prototype merged and feature-flagged with unit and e2e tests in runtime-1.22 branch.
New Console metrics and alerting present: per-reservation burst-credit usage and reservation headroom percentage.
Runbook appended with step-by-step tenant throttling and a post-escalation checklist; SRE on-call runbook drill completed.
Customer-facing incident summary drafted and reviewed with legal/PR for affected customers.

(Priya) Add per-reservation burst metrics to Grafana and create alert runbook (target 2026-03-18).

(Product) Propose pricing options for Guaranteed Headroom tier and send to revenue ops for modeling (target 2026-04-01).

[KV cache prefetch contamination leading to memory spiral and eviction instability]
description:
Follow-up ticket for the March 2026 incident where background prefetch logic contaminated shard metadata and triggered a cascading memory growth and eviction instability. This ticket tracks remediation, short-term mitigations, instrumentation additions, and follow-on hardening work to prevent recurrence and restore predictable tenant isolation.

incident_summary:
At ~2026-03-01T03:40Z a surge in tenant A's request rate plus a new prefetch heuristic caused stale 'prefetch' entries to be inserted without proper TTLs and reference accounting. Over 18 minutes shards experienced progressive slab fragmentation and an eviction score amplification loop: eviction mis-sampling dropped hot entries while prefetch floaters prevented compaction, causing memory consumption to exceed safe thresholds and triggering capacity throttles and elevated 5xx rates for affected tenants.

timeline:
2026-03-01T03:38Z - Canary alert: elevated slab utilization on shard-17
2026-03-01T03:41Z - Autoscaler and request-throttles kicked in for tenant A; first user-facing errors observed
2026-03-01T03:50Z - On-call paged; initial mitigation: reduce prefetch worker concurrency and enable per-tenant soft caps
2026-03-01T04:10Z - Root-cause hypothesis formed: prefetch inserted entries with missing TTL & zero refcount leading to compaction skipping
2026-03-01T04:35Z - Temporary rollback of prefetch heuristic deployed; memory usage began to trend down
2026-03-01T05:05Z - Traffic normalized; incident declared mitigated; ticket created for follow-ups

investigation_notes:
Repro locally by simulating a high-rate tenant with prefetch enabled; observed two failure modes: (1) prefetch inserting marker entries without namespace TTL causing namespace-level GC to ignore them, (2) compaction path skipping entries flagged as 'prefetch_candidate' because flag combined with 0 refcount produced a tombstone race. Telemetry gaps slowed diagnosis: missing per-shard prefetch origin histograms and no compact-pass skip counters. We also found that eviction scoring used stale approximate counters which were biased by prefetch churn, amplifying eviction of valid hot entries.

root_cause:
A regression in the prefetch worker (runtime change in 1.21) failed to assign TTL/refcount properly for some warmed entries and introduced a 'prefetch_candidate' tag that inadvertently made compaction treat entries as ephemeral. This plus an eviction score calculation that did not account for prefetch-originated churn produced a positive feedback loop: more prefetch -> more fragmentation -> worse eviction scoring -> more misses -> more prefetch.

impact:
High: multiple tenants experienced increased 5xxs and latency; autoscaler consumed reserve capacity causing pressure on Dedicated pools for ~25 minutes. No data loss observed, but cache state required forced compaction for some shards.

action_items:
A: Emergency rollback landed for prefetch heuristic (completed) - OWNER: Marco Reyes - ETA: Done
B: Add strict TTL/refcount validation in prefetch path with unit + integration tests to fail CI on missing TTLs - OWNER: Priya Nair - ETA: 2026-03-12
C: Instrument per-shard prefetch-origin counters and compaction-skip metrics; expose dashboard + alert when compaction_skip_rate > 0.5% - OWNER: Jamal Ortiz - ETA: 2026-03-08
D: Adjust eviction score to discount prefetch-origin churn and add smoothing window to avoid amplification spikes - OWNER: Chen Li - ETA: 2026-03-18
E: Implement per-tenant soft memory caps that shed prefetch work before global eviction starts; include tenant-priority override for enterprise tenants - OWNER: Marco Reyes & SRE - ETA: 2026-03-22
F: Build a repair tool to recompact affected shards offline and reconcile metadata (runbook + playbook) - OWNER: Infrastructure Tools - ETA: 2026-03-25
G: Post-deployment canary plan: synthetic workload that exercises prefetch+compaction loop and validates metrics before scaling - OWNER: QE - ETA: 2026-03-10

I: Run retrospective and update runbook with checklist for similar memory-growth incidents, include quick rollback steps and emergency compaction commands - OWNER: Incident Lead (Aisha Patel) - ETA: 2026-03-09

notes:
This ticket captures both short-term safety mitigations and longer-term architectural changes (eviction smoothing and tenant soft caps). Avoid re-introducing the previous prefetch heuristic until validation gates (canary + synthetic) exist. Consider backporting safe TTL/refcount checks to 1.21-1.22 maintenance branches.

[Trailing silence and incomplete final JSON when re-establishing SSE after iOS connection warm-up behind Apple HTTP proxy]
description:
Issue summary: Customer reports SSE streaming sessions ending with a trailing silence and an incomplete final JSON object after an iOS client (managed device) reconnects. The client receives a partial JSON payload (closing bracket missing or truncated final text) but the stream does not emit an explicit terminal event. Impact: Customer's app shows 'incomplete' responses for ~5-15% of long-running streams on iOS 15/16 devices behind the Apple HTTP proxy used in their MDM. This affects Generation and Chat endpoints and causes user-visible corruption in message endings. Environment: prod-us-west, customer using our hosted API via SDK v1.12.0, mobile network: corporate Wi-Fi with Apple HTTP proxy/transparent caching. Observed: - Session logs show a short idle period then a socket rebind/hand-off from device path manager. - Edge logs include: "connection: id=sk-8765 partial_close=true late_fin=true" and serving-runtime logs show "stalled-flush: true" for the stream session. - Client-side: SDK reports reconnect, normal resume handshake, then receives no explicit "[DONE]"-like event or end-of-stream marker; final JSON block is truncated. Steps to reproduce (customer-provided): 1) Start a long streaming generation (>120s) on iOS device on corp Wi-Fi. 2) Background the app for ~10s then bring it to foreground. 3) Observe stream reconnect and final payload missing trailing characters. Expected: stream resumes and emits final terminal event or complete JSON. Observed: trailing silence and truncated final object. Additional notes: Issue more frequent when device OS performs a connection warm-up (path negotiation) or when Apple HTTP proxy inserts an intermediary probe. This appears different from standard proxy chunking issues we've seen previously because the connection close code sequence is unusual (delayed FIN coalesced with keepalive).

logs:
[edge-2026-03-12T14:02:11Z] x-request-id=7f9c2a session=ss-04f3
[edge-2026-03-12T14:02:12Z] connection: id=ss-04f3 partial_close=true reason=idle_probe_coalesce code=SOCKET_MIGRATE
[serve-2026-03-12T14:02:12Z] stream_id=ss-04f3 stalled-flush=true kvcache-primed=true last-frame-offset=18432
[client-logs] sdk.v1.12.0: reconnecting, resumeToken present
[client-logs] received chunk: "{\"choices\": [{\"text\": \"...and finally we recommend\"}\n\n(EOF)\n"

investigation_notes:
Initial hypothesis: Apple HTTP proxy on managed networks sometimes coalesces an idle-probe FIN with a subsequent TCP migration, which the edge treats as a definitive stream close before the serving-runtime has flushed the trailing buffered tokens. Differences vs known issues: not classic proxy truncation or chunk reordering; here the edge emits partial_close marker and we see a stalled flush rather than an explicit RST. Reproducer verification: Support able to reproduce locally using an iOS device simulator + a transparent proxy that delays ACKs. Correlation: request ids with partial_close show higher incidence when keepalive interval on client > 20s. Temporary mitigation: instruct customer to enable websocket fallback in SDK or set keepalive to 15s. Observed workaround success: websocket fallback avoided truncation in 30 test runs (0/30 truncations).

[SSE session-handoff causes trailing silence + JSON fragment split when reconnecting behind enterprise proxy]
description:
Issue summary: Customer reports that when a browser client behind an enterprise reverse proxy (corporate NGN/inspect proxy) reconnects an SSE stream, the final JSON choice is sometimes split across two fragments and the stream ends with 4-6s of trailing silence before an EOF event. Impact: downstream application shows 'incomplete assistant response' and discards last sentence in 12% of reconnect events.

Impact: BrightChat AI's customer-facing chat widget is intermittently missing the last sentence after network blips, causing UX regressions for end-users. Several paid enterprise customers noticed degraded conversational quality.

Environment: prod traffic routed through customer's corporate proxy chain -> customer edge -> Redwood API Gateway -> serving runtime. Client SDK: web-sdk@1.8.2 (EventSource-based SSE).

Observed behavior: on reconnect, server emits resume event and then a sequence of data chunks. A JSON metadata chunk that includes 'finish_reason' sometimes arrives split (e.g., '{"choices":[{"text":"...","finish_reason":"' then 'length"}]}'), causing client JSON parse errors or partial choice rendering. Additionally, there is a multi-second gap (4-6s) of no data before final EOF event in a subset of sessions.

Expected behavior: resume and finalization messages should be emitted as complete JSON tokens and the stream should deliver EOF promptly (sub-second) after final content.

Steps to reproduce: 1) Use web-sdk@1.8.2 behind an enterprise transparent proxy that performs TLS inspection and connection pooling. 2) Initiate long streaming generation (approx 400-800 tokens) with SSE. 3) Simulate short network blip (TCP FIN then reconnect, or client re-establish EventSource). 4) Observe client-side partial JSON parse or silent gap before EOF.

Notes: Customer provided an HAR, tcpdump slices from their edge, and a minimal reproduction app. The problem is not consistently reproducible in staging where proxy chain is absent.

steps_to_reproduce:
Open BrightChat web widget (web-sdk@1.8.2) behind corporate proxy
Send a long prompt to trigger streaming (>400 tokens)
Force a short network disconnect (toggle client network or simulate FIN)
Allow client to reconnect automatically and observe final JSON and EOF timing

observed_behavior:
Final JSON metadata chunk sometimes arrives split across multiple SSE data frames; client JSON.parse fails or truncates last sentence. In ~12% of reconnects, there is a 4-6s gap of no bytes before server sends EOF event.

expected_behavior:
Resume and terminal events arrive intact in the same data frame(s) or in-order without mid-fragment splits. EOF emitted within 500ms of final token under normal path.

client-har: request id 9a3b-20260309.har (attached) - shows two 'data:' lines splitting terminal JSON
tcpdump-slice: edge-9a3b-20260309.pcap (attached) - shows proxy reusing keepalive connection and 2nd fragment delayed
gateway-log: gw-req-2026-03-09-9a3b - upstream resumed, served resume_token=xyz, final_sent=true

03/10 13:40 - SRE (Liam): observed that our HTTP/1.1 SSE framing uses chunked encoding; some corporate proxies coalesce and re-chunk payloads causing split JSON sequences across TCP writes.
03/10 15:05 - Eng (Marta): hypothesis: proxy connection pooling + buffering leads to artificial pause before final chunk is flushed. Also saw keepalive COALESCE behavior on proxy (github.com/proxy-vendor/issue/432).

[Proxy buffering causes prolonged stream silence then duplicated metadata and split final choice on reconnect]
description:
Issue summary: Customer reports that long-tail buffering on their corporate proxy results in a silent period mid-stream. The client reconnects and the resumed session receives duplicated metadata events and the final choice is split across two fragments, effectively truncating the last sentence. Impact: Multiple calls from a production webhook pipeline drop the terminal punctuation and sometimes receive a duplicate 'choice_meta' block. This corrupts downstream JSON parsing in their ingestion pipeline and caused a production rollback for one service. Environment: Production calls from ClearView HealthTech, routed through an on-prem NGINX reverse proxy (company-managed) to our hosted Redwood API in us-east-1. Uses SSE streaming for chat completions with model gpt-open-7b-quant and heartbeat enabled every 15s. Steps to reproduce: 1) Configure a reverse proxy with proxy_buffering on and a small proxy_buffer_size so bursts are coalesced (we used nginx with proxy_buffering=on and proxy_buffer_size=4k). 2) Start a streaming chat request that emits a ~3KB terminal packet followed by heartbeat messages. 3) Introduce a short upstream latency spike (150-400ms) that triggers the proxy to flush buffered packets as a single chunk. 4) Simulate client reconnect logic that opens a new SSE session before the previous session's final chunk is fully delivered. Expected: seamless resume with single terminal chunk and intact metadata. Observed: silent period (~6-12s), then client reconnect; the resume delivers two metadata blocks (one repeated) and final text split mid-sentence across the two chunks. Logs/observations: - Request IDs: req-20260310-84a2 / upstream-req-7f1c - Server delivered final chunk at 2026-03-10T15:22:41.972Z. - Proxy flushed combined heartbeat+terminal payload at 2026-03-10T15:22:48.014Z after coalescing. - Client reconnected at 2026-03-10T15:22:49.129Z and received duplicated metadata header. Workaround used by customer: disable proxy_buffering or increase proxy_buffer_size; add client-side guard to wait 3s before issuing reconnect. Next steps: SRE + runtime team to reproduce in our lab with an nginx proxy; consider server-side change to include explicit sequence numbers and terminal flag that survive proxy coalescing. Also evaluate a small SDK change to detect duplicate metadata blocks and stitch split final choices.

comments:
2026-03-10 16:05 - Maya Chen (Support): Customer filed after rollback of webhook consumer; attached traces and proxy config snippets.
2026-03-10 17:22 - Liam O'Connor (SRE): Reproduced locally using nginx proxy config from customer; observed buffering/coalescing behavior matches report. Logged reproduction script and packet captures to the investigation notes.
2026-03-11 09:10 - Nora Patel (Client SDK): Confirmed that current JS SDK treats metadata events as idempotent but does not guard against duplicated 'terminal' metadata. Proposed small client-side patch to de-duplicate metadata by event id.
2026-03-11 14:40 - Priya Singh (Runtime): Observed that multipath flushing can merge keepalive and terminal lines; propose adding explicit 'seq' and 'terminal' fields to stream events to make resume deterministic. Raised PR idea and linked draft design in Confluence.
2026-03-12 11:01 - Liam O'Connor (SRE): Created test harness and confirmed two mitigation paths: 1) configuration guidance for customers (disable buffering or increase buffer). 2) runtime change to add sequence+terminal fields; initiated PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/12345.

investigation_notes:
Repro harness: nginx 1.22 with proxy_buffering=on, proxy_buffers=4 4k reproduces duplicate metadata when a final chunk is coalesced with keepalive and then flushed in one packet.
Packet capture shows terminal JSON split boundary moves when proxy appends keepalive bytes before flush, resulting in two JSON fragments sent back-to-back; client reconnect logic can consume both fragments but treats the second metadata block as new.
Hypothesis: Without explicit per-event markers the client cannot disambiguate a buffered-flush duplicate metadata event from a genuine new metadata event on resume.
Mitigation tested: delay reconnect in client by 3s reduces occurrence from 100% to ~2% in our lab; disabling proxy_buffering eliminates the issue.
Runtime mitigation candidate: augment SSE/event stream with 'event_seq' integer and 'terminal': true/false flags in metadata events to allow idempotent resume and reassembly logic.
Impact scope: primarily enterprise customers behind aggressive reverse proxies (on-prem NGINX, some F5 configs). Self-serve customers using cloud front proxies less affected.
Related: SUP-314159 (multiplexed session rotation truncation) shows similar boundary-splitting symptoms but different root cause; cross-referencing for potential common fixes.

resolution:
Mitigation in-progress. Short-term guidance provided to customer: increase proxy_buffer_size or disable proxy_buffering and apply client reconnect backoff. Medium-term: runtime PR #12345 to add event_seq + terminal flags submitted; client SDK de-dup patch under review. Will update when PR merges and we validate in staging.

[Final SSE event merged with health probe on edge layer causing unclosed JSON and truncated image embed]
description:
Issue summary:
Customer NoteServe reports intermittent truncation of the final SSE event when reconnecting after a short edge-level probe. The final JSON choice is left unclosed and an inline image URL (base64/attachment) is missing. The customer observed this with our JS SDK behind their corporate gateway.

Impact:
- Affected users see final paragraph missing or truncated image/attachment in ~0.7% of reconnects for long outputs (>4k tokens).
- Causes downstream parsing errors in customer app (JSON.parse errors or missing attachments).
- Reported by a production customer on Dedicated plan; affects live user workflows.

Environment:
- Redwood hosted endpoint in us-west-2, dedicated cluster (cust-dc-7).
- Customer uses our JS SDK v1.4.2 behind an internal HTTP/2 reverse proxy (company gateway v2.9) that performs active health probes.
- Models: redwood-3b, streaming SSE mode with keepalive heartbeats every 20s.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1. Start a long streaming generation that includes an inline image URL at the end (embedding produced as base64).
2. Simulate a short edge-level health probe during the final 1-2 seconds of generation (their gateway does this automatically).
3. Client reconnects (SSE re-establish) and receives output; final JSON block is unclosed or missing image field.

Observed behavior:
- The last SSE event appears concatenated with a small health-probe frame from the gateway. The client-side parser sees a malformed final JSON chunk (trailing comma/no closing bracket) or missing "attachments" field. The generation content itself appears complete on the server but gets truncated on the client.

Expected behavior:
- Final SSE event should be delivered intact across reconnects. Heartbeat/probe frames should not be merged into payload frames in a way that corrupts JSON boundaries.

Logs & attachments:
- Customer provided client-side console log: "Uncaught SyntaxError: Unexpected end of JSON input" with SSE payload snippet.
- Server trace from prod (partial): "stream:choice:finalized id=... status=ok size=... flush_ts=2026-03-12T17:45:03Z"
- Edge capture (pcap excerpt) attached by SRE shows two minimal frames coalesced at the proxy.

Reproduction note:
- We can reproduce locally by inserting a small TCP-level delay and running an HTTP/2 multiplexing proxy configured to aggressively batch small frames; leads to the same corrupted final event.

[Intermittent stream chunk reordering and lost final choice after short websocket disconnect behind corporate proxy]
description:
Issue summary:
Customers using the Redwood websocket streaming API behind a corporate proxy observe that, after short network blips (2-5s), the resumed stream sometimes reorders intermediate chunks and drops the final 'choice/end' marker. The resulting output either contains duplicated trailing whitespace tokens or never emits the final end event, causing client-side completion logic to stall.

Impact:
- Production traffic for Acme Payments chat assistant experiences ~0.8% incomplete responses during business hours in us-east.
- Client SDKs report hung streaming sessions that require manual reconnects.
- Affects dedicated customers behind middlebox proxies; not reproducible in simple NAT environments.

Environment:
- Platform: Redwood Dedicated (reserved pool)
- Region: prod-us-east
- Client: Browser apps (React) behind corporate HTTP/WS proxy (Squid/NGINX as TLS-terminating reverse proxy)
- Model: gpt-embed-4k serving via streaming websocket endpoint v1/stream

Steps to reproduce (customer-supplied):
1) Start a streaming generation via the JS SDK from a browser inside the corporate network.
2) Force a short network interruption (e.g. disable Wi-Fi for ~3s) or simulate transient proxy hiccup.
3) Allow reconnection; the SDK attempts resume.
4) Observe that some intermediate chunks are reordered and final end event is either delayed indefinitely or never seen.

Observed behavior:
- Reconnected stream resumes with chunks that appear out-of-order compared to original sequence numbers logged on the server.
- Final choice/end event absent ~0.8% of attempts, or duplicates of trailing whitespace tokens emitted.
- Server logs show resume token accepted and a follow-up stream session created, but downstream WebSocket frames logged from the proxy show intermittent fragment coalescing.

Expected behavior:
- Resume should preserve original token ordering and always include final choice/end event once generation completes on the server-side.

Initial hypothesis:
- Corporate proxy or TLS-terminating reverse proxy is re-fragmenting or buffering websocket frames and delivering them out of sequence to the backend after a short disconnect.
- SDK resume handshake may be interpreted as a new session by the proxy, which merges buffered fragments from both the old and new TCP streams in a way that reorders payloads.

Attachments/logs:
- Customer supplied client-side debug logs (attached link in ticket)
- Server-side streaming session logs and sequence numbers (anonymized)
- Proxy logs showing TCP-level retransmits and frame coalescing timestamps

Customer impact statement:
Acme requires reliable chat completions for payment support flows; missing final tokens cause their UI to show an eternal "thinking" spinner and occasionally submit incomplete instructions to downstream systems.

Created small test harness and confirmed that coalesced frames from proxy can reorder payloads across short reconnects.
2026-02-24 10:10 - Marco Rivera (SRE): Proposed a mitigation: make server resume handshake include per-message monotonic counter and drop any frames with lower-than-expected counters on resume; updated engineering ticket with proposed fix plan.

investigation_notes:
Repro environment: local NGINX with proxy_buffering on reproduces reorder when resume allowed. Switching to proxy_buffering off eliminated reorder in tests.
Server-side logs: resume token accepted, resume session created, sequence_number during original session up to 3487, new session accepted frames with sequence 3482-3490 but timestamps indicate overlap/duplication from proxy.
Network trace: pcap from patient customer shows proxy replays buffered websocket frames after TCP reconnect causing interleaving from old and new stream fragments.
SDK behavior: resume attempts to patch prior message index; when backend receives interleaved fragments with lower counters, it previously appended them rather than discarding which allowed reordering/duplicates.
Similar tickets: SUP-4721 and SUP-20347 indicate other proxy-related resume edge cases; however this case shows explicit re-injection of buffered frames rather than simple truncation.
Risk assessment: high for dedicated customers behind enterprise proxies; low for customers on straightforward NATs or cloud load balancers with websocket passthrough.
Mitigation options evaluated: 1) Client-side: force full reconnect on resume failure; 2) Server-side: enforce monotonic message counters and drop stale frames on resume; 3) Ops: guidance to proxy admins to disable buffering/tuning tcp_nodelay.
Chosen short-term mitigation: provide customer with client-side flag to disable resume and documentation for proxy tuning. Long-term fix: server-side monotonic counter enforcement (PR-4321).

2026-03-10 - Rollout: fixed behavior verified in canary; post-rollout monitoring for 72h shows no recurrence in prod-us-east for repro scenarios. Notified customer and ops channels.
Follow-ups: add a note in streaming runbook about proxy tuning and include resume-safe headers for customers who must keep buffering enabled.

[Dependency Failure Containment and Customer Communication Cookbook]
Summary:
This cookbook describes standard procedures for containing, mitigating, and communicating incidents caused by external dependencies (third-party APIs, cloud managed services, vendor models, and shared infra components). It focuses on rapid containment patterns, safe degradations, and customer-facing communications. The goal is fast, predictable response with clear ownership and minimal customer surprise.

Scope:
- Applies to incidents where a Redwood customer-visible failure is caused primarily by a non-Redwood dependency (e.g., upstream model host, cloud DB region, vendor auth provider, CDN outage).
- Does NOT replace generic service outage runbooks; it augments them with dependency-specific checks, routing options, and communication templates.
- Intended audience: on-call SREs, service owners, incident commanders, and customer success leads.

TL;DR Playbook (one-page):
1) Detect: confirm alerts and customer signals (pager, dashboards, support queue). Note root-suspect dependency.
2) Contain: apply traffic routing & circuit breakers; switch to cached responses or degraded mode; disable non-critical feature paths.
3) Communicate: publish a short-status page message and notify customer success for high-impact customers. Use the "Partial degraded experience" template (see below).
4) Mitigate: apply vendor workarounds (retry policies, alternate endpoints), escalate to vendor/partner.
5) Restore: re-enable normal routing once metrics recover for min-stability window (see thresholds).
6) Post-incident: capture timeline, evidence (metrics/traces/logs), and owner action items; schedule a dependent-party RCA with vendor if needed.

Detection and Triage:
- Primary signals:
  - Service 5xx spike correlated with a single upstream hostname or SDK (tagged in traces).
  - P95/P99 latency jump on specific call site (example: /models/embeddings endpoint to vendor X).
  - Customer support tickets referencing new errors or timeouts.
- Quick triage checklist (first 10 minutes):
  1. Confirm alert and scope (regions, clusters, customer segments).
  2. Identify upstream hostnames/IPs and SDK version.
  3. Check circuit-breaker metrics and existing retry logs.
  4. Look for vendor status page updates or security advisories.
  5. If high-impact (SLO-blow or large customer swarm), declare an incident and assign IC.

Initial responder checklist (immediate actions):
- Mark affected services and set incident priority.
- Gather key artifacts: one representative failing request/trace, recent deploys, configuration changes.
- Flip read-only toggles if applicable.
- Rate-limit or disable background jobs making heavy upstream calls.
- Enable increased logging around dependency call sites (short-lived).

Containment patterns (choose based on topology):
1) Fail-fast/circuit-breaker: open the circuit for the dependency when error rate > 5% for 2 minutes. Return graceful fallback or cached response.
2) Regional re-routing: if only one cloud region affected, shift traffic to unaffected region (with capacity guardrails).
3) Graceful degradation: turn off non-essential features that rely on the dependency (e.g., re-ranking or non-critical embeddings).
4) Local cache fallback: serve from last-known-good embeddings/search index for up to 30 minutes.
5) Rate limiting & admission control: reduce per-user token budget for generation features to preserve throughput.
6) Alternate vendor endpoint: switch to known-compatible model variant or vendor endpoint if validated during runbook authoring.

Decision matrix (short):
- If >10% customers affected OR SLO breach: containment + status page + CSM notify + vendor escalation.
- If <10% and degraded only for non-critical ops: monitoring and vendor ticket; update customers if it persists >30m.

Customer-facing comms templates
- Status page short (initial):
  "Summary: We are investigating increased error rates for [service-name] that appear related to an external partner (vendorX). Impact: some API requests may return errors or experience increased latency. Mitigation: we've applied temporary traffic controls and fallback paths. Next update: in 15 minutes."
- Status page update (post-containment):
  "Update: We have implemented a failover and reduced feature surface to limit customer-facing errors. Error rate down from 18% to 3% in the last 10 minutes. We continue to monitor and are working with vendorX. ETA for full restoration: unknown; next update in 30 minutes or sooner."
- Customer success email (high-impact customers):
  Subject: Incident affecting [service-name] — current status
  Body: Hello [CustomerName], we are currently investigating an issue affecting [service-name] that may impact [exact features]. We have applied temporary mitigations (failover/degraded mode). Our engineering team is actively working with the upstream provider (vendorX). We will provide a technical timeline and postmortem after resolution. If you require a workaround or status call, reply to this thread and we'll prioritize.
- Internal incident Slack snippet (IC → #oncall):
  "INCIDENT: Dependency degradation on [service-name]. Vendor: vendorX. Impact: ~20% error rate for customers in us-east-1. Containment actions: opened circuit, enabled local cache, reduced model precision. IC: @<name>. Contact: @CSM-Team for VIP customers."

Internal comms and vendor escalation checklist:
1. Collect evidence: representative request IDs, trace IDs, timestamps, SDK versions, and full error payloads.
2. Open vendor ticket: include rate graphs, p95/p99 latency, sample traces, and a clear desired action (e.g., "please confirm whether your control plane reported quota throttles for our API key between T1 and T2").
3. Share incident channel link and SRE contact with vendor escalation engineer.
4. If vendor can't respond within SLA and customer impact is severe, trigger backup plan (alternate vendor or model variant).

SLO / Metrics to record in incident timeline:
- Error rate for affected RPC (1m/5m/15m).
- p95/p99 latency before and after containment.
- Fraction of requests served from cache/fallback.
- Customer seats affected and list of enterprise customers with errors.
- Duration from detection to containment and to full restore.

Restoration criteria and stability window:
- Restoration considered successful when:
  1. Error rate < SLO-threshold for 15 continuous minutes (default: error rate <= 1% for user-facing RPCs) AND
  2. Latency p95 within 20% of baseline for 15 continuous minutes.
- Post-restore steps: gradually remove rate-limits and feature toggles over 30–60 minutes while monitoring.

Post-incident responsibilities (30/60/90 day actions):
- 0–3 days: IC writes timeline and preliminary RCA draft; notify customer success for impacted accounts.
- 3–14 days: schedule vendor RCA call; collect vendor evidence and ticket closure.
- 14–30 days: implement mitigations (circuit-breaker tuning, cache TTL changes, model fallback path testing).
- 30–90 days: schedule a game day to rehearse the same failure mode and validate automation.

Postmortem template (starter fields):
- Title, date, IC and authors.
- Summary (one-paragraph impact).
- Timeline (minute-granular for first hour, 5–15 minute thereafter).
- Root cause hypothesis and evidence.
- Customer impact and severity classification.
- Corrective actions (owners + ETA).
- Preventive actions and verification plan.
- Vendor follow-up and SLA changes (if any).

On-call rotation and ownership notes:
- Primary on-call: owns rapid containment actions and status page updates.
- Secondary: vendor escalations and CSM handoffs.
- Engineering lead (post-incident): leads RCA and remediation prioritization.
- Rationale: keep action items close to the code owners; keep vendor comms centralized through a rotated escalation owner.

Game day scenarios (playbook exercises):
1) Vendor auth service returns 403 for 50% of requests for 30 minutes: practice failover to cached tokens and vendor ticket escalation.
2) Cloud region DB latency spikes causing model store timeouts: practice regional reroute and degraded-mode ranking.
3) Embedding vendor goes into degraded throughput: rehearse switch to low-cost local embedding quantization profile + customer notice cadence.

Example runbook snippets and commands:
- Toggle a circuit breaker (k8s annotation example):
  kubectl annotate deployment service-a rdb-circuit-breaker=open --overwrite
- Re-route traffic (Istio route weight example):
  kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
  apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1alpha3
  kind: VirtualService
  metadata:
    name: service-a-routing
  spec:
    hosts: ["service-a.internal"]
    http:
    - route:
      - destination:
          host: service-a-primary
          subset: v1
        weight: 0
      - destination:
          host: service-a-secondary
          subset: v1
        weight: 100
  EOF
- Sample status page JSON for short update:
  {
    "component": "Model Embeddings API",
    "status": "degraded_performance",
    "message": "We are investigating elevated error rates likely due to vendorX. Temporary mitigations are in place."
  }

Thresholds and configuration table (reference):
- Error-rate-open-circuit: 5% sustained for 2 minutes
- Cache-TTL-fallback: 30 minutes by default
- Min-stability-window-before-restore: 15 minutes continuous
- Customer-notify-threshold: >10% customers impacted OR >5 enterprise accounts affected

Ownership and contact matrix:
- Service owner: @service-a-team (oncall rotation link: https://pager/rosters/service-a)
- SRE escalation: @eng-sre-oncall (primary phone tree)
- CSM lead for VIPs: Customer Success team rotation (contact: csm-rotation@redwood.com)

Guidance for vendor contracts and SLAs:
- For critical dependencies, contractually require: 24/7 escalation path, dedicated escalation engineer for P1s, and uptime SLA with credit terms.
- Track vendor incident frequency and renegotiate if recurring incidents exceed N per quarter.

Appendix: sample escalation message to vendor
Subject: URGENT: Production errors from Redwood account [account-id] — request immediate escalation
Body:
We are experiencing production errors impacting multiple customers. Evidence attached: error logs, trace IDs, timestamps. Impact: 20% of API calls failing in us-east-1. Please escalate to your on-call escalation engineer and confirm whether this is caused by quota throttling, control plane issue, or a degradation in downstream service. Required: callback within 15 minutes and summary within 60 minutes.

Appendix: Game day checklist for exercise facilitators
- Pre-game: pick a target dependency and failure mode; create simulated vendor silence or degraded responses.
- During: measure detection time, containment actions, and status page latency.
- Post: score the run on RTO, communication clarity, and completeness of postmortem artifacts.
- Follow-up: convert findings into 1–3 prioritized action items and assign owners.

Related reading and links:
- Runbook governance and post-incident cadence (policy)
- Incident communication and postmortem framework
- Vendor management playbook and SLA negotiation checklist
