[First-Hour Stabilization SOP and Executive Incident Brief]
Overview:

Purpose: This document codifies a repeatable, auditable first-hour stabilization SOP for operator teams (SRE, serving runtime, product support) and provides a template executive incident brief. The goal is to restore customer-visible service levels quickly, gather forensic evidence, and produce an actionable post-incident plan.

Audience: SREs, on-call engineers, incident commanders, support leads, and engineering managers.

Scope: Applies to production inference service incidents impacting latency SLOs, error-rate regressions, large-scale capacity failures (regional or multi-tenant), and model-quality degradations that require cross-team coordination. Does NOT replace service-specific runbooks but provides a universal first-hour ladder and comms templates.

Quick reference:
- Severity mapping: P0 (system-wide outage), P1 (SLO breach impacting many tenants), P2 (single-customer impact or degraded quality), P3 (minor/non-customer-facing degradations).
- Primary contact channel: #ops-bridge Slack channel and incident Zoom bridge (automatically created by pager).
- Required immediate outputs in first 60 minutes: triage summary, mitigation action(s) in flight, customer-visible status published, executive brief stub created.

Roles & responsibilities:

- Incident Commander (IC): Owns coordination, decisions, and the executive brief. Typical IC rotation: senior SRE on-call.
- Service Steward: Owner of the impacted service (e.g., serving-runtime lead). Responsible for technical diagnosis and runbook execution.
- Bridge Operator: Manages comms, runbook links, status page updates.
- Escalation Engineer: SME (runtime/kernel/model) pulled for deep technical fixes.
- Customer Liaison (for P1/P0): Support/CS rep for customer notifications and impact assessment.

Severity decision ladder (short):
1) Confirm alert signal (AlertName, count, query) and scope (region, model, tenant).
2) Check SLO dashboards: 99th latency, error-rate, request-success ratio for the last 5m and 1h.
3) If ≥ 50% of global requests show SLO violation OR > 3 enterprise customers affected -> escalate to P0/P1.
4) If single-customer only AND mitigations exist (route/disable) -> P2.

First-hour stabilization checklist (step-by-step, numbered):

1. Acknowledge and declare incident (0-2 minutes)
   - IC acknowledges pager, moves to #ops-bridge, and posts initial one-line incident declaration: "Investigating elevated 99p latency for text-generation (region: us-west-2)."
   - Bridge operator documents alert name, originating alert rule, pager time, and initial SIG (SLO/availability/quality).

2. Rapid scope & safety checks (2-8 minutes)
   - Validate whether the alert is synthetic or real (look for matching synthetic failures).
   - Confirm telemetry: traces, sample error logs, and load metrics (RPS, queue length, GPU util, KV cache hit rate).
   - If throttling/backpressure is present, enable pre-approved escape hatch (eg: bump per-customer concurrency limits for critical customers).

3. Apply immediate mitigations (8-20 minutes)
   - Hotfix options (choose the least invasive first): 1) Route traffic to warm standby region; 2) Scale dedicated pool for high-impact customers; 3) Roll back recent model/config rollout; 4) Engage fallback model variant (quantized/cheaper).
   - Document chosen mitigation, operator, ETA for effect, and metrics to watch.

4. Contain & preserve evidence (20-35 minutes)
   - Freeze relevant autoscaling and deployment operations to prevent noisy artifacts.
   - Increase retention for traces/logs for impacted services for at least 72 hours (evidence TTL).
   - Snapshot key runtime state: KV cache eviction counts, model KV cache keys for affected sessions, and GPU kernel traces.

5. Customer & status communications (30-45 minutes)
   - Publish initial customer-facing status page entry (template below) and post a short note in the account-level status channels for affected enterprise customers.
   - If P0/P1, prepare an exec brief stub and circulate to leadership list (email + Slack).

6. Stabilize and handoff to long-running remediation (45-60 minutes)
   - If mitigation restores SLOs, build a rollback/cleanup plan and assign owners for full root-cause analysis (RCA).
   - If SLOs are not restored, escalate to extended incident (schedule additional escalation cadence and mobilize postmortem team).

Forensic evidence checklist (must be collected within first hour):
- SLO time series (1m/5m/1h) for latency (p50/p95/p99), error-rate, and success ratio.
- Trace samples covering at least 100 failed/spike requests.
- GPU telemetry: GPU util, memory, kernel error counters, and process-level metrics.
- Autoscaler and scheduling events with timestamps.
- Recent deployments and model-rollout hashes (git commits, model version IDs).
- KV cache metrics: hit/miss/evict counts and notable prefix keys.
- Model-quality signals: eval-set regressions and recent production prompt-eval deltas (if available).

Escalation matrix & time targets:
- 0 minutes: Pager fired and primary on-call acknowledges.
- 5 minutes: IC declared if multiple signals confirmed.
- 15 minutes: Escalation engineer (runtime/model) paged for P0/P1.
- 30 minutes: CS Customer Liaison engaged for any enterprise-impacting incidents.

Communication templates:

1) Internal bridge headline (post on #ops-bridge):
   - Subject: [INCIDENT] One-line summary | SEV | region | impact
   - Body: Timestamp (UTC), IC name, short problem statement, primary mitigation in flight, immediate next-check (time).

Example: "[INCIDENT] P1: Elevated p99 latency for text-gen in us-west-2 — 2026-02-03T17:24Z — IC: Maya Chen — Routing traffic to warm standby region (eta 6m) — next check 17:30Z."

2) Customer-facing status page template (short):
   - Title: Service Degradation — Text Generation — us-west-2
   - Impact: Some requests are seeing increased latency (> p99 target of 450ms).
   - Start time: 2026-02-03T17:18Z UTC
   - What we're doing: Investigating root cause; routing traffic to alternative region and scaling affected pools.
   - Next update: 30 minutes

3) Executive incident brief stub (one page):
   - Incident ID: INC-YYYYMMDD-####
   - Summary (3 lines): What happened, customer/system impact, high level mitigation.
   - Current status: Contains live metrics snapshot (p99, error-rate, capacity) and mitigation in-flight.
   - Owners: IC, Service Steward, Escalation SME, Customer Liaison.
   - Near-term actions (0-4h) and decision points.

Postmortem skeleton (to be completed after stabilization):

[Incident Cadence Architects: Field Guide to On-call Rhythm, Drills, and Customer Notices]
Title: Incident Cadence Architects: Field Guide to On-call Rhythm, Drills, and Customer Notices\n\nIntroduction\nThis guide describes the intended operational rhythm for on-call teams at Redwood Inference, and provides repeatable artifacts for designing incident cycles, game-day drills, customer status updates, and post-incident synthesis. It is intended for SREs, service owners, and engineering leads responsible for reliability and customer communication.\n\nPurpose and scope\n- Purpose: Define a repeatable cadence (detection -> stabilization -> restore -> learn) and provide concrete templates and metrics so teams can safely run experiments, measure improvement, and maintain customer trust.\n- Scope: Applies to all Redwood customer-facing inference services (hosted API, Dedicated routing, Private control plane). Internal developer tools (CI runners, build cluster) should align but may have separate SLAs.\n\nTable of contents\n1) Principles\n2) Roles and responsibilities\n3) Incident cadence (detailed lifecycle)\n4) Standard runbook template\n5) On-call rotation patterns and handoff rules\n6) Game-day and SLO-drill design\n7) Customer status page and comms templates\n8) Postmortem rubric and evidence checklist\n9) Runbook maintenance and measurement\n10) Appendices: CLI snippets and example escalation policy\n\n1) Principles\n- Prioritize user impact over internal alerts: categorize signals by customer-visible symptom first (API errors, latency increase, embedding quality regression).\n- Keep the bridge lean: limit participants to necessary roles early; scale as severity requires.\n- Safe experimentation: game days should be scripted with rollback plans and a pre-approved quiet window.\n- Measure outcomes not effort: drills and postmortems should link to objective changes (SLOs, MTTR, automation coverage).\n\n2) Roles and responsibilities\n- Incident Commander (IC): owns decisions until handoff. Responsibilities: triage priority, approve temporary mitigations, coordinate external comms. Typical owner: senior SRE on rotation.\n- Primary responder (Primary): first on-call engineer handling triage and initial mitigation.\n- Secondary/Backup: supports primary, takes over for escalations and extended incidents.\n- Service Owner / Product Liaison: provides feature/context and customer impact guidance.\n- Communications Lead (Comms): crafts status page and external messages; often a member of CS or a designated SRE.\n- Evidence Collector: records timestamps, commands run, metrics dashboards, and links to traces for later postmortem.\n\n3) Incident cadence (detection -> closure)\n1. Detection & Initial validation (0-5 minutes):\n   - Alert fires (source: Prometheus, tracer-based SLI, customer report).\n   - Primary acknowledges within 5 minutes. If no ack, PagerDuty escalates to Secondary.\n   - Quick verification: run defined smoke-check commands (see Appendix A).\n2. Triage & impact assessment (5-20 minutes):\n   - IC identifies customer-visible symptoms, affected regions/tenants, estimated blast radius.\n   - Categorize severity: Sev1 (customer-facing outage), Sev2 (degradation affecting >5% customers or p95 latency regression > 5x), Sev3 (minor or internal).\n   - Record start time and notify stakeholders per escalation matrix.\n3. Containment & mitigation (20-60 minutes):\n   - Apply safe mitigations: routing fallbacks, capacity scaling, circuit breakers, or temporary feature disablement.\n   - If mitigation requires cross-team action (DB, infra, routing), spin up bridge and assign owners.\n4. Restore & verification (60-240 minutes):\n   - Gradual roll-forward fixes with canary traffic where possible.\n   - Monitor SLIs closely; when service meets recovery criteria (see SLI thresholds below), begin stakeholder notification of recovery.\n5. Recovery & post-incident transition (240+ minutes):\n   - Prepare a 1–2 paragraph incident summary for the status page.\n   - Assign a postmortem owner within 48 hours.\n6. Postmortem & follow-up (1–14 days):\n   - Conduct blameless postmortem using the rubric below.\n   - Publish action items and assign owners with due dates; tie to backlog and track until resolved.\n\nMinimum SLIs and thresholds (example)\n- Availability SLO (hosted API): 99.9% monthly availability. Error budget: 0.1% of requests per calendar month.\n- Latency SLO: p95 generation latency < 200ms for short prompt workloads (<= 128 tokens); p99 < 700ms.\n- Embedding throughput SLO: 99% requests complete within 800ms.\n- Alert thresholds (examples): p95 latency increase > 2x baseline for 3m -> Severity 2 alert; error rate > 0.5% for 5m -> Severity 1 if customer impact confirmed.\n\n4) Standard runbook template (use for service-level incidents)\n- Title: short descriptive name (e.g., "api-inference-error-5xxs").\n- Purpose: one sentence describing symptom being remedied.\n- Owner: primary oncall and service team.\n- Detection checks: list of dashboards/queries to run. Example: `curl -sS https://api.redwood.ai/health | jq .status` and `promql: sum(rate(http_request_errors[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests[5m]))`\n- Quick mitigation steps (ordered):\n  1. Identify if the problem is regional or global via region filtering.\n  2. If caused by recent deploy, roll back the deploy (documented rollback command).\n  3. If caused by capacity, scale Dedicated pool by +20% in the autoscale UI or use cli: `redwood scale --pool inference --delta 0.2` (example).\n  4. If caused by model OOMs, switch traffic to quantized variant or compatible fallback model.\n- Verification: list of metrics and thresholds to watch post-mitigation.\n- Post-incident tasks: add test cases, update alert thresholds, create runbook improvements.\n\n5) On-call rotation patterns and handoff rules\n- Pattern A (default): 1-week primary shifts, weekday coverage 9am-6pm local, nights and weekends on-call with 24/7 rotation.\n- Pattern B (high-intensity services): 2-week primary shifts with 24/7 on-call and a secondary for the first week of handover.\n- Handoff checklist (must be completed for every shift change):\n  1. Confirm completed incidents and outstanding action items.\n  2. Review active alerts and silenced notifications.\n  3. Share any planned maintenance or expected traffic spikes.\n  4. Confirm escalation contact list and bridge URLs.\n- Warm handoff protocol for long incidents: the outgoing primary briefs incoming primary in a 10-minute synchronous call and stays in observer role for first 30 minutes.\n\n6) Game-day and SLO-drill design\n- Objective: exercise the detection and mitigation workflow and measure time-to-first-action, MTTR, and false-positive tolerance.\n- Planning steps:\n  1. Define a scope and blast radius safe for production or use a staging mirror.\n  2. Create a script with a clear failure injection and a documented rollback.\n  3. Identify stakeholders and a Comms lead; schedule a quiet window where customer-impacting drills are allowed.\n- Example drill: KV cache eviction and traffic spike\n  - Expected learning: verify KV-cache warming strategy, observe autoscaler behavior, and validate alert thresholds for p95 latency.\n  - Measured metrics: time to detect, time to mitigation, time to restore, number of manual steps.\n- Post-drill: publish a short after-action report with measurable improvements and update runbooks.\n\n7) Customer status page and comms templates\n- Status page principle: fast, factual, and respectful. Use the template below and avoid speculative technical details.\n- Message states (short forms used on status.redwood.ai):\n  1. Investigating: We are aware of reports of [symptom]. Our team is investigating. (Examples: \"Investigating: Increased API errors for text generation in us-west-2\")\n  2. Identified: We have identified a root cause and are implementing mitigation. (E.g., \"Identified: Infrastructure routing misconfiguration affecting inference traffic\")\n  3. Mitigating: We are actively applying mitigations; service may be partially available.\n  4. Restored: Service availability is restored; we are monitoring for stability.\n  5. Postmortem published: A postmortem with findings and actions is available at [link].\n- Status message template (short public update)\n  - Title: Investigating: [short symptom]\n  - Body: We are investigating reports of [symptom]. Affected customers may experience [impact]. We will provide an update within [timeframe].\n- Escalated customer notice (to CS/enterprise)\n  - Subject: Incident update – [service] – [time range]\n  - Body: Hello (Customer Name),\n    We are investigating an issue affecting [service]. Impact: [concrete symptom]. Mitigation in progress: [high-level steps]. We will share a timeline for resolution within [x] minutes and will follow up with a summary and corrective actions.\n\n8) Postmortem rubric and evidence checklist\n- Postmortem timeline: draft published within 72 hours.\n- Required sections:\n  1. Summary (1–2 paragraphs)\n  2. Impact (customers, regions, tenant count)\n  3. Root cause analysis (what happened and why)\n  4. Timeline of actions (timestamps and actors)\n  5. Mitigations and rollbacks applied\n  6. Action items (owner, priority, due date)\n  7. Lessons learned and preventive measures\n- Evidence checklist (must be attached or linked):\n  - Alert payloads and Prometheus query results.\n  - Relevant logs and sampling of trace IDs.\n  - Deployment diffs (commit IDs) if deploy-related.\n  - PagerDuty timeline and acknowledgement logs.\n  - Customer support tickets and status page history.\n\n9) Runbook maintenance and measurement\n- Runbook ownership: every runbook has an owner and an annual review date. Owners will tag runbooks with `last-tested` after any game day or real incident.\n- Key metrics to track annually per service:\n  - Mean time to acknowledge (MTTA) target: < 5 minutes.\n  - Mean time to mitigate (first effective mitigation): < 30 minutes for Sev1s.\n  - Mean time to restore (MTTR): < 120 minutes for Sev1s.\n  - Automation coverage: % of mitigation steps executable via documented CLI or playbook target > 70%.\n- Quarterly cadence: each service must run at least one SLO-drill or game day per quarter. Results are summarized during the reliability review.\n\n10) Appendices\nA) Quick validation commands (examples)\n- Health check: `curl -sS https://api.redwood.ai/health | jq .status`\n- Error rate (Prometheus): `sum(rate(http_request_errors[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests[5m]))`\n- Check model serving pool occupancy: `redwood-admin pool list --service inference`\n\nB) Example Slack public-facing status snippet (30 minute update)\n- `@channel: INVESTIGATING: We are aware of increased 5xx errors for inference in us-west-2. Engineers are investigating. We will update in 30 minutes. Link: <status.redwood.ai/incident/xxxx>`\n\nC) Example escalation policy (pseudo-YAML)\n- `escalation_policy:`\n  - `- after: 5m -> notify: secondary`\n  - `- after: 15m -> notify: oncall-lead and IC`\n  - `- after: 60m -> page: director-oncall`\n\nD) Measuring improvement: example post-drill KPIs\n- Reduction in manual steps required in runbook (baseline vs post-action).\n- Decrease in MTTR across three subsequent incidents.\n- Increase in automation coverage (playbooked steps).\n\nOwner and next steps\n- Document owner: Maya Chen (SRE).\n- Next review scheduled: 2024-05-01.\n- Action: Teams should use this guide to plan their next quarterly SLO-drill and tag runbooks with `last-tested` when complete.\n\nRelated pages and references\n- See also: service-level runbooks in the runbook library, incident evidence standard, and the operator training syllabus.\n\nFeedback\nPlease add suggestions directly to the page comments or file a PR against the runbook template in the operations docs repo.

[Incident Orchestration Decision Canvas and Runbook]
Overview\n\nThis page documents a combined decision canvas and runnable playbook for on-call responders at Redwood Inference. The intent is to give a clear, SLO-driven decision process that: 1) shortens time-to-containment, 2) reduces noisy escalations, and 3) improves evidence collection for post-incident analysis. Use this page as the primary guide when an active incident affects customer-facing inference services (hosted API, Dedicated, or Private control plane).\n\nScope\n\n- Applies to incidents that impact latency, availability, correctness (quality regressions), or billing/quotas for inference endpoints.\n- Does NOT replace service-specific runbooks for deployment, onboarding, or infra reconfiguration; it is the orchestration layer to choose which runbook and communications path to use.\n\nQuick facts and SLO thresholds (production)\n\n- Availability SLO: 99.95% (per-region, 30d rolling).\n- Latency SLO: p99 < 350ms for short-form generate endpoints; p99 < 700ms for long-sequence pipelines.\n- Error budget alert: Trigger when 7-day rolling availability drops below 99.9% or error-rate increase > 2x baseline for 30 minutes.\n- Severity mapping:\n  - Sev-0: Global outage impacting >50% of traffic or all control plane requests – page exec & Exec Bridge.\n  - Sev-1: Major degradation (SLO breach risk within 1 hour) impacting production customers – Incident Bridge.\n  - Sev-2: Partial degradation or isolated customer impact – Slack triage and owner-led response.\n  - Sev-3: Minor non-customer impacting issues, backlog tickets.\n\nRoles & ownership\n\n- First Responder (Pager): Acknowledge within 5 minutes. Primary responsibilities: initial triage, evidence collection, stabilize or escalate.\n- Incident Lead (IL): Assumes orchestration for incident run until handoff. Owns timeline, communications cadence, and action tracking.\n- Engineering SRE: Implements mitigations, applies capacity or routing changes, validates fallbacks.\n- Product/CS Liaison: Drafts customer-facing messages and pulls impacted customer list.\n- On-call Manager: Ensures correct escalation, rotates relievers if incident extends beyond shift.\n\nDecision Canvas: How to pick the remediation path\n\nUse the following questions in order. Answer quickly and use the branching guidance to select the right runbook and comms path.\n\n1) Detect: Is this an alert (automated) or a customer report?\n  - If alert and metric crosses severity thresholds (see Quick facts), continue.\n  - If customer report and localized: start Sev-2 triage; verify scope via request logs.\n\n2) Scope: Is impact region-wide or customer-scoped?\n  - Region-wide -> consider routing, capacity, or control-plane failure runbooks.\n  - Customer-scoped -> follow escalation matrix to platform & account teams; consider temporary exception or throttling.\n\n3) Velocity: Is the degradation rapidly worsening (exponential error growth or rising latency trend)?\n  - If yes -> escalate to Incident Lead and open a dedicated bridge.\n\n4) Containment feasibility: Can we reduce blast radius with routing flags, model-fallback, or circuit-breakers?\n  - If yes -> implement containment (see Containment steps). If not, escalate to infrastructure leads.\n\n5) Recovery path: Is a fast rollback or failover available (canary rollback, previous model version, or alternate region)?\n  - If yes -> run Recovery Execution template.\n  - If no -> run Mitigation & Stabilization template and plan RTO > 1 hour.\n\nRunbook templates (copyable blocks)\n\nA) Containment (apply immediately if feasible)\n1. Toggle prefix/KV cache passthrough for the affected model pool (console CLI: redwood cache set --pool <pool> --mode passthrough).\n2. Apply route-level throttles to limit new sessions to 30% of normal traffic for the affected pool.\n3. Activate model-fallback: route low-priority traffic to quantized/compatible variant.\n4. If OOM or GPU errors present, drain impacted nodes from serving group and shift traffic to standby capacity.\n\nB) Recovery Execution (rollback/failover)\n1. Verify available previous model or deployment snapshot timestamped in the catalog.\n2. Initiate canary rollback using the Console: rollouts create --service <svc> --target <version> --canary 10%.\n3. Monitor p95/p99 latency and error-rate for 5 minutes. If stable, ramp to 50% for 3m, then full.\n4. If rollback fails, revert and fallback to circuit-breaker + staging capacity.\n\nC) Mitigation & Stabilization (when rollback not possible)\n1. Temporarily increase autoscale target for Dedicated pools by +25% (owner: infra).\n2. Reduce model max_tokens/sequence on heavy pipelines to reduce per-request work.\n3. Enable degraded-mode responses: include structured field \"warning\": \"degraded_serving\" for downstream clients.\n4. Open ticket for engineering change and assign immediate action items with owners and ETA.\n\nContainment checklist (evidence to collect before modifying production)\n\n- Incident timestamp, originating alert ID, scope (regions/tenants), and request sample.\n- Relevant metric graphs (latency p50/p95/p99, errors, qps) and trace ids for 3 sample requests across affected timeframe.\n- Cluster/node logs (stderr/stdout), GPU OOM messages, scheduler traces.\n\nStatus page & customer comms templates\n\nUse these templates on the Status Page (internal canonical copy) and for customer emails/CS messages. Personalize the placeholders (<...>).\n\nInitial acknowledgement (public status page and customer CS)\n\"We are aware of an issue affecting the Redwood inference API in <region>. Our engineering team is investigating. Impact: increased latency and request failures for some customers. We will provide an update within 30 minutes. Reference: <incident-id>.\"\n\nStatus update (20-60 minute cadence while active)\n\"Update: Engineering identified a high-error-rate condition tied to <root_cause_short>. We’ve applied a containment step to reduce customer impact by <percent_reduction>% and are validating service behavior. Next update in 30 minutes or after major progress. Impacted customers: <list or 'subset of customers'>. Reference: <incident-id>.\"\n\nResolution (final)\n\"Resolved: The issue affecting inference requests in <region> has been resolved at <time>. Root cause: <short_rca>. Mitigation: <actions taken>. If you continue to experience problems, please contact support with reference <incident-id>. A technical postmortem will be published to customers within 48 hours if they were materially affected.\"\n\nInternal incident comms cadence (recommended)\n- 0-10m: Acknowledgement to core Slack incident channel and create bridge.\n- 10-30m: First status update with containment steps completed.\n- Every 30m while active: update with metrics and current next-action.\n- On resolution: brief summary and link to postmortem draft.\n\nOn-call rotation, escalation matrix and shadowing\n\n- Primary responder: 8-hour rotation (08:00–16:00; 16:00–00:00; 00:00–08:00). Relievers shadow for first 48h of a long-running incident.\n- Escalation contact order: Primary Pager -> On-call team lead -> SRE Principal -> Head of Infra. Contact details are maintained in the oncall roster.\n- Shadowing policy: New responders shadow for 2 full shifts and run tabletop drills before independent paging.\n\nGame days and readiness drills\n\n- Frequency: Quarterly game days per region; monthly tabletop for new hires.\n- Exercise types: network partition simulation, multi-model quality regression, capacity exhaustion, and downstream dependency failure.\n- Scoring: time-to-detect, time-to-contain, customer-impact reduction, and completeness of evidence collected.\n\nPostmortem and action tracking (must-haves)\n\n1. Postmortem timeline with timestamps for detection, triage, containment, full recovery, and communications.\n2. Root cause analysis: a clear causal chain (not just symptoms).\n3. Corrective actions: owner, ETA, and verification steps.\n4. Customer impact summary and whether credits/notifications are required.\n5. Postmortem review meeting scheduled within 7 days and linked in the document.\n\nEvidence collection template (minimum)\n\n- Alert IDs and monitoring graphs (PNG links).\n- 3 representative request traces with full call-stack and headers redacted.\n- Configuration snapshot (model version, routing rules, autoscale parameters).\n- Deployment history for last 24 hours.\n\nWhen to convert to a public postmortem\n\n- Convert when > 10% of customers or any enterprise customer experienced latency or failures for more than 1 hour, or if the incident required a region-level failover. Publish a customer-facing summary within 48 hours and a full internal RCA within 7 days.\n\nOperational notes & dos-and-don’ts\n\n- Do: Keep the Incident Lead role single-threaded for coordination.\n- Do: Avoid broad-spectrum rollbacks without canary validation.\n- Do: Use structured ‘degraded-mode’ flags in responses to allow downstream graceful degradation.\n- Don’t: Make unilateral security or data-retention changes during an incident.\n- Don’t: Use the status page for internal technical noise; keep it high level and customer-centric.\n\nAppendix: CLI snippets and common commands\n\n- Create bridge: redwood bridge create --incident <incident-id> --severity <sev> --owner <il-name>\n- Toggle model fallback: redwood routes update --route <route> --fallback-version <id>\n- Snapshot deployment: redwood deployments snapshot --service <svc> --out /tmp/snapshot-<ts>.json\n\nRelated pages and references\n\n- SLO and error budgeting guidance: /confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets-2024\n- Incident lifecycle templates: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-lifecycle-orchestration-templates-2025\n- Runbook maintenance policy: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/runbook-retention-and-responder-onboarding-handbook-2026\n\nDocument maintenance\n\n- Owner: Engineering (oncall-playbooks squad). Review cadence: quarterly or after any Sev-1 incident.\n- Last reviewed: 2025-02-03.\n\nEnd of document."

[Swarm coordination runbook and customer notice patterns]
Summary
-------
This document defines the "swarm" coordination pattern for incidents that require rapid cross-team engagement (multi-service degradations, noisy neighbors, regional capacity events). It includes a short, time-boxed containment checklist, step-by-step coordination flows, role definitions, customer notice and status-page templates, and the post-incident investigation cadence. Use this runbook for incidents that meet the Swarm criteria (see section below).

When to use this runbook
-----------------------
- Use for multi-service or multi-team incidents (3+ teams impacted).
- Use when SLO impact is: availability drop >= 3% or error rate spike (5xx) above 1% for 5+ minutes.
- Use when a regional or capacity constraint causes cascading failures (e.g., GPU farm / routing tier / cache invalidation).

Swarm criteria checklist (quick assessment)
------------------------------------------
1. Impact breadth: are >2 product routes or services degraded? (yes/no)
2. Customer impact: are paid customers experiencing errors or latency above SLA thresholds? (yes/no)
3. Time sensitivity: is the incident actively growing? (yes/no)
If two or more answers are yes, escalate to Swarm.

Roles and responsibilities
--------------------------
- Incident Lead (IL): owns triage decisions, customer comms cadence, and bridge coordination. Typically Senior SRE on-shift.
- Bridge Operator: runs the conference bridge, collects evidence, updates status.
- Service Leads: owners for each affected service; responsible for containment and short-term mitigations.
- Platform Capacity Lead: evaluates capacity, autoscaling, and hardware pool health.
- Communications Lead: drafts public and customer-specific messages (CS/AE-run).
- Engineering Liaison (per team): implements fixes, rollbacks, or configuration changes.
- Postmortem Author: appointed during incident close; drives RCA timeline.

Immediate containment checklist — first 15 minutes
------------------------------------------------
1. Acknowledge and classify (0–2 min)
   - Pager acknowledged in Slack / PagerDuty.
   - IL assigned on the bridge.
   - Short headline: impact, region, estimated customers (post to #incidents).
2. Stabilize (2–10 min)
   - Apply traffic-limiting rules or throttles to noisy routes.
   - Temporarily disable non-essential background jobs or batches.
   - If CPU/GPU saturation suspected: route traffic to alternate pool or enable burst capacity.
3. Evidence capture (2–10 min)
   - Capture SLO dashboards: 1m/5m error rates, p95/p99 latency, request volume.
   - Collect recent deploys, config changes, autoscaler events (last 60 minutes).
   - Snapshot relevant logs and stack traces (link to centralized log view).
4. Customer triage (10–15 min)
   - Communications Lead posts initial status (see templates below).
   - Identify top affected customers and flag AE/CS.

Investigation run loop — 15–90 minutes
-------------------------------------
- Timebox 15-minute investigation sprints with short syncs on the bridge.
- Typical checks (parallel across Service Leads):
  - Dependency health: Redis/memcache hit rates, DB connection pool errors.
  - Model-serving queues: KV cache misses, OOMs on GPU nodes, quantization mismatch errors.
  - Autoscaler: scaling events, cooldowns, throttling logs.
  - Networking: LB error codes, TLS handshake failures, regional routing spikes.
- Use the evidence matrix to mark implicated components. Update the IL every sprint.

Restoration & mitigation steps
------------------------------
1. Priority mitigations (apply in order of least to most impactful):
   - Route around: shift traffic to healthy region or model variant.
   - Config rollbacks: revert the most recent deploys for implicated services.
   - Increase capacity: temporarily add burst nodes or expand GPU pool (with capacity lead).
   - Feature gates: flip off heavy features (large-context generations, long-streaming sessions).
2. Validation: confirm SLO and throttling metrics recovering for 2 consecutive 1-minute windows.
3. Gradual restore: reintroduce features / routes in canary stages, monitor for regressions.

Customer communications patterns and templates
-------------------------------------------
Principles: be timely, transparent, and measurable. Provide next steps and expected updates.

Status snippet templates (short)
- Initial (within 15 min):
  "We are investigating increased error rates for text generation in us-west-2. Customers may see timeouts or 5xx responses. Our engineers are actively triaging and we will provide an update within 30 minutes. Impacted customers: internal estimate ~8% of requests."
- Update (every 30–60 min):
  "Progress update: root cause narrowed to GPU autoscaler failing to add nodes after burst threshold. We have routed traffic to a healthy region and are seeing partial recovery (errors down from 7% to 2%). Next update in 45 minutes or earlier for major changes."
- Resolution/Close:
  "Resolved: services restored and error rates are back within SLO. We are performing a post-incident review and will publish a summary within 72 hours. If you continue to see issues, contact support@redwood.example.com."

Customer-specific template (for high-touch customers)
- Subject: Incident update — service degradation impacting model inference
- Body: "We detected degraded inference performance impacting X% of requests in us-west-2. Our engineering team placed a temporary traffic reroute and reduced batch sizes to limit timeouts. We expect further improvement in the next hour. Your account team (cc'd) will follow up with any mitigation options for your workloads."

Status page examples (markdown-friendly)
| Component | Status | Impact | Next update |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Inference API (us-west-2) | Degraded | 8% of requests | 30m |
| Model-serving pool (g4dn) | Recovering | Partial saturation | 30m |

Postmortem and RCA cadence
--------------------------
- Postmortem timeline (mandatory for Sev 2+ incidents):
  - 0–72 hours: Postmortem draft created. Evidence attached (dashboards, logs, deploys).
  - 72–120 hours: Root cause analysis and action items finalized. Assign owners and due dates.
  - 7 days: Postmortem published and shared with stakeholders; action items entered into the tracking board.

[Egress transit provider dropping 'fragmentation-needed' ICMP causing large HTTP/2 model-shard streams to stall in private deploy]
description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports intermittent stalls when streaming large model shard downloads and long-lived gRPC/http2 connections from their Private deployment. The problem started after an on-prem network change from their transit provider two days ago.

Impact:
- Models fail to fully stream for larger shards (>64KB) causing inference requests to stall and time out after ~30s.
- Affects production traffic for FinData Analytics (private deployment, single VPC peered to our control plane).
- Observed in us-east-1 only.

Environment:
- Private deployment (customer-managed VPC) peered to Redwood control plane via TGW.
- Worker nodes: t3.large-equivalent instances with custom MTU 1500 by default.
- Presigned S3 artifact fetches used with range requests (HTTP/2 multiplexed).

Steps to reproduce (observed by customer):
1) Trigger a model load that requires range fetches (large model shard).
2) Observe initial TLS handshake completes. HTTP/2 connection established.
3) After a few KBs, the download stalls and the HTTP/2 stream is left in a half-open state; no further DATA frames from server are delivered.
4) Retry with smaller range window or reduce request size -> succeeds.

Observed behavior:
- tcpdump on worker shows server sending TCP segments but client stops ACKing after a certain MSS-sized segment. No ICMP "Fragmentation Needed (Type 3, Code 4)" is seen reaching the customer edge.
- When we instrumented a capture at the customer-VM side we do see an ICMP type 3 code 4 originating from the downstream router, but it disappears before reaching the customer's transit provider egress (suggesting provider filtering/rate limit).
- HTTP/2 stream state: initial SETTINGS/HEADERS exchange ok, partial DATA frames delivered, then stall; client eventually times out and triggers a reconnect.

Expected behavior:
- If path MTU requires fragmentation adjustments, ICMP "Fragmentation Needed (Type 3, Code 4)" should be delivered to endpoints so PMTU can adjust and streaming continues without stalls.

Additional logs / captures:
- Attached pcap snippets (provided by customer): "pcap_worker_side.pcap" shows server DATA up to a segment then no further ACK progression.
- Worker logs: serving-runtime reported repeated stream timeouts with code 14 (UNAVAILABLE) and downstream transport errors referencing ECONNRESET after timeouts.
- Console trace: Model shard fetch request id=shard-20260312-34 produced 0 bytes after 18s then retried and succeeded with MTU reduced.

Immediate customer workaround performed:
- Customer set worker node MTU to 1400 (temporary) — this prevented the need for ICMP fragmentation and streaming resumed successfully.

Notes:
- This only reproduces on large sequential downloads (range-based) or larger gRPC frame payloads; small requests and embeddings flows unaffected.
- The control plane auth and presigned URL generation are not implicated (we can generate working presigned URLs that still stall when path MTU issues present).


investigation_notes:
2026-03-12: Initial triage by Support (Aisha). Collected tcpdump + HTTP/2 trace. Customer confirms transit provider changed perimeter firewall/policy on 2026-03-11.
2026-03-12: SRE (Marco) requested pcap from customer and reproduced stalls by issuing range requests to the same object; pcap at worker shows missing ICMP fragments and stalled TCP sequence progression.
2026-03-13: We set up controlled repro from an EC2 in the customer's VPC and instrumented packet captures at three points: (a) worker VM, (b) customer edge router, (c) provider egress (captured by customer but provider did not provide mirrored capture). The VM saw ICMP type 3 code 4 originate from edge router; there is a gap at the provider handoff.
2026-03-13: Opened inbound ticket with customer's transit provider (ticket TP-44821) — provider response indicates they apply ICMP rate-limiting and drop some Type 3 messages under heavy NAT; they are investigating.
2026-03-14: SRE confirmed MTU-lowering on worker (1400) is an effective mitigation. We tested increasing TLS record granularity (server-side capping to 1200) and that also mitigates but requires runtime change.

Hypothesis:
- Transit provider's egress filtering/rate-limiting is preventing delivery of ICMP Fragmentation Needed messages to the customer's VMs, causing PMTU discovery to fail and resulting in a blackhole for packets larger than path MTU. HTTP/2/HTTP/2-over-TLS tends to push larger frames which triggers the failure more evident for large shard downloads.

Next steps / action items:
- SRE: Collect signed pcap evidence to include in provider escalation (assigned Marco Alvarez).
- Support: Document workaround steps for customer (MTU 1400 or server TLS record size cap).
- Customer: Keep transit provider ticket open and request allowing ICMP Type 3 Code 4 or otherwise enable PMTU transparency.
- Product: Consider adding an automatic fallback to smaller TLS record sizes for private deployments when PMTU probes fail (follow-up RFC).

Workaround: Customer lowered worker MTU to 1400 which restored streaming. Alternative workaround: cap TLS record sizes/server-side chunking to avoid packets exceeding Path MTU.
Root cause: Provider-level ICMP (Fragmentation Needed) filtering/rate-limiting preventing PMTU discovery; provider ticket TP-44821 opened by customer.

[On-prem BGP host-route leak routes return traffic to wrong ENI causing presigned artifact fetches to hang and TLS stalls]
description:
Issue summary:
Customer (FintechCo - private deployment) reports intermittent hangs when Redwood serving nodes attempt to download model artifacts using presigned S3 URLs. The control plane shows long-lived TCP sessions without TLS application progress (TLS '0-RTT' or zero-window events observed). Artifact fetches appear to succeed sometimes but intermittently hang in a half-open state for ~30-90s and then recover when connections are retried.

Impact:
- Artifact fetch failures during model start/scale cause model-pull timeouts and degraded request throughput for the customer's private cluster.
- Affected traces show long tail cold-start times and increased request latency.
- Customer-facing: some inference requests returned 502/504 during scale events.

Environment:
- Private deployment (customer-managed VPC peered to Redwood control plane via TGW/VPC peering).
- Region: us-west-2.
- Customer network: on-prem router advertises host-routes into their cloud VPC via BGP over Direct Connect.
- Serving nodes: g4dn-like instances in private subnet behind ENIs.

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) Trigger model scale-up (deploy new model version or restart serving process).
2) Serving node downloads artifact via presigned S3 URL from Redwood artifact storage (control plane presigned URL).
3) TCP connection established, TLS client hello observed from serving node.
4) Server responds; however, return packets for that TCP flow are routed to a different ENI (same AZ but different instance) and do not reach the original socket.
5) Original connection stalls (zero window / retransmits), artifact download times out after retries.
6) If customer BGP peer withdraws the leaked host-route or a quick route flap occurs, flow returns to expected ENI and downloads complete.

Observed behavior / logs / metrics:
- tcpdump from serving node: initial SYN, SYN-ACK, Client Hello, then ACKs continue but no TLS application data progress. Retransmits and duplicated ACKs observed.
- VPC flow logs: packets for response path show destination ENI different from source ENI for the flow hash.
- Control plane log: presigned URL access attempts show CONNECT events with long round-trip and then final timeout at ~45s.
- Customer's edge router BGP table snapshot attached via support upload: shows /32 host routes for specific on-prem IPs leaked into their VPC CIDR.
- Cloud route table snapshot: route priority shows host-routes learned via TGW which take precedence over instance primary subnet routes.

Initial investigation notes:
- Hypothesis A: On-prem BGP speaker is leaking /32 host routes that overlap the ephemeral source addresses used by serving nodes or the artifact endpoints. When those host routes are installed in the VPC/TGW route table, return traffic for specific flows is sent to the on-prem path (or to a different ENI implementing that route) instead of the originating ENI, causing asymmetric routing and TCP stalls.
- Hypothesis B: ECMP/hash interaction with TGW and host-routes causes inconsistent flow steering; the underlay forwards responses to a different instance which lacks the matching socket, leading to RST or retransmits.
- We reproduced asymmetric return path in lab by advertising a /32 host route from a BGP speaker and observing identical stalled TLS behavior.

What we've tried so far:
- Confirmed via tcpdump and VPC flow logs that responses were misrouted to a different ENI.
- Asked customer to temporarily withdraw the leaked host-route; artifact fetches resumed normally.
- Applied temporary iptables DNAT on serving instance to force return path through same ENI (workaround proof-of-concept) — mitigated the stall in short term but not a long-term solution.
- Requested edge team to show BGP config; discovered an automation script leaking host-specific routes for internal monitoring IPs.

Workaround / Mitigation provided to customer:
- Immediate: Withdraw the leaked /32 host route(s) on the on-prem BGP speaker (customer confirmed). Downloads and model pulls recovered within 2 minutes after withdrawal propagated.
- Short-term: Customer to add route-policy on border router to prevent advertising host-prefixed routes into the cloud VPC (explicit deny on /32 / host ranges).
- Temporary: If withdrawal is not possible, configure instance-level source/destination check adjustments plus a NAT gateway path for artifact fetches to ensure symmetric return via NAT. (Documented caveats: may increase cost and change source IP in presigned URL access checks).

Resolution plan / next steps:
- Customer action (required): Implement BGP export filters to block /32 host-route advertisement into their cloud VPC and test route stability for 24 hours.
- Redwood action: Add automated detection to control plane that alerts when a newly learned route is a /32 host route and logs potential asymmetric-route risk for private deployments. Create runbook escalation that correlates flow logs + route table to detect misrouted flows quickly.
- Follow-up change: Investigate whether TGW route priority/longest-prefix interplay can be surfaced in our console for private deployments and flag host-route anomalies.

Postmortem notes / follow-ups assigned:
- Runbook task: NETOPS-129 (create detection playbook and alert).
- Engineering task: INFRA-412 (console UI flag for host-route anomalies and automated heuristic).
- Customer success: CS-74 (confirm customer's BGP filters applied and monitor for 72 hours).

Attachments / references:
- Slack thread: #support-private-deploys (https://slack.redwood.com/archives/C09ABC123)
- tcpdump snippets uploaded to ticket attachments: tcpdump-servingnode-20260312.pcap (redacted)

2026-03-12 15:01 - NETOPS (Liu): Confirmed via VPC flow logs. Flows are returning to an ENI that matches the leaked host route. Customer was asked to withdraw the route — they did and we saw recovery within two minutes.
2026-03-12 16:30 - Customer (FintechCo NetEng, Rajiv): We ran our automation and found an old monitoring script that advertised host-routes for probe IPs. We're rolling a config change to stop advertising those. Requesting recommended verification steps from Redwood.

resolution:
Workaround implemented by customer (removed leaked /32 routes). Long-term fixes planned: BGP export filters on customer border, Redwood detection/alerting for host-route anomalies, and console UI flag. Ticket will be closed after 72-hour quiet window without recurrence.

notes:
This issue differs from typical VPC DNS/TLS/MTU problems: root cause here was route leakage from an on-prem BGP speaker creating asymmetric routing to cloud ENIs, leading to TCP/TLS stalls for long-lived artifact fetch flows. Recommend adding this scenario to our Private Deploy runbook and including it in onboarding checklists for customers using BGP/Direct Connect.

[Conntrack hash rewrite by perimeter firewall causes ephemeral port collisions and OCSP/STS token stalls on private deployment]
description:
Issue summary:\nCustomer reports intermittent control-plane authentication failures and long model download latencies from private deployment behind their perimeter firewall. Failures correlate with bursts of outbound artifact fetches (nightly batch jobs). Impact: model pulls stall, control-plane heartbeats delay, and client token refreshes (STS/OAuth) see multiple retries and occasional 401s.\n\nImpact:\n- Multiple serving nodes in the customer's VPC observed KV cache heartbeats delayed (leading to increased cold starts).\n- Control-plane auth attempts show OCSP lookup timeouts and STS token refresh retries, causing customer application errors and elevated latencies.\n- Reproducible during high parallel shard downloads (batch jobs).\n\nEnvironment:\n- Redwood Private deployment (VPC + VPCE)\n- Customer firewall / NGFW in egress path performing conntrack and port-preserving NAT (partner device vendor: Fortinet 7.x series)\n- Region: us-west-2\n- Affected subset of serving fleet behind NAT64/dual-stack branch office peers.\n\nSteps to reproduce (customer supplied):\n1) Trigger nightly batch that downloads ~500 parallel model shards from S3-presigned URLs via VPCE.\n2) Observe sustained high ephemeral port churn on egress NAT pool for ~5–8 minutes.\n3) During peak, control-plane requests begin retrying; OCSP queries fall back to TCP53; some STS token exchanges report 502/504 timeouts.\n4) After churn subsides, normal operation resumes.\n\nObserved behavior:\n- Conntrack tables on the customer's firewall show high hash bucket collisions and frequent entry churn (logs attached by customer).\n- Firewall rebalancing algorithm appears to rewrite source port hashing (conntrack hash normalization) causing ephemeral source port aliasing between concurrent flows.\n- OCSP/TLS handshakes occasionally return truncated or retried responses; downstream Redwood control-plane logs show 3x increased auth latency and sporadic 401s during the window.\n\nExpected behavior:\n- Egress NAT should preserve unique ephemeral source ports per concurrent flow; no port aliasing between unrelated connections.\n- OCSP and token exchange flows should use stable source ports long enough to complete TCP/TLS handshakes without mid-flow rewrite.\n\nLogs and evidence provided:\n- Packet capture snippets from customer showing SYN/SYN-ACK/SYN duplicate and reused source ports (pcap snippets attached).\n- Firewall conntrack stats: high bucket collision counters and seen ConntrackHashReset events.\n- Redwood control-plane auth traces (trace IDs included) showing timeouts correlated to the time windows.\n\nInitial hypotheses:\n- Perimeter firewall is using a hash normalization/connection-bin collapse algorithm under load that rewrites source-port assignment, causing in-flight collisions and TCP/TLS session disruption for long-lived handshakes (OCSP, STS).\n- Asymmetric routing / ECMP could amplify reuse, but the customer's topology indicates single egress appliance.\n\nWorkaround in place (customer):\n- Customer temporarily reduced parallelism of shard download jobs to limit ephemeral port churn; immediate reduction in failures observed.\n- Customer also applied a short-lived firewall tuning (increase conntrack table size) — mitigates but not a full fix.\n\nRequested action from Redwood Support:\n- Confirm whether control-plane expects consistent source-port behavior for OCSP and STS flows (yes, for some long-lived handshakes we rely on stable TCP/TLS).\n- Provide guidance on defense-in-depth: whether VPCE or service-level retries can be tuned to be more resilient to ephemeral port reassignments, and whether we should add specific retry idempotency headers for presigned artifact downloads.

[TGW IP-in-IP encapsulation + MSS clamping causing TLS record fragmentation and HTTP/2 frame split, corrupting presigned shard downloads]
description:
Issue summary: Customer reports intermittent 403/Range mismatch errors when fetching large sharded model artifacts from Redwood control plane. Failures correlate with network path through customer's Transit Gateway (TGW) where IP-in-IP encapsulation and an inline WAN appliance perform MSS clamping. Impact: model pulls fail during model boot, causing degraded serving and elevated latency for customer-facing inference.

impact:
Model pull failures for ~20% of attempts during nightly scaling; serving nodes fall back to older cached weights, causing slower cold-start and a small percentage of inference errors.

environment_details:
Private deployment with TGW-attached branch sites using IP-in-IP (IPIP) encapsulation for site-to-site tunnels. Egress path traverses branch WAN appliance that applies MSS clamping to avoid PMTU blackhole on legacy MPLS links. Control plane and object storage endpoints reachable via VPCE gateway.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Provision a serving node in customer's private deploy in us-west-2 with model gpt-large-3b-sharded pinned to version v2026-02-28.
2) Trigger a cold start by scaling from 0 -> 3 replicas during nightly batch window (large shard downloads).
3) Observe artifact presigned range GETs failing intermittently with HTTP 206/416/403 or aborted HTTP/2 stream resets in curl/nghttp2 logs when path traverses branch TGW -> appliance -> internet egress.
4) Re-run with tcpdump on serving node and packet capture on branch appliance to correlate MTU, IPIP headers, and TCP segments.
5) Reproduce is time-correlated with branch appliance applying MSS clamp to 1200 bytes for tunneled flows.
6) Disabling IPIP (or bypassing the appliance) removes the failure consistently.

logs:
[serving-node] 2026-03-10T03:14:22Z GET /shards/part-12 Range: bytes=0-1048575 -> HTTP/2 stream error: PROTOCOL_ERROR (frame size mismatch)
[serving-node] 2026-03-10T03:14:23Z curl: (18) transfer closed with outstanding read data
[appliance] 2026-03-10T03:14:21Z TCP: mss clamp applied: original 1460 -> 1200 for conn src=10.1.22.5 dst=54.239.12.10 (IPIP)
[pcap] seq 0x1a2b3c TCP payload sizes: 600, 600, 300 (after IPIP header) -> observed TLS record boundaries crossing frames leading to HTTP/2 HEADERS+DATA split and nghttp2 frame reassembly error

comments:
Aisha Patel (Support) 2026-03-10: Initial triage — customer reports shard validation failures on 0->3 scale-up. Asked for packet captures and appliance config screenshots.
Customer (DataSense SRE) 2026-03-10: Uploaded tcpdump and appliance syslogs to shared S3 (link in ticket). Note: this started after TGW attachment to new branch hub and enabling IPIP with legacy WAN appliance.
Marco Nguyen (SRE) 2026-03-11: Observed consistent MSS clamp to 1200 bytes post-IPIP encapsulation resulting in TLS records spanning multiple TCP segments. Hypothesis: TLS record fragmentation + HTTP/2 frame splitting triggers nghttp2 frame length mismatch leading to stream resets and partial range reads, which artifact client treats as corruption and retries with invalid range -> 416/403.
Marco Nguyen (SRE) 2026-03-11: Requested customer to temporarily disable MSS clamp on appliance or route traffic around the appliance. Customer agreed to test bypass during maintenance window.
Customer (DataSense SRE) 2026-03-12: Bypassed appliance for VPCE egress path during 02:00-03:30 UTC; artifact downloads completed without error for 2000+ pulls. Re-enabling appliance reproduced failures. Will coordinate WAN vendor to change clamp policy.
Marco Nguyen (SRE) 2026-03-12: Created infra PR to add additional guardrails: increase artifact client retry validation, and detect HTTP/2 frame reassembly errors to initiate TLS renegotiation fallback (gh PR #1289).

investigation_notes:
Reproduced locally using network emulation: adding 20 bytes of IPIP header + mss clamp to 1200 reproduces the nghttp2 frame error under HTTP/2 multiplexed shard fetches.
TLS stack (OpenSSL 3.1) preserves record boundaries but TCP segmentization from clamp causes a HEADERS frame split; nghttp2 treats illegal split as PROTOCOL_ERROR.
S3 presigned range behaviour: partial range retries with adjusted Range header contain offset mismatches when client received truncated payload leading to validation checksum mismatch -> server 403 on second attempt (presigned token replay semantics).
No evidence of model artifact corruption on S3 side; validation failures are client-side partial-read reassembly issues.
Related to path MTU/encapsulation interplay; existing docs mention PMTU but not interactions with MSS clamps on encapsulated flows.
Customer TGW route propagation timing and traffic steering to hub appliance exacerbated the window where this surface area affected scale-ups.

resolution:
Workaround: Instructed customer to disable MSS clamping for VPCE-bound flows or to adjust clamp to MTU 1350 (accounting for IPIP overhead) until WAN vendor can patch. Implemented client-side mitigations: increased HTTP/2 reassembly tolerance and added explicit detection of truncated TLS records to trigger connection restart in PR gh.com/redwood/infra/pull/1289. Post-change verification: customer reported 0 failures during bypass window and subsequent test with adjusted clamp=1350 showed successful pulls for 5000 sequential shard downloads.

postmortem_followup:
Confluence runbook update: add section on 'Encapsulation-aware MSS guidance' with recommended clamp values per encapsulation type.
Cloud infra task: add an early-detection metric for nghttp2 PROTOCOL_ERRORs during shard fetches and alert at >0.5% of shard pulls per minute.
Customer-facing docs: updated Private Deploy network checklist to call out TGW+IPIP interactions and VPCE egress validation steps.
Engineering: track gh issue #1290 to harden artifact client reassembly and add a test harness that injects small MTU and encapsulation headers.

[HTTP/2 → HTTP/1.1 proxy translation closes chunked POSTs, causing intermittent model artifact download failures on private deployment]
description:
Issue summary: Customers on Vidra Labs private deployment experience intermittent failures when the control plane or worker nodes attempt to download model artifacts. The failure correlates with an on-prem HTTP proxy that translates inbound HTTP/2 requests to an upstream HTTP/1.1 caching tier.

Impact: Artifact downloads (POST with chunked transfer) fail partway through with connection closed by proxy, causing model pulls to retry and sometimes fall back to older pinned model versions. Customer reports increased cold-start latency and occasional task failures for in-flight inferences.

Environment: Private deployment in customer VPC peered with Redwood private control plane. Traffic path: worker instance -> local HTTP/2 proxy (Envoy-based) -> corporate perimeter appliance -> caching gateway (HTTP/1.1) -> artifact storage. TLS terminates at the Envoy proxy (mTLS to Redwood); downstream hop to caching gateway is plaintext HTTP/1.1.

Observed behavior: Upstream (artifact storage) logs show truncated POST bodies. Worker-side error messages: "EOF during chunked upload" and gRPC error code UNAVAILABLE when fetching artifacts over our artifact-fetcher service. The proxy logs show it rewrites HTTP/2 frames to HTTP/1.1 and then emits a "downstream connection closed" after a short idle during chunked transfer. No consistent packet loss or conntrack exhaustion observed.

Expected behavior: Chunked POSTs should be translated to chunked Transfer-Encoding: chunked on HTTP/1.1 without terminating the connection mid-stream. Model artifact download should complete reliably.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Deploy private worker in Vidra Labs prod-us-west with artifact_fetcher enabled and model version set to 'redwood-compat-v1'
2) Simulate cold start by clearing local cache and trigger a model pull via a single long-running inference that causes a chunked POST of 50+ MB
3) Observe worker-side logs for 'EOF during chunked upload' and artifact-fetcher retries
4) Correlate with proxy logs showing HTTP/2 -> HTTP/1.1 translation and an upstream connection close during request body streaming

logs:
worker: 2026-03-10T14:22:11Z artifact-fetcher ERROR fetch failed: rpc error: code = Unavailable desc = transport is closing
envoy-proxy: 2026-03-10T14:22:11Z warning HTTP/1.1 upstream closed while decoding request body
upstream-cache: 2026-03-10T14:22:11Z warning truncated request body, bytes_received=2374184 expected=52428800

investigation_notes:
03/10 - Initial triage by support: Reproduced failure in customer test harness. Failures only when proxy translation is in the path; bypassing the corporate perimeter (direct routing to upstream gateway) completes successfully.
03/11 - SRE ran tcpdump on worker and observed continuous TCP stream until proxy signals FIN; no resets visible on worker side. Packet sizes consistent with HTTP/2 DATA frames prior to proxy. Suggests translation layer triggers close upstream.
03/11 - Inspected Envoy config provided by customer: http2 to http1 bridge uses 'half-close' semantics with idle_timeout=30s. Customer reported intermittent pauses in chunks caused by their gateway's per-connection throughput shaping (bursts). Combination likely triggers idle timeout on bridge and results in upstream close.
03/12 - Reproduced with a local Envoy + a simulated HTTP/1.1 gateway that intentionally delays chunk bodies: when delayed beyond 25s gap between data frames, Envoy bridge issues a downstream idle close, upstream receives truncated body. This matches customer symptom timing.
03/12 - Hypothesis: Envoy's default idle/stream timeouts for bridging HTTP/2->HTTP/1.1 consider gaps between HTTP/2 DATA frames as idle and close the stream; an intermediate gateway that buffers/delays chunk flushes causes bridging timeout and upstream close, leading to EOF on worker.

workaround:
Customer temporarily disabled the HTTP/2->HTTP/1.1 translation for artifact endpoints by adding a bypass route on their perimeter appliance. This allowed direct HTTP/2 to upstream gateway (or direct https) and eliminated truncation. Alternative workaround: increase envoy 'stream_idle_timeout' and 'idle_timeout' values on the translation proxy to >90s and disable half-close behavior for artifact endpoints.

resolution:
In Progress - No permanent fix applied yet. Recommended permanent mitigations:
1) Customer to update Envoy translation config for artifact endpoints: set stream_idle_timeout to 120s and 'drop_idle_connection' to false for the route handling large chunked uploads.
2) Add explicit keepalive/ping from worker during long uploads to prevent perceived idle gaps.
3) Long-term: update artifact-fetcher to use ranged GET with retry-friendly semantics for large artifacts instead of chunked POST where possible.

Next steps:
- Diego to coordinate with Vidra networking team to schedule a change window to adjust Envoy timeouts (ETA 2026-03-15).
- Platform engineering to evaluate making artifact fetch use range-based GETs (RFC/PR created: see related_github_prs).

[Compact Shift Digest: Contextual Alert Summaries & Postmortem Shortcuts]
description:

Current incident tiles in the console are too verbose, require multiple clicks to reach runbooks/postmortems, and do not surface SLO delta context alongside cost/latency trends. Goal: Design a compact 'Shift Digest' card that surfaces the top 3 active alerts, an SLO delta sparkline, quick actions (acknowledge, escalate, snooze), and a one-click Postmortem/Runbook shortcut. The digest should fit in a single-line card for lists and expand into a contextual drawer without losing keyboard focus. Key UX properties: - density: compact by default; expanded drawer for deep actions - contextual linking: direct link to latest postmortem for an alert when available - SLO delta: small sparkline with hover tooltip for 1h/6h/24h - cost awareness: optional token showing recent cost delta for the service - privacy: redact sensitive incident metadata in shift exports - keyboard-first: first-class quick actions via single-key hotkeys - performance constraint: avoid loading full postmortem or heavy SLO queries on list render (use cached payloads and lazy fetch)

acceptance_criteria:
Compact Shift Digest card shows up to 3 top alerts with severity badges and short summaries (<=80 chars)
Each alert row has an inline SLO delta sparkline and a one-click Postmortem shortcut when a postmortem exists

Quick actions (Acknowledge/Escalate/Snooze) available from collapsed state via kebab menu or keyboard hotkeys
Design includes microcopy for privacy mode and export behavior; meets AA color contrast for badges and actions

Hand-off flows include links to the canonical postmortem doc, related GitHub PRs, and the incident timeline URL
Engineering design notes include caching strategy and fallback behavior if SLO query times out

Use sparklines for SLO deltas instead of numeric-only deltas to give trend context at a glance
Expose postmortem shortcut only when a linked postmortem exists; otherwise show 'File postmortem' CTA
Avoid preloading full postmortem bodies on list render to reduce load; use cached metadata and lazy fetch on expand
Built-in keyboard shortcuts (A = acknowledge, E = escalate, S = snooze) to reduce mouse travel during handoff

[Compact Cluster Network Health & Cost Insights: compact dashboard prototype for Private/VPC clusters]
description:
Design and prototype a compact cluster-level dashboard card that surfaces networking health, upgrade status, and per-cluster cost insights for Private/VPC deployments. The card should be usable on the cluster listing page and in a cluster detail header; it must be compact, scannable, and actionable with RBAC-aware quick actions (drain, drain-and-upgrade, open network debug).

background:
Teams running Redwood Private want a single glance view that shows whether a cluster's network configuration and connectivity are healthy, whether any nodes are mid-upgrade, and a lightweight cost estimate for that cluster. Current console pages are large and siloed (separate network topology, cluster status, and cost pages). This ticket aims to consolidate key signals into a single compact UI card to reduce context switching.

goals:
Create a compact card (desktop and wide tablet) that fits on cluster list rows and on cluster overview header
Surface three primary signals: Network Health, Upgrade Status, Estimated 24h Cost
Provide two contextual quick actions with permission gating: Open Network Debug, Start Cluster Upgrade (canary)
Ensure data freshness indicators and fallback states for disconnected control planes
Prototype interactions for inline rollouts status and cost breakdown hover

non_goals:
Replace full topology canvas or deep cost reports
Implement full RBAC backend (this ticket is design + front-end prototype; engineering will wire auth)

proposed_components:
Compact card layout (left: 48px cluster badge + name; center: three horizontal mini-tiles; right: quick actions)
Network Health mini-tile: color-coded band + micro-sparkline for packet loss/latency
Upgrade Status mini-tile: small progress bar + textual state (Idle / Canary / Rolling / Failed)
Cost mini-tile: estimated 24h USD + percent change vs baseline
Hover panel: expanded cost breakdown and last 5 rollout events
AR/AT (accessibility) labels for all status indicators and tooltips

prototypes:
Figma: https://www.figma.com/file/abcd1234/compact-cluster-network-cost-dashboard
Clickable prototype (play): https://www.figma.com/proto/abcd1234/cluster-compact-play
Front-end demo branch: https://github.com/redwood-inference/console/pull/2784 (WIP)
Design spec (Confluence): https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENG/pages/78901234/Compact+Cluster+Card+Spec

usability_notes:
Prefer short numeric values (e.g., 12ms / 0.03% packet loss) with tooltips for trend context
Default to aggregated cluster-level health; allow drill into node list from hover
When control plane unreachable show 'stale' badge and last-seen timestamp
Test compact card at 820px width (cluster list) and 1280px (cluster header)

engineering_feedback:
ENG review 2026-03-02: backend must expose node-level latency histogram and a cluster-level aggregate to avoid per-cluster O(N) calls
ENG note: cost estimate should be computed server-side and cached for 5 minutes to keep API load reasonable
Infra concern: network health metrics rely on synthetic probes that currently run every 30s; consider adding last_probe_age field
Security: quick actions must call endpoints that validate RBAC and MFA status for destructive ops

design_decisions:
Use 3-tile layout to maximize scannability and reuse on list and detail pages
Color semantics: green/yellow/red with accessibility-contrast-checked icons (not color-only), and numeric text
Show cost as a lightweight estimate (rounded) with a hover showing amplification factors (gpu-hours, storage)
Keep topology link separate from card to avoid rendering heavy canvases in list views

risks:
Misleading cost estimates if customers have custom billing adjustments; include 'estimate' label prominently
Premature exposure of sensitive network metadata; omit IP-level details in list view
Overloading the card with metrics causes cognitive noise; prioritize three primary signals

Incident learnings: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENG/pages/654321/Cluster+network+outage+postmortem
