[Surface Pro (ARM) dual-radio metric flip during roam causes WireGuard split-tunnel to lose internal routes]
description:
Issue summary: Multiple Surface Pro (ARM) devices reporting sudden loss of access to internal services immediately after roaming between 2.4GHz and 5GHz SSIDs. VPN (WireGuard) remains 'connected' but traffic to internal subnets (10.10.0.0/16) no longer flows. Impact: several engineers working on private repos and internal dashboards were blocked. Scope: 6 confirmed machines in SF office, same Wi-Fi AP cluster, mixed OS build 22H2 on ARM.

Expected behaviour: roam completes, VPN stays connected and internal routes remain pinned via split-tunnel rules.

Observed behaviour: after roam, Windows chooses different physical adapter and flips interface metrics; WireGuard continues with handshake but system route table places default for internal subnets via physical adapter that has no corporate VLAN reachability, causing traffic to leave on guest VLAN and be dropped by edge firewall.


steps_to_reproduce:
1) Start WireGuard client connected to corporate split-tunnel config (internal subnets pinned).
2) On Surface Pro ARM device, trigger 2.4GHz->5GHz roam (walk between APs or toggle radio to force handoff).
3) Observe Windows network interface metric and route table immediately after roam (use `Get-NetIPInterface` / `route print`).
4) Attempt to reach internal service (e.g., git.redwood.internal:22 or 10.10.5.12) — connect fails despite WireGuard reported as connected.
5) Compare traffic path with packet capture on client (Wireshark) and AP logs.
6) Reboot or manually set interface metric back and confirm connectivity returns.

logs:
Selected excerpts: 
- WireGuard status: peer=corp-peer latest-handshake=0s transfer=12.4 MiB/1.2 MiB
- Windows Event Log (NetworkProfile) 2026-02-24 09:18:12: Interface metric changed: InterfaceIndex=23 old=25 new=2
- netsh interface ip show config (post-roam): Ethernet 23 (Wi-Fi-5G): Metric 2, IPv4 DHCP, DNS suffix not set
- route print (post-roam): 10.10.0.0 mask 255.255.0.0 192.168.50.1 if 23 metric 2
- AP Controller logs: client A: roam success to AP-B bssid=aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff, assigned VLAN guest (300) due to NDP mismatch


investigation_notes:
2026-02-24 09:40 - Triage: Confirmed 3 devices reproducing sequence in SF office. WireGuard shows active encryption, but system route points to wrong gateway (guest VLAN). Hypothesis: driver or Windows automatic metric change after roam causing routes to prefer a non-corporate interface.
2026-02-24 11:15 - Network Eng (Diego): AP controller performed VLAN reassignment for those client sessions on roam due to sticky client policy; observed DHCP lease refresh mapping client to guest VLAN for short window (30s) before corporate VLAN restored.
2026-02-24 14:05 - Windows sysadmin (Liam): Verified Windows behavior: on ARM build 22H2 with specific Qualcomm driver v4.2.0.13, `Automatic metric` flag toggles on roam, recalculating interface metric and reordering route table. Confirmed that persistent split-tunnel routes remain but traffic egresses via interface with lower metric to non-corporate gateway.
2026-02-25 09:12 - Repro test: Disabled 'EnableReassociation' on AP and forced roam — metric flip still occurs but VLAN remains corporate; suggests dual contribution: both AP transient VLAN assignment and client metric recalculation necessary to cause outage.
2026-02-26 10:00 - Vendor engagement: Opened ticket with Qualcomm driver team; they acknowledged a known issue where NDIS 6.70 events trigger metric recalculation on 802.11r handoff for certain NIC firmware. Vendor provided a beta driver that pins interface metric.
2026-02-27 16:30 - Mitigation test: Applied local Group Policy (script) to set interface metrics to higher priority for corporate SSID; confirmed successful mitigation on 5 test devices.
2026-03-01 08:00 - Rollout: Deployed updated WireGuard client (1.2.3) which ignores ephemeral route replacements for pinned subnets, and pushed GPO to fleet to set explicit interface metrics for corporate SSIDs. Monitoring shows no recurrences in SF cluster after change.

comments:
Asha Patel (2026-02-24 09:25): Reported by eng team after losing access to internal dashboards post-meeting roam. Attached Wireshark capture and `route print`.
Support - Liam O'Connor (2026-02-24 09:35): Acknowledged, investigating. Asking for affected device model list and timestamps.
Network - Diego Ramos (2026-02-24 11:20): Looked into AP controller logs; saw transient VLAN assignment during reassoc. Noted sticky-client policy triggered on AP-B.
QA - Mei Chen (2026-02-25 10:10): Reproduced with debug build; metric flips observed only on Qualcomm NICs on ARM Surface. Intel x86 devices unaffected.
Qualcomm Vendor Rep (2026-02-26 13:04): Confirmed similar reports; provided driver beta and will include long-term fix in upcoming firmware.
Liam O'Connor (2026-02-27 17:00): Deployed GPO with interface metric script to 200-device pilot (SF office + remote ARM devices). Please validate if anyone still sees issue.
Asha Patel (2026-03-01 08:12): Confirmed fixed for previously impacted machines. Thanks for the quick turnaround.

resolution:
Root cause: Interaction between AP controller transient VLAN reassignment during roam and Qualcomm Wi-Fi NDIS driver behavior on ARM devices that triggers automatic interface metric recalculation. This allowed split-tunnel routes to be overshadowed by a lower-metric gateway on the guest VLAN.

Immediate remediation: 1) Deployed a client-side mitigation: Group Policy to set explicit interface metric for corporate SSID and a PowerShell script to re-assert routes for 10.10.0.0/16 on network change. 2) Updated WireGuard client to 1.2.3 which rejects ephemeral route replacements for pinned subnets. 3) Adjusted AP controller sticky-client policy to avoid transient VLAN flips during 802.11r handoffs on the affected AP cluster.

Permanent fix / follow-up: Qualcomm to release driver firmware with NDIS fix (vendor ticket QC-29812). IT will monitor and schedule driver rollout after vendor QA. Created follow-up internal task INT-356802 to track vendor driver validation and fleet upgrade.

[Intermittent SF HQ Wi-Fi disconnects and corporate VPN DNS resolution failures (split-tunnel)]
description:
Issue summary:
Multiple SF office users report intermittent Wi-Fi disconnects over the past 48 hours. Users who subsequently reconnect via the corporate VPN experience DNS resolution failures for internal services (e.g., vault.redwood.local, internal-console.redwood.local). Root cause unknown; appears correlated with a configuration change on the office firewall or DHCP/DNS behavior when clients switch networks.

Impact:
- ~12-18 users affected sporadically during business hours (engineering, sales desks on 4th floor).
- Developers cannot access internal-only services after connecting to VPN until DNS cache/route is cleared or laptop rebooted.
- Productivity impact: medium-high during intermittent windows.

Environment:
- SF HQ office Wi-Fi (SSIDs: Redwood-Employee, Redwood-Guest) managed by Meraki MS/ MR stack behind Palo Alto PA-5260 firewall.
- Corporate VPN: OpenVPN server cluster (private), split-tunnel enabled for internet traffic; internal subnets routed via VPN.
- Timeframe first reports: 2026-03-09 09:40 PST.

Observed behavior:
- Wi-Fi disconnects: client reports 'Disconnected' then reconnects to same SSID; DHCP lease renewals logged on Meraki controller.
- After rejoin and VPN connect: client resolves public DNS but not internal short names; nslookup against 10.0.0.10 (internal DNS) times out intermittently.
- Some clients require ipconfig/flushdns + dhclient restart or full reboot to restore internal name resolution.

Expected behavior:
- Seamless reconnection to Wi-Fi and VPN without loss of internal DNS resolution; split-tunnel should still route internal domains to 10.0.0.10 DNS.

Temporary workaround:
- Instruct affected users to run: "sudo systemd-resolve --flush-caches" (Linux) or "ipconfig /flushdns" (Windows) and then restart the VPN client. Reboot if that fails.

Notes about scope:
- Guest SSID is unaffected. Wired clients do not report issues. Problem appears tied to Wi-Fi client state transitions and DNS server reachability immediately after VPN bring-up.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Connect a laptop to Redwood-Employee SSID in SF HQ (4th floor).
2) Authenticate and obtain DHCP lease.
3) Establish OpenVPN connection with split-tunnel enabled.
4) Attempt to resolve an internal hostname (vault.redwood.local) or access internal-console URL.
5) If Wi-Fi disconnects and reconnects during the session, note DNS failures immediately after reconnection.

Observed: DNS timeouts or NXDOMAIN for internal names until local cache cleared or network restarted.

logs:
Meraki event snippets (times in PST):
- 2026-03-09T09:38:12: Client AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF association failure: DHCP timeout
- 2026-03-09T09:38:19: Client AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF re-associated, DHCP assigned 10.88.45.102

OpenVPN client log (example):
- Tue Mar 09 09:39:05 2026 ERROR: RESOLVE: Cannot resolve host address: 10.0.0.10: DNS lookup failed
- Tue Mar 09 09:39:07 2026 NOTE: sequence of routes added: 10.0.0.0/16 -> tun0
- Tue Mar 09 09:39:08 2026 WARNING: DNS push failed, fallback to system resolver

System DNS resolution trace (from affected laptop):
- dig +short @10.0.0.10 vault.redwood.local -> ;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached
- dig +short @1.1.1.1 vault.redwood.local -> 203.0.113.50 (public) -> incorrect; internal name leaked to public resolver

investigation_notes:
- 2026-03-10: Support confirmed 12 initial reports from SF; reproduced on MacBook Pro (macOS 13.6) and Ubuntu 22.04.
- Hypothesis 1: Meraki controller DHCP reassignments are briefly dropping local route advertisement; clients rebind with DNS search domain lost.
- Hypothesis 2: Palo Alto firewall policy update (2026-03-09 02:00 UTC) altered NAT rules for split-tunnel, causing internal DNS traffic to be NATed to public interface resulting in dropped packets.
- Collected packet captures from affected client (pcap attached to INT-4102) showing DNS queries leaving tun0 but no replies from 10.0.0.10 during failure window.
- Verified OpenVPN server config pushes DNS 10.0.0.10 and route 10.0.0.0/16; server logs show successful push but some clients log 'DNS push failed'.
- Meraki telemetry shows spikes in DHCP handshake failures coincident with the times users reported drops (see Meraki dashboard link).
- Quick test: creating a temporary static DNS entry in laptop /etc/hosts allowed access to internal-console immediately after reconnect, indicating name resolution is primary failure, not routing entirely.

comments:
Aisha Patel (2026-03-10 10:02 PST): Notified office support desk to collect affected MACs and seat locations. Pls escalate to networking team - several engineers blocked.
Diego Alvarez (2026-03-10 11:45 PST): I pulled PA firewall audit logs for 2026-03-09 01:30-03:30 UTC. Found a config commit at 2026-03-09 02:05 UTC titled 'egress nat policy tweak' by network-admin. Will coordinate rollback window.
Morgan Chen (SRE) (2026-03-10 12:10 PST): Packet captures received (linked INT-4102). I see DNS queries to 10.0.0.10 with no response; traceroutes show tun0 present. Suggest testing with split-tunnel disabled to confirm whether issue is DNS over VPN only.
Diego Alvarez (2026-03-11 09:08 PST): Rolled back the egress NAT change in a controlled window (09:00-09:15 PST). Post-rollback initial checks show fewer DNS timeouts; monitoring continues.
Riley Brooks (Office IT) (2026-03-12 16:20 PST): Collected additional user reports after rollback — two users still had problems after afternoon hotspot maintenance. We swapped APs for those desks; both recovered. Could be flaky AP and concurrent firewall change made it visible.
Diego Alvarez (2026-03-14 08:39 PST): Follow-up: request to schedule a deeper config audit for Meraki <-> Palo Alto interactions and to add a health-check monitor for internal DNS reachability over VPN. Assigned INT-4199 for monitoring task.

next_steps:
1) Run controlled tests with split-tunnel disabled on a set of affected clients to confirm DNS behavior (SRE + Networking).
2) Audit Meraki DHCP lease churn on 4th floor APs and check for firmware updates; replace flaky APs (Office IT).
3) Add active health check that queries internal DNS (10.0.0.10) over VPN for SF office and alert on failures (Monitoring / Observability).
4) Create a firewall rule test plan: replay NAT change in staging and validate DNS packet handling (Network team).
5) Follow-up ticket INT-4199 created for long-term monitoring and INT-4200 for Meraki firmware rollout.

resolution:
In progress - temporary rollback of egress NAT rule reduced incidents. Ongoing follow-ups: AP replacements and DNS health-checks scheduled. No permanent root-cause confirmed yet.

[Mesh AP band-steer + DHCP suppression causes VPN (WireGuard) handshake stall during client roaming]
synthesis:
Summary: Several employees on the SF office mesh network report short (5-20s) VPN stalls when their device transitions between APs or switches bands. The corporate WireGuard-based zero-trust agent fails to re-establish a fully functional tunnel promptly; upper-layer connections stall and some TCP flows reset. Issue appears correlated with mesh band-steering + DHCP lease behavior when the AP suppresses DHCP renewals during fast L2 handover.

impact:
Multiple employees are losing access to internal services briefly during office roaming/hotdesk movements. Affects developer productivity (git pushes/timeouts) and internal dashboards for ~5-10% of devices observed in sampling. Not a full outage but disruptive to interactive workflows.

description:
Issue summary:
- Symptom: During roaming or when client is steered between 5GHz and 2.4GHz SSIDs by the mesh controller, the WireGuard tunnel remains in a 'connected' state but user traffic stalls for 5-20s. After stall, traffic resumes without user intervention.
- Observed at: SF office, floor A-corridor, APs: mesh-zone-3 & mesh-zone-4.
- Client platforms: macOS 13/14, Windows 11, Android 12/13.
- Temporary workaround: manual disable/enable of Wi-Fi or force-wireguard-restart on some clients.

Why this is notable: The agent stays 'up' and handshake messages continue intermittently, but route or DNS state on the client is inconsistent which blocks traffic until timers expire or agent resets. This differs from a full tunnel down (no peer).

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Join corporate SSID on a device near mesh-zone-3 (5GHz). 2) Walk towards coverage overlap with mesh-zone-4 where controller enforces band-steer to 2.4GHz. 3) Observe short stall in ssh/git/IDE connections. 4) Run tcpdump on client or capture wireguard logs. 5) Repeat with DHCP debug logging enabled on AP controller.

observed_behavior:
- TCP flows show long retransmit bursts then a few successful packets; many sessions reset by client apps.
- WireGuard user-space logs show repeated keepalive packets from client but no immediate rekey/handshake; peer keeps old endpoint for ~8-12s.
- Client DNS resolver cache shows transient inability to resolve internal hostnames until /etc/resolv.conf (or equivalent) rebinds to correct DNS server.
- DHCP logs on controller show 'suppressed renewal' events during handover windows.

expected_behavior:
During fast AP transition the zero-trust agent should quickly rebind routes, maintain peer endpoint mapping, and internal DNS should remain reachable without stall longer than normal roaming (<1s).

logs:
Sample client log (macOS) excerpt:
[2026-03-10T09:12:11.123Z] wg-quick[pid]: Sending keepalive to 52.36.91.12:51820
[2026-03-10T09:12:11.130Z] kernel: en0: link state change, BSSID switch
[2026-03-10T09:12:11.140Z] resolver[scutil]: DNS servers updated -> 10.0.5.2 (suppressed)
[2026-03-10T09:12:18.450Z] wg-quick: handshake attempt failed: timeout waiting for response
[2026-03-10T09:12:21.678Z] app/browser: tcp retransmit, 8 retries

Controller DHCP excerpt:
2026-03-10 09:12:11 SLOW_RENEW client=AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF suppressed renewal during fast roam to mesh-zone-4
2026-03-10 09:12:20 RENEW_GRANTED client=AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF lease=10.0.5.123

WireGuard capture (server side):
10:12:11.123 IP 10.0.5.123.51820 > 52.36.91.12.51820: IP payload (keepalive)
10:12:18.430 IP 10.0.5.123.51820 > 52.36.91.12.51820: UDP, len 60 (retransmit)


investigation_notes:
Actions taken so far:
- Collected pcap from client and server (tcpdump -i en0 'port 51820') and compared timestamps.
- Reproduced with macOS and Surface; both show same pattern.
- Verified mesh controller is configured for aggressive band-steer and has DHCP 'suppress renewals' option enabled to reduce DHCP storm during roam.
- Tested disabling suppression on a staging AP — when suppression disabled, client roam completed with <1s stall.
- Hypothesis: DHCP suppression delays client refresh of DHCP options (DNS and route push), leaving resolver pointed at an AP-local DNS proxy that is momentarily unreachable, while WireGuard keepalives continue but subsequent traffic fails until lease/route state is reconciled.
- Additional hypothesis: AP's client isolation during micro-handoff briefly blocks UDP flows from reaching local gateway, causing WG handshake timeouts and route flaps.
- Slack thread: #it-support with captures: https://slack.redwood.com/archives/C0FFEE12/p1678470000000
- Related infra PR to change AP DHCP behavior: github.com/redwood/infrastructure/infra-config/pull/1983
- Reproduction notes: increase AP roam aggressiveness and enable DHCP suppression to trigger in ~3/5 attempts.

temporary_workaround:
1) Disable aggressive band-steer on affected APs (mesh controller setting).
2) If user affected, instruct to toggle Wi-Fi or restart zero-trust agent; this rebinds routes.
3) Short-term: reduce DHCP suppression timer on controller for office zones.
Workaround status: controller change rolled to mesh-zone-4 for experiment; preliminary reduction in reports.

next_steps:
- Coordinate with network team to roll a config change that reduces DHCP suppression window in high-roam areas.
- Evaluate firmware patch or controller upgrade that alters client path pinning during handover.
- Add targeted telemetry to zero-trust agent to surface endpoint rebind events and DNS switch events for future triage.
- Create follow-up INT to track rollout of config across sites if experiment successful.
- Notify workspace ops to monitor for collateral increase in DHCP traffic.

comments:
Ava Park (reporter) 2026-03-10: Collected 5 captures, all show the same 8-12s stall window. User reports 2-3 incidents/day while hot-desking.
Liam Chen (assignee) 2026-03-11: Confirmed reproducible. Disabled suppression on mesh-zone-4 and stalled reproductions dropped from ~60% to ~10% in 30 trials. Need ops signoff for broader rollout.
Nina Patel (network) 2026-03-12: Controller change proposal: reduce suppression window from 10s to 1s for office zones tagged 'high-roam'. Opens possible DHCP storm; will add rate-limiter. Planning canary of 3 APs.
SRE (2026-03-13): Observed no increase in DHCP requests post-canary. WireGuard server logs show handshake latency drop from median 9.8s -> 0.9s for canary clients.

[Office Wi‑Fi client aggregation interacts with NAT timeouts causing ephemeral port reuse and SSH connection resets to internal hosts]
description:
Several engineers in the SF office reported intermittent SSH resets and failures when connecting to internal build hosts (10.3.4.0/22) while connected to the corporate Wi‑Fi. Connections over wired ethernet to the same hosts are stable. Initial hypothesis: wireless aggregation/A-MPDU interaction with the branch NAT and our UDP hole-punching for VPN is leading to ephemeral port reuse and mid-session TCP/SSH resets.

impact:
Multiple engineering users in office unable to maintain stable SSH sessions to internal build/test infrastructure. CI jobs running from laptops occasionally drop during deploys. Affects productivity; no public customer impact detected.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Connect a laptop to corp‑wifi (SF office, 802.11ax APs). 2) Establish site-to-site VPN via corporate edge (WireGuard client from laptop). 3) SSH to an internal build host behind branch NAT (10.3.4.x). 4) Start an interactive session and run a long-running command (e.g., tail -f + large scp). 5) Observe intermittent SSH disconnects after ~300-1200s. Repeat with wired ethernet — issue does not reproduce.

observed_behavior:
SSH sessions drop with 'Connection reset by peer' or 'Broken pipe'. netstat on branch edge shows ephemeral port mappings being reclaimed and reused rapidly. AP telemetry shows high A-MPDU aggregation sizes and bursty TX patterns for affected clients. NAT table entries time out unusually quickly for UDP/VPN flows on the branch gateway during the bursts.

expected_behavior:
SSH sessions should remain stable over Wi‑Fi; NAT should preserve ephemeral mappings for the negotiated lifetime; wireless aggregation should not trigger premature NAT eviction.

logs:
branch-gateway/syslog: Mar 10 10:42:11 natd[1223]: evicting entry UDP 10.3.4.23:51734 -> 34.67.12.9:51820 (age 8s)
ap-telemetry: client 02:11:22:33:44:55 a-mpdu: avg 64k, bursts: 12 in 60s
laptop dmesg: wireguard: peer 34.67.12.9 handshake OK; keepalive every 25s
ssh client: Mar 10 10:49:21 packet_write_wait: Connection to 10.3.4.45 port 22: Broken pipe

investigation_notes:
- Reproduced with two different laptop models and two different APs in SF office.
- Packet captures show that when AP sends large aggregated frames, bursts of ACK-less UDP keepalives are delayed (driver coalescing), causing branch gateway to see no activity for VPN UDP mapping and prune it.
- NAT eviction policy on branch gateway uses inactivity thresholds of 10s for UDP by default; aggressive pruning combined with delayed keepalives leads to a race where ephemeral ports are reclaimed and later reassigned to new flows. When reassigned, inbound packets land on the wrong TCP tuple causing upstream TCP resets.
- Wired path shows no aggregation; keepalives are timely and NAT entries persist.
- Configuring laptop wireguard keepalive to 10s reduced occurrence but did not eliminate it under heavy aggregation bursts.
- No related recent code deploys in networking infra; change window: AP firmware update two weeks ago that enabled higher TX aggregation sizes on 802.11ax under heavy client load.
- Correlated increase in incidents with AP firmware rollouts (ticket AP-FW-2026-02-25).

actions_taken:
1) Temporarily adjusted branch NAT UDP inactivity timeout from 10s -> 60s for SF office gateway (mitigated immediate flapping).
2) Contacted wireless team to throttle A-MPDU max aggregation per-client to default levels on affected APs (rolled back recent aggressive setting).
3) Recommended laptop-side workarounds: set WireGuard PersistentKeepalive to 15s and reduce driver TX coalescing (sysctl/net driver knobs) where feasible.
4) Scheduled follow-up: firmware vendor validation of aggregation vs keepalive interplay and vendor bug report ID: VENDOR-1823.

Mitigation applied: NAT UDP inactivity timeout increased and AP aggregation parameter rolled back. Short-term workaround documented for engineers (set persistent keepalive). Long-term fixes: vendor patch expected to address interaction; plan to add a NAT heuristic to avoid reclaiming recently used UDP mappings for flows identified as VPN tunnels.

- Implement NAT heuristics in branch gateway to detect and protect VPN UDP mappings.

[Sticky captive portal sessions keep devices on guest VLAN, causing split-tunnel VPN traffic failures]
description:
Issue summary: Several employees report intermittent failures when their MacBooks (macOS 13/14) connect to the corporate wifi after being offsite or using a hotspot. Affected devices appear to remain on the guest VLAN with a captive-portal binding even after successful SSO authentication, so split-tunnel VPN traffic to internal services is routed incorrectly and is blocked by firewall rules.

Impact: ~12 users in the SF office and some remote users experienced loss of access to internal services (internal API, dev dashboards) while appearing connected to wifi and VPN. Productivity impact for those users is high; they must use mobile hotspot or wired connection to restore full access.

Environment: Production corporate SSID (corp-ssid) with per-user auth and split-tunnel VPN policy. Wireless controller version 8.2.3, AP firmware 5.14, firewall NAT and conntrack on edge appliances. Mac clients (macOS 13/14) and a handful of Linux laptops observed.

Observed behavior: After SSO success users still get an HTTP redirect to captive portal for some internal addresses; VPN establishes but internal traffic is NAT'd on guest VLAN and firewall denies it. Wireless controller console shows a persistent captive-session mapping tied to client MAC that is not cleared by reauth or DHCP renew.

Expected behavior: Successful auth moves client to corporate VLAN, split-tunnel routes internal destinations over the corporate path and the VPN tunnel as expected.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Join corp-ssid from macOS 14 client that was previously connected to guest or a different AP.
2) Authenticate via SSO captive portal when prompted (Microsoft SSO).
3) Observe client receives corporate VLAN IP and attempts to start split-tunnel VPN (WireGuard).
4) Attempt to access internal API (https://internal.api.redwood/) — client is redirected to captive portal instead of receiving a 200, and packets show NAT via guest VLAN.
5) Check wireless controller: captive session entry remains bound to MAC and AP, even after reauth, DHCP renew, and client roaming.

investigation_notes:
Initial triage (Support): Confirmed pattern across multiple users, reproduced on macOS 13 and 14 with vendor APs in SF office.
Wireless team (Lucas Ortega): Controller shows captive-session sticky flag set; controller config has 'sticky-client' enabled for faster roaming. Suspect sticky assignment kept client on guest VLAN when AP switched contexts.
SRE (Priya Rao): Conntrack entries on the firewall showed NAT mapping to guest-zone IPs. Long conntrack timeouts (~600s) mean stale NAT mappings persist after VLAN move.
Hypothesis: Combination of controller's sticky-client + aggressive AP band-steering + long conntrack NAT timeouts leads to clients being authenticated but their IP/MAC binding still associated with guest-zone NAT path, causing split-tunnel traffic to be misrouted/blocked.
Packet captures: Showed SYNs from client going out with guest-zone source IP and firewall dropping because policy expects corporate subnet. AP logs indicate an incomplete VLAN reassignment event followed by auth success.
Reproduce notes: Forcing DHCP release on client occasionally clears the state; disabling sticky-client on a test AP prevented the issue during a 4-hour window.
Temporary mitigation attempted: Reduced conntrack timeout for established TCP from 600s to 120s on edge firewall (quick test) — some clients recovered after timeout expiry; not ideal for long-term.
Controller vendor advised there is a known edge-case with sticky-client and captive portal handoff in firmware <=5.14; recommended firmware 5.16+ where captive mappings are cleared on VLAN change.
User impact estimate: ~0.5% of daily connections based on AP session logs over last 48 hours, concentrated in SF and some remote clients using hotspot-to-wifi handover.

Workaround applied: disabled sticky-client on affected AP groups and reduced firewall conntrack timeout to 180s to reduce impact while vendor firmware upgrade is scheduled. Long-term fix: staged AP firmware upgrade to 5.16 and enable controller option to clear captive-session on VLAN change. Follow-up action: verify rollout during maintenance window and monitor session churn metrics for 72 hours.

[soft-termination-tombstone-and-resume-negotiator-openai-compat]
description:
Context and motivation: Streaming client disconnects during multi-step tool/function calls result in partial side-effects and poor developer experience: clients either lose progress or trigger duplicate tool calls on reconnect. This PR introduces a soft-termination 'tombstone' mechanism plus a handshake-based resume negotiator so clients can rejoin or safely abort without inducing duplicate effects. This is implemented as a compatibility-layer extension (opt-in via the OpenAI adapter header) and defaults to conservative behavior to avoid breaking existing contracts.

What this changes (single continuous description): Implements a server-side tombstone marker for streams that have been soft-terminated by the server after a grace window. A tombstone is a short-lived, idempotency-friendly marker recorded for an in-flight session that (1) records the last-acknowledged stream offset, (2) encodes any pending tool-call signatures (non-sensitive hashes used for idempotency), and (3) exposes a resume_token to the client. On reconnect, the client sends resume_token + last_received_offset in the OpenAI-compat resume handshake. The server negotiator validates the token against the tombstone; if valid, the server resumes by streaming from the negotiated offset and replays any structured-output markers necessary to reconstruct the partial call context. If tombstone TTL has expired or validation fails, the server falls back to either: (A) returning a hard-abort error that includes a safe re-run suggestion, or (B) offering a server-side replay path (controlled by customer policy).

Design highlights: - Soft-termination grace_window: configurable per-customer; default 30s. During grace window the server keeps a small in-memory KV entry with tombstone metadata and writes a condensed tombstone entry to the durable session store on soft-termination. - Tombstone contents: last_offset (int), stream_version (v2), tool_call_signature_hash (sha256 of tool id + args fingerprint), structured-output boundary markers (byte offsets), and expiry timestamp (ISO8601). Tombstones intentionally do NOT store plaintext inputs/outputs to avoid PII/Audit surface. - Resume negotiator: new state machine in api/openai/compat_streaming.go that accepts resume tokens and performs deterministic validation. Validation includes timestamp TTL check, stream_version compatibility, and tool_call_signature collision checks. - Idempotency: tool runtimes check tombstone signature hash to ensure re-run safety. If a tool is non-idempotent and tombstone suggests it may have executed, negotiator responds with 'resume_not_safe' and client can choose to force a re-run with acknowledgement header. - Structured output: streaming markers were extended to include a continuation boundary tag (CONT-BND:v2) so SDKs can reconstitute partial JSON/structured blobs across resume. This keeps the OpenAI-style streaming framing, but adds metadata that Redwood SDKs interpret for safe restarts.

Implementation notes: - Files added/changed (high level): src/streaming/terminate_manager.go (new tombstone writer + TTL sweeper), api/openai/compat_streaming.go (resume handshake and token validation), runtime/tool/idempotency.go (signature helpers), docs/api/streaming.md (spec), tests/integration/stream_resume_test.go (end-to-end). - Resume token format: base64url(JSON{session_id, tombstone_id, mac}). Tokens are MACed using per-tenant signing key; signing is pluggable through KMS. - Backwards compatibility: clients that do not pass the new header receive existing behavior; the tombstone/resume flow only activates when either: (a) client sends header X-Redwood-Resume: 1 on initial handshake, or (b) customer opts-in via tenant flag. - Security and privacy: tombstones avoid storing payloads; signing and TTL prevent replay attacks. We added KMS-backed signing for production tenants. - Observability: new metrics (stream.tombstone.created, stream.resume.attempts, stream.resume.succeeds, stream.resume.failures, stream.tombstone.ttl_expired) and tracing spans for the negotiation path.

Testing and rollout: unit tests for terminate_manager + negotiator, integration test covering resume success/failure, fuzz test for malformed tokens. Canary rollout plan: feature flagged by tenant; start with internal Redwood tenants, then 5 customers in canary cohort, ramp to 50% of traffic with monitoring thresholds on resume failure rates and tool duplicate signals.

Checklist: - [x] Tombstone writer and TTL sweeper implemented - [x] Resume handshake implemented in OpenAI adapter - [x] Tool signature and idempotency checks added - [x] Structured-output continuation markers finalized - [x] Tests added (unit + integration) - [x] Docs updated with example handshake and SDK guidance - [x] Metrics and tracing added - [x] Canary rollout plan documented

Compatibility and SDK work: Redwood SDKs will add helpers to: (1) detect CONT-BND:v2 markers and buffer structured payloads, (2) automatically send resume_token on reconnect when available, and (3) expose resume prompts in higher-level chat/session objects. This PR includes the API-side compatibility bits and docs examples; SDK PRs will follow.

Risks and mitigations: - Risk: Tombstone retention increases memory/storage pressure. Mitigation: tombstones are condensed metadata only; sweeper and TTL aggressive by default (30s) and configurable. - Risk: Incorrect tool signature collisions could prevent safe resume. Mitigation: signature includes arg fingerprinting + tool runtime id; we also log collision diagnostics and expose developer-facing reason codes. - Risk: Behavior drift for older clients. Mitigation: opt-in via header and tenant flag; default unchanged.

Related work items: Linear ENG-1982 (streaming resume design), ENG-2045 (tool idempotency upgrades), SUP-482 (customer incident that motivated tombstone approach).

Commit summary: - add terminate_manager and tombstone format - implement resume_negotiator in compat adapter - add idempotency helpers to tool runtime - wire metrics and tracing - docs and integration tests

Changed files (high level list): src/streaming/terminate_manager.go, api/openai/compat_streaming.go, runtime/tool/idempotency.go, docs/api/streaming.md, tests/integration/stream_resume_test.go, go.mod

CI and rollout history: Initial CI run failed on a race in terminate_manager sweeper (flaky test). Fixed by adding a deterministic clock in tests and reworked sweeper locking. CI green after rerun; e2e integration in staging passed. Canary started 2025-01-20 with internal tenants; no duplicate tool signals observed in first 48h.

Merge notes: squashed commits to keep history concise. Feature lives behind tenant flag + opt-in header; not enabled by default for all customers. SDK teams notified to prepare adapters.



release_notes:
Adds soft-termination tombstone markers and a resume-negotiation handshake to make client disconnects and reconnects more resilient for streaming API calls; OpenAI compatibility adapter updated to expose continuation tokens and structured-output markers.

[streaming-session-snapshot-client-ack-add-resume-token-openai-compat]
description:
Motivation: Improve streaming resilience for mobile/unreliable clients and make client-initiated cancel behavior idempotent while preserving OpenAI compatibility. This PR introduces a 'streaming session snapshot' model and explicit client ACK semantics so disconnected clients can reconnect and resume without inconsistent tool calls or duplicate function invocations. Includes small API surface additions (resume_token, session_id, seq) exposed in the OpenAI-compatible streaming adapter.

Summary of changes: 1) Protocol: add optional query/header parameters: X-Redwood-Session-Id (UUID), X-Redwood-Resume-Token (opaque token), and X-Redwood-Seq (monotonic integer). Server will emit a resume_token event at checkpoint boundaries (full structured object flush points) to allow resumption. 2) Client ACK semantics: streaming responses now include an ACK event type ("ack") that clients can send to confirm they received the last checkpoint; server holds tool-call/side-effect commits until ACK or until server soft-timeout expires. 3) Idempotent cancel: client-initiated cancel now accepts a cancel-with-reason payload and returns an idempotency token; repeating cancel requests with the same idempotency token is a no-op. 4) Server-side grace window: implement a configurable soft grace period (default 30s) after disconnect where session state and pending tool call fences are retained to allow resume. After grace window expiration the session is garbage collected. 5) Function-calling/structured output: ensure structured JSON blocks are flushed at checkpoint boundaries; add deterministic boundaries to avoid partial structured chunks on reconnect. 6) OpenAI compatibility layer: expose resume_token as a top-level SSE event named "resume_token" and support incoming resume headers for existing SDKs; keep the text/event-stream framing compatible with existing clients.

Why this is different from previous proposals: previous work focused on reconnect/retry-backoff and teardown safety. This PR couples explicit checkpoint metadata and client ACKs to avoid duplicate function calls and to provide a concrete resume point that is safe across network blips. It is optimized for tool calling workloads where side effects must be constrained to once semantics.

Commits (high-level): [1] protocol: add session id and resume token headers and wire through adapter; [2] runtime: checkpoint serializer and resume token generation; [3] runtime: hold-and-commit mechanism gated by client ACK and grace window; [4] api: idempotent cancel endpoint and cancel idempotency token; [5] openai-adapter: SSE event renames and backward-compatible parsing; [6] tests: end-to-end resume and duplicate-cancel tests; [7] docs: streaming lifecycle migration guide and SDK hints.

Files changed (high-level): api/streaming_adapter.py (protocol parsing and headers), runtime/checkpoint_manager.rs (checkpoint persistence and GC), runtime/tool_fence.rs (hold/commit logic), openai_compat/sse_adapter.go (resume_token event), stdlib/net/ack_client.py (SDK helper), tests/integration/test_resume.py, docs/streaming-lifecycle.md.

Small illustrative snippets: - in SSE stream: event: resume_token

  data: {"token":"<opaque>","seq":42,"session_id":"..."}

- cancel endpoint: POST /v1/streams/:id/cancel {"reason":"user_abort","idempotency_token":"abc123"} -> 202 {"cancelled":true,"token":"abc123"}

Testing: added deterministic unit tests for checkpoint boundaries and a flaky-network harness that simulates TCP drops and validates resume semantics across reconnects. End-to-end tests ensure that function-calling side-effects execute exactly once when clients follow ACK/resume contract. Performance: microbenchmark shows ~3% p99 overhead for sessions with frequent checkpoints (configurable), negligible for typical chat flows.

Migration notes: - Backwards compatible: clients that do not send session headers keep existing behavior. Resume support is opt-in (server issues resume_token only when session_id provided). - SDKs: quick helper added in python/ts/go SDKs (std ack helper) and docs updated with example reconnect flow. - Operators: new config runtime.streaming.grace_window_seconds (default 30) and runtime.streaming.max_session_persist (default 10m).

Rollout plan: feature-flag rollout behind 'stream_session_snapshot' flag. Start with internal beta, then enable for hosted customers on request, then GA after 3 weeks of monitoring. Alerts: added SLO-level alert if resumed session failure rate > 1% over 1h.

Known limitations & follow-ups: - Resume requires client to retain resume_token; tokens are opaque and ephemeral. We will later add signed tokens for cross-region resume. - Tool-call fences add memory pressure while session is in grace window; follow-up to add spill-to-disk for very large pending calls (ENG-2210).

Checklist: [x] design doc linked, [x] unit tests, [x] e2e tests, [x] docs updated, [x] SDK helpers, [x] load test run, [x] security review (RBAC/headers sanitized).

Release notes: Introduces optional streaming session resume through session_id/resume_token and client ACK semantics to avoid duplicate tool invocations on reconnects. Backwards compatible by default. See docs/streaming-lifecycle.md for usage and SDK examples.

review_comments:
Leo Zhang: Can we avoid holding tool fences in memory for >grace_window? Suggest spill-to-disk or bounded queue. (addressed in follow-up ENG-2210).
Aisha Gomez: Edge-case: what happens if client ACK is lost and resume_token used? Proposed server-side re-emit on reconnect if session still valid. Implemented and covered by e2e tests.
Tomás Ribeiro: Please document the backward compatibility with existing SSE parsers. Added details to docs and openai adapter contains toggles to keep legacy event shapes.

[introduce-gradual-schema-flag-and-streaming-fallback-shim]
description:
Motivation: We need a low-friction path to introduce a schema v3 (structured output / tool-calling harmonization) while preserving existing OpenAI-compatible clients and streaming semantics. This PR adds a conservative, opt-in compatibility flag and a server-side shim that gracefully falls back streaming to a polling pathway when a client/server schema mismatch prevents stable event streaming.

Summary of changes (single-line summary): introduce X-Redwood-Schema header, 'Prefer: schema=v3-beta' opt-in, server shim that maps v2->v1 fields for compatibility, streaming handshake fallback, updates to function-call and structured-output mapping in the openai-compat layer, tests and docs.

Checklist: - [x] Add opt-in request header parsing (X-Redwood-Schema / Prefer) - [x] Implement server-side mapping shim (turns/messages, json_schema/structured_output) - [x] Streaming handshake: detect schema-negotiation mismatch and emit fallback control event - [x] Add telemetry events for fallback occurrences - [x] Unit/integration tests across Go runtime + TS SDK mapping - [x] Docs: migration notes + deprecation timeline - [x] E2E compatibility tests with legacy clients

Commits (high-level): 1) Add header parsing and schema negotiation in compat handler 2) Implement v3->v2 field mapping shim and canonicalizer 3) Streaming handshake: add 'schema-compatible' probe, streaming-fallback route and polling link 4) Function-calling adapter: accept both function_call and call_instruction shapes, normalize to runtime shape 5) Structured-output adapter: map json_schema -> structured_output and vice versa, sanitize extra_properties 6) Tests + fixtures 7) Docs and changelog

Files/areas touched (high-level): - server/compat/negotiation.go (new) - server/compat/shims.go (new) - server/compat/streaming_fallback.go (new) - runtime/handler.go (compat hooks) - openai-compat/adapter.ts (mapping helpers) - sdk/ts/tests/compat_streaming.test.ts - docs/migrations/schema-v3-beta.md - ci/workflows/compat-tests.yml

Small illustrative snippet (compat negotiation pseudocode):

// on request
// 1) parse headers: X-Redwood-Schema OR Prefer: schema=v3-beta
// 2) if request asks for v3 semantics but server not yet capable -> attempt shim
// 3) if streaming handshake fails due to structural mismatch -> return 204 + Link: <polling>/status and emit telemetry

Review conversation (abridged, in-thread):
- Arjun: "Can we guarantee no change for existing clients when no header is provided? Add explicit opt-in tests."
- Maya: "Yes — default behaviour is unchanged. Added integration tests that exercise blank header and Prefer header negative case (tests/compat_default_blank_header)."
- Lena: "Streaming fallback is clever but we need to measure latency tax. Please add a metric: streaming.compat.fallback.latency distribution."
- Maya: "Added telemetry event streaming.compat.fallback.{count,lat_p50,p95} and a dashboard note in docs."
- Diego: "Function calling adapters must preserve original user-visible signatures for OpenAI-compat clients. Validate no loss of argument typing."
- Maya: "Adapter preserves argument blob; when converting between JSON-string and object we include original raw_arguments on the runtime context for audits."

CI notes: initial run showed an e2e flake in the TS SDK streaming harness (race in event buffer). I fixed by adding a short retry in the harness and hardened the mock server to assert schema-negotiation header ordering. Final run: all checks passed (unit, integration, e2e, lint, benchmarks).

Design/behavior details: - Header surface: X-Redwood-Schema: v1 | v2 | v3-beta (canonical). We also honor Prefer: schema=v3-beta for HTTP clients. Absent header = v2 compatibility. - Opt-in semantics: v3-beta enables stricter structured output enforcement, canonical variable names for tool-calling, and explicit schema-driven streaming events (delta types). Servers accept v3-beta only when runtime feature-flag enabled; otherwise respond with 412 + guidance or silently shim (configurable per-deployment). - Shim behavior: When a v3-beta request arrives at a runtime not fully v3-capable but our compat layer can do a safe mapping, we apply the shim to translate request/response shapes. For streaming: we attempt the normal streaming handshake; if an early mismatch is detected (response frames not parseable by client schema), we abort server-sent events stream and emit a small control event to the client with "streaming_fallback": true and a Link header to a compensating polling endpoint (/compat/poll/<id>). The client receives a 204 No Content body for the stream and can continue by polling; meanwhile we schedule the full response to be available at the polling route. - Telemetry: new events streaming.compat.fallback.count, streaming.compat.fallback.latency_p50, streaming.compat.fallback.latency_p95, compat.schema.negotiation.failure. - Deprecation timeline: v1 behaviour (implicit 'messages' only) is now marked deprecated in favor of v2 canonical names. We will send X-Schema-Deprecation: v1; will not break existing clients for 12 months. Docs include migration recipe and code samples.

Backward compatibility notes: - No changes for clients that do not opt into v3-beta headers. - For opt-in clients, the shim aims to preserve semantics; however, because some v3 features (schema-validated streaming frames) are newer, we provide the fallback so production users don't observe silent truncation.

Testing: added 18 new unit tests and 5 e2e scenarios exercising streaming fallback with mismatched shapes, function_call shapes, and structured-output edge cases. Load bench: added a micro-bench that simulates 1000 small streaming requests; fallback path measured additional median latency of ~18ms for negotiated fallbacks (telemetry recorded in benchmark harness).

Docs: docs/migrations/schema-v3-beta.md includes recommended headers, server responses to expect, and sample code in Python and TS for doing graceful client-side fallback handling.

Follow-ups (future work captured in ENG-2160): - Server can advertise supported schema versions in OPTIONS /status endpoint - Automated rollout gating: only enable shim for a percentage of users initially - SDK helpers: client-side automatics to retry as polling when receiving a fallback control event - Consider making fallback link a resumable websocket handle for lower-latency recovery

Merge notes: Squashed and merged to main after reviewer approvals. No prod config flip was performed in this PR; deployment requires runtime feature-flag enablement per-cluster.

If you want to test locally: see docs/migrations/schema-v3-beta.md and run `make compat-test` in the openai-compat package.

References: Linear ENG-2147 (schema v3 rollout), ENG-2160 (streaming compatibility plan).

release_notes:
Adds opt-in schema header and server-side compatibility shim with streaming fallback. Deprecation warnings for legacy schema behavior. No user-visible breaking changes if opt-in not used.

notes:
This PR is intentionally conservative: opt-in, telemetry-first, with a clear fallback path to preserve production stability for streaming and tool-calling clients.

[Ordered Toolcall Reconciliation & Disconnect Splay for Streaming Resilience (OpenAI compat)]
description:
Motivation: customers running multi-tool conversations saw non-deterministic toolcall ordering after client disconnect + rapid reconnects which caused out-of-order side effects in third-party systems. This PR introduces server-side ordering guarantees for tool/function calls across reconnect/resume boundaries plus a client disconnect splay (randomized small backoff applied server-side to accept/reconcile reconnects) to avoid thundering reconnections. Design: 1) Sequence numbers: each stream session assigns a monotonic sequence number to each emitted event that can invoke a tool. Sequence numbers are signed by the server lease and attached to events sent to the client. 2) Reconciliation window: on reconnect the client can provide latest-acked-seq; server replays pending events in-order and drops duplicates. 3) Idempotency + ordered-apply: tool call invocations include an ordered_id composed of session_id:seq so downstream adapters (and the OpenAI compat shim) can apply tools in sequence. 4) Disconnect splay: when many clients disconnect during scale events we introduce a small randomized acceptance delay (0-300ms configurable) before reattaching the session lease to avoid simultaneous inflight reconnections overwhelming the tool adapters. 5) Config and compatibility: the OpenAI compatibility layer now accepts and emits ordered_toolcalls metadata on streaming endpoints and falls back to previous behavior when the flag is off. 6) Safety: added checks so that a resumed stream with an older lease is rejected; client must re-negotiate if server lease id mismatches. Rollout plan: feature gated behind streaming.reconnect.ordered_toolcalls, enabled for canary customers for 48 hours, metric-driven rollouts tied to toolcall error-rate and tail-latency. Tests: unit tests for seq assignment and validation, integration tests simulating N concurrent reconnects with artificial clock skew, e2e tests validating toolcall ordering against a mock adapter. Docs: docs/streaming/reconnect.md updated with semantics and migration steps. Implementation notes: implementation touches the session manager, ack manager, and OpenAI adapter layers to wire ordered ids into structured output. Commits are small and focused to ease bisecting. Backwards compatibility: when the client does not provide ordered metadata we maintain existing behavior; SDKs are updated to opt into the new behavior. Observability: added metrics streaming.reconnect.splay_applied and streaming.reconcile.ordered_replays to monitor adoption. 

release_notes:
Adds ordered reconciliation for tool/function calls during stream reconnects and introduces a randomized disconnect splay to reduce reconnect storms. OpenAI compatibility layer now preserves toolcall ordering and surfaces deterministic idempotency tokens. Behavior is opt-in via streaming.reconnect.ordered_toolcalls config; rollout staged behind a feature flag.

review_comments:
Ethan Cole: Nice focused change. Can we ensure the sequence number fits in 64 bits across long-lived sessions? Also request an extra unit test for seq wrap-around detection.
Maya Patel (author): Seq is u64 currently; added a test for wrap-around detection and defensive error path that forces session renewal when seq would overflow.
Ravi Singh: The disconnect splay param seems low for high fan-out events. Suggest making the upper bound configurable per deployment and exposing metric when splay is applied.
Maya Patel (author): Made upper bound configurable via streaming.reconnect.splay_max_ms and added streaming.reconnect.splay_applied metric and dashboards in observability pack.
Priya Nair: Integration test flaked in the first run due to timing; can we add a deterministic clock or retries to stabilize? Also ensure SDK changes have clear migration notes.
Maya Patel (author): Switched integration harness to use fake clock for deterministic behavior and added migration note in docs/streaming/reconnect.md. Marking as ready-for-merge after CI green.

merge_outcome:
Merged via squash on 2026-02-24 by Maya Patel after approvals from reviewers. Feature gated; no immediate global rollout. Canary enabled for 3% of streaming traffic and monitored for 48 hours.

notes:
Behavior is opt-in via streaming.reconnect.ordered_toolcalls; default remains backwards compatible.
SDKs: python/ts updated to include helpers for reconstructing ordered toolcall ids; patch released in minor versions.
Observability: new metrics added; dashboards updated in observability-pack repo.
Operational: when enabling globally, consider raising tool-adapter concurrency limits for first 24 hours to absorb ordered replays.

[Add client-hiatus reconnect orchestration and soft-cancel window for streaming API]
description:
Motivation: Unreliable client networks and transient disconnects were causing noisy aborts and duplicate tool/function calls in the streaming OpenAI-compat layer. This PR introduces a first-class client-hiatus orchestration mechanism and a "soft-cancel" grace window so that short client disconnects do not immediately finalize sessions or replay tool calls. Design summary: (1) server-side ephemeral lease with configurable 'hiatus_ms' and 'grace_ms' to hold inflight sessions for a short period; (2) an explicit resume handshake: clients present a session token plus a monotonically increasing session-echo to safely rejoin and continue a stream; (3) soft-cancel semantics: when a client disconnects, the server marks a session as 'soft-cancelled' and continues producing a short terminal delta that allows downstream toolcall idempotency guards to commit safely, but it refrains from hard-finalizing model state until grace window expires; (4) lease refresh: long-running streams periodically refresh the ephemeral lease to avoid premature eviction; (5) backoff/jitter tuning: reconnect backoff uses capped exponential with randomized jitter to avoid thundering herd. Implementation notes: added a lightweight orchestrator (server/streaming/hiatus_orchestrator.go) that implements the lease state machine and exposes hooks for the adapter layer. The OpenAI-compat adapter (api/openai_adapter/stream_controller.py) was updated to (a) translate WebSocket disconnects into soft-cancel state, (b) accept resume() calls with session token and session-echo, and (c) enforce idempotent toolcall dedup keys derived from the session-echo + tool-call-id. SDK changes: python SDK exposes Stream.resume(session_token, echo_id) and a new Stream.hiatus_config to mirror server defaults. Console change: admin UI shows 'hiatus_age' and 'soft_cancel' metrics and a toggle for lowering the default grace window per-organization. Backwards compatibility: defaults preserve current behavior for most customers (default grace_ms=20000). Operators can lower to 0ms to restore immediate cancels. Testing: unit tests for state transitions, a deterministic integration harness that simulates network pauses, and end-to-end validations against the python SDK that assert no duplicate toolcall side-effects across reconnects. Rollout plan: feature flagged off by default; staged rollout to Canary (internal), then Dedicated customers with opt-in, then full enable. Metrics to monitor: session_reclaims, resume_success_rate, duplicate_toolcall_rate. Related work: follows ENG-5823 (stream durability) and ENG-5890 (openai-compat reconcilers).

release_notes:
Adds a configurable client-hiatus window and soft-cancel semantics for streaming sessions; introduces server-side lease refresh and reconnect orchestration. Backwards compatible by default; operators can tighten defaults via config.

Marco Li (reviewer): The overall approach looks good. Request: tighten the default grace window to 15s instead of 30s — we've seen cases where 30s holds resources too long. Also please add a metric for 'soft_cancel_count' and tag by model.
Ayesha Patel (author): Acknowledged. I've changed the default to 20s to balance operator burden and flaky mobile networks. Added 'soft_cancel_count' and 'hiatus_age_ms' histograms tagged by_model in aa00bb. Willing to make the default configurable via env/values.yaml.
Sofia Nguyen (reviewer): Can you ensure we don't break function/tool call ordering guarantees when a resume happens mid-toolcall? Also add an integration test that simulates duplicate delivery and asserts idempotency guards prevent double-commit.
Ayesha Patel (author): Implemented an idempotent dedupe key using session-echo + tool-call-id and added a deterministic integration in 778899 that replays delivery twice; asserts no duplicate side-effect. Documented the idempotency heuristic in docs/openai_compat_streaming_lifecycle.md.
Daniel Ortiz (reviewer): Code looks good, minor nit on log level for lease refresh telemetry. Approving after nits are addressed.
Ayesha Patel (author): Addressed the logging nit (reduced lease refresh logs to DEBUG) and squashed fixup commits. Ready to merge.

notes_on_upgrade:
Default behavior is backward compatible. Operators running private/Dedicated should review charts/values.yaml to lower grace_ms if they have tight GPU capacity constraints. SDK consumers: bump python SDK to v0.8.4 to get resume() helpers. Release flagged; enable via rollout UI or env flag 'STREAM_HIATUS_ENABLED=true'. Monitor resume_success_rate and duplicate_toolcall_rate post rollout.

[tool-result-merge-policy-and-exponential-backoff-for-parallel-calls]
description:
Summary: Introduces a configurable tool result merge policy and a per-invocation exponential backoff/retry budget aimed at improving ergonomics and determinism for parallel/multi-tool calls. Motivation: the previous default (inject-first-returned) caused nondeterministic structured-output injection when multiple tools returned overlapping JSON fragments or produced idempotent but out-of-order updates. This led to subtle regressions in downstream parsers and customer incidents (SUP-9021). Design: add three merge strategies: first_wins (legacy), last_wins, and merge_patch (depth-aware JSON/struct merge that preserves keyed identities and deduplicates array items when an id key is present). Merge order is deterministic by explicit priority then monotonic timestamp. Implement a per-call RetryPolicy that exposes base_delay_ms, factor, max_attempts, max_delay_ms, jitter_pct and an overall retry_budget_ms to avoid retry storms that starve streaming tokens. The runtime applies exponential backoff with jitter and a budget check before scheduling retries; when budget is exhausted we surface a partial-injection event and optionally trigger a fallback model or canned response based on caller policy. API surface: ToolInvocationOptions gains result_merge_policy and retry_policy fields. OpenAI compatibility: map legacy tool_call behavior to result_merge_policy=first_wins by default and emit a single deprecation notice per workspace when user libraries request explicit tool_call hints. SDKs: TS/Python/Go helpers to opt-in and a migration linter rule that flags ambiguous tool call patterns. Rollout: default behavior remains first_wins to preserve backwards compatibility; merge_patch is enabled behind a gate and will be rolled out to 10% traffic for initial experiments. Observability: new metrics added tool_result_merge.policy{policy} count, tool_result_merge.conflicts, tool_result_merge.resolved_by and retry metrics retries_per_invocation and retry_budget_exhausted. Dashboards updated under "Tooling / Result Merge" to show conflicts over time and the fraction of calls that used merge_patch. Testing: unit tests for conflict resolution, array deduping, id-key heuristics and integration tests that simulate 3 parallel tool calls with conflicting ids and transient failures. Performance: microbenchmarks show a median 7-12% extra CPU latency on 3-way merges with merge_patch but end-user parser error rate drops by 18-42% depending on workload. Backwards compatibility: no breaking change by default; customers can opt into alternate policies per-route or globally. Docs: added migration guide and examples showing how to express merge policies for common tooling patterns. CI/QA: initial CI run failed lint and a flaky time-sensitive test; fixed by mocking monotonic clock and adding unit test coverage for jitter. Merge and deployment: feature-flagged implementation, gradual ramp to 100% after 2-week smoke window, emergency kill switch in Console. Related work: ties to ENG-2431 and earlier speculative affinity work; addresses SUP-9021 incident. See commits for implementation details and changed files for exact locations of changes.

review_comments:
Eleni Strauss: This looks very helpful. Two asks before approving: 1) can we avoid copying large JSON blobs when doing merge_patch? 2) add metric for bytes_copied_by_merge. Priya Kulkarni: switched to in-place shallow diffs where possible; added bytes_copied_by_merge metric and tests for large payloads.
Marcus Li: The merge_patch name is slightly ambiguous. Can we document the semantics explicitly and add a deterministic tie-breaker for identical priorities? Also please ensure this does not change KV cache keys' semantics. Priya Kulkarni: added explicit priority then timestamp tie-breaker and updated KV cache key tests to assert no change in behavior.
Jonah Rivera: Request to add a visible retry_budget_exhausted alert and an emergency kill-switch in Console. Also asked for an example showing how to opt-out per-route. Priya Kulkarni: added alert to SLO dashboard and a Console toggle; included route-level opt-out example in migration doc.

release_notes:
Add configurable tool result merge policies and per-invocation exponential backoff for parallel tool calls. Default behavior unchanged; opt-in merge_patch provides deterministic depth-aware JSON merging and deduplication by id keys. New metrics and dashboard panels for policy usage and conflict resolution. SDKs include helpers and a linter to assist migration.

notes:
This PR is intentionally conservative: default is legacy behavior to avoid breaking users. The implementation is feature-flagged and rollout is gradual. We measured correctness improvements in end-to-end parser tests which motivated prioritizing this change over low-latency micro-optimizations. The team will follow up with a smaller perf-optimization PR that trades some CPU for lower median latency when merge_patch is used.

[Toolchain invocation ergonomics: async hydration, parallel backoff, and structured result merging]
description:
Motivation: Customers are using multi-tool call graphs (chain-of-tools + parallel tool fans) and need safer, more ergonomic ways to hydrate tool outputs back into downstream tool inputs while preserving deterministic structured output shapes. This PR adds an async hydration layer on the tool invocation path, a deterministic merging strategy for structured results (JSON schema merging + conflict resolution policy), and robust retry/backoff semantics for tools invoked in parallel. Goals: 1) Make multi-tool flows less error-prone for app developers; 2) Reduce silent races when parallel tool calls return at different times; 3) Keep OpenAI-compatibility for function/tool calling while exposing more explicit ergonomics for engineering teams.

release_notes:
Improves tool-calling ergonomics: introduces async result hydration for multi-tool graphs, deterministic merge strategy for structured outputs, and exponential backoff/retry plumbing for parallel tool invocations. Backward-compatible with existing OpenAI-style function-calling semantics.

notes:
Implementation details: the async hydration layer attaches a hydration token to each tool invocation; results are streamed back into a per-request ledger, which the merger consumes when either all expected results arrive or a soft timeout triggers. Retry semantics: parallel fanouts use exponential backoff with jitter and a shared circuit-breaker per tool type to avoid thundering herds. OpenAI compatibility: preserved function-calling signature; hydrateToolResults returns outputs in both OpenAI-style 'arguments' and Redwood's structured result wrapper. Backwards compatibility: default merge policy is 'prefer-schema' which preserves stable behavior for existing customers while surfacing conflicts to the application via telemetry and structured error payloads.

migration_guide:
For most customers: no action required. To opt into experimental stricter merging, set config 'tool.merge.policy=strict-error' in console or private config. SDKs: new helper hydrateToolResults() available in TS SDK; Python SDK shim to follow in subsequent PR. Note: if you rely on non-deterministic merge behavior, test with the new harness first.

[multi-tool-execution: ergonomic API + parallel tool runner + result injection + retry policies]
description:
Motivation: Improve ergonomics and reliability for tool/function-calling in the OpenAI-compat layer and native Redwood API. Customers asked for easy multi-tool invocations, deterministic injection of tool results into continuations, safe parallel tool execution, and more robust retry/backoff for transient tool failures. This PR introduces a small, backwards-compatible API extension plus a new parallel tool-runner implementation and runtime wiring for result injection and structured output hints. Summary of changes: 1) API: add `tools` invocation signature that supports multiple tool calls in a single step and an optional `parallel` flag. 2) Runtime: implement ParallelToolRunner with optimistic concurrency, coordinated token streaming, and ordered result injection points. 3) Retry semantics: add configurable retry/backoff policies per-tool with circuit-breaking thresholds and idempotency markers. 4) Structured output: expand function-calling schema to include `injection_point` and `merge_strategy` hints for deterministic consolidation of parallel results. 5) OpenAI compatibility: surface the new multi-tool signature through the OpenAI-compat endpoint with feature gating and compatibility warning headers. 6) SDK: Python and TS client updates for ergonomics and typed helpers. 7) Tests & docs: unit + integration tests for parallel tool execution, backpressure scenarios, and streaming stability; docs and migration guide. Implementation notes and tradeoffs: - Parallel execution is best-effort: by default the runner executes tools concurrently and injects results in the order of `injection_point` when present. If tools have cross-dependencies, callers should use explicit sequential mode or `depends_on` fields. - Streaming: we added a coordinator that merges streaming outputs from active tools into a single response stream while preserving token interleaving semantics. This required a small amount of additional buffering (configurable via runtime flags) to avoid head-of-line blocking. - Retries: only idempotent-marked tools will be automatically retried; non-idempotent tools can opt into safe-retry wrappers. Retries use exponential backoff with jitter and a per-tool max attempt limit. - Backwards compatibility: existing function-calling calls remain unchanged. The new fields are optional and gated behind an SDK flag and an OpenAI-compat header for the next release window. Checklist: - [x] Design doc reviewed by runtime and API teams (ENG-8341) - [x] Prototype validated in perf-canary with small synthetic workload - [x] Unit tests for ParallelToolRunner and retry policies - [x] Integration tests for streaming merge and structured injection - [x] Python + TS SDK helpers + docs snippets - [x] Compatibility guard and migration notes in docs - [x] Load test showing <5% median latency regression on typical chat workloads Known limitations: - Result consolidation for very large tool outputs can increase memory usage; we recommend streaming-friendly tool outputs or chunking. - Deterministic ordering across parallel calls is only guaranteed when callers provide explicit injection points. Related: ENG-8341 (tool ergonomics), PM-412 (product requirements), SUP-2023 (support case that drove retries). See inline changed files for details.

release_notes:
Add multi-tool invocation API and ParallelToolRunner: clients can invoke multiple tools in one call with optional parallel execution. Improvements include result injection points, merge strategies for structured output, and per-tool retry/backoff. Backwards compatible; gated behind feature flag for OpenAI-compat clients.

[parallel tool returns reconciliation and retry choreography for OpenAI-compat]
description:
Motivation: Customers are building multi-tool workflows where the model fan-outs tool calls in parallel and expects a single, deterministic structured injection back into the next model turn. We observed two classes of problems in production: (1) non-deterministic ordering and partial/overlapping streamed tool outputs which break structured output parsing, and (2) retry storms and duplicated results when a subset of parallel tool calls fail transiently. This PR introduces a reconciliation layer and retry choreography to make parallel tool-calling ergonomics reliable and OpenAI-compat friendly.

What this PR does (high-level): Adds a Reconciler component that: 1) accepts concurrent tool responses (streamed or final) and materializes a canonical merged representation; 2) enforces deterministic injection ordering via a reconcile_id and explicit injection_strategy; 3) implements per-tool retry/backoff and a short-circuit policy for "first-success" strategies to reduce tail latency and cost. On the API surface we add opt-in request flags for OpenAI-compat requests: "reconcile_id", "injection_strategy" (values: "merge", "first-success", "serial"), and "max_retries_per_tool". SDK helpers expose an ergonomic call_tools(...) helper that returns the reconciled structured output and metadata for diagnostics.

Key design points: - Deterministic ordering: callers can opt to preserve the generation order with "serial" or allow a merge strategy that combines outputs by semantic slot. Reconciler uses a stable slot ordering derived from the call graph to avoid flakiness. - Streaming stability: partial streamed chunks from tools are buffered and reassembled in a small in-memory window (configurable via reconcile_window_ms) before they are forwarded as a single atomic injection event to the language model. This prevents the model from seeing interleaved partial payloads. - Retry choreography: per-tool backoff is jittered and bounded; the reconciler tracks idempotency keys provided by tools to dedupe retries. For "first-success" strategy we short-circuit remaining tools once a minimum-success threshold is reached. - OpenAI compatibility: function-calling style metadata is preserved; reconciled outputs are emitted as valid function-call payloads (name + arguments) so existing OpenAI-compat clients can consume results without extra parsing changes. - Observability: events, per-tool latencies, retry counts, and reconciliation decisions are emitted to existing traces/metrics. We added tracing tags reconcile_id and injection_strategy.

API changes and backwards compatibility: - New optional fields on the inference request JSON: "reconcile_id" (string), "injection_strategy" (string), "max_retries_per_tool" (int), "reconcile_window_ms" (int). Defaults maintain current behavior (no reconciliation; naive injection) so this is opt-in and non-breaking. - SDK helpers: python and typescript convenience functions wrap the new fields and handle streaming reassembly. Existing SDK call sites that don't opt in see no change.

Implementation notes and tradeoffs: - Reconciler lives in runtime/reconciler.py and sits between the tool-runner and the streaming response multiplexer. It maintains an ephemeral in-memory buffer keyed by reconcile_id; for large outputs we spill to disk using the existing chunk-store utility to avoid OOM. - To avoid increased tail latency we aggressively favor optimistic short-circuits under "first-success" and expose per-request thresholds. - We added integration tests that replay production failures (partial stream cuts, duplicated tool callbacks) to assert deterministic reconciled outputs.

Benchmarks: microbenchmarks on a 4xA100 stack show median additional latency of ~4ms for reconciliation in the common case (small tool outputs) and 95th percentile increase of ~12-18ms when buffering larger streamed payloads. Cost/regressions: we observed negligible tokenization overhead; the main cost is slightly increased CPU for reassembly under heavy fan-out which is bounded by a configurable concurrency limit.

Rollout plan: - Feature gated behind runtime flag reconcile.enabled=false by default. - Canary rollout to 10% of hosted traffic with a revert window of 48 hours. - SDK release (python/ts) coordinated: minor semver bump with new helper exposed. - Docs/compat: update OpenAI-compat page with examples showing function-call style reconciled results and migration notes.

Testing: Unit tests for reconciler logic, end-to-end integration tests that validate deterministic injection and retry backoff behavior, and performance runbooks added to benchmarks/. CI: added a new workflow to exercise long-lived streaming reconnection scenarios.

Notes for reviewers: focus on idempotency/dedupe correctness (reconciler/keys), spike protection under many concurrent reconcile_ids, and the SDK ergonomics (is call_tools intuitive?). Also validate the OpenAI-compat output shape in docs/openai_compat/tool-calling.md.

Related: ENG-9876 (design), SUP-2219 (customer incident), ENG-10012 (retry policy work).

Liam O'Connor: Can you explain how we guarantee stable ordering across retries? Stateful slot ordering looks tricky when callers fan-out dynamically.
Author (Aisha Khan): We derive the stable slot order from the call graph emitted with the request (tools are assigned deterministic indices). Retries are keyed to the original slot index so dedupe is deterministic.
Ravi Singh: Need circuit-breaker so a misbehaving tool doesn't drag reconciler memory. Also prefer upper bounds on in-flight reconcile_ids.
Author: Added a per-reconciler in-flight cap and eviction policy; spelled this out in runtime/reconciler.py and added metrics. See commit b27d4f1.

Author: Added expanded examples and a migration snippet in docs/openai_compat/tool-calling.md.
Nadia Chen: CI flake on streaming reconnect test; was due to test harness timing. I reran and all checks passed.
Liam O'Connor: Approve after the small nit on naming (reconcile_window_ms -> reconcile_window_ms) fixed.
Author: Fixed naming nit and added a one-line changelog entry.

release_notes:
Add reconciler for deterministic multi-tool injection and retry choreography. Opt-in via request flags: reconcile_id, injection_strategy, max_retries_per_tool. SDK helpers provided for python and typescript.

notes:
Feature gated; will monitor per-tool retry metrics and reconcile buffer memory during canary.

[Convergent toolflow ergonomics: deterministic injection, parallel reconciliation, and retry surface]
description:
Context and motivation: We have several customer patterns that combine multiple tool calls inside a single chat turn: parallel lookups (user profile + permissions), speculative enrichment (NER + web search), and chained transforms (summarize -> format). In some of these cases, the runtime previously returned non-deterministic injection ordering and duplicate re-injections after retries, which caused frontend flakiness and made downstream structured-output validation brittle. This PR introduces a cohesive ergonomics layer for multi-tool flows that focuses on three goals: 1) deterministic injection semantics (order and idempotency keys), 2) a reconciliation strategy for parallel tool results that constrains fanout and attaches provenance metadata, and 3) an explicit developer-facing retry surface that avoids duplicate payloads and maintains streaming stability.

What this changes (high-level): - Adds a deterministic injection protocol: tools are assigned stable invocation IDs, and the runtime tracks insertion points so that on resume/retry the same logical positions are used. This prevents content shuffling when partial streaming responses are resumed. - Parallel reconciliation operator: a new executor that accepts multiple tool futures, applies configurable merge policies (first-wins, priority-map, merge-by-field), and emits a single canonical injection block with provenance headers. - Retry surface: explicit retry annotations on tool descriptors (max_retries, backoff_policy, idempotency_hint) and centralized retry coordinator that deduplicates in-flight retries using the invocation ID and at-most-once commit semantics for side-effecting tools. - Compatibility shim: small OpenAI-compat layer change to preserve function_call ordering when tools are returned as an array; structured output helpers expanded to attach tool provenance (tool_id, invocation_id, latency_ms) so downstream evals can assert stability.
