[Cross-functional dependability sprint heuristics and comms diary]
Purpose:
This document is a working sprint diary and tactical checklist for a 10-week cross-functional dependability program focused on defining and operationalizing SLOs for model-serving endpoints. It’s intentionally informal — notes, hypotheses, comms templates, and handoff scripts we can iterate in the open.

Background/context: quick bullets
- Goal: get 6 product-serving teams to a baseline SLO (latency P95 and error-rate) + runbooks + rollout gating within 10 weeks.
- Motivation: recent production regressions in hosted API (Dec 2025) highlighted gaps: inconsistent ownership, missing observability for model variants, and unclear rollback policies.
- Success criteria (working): onboarded teams show a measurable drop in P95 tail and a documented runbook; at least 2 teams use canary + automatic fallback.

High-level approach
1) Week 0-2: discovery + telemetry hardening
   - Audit: each service/microservice owning model endpoints (list owners and current signal coverage)
   - Fill telemetry gaps: add request-id propagation, tokenized latency buckets, KV-cache hit metrics; short spike alert M: SRE-telemetry-ops
   - Deliverable: minimal observability checklist per team + shared dashboard template

2) Week 3-6: SLO design + experiment lab
   - Run SLO design workshops with product & infra: define consumer-impact metrics (auth failure vs model runtime error), map to error budget policy
   - Hypotheses: 1) prefix caching reduces P95 by 15% for chat-heavy routes. 2) Route-level failover to quantized model reduces error-rate at cost of quality degradation detectable by evals.
   - Small experiments: enable prefix cache for 15% of traffic on test cluster; pilot quantized variant in a canary pool.
   - Deliverable: SLO config PRs (repo: infra/slo-config), experiment result log, decision flags (promote/rollback)

3) Week 7-10: rollout + handoff + runbooks
   - Canary-to-gradual rollouts with automatic fallback per policy (traffic split, thresholds, time windows)
   - Oncall handoff runbooks: escalation tree, verification script, rollback playbook (short commands + run outputs)
   - Post-mortem template and acceptance checklist for SLO adoption
   - Deliverable: per-service runbook in docs repo, merged SLO configs, training session recordings

Operational heuristics (quick reference)
- SLO composition: prefer consumer-impact over infrastructure-only signals. If consumer signal missing, create a proxy signal (e.g., inference-response-with-error-field).
- Error budget policy: soft-threshold alert at 40% burn in 1h, action at 70% burn in 6h (notify product + SRE), auto-fallback trigger at 90% burn for 15m window.
- Latency SLOs: use P95 for interactive routes, P99 for batch inference endpoints.
- Canary windows: 30m ramp for new model variant, require <10% relative increase in error-rate and <5% P95 regression to proceed to 2h ramp.

Cross-functional roles + responsibilities (working)
- Product owner (PO): clarifies customer-impact windows and approves SLO targets; owns rollback decision when quality tradeoffs hit.
- SRE lead: owns observability baseline, alerting, runbook template, and rollout automation.

[Reliability Covenant — 12-week cross-team sprint playground and run-to-stable plan]
Purpose

This doc captures a practical, lightweight cross-team plan for a 12-week reliability sprint we’re calling the "Reliability Covenant". The goal: converge on pragmatic SLOs, test orchestration patterns (routing/fallback), and prove an operational handoff that reduces incident toil by 30% for model-serving flows.

Why a "covenant"?
- Emphasizes shared commitments across product, serving-runtime, SRE, and platform teams.
- Keeps it social and contractual (small, signed agreements per service).

Scope
- Primary surface: model-serving (text generation + embeddings) endpoints and routing layer.
- Included teams: platform-engineering (owner), serving-runtime, site-reliability, product-hosted-api, devexp for SDK hooks.
- Out of scope (for this 12-week run): private deploy installs beyond internal QA, experimental model weights onboarding.

Success criteria (end of 12 weeks) — measurable outcomes
- SLOs defined and agreed for 3 representative services (baseline: p50/p95 latency, availability window, error-rate).
- Automated SLO dashboard (per-route) with live alerts ≠ pager noise (<= 2 false alarms/week).
- Two safety-net playbooks implemented: regional fallback + model-variant fallback with smoke tests.
- Incident toil reduced (hand tracking) by >= 30% on those services (compare 30-day before/after).

Top-level milestones (12-week cadence)
- Week 0–2: Discovery + Service selection + baseline metrics collection
  - Identify 3 candidate services (low, med, high QPS)
  - Pull historic traces: latency distributions, error classes, traffic shape (seq len)
  - Draft SLO proposals per service (owner: product + SRE)

- Week 3–5: Agreement & instrumentation
  - Finalize SLO thresholds + error budget policy (burn-rate windows)
  - Implement/enable metric collection (latency buckets, request-level tags) and add to dashboard template
  - Add simple synthetic canaries for model-variant fallback

- Week 6–8: Orchestration experiments & canary rollouts
  - Run traffic-split experiments (10/90 -> 50/50) for fallback patterns
  - Test automatic fallback triggers (e.g., sustained p95 > threshold for 2m)
  - Evaluate cost vs latency trade-offs for quantized model variant fallback

- Week 9–12: Stabilize + runbook + handoff
  - Freeze SLOs & publish operational covenant docs
  - Run cross-team tabletop + simulated outage walk-throughs
  - Handoff steady-state ownership and QBR metric checkpoints

Roles & responsibilities (lightweight)
- Platform-engineering (lead): coordinate timelines, host dashboards, manage infra changes for routing experiments.
- Serving-runtime: provide model-variant compatibility guarantees, KV cache implications, and runtime flags for fallbacks.
- Site-reliability: define SLI collection, alert thresholds, and ownership for pagers.

[SLO Cadence Bootcamp & Cross-functional Rehearsal Notebook]
Purpose:
This is a working notebook for a compact, operational-first SLO cadence bootcamp aimed at product, infra, platform, and support partners. The goal is not to write another policy doc — its to rehearse precise handoffs, validate signals, and train responders on the SLO rhythm we expect teams to run for model-serving features (hosted API, dedicated, private).

Objective (measurable):
- Run a 10-person cross-team rehearsal and complete 3 tabletop-to-live escalation handoffs within 2 weeks.
- Validate the SLO signal chain end-to-end (client metric -> aggregators -> alert -> incident bridge -> postmortem starter).
- Produce 5 small, actionable changes to the SLO observability checklist and 2 quick configuration changes (alert thresholds, runbook links).

Audience:
- SREs, Feature Engineers owning model endpoints, Platform Engineers, Customer Success on-call leads, Product PMs for priority features.

High-level bootcamp plan (2 weeks):
Week 0 (prep)
- Day -7: Invite list, pre-reading, attach current SLOs + incident runbooks, mapping doc.
- Day -5: Data sanity check run: make sure metrics exporter, rollups, and alerting queries are returning expected values.
- Day -3: Quick sync with observability infra to enable synthetic tests and a short-lived alert channel for the rehearsal.

Week 1 (rehearsals)
- Day 1: Orientation (1 hour): cadence overview, roles, how to read SLO dashboards.
- Day 2-3: Tabletop sessions (2x 90m) focused on: slow tail latency (P95->P99 divergence) and token-cost regression. Use incident-sculpting templates (see exercises section).
- Day 4: Live mini-sim (4 hours): inject synthetic latency to a staging model pool and exercise automated fallback routing. Observe system kinetics, KV cache warm-up effects, request batching shifts.
- Day 5: Debrief and quick fixes (2 hours): triage suggested changes and apply 2 configuration items in staging.

Week 2 (handoff & measurement)
- Day 8: Canary failure escalation (full replay): simulate a sustained GPU pool failure in a single region and route traffic to fallback variant. Walk the oncall rota through the escalation.
- Day 10: Customer-impact tabletop (90m): product PM and CS run prioritization decisions (who to call, customer comms).
- Day 12: Postmortem starter & metrics audit (2 hours): ensure the postmortem stub has required SLO evidence and signal artifacts.

Session roles and responsibilities (short form):
- Incident Commander (IC): SRE oncall (primary). Starts bridge, drives tl;dr, ensures runbook steps executed.
- Observability Lead: platform-observability engineer. Owns dashboards, ensures alerts fired and screenshots are captured.
- Feature Owner: product/feature engineer for the affected endpoint. Executes rollback/fallback if required, decision authority for product trade-offs.
- Routing/Fallback Engineer: serving-runtime engineer. Validates model variant/fallback routing and capacity changes.
- CS Rep: customer-success oncall lead. Prepares communication template and customer impact assessment.
- Recorder/PM: takes notes, timestamps key signal artifacts for postmortem.

Exercises (unique, repeatable):
1) Incident Sculpting: P95->P99 Divergence
- Scenario: After a model update, P95 stays stable but P99 latency spikes for long-tail queries. No immediate request drop, but error budgets are bleeding.
- Steps:
  - Observability Lead runs the "tail-sampler" query (provided snippet) to collect full-request histograms.
  - IC declares SLO burn threshold; Feature Owner decides between throttling long queries or rolling back.
  - Routing Engineer toggles prefix-KV caching to test mitigation; measure 15-minute impact.
- Learning targets: how quickly can teams identify root-cause (model complexity vs batching behavior), and can fallback routing prevent escalation within 20 minutes.

2) Model Serving Cost Spike (token-cost regression)
- Scenario: A change increases token churn for a set of prompts causing 2x cost on a mid-tier route and a steady SLO burn on latency under load.
- Steps:
  - Use recorded traffic replay in a staging pool for 30 minutes.
  - Observability Lead shows token-cost attribution per route; CS flags customers at risk.
  - Quick mitigations: reduce max_tokens, enable quantized variant for that route, or apply rate limiting.
- Learning targets: map cost signal to SLO choices and runbook entries.

3) Partial-region GPU Failure + Fallback Validation
- Scenario: One region's dedicated pool loses 60% capacity over 10 minutes (simulated), autoscaler triggers but not fast enough.
- Steps:
  - Routing/Fallback Engineer force-routes 20% traffic to secondary region/model variant.
  - IC checks latency and errors on radar; if customer-impacting, CS drafts comms.
- Learning targets: time-to-fallback, warm-up cost, and customer impact communication template timing.

Rehearsal scripts (short snippets you can read out):
- "Bridge open. We see P99 at 2.4s for route X, error rate stable. Token cost has increased 2.1x for the last 10m. IC asks: Feature owner, do you own rollback or do we throttle?"
- "Observability: attaching dashboard snapshot and flame graph link. Routing, can you confirm fallback candidate is ready?"

Artifacts to capture during runs (must be saved to the incident folder):
- Dashboard screenshots with timestamped queries.
- Alert firing history (raw JSON).
- Sampling of raw traces and the input prompts that caused the tail.
- Command history for any toggles (rolling back, routing changes).

Success metrics and acceptance criteria:
- All alert-to-bridge times <= 5 minutes for synthetic tests.
- At least 1 successful automated fallback during live mini-sim with < 15% customer-impact traffic diverted.
- Post-bootcamp: 80% of participants can list the SLO signal chain in a 3-point checklist test.

Quick runbook checklist (bite-sized items):
- Is the correct SLO policy attached to the route? (yes/no)
- Can synthetic tests be triggered in < 10m? (who owns it)
- Alert severity mapping set: P99 latency -> page; error-rate -> page; cost-spike -> slack only.
- Postmortem stub created with links to dashboards, alert JSONs, and timeline.

[Stability Orienteering: Field Guide and Cross-Team Collab Sprint]
Purpose and intent:\nThis is a practical, bottom-up field guide to run a 6-week cross-functional stability sprint focused on SLO operationalization for model-serving endpoints. The intent is not to re-specify SLOs but to create repeatable, low-friction runbooks, quick experiments, and escalation handoffs so feature teams can adopt service-level thinking with minimal friction.\n\nWho should read this:\n- SREs partnering with feature teams owning model endpoints\n- Platform engineers (serving/runtime) who need clearer guardrails\n- Product/PMs who depend on predictable latency/cost SLAs\n- Solutions & Customer Success for high-touch customer onboarding\n\nHigh-level goals (6 weeks):\n1) Get 3 pilot model-serving routes from \"no SLO\" to \"observable + error budget policy\".\n2) Deliver a lightweight synthetic test harness and a canary policy per route.\n3) Reduce P99 tail risk exposure via targeted mitigations (KV caching, prefix cache, batching settings).\n4) Create an ops playbook for brownouts + automatic fallback chaining for model variants.\n\nSprint cadence and roles:\n- Sprint length: 6 weeks (12 x 1-week iterations = 6 two-week workblocks but run weekly checkpoints)\n- Core leads: SRE lead (Ethan), Platform lead (Aisha), Feature PM (Daniel)\n- Weekly 30m sync (Mon 09:30) + triage (Fri 16:00)\n- Oncall coordination: SREs rotate 2-week shadow with the feature team (explicit handoff doc)\n\nDefinitions we use here:\n- SLO: availability measured at request-level success (HTTP 2xx + model-safe-response) and latency percentiles per route.\n- Error budget: monthly budget derived from SLO; policy defines when rollouts are paused or when capacity increases are triggered.\n- Route: a logical API surface (e.g., /v1/generate-chat - gptx-medium-prod)\n\nPilot route selection criteria (pick 3):\n- High request volume (top 30%),\n- Externally customer-affecting (non-internal),\n- Different failure modes (memory pressure, slow KV, downstream scoring)\n\nSprint plan (high level)\nWeek 0 (prep) - discovery and instrument sweep:\n- Inventory: owners, deployed variants, existing alerts, dashboards (SREs + platform)\n- Quick telemetry gap map: what metrics are missing (trace sampling, per-route latency histograms, kv cache hit rate)\n- Deliverable: route inventory sheet + minimal dashboard templates\n\nWeek 1-2 - observability and baseline:\n- Add per-route tagging to logs (request_id, route, model_version, quantization_profile)\n- Deploy synthetic checker (local harness) that hits each route with realistic prompt shapes\n- Baseline metrics for 7-day p50/p90/p99, tail latency histograms, and 5xx distribution\n- Deliverable: baseline report + proposed SLO targets for each route (example: availability 99.9% monthly, p99 latency 800ms)\n\nWeek 3 - error budget automation + rollback policy:\n- Implement simple error budget counter (daily rolling window) with alert thresholds: warning at 25% burned, action at 50%, emergency at 80%\n- Define automatic rules: pause canary rollouts when burned > 50%; auto-evacuate traffic to fallback when burned > 80%\n- Deliverable: error budget alerts in PagerDuty + rollback playbook (doc + checklist)\n\nWeek 4 - performance experiments and mitigations:\n- Run targeted experiments (one at a time):\n  - Enable prefix/KV caching for frequent prompts\n  - Adjust batching delta thresholds on serving runtime\n  - Try a quantized fallback model for long-tail prompts\n- Measure unit-cost delta and latency impact for each change\n- Deliverable: experiment log (measurements, configs, links to PRs)\n\nWeek 5 - canary + traffic shaping:\n- Canary config: 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% with 24h at each step and automatic rollback on error budget triggers\n- Test outage scenarios: simulate KV outage, node OOM, cold-start storms\n- Deliverable: canary runbook + run results\n\nWeek 6 - handoff, docs, and playbook publication:\n- Finalize step-by-step runbook for each route (how to read SLO dashboards, how to trigger fallback, how to patch runtime configs)\n- Publish: Confluence + link from Console guide + add to oncall runbook index\n- Deliverable: public playbook, 1 pager for execs summarizing impact and risks removed\n\nOperational primitives we insist on (minimum viable):\n- per-route metric tags and tracing\n- synthetic checker that mirrors production distribution (not just ping)\n- automatable error budget state visible in console + PD alerts\n- documented fallback chain (model_variant -> quantized -> cached_response)\n\nEscalation and decision matrix (quick reference):\n- Warning (25%): SRE + Feature PM notified, triage in 24h\n- Action (50%): Pause rollouts, increase sampling for traces, re-run synthetic test with heavier load\n- Emergency (80%): Auto-failover to fallback model & reduce traffic, oncall bridge + customer comms (Customer Success lead notified)\n\nChecklist templates (copy into issues):\n- Pre-launch: inventory, baseline metrics, synthetic test green, alerting wired, rollback policy reviewed\n- Canary step: monitor p99 and error budget every 6h, snapshot mem/cpu/gpu utilization\n- Incident: run brownout script -> escalate -> run fallback -> confirm customer-impact metrics recover\n\nOpen questions / trade-offs we must decide quickly:\n- SLO cadence: monthly vs 30d rolling. (Recommendation: start with 30d rolling for faster signal.)\n- Cost vs latency trade-offs: when to accept higher latency to reduce GPU cost vs maintain p99. (Decision owned by product+finance for each route.)\n- Synthetic checker fidelity: how many prompt templates needed to be representative? [Service energy and cost accounting metadata standard (v2)]
Overview

This page defines the company-wide standard for per-request energy and cost accounting metadata. The goal is to provide a consistent, compact envelope that services and proxies attach to requests and emitted telemetry so downstream billing, cost-optimization, SLO reconciliation, and sustainability metrics can reliably attribute spend and estimated energy consumption to tenants, models, and workload features.

This 2026 revision introduces cost_version=v2 and clarifies header propagation, typing, and privacy rules based on the 2025 rollout learnings.

Why this standard matters

- Unifies cost attribution across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
- Enables low-latency routing decisions using cost hints without leaking raw pricing data.
- Provides the data foundation for chargeback, forecast, and energy-conscious routing features.
- Supports audits and compliance with per-tenant retention and redaction policies.

Goals and constraints

1. Keep the per-request envelope small (<= 3KB) to avoid adding significant network or serialization overhead.
2. Include stable, well-documented keys (snake_case) rather than free-form tags.
3. Ensure values are typed and bounded (e.g., currency amounts in micro-units; energy in millijoules).
4. Make the envelope forward-compatible: allow vendor-specific extensions under a reserved prefix.
5. Avoid embedding per-token usage details in the routing envelope; use async telemetry for high-granularity events.

Scope

- Applies to: edge proxies (edge-router), API gateway (api-gateway), inference routers (inference-router), runtime sidecars (runtime-sidecar), batch job submitters, and telemetry collectors.
- Does not mandate billing rates or conversion tables — those live in the billing service and are referenced by id.
- Includes both real-time headers for short-lived routing decisions and persisted JSON envelopes for telemetry records.

Metadata fields (canonical envelope)

Use the following canonical keys in the JSON envelope attached to telemetry events and the corresponding HTTP headers for routing. Types and example values are provided. Services must include the required fields; others are optional.

Notes (v2):
- Numeric fields MUST be emitted as JSON numbers in persisted telemetry. For headers, the base64 envelope must preserve types.
- tenant_id remains required for internal telemetry; for cross-team aggregate pipelines, use hashed_tenant_id and omit tenant_id.

| Field | Required | Type | Description | Example |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| request_id | yes | string | Global request UUID (trace-friendly). | "req_123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000" |
| tenant_id | yes* | string | Tenant (customer) identifier used for billing. *Required for internal telemetry; must be omitted in "public-aggregate" pipelines. | "acme-corp" |
| hashed_tenant_id | no | string | Stable, salted tenant hash for aggregate analytics. Required when tenant_id is omitted. | "ht_9f2a0c..." |
| model_id | yes | string | Canonical model identifier (catalog/model-hash). | "redwood/gptx-7b:2025-03-01" |
| deployment_id | no | string | Deployment or cluster identifier for private/dedicated installs. | "dep_priv_usw1_003" |
| estimated_energy_mJ | no | integer | Estimated energy consumed by request in millijoules (best-effort). | 4120 |
| compute_microdollars | no | integer | Estimated compute cost in micro-dollars (USD * 1e6). | 125000 |
| currency | no | string | ISO currency code for compute_microdollars when non-USD (rare; telemetry-only). | "USD" |
| cost_version | yes | string | Version of the cost-accounting envelope schema (v1, v2...). | "v2" |
| pricing_ref_id | no | string | Billing service reference to the pricing table used (opaque id). | "price-table-prod-2026-01" |
| priority_class | no | string | One of: realtime, interactive, batch, bulk. Used for routing decisions. | "interactive" |
| cache_hit | no | boolean | True if the request was served from a cache (impacts cost). | true |
| gpu_tier | no | string | GPU tier hint (e.g., a100-80gb, h100-80gb, b200-80gb). | "h100-80gb" |
| inference_tokens_est | no | integer | Optional token estimate used for cost modeling (approx). | 120 |
| appended_by | yes | string | Service that appended/last-modified this envelope (service-name). | "inference-router" |
| routed_region | no | string | Region code used for routing (e.g., us-west1). | "us-west1" |
| cost_finalized | no | boolean | True if the envelope reflects finalized accounting (telemetry-only). | true |

Header mapping for real-time routing

- Preferred: X-RW-ACCT (base64-encoded JSON envelope).
- Minimal header set (when envelope is not available):
  - X-RW-REQ-ID
  - X-RW-TENANT (internal-only; must not be forwarded to customer-controlled hops)
  - X-RW-MODEL
  - X-RW-PRIORITY
  - X-RW-COST-VERSION

Header and forwarding rules (updated)

1. Runtime proxies must not forward tenant_id or pricing_ref_id outside Redwood-controlled networks. When traffic crosses a customer-controlled boundary, scrub X-RW-TENANT and any envelope fields containing tenant_id or pricing_ref_id.
2. pricing_ref_id MUST NOT appear in any externally-forwarded header. It may appear in internal telemetry.
3. If a service cannot safely attach headers (protocol limitation), it must attach the envelope only to telemetry.

Telemetry propagation and mutation rules

1. The first ingress service (edge-router or api-gateway) must create request_id and populate tenant_id and model_id.
2. Each service that materially changes estimated_energy_mJ or compute_microdollars must update appended_by to itself and emit a telemetry-only delta record (delta fields are telemetry-only and must never be included in routing headers).
3. runtime-sidecar may update compute_microdollars after final token counts; it must emit a separate telemetry record with final accounting and set cost_finalized=true.
4. If a proxy cannot compute estimated_energy_mJ, it must omit the field (do not set 0).

Schema versioning and compatibility

- Use the cost_version field to determine compatibility. Consumers must ignore unknown fields.
- v2 changes:
  - Clarifies numeric typing (JSON numbers in telemetry; preserve types in base64 envelope).
  - Adds hashed_tenant_id and deployment_id.
  - Deprecates the name X-RW-COST in favor of X-RW-ACCT (X-RW-COST is accepted until 2026-09-30).

SLOs and accuracy expectations (updated targets)

- Energy estimate accuracy: median absolute error <= 15% for production real-time estimates vs finalized telemetry for 95% of requests over a rolling 7-day window.
- Cost estimate accuracy: median absolute error <= 8% for compute_microdollars vs billing-service reconciliation for 99% of requests within 24 hours.
- Envelope propagation SLA: 99.95% of in-flight requests must carry either the minimal header set or the base64 envelope between edge-router/api-gateway and runtime-sidecar.

Storage, retention and redaction

- Telemetry envelopes stored in observability must omit tenant_id for analytics buckets labeled "public-aggregate". Use hashed_tenant_id when sending to cross-team aggregate pipelines.
- Raw envelopes with tenant_id and pricing_ref_id are PII-adjacent; retention default is 120 days unless tenant contract requires longer retention.
- For privacy-sensitive tenants, support redaction at ingress: redact_fields=["pricing_ref_id","estimated_energy_mJ"].

Rollout plan (recommended)

1. Week 0: Publish spec and unit tests in infra-standards repository; publish decoder for X-RW-ACCT.
2. Week 2: edge-router and api-gateway generate minimal headers and X-RW-ACCT. Keep emitting X-RW-COST for backward compatibility.
3. Week 4: inference-router and runtime-sidecar adopt v2 mutation rules and emit finalized telemetry with cost_finalized=true.
4. Week 6: billing-service consumes finalized telemetry and runs reconciliation; enforce updated accuracy metrics.
5. Week 8: Enable opt-in energy-based routing experiments for a small percentage of traffic (5%) using estimated_energy_mJ.

Validation and testing

- Unit test: schema validator that rejects envelopes with wrong types or missing required fields for the declared cost_version.
- Integration test: synthetic workload where compute_microdollars from runtime matches the billing-service computed microdollars within <8%.
- Smoke test: request roundtrip through edge -> runtime -> telemetry collector must include X-RW-REQ-ID and the envelope in the final event.

Example envelopes

Minimal header-encoded JSON (for routing):

X-RW-ACCT: eyAicmVxdWVzdF9pZCI6ICJyZXFfMTIzZSIsICJ0ZW5hbnRfaWQiOiAiYWNtZSIsICJtb2RlbF9pZCI6ICJyZWR3b29kL2dwdHgtN2I6MjAyNS0wMy0wMSIsICJjb3N0X3ZlcnNpb24iOiAidjIiLCAicHJpb3JpdHlfY2xhc3MiOiAiaW50ZXJhY3RpdmUiIH0=

Example telemetry JSON envelope (persisted):

{
  "request_id": "req_123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000",
  "tenant_id": "acme-corp",
  "model_id": "redwood/gptx-7b:2025-03-01",
  "estimated_energy_mJ": 4120,
  "compute_microdollars": 125000,
  "cost_version": "v2",
  "pricing_ref_id": "price-table-prod-2026-01",
  "priority_class": "interactive",
  "appended_by": "runtime-sidecar",
  "routed_region": "us-west1",
  "cost_finalized": true
}

Operational runbook snippets

- Problem: Missing tenant_id in envelopes for a subset of traffic.
  1. Check edge-router logs for header generation failures (service: edge-router, log key: cost-envelope-generation).
  2. Validate ingress auth middleware configuration: ensure tenant extraction rules are up-to-date.
  3. If using hashed_tenant_id fallback, verify the target pipeline is "public-aggregate" and that tenant_id is intentionally omitted.

- Problem: compute_microdollars differs from billing-service by > 15% (daily reconcile).
  1. Pull a sample of requests with request_id and compare runtime token counts vs billing charge pipeline.
  2. Verify pricing_ref_id mapping in billing-service and whether a new price-table was rolled without updating pricing_ref_id.
  3. Temporarily mark the envelope with telemetry-only debug fields (e.g., cost_override_reason="investigation") and ensure they do not appear in headers.

Governance and ownership

- Spec owner: Eng Infra Standards (primary: Aisha Kapoor; delegate for observability alignment: Evelyn Chen).
- Implementation owners: edge-router (team: eng-platform), inference-router (team: eng-serving-runtime), runtime-sidecar (team: eng-private-deployments), telemetry collector (team: eng-observability).
- Review cadence: Quarterly review or when cost_version increments.

Backwards compatibility guidance

- Producer-first approach: when introducing new fields, producers may emit them flagged as optional. Consumers must tolerate absent fields.
- Deprecation: announce deprecation of a key at least 8 weeks prior and publish a migration playbook.
- Header deprecation: X-RW-COST is deprecated in favor of X-RW-ACCT; dual-emit until 2026-09-30.

Open questions and future work

- Integrate energy models that use hardware telemetry (PState/PMU) for improved estimated_energy_mJ accuracy.
- Standardize hashed_tenant_id algorithm and key rotation guidance for cross-tenant analytics with privacy guarantees.
- Add support for per-region pricing overrides without increasing header cardinality.

[Traffic mirroring for SLO validation and capacity-impact testing]
Summary:
This playbook describes a standardized approach to using traffic mirroring (traffic shadowing) to validate SLO compliance and measure capacity impact without affecting production traffic. It focuses on safe mirroring pipelines, measurement methodology, telemetry collection, and decision gates for progressing from shadow tests to gradual rollouts.

Why this exists:
- SLO-driven decisions require realistic load and production-like request patterns.
- Full canaries change user-visible state; mirroring lets teams exercise the stack end-to-end in a read-only fashion.
- Mirroring enables: regression detection, resource usage profiling (CPU/GPU/memory), KV/DB read amplification analysis, and cache-hit behavior insights.

Scope and applicability:
- Services backed by stateless inference endpoints (text-gen, embeddings) and stateful control planes are both supported, but write-side effects must be blocked or replayed to test sandboxes only.
- Intended for feature/variant validation prior to any write-enabled canary or rollout.
- Not suitable for migrations that rely on side-effect behavior (e.g., payments) unless a safe sandbox exists.

Definitions and key metrics:
- Mirror target: non-production replica of the real service (cluster or namespace) receiving mirrored requests.
- Source service: the production ingress or routing proxy that supports mirroring (e.g., envoy/redwood-edge).
- Important metrics to collect (examples):
  - redwood.request.latency_p50/p95/p99 (ms)
  - redwood.request.success_rate (OK codes / total)
  - redwood.request.cpu_seconds_per_1k_requests
  - redwood.kv.cache_hit_ratio
  - redwood.gpu_utilization_percent
  - redwood.error.type_counts (per-class)
  - redwood.request.queued_length

Preconditions and safety controls (must be satisfied before mirroring):
1. Ownership: Each mirror run must declare an SLO champion (oncall or service owner) and a safety lead.
2. Read-only enforcement: Mirror target must be configured to reject or sandbox any requests that mutate state. If sandboxing is impossible, mirror only read requests.
3. Resource isolation: Mirror cluster must have separate quotas and alerts to prevent accidental autoscaler interactions with production.
4. Throttling policy: Mirrored traffic should be initially limited (suggested 0.5% of production QPS) with hard caps enforced by the proxy.
5. Observability: Mirror target must expose the same telemetry schema and labels as production.
6. Abort window defined: a time window and explicit abort criteria (see Escape hatch).

High-level architecture:
- Production ingress (envoy/redwood-edge) receives real requests.
- Mirroring rule duplicates a subset of traffic to the mirror target asynchronously (no response path changes).
- Mirrored requests are instrumented with header X-Redwood-Shadow: <run-id>.
- Mirror target writes telemetry to a separate metrics namespace and logs to an isolated index for analysis.
- Post-processing jobs compute per-run SLO deltas and resource deltas.

Step-by-step procedure to run a mirror test:
1) Plan the run
   - Define scope: endpoints, request sampling percentage, duration, and run-id (format: mirror-YYYYMMDD-service-feature).
   - Identify hypothesis: e.g., "variant A increases p99 latency by <10ms and does not increase GPU utilization >5% at 95th percentile."
   - Delete or sandbox any downstream write-side integrations.
   - Notify SRE channel and affected teams with run details and abort criteria.

2) Prepare mirror target
   - Create a dedicated namespace/cluster using the latest build or the specific model/quantization under test.
   - Ensure the deployment config sets READ_ONLY=true, DB_RW_PROXY=disabled, or uses replay proxy.
   - Configure autoscalers to deterministic min/max to avoid unbounded scaling interacting with mirrored load.

3) Configure the ingress mirroring rule (example for Envoy v3):

   # envoy mirror config (pseudo-YAML)
   listener:
     name: ingress-ingress
     filter_chains:
       - filters:
           - name: envoy.filters.network.http_connection_manager
             typed_config:
               http_filters:
                 - name: envoy.filters.http.router
               route_config:
                 virtual_hosts:
                   - name: prod-host
                     routes:
                       - match:
                           prefix: "/v1/generate"
                         route:
                           cluster: production-cluster
                           request_mirror_policies:
                             - cluster: mirror-cluster
                         # Percentage controlled dynamically by x-rate-limit header or feature flag

4) Throttle and ramp
   - Start with 0.1% of production QPS mirrored for 30 minutes. Validate telemetry ingestion and label propagation.
   - Ramp to 0.5% for 60 minutes if no alerts, then to 2% for a single stress window (if allowed).
   - Never mirror more than the defined hard cap (default 5% unless approved).

5) Monitor during run
   - Real-time dashboards: Mirrored vs production side-by-side charts for p50/p95/p99 and error breakdowns.
   - Resource dashboards: CPU, GPU, memory, ephemeral storage and network egress.
   - Alerts: Fail-on-delta alerts configured for quick abort:
     - p99_latency_mirror_exceeds_prod_by_ms > 50ms sustained for 5m
     - error_rate_mirror - error_rate_prod > 0.5% sustained for 5m
     - mirror_gpu_utilization > 95% or mirror_cpu > 90% sustained 5m
   - Use a runbook channel pinned message containing run metadata and links to dashboards.

6) Post-run analysis (automated and manual)
   - Compute SLO deltas: for each metric compute absolute and relative deltas between mirror target and production baseline over the run window.
   - Resource profiling: produce per-request resource cost estimates (e.g., tokens -> GPU-ms).
   - Failure mode classification: correlate increased latencies or error types with code paths and model artifacts.
   - Produce a short report with: run-id, hypothesis, traffic % mirror, duration, pass/fail against abort criteria, key metrics table, recommendations.

Validation checklist (pass conditions):
- Latency: p99_mirror <= p99_prod + 25ms (unless hypothesis specifies otherwise).
- Success rate: delta <= 0.2% absolute or within hypothesis bounds.
- Resource overhead: median GPU-ms per request delta <= 10% unless testing a more expensive quant/model.
- No new error classes introduced (>=50 occurrences) without triage.
- Observability completeness: all mirrored requests are present in the mirror metrics index and flagged with the run-id.

Abort criteria and escape hatch:
- Abort immediately if any of the following occur during the run:
  1. p99 latency delta > 50ms sustained for 5 minutes.
  2. Error rate delta > 1% absolute sustained for 5 minutes.
  3. Mirror target saturates (GPU or CPU > 98% for 1 minute).
  4. Any production impact is observed (e.g., increased production latency correlated with mirroring agent).
- Aborting steps:
  - Disable mirror rule at the ingress control-plane (document the exact command in the run comment).
  - Notify channel, set incident-to-incident-review if impact was observed.
  - Collect and preserve all telemetry for postmortem.

Integrating mirror runs into SLO lifecycle and capacity planning:
- Mirror runs are required for: major model/quantization changes, architecture swaps (e.g., offloading KV cache), and rollout of new GPU instance types.
- Results feed into capacity plans: per-request GPU-ms and queueing profiles inform autoscaler target changes and reserved capacity sizing.
- SRE-run mirror reports must be attached to the corresponding SLO change request (Jira/PR) before approving production rollout.

Operational tooling and automation suggestions:
- Feature flag toggle: use a dynamic feature flag to adjust mirror percentage without config deploys.
- Mirroring-run registry: lightweight service that registers run-id, owner, hypothesis, and status. Exposes REST endpoints for automation and a UI table.
- Automated delta calculators: scheduled job that computes metrics deltas and attaches charts to the run record.
- Canary-to-mirror transition script: after successful mirror run, script generates a canary rollout plan with percent traffic batches.

Ownership and roles:
- SLO Champion: approves hypothesis and pass/fail criteria (typically product or reliability PM).
- Safety Lead: has authority to abort the run and is responsible for rollback decisions.
- Mirror Engineer: configures mirror rules and ensures read-only enforcement.
- Observability Engineer: ensures dashboards, metric names, and alerts are correct.

Example run report template (to be attached to run record):
- Run-id: mirror-20250215-textgen-quantA
- Owner: @aisha.bennett
- Duration: 2025-02-15T09:00Z to 2025-02-15T13:00Z
- Traffic mirrored: 0.5% steady
- Hypothesis: p99 latency increase < 10ms and GPU-ms per request delta < 5%
- Result: PASS/FAIL
- Key deltas: p50/p95/p99 tables, error deltas, gpu-ms delta
- Recommendation: proceed to 2% mirror and then canary/gradual rollout OR investigate X cause and re-run.

Appendix A — Example commands and snippets:
- Disable mirroring on the envoy control plane (kubectl patch example):
  kubectl patch configmap envoy-config -n ingress --type merge -p '{"data":{"disable_mirror":"true"}}'

- Query example (PromQL sample):
  # p99 latency delta
  (histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(redwood_request_duration_seconds_bucket{cluster=\"mirror\",run_id=\"mirror-2025\"}[5m])) by (le)) - histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(redwood_request_duration_seconds_bucket{cluster=\"production\"}[5m])) by (le)))

- Grafana dashboard panels to include:
  - Mirrored vs Production p50/p95/p99 latency (time-series)
  - Error-class waterfall (stacked bar)
  - GPU-ms per request heatmap by request type
  - Request path distribution (to detect skew in mirrored sample)

Appendix B — Common pitfalls and mitigations:
- Pitfall: Mirrored traffic is not representative (biased sampling).
  Mitigation: Use sampling keyed on request path and user cohorts or run multiple runs across different windows.
- Pitfall: Downstream systems accidentally observe mirrored write intents.
  Mitigation: Enforce read-only mode and replay with a separate queue if necessary.
- Pitfall: Telemetry label mismatch causing aggregation errors.
  Mitigation: Use a metrics schema validator that runs pre-flight checks.

Governance and retention:
- Run records and associated telemetry must be retained for 90 days for audit and SLO regression analysis.
- High-risk runs (those that fail or trigger aborts) must be retained for 365 days and attached to the post-incident review.

Contact and escalation:
- Primary contact: @aisha.bennett (SRE lead)
- SRE escalation channel: #sre-mirroring-runs
- Pager: SRE oncall rotation (see /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-and-incident-response/oncall-rotations)

[Adaptive Quantization and Runtime Fallback Standards]
Summary:

This document defines the standards for adaptive quantization profiles and the runtime fallback policy used by Redwood's serving runtime. The goal is to allow aggressive cost-optimizing quantization for production traffic while guaranteeing detectable quality regressions are automatically mitigated by deterministic fallback actions.

Scope:

- Applies to all model variants served by Redwood-hosted and Dedicated runtimes.
- Covers quantization profile metadata, runtime quality checks, automated fallback routing, SLOs, testing, and operational monitoring.
- Does NOT replace model onboarding QA; it complements pre-deployment validation with production guards.

Motivation:

Quantization is a major lever for inference cost reduction but can introduce subtle quality regressions that only surface under real traffic. These standards ensure teams can deploy quantized variants safely and recover automatically with documented ownership and observability.

Definitions:

- Quantization profile: A named set of numeric transformations and runtime flags (e.g., int8-aq, int4-ema, q4_0) attached to a model variant.
- Canary prompt-set: A small representative set (default 150 prompts) used at runtime to detect quality drift.
- Quality signal: Metric(s) computed against the canary prompt-set, e.g., token-level perplexity delta, semantic similarity (cosine) for embeddings, or task-specific eval scores.
- Fallback: Automatic routing away from a quantized variant to a less-quantized/FP16 variant or a different model family when thresholds are exceeded.

Standards (high level):

1) Quantization Profile Metadata

- Every quantized model variant MUST include the following metadata fields:
  - profile_name (string): short, kebab-case, e.g. "int8-latency-optimized"
  - compress_rate (string): estimated token-cost reduction, e.g. "~2.6x"
  - expected_p50_latency_ms (string): representative p50 at standard load, e.g. "85ms"
  - predeploy_eval_hash (string): SHA256 of the canonical predeploy eval run
  - fallback_targets (list of strings): ordered model variants to try on fallback, e.g. ["fp16-stable", "int8-conservative"]

- Profiles SHOULD be versioned (profile_name + semantic suffix) when microarchitectural changes occur, e.g. "int8-latency-optimized-v2".

2) Runtime Quality Checks

- The serving runtime MUST execute a lightweight canary evaluation every 60s per model-shard using the canary prompt-set (default: 150 items).
- Quality signals to compute (select at least one per model class):
  - generation: mean normalized perplexity (MNP), normalized against baseline FP16 MNP;
  - semantics/embeddings: mean cosine similarity versus baseline embeddings;
  - classification/regression: micro-F1 or task-specific metric from the suite.
- Check frequency and sample size are configurable per customer model (min interval 30s, max interval 300s).

3) Thresholds and Decision Logic

- Alert threshold (soft): any single 60s canary run that shows:
  - generation: MNP increase >= 7% relative to baseline OR
  - embeddings: mean cosine drop >= 0.06 OR
  - task-F1 drop >= 3% absolute.
- Failure threshold (hard, triggers fallback): aggregated over a 5-minute rolling window: at least 3/5 checks meeting or exceeding the alert thresholds above.
- Safety net: if request error-rate > 0.5% or tail latency (p99) increases > 40% relative to baseline, trigger immediate fallback regardless of canary signals.

4) Fallback Policy (automated)

- When the failure threshold is met, runtime must execute the following deterministic steps in order:
  1. Switch 100% of new traffic for the affected model-shard to the first available fallback_target in metadata.
  2. Maintain sticky in-flight request completion on the original variant for up to 60s to avoid partial-response errors.
  3. Mark the incident in runtime metadata and emit an event to the incident stream with tags: model, profile_name, shard_id, reason, metric_series (last 10 canary runs).
  4. Notify owning team via configured paged channel if the incident persists after 10 minutes.

- Rollback: a successful sequence of 10 consecutive canary checks (per-shard) within 80% of baseline metric values is required before attempting a re-enable of the quantized variant. Re-enable is performed as a canary rollout (5% -> 20% -> 50% -> 100%) with 10-minute stabilization windows.

5) SLOs, Metrics and Alerting

- SLOs to maintain for quantized traffic:
  - Quality SLO: no more than 0.2% of quantized-shard-minute windows per month may exceed the Failure threshold (soft tolerable regressions).
  - Availability SLO: quantized-variants must not cause model-level availability decrease of >0.1% compared to baseline FP16 for the month.

- Required telemetry (emitted per model-shard):
  - canary_mnp_ratio (time-series string), canary_cosine_mean, canary_task_f1, fallback_events.count, fallback_duration_seconds, p50_latency_ms, p95_latency_ms, p99_latency_ms, error_rate

- Alerts:
  - Paging: fallback_events.count > 0 for > 10 minutes AND owning_team != "opt-out" triggers page.
  - Ops-only: per-shard p99 latency increase > 40% triggers runbook.

6) Testing and Predeploy Requirements

- Predeploy checklist for any quantized profile:
  1. Run the canonical predeploy eval (1500 prompts) and record predeploy_eval_hash.
  2. Run a micro-benchmark of 1000 production-simulated requests to estimate p50/p95/p99.
  3. Confirm functional parity on a golden prompt-set (team-owned, 300 prompts) with metric deltas under the alert thresholds.
  4. Document fallback_targets and ownership in model manifest.

- Canary prompt-set construction guidance:
  - Minimum 150 items, representative across top 10 intents by traffic, include edge-case prompts known to be fragile.
  - Keep as immutable artifact stored in model revision history.

7) Ownership and Roles

- Owning team: the team that owns the model variant is the primary on-call for fallback notifications.
- Runtime team: implements the canary execution, telemetry, and automatic routing logic.
- SRE: owns the alerting rules and cross-service incident escalation.

8) Operational Runbook (short):

- Trigger: Automatic fallback event emitted for a model-shard.
- Immediate steps (0-10m):
  1. Verify incident details in the runtime incident event.
  2. Check recent canary metric plots for canary_mnp_ratio / canary_cosine_mean.
  3. If fallback restored service and metrics are within baseline, annotate incident and close.
- Remediation (10-60m):
  1. Reproduce failure locally using the canary prompt-set against both quantized and fallback variants.
  2. If reproduction succeeds, collect model logs, kernel traces, and hardware telemetry; open an engineering ticket.
  3. If not reproducible, consider expanding canary set and run a 5k request smoke test.

9) Telemetry retention and privacy

- Canary artifacts and derived metrics are retained for 90 days by default. Raw user inputs used to construct canary prompts must follow the data-retention policy: remove PII and follow the customer data residency constraints.

10) Example configuration snippet (YAML)

  model_id: text-redwood-23b
  variant: int8-latency-optimized-v1
  quantization_profile:
    profile_name: int8-latency-optimized-v1
    compress_rate: "~2.4x"
    expected_p50_latency_ms: "88ms"
    fallback_targets: ["fp16-stable-v3", "int8-conservative-v1"]
    canary_prompt_set_ref: "gs://redwood-canaries/text-redwood-23b/int8-v1/150.json"
    canary_interval_seconds: "60"
    canary_sample_size: "150"
    alert_thresholds:
      generation_mnp_pct: "7"
      embeddings_cosine_drop: "0.06"
      task_f1_drop_pct: "3"

11) CLI / debug commands (examples)

- Trigger a manual canary run:
  rwdctl runtime canary-run --model-id text-redwood-23b --variant int8-latency-optimized-v1 --shard shard-2

- Force fallback for a shard:
  rwdctl runtime fallback --model-id text-redwood-23b --shard shard-2 --target fp16-stable-v3 --reason "manual-testing"

- Inspect last 20 canary results:
  rwdctl runtime canary-list --model-id text-redwood-23b --variant int8-latency-optimized-v1 --limit 20

- Model slicing and fallback routing guidelines (internal): /confluence/architecture-and-standards/model-serving-standards/model-slicing-and-fallback-routing-guidelines-2026

Appendix A: Example incident event payload (abbreviated JSON for diagnostics)

{
  "event_type": "quant-fallback",
  "model_id": "text-redwood-23b",
  "profile": "int8-latency-optimized-v1",
  "shard": "shard-2",
  "reason": "canary_mnp_rolling_failed",
  "last_canary_metrics": "[...series values omitted here ...]"
}

Notes and rationale:

- Thresholds were chosen to prioritize user-visible quality while allowing meaningful cost reductions; teams operating high-sensitivity verticals (finance/medical/regulatory) should override alert thresholds to be more conservative (e.g., 2–3% generation MNP threshold).
- This standard assumes the runtime can execute lightweight canary evaluations with <1% additional CPU/GPU overhead per-shard; measurement and optimization of that overhead is tracked in a separate infra standard.

[PRD: Internal Unit Economics Dashboard (v1)]
h1. Internal Unit Economics Dashboard (v1) — Product Requirements Document

h2. Summary
Redwood Inference will build an internal-only “Unit Economics” dashboard in the Redwood Console to make inference cost drivers visible and actionable across Product, Engineering, and Finance.

The dashboard’s primary KPI is *Blended $/1M output tokens*, with drilldowns by:
* Model (including model version and quantization profile)
* Region (canonical normalized region)
* Customer tier (Self-serve / Dedicated / Private / Enterprise)

The dashboard is intended to support Cost Optimization Automation efforts (batching, caching, quantization) by:
1) quantifying impact, 2) identifying regressions, and 3) enabling prioritization of runtime/infra work.

h2. Goals (v1)
* Establish a *trusted, finance-aligned* definition of “Blended $/1M output tokens” that reconciles with infra spend inputs and platform metering.
* Enable interactive drilldowns and comparisons to identify unit-cost outliers by model/region/tier.
* Surface contributing signals to support diagnosis: cache hit rate, batching efficiency, average output length, streaming vs non-streaming, and quantization profile.
* Operationalize metric reliability via data quality checks, SLOs, alerts, and an on-call playbook so the KPI is dependable for exec reporting.

h2. Non-goals (explicit, v1)
* External/customer-facing cost dashboards.
* Fully automated optimization actions (the dashboard provides measurement/diagnostics that feed automation).
* Per-customer or per-request identification in the UI (avoid customer-identifiable drilldowns; only aggregated views).
* Real-time cost reporting (v1 targets hourly aggregation and near-real-time freshness, not second-level).

h2. Personas + Use Cases
h3. Finance (CFO / FP&A)
* Primary users: Laura Bennett (CFO), Rishi Malhotra (FP&A)
* Use cases:
  * Quarter-to-date / month-to-date unit cost trending for exec reporting.
  * Reconciliation of KPI vs infra spend (rate card) and token metering.
  * Understand how mix shifts (region/model/tier) change blended unit cost.

h3. Engineering (Telemetry/Analytics, Serving Runtime, Infra)
* Primary users: Logan Wright (Telemetry/Analytics), Nadia Rahman (Token metering), Sean Gallagher (SRE)
* Use cases:
  * Detect regressions (e.g., output token undercounting, region mapping gaps, sudden cost spikes).
  * Attribute cost changes to signals (cache hit rate, batching utilization, quant profile changes).
  * Verify improvements from runtime changes and infrastructure optimizations.

h3. Product (Console, Optimize)
* Primary users: Marissa Cole (Console), Aditya Rao (Optimize)
* Use cases:
  * Prioritize optimization roadmap based on largest cost opportunities.
  * Validate that optimization launches reduced blended cost without hidden regressions.
  * Communicate cost drivers to GTM/CS with appropriate caveats and aggregation.

h2. Key Definitions (v1)
This section defines the canonical metric as displayed in the dashboard. For full methodology and reconciliation rules, see “Blended Cost Methodology v1” and ADR-034.

h3. KPI: Blended $/1M Output Tokens
*Display name in Console:* “Blended cost ($/1M output tokens)”

*Definition (high level):*
Blended $/1M output tokens = (Allocated inference cost in USD / Total output tokens) × 1,000,000

h4. Numerator: Allocated inference cost (USD)
Cost is computed from a finance-owned GPU hourly rate card and allocated to usage based on the adopted attribution model (ADR-034). v1 includes:
* GPU compute costs (fleet spend applied via hourly rate card)
* Region/provider-specific rates (e.g., us-east, eu-west)
* Capacity-type handling (hosted shared pools vs reserved/dedicated pools)
* Idle capacity treatment per ADR-034 (v1 will display *blended* cost, inclusive of allocated idle, not marginal)

Explicit exclusions in v1 (unless specified by Finance methodology):
* Non-GPU costs (e.g., general SaaS tools) unless included as a fixed overhead allocation in the finance methodology
* One-time credits/promotions (these affect revenue/billing, not cost)

h4. Denominator: Output tokens
*Output tokens* are the platform-metered tokens generated by the model as completion output.

Inclusions:
* Tokens produced in non-streaming responses
* Tokens produced in streaming responses (requires parity across streaming code paths)

Exclusions/notes:
* Input/prompt tokens are *not* in the denominator for this KPI (v1 is output-token-centric for comparability across workloads).
* Tool call payload tokens are included only if they are counted by the canonical tokenizer in the serving path; v1 will follow metering standard and document known edge cases.
* Truncation behavior must be consistent: count tokens actually emitted to the client (or logically generated if streaming partial emissions are retried), per metering spec.

h4. Dimensions (grouping keys)
All drilldowns and filters must use canonical normalized dimensions to keep results stable.

Required dimensions in v1:
* Model identifier (canonical): model_family + model_name + model_version
* Quantization profile: controlled vocabulary (e.g., fp16, int8, w4a16) with guardrails against high-cardinality tags
* Region: canonical region mapping table (normalize cloud regions/internal labels)
* Customer tier: Self-serve / Dedicated / Private / Enterprise derived from authoritative sources (billing plan + contract flags + routing context)

Optional dimensions (not first-class in v1 UI, but may exist in the warehouse):
* Route, endpoint, streaming flag, request class

h3. “Blended” vs “Marginal” cost (user-facing guidance)
The v1 KPI is *blended*, not marginal.
* Blended includes allocated shared overhead and idle per ADR-034.
* Users must not interpret short-window changes as purely causal; the dashboard will include tooltip guidance and (where available) a confidence/coverage indicator.

h2. User Experience Requirements (v1)
(See UX spec for layouts; this PRD defines functional requirements.)

h3. Entry points
* Redwood Console (internal-only) → “Unit Economics” page under internal tooling section.
* Direct deep link URLs must preserve filter state for sharing internally.

h3. Default view
Default filter state (v1):
* Time range: Last 7 days
* Grouping: Overall (no grouping) with a supporting breakdown (Top models)
* Customer tier: All
* Region: All
* Model: All

The dashboard must prominently show:
* KPI value for selected time range
* Time series chart (hourly or daily aggregation, depending on range)
* Top-N breakdown tables (models, regions, tiers)
* Coverage/data-quality indicator (see Data Quality)

h3. Filters (must-have)
* Time range selector with presets: 24h, 7d, 30d, QTD, custom
* Model selector (supports model family/name; advanced toggle for model version)
* Region selector (canonical regions)
* Customer tier selector (self-serve/dedicated/private/enterprise)

h3. Drilldowns
v1 drilldown behavior:
* Clicking a Top-N row navigates to a drilldown view with that dimension pinned and secondary breakdowns available.
* Drilldowns supported in v1:
  * Model → Model version → Quantization profile
  * Region → (optional) Provider/capacity type if available in warehouse
  * Customer tier → (no deeper drilldown by customer)

h3. Contributing signals (diagnostic overlays)
The dashboard must display (at minimum) the following signals alongside cost to support diagnosis:
* Cache hit rate (prefix/KV cache) — aggregated
* Batching efficiency/utilization — aggregated
* Avg output length (tokens/output) — aggregated
* Streaming share (% requests streaming)
* Prefill/decode ratio (if available by v1; otherwise mark as v1.1)

Each signal must have:
* A clear definition tooltip
* A statement of known limitations (e.g., only available for certain runtimes/regions)

h2. Functional Requirements
h3. Computation and freshness
* Aggregation cadence: hourly computation with availability in Console within defined freshness SLO.
* Support daily rollups for longer ranges (e.g., > 30 days) to keep queries fast.
* Provide two “views” of freshness in v1:
  * “Live” view (fast updates, may be preliminary)
  * “Finance reporting” view (stable, reconciled, uses versioned rate card and allocation rules)

h3. Reconciliation
* Provide a reconciliation report/view that compares:
  * Total allocated cost (USD) for period
  * Total output tokens for period
  * Derived blended $/1M output tokens
  * Differences vs finance reporting totals (with explained deltas)

Acceptance criteria for Finance signoff (v1):
* QTD blended $/1M output tokens matches Finance’s methodology within an agreed tolerance for at least 2 consecutive weekly checks.
* Rate card provenance and version used for each period is visible (metadata).

h3. Access control and auditability
* Internal-only feature flag gate.
* RBAC: allowlist initial groups (Finance, Exec staff, Eng leads for telemetry/runtime, Product Console/Optimize).
* Audit log access (who viewed the page and when) is required because the metric is sensitive.

h3. Privacy and safe aggregation
* No customer-identifiable data in tables or drilldowns.
* No raw request IDs.
* Minimum thresholding: suppress rows with extremely low volume (tokens or cost) if it increases re-identification risk. Threshold values to be set with Security + Finance.

h2. Data Quality and Reliability Requirements
h3. Data quality gates (v1)
The dashboard must expose a coverage indicator and enforce data quality checks before broad rollout.

Minimum checks:
* Completeness: hourly rows present for required dimensions (model, region, tier) above threshold.
* Streaming parity: output tokens for streaming paths are not systematically undercounted vs non-streaming.
* Cardinality guardrails: quantization_profile, model_version values do not explode beyond expected controlled vocab.
* “Unknown” bucket monitoring: unknown region/tier/model must remain below agreed threshold.

h3. SLOs (initial targets)
(Owned by SRE/Telemetry; see SLO doc for final numbers. v1 targets below are used for launch gating.)
* Freshness: 95% of hours available within 2 hours of hour-end.
* Completeness: for each hour, >= 99% of output tokens have non-null canonical model + region + tier.
* Correctness: automated checks show streaming/non-streaming token parity within agreed tolerance over 7d windows.

h3. Incident response
* Alerts route to Eng Platform/SRE on-call, with escalation to Telemetry/Analytics and Finance when reconciliation is affected.
* Runbook must include validation queries, backfill procedure, and comms template for Finance.

h2. Success Metrics
h3. Adoption (internal)
* Weekly Active Viewers (WAV):
  * Week 2 after internal dogfood: >= 15 unique viewers
  * By v1 launch + 4 weeks: >= 40 unique viewers across Finance/Product/Eng
* Finance usage: at least 1 recurring weekly Finance review that uses the dashboard as the source of truth for QTD unit cost.

h3. Effectiveness
* Time-to-diagnosis: reduce median time to identify top driver of a unit-cost change from >1 day to <2 hours (measured via internal survey + incident notes).
* Regression detection: catch at least 2 unit-cost regressions via dashboard signals/alerts within the first 60 days post-launch.

h3. Data trust
* Finance signoff achieved (methodology + reconciliation) before enabling the dashboard beyond the initial allowlist.
* SLO compliance: meet freshness/completeness SLOs for 14 consecutive days post-launch.

h2. Scope (v1)
Included:
* Canonical metric definition and warehouse views/tables
* Hourly aggregation job + backfill tooling for 2025 Q1
* Console APIs for time series and breakdowns (Top-N)
* Console internal UI (filters, charts, breakdown tables, drilldowns)
* Alerts, SLO dashboards, runbooks, and access controls

Excluded:
* Per-customer drilldowns
* Revenue/margin views (cost-only unit metric)
* Fully real-time streaming dashboards

h2. Milestones and Rollout Plan
h3. Phase 0 — Definition + alignment (Weeks 1–2)
Deliverables:
* Finance-aligned metric definition and methodology references
* Dimension definitions (model/version/quant, region normalization, tier mapping)
* Gap analysis (streaming parity, missing dims)
Exit criteria:
* Rishi (FP&A) + Laura (CFO) approve the methodology draft for implementation

h3. Phase 1 — Telemetry + aggregation (Weeks 3–6)
Deliverables:
* Streaming output token metering parity fixes
* Hourly aggregation tables + initial warehouse views
* Reconciliation prototype report
Exit criteria:
* 7-day backtest with stable results; unknown-dimension rates within thresholds

h3. Phase 2 — Console API + UI (Weeks 5–8)
Deliverables:
* Query endpoints (time series + breakdowns + drilldowns)
* Console internal page with filters + top-N tables + drilldowns
Exit criteria:
* Dogfood with Product/Eng; performance targets met (p95 dashboard query < 2s for default views)

h3. Phase 3 — Hardening + access controls (Weeks 8–10)
Deliverables:
* SLO dashboards/alerts wired to on-call
* Runbook and escalation policy
* RBAC + feature flag + audit logging
Exit criteria:
* SLOs met for at least 7 consecutive days in dogfood

h3. Phase 4 — Staged rollout + exec readiness (Weeks 10–12)
Rollout steps:
1) Expand allowlist to Finance + Product leads + Eng managers
2) Weekly reconciliation check with Finance for two cycles
3) Publish internal announcement + feedback channel

Go/No-Go criteria:
* Finance signoff complete
* Reconciliation report shows agreed tolerance vs Finance totals for QTD
* Alerts tested; runbook validated by on-call

h2. Risks and Mitigations
*Risk:* Streaming output token undercount leads to inflated blended cost.
*Mitigation:* Parity tests + canary checks; explicit dashboard warning if parity check fails.

*Risk:* Tier mapping ambiguity (resellers, pilots, credits) makes tier drilldowns untrustworthy.
*Mitigation:* Define authoritative tier source; default to “Unknown” with alerting if mapping coverage drops.

*Risk:* Region normalization mismatches between billing/infrastructure labels and request telemetry.
*Mitigation:* Canonical mapping table with versioning; monitor “unknown region” bucket; backfill mechanism.

*Risk:* High-cardinality tags (model version / quant profile) degrade metrics stability and cost.
*Mitigation:* Allowlisted values + validation at ingestion; periodic audits.

*Risk:* Misinterpretation of blended cost as marginal cost by stakeholders.
*Mitigation:* UI copy/tooltips + documentation; separate “live” vs “finance reporting” view.

h2. Open Questions
1) Idle capacity allocation: confirm final treatment and how it’s explained in the UI (tooltip text and examples). Owner: Rishi Malhotra.
2) Overhead allocation: which overhead categories (if any) are included in v1 blended cost. Owner: Laura Bennett.
3) Thresholding/redaction: what minimum volume thresholds should be enforced to avoid re-identification risk. Owners: Marcus Lin + Finance.
4) “Finance reporting” view definition: what constitutes “stable” (rate card version lock; backfills allowed; revision policy). Owners: Finance + Telemetry.
5) Prefill/decode ratio availability: confirm instrumentation readiness and whether it ships in v1 or v1.1. Owner: Nadia Rahman.

h2. Appendix: Acceptance Criteria (v1)
* The dashboard displays blended $/1M output tokens with correct units and consistent definitions.
* Users can filter by time, model, region, customer tier, and drill down to model version and quantization profile.
* Top-N tables for models/regions/tiers match the time series totals (within rounding).
* Data quality indicator reflects missingness and updates as checks fail/pass.
* Access is internal-only with RBAC and audit logging.
* Finance can use QTD view for KPI reporting with documented reconciliation and rate card provenance.


[latency-tiered-routing-and-shape-spec]
Overview

This design spec defines the Latency-Tiered Routing and Request Shaping (LTRS) system: a policy-driven routing layer that classifies incoming inference requests into latency tiers (instant, interactive, batch) and applies per-tier shaping, model selection, and fallback policies to meet customer SLAs while optimizing cost. LTRS is intended to sit in the request plane immediately upstream of the serving runtime and integrate with Router, Autoscaler, and Billing subsystems.

Goals

- Provide deterministic latency behavior for 90th/95th percentile requests by enforcing per-tenant per-route latency tiers.
- Enable automated cost/latency trade-offs with measurable unit economics per tier.
- Support gradual rollout and runtime configuration without service restarts.
- Maintain compatibility with Dedicated and Private deployments.

Non-goals

- LTRS will not replace lower-level kernel or scheduler optimizations in the serving runtime.
- LTRS will not attempt to infer semantic equivalence or rerank model outputs (that remains higher-level)

Personas and Stakeholders

- Product Engineers: configure per-route latency tiers and budgets.
- Platform Engineers: monitor LTRS metrics and tune autoscaling knobs.
- Customer Success: advise customers on trade-offs and migration.
- Billing/Finance: compute per-tier unit economics for pricing.

High-level Requirements

Functional requirements (must):
1. Accept route-level configuration with: latency_tier, max_allowed_queue_ms, preferred_model_list, fallback_models, tenant_capacity_tag.
2. Classify requests into "instant" (p95 <= 120ms), "interactive" (p95 <= 500ms), "batch" (no strict latency SLO).
3. Enforce per-tier queueing and admission control to protect latency SLOs.
4. Route to preferred models when capacity allows; automatically fall back to quantized/cheaper models when constrained.
5. Emit structured traces and metrics to Console: per-tier latency histogram, queue depth, admission_drop_rate, fallback_rate, per-token-cost.

Non-functional requirements:
- Support 99.99% availability for routing control-plane changes in Hosted/Dedicated clusters.
- Configuration changes should propagate within 60s (target 15s) to edge routers.
- Support 100k RPS across regions with <5ms median routing overhead.
- All routing decisions must be auditable for compliance: log policy version and decision reason.

Design overview

Components
- LTRS Control Plane: stores policies, validates schemas, exposes API for product/config UI.
- LTRS Data Plane (routers): enforces per-request classification, admission, model selection, and emits telemetry.
- Admission Service: per-tenant token bucket + priority queues + backpressure signal to client SDKs.
- Fallback Engine: model compatibility matrix and conversion rules (e.g., float32 -> int8 quantized) with estimated quality delta.

Flow (high level)
1. Request arrives at API gateway with route_id and tenant_id.
2. Router fetches cached policy (expires ~15s) from LTRS Control Plane.
3. Request is classified into a latency tier using route policy and request headers (e.g., priority_hint).
4. Admission Service decides: accept -> forward to model endpoint; queue -> buffered with per-tier max queue time; reject -> return structured 429 with retry-after and 'fallback_suggestion' field.
5. If accepted but preferred model is saturated, Fallback Engine selects next compatible model and annotates the response with fallback_reason.

Policy model and schema

Example policy YAML (for route-level config):

---
route_id: chat-completions-v1
latency_tier: interactive
max_allowed_queue_ms: 300
preferred_model_list:
  - redwood-alpha-2b-fp16
  - redwood-alpha-4b-q8
fallback_models:
  - redwood-alpha-4b-q4\  - redwood-legacy-3b\priority_mapping:
  low: batch
  default: interactive
  high: instant
autoscale_hint:
  min_replicas: 2
  max_replicas: 50
  target_utilization_pct: 70
---

Policy fields explained:
- latency_tier: one of [instant, interactive, batch] and maps to target p95 latency and admission parameters.
- max_allowed_queue_ms: how long a request may be queued before being rejected.
- preferred_model_list: ordered list of model variants to try before fallback.
- fallback_models: models acceptable as degraded-quality alternatives.
- priority_mapping: maps client-side priority hints to latency tiers.
- autoscale_hint: non-binding signals for the Autoscaler; policy does not replace autoscaler logic.

Admission and queueing semantics

- Instant tier uses strict admission (tiny token bucket) and no queueing except a micro-buffer for prefetch operations.
- Interactive tier allows small queues (max_allowed_queue_ms) and organizes requests by estimated compute cost (tokens * model_cost_multiplier).
- Batch tier permits large queues and background capacity.

Backpressure and graceful degradation

When capacity is constrained:
- Step 1: Apply admission thresholds; lower-priority requests are rejected with Retry-After header.
- Step 2: For accepted but unschedulable requests, attempt fallback model in preferred order.
- Step 3: If no compatible fallback exists, respond with deterministic error and a link to customer guidance.

Fallback decision logging

Every fallback event must log: timestamp, tenant_id, route_id, original_model, selected_model, decision_reason, policy_version. This is required for quality regression triage and billing reconciliation.

Model compatibility and quality budgeting

- Compatibility matrix owned by Applied ML: maps model families to compatibility score and expected quality delta per task class (chat/summary/embedding).
- LTRS consults matrix to enforce per-request maximum allowed quality delta (configurable per-route as quality_budget_pct).

Telemetry and SLOs

Metrics to emit (per-route, per-tenant, per-region):
- ltrs.latency.histogram (p50/p95/p99)
- ltrs.queue_depth.gauge
- ltrs.admission_drop_rate
- ltrs.fallback_rate
- ltrs.estimated_cost_per_request_usd

SLO targets (default):
- Instant: p95 <= 120ms, fallback_rate <= 1%
- Interactive: p95 <= 500ms, fallback_rate <= 5%
- Batch: availability 99.9% (latency not bound)

Operational runbook (summary)

1. Detect: Alert on ltrs.admission_drop_rate > 0.5% sustained for 5 minutes or p95 latency SLO violation.
2. Diagnose: Check policy version, current replica counts for models in preferred_model_list, and queue depths.
3. Mitigate: Increase model replicas (scale-up), adjust tier thresholds (widen interactive window), or enable auto-fallback to next model.
4. Post-incident: Create a regression ticket with fallback logs and sample request IDs for Applied ML review.

Migration and rollout plan

Phase 0 (canary - 2 weeks):
- Deploy LTRS data plane to staging and one small hosted region.
- Enable for internal product routes only (no customer traffic).
- Validate metrics and decision latency.

Phase 1 (limited customer opt-in - 4 weeks):
- Invite 10 low-risk customers to opt in.
- Observe per-tenant cost delta and fallback rates.

Phase 2 (gradual ramp - 6 weeks):
- Enable for 30% of traffic by routing fraction in Router.
- Monitor SLOs, regressions, and billing attribution.

Phase 3 (full rollout):
- Default-enable for interactive and batch routes with escape hatch flags.

Rollout safety checks

- Automatic rollback triggers: sustained p95 SLO breach or increase in customer-facing errors by >0.5%.
- Config gating: policy changes require signed-off validation in staging before production deployment.

Backward compatibility

- If a route has no policy, LTRS defaults to legacy behavior: first-fit model routing with no admission enforcement.
- Policy versioning: policies are immutable; edits create a new version with a changelog field.

Security and compliance considerations

- All policy modifications are audited; store diff with author and timestamp.
- Fallback decisions do not send model payloads outside customer region in Private deployments.
- Sensitive fields (customer_tier tags, quotas) are restricted to owners and platform-admin roles.

Billing and pricing implications

- Each latency tier will map to an internal cost multiplier used for visibility (not necessarily public pricing at launch). Example: instant x1.8, interactive x1.0, batch x0.45.
- Billing team will provide recommended public pricing bundles in Q4 2026 that reflect per-tier SLO guarantees.
- For Dedicated customers with reserved capacity, LTRS will prefer capacity-tagged model pools to avoid cross-tenant cost leakage.

Example billing annotation (response header JSON):
{"estimated_cost_usd":"0.0014","latency_tier":"interactive","policy_version":"v13"}

Open questions (needs product/finance decision)

- Whether to expose latency tiers as first-class billable product (premium SLA for instant).
- How to present fallback quality deltas to customers and whether to offer credit/refund for measurable regressions.
- Pricing for Private deployments where model pool cost accounting is opaque.

Testing strategy

- Unit tests for policy validation and admission logic.
- Load tests that simulate mixed-tier traffic and verify p95 SLOs under stress.
- Chaos tests that kill model replicas to verify fallback behavior and audit logging.

Release notes (planned for 2026-07-15)

- Feature: Latency-Tiered Routing and Request Shaping (LTRS) initial launch (canary).
- API: route policy CRUD endpoints: POST /policies, GET /policies/{id}, PATCH /policies/{id}.
- Metrics: new ltrs.* metrics in Console with dashboard template.
- SDK: client SDKs return structured 429 with retry-after and fallback_suggestion.

Ownership and contact

- Engineering lead: Ethan Myers (eng-serving-runtime).
- Applied ML owner (compatibility matrix): Lina Alvarez.
- On-call rotations: refer to eng-sre/runbooks/ltrs-oncall (planned).

Appendix A: sample validation errors (human-friendly)

- invalid_policy: "preferred_model_list must include at least one model"
- unsupported_tier: "latency_tier must be one of instant, interactive, batch"
- quality_budget_violation: "requested fallback would exceed allowed quality_delta for route"

Appendix B: small config table (text)

| Field | Type | Meaning | Default |
| latency_tier | enum | tier that determines SLOs | interactive |
| max_allowed_queue_ms | int | max permitted queue time | 300 |
| preferred_model_list | list | ordered model variants | [] |
| fallback_models | list | acceptable degraded models | [] |
| quality_budget_pct | int | max allowed quality delta | 10 |

Feedback / next steps
