[Consolidate retry/deadline semantics, client idempotency, and hedging defaults across runtime + SDKs]
description:
Problem: Multiple services and SDKs expose different retry/backoff and deadline semantics. Some clients use naive exponential backoff, others rely on hedged requests; idempotency headers are inconsistently applied, causing duplicate side-effects in Dedicated and Private deployments during partial failover. This leads to SLO violations and customer-facing errors during multi-region failovers and sudden load spikes.

Goal: Define a single 'retry contract' that spans server runtime and official SDKs: clear deadline propagation, default retry/backoff profiles by route class, opt-in hedging with a configurable hedge-window, and a canonical idempotency key format to allow safe retries and hedged requests. Provide a migration path and rollout with telemetry and circuit-breaker integration so we can load-shed gracefully under overload and keep tail latency within SLOs.

Scope: runtime (kernel selection + request router), hosted API, official SDKs (python/js/go), console rollout controls, and docs. Excludes: third-party partner SDKs (will provide compatibility guidance).

Design summary:
- Deadline propagation: clients may send X-Redwood-Deadline-ms; runtime enforces and translates to per-model token budget. Servers must reject requests when remaining deadline < 20ms.
- Retry policy surface: routes labeled 'idempotent-by-default' (embeddings, rerank) get safe retries up to 2 attempts; 'stateful' routes (fine-tune, admin) default to no automatic server-side retry. The SDKs expose RetryPolicy objects and a single default: "balanced" (initial 20ms jitter, exponential backoff factor 2, max interval 500ms, overall attempt cap 3).
- Hedge window: hedging is opt-in per-request via Hedge-Mode header. Default SDK behavior: hedging disabled. For low-latency routes we provide an explicit HedgePolicy: start a speculative second request at t = max(1.2 * p50_latency, 35ms) if first request hasn't started streaming. Hedge responses are deduped via canonical idempotency key.
- Idempotency key: canonical header: Idempotency-Key. SDKs will generate V2 keys: prefix "rid-v2-" + base64(uuid+client-ts+SIG). Servers verify format but accept older keys. Keys should be stored in the runtime KV cache with 24h TTL for dedupe.
- Circuit breakers & load shedding: add a per-route token-bucket-based shedder that consults runtime queue length, GPU availability, and per-customer SLA. When shed, server returns 429 with Retry-After and 'X-Redwood-Shed-Reason' header. SDKs should interpret 429 as non-fatal for idempotent routes and may queue a single retry subject to backoff and remaining deadline.

[Staged region switchover with heterogeneous variant hedging and cold-cache seeding]
description:
Objective: Implement a staged multi-region switchover workflow that (1) progressively shifts traffic across regions using tier-aware fences, (2) hedges model fallback risk by routing initial traffic to heterogeneous model variants, and (3) seeds cold KV caches with prioritized snapshots to reduce cold-start tail latency. This ticket covers orchestration logic, readiness gating, instrumentation, and an automated rollback window.

acceptance_criteria:
1) Orchestrator can execute a staged switchover across three regions: primary -> transit -> target with configurable stage durations and percent ramps. 2) For each stage, routing policy prefers same-tier capacity but will route up to a configurable percent of traffic to fallback model variants (heterogeneous hedging). 3) KV cache seeding runs before any stage traffic reaches >1% of target region capacity and exposes preflight metrics (prefetch_success_rate, snapshot_apply_latency, cache_warmth_percent). 4) Readiness gates evaluate: p95 latency delta <= 20% vs baseline, error rate <= 0.5%, cache_warmth_percent >= 35% or prefetch_success_rate >= 85%. 5) Canary stage with 1% traffic must be reversible within 30s and auto-rollback triggers if metrics cross thresholds. 6) End-to-end integration tests and chaos tests (network partition and degraded GPU) run in the lab environment and pass. 7) Playbook and Confluence runbook updated with step-by-step operator commands.

technical_notes:
Design: New Switchover conductor service (stateless controller) will emit staged routing plans to Smart Router. Each plan includes: region sequence, per-stage traffic percent, tier constraints, fallback_variant_list (ordered), snapshot_id for KV seeding. Hedging: Smart Router forwards hedged requests to model variants using probabilistic sampling with deterministic hashing for sticky sessions. Cache seeding: snapshot replays use prioritized keys (high-frequency prefixes) and a prefetch queue capped by target GPU working memory. Readiness scoring: composite score = weighted(sum of normalized metrics) with weights configurable by project. Telemetry: Introduce 'switchover.*' metrics, per-variant latency histograms, and per-region cache_warmth_percent gauge.

runbook_snippets:
Pre-switchover checks: circuit-health OK, model-variant compatibility matrix validated, backup snapshot exists. Execution: 1) stage0: dry-scan (0% traffic) to validate snapshot apply. 2) stage1: 1% target traffic with hedging 10% to fallback variants. 3) stage2: 10% target traffic, increase cache prefetch parallelism. 4) stageN: full ramp if all gates pass. Rollback: set routing to previous region and invalidate warmed keys from failed region to avoid stale KV inconsistencies. Postmortem steps recorded in confluence. Operator CLI: `rdw switchover start --plan-id <id> --dry-run|--execute`.

test_plan:
Unit tests for controller plan generation and validation. Integration tests: simulate snapshot apply + prefetch and measure cache_warmth_percent. E2E lab: run staged switchover between us-east1, europe-west1, asia-south1 with injected 200ms cross-region latency and measure p99 tail behavior. Chaos: disconnect primary mid-stage and assert automatic rollback occurs and traffic returns to last stable region. Automation: nightly synthetic test runs as a Canary pipeline.

risk_and_mitigation:
Risk: Hedging increases cost and could mask model regression. Mitigation: limit hedging to <10% traffic initially, enable detailed per-variant quality logs and automated quality regression alerts. Risk: Snapshot replays spike GPU memory/IO. Mitigation: prioritize keys and rate-limit prefetch; use backpressure metrics to throttle. Risk: Inconsistent KV state across regions. Mitigation: tag prefetched keys with switchover epoch and ensure read-path honors epoch mismatch until consistency achieved.

metrics_to_monitor:
switchover.stage.duration_seconds, switchover.stage.composite_readiness_score, region.<region>.p95_latency_ms, region.<region>.error_rate, region.<region>.cache_warmth_percent, variant.<variant>.latency_p95, hedging.request_fraction, prefetch.snapshot_apply_latency_ms, rollback.trigger_count

dashboards_and_alerts:
Dashboard: Switchover overview with stage timeline, readiness score, cache warmth heatmap, and per-variant quality panel. Alerts: readiness_score < 0.7 for 2m -> pager, rollback_count > 0 -> ticket auto-open. Latency spike guard: region.p95 > baseline*1.5 -> auto-scale and notify.

[Retry & Backoff Policy Spec + SDK Compatibility Matrix]
description:
Problem statement: We have divergent retry/timeout/backoff behaviors across services and client SDKs that undermine SLOs and complicate multi-region failover and incident response. Some clients retry aggressively without idempotency keys; others rely on hedged requests inconsistently. This ticket defines a cross-service runtime + SDK contract for safe retries, standardized timeouts/backoffs, idempotency key rules, hedged request guardrails, circuit breaker signals, and load-shedding behavior. Goals: 1) prevent duplicate side-effects when clients retry; 2) ensure predictable latency/cost trade-offs for hosted and dedicated customers; 3) provide a migration path for older SDKs without breaking production; 4) enable multi-region failover with coordinated retry/backoff to avoid synchronized storms.

acceptance_criteria:
Authoritative spec published in Confluence: 
SDK compatibility matrix published and reviewed by SDK owners
Runtime implements server-side idempotency token handling for retryable endpoints with a 24h dedup window and configurable storage backend
SDKs (python/js/go) implement the default policy flags and unit + integration tests
Canary traffic rollout (10% -> 50% -> 100%) behind feature flag with rollback plan
Monitoring: dashboards for client retry rates, idempotency conflicts, hedged request ratio, circuit-breaker state, and P95/P99 tail latencies
Runbook updated with failure modes and escalation steps
No regressions on core SLOs in canary (availability >= 99.9%, P95 latency within 10% of baseline)

spec_summary:
Core proposal (high level): Default client retry policy: up to 2 retries for idempotent-safe operations (total attempts = 3), exponential backoff with base 100ms, multiplier 2, full jitter, max_backoff 3000ms, and an overall client-side deadline of 8s. For non-idempotent endpoints, retries are allowed only when an Idempotency-Key header is supplied (UUIDv4 recommended) and server advertises idempotency support. Server deduplication TTL default = 24 hours. Hedged requests are opt-in per endpoint: allow a single hedged duplicate when observed tail latency exceeds configured P95 threshold for that model/route; hedged attempts must be limited per-client and globally rate-limited to avoid amplification. Circuit breaker signals: open when 5xx rate > 5% or error rate increases by >x2 over baseline in a 1-minute sliding window, with exponential cooldown and progressive reopen checks. Load-shedding: runtime should reject the lowest-priority requests first with 429 + Retry-After and provide a clear Failover header indicating alternative regions if available.

detailed_policies:
Timeouts: Client socket timeout = 8s default, connect timeout = 500ms. Servers respect X-Client-Deadline when provided; runtime enforces per-request server timeout and cancels background work beyond server deadline.
Backoff: Exponential backoff formula t = base * (2^attempt) with full jitter. Base=100ms, max_backoff=3s, attempts=2 (client retries). Total retry budget per logical request <= 8s.
Idempotency key semantics: Header: Idempotency-Key: <UUIDv4>. Tokens are opaque to runtime and used to dedupe side-effects. Server returns Idempotency-Status header with values {replayed, accepted, conflict}. Dedup window default 24h; configurable per-customer. Keys MUST be unique per logical user operation (do not reuse across distinct operations).
Hedging: Condition for hedged duplicate: request latency > route-configured p95_latency_threshold OR explicit client flag hedged=true. Hedged attempts launched after a hedging_delay = max(50ms, p95_latency_threshold * 0.5). Limit 1 hedged attempt per original request. Hedged attempts are counted separately in metrics and can be rate-limited by runtime feature flags.
Circuit breakers: Per-route and per-tenant breakers. Open threshold: 5xx_ratio > 5% in 1m window AND error_count > 100. Half-open probation: allow 5 requests every 10s. Breaker state exposed through admin API and dashboards.
Load shedding: Runtime drops requests by priority. Default priority: auth > inference > background. When overloaded, return 429 with Retry-After. Provide lightweight rejection path for unauthenticated/anonymous workloads to protect authenticated premium traffic.
Telemetry: Clients MUST emit retry metadata (attempt number, reason, idempotency key) as headers for runtime consumption and observability. Runtime records dedupe hits, idempotency conflicts, hedged wins/losses, and aggregated cost impact.
Backward compatibility: If server responds with 501 or header Idempotency-Supported: false, SDKs MUST disable retry for non-idempotent endpoints and surface a clear warning in logs. Old SDKs without the new behavior are subject to increased request failures; we will provide a compatibility library shim for users on unsupported SDK versions.

sdk_compatibility_matrix:
Python SDK v3.1+: full support for idempotency header, default retry policy, and hedging opt-in flag
JS SDK v2.8+: supports idempotency and retry flags; browser build will disable hedging by default due to concurrency constraints
Go SDK v1.6+: lightweight header-only implementation; hedging is opt-in and behind runtime feature flag
Other clients: fallback behavior documented; server will return explicit headers when features are not supported and SDKs should respect them

rollout_plan:
Week 1: Publish spec and compatibility matrix; SDK owners to open PRs with feature-flagged changes
Week 2: Runtime feature gated rollout to canary region; enable idempotency token storage using Redis cluster (replicated) for canary tenants
Week 3: Canaries with 10% production traffic for selected internal customers; monitor dedupe hit rate and P95/P99 latency
Week 4: Expand to 50% after SLO verification; update public docs and migration guide
Week 5: 100% rollout and deprecation notice for legacy retry behavior in 90 days

testing_plan:
Unit tests for SDKs to validate header wiring, backoff timing, and retry counters
Integration tests: staged failure injection to verify dedupe semantics and hedged request winners/losses
Chaos tests: region-level partition to confirm multi-region failover and that coordinated backoffs avoid cascading overload
Load tests: ensure circuit-breaker thresholds and load-shedding behavior preserve high-priority traffic under stress

risks_and_mitigations:
Risk: Clients may accidentally reuse Idempotency-Keys causing unintended dedupe. Mitigation: document best practices, SDKs auto-generate UUIDs unless caller supplies one, and add a warning when reused frequently.
Risk: Hedging amplifies load during partial outages. Mitigation: hedging is opt-in per route with a global rate limiter and conservative defaults; monitor hedged amplification ratio and disable if >1.2x amplification.
Risk: Increased state/storage for idempotency dedupe. Mitigation: configurable TTLs per customer, efficient Redis schema, and optional spillover to blobstore for long-term entries.
Risk: Backwards compatibility break with older SDKs. Mitigation: compatibility matrix + shim library + clear deprecation timeline and telemetry to detect old SDK usage.

[Regional switchover controller for zero-downtime Hosted API upgrades]
description:
Objective: Implement a regional switchover controller and upgrade tooling to enable zero-downtime Hosted API upgrades across regions with deterministic traffic attenuation, LTS channel awareness, and automated rollback triggers.

Background: We have frequent incidents where multi-region upgrades expose edge cases in routing, leading to partial outages or elevated error rates in some regions. Current traffic shifting primitives are ad-hoc and tied to individual deploys. We need a centralized controller that understands version semantics (major/minor/patch + LTS flags), cross-region dependency graphs, and rollout gates tied to SLO/health signals.

Scope:
- Controller service that orchestrates coordinated switchover across regions using a sliding-window traffic attenuation algorithm (percent-based schedule with health gates).
- Support for LTS channels: stable, lts, experimental; ability to prefer LTS builds for enterprise tenants and pin versions per-customer during switchover.
- Integration with runtime-1.21 release pipeline and Redwood Console rollout UI (hooks for visualizing state and manual overrides).
- Upgrade CLI (redwoodctl rollout) to create, preview and promote switchover plans.
- Telemetry and SLI mapping for rollout gates: 99th percentile latency, 5xx rate, token-throughput variance, downstream error amplification.
- Automatic rollback policies and a "lifeboat" fallback route that routes traffic to the last-known-good variant in case of severe health degradation.

Non-goals: Full rework of scheduler/k8s autoscaler or replacing existing per-region autoscaling. We won't change model variant packaging or image build pipelines in this ticket.

Design notes:
- Versioning: controller uses semver-like tags and an LTS boolean. Each deployment publishes a manifest with version, variant-id, compatible-kernel-hash, and capacity profile. Controller validates compatibility before scheduling traffic.
- Traffic attenuation: schedule expressed as array of steps (time-window, target-percentage). Controller applies per-gateway roll rates with jitter to avoid synchronized cutovers.
- Health gates: windowed anomaly detector compares current SLI to baseline using a short-term median absolute deviation. If gate fails for >2 consecutive windows, controller pauses and triggers automated mitigation.
- Policy engine: supports global policies (SLO thresholds), tenant exceptions (enterprise LTS pinning), and manual holdpoints with runbook references.

Migration plan: Start with a single non-critical region (eu-west-3) and synthetic load test. Then roll to secondary regions (us-west-2, eu-central-1) with staged ramp. After 2 successful runs, enable for a small percentage of production traffic for Canary customers, then full rollout.

Runbook links and artifacts:
- Design spec: https://confluence.redwood.ai/designs/regional-switchover-controller (draft)
- Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/9123
- Console mockups: https://drive.redwood.ai/drive/folders/1SwitchoverUI


acceptance_criteria:
1) Controller can create and execute a regional switchover plan that moves 100% of traffic from version A to version B with no increase in 99th percentile latency beyond configured SLO for >5 minutes.
2) LTS channel selection works: enterprise tenants with 'lts' flag remain on pinned LTS versions during a default switchover.
3) Automated rollback triggers on: 5xx rate >0.5% absolute increase OR 99p latency regression >30% sustained for 2 windows.
4) redwoodctl rollout preview shows a dry-run with region-by-region timeline and estimated impact.
5) Console displays plan state, per-region health metrics, and provides manual pause/rollback actions.
6) Two successful canary runs in non-prod and one controlled production run with traffic shaping completed without manual intervention.


tasks:
- Build controller API and state machine for plan lifecycle (create/preview/execute/pause/rollback).

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-10 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Nina Park (Redwood AE), Lucas Reed (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (CISO, Auriga), Ravi Patel (Infra Lead), Lena Ortiz (ML Platform Lead)

Summary (auto): initial security intake to surface gating controls for production inference. Need to confirm KMS model, SSO integration path, RBAC granularity, audit log retention windows and encrypted at-rest/backups.

[00:00] Nina (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for making time, i think we've got about 50 minutes, i'll do a quick intro then pass to Lucas for the technical bits. Maya, thanks for coordinating on your side.
[00:12] Maya (Auriga CISO): yep thanks, our execs want to move fast but we have strict controls; i'm here to make sure we don't miss compliance gates.
[00:18] Nina: perfect. quick context - Auriga's eval is around running inference for prod customer-facing features. you flagged a few big areas — encryption keys, sso, and audit logs? is that the right triage?
[00:27] Maya: yes exactly. also retention windows because some of our data is regulated under e-privacy and certain European regs.
[00:33] Ravi (Auriga Infra): and from infra, network topology and ability to use our KMS is huge; we prefer customer-managed keys if possible.
[00:38] Nina: understood. i'll hand off to Lucas to walk through hosting options and where the controls map.
[00:42] Lucas (Redwood SE): cool — hi all. i'll keep it high level then dig in. Redwood supports three deployment modes: hosted (our cloud API), dedicated (reserved GPU pools in our infra), and private (VPC or on-prem package). For each we can surface different controls.
[01:05] Lucas: hosted — easiest to get started, but by default keys are managed by Redwood. we do have envelope encryption and we can enable customer v-managed keys for enterprise tiers, though that has additional network/auth steps. some customers call that "bring-your-kms".
[01:25] Maya: when you say "bring-your-kms" do you mean we can point to our AWS KMS key? or do you require bringing HSM appliances?
[01:33] Lucas: good question — we support AWS KMS and GCP KMS integrations for keys at rest via a key wrap model. we also have an HSM-backed option for Private deployments where we can integrate with on-prem HSMs, but that typically requires a private package and some SAs to wire it into the key establishment flow.
[01:47] Ravi: so for hosted we could do an AWS CMK; is the key material ever held by Redwood?
[01:53] Lucas: in the envelope pattern, raw key material stays in your KMS; Redwood gets the wrapped key and uses it for short-lived decryption in memory. we don't persist unwrapped key material to disk. (note: some transcript words may be a little off - "envelope" sometimes spoken fast)
[02:08] Lena (ML Lead): and what about KV cache — we rely on prefix caching for latency. do cached tokens or KV store contain PII?
[02:15] Lucas: KV cache contains model context, which can include user input. for private/dedicated you can opt to keep caches in your VPC or ephemeral memory only. for hosted we have configurable retention and redaction.
[02:27] Maya: configurable retention — how granular? we need 90 days for debug logs, but anything with PII should be deleted in 7 days.
[02:32] Nina: quick note — we'll put that on the retention matrix action item, and Lucas will call out where logs vs payloads live.
[02:39] Lucas: sounds good. audit logs — we emit request-level logs, token counts, model versions, and access events. for enterprise tiers we can ship logs to customer S3 or to a SIEM via syslog/forwarder. retention and deletion policies can be set on the storage side.
[02:58] Ravi: SIEM forwarding is good — what about redaction? we want sensitive fields stripped before logs leave our environment.
[03:05] Lucas: we offer pre-shipping redaction hooks and a scrubber pipeline that can mask common PII patterns. it's rule-driven but we recommend customers run their own final scrubbers as well.
[03:16] Maya: SSO is another gate — we need SAML 2.0 with SCIM provisioning ideally, plus SSO enforced for system admins.
[03:24] Nina: we support SAML SSO and SCIM for user provisioning; for RBAC we have role templates but also custom roles. Lucas, can you share how RBAC maps to tokens and route-level controls?
[03:36] Lucas: sure — RBAC in the console maps to API tokens and role scopes. for example you can have "model-readonly", "deploy-admin", and "billing" roles. tokens can be restricted to endpoints and models. for Private deployments tokens can be further scoped to IP ranges.
[03:51] Lena: are tokens human-issued? or do you integrate with our OIDC provider for short-lived tokens?
[03:56] Lucas: both — we can mint short-lived tokens via our STS with OIDC or SAML assertion flows and issue ephemeral tokens that expire. that's standard for dedicated/private setups.
[04:09] Ravi: network — for private we need explicit egress rules and cert pinning; what's your recommended VPN/peering pattern?
[04:16] Lucas: commonly we do VPC peering or AWS PrivateLink; for stricter setups customers use an on-prem package where the inference runtime runs inside their network and only management plane talks out to Redwood. that removes egress concerns.
[04:30] Maya: for SOC2/ISO, can you send your attestations? we need the latest reports as part of vendor assessment.
[04:36] Nina: absolutely — i'll send SOC2 Type II and ISO27001 snapshots. note: sometimes the naming in our docs is older, but i'll include the attestation PDFs and a short matrix mapping controls to your requirements.
[04:48] Maya: retention of logs and how long you retain query payloads for hosted mode — can customers force delete?
[04:54] Lucas: in hosted there is a standard retention policy (30 days for request payloads by default) but enterprise tiers let you set custom retention or opt out of retention entirely by enabling no-persist mode, though that impacts traceability and debugging. for dedicated/private it's controllable on your side.
[05:11] Maya: is there a way to request deletion for a particular user event (like a right-to-be-forgotten flow)?
[05:16] Lucas: yes — we support subject access deletion requests; for hosted we have a ticketed workflow where we validate and remove across indexed stores. for private, customers handle deletion locally.
[05:27] Ravi: backups — if you integrate with our KMS do backups get encrypted under our CMK as well?
[05:33] Lucas: yes, when integrated with a customer CMK, snapshots and backups are wrapped with the same key material per the envelope model.
[05:40] Lena: audit evidence — can we get raw access logs for a rolling 12 months?
[05:44] Lucas: we generally provide access logs for 12 months for enterprise customers; long-tail retention can be configured but may incur costs.
[05:51] Maya: we also have vendor requirements around penetration tests and vuln disclosure. do you do third-party pen tests?
[05:57] Nina: we do periodic third-party pentests and maintain a vuln disclosure program with a security@ email. i'll include the latest pentest summary in the packet.
[06:07] Maya: okay good. are there any roadblocks you expect for us to use customer-managed KMS in hosted?
[06:13] Lucas: the main work is network auth between Redwood's control plane and your KMS, and ensuring roles/assume-role patterns are set up. it can be done, but there are a couple of ops steps; we'll document them.
[06:24] Ravi: latency implications — if the key wrapping call adds round trips at init is that significant?
[06:30] Lucas: we cache the unwrapped symmetric key for short-lived sessions in memory; the extra handshake is minimal and amortized over many requests. worst case you see a small cold-start on a model host.
[06:41] Lena: model rollback and canary — we want to make sure audit trails show which model version served which request.
[06:47] Lucas: we surface model version in the logs and traces and can pin model versions per route; canary deploys are supported and marked in audit logs.
[06:56] Maya: any compliance certifications for Dedicated nodes?
[06:59] Lucas: dedicated pools come under our corporate SOC and we extend control evidence for customer-dedicated instances; for private, you get even more control because runtime is in your network.
[07:10] Nina: quick check — are there specific red flags that would force you to insist on private/on-prem? Maya?
[07:17] Maya: if we can't get customer-managed keys and we can't ensure PII redaction before logs egress, that's a showstopper. also, inability to SCIM + enforce SSO for admin users is a big no.
[07:29] Ravi: and for infra — if network ports/peering patterns require unsupported changes to our VPC, we might prefer the on-prem appliance.
[07:36] Nina: understood. i'll capture that as acceptance criteria.
[07:40] Lucas: one operational note — for private deployment we provide the runtime bundle and a management agent; we still provide the control plane for model catalog and rollouts but the control plane can be run in a customer VPC for strict air-gap needs.
[07:55] Lena: what about data residency — we have customers in EU and APAC and need region-specific hosting. can you guarantee region pinning?
[08:02] Lucas: yes, we support region pinning via deployment policies — hosted models can be pinned to specific region clusters; dedicated/private gives you stronger guarantees.
[08:12] Maya: anything else about audit logs? specifically chain-of-custody for logs if requested in an audit.
[08:18] Lucas: we can provide signed log exports and integrate with your SIEM for immutable storage; for deeper chain-of-custody we recommend storage in your own S3 with object-lock enabled.
[08:30] Nina: okay we're about midway through — any other controls?
[08:34] Maya: one more — staff access for Redwood engineers. do you have jumpbox access or do you use bastion with MFA?
[08:40] Lucas: Redwood support accesses customer instances through a gated bastion with SSO + MFA and just-in-time access workflows; all sessions are recorded and logged. for private on-prem installs we can adapt to your access model.
[08:53] Ravi: can you show evidence of that? session logs or an example audit?
[08:58] Nina: yes i'll include sample support access audit excerpts.
[09:02] (short crosstalk, someone briefly muted)
[09:10] Maya: timeline — we're looking at a pilot in Q1. decision criteria: keys must be customer-managed or private, SSO must be enforced for admins, audit logs retention 12 months with 90-day quick access, and data retention rules respected per user type.
[09:29] Nina: sounds actionable. i'll summarize next steps: send attestation docs, schedule Lucas + Ravi deep dive about networking and KMS wiring, and Maya will share retention matrix.
[09:40] Lucas: i'll also draft the change list for the private package if you end up on that path.
[09:45] Lena: any rough cost delta between dedicated with BYOK and private?
[09:50] Nina: quick thumb — dedicated with BYOK typically 15-30% premium over hosted enterprise pricing; private/on-prem has a higher base fee and professional services. we'll follow up with numbers.
[09:59] Maya: ok thanks everyone.
[10:02] Nina: one last thing — security contact? i'll send to security@auriga and to your procurement.
[10:08] Maya: please copy me and Ravi.
[10:10] Nina: will do. thanks all.

Recap / explicit next steps (auto):
- Redwood (Nina) to send SOC2 Type II + ISO27001 snaps, pentest summary, support access audit excerpts, and security whitepaper.
- Redwood (Lucas) to prepare network diagram and KMS integration steps for AWS KMS and HSM notes.
- Auriga (Maya) to provide data classification and retention requirements spreadsheet.

[Hybrid slab arena and adaptive checkpoint scheduler to reduce GPU workspace]
description:
Summary: This PR introduces a hybrid slab-focused arena allocator plus an adaptive activation checkpoint scheduler that cooperates with per-kernel scratch throttling and KV-cache LRU hints to materially reduce peak workspace and overall device allocation for long-context chat workloads. Motivation: customers running 100k+ token sessions and multi-turn chat were hitting OOMs on medium GPUs due to worst-case scratch+arena peaks; previous approaches (pure checkpointing or global arena caps) either increased latency or underutilized GPU memory. The goal here is to reduce worst-case workspace while preserving p95/p99 latency and throughput. What changed: 1) Arena allocator: add slab reservation for transient kernel scratch (slab_reserve_ratio tunable) so short-lived scratch allocations get carved from a temporary slab instead of the global arena; introduce slab eviction heuristics to free slabs when sustained memory pressure detected. 2) Hybrid checkpoint scheduler: new scheduler defers some activation checkpoints from the hot microbatches to colder microbatches within the same request when safe, reducing simultaneous checkpoint buffers; it uses a cheap cost model keyed by sequence-length and layer-flops to decide which layers to checkpoint eagerly versus deferred. 3) Scratch pool throttling: per-kernel scratch quotas that bias kernel selection toward low-scratch variants under pressure; integrates with kernel selector to prefer fused-attention paths that use smaller temporary buffers when sequence-length distribution suggests benefit. 4) KV-cache coalescing: KV manager now coalesces identical prefix KV handles across concurrent requests from the same conversation id to avoid duplicate KV allocations; LRU hinting reduces retention of rarely-reused past-turn keys. 5) Runtime knobs and telemetry: new tunables (slab_reserve_ratio, checkpoint_deferral_threshold, scratch_quota_ms) and metrics (arena.slabs.active, checkpoint.deferrals, scratch.throttled_count) added to Console and traces. Benchmarks: Internal p50/p95/p99 latency changes on rw-llama-7b loadtest with batch=8 and 4 concurrent streams: peak device allocations down 28% (from 9.8GB to 7.0GB), average device footprint down 18%, p95 latency +2.3%, p99 latency +3.8% on worst-case mixed-length traces; throughput unchanged within noise. Safety/perf tradeoffs: some microbatched requests may force checkpoint deferral causing slightly higher recompute on tail cases; knobs default conservatively to minimize recompute for latency-sensitive tiers. Commits: "alloc: add slab reserve allocator and eviction policy"; "sched: hybrid checkpoint scheduler and cost model"; "kernel: scratch quota enforcement + selector hints"; "kv: coalesce conversation kv handles and LRU hints"; "telemetry: arena and scheduler metrics + console panels"; "tests: add unit/integration tests for slab/deferral behaviour". Files changed (high level): runtime/allocator/slab_arena.{h,cpp} - new slab reserve implementation; runtime/scheduler/checkpoint_scheduler.cpp - new scheduler and cost model; runtime/kernel/scratch_pool.cpp - quota enforcement and selector hooks; runtime/kv/kv_cache_manager.cpp - coalescing logic and LRU hint flow; runtime/selector/kernel_selector.cpp - prefer low-scratch kernel variants when quota triggered; console/metrics/arena_dashboards.yaml - new panels; tests/allocator/test_slab_eviction.cpp - unit tests; integration/bench/long_context_memory.yaml - benchmark harness. Small illustrative snippet (updated allocator heuristic): "if (current_pressure > slab_threshold) slab->evict_least_recently_used(); else reserve_from_slab(requested)". Review conversation: Jordan Kim (reviewer) requested clearer invariants around deferral: "How do we ensure correctness when deferring checkpoint writes across microbatches?"; Anika replied: "We only defer within the same parent request boundary and track dependency fences per-layer; added assertion coverage and integration tests to validate tensor liveness across deferral windows." Priya Desai asked for telemetry gating and signal names; Anika: "Added metrics and Console panels and documented tunables in runtime/README.md; default values set to conservative for hosted API." Liam O'Connor raised concern about KV coalescing for multi-tenant Dedicated pools: "Could coalescing leak state across tenants?"; response: "Coalescing keyed by conversation-id + tenant-id; no cross-tenant sharing. Added unit tests and an audit log entry when coalescing occurs." CI status: initial lint failure (allocator header include order), tests flaky on integration bench (timing sensitivity) causing a failed run; fixes applied and CI green on re-run. Rollout plan: feature gated under runtime.tunable.hybrid_checkpoint enabled=false by default for hosted main, enabled in internal perf clusters and Dedicated with opt-in; gradual rollout to all Dedicated pools after two-week soak. Related work: follows ENG-742 and builds on previous arena and checkpoint experiments (see PRs reducing arena/checkpoint footprint) but differs by combining slab-reservation with a cost-driven deferral scheduler and KV coalescing. Merge: squash and merged by Anika Rao; merge commit message: "hybrid slab arena + adaptive checkpoint scheduler - reduce workspace and scratch peaks". Notes for ops: if customers report increased recompute tail, recommend lowering checkpoint_deferral_threshold or disabling hybrid_checkpoint for that pool. Checklist: [x] unit tests added, [x] integration bench added, [x] telemetry panels, [x] docs updated, [x] feature gated for gradual rollout.

release_notes:
Reduced peak GPU workspace by ~28% and end-to-end GPU footprint by ~18% for typical chat workloads; no API changes. Rollout: gradual on Dedicated pools with new arena tunables defaulting to safe limits.

[paged-kv: reallocator + pinning to reduce fragmentation, reuse hot blocks, and cut GPU-host transfers]
description:
Context: the paged KV cache has shown increasing memory fragmentation and allocation overhead under bursty, high-concurrency workloads. That leads to extra memcpy/transfer work between CPU and GPU when blocks are evacuated, and observable p95 latency regressions on serving paths that rely on long KV chains. Motivation: reduce allocation churn and unnecessary evictions, make hot pages stay resident, and provide deterministic reuse to reduce worst-case tail latency.

Summary of changes: implemented a new block reallocator and pin manager for the paged KV cache. Key pieces: BlockAllocator (size-classed free lists + contiguous free spans), BlockPool (per-device pool for reuse to avoid cross-device allocations), PinManager (reference-counted pinning of blocks used by in-flight requests), and an atomic reservation API to avoid races during concurrent alloc/free. Integration touches the existing kv/paged_cache.cc to wire allocation/reuse paths and the scheduler heuristics so the runtime prefers pinned blocks for hot KV prefixes. A feature flag (pinned_kv_v2) gates the rollout.

Design notes: - Size classes tuned for observed page sizes (128B/512B/2KB/8KB) to reduce internal fragmentation. - Reallocator attempts to coalesce adjacent free blocks to satisfy larger requests and keep fragmentation low. - Pinning is lightweight: a block can have a short-lived pin (auto-unpin on request completion) or a long-lived lease (for cache warmups). Pins prevent eviction and skip expensive GPU->host transfers. - Eviction now uses a two-pass policy: prefer unpinned cold blocks, and when forced, write-back/push hot pinned blocks to a spill region instead of synchronous host copies. - Atomic reservation ensures that two concurrent request threads don't both allocate and then race to copy into the same block; a reservation token is returned and either converted to a block or released.

Testing and CI: added unit tests for BlockAllocator coalescing and reservation semantics, integration tests exercising pin/unpin with concurrent alloc/free, and added a stress job in perf-canary that simulates high-QPS KV churn. One flaky test (kv_allocator_concurrency) surfaced on first CI run; root cause was a missing memory barrier in the reservation path and was fixed in subsequent commit. CI summary below.

Benchmarks: microbenchmarks on a 4-GPU Dedicated node under our "ask-heavy" synthetic trace show: - p95 latency: -9% (from 138ms to 126ms) - throughput: +12% sustained under 2k concurrent requests - memory fragmentation (estimated wasted bytes): -18% - block reuse rate (requests satisfied from free pool without fresh allocation): +34% Real-world canary in us-west-2 (20% of traffic, green path) confirms ~6% p95 improvement on customer traffic with no error increase. Details in the perf artifact link (see checks).

Rollout plan: enable pinned_kv_v2 behind config flag. Phases: (1) internal canary on dev cluster (done), (2) Dedicated canary 5% traffic for 48h, (3) ramp to 50% for a week, (4) full rollout. Fallback: flip pinned_kv_v2 off to revert quickly. Metrics to watch: kv_page_hits, kv_pin_evictions, kv_reservation_conflicts, mem_fragmentation_estimate, and end-to-end p95.

Backward compatibility: no API changes. Runtime option only.

Notes/links: Linear: ENG-3152 (reallocator design), ENG-3221 (pinning instrumentation). Support ticket SUP-4123 reported observed tail latency in production and motivated canary. Perf artifacts: ci/perf/artifacts/paged-kv-reallocator-2026-03-02.

Checklist: - [x] Design doc and benchmark plan - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] Perf canary run - [x] Feature flag + rollout plan - [x] Docs updated (architecture KV page)

Small migration note: the existing on-disk spill format is unchanged but spill ordering differs slightly because pinned blocks are moved to the front of the spill queue to preserve hotness.

review_comments:
Diego Ramos: Nice end-to-end work. Two asks: (1) add a metric for reservation_conflicts and (2) ensure the reservation path is non-blocking in hot loops.
Asha Patel: Added kv_reservation_conflicts and made reservation switch to try-reserve w/ fast-fail; updated tests.

[split-fused-qkv-kernel-and-rope-swap-prefetch-scheduler]
description:
Motivation: reduce tail latency and improve per-GPU throughput for common small-batch streaming workloads by separating concerns in the attention path. This PR decouples the fused QKV arithmetic from rotary/rope application and introduces a lightweight rope-swap stage plus a GPU-side KV prefetch streamer integrated with the continuous-batching scheduler. Rationale: tightly fused QKV+rotary kernels are fast on steady, large-batch workloads but cause memory layout churn and head-of-line blocking for bursty single-request streams and mixed sequence lengths. By splitting the fused kernel and moving rotary application to a deterministic post-QKV pass we can reuse packed QKV buffers across nearby requests and prefetch remote KV shards before decode starts. What this PR does: 1) Introduces a new tiled QKV kernel (FlashLoop wrapper) that focuses exclusively on Q/K/V matmuls and packing; it accepts an optional packed-output flag so the scheduler can keep buffers GPU-resident for a short window. 2) Adds a rope-swap stage (device and CPU fallbacks) that applies rotary/rope in-place or in a streaming chunked mode for very long sequences. 3) Implements a KV prefetch streamer in the continuous-batching scheduler that issues async copies for predicted hot KV shards while request tokens are being decoded; integrates with the existing cache eviction heuristics. 4) Adds runtime toggles and telemetry for the new stages (opt-in via config and feature flag for canary customers). Backwards compatibility: default behavior on main is unchanged until feature-flag rollout completes; new kernel is gated by runtime config so we can A/B or do canary rollouts. Testing: unit tests for kernel correctness (compare against fused QKV+rotary baseline), integration tests for scheduler prefetch logic, and microbench harness results included below. Benchmarks (A100, fp16, seq=1024 unless noted): - Small-batch streaming (batch=1, token-by-token): p50 latency down 7%, p95 down 14%, end-to-end throughput up 8-12% depending on model width. - Mixed-batch steady-state (batch 8-16): throughput neutral to +3% (depends on quantization path). - KV-heavy rerank workload (large cache churn): effective GPU utilization improved by ~15% due to prefetch overlap. - Worst-case long-seq (seq>8192): rope-swap chunked path shows 10% lower memory overhead vs fused kernel. CI notes: one flaky integration test (scheduler/eviction_test) failed on first run, was rerun and passed; no test regressions after fixes. Rollback plan: toggle feature-flag to false and revert canary pool; kernel code is additive and default path unchanged. Risks and mitigations: slight increase in code surface for kernel staging; mitigated by conservative defaults, telemetry, and canary rollout. Release notes: improved small-batch streaming latency and KV-heavy workload throughput via new split-QKV kernel and rope-swap prefetching. Additional context and links: Linear ENG-3789 for rollout plan, perf-canary dashboards attached in the PR comments.

[Pageable activation tiling and cooperative kernel preempt scheduler to reduce GPU working set]
description:
Motivation: Large-context streaming cases and some batched workloads were causing unbounded growth of the GPU working set due to monolithic activation allocation and conservative kernel scheduling. This PR introduces a pageable activation tiling layout and a cooperative kernel preemption scheduler to keep active GPU memory bounded while preserving end-to-end latency targets.

Summary of changes: Implements a lightweight OS-like paging layer for activations (tile units ~64KB) that allows lazy page-in and eviction of cold tiles; introduces cooperative kernel preemption points so long-running kernels yield control to page-in hot tiles without full kernel termination; updates KV cache manager to pin small hot windows and integrate with tile eviction policy; adds batching compatibility so continuous-batching keeps prefetched tiles pinned for expected next requests. All changes are feature-flagged behind runtime config `GPU_PAGEABLE_TILING` and `COOP_PREEMPT_SCHEDULER` and default to OFF for now.

Implementation details: 1) runtime/memory/paging.{cc,hh}: new pageable allocator that splits activations into fixed-size tiles, maintains a two-tier LRU (tile-level hotset + activation metadata). 2) runtime/kernel/scheduler.cpp: cooperative preempt scheduler that instruments safe yield points in attention and MLP kernels; uses lightweight state checkpoint so kernels can resume without full restart. 3) runtime/kv_cache/kv_manager.py: KV cache now tracks tile residency and charges pin cost back to routing decision. 4) continuous batching glue updated to prefetch next-request tiles when batch composition is stable for 2+ requests. 5) tests/perf and benchmarks added.

Testing & validation: Unit tests for allocator invariants and tile eviction; microbenchmarks for page-in latency; integration tests validating correctness of resumed kernels (deterministic outputs compared to baseline); production perf canary run on dedicated pool (see perf summary).

Rollout plan: landed behind feature flags. After merge we'll run a 48h canary on dedicated-xx region with 10% traffic and monitor token latency p50/p95, page-in latency histogram, and memory high-water marks. If stable, flip default to ON for Dedicated customers and enable opt-in for Hosted with per-tenant guardrails.

Notes: This PR intentionally avoids aggressive compression and instead focuses on predictable memory bounds. Follow-ups planned: adaptive tile sizing, intra-GPU prefetch heuristics, and kernel codegen hooks to reduce resume cost.

[Drift‑resilient collective scheduler and KV slab consolidation to reduce NCCL contention]
Context and motivation: In production we continue to see sporadic tail latency spikes on multi‑GPU TP workloads correlated with short windows of NCCL congestion and many small KV cache allocations from continuous batching. This PR introduces two coordinated runtime changes: (1) a drift‑resilient collective scheduler that perturbs and staggers NCCL launches to avoid pathological synchronization across tensor slices, and (2) a KV slab consolidation pass that reduces small allocation churn and improves L2/L3 locality for the KV cache allocator. The combined change targets multi‑GPU tensor‑parallel inference paths (TP runtime) and the continuous‑batching code path used by the API router.

What this PR does (high level): - Adds Scheduler::PerturbationWindow, a lightweight jittering layer that applies per‑peer launch offsets within a configurable window to break lockstep NCCL launches while preserving ordering and progress guarantees. The scheduler also tracks per‑peer outstanding credits and backs off launches when cumulative outstanding bytes exceed a runtime threshold. - Adds KVSlab::Consolidate and a consolidation task that merges hot small slabs into larger contiguous slabs at low priority, reducing per‑token allocation overhead and fragmentation. Consolidation is gated by memory pressure and configurable thresholds so it won’t interfere with SLOs. - Adds a small admission tweak to continuous batching: older requests receive a priority boost in the batch selector to reduce head‑of‑line latency under high QPS. - Benchmarks and regression tests: microbenchmarks for NCCL launch variance, end‑to‑end tp inference perf harness, and an integration test that exercises slab consolidation under load.

Design notes and rationale: - We intentionally avoid deterministic reordering. The perturbation window is randomized per launch but bounded; this prevents pathological worst‑case alignments while keeping collectives efficient. - Consolidation is incremental and infrequent; it uses a background worker with a budgeted runtime slice to avoid interfering with token service. - The NCCL perturbation is conservative: on rigs where we observe no contention, the perturbation window defaults to zero. Operators can tune the window via runtime flags and per‑cluster policies. - The combined effect reduces contention-caused retries and kernel stalls while also lowering memory allocation overhead that exacerbates NVLink traffic.

Commits (summary): - 1a2f3b4: Introduce perturbation scheduler hooks and config knobs; add unit tests for scheduling invariants. - 2b3c4d5: Implement KV slab consolidation pass, background worker, and new allocator stats. - 3c4d5e6: Integrate with continuous batching admission, add perf test harness and perf metrics, update docs and changelog.

Files changed (high level): - runtime/scheduler/perturbation_scheduler.{cc,h} - runtime/kv_cache/kv_slab_consolidator.{cc,h} - runtime/kv_cache/allocator_stats.{cc,h} - runtime/batching/batch_selector.{cc} (priority tweak) - tests/perf/tp_nccl_stress_test.py - ci/perf/benchmarks/launch_variance.yaml - docs/release_notes/2026-02-03-kv-nccl-optimization.md - examples/perf/tuning/README.md

Tiny illustrative snippet (informational only): "Scheduler::PerturbationWindow" accepts a window_ns and seed; when >0 it computes offset = rng.uniform(0, window_ns) and schedules NCCL launch at planned_time + offset. KVSlab::Consolidate scans slab list for contiguous small slabs with same owner and merges them under lock.

Review conversation (highlights): - Ethan Park (reviewer): "Nice isolation of perturbation logic. A few requests: make the default window configurable via env var, and add a per‑node debug metric for perturbed launches." Author reply: "Added RW_SCHED_PERTURB_NS env and metric runtime.scheduler.perturbed_launches_count; updated tests." - Lucia Ramirez: "Concern about consolidation causing a stop‑the‑world when merging many small slabs." Author reply: "Consolidation uses a background budgeted worker; added unit test and a runtime flag to disable consolidation during low latency SLO periods." - Owen Patel: "Can we get a perf comparison on a 8xA100 TP run?" Author reply: "Included 8x A100 numbers below; will add CI perf job once this merges." - Followups: minor doc edits, one flaky test disabled and a TODO added to re-enable after allocator lock refactor.

CI summary: - Linux unit tests: pass - Integration perf harness (short): pass - Lint: pass - Extended perf run (internal): nominal but required one rerun due to infra transient. Overall status: pass.

Benchmarks (selected results, end‑to‑end TP inference harness, 8x A100, mixed sequence lengths): - Baseline (main): median throughput = 1000 infer/s, p99 latency = 210ms, peak NVLink utilization = 78% - This PR: median throughput = 1140 infer/s (+14%), p99 latency = 185ms (-11.9%), peak NVLink utilization = 66% (-15.4%) - KV memory fragmentation (tracked via allocator_stats.hot_slab_frag): baseline 0.18, this PR 0.09 (-50%) Notes: numbers averaged across 20 runs with warm‑up. Workloads with many small prefixes saw larger gains.

Backward compatibility and operator impact: - Defaults keep behavior unchanged (window defaults to 0, consolidation disabled under heavy SLO by default). - Operators can enable the window and consolidation via flags or cluster policy in the console. - Added new runtime metrics and two flags: RW_SCHED_PERTURB_NS and RW_KV_CONSOLIDATE_ENABLED documented in docs/release_notes.

Follow‑ups and TODOs: - Add an operator dashboard tile to surface perturbed launch counts and consolidation activity. - Extend consolidation heuristics to account for pinned memory slabs. - Add a canary rollout in Dedicated environments to validate across different network topologies.

Flags: RW_SCHED_PERTURB_NS, RW_KV_CONSOLIDATE_ENABLED."

Identity-proxy currently rejects tokens whose 'iss' does not match configured accepted_issuers list (single value).
Support Console's approval token generator signs a short-lived JWT with an 'iss' claim set to the Okta issuer configured at time of generation. Some queued approvals were created before migration and delivered post-migration.
RBAC datastore keys: grants are indexed by (principal_id, issuer). When issuer changes, previously-created grants are still stored under old issuer namespace; provisioning call attempts to read grants using issuer from assertion.
Attempted local repro by forging approval JWT with old issuer and calling provisioning endpoint — repro'd 403 with same logs as production.

resolution_notes:
Short term mitigation: Deployed identity-proxy update to accept both https://okta-new.redwood and https://okta-old.redwood on the access-request/provisioning endpoint only. This allowed in-flight approvals to complete normally without touching global token acceptance.
Medium term fix: Backfilled RBAC grants for recently-approved requests by running migration job that normalizes grant keys from old issuer to new issuer for approvals in the migration window (2026-03-09 22:00 -> 2026-03-10 04:00). PR: github.com/redwood-inference/rbac-tools/pull/57
Long term: Update approval token generation to include an 'orig_iss' claim and update provisioning to canonicalize issuer during lookup. Add explicit migration step to retirement playbook for future issuer changes. Added unit tests for multi-issuer acceptance in identity-proxy.
Follow-ups:
- Security to review acceptance window (Ethan & Claire).
- Rotate any long-lived service tokens that may embed old issuer references.
- Run additional audit to ensure no external tokens accepted accidentally.

[Post-approval race condition: UI shows access granted for Model Insights but 403 persists]
description:
Issue summary:
Several internal users report that the Model Insights app shows their access request as "Approved" in the self-service UI, but they receive 403 Forbidden when loading dashboards or running queries. This started being reported after the cross-region IdP rollout last week.

Impact:
- Affects internal analytics and platform engineers using Model Insights (approx 12 confirmed users across teams).
- Blocks debugging and incident work for these users when they don't actually get role bindings despite the UI state: 'Granted'.
- Intermittent: ~20% of approvals processed in the last 48h ended up in this state.

First observed:
2026-03-11 09:40 UTC in us-east region after a staged Okta tenant update and scaled approval queue processing.

Additional context:
- Model Insights uses the standard access-request flow: approval -> webhook to provisioning service -> RBAC service creates role_binding -> auth-proxy cache pick-up -> user can access.
- After the Okta change there were duplicated approval webhook deliveries (same approval id delivered twice to different regional endpoints). The UI shows a successful approval acknowledgment but the downstream RBAC binding sometimes lacks the internal role_id mapping required by auth-proxy.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Submit an access request for Model Insights from internal console for a user in us-east.
2) Approve the request via the approval queue (canary approver account used).
3) Observe approval webhook delivery logs in provisioning service. If duplicate webhook deliveries occur across regions, sometimes role_binding created with missing role_id mapping or created before role mapping reconciliation completes.
4) User refreshes Model Insights; UI shows "Granted" but request to /v1/dashboards returns 403 with X-Auth-Reason header 'role-mapping-missing'.

logs:
2026-03-11T09:42:12Z provisioning-service INFO Received approval id=appr-9c1f
2026-03-11T09:42:13Z provisioning-service WARN Duplicate approval id=appr-9c1f delivered to regional endpoint us-west while us-east still processing
2026-03-11T09:42:13Z rbac-service ERROR create_role_binding failed: missing_internal_role_id for external_role='model_insights_viewer' request_id=req-77f
2026-03-11T09:42:14Z auth-proxy DEBUG cache-refresh skipped: no mapping for role_binding rb-443
2026-03-11T09:42:15Z model-insights ERROR /api/dashboards 403 user=alice@example.com reason=role-mapping-missing

investigation_notes:
Initial triage by Support and SRE: 
- Confirmed duplicate webhook deliveries originating from the approval queue fanout to regional provisioning endpoints.
- Observed a time window where the SCIM/role-mapping table (role_mappings) is being asynchronously reconciled after an Okta canonicalization change; if provisioning creates a binding before reconciliation completes, role_binding.row.role_id stays NULL and auth-proxy rejects requests.
- The provisioning service does not currently provide a strong idempotency guarantee across regions; duplicate deliveries can race with background reconciliation jobs.
- Auth-proxy relies on role_id (internal numeric id) instead of external_role slug; missing role_id causes 403 with 'role-mapping-missing'.

Hypothesis: missing idempotency / race between regional webhook processing and background role mapping reconciliation after the IdP attribute normalization change.

Data points:
- 12 affected users all had access requests processed within a 10s window of the SCIM reconciliation job run.
- When we manually re-bound the role_binding (populate role_id and re-send cache invalidation), users immediately regained access.

Temporary mitigation executed:
- Added a short retry+reconcile step in provisioning service for pending bindings (backfill job) scoped to last 1 hour which fixed ~8/12 cases so far.
- Added alert rule to detect create_role_binding failures with 'missing_internal_role_id' and to escalate to SRE.

comments:
Support (Aisha): Added initial report and reproducer; collected affected user list and first set of logs.
SRE (Samir): Investigating provisioning fanout. Found duplicate webhook deliveries between us-east and us-west; suspect idempotency key not set on regional fanout.
Eng (Priya, SCIM): We rolled Okta canonicalization patch 2026-03-10 that introduced a delayed reconciliation job to normalize external_role slugs. We will prioritize making reconciliation synchronous for new role definitions or add blocking to provisioning until mappings exist.
SRE (Samir): Applied a temporary backfill to populate missing role_id for affected role_bindings and triggered auth-proxy cache invalidation for those user sessions (recovered 8/12).
Support (Aisha): Notified affected users and asked for verification; two users still report 403 after backfill.
Eng (Priya): For the remaining users, found a separate code path that writes role_binding before creating the external_role row in the role_mappings table due to a rare migration ordering issue. Preparing fix PR to enforce transactional create-or-wait semantics.

resolution:
Workaround in place: manual backfill job and cache invalidation restores access for most users. Next steps (in progress):
- Engineering to land PR that adds region-safe idempotency keys to the approval webhook fanout (expected 2026-03-15).
- Change provisioning service to block short-lived bindings until role_mappings confirms existence (or perform an inline reconciliation).
- Add a reconcile-and-retry step to provisioning for 30s with exponential backoff to reduce races.
- Post-deploy: run a one-off audit to find any stale bindings with NULL role_id and fix.
- Add monitoring: metric 'rbac.bindings.missing_role_id' and alert threshold > 1/min.

Pending: final fix PR, QA on canary region, and a postmortem to be filed on Confluence.

[Intermittent 403 when submitting delegated access requests from Electron portal]
description:
Issue summary: Several Support and Platform engineers intermittently receive 403 Forbidden when clicking 'Request Access' (delegated role request) from the Electron-based internal portal. The button appears to succeed for a moment (UI shows spinner) and then a toast "Request failed: 403" appears.

Impact: Affects internal tooling access flows for ~10% of requests during observed windows; prevents engineers from obtaining temporary delegated roles and blocks on-call runbook access. No reported customer-facing impact, but causes operational delays during incidents.

Observed characteristics: failures are intermittent (not tied to a single user), correlate with times of autoscaler events on the auth-proxy pool, and appear to surface only when users' requests route across upstream auth-proxy instances that have recently cycled. Requests routed to a warm auth-proxy instance succeed consistently.

Initial hypothesis: 403s caused by CSRF/session validation failure due to stale server-side session state / CSRF token cache being evicted or lost after memcached eviction or container restart; when load-balancer stickiness flips between backends the Electron portal submits a token that is no longer valid on the new backend.

Environment details: Electron v2.5.1 (internal); auth-proxy (k8s deployment auth-proxy-prod, HPA autoscaler triggers), session-store uses memcached-cluster-1 (managed), RBAC service v1.14.2. Okta SSO is the identity provider; session cookie is SameSite=None; auth-proxy sets an app-specific CSRF token in server-side cache keyed by session id.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Sign in to Electron portal (Okta SSO) and confirm role is unstaged for delegation.
2) Trigger a role delegation request via the portal UI (Request Access → choose role → submit).
3) Repeat submit while watching which auth-proxy pod handles requests (kubectl get pods -n auth | kubectl describe endpoints to correlate), or while an HPA-induced pod churn is happening.
4) Observe that some submissions return 403 and corresponding errors in auth-proxy logs; submissions routed to a different pod often succeed.
5) Reproduce window correlates with memcached evictions and k8s scaler events (scale up/down).

logs:
auth-proxy[2026-03-12T15:14:21Z] WARN csrf: validation failed for session=abc123, expected token missing (cache-miss)
rbac-service[2026-03-12T15:14:21Z] INFO delegation-request denied user=leah.chen@redwood.com reason=csrf_validation_failed
memcached[2026-03-12T15:14:20Z] NOTICE evicting key=session:abc123 due_to=slab_rebalance
ingress-lb[2026-03-12T15:14:22Z] INFO backend-change client_ip=10.32.5.18 from=auth-proxy-7ff4d -> auth-proxy-9d1c3

investigation_notes:
- Reproduced in staging by forcing auth-proxy pod recycle + memcached eviction; observed same 403 and csrf cache-miss entries.
- Correlation between HPA pod churn and higher 403 rate (spike from baseline 1% -> 12% during churn window).
- Session cookie binding is fine; issue is server-side CSRF cache keyed by session id and not replicated across instances.
- Auth-proxy currently uses local in-memory CSRF token cache fallback to memcached; memcached eviction/eviction race window leads to cache-miss and immediate 403.
- Electron client does not retry on 403; UX shows immediate failure.

Next steps: (1) Add request-level retry in Electron for transient 403s on delegation endpoints (short-term mitigation). (2) Update auth-proxy to persist CSRF tokens in a strongly-consistent store or implement double-submit cookie pattern to remove server-side dependency (design RFC). (3) Add metric + alert for csrf_cache_misses / delegation_403_rate. (4) Patch memcached eviction settings and review HPA cooldown to reduce chop frequency.

comments:
Leah Chen (reporter) 2026-03-12: Noticed this during an on-call rotation when I couldn't request a delegated role after a pager. The portal showed the spinner and then 403 toast. I retried twice and then it worked once (after a minute).
Marco Ruiz (assignee) 2026-03-12: Confirmed similar traces in prod logs. Spun up a staging test to simulate HPA churn; can reproduce. Will prototype client-side retry while we design server fix.
SRE #internal-access 2026-03-12: Observed memcached slab rebalances during the same window; investigating eviction patterns. Suggest temporarily increasing memcached memory and adding eviction metrics.
Security 2026-03-13: CSRF change must preserve protection guarantees. Double-submit cookie approach acceptable but coordinate with security review.

[Just-in-time access shows approved but user lacks console roles after approval]
summary_long:
A developer used Just-In-Time (JIT) access to elevate for a support task; Okta approval flow completed, but the console still returns 403 and the user has no elevated roles in the UI or token claims.

description:
Issue summary: A developer requested temporary elevation via the internal JIT access flow. The approval email was clicked, approval registered in Okta (approval log entry present), but the user remains unable to access the support console and receives 403 errors when attempting role-protected routes.

Impact: Blocks a support engineer from accessing runbooks and incident dashboards for ~30 minutes. Internal impact only, affects a single on-call engineer.

Environment: Production (us-east), Console v2.34, Auth proxy v1.8, Okta org: redwood-prod.okta.com.

Observed at: 2026-03-10T14:22:00Z (first report).


steps_to_reproduce:
1) User initiates 'Request Temporary Elevation' from internal console.
2) Manager approves via Okta approval email.
3) User clicks approve and sees Okta confirmation.
4) User attempts to open /runbooks and /incidents in console and receives 403.
5) Token exchange logs show successful grant but console RBAC check fails.


expected_behavior:
After Okta approval, the user's session and tokens should include the elevated role claims and the console should allow access to role-restricted pages within 30s.

actual_behavior:
Okta logs show approval event and JIT service recorded a successful approval; however, the console shows '403 Forbidden' and the user's token does not include the temporary elevated roles. A manual re-login sometimes fixes the issue for affected users.


logs_and_evidence:
- Okta System Log entry: eventType=approval.task.approved id=0oab12345XYZ timestamp=2026-03-10T14:23:05Z
- JIT service log: approval_handler: processed approval id=apr-789, status=applied, assigned_role=oncall-temporary
- Auth proxy token-exchange log: token_exchange request id=te-456 status=200 claims=[base_roles] (missing oncall-temporary)
- Console audit: 403 on GET /runbooks for user maya.chen@redwood.com at 2026-03-10T14:24:21Z


investigation_notes:
Initial hypothesis: race between approval propagation to RBAC cache and token exchange.
Findings: JIT service emitted 'status=applied' but role propagation worker showed spike of errors connecting to role-store (ETCD) between 14:23:30 and 14:24:10 (connection refused transient).
Second hypothesis: token issued before role write committed, so token lacks new claim. Evidence: token timestamp 14:23:40, role-store write commit at 14:24:05.
Added a temporary mitigation to refresh user session after approval to force re-fetch of claims.


temporary_workaround:
Support instructs affected users to perform a full sign-out and sign-in after approval (or force token refresh). This restores access in >90% of cases. For the on-call engineer in this ticket this resolved the issue at 14:32 after sign-out.


root_cause:
Propagation lag between JIT approval commit and RBAC store leading to tokens minted before role write completion. Underlying cause appears to be transient ETCD connectivity errors on role-store write worker during a brief network hiccup.


resolution:
- Restarted role-store write-worker to clear transient connection failures (14:50 UTC).
- Added a short retry/wait in the approval handler: after write commit verification, approval handler now polls role-store up to 3s to ensure role visible before returning success to token exchange.
- Instrumented a metric for approval-to-claim latency and alert if >5s.
- Follow-up: SRE to investigate ETCD networking noise in us-east (ticket INT-100215 linked).


comments:
2026-03-10 14:30 - Maya Chen (reporter): I approved the request and saw Okta confirmation. Console still 403. Tried refresh, no luck.
2026-03-10 14:35 - Ravi Patel (assignee): Acknowledged. Collecting logs and checking JIT approval flow. Can you confirm sign-out/sign-in?
2026-03-10 14:37 - Maya Chen: I tried sign-out then sign-in at 14:32 and access was restored. Attached screenshots in ticket.
2026-03-10 15:05 - SRE (Anita Gomez): Noted transient ETCD connection errors in write-worker during window 14:23-14:25. Grabbed logs, opening follow-up INT-100215.
2026-03-11 09:10 - Ravi Patel: Rolled out a small fix to the approval handler (PR linked). Adding metric for approval-to-claim latency. Monitoring for recurrence.
2026-03-11 12:40 - Maya Chen: Confirming final fix — re-approval test passed and no 403 observed. Marking as resolved pending SRE postmortem.


[Service-broker UI 403 after SSO login due to session cookie path mismatch]
description:
Issue summary: Several internal users report 403 Forbidden when opening the service-broker UI immediately after completing Okta SSO. The main Redwood console and most services authenticate fine; the service-broker UI (path /services/broker) is the only product page consistently returning 403 after a successful Okta redirect. Impact: ~12 engineers reported inability to access service-broker workflows; blocks a small number of oncall tasks that require approving dedicated capacity requests. Environment: prod us-east, observed from browser sessions on Chrome and Firefox. Steps to reproduce: 1) Sign in via Okta SSO to console.redwood.ai 2) Click the Services -> Broker entry (navigates to console.redwood.ai/services/broker) 3) Observe redirect to /auth/callback then immediate 403 on /services/broker Expected behavior: SSO redirect results in an authenticated session and the browser should include the Okta session cookie so the /services/broker route allows access. Actual behavior: The browser receives Set-Cookie on auth callback with Path=/console but requests to /services/broker do not include that cookie, resulting in a 403 from the backend. Temporary observations: - Network tab shows Set-Cookie: Redwood-SSO=...; Path=/console; Secure; HttpOnly - Subsequent GET to /services/broker does not include Redwood-SSO header. - Other console paths under /console/ include cookie and work normally. - This started after last ingress gateway deployment on 2026-03-08. Logs: - proxy logs show cookie rewrite for paths outside /console - backend reports 401->403 mapping when session missing Additional context: Several users used Incognito and cleared cookies with same result. Issue appears to be an ingress-side regression that changed cookie path or rewrote path attribute for SSO sessions.

investigation_notes:
- 2026-03-10 10:15: Reviewed network traces from affected user (user: amanda.liu@redwood). Confirmed Set-Cookie Path=/console. - 2026-03-10 11:05 Pulled ingress-gateway helm chart diff vs previous: found new annotation ingress.kubernetes.io/cookie-path: /console added in 2026-03-08 deploy. - 2026-03-10 13:30 Reproduced locally by toggling cookie-path annotation: when cookie-path=/console access to /services/* fails. - Hypothesis: ingress-gateway change scoped Okta session cookie to /console only; service-broker lives at /services so cookie not sent. - Cross-checked with auth-service: session validation expects Redwood-SSO cookie present on all console subpaths; currently validation middleware checks cookie regardless of request path which means scoping cookie to /console prevents access to /services endpoints. - Noted linked request INT-11205 had a concurrent SCIM/role propagation change but unrelated to cookie behavior. - Captured proxy config and exported for GH PR 447 which contains proposed fix to remove cookie-path scoping and restore path=/.

comments:
Support (2026-03-10) - Jonah Kim: Initial triage done; reproduced in staging with cookie-path annotation present. Marking P1 due to oncall impact.
SRE (2026-03-10) - Maria Torres: Ingress change in rollout on 2026-03-08 added cookie-path annotation during a refactor (PR 432). Rolling back that annotation in a canary should validate hypothesis.
Eng (2026-03-11) - Priya Singh: Created github.com/redwood-inference/ingress-gateway/pull/447 to remove the annotation and consolidate cookie scoping logic. Running integration tests against staging now.
Support (2026-03-12) - Jonah Kim: Customers on Dedicated reported no impact; this is internal-only because service-broker is internal path. Keep internal comms updated in #internal-support.
SRE (2026-03-12) - Maria Torres: Canary rollback applied to cluster staging-us-east-1. Verified that Set-Cookie now uses Path=/ and /services/broker accepts authenticated requests in the canary. Scheduling prod rollback pending approvals.

resolution:
Workaround: Engineers can access the service-broker UI by using the console entrypoint under /console/services/broker or by logging in and manually setting the cookie scope via developer tools (temporary and not recommended). Permanent fix: Revert ingress annotation that scoped the session cookie to /console and update integration tests to assert cookie path = /. A PR with the change (ingress-gateway PR 447) is open; plan is to deploy rollback to prod during low-traffic window and then follow with a forward-compatible change that centralizes cookie scoping logic in auth-service. Post-deploy verification steps documented in related_confluence_pages.

[Introduce per-tenant rollback token planner and helm-diff apply sanity guard]
description:
Context and motivation:
Upgrades in multi-tenant private deployments can result in partial rollouts where some tenants are migrated while others fail partway, leaving state skew. This change introduces a coordinated, tenant-scoped rollback token planner plus a Helm diff-based apply sanity guard to reduce the blast radius of failed upgrades. The planner produces an idempotent rollback token and an ordered plan per-tenant so operators can safely abort or rewind upgrades without manual state reconstruction.

What this PR does (high level):
- Adds a rollback token generator that captures release manifest fingerprints, schema migration checkpoints, and operator epoch metadata per-tenant. The token is stored in the cluster (sealed secret) and can be used for automated rollback playbooks.
- Implements a Helm-apply sanity guard that runs a pre-apply "helm-diff" check and rejects applies if required invariants (CRD compatibility, PV claim changes, forbidden schema downgrades) are detected unless manual override is passed.
- Adds a dry-run path that emits a tenant rollout plan (JSON) and a signed token; this enables safe rehearsals and automated acceptance tests.
- Pins the operator Terraform module version when doing plan+apply to prevent drift during upgrade windows and adds a preflight terraform-state lock verification.
- Small helpers and docs: CLI subcommands (installer rollback-plan, installer apply-check), examples in the upgrade runbook, and unit tests for plan generation and token validation.

Checklist (manual testing / acceptance):
- [x] Generate rollback token for a three-tenant cluster and validate token idempotency (installer rollback-plan --dry-run).
- [x] Run helm-diff warning-only mode against example charts; ensure rejects on CRD incompatible change.
- [x] Simulate partial failure case and confirm rollback playbook consumes token to return cluster to previous manifest set.
- [x] Terraform operator pin validated with plan locking test.

Commits (summary):
- feat(rollback): add tenant-scoped rollback token generator and serializer
- feat(installer): CLI: installer rollback-plan and installer apply-check subcommands
- feat(helm): integrate helm-diff pre-apply guard with invariant ruleset
- infra(terraform): pin operator module and add plan lock verification
- test: unit + integration tests for plan generator and helm guard paths
- docs: upgrade runbook section and examples for rollback-token recovery

Files changed (high level):
- cmd/installer/rollback_plan.go (new)
- pkg/rollback/token.go (new)
- pkg/rollback/plan_builder.go (new)
- pkg/helm/apply_guard.go (new)
- charts/operator/values.schema.json (small validation additions)
- terraform/modules/operator/versions.tf (pin)
- docs/upgrade-runbook.md (add example and recovery steps)
- test/integration/rollback_plan_test.go (new)

Review notes and edge cases:
- Token storage is designed to be tenant-scoped and sealed; immediately call out that operators must have KMS configured for private installs to ensure token confidentiality. The token contents are minimal and include release manifest sha256, migration checkpoint id, and operator epoch.
- Helm diff rules are intentionally conservative; they surface as a hard reject only for known-dangerous changes (CRD major version bump, persistent volume claim size shrink, and explicit schema downgrades). Other diffs are warned. Manual override requires an operator token to prevent accidental bypass in automation.
- Rollback plan generation is deterministic but depends on cluster-read estate; in highly dynamic clusters the plan is snapshot-based and carries a plan timestamp to detect staleness. The installer will refuse to execute a stale plan unless explicitly forced.

Testing and CI:
- Unit tests cover token serialization, signature verification, and plan ordering invariants.
- Integration test exercises a simulated three-tenant Helm upgrade and uses the rollback token to restore previous manifests.
- CI includes: lint, unit, integration smoke, helm-validate, terraform-plan-check. All checks passed prior to merge.

How to exercise locally (short):
1) Build installer binary: make cli-build
2) Create dry-run plan: ./bin/installer rollback-plan --cluster kubeconfig.yaml --tenants t1,t2,t3 --dry-run > plan.json
3) Verify helm-diff guard: ./bin/installer apply-check --chart ./charts/app --kubeconfig kubeconfig.yaml
4) Perform playbook rollback: ./bin/installer rollback-exec --token <sealed-token>

Related work and references:
- Linear: ENG-1842 (tenant rollback orchestration)
- RFC: https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-1899/rollback-token-rfc
- Previous PRs: follow-on from "staged-rollback" work but uses a different token-based coordination model to avoid centralized state machine contention.

Merge strategy:
- Squash and merge; release notes added. Backwards compatible for existing private installs but operators should schedule a maintenance window to enable KMS and test the dry-run path.
