[Introduce migration-preview mode and safe-commit hook for installer]
description:
Motivation: Upgrades for private deployments (VPC/on-prem) require predictable, auditable state transitions and a low-risk path to roll back when migrations touch DB schemas or object-store layouts. This PR adds two orthogonal safety primitives: 1) migration-preview mode — a dry-run path that validates planned migration actions (DB DDL/DML, helm chart template diffs, terraform plan artifacts, and file-store transforms) against a snapshot of the cluster and returns a deterministic report; 2) safe-commit hook — an idempotent final-state checkpoint written at the end of a successful install/upgrade that records applied migrations, checksumed manifests, and a compact failure-containment plan so rollbacks can pick up cleanly. Summary of changes: - installer/cli: new `--migration-preview` flag; preview writes a human-readable report and machine-friendly artifact to <artifacts>/migration-preview/<run-id>. - installer/hooks: implement `safe-commit` hook executed only when `--safe-commit=true` and the run completed successfully. The hook writes final-state.json and a signed lockfile to the configured artifacts backend (S3/GCS/MinIO). - helm/redwood-core: chart hook annotations to gate post-upgrade finalization, avoid Helm completing release until safe-commit artifact persisted. - terraform/modules: add `migration_plan_output` optional output and a `plan_checksum` export; wiring plumbed to the installer so preview compares planned vs applied. - db/migrations: add schema-compatibility checker (non-destructive compatibility ruleset) that runs during preview and actual run; it prevents downgrade-only-unsafe operations unless explicitly allowed by `--allow-destructive`. - upgrade-playbooks: document a rollback sequence that uses final-state.json to produce a restore playbook and automated sanity checks. Design details: - Preview semantics: preview runs all code paths except executing destructive DDL/DML and object-store movers; instead it simulates them using a mutable snapshot in a temp namespace or a locally mounted copy. It records the exact set of files/SQL statements/k8s manifests that would be applied and computes a deterministic checksum for each artefact. - Safe-commit semantics: safe-commit writes {run_id, timestamp, base_branch, head_commit, migration_checksums[], terraform_plan_checksum, helm_chart_checksum, validation_summary, rollback_hint} plus a cryptographic HMAC when KMS key present. The hook is resilient: retries with backoff, and on repeated failure marks release as `finalization_failed` with instructions for manual salvage. - Rollback/restore: a new script `installer/bin/restore-from-final-state` reconstructs a minimal cluster snapshot and runs the inverse actions for non-destructive rollbacks; for destructive changes it emits a guided manual path. Testing performed: - Unit tests for schema checker rules (db/migrations/test_schema_checker.py). - Integration tests using KIND + MinIO to exercise preview and commit (test_migration_preview_e2e.sh). - Manual dry-runs against customer-like manifests (two internal lab clusters). - CI: added a matrix job (preview, safe-commit) that runs the simulated path and validates artifacts are produced. Backwards/compatibility notes: - Default behavior is unchanged; both migration-preview and safe-commit are opt-in flags. - Safe-commit artifacts are compact JSON + gzip; we provide a migration tool to import legacy backups when present. Rollout plan: - Stage feature behind feature-flag in release channel A for 2 weeks; invite early-adopter customers for Private channel testing. - After no critical issues, flip to default-available (not enabled) in the console and add to upgrade checklist. Related: Linear ENG-4123 (migration preview), ENG-4199 (safe commit hooks). Links: internal design doc: /docs/private/upgrade-safety/migration-preview.md. Full implementation here includes small Helm chart updates and Terraform outputs to carry checksums. See changed_files for specifics.

[Session-coordinated shadow promotion with rollback playbook]
description:
Context & motivation: customers running shadow traffic into new model variants frequently see noisy short-lived regressions that are hard to correlate with session state (sticky sessions, multi-request flows). This PR implements a session-coordinated promotion path: when a model variant shows stable behavior on shadowed sessions for a configurable observation window, we automatically promote a controlled subset of those same sessions into a canary lane rather than random users. The goal is to reduce promotion flakiness, increase signal fidelity for multi-request flows, and provide deterministic rollback hooks when regressions emerge.

Design summary: 1) Session fingerprint capture: the shadow bridge records a compact session fingerprint (hash of session-id, user-metadata-sanitized, request-seed) in the shadow telemetry blob; fingerprints are stored in the short-lived promotion cache (TTL configurable, default 10m). 2) Promotion eligibility: a variant becomes eligible for session-promotion after meeting coverage and success thresholds on shadowed sessions (configurable metrics: per-session success rate, median latency, absence of catastrophic errors). 3) Controlled promotion: eligible session fingerprints are used to seed canary routing so those same sessions are routed to the candidate variant (seeded canary allocation) keeping session affinity intact across multi-request flows. 4) Safety gates & rollback: we wire automatic rollback triggers (latency delta > 30% p50, error rate spike > 1.5x baseline, regression on key quality evals). When a trigger fires we immediately 1) pause new promotions, 2) drain candidate variant from promoted sessions, 3) escalate via the embedded rollback playbook (automated notifications, runbooks with one-click revert in Console). 5) Observability: new telemetry tags (session_promoted=true/false, promotion_reason, promotion_window_id) and per-session traces for promoted flows.

Configuration: new API in rollout policy: "promotion_mode: session_promote", keys: observation_window, session_ttl, min_session_coverage, success_thresholds, rollback_triggers, promotion_rate.

Migration and compatibility: default behavior is off. Operators can opt-in at rollout creation; we also include a CLI migration helper to convert existing canary definitions to session-promote-enabled templates.

Testing & safety: unit tests for controller logic, integration tests simulating multi-request flows, and a canary-sim harness that runs 10k synthetic sessions with injected latency/error faults to validate rollback conditions. We added a small staged e2e run on perf-canary lab.

Implementation notes: primary implementation lives in serving/orchestrator/promotion_controller.go and serving/bridge/shadow_bridge.go; a light-weight cache backed by redis (configurable to in-memory for dev) stores session fingerprints; telemetry is emitted via observability/telemetry_v2.

Backwards compatible: other rollout modes unchanged. Related: builds on ENG-7812 (shadow telemetry pipeline) and ENG-7824 (canary routing seeds).

Motivation story: this surfaced during a customer incident where a model change was promoted globally after shadow metrics looked stable, but multi-request checkout flows failed only for sessions that had been shadowed; session promotion reduces that risk by promoting the same sessions that were exercising the flow.

Rollout plan: 1) land as a feature-flag off, 2) enable in internal staging and run 72h synthetic session run, 3) enable for a small set of customers via Dedicated testing, 4) open opt-in in Console and document playbook.

Risks & mitigations: fingerprint collisions addressed with 128-bit HKDF-based fingerprints plus per-window salt; privacy: no PII is stored and we provide a built-in sanitizer for common identifiers; operational complexity: promotion cache TTL defaults conservative.

Ask from reviewers: please validate the rollback thresholds, the runbook phrasing, and the upgrade path for Private deployments.

release_notes:
Adds a session-aware promotion path from shadow to canary with automated rollback triggers and an operational playbook. No user-facing API changes.

[unify-tfstate-backend-and-gpu-nodepool-labeling-for-private-deploys]
description:
Motivation: Private deployments have diverged across customers: some clusters used per-VPC tfstate buckets, others used per-cluster keys, and GPU node pools lacked consistent labels that our autoscaler and cost tooling rely on. This PR unifies the tfstate backend layout, introduces canonical GPU nodepool labels/metadata, and modularizes IAM role surfaces to reduce blast radius and make upgrades/rollbacks safer.

Changes (high level):
- modules/state/backend.tf: new unified backend key pattern (bucket /<org>/<env>/redwood-private.tfstate) with an optional legacy migration flag. Supports both S3 and GCS via provider-agnostic variables.
- scripts/tfstate-migrator/migrate.sh: helper to detect legacy state objects and perform terraform state mv/import under a dry-run flag. Adds consistent locking hints and post-migration verification steps.
- modules/gpu-pool/*: node pool module now injects standardized tags/labels: redwood.org, redwood.env, redwood.pool-type=gpu, redwood.gpu-class; exposes optional node taints and kubelet args for NUMA/mtune. Readme documents compatibility with cluster-autoscaler label selectors.
- modules/iam/*: split into iam/nodepool_role and iam/admin_role abstractions; least-privilege defaults and a documented opt-out for legacy workflows. Added policy attachment moving from monolithic role to smaller role-per-responsibility.
- modules/network/shared_vpc_peering.tf: optional module to configure cross-project VPC peering and route propagation for air-gapped hybrid customers.
- docs/private/state-migration.md: step-by-step runbook and rollback instructions, including sample terraform commands and S3/GCS object snapshots.

Checklist: (x) unit/integration plan checked locally; (x) migration script tested against a staging bucket; (x) reviewers added; (x) docs updated.

Testing / Validation:
- Ran terraform plan/apply against a staging project using the migrator in dry-run mode, validated that state mv commands map resources to the new key layout without resource replacement.
- Deployed a GPU nodepool to a test cluster and verified labels appear on Node objects and that cluster-autoscaler picks them up with selector redwood.pool-type=gpu.
- IAM module unit tests validated with kitchen/inspec (policy lint) and validated that node instance profile permissions are sufficient for kubelet and NVIDIA driver provisioner only.

Upgrade path and migration plan:
1) Run scripts/tfstate-migrator/migrate.sh --dry-run against your existing state to collect candidate keys.
2) Review generated mapping and run migrate.sh (non-dry-run) to copy/move state into the new backend key. The script performs a terraform init -migrate-state under the hood.
3) Run terraform plan against the new backend; expect no resource diffs if migration succeeds.
4) If anything fails, follow rollback: restore bucket snapshot (instructions in docs/private/state-migration.md) and revert the backend config.

Rollback considerations:
- We explicitly do NOT attempt in-place live renames of provider-managed resources. The migrator is conservative: it moves terraform state only, leaving cloud resources untouched. Snapshots are required before running any state migration.
- If a migration partially completes, the runbook includes steps to re-run the migrate script referencing the checkpoint manifest.

Security notes:
- IAM changes reduce iam:PassRole and wide admin bindings; default new roles are narrower. Customers with custom bindings must opt-out and provide a mapping.

Related tickets / context: Linear ENG-1124 (private deployment state drift) and INF-78 (GPU autoscaler label standardization). Support case SUP-4321 reported a migration failure; this PR includes the fix.

Why this approach? Centralizing the backend key namespace avoids dozens of ad-hoc state keys we've accumulated and makes user-facing runbooks simpler. Canonical GPU labels simplify autoscaling, cost attribution, and cross-team policies. Modular IAM reduces blast radius during upgrades.

Diego Ramos: +1 on the labeling change — can we make redwood.gpu-class optional with a default of 'nvidia-a100' so older clusters don't break?
Anita Kaur: Good call; made redwood.gpu-class optional with default and added a note to README about explicit overrides.
Priya Menon: Migration script looks good. One request: add a --backup-bucket flag for customers who want state snapshots in a different bucket.
Anita Kaur: Added --backup-bucket and updated docs with examples. Also added a safety check to prevent migration if lock TTL is too low.
Ethan Zhou: IAM policy change is safer; recommend an automated policy diff as part of CI to avoid surprise privilege escalation in enterprise upgrades.

Private deploy: unified tfstate backend key schema; migration helper for legacy states; standardized GPU nodepool labels for autoscaler and cost tooling; modular IAM roles to minimize privileges; optional shared VPC peering module. See docs/private/state-migration.md for migration/runbook.

[Introduce slate-constructor and kernel-fingerprinter for cross-model throughput steering]
description:
Motivation: We need a lightweight, reproducible way to probe multi-model throughput behavior and attribute tail events to kernel-level signatures without running full long-running workloads. This PR introduces two components: (1) a 'slate-constructor' workload generator that builds compact multi-request slates representative of customer traffic slices, and (2) a 'kernel-fingerprinter' exporter that captures per-kernel execution fingerprints (kernel time histogram + op shapes) from short probes and converts them into a compact signature for attribution and routing models.

What this PR changes (summary): compact workload runner (slate-constructor) that supports per-model mixing, ordered/parallel slate layouts, and conditional KV priming; a kernel-fingerprinter service that hooks into the profiler API, produces tiled histograms, and emits a protobuf-compatible JSON exporter; an analysis utility that maps fingerprints to the kernel performance catalog used by the scheduler.

Why this is useful: teams can run short, deterministic slate probes (10-30s) and obtain stable kernel fingerprints to guide throughput-steering decisions (route to alternative model variant or split traffic). This avoids relying purely on long-running synthetic runs or noisy production traces for kernel attribution.

Design notes (single-string): Slate: each slate is a compact batch of 6-48 requests (configurable) assembled from a lightweight corpus sampler. Slates encode sequence length distributions, token mixes, and optional KV cache preconditions. The slate-constructor can emit both synchronous and async probe patterns and supports controlled inter-slate gaps to exercise concurrency windows. Kernel-fingerprinter: uses the existing traced kernel timing hooks, aggregates per-kernel latency buckets (0-1us,1-5us,5-20us,20-100us,100us+), and records op shape signatures (tensor dims, dtype buckets). The exporter compresses the fingerprint into a 128-byte base64 token for storage and transmission. Mapping: a small nearest-neighbor mapper correlates new fingerprints against historical catalog entries to suggest likely kernel hotspots and an estimated throughput delta.

Checklist: - [x] Slate generator implementation (python runner + CLI) - [x] Kernel fingerprinter profiler hooks and exporter - [x] Fingerprint -> catalog mapper service + unit tests - [x] Integration smoke: run slate probe against local mini-cluster and verify exporter output - [x] Bench harness: end-to-end benchmark showing attribution precision and throughput impact estimates - [x] Docs: README + usage examples + examples/recipes/slate-templates.md

Performance summary (selected): - Mixed-model probe (A: long-form encoder-decoder, B: decoder-only) at 8 concurrent slates for 30s: baseline scheduler attribution accuracy 58% -> with fingerprint mapper 78% ( +20% abs ) - Tail throughput under mixed traffic (p95 tokens/sec aggregate) improved 12% when steering rules informed by fingerprints vs heuristic routing - Typical probe duration: 12s (median), data payload per fingerprint: 180 bytes after compression

Commits: ["init: add slate-constructor runner and CLI (elena/2026-01-14)", "feat: kernel-fingerprinter and exporter + proto (elena/2026-01-21)", "feat: mapper service and NN index (elena/2026-01-28)", "test: add unit/integration tests for mapper and exporter (elena/2026-02-05)", "docs: usage, examples, and cookbook templates (elena/2026-02-10)", "fix: reduce exporter serialization overhead (elena/2026-02-18)", "ci: bench pipeline tweaks and flake fixes (elena/2026-02-24)"]

Files changed (high level): ["benchmark_lab/slate_constructor/runner.py", "benchmark_lab/slate_constructor/cli.py", "benchmark_lab/slate_constructor/templates/default_slate.json", "benchmark_lab/fingerprinter/profiler_hook.py", "benchmark_lab/fingerprinter/exporter.py", "benchmark_lab/fingerprinter/proto/fingerprint.proto", "benchmark_lab/mapper/nn_index.py", "benchmark_lab/mapper/service.py", "benchmark_lab/tests/test_fingerprint_mapping.py", "benchmark_lab/tests/test_slate_generation.py", "docs/benchmark_lab/slates.md", "examples/recipes/slate-templates.md"]

Changed snippets (illustrative): - runner.py: added Slate class with sample method: 'def sample(self, corpus, seq_dist): return [Request(prompt, seq_len) for ...]' - exporter.py: compress_fingerprint(f) -> base64.b64encode(zlib.compress(json.dumps(f).encode()))[:].decode() - mapper/nn_index.py: uses cosine embedding of histogram vector and tiny FAISS-like in-memory index (fallback to brute force for <1024 entries).

Testing and CI: unit tests for mapping and exporter run in ~45s. Bench integration pipeline executed a 30s probe suite on the GPU smoke harness. CI checks: unit-tests: pass, flake8: pass, bench-integration: pass with a single warning re: ephemeral telemetry retention. Full CI summary included below in ci_checks.

Review notes and decisions: 1) Memory/space: fingerprints limited to compressed 512B in practice; we store the compact token only in the catalog to keep catalog size small. 2) Privacy: fingerprints are structural and do not include raw prompt text; templates are configurable to use anonymized corpora. 3) Forward compatibility: proto includes a version field; mapper tolerates missing/extra fields.

Integration instructions: see docs/benchmark_lab/slates.md for running: 'benchctl slate run --template examples/recipes/slate-templates.md --duration 30s --exporter fingerprinter://local' and then inspect catalog via 'benchctl fingerprinter list --recent'.

Release notes: Adds slate-constructor and kernel-fingerprinter for short deterministic probes and a mapper service to correlate fingerprints to kernel catalog entries. Useful for throughput steering and routing decisions.


review_comments:
Marco: Nice pattern. Can we reduce the default slate size to 12 for faster CI? (response: adjusted in cli default and documented)
Priya: How do we guarantee fingerprints don't leak PII? (response: fingerprint explicitly excludes prompt tokens and includes only shape+timing histograms; docs updated)
Alan: Mapper fallback when catalog small? (response: added brute-force fallback up to 1024 entries; included unit test)
Marco: Please add a test that verifies exporter output size < 1KB (response: added test_fingerprint_size assertion)
Priya: integration flake caused by ephemeral telemetry; CI job retried and passed

release_notes:
Adds a lightweight slate generator and kernel fingerprinter exporter to produce compact per-probe kernel signatures. Includes mapping service to correlate signatures with kernel catalog entries to improve routing and throughput steering decisions. Backwards-compatible proto with versioning. No user-facing breaking changes.

notes_for_followup:
Follow-ups planned: (1) catalog clustering job to deduplicate similar fingerprints (ENG-6501), (2) dashboard panel for fingerprint drift over time (ENG-6520), (3) integrate with autoscaler to surface steering suggestions in Redwood Console.

risk_and_mitigation:
Risk: misclassification of fingerprint may cause suboptimal steering. Mitigation: conservative default policy (suggest-only), ship telemetry to validate with canary before automatic rollout. Added canary flags and opt-in via benchctl config.

manual_test_steps:
1) benchctl slate run --template examples/recipes/slate-templates.md --duration 30s --exporter fingerprinter://local 2) benchctl fingerprinter list --recent 3) benchctl mapper lookup --token <token> --top 5

[LuminaForge — Marketplace governance & runtime integration sync]
summary:
High-level technical sync between Redwood and LuminaForge to align on marketplace packaging, governance requirements, runtime integration patterns (VPC, KMS, image signing), and joint pilot workloads. Agreed next steps on artifacts to exchange and a pilot timeline in early December.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-27 14:00 PT
Duration: 62 minutes
Recorded: yes
Attendees: Alicia (Redwood AE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood PM), Dana (LuminaForge Head of Partnerships), Owen (Platform Eng), Simone (Security), Leo (Product)

[00:00] Alicia: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick roll call — Marcus and I from Redwood, Priya joining to capture any product-level constraints. Dana, Owen, Simone, Leo from LuminaForge?
[00:11] Dana: Yep, all here. Thanks. Wanted to move quickly through the packaging and then deep dive on the runtime pieces.
[00:18] Marcus: Sounds good. I'll start with a quick overview of how Redwood usually packages for marketplace listings — then we can map to LuminaForge's ops.
[00:25] Marcus: So our typical offering has two artifacts: a lightweight listing that points to a container image plus a helm chart for self-managed installs. We also support an operator path but most partners start with helm. The chart includes RBAC templates, K8s resources, and a simple values.yaml that lets you choose between hosted endpoints, Redwood Dedicated, or an on-prem runtime.
[00:45] Owen: Just to clarify — when you say "container image," are we expected to host the image in our registry or do you support pull-through from Redwood's registry?
[00:52] Marcus: Both patterns are supported. For marketplace listing we prefer partners to host the image in their registry and use image signing (cosign) with attestation. We can also provide a signed image from Redwood in certain co-managed cases.
[01:07] Simone: On the security side we need to validate the signing flow and KMS integration. Does Redwood require customer-managed KMS (bring-your-own-key) for private deployments?
[01:17] Marcus: For Redwood Private and Dedicated, we integrate with customer KMS — KMS or HSM — yes. For the hosted listing, the control plane may use Redwood's keys but we support envelope encryption with customer keys for data at rest. There's some nuance: if you need HSM-backed keys for attestation, that's something we'll validate with our security team.
[01:35] Leo: For our compliance team it's important that the listing can be deployed into our customer's VPC and that we can pass through SAML assertions for SSO to the console.
[01:44] Priya: We have a marketplace pattern that includes SAML integration for the management console and an RBAC mapping layer. The helm chart exposes a pluggable SSO adapter; we can provide sample SAML config and a template.
[01:56] Dana: Great. On billing and metering — how granular is the meter when deployed through the marketplace? We have two SKU models: per-instance reserved, or usage-based per token for hosted.
[02:06] Marcus: Marketplace metering usually depends on the marketplace vendor. For our standard integration we provide two flavors: a metered usage webhook for token-level billing, or a monthly seat/instance reporting endpoint. We provide reporting hooks and a CSV export; for tighter integrations we can add custom billing events.
[02:22] Owen: Will we need to run any special telemetry agents to get token-level counts?
[02:26] Marcus: No special agent. The runtime emits token counts and request metadata to a metrics endpoint; the helm chart wires a sidecar that batches and ships events. If you want token-level per-customer tagging we'll need to pass the tenant headers from the platform.
[02:39] Simone: Quick question — for image attestation, you said cosign. Do you also support sigstore-based provenance attestation? Our compliance prefers full provenance.
[02:49] Marcus: We can accept sigstore attestations; our release pipeline integrates with Cosign and Rekor. We'll include the recommended provenance format in the checklist.
[02:57] [00:03:00] Dana: Ok can we talk about runtime compatibility? Our platform currently runs mixed nodes — x86 with A100s and a small set of H100s for customers that request it, plus a couple of AMD MI300 nodes in staging. We need to be sure the model builds you recommend run across these.
[03:20] Marcus: Important detail. Redwood's runtime has multi-arch kernels and supports common quantization profiles. We usually publish a compatibility matrix: sequence length, recommended batch sizes per GPU family, and whether to use float16 vs int8 kernels. For AMD MI300 there are a few kernels that are still experimental; we'd want to run a tiny benchmark.
[03:38] Owen: Benchmark would be great. We can carve out a 24-hour window in staging. What should the workload be?
[03:44] Marcus: If you can provide two workloads: (1) low-latency chat (approx 512 token window) and (2) batch embeddings for 1536 token inputs. That will exercise both streaming low-latency paths and batch throughput.
[03:56] Leo: Do you have recommended model variants for cost-sensitive customers?
[04:00] Marcus: Yes — we usually suggest a performance tier (FP16, larger context) and a cost tier (int8 quantized). Redwood Optimize can recommend the quantization profile and expected cost delta. We'll put those profiles in the checklist.
[04:11] [00:04:20] Simone: On encryption and key management — for marketplace deployments some customers demand that private keys never leave their KMS. How does token caching or KV cache encryption work in that scenario?
[04:25] Marcus: The KV cache can be encrypted at rest and we support envelope encryption where the customer-managed KMS only holds the data keys. The runtime never exports plaintext keys; the unsealing happens locally in the node's runtime and keys are rotated per policy. We'll share our KMS integration docs.
[04:40] Dana: Any gotchas around network egress or connectivity when a listing is deployed into a customer's VPC? Guardrails, NATs, etc?
[04:47] Marcus: The main thing is outbound webhook endpoints for billing/telemetry and optional callbacks to Redwood-hosted services for model fallback. We support a fully air-gapped install but that requires shipping the model artifacts and disabling outbound health checks. Standard installs need at least one egress route to the metrics endpoint.
[05:04] Owen: About model fallback — if a customer wants to fallback to Redwood Hosted for spikes, how is traffic routed?
[05:10] Marcus: We have a routing shim in the helm chart that respects a policy — local preferred, fallback to a compatible hosted variant. It also supports weights for A/B style rollouts.
[05:20] [00:05:40] Leo: Can you explain the listing security review process for marketplace certification? We've had previous vendors fail due to missing attestation or insufficient audit logs.
[05:29] Priya: From Redwood's side the flow is: we run a pre-cert checklist (image signing, provenance, RBAC, telemetry), then an optional penetration test if the marketplace requires it, and finally a governance review. We'll share the exact gating doc.
[05:43] Simone: Does Redwood provide the audit log format? Our SIEM needs a particular JSON schema for events.
[05:49] Marcus: Yes we can provide a mapping or an example events export. We'll include a sample Splunk/ELK JSON payload.
[05:57] [00:06:00] Dana: One operational question — for upgrades, do you support in-place rolling updates of the runtime with zero-downtime KV cache migration?
[06:06] Marcus: We support rolling upgrades. KV cache migration is controlled via a compatibility flag; usually we rehydrate caches and support golden path fallbacks. There can be a small warmup latency during the first traffic after upgrade.
[06:18] Owen: For the pilot, what's the recommended minimum cluster size?
[06:21] Marcus: For a pilot with one low-latency and one batch workload, we'd recommend at least 2 GPU nodes: one A100/H100 for latency and one for batch throughput. If you want to mimic multi-tenant behavior add a smaller CPU node for control plane services.
[06:35] [00:06:40] Simone: Any special requirements for FIPS or HSM integrations? We use a vendor that requires PKCS#11 interface.
[06:44] Marcus: We support PKCS#11 for HSMs in the private deploys; for marketplace listing you can document the HSM connector and we'll validate in the pre-cert.
[06:52] Dana: What about commercial terms on the marketplace listing — revenue share, discounts, support SLAs — can we align on a standard?
[06:58] Alicia: I'll push a standard listing term sheet — it's our usual marketplace msla and revenue share templates. We can treat custom requests as addenda.
[07:07] [00:07:10] Leo: Any known edge cases when the partner wants to enable model fine-tuning on-prem?
[07:13] Marcus: Fine-tuning on-prem introduces data locality and checkpoint storage complexity. We support training-light use cases (adapter-based fine-tuning) but full-finetuning would require additional storage and possibly different kernel paths. For marketplace listings we generally recommend inference-only packages unless you explicitly want a training offering.
[07:30] Owen: Ok that helps.
[07:33] [00:07:40] Dana: Let's do a quick timeline — would a mid-December pilot be reasonable?
[07:39] Alicia: If you can get the shortlist of workloads and cluster inventory by Dec 1, we can aim for a rolling pilot starting Dec 8 with a 2-week validation window.
[07:47] Dana: Sounds good.
[07:48] [00:08:00] Marcus: I'll attach the packaging checklist, the helm chart sample, and the quantization profiles to the follow-up. Also the KMS integration doc and the provenance example.
[08:00] Simone: We'll need to confirm whether our compliance requires a third-party pen test before listing. If so we'll alert you.
[08:06] Priya: Noted — we'll hold a follow-up SOC2/HSM session if needed.
[08:11] [00:08:20] Dana: Anything else?
[08:23] Leo: One last: on-region availability — some of our enterprise customers require EU-only deployments. Is there any restriction on region-specific packaging?
[08:31] Marcus: No restriction; the chart is region-agnostic. For regional listing you just pick the image registry and KMS region. We'll document best practices for data residency in the checklist.
[08:43] [00:08:50] Dana: Great. Thanks all.
[08:52] Alicia: Quick recap — Marcus sends artifacts, LuminaForge provides workloads and cluster inventory, Simone flags compliance items, and Alicia follows up on legal. We'll sync again once artifacts are shared.
[09:05] Meeting end.

Meeting Header: 2026-07-08 16:00 UTC — Duration: 53 minutes — Attendees listed above.

00:00 Samira Patel: All right, everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda — align the three deals we pre-scored, decide pilots, and list what we need for procurement.
00:15 Olivia Park: Thanks Samira, appreciate it. We want to move the biggest one, Deal A, through sales in the next 6 weeks if possible. we've got exec sponsor locked but need a clearer co-sell plan.
00:30 Marco Ruiz: Yeah one note — our legal team flagged data residency for a few customers, also pricing band concerns.
00:45 Ethan Hughes: Just to call out, from a technical side, the main question is hosted vs private for each use-case. latency sensitivity on Deal A means we probably want a dedicated cluster or private VPC.
01:10 Jian Li: latency is non-negotiable on the real-time routing use-case, we need <80ms p95. what's your experience running that on Redwood hosted versus dedicated?
01:30 Ethan Hughes: In our perf runs, hosted with smart batching and prefix cache hits often sits in the 60–90ms range for short prompts, but variability can spike. Dedicated pools give a tighter SLA but cost more. you trade predictability for unit economics.
02:05 Hector Morales: When you said prefix cache, do you mean KV cache? I think the ops team called it something else in the doc. transcribed earlier as key cache so want to make sure we align.
02:22 Samira Patel: yes KV cache — sometimes mirror text in the docs as key-value cache, the docs are a bit inconsistent, sorry about that. we'll share a clarified glossary.

06:30 Samira Patel: discounts are negotiable within certain bands; instead of competing on pure discount we can offer a bundled pilot credit and a dedicated SE day to accelerate implementation which is often more convincing.

08:25 Hector Morales: is there a way to route cold-class requests to a cheaper model variant automatically? we have cost constraints at scale.
08:40 Ethan Hughes: yes — smart routing policies can route by latency budget or cost tiers; we can set fallback to a lower-cost quantized variant for non-critical paths.

10:30 Samira Patel: quick recap so we all line up: Deal A — pilot private cluster for latency-sensitive customer; Deal B — hosted pilot focused on embeddings and quantization; Deal C — hosted trial with options to scale. will we agree on that?

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-08
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 54m
Attendees: Alex Rivera (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Sam Cho (Redwood GTM), Mark Holden (StratusAI - Head of Alliances), Lina Gomez (Partner Sales Lead), Ibrahim Khan (Solutions Architect)

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check—can you see my screen? I pulled the draft co-sell worksheet and a one-pager for the sprint.

[00:12] Mark: Yep, seeing it. Thanks Alex. We got Lina and I on this side, and Ibrahim is dialed in from the east coast.

[00:20] Priya: Cool. I wanna be explicit up front — goal for this call is to agree on how we route, qualify, and pilot three joint accounts over the next 6 weeks. Sound right?

[00:30] Lina: Yes. We have a couple of marketing events looming so we also want to scope what assets we need.

[00:36] Alex: Great. So first slide — ownership model. We propose a shared tracker where Stratus logs inbound leads and Redwood tags product-fit level A/B/C plus model preference. Then we route based on lead score.

[00:50] Mark: How do you define product-fit A? For us, A means customer is actively evaluating inference infra, has >$100k ARR potential and needs VPC or dedicated options.

[01:06] Alex: That aligns well. Our suggested A is: production LLM usage required, privacy/regulatory needs or SLA requests, and ACV over $75k. B is pilotable but not immediate spend. C is marketing nurture.

[01:20] Ibrahim: Quick technical question — when you say \"dedicated\" how strict is the requirement on VPC? A lot of our customers want private tenancy or on-prem.

[01:30] Priya: Good point. Redwood Dedicated supports reserved GPU pools and our Private deploy supports VPC or on-prem installs. For pilots we'll usually start hosted for speed unless data residency or SOC2 controls require Private.

[01:44] Ibrahim: Ok. And about latency — we had a lead concerned about kv cache performance on long context windows.

[01:52] Priya: (laughs) We sometimes see \"kay vee cash\" in notes — that's KV cache. Our baseline tests will include 8k and 32k context runs; we'll capture p99 latency and token cost.

[02:05] Sam: On the GTM side, the ask is simple: for A deals Stratus owns initial conversation and Redwood supports with SE + pricing. For B deals we want a joint outreach with Stratus listing the partner value-add.

[02:18] Mark: Works. Question — revenue split discussion? Our legal wants a simple referral fee on the first year and then a smaller sharing if we close more deeply.

[02:28] Alex: We can do a referral -> motion where initial introduction yields a finder fee (standard percentage), then for larger deals we move to an MSA addendum with co-sell terms. I can share a template, but legal will need to confirm.

[02:40] Lina: Please share the template. Also, do you have any measurement for how Redwood credits leads when there are multiple touches? Our CRM processes need that.

[02:52] Alex: We'll use first-touch in the tracker but can flag when Redwood expands the opportunity to full close and then update attribution. We can add a column for 'owner at close' in the sheet.

[03:03] Mark: Makes sense. Let's switch to the pilot plan — Priya?

[03:08] Priya: Sure. Technical pilot is two parts: 1) a quick functional demo and 2) a 1-week benchmark. For benchmark we collect throughput/latency, cost per 1k tokens, and stability under a ~2k qps simulation for a short burst. We'll also test prefix caching for conversational flows.

[03:26] Ibrahim: For the qps sim — do you simulate streaming and non-streaming? Many customers stream to reduce perceived latency.

[03:32] Priya: We'll include both. Streaming adds complexity, and we'll measure end-to-end TTFF (time to first token) and time-to-complete for 1k token responses.

[03:44] Mark: Any restrictions on datasets for benchmarking? Some customers won't share production prompts.

[03:50] Priya: We can use synthetic prompts or a sanitized prompt set. The important part is distribution shape — avg length, tail length percentiles. We can also run with the customer's anonymous prompts if they prefer.

[03:59] Alex: For timeline, proposal: Mark picks three opportunities this week — ideally a mix (1 enterprise SOC2-heavy, 1 mid-market chat use-case, 1 ISV embedding use-case). Then Priya runs two pilot benchmarks (one hosted baseline, one dedicated/private if customer needs). Priya, can you do those in the week of 4/14?

[04:18] Priya: Yes, that works. I’ll need access to sample prompts and an estimated seq length distribution. Also an AE owner on the customer side to help with signoff for load tests.

[04:30] Mark: Lina will coordinate on the sample sets. Ibrahim will help prepare the sandbox for the one on-prem trial.

[04:36] Lina: We'll also want a short joint one-pager for sales enablement — message map, key objection handling (latency vs cost), and the co-sell pitch.

[Talent acquisition and first-120-days handbook]
Summary
This handbook consolidates Redwood Inference’s standard hiring workflow, interviewer calibration guidance, candidate SLAs, offer/negotiation guardrails, and the structured first-120-days (manager + new-hire) ramp plan. It is intended for hiring managers, interviewers, recruiters, and people-ops partners.

Purpose and scope
- Purpose: Reduce variability in hiring outcomes, accelerate new-hire productivity, and provide managers pragmatic checklists to own execution.
- Scope: All full-time and core contractor hires across engineering, product, and go-to-market teams. Excludes contingent vendors and agency contractors (see vendor onboarding doc).

Principles we follow
1) Candidate experience matters: respond within SLA windows, transparent feedback, respectful scheduling.
2) Evidence-based hiring: decisions rely on rubric scores + hiring manager calibration.
3) Manager ownership: hiring, onboarding logistics, and performance signals are manager responsibilities with people-ops support.
4) Continuous calibration: interviewers attend quarterly calibration sessions and update rubrics.

Roles & responsibilities (quick reference)
- Hiring manager: role definition, interview panel selection, final decision, first-120-days plan, career conversation at 90/120 days.
- Recruiter: sourcing strategy, scheduling, offer preparation, candidate communications, diversity sourcing targets.
- Interviewers: complete rubrics, provide written feedback within 48 hours, surface concerns early.
- People Ops: compensation bands, background checks, documentation, onboarding logistics, run manager calibration training.

Standard hiring workflow (timeline expectations)
1) Role kickoff (Day 0–3)
   - Manager completes role brief template (template link) and must attach: job mission, top 3 success metrics for first 6 months, required vs nice-to-have skills, proposed interview loop.
2) Sourcing and sieve (Day 1–14)
   - Recruiter returns shortlist within 7–10 business days for active reqs. Diversity-sourcing target: at least 30% of longlist from underrepresented groups where feasible.
3) Interview loop (Day 7–21)
   - Interview panel: 4–6 interviews (technical, design, system sense, collaboration/culture) recommended. No more than 2 back-to-back interviews without a 15-minute break.
4) Decision and offer (Day 21–28)
   - Hiring manager submits hire memo with anonymized rubric summary. Recruiter prepares offer within 48 hours of approval.
5) Acceptance to start (Day 30–60)
   - Standard notice period target: 30 days. Escalate if longer to people-ops for special onboarding support.

Candidate experience SLA (service-level agreements)
- Recruiter initial reply to inbound application: 2 business days.
- First interview scheduled after initial screen: within 7 business days for active roles.
- Interview feedback provided to candidate: within 7 business days of final interview.
- Offer response window: standard 7 calendar days (extendable with recruiter approval).

Interview rubric (scoring and guidance)
- Scoring scale: 1–5 (1 = does not meet, 3 = meets expectations, 5 = outstanding).
- Dimensions (apply per role):
  - Core competency (domain knowledge / technical skill)
  - Problem solving & debugging
  - System design / architecture (if applicable)
  - Collaboration & communication
  - Ownership & execution
  - Role-specific signals (product sense, sales aptitude, security mindshare)
- Minimum hire thresholds (guideline): average score >= 3.5 AND no single dimension < 2 unless hiring manager documents a compelling exception.

Example rubric table (paste into interview form)
| Dimension | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Problem solving | Incorrect approach, cannot reason about tradeoffs | Basic solution with gaps | Solid approach, some clarity issues | Strong approach with good tradeoffs | Exceptional insight and tradeoff analysis |
| Collaboration | Unable to accept feedback | Limited examples of teamwork | Clear examples of cross-team work | Drives collaboration proactively | Influences cross-org outcomes |

Calibration & training
- Quarterly calibration sessions run by people-ops (60 minutes). Attendance required for interviewers who did >6 interviews that quarter.
- Calibration agenda: 3 anonymized debriefs, rubric edge cases, signal alignment for leveling.

Offer & comp guidelines
- Compensation anchors: use current comp bands (see related_pages). Compensation must be approved by people-ops for any offer above band midpoint + 15%.
- Equity: recommended grants for ICs and managers based on level (see comp bands doc).
- Counter-offer handling: recruiter and manager coordinate; avoid incentivizing multiple-stage counter cycles.

Background checks & compliance
- Standard pre-hire checks: identity verification, employment verification, and reference check for ICs at level 4+.
- For hires in regulated markets (EU data residency or healthcare customers): initiate enhanced checks (people-ops will advise).

First-120-days structured ramp (manager + new-hire checklists)
Manager checklist (pre-boarding) — 2 weeks before start:
- Confirm offer acceptance and start date in HRIS.
- Add to team calendar, assign buddy, confirm hardware & network access, create agenda for day 1.

Day 1–14: orientation & context
- Week 1 objectives:
  - Orientation: company mission, code of conduct, security basics (complete security course by day 5).
  - Team orientation: context doc, architecture tour, current roadmap, key stakeholders.
  - Quick win: assign a read-only task and a small actionable task to deliver in week 2.
- Manager deliverables: 30-minute daily check-ins for week 1, assign a mentor, set expectations for 1:1 cadence.

Day 15–60: ownership & delivery
- Objectives:
  - Deliver the small project and present findings.
  - Shadow main workflows (deploys, triage, design reviews).
  - Complete two cross-functional introductions.
- Manager deliverables: weekly 1:1s, feedback at 30-day checkpoint.

Day 61–120: impact & career conversation
- Objectives:
  - Lead a medium-scope project or feature.
  - Demonstrate independent execution and cross-team coordination.
  - Prepare a 90–120 day review packet: accomplishments, blockers, and development goals.
- Manager deliverables: 90 and 120-day review conversations; align on success metrics and development plan.

90/120-day evaluation rubric (manager uses to guide conversation)
- Signals of success (examples): delivered assigned scope, communicative and responsive, adopted team practices, positive peer feedback.
- Areas requiring attention: needs additional mentorship, performance gaps, cultural/behavioral concerns.

Performance & feedback cycles integration
- New hires are added to the standard performance cadence after their 90-day checkpoint. For levels with probationary reviews, managers must document progress and escalate to people-ops if risk of separation is >30% at day 90.
- Feedback cadence: 1:1 weekly for first 90 days, then standard 1:1 cadence per team. People-ops recommends documented 1:1 notes stored in manager wiki.

Onboarding success metrics (people-ops will track quarterly)
- Time to first PR/merge (goal: <= 30 days for engineering ICs).
- Time to independent ownership of a component (goal: <= 90 days).
- New-hire onboarding NPS (survey at day 14 and day 90; target NPS >= +40).

Escalation and separation guidance
- If a new-hire shows sustained performance issues between day 30–90, manager must: 1) document examples, 2) run an improvement plan with clear milestones (30 days), 3) loop in people-ops for coaching.
- People-ops will provide legal/termination checklist if separation proceeds.

Manager quick-start guide (5-minute read)
- Before offer: write a crisp success profile (3 success metrics).
- Before day 1: assign buddy, create 30/60/90 outcomes, reserve 1 hour for architecture deep dive.
- Weekly: document one piece of feedback, schedule a short peer sync for cross-team visibility.

Templates and examples

[Talent intake, time-to-hire SLAs, and manager responsibilities]
Overview

Purpose
This document defines the standardized talent intake workflow, time-to-hire SLAs, interview loop design expectations, and explicit manager responsibilities for hiring and for the first 90 days of onboarding. It unifies recruiter and manager handoffs, reduces time-to-fill variability, and creates clear escalation points to preserve candidate experience and enable predictable capacity planning.

Audience
- Hiring managers
- Recruiters
- People Partners
- Hiring committee members
- People-ops leadership

Context and goals
- Reduce average time-to-offer from 52 days to target SLA of 21 days for IC roles and 30 days for manager roles.
- Ensure every role has a signed intake and a calibrated scorecard before candidates are sourced.
- Define manager commitments during hiring and onboarding so People-ops can measure compliance and coach where needed.

Key definitions
- Time-to-hire (TTH): Days from Approved Intake (see step 2) to Offer Acceptance.
- Time-to-offer: Days from Approved Intake to Offer Extension.
- Approved Intake: Recruiter + Hiring Manager + Finance signoff documented in Greenlight Intake form.
- Calibrated scorecard: Role rubric with top-3 success criteria and interview question mapping.

1) Intake and approvals (owner: Hiring Manager, recruiter as co-owner)
1.1 Intake submission\- Manager opens Position Intake form in Greenlight within 3 business days of hiring need discovery. Include:
  - Role brief (one-paragraph), mission, org placement
  - Required vs. nice-to-have skills
  - Scorecard: top 3 success indicators and examples of evidence
  - Expected compensation band and remote/location constraints
  - Resourcing priority (replace/scale/new)

1.2 SLAs for approvals\- People-ops will respond to new intake submissions as follows:
  - Manager acknowledgement: immediate auto-receipt from Greenlight (0 days)
  - Recruiter assignment: within 2 business days
  - Finance compensation check: within 3 business days
  - Final intake approval (Recruiter + People Partner): within 5 business days

1.3 Reject/iterate criteria\- If salary/level misalignment or unclear scorecard, intake returns to manager with clear comments and expected revision window of 3 business days.

2) Interview loop design and calibration (owner: Recruiter + Hiring Manager)
2.1 Minimum standards for interview loops (applies to all IC and manager hires)
  - Screening call (30m) + technical or role assessment (take-home or pair; if used, include clear success rubric)
  - 3–5 onsite/virtual interviews capped at 4 hours total for ICs; manager loops may be up to 5 hours
  - Each interviewer receives the calibrated scorecard and explicit question mapping at least 24 hours before interview
  - Diversity of perspectives: at least one cross-functional stakeholder and one peer-level interviewer

2.2 Interviewer training and calibration\- People-ops runs quarterly interviewer calibration sessions. Managers must certify at least 2 interviewers per role as calibrated in Greenlight before scheduling onsite loops.

2.3 Interviewer no-no list
  - Do not ask for compensation history
  - Avoid hypothetical leading questions that are not scored on the rubric
  - Do not make offers or commitments outside Offer Authority matrix

3) Time-to-hire SLAs (owner: People-ops; metrics surfaced to manager dashboards)
3.1 Target metrics (measured per role family and level)
  - Target time-to-offer (IC): 14 business days from Approved Intake to Offer Extension
  - Target time-to-offer (Manager): 21 business days from Approved Intake to Offer Extension
  - Target time-to-accept (all roles): 7 business days from Offer Extension to Candidate Acceptance
  - Target time-to-start: 21 days from Offer Acceptance to Employee start date for internal hiring; 28 for external candidates

3.2 Escalation thresholds
  - Warning: role exceeds 14 business days (IC) without an offer — auto-notification to Hiring Manager + Recruiter
  - Escalation: role exceeds 21 business days (IC) — People-ops flags on weekly hiring review and schedules a triage meeting
  - Executive escalation: roles open > 45 calendar days for mission-critical positions

3.3 Measurement and dashboards\- Data sources: Greenlight intake metadata, ATS pipeline timestamps, compensation approvals. KPIs updated daily on People-ops hiring dashboard and available to managers via Manager Portal.

4) Offer approvals and negotiation playbook (owner: People-ops + Finance)
4.1 Offer checklist before extension
  - Approved budget and comp band documented
  - Background check / compliance required (role-dependent) flagged
  - Offer packet with role summary, manager expectations, and onboarding start window ready

4.2 Negotiation guardrails
  - Manager may approve up to +10% above midpoint for IC roles with People-ops signoff; >+10% requires VP/Finance approval
  - For counter-offers, maintain transparency and re-run basic reference checks if >15% variance from original terms

5) Manager responsibilities during hiring and first 90 days (owner: Hiring Manager)
5.1 Commitment windows
  - Intake completion: 3 business days from need identified
  - Interview feedback submitted: within 48 hours of interview completion
  - Final decision communicated to recruiter: within 2 business days after last onsite

5.2 Onboarding and first 90-day plan (must be published in Greenlight Onboard tab prior to start date)
  - Week 0: Welcome logistics, hardware, account provisioning checklist, first-day agenda
  - Week 1: 1:1 daily check-ins for ICs new to role; manager hires: daily plus 90-day goals discussion
  - Week 2–4: Role immersion — product demos, team pairing schedule, top-priority deliverables mapped to scorecard
  - Month 2: Mid-probation review (documented evidence vs. scorecard)
  - Month 3: Probation closeout and permanent goals set, or extension plan defined with concrete success criteria

5.3 Evaluation evidence required at checkpoints\- For every mid-probation and probation closeout, provide 3 artifacts of evidence mapped to the calibrated scorecard (examples: code review snapshots, sales calls recorded with consent, project summaries).

6) Performance feedback cadence alignment (owner: People-ops + Manager)
6.1 Tied to hiring scorecard\- First-cycle feedback must reference the original calibrated scorecard. Managers should avoid ad-hoc criteria that were not in the scorecard during hiring.

6.2 Coaching cadence during probation
  - Weekly 1:1s for first 60 days with a documented short note (one-paragraph) in Greenlight after each session
  - People-ops will auto-request a probation checkpoint report at Day 45 and Day 85

7) Failures, remediation, and role cancellation
7.1 Cancellation before offer
  - If headcount is paused, recruiter or People Partner changes intake state to "Paused" and notifies candidate slate within 48 hours.

7.2 Remediation plans after hire
  - If midpoint evidence at Day 45 is failing, manager creates a 30-day remediation plan with clear success criteria and a weekly review schedule. People-ops supports calibration and, if needed, escalates to HR for policy review.

7.3 Offboarding within probation
  - If termination is required during probation, follow the people-ops termination checklist and record decisions with evidence. People-ops will coordinate exit logistics and reallocation of budget.

8) Templates and artifacts (attached in Greenlight)
  - Intake template (required fields)
  - Calibrated scorecard template (3 success criteria, evidence mapping, interview question bucket)
  - Offer packet template
  - First-90-days plan template
  - Probation checkpoint report template

9) Operational handbook for recruiters and managers (short procedures)
9.1 Recruiter daily ritual
  - T+0: validate new intakes and schedule stakeholder alignment within 2 business days
  - T+2: pipeline kickoff with sourcers and initial candidate outreach
  - Weekly: Hiring review sync with manager to review top-5 slate

9.2 Manager interview and feedback procedure
  - Run calibration readout with interviewers before loops start
  - Submit feedback using the structured scorecard (numerical + narrative) within 48 hours
  - If an interviewer misses feedback window, recruiter has authority to accept late feedback up to 5 business days, after which interviewer is excluded from final decision unless escalated

10) Exceptions and fast-path for critical hires
  - Fast-path criteria: critical bug-fix roles, revenue-impact hires, legal/compliance escalations
  - Fast-path process: 24–48 hour intake vetting, accelerated interview loop with pre-approved interviewers, and Offer Authority delegated to VP+People-ops for same-day offers when warranted

11) Governance, audit, and continuous improvement
  - Quarterly audit of 10 random closed requisitions for compliance with intake, scorecard, and feedback SLAs. Findings published to People-ops readout.
  - Quarterly feedback loop with Hiring Managers to revise SLAs and reduce bottlenecks.

Appendix A — SLA table
| Metric | Target | Owner | Escalation threshold |
|--------|--------|-------|----------------------|
| Recruiter assignment | 2 business days | People-ops | 5 business days |
| Intake approval | 5 business days | People-ops | 10 business days |
| Time-to-offer (IC) | 14 business days | Hiring Manager + Recruiter | 21 business days |
| Time-to-offer (Manager) | 21 business days | Hiring Manager + Recruiter | 30 business days |
| Offer acceptance | 7 calendar days | Candidate | 14 calendar days |
| Time-to-start (external) | 28 calendar days | Hiring Manager | 45 calendar days |

Appendix B — Quick checklist (for hiring manager)
- [ ] Submit intake within 3 business days
- [ ] Draft calibrated scorecard and evidence mapping
- [ ] Certify 2 interviewers in Greenlight
- [ ] Commit to feedback timelines and weekly hiring sync
- [ ] Publish first-90-days plan before start date

[PLG Signal Follow‑Up Playbook (Hosted → Dedicated/Private)]
## Purpose
This playbook defines how AEs/SDRs/SEs/CSMs should follow up on product-led growth (PLG) signals that indicate a self-serve customer is a strong candidate for a sales-assisted upgrade to **Redwood Dedicated** or **Redwood Private**.

The goal is to:
- Respond quickly to real need (scale, reliability, security/compliance) without spamming customers.
- Standardize messaging and discovery so we qualify consistently.
- Ensure clean handoffs to SE and CS and consistent outcome logging for attribution.

**Pilot scope (Phase 2):** NA self-serve cohort only; HubSpot task-based execution (no automated sequencing beyond task templates).

---

## Quick start (what to do when you get a PLG Signal task)
1) **Open the HubSpot Company record → “PLG Signals” section** and read:
   - Latest signal type(s) and score
   - The “Why routed” summary (top contributing metrics)
   - Suppression history (to avoid duplicate touches)

2) **Determine motion (choose one):**
   - **Scale motion (Dedicated)**: sustained usage/spend growth, multi-workspace/team expansion
   - **Reliability motion (Dedicated)**: repeated 429s/timeouts/latency regressions, SLO risk
   - **Compliance motion (Private or Dedicated+security add-ons)**: security doc intent, residency, VPC/on-prem interest

3) **Check guardrails before outreach** (see “Outreach guardrails & suppression” below).

4) **Send the Day 0 email + optionally call** if signal is high confidence (see scoring guidance). If compliance-driven, loop SE early.

5) **Log outcomes** in HubSpot within 24 hours (Meeting booked / Nurture / Disqualified / Already engaged / Existing customer managed by CS).

---

## Signal taxonomy (what counts, and what we do)
Signals are grouped into two categories:
- **Threshold signals (behavior at scale):** quantitative usage/spend/error thresholds.
- **Intent signals (stated interest):** pricing, Dedicated/Private docs, security content consumption, residency/VPC/on-prem exploration.

### Canonical signal types and recommended motions
**A) Scale (upgrade to Dedicated)**
Trigger examples (any one can qualify; multiple raise priority):
- Sustained token volume growth over a 7–14 day window.
- Spend velocity increasing week-over-week.
- Multi-workspace creation or rapid org member invites (team expansion).
- High throughput embeddings usage with consistent daily load (predictable reserved capacity fit).

Recommended motion:
- Primary offer: **Dedicated** (predictable throughput + isolation + cost control).
- Secondary: keep Hosted with optimization guidance if customer is early-stage / spiky traffic.

**B) Reliability (stabilize + Dedicated)**
Trigger examples:
- Repeated **429 (rate-limit)** responses over multiple days.
- Elevated p95/p99 latency vs baseline for that model route.
- Increased retries/timeouts that correlate with production errors.

Recommended motion:
- Primary offer: **Dedicated** (capacity guarantees + routing control + higher limits).
- Secondary: short-term mitigations (quota adjustments, batching/caching guidance) with a clear path to Dedicated.

**C) Compliance / Security (Private or Dedicated with enterprise controls)**
Trigger examples:
- Security FAQ / SOC2 / DPA / audit log documentation views.
- VPC / Private deployment docs views.
- EU data residency signals or region-specific concerns.
- Evidence request language in inbound messages or support tickets.

Recommended motion:
- Primary offer: **Private** for VPC/on-prem, strict residency, or regulated workloads.
- Alternative: **Dedicated** when the need is isolation + SLA but not full private control plane.

---

## Scoring + prioritization (how to triage)
Signals are routed with an internal score (0–100) based on volume, duration, and intent strength. Use this to decide whether to call immediately or start with email.

**Priority bands**
- **P0 (Score 80–100):** Contact same business day. If compliance-driven, schedule SE within 72 hours.
- **P1 (Score 60–79):** Day 0 email; call within 48 hours.
- **P2 (Score 40–59):** Email only; monitor; convert to nurture if no reply.
- **Below 40:** No direct outreach unless additional context exists (inbound request, support escalation, known ICP).

**Important:** The score is a guide. If the company is already in a live sales cycle or is owned by CS, follow the ownership/handoff rules.

---

## Outreach guardrails & suppression (do not spam)
Before reaching out, confirm:
- **No recent sales outreach:** If any AE/SDR touch occurred in the last **14 days**, do not re-trigger without a materially new signal.
- **Marketing nurture conflict:** If the customer is in a high-touch lifecycle campaign, coordinate with Marketing Ops (Tyler Benson) or apply the “sales-first” suppression rule for P0/P1 signals.
- **Existing customer expansion:** If there is an assigned CSM (Customer Success), notify CS and coordinate a joint plan (see handoff section). Do not run an SDR cadence that conflicts with QBR/renewal.
- **Customer complaint history:** If the account previously reported unwanted outreach, require AE manager approval before re-contacting.
- **Data minimization:** Do not reference precise internal telemetry (“we saw X tokens/day”) in outbound. Use customer-centric language (“teams often hit scaling limits at this stage”).

---

## Messaging framework (by signal type)
Use the same structure across all motions:
1) Observation (non-creepy) + hypothesis
2) Value proposition
3) Ask for a short working session
4) Clear agenda

### A) Scale messaging (Hosted → Dedicated)
**What we’re trying to learn:** Is their usage stable/predictable enough for Dedicated, and are cost/latency/throughput constraints becoming product constraints?

**Email opener examples**
- “Noticed your team is scaling Redwood usage—wanted to share a few patterns we see when teams move from self-serve to a more predictable capacity setup.”
- “If you’re planning to expand usage beyond a single team/workspace, we can help you lock in throughput and simplify rollout and governance.”

**Value props to emphasize**
- Predictable throughput and latency targets
- Higher limits + reduced throttling risk
- Better unit economics via batching/caching + reserved capacity
- Isolation and control (without running your own inference stack)

**CTA**
- “Open to a 20-minute working session this week? We can map your workload (peak TPS, seq lengths, model mix) to a Dedicated configuration and pricing range.”

### B) Reliability messaging (429s/latency/timeouts)
**What we’re trying to learn:** Are reliability issues impacting production SLAs and customer experience? Is Dedicated the clean fix vs tuning quotas/rate limits?

**Email opener examples**
- “A few teams reach a point where self-serve limits and bursty traffic create reliability headaches (throttling, retries). If that’s happening, we can help stabilize quickly.”
- “If latency and throttling are starting to affect product experience, we can review options to get consistent headroom.”

**Value props to emphasize**
- Capacity headroom and dedicated routing
- SLA-backed uptime/latency options
- Clear escalation path + operational tooling (dashboards, rollouts, fallbacks)

**CTA**
- “Can we do a quick reliability review? We’ll cover current limits, traffic patterns, and what ‘good’ looks like for p95/p99.”

### C) Compliance/security messaging (Dedicated/Private)
**What we’re trying to learn:** What specific control is required (SSO/SAML, audit logs, retention, residency, VPC/on-prem), and what timeline is driving it (procurement, customer demand, regulatory milestone)?

**Email opener examples**
- “If you’re evaluating security/compliance requirements for expanding LLM usage, we can walk through Redwood’s controls (audit logs, retention, key management, deployment options).”
- “Some teams need VPC/private deployment and stronger governance as they move into regulated workflows—happy to compare options and share evidence artifacts.”

**Value props to emphasize**
- Private deployments (VPC/on-prem options)
- Audit logs, retention controls, KMS/HSM integrations
- Data residency / region routing options
- Security review process + evidence package readiness

**CTA**
- “If helpful, we can schedule a 30-minute security overview with an SE and share the relevant SOC2/audit materials under NDA.”

---

## Discovery questions (use in first meeting)
Aim for a tight discovery to validate fit and route to the right SKU.

### Universal (ask every time)
- What user experience are you protecting? (latency, reliability, output quality)
- What’s the business-critical workflow? (support agents, search, content generation, internal tooling)
- What models/routes are you using today? Any planned changes?
- What’s the traffic pattern: steady vs bursty; time-of-day peaks; region distribution?
- What are the top constraints right now: cost, limits, latency, governance, procurement?

### Scale-specific
- How many teams/workspaces will be using this in the next 90 days?
- Are you optimizing for lowest cost per token or for consistent latency under peak load?
- What are success metrics for an upgrade? (throughput, p95 latency, max concurrency, unit cost)

### Reliability-specific
- Where do errors show up (429, timeouts, internal app retries)? How does it impact end users?
- What’s your current retry/backoff strategy?
- Do you need per-route guarantees or global org-level capacity?

### Compliance/security-specific
- Which requirement is driving this? (SOC2, HIPAA, GDPR, internal policy, customer questionnaire)
- Do you need VPC, on-prem, or is dedicated isolation sufficient?
- Data retention needs: default, maximum retention, deletion requests.
- AuthN/AuthZ requirements: SSO/SAML, SCIM, role-based access.
- Evidence timeline: when do you need a security review completed?

---

## Meeting goals + next steps (what “good” looks like)
### First call goals (20–30 minutes)
- Confirm the trigger problem (scale/reliability/compliance) in the customer’s words.
- Identify the correct motion (Dedicated vs Private vs optimize self-serve).
- Secure agreement on a concrete next step:
  - **Dedicated:** benchmark plan + sizing inputs + pricing range
  - **Private:** security review + deployment requirements checklist
  - **Not ready:** nurture plan with explicit re-check timing

### Outputs to capture (in HubSpot)
- Workload summary: model mix, peak concurrency, regions, critical latency target.
- Constraints: compliance checkboxes, procurement timeline, budget signals.
- Stakeholders: Eng owner, security owner, procurement/legal.
- Next meeting date + owner.

---

## Handoff points (when to loop in SE/CS/Security)
### When to involve an SE (Markus Klein’s team)
Loop in Solutions Engineering immediately if any of the following are true:
- Private/VPC/on-prem interest signals or explicit questions.
- Security/compliance discovery is non-trivial (audit logs, KMS/HSM, residency commitments, DPA redlines).
- Reliability issues are production-impacting and require architecture guidance.
- Customer requests benchmarks, performance proof, or a mutual action plan.

**SE handoff package (paste into internal notes):**
- Signal type + short context
- Current usage pattern (qualitative; avoid exact telemetry in shared customer channels)
- Customer objective and deadline
- Known blockers + stakeholders

### When to involve Customer Success (Jasmine Liu)
Notify CS and coordinate outreach when:
- The account is already a paying customer with a CSM assigned.
- The signal indicates multi-team rollout or expansion inside an existing org.
- The customer’s message reads like “support escalation” rather than “sales interest.”

**CS coordination rule:** If there is a CSM, the CSM owns the primary relationship. AE should align on joint messaging and avoid parallel cadences.

### When to involve Security/Compliance
Engage Security/Compliance reviewers (Dr. Aisha Rahman / Marcus Lin / Olga Petrov) when:
- Customer requests specific evidence artifacts beyond the standard package.
- There are atypical data handling requirements (custom retention, data residency, audit log export constraints).
- There is an escalation risk (regulated healthcare/fintech + tight timelines).

---

## Cadence (tasks + timing)
Use HubSpot task templates (do not freestyle high-volume outreach during pilot).

### Standard cadence (P0/P1)
- **Day 0:** Email + (optional) call
- **Day 2:** Follow-up email with a specific agenda and two time options
- **Day 5:** Short call attempt + concise email (“close the loop”)
- **Day 10:** Final check-in + offer to route to self-serve optimization resources

**Exit criteria (stop the cadence):**
- Meeting booked
- Customer replies “not interested” / “stop”
- Disqualified (student project, internal/test, non-ICP)
- Ownership is reassigned to CS or active opportunity exists

### Nurture cadence (P2)
- Single email with a helpful resource (Dedicated overview, scaling guide, security FAQ)
- Set a reminder in 30 days to re-check signals

---

## Objections + recommended responses
**“We’re fine on self-serve.”**
- “Totally—many teams stay on self-serve. The main reason teams switch is when throughput and reliability start to become product constraints. If it’s helpful, we can sanity-check future growth and share what thresholds typically change the economics.”

**“We don’t want sales outreach.”**
- “Understood. We reached out because teams at your stage sometimes want help avoiding scaling issues. I can close the loop and only re-engage if you request it. If you’d like, I can share one resource and step back.” (Then mark suppression / opt-out clearly.)

**“We need enterprise security controls.”**
- “We can help. The fastest path is a short security overview to map which controls you need (SSO, audit logs, retention, residency, VPC). Then we’ll recommend either Dedicated with the right controls or Private deployment.”

**“Pricing?”**
- “We can share a range once we understand workload shape (model mix, peak concurrency, seq lengths). Dedicated is usually driven by capacity and SLO needs. If you share a few parameters, we can come back with a sizing + pricing estimate and options.”

---

## How to log outcomes (required)
In HubSpot, update the latest PLG Signal task with one outcome:
- **Contacted** (email/call completed)
- **Meeting booked** (add meeting link)
- **Evaluation started** (POC defined)
- **Opportunity created** (Dedicated/Private)
- **Nurture** (set follow-up reminder)
- **Disqualified** (include reason)
- **False positive / Suppress** (include the reason and recommended rule)

This logging is required for attribution and for improving suppression/noise rules.

---

## Privacy and “don’t be creepy” guidelines
- Do not cite exact internal metrics (tokens/day, spend) in outbound.
- Avoid “we saw you reading X page at Y time.” You may reference broad categories (“security documentation” / “deployment options”).
- If asked how we knew, say: “We use aggregated, privacy-aware product signals to offer help when teams may be running into scaling or compliance requirements. We can stop these prompts if you prefer.”

For data handling details, see: **PLG Signal Data Handling and Retention**.

---

## FAQ
**Q: Who owns the account if it’s unowned in HubSpot?**
A: Ownership is assigned via region/tier rules with round-robin fallback (see routing ADR). If you believe ownership is wrong, tag Sales Ops (Isabelle Laurent) and do not outreach until resolved.

**Q: What if the signal is clearly a support issue (errors/429s) and customer is angry?**
A: Treat it as support first. Loop in CS/Support and offer an SE reliability review; do not pitch upgrades in the first response.

**Q: What if the customer already opted out of sales outreach?**
A: Respect the opt-out. Mark the signal as suppressed and coordinate with CS for relationship-safe engagement only if requested.

---

Short answers:
- Throttling: We do NOT immediately hard-throttle at commit breach. We use a tiered approach: a soft-burst window (default = 24 hours) that lets traffic exceed commit by up to 2x without hard drops; after the burst window we apply either metered overage billing or gentle traffic shaping depending on the contract.
- Metering: Overage is metered at a per-GPU-hour equivalent for Dedicated pools, calculated from per-minute scheduling usage and normalized to our A100-equivalent GPU-hour. We also provide token-based costing only for hosted workloads (not Dedicated).

Details: how it works operationally
- Metering granularity: native sampling every 60s per node. We aggregate to GPU-minute and convert to GPU-hours for billing (sum of GPU-minutes / 60). This gives predictable month-end numbers while remaining sensitive to short bursts.
- Burst policy: default 2x committed capacity for up to a rolling 24-hour window. The burst bucket refills slowly (policy: % of commit per day) to avoid constant sustained overuse.
- Throttling & shaping: if sustained usage remains > commit after the burst window, the platform applies a tenant-configurable shaping policy (aggressive: immediate traffic shaping to 100% of commit; gentle: shaped down in steps over 6 hours). We recommend gentle for production-critical customers.
- Pricing math: overage price = committed unit price * overage multiplier. Standard multiplier = 2.5x of committed per-GPU-hour. Tiered discounts can reduce the multiplier down to 1.5x depending on committed size and contract length.

Region & multi-zone behavior
- Multi-region replication: overage is metered per Dedicated pool (region). If you have identical commits in two regions, each pool's usage is measured independently. If you use Redwoods automated failover across regions and spike into a secondary, that secondary's pool will apply its own burst bucket/overage rules. - Annual true-up and credit for sustained underuse
