[SRE After-Action Framework and On-call Mentoring Guide]
content:
Overview

This document defines a repeatable After-Action Review (AAR) process tailored to Redwood Inference incident lifecycles, and pairs it with a practical on-call mentoring and succession program. It is intended for SREs, on-call engineers, support leads, and engineering managers who participate in incident response, runbook maintenance, and readiness drills.

Goals
- Produce concise, action-oriented post-incident artifacts that reduce repeat incidents.
- Shorten mean time to recovery by improving knowledge transfer across rotations.
- Grow on-call confidence through structured shadowing, feedback, and remediation coaching.

Scope
- Applies to production incidents (Sev1–Sev3) and to any multi-team incident escalations.
- Includes runbook updates, postmortem/AAR, incident communication templates, and game day design.
- Does NOT replace legal/security-required incident handling for data breaches (see security incident procedures).

1) Incident lifecycle and AAR timeline

Summary timeline (targeted SLAs)
1. Detection & triage (T0–T10m): Pager fired; initial ack within 5 minutes.
2. Stabilization & mitigation (T10m–T2h): Contain blast radius; apply short-term mitigation.
3. Recovery & verification (T2h–T24h): Restore service and validate correctness.
4. Post-incident AAR kickoff (T+24–72h): IC schedules AAR, invites stakeholders.
5. Postmortem published (T+7 days target): Draft circulated; action items created.

Roles & responsibilities
- Incident Commander (IC): Drives triage and timelines.
- Communications Lead: Publishes status page and customer updates.
- Tech Lead / Owner: Implements fixes, verifies root cause.
- Scribe: Captures timeline and decisions in shared doc.
- Mentoring Buddy: Assigned mentor for the on-call engineer handling the incident (see section 3).

Severity classification (summary)
| Severity | Definition | Detection/Impact threshold | Response window |
|---------|----------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------|------------------|
| Sev1 | System-wide outage or data loss affecting >25% customers | Major SLO breaches (>99.9th pct tokens error) | Immediate (timer start T0) |
| Sev2 | Partial outage or major degradation for subset of customers | Latency/throughput degradation causing elevated error rates | Acknowledge within 10m |
| Sev3 | Service degradation with low customer impact or single-customer issues | Isolated errors, non-critical regressions | Acknowledge within 1 hour |

2) Containment & runbook update pattern

Containment checklist (first responders)
- Confirm scope (services, regions, customer impact).
- Switch traffic to fallback model/region if configured.
- Disable automated rollouts (if active).
- Apply rate-limiting mitigation keys or throttles.
- Capture relevant logs and full KV cache markers; preserve for analysis.

Runbook update rules (post-incident)
1. The engineer who executed any manual mitigation must add a section to the runbook within 48 hours explaining steps and rationale.
2. Runbook edits require a short review by the owning team and the SRE mentor.
3. If an ad-hoc mitigation becomes recurring, convert to a permanent operational step and add a rollback path.

Example quick mitigation snippet
```
# Example: drain a problematic node and restart replica
kubectl cordon gpu-pool-node-42
kubectl drain gpu-pool-node-42 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data
kubectl rollout restart statefulset/model-inference-pool
```

3) On-call mentoring and succession program

Objective: Turn incident experience into organized learning and reduce tribal knowledge risk.

Program components
- Shadow Week (first rotation): New on-call engineers shadow a senior mentor for at least three incidents or for five shift-hours.
- Mentoring Buddy: Every on-call has an assigned buddy for the rotation who reviews post-incident notes and provides feedback within 72 hours.
- Rotation Succession Plan: Engineers must nominate a successor two weeks before planned PTO; manager confirms coverage.
- Knowledge Artifacts: Each incident must produce a one-paragraph learning note ("what I learned") added to the team wiki within 7 days.

Mentor checklist (for each incident)
1. Review the timeline and key decisions.
2. Provide 30–60 minute synchronous review if the incident was Sev1/Sev2.
3. Suggest two runbook edits or test cases to reduce recurrence.
4. Sign off on runbook changes as reviewer.

4) AAR / postmortem template (required fields)
- Title: [Service] — [Short summary of impact]
- Incident date/time: Start / End (UTC)
- Severity: Sev1|Sev2|Sev3
- Summary (2–4 sentences): What happened, customer impact, current state.
- Timeline: Ordered events with timestamps and actor names.
- Root cause analysis: Summary and evidence.
- Detection & tooling gaps: Why pager fired and where detection failed (if applicable).
- Mitigations & recovery steps: Short-term actions taken and owners.
- Long-term corrective actions: Action items with owner and due date.
- Learnings & impact on runbooks: What to change in runbooks, dashboards, or alerts.
- Postmortem review notes: Feedback from reviewers and final sign-off.

Action item format (table inserted into the postmortem)
| Action ID | Owner | Description | Due date | Status |
| A-2025-001 | Jane Doe | Add synthetic test for KV cache expiry | 2025-04-15 | open |

Delivery expectations
- Draft circulated to reviewers within 5 business days.
- Finalized and published on the incident tracker within 7 business days.
- All action items tracked in the team’s task board; overdue items escalated during retro.

content_continued:

5) Game days and simulation curriculum

Design principles
- Simulate real traffic shapes and alert triggers rather than toy faults.
- Rotate roles (IC, comms lead, tech lead, scribe) so everyone practices different responsibilities.
- Include a post-exercise AAR with the same template as a production incident.

Quarterly game day template
- Pre-brief (30m): Objectives and environment snapshot.
- Scenario run (90m): Inject failure, allow teams to discover and mitigate.
- Recovery verification (30m): Validate service and customer-facing checks.
- AAR (60m): Capture learning notes, update runbooks.

Sample scenarios
- Model-serving KV cache corruption under burst load.
- Cross-region failover with stale routing rules.
- Canary rollout causing 20% error rate on a critical endpoint.

6) Status page and customer communications (templates)

Initial acknowledgement (use in first 15 minutes)
Subject: [Redwood] Incident detected: [service] — Investigating
Body:
We are investigating an issue affecting [service]. Customers may experience [symptoms]. We will provide an update within 30 minutes or sooner. Impacted regions: [us-west-2, eu-central].

Hourly update (use when active)
Subject: [Redwood] Update: [service] incident — [ETA or progress summary]
Body:
Current status: [mitigations in progress / traffic rerouted / partial recovery]
What we are doing: [short bullets]
Next update: [time or condition]

Resolved message (use when fully recovered)
Subject: [Redwood] Resolved: [service] incident
Body:
Summary of impact: [what happened, who was affected]
Root cause: [short phrase]
Customer guidance: [any user actions required or none]
Link to postmortem: [link]

Status page policy
- The Communications Lead must publish an initial status page entry within 30 minutes of incident escalation.
- Updates should be posted at least hourly until recovery or when materially new info is available.
- Resolved entries must include a link to the AAR within 7 business days.

7) Post-incident closure and metrics

Closure checklist
- Verify all actions in postmortem have owners and due dates.
- Confirm runbook edits merged and reviewed.
- Mark incident as closed in the incident tracker only after corrective tests pass in staging.

Key metrics to track per incident
- MTTR (time to first mitigation, time to full recovery)
- Number of on-call handoffs during the incident
- Number of runbook edits created from the incident
- Recurrence rate (repeat incidents with same RCA within 90 days)

8) Governance & ownership

- Each service must have a designated runbook owner and an SRE mentor assigned quarterly.
- The on-call rotation manager (engineering operations) is responsible for scheduling shadow weeks and confirming successors for PTO.
- The incident review board meets monthly to triage overdue action items and evaluate systemic trends.

Related references
- Incident command playbook and escalation matrix (link)
- On-call simulation cookbook and rotation guidelines (link)
- Security breach handling procedures (link to security-and-compliance)

Appendix: Quick checklist for a new on-call engineer
- Read the team runbook and open the latest 3 AARs for your service.
- Complete one shadow shift with your mentoring buddy.
- Verify ICS access: pager, status page, runbook editor, incident tracker.
- Run the local recovery smoke test (script path: ops/scripts/smoke-recover.sh).

Document history
- 2025-03-18: Created by Aisha Patel (initial draft).
- 2025-05-02: Added mentoring buddy rubric and sample mitigation snippet (reviewer: Connor Lee).
- 2025-11-02: Updated AAR delivery SLA and quarterly game day template (reviewers: Maya Rangan, Diego Alvarez).

[Accelerator chaos and profiling playbook]
Overview

Purpose:
This playbook describes a controlled experiment and incident-response process for exercising and profiling heterogeneous accelerator configurations (mixed GPU types, CPU-only fallbacks, and experimental NPU/TPU-like devices) in Redwood's serving runtime. The goal is to surface scheduling, kernel-selection, KV cache, and memory-pressure behaviors that do not appear under homogeneous, baseline load, and to capture high-fidelity telemetry for triage and optimization.

Scope:
- Applies to internal test and canary clusters only, never to production customer-facing instances unless explicitly scheduled and approved.
- Targets mixed-accelerator nodes, runtime scheduler, kernel mapper, and KV cache layers.
- Includes both active chaos (throttling, device evictions) and passive profiling (high-sample tracing, microbenchmarks).

Owner and contact:
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime (runtime quality team)
- On-call contact for experiments: @miguel-torres (pager)
- Slack channel: #runtime-qa-experiments

Timebox and safety:
- All chaos windows must be scheduled in the team calendar and registered with SRE 72 hours before start.
- Max experiment duration per cluster: 2 hours.
- Abort condition: any production SLO deviation >2% in linked staging-prod shadow traffic metrics or alerting on GPU driver/host watchdog (see Abort conditions section).

Pre-run checklist (must be completed before any active injection):
1) Approvals: experiment approved by eng-serving-runtime lead and SRE duty engineer. Approvals recorded on the experiment ticket.
2) Snapshot configs: capture current scheduler profiles, kernel-mapper table, and deployment manifests. Commands: 
   - git rev-parse HEAD (runtime-config repo)
   - kubectl get configmap runtime-scheduler -n runtime -o yaml > runtime-scheduler.snapshot.yaml
3) Canary targets: select a dedicated canary pool labeled runtime-chaos=true with no customer traffic.
4) Backups: ensure model KV cache checkpoints and stateful store snapshots have been saved.
5) Alert hooks: add temporary dashboards and high-priority alerts (see Telemetry & dashboards).
6) Rollback plan: documented step-by-step (see Rollback section).

Experiment types and procedures:
The playbook defines three canonical scenarios. Each scenario includes the purpose, exact commands, expected observability signals, and failure modes to watch for. Always run in sequence: Profiling -> Degraded scheduling -> Forced eviction.

A) High-sample profiling (no chaos)
Purpose: collect high-fidelity traces and kernel timings under controlled synthetic load.
Steps:
1. Deploy the profiling harness on canary pool: `kubectl apply -f profiles/harness-canary.yaml`
2. Start load generator with shape file: `./perfgen --shape mixed-latency-burst.json --qps 150`
3. Enable tracing at 1000Hz sampling for 5 minutes: set runtime flag `telemetry.sampler_rate=1000` via ConfigMap patch.
4. Capture GPU kernel traces and nvprof logs (or nsys):
   - `nsys profile --output=trace-canary --sample=cpu,cupti --duration=300s --target PID`
5. Collect KV cache hit/miss histogram and sequence length distribution from internal endpoints: `curl http://runtime-metrics/kvcache?range=5m`
Expected signals:
- Kernel latency heatmap should show stable distribution; abnormal long tails indicate kernel contention or inefficient kernel selection.
- KV cache cold-start rates after model reloads should be < 0.5% for steady-state load.

B) Degraded scheduling (soft chaos)
Purpose: validate scheduler priority inversion handling and kernel credit accounting when a subset of devices are throttled.
Steps:
1. Limit GPU SM frequency on 30% of nodes using device driver throttling (requires driver-level privileges). Example command (NVIDIA):
   - `sudo nvidia-smi -i 0 -pl 120`  # reduce power limit to 120W on device index 0
2. Introduce a slow background job pinned to those GPUs (long-running attention microkernel). Use `kubectl run` with nodeSelector runtime-chaos-slow=true.
3. Monitor queue length, kernel credits, and request latencies.
Expected signals:
- Scheduler should demote low-priority jobs and preserve SLO for high-priority tiers.
- Kernel credit reserves should decrease gracefully without causing node-wide starvation.
Failure modes:
- Priority inversion observed as sustained latency increase > 20% for high tiers.
- Kernel queue growth that triggers preemption thrashing.

C) Forced eviction (hard chaos)
Purpose: verify graceful fallback, model variant switching, and session KV cache reconciliation when GPUs are evicted or removed unexpectedly.
Safety note: this is the riskiest scenario; keep duration < 10 minutes per node, and have rollback plan ready.
Steps:
1. Coordinate with SRE to cordon nodes and then trigger device offline event (simulate with `kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data`).
2. On the runtime control plane, reduce available slot counts to simulate sudden capacity loss: patch autoscaler minReplicas down by 40% for test pool.
3. Observe the tiered fallback: do requests automatically route to CPU-only or smaller quantized variants? Check model_variant_switch metric.
4. Validate KV cache consistency: confirm that new sessions warm KV caches appropriately and that previous sessions are either migrated or invalidated according to policy.
Expected signals:
- 95th percentile tail latency for critical routes should degrade no more than 2x for the duration, and error rate < 1%.
- Model switch events should be recorded with reason=eviction and an associated decision trace id.

Telemetry & dashboards (quick setup)
Create temporary dashboards tagged `chaos-run-<ticket-id>` with the following panels:
- Per-route p50/p95/p99 latencies (segmented by priority)
- Kernel latency heatmap (kernel-name x device-type)
- Kernel credit utilization by node
- KV cache hit ratio and per-model warmup curve
- Device driver errors and watchdog resets
- Scheduler decision traces: counts of preemptions, demotions, and fallback decisions

Alerts to enable for experiment window:
- latency.p95.critical_route > baseline * 1.5 for > 1m -> paging
- kernel.queue_length > 500 on any node for > 2m -> ops-crit
- device.watchdog.reset > 0 -> paging

Observability snippets (examples)
- Kernel-level metric query (promql): `histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(kernel_latency_seconds_bucket[1m])) by (le, kernel, device_type))`
- KV cache warmup: `increase(kv_cache_warmups_total[10m]) / increase(kv_cache_requests_total[10m])`

Data retention and artifact collection
- Traces and nsight captures must be uploaded to S3 prefix: s3://redwood-telemetry/experiments/<ticket-id>/traces/
- Prometheus: take a snapshot using `tsdbctl snapshot` and link in the experiment ticket.
- Runtime logs: `kubectl logs -l app=runtime -n runtime --since=30m > runtime.<ticket-id>.log`

Analysis checklist (post-run)
1. Confirm that raw artifacts exist in S3 and are readable.
2. Run automated correlation job: `python tools/chaos_correlation.py --ticket <id> --out report.html` which links kernel tails to scheduler events.
3. Annotate release notes or kernel hints if a material regression is discovered.
4. If mitigation or code changes are required, create an ADR or tactical patch and specify rollout strategy (canary -> progressive -> global).

Rollback and remediation steps
- Immediate rollback: revert autoscaler/minReplica patch, uncordon nodes (`kubectl uncordon <node>`), and restore driver power/ frequencies.
- KV cache reconciliation: run `kubectl exec -it runtime-admin -- /opt/runtime/tools/kvcache-reconcile --model <id>` if mismatches are detected.
- If preemption thrash observed: temporarily increase kernel-credit-per-slot for affected pool via configmap and re-evaluate.

Abort conditions (must abort and remediate immediately):
- Any customer-facing cluster shows p99 latency > 2x baseline for > 2 minutes.
- Persistent driver or host-level watchdog resets on >3 nodes.
- Error rate for critical routes > 2% and trending upwards.

Postmortem and artifact requirements
- Within 24 hours: publish an experiment write-up with summary, artifacts links, hypothesis vs outcome, and recommended actions. Use template: Experiment write-up - <ticket-id>.
- Within 72 hours: if the experiment revealed a regression, propose a mitigation PR with test plan and include benchmark numbers pre/post.

Kernel and scheduler knobs to inspect (quick reference)
- scheduler.priority_decay_seconds: default 30
- kernel.credit_per_slot: default 1000
- kernel.max_concurrent_kernels_per_device: default 32
- telemetry.sampler_rate: production default 10, test default 1000
- kvcache.max_entries_per_model: default 512k
(Note: change via runtime-config repo and apply as a canary)

Run-specific config examples (YAML snippet)
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: runtime-experiment-config
  namespace: runtime
data:
  telemetry.sampler_rate: "1000"
  scheduler.priority_decay_seconds: "10"
  kernel.credit_per_slot: "1500"
```

Known limitations and caveats
- Driver-level throttling is vendor-specific; behavior differs dramatically across GPU families. Documented differences must be updated after each major driver release.
- NPUs/TPUs in lab mode may not expose full tracing; fallback to request-level tracing for those devices.
- Some kernel contention modes are only reproducible with sequence-length distributions that match production—use real request traces where possible.

[Evidence Retention and Emergency Access Playbook]
Overview

This playbook defines the company standard for packaging, retaining, and granting emergency access to security and compliance evidence. It covers: RBAC emergency elevation, audit log preservation, evidence manifests and packaging, data residency considerations for retained artifacts, handoff to legal/forensics, and linkage to the secure SDLC and incident response process.

Intended audience

- Security responders and on-call engineers
- Platform/SRE engineers who operate logging and storage systems
- Legal/Compliance teams preparing for audits
- Engineering managers approving emergency access

Scope and applicability

- Applies to all production and customer-facing systems (hosted, dedicated, private) and their supporting infra (control plane, build artifacts, CI systems).
- Covers artifacts needed for compliance evidence and forensics: auth logs, API request traces, model-serving telemetry, deployment manifests, key rotation events, and chain-of-custody records.
- Does NOT replace standard data-retention policies for customer data; those are covered under data-residency-and-retention policies.

Definitions

- Evidence artifact: any log, binary, manifest, or snapshot retained for audit or forensic purposes.
- Emergency access: time-bounded, audited temporary elevation of permissions to retrieve or preserve evidence when normal processes cannot be used.
- Evidence manifest: canonical JSON file describing included artifacts, retention rationale, and custody history.

Roles and responsibilities

- Incident Commander (IC): declares emergency retention or access requirement.
- Security On-call: executes preservation steps and coordinates packaging.
- Platform/SRE Owner: provides access to logs, snapshots, and storage buckets.
- Legal/Compliance Lead: approves retention beyond baseline and initiates legal holds.
- Approving Manager (Engineering or Security): grants emergency RBAC elevation when required.

SLOs and thresholds

- Time-to-preserve: first snapshot of relevant artifacts within 60 minutes of IC declaration.
- Immutable packaging: evidence must be sealed (hash-signed) within 4 hours.
- Access audit: any emergency access must include an approval ticket in the change system and recorded justification.

Minimum evidence inventory (by scenario)

1) Authentication/Authorization incident
- AuthN logs (last 90 days or window as requested)
- RBAC policy change history (git commit + PR metadata)
- JIT activation events and approval tickets
- Affected principal session traces

2) Data residency or leakage suspicion
- Object storage access logs with signed URLs and presigned token traces
- Network egress logs for VPCs/regions in scope
- If relevant, copy of the object(s) (isolated and hashed) subject to retention policy and legal approval

3) Model-serving integrity event
- Model binary/artifact manifest + checksum
- Serving runtime logs and kernel-level traces for time window
- Deployment pipeline logs (CI/CD run artifacts)

Retention schedule (baseline)

| Artifact Type | Baseline Retention | Storage Class | Custody Owner | Notes |
|---------------|--------------------|---------------|---------------|-------|
| Auth logs (structured) | 2 years | encrypted-archive | infra-logging | Can be shortened by legal order |
| API request traces | 1 year | hot/nearline | infra-telemetry | redact PII before sharing |
| Deployment manifests | 5 years | hot | eng-platform | Include commit + tag |
| CI/CD run artifacts | 1 year | nearline | eng-platform | Keep minimal logs; full artifacts on legal request |
| Forensic snapshots | 7 years (case-by-case) | sealed-archive | security | Requires legal hold to extend |

NOTE: For customer-specific or region-bound artifacts, apply data-residency rules from data-residency-and-retention policy.

Emergency RBAC elevation: procedure

1. IC identifies need and creates an emergency request ticket in the change system with: incident id, short rationale, artifacts required, expected duration.
2. Approving Manager (security or eng manager) must acknowledge and approve within the ticket. Approval must include explicit expiration time (max 12 hours without extension).
3. Platform/SRE grants JIT role via the attribute-broker (or cloud provider IAM) for the requested time window. All activations must be logged with a correlation id.
4. Security On-call executes preservation steps and records actions in ticket.
5. After task completion or timeout, platform revokes temporary roles and documents revocation time and hash of sealed package.

Required approvals and evidence for retrospective review

- Approval ticket URL and approver username
- Justification narrative (minimum 100 characters)
- List of artifacts accessed and hashes generated
- Time window and IP/address used for access

Evidence manifest template (required inside every package)

{
  "manifest_version": "1.0",
  "incident_id": "INC-2025-1234",
  "created_by": "security-oncall@redwood.com",
  "created_at": "2025-11-30T14:12:00Z",
  "artifacts": [
    {"path": "auth-logs/2025-11-30/auth-structured-2025-11-30.ndjson.gz", "sha256": "<hex>", "retention_reason": "investigation"},
    {"path": "snapshots/instance-xyz-disk.img.gz", "sha256": "<hex>", "retention_reason": "forensic"}
  ],
  "chain_of_custody": [
    {"actor": "s.oncall@redwood.com", "action": "created_snapshot", "timestamp": "2025-11-30T14:22:00Z"}
  ]
}

(Replace placeholders with actual values. The manifest must be stored as a top-level file named evidence-manifest.json inside the sealed package.)

Packaging and sealing

- Packaging format: tar.gz or zip with AES-256 encryption. Use corporate key management (KMS/HSM) for envelope keys.
- Sealing: generate a manifest, compute per-file sha256, sign the manifest with the security key (pgp or HSM signature), then store the signature as manifest.sig.
- Store sealed package in sealed-archive storage class. Ensure immutability flags or retention locks are enabled.

Chain of custody and audit log requirements

- Log every action in the evidence lifecycle: create_snapshot, export_logs, package_artifact, sign_manifest, store_package, grant_temp_access, revoke_temp_access.
- Each log entry must include actor, correlation_id, timestamp, and authorization ticket id.

Forensic snapshot checklist (minimal)

- Verify snapshot consistency (fs freeze or filesystem-aware snapshot)
- Verify running process list and loaded kernel modules (if virtualization allows)
- Capture network connection table and open sockets
- Capture in-memory secrets cache indicators (note: handle secrets per secret management guidance)
- Compute sha256 of the snapshot and record in manifest

Data residency and retention notes

- When artifacts include customer data or cross-border metadata, route preservation requests through Legal and Data Residency Owner. Do not copy exported objects to regions not permitted by contractual obligations.
- If evidence must be retained beyond baseline for legal hold, Legal must file a formal legal hold and notify the Records Manager.

Integration with Secure SDLC and CI/CD

- CI systems must tag build artifacts with immutable commit hash and the signing identity. When a deployment is included in evidence, include the build tag, pipeline run id, and storage location.
- PRs that change RBAC policies must include an automated evidence snapshot trigger that records pre-change policy and the diff. This snapshot is retained for 90 days unless converted to formal evidence.

Audit and retrospective process

1. Within 7 days of package sealing, Security performs a technical review to validate manifest accuracy.
2. Within 30 days, Legal/Compliance confirms retention appropriateness and flags any additional hold requirements.
3. Quarterly, the Evidence Council reviews sealed packages with high risk and recommends policy changes.

Tooling and CLI examples

- Snapshot (example):
  - ./tools/snapshotter --instance i-abc123 --out snapshots/i-abc123-20251130.img.gz --freeze

- Compute checksum:
  - sha256sum snapshots/i-abc123-20251130.img.gz > snapshots/i-abc123.sha256

- Seal and encrypt (example):
  - tar -czf package.tar.gz evidence-dir/
  - ./tools/encrypt-with-kms --input package.tar.gz --output package.sealed --kms-key projects/redwood/kms/evidence-key

- Sign manifest (example):
  - ./tools/hsm-sign --key evidence-signing-key --in evidence-manifest.json --out evidence-manifest.json.sig

Escalation and exceptions

- Exception window: if approving manager is unavailable, IC may escalate to the Head of Security for approval. All escalations must be recorded and justified.
- Exception retention beyond the baseline requires Legal approval within 48 hours.

Metrics and monitoring

- Key metrics to track: time-to-preserve, percent sealed within SLA, number of emergency RBAC activations per quarter, percentage of packages with complete manifests.
- Dashboards: Security will maintain a dashboard in the Console that surfaces active evidence packages and their retention expiration.

Related policies and references

- data-residency-and-retention (apply geographic controls)
- rbac-and-auth (JIT activation and role lifecycle)
- incident-response-security (playbooks for triage and evidence collection)
- secure-sdlc (artifact signing requirements)

Change history

- 2025-04-15: Document created by Priya Malhotra.
- 2025-11-30: Added manifest template and packaging steps after IR-2025-11 review.
- 2026-01-21: Aligned retention baselines with Records Manager and updated approval windows.

Appendix: quick checklist for on-call

- Create emergency ticket referencing incident id.
- List artifacts and owners in ticket.
- Request JIT access and obtain approval.
- Snapshot logs and compute checksums.
- Create evidence-manifest.json and sign it.
- Encrypt and store sealed package in sealed-archive.
- Record final hashes, revocation time, and close ticket.

For questions or playbook improvements, contact security@redwood.com or open a PR against the confluence source page.

[Assurance Convergence Protocol: Controls Alignment for Auth, Logging, Residency & SDLC]
Summary
This document defines the Assurance Convergence Protocol (ACP): a single operational rubric that aligns RBAC and authentication controls, audit logging guarantees, data residency and retention schedules, secure SDLC gates, and incident-response evidence workflows. The ACP exists to reduce control gaps, accelerate audit preparation, and make exception and risk decisions traceable and reversible.

Scope
- Applies to hosted, dedicated, and private deployments (Redwood API, Dedicated capacity, and Private/VPC builds).
- Covers: role/permission lifecycle, authn/authz telemetry, audit-log schema & ingestion, retention/residency mapping for customer and telemetry data, SDLC release gates that require security evidence, and incident evidence capture & handoff.
- Excludes product feature design decisions; those are covered in product PRDs but must reference the ACP when they introduce new control requirements.

Guiding principles
1) Single source of truth for control ownership and artifacts. Every control references: owner team, canonical artifact location, retention policy, and review cadence.
2) Minimum viable evidence for audits. Evidence artifacts are pragmatic: attestations, logs, manifests, and linkable references (no bulky ad-hoc exports).
3) Traceable exceptions. Any deviation uses the exception workflow with explicit mitigation and automatic expiration.
4) Recovery-first: incident evidence collection must preserve forensic fidelity while minimizing service impact.

Controls matrix (operational view)
Control | Owner | Canonical artifact(s) | Retention | Review cadence | Escalation on failure
--- | --- | --- | --- | --- | ---
RBAC (role binding + approval history) | identity-team | s3://redwood-secure-artifacts/rbac/attestations/{YYYY-MM}.json, identity-db change log | 7 years for audit roles; 1 year for ephemeral roles | Quarterly automated attestation; manual if unusual changes | Pager to identity-team; escalation to Security on failed attestation
AuthN (SSO + service tokens) | identity-team | oidc-logs (Kafka topic), service-secret-rotation-manifest | 2 years for auth events; secrets rotated per policy | Monthly rotation verification | Immediate rotate + token invalidation SOP
Audit logging (ingestion + schema) | infra-sre / observability | audit-index (clickhouse/olap), immutable-s3: s3://redwood-audit/immutable/{date}.ndjson | 7 years (prod); 1 year (dev/staging) | Continuous ingestion SLA checks; schema contracts validated on deploy | Fallback to immutable-s3 + backlog reingestion; SEV2 if >5% missing
Data residency mapping (customer data tag & location) | legal-compliance / infra-sre | residency-manifest.csv, residency-mapping-api | 7 years or per contractual obligations | Annual and on-new-region deploy | Block new deployment until mapping verified
Secure SDLC gate evidence (pre-release) | eng-platform / sec-ops | pre-release-evidence bundle (tests, SCA, attestation) | 3 years (release artifacts) | Per-release gating | Release hold and security review board (SRB) for failed gates
Incident evidence capture | sec-ops | incident-evidence-manifest.json + forensic bundles in s3://redwood-forensics/{incident-id}/ | 10 years for high-severity incidents; 2 years for medium | After-action review (14 days) | Immediate forensic preservation + legal notification as required

Operational thresholds and SLA examples
- Audit log ingestion SLA: 99.9% of events indexed within 5 minutes of generation.
- Auth event retention for realtime detection: events must be queryable for 90 days with sub-10s query latency.
- RBAC attestation pass rate: 100% of owners respond to quarterly attestations; exceptions automatically auto-expire after 30 days.

How artifacts are named and stored (convention)
- Naming convention: <control>-<artifact-type>-<YYYYMM>-<short-id>.ext
  - Example: rbac-attestation-202603-identitydb.json
- Canonical storage: secure S3 (KMS-encrypted) buckets with object-lock enabled for immutable audit buckets. Buckets: redwood-secure-artifacts, redwood-audit, redwood-forensics.

Evidence manifest example (artifact-level index)
{
  "incident_id": "IR-2026-0427-01",
  "artifacts": [
    {"path": "s3://redwood-forensics/IR-2026-0427-01/conntrack.ndjson", "type": "network-capture", "hash": "sha256:..."},
    {"path": "s3://redwood-forensics/IR-2026-0427-01/rbac-attestation-202603.json", "type": "attestation"}
  ],
  "collected_by": "sec-ops@redwood.com",
  "collected_at": "2026-03-05T14:22:31Z"
}

Automated checks and CI integration
- Code-level gates (SDLC): every merge to main must pass security-oriented checks documented below. The pre-release-evidence bundle is produced by the CI pipeline (build artifact + SCA report + unit/integration test summary) and uploaded to the canonical artifact location.
- Example pre-release policy (yaml snippet):
policy:
  ssa_threshold: 0.0
  sca_blocking: true
  required_artifacts: ["sast-report.json","dependency-sbom.json","qa-eval-summary.json"]

Exception & risk approval workflow (operational steps)
1) Submit exception ticket in Jira component: SECURITY-EXCEPTIONS with fields: control-id, risk-rating (low/med/high), mitigation, expiration date.
2) Auto-attach required artifacts: short risk memo, compensating controls evidence, mitigation acceptance checklist.
3) Security reviews within 5 business days. For high risk: SRB convenes within 48 hours.
4) If approved, exception is timeboxed and a webhook populates enforcement rules (e.g., rate-limiting, increased monitoring) for its duration.
5) Expired exceptions auto-revoke; owners must re-request or system reverts to default control state.

Incident evidence collection: step-by-step (for sec-ops)
1) Triage: identify incident ID and severity. Assign an evidence custodian (person) in PagerDuty incident.
2) Preserve: enable object-lock and snapshot affected systems. If possible, pause log rotation and create immutable copy:
   - CLI: aws s3 cp s3://service-logs/prod/2026-03-05/ s3://redwood-forensics/IR-2026-0427-01/ --recursive --sse aws:kms
3) Collect: gather RBAC change logs, auth events (time window +/- 30 minutes), deployment events, and model-serving runtime traces.
4) Hash & catalog: compute sha256 for each artifact and add to incident-evidence-manifest.json.
5) Share: handoff to Legal/Compliance via the secure evidence portal; include a minimal chain-of-custody statement.

Audit readiness playbook (quarterly)
1) Run artifact discovery job across canonical buckets; produce a gaps report.
2) Resolve high-priority gaps within 7 business days.
3) Perform sample replays: validate that audit logs can be reconstructed and that telemetry maps to control events.
4) Produce an audit readiness attestation signed by owners; store at s3://redwood-secure-artifacts/audit-attestations/{YYYY-MM}.json

Monitoring and alerting (examples)
- Metric: audit_ingest_lag_p50/p95/p99. Alert if p95 > 300s for more than 5 minutes (SEV2).
- Metric: rbac_attestation_response_rate. Alert if < 80% 7 days after attestation launch (SEV3).
- Metric: exception_count_by_risk. Pager duty if any high-risk exception active longer than 14 days.

Operational responsibilities (owners at a glance)
- identity-team: role lifecycle, SSO, service account policy, attestation orchestration.
- infra-sre: audit log pipeline, immutable storage, region mapping.
- sec-ops: incident evidence collection, chain-of-custody, SRB coordination.
- legal-compliance: residency mapping decisions, regulatory evidence requirements.
- eng-platform: CI gate enforcement and pre-release artifact generation.

Appendix A — Evidence templates and quick CLI snippets
- RBAC attestation retrieval (Athena):
  SELECT * FROM rbac_attestations WHERE month = '2026-03';
- Audit bucket immutable copy (example):
  aws s3api put-object-lock-configuration --bucket redwood-audit --object-lock-configuration '{"ObjectLockEnabled": "Enabled","Rule":{"DefaultRetention":{"Days":3650}}}'
- Minimal chain-of-custody text: Collector: <name> | Collected at: <timestamp> | Method: snapshot/s3-copy | Notes: <short description>

Appendix B — Frequently asked questions
Q: When should a product change trigger residency re-review?
A: Any feature that stores or indexes customer-provided data in a new region or service tier requires a residency-mapping change request and legal signoff prior to rollout.

Q: Who signs the pre-release evidence bundle?
A: The engineering release lead plus the eng-platform and sec-ops approvers must sign; legal only signs when the release affects residency or contractual controls.

[Responder rotation synthesis and deferred postmortem protocol]
Overview:

This playbook describes Redwood's responder rotation synthesis process and a lightweight Deferred Postmortem (DPM) protocol for incidents that meet defined criteria. It combines on-call scheduling practices, a structured bridge handoff procedure, and customer-facing messaging templates designed for speed and clarity. The goal is to reduce cognitive load during high-impact events and to ensure timely learning when full postmortems are not immediately practical.

Scope:
- Applies to: SRE, Serving Runtime, Platform, and Incident Response stakeholders.
- Excludes: low-priority alerts that resolve without human intervention (see 'Auto-resolved alerts' below).

Definitions:
- Responder rotation synthesis: periodic review and rebalancing of on-call shifts, handoffs, and escalation ladders to maintain equitable load and coverage.
- Deferred Postmortem (DPM): a time-boxed post-incident review that defers non-critical analysis until stakeholders are available, while still capturing root evidence and action items immediately.

Key principles:
1) Fast stabilization first: prioritize containment and customer impact minimization.
2) Minimal friction handoffs: standardized bridge transfer reduces repeated context overhead.
3) Continuous learning: short DPMs for low-severity incidents; full postmortems for Sev1/Sev2.
4) Equity in rotations: no responder assigned >36 hours continuous duty without relief.

On-call rotation design (synthesis process):
1. Quarterly synthesis review (owner: SRE lead):
   - Pull the last quarter's on-call logs and pager counts.
   - Calculate median and 95th percentile pager counts per responder.
   - Identify top-10% busiest windows and common root causes.
2. Rebalance rules:
   - Move noisy services to a dedicated micro-rotation if they account for >25% of pages.
   - Limit night-weekend primary duty to volunteers in the rotation unless emergency staffing required.
3. Local fairness check (monthly):
   - Team leads run a 15-minute review in the first week of each month to confirm schedule fairness and swap if needed.

Rotation constraints (config):
| Constraint | Value | Rationale |
|---|---:|---|
| Max continuous on-call | 36h | Prevent fatigue and degraded decision-making |
| Minimum handoff overlap | 15m | Time to summarize bridge state and outstanding actions |
| Max weekly duty | 56h | Prevent single-responder overload across teams |
| Handoff notes retention | 90d | Auditability and incident reconstruction |

Bridge handoff procedure (step-by-step):
1) Pre-handoff checklist (outgoing):
   - Summarize incident timeline, current hypotheses, mitigation steps in progress, and customer impact.
   - Confirm runbook page(s) in Bridge tab are current and link to traces/log queries.
2) Live handoff (over bridge):
   - 5–15 minute verbal summary; ensure incoming acknowledges critical mitigations.
   - If unresolved customer-impacting work remains, assign an owner and ETA.
3) Post-handoff (incoming):
   - Record a 1-line status in the incident timeline and attach a minimum evidence set (logs, traces, alert IDs).

Incident lifecycle and DPM decision matrix:
- If incident is Sev1 or multi-tenant Sev2 -> full postmortem required within 72 hours of remediation.
- If incident meets ALL of the following, use DPM: single-tenant, <30 minutes customer-visible impact, known cause, effective mitigation applied at resolution.
- Otherwise triage for full postmortem.

Deferred Postmortem (DPM) protocol (when to use and how):
Purpose: capture essential facts and actions quickly when resource constraints or ongoing high operational tempo would make a full postmortem impractical in 72 hours.
DPM steps (owner: incident lead):
1) Within 8 hours of incident resolution: populate DPM template with
   - 1-line summary, impact window (start/end), services affected, severity, and customer impact.
   - Evidence snapshot (link to logs, runbook used, mitigation commands).
2) Create action items with clear owners and SLAs (default: 14-day action SLA).
3) Flag DPM for follow-up in the next synthesis meeting.
4) If DPM reveals systemic risk or unresolved unknowns, escalate to full postmortem.

DPM template (minimum fields):
- Title (1 line)
- Date/time window
- Affected services and teams (comma-separated)
- Immediate mitigations executed
- Evidence links (logs, traces, alert IDs)
- Action items (owner | due date | description)
- Decision to close DPM or escalate (yes/no)

Escalation and timeline expectations:
- Immediate: severity declaration and customer status update within 30 minutes of detection for Sev1/Sev2.
- Short window: initial triage and bridge stand-up within 60 minutes.
- DPM creation: within 8 hours.
- Full postmortem: published within 72 hours for Sev1/Sev2.

Customer communications templates (for bridge operator use):
- Initial status (first 30m):
  "We have identified an issue affecting [feature/service]. Our team has engaged and is investigating. We will provide an update within 30 minutes."

- Follow-up status (post-triage):
  "Update: The issue is caused by [brief cause]. Mitigations underway include [actions]. Current impact: [scope]. Next update scheduled at [time/ETA]."

- Resolution notice:
  "Resolved: The issue affecting [service] has been mitigated at [time]. Root cause and next steps will be published in a follow-up note or postmortem."

- SLA-credit preliminary message (if applicable):
  "We are assessing impact against our SLA commitments. If you are eligible, we will follow up with credit details once our postmortem is complete."

Game day design and schedule (90-minute template):
- Goal: validate handoff, DPM creation, and customer comms speed.
- Attendees: 1 bridge operator, 2 responders, 1 product EM, 1 customer success observer.
- Timeline:
  00:00 — Inject alert and distribute pager
  00:05 — Bridge up and first customer status sent
  00:20 — Handoff simulation between responders
  00:45 — DPM skeleton completed and action items assigned
  01:05 — Demo of status page update flow and mock SLA notice
  01:20 — 15-minute retro and lessons logged

Runbook snippets (examples):
- Quick KV-cache eviction (serving-runtime):
  "# Commands
  kubectl exec -n runtime svc/cache-operator -- cache evict --pattern=*
  # Verify: tail logs for 200 responses to health endpoint for 5m"

- Throttle mitigation (traffic spike):
  "1) Move non-critical traffic to burst_throttle=true route.
   2) Increase instance headroom by policy 'scale-now' for model-serving service.
   3) Notify customers via status page if >5% error rate persists after 5m."

Ownership and metrics (who owns what):
- On-call synthesis owner: SRE manager (quarterly cadence).
- DPM governance: Incident review council (product + SRE rep)
- Bridge operator: maintains status templates and runbook links.
- Metrics to track: mean time to ack (MTTA), mean time to remediate (MTTR), percentage of incidents resolved with DPM, action-item closure rate within 14 days.

Audit and retention:
- DPMs and postmortems retained for 2 years in the incident archive.
- Handoff notes retained for 90 days.

Related pages and references:
- Link: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-evidence-collection-standard (internal)
- Link: /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/kv-cache-eviction (internal)

Appendix: triage decision quick chart:
- High latency + multi-tenant -> Sev1 -> full postmortem
- Short outage <30m + single-tenant + known fix -> DPM
- Repeated flapping events -> escalate to hypothesis-driven postmortem

record_body:
Account summary (Northlake Customer Support AI)

Firmographics / context
- Mid-market support platform building AI agent add-on for live chat + email. They sell to SaaS + fintech; have a few customers that demand tighter audit + retention controls.
- Stack today: mix of vendor LLM APIs + some self-hosted experimentation. They want to standardize on one inference platform and stop hand-tuning batching.
- Deployment: prefers VPC for production (customer expectations + data isolation). Open to starting hosted API for POC.

Primary use case
- Support-agent chat (streaming) with tool calling.
  - High sensitivity to time-to-first-token (TTFT) and streaming smoothness (chunk cadence).
  - They explicitly said: "If the agent pauses for 2–3 seconds mid-stream, our users think it broke." 
- Secondary: summarization of long tickets, embeddings + reranking for internal KB retrieval.

Requirements (captured across discovery + demo)
- Latency
  - Streaming endpoints are the critical path. They asked for a clear 'FAST' tier that they can set-and-forget.
  - Targets they mentioned (not formally committed yet): TTFT < ~350–500ms p95 (region-dependent), and p99 "no multi-second stalls" during decode.
  - Concern: under bursts, they see tail latency spikes with other providers (queue depth grows; token streaming becomes bursty).
- Traffic shape
  - Concurrency: normal 50–120 concurrent chats; peak events 300–600 concurrent (product launches / incident storms).
  - Prompt lengths: mix of short chat turns + occasional long context (ticket history + KB snippets). They admitted their worst-case prompts are "ugly" (copy/paste logs).
  - Mix: streaming chat dominates daytime; summarization batch jobs off-hours.
- Cost
  - Cost sensitive but not at the expense of perceived responsiveness. They like the idea of cost-efficient tier for async summarization, but want guardrails.
  - Asked whether tier defaults can be applied per-route (streaming chat fast; summarization cost-efficient).
- Model preferences
  - They’re model-agnostic but asked about strong 8B/70B class options for agent chat; they want fallback behavior if a model family is constrained.
  - They care about output stability during rollouts; asked how Redwood detects regressions when changing batching defaults.
- Controls / ergonomics
  - Key request: "Fast as the default for streaming." They do not want to tune max_batch_tokens / wait_ms knobs directly.
  - Wants visibility into the effective profile + why it was chosen (override vs default vs overload mode). Reason codes resonated.
  - Wants an easy override mechanism for enterprise: route-level policy in Console, plus a header/SDK param for experiments.

Security / compliance notes
- Asked for: SSO/SAML for Console, audit logs (who changed policies/tiers), retention controls, and KMS integration for any stored config/telemetry.
- Confirmed that tier selection should not change data handling/logging; they were sensitive to "does fast tier log more?" Answer: no; runtime behavior only.

Buying / stakeholders
- Champion: Head of Product (agent experience) + platform lead (infra). Procurement will care about VPC + SLA.
- They want a concrete rollout story: start hosted, then Dedicated VPC once metrics prove out.

Open questions / follow-ups
- Need their real workload stats: prompt-length distribution (prefill tokens), response length distribution (decode tokens), and streaming on/off split per route.
- Need to align on which SLO tier maps to which endpoints (fast for streaming agent chat; standard for internal tools; cost-efficient for async summarization).
- They asked for guidance on overload behavior per tier (shed load vs increase batching). We should propose a default overload policy for their agent route and show what happens at peak.

Risks
- Mixed workloads on same capacity: they may run streaming chat and summarization concurrently; if they do, we need clear route separation or policy precedence to avoid chat p99 getting dragged.
- Tail latency expectations are aggressive; we should set expectations with published tier definitions and highlight that fast-tier protects tail via tighter wait budgets + admission control.

Next steps (agreed)
1) Northlake sends: 7-day traffic shape snapshot (tokens in/out, prompt buckets, concurrency over time, streaming ratio).
2) Redwood (Ethan Park) provides: POC plan + how to force FAST tier for streaming endpoints (include SDK/header example) and how to monitor TTFT + p99.
3) Redwood to propose Dedicated VPC sizing + override/precedence approach for peak-hour protection.
4) Schedule security checklist review (SSO/SAML, audit log export, retention controls) once POC metrics are positive.

[Transient affinity break during gradual rollout triggers routing fallback loop]
description:
Issue summary:
During a scheduled gradual rollout of redwood/open-qa-v1 for BrightForms, a subset of pinned sessions experienced transient loss of version affinity which caused the routing layer to trigger fallback paths repeatedly. The loop manifested as accelerated canary traffic eviction and intermittent 5xx errors for affected sessions.

Impact:
- ~12% of BrightForms production requests returned 5xx or were redirected to older model variants for short windows (2-5 minutes).
- Customer observed degraded chat UX and increased error alerting.
- No broad platform outage; localized to their dedicated pool in us-east.

Environment:
- Dedicated capacity (dedicated GPU pool), prod-us-east (us-east-1)
- Customer pinned some long-lived sessions to open-qa-v1 via the session pin API

Observed behavior:
- During the rollout weight shift (canary -> primary), session affinity TTLs were reset for a cohort of sessions, causing them to lose their pinned binding. The router immediately attempted fallback to a compatible model variant, but health-check timing and quick subsequent retries created a short loop where affinity was re-evaluated and lost again.

Expected behavior:
- Pinned sessions should retain their version affinity for the configured TTL across gradual weight changes; router fallbacks should be rate-limited to prevent oscillation.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Customer creates pinned sessions pointing to redwood/open-qa-v1 (session-ttl=30m).
2) Start a gradual rollout increasing primary weight to 100% over 10 minutes.
3) Observe session-affinity metrics and router logs for sessions in the pinned cohort.
4) Reproduce by adjusting affinity-ttl downward to 60s in a staging pool to trigger faster cycles.

Notes: repro is non-deterministic in prod; a staging test with controlled TTL reliably reproduces the loop.

logs:
Excerpt from router logs (us-east-1) around 2026-03-10T15:24:03Z:
- [15:23:58Z] session_id=abc123 aff_ttl=1800 pinned_version=open-qa-v1 route=canary weight=20%
- [15:24:01Z] session_id=abc123 aff_ttl=0 affinity-mapper:evicted -> trigger fallback to open-qa-v0
- [15:24:02Z] router:health-check returned healthy for open-qa-v1
- [15:24:03Z] session_id=abc123 reconnect aff_ttl=1800 rebind attempt failed (race)
- Repeat observed for ~250 unique session IDs over a 3 minute window.
Relevant console trace: https://console.redwood.ai/traces/trace-2026-03-10-1524 (internal link)

investigation_notes:
Initial hypothesis: affinity TTL reset came from the session-affinity cache invalidation triggered by a side-effect of canary weight recomputation.
- Checked scheduler: no worker restarts coinciding with event.
- Router code path: identified a race between the 'commit weight' hook and cache refresh that marks sessions as stale when weights cross a threshold.
- Reproduced locally by toggling weight-change debounce to 0s: affinity TTLs were zeroed for sessions that had pending rebinds.
- Related to previous issues: SUP-31147 (session-resume drops version affinity) had similar symptoms but different root cause (proxy timeout).
- Customer reported they had several long-lived pinned sessions; this increases surface area for the race.

Temporary mitigation applied 2026-03-10 16:10Z:
- Rolled back weight-change debounce to last-known-good value for BrightForms pool.
- Increased affinity-ttl for pinned sessions via API for BrightForms (from 30m to 2h).
- Enabled soft-rate-limit on fallback attempts at router edge for the pool.

comments:
2026-03-10 15:40 Priya Singh (Support): Notified customer and requested traffic snippets and sample session IDs. Customer provided session ids and spike timestamps.
2026-03-10 16:05 Diego Alvarez (SRE): Identified race in weight recompute -> cache invalidation path. Applying temporary debounce change for affected pool.
2026-03-10 16:15 Maya Chen (Customer Success): Customer acknowledged workaround; reported immediate reduction in errors after debounce rollback.
2026-03-11 09:00 Rahul Mehta (Eng): Opened PR to add stronger guard and test for session-affinity retention during rollouts: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/2410
2026-03-12 14:22 BrightForms Engineering Lead (customer): Thank you — screenshots show much improved behavior. Please share permanent fix ETA.

resolution_notes:
Short-term fixes applied:
- Restore rollout debounce for affected dedicated pool (2026-03-10 16:10Z).
- Increased pinned session TTL for BrightForms to 2 hours via tenant config.
- Applied router edge soft-rate-limit on fallback (50rpm per session bucket).

Long-term fix (in flight):
- PR #2410 adds an atomic commit to the weight-change path so cache invalidation does not zero affinity TTLs for pinned sessions. Includes unit and integration tests that reproduce the timing window. Target merge and canary deploy: 2026-03-14.

Follow-ups / action items:
- Post-deploy monitor: add a short-lived dashboard for pinned-session affinity retention and fallback rates (owner: Observability team).
- Update rollout playbook to include affinity-ttl checks before changing weights (owner: Product + SRE).
- Notify other customers with long-lived pinned sessions about the planned fix and scheduled maintenance window.

Ticket remains open until PR merges and canary verifies fix in BrightForms pool.

[Affinity lease renewal lag triggers mixed routing and unintended fallback during gradual canary rollout]
description:
Issue summary:
Customer (BrightMap Analytics, dedicated tenant) reported seeing mixed model outputs and a sudden spike in fallback routing to the canary variant during a slow, weighted rollout. Tenant had a model version pinned for a subset of sessions; several of those sessions received responses from the new canary variant for short windows (~10-30s) before affinity restored. Impact: inconsistent inference outputs, user-visible quality regressions for affected sessions, and a brief increase in token costs due to replayed requests.

Impact:
- ~120 sessions observed mixed routing over a 24-minute window (2026-03-13 02:08–02:32 UTC).
- Customer reports downstream quality alerts and a rollback request.
- No full outage; requests completed with increased latencies and occasional 5xx spikes correlated with the event.

Environment:
- Redwood prod (us-east-1) - dedicated capacity pool: dp-09b4
- Edge tier: edge-v3-proxy cluster (ASG edge-us-east-1-3)
- Canary rollout: weighted rollout 5% -> 25% over 2 hours; affected sessions were meant to remain pinned to stable variant via session affinity (lease TTL 60s).
- Customer pinned version: rw-infer-v2-medium@2026-03-10, canary variant: rw-infer-v2-medium@2026-03-13-canary

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) Begin weighted rollout and verify canary weight increasing (5% at 01:50 UTC).
2) Simulate long-running sessions that rely on affinity (session token kept alive).
3) Introduce a synthetic edge-proxy restart/rolling restart (we observed an internal edge-restart job at 02:06 UTC).
4) Within ~2 minutes after the restart, sessions intermittently lost affinity and routed to canary for a single request before re-binding to original pinned variant.

Logs / Observations:
- edge-proxy logs (edge-us-east-1-3) show lease_renewal_rpc latency spikes from ~12ms baseline to 1.2s at 2026-03-13 02:07:34 UTC.
- Router metric `session_affinity_miss` spiked from 0.3/min to 18/min during the window.
- Serving-runtime returned canary variant for requests that carried the original session token; token verification succeeded but affinity lookup returned 404 for a short period.
- No auth/SSO rotation events for the tenant in the timeframe.

Hypothesis:
Primary: Edge-proxy lease renewal requests timed out due to transient RPC backpressure during the rolling restart, causing the affinity store to drop or fail to return binding for a narrow window. Router fallback policy allowed requests without confirmed binding to be routed via the canary path (safe default), resulting in mixed outputs.
Secondary: A TTL/lease-reconciliation race between the canary-controller's cohort rebalancer and the edge's lease-renewal path surfaced because of accelerated canary weight change combined with pod restarts.

Temporary mitigation / Workaround applied:
- Support manually pinned the tenant at the router layer to force stable variant for 30 minutes and initiated a controlled drain of edge-proxy hosts that exhibited high lease latency.
- Canary rollout paused (canary weight set to 0%) and an emergency config was applied to increase affinity lease TTL to 180s for all dedicated tenants.
- Customer notified and asked to hold heavy evaluation traffic for 1 hour.

Next steps / Action items:
1) SRE: Investigate edge-proxy restart job logs and autoscaler activity around 02:05–02:10 UTC (Omar).
2) Runtime: Add additional logging around affinity-store RPC failures to capture call path and error codes (Maya + Helena).
3) Reconciler: Review lease-reconciliation logic for races when pod restarts coincide with weight change events; propose a backoff or hold window (PR referenced).
4) Product: Consider defaulting to rebind-to-stable policy for pinned sessions during rollout windows for dedicated tenants.
5) Follow-up: Run a controlled repro in staging simulating edge rolling restarts + gradual rollout to validate fixes.

Owner: Omar Patel (SRE)
Priority: P1 / Sev1

Attachments / Links:
- Grafana: https://dashboards.redwood.com/d/affinity/lease-renewal?orgId=1&from=2026-03-13T02:00:00Z&to=2026-03-13T02:40:00Z
- Edge logs (scrubbed): s3://redwood-support-logs/SUP-402321/edge-proxy-us-east-1-3-02-07.gz
- Reconciler PR for investigation: https://github.com/redwood-inference/reconciler/pull/1427

[Prewarm swap exposes shadow routing and breaks tenant pin affinity during canary rollout]
description:
Issue summary: During a scheduled canary promote for KiteMaps' dedicated pool we observed an unexpected split in model-version pin affinity across tenant sessions after the 'prewarm swap' step completed. Impact: ~18% of requests for a pinned tenant cohort were routed to fallback model variants resulting in inconsistent outputs and several user-reported mismatches. Environment: prod (us-east), dedicated pool id: dp-34-km, canary cohort weight: 10% -> 50% planned gradual rollout, prewarm_swap flag enabled. Steps to reproduce: 1) Create dedicated pool with tenant pin to redwood-v1.3. 2) Schedule a canary promote with prewarm_swap enabled and default healthprobe (200ms). 3) At promotion step, trigger a synthetic traffic surge (concurrent requests ~3x baseline) while letting prewarm hosts enter service. 4) Observe routing cache snapshots and session tokens. Observed behavior: - After prewarm swap completed, ~18% of sessions lost version affinity and began hitting fallback model variant redwood-v1.2. - Edge logs show X-Tenant-Session header missing on some requests forwarded to the new prewarm hosts. - Routing cache shows duplicate cohort entries for the tenant (one with pin, one without). - Health probes for prewarm hosts returned success but their session-handshake path skipped affinity initialization. Expected behavior: prewarm swap should not cause loss of tenant pin affinity; new hosts should initialize routing state before receiving production traffic. Logs/metrics attached: - edge-router logs (snippet): "WARN: missing-session-token; host prewarm-12 accepted request without session init" - canary-coordinator timeline: prewarm_swap completed at 14:12:06Z, cohort-weight adjustment started at 14:12:09Z - routing-cache dump: tenant_km_23 -> [pin:redwood-v1.3 (count:82), pin:unset (count:18)] Preliminary hypothesis: The prewarm swap flow is introducing a race where the edge sidecar forwards a small portion of traffic to newly promoted prewarm hosts before the routing-cache / cohort-affinity reconciliation completes. A secondary factor: a recent sidecar header sanitizer change (PR referenced above) removes empty cookies/headers and may be stripping the X-Tenant-Session on certain keepalive connections created during prewarm. Combined, this results in newly promoted hosts processing requests without establishing the tenant pin and therefore triggering fallback routing logic. Mitigation/workaround applied: - Immediately rolled back prewarm_swap flag for KiteMaps rollout and paused the canary progression. - Forced a routing-cache reconciliation job for tenant_km_23 which re-established pins for affected session IDs. - Customer advised to retry affected requests; provided temporary rate-limit increase window for retries. Next steps (in progress): - SRE to reproduce race in staging with prewarm_swap + header sanitizer toggled (assigned to Lena). - Engineering to review sidecar header sanitizer PR and add explicit pass-through for X-Tenant-Session during prewarm handoffs. - Add ordering gate in canary-coordinator: only switch traffic to prewarm hosts after routing-affinity confirmation. - Postmortem and follow-up changelog entry scheduled after resolution.

[Residual version-lock remains after shadow-mirroring abort, causing implicit legacy routing]
description:
Issue summary:
Customer BrightRoute AI reported that after an attempted canary + shadow-mirroring rollout (promote -> shadow traffic -> abort), a subset of tenant requests continued to be routed to the legacy pinned version despite the canary being rolled back.

Impact:
- ~8% of requests from BrightRoute's production tenant were served by the legacy variant for ~30 minutes after the abort.
- Observed mixed outputs and intermittent tokenization deltas leading to downstream application errors and a brief billing discrepancy.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool for BrightRoute in us-west-2.
- Orchestrator version: v1.12.7.
- Edge-proxy: v3.4.2.
- Serving runtime: release-2025-11.

Steps to reproduce (customer report + internal repro):
1) Customer requested a canary rollout of redwood-v2-compat-7B with shadow-mirroring enabled for 10% traffic.
2) Prewarm and shadow started successfully; traffic mirrored to community-llama-70b-q4 for profiling.
3) At 10:23 UTC, customer aborted the rollout due to quality regression. Abort sequence initiated via console (rollout abort).
4) Control-plane reported abort complete at 10:24 UTC, but edge-mesh continued to serve legacy variant for ~30 minutes for a cohort of session tokens.
5) Repro by replaying session tokens from request logs shows consistent legacy variant routing for those tokens until a manual cache flush at 10:55 UTC.

Observed behavior / logs:
- Orchestrator logs show a successful abort and snapshot commit: "snapshot_commit: rollback -> epoch 8421".
- Edge-proxy logs show repeated 200 responses but with header X-Model-Version: redwood-v1-locked (legacy) for token cohort.
- Routing-mesh trace for a sampled request: "route-lookup -> route-cache hit -> affinity-token resolved to cohort-A -> model-binding: legacy" despite control-plane snapshot pointing to non-legacy binding.
- KV cache metrics show mismatched TTLs between edge cache and orchestrator snapshot: edge TTL remained at 12h, orchestrator snapshot epoch had a TTL of 30s for ephemeral binds.

Initial hypothesis:
- Shadow-mirror abort triggered a fast commit on the control plane, but the edge routing-mesh retained a stale affinity cache entry for a cohort of session tokens because prewarm shadowing wrote a long-lived binding in the edge cache. The longer TTL prevented expected unpin/unbind flows, causing implicit legacy routing.
- Possible race between cache-invalidation messages and the orchestrator's epoch bump, where the edge accepted the shadow prewarm write (with an undocumented TTL override) and ignored the subsequent rollback invalidate due to backpressure on the invalidation queue.

Immediate mitigation taken:
- Support triggered a targeted cache invalidation for BrightRoute tenant cohort via edge admin API at 10:55 UTC which restored expected routing.
- We notified customer and opened this ticket for root-cause and broader mitigation.

Next steps:
- Engineering to verify invalidation queue metrics and whether backpressure led to dropped invalidation messages.
- Add telemetry to detect cohort-level routing divergence within 5 minutes of rollout abort.
- Short-term: tighten prewarm shadow write TTLs to 1 minute for dedicated-rollouts to avoid long-lived bindings.
- Postmortem to propose control-plane -> edge invalidation acknowledgements for committed rollbacks.

Notes:
- Customer reported a small billing spike due to additional served tokens while legacy variant was active; finance notified for adjustment pending final RCA.
- See linked GH PRs for an in-progress change to edge invalidation handling.

18:18 UTC: SRE (Ethan) confirmed elevated apigw 502s, traced to routing to srw-usw-3 pool nodes showing runtime restarts.
18:25 UTC: Correlation found between ClarionMaps bulk-job bursts and sudden KV-cache hot-locks on a subset of partitions (partition id range 1024-1280).
18:33 UTC: Observed retries from client increased connection churn; autoscaler added 4 nodes but prefetch + model initialization increased load and cold-start memory pressure.
18:45 UTC: Applied temporary rate-limit rule for ClarionMaps tenant at edge (conn/concurrency cap = 40) which reduced immediate 5xx spike; error floor persisted at ~1% for 30m after due to cache thrash and pipeline recovery.
19:30 UTC: Eng runtime team confirmed a bug in KV-cache lock path under heavy concurrent prefix invalidation that can cause lock inversion and long hold times (internal issue created: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/issues/9876).
20:10 UTC: Deployed emergency mitigation (kv-cache backoff tuning and lock timeout enforcement) to a canary subset of runtime pool; saw p95 lock wait drop from 420ms to 12ms on canary nodes and 5xx rate drop to ~0.6% for that slice.
21:00 UTC: Gradual rollout of mitigation across us-west serving pool completed; customer notified and asked to retry imports. Monitoring shows stabilization but a small residual error-floor remains while background prefetch eviction completes.

hypothesis:
Primary: Large concurrent embedding bulk uploads triggered concentrated hot-key access patterns in KV-cache partitions, causing lock contention that blocked request handling goroutines and cascaded into runtime panics under memory pressure.
Secondary: Client retry amplification and autoscaler cold-starts amplified resource pressure, leading to intermittent GPU preemption and runtime process restarts, producing upstream 502/503 responses at the gateway.

temporary_workaround:
Applied tenant-level connection/concurrency cap (conn cap 40) at edge for ClarionMaps and increased kv-cache lock timeouts plus backoff on lock acquisition. Recommended customers stagger large bulk-upload jobs and use smaller batches (<=1k items) until fix is rolled out.

resolution:
Mitigation rolled to canary then full us-west pool: updated kv-cache lock backoff and introduced lock acquisition timeout with graceful fallback to a soft-cache-miss path. Runtime crash target fixed by guard against nil pointer during cache fetch (runtime PR merged: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4221). Monitoring shows 5xx back to baseline by 2026-03-11 02:15 UTC for us-west.

postmortem_followup:
Create a throttling guidance doc for large embedding bulk imports and add to public docs and quickstart (owner: Devex, due 2026-03-20)
Implement tenant-level adaptive batching to detect hot-key patterns and automatically shard KV-cache keys to reduce single-partition contention (owner: Serving Runtime team, epi: INT-4021)
Add pre-deploy chaos test that simulates large concurrent embedding uploads to catch regressions in lock paths (owner: QA, due 2026-04-05)
Add an alert rule for kv.lock.wait_ms_p95 > 200ms in any region (owner: Observability)
Customer CS follow-up: ClarionMaps to receive incident summary and recommended import best practices; offer 2 weeks of Dedicated throughput credit for remediation impact (owner: CS)

[Ingress sidecar backpressure amplification causing sustained server-error spike and runtime restarts]
description:
Issue summary: Beginning ~2026-03-12 09:30 UTC Acme Retail observed a sustained spike in 500-class responses on their streaming and short-poll routes. Traffic showed elevated error-rate (~18% 5xx) and increased end-to-end latency. Support engagement requested immediate mitigation and root-cause investigation.

Impact: Multi-tenant dedicated cluster serving Acme Retail experienced degraded availability for conversational and embedding endpoints resulting in customer-reported client errors and retry amplification. Critical flows for order chatbots and embedding lookups affected.

Environment: prod-us-east, Dedicated pool (tenant: acme-retail-01), API gateway fronted by ingress-sidecar proxies deployed as a daemonset on edge nodes.

Observed at: 2026-03-12 09:28 UTC first alert from customer dashboard (high 5xx and latency).


steps_to_reproduce:
1) Customer issues a mix of short chat requests and streaming sessions to the tenant endpoint under sustained high healthcheck/backchannel load
2) In parallel the ingress-sidecar receives a spike of internal healthcheck/backchannel polling (from an internal monitoring job),
3) Connections saturate accept queue and HTTP/2 stream slots; gateway begins returning 502/503/504 while runtimes trigger watchdog restarts
4) Client retries amplify load, maintaining high error rate until throttles are applied

investigation_notes:
Initial hypothesis: kvcache thrashing or GPU OOMs. Verified: no OOMs on host; NVML logs clean.
Detailed traces show majority of 5xx were proxy-layer (502/503) with upstream runtime restarts following proxy accept-queue saturation.
Ingress-sidecar metrics: connection_accept_rate jumped x6, keepalive churn increased, pending-accepts queue grew to 95th percentile of configured max leading to early connection drops.
TLS renegotiation attempts from healthcheck client detected — increased CPU load on proxy and caused HTTP/2 window stalls.
Runtime threadpool starvation correlated with heavy TLS processing on sidecar leading to delayed runtime wakeups and watchdog restarts.
Customer traffic pattern: long-poll streaming + frequent healthcheck/backchannel from internal monitoring job that uses short-lived connections. These combined to create head-of-line blocking on edge accept queues.

2026-03-12T09:31:05Z ingress-sidecar[proxy]: accept_queue length=512->overflow; dropped_streams=37
2026-03-12T09:32:10Z serving-runtime[worker-7]: watchdog: cpu_spike_detected, threadpool starved, restarting runtime (pid=8421)
2026-03-12T09:33:45Z autoscaler: ephemeral-pool-shed trigger for tenant acme-retail-01 due to backpressure_missmatch

comments:
2026-03-12 09:40 - Asha Mehta (Support): Acknowledge ticket and opened investigation. Asked customer to provide client-side timestamps and a pcap of failing sessions.
2026-03-12 09:55 - Diego Morales (SRE): Observed accept-queue saturation on three edge nodes. Spinning up temporary extra proxies to relieve load. Linking logs: https://dashboards.internal/redwood/edge/accept-queue?range=1h
2026-03-12 10:05 - Acme Support Contact (Jordan Lee): Provided client traces and confirmed healthcheck job ran at 09:29 with aggressive parallelism (50 threads).
2026-03-12 10:20 - Diego Morales (SRE): Applied emergency mitigation: rate-limit healthcheck path via ingress-sidecar config and increased accept_queue size on edge nodes. Observed 5xx drop from 18% -> 3% within 6 minutes.
