resolution:
Mitigation: Applied ingress-sidecar healthcheck rate-limit (temporary ACL) and increased accept_queue on affected edge nodes; rolled back a recent aggressive keepalive-prune config. Result: error-rate reduced to baseline and runtimes stablized.
Long-term: Engineering will implement a sidecar-level backpressure window, add prioritized control plane healthchecks, and harden watchdog thresholds to avoid cascading restarts. Scheduled follow-up: INT-3782 (sidecar backpressure redesign).

[Gradual 5xx drift from prefetch queue growth causing intermittent circuit-trips in prod us-east]
description:
Issue summary: BrightWrite reported a steady rise in 5xx responses and degraded throughput beginning ~2026-03-10 02:00 UTC in us-east. Errors escalate slowly over several hours (5xx rate rising from ~0.2% to ~6%) and occasionally trigger api-gateway circuit-breaker marks against upstream serving clusters, resulting in short windows of routing to fallback variants. Impact: customer reports increased failed requests for embeddings and streaming generation, elevated tail latency, and intermittent session resets during business hours. Environment: prod (us-east), dedicated tenant BrightWrite. Observed timeline: 2026-03-10 01:45 UTC — first uptick in prefetch queue length on tenant shards. 2026-03-10 02:10 UTC — p95 prefetch latency increases from ~40ms to ~280ms; api-gateway 5xx begins to climb. 2026-03-10 04:20 UTC — gateway marks 2/6 upstream endpoints UNHEALTHY and triggers short circuit; traffic directed to fallbacks for ~30-90s. 2026-03-10 06:00 UTC — partial mitigation when prefetch-service recycle restored per-shard throughput. Steps to reproduce: 1) Run sustained small-batch embedding and short-chat generation mix targeting BrightWrite tenant with connection churn to emulate multiple clients. 2) Observe prefetch queue length and prefetch-service latency. 3) Track api-gateway health checks and circuit-breaker events. Logs/metrics: prefetch-service traces (grafana/dashboard/prefetch/tenant/BrightWrite), api-gateway health events (grafana/dashboard/apigw/health), runtime logs pointing to repeated kvcache shard lock attempts (logs.storage/kvcache/shard-47), support ticket timeline thread (#support-brightwrite on Slack).

investigation_notes:
Hypothesis 1: Prefetch-service queue growth per tenant causes blocking on kvcache shard locks, increasing request latency and causing api-gateway health checks to fail intermittently.
Hypothesis 2: Long-tail prefetch latency cascades into serving-runtime thread starvation under mixed workloads (embeddings + streaming) for dedicated tenants with pinned model instances.
Findings: p95 prefetch latency correlated strongly with increase in 5xx rate. kvcache logs show repeated lock retry backoffs on shard-47 and shard-53 belonging to BrightWrite. No NVML resets observed. Runtime GC pauses were normal range but thread pool utilization was at 92% during peak.
Experiment: Increased prefetch worker count for tenant and applied jitter to prefetch retry loop; this reduced immediate queue length but uncovered kvcache contention at the storage layer.
Related: prefetched keys show hot-key skew for a small set of prompt templates used by BrightWrite; suggests application-level access pattern causing kvcache hotspotting.
Linked prior incidents: SUP-214567 (backpressure propagation) contains similar kvcache contention notes but at cross-tenant scale.
Next investigative actions: capture flamegraphs from prefetch-service threads during the next peak window, enable per-shard lock telemetry for kvcache, and run a controlled load test that reproduces hot-key access patterns.

comments:
Support (2026-03-10 03:05) - Aisha Patel: Initial customer report received. Asked for request IDs and approximate time window. Customer provided sample request IDs and a short kinesis of errors.
Customer (BrightWrite) (2026-03-10 03:20) - Sara Liu: Confirmed failures across multiple users; attaching example request IDs: req_20260310_az1, req_20260310_bx9.
SRE (2026-03-10 04:00) - Miguel Torres: Noted correlated growth in prefetch queue size for BrightWrite shards; opened investigation into prefetch-service threadpool saturation.
SRE (2026-03-10 05:10) - Miguel Torres: Observed kvcache shard lock contention logs and a pattern of slow prefetch downstream acknowledgements. Temporarily increased prefetch concurrency for tenant to see effect.
Support (2026-03-10 06:30) - Aisha Patel: Communicated temporary mitigation to customer (restarted prefetch workers for tenant). Customer reports partial recovery; still seeing elevated p95.
Eng (2026-03-11 09:00) - Priya Desai: Deployed a canary that adds backoff jitter and reduces aggressive prefetch cancelation; monitoring for regressions.
Customer (2026-03-11 11:12) - Sara Liu: Noted much improved stability overnight; requests still show occasional 502s at peak times.

resolution:
Workaround (2026-03-10): Recycled prefetch workers for BrightWrite tenant and temporarily increased prefetch concurrency to reduce queue buildup. This brought 5xx rate back toward baseline but did not eliminate spikes at peak.
Mitigation (2026-03-11): Deployed a canary patch to prefetch-service that adds randomized jitter to retry backoffs, caps per-tenant prefetch inflight, and adds backpressure metrics to Prometheus. Also scheduled a maintenance window to redistribute hot kvcache keys across shards.
Permanent next steps: 1) Implement adaptive per-tenant prefetch throttling driven by kvcache lock contention signals. 2) Add hotspot detection and automatic shard rebalancing for kvcache. 3) Update runbook to include explicit checks for prefetch queue growth as a leading indicator. 4) Follow up with BrightWrite on client-side prompt fanout patterns and recommend minor batching to reduce hot-key frequency.
Postmortem/Follow-up: Assign an action owner in SRE to track kvcache rebalancer RFC and schedule a cross-team review with Storage and Serving by 2026-03-25.

[Autoscaler backoff due to false GPU thermal flags causing batched throughput loss]
description:
Issue summary:\nByteStream Analytics (dedicated tenant) reported a sudden drop in sustained batched throughput on their reserved pool during midday traffic on 2026-03-10. P50/P95 token throughput dropped ~30% and p99 saw large variance, with a sharp increase in queued/batched requests and autoscaler entering repeated backoff cycles.\n\nImpact:\n- Customer-facing inference latency and throughput degradation for production routes pinned to dedicated pool.\n- Visible dropped throughput for long-lived batched streams (LLM chat workloads) and increased request queuing.\n- No token-level errors returned to customer (most requests eventually succeed but with higher latency and throttling).\n\nEnvironment:\n- Prod (us-east) dedicated pool; customer reserved capacity; models: redwood/llama-13b-quant and open/opt-6.7b; traffic pattern: sustained batched chat with periodic long-lived checkpointing sidecar jobs.\n\nTimeline: (local times UTC)\n- 2026-03-10 14:03: Customer reports throughput drop via support portal.\n- 2026-03-10 14:07 Support triage: observed autoscaler backoff events and repeated GPU unhealth annotations.\n- 2026-03-10 14:12 On-call SRE pulled telemetry and saw rapid series of GPU thermal alerts for a subset of hosts, coincident with increased sidecar IO.\n- 2026-03-10 14:30 Autoscaler reduced attach rate/backed off; queued requests spiked.\n\nSteps to reproduce (investigation):\n1) Replay customer traffic pattern (sustained batched chat + a utility sidecar that writes periodic large checkpoint files every 90s) against a reserved pool replica in staging.\n2) Run synthetic load with intermittent high sidecar disk/IO on several nodes.\n3) Observe metrics: gpu_temperature_alerts, gpu_attach_failures, autoscaler_backoff_count, batch_queue_length.\n\nLogs / metrics observed:\n- Increase in metric cluster.gpu.temperature_alerts on 3 hosts between 14:05-14:20.\n- Autoscaler log: \"backoff: host_marked_unhealthy: gpu_thermal_alert\" repeated with 5-10s cadence.\n- node-exporter logs show thermal-sensor reads timestamped but with repeated identical values and occasional read-timeouts from the thermal sensor process.\n- Sidecar process (checkpoint writer) logs show concurrent NVME write bursts correlating with the timestamps of the thermal alerts.\n- No driver OOPS or kernel panic present; no GPU ECC errors.\n\nInvestigation notes / hypothesis: \n- Initial hypothesis: real thermal excursions from NVMe-sidecar IO causing GPU thermal rise.\n- Secondary hypothesis (stronger): sensor read subsystem on affected hosts is intermittently returning stale/malformed values (stuck high) when IO scheduler is saturated, causing our health checks to interpret those as thermal faults. The autoscaler treats repeated thermal alerts as an unhealthy GPU and applies backoff/attach reduction.\n- Evidence supporting secondary hypothesis: 1) GPU core/PCIe telemetry does NOT show matching continuous high power or frequency throttling; 2) temperatures spike in metrics but hardware counters (fan speed, GPU utilization) remain normal; 3) sensor read errors/timeouts in node logs align with NVMe write bursts from the sidecar.\n\nImpact analysis: \n- Autoscaler behavior: when a host emits >N thermal alerts in T seconds, controller reduces attach concurrency and triggers conservative backoff for the tenant; this protected other tenants but caused reserved capacity under-utilization for ByteStream.\n- The behavior amplified due to many sidecars performing scheduled checkpoint writes at similar intervals (coordinated by customer cron), creating a correlated IO burst (noisy-tenant pattern).\n\nImmediate mitigation performed: \n- At 14:40, SRE applied a temporary autoscaler rule override for ByteStream's pool to ignore gpu_thermal_alert for 10 minutes (mitigates customer impact while we investigate).\n- We instructed customer to stagger their checkpoint writes as a short-term workaround.\n\nProposed remediation / next steps: \n1) Short-term (<=24h): keep autoscaler override in place; advise customer to stagger heavy sidecar IO. Schedule a coordinated rollout to re-enable after fixes.\n2) Medium-term (<=1 week): add debouncing logic to thermal-alert pipeline to require corroborating hardware telemetry (fan speed or power) before marking GPU unhealthy.\n3) Long-term: harden node sensor read path to avoid spurious high-values due to IO-timing edge cases; consider moving sensor reads to a lower-priority thread to avoid being affected by NVMe saturation.\n\nNotes:\n- Related: this appears distinct from standard noisy-tenant GPU hogging; the root cause is interplay between sidecar IO bursts and sensor-read timing producing false positives.\n- Affected hosts: list provided to infra in private logs (not included here).\n

comments:
Support (Aisha): Acknowledged customer report and collected initial metrics; created ticket and escalated to on-call SRE.
SRE (Marco): Pulled node/exporter logs and autoscaler traces; observed repeated thermal-alert events without corroborating hardware throttling — leaning toward sensor-read failures tied to IO bursts.
Customer (ByteStream Ops): Confirmed they run a checkpoint sidecar that writes multi-GB checkpoints every 90s; agreed to temporarily stagger schedule.
SRE (Marco): Applied temporary autoscaler override to ignore thermal-alerts for this tenant's pool for 10 minutes to relieve immediate customer impact (change logged in deployment history).

resolution:
Triage complete; temporary override applied to restore throughput. Medium- and long-term fixes proposed: introduce debouncing/corroboration for thermal alerts and harden sensor read path. Engineering ticket to follow for code changes (tracking PR added).

[Sustained 5xx elevation from asymmetric upstream restart and HTTP/2 stream-slot starvation during mixed embed/chat burst]
description:
Issue summary: Customers started seeing a sustained elevation in 5xx responses for streaming and short-chat requests beginning 2026-03-12 10:50 UTC. Errors primarily reported as 502/503 from the API gateway with 'upstream reset' and 'stream slot unavailable' symptoms.

Impact: NovaDocs (dedicated tenant) observed 30-45% error rate on streaming chat routes for ~2 hours, causing real user failures and increased retry traffic. Other tenants on the same pool experienced degraded tail latency.

Environment: prod/us-east, Dedicated GPU pool (reserved), hybrid streaming+embedding workload (mix ratio ~60/40).

Steps to reproduce:
1) Start a burst of concurrent streaming chat sessions (50-80 concurrent streams) mixed with medium-size embedding uploads (batch size ~128).
2) Observe API gateway returning intermittent 502/503 and aborts within 30s.
3) Checking runtime shows frequent short-lived restarts on a subset of replicas and many HTTP/2 streams stuck in HALF-CLOSED_LOCAL state.

Observed logs/snippets:
- apigw: "upstream reset before response completed" / "502 upstream connection reset"
- runtime: "runtime: panic at kv_prefetch.go:482" followed by fast restart and subsequent "http2: stream slot unavailable" warnings
- autoscaler: flurry of scale-up/scale-down events within 10m window (oscillation)

Customer notes: NovaDocs reported that failures aligned with a product campaign spike and asked for priority remediation and mitigation while we investigate.

Urgency: Customer-facing impact for a paying dedicated tenant during business hours. Escalated to SRE oncall.

comments:
2026-03-12 11:05 - NovaDocs (CS contact): 'We're seeing 50% of chat requests fail with 502s since ~10:50 UTC. Can you route us to another pool? This is blocking our customers.'
2026-03-12 11:12 - Support (Aisha Khan): Acknowledged. We're investigating and will provide mitigation steps within 15 minutes. Asked for tenant id and example request IDs.
2026-03-12 11:28 - SRE (Jonah Park): Early telemetry shows a localized restart pattern on 3/12 runtime replicas and HTTP/2 stream slot exhaustion. Temporarily routed NovaDocs to a warmed fallback pool and disabled hedged retries for their tenant. Error rate dropped to ~8% after routing change.
2026-03-12 12:10 - Support (Aisha Khan): Customer confirmed partial recovery after routing. They still see intermittent 503s on long-lived streams.
2026-03-12 13:40 - SRE (Jonah Park): Collected core dumps and runtime logs from affected replicas. Uploaded artifacts to internal S3: s3://redwood-incident/SUP-277338/ and created trace links. Hypothesis added to investigation notes.
2026-03-13 09:15 - Engineering (Priya Desai): Reproduced stream-slot leak locally with a mixed workload harness. Found a race in prefetch cancellation that prevented HTTP/2 stream closure on restart. Draft patch PR opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/2314
2026-03-14 08:30 - SRE (Jonah Park): Patch approved for canary rollout. Plan: deploy patch to 10% of pool, monitor stream slot metrics and 5xx rate for 30m before wider rollout.

investigation_notes:
Timeline of actions and findings:
- 10:50 UTC: Error elevation begins correlated with NovaDocs campaign spike.
- 11:00 UTC: API gateway shows high upstream reset rates and increased connection re-establishments.
- 11:12 UTC: SRE observed three runtime replicas restarting repeatedly; their restart cadence aligned with prefetch worker failures in logs.
- 11:30 UTC: Evidence of HTTP/2 stream slot saturation: large number of HALF-CLOSED_LOCAL streams around affected replicas, preventing new stream allocation.
- 11:40 UTC: Autoscaler reacted to perceived capacity shortage then backfilled; rapid scale events amplified the issue via transient cold starts.
Hypotheses considered:
H1: Runtime prefetch cancellation race causes panic and restart, leaving half-closed streams -> downstream apigw 502s (most likely).
H2: Autoscaler cooldown misconfiguration causing oscillation that amplifies transient restarts (contributor).
H3: Client retry amplification (hedged retries) increased concurrent open streams (contributor).
Evidence: core dumps show prefetch goroutine stack consistent with known race. Canary reproduction confirms leak under mixed streaming+embed load.
Temporary mitigations applied:
- Rerouted NovaDocs to warmed fallback pool which significantly reduced 5xx rate.
- Disabled hedged retries at the tenant-level for NovaDocs.
- Increased HTTP/2 max-concurrent-streams soft limit on the gateway for the pool to reduce immediate rejections.
Next steps: roll out runtime patch to fix prefetch cancellation, adjust autoscaler cooldowns to prevent oscillation, update hedged retry defaults and add tenant-level backoffs.
Monitoring: dashboards updated (grafana link: https://grafana.redwood/s/incident/SUP-277338), alert thresholds lowered for stream-slot utilization.

resolution:
Workaround implemented: NovaDocs routed to fallback pool and hedged retries disabled for the tenant; HTTP/2 soft limit temporarily increased.
Permanent fix: merged runtime patch to properly cancel prefetch and ensure stream closure (PR merged 2026-03-13). Canary rollout completed 2026-03-14 09:10 UTC with success (5xx down to baseline).
Follow-up actions assigned:
- Adjust autoscaler cooldown and add jitter to reduce oscillation (owner: infra-autoscale team).
- Add automated acceptance test in the mixed-workload harness to detect stream-slot leaks (owner: runtime QA).
- Update runbook with steps for tenant routing during asymmetric restarts and document hedged retry opt-outs for large embedding/chat mixes.
Customer communication: NovaDocs informed of mitigation and planned fixes. They requested postmortem and we agreed to provide within 3 business days.

[Intermittent timeouts and doubled latency for repeated prompts: stale prefix / KV cache misses during streamed retry path]
description:
Issue summary: Customer (AtlasWrite, Dedicated) reports intermittent per-request latency spikes (1.8-2.5x baseline) and occasional streaming timeouts when users resubmit identical prompts or when client SDK retries a broken stream. Impact: Several customer-facing flows (autosummarize & chat history replay) experience user-facing slowdowns and ~5-10% request failures during peak traffic windows. Environment: prod/us-east, dedicated pool id d-pool-12. Observed primarily on gptx-13b-quantized and gptx-8b-finetune. Steps to reproduce: 1) Send a multi-turn conversation with a repeated prompt token prefix. 2) Force a transient stream disconnect on the client to trigger retry logic (SDK exponential backoff). 3) Observe server-side logs and latency metrics for repeated prompt ID. Expected behavior: Repeat prompt should hit warmed prefix/KV cache and return near-baseline latency with streaming retry preserving KV cache. Actual behavior: First retry shows KV cache miss, full KV lookup or cold fetch (~150-300ms extra) and in some cases the retry path times out after streaming proxy backpressure, producing a 504 to the caller. Recent change: Queryable prefix indexing refactor (serving-runtime v2.8.0) rolled 2026-03-08 suspected to coincide with regression window. Attachments: customer traces, sample request headers, and timing graphs uploaded to ticket attachments.

Logs / snippets: Error patterns observed in logs (prod us-east): "kv-cache: prefix-miss for key=prefix_0x4f2a" followed by "kv-fetch: cross-pool fetch latency=210ms" and then "streaming-proxy: retry-forward - client-side disconnect, initiating retry path". Several entries show the serving node evicting prefix entries after background compaction even when traffic indicates hot prefixes.

investigation_notes:
2026-03-10 10:20 - Support: Confirmed customer reproducible with SDK simulated disconnect. Collected p95/p99 latency traces and raw streaming logs.
2026-03-10 12:05 - SRE: Correlated latency spikes to increased KV miss rate for prefix keys during retry windows. KV eviction rate spiked after compaction window in pool d-pool-12.
2026-03-10 14:30 - Eng (serving-runtime): Found that refactor introduced a race where prefix entries marked as 'candidate-for-evict' were eligible for eviction earlier, but retry path assumes presence of warmed prefix and skips prefetch.
2026-03-11 09:10 - Hypothesis: Streaming retry path does not trigger prefix pre-warm when it attaches to existing request context; combined with aggressive eviction this yields cold lookup latency and occasional streaming backpressure leading to timeouts.
2026-03-11 13:45 - Repro test: In staging, toggling eviction threshold + enabling pre-warm on retry reduced p95 from 420ms to 180ms for repeated prompts.
2026-03-12 08:00 - Risk: If rollout continues, more dedicated pools with high retry rates may see increased user errors; customer impact likely for high-frequency repeat prompts (chatbots, summarizers).

comments:
2026-03-10 10:45 - Ava Chen (Support): Notified AtlasWrite success team and requested sample trace ids. They provided traces: trace-az-8912 and trace-az-8919.
2026-03-10 12:25 - Diego Martinez (SRE): Spun up targeted flamegraphs for d-pool-12 and confirmed elevated kv-fetch latencies aligning with customer traces.
2026-03-11 11:00 - Priya Nair (Serving Eng): Identified race in prefix eviction logic introduced in v2.8.0. Created a branch to add an explicit pre-warm on the retry hot-path and to reduce eviction aggressiveness for 'recently-accessed' prefixes.
2026-03-11 16:35 - Customer (AtlasWrite, support@atlaswrite.example): Provided user impact report. They requested immediate mitigation or a config knob to reduce timeouts on their dedicated pool.
2026-03-12 09:20 - Diego Martinez (SRE): Deployed a temporary config to d-pool-12 to extend prefix TTL and enabled retry pre-warm. Monitoring shows p95 latency back to baseline and streaming errors falling to ~0.8% from 6%.
2026-03-12 12:00 - Ava Chen (Support): Informed customer of temporary mitigation and ETA for full patch (see resolution). Customer accepted mitigation and requested postmortem once resolved.

root_cause:
A race introduced in the prefix/KV cache refactor caused aggressive eviction of recently used prefix entries while the streaming retry code assumed warmed prefixes. Retry path did not trigger prefix pre-warm, resulting in cold KV fetches; the extra latency combined with streaming proxy backpressure caused retries to hit timeouts.

workaround:
Temporary config change applied to d-pool-12: increase prefix TTL and enable explicit pre-warm on streaming retry path. This reduces cold fetches and drops streaming timeouts for the customer.

resolution:
Patch accepted: serving-runtime PR #3124 adds explicit prefix pre-warm on retry path and tightens eviction gating for recently-used prefixes. Patch scheduled for canary in prod on 2026-03-13 and full rollout on 2026-03-14 after monitoring window. Post-deploy: confirm with AtlasWrite that their observed errors are resolved and close ticket.

follow_up_tasks:
Post-deploy: run 48h regression tests on dedicated pools with synthetic retry storms to validate no hidden perf regressions.
Add an observability alert: sustained increase in kv-miss-rate for hot-prefixes tied to streaming retry counts.
Confluence: Draft a short postmortem and add preventative checklist for future prefix refactors.
Customer communication: Schedule a 30-min review with AtlasWrite success team to walk through fix and confirm SLA satisfaction.

[Exception process: emergency unsigned (hotfix) offline bundle for Redwood Private]
## Purpose
This page defines the **break-glass exception process** for shipping an **emergency unsigned offline bundle** ("unsigned hotfix bundle") for **Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem)** when the standard bundle signing process is unavailable.

**Default policy:** All Redwood Private offline bundles MUST be signed and must fail closed in the installer when signature verification fails.

**Exception:** An unsigned bundle may be shipped only under the strict conditions and approvals below, with mandatory compensating controls, customer communication, and follow-up remediation.

This process exists to:
- Enable urgent customer impact fixes when signing is temporarily blocked.
- Control and document supply-chain risk.
- Produce auditable evidence for customers and internal compliance.

---

## Scope
Applies to:
- **Offline bundles** distributed to customers for air-gapped or restricted-network environments.
- **Hotfix** releases required for security vulnerabilities, data loss risk, severe availability incidents, or legal/compliance blockers.

Does not apply to:
- Standard signed releases.
- Customer-controlled internal artifact repackaging (customer actions outside Redwood distribution).
- Break-glass install flags on the customer side (covered in installer policy and runbooks).

---

## Definitions
- **Offline bundle:** The packaged set of artifacts used to install/upgrade Redwood Private (installer, charts/manifests, image references, runtime artifacts, model/runtime dependencies, SBOM pointer, etc.).
- **Unsigned hotfix bundle:** An offline bundle that is distributed **without Redwood’s cryptographic signature** due to an exception.
- **Compensating controls:** Additional verification steps (hash validation, controlled distribution, access restrictions, enhanced audit logging) required when signature-based integrity verification is not available.

---

## Policy statement
1) **Unsigned offline bundles are prohibited by default.**
2) **Unsigned offline bundles may be shipped only under an approved exception** and must:
   - Be limited in scope, time, and recipients.
   - Use compensating controls described in this document.
   - Include a committed plan and deadlines for a **signed replacement**.
3) Any use of this exception is treated as a **Security/GRC event** and must be recorded for audit purposes.

---

## Acceptable reasons (eligibility criteria)
An exception request is eligible only if ALL of the following are true:
- **Customer impact is high/urgent**, e.g.:
  - Critical security vulnerability (actively exploited or high confidence risk).
  - Severity-1 incident impacting production installs/upgrades.
  - Data corruption/loss risk.
  - Regulatory/legal deadline where delay would materially harm customer.
- **Standard signing is blocked** due to one of:
  - Signing key infrastructure outage/unavailability (HSM/KMS access failure).
  - Release pipeline break preventing signing with no timely workaround.
  - Emergency incident response requiring immediate patch distribution before signing path can be restored.
- **No safe alternative exists**, such as:
  - Shipping a signed bundle via an alternate signing environment.
  - Reverting to last known good signed bundle.
  - Using a signed minimal mitigation release.

Not eligible:
- Convenience, schedule pressure, non-urgent feature delivery.
- Avoiding a normal security review.
- Shipping unsigned because the signing process is “not finished”.

---

## Approval matrix (who must approve)
The approvers below provide explicit, recorded approval (ticket + written acknowledgment). Approvals may not be delegated without Security leadership consent.

| Decision / Step | Required approvers | Optional / FYI |
|---|---|---|
| Open exception request + initial triage | Release Eng Lead (Connor O'Brien), Security Eng Lead (Marcus Lin) | Product Owner Private (Vivek Kulkarni), SRE Lead (Sean Gallagher) |
| Risk acceptance to distribute unsigned bundle | Security Exec Sponsor (Dr. Aisha Rahman), GRC Lead (Olga Petrov), Release Eng Lead (Connor O'Brien) | Infra/SRE Exec Sponsor (Neha Kapoor) |
| Customer communication approval (template + recipients) | Product Owner Private (Vivek Kulkarni), Support Readiness Lead (Dev Patel), GRC Lead (Olga Petrov) | Customer Success Lead (Rachel Kim), Solutions Lead (Fatima Noor) |
| Final “go/no-go” on distribution | Security Exec Sponsor (Dr. Aisha Rahman) AND Release Eng Lead (Connor O'Brien) | CEO/Legal only if contractually required |

**Quorum rule:** If any required approver is unavailable, the exception is blocked unless Dr. Aisha Rahman and Connor O’Brien both approve an alternate approver in writing.

---

## Required artifacts and evidence (must be produced)
For each unsigned bundle exception, the release owner (Release Eng) must produce and store the following:

1) **Exception ticket** (single source of truth)
- Title format: `EXC-UNSIGNED-BUNDLE: <Customer/Segment> <Bundle version> <Reason>`
- Must include: impact, timeline, affected customers, mitigation plan, and risk acknowledgment.

2) **Bundle identity + immutable metadata**
- Bundle version (e.g., `private-2026.01.0-hotfix.1`)
- Build ID / CI run ID
- Git commit SHAs for installer/charts/runtime as applicable
- Artifact list (what is included)
- Intended recipients (named accounts)

3) **Compensating integrity verification package (hash manifest)**
Because signature verification is not available, Redwood must provide a **separate integrity verification package**:
- `SHA256SUMS` (or equivalent) covering:
  - Offline bundle archive
  - Internal bundle manifest
  - Installer binary (if shipped separately)
  - Any chart tarballs or dependency packages
  - SBOM file/pointer artifact if included
- Hashes must be generated on a controlled build runner and verified by a second operator.

4) **Two-person verification record**
- Operator A generates hashes and attaches them to the ticket.
- Operator B independently recomputes hashes from the staged artifacts and confirms match.
- Both sign off with timestamp and workstation/build environment identifier.

5) **Distribution controls record**
- Where the bundle is hosted (internal restricted bucket/release portal)
- Access control list (ACL) snapshot: who can download
- Expiration date for access

6) **Customer communication record**
- Approved message sent, time sent, recipients, and acknowledgement if required.

7) **Remediation plan with deadlines**
- Target date for restoring signing pipeline
- Target date for issuing a signed replacement bundle
- Plan for revocation/withdrawal of unsigned bundle

---

## Compensating controls (required)
When shipping an unsigned bundle, Redwood must apply ALL of the controls below.

### 1) Strict distribution limitations
- **Limit recipients** to explicitly approved accounts/environments.
- **Limit time window**: bundle access should expire within **7 calendar days** unless re-approved.
- Do not post unsigned bundles to broad download portals or public locations.

### 2) Out-of-band integrity verification instructions
Provide customers with:
- A hash file (e.g., `SHA256SUMS`) and verification steps.
- A clear statement: “Integrity must be verified before install; do not proceed if hashes do not match.”

Recommended customer commands (Linux example):
- `sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS`
- Or `sha256sum <bundle>.tar.zst` and compare with provided value.

### 3) Controlled transport guidance
Customers must be instructed to:
- Avoid tools known to mutate archives.
- Prefer binary-safe transport (e.g., secure copy to removable media, verify hashes after transfer).

### 4) Explicit risk labeling in artifacts
- Bundle filename must include `UNSIGNED` (example):
  - `redwood-private-2026.01.0-hotfix.1-UNSIGNED-offline-bundle.tar.zst`
- Include `UNSIGNED_README.txt` at bundle root stating:
  - Why unsigned
  - Required verification steps
  - Expiration / replacement plan

### 5) Installer behavior
- The installer must continue to **fail closed** on signature verification by default.
- If the customer must proceed without signature validation, this must be handled via the installer’s documented break-glass path (separately governed), and must be logged locally as a break-glass event.

---

## Risk acknowledgment (required language)
Approvers must acknowledge the following in the exception ticket:

- “We understand that shipping an unsigned offline bundle increases the risk of undetected tampering in transit or at rest.”
- “We confirm that the signed-bundle pipeline is currently blocked and that no safe signed alternative is feasible within the required timeline.”
- “We commit to issuing a signed replacement bundle by <DATE> and to withdrawing the unsigned bundle from distribution by <DATE>.”
- “We confirm compensating controls are in place: restricted distribution, hash-based verification, two-person verification, and documented customer communication.”

---

## Procedure
### Step 0 — Initiate exception
Owner: Connor O'Brien (Release Engineering) or delegate on the release train.

Create the exception ticket and include:
- Severity/impact summary
- Root cause of signing blockage (what failed)
- Why delay is unacceptable
- Proposed unsigned bundle version + recipients

### Step 1 — Security triage
Owner: Marcus Lin (Security Engineering)

Validate:
- Eligibility criteria
- Threat considerations (tampering, replay/downgrade risk)
- Whether additional controls are required for the specific customer environment

### Step 2 — Prepare unsigned bundle + hash manifest
Owner: Release Engineering

- Produce the bundle using deterministic build steps as usual.
- Generate `SHA256SUMS` for all required artifacts.
- Complete two-person verification.

### Step 3 — Obtain approvals
Owner: Olga Petrov (GRC) to coordinate approvals

- Collect approvals per matrix.
- Ensure risk acknowledgment language is included verbatim.

### Step 4 — Customer communication
Owner: Vivek Kulkarni (Product Private) + Dev Patel (Support)

Send approved message before sharing download links.

Minimum content:
- Reason for unsigned distribution
- Required hash verification steps
- Support contact path
- Replacement plan and expected timeline

### Step 5 — Distribute with access controls
Owner: Release Engineering

- Host in restricted location.
- Provide customer with:
  - Bundle
  - `SHA256SUMS`
  - Verification instructions
  - `UNSIGNED_README.txt`

### Step 6 — Track completion + remediation
Owner: Release Engineering + Security

- Confirm customer verified hashes and completed install/upgrade.
- Restore signing pipeline.
- Ship signed replacement bundle.
- Withdraw access to unsigned bundle.

---

## Customer communication templates
### Template A — Initial notice (email)
Subject: `[Action required] Redwood Private hotfix bundle integrity verification (unsigned emergency release)`

Body:
- We are providing an emergency hotfix bundle to address <ISSUE>.
- Due to <SIGNING BLOCKER>, this bundle is **unsigned**. This is an exception to Redwood’s standard signed-bundle process.
- Before installation, you must verify integrity using the provided `SHA256SUMS` file:
  1) Transfer both the bundle and `SHA256SUMS` to your offline environment.
  2) Run: `sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS`
  3) Do not proceed if any verification fails.
- We will provide a **signed replacement** by <DATE> and will retire this unsigned bundle by <DATE>.
- If you have any questions or verification failures, contact <Support alias/SE contact> and include the verification output.

### Template B — Follow-up (signed replacement available)
Subject: `Signed replacement available: Redwood Private <version> offline bundle`

Body:
- A signed replacement bundle is now available: <LINK/DELIVERY METHOD>.
- Please prefer the signed bundle for any new installs/upgrades.
- The previous unsigned bundle will be removed from distribution on <DATE>.

---

## Remediation requirements (mandatory)
Within **5 business days** after distribution of any unsigned bundle, Release Engineering must schedule and complete a remediation review with Security + GRC.

### Remediation checklist
- [ ] Root cause analysis: why signing was blocked (technical + process)
- [ ] Confirm the signed pipeline is restored OR a permanent workaround exists
- [ ] Issue a signed replacement bundle and validate verification end-to-end
- [ ] Withdraw unsigned bundle distribution and document withdrawal date/time
- [ ] Confirm customer has migrated (or documented why not)
- [ ] Update runbooks/tests to prevent recurrence
- [ ] File follow-up tickets for any process gaps (approvals, evidence, access controls)

### Evidence to attach after remediation
- Link to signed replacement release artifact
- Confirmation of unsigned bundle removal
- Summary of customer outcome (install success + any issues)

---

## Audit and retention
- Exception tickets and evidence must be retained for **7 years** (or longer if customer contract requires).
- All approvals must be recorded in writing (ticket comments are acceptable if identities are validated).
- Access logs for downloads must be retained for at least **1 year**.

---

## Escalation and incident handling
If an unsigned bundle is suspected to be tampered with, leaked, or redistributed beyond approved recipients:
1) Notify Security on-call and Release Engineering immediately.
2) Stop distribution (revoke links/credentials).
3) Initiate an incident: “Potential supply-chain compromise (unsigned bundle exception)”.
4) Provide customers with new verified artifacts and guidance.

---

## FAQ
**Q: Can we ship an unsigned bundle to keep a release train on schedule?**
No. Schedule pressure is not an eligible reason.

**Q: Can we provide only a single hash of the bundle archive?**
No. At minimum, provide a hash for the archive and the internal manifest; additionally provide hashes for critical install components (installer, charts/deps) to support targeted verification and troubleshooting.

**Q: Can Support approve this exception?**
No. Support participates in readiness and communication, but Security leadership, GRC, and Release Engineering approvals are mandatory.

**Q: Does this change the installer verification policy?**
No. The installer must continue to treat missing/invalid signatures as a failure by default; any customer-side override remains separately governed and must be audited.


[On‑prem upgrade bundle format (air‑gapped) — Redwood Private]
## Purpose
Redwood Private on‑prem (including fully air‑gapped environments) upgrades are delivered as a **single, self‑contained upgrade bundle**. The bundle includes all artifacts required by the installer to validate, plan, and execute an upgrade **without reaching the public internet**.

This document defines:
- Bundle packaging requirements and directory layout
- The **manifest** (what it must contain and how it’s validated)
- Checksums and signature verification requirements
- Offline dependency handling (container images, Helm charts, CLIs)
- How `redwood-private-installer` locates, verifies, and uses bundles

## Terminology
- **Bundle**: A `.tar.zst` (preferred) or `.tar.gz` archive containing a manifest and all upgrade artifacts.
- **Artifact**: A file or OCI object required for upgrade (charts, images, binaries, migration jobs).
- **Mirror**: Customer-managed offline registry/repository (e.g., Harbor, Artifactory, Nexus).

## Supported bundle types
We publish two bundle flavors. Both share the same manifest schema.

1) **Offline bundle (recommended)**
- Contains **all** OCI images (as tar archives) and Helm charts.
- Installer can load/push images to a local registry and install charts without any external fetch.

2) **Mirror-assisted bundle**
- Contains charts and metadata, but images are expected to already exist in the customer mirror.
- Manifest includes required image digests; installer verifies presence by digest.

## High-level invariants (must hold)
1) **Deterministic**: A bundle uniquely identifies the release and artifact digests.
2) **Verifiable**: Bundle must pass checksum + signature verification before use.
3) **Complete**: For Offline bundles, no network fetch is required after verification.
4) **Auditable**: Installer writes verification and consumption results into the upgrade audit trail.

## Bundle file naming
Recommended naming convention:
- `redwood-private-upgrade-bundle_<privateVersion>_<k8sMinor>_<arch>_<buildId>.tar.zst`

Example:
- `redwood-private-upgrade-bundle_1.18.0_k8s-1.29_amd64_b20250614.3.tar.zst`

## Bundle directory layout
After extraction, the bundle must have this top-level structure:

```
./
  manifest.json
  manifest.sig
  checksums.sha256
  charts/
    redwood-private-<version>.tgz
    redwood-private-crds-<version>.tgz
  images/
    index.json
    oci/
      redwood-control-plane_@sha256-....tar
      redwood-data-plane_@sha256-....tar
      redwood-migrations_@sha256-....tar
      ...
  binaries/
    redwood-private-installer_<version>_<os>_<arch>
    kubectl_<version>_<os>_<arch>   (optional)
    helm_<version>_<os>_<arch>      (optional)
  docs/
    release-notes.md
    upgrade-notes.md
  licenses/
    THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt
```

Notes:
- `manifest.json`, `manifest.sig`, and `checksums.sha256` are mandatory.
- `images/` is mandatory for Offline bundles; optional for Mirror-assisted bundles.
- `binaries/` may include a pinned installer build, but the bundle can also be consumed by a separately distributed installer as long as compatibility checks pass.

## Manifest
### Format
- File name: `manifest.json`
- Encoding: UTF‑8
- JSON object (schema validated by installer)

### Required fields
The installer treats these fields as required and **blocking** if missing.

- `bundle_format_version`
  - String; current value: `"1.0"`
- `bundle_id`
  - String; unique id (e.g., build id)
- `created_at`
  - RFC3339 timestamp
- `private_version`
  - The Redwood Private platform version contained in this bundle
- `upgrade_paths`
  - Supported source versions (initially N‑1 → N is the default)
- `kubernetes_compatibility`
  - Supported K8s minor versions (e.g., `1.28`, `1.29`)
- `artifacts`
  - Lists charts/images/binaries by name, version, and digest
- `signing`
  - Signature metadata (key id, algorithm)

### Recommended fields
- `release_channel` (e.g., `stable`, `beta`)
- `notes` (short summary)
- `known_issues` (links/ids)
- `support_bundle_tags` (what to include in support bundles)

### Manifest example (abridged)

```json
{
  "bundle_format_version": "1.0",
  "bundle_id": "b20250614.3",
  "created_at": "2025-06-14T21:03:11Z",
  "private_version": "1.18.0",
  "release_channel": "stable",
  "upgrade_paths": {
    "supported_sources": ["1.17.0", "1.17.1"],
    "blocked_sources": ["<=1.16.x"],
    "notes": "Default supported path is N-1 -> N. Multi-hop requires manual plan."
  },
  "kubernetes_compatibility": {
    "supported_minors": ["1.28", "1.29"],
    "notes": "K8s 1.27 is EOL for this release."
  },
  "artifacts": {
    "charts": [
      {
        "name": "redwood-private",
        "version": "1.18.0",
        "path": "charts/redwood-private-1.18.0.tgz",
        "sha256": "<sha256>"
      },
      {
        "name": "redwood-private-crds",
        "version": "1.18.0",
        "path": "charts/redwood-private-crds-1.18.0.tgz",
        "sha256": "<sha256>"
      }
    ],
    "images": [
      {
        "name": "redwood/control-plane",
        "digest": "sha256:<digest>",
        "tar_path": "images/oci/redwood-control-plane_@sha256-<digest>.tar"
      },
      {
        "name": "redwood/migrations",
        "digest": "sha256:<digest>",
        "tar_path": "images/oci/redwood-migrations_@sha256-<digest>.tar"
      }
    ],
    "binaries": [
      {
        "name": "redwood-private-installer",
        "version": "0.31.0",
        "path": "binaries/redwood-private-installer_0.31.0_linux_amd64",
        "sha256": "<sha256>"
      }
    ]
  },
  "signing": {
    "algorithm": "ed25519",
    "key_id": "redwood-release-key-2025-01",
    "signature_file": "manifest.sig"
  }
}
```

### Schema validation rules (installer)
The installer MUST:
- Reject unknown `bundle_format_version` values.
- Reject bundles whose `private_version` is not compatible with the installer’s supported range.
- Enforce `upgrade_paths.supported_sources` / `blocked_sources` (see compatibility policy).
- Validate that every artifact referenced exists and matches the expected digest.

## Checksums
### checksums file
- File name: `checksums.sha256`
- Format: standard `sha256sum` output (`<sha256>  <relative-path>`)
- Must include:
  - `manifest.json`
  - All chart tarballs under `charts/`
  - All image tars under `images/oci/` (Offline bundles)
  - Any binary under `binaries/` shipped in the bundle
  - Any `docs/` content is optional (non-blocking if missing unless referenced by manifest)

Example:

```
9f2d...  manifest.json
b18a...  charts/redwood-private-1.18.0.tgz
c91c...  charts/redwood-private-crds-1.18.0.tgz
0d77...  images/oci/redwood-control-plane_@sha256-....tar
f3a1...  binaries/redwood-private-installer_0.31.0_linux_amd64
```

### Verification behavior
- The installer verifies SHA256 for each referenced artifact.
- Any mismatch is **blocking** and must fail before prechecks/plan generation.

## Signing
### Signature file
- File name: `manifest.sig`
- Signature covers the bytes of `manifest.json` (exact file contents).
- Signature algorithm: **ed25519**

### Trust model
- Redwood publishes release public keys out-of-band to on‑prem customers as part of the Private onboarding package.
- Customers configure trusted keys on the operator host (or inside the installer container) prior to upgrade.

### Installer key configuration
The installer searches keys in this order:
1) `--trusted-keys <path>` (file containing one or more public keys)
2) `REDWOOD_PRIVATE_TRUSTED_KEYS_PATH` (env var)
3) Default path: `/etc/redwood-private/trust/keys/`

Verification requirements:
- Signature verification is **blocking**.
- `signing.key_id` in the manifest must match an available trusted key id.
- Installer records key id and verification result in upgrade audit logs.

## Offline dependencies
### Container images
#### Offline bundle
- `images/oci/*.tar` are OCI image tarballs.
- `images/index.json` maps human names to digests and tar paths (installer uses this for fast validation).
- Installer can either:
  - Load into container runtime (e.g., `containerd`) and re-tag, or
  - Push directly to a customer registry mirror.

Required: all images referenced by charts must be present by digest.

#### Mirror-assisted bundle
- Bundle omits image tar files.
- Manifest lists all required images + digests.
- Installer verifies images exist in the configured mirror registry **by digest**.
- If the mirror serves tags only, operator must ensure tags resolve to the declared digests.

### Helm charts
- Must be shipped as `.tgz` under `charts/`.
- The bundle should include a CRDs chart separately (`redwood-private-crds`) when CRDs must be applied ahead of control plane rollout.

### CLIs and tools
- For air‑gapped environments, we recommend shipping a pinned installer binary in `binaries/`.
- Optional: include `kubectl` and `helm` to avoid relying on host tooling.

## How the installer locates bundles
The installer supports two primary modes: **path-based** and **directory discovery**.

### Path-based (recommended)
Operators provide the bundle archive or extracted directory:

- Archive:
  - `redwood-private-installer upgrade --bundle /path/to/bundle.tar.zst`
- Extracted dir:
  - `redwood-private-installer upgrade --bundle-dir /path/to/extracted/`

Rules:
- If `--bundle` is provided, installer extracts to a working directory under:
  - `${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-~/.cache}/redwood-private/bundles/<bundle_id>/`
- If `--bundle-dir` is provided, installer uses it read-only and writes state elsewhere.

### Directory discovery (fallback)
If no explicit bundle flag is passed, installer searches:
1) `REDWOOD_PRIVATE_BUNDLE_DIR`
2) `/opt/redwood-private/bundles/current/`

Discovery requires `manifest.json` at the root.

## Verification and consumption flow
Installer performs these steps in order (all are auditable):

1) **Locate bundle** (path/discovery)
2) **Read manifest** and validate schema
3) **Verify signature** of `manifest.json`
4) **Verify checksums** of referenced artifacts
5) **Compatibility gate**
   - Source version must be in `supported_sources` and not in `blocked_sources`
   - K8s minor must be supported
6) **Artifact availability checks**
   - Offline bundle: ensure all required `images/` and `charts/` exist
   - Mirror-assisted: verify mirror contains all required digests
7) **Proceed to prechecks / plan**

If any step fails, the installer must stop before making changes.

## Operator configuration: offline registry and mirrors
For on‑prem, images typically must be pushed to a local registry.

Installer flags (common):
- `--registry-mirror <host:port>`
- `--registry-username <user>` / `--registry-password-file <path>`
- `--registry-ca-file <path>` (private CA)
- `--registry-insecure` (not recommended; restricted environments only)

Expected behavior:
- For Offline bundles, installer loads and pushes **by digest**, then configures chart values to reference the mirror.
- For Mirror-assisted bundles, installer validates image digests exist before continuing.

## Failure modes and operator remediation
| Failure | What it means | Typical remediation |
|---|---|---|
| `SIGNATURE_VERIFICATION_FAILED` | Bundle may be tampered with or wrong key configured | Confirm trusted key set; re-download bundle; verify key id; avoid copying through systems that modify files |
| `CHECKSUM_MISMATCH` | A file differs from expected SHA256 | Re-transfer with binary-safe method; validate storage integrity; re-fetch bundle |
| `MISSING_ARTIFACT` | Manifest references a file not present in the bundle | Wrong bundle version or incomplete extraction; re-download and re-extract |
| `UNSUPPORTED_UPGRADE_PATH` | Source version not supported | Use supported N‑1 release first or contact Support for an assisted multi-hop plan |
| `MIRROR_DIGEST_NOT_FOUND` | Mirror does not contain required image digest | Push images to mirror (or use Offline bundle); ensure digest retention is enabled |

## Operational guidance
- Store bundles in a WORM-capable or access-controlled location (auditors frequently request evidence of what was installed).
- Keep `manifest.json`, `checksums.sha256`, and `manifest.sig` together; do not rename files.
- Prefer `.tar.zst` for large bundles (faster and smaller for offline transfer).
- Ensure your transfer mechanism preserves file integrity (avoid email/IM attachments; use SFTP, signed artifact channels, or physical media with verification).

## Security and compliance notes
- Bundle signatures are the primary integrity control; checksums provide defense-in-depth and earlier corruption detection.
- Customer environments may require that bundles are scanned prior to import. The manifest can be used as an input inventory for scanners.
- The installer must emit audit events for: bundle verification start/finish, key id used, and bundle id/private version consumed.

## Appendix A: Recommended extraction and validation commands
On an operator workstation:

```
# Extract (tar.zst)
tarzstd -d -c bundle.tar.zst | tar -xvf -

# Quick local checksum verification
sha256sum -c checksums.sha256

# Optional: inspect manifest
cat manifest.json | jq .
```

## Appendix B: Bundle compatibility with installer versions
- Bundles are forward-compatible within a major installer line when `bundle_format_version` is unchanged.
- If the installer reports `UNSUPPORTED_BUNDLE_FORMAT`, update the installer to the minimum version referenced in release notes.

(Installer compatibility enforcement is described in the upgrade plan / rollback ADR and the Private release gating policy.)


[ADR-021: Private Observability Minimum Pack — Scope, Stack Dependencies, and Export Integrations]
## Status
Published (effective starting Redwood Private release line: 2025.07)

## Context
Redwood Private (VPC + on-prem) deployments have historically had bespoke observability setups depending on the customer’s cluster standards and their preferred tooling. This creates recurring issues:
- Support/SRE cannot rely on consistent signals, dashboards, or alert semantics across installs.
- Customers experience time-to-diagnose delays (missing dashboards, inconsistent metric names, no runbook links, noisy/unbounded alerts).
- Air-gapped/on-prem installs require deterministic packaging of artifacts (dashboards/rules/config), which ad-hoc setups do not provide.

The “Private Observability Minimum Pack” project standardizes the lowest viable, supported observability bundle that ships with Redwood Private via Helm charts and the private installer.

This ADR defines:
- What is in scope vs out of scope for the minimum pack (v1)
- The required dependencies (Prometheus/Grafana baseline) and what “supported” means
- How export integrations (logs/metrics, and limited traces where feasible) are handled in private environments

## Decision summary
1) **Prometheus + Grafana are the supported baseline for the minimum pack** (dashboards + alert rules + recording rules), delivered as versioned artifacts and wired into Redwood’s Helm charts/installer.

2) **The minimum pack is an integration bundle, not a full observability platform.** We provide:
- Redwood metrics endpoints and a curated set of alerts/dashboards
- A recommended deployment path for Prometheus/Grafana (customer-managed or Redwood-provisioned where allowed)
- Log collection defaults and supported exports (see ADR-022)

We do **not** build or operate a Redwood-specific metrics backend, log SIEM, or tracing backend for Private.

3) **Exports are supported via documented configuration paths and tested reference configurations**, not via bespoke per-customer engineering:
- Logs: Loki, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, Splunk HEC, and optional OTLP logs (where customer has an OTEL collector)
- Metrics: Prometheus remote_write as an integration path (customer-managed destination)
- Traces: best-effort (v1), optional OTLP tracing enablement where runtime components emit spans; no guaranteed end-to-end tracing in v1

4) **Scope is explicitly SLO- and incident-driven:** cover the highest-impact failure modes for inference serving and private control plane health, with bounded cardinality and upgrade-safe artifact versioning.

## Goals (what success looks like)
- A Private install has usable dashboards/alerts within 30 minutes of install/upgrade, without bespoke setup.
- Redwood Support/SRE can ask for a consistent “minimum pack” dashboard/alert set during escalations.
- Air-gapped installs can validate artifacts (dashboards/rules/config/images) are present and versioned.
- Metrics and labels are bounded to avoid customer Prometheus overload.

## Non-goals
- Full “premium observability” (long retention, federation, cross-cluster aggregation, advanced tracing controls, bespoke dashboards).
- Supporting every monitoring stack (Datadog, New Relic, proprietary APMs) in v1.
- Creating a new Redwood-managed SIEM or log storage for Private.

## In scope (v1 minimum pack)
### A) Metrics + alerts
- Standardized metrics naming/labels for Private (see metrics/alerting standards)
- Recording rules for runtime golden signals:
  - Request rate (RPS) and token throughput
  - Error rate (5xx, timeouts, upstream dependency errors)
  - Latency p50/p95/p99 (request + token generation where applicable)
  - Saturation indicators (GPU utilization, queue depth, batch size, cache hit rate)
- Prometheus alert rules mapped to Private SLO guidance:
  - Availability / error budget burn (page-worthy vs ticket-only)
  - Latency SLO burn (p95/p99) and sustained degradation
  - GPU/CPU/memory pressure, OOMKills, restart loops
  - Scrape failures (Prometheus target down), exporter health, TSDB issues (disk filling)

### B) Dashboards (Grafana)
Curated “minimum supported” dashboards (names are normative; exact panel composition may evolve with versions):
- Private Runtime Overview (golden signals + batching/KV cache + GPU panels)
- Control Plane Health (API gateway, routing/policy engine, auth/RBAC integration points, installer/upgrade controller)
- Kubernetes/Infra Summary (node/pod health, persistent volume usage for Prometheus/Grafana, scrape health)

### C) Logs (operational)
- Baseline log collection configuration shipped with the installer/Helm charts
- Structured log fields aligned across control plane and data plane (e.g., request_id, component, severity, model, route; tenant identifier must be hashed)
- Safe-by-default redaction posture (no request payload logging by default; secrets never logged)
- Export configuration patterns for supported sinks (details governed by ADR-022)

### D) Packaging + installation
- Versioned “observability-pack” artifacts (dashboards, rules, configs) pinned to Redwood Private releases
- Installer preflight checks relevant to observability readiness (storage class, network policies, resource requests)
- Post-install validation steps (scrape targets present, dashboards loaded, critical alerts not firing)
- Air-gapped bundle support: all images and artifacts included, with checksums/signing where required by the offline packaging process

## Out of scope (explicitly)
- Shipping a fully managed, Redwood-operated Prometheus/Grafana service inside customer environments.
- Long-term log/metric retention beyond default recommendations (customers can configure retention and storage).
- Multi-cluster federation, Thanos/Cortex/Mimir architecture design and support as part of v1.
- Guaranteed end-to-end distributed tracing across every component.
- Customer-specific dashboard customization as a supported offering (customers may clone dashboards, but it is not supported for troubleshooting unless they reproduce issues on minimum-pack dashboards).

## Options considered
### Option 1: Support multiple monitoring stacks (Prometheus/Grafana + vendor APMs) in v1
**Rejected.** Increases combinatorial support burden and makes “minimum supported” ambiguous. Private customers have highly variable constraints, and supporting multiple vendor-specific solutions would slow delivery and reduce reliability.

### Option 2: Redwood Private ships with kube-prometheus-stack as a hard dependency
**Partially accepted (recommended, not mandatory).**
- We will document and validate against kube-prometheus-stack as the reference installation.
- We will not require customers to run the exact chart if they already have Prometheus/Grafana; however, they must meet compatibility requirements (scraping, Grafana dashboard provisioning, PromQL support).

### Option 3: Use OpenTelemetry Collector + OTLP as the primary standard for everything (metrics/logs/traces)
**Rejected for v1 as the primary baseline.**
- OTLP is a useful integration path, but many Private customers are standardized on Prometheus + Grafana for metrics and alerting.
- Prometheus-native alerting (PromQL) is the fastest path to deliver the minimum pack and to align with existing SRE muscle memory.
- OTLP remains an optional export/integration path (especially for logs and traces) where customers already operate an OTEL pipeline.

## Decision details
### 1) Supported baseline: Prometheus + Grafana
The minimum pack’s dashboards and alert rules are delivered as:
- Grafana dashboards (JSON) provisionable via ConfigMaps or Grafana sidecar provisioning
- PrometheusRule resources (or equivalent rules files) containing:
  - Recording rules (to stabilize dashboard queries and reduce repeated expensive PromQL)
  - Alerting rules with consistent labels and annotations

**Support policy:**
- If a customer uses Prometheus + Grafana (or compatible equivalents) and deploys the minimum pack artifacts unmodified, Redwood Support will treat the signals as canonical.
- If a customer uses alternative stacks, Support will request they enable the Prometheus-compatible endpoints and provide equivalent evidence; best-effort support applies.

### 2) Definition of “minimum supported”
“Minimum supported” means:
- The artifacts are shipped, versioned, and tested in reference environments (VPC + on-prem-like)
- Alert rules include:
  - severity taxonomy (Sev0/Sev1/Sev2 or page/ticket classification per Private on-call policy)
  - runbook links in annotations
  - noise controls (for example: for 5xx, require sustained burn or minimum traffic)
- Metric names/labels are stable across minor releases; breaking changes require documented migration and upgrade checks

### 3) Export integrations (how we handle customer toolchains)
We support exports by providing:
- A default collector configuration (logs) with documented toggles and examples
- A “supported sinks” list with validation coverage and known limitations
- A matrix of prerequisites per sink (network egress, auth, certificates, buffering)

**We do not**:
- Operate or host the destination systems
- Write one-off transformations for customer-specific field mappings beyond documented examples

**Metrics exports:**
- Primary mode is scrape by Prometheus
- Supported integration path: Prometheus remote_write to a customer-managed backend (implementation and operations are customer-owned)

**Logs exports:**
- Governed by ADR-022; minimum pack includes tested reference configs for Splunk HEC and Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, plus Loki as a common in-cluster option

**Traces:**
- v1 is “best effort” and optional; where spans exist, OTLP export may be enabled, but absence of traces is not considered a minimum-pack failure

### 4) Cardinality and privacy constraints
Private environments can have strict resource envelopes. Therefore:
- Labels with high cardinality (tenant identifiers, request_id, raw route/model strings) must be bounded or hashed/normalized.
- Default dashboards/alerts must rely on aggregated signals.
- Any “per-model” or “per-route” breakdown must be limited to allowlists/top-K patterns, not unbounded label explosion.

Security constraints:
- No secrets, API keys, or request prompts/completions in operational logs by default.
- Tenant identifiers must be hashed (non-reversible) unless explicitly enabled by the customer and approved by Security & Compliance.

## Consequences
### Positive
- Clear, repeatable support posture for Private escalations.
- Faster installation validation and fewer “no dashboards/no alerts” incidents.
- Reduced operational variance across VPC and on-prem installs.

### Negative / tradeoffs
- Customers on vendor-only monitoring stacks may require extra integration effort.
- Some advanced visibility (deep tracing, long retention, federation) remains out of scope and may be requested by large enterprises.

### Risks and mitigations
- **Risk:** Alert noise causes customers to disable alerts.
  - **Mitigation:** Ship conservative defaults; separate paging vs ticket alerts; include tuning guidance.
- **Risk:** Prometheus TSDB sizing issues in higher-throughput Private clusters.
  - **Mitigation:** Provide sizing/retention guidance and installer preflight warnings; recommend recording rules.
- **Risk:** Air-gapped artifact drift across versions.
  - **Mitigation:** Version-pin artifacts; include in offline bundle with checksums; add post-install validation.

## Implementation notes (normative requirements)
- Dashboards and rules must be versioned and referenced by the Redwood Private release version.
- Every alert must include:
  - `summary` and `description`
  - `runbook_url`
  - `severity` or `paging` label aligned with Private paging policy
- Installer must provide:
  - Preflight checks: storage class availability, expected ports/NetworkPolicy compatibility, minimal CPU/memory requests
  - Post-install checks: Prometheus targets UP for Redwood services; Grafana dashboards present; rule groups loaded

## Rollout plan
- Ship as opt-out enabled-by-default in new installs.
- For upgrades, enable by default but allow customers to keep existing external Prometheus/Grafana and only import Redwood artifacts.
- Backport critical fixes (dashboards broken, invalid rules, excessive cardinality) to supported Private release branches.

## Open questions (tracked separately)
- Do we standardize on a single “recommended” Helm stack (kube-prometheus-stack + Grafana) as a Redwood-supported deployment profile in a future release?
- Should OTLP traces become a minimum requirement once runtime tracing coverage reaches a defined threshold?
- Should we ship optional Thanos sidecar + object storage guidance as a documented “extended retention” profile (still customer-operated)?

## Appendix: Compatibility requirements (Prometheus/Grafana)
Customers bringing their own stack must support:
- Prometheus scraping Kubernetes service endpoints (TLS optional, configurable)
- PromQL features used by shipped rules/dashboards (recording rules, histogram_quantile where applicable)
- Grafana dashboard provisioning from JSON, and Prometheus datasource access

If these requirements are not met, Redwood Support will request deployment of the reference setup for troubleshooting.


[Serving surface PRD: product-level requirements, packaging, and release plan (H1 2026)]
Overview

Purpose
- This PRD defines the product surface for Redwood Inference’s hosted and dedicated serving APIs for H1 2026. It unifies the request surface, packaging options, and the coordinated release plan and pricing experiments. The goal is to improve developer productivity, make cost/latency tradeoffs explicit, and enable predictable enterprise adoption.

Scope
- Host: Redwood API (hosted + dedicated capacity).
- Features: unified inference endpoints, routing-level quality tiers, bundled latency/cost SKUs, rollout plan to customers on trial and enterprise tiers.
- Out of scope: Private on-prem installer packaging (will get a compatibility spec in a follow-up doc).

Background and motivation
- Customers report confusion between per-token pricing, dedicated commitments, and the cost/latency payoff of quantization and batching. Engineering and sales need an aligned product that: (1) exposes clear choices to developers, (2) enables reliable performance SLOs per SKU, and (3) supports cheap experimentation via feature flags.

Personas
- ML Engineer: needs predictable latency and model versioning for product features.
- Platform Engineer: wants to allocate budget across teams and enforce quotas.
- Startup founder/Developer: wants a simple price ladder and a quick path to production.
- Enterprise CS / Sales: needs SLAs and an upgrade path to dedicated capacity.

Goals (measurable)
1) Reduce upgrade friction: 30% fewer support tickets about pricing/latency choices in Q2 2026 vs Q4 2025.
2) Increase enterprise conversions: 15% lift in Dedicated leads attributable to clearer packaging by end of H1 2026.
3) Developer clarity: >90% of new signups pick a recommended SKU within first 15 minutes (post-checkout funnel metric).
4) Maintain median hosted generation latency <= 220ms for the Standard tier at 512 tokens.

Key product decisions (summary)
- Introduce three quality/latency tiers on the public API: Economy, Standard, and Premium. Each tier maps to a routing policy and default model/quantization profile.
- Offer two packaging paths: self-serve metered (per-token + tier surcharge) and committed Dedicated bundles (monthly reservation + reduced per-token).
- Feature-flagged rollout for routing fallbacks and progressive rollout to high-volume customers.

Requirements
Functional requirements (FR)
FR-01: Single POST /v1/generate endpoint with optional query param tier={economy|standard|premium}.
FR-02: Default behavior: if no tier specified, backend selects Standard.
FR-03: Tier-to-model mapping documented and editable in product config.
FR-04: SDKs (Python/Node/Go) must expose a 'preferred_tier' client option and a helper to estimate cost for a prompt.
FR-05: Admin console: ability to create packaged bundles and assign to accounts.

Non-functional requirements (NFR)
NFR-01: SLOs per tier (target):
- Economy: P95 latency <= 450ms for 256 tokens; availability 99.5%.
- Standard: P95 latency <= 220ms for 512 tokens; availability 99.9%.
- Premium: P95 latency <= 120ms for 1024 tokens; availability 99.95%.
NFR-02: Price estimation API must respond <= 40ms 95% of the time.
NFR-03: Pricing and tier selection controls in the console must load within 1.5s on a 100ms RTT network.
NFR-04: Rollout system must support canary at 0.5%, 1%, 5%, 25%, 100% and automatic rollback based on error budget triggers.

Acceptance criteria (AC)
- AC-01: Integration tests demonstrate endpoint with tier parameter routes to expected model and returns tokens with stream support in SDKs.
- AC-02: Benchmarked invoices: cost estimator matches actual per-token billing within 3% on test billing runs.
- AC-03: Performance tests show Standard tier meets NFR-01 in the staging environment with production-like hardware.
- AC-04: Admin console can provision a Dedicated bundle and enforce quota isolation for a test account.

Design notes
Routing and policy
- Each incoming request is annotated with tier metadata and hashed to routing bucketing. A policy engine (policyd) decides model variant, region preference, and fallback sequence.
- Fallback order example for Standard: Standard-quantized -> Standard-full -> Economy-quantized (if compatibility). Fallback policies are versioned and controlled by flags.

Model/quantization mapping (recommended default)
| Tier | Model family | Quantization | Target hardware |
| Economy | open-m-7b | int8/4 | cpu-burst/gpu-low |
| Standard | open-m-13b | int8 | A10/A16 or comparable |
| Premium | open-m-70b | fp16 | H100/V100-style fast GPUs |

Pricing and packaging (product recommendation)
- Metered (public): base per-token unit + tier multiplier for latency premium. Example (proposal for experiment):
  - Tokens unit: $0.0008 / 1k tokens (base).
  - Economy multiplier: x0.8 (cheaper inference but higher latency).
  - Standard multiplier: x1.0 (base).
  - Premium multiplier: x2.5 (fast path and priority routing).
- Dedicated bundles: monthly reservation tiers with discounted included units and overage rates. Example bundle table:
| Bundle | Monthly commitment | Included tokens | Effective per-1k price (if used fully) | Notes |
| Dev  | $2,500 | 400M tokens | $0.0006 | For small teams, limited to Standard tier |
| Growth | $12,000 | 2.5B tokens | $0.00048 | Optional burst capacity into Premium at +30% surcharge |
| Enterprise | $60,000 | 15B tokens | $0.00035 | SLA 99.95% and named support engineer |
- Upsell mechanics: free trial credits for Premium trials (30M tokens) and automated usage report highlighting latency/cost tradeoffs after 7 days.

Billing and metering details (implementation notes)
- Metering window: per-request token counts + model variant metadata. Billing pipeline must tag events with tier and bundle_id.
- Rate limiting: default per-account QPS for Standard = 50 requests/sec. Dedicated bundles may assign higher QPS and token concurrency.

Rollout plan and timeline (Q1–Q2 2026)
1) Pilot (Q1 start, 6 weeks): enable tier param in API and SDKs for internal feature teams and 3 external pilot customers. Collect latency and cost telemetry. Owner: Product + Eng Platform.
2) Closed beta (Q1 mid, 4 weeks): open to selected self-serve signups with dedicated dashboard and billing telemetry. Owner: Product, SRE.
3) Pricing experiment (Q1 end – Q2 start, 8 weeks): run A/B experiment comparing per-token multiplier vs flat price tiers to measure conversion and revenue impact. Owner: Growth & Finance.
4) Public launch (Q2): full documentation, console UI, marketing materials, and gradual rollout for all new signups. Owner: Product + GTM.

Canary and rollback rules
- Canary cohorts: 0.5% internal -> 1% alpha customers -> 5% early adopters -> 25% general -> 100%.
- Automatic rollback triggers: error rate spike > 2x baseline OR P95 latency breach for tier beyond configured SLO for > 10 minutes.

SDK and docs deliverables
- SDK updates: Python/Node/Go: new Client.preferred_tier option, cost_estimate(prompt, length), and sample code for migration.
- Docs: tutorial ‘Picking the right tier’, developer FAQ comparing cost/latency, migration checklist for Dedicated customers.

Release notes (initial public launch summary)
- Feature: tiered inference surface with Economy / Standard / Premium options.
