[Private Observability Minimum Pack — Product Requirements (v1)]
## Summary
Redwood Private customers frequently ask “what’s the supported way to run observability?” Today, installs are inconsistent: some customers integrate Prometheus/Grafana and logs cleanly; others ship no dashboards, have incomplete scrapes, or produce unsafe/unstructured logs. This creates Support/SRE escalations and increases time-to-resolution.

The **Private observability minimum pack** defines and ships a **baseline, supported** observability bundle for Redwood Private installs (VPC and on-prem), packaged with the installer/Helm charts and validated in reference environments.

This page is the **v1 PRD**: personas, requirements, non-goals, and acceptance criteria.

---

## Goals
1. **Turnkey baseline observability** for Redwood Private installs with minimal customer configuration.
2. **Standardize** the minimum set of dashboards + alerts that Redwood Support/SRE will rely on during incidents.
3. Provide a **supported log pipeline** with safe defaults (structured logs + redaction guidance) and **export options** for common private environment sinks.
4. Ensure the pack is **upgrade-safe** (dashboards/alerts continue to work or have documented migrations) and **air-gap compatible**.

## Non-goals (v1)
- Building a “premium observability” offering (multi-cluster federation, long retention, customer-specific dashboards, advanced tracing controls, deep historical analytics).
- Replacing customer-standard tooling (e.g., “Redwood SIEM”). We integrate with it.
- Guaranteed cross-vendor parity with Hosted/Dedicated Redwood Console observability. v1 focuses on a supported minimum for Private.
- Full distributed tracing for all components in all environments. (Traces are “best-effort / optional” in v1; metrics + logs are the baseline.)

---

## Personas & primary use cases
### Persona A: Customer Platform/Infra team (primary)
**Who:** Engineers operating Kubernetes, observability, and security controls for the customer.

**Needs / jobs-to-be-done:**
- Install Redwood Private and know it is “healthy” without building custom dashboards.
- Integrate logs/metrics with existing monitoring/SIEM.
- Operate upgrades/rollbacks safely and verify monitoring still works.
- Avoid high-cardinality metrics, excessive resource usage, and unsafe logs.

### Persona B: Redwood Support & SRE (primary)
**Who:** Redwood Support engineers and on-call SREs assisting customers.

**Needs / jobs-to-be-done:**
- Diagnose common failures quickly (scrape failures, saturation, OOM/restarts, network policy issues).
- Have **consistent** dashboards and alert semantics across customer installs.
- Avoid alert noise and unclear “what do I do now?” next steps.

### Persona C: Solutions Engineering / Professional Services (secondary)
**Who:** SE/PS deploying Private in complex customer environments.

**Needs / jobs-to-be-done:**
- Reference architectures and sizing guidance.
- Clear “supported vs customizable” lines.
- Export recipes for Splunk/ELK/Loki/OTLP where applicable.

---

## Definitions
### What “minimum supported” means
A Private install is considered **minimum-pack supported** when:
- The customer deploys the observability components using Redwood-provided Helm/installer integration (or provides equivalent endpoints and wiring), and
- The default dashboards render data, and
- The baseline alert rules are installed (even if some are disabled by default per policy), and
- Logs are collected in a supported structured format with recommended redaction settings.

### Components in scope
**In-scope (v1):**
- Private control plane services (auth/RBAC integration points, config/policy service, upgrade controller)
- API gateway / ingress
- Routing/policy engine
- Serving runtime pods (inference)
- Model registry integration points
- Installer/upgrade controller

**Out of scope (v1):**
- Customer-managed apps that call Redwood API
- Customer model hosting outside Redwood runtime

---

## Supported deployment environments (v1)
The minimum pack must work (validated) in:
- **VPC Private** (customer-managed cluster)
- **On-prem / air-gapped** (offline image mirroring and artifact bundling)

Assumptions / compatibility targets:
- Kubernetes: supported Redwood Private versions (see Private release notes); validate at least two recent minor versions in CI/staging.
- Metrics: Prometheus-compatible scraping (Prometheus operator or standalone Prometheus).
- Dashboards: Grafana-compatible JSON dashboards.
- Logs: Kubernetes DaemonSet/sidecar-based collection where appropriate.

---

## Requirements

### R1. Packaging & installation (must-have)
**R1.1** Observability pack ships as a **versioned artifact bundle** (dashboards + alert rules + log collector config) that is included with:
- `redwood-helm-charts` (values + templates)
- `redwood-private-installer` (preflight + postinstall validation)

**R1.2** Air-gapped installs must be supported:
- All required images must be mirrorable
- All dashboards/rules/config must be packaged in the offline bundle
- Checksums/signing must be compatible with existing installer bundle verification

**R1.3** Defaults must be “safe” for typical customer clusters:
- Bounded metric cardinality
- Conservative resource requests/limits for observability components
- Log redaction defaults that avoid secrets/PII

**R1.4** Easy opt-out/override:
- Customers can disable specific exporters/collectors (where permissible) and still run Redwood
- Customers can point to existing Prometheus/Grafana/log sinks instead of installing bundled ones

### R2. Metrics requirements (must-have)
Metrics must cover golden signals across key planes:
- **Data plane / runtime:** request rate, error rate, latency (p50/p95/p99), token throughput, batching/queueing signals, saturation (GPU utilization, memory), OOM/restarts
- **Control plane:** API availability/latency, auth failures, policy/routing health, registry integration errors
- **Infra integration:** scrape health, TSDB ingestion health, exporter health

Constraints:
- Must follow Private metric naming and label standards (see standards page).
- Labels must be cardinality-safe for customer Prometheus. Avoid unbounded `tenant_id`, `request_id`, raw `prompt`, full model identifiers if high-cardinality. Prefer aggregated labels and allow explicit opt-in for more detailed labels.

### R3. Dashboards (must-have)
The pack must include a curated set of dashboards with consistent taxonomy, quick links to runbooks, and “top-of-page health summary” panels.

**Required dashboard set (v1):**
1. **Runtime Overview (Private)**
   - Latency (p50/p95/p99), error rate, request volume
   - Token throughput, generation speed
   - Batch size distribution / continuous batching effectiveness
   - Queue depth / backpressure signals
   - KV cache hit rate / utilization (where available)
   - GPU utilization + GPU memory utilization; CPU/memory basics per pod

2. **Control Plane Health (Private)**
   - API gateway availability and latency
   - Auth/RBAC integration failures (e.g., OIDC/JWT validation errors)
   - Routing/policy engine health and configuration reload errors
   - Model registry integration (sync failures, fetch errors)
   - Installer/upgrade controller health (reconcile errors)

3. **GPU / Node Capacity (Private)**
   - GPU saturation over time
   - GPU OOM events / throttling indicators
   - Node-level CPU/memory/disk pressure for nodes hosting runtime pods

4. **Kubernetes Workloads (Private)**
   - Pod restarts and crash loops for Redwood namespaces
   - Pending pods / scheduling failures (resource constraints)
   - Network policy / service discovery indicators (e.g., missing endpoints)

5. **Observability Pipeline Health (Private)**
   - Prometheus scrape success for Redwood targets
   - TSDB ingestion and storage pressure
   - Log collector health: dropped logs, queue/backpressure, retry errors

Dashboard design requirements:
- Dashboard variables must not cause high-cardinality queries by default.
- “Last 15m” view should be actionable for incidents; include longer windows for trend triage.
- Each dashboard includes a “What changed?” section: deploy version/installer version panels when feasible.

### R4. Alerting (must-have)
The pack must include Prometheus alert rules aligned to SLOs and “highest-impact failure modes.”

**Alert philosophy:**
- **Page-worthy (Sev2/Sev1)**: customer-facing availability/latency SLO burn, widespread errors, capacity exhaustion causing request failures.
- **Ticket-only (Sev3/Sev4)**: early warning signals (disk filling, scrape flakiness) with sufficient time to remediate.
- Alerts must include: summary, impact, likely causes, and a **first 3 steps** section + runbook link.

**Required alert families (v1):**
1. **Availability & error rate**
   - API request error rate above threshold (fast burn)
   - Elevated 5xx from gateway/runtime

2. **Latency SLO burn**
   - Multi-window burn rate for p95 latency where SLO guidance exists

3. **Saturation / resource pressure**
   - GPU sustained saturation above threshold (actionable)
   - GPU memory near capacity / OOM kill detected
   - Pod restart loops (CrashLoopBackoff) for runtime/control-plane
   - CPU/memory pressure for critical components (only if actionable; avoid noisy “>80% CPU” by default)

4. **Queueing/backpressure**
   - Queue depth sustained above threshold causing latency impact

5. **Observability failure**
   - Prometheus scrape failing for Redwood targets
   - Log collector dropping >X% logs or persistent send failures

**Noise controls:**
- Provide default thresholds tuned for typical Private footprints.
- Allow customer override via Helm values.
- Some alerts may be **disabled by default** if they are known to be noisy without customer-specific thresholds (must be documented and still shipped).

### R5. Logs: collection, structure, redaction, exports (must-have)
**R5.1 Structured logging**
- Redwood services must emit structured logs (JSON) with a consistent core schema.

Minimum required fields (where applicable):
- `timestamp`, `level`, `service`, `component`, `namespace`, `pod`, `node`
- `request_id` (generated ID; do not log full payload)
- `route` (bounded set or hashed/normalized per standards)
- `model` (bounded/normalized name; avoid per-request unique identifiers)
- `tenant` as a **non-reversible hash** if needed for debugging (must be optional / per standards)
- `error_code` / `grpc_code` / `http_status`
- `latency_ms` (for key request logs)

**R5.2 Redaction / safety**
- Default config must not log raw prompts, completions, authorization headers, tokens, cookies, or customer secrets.
- Provide documented guidance for safe debug escalation (e.g., short-lived debug modes with explicit customer approval).

**R5.3 Supported export sinks (v1)**
The pack must include validated configurations/examples for exporting logs from Private to:
- **Loki** (Grafana stack)
- **Elasticsearch/OpenSearch**
- **Splunk HEC**

Optional / best-effort (documented, not a hard requirement for GA):
- **OTLP logs endpoint** (if included, must be clearly labeled “experimental” for v1)

**R5.4 Backpressure/durability defaults**
- Collector config must define queue sizes, batching, retry policies, and an explicit drop behavior.
- Defaults prioritize **cluster safety** (do not OOM nodes) while making drops visible via metrics and alerts.

### R6. Validation, smoke tests, and supportability (must-have)
- Installer must include **preflight checks** for common breakages:
  - Storage class availability (PVC provisioning)
  - Network policies that would block scraping/collector egress
  - Minimal resource availability
- Post-install validation must verify:
  - Prometheus can scrape Redwood targets
  - Dashboards are installed and queryable
  - Baseline alerts are loaded
  - Log pipeline is running and can deliver to the configured sink

- Provide a smoke test harness suitable for CI and customer-like staging.

---

## Requirements table (condensed)
Priority levels: P0 = must-have for v1 GA; P1 = should-have; P2 = nice-to-have.

P0
- Bundle versioned dashboards + rules + log config into Helm/installer, including air-gap support.
- Runtime Overview dashboard and Control Plane Health dashboard.
- Baseline alert families for availability, latency burn, GPU OOM/restarts, scrape failures.
- Structured logs + redaction defaults + validated exports to Splunk HEC and Elasticsearch/OpenSearch and Loki.
- Installer preflight + postinstall validation + CI smoke tests.

P1
- Observability Pipeline Health dashboard with collector drop metrics.
- Optional OTLP export (best-effort; clearly labeled).
- Automated “runbook links required” linting for alert annotations.

P2
- Tracing end-to-end with sampling controls and exemplars.
- Multi-cluster federation and long retention guidance beyond sizing defaults.

---

## UX / Documentation requirements (must-have)
- Publish a customer-facing (or customer-shareable) install/config guide for enabling the pack.
- Provide clear instructions for:
  - Using customer-provided Prometheus/Grafana vs deploying bundled components
  - Exporting logs to each supported sink
  - Tuning retention, resources, and thresholds
- Provide Support-facing known issues + workarounds and day-2 runbooks.

---

## Acceptance criteria (GA)
A release is GA-ready when all items below are true:

### Installation & packaging
1. Observability artifacts (dashboards, rules, log collector configs) are versioned and shipped with the Private installer/Helm charts.
2. Air-gapped bundle contains all required images and artifacts; install completes without internet access.
3. Upgrade and rollback across at least one prior supported Private version does not break dashboards/alerts (or provides documented migrations).

### Dashboards
4. The required dashboards render data in reference environments (VPC + on-prem-like), with no empty panels due to missing metrics.
5. Dashboard variables and default queries do not generate unbounded cardinality or overload Prometheus in typical cluster sizes.

### Alerting
6. Baseline alerts load successfully and include: severity, summary, impact, and runbook link.
7. Alert noise is reviewed in staging: page-worthy alerts are not firing during normal steady-state, and any disabled-by-default alerts are documented with rationale.

### Logging
8. Logs are structured, include the minimum required fields, and do not include prohibited sensitive data by default.
9. Export configurations for Splunk HEC + Elasticsearch/OpenSearch + Loki are documented and validated in at least one reference environment each.
10. Log pipeline metrics exist for dropped logs/backpressure and are surfaced on a dashboard and (where appropriate) an alert.

### Validation & supportability
11. Installer preflight checks catch common misconfigurations (storage, network policies for scrapes/egress).
12. Postinstall validation provides a clear pass/fail signal for scrapes, dashboards, and alert loading.
13. CI smoke tests run on every release branch and include failure-injection for at least: scrape failure, runtime pod crash loop, and GPU OOM simulation (or closest feasible proxy).

---

## Dependencies
- Observability standards for metric naming/labels and alert severity taxonomy (Owner: SRE/Architecture).
- Runtime/control plane instrumentation changes to ensure required metrics exist and are cardinality-safe.
- Installer/Helm integration work for packaging + toggles + validations.
- Security review for logging schema, redaction defaults, and retention guidance.

---

## Risks & mitigations
1. **Metric cardinality explosion** (models/routes/tenants). Mitigation: enforce label constraints, provide recording rules and aggregation; default dashboards use aggregated views.
2. **Alert noise** in heterogeneous customer environments. Mitigation: multi-window burn alerts, conservative defaults, disable certain alerts by default with documentation.
3. **Air-gap packaging misses artifacts** (dashboards/rules/config). Mitigation: bundle manifest + automated bundle verification test in CI.
4. **Customer network policies block scrape/egress**. Mitigation: installer preflight checks and a documented minimal NetworkPolicy exception set.
5. **Security concerns over log content**. Mitigation: explicit prohibited fields list, redaction defaults, and documented debug escalation process.

---

## Open questions
1. Do we make OTLP export a v1 requirement or “documented best-effort”? (Current: best-effort / optional.)
2. Which alerts should be disabled by default for GA (if any) and what is the exact policy for enabling them?
3. Do we ship a bundled Prometheus/Grafana stack by default, or default to integrating with customer tooling (with an optional bundled deployment)?

---

[VectorLane — Hosted Embeddings + Rerank API Walkthrough]
summary:

transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood Inference, AE on the account. we got Owen from solutions here too. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Priya Nair: Hi, Priya here — head of search at VectorLane.
[00:11] Ethan Cole: Ethan, CTO.
[00:12] Jamal Ortiz: Jamal, data eng.
[00:13] Sofia Ruiz: Sofia, PM.
[00:16] Owen Reyes: Hey all, Owen — I'll run the demo. Quick agenda, we'll do a short intro, show hosted embeddings + rerank flow with console tuning tips, then Q&A and next steps.
[00:28] Maya Chen: Goals from our side: show an end-to-end hosted pipeline, highlight latency/cost levers in Optimize, and answer security questions you flagged.
[00:35] Priya Nair: Sounds good. main thing for us — we have a global product, strict p95 latency targets for search, and cost matters — we serve a lot of queries. We also use Pinecone today for vectors, and want to know how Redwood fits without ripping out infra.
[00:49] Owen Reyes: Great. quick architecture — hosted API handles embeddings generation, then candidate fetch from your vector DB (like Pinecone/Weaviate), then Redwood reranker endpoint takes top-K candidates plus query and returns ranked results. We support both dot/FAISS-derived vectors and you can keep your vector store as-is.
[01:10] Jamal Ortiz: So our flow today: client -> frontend -> our API -> Pinecone -> we rerank clientside using a small transformer. We're trying to move ranking closer to the server to reduce client complexity and improve feature-rich reranking. latency target p95 ~ 220ms end-to-end for rerank path.
[01:27] Owen Reyes: Okay that helps. Demo will use a small dataset so numbers won't be production, but we'll point to how batching, prefix/KV cache, and smaller model variants reduce token cost and improve tail latency.
[01:38] [02:00] Owen Reyes: (screen share) starting in Console — here's the API Playground. We have an embeddings endpoint and a rerank endpoint. I'll show a sample call. first, embeddings: POST /v1/embeddings with model redwood-embed-compact, payload query text. simple JSON, returns vector.
[02:22] [02:30] Owen Reyes: Now candidate fetch mock: we send vector to Pinecone and get top 50 ids, then call Redwood reranker with the query and the 50 doc snippets. here's the rerank call — note fields: query, candidates[], schema for document metadata, and optional model hints (we'll select redwood-rank-2-small).
[02:48] Priya Nair: Do you stream rerank results? what about partial scores?
[02:52] Owen Reyes: Rerank returns a scored list; we don't stream tokens like generation. it's a single response with ranks and scores. our Console shows token-level breakdown for embeddings generation cost and rerank inference cost separately so you can attribute money to each stage.
[03:10] Ethan Cole: For 220ms p95, what's realistic? our client is in us-east.
[03:14] Owen Reyes: With hosted, typical rerank p95 for redwood-rank-2-small with top-50 is around 80-150ms depending on snippet length; embeddings call ~15-35ms. But that's model-dependent and influenced by batching. Our Optimize tab will recommend batch size and KV cache (prefix caching) based on your query distribution.
[03:34] Sofia Ruiz: What's prefix/KV cache?
[03:36] Owen Reyes: It's the KV cache for autoregressive models — for rerank models it's more like cached embeddings for repeated queries or cached doc embeddings on our side if you choose to pin them. For LLM generation, KV cache avoids recomputing earlier tokens. For rerank we support document embedding caching so you only generate embeddings for changed docs.
[03:58] Jamal Ortiz: We already store document embeddings in Pinecone. if we keep that, is there double-cost?
[04:02] Owen Reyes: No, if you keep embeddings in Pinecone, you can skip Redwood embeddings step and only call reranker. Alternatively, you can use Redwood embeddings to replace your vector store pipeline and store in your DB — options are flexible.
[04:14] [04:30] Owen Reyes: Demo call — I'll run a real rerank with a mock top-10. (runs) Here's a sample response: list of doc ids and rerank scores, with brief explanation on why the model bumped doc X (Console highlights attention).
[04:50] Priya Nair: Console shows "explain"? that's helpful for triaging.
[04:53] Owen Reyes: We have a simple explain feature that surfaces tokens or phrases the model attended to most — it's heuristic and sometimes noisy.
[04:59] Ethan Cole: Security — what about data retention and encryption? we need SOC 2 plus KMS integration, and logs for audits.
[05:06] Maya Chen: Redwood is SOC 2 Type II. We provide KMS integration for private deployments and hosted with BYOK for enterprise customers; audit logs and request-level tracing are in Console. I'll attach the SOC2 summary and our security whitepaper.
[05:22] Priya Nair: Are request payloads stored? we have to avoid storing customer queries in plaintext for 90 days.
[05:27] Maya Chen: By default we retain logs for short windows for debugging, but enterprise pilots can opt out of retention, or set redaction. We also offer Private (VPC) deployments if retention policy can't be relaxed.
[05:40] Jamal Ortiz: On infrastructure — how does fallback work if a model variant is down? we need graceful degradation.
[05:45] Owen Reyes: Smart routing: requests can failover from a high-perf replica to a smaller cheaper variant. Redwood supports canarying and automatic fallback to compatible quantized models so your app sees a result even if perf model is overloaded.
[05:59] Priya Nair: And billing — is it per token for reranker?
[06:03] Maya Chen: Rerank is priced per API call plus per-token compute for the embedding/generation portion. We'll provide an example pricing sheet. For pilots we often cap spend and provide trial credits.
[06:15] [06:30] Owen Reyes: Back to Console: Optimize tab here suggests batch size 8 for our traffic pattern, and cache TTL of 12 hours for doc embeddings. It estimates 27% cost savings and 18% p95 improvement for the sample workload.
[06:45] Priya Nair: How do you measure quality/regression? we can't afford rank regressions when changing models.
[06:51] Owen Reyes: We have evals tied to prompt sets — you can upload a labelled validation set (query + ideal doc ranking) and Console will run A/B tests and monitor NDCG/precision changes across model rollouts. It will block a rollout if quality drops beyond threshold.
[07:09] Ethan Cole: Integrations — we run k8s on GCP with private networking. can Redwood call into our Pinecone instance over VPC peering?
[07:16] Maya Chen: For hosted API we support private networking options through Redwood Dedicated or Private (VPC) with secure connectors. For pilot we often use mutual TLS and IP allowlists; for production we recommend VPC connectors.
[07:30] Jamal Ortiz: Latency with a VPC connector — any overhead?
[07:33] Owen Reyes: Minimal. There's an extra hop but usually within a 5-15ms window depending on region. We'll quantify during pilot.
[07:42] [08:00] Priya Nair: Show us an example where we keep Pinecone and call Redwood only for reranking — how do we pass metadata?
[08:06] Owen Reyes: In the rerank payload you can pass an array of candidate objects: {id, text, metadata}. We'll accept up to 100 candidates inline; larger sets can be referenced by id and Redwood will fetch if you give us a read-only connector.
[08:22] Sofia Ruiz: Connector — is that a service account we hand you?
[08:25] Maya Chen: It's read-only credentials with limited scope. We can also accept pre-signed fetch URLs for docs.
[08:32] [09:00] Owen Reyes: (runs a small script) here's a notebook run: 1) embed query (if desired), 2) fetch top 50 from Pinecone, 3) call rerank endpoint with top 50 docs. I'll paste the exact curl/snippet to the chat.
[09:20] Jamal Ortiz: If we have long documents, do you chunk?
[09:23] Owen Reyes: Yes, we recommend chunking at ingestion and storing chunk embeddings. Reranker can accept score-collapsed results to map chunk scores back to parent doc. Console has a chunking template and recommended chunk size per domain.
[09:38] Priya Nair: We have a multi-lingual dataset — will rerank work for non-english?
[09:43] Owen Reyes: We support multiple languages in our embeddings models. Reranker models are trained primarily on english but we have multilingual variants; quality varies. We'll run a quick evaluation if you share a sample set.
[09:56] [10:30] Ethan Cole: Benchmarks — can you run our 1k sample queries against your hosted instance? we want real p95 numbers.
[10:35] Maya Chen: Absolutely — that's a standard pilot step. Owen will help run the benchmarks; we'll need your sample set and an account or temporary API key.
[10:45] Owen Reyes: For the pilot we usually do a 30-day sandbox with capped spend. We'll use your sample queries, pin a model variant, and gather p50/p95/p99 plus cost estimates.
[10:56] Priya Nair: How do we handle personalization signals? we enrich candidate docs with feature metadata — can reranker consume those features?
[11:02] Owen Reyes: Yes, candidate objects can include metadata fields, numeric features, recency, user-level signals. Reranker can accept structured features and we can pass them into the scoring architecture. Note: features affect tokenization overhead slightly if embedded as text.
[11:20] Jamal Ortiz: Any limit on candidate size?
[11:23] Owen Reyes: There's a practical size: up to ~100 candidates inline with reasonable snippet lengths. We recommend returning short snippets and the rest of doc in metadata.
[11:34] [12:00] Priya Nair: What's the friction for rolling to production? we want to start with a small endpoint, then scale.
[12:06] Maya Chen: You can start with hosted pilot (no infra changes), then move to Dedicated once you need reserved capacity and tighter SLAs, or Private for VPC/on-prem. Rolling is a config change — you pin model versions and set rollout policies in Console.
[12:18] Sofia Ruiz: Do you support canarying by percent of traffic?
[12:21] Owen Reyes: Yes, Console supports per-route canarying and automatic rollback if metrics degrade.
[12:27] [13:00] Owen Reyes: Quick note about cost optimization: choose smaller rerank models for lower-latency use cases, use cached doc embeddings to skip recompute, and batch rerank requests when feasible. Optimize will simulate cost savings and show token-level breakouts.
[13:20] Priya Nair: For mobile clients, can we batch multiple queries from a session?
[13:24] Owen Reyes: You can create batched rerank requests server-side; client should send session-level hints. Batching improves throughput but may add latency for small QPS.
[13:36] [14:00] Ethan Cole: Any customers who've migrated from using only Pinecone + client-side rerank to your hosted rerank?
[14:05] Maya Chen: Yes — a retailer moved rerank server-side and saw 30% lower client complexity and 20% improvement in ranking quality due to richer model features. I'll get you a reference.
[14:15] Priya Nair: Ok that helps.
[14:18] [14:30] Owen Reyes: Now I'll show the Console Relevance Lab: you can upload eval sets, run A/B, and get NDCG plots. here's a run where model B slightly improved NDCG@10. you can set alert thresholds.
[14:48] Jamal Ortiz: Will you run continuous evaluation?
[14:50] Owen Reyes: Yes, Console can run scheduled evaluation jobs or ad-hoc. You can wire alerts to Slack.
[14:57] Sofia Ruiz: Are alerts per-route?
[15:00] Owen Reyes: Per-route and per-model.
[15:04] [15:30] Priya Nair: One more on security — SSO, RBAC? we have internal access controls.
[15:34] Maya Chen: We support SSO/SAML, SCIM for provisioning, role-based access controls in Console, and audit trails.
[15:42] Ethan Cole: For compliance we'll need encryption-at-rest and in transit.
[15:45] Maya Chen: AES-256 for rest, TLS1.2+ in transit, and KMS for key management. We'll include the cryptography section in the package.
[15:57] [16:00] Owen Reyes: Quick Q&A lightning:
[16:03] Jamal Ortiz: Are retries idempotent?
[16:05] Owen Reyes: Yes, requests include idempotency keys for most write operations.
[16:08] Priya Nair: Can we run a smoke test in our staging?
[16:10] Maya Chen: Yes — we'll provide staging credentials for pilot.
[16:12] [16:30] Owen Reyes: I'll paste the notebook, the curl examples, and a link to Console Relevance Lab into the chat now. (pastes)
[16:42] Priya Nair: Seeing the examples is helpful. question — do you support rerank explanations as structured tokens or just text blobs?
[16:50] Owen Reyes: Mostly text heuristics today; structured saliency is on the roadmap. Some customers export token-level saliency via the SDK.
[16:58] Sofia Ruiz: Timeline — if we approve the security docs this week, can pilot start next week?
[17:02] Maya Chen: Yes, timeline is tight but doable — pilot kick-off next Tuesday possible.
[17:12] Ethan Cole: Any risks for us?
[17:14] Maya Chen: Main risk is model quality mismatch; we'll mitigate via evals and pinned rollouts. Also network setup for connectors might take a few days.
[17:26] [17:30] Owen Reyes: Recap: demo'd embeddings + rerank flow, Console Optimize recommendations, evals and monitoring, and security options. We'll run benchmark with your 1k sample once you share it.
[17:42] Priya Nair: Next steps noted. we'll get the sample set and security questionnaire back.
[17:48] Maya Chen: Great — I'll share the SOC2, security whitepaper, pilot pricing, and Owen's rerank notebook. Thanks everyone.
[17:55] Ethan Cole: Thanks.
[18:00] Jamal Ortiz: Thanks all.
[18:04] Sofia Ruiz: Bye.

[Neon-orchestrated attention: hybrid Flash + kernel tiler with lazy-KV streaming]
description:
Summary: Introduces a neon-orchestrated hybrid attention path that combines a lightweight FlashAttention-style fast path with a tiled microkernel fallback. The patch adds a tiler that decides at runtime between (1) the optimized Flash micro-path for dense short sequences and (2) a new neon-prefetch tiled kernel for long contexts and odd sequence-lengths. Additionally this PR implements a lazy-KV streaming integration: instead of allocating/evicting large KV pages eagerly, the runtime streams KV slabs on demand and performs background prefetch with priority hints from the batcher. Motivation: our production traces show two dominant sources of per-token latency and cost: kernel selection overhead for mixed-length workloads and expensive full-KV swaps on long-context workloads. The hybrid path reduces kernel dispatch overhead and keeps the fast Flash path density benefits while the tiler maintains throughput on longer sequences. Design notes: - Kernel Tiler: a lightweight heuristic that computes tile sizes based on seq_len, k/v cache hits, and device utilization. Tiler exposes hints to the scheduler (tile_size, prefetch_priority, use_flash_path). - Flash micro-path: minimal changes to the existing Flash bridge to support neon-friendly memory layout and allow partial-row processing for non-4x head dims. - Neon tiled kernel: a new microkernel optimized for moderate tile sizes (32..256) with streaming prefetch and FP16 accumulation; includes an in-kernel rotary index remap to avoid extra memory passes. - Lazy-KV streaming: KV is broken into logically contiguous slabs. When a request needs a slab not present, we schedule an async prefetch and continue with partial KV (best-effort) to maintain tail latency. Background prefetching uses LRU+priority hints from the tiler. - Scheduler integration: continuous-batcher emits per-request hints (hot_token_prefix, expected_future_tokens) so the runtime favors coalescing requests that share KV slabs. - Fallback semantics: graceful fallback to the tiled kernel if flash_path fails or when the tiler estimates minimal benefit. Implementation touches: serving/runtime/tiler/* (core tiler & heuristics), serving/runtime/kvcache/streamer.* (lazy slab manager + prefetch worker), serving/runtime/kernels/neon_tiled_attn.* (new kernel), serving/runtime/kernels/flash_bridge adjustments, tests/perf/bench_attn_tiler.py, docs/attn_tiler.md. Testing & benchmarks: - Microbenchmarks across sequence lengths 8..16384, heads 8..64, model dims 1024..6144. - Canary on dedicated pools (pool-attn-4g). Results (canary): p50 latency -6%, p95 latency -12% on mixed-length workloads (avg seq ~512), throughput +18% on long-context workloads, token-cost -9% (due to fewer KV churns). Rollout plan: canary to 5% dedicated capacity for 48h, monitor tail latency, KV cache miss rate, memory OOMs. If no regressions, gradual increase over 7 days. Migration notes: no API changes. Config flags: runtime.tiler.enabled (default: true), kvcache.lazy_streaming (default: false) — kvcache.lazy_streaming off by default during initial rollout. Checklist: - [x] Design doc (ENG-1842) - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] Perf harness runs - [x] Canary plan - [x] Docs update - [x] Security review (no new surface) Known limitations: streaming introduces additional background IO which can increase memory churn under extreme concurrency; tiler heuristics are intentionally conservative and will be tuned as we gather telemetry. Backwards compatibility: existing model pins and rollouts remain unaffected.

[adaptive-kernel-selection-and-fused-rotary-reshape-with-kv-reservation]
description:
Motivation: long-tail inference workloads (mixed sequence lengths and multi-tenant bursts) expose inefficiencies in a single-kernel dispatch strategy and occasionally trigger noisy KV cache pressure. This PR implements an adaptive kernel selector that chooses between two optimized attention kernels at runtime (small-seq fastpath + wide-seq streaming fastpath), introduces a small fused rotary-reshape CUDA kernel to remove redundant transposes when rotary embeddings are used, and adds a lightweight KV reservation mechanism to reduce eviction churn under bursty continuous-batching.

What this PR does (high level):
- Runtime kernel selector: heuristics based on sequence length, batch shape distribution, and available SM occupancy to pick best kernel per request group. Selector lives in serving/runtime/attn/kernel_selector.cpp and exposes a stable decision API so other schedulers can consult it.
- Fused rotary-reshape: new CUDA kernel fused_rotary_reshape.cu removes an intermediate permute and reduces memory traffic for rotary-enabled models (~1.6x reduction in transient mem ops on long sequences). Hooked into the kernel code path when rotary flags are detected.
- KV reservation: add kv_reservation.h/.cpp that lets the continuous batcher reserve a bounded KV budget for in-flight canary/cold requests so we avoid evicting hot prefixes during transient spikes. Implemented conservative default: 8% reservation per model instance, configurable in runtime config.
- Batching/backpressure tweaks: continuous_batcher now exposes a backpressure token check and will fall back to the small-seq kernel earlier to meet p95 latency SLOs for short requests.

Checklist: 
- [x] Kernel selector implementation + unit tests
- [x] CUDA fused rotary-reshape implementation + correctness tests
- [x] KV reservation mechanism + e2e smoke test
- [x] Bench harness changes and new benchmarks
- [x] Docs: perf rationale and flags in docs/perf/attn_kernels.md

Performance summary (bench running on p4d-like staging infra, mixed workload):
- End-to-end token throughput +13-17% on 2048-8192 seq mix for a 16-GPU pool when selector chooses wide-seq kernel.
- Memory transient traffic reduced ~1.6x for rotary models when fused kernel engaged.
- p95 latency for short seq requests unchanged (<2% regressions in noise runs).
- KV eviction events under bursty load reduced ~45% in microbench.

Compatibility and rollout: changes are backward-compatible. Selector defaults to conservative thresholds and can be disabled with runtime flag REDWOOD_ATTN_KERNEL_SELECTOR=off. Fused rotary kernel used only when model metadata reports rotary format. KV reservation is conservative and tunable. Rollout plan: gradual canary (10% traffic) for 48h then 50% -> 100% after monitoring.

[vector-bridge tiled Q/K batching and rope rematerialization for lower-latency attention]
description:
Motivation: reduce tail latency for medium-length sequences (128-1024) on multi-model serving by combining tiled Q/K micro-batching with a lightweight 'vector-bridge' rematerialization for rotary/rope state. This PR introduces a runtime-attention path that trades negligible peak memory for consistently lower p95 latency when continuous batching is active and KV cache occupancy is moderate.

What changed (high level): introduced a new attention execution path (vector-bridge) that: 1) tiles Q/K into fixed-size micro-tiles to better utilize SIMT on Ampere+ GPUs, 2) applies a compact rematerialization for rotary/rope phase factors to avoid storing large precomputed tensors in the KV cache, and 3) adds a scheduler hint so continuous-batcher can preferentially group compatible sequence-length requests into the same micro-batch.

Design notes: the vector-bridge is not a wholesale replacement for existing fused attn kernels. It is registered as a selectable kernel and chosen by the kernel-selector when (a) sequence length distribution matches tiled thresholds, (b) model metadata lists rope/rotary usage, and (c) the container has >= 2 concurrent streams. The rematerialization computes per-head sin/cos on-the-fly using a compact 1D table + linear interpolation for frequencies that fall between table entries; we validated numerical parity within 1e-5 for typical rotary implementations.

Implementation summary: single PR that touches the runtime, kernel registry, scheduler, and a lightweight CUDA microkernel: commits include a microkernel implementation (vector_bridge_attn.cu), a kernel selector heuristic (kernel_selector.cpp), scheduler hint plumbing (continuous_batcher.cpp), updates to the KV cache layout to hold a compact rope token descriptor (kv_cache.h), and tests/bench harness updates. A new unprivileged integration test drives mixed sequence workloads and asserts latency and correctness.

Benchmarks (representative): on p4d-like instance, BPE tokenizer workloads: - median latency: -8% vs current best fused kernel, - p95 latency: -18%, - throughput at 99ms SLO: +12% effective throughput. Memory: peak GPU working set increased by ~3-6% depending on batch packing. Bench harness and raw data included under test/bench/vector-bridge/bench-2026-02-17.log.

Compatibility & rollout: kernel is opt-in via a runtime feature flag (--enable-vector-bridge). Default kernel selector will only pick it for models that opted-in via model metadata (model.yaml: runtime-kernels: [vector-bridge]) to avoid surprise behavior. We included a canary rollout plan in the PR checklist.

Testing & CI: unit + integration + small-scale GPU smoke tests included. Long-running perf suite executed in CI as a separate gated job.

Rollback plan: revert selector registration if any correctness/regression is observed; fallback to fused-attn or flashbridge kernels automatically if numerical checks fail at runtime.

Checklist: - [x] Kernel implementation and tests - [x] Kernel selector heuristic - [x] Scheduler hint + continuous-batcher integration - [x] Model metadata opt-in - [x] Benchmarks and logs attached - [x] Docs snippet for operators guide

Related: links to linear tickets: ENG-4821, ENG-5073.

Notes: this PR focuses on medium sequence workloads; large sequence (>4096) still prefer the tiled long-attn path and small (<64) prefer scalar-fused path.

[Introduce non-blocking FlashBlit attention kernel with hybrid prefetch and rotary rematerialization]
body:
Summary: This PR introduces a new attention execution path (FlashBlit) and a scheduler hinting flow that together reduce tail latency and improve throughput for mixed-length workloads. FlashBlit is a hybrid FlashAttention-like microkernel that implements a non-blocking prefetch strategy, lightweight rematerialization of rotary embeddings (rope), and a KV warmup path for continuous batching. The change is opt-in via the kernel selector and gated by a rollout feature flag. Motivation: Production traces show a disproportionate number of short/medium requests blocking on heavy kernel launches and KV warmups during bursty traffic. Existing kernels are highly optimized for single-call throughput but exhibit stalls in continuous-batching scenarios and when rotary rematerialization occurs for long sequence offsets. FlashBlit targets the hot path to avoid stalls by overlapping memory operations, reducing global synchronization, and reducing rematerialization overhead on rotary/rope.

What this PR does (high level):
- Adds flashblit/ directory with the FlashBlit kernel interface and CUDA/C++ microkernel glue (non-blocking prefetch + fused qkv layout path).
- Introduces a new scheduler hint "stride_prefetch" that tells the batcher when to issue non-blocking staged prefetches for upcoming KV strips.
- Implements rotary rematerialization helpers that avoid full KV reconstruction by applying compact rotary deltas on the fly (rope-remat.cu).
- Adds a KV warmup async path that performs background KV population for continuous-batching sessions (KV warmup broker and TTL heuristics).
- Kernel selector updates: detection heuristics prefer FlashBlit for seq_len in [64,2048] when stride_prefetch is available and when model layout matches fused-QKV.
- Adds unit and integration tests, microbenchmarks, and a rollout plan in the console configuration.

Commits (summary):
- commit 1: core: add FlashBlit kernel interface, registration, and initial CPU fallback (ava/flashblit/init)
- commit 2: cuda: non-blocking prefetch implementation, rope-remat helpers, fused qkv path (ava/flashblit/cuda)
- commit 3: scheduler: stride_prefetch hint and kv-warmup broker + metrics (ava/flashblit/scheduler)
- commit 4: tests/bench: microbench harness for FlashBlit, perf targets and CI checks (ava/flashblit/tests)
- commit 5: docs: runtime notes and rollout flags (ava/flashblit/docs)

Files changed (high level):
- src/runtime/kernels/flashblit/{flashblit.h,flashblit.cu,rope-remat.cu} (new)
- src/runtime/scheduler/stride_prefetch_hint.cc (new)
- src/runtime/kv/kv_warmup_broker.cc (new)
- src/runtime/kernel_selector/selector.cc (updates to prefer flashblit under heuristics)
- tests/perf/flashblit_microbench.cc (new)
- docs/runtime/flashblit.md (new)
- build/BUILD.bazel and CMakeLists.txt updates for new targets
- python/tests/test_flashblit_integration.py (adds an end-to-end smoke test)

Benchmarks (internal):
- Setup: A2 medium GPU (8x A100-sim), mixed conversational workload with 60% short (<64), 30% medium (64-512), 10% long (>512). Continuous-batching enabled with batch window 16ms.
- Baseline: current flashbridge kernel with lazy-kv prefetch and standard rotary path.
- FlashBlit results: P50 ~ -4% latency, P95 ~ -9% latency, P99 ~ -11% latency for medium sequences. Token cost reduced ~15% measured via per-token GPU time breakdown. For long sequences (>1024) FlashBlit falls back to existing FlashBridge path (no regression observed at 95th percentile in those cases).
- Microbench: single-GPU token generation throughput improved 6-10% on fused-QKV models when non-blocking prefetch triggers were hit.
- Note: We measured a small (~1.5%) increase in CPU-side scheduling overhead due to background KV warmup management; this is within acceptable bounds for the throughput improvements.

Compatibility and rollout: FlashBlit is behind the runtime kernel selector. Default behavior on main remains unchanged. Admins can toggle feature flag 'runtime.enable_flashblit' in the console/rollout config. Initial rollout plan: 10% traffic -> 25% -> 50% -> 100% across dedicated pools with canary metrics watching P99 and generation correctness.

Correctness and tests: Unit and integration tests added. We added a randomized reference test comparing outputs between flashblit and the canonical CPU attention to ensure numerical fidelity within FP16 tolerances. Additional regression suite compares token-level logits for a set of canonical prompts (seeded RNG).

Metrics and observability: New metrics exported:
- runtime.flashblit.prefetch_attempts_total
- runtime.flashblit.prefetch_hit_ratio
- runtime.flashblit.rope_remat_invocations
- runtime.kv.warmup_jobs_active
We added per-request tagging to allow per-model rollout visibility in the console.

Review conversation (high level, chronological):
- Marcus Lee: "Interesting approach — non-blocking prefetch should help tails. Two asks: add a synthetic test that simulates bursty arrivals and show the KV warmup doesn't cause memory pressure; and ensure the rope-remat path has a fallback when rotary base offsets are nonstandard."
- Ava (author): "Added bursty-arrival synthetic test (tests/perf/flashblit_bursty_test) and KV warmup uses soft caps with LRU evict TTL. rope-remat now detects nonstandard offsets and falls back to full remat. See commit 3 and tests."
- Priya Raman: "Can we avoid a behavioral change for streaming APIs? Also, please add metrics for prefetch failures so we can instrument rollout."
- Ava: "Streaming APIs unchanged; prefetch hints are only used at scheduler level and do not alter streaming control flow. Added runtime.flashblit.prefetch_failures_total."
- Diego Alvarez: "Small nit on API names and a race I found in the warmup broker shutdown path."
- Ava: "Fixed broker shutdown race by introducing a drain barrier and added unit test for broker shutdown (tests/kv/test_broker_shutdown.cc)."
- Priya: "Approving after CI pass and benchmark numbers are reproduced in the canary cluster."

CI and gating: All CI checks pass on mainline (unit tests, python integration smoke tests, and microbench correctness). GPU integration runs required rerun once due to transient docker pull timeout; rerun green. Performance regression checks run as part of a separate microbench job and indicated improvements above. The repo-level pre-merge lint and static analysis flagged a missing CUDA kernel comment — fixed in follow-up commit.

Risk assessment and mitigations: Risk: new kernel may introduce subtle numerical divergence for FP16 models; Mitigation: randomized numerical comparison test and canary rollout. Risk: KV warmup could increase memory footprint; Mitigation: soft caps, TTL-based eviction, metrics, and immediate rollback flag in console.

Rollout checklist (in PR):
- [x] Unit tests for kernel interface and remat helpers
- [x] Integration smoke test (python)
- [x] Performance microbench reproducing baseline improvements
- [x] Metrics instrumented and dashboards added (docs/runtime/flashblit.md)
- [x] Rollout flag implemented in console config
- [x] Docs and runtime notes

Merge outcome: Merged to main via squash on 2024-11-12 after approval from two reviewers and green CI. Follow-ups: 1) add more kernel tiling options (ENG-1491), 2) extend flashblit for bfloat16 paths (ENG-1499).

Notes for release engineers: This is opt-in; no infra changes required for main. Add new kernel artifacts to the GPU packaging manifest when cutting runtime images. See docs/runtime/flashblit.md for feature flags and metric dashboards. If any stability regression is observed, flip 'runtime.enable_flashblit' to false in the console to disable dynamically.

release_notes:
Adds FlashBlit attention kernel with non-blocking prefetch and rotary rematerialization. Improves P99 latency by ~8-12% and token cost by ~15-20% on medium-length conversational workloads; opt-in behind kernel selector and a rollout flag.

[low-precision-path-allocator-and-kernel-hookups]
description:
Motivation: Continued work to reduce per-token cost and tail latency for low-precision inference. Prior PRs added isolated INT8/FP8 kernels and dequant fusion primitives; this change weaves those pieces into the serving runtime with a small, deterministic allocator and dispatch layer that routes requests to the best low-precision execution path based on model variant, sequence-length distribution, KV-cache state, and batching profile. The goal is pragmatic: improve throughput and p99 latency for production workloads while preserving correctness and fast fallback to FP16/FP32 when numerical risk is detected.

Summary of changes (single-shot): adds a LowPrecisionPathAllocator that makes per-request routing decisions, wires kernel dispatch tables for INT8 and FP8 fused-dequant paths, introduces lightweight per-worker hints to the continuous-batching scheduler to avoid head-of-line blocking when long sequences and small batches mix, and optimizes KV cache hot-path bookkeeping to reduce CPU overhead on cache-miss heavy workloads. Also includes microbench harness changes and canary rollout config for safe production enablement.

Why this is different: previous PRs provided kernels and fusion infra in isolation; this PR focuses on connecting those kernels into runtime scheduling and KV-cache-aware routing so that benefits are realized in end-to-end serving. It emphasizes deterministic allocation (no global locks), low-overhead decision logic, and explicit fallback rules when stability checks fail.

Behavioral details and invariants: allocator decisions are per-request at enqueue time and are stable for the request lifetime; dequant fusion is only selected when the model variant metadata marks weights as stable for fusion and dynamic range checks pass for the first token; KV cache uses an additional small per-request bitmap to avoid expensive lookups for fully warmed prefixes. Fallback to FP16 is immediate and logged when a numerical anomaly (NaN/Inf or outlier token likelihood shift exceeding a threshold) is detected.

Benchmark highlights (internal perf harness, 8xA100 p4d-like profile, mixed sequence lengths): INT8 fused-dequant path: +12% throughput, p99 latency -18% on chat-like traffic compared to baseline FP16 runtime; FP8 path: +8% throughput, p99 -10% for short-sequence-only workloads; KV cache bookkeeping optimization reduces CPU-side cache-miss accounting overhead by ~25% in high-concurrency tests. End-to-end cost projection (model-dependent) shows unit token cost reduction up to 20% in aggressive INT8 mode under production batching distributions. Full benchmark run artifacts attached to the PR.

Compatibility and safety: feature gated behind runtime flag low_precision.path_enabled and staged via canary config (release/ops/rollouts). No model format changes required. Contains extensive checks that prevent low-precision selection for models listed in a denylist or when model metadata lacks quant-stability hints.

Testing: unit tests for allocator heuristics, kernel routing, and fallback; integration tests with the continuous-batching scheduler and KV cache; regression tests exercising numerical stability thresholds. CI includes microbench regression checks on the perf lab.

How to exercise locally: run tools/perf/harness --profile=canary-int8 --model=gpt-medium --seq-distribution=chat-mix; the harness supports toggling low_precision.path_enabled. See docs/perf/low_precision_readme.md for experiment configuration and metrics artifacts.

References: related Linear ticket ENG-2145, earlier kernel PRs that added fused-dequant primitives and FP8 kernels.

Release strategy: deploy to a 5% canary for 48h with end-to-end latency/cost monitors and automatic rollback if p99 regresses beyond the configured SLO delta.

Checklist:
- [x] runtime allocator and dispatch implemented
- [x] kernel hookups and fused-dequant path enabled behind flag
- [x] KV cache bookkeeping optimization implemented
- [x] unit and integration tests added
- [x] perf harness runs and artifacts committed

Notes: this PR intentionally avoids aggressive auto-quant decisions; quant selection remains model-owner controlled until we have more confidence from cross-customer benchmarks.

review_comments:
Priya Menon: Can you add a short experiment that shows when the allocator would prefer FP16 despite INT8 availability? Reason: we need a clear example to justify operator overrides.
Luca Ortega: Added a test case that simulates a model with unstable dynamic ranges and verified the allocator chooses FP16; expanded the readme with an operator override note.
Sara Kim: The continuous-batching hint looks good; are there pathological cases where this increases tail latency? Suggest a stress test with interleaved very long sequences.
Luca Ortega: Added a stress bench in tools/perf and updated scheduler comments. Stress tests show minimal regression when long sequences are rare; if long sequences dominate, we fallback to a conservative scheduling mode.
Daniel Park: KV cache bitmap is elegant — can you confirm memory overhead per worker?
Luca Ortega: Bitmap is 64 bytes per request slot by default (configurable); added comment and a unit test asserting memory bounds.
Priya Menon: Approved after perf data added.

release_notes:
Introduces a runtime-low-precision allocator that routes requests to INT8/FP8 fused-dequant kernels when safe, reduces p99 latency and improves throughput for many production batching patterns; gated behind feature flag and staged via canary rollout. See docs/perf/low_precision_readme.md for usage.

description:

The package must be suitable for handoff to an external incident response vendor and include: a canonicalized newline-delimited JSON export, SHA-256 manifests for each file, a signed index file (timestamped and KMS-attested), and a short verification guide. Impact: Customer needs this for an ongoing third-party incident response and regulator notification. They cannot proceed with containment and reporting without a verifiable audit bundle. Environment: prod/us-east (multi-tenant org with four sub-tenants). Requested format: NDJSON (UTF-8), UTC timestamps canonicalized to RFC3339, per-record event IDs retained, and per-tenant envelope. Delivery method: Pre-signed S3 objects in a customer-provided bucket (they will provide a cross-account role), plus an additional gzip-compressed tarball signed with Redwood's code-signing key. Security requirements: do not include full message payloads for events flagged PII-SENSITIVE; instead include a redaction manifest showing which fields were removed and a reversible pseudonymization map accessible only to Peregrine under an HMAC-wrapped envelope. Steps to reproduce / produce request: 1) Customer asked through account team with incident reference PEREG-IR-2026-02; 2) Support to validate retention window and tenant scoping; 3) Support to coordinate with SRE/archiving to generate export and KMS-signed index. [Per-tenant sequenced audit delivery with gap proof, signed resume tokens, and security questionnaire bundle for EU banking review]
description:
Issue summary:
Customer requests a formal evidence bundle and delivery verification for per-tenant sequenced audit events. [SmartPath: hybrid runtime heuristic for kernel allocation balancing prefill priority and tail-latency in mixed-length workloads]
description:
Goal: Reduce 95th/99th-tail latency for mixed workloads (short chat turns + long prefill jobs) while minimizing per-token cost. SmartPath is a hybrid heuristic that combines a compact runtime fingerprint with a lightweight online cost model to pick kernel implementations and prefill/decode scheduling decisions per GPU node and per-request.

Problem context: Our fleet frequently serves mixed traffic where the distribution of sequence lengths changes quickly (e.g., bursts of short chat with occasional long-context completions). Current static kernel routing or global seqlen buckets either overprovision for worst-case (increasing cost) or under-provision for tail latency (causing SLA violations). We need a per-worker, low-overhead tuner that: 1) recognizes transient shifts in seqlen distribution, 2) prefers low-latency kernels for short-decode paths, and 3) safely falls back to throughput-optimized kernels for sustained long-prefill workloads.

Approach summary:
- Runtime fingerprint: stream lightweight metrics per-worker (recent 1k requests): median and 90th/95th seqlen, recent decode token rate, average KV cache hit ratio, and short-job fraction. These are encoded into a 6-d fingerprint vector stored in shared memory (small fixed-size).
- Cost model: approximate per-kernel cost surfaces built from microbenchmarks (tokens/sec, warmup penalty, memory headroom) per architecture class (A100, H100, L4). We compress the empirical tables into a small lookup grid plus linear interpolation to keep evaluation cheap.
- Decision rules: a two-stage policy. First, map fingerprint -> kernel candidate set using thresholded rules (short-high-priority, long-throughput, mixed-hybrid). Second, run a policy comparator that factors in estimated latency impact, rollback risk, and expected unit cost. Includes a fast safety-check that prevents switching if there are >N active long-prefill jobs.
- Prefill/Decode scheduling: when a kernel switch is expected to increase prefill throughput at the cost of decode latency, SmartPath can schedule long-prefill jobs into a separate per-node queue processed during idle intervals or routed to reserved dedicated pools if configured.

Why different from previous work: Many existing tickets focus on global or seqlen-bucketed autotuners. SmartPath favors per-worker transient detection and explicit prefill scheduling with a small safety envelope for rollback. The emphasis is on low memory and compute overhead so the heuristic can live in the hot path of the serving agent without adding tracing or heavy profiling cost.

acceptance_criteria:
Proof-of-concept SmartPath enabled on 2 dev clusters (A100 & H100) with runtime flag
Measured 20-40% reduction in 95th latency for a synthetic mixed workload (50k reqs) vs baseline kernel routing
No more than 5% increase in mean cost per token across mixed workload experiments
Safe rollback path implemented (configurable cooldown and active-job threshold)
Unit + integration tests covering fingerprint stability and decision-rule boundaries
Design doc (Confluence) and benchmarking notebooks published and linked from ticket

[Hybrid tiered prefill-decode arbiter with opportunistic fast-paths and fairness budgets]
description:
Background: current prefill/decode arbitrator favors strict token-based fairness and coarse timeout heuristics. That approach provides good long-term throughput but causes noticeable latency spikes for latency-sensitive customers during mixed workloads (short chat vs long-completion). Proposal: implement a hybrid, tiered arbiter that classifies incoming requests into latency tiers and applies an opportunistic fast-path plus a budgeted fairness mechanism to avoid starvation of high-cost requests. Goals: 1) reduce P50/P95 latency for tiered-latency requests by 20-30% without increasing cluster token cost by more than 5%; 2) prevent >1% increase in long-request tail (>1k tokens) completion time; 3) keep scheduler overhead CPU <3% of runtime process.

design_decision_summary:
We will not pursue a pure priority queue because it leads to starvation. Instead, requests get a latency_tier label (L0: latency-sensitive, L1: balanced, L2: throughput/batch). Each tier receives an initial token budget per sliding window and a soft deadline. The arbiter grants prefill and decode slots preferentially to L0 up to budget, but allows opportunistic fast-paths: short-prefill fast-pass for requests whose estimated prefill tokens < X and expected decode length < Y. Long requests can be 'stealed-from' no more than Z tokens per window to satisfy L0 demands. The arbiter runs a lightweight scoring function: score = base_priority + urgency_boost - cost_penalty, with tunable coefficients. We will implement the arbiter as a runtime plugin to keep rollout safe and enable A/B tests.

tradeoffs_and_risks:
Risk: extra context switches if the arbiter preempts decode streams too aggressively — mitigation: limit preemptions per-request and prefer cooperative handoffs.
Tradeoff: short-prefill fast-path improves latency but may reduce batching efficiency; mitigation: fast-path only for requests where batching benefit < threshold and when CPU headroom exists.
Risk: KV cache thrash from interleaving many small prefills and large decodes — mitigation: sticky allocation for active contexts and cache-aware scheduling heuristics.
Tradeoff: fairness budgets introduce complexity in debugging billing spikes — mitigation: dashboarding and per-tenant budget traces, plus opt-out per-customer flag.
Risk: incorrect token cost estimates leading to misclassification — mitigation: use conservative estimates from model profiles and runtime feedback loop to recalibrate.

proposed_metrics:
prefill_latency_ms.P50/P95
decode_latency_ms.P50/P95/P99
tokens_per_request.average
batch_size_distribution
steal_count_per_window
budget_exhaustion_rate
cpu_overhead.scheduler_percentage
kv_cache_miss_rate

implementation_notes:
Componentization: 1) Classifier module (assigns latency_tier, estimates token cost) 2) Budget manager (sliding-window counters, per-tenant or per-route budgets) 3) Arbiter core (scoring + grant/steal logic) 4) Fast-path executor (short-prefill optimized flow) 5) Observability hooks (granular traces and budget metrics). We'll add feature flags and rollout gates: feature_flag.hybrid_arbiter and feature_flag.fastpath. Config surface: per-route latency_tier, budget_tokens_per_minute, steal_limit_per_window, fastpath_max_prefill, cost_coefficients. Implementation will live in runtime/arbiter plugin and expose a REST/Console page for threshold tuning.

experiment_plan:
Phase 1 (prototype): implement classifier + budget manager + simple grant logic in sandbox container and run synthetic mixes (80/20 short/long, uniform, heavy-long). Compare with baseline scheduler. Phase 2 (dogfood): enable on internal tenants with feature flag for 5% of traffic; collect metrics for 2 weeks. Phase 3 (ramp): A/B test against baseline in region us-west-2 for 25% traffic for 1 week. Success criteria: latency-sensitive P95 reduced >=20% and no >5% regression in long-request P99. Rollback if budget_exhaustion_rate > 10% or customer complaints > threshold.

prototyping_results:
Synthetic 80/20 short/long: P95 latency for L0 dropped 28% in prototype; average batch size decreased 12% leading to 3.7% token cost increase in microbenchmarks on A100-80GB nodes.
KV-cache miss rate rose initially by 0.9pp in worst-case mixes; adding sticky allocation reduced this to 0.2pp.
Scheduler CPU overhead measured at ~1.8% in prototype run at 5000 qps; acceptable for runtime-1.22 target.
Edge case: very-high-concurrency long-requests (>10k tokens) saw a small tail regression; we added 'long_request_protection' which reduces steal rate for requests flagged as important.

[Kernel concierge for bursty traffic with lightweight seqlen estimator and attention-lane optimizations]
description:
We need a lightweight, low-overhead kernel selection agent ("kernel concierge") that runs per-GPU instance and does fast per-request micro-profiling plus a burst-aware sequence-length estimator. The goal is to reduce 95th/99th percentile latency regressions during mixed workloads without heavy offline autotuning or full-stack re-profiling on every deployment. The concierge should: 1) use a tiny sampling prober on a small subset of requests to pick between attention implementations (blockwise, tiled, dense-optimized, quantized fallback), 2) incorporate a short-horizon seqlen predictor trained on request header histograms and recent traffic, 3) decide prefill vs decode kernel split points to reduce tail latency for short-prefill long-decode workloads, and 4) expose a trace tag for rollouts and diagnostics. This ticket scopes the design, prototype, and a non-invasive canary rollout on hosted infra.

acceptance_criteria:
Prototype implements a per-GPU agent that samples <=1% of traffic for microbenchmarks and logs selection decisions
Seqlen estimator achieves <10% median absolute error on recent traffic traces and is bounded in CPU usage (<2% on inference nodes)
95th percentile latency for mixed short-prefill workloads improves by >=8% in the canary cohort vs baseline for the same model/version
Fallbacks in the concierge prevent any latency degradation >2x for edge cases and are covered by automated tests
Logs include kernel_choice, seqlen_bucket, reason_code, and probe_id for every sampled request and are visualized on the runtime dashboard

Draft design doc and decision matrix for acceptable microprobe overhead
Implement lightweight microprobe harness and integrate with runtime kernel chooser API
Build a small seqlen estimator using exponential smoothing + histogram bucketing; collect training traces
Add prefill/decode split heuristic and safety throttles to concierge
Create unit and perf tests; run microbench suites on dev GPU farm
Instrument logging and dashboard panels for canary rollout
Run a two-week canary in hosted beta with 5% traffic; collect metrics and iterate

design_notes:
Trade-offs considered: 1) full per-model offline tuning vs lightweight online concierge. Chosen: concierge for faster adaptation and lower ops cost.
Microprobe design: warm up with 8 synthetic micro-batches that mimic observed seqlen buckets; measure decode and prefill kernels separately.
Seqlen estimator: use two-tier approach: short-term EWMA for immediate bursts and long-term histogram for bucket priors to avoid cold-start flips.
Safety nets: max_kernels_change_per_minute, probe_rate_decay_on_error, and quantized_fallback enforced to avoid regressions.
Memory/cpu budget: concierge must not exceed 512MB nor 2 CPU threads under typical load; probes limited by rate-limiter tied to tenancy tier.

risks:
Probe-induced noise on latency if sampling not isolated; mitigated by in-process probes and strict rate limits
Seqlen estimator mispredicts rare long-tail requests causing suboptimal kernel pick; mitigated by conservative fallback and decaying weight on estimator
Complexity of kernel matrix increases with new implementations (sparse, fused attn); maintainability concern
Telemetry volume increase from per-request tags; will add sampled logging only and aggregated counters

[Variance-Aware Slot Packing for Prefill/Decode to Reduce Padding Waste]
description:
Reduce token-padding overhead and improve throughput by introducing a variance-aware slot packing algorithm that coalesces prefill and decode requests into tightly-packed runtime slots based on sequence-length variance and latency targets.

background:
Current request coalescing uses coarse buckets by approximate length ranges. High variance within buckets leads to wasted tokens due to padding, especially on mixed workloads (short prompts + long context). This increases per-token cost and decreases effective throughput on Dedicated pools. Existing efforts (ENG-4721, ENG-62045) focus on bucket shaping; this ticket explores a different axis: slot-level packing with a lightweight scoring function that balances padding waste vs. scheduling latency.

proposed_solution:
Implement a slot packing layer in the prefill scheduler that: (1) computes a variance score for pending requests in short windows, (2) forms slots by merging requests with complementary lengths to reduce max-seqlen padding, (3) applies a latency-aware penalty so we don't hold short requests beyond a soft deadline, and (4) exposes a small kernel-selection hint (kernel_score) to the runtime to prefer single-kernel execution when effective sequence-length dispersion is low.

technical_notes:
Slot packing algorithm: greedy merge with max-slot-size cap and slack budget; compute benefit = sum(max_len_before - new_max_len) - latency_penalty
Latency penalty: exponential function of wait_time/soft_deadline (configurable per route) to avoid long-hold of short requests
Kernel hint: slot produces kernel_score vector {single_kernel_prefer: bool, preferred_block_size: int} written into RequestMeta passed to runtime scheduler
KV cache implications: prefill merges must preserve request->response KV index mapping; we will annotate slots with offsets and validate after decode
Backpressure: if slot formation delays cause queue growth past threshold, fallback to immediate dispatch (disable slot pack) for oldest items
Telemetry: emit slot_metrics (num_requests, max_len, wasted_padding_tokens, wait_time_ms, kernel_score) to Console metrics endpoint

acceptance_criteria:
Implemented slot-packing scheduler component behind a feature flag (runtime.slot_packing.enabled)
Integration tests validate correctness: no token duplication/lost KV cache, deterministic slot assignment under same seed
Observed >=10% reduction in median padding tokens per batch on mixed demo workload (short+long), measured on dedicated-gpu-small benchmark
P95 decode latency for short requests increases by <=5% compared to baseline (with flag off)
Kernel-selection hint flows end-to-end to runtime and produces same outputs as baseline when kernel choice differs (sanity test passed)

success_metrics:
padding_tokens_saved_percentage >= 10% on mixed workloads
overall tokens/sec improvement >= 6% on average across benchmarks
p50/p90 latency regressions < 3% for long requests and <5% for short requests
no user-facing error spikes or increased 5xx rate after rollout

testing_plan:
Unit tests for slot merge heuristics (edge cases: single very long request, many tiny requests, equal-length all)
Integration tests with runtime sim that verifies KV indexing and decode correctness
Performance bench: run mixed-synthetic workload (50% short <50 tokens, 50% long 800-1200 tokens) comparing baseline vs slot-packing on dedicated-gpu-small
Chaos test: induce transient load spike to ensure rollback kicks in and no request starvation occurs
A/B experiment runbooks and dashboards: latency buckets, padding token histogram, tokens/sec by model
Security review: ensure kernel_score does not leak sensitive user data (it's derived from length/variance only)

rollout_plan:
Phase 0: feature flagged rollout to internal canary only (redwood-dev cluster) for 72 hours
Phase 1: enable on 5% of hosted traffic + Dedicated low-traffic pool for 1 week, collect metrics
Phase 2: increase to 25% with automatic rollback on threshold breach (error rate or latency SLO violations), run A/B kernel performance measurement
Phase 3: full rollout to eligible Dedicated pools if metrics are green and SOCs approved

[Hybrid windowed coalescer for mixed-sequence workloads (continuous batching + KV reservation)]
description:
Design and implement a hybrid windowed coalescer (HWC) to improve end-to-end token throughput and tail latency for mixed prompt/response length workloads. HWC combines an entropy-based short-window coalescer for low-latency short prompts with an opportunistic long-window consolidator that absorbs long-response requests for GPU memory packing and KV reservation. The feature integrates with the KV cache watermarking system and GPU slab-aware allocator to reduce memory fragmentation and unnecessary evictions.

motivation:
Observed production workloads show highly skewed request length distributions (many short prompts interleaved with fewer very long responses). Existing continuous batcher either favors latency (thin windows) or throughput (thicker windows), leading to either wasted GPU cycles or long tail latencies and repeated KV evictions. HWC aims to adaptively split the request stream into short-latency lanes and throughput lanes while coordinating KV reservation and GPU slab packing to preserve SLOs and reduce unit cost.

technical_design:
HWC has three main components: (1) entropy estimator that computes a lightweight sequence-length and token-variance score per request to classify into lanes; (2) a dual-window coalescer: a fast-pass window (5-15ms) for low-entropy/short requests and a slow-pass window (20-80ms) for high-entropy/longer responses; (3) KV reservation & GPU packer that reserves a soft KV slab per slow-pass batch and requests GPU slab compaction when cross-batch packing improves utilization. The scheduler exposes per-route knobs: short_window_ms, long_window_ms, entropy_threshold, kv_soft_reserve_tokens, and slab_pack_aggressiveness. Watermarking: two thresholds (soft, critical) trigger different behaviors: soft watermark starts early eviction but prefers reservation for in-flight slow-pass batches; critical watermark disables slow-pass and forces short-pass only.

design_tradeoffs_decisions:
Use entropy estimator instead of strict token-count heuristics to better handle variable response lengths in streaming chat use-cases.
Short-window upper bound chosen as 15ms to maintain perceived interactivity; measured regression risk and kept conservative to avoid user-facing latency.
KV soft reservation is optimistic (pre-allocate logical tokens) rather than hard allocation to avoid blocking high-throughput lanes; this reduces worst-case reservation overhead but requires robust early-release logic.
GPU slab compaction may increase CPU orchestration overhead; we bias aggressiveness toward customer tiers with higher unit-cost sensitivity.
Fallback logic prioritizes availability over throughput: on critical memory pressure we revert to existing batching behavior to avoid OOMs.

success_metrics:
p50 token latency <= baseline+5% for short prompts
p99 request latency reduced by >= 15% for mixed workloads
GPU memory fragmentation (free slab ratio) reduced by >= 20% during long-response bursts
KV eviction rate down by >= 30% for customers with mixed-length dialogs
tokens/sec per GPU increased by >= 8% on representative benchmarks

acceptance_criteria:
HWC can be toggled per runtime via runtime config flag
Automated experiments show improved metrics on benchmark harness (see links)
No regression on existing latency-sensitive routes (canary tests passed)
Graceful fallback to current continuous-batcher when KV pressure > critical watermark
Documentation and console controls added for lane thresholds and KV reservation parameters

rollout_plan:
Feature branch merged behind feature flag (runtime.hwc.enabled)
Unit + integration tests in CI covering lane classification edge cases
Canary on internal dev cluster with synthetic mixed-length traffic
Gradual rollout to 5% production region traffic for non-SLA routes
Monitor metrics for 48 hours; if no regressions, expand to 25% and then 100% for candidate routes
Expose per-customer override and opt-out in Console until feature matures

testing_plan:
Synthetic harness: replay of mixed-dialog traces (internal dataset) against baseline and HWC; compare p50/p95/p99 latencies and KV eviction traces
Chaos tests: force KV cache pressure and ensure HWC disables slow-pass correctly
GPU memory profiling: measure slab fragmentation with and without slab compaction
A/B tests on a sampled set of accounts with telemetry for perceived latency and cost metrics
Load test: peak QPS with long-response bursts to verify no increase in error-rate or OOMs
