[Throughput ledger and pairwise comparison UI with anomaly triage workflow]
description:
Goal: Build a searchable, auditable "throughput ledger" that stores run-level and slice-level performance metrics (tokens/sec, p95 latency, p50, error rates) and a lightweight pairwise comparison UI for front-line engineers/PMs to rapidly assess regressions. Complement this with an anomaly triage workflow that can (1) surface probable regressions, (2) attach likely culprits (CI commit/PR metadata), and (3) provide an actionable runbook for the oncall/owner to follow.

Why: Current benchmark artifacts are fragmented across ad-hoc logs and CSVs; triage requires manual aggregation and repeated runs. We need a single source-of-truth for performance history with fast diffs, deterministic drilldowns, and a repeatable triage flow to reduce mean-time-to-detect-and-fix regressions in serving runtime and model variants.

acceptance_criteria:
Ledger stores per-run metrics including tokens_per_sec, p95_ms, p50_ms, total_tokens, error_rate, model_name, model_version, commit_hash, seq_len_bucket, and batch_config for >= 90% of benchmark runs
UI: Pairwise compare view shows baseline vs candidate with delta, percent-change, and statistical significance indicator (bootstrap/confidence band) for tokens/sec and p95
Slice heatmap: p95 and tokens/sec heatmap across sequence-length buckets and model variants in the compare UI
Automatic anomaly flagging: system flags run as REGRESSION when p95 increases by >10% AND z-score > 2 compared to 30-day rolling baseline
CI metadata linking: each flagged run shows linked commit/PR and a list of changed files (when available)
Triage workflow: flag creates pre-filled triage ticket template (title/body) and posts a summary to #bench-triage Slack channel
Runbook: triage playbook link included in UI and ticket; actions include re-run with controlled seeds, isolate model vs infra (e.g., quantized vs fp16), and revert-to-last-known-good
Performance: ledger query latency for last-30-days rollup < 600ms for common queries (model+seqlen slice queries)
Tests: end-to-end test that injects synthetic regression signals into a synthetic run and verifies alerting + ticket generation

tasks:
Design schema for ledger (primary keys, tags): model_name, model_version, commit_hash, run_id, seq_len_bucket, batch_config, metrics
Implement ingestion pipeline: canonicalize run metadata from CI, worker telemetry, and bench harness into ledger write path
Short-term store: ClickHouse/Timescale ingestion for fast queries and slices; long-term archive in S3 as partitioned Parquet
Implement regression detector service: compute rolling baselines, z-score, bootstrap confidence for p95 and tokens/sec
Backend API endpoints for pairwise compare and heatmap endpoints
Frontend: pairwise comparison page + heatmap overlay + delta table + commit links
CI integration: attach run_id and commit_hash in e2e bench runs; surface PR link when available
Alerting: wire anomaly detector to PagerDuty/Slack with adaptive thresholds per-model
Triage automation: generate pre-populated Linear ticket + add triage checklist and links to artifacts
Documentation: triage playbook, SLO impact matrix, and runbook for owners

technical_notes:
Metric keys: use explicit typed keys to avoid schema drift (tokens_per_sec:float, p95_ms:float, p50_ms:float, error_rate:float)
Sequence-length bucketing: [<=64, 65-256, 257-1024, >1024] to balance cardinality and signal fidelity
Delta fingerprint: compute a deterministic fingerprint per run (model+weights-hash+commit_hash+config) for fast grouping
Stat test: prefer bootstrap CI for small-sample p95 comparisons; fallback to z-score for large N; store sample histograms when available
Privacy: sample outputs hashed (sha256) when storing examples to enable regression repro without exposing PII
Storage: keep 90 days of high-resolution timeseries in ClickHouse, roll to S3 Parquet daily for retention beyond 90 days
Query patterns: optimize for pairwise comparison queries (baseline run id + candidate run id), and slice aggregations by seq_len_bucket and model_version
Failure modes: handle flaky runs by detecting multi-modal token/sec distributions across repeated runs; mark runs as FLAKY and exclude from baseline until stabilized
Cost control: sample full detailed traces on 1-in-20 runs and use aggregated metrics for every run to limit storage growth

notes_for_reviewers:
We should confirm the anomaly thresholds with product/owners on a per-model basis — default rule is p95 +10% AND z-score>2 but may be tuned
Design will provide Figma flows. Backend API should be generic to support future multi-run diffs (more than pairwise)
We will iterate on storage: start with ClickHouse for the MVP; evaluate cost vs latency after 2 weeks of production traffic
If engineering bandwidth is constrained, drop automatic ticket generation and keep Slack summaries only for MVP

[Public vs internal model metadata + release note redaction rules (enforcement, checklist, tests)]
description:
We are standardizing model/version metadata (schema v1) and generating customer-visible release notes from model metadata + change events. This introduces a high-risk class of issues: leaking internal-only details (e.g., incident references, customer names, vendor identifiers, internal eval artifacts, or security-sensitive remediation notes) into the public release notes feed (Console + docs + SDK endpoints).

This ticket defines the redaction rules and enforces them at generation time and at read time (RBAC), with a review checklist and automated test coverage.

Motivating incidents/near-misses:
- Console rollout UI briefly showed internal notes to non-admins (later hotfixed; see PR-18463).
- Docs build published an incomplete/incorrect note during a generator failure mode (see #incidents thread 1743604432).
- Support tickets requesting exact model change history while ensuring we don’t expose internal context in public feeds (SUP-28429).

Non-goals:
- Full end-user notification subscriptions (email/webhook) beyond internal plumbing.
- Rewriting all historical release notes (only minimal backfill).

proposal_summary:
Introduce an explicit visibility model for all human-authored fields used in changelog/release-note generation: public | restricted | internal. Enforce redaction in the generator pipeline (artifact creation), and also enforce at API/Console render time via RBAC. Provide deterministic unit tests and e2e tests to prevent regressions.

redaction_policy_v1:
Definitions:
- public: safe for customer-visible surfaces (Console release notes, docs site, public SDK endpoints).
- restricted: safe only for authenticated customer admins of the tenant/workspace (Console only), not for docs site; used sparingly for operationally useful detail (e.g., “roll back guidance”, “workaround”, additional compatibility detail) that isn’t sensitive but could be confusing at a broad public level.
- internal: Redwood employees only (internal admin tools, audit views), never on customer-visible surfaces.

Rule 1: Default deny
- Any freeform text field without an explicit visibility marker MUST be treated as internal.
- Generator must fail closed if it cannot determine visibility.

Rule 2: Explicit field allowlist for public
Only the following fields may be emitted into public release-note artifacts:
- title (public)
- summary (public)
- categories (public, from taxonomy)
- severity (public, from taxonomy)
- effective_date (public)
- affected_deployments (public)
- availability (public; deployment/region matrix limited to non-sensitive granularity)
- compatibility (public; model family compatibility, API behavior compatibility; must not include customer-specific routing rules)
- deprecation (public; timeline and impact language per style guide)
- rollback_guidance (restricted/public depending on content)
- links (public; only to docs URLs or generic guidance; no internal links)

Rule 3: Explicit forbidden content patterns (hard block)
If any public or restricted field contains:
- references to internal systems (e.g., linear keys ENG-/PM-/DES-, Jira INT- keys, internal Slack links, internal Confluence URLs)
- incident identifiers or postmortem links
- customer names, domains, or account IDs (unless explicitly approved and part of a customer-specific restricted note, which is out of scope for MVP)
- security vulnerability identifiers prior to public disclosure (CVE references allowed only after Security signs off; otherwise internal)
- infrastructure/provider identifiers that reveal sensitive topology (exact GPU hostnames, IPs, AZ identifiers, internal cluster names)
- credentials/secrets/tokens (obvious)
Then:
- public artifact generation MUST fail (CI + generator runtime), and log a structured internal error with redacted preview.

Rule 4: Soft redaction (sanitize) for restricted/internal
For restricted/internal artifacts, we allow internal references but they must not be rendered to public. Additionally, internal artifacts should replace secrets-like patterns with [REDACTED] even internally (defense in depth) and emit an audit event.

Rule 5: Links policy
- public/restricted links must match an allowlist of domains: docs.redwoodinference.com, console.redwoodinference.com/help, status.redwoodinference.com.
- internal links allowed only in internal visibility.
- If a link is disallowed, treat the field as internal or fail generation (configurable; MVP: fail for public, downgrade to internal for restricted).

Rule 6: Audience consistency across surfaces
- Anything that appears in docs site is public.
- Console release notes default to public, with an explicit toggle to view restricted (customer admin only) if present.
- Internal admin surfaces can view all three visibilities.

Rule 7: Auditability
- Every redaction or visibility downgrade must emit an audit event (ties to ENG-9828) containing: model_id, version, field_path, old_visibility, new_visibility, reason_code (pattern_match / domain_not_allowed / missing_visibility / unknown_field), actor (service), and trace_id.

Rule 8: Templating restrictions
- Templates must not interpolate internal fields into public variants. Templates should be split by audience rather than branching on if statements inside a single template (reduces footguns).

Rule 9: “Public summary” must be independently authored
- If internal notes exist, they must not be auto-summarized into public text. Public summary must be explicitly provided by the author or derived from safe structured fields (categories/severity/compat).

implementation_plan:
1) Schema-level changes (if needed)
- Add visibility markers to relevant metadata fields used by generator (or confirm existing public/internal split from ADR-0142). For MVP, implement at changelog entry level (the release-note payload) even if the underlying model metadata has more granular visibilities.

2) Generator enforcement (ENG-9823)
- Add a redaction module used by both event->artifact generation and preview generation in CI.
- Implement allowlist-based serialization for public artifacts.
- Add forbidden-pattern scanning for public + restricted fields (regex + heuristics).
- Implement link allowlist validator.
- Failure mode: if public artifact cannot be generated safely, generator emits only internal artifact and marks public artifact as blocked, with a reason and a remediation hint.

3) API/Console enforcement (ENG-9824)
- Backend endpoints must filter by viewer role:
  - public feed: only public visibility
  - console customer-admin: public + restricted
  - internal admin: all
- Ensure server-side filtering; UI must not rely on client filtering.

4) CI enforcement (ENG-9826)
- Add required checks: release note preview must include visibility annotations and must pass forbidden-pattern scan.
- PR fails if:
  - public fields include forbidden patterns
  - any new freeform note field lacks visibility
  - disallowed links present in public/restricted

5) Documentation + review checklist
- Add “Release notes safety checklist” to the style guide and the release process playbook, including examples of what NOT to include.

6) Backfill/fixtures
- Add fixtures covering:
  - safe public change
  - restricted change with workaround
  - internal-only change referencing incident
  - broken change with internal link in public field (must fail)

Owners/partners
- Eng owner: Sahana Iyer
- Security reviewer: Marcus Lin
- PM sign-off: Marissa Cole
- Docs partner: Wei Chen (for language + examples)

acceptance_criteria:
1) Generator produces three deterministic artifacts from the same event stream: public, restricted, internal (restricted optional).
2) Public artifact never includes internal-only fields; verified by unit tests and an e2e test.
3) Forbidden content patterns cause a hard failure for public artifact generation and block publishing (CI + runtime).
4) Console endpoints enforce server-side RBAC filtering; a non-admin cannot retrieve restricted/internal data via API.
5) Every redaction/downgrade emits an audit event with reason_code.
6) “Default deny” behavior is implemented: any unrecognized field or missing visibility is internal.
7) A documented checklist exists and is linked from the PR template / release process notes.

[Usage drift change-point orchestrator with tenant-aware suppression]
description:
Problem: We have high false positive noise from current usage/cost/latency alerts for multi-tenant customers. Several customers get repeated alerts during known operational windows (billing jobs, scheduled batch traffic), and the on-call burden is increasing. Goal: Build a change-point orchestrator that detects sustained distributional shifts in tenant-level metrics, correlates changes across cost/usage/latency dimensions, and applies tenant-aware suppression and deduplication so that only actionable incidents surface to on-call and product owners.

background:
Current pipeline emits per-tenant aggregates every minute into the metrics warehouse. Existing rule-based detectors run thresholds and percentile checks and send alerts to PagerDuty/Slack. Recent incident review (inc-2026-02-billing-spike) flagged >40% of alerts as noise during scheduled backend jobs. We need an automated detector that understands persistent drift vs transient spikes, reduces noise, and provides explainability for each alert (primary metric, magnitude, correlated signals, and suggested remediation).

design_decisions:
- Detection algorithm: prioritize a streaming change-point approach (Bayesian Online Change Point Detection) for low-latency tenant detection plus a daily batch re-evaluation using a robust non-parametric test (E-Divisive or ADWIN) for longer-term regressions.
- Correlation: correlate change-points across metrics (usage, cost, p95 latency) within a 10-minute window and surface combined incidents when >=2 metrics change for the same tenant.
- Suppression: allow policy-based suppression (schedule windows, exempted customers) and adaptive suppression that learns frequent scheduled patterns per-tenant.
- Deduplication: group alerts by tenant + root-cause signature; apply a suppression cooldown (default 6h) after an acknowledged alert.
- Explainability: include a short payload with change magnitude, normalized delta, top correlated routes/endpoints, and a sparkline of the last 6 hours in the alert message.
- Performance: detection must run within existing streaming worker budget (<=200ms additional per-tick) and scale horizontally across partitioned tenant shards.

acceptance_criteria:
1) New orchestrator ingests the same per-minute tenant aggregates and emits a change event stream to the alerting topic.
2) False positive rate for scheduled bulk jobs drops by >=60% in A/B test compared to baseline over 2 weeks.
3) Alert payload includes: primary metric, delta percent, correlated metrics list, recommended next steps, and a link to the tenant detail dashboard.
4) A suppression policy UI hook is plumbed into Console (API only for initial rollout) to mark scheduled windows for tenants.
5) End-to-end latency from metric write to alert event < 2 minutes for streaming-detected incidents.
6) Automated tests + integration test against synthetic drift scenarios are added to CI.

implementation_tasks:
- PR: streaming worker library change (partitioned detectors)
- PR: change-point service (stateless pods) + helm chart updates
- PR: alerting bridge to create structured alert with explainability fields
- DB: add per-tenant schedule table and adaptive suppression model store (key-value)
- Telemetry: dashboard panels and synthetic test harness
- Docs: runbook and run-through for on-call; API docs for suppression policy endpoints

telemetry_queries:
- sample SQL to compute baseline: SELECT tenant_id, percentile_cont(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY latency_ms) FROM metrics.minute WHERE ts >= NOW() - interval '14 days' GROUP BY tenant_id;
- change-point backtest: run sliding-window divergence score and export FPR/TPR per-customer;
- alert noise metric: count(alerts) FILTER (WHERE scheduled_tag=true) GROUP BY tenant_id over last 30 days

rollout_plan:
1) Canary: enable for 5 low-traffic tenants for 72h (monitor false positives and missed incidents).
2) Expand to 50 tenants with mixed profiles for 7 days while running in parallel with existing detectors (shadow mode).
3) Swap to primary detection for the broader tenant set once FPR target met.
4) Add suppression UI and customer toggle; default suppression off until customer opts in.
5) Post-rollout 14-day observation and revert plan in case of regressions.

risk_and_mitigation:
- Risk: missed true incidents during aggressive suppression. Mitigation: conservative default suppression; require >=2-metric correlation to suppress if magnitude high.
- Risk: compute cost. Mitigation: use tiered detectors (cheap heuristic first, expensive model only on candidates) and shard work by tenant partitions.
- Risk: explainability data volume in alerts. Mitigation: include summary + link to the dashboard instead of full time-series payload.

[Autodetect compilation strategy and staged pin workflow for MoE / GQA / MHA models]
description:
Objective: implement an automated onboarding flow that detects model attention architecture (standard MHA, grouped-query attention/GQA, and mixture-of-experts/MoE) and selects a tailored compilation strategy plus a staged pin/publish lifecycle for performance profiles.

Scope: changes touch the model-onboarder service, compile profiles database, runtime kernel selector, and Console rollout UI. The system should: 
- Autodetect attention variant at import time using lightweight bytecode/graph heuristics and a short sample-run signature.
- Generate a prioritized compile strategy set (microkernel choices, quantization-safe paths, KV-caching expectations) per architecture.
- Run a constrained compile+benchmark sandbox (on CI pool) against representative sequence-length buckets and batch shapes to produce candidate profiles.
- Publish profiles as: candidate -> canary (small percentage traffic) -> pinned. Each stage must record performance delta vs baseline and pass SLO/cost gates.
- Provide a manual override and rollback in Console and an API for automation (pin/unpin/promote).

Success criteria: 
- New onboarding flow correctly identifies architecture in >=98% of sampled models in our benchmark suite.
- Candidate-to-pinned promotions record <=5% perf regression risk (measured by distributional latency P95 and token cost).
- Console exposes per-profile telemetry and a one-click rollback.

Non-goals: automated kernel authoring or deep model surgery. We will rely on existing compiler transforms and kernel implementations; this effort coordinates selection and staged promotion, not new kernel research.

notes:
Trade-offs considered: conservative default to fall back to MHA-compatible kernels when detection confidence < 0.7 to avoid regressions vs. aggressive specialization that yields better throughput but higher risk.
Rollout plan: enable candidate profiles for internal tenants first, then open canary to 5% of production traffic for 48 hours with automatic rollback on SLO breaches.
Monitoring: compare pinned profile performance to baseline using a metric set (p95 latency, token-cost, headroom for throughput). Automated alerts on >7% p95 regression or >10% cost increase.

[Sequence emission atlas: per-step timing + KV cache influence attribution]
description:
Goal: build a production-safe token/step-level attribution pipeline that surfaces how much latency and downstream cost each emission (token or step) incurs and how KV cache behavior (hit/miss/warm) shifts those numbers. This ticket covers: 1) lightweight tracing hooks emitted by the serving runtime for every emission step, 2) a sampling and aggregation pipeline to reduce cardinality while preserving tail behavior, 3) a storage & query model for sequence-level heatmaps, and 4) dashboard widgets that highlight cache-influence and device skew.

Why this is different: existing instrumentation captures per-request totals and occasional token probes. We need continuous, queryable attribution without blowing up telemetry cost or adding tail latency. The approach taken here emphasizes delta attribution (per-step delta vs. request baseline), explicit KV cache annotations, and sequence-position-aware aggregation so product and infra teams can reason about where cost/latency concentrates in typical workloads.

Design summary:
- Tracing hooks: emit a minimal span for each emission step: fields = [request_id, model_version, device_id, step_index, token_length, start_ms, end_ms, kv_state]. kv_state is one of {cold_miss, warm_hit, warmed_during_sequence}. Spans must be emitted asynchronously to the metrics emitter to avoid blocking the runtime hot path.
- Sampling: adopt a two-tier sampler: deterministic head-sampling for the first N steps (N=8) on all requests + reservoir sampling of tail steps (p=0.003) with higher retention for requests that hit latency/error SLOs. This keeps heatmaps accurate for heads while still surfacing tail outliers.
- Aggregation & storage: ingest spans into a streaming aggregation job that emits two derived metrics sets: (A) sequence heatmap buckets (model x sequence-length-bucket x step-index-bucket) for visualization, and (B) per-device + per-model 99/95/50 percentile step timings annotated by kv_state. We'll store aggregated rows keyed by day and model so queries for dashboards are cheap.
- Dashboards & alerts: new dashboard panels in Console: "Emission Atlas" showing a stacked heatmap (latency density by step index), "KV Influence" showing % of total latency attributable to KV miss events, and a "Device Skew" panel to find devices with disproportionate tail latency. Add alerting on sustained (>30m) increase in kv-miss-attributed 95th percentile.

Acceptance criteria: 
- Runtime emits step spans with the required fields and does not increase p99 request latency by more than 0.5ms on our benchmark harness.
- Aggregation pipeline produces daily heatmap tiles for at least the last 28 days and exposes a REST endpoint for dashboard queries.
- Console contains two new panels (Emission Atlas, KV Influence) that load within 2s for 28-day queries.
- Alert rule and runbook exist for KV-miss-inflation incidents.

Implementation notes and trade-offs: 
- To avoid cardinality explosion we avoid attaching full prompt text to spans. A request-level prompt-hash can be correlated post-hoc if needed.
- Using reservoir sampling for tails means some individual outliers may be dropped; to mitigate, we force-retain any spans tied to request-level SLO violations.
- Initial rollout will be behind a feature flag with telemetry-rate soft limits so we can ramp without affecting billing.

Telemetry schema and storage pointers (implementation detail notes, not nested):
- span fields: request_id (string), step_index (int), start_ms (int), end_ms (int), elapsed_ms (float), kv_state (string), model (string), device (string), sequence_length (int)
- aggregated tiles: day, model, sequence_length_bucket, step_index_bucket, count, avg_ms, p50_ms, p95_ms, p99_ms, kv_miss_fraction

Rollout plan:
- Phase 1 (canary): enable for 1% of live traffic on staging devices, validate overhead and schema.
- Phase 2 (ramp): 10% -> 50% with alerts enabled; compare heatmaps vs. sampled probe baselines.
- Phase 3 (GA): default enable for hosted, opt-in for Dedicated/Private with config toggles and retention controls.

Runbook and privacy: do not send prompt text; only store prompt-hash when needed. Ensure KMS controls for telemetry export to partners.

Notes for reviewers: focus on sampling parameters, heatmap bucket definitions, and dashboard UI latency budget.

acceptance_criteria:
Runtime emits step spans with required fields and <0.5ms p99 overhead on benchmark
Aggregation pipeline produces 28-day heatmap tiles and REST query endpoint
Console panels (Emission Atlas, KV Influence) load within 2s for 28-day queries
Alert rule + runbook for sustained KV-miss 95th percentile regression

[Introduce workload deglitcher + tail-response smoothing and cost-tuner CLI]
description:
Context: production traces showed recurring short-duration high-concurrency spikes ('glitches') that push the serving stack into suboptimal batching and cache-miss behavior, increasing unit cost for low-traffic routes while degrading p95 latency for tail requests. Motivation: existing econ defaults are great for steady-state workloads but oscillate badly on bursty tails; operators end up widening SLAs or creating ad-hoc route overrides. This PR introduces a two-pronged, conservative change set to reduce unit-cost oscillation and make defaults safer for bursty, low-volume routes: 1) A lightweight 'workload deglitcher' signature detector integrated in the request router that detects short spikes (configurable 1-5 minute windows) and applies a transient smoothing policy: prefer smaller micro-batches, enable conservative KV prefix caching prioritization, and temporarily pin to a lower-quantization fallback when latency SLOs are relaxed. 2) A 'tail-response smoothing' module in the runtime scheduler that stretches the effective batching window only for detected glitch windows to trade a few ms of median latency for dramatically lower per-token cost at the tail. 3) A small companion CLI tool (redwood-cost-tuner) and library under tools/econ-sim that lets SREs/Platform engineers run fast Monte Carlo simulations of route-level unit economics across combinations of batch_size, kv_cache_policy, and quant_profiles; the tool includes presets and an automated 'safe-default' suggester that writes YAML snippets for per-route defaults. Changes: added workload_deglitcher.py (router integration), tail_smoother.py (scheduler hook), a new conservative quant profile (qsafe-i16) with runtime gating, the cost-tuner CLI (tools/econ-sim/cli.py) and a lightweight simulation engine (tools/econ-sim/sim.py), and docs + smoke tests. Backwards compatibility: all behavior is opt-in by default; the global config flag runtime.enable_deglitcher is false unless set by ops or via the safe-default suggester. Rollout plan: feature gate off, deploy to staging; run cost-tuner against staging traffic and generate suggested per-route configs; flip feature gate to enabled only for routes in a canary list for 72 hours and monitor p50/p95/units-per-req. Observability: new tracing spans (router.deglitch.detect, scheduler.tail_smooth.apply) and metrics (deglitch.window_count, tail_smooth_applied, econ_sim_recommendations) included. Risks & mitigations: initial perf run indicated qsafe-i16 caused a 2% token throughput regression on LLM-7B float paths; we narrowed the runtime gate for qsafe-i16 to routes with sequence_length < 1024 and added a GC-friendly quant fallback. Tests: unit tests for detection heuristics and simulation engine; integration smoke for router->scheduler wiring. Deployment notes: config schema bump (runtime.enable_deglitcher boolean, econ_suggester.bucket_ms int). Related: ENG-1423 (workload stability), ENG-1487 (unit econ tooling).

[Targeted kernel paths and continuous-batch coalescing for Mistral GQA quirks]
description:
Motivation: Mistral models with GQA (grouped query attention) patterns expose two recurring runtime inefficiencies in our serving stack: 1) kernel selection often picks the generic attention kernels for layers where narrow head widths would benefit from a specialized head-stride kernel; 2) continuous batching produces many small ephemeral batches that do not coalesce across short inter-arrival gaps for the common Mistral workload, leading to increased kernel launch overhead and KV cache pressure. This PR introduces two coordinated changes: (A) targeted kernel path hints (per-layer metadata and runtime heuristics) to prefer head-stride and planar attention micro-kernels when group sizes are small, with a runtime fallback to generic kernels; (B) a continuous-batch coalescer that extends the batching window by a configurable micro-delay and opportunistically merges compatible requests (same model/version, compatible max-seq and sampling flags) into a single execution batch while preserving latency SLOs via deadline-driven flushing.

Design:
- Per-layer kernel hints: model loader reads a new optional \"kernel_hints\" field emitted by model packaging (and falls back to statistical heuristics if absent). Hints include preferred kernel family and a conservative activation threshold. At runtime the scheduler evaluates hint + real-time seq/head distribution to pick a kernel function pointer.
- Coalescer: a lightweight per-worker coalescing queue holds incoming requests for up to micro_delay_ms (default 2ms). Requests are tag-matched by signature {model_id, model_version, max_seq_bucket, sampling_mode}. When coalesced, KV cache and prefix caching are unified so that shared prefixes are emitted once and fed into the batched kernel path. Safety: coalescer is disabled when requests set strict latency tags or when any incompatible function-call features are present.

Implementation highlights:
- runtime/scheduler: introduced KernelHintSelector and updated KernelRegistry to support prioritized families and graceful fallbacks.
- runtime/batching: added ContinuousCoalescer with a pluggable delay param and visibility into token-level deadlines.
- model/packaging: added README and schema addition (optional) for kernel_hints and sample hint generator in model tools.
- extensive unit and integration tests, plus a canary rollout plan.

Performance: microbenchmarks on Mistral-7B with GQA pattern (grouping 4, head-width 64) show:
- median p50 latency at 1rps workload decreased by 8% (kernel hint path)
- tail latency p99 at 100rps improved by 15% due to coalescing overhead reduction
- end-to-end tokens/sec at steady-saturation improved by 12% with coalescing enabled and conservative micro_delay_ms=2.

Rollout and safety:
- Canary rollout: enable on 10% of serving capacity for two days with A/B metric gating (p95 latency, error rate, token cost).
- Automatic rollback triggers on >5% p95 regressions or >1% increased error rate.

Backwards compatibility: kernel_hints are optional; when absent we fall back to heuristics. The change is non-breaking to the public API.

Related: ENG-4821 (GQA perf investigation), ENG-5098 (continuous batching experiment).

- [x] Integration tests for coalescer with KV cache semantics
- [x] Canary pipeline + dashboard widgets

[Introduce stepped batching policy, quant-safety linter, and unit-econ smoke tests]
description:
Motivation and summary:\n\nWe observed that single-threshold batching (max-batch-size only) can yield large cost variance across mixed workloads: small short requests suffer latency when waiting for large batch thresholds, but lowering thresholds increases per-token cost under high QPS. This PR introduces a small, operationally conservative stepped batching policy that trades off a couple of microseconds of scheduling overhead for much more stable unit economics across variable request size/QPS.\n\nWhat this PR does (single-string summary):\n- Implement 'stepped' batching policy in the serving runtime: the scheduler can be configured with an ordered list of candidate batch sizes (e.g., [1, 4, 16]) and per-step latency bounds. The runtime opportunistically serves smaller batches when latency SLOs are tight and ramps to larger steps when throughput allows.\n- Add a `quant-safety` static linter that inspects quantization profiles and model graph ops to catch unsafe combinations (e.g., per-channel quant on ops we don't support in the CUDA/XT kernels, or FP16-only fused ops missing fallback). The linter emits warnings and suggested safe profiles.\n- Add 'unit-econ smoke tests' to the CI: lightweight workload simulator that runs short generation workloads across a small matrix of batch sizes, quant profiles, and cache settings, and verifies cost-per-token regressions are within expected bands. Smoke tests run in ~8 minutes and gate regressions for perf/infra changes.\n\nImplementation notes and commits (high-level):\n- commit 1: runtime: stepped batcher core + scheduler hooks (api contract unchanged; new config block under route->batching)\n- commit 2: runtime: careful backpressure handling and metrics (per-step latency histograms, step_transition_counter)\n- commit 3: tooling: quant-safety linter as a CLI subcommand and CI check (bin/quant-linter)\n- commit 4: tests: unit-econ smoke test harness + CI job + small golden baselines (ci/smoke/unit-econ/)\n\nFiles touched (high level):\n- services/serve/scheduler/stepped_batcher.rs (new)\n- services/serve/config/batching.yaml (docs + examples updated)\n- runtime/metrics/registry.rs (added step-level metrics)\n- tools/quant-linter/main.go (new)\n- tools/quant-linter/rules/*.go (rules for op compatibility and fallbacks)\n- ci/smoke/unit-econ/run_smoke.py (new harness)\n- ci/.github/workflows/unit-econ-smoke.yml (CI job)\n- sdk/python/examples/bench/stepped_batch_example.py (example config)\n- docs/observability/batching.md (explain metrics and when to use stepped batching)\n- tests/integration/serve/stepped_batcher_endtoend.test (integration test)\n\nSmall config example included in docs (snippet):\n\n  batching:\n    strategy: stepped\n    steps:\n      - size: 1\n        max_latency_ms: 20\n      - size: 4\n        max_latency_ms: 50\n      - size: 16\n        max_latency_ms: 200\n\nNotes on design choices: we intentionally keep the default step set conservative (1,4,16) to avoid surprising throughput regressions for large sustained QPS. The scheduler uses a tiny state machine to avoid flip-flopping between steps: a step transition requires a short stabilization window (configurable, default 50ms).\n\nQuant-safety linter details:\n- Static analysis of exported model graph + quant profile.\n- Rules added: unsupported op-quant combos, precision funnel points (places where FP32->INT8 may lose critical dynamic range), and kernel mismatch with our CUDA kernels.\n- Linter outputs machine-readable JSON and human-friendly summaries used by CI to annotate PRs. Example output: \"WARN: op=matmul, quant=per_channel_int8 -> kernel_fallback_needed\"\n\nUnit-econ smoke tests:\n- Simulate 1m equivalent tokens split across generated short (avg 12 tokens) and long (avg 160 tokens) requests to mimic chat + summarization mixes.\n- Measure median latency, p95, and cost_per_1000_tokens. Failures trigger an artifact dump with token/time traces to help reproduce locally.\n\nReview conversation (high-level transcript):\n- Miguel: \"Nice approach. Can we make the step list hierarchical per-route? Some customers want different steps for embeddings vs generation.\"\n- Author (Asha): \"Yes — config supports per-route batching blocks. Examples added to docs and example config file.\"\n- Jade: \"Quant-linter looks solid; add an allowlist for customers with known model exceptions.\"\n- Author: \"Added allowlist file support and tests for the allowlist behavior (tools/quant-linter/allowlist_test.go).\"\n- Evan: \"CI time looks okay, but make sure smoke tests don't flake on low-QPS CI runners.\"\n- Author: \"Added retry + seeding and reduced variance; smoke runs ~8 minutes on our CI images.\"\n- Miguel (approval): \"Approve after green CI and one more perf run on canary infra.\"\n\nCI summary: initial run had one transient failure in smoke tests on ubuntu-latest runner due to clock skew; rerun succeeded. All checks now green.\n\nBackward compatibility and rollout:\n- No breaking API changes. The batching config is additive; if customers omit strategy, existing behavior (legacy max-batch-size) remains.\n- Enabled stepped batching only when explicitly configured. We plan to roll out conservative defaults in the Dedicated face as an opt-in for early customers.\n\nTesting and perf numbers (representative):\n- Mixed workload (40% short, 60% long) on g4dn.xlarge: median latency improved ~6% vs single-threshold tuned for throughput and cost-per-token reduced ~12% compared to always-on small-batch strategy. p95 latency was within the configured budgets for the step set above.\n\nFollow-ups and todos (post-merge):\n- ENG-2101: automatic step-suggestor that profiles live traffic and proposes step tuples per-route.\n- Add telemetry to Redwood Console to visualize step transition heatmaps per-route.\n- Expand quant-linter rules to cover model conversion tooling and add auto-fix suggestions where safe.\n\nMerge details:\n- Merge method: squash and merge.\n- Final merge commit: \"squash: stepped batching + quant-linter + unit-econ CI (Asha Patel)\"\n\nIf you want to run locally: see sdk/python/examples/bench/stepped_batch_example.py and tools/quant-linter/README.md for quickstart.\n

Adds a stepped batching policy with conservative defaults, a static quantization-safety linter to catch incompatible quant profiles, and a new suite of unit-econ smoke tests for CI. No user-facing API changes; operational defaults improved.

[Add prompt_set_v3 “production mix” (prefill-heavy + decode-heavy) and update benchmark defaults]
body:
## Summary
This PR introduces a new benchmark prompt set, `prompt_set_v3` (“production mix”), intended to better reflect real production request shapes on Redwood: a mix of prefill-heavy workloads (e.g., RAG / long context + short answer) and decode-heavy workloads (e.g., chat / shorter context + longer generation). It also updates the benchmark harness defaults to use v3 for the latency/$ report pipeline, while keeping v2 available for back-compat and comparison.

## Why
The existing prompt set (v2) over-indexes on decode-heavy chat flows and under-represents long-context prefill behavior. In production, cost/latency is frequently dominated by prefill and KV-cache pressure (especially at higher concurrency), which can materially change latency/$ rankings across models/regions. We need a prompt distribution that:
- more closely matches observed traffic shapes (context length, output length, prefill:decode ratio)
- keeps prompts non-sensitive + publishable (no customer content)
- is stable/reproducible across runs and regions

## What changed
- Added `prompt_set_v3` with two components:
  - `prefill_heavy`: long-ish context with short completions (simulates retrieval + summarization, doc Q&A, tool result formatting)
  - `decode_heavy`: moderate context with longer generations (simulates assistant replies / chat)
- Added weighting + sampling rules so v3 produces a consistent token-shape mix:
  - target distribution (by requests): 60% prefill-heavy / 40% decode-heavy
  - target distribution (by tokens): approximately balanced across prefill vs decode at the dataset level (so one category doesn’t dominate aggregate cost)
- Updated harness defaults used by the `latency_per_dollar` pipeline to v3 (flag override preserved)
- Added dataset “shape report” emitted into run artifacts so we can validate the realized distribution per sweep (context/output token histograms + realized prefill:decode ratio)

## Prompt set design details
All prompts are synthetic and/or derived from public domain sources (with paraphrasing where needed). We avoid any customer-like identifiers and keep content generic. Prompts are stored with explicit license/attribution notes where applicable.

**Prefill-heavy bucket (examples of shapes, not raw text):**
- context tokens: p50 ~2.5k, p95 ~7k
- output tokens: p50 ~120, p95 ~280
- includes: long context summarization, Q&A over a provided passage, structured extraction to JSON (schema provided)

**Decode-heavy bucket:**
- context tokens: p50 ~500, p95 ~1.2k
- output tokens: p50 ~650, p95 ~1.6k
- includes: multi-turn chat continuation, reasoning-lite assistance, instruction following with constrained style

## Validation
We ran A/B sweeps (v2 vs v3) on 3 models across 2 regions with the same concurrency + batching settings.

Results summary:
- v3 increases prefill share in aggregate token accounting from ~28% (v2) to ~49% (v3) on the sampled sweep
- overall latency/$ becomes more sensitive to kernel selection and prefill throughput; variance across repeats did not regress
- p95 latency stability: no statistically significant increase in run-to-run variance after enabling v3 (see artifact `shape_report.json` + `stability_summary.md` in the run output)

Notes:
- We intentionally did not tune any runtime parameters for the new dataset in this PR. The goal is measurement fidelity, not optics.
- Exclusions/guardrails are unchanged (same warmups, same max prompt length caps, same timeouts).

## Backward compatibility
- `prompt_set_v2` remains available and unchanged.
- Default changed only for the `latency_per_dollar` report pipeline config (CLI flags can still pick v2).

## Files / areas changed (high level)
- `prompt_sets/prompt_set_v3/` new prompts + metadata
- `configs/report/latency_per_dollar.yaml` default prompt set switched to v3
- `runner/shape_report.py` new artifact generator
- `docs/prompt_sets.md` updated with v3 rationale and token-shape targets

## How to test
1) Unit tests: `pytest -k prompt_set_v3`
2) Local dry-run (no GPU): `bench run --prompt-set v3 --dry-run --emit-shape-report`
3) Small sweep: `bench sweep --models <m1,m2> --regions <r1> --prompt-set v3 --concurrency 8 --warmup 2m`

## Risks / mitigations
- Risk: dataset drift or accidental sensitivity in prompt text. Mitigation: prompts are synthetic/public + reviewed; add lint rule for disallowed patterns.
- Risk: changing defaults could affect longitudinal comparisons. Mitigation: artifact schema includes prompt_set_version and shape report; dashboards can filter by prompt set.

## Checklist
- [x] Added prompt set + metadata
- [x] Added shape report artifact + tests
- [x] Updated docs
- [x] Re-ran representative sweeps and attached summaries

Refs: ENG-18442 (region sweep automation), ENG-18521 (stability gates).

Rina Kobayashi (author): Added `targets:` section to `metadata.yaml` (request-level + token-level goals) and wired that into the shape report output. Also added a sanity test asserting realized contexts stay under `max_prompt_tokens - 256` with current caps; the few longer examples were trimmed.

[kv: windowed compactor and spill regulator for tenant-aware memory coordination]
description:
Motivation: We observed recurring tenant-level memory amplification and transient OOMs during mixed workloads (small chat requests + occasional long generation). Root causes were fragmented KV slabs and uncoordinated spill decisions that created cascading I/O pressure. This PR introduces a tenant-aware memory coordinator that schedules a windowed compaction pass and a rate-limited spill regulator to reduce fragmentation, smooth spill throughput, and improve tail latency. Design summary: 1) Windowed compactor: background compaction runs in configurable time windows per-tenant to coalesce fragmented segments without impacting short-lived latency SLOs. Compaction work is budgeted in CPU + device-time and yields are inserted to keep p99 latency stable. 2) Spill regulator: spill decisions are rate-limited and smoothed by a token-bucket style regulator per-device and per-tenant. Regulator exposes backpressure signals to the scheduler so batching and placement can prefer warm KV regions. 3) Tenant memory coordinator: centralizes fragmentation metrics and admission signals so we avoid simultaneous heavy compaction + spilling across tenants on the same GPU. 4) Evictor changes: eviction ranking now includes fragmentation risk score and recent compaction history to avoid repeatedly evicting the same hot prefixes. Implementation notes: - New modules: src/kv/compactor.rs, src/kv/spill_regulator.rs, src/kv/memory_coordinator.rs. - Metrics: kv.fragmentation_pct, kv.compactor.window_secs, kv.spill.regulator_fill, kv.spill.backpressure_events (per-tenant labels). - Config knobs: compaction_window_seconds (default 30s), compaction_cpu_budget_ms (default 25ms/interval), spill_regulator_rate_tokens (default 4/s), aggressiveness per-tenant. - Feature flag: kv.windowed_compactor (off by default for older deploys). Observability/telemetry: dashboards added in docs/ops/kv_compaction.md and console runbooks included for when kv.spill.backpressure_events > 50/min. Performance summary (canary): - Median token latency unchanged. - p95 generation latency reduced by ~6-9% under mixed workloads. - Memory churn (allocation hotpath) down ~18% in canary tenants. - In cluster soak we saw 62% fewer transient tenant OOMs during bursty load compared to baseline. Rollout plan: 1) Deploy as feature-flagged to canary nodes (10% traffic) for 48h. 2) Monitor kv.spill.backpressure_events and p95 serve latency; regress if p95 increases by >3x or spill regulator fill > 90% for >5m. 3) Gradual ramp to 100% over 7 days if stable. Backwards compatibility: default knobs safe; compactor disabled unless feature flag explicitly enabled. TODO/checklist: - [x] Add unit tests for compaction scheduling and spill regulator token logic - [x] Add integration test to validate coordinator prevents simultaneous compactions on same GPU - [x] Add metrics and docs - [x] Perform perf bench harness runs - [x] Feature-flag gated rollout - [x] Added migration notes for config defaults

review_comments:
Daniel Park: Can we add a safety cap so compaction can't starve inference threads? Suggest compaction_cpu_budget_ms default of 25ms/interval.
Asha Mehta (author): Added cap and explicit yield points; clarified in the compactor code comments and tests.
Marta Alvarez: How does the spill regulator react to transient I/O spikes? Will it delay required spill and cause memory pressure?
Asha Mehta (author): Regulator is conservative: on sustained I/O spikes it will raise a backpressure signal to the scheduler and accelerate eviction ranking for low-value prefixes. Added integration test to simulate I/O spike.
Ravi Singh: Please ensure tenant labels are included on new metrics and the console dashboards show top-10 tenants by fragmentation.
Asha Mehta (author): Metrics now include tenant_id labels and dashboard JSON updated.

release_notes:
Introduce tenant-aware windowed compaction and spill regulator to reduce KV fragmentation and smooth spill throughput. Feature gated; default disabled. Observable via new metrics (kv.fragmentation_pct, kv.spill.regulator_fill, kv.spill.backpressure_events). Can reduce p95 under mixed workloads and significantly lower transient tenant OOM rate when enabled.

notes_for_ops:
Feature flag kv.windowed_compactor is off by default. If enabling, follow rollout plan in docs/ops/kv_compaction.md. Watch kv.spill.backpressure_events and p95 generation latency; if backpressure_events persist, reduce compaction aggressiveness or lower spill_regulator rate. Console dashboard added under Storage > KV > Compaction.

[Add export checksum and anomaly flagging to detect proration drift]
description:
Summary: Several customer investigations in Q4 and ongoing reconciliations indicate small, silent proration drift in the nightly Stripe/NetSuite billing export pipeline. These drifts are often under the alerting threshold and only show up as invoice differences during manual audits. This ticket implements an auditing layer: deterministic checksums and anomaly flagging at each export stage to detect silent offset drift and stop bad exports before they reach accounting systems.

Problem details: The export pipeline has multiple stages (hourly usage rollups -> proration merger -> invoice line generation -> Stripe/NetSuite payload builder). Multiple failure modes can silently alter totals: eventual-consistency reorders from delayed webhooks, racey invoice-line merges that drop fractional cents, and non-deterministic map iteration in an older aggregation job. These cause subtle mismatches between the canonical usage ledger and the final export (e.g., -$0.25 to +$1.10 per invoice) which are hard to trace after export.

Root cause hypothesis: We observed cases where the aggregation step and the invoice-line merge operate on slightly different input sets due to late-arriving usage, and there is no end-to-end invariant check between the canonical ledger and exported totals. The export writes only final line items; there is no cryptographic or checksum metadata attached at intermediate stages.

Proposed solution: 1) Add deterministic, stage-stable checksums to every export artifact (hourly-usage bundle, proration diff, invoice-line bundle) computed using a stable canonicalization method (sorted keys, normalized currency rounding, UTF-8 stable serialization) and a fast checksum (CRC32 or xxhash64). 2) Persist checksum and a small export manifest (counts, sum_in_cents, currency, exported_ids) alongside artifacts in export storage. 3) Produce an end-to-end reconciliation check that verifies manifest.sum_in_cents equals the canonical ledger's sum within configured tolerance and checksum equality for the canonicalized payload. 4) If mismatch > tolerance or checksum mismatch, mark the export as FAILED, raise PagerDuty, write a blocking marker to prevent downstream pushing to Stripe/NetSuite, and create a reconciliation ticket with links to artifacts. 5) Add anomaly metrics and dashboards: export_checksum_mismatch_count, export_sum_delta_cents, export_blocked_count; retention for 90 days.

Design constraints and trade-offs: - Checksums must be computed deterministically and cheaply; we avoid heavyweight crypto HMACs to keep cost low, but will include optional signing in a follow-up if adversarial tampering is a concern. - Must not change existing exported payload schema (so Stripe/NetSuite consumers unaffected). The manifest will be stored alongside artifacts in S3 and referenced by the export job. - Tolerance should be configurable per-customer (default 100 cents or 0.5% whichever is greater) to avoid blocking noisy small customers.

Acceptance criteria: - New export pipeline emits manifest files for 100% of exports in staging and prod canary. - When we intentionally inject a single-cent discrepancy in test data, the system flags the export and prevents a downstream push. - Dashboards surface checksum_mismatch_count with drilldowns to manifest S3 keys. - Runbook documented for investigation/playbook and one retrospective after first blocked export. - Integration tests cover canonicalization changes and checksum computation.

Rollout plan: 1) Implement manifest writer and checksum logic in export-worker (feature-flagged). 2) Enable read-only sanity checks in prod for 2 weeks (no blocking) while we observe metrics. 3) Enable blocking behavior in a single region and particular tenant cohort (canary customers) for 1 week. 4) Gradual ramp to all exports. 5) Post-rollout: run a full backfill check for past 30 days and create remediation tickets for any mismatches.

Operational notes: - Alerts should page on high-severity mismatches (>= $10 or >1% of invoice) and write to an internal Slack channel for lower severity. - Add a lightweight endpoint to query a manifest by export_id and present sums/checksums for manual review (console integration later).

Security and privacy: Manifests contain only export metadata and aggregated sums and exported IDs; no raw customer PII or usage text will be included. If additional signing is needed, follow-up will go through security review.

Related: This is complementary to the existing late-webhook and proration fixes but focuses on detection and automated blocking so human auditors can remediate before invoices are sent.

2026-01-18 Liam Chen: Investigation - replayed 90 days of exports in staging and found 18 exports with >20 cents delta due to non-deterministic map order in legacy aggregator. POC checksum generator implemented in staging branch. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/billing/pull/3412

2026-02-05 Dev (Liam Chen): Feature-flagged manifest writer merged to main with unit + integration tests. End-to-end test harness updated to validate manifest roundtrip. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/billing/pull/3479
