[Unexpected variant tilt to low-memory replica causing prolonged KV warmup and 504s]
description:
Issue summary: During the 2026-03-10 09:15 UTC traffic spike for HyperRetail's dedicated pool, a routing decision caused a subset of requests to be routed to a low-memory variant (sparse-mem-replica) that was not sufficiently warmed. Impact: ~10-15% of requests for the customer returned 504/timeouts or experienced multi-second token wait times for ~20 minutes. This affected storefront search latency and caused customer alerts.

Impact: Customer-reported elevated error rate and slow inference for critical search endpoints during peak traffic. No customer data leakage observed.

Environment: Dedicated pool for HyperRetail in prod-us-east. Autoscaling events were in-flight; new replicas launching. The routing policy includes a capacity-aware fallback that prefers low-cost variants under contention.

Expected behavior: Under capacity pressure the platform should route to warmed fallback variants or gracefully queue with backpressure, not shift a significant fraction of live traffic to replicas that require prolonged KV cache warmup.

Observed behavior: A traffic shift (tilt) routed ~12% of requests to a low-memory replica type which had cold or partially-cold KV caches, causing long per-request warmup stalls and 504s.

Steps already taken: throttled customer burst, temporarily disabled the low-memory fallback for the HyperRetail pool, coordinated with SRE to increase target warm replicas.


steps_to_reproduce:
Provision a dedicated pool with mixed-capacity variants (high-memory and low-memory replicas)
Simulate a sudden traffic surge that triggers autoscaler and fallback routing (5000 req/min for 5 minutes)
Observe routing decisions in router logs: look for >10% traffic to sparse-mem replicas that recently transitioned from initializing
Inspect serving-runtime traces for KV cache misses and long warmup durations

observed_behavior:
Requests were diverted to sparse-mem replicas that returned intermittent 504s and showed long wait times due to synchronous KV warmup operations. Latency plots show a step increase in tail latency aligned with the autoscaler add events.

expected_behavior:
Platform should maintain traffic on warmed replicas, or use a staged ramp/fan-out to new replicas that pre-warm KV caches without taking live traffic until warm. Fallbacks should prefer replicas with warm KV cache or use queued warmup prior to routing production traffic.

investigation_notes:
Router decision logs indicate the capacity-aware fallback policy weights low-cost variants when available_capacity < threshold
Sparse-mem replicas were marked 'ready' by the scheduler once container started but before KV prefetch completed
Serving-runtime traces show synchronous KV prefetch running on first requests, blocking token generation for ~1.2-2.5s per affected request
Autoscaler events: 3 new sparse-mem replicas spun up between 09:12-09:18 UTC; router immediately included them in candidate pool
Hypothesis: readiness gating currently checks container liveness only; KV cache readiness is not gated leading to early routing
Related runbook: routing/fallback-policy.md suggests a warmup probe feature but it was not enabled for this customer's deployment

[CardinalPay: fallback amplification causing repeated streaming truncation and billing spike - post-incident review]
description:
Issue summary: Between 2026-02-14 09:12 and 2026-02-14 11:03 UTC CardinalPay experienced repeated streaming truncations and an unexpected billing spike. The root trigger was a rollout of a quantized model variant plus an autoscale event on Dedicated capacity that caused the smart-routing fallback loop to amplify requests to higher-cost model variants and retried streaming sessions, producing duplicate billable tokens and truncated streams. Impact: customer-facing degradation (failed or truncated streaming responses), elevated 5xx for long-tail requests, and a ~3.7x increase in billed tokens for the customer during the window.

impact:
All CardinalPay production tenants in us-east saw ~12% of streaming sessions truncated mid-response and a sudden 370% token billing spike for the 2-hour window. Latency SLOs breached for 98th/99th percentiles. Customer reported partial failures in live checkout flows and escalated to C-suite. Revenue-impacting and high-severity escalation.

investigation_notes:
Timeline: - 09:05: canary of quantized variant enabled. - 09:11: Dedicated pool autoscaled (new nodes registered slowly; scheduling jitter observed). - 09:11-09:20: multiple routing decisions returned 'capacity_unavailable' transiently which triggered smart-routing to cascade fallbacks. - 09:12-09:45: API gateway retried streaming session startups on client reconnect which produced repeated partial streams. Hypothesis: the combination of slow node warm-up (KV cache coldness), scheduler churn, and an aggressive gateway retry policy led to duplicate requests being routed to fallback variants. Gateway retry and streaming reconnection logic did not de-duplicate session restarts. Confirmed by correlating session IDs and connection-attempt counters in gateway traces. Billing spike path: duplicate token accounting occurred because early-session partial outputs were counted as billable tokens before retries produced final responses; some retries were billed again by downstream accounting before final reconciliation.

resolution_summary:
Root cause: interaction between quantized model canary rollout, Dedicated pool autoscale churn, and aggressive gateway retry behavior that led to repeated fallback routing and duplicate billable sessions. Fixes applied: 1) API gateway dedupe logic for streaming session restarts (patch deployed). 2) Scheduler tuning: increased node warm-up parallelism and image pull retry limits to reduce registration delay (PR merged). 3) Smart-routing change: temporary cooldown on consecutive fallbacks per-tenant to avoid amplification. Billing action: provisional credit approved and will be applied to CardinalPay March invoice.

follow_up_actions:
1) Postmortem doc created and linked: confluence.redwood.com/display/OPS/CardinalPay+INC+2026-02-14+Postmortem (owner: Marco Ruiz, due 2026-02-20). 2) Add automated test in CI that simulates canary rollout + autoscale to assert no routing amplification (owner: runtime team). 3) Billing: reconcile double-counted tokens and apply credit (owner: Sofia Park, ticket BILL-9876). 4) Product: review default gateway retry policy for streaming APIs and consider safer defaults (owner: Product infra). 5) Runbook update: add explicit guidance for coordinated model canary + autoscale during peak windows.

Initial detection: 2026-02-14 09:32 UTC (support notified). Customer escalation call held 2026-02-14 11:00 UTC with VP Eng & Head of Operations. We committed to: immediate mitigation, a technical postmortem within 3 business days, and a billing credit. Final postmortem shared 2026-02-18 and credit agreed. Customer is satisfied with remediation and monitoring improvements; case closed.

[Graceful overflow: model-pin overflow causing instantaneous 429s and request drop without fallback]
description:
Issue summary: Beacon Health is seeing immediate 429 responses when a pinned model route exceeds capacity. Instead of being routed to a fallback model variant or queued briefly, requests are rejected and surface to the application. Impact: client-facing health-app backend receives 429s for ~30s during daily morning spike (03:42-03:46 UTC) causing degraded UX and error alerts. Timeline: 2026-03-12 03:42 UTC - first surge; 03:43-03:46 - sustained 429s; 03:46 - partial recovery once queued tokens cleared. Observed behavior: requests to route /v1/generate pinned to redwood-llama-70b-v2 are immediately answered with 429 and X-RateLimit-* headers show per-route bucket exhausted; fallback rules exist in their console but appear not to trigger. Expected behavior: seamless overflow to pre-configured fallback (rlhf-quant-8bit) or short queueing/spillover policy instead of hard 429 during short warmup of fallback pool. Customer asks for explanation of why fallback did not trigger, and configuration guidance to allow transient overflow without large billing spikes.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) On a dedicated pool with route pinned to redwood-llama-70b-v2, configure fallback route to rlhf-quant-8bit (console: Routes > Edit > Fallback) but leave fallback weight default
2) Send 150 parallel short requests (avg 120 tokens) to /v1/generate from a single API key over 30s to emulate morning fanout
3) Observe immediate 429s for a subset of requests; check response headers for X-RateLimit-Remaining and X-RateLimit-Reset
4) Watch dedicated-autoscaler and fallback pool metrics in console; fallback pool shows cold start and then scales but after initial 429 window

2026-03-12T03:43:01Z request_id=0a1f3e route=pinned/redwood-llama-70b-v2 status=429 X-RateLimit-Remaining=0 X-RateLimit-Reset=2026-03-12T03:44:10Z
2026-03-12T03:43:05Z request_id=0a1f6b route=pinned/redwood-llama-70b-v2 status=429 quota=route:tokens exhausted
2026-03-12T03:43:09Z request_id=0a1fbb routing_decision=fallback-check skipped=policy-disabled reason=exact-match-pin
2026-03-12T03:44:22Z request_id=0a2003 route=rlhf-quant-8bit status=200 latency=180ms scaled_from=0->2

investigation_notes:
Initial triage: per-route token bucket consumed rapidly due to many parallel short requests; console fallback was configured but route-level pin appears to block normal fallback path (design: exact-pins avoid automatic spillover to preserve determinism for enterprise customers)
Autoscaler behavior: fallback pool cold-start latency ~35-45s in us-east observed in metrics; autoscaler does not preemptively warm a fallback if pinned route is considered authoritative
Quota accounting: requests counted against route token bucket before routing policy evaluation in current config; when bucket is zero the request is rejected instead of being forwarded to fallback or queued
Hypothesis: policy combination 'model pin + strict per-route quota' leads to hard 429; customer expected 'graceful spillover' but pin semantics intentionally prioritize strict routing
Risk note: enabling transparent spillover can increase footprint on fallback pool and lead to unexpected billing; recommend rate-limited spillover with token-weight cap

resolution:
Short-term workaround (applied): temporarily increase route token quota for pinned route and enable short-lived burst credits in console (Routes > Quotas > Burst window + extra tokens) to absorb morning spike
Medium-term recommended config changes:
- Configure a controlled fallback policy: Console -> Routes -> Edit routing policy -> set 'Fallback mode' to 'allowed-with-rate-limit' and specify token ceiling (e.g., 10k tokens/min)
- Enable 'pre-warm fallback' for critical routes: set fallback pool min-replicas=1 during known daily windows to reduce cold-start 35s overhead
- Use token-weighted spillover so requests get forwarded only if per-request token estimate <= spillover_threshold
Operational guidance: add a canary policy that routes 2% of requests to fallback during quiet hours to keep cache/weights warm without large cost impact
Follow-ups: SRE to propose UI change for clearer pin+fallback semantics; Engineering to evaluate route evaluation order (quota vs fallback) for possible safe reorder
Customer communicated acceptance of temporary quota bump; ticket to remain open for config follow-up

[Model catalog: add interoperability flags, streaming resilience hints, and function-call shaping]
description:
Context: Customers frequently need to discover models by how they interoperate with OpenAI-style clients (function/tool calling, strict structured output, streaming backpressure characteristics) and by practical limits (per-request tokens, tool concurrency). Motivation: expose lightweight interoperability flags and numeric hints in the model catalog so client-side shims and the openai-compat layer can make better routing/formatting decisions without a heavyweight schema migration. This PR adds: 1) new capability flags on the catalog API (tool_support, structured_output: [strict|lenient], openai_compat_level) 2) numeric hints (max_tools_concurrent, max_tokens_per_request, baseline_cost_1k_tokens, streaming_reliability_score) intended as advisory fields only 3) streaming resilience hints to suggest preferred chunking/batch sizes and fallback policies for slow consumers 4) function-call shaping metadata to help the OpenAI-compat shim choose whether to synthesize tool manifests or fallback to text-only outputs 5) query filters for listing by these capabilities (e.g., ?tool_support=true&structured_output=strict&min_streaming_reliability=0.8) Checklist: - [x] API schema additions (catalog schema + openapi docs) - [x] Listing filters and query parsing - [x] Backward-compatible behavior when flags are absent - [x] Unit tests for filtering logic and JSON schema validation - [x] Integration tests exercising openai-compat shim routing - [x] API docs + examples for SDKs - [x] Release notes Draft/Notes: This is intentionally advisory: fields are not enforced by runtime; they are hints for routing and SDK behavior. The streaming_reliability_score is a 0.0-1.0 heuristic combining observed tail-latency, chunk-drop rate, and historical reconnects; it will be refined in follow-ups. Related: RFC: internal rfc/catalog-interop-2024 (link: https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-5412/catalog-interoperability-flags), depends on ENG-5231 (streaming-slo-metrics). Migration: old clients continue to work unchanged. New query parameters are additive.

Aisha Patel (author): I considered nesting but chose top-level for lookup simplicity in the catalog queries. We keep names short and prefixed to reduce collision risk. If storage cost is a concern we can collapse in follow-up.

Aisha Patel (author): Added doc section in docs/api/model-catalog.md that explains the heuristic (tails, drops, reconnects) and notes it's advisory.
Jonas Meyer (approver): LGTM after small nits fixed around openapi examples. Approving to unblock release.
Release lead (comment): Targeted for next minor (v0.18.0); watch rollout of openai-compat edgecases.

release_notes:
Model catalog now exposes advisory interoperability hints and capability flags. New listing filters: tool_support (boolean), structured_output (strict|lenient), min_streaming_reliability (0.0-1.0). SDKs updated to surface optional fields. These fields are advisory; clients should treat them as hints, not guarantees. See docs/api/model-catalog.md for examples and migration notes.

[Introduce scoped model-list filters, OpenAI preview flag, and pricing hint fields]
description:
Motivation: product teams want richer discovery from the model catalog without having to pull the entire model index into client-side logic. This PR extends the public model-listing API with: 1) scoped filter profiles that encode common filter sets (latency-sensitive, cost-sensitive, structured-output-first), 2) an opt-in OpenAI-compat preview flag on model entries so clients can discover which models currently support the OpenAI-style function-calling/structured-output shim, and 3) a lightweight pricing_hint/pricing_tier field to help routing decisions.

What changed (high level):
- API: GET /v1/models supports new query params: filter_profile (string), include_compat (boolean), pricing_hint (string) and streaming_safe (boolean) to annotate model capabilities for streaming callers. Responses include model.metadata.compatibility_preview (enum: none|openai|openai_partial), model.metadata.filter_profiles (list), and model.metadata.pricing_tier (string).
- Backend: catalog indexer updated to compute and persist filter profiles based on model performance metadata (latency P50/P95, kv-cache-friendly indicator, memory footprint). Added a lightweight compatibility-check pipeline that runs smoke checks for OpenAI function-calling semantics and sets the compatibility_preview flag.
- Server: model-list handler uses scoped profile templates to expand into query predicates; added caching for profile-expanded queries to avoid repeated index scans.
- Docs & SDKs: added examples and typing updates in Python/TS SDKs (backwards compatible: old fields untouched).

Compatibility notes: default behavior preserves the existing model-list response when filter_profile is absent. compatibility_preview defaults to 'none' until the smoke-check pipeline has run for a model. Pricing hints are advisory (routing may still consult explicit price tables).

Testing: unit tests for profile expansion, compatibility flagging, and JSON schema changes; integration test that validates streaming_safe semantics with the streaming router.

Related: Linear ENG-6125 tracks follow-up work for exposing filter_profile UI in Console; PM-187 documents product requirements for pricing tiers.

Checklist:
- [x] API + schema changes implemented
- [x] Indexer and pipeline to compute fields
- [x] SDK surface annotations updated (Python/TS)
- [x] Unit and integration tests added
- [x] Migration notes and release notes prepared

Notes for reviewers: pay attention to the compatibility_preview state machine (we keep an explicit 'pending' transitional window in the pipeline) and the cache TTL chosen for profile-expanded queries (30s by default).

[Enrich model listing endpoints with runtime hints, pricing/limits and OpenAI-compat shim]
description:
This PR extends the model listing and capability endpoints to expose runtime hints (streaming stability hints, recommended kv-cache policies, batching/latency profiles), explicit compatibility flags for OpenAI-style features (function_calling, structured_output, streaming), and per-model pricing/limits metadata (tokens_per_second_estimate, max_context_tokens, soft_rate_limit, burst_capacity). Motivation: product teams need a single discovery API to make deterministic routing and graceful fallback decisions at runtime; SDKs and the OpenAI-compat shim need canonical fields to drive feature negotiation without brittle heuristics. The change includes: 1) schema additions to /v1/models and /v1/model-catalog with new flat fields; 2) a compatibility map that lists boolean flags and a deprecation & aliases map for older capabilities; 3) streaming stability hint tokens that indicate recommended chunking size and backoff policy; 4) pricing/limits fields surfaced for billing and client-side throttling; 5) an OpenAI compatibility layer update that maps Redwood capability names to OpenAI equivalents and exposes a single compatibility_score to help automated routing. Backwards compatibility: added fields are optional and default to safe values to avoid client breakage. See release_notes for migration guidance.

testing_and_validation:

Load test validated tokens_per_second estimates under mixed batch sizes and reported within 10% of observed throughput.

New fields: compatibility_flags (function_calling, structured_output, streaming), compatibility_score, streaming_hints (chunk_size, recommended_backoff), tokens_per_second_cpu/gpu, max_context_tokens, soft_rate_limit, burst_capacity. [catalog: surface model capability flags, pricing and limits for OpenAI-compat clients]
description:
Motivation: Clients using the OpenAI-compat layer and our public model listing need a single, predictable surface to discover per-model capabilities (streaming stability, function/tool-calling support, structured-output specializations) and unit economics (pricing per token, soft/hard limits and concurrency). This PR extends the model catalog API and internal catalog objects to include capability and pricing metadata, plus server-side filters that power the console and SDKs.

Summary of changes: added explicit capability flags (openai_compat, supports_streaming_stable, supports_function_calling, structured_output_profiles) to the model listing; exposed priced_units and limits metadata (cost_per_input_token, cost_per_output_token, max_tokens_per_request, recommended_concurrency, rate_limit_tier). Implemented new query params for the GET /v1/models endpoint to filter by capability, max_estimated_cost_per_k, min_stability_score, region, and quantization support. Updated the OpenAI compatibility layer to prefer models with openai_compat=true for compatibility endpoints and to fall back predictably to compatible variants when a requested capability is not available. Added docs, SDK bindings, and tests.

Why this is safe: fields are additive. No breaking schema changes for existing consumers. Default behavior for compatibility endpoints is unchanged unless clients explicitly query the new fields or filtering. We included a migration path for older model entries missing cost metadata (defaults used and surfaced as "unknown").

API additions (examples):
- GET /v1/models?capability=function_calling&region=us-east-1&max_estimated_cost_per_k=0.50 -> returns models that advertise function calling and whose cost_per_1k_tokens <= 0.50.
- New model-listing response includes keys: capabilities (list), pricing (object), limits (object), compatibility_flags (list). Example snippet in response body (condensed for PR):
  "models": [{"id": "redwood-slim-1b", "capabilities": ["embeddings","streaming"], "pricing": {"cost_per_input_token": "0.00005", "cost_per_output_token": "0.00006", "currency": "USD"}, "limits": {"max_tokens": "4096", "recommended_concurrency": "4"}, "compatibility_flags": ["openai_compat"]}]

Implementation notes:
- internal/catalog/store: extended ModelRecord with flattened string lists for capabilities and compatibility_flags; pricing/limits stored as strings to avoid schema churn in metadata blobs.
- api/handlers/models: added parsing for new query params and server-side filter combinators; implemented pagination and estimation of cost-per-request for the max_estimated_cost_per_k filter.
- openai-compat layer: updated selection logic to prefer exact capability matches, then compatibility-flagged fallbacks, then nearest-latency alternative. This avoids regression for streaming clients while giving a predictable fallback path.
- SDK updates: python and ts SDKs gain ModelCatalog.list_models() optional filters.
- docs: new reference doc with examples and migration guidance.

Testing: Added unit tests for filter logic, integration tests exercising the openai-compat routing, and a small perf smoke to ensure the filter path does not add >1ms median overhead. CI initially caught a flaky kv-cache test unrelated to the change; rerun resolved it.

Rollout plan: Feature is behind a feature flag (model_catalog_capabilities_v2) and enabled for internal and canary tenants first. Console uses the new fields only when the flag is on. After 2 weeks of canary telemetry (stability and no client errors), we will flip default and update external SDK releases.

Related: ENG-4821 (catalog UX for capability discovery), SUP-188 (customer reported mismatch between advertised function calling and actual routing), docs PR will follow to expand examples.

Notes for reviewers: focus on the filter combinator correctness (api/handlers/models/filter.go), openai-compat selection priority (pkg/openai/selector.go) and the SDK bindings. The JSON snippet above is illustrative; exact field names are in the updated API doc file.

release_notes:
Expose model capabilities and pricing in the model listing. New filters for capability, region, quantization, and estimated cost per 1k tokens. Additive API change; default behavior unchanged. Clients should opt into new fields via filters or SDK updates.

[introduce capabilities_query endpoint + structured-output and function-call profiles in model catalog]
description:
Motivation: Product teams need a single, efficient query surface to discover model capabilities and runtime hints that drive API behavior (streaming vs non-streaming, structured-output templates, function-calling profiles and per-model pricing/limits). This PR adds a new endpoint /v1/model_catalog/capabilities_query that returns a normalized capability document for each model and expands the model index with structured-output and function_calling profiles plus optional per-route pricing hints. The change is designed to be backward-compatible with the existing /v1/models listing and the OpenAI compatibility shim.

What this PR does: Adds a query-focused catalog endpoint that accepts flexible filters (capability flags, max_sequence, supports_streaming, openai_compat_level) and returns a compact capability payload. Introduces two first-class capability families: structured_output_profiles (named templates + JSONSchema hints + stability score) and function_calling_profiles (preferred calling semantics, argument mapping, and failure_fallback policies). Adds a pricing_limits field (per-1000-token cost_hint and soft_rate_limit) to model entries to aid routing/costing decisions at the gateway. Updates the OpenAI shim to map compatibility_level -> openai_deprecation_hints so older clients get migration guidance. Includes tests, docs, and console list adjustments to surface the new query filters.

Compatibility and migration: Existing consumers of /v1/models are unaffected. The new endpoint is additive. The OpenAI shim will continue to expose the current compatibility flags but now emits an additional deprecation hint if a model's openai_compat_level is below the requested threshold. Operators should review release notes for telemetry changes: new metrics were added (catalog.query.latency, catalog.query.result_size, catalog.query.filtered_count).

Checklist:
- [x] API endpoint implementation server-side (HTTP + SDK bindings)
- [x] OpenAPI/SDK docs updated
- [x] Unit and integration tests for filtering and profile shapes
- [x] Console UI: add capability filter and pricing column
- [x] Migration notes and telemetry added

Rollout plan: Feature-gated via feature_flag:capabilities_query. Default off for Dedicated customers in the initial rollout window; enabled in hosted after 72-hour dark-traffic validation.

Notes: This PR intentionally keeps profile schemas minimal (string identifiers + lightweight JSONSchema references) to avoid inflating catalog payloads; future work (ENG-2089) will add a cached profile store for richer profiles.

Added a new /v1/model_catalog/capabilities_query endpoint to fetch compact capability documents. [Residency ops runway and incident vignettes]
summary:
Working notes for operational readiness (runway) and a set of short incident vignettes to validate region-anchoring/fallback behavior. Intended for SREs, oncall, and solutions eng to run tabletop exercises and pre-flight checks before customer rollouts.

body:
Purpose:
- Create a compact, ops-friendly checklist and a handful of realistic incident vignettes to exercise region anchoring ("anchors") and fallback behavior for private deployments.
- Make sure the team has concrete evidence artifacts and comm templates for audits and customers.

Scope:
- Applies to Private (VPC/on-prem) and Dedicated customers who require region pinning or strong site affinity.
- Does NOT cover fine-grained KMS/GDPR legal analysis (see legal / product contract templates).

Operational runway (pre-rollout checklist) — quick runway items we should validate before enabling "hard anchors":
- Tenant mapping sanity: validate tenant -> region mapping table (sample 100 tenants across EU/US/APAC).
- Telemetry gating: make sure residency-evidence metrics are present for +ve and -ve cases (requests_local, requests_fallthrough, cache_hits_by_pin).
- Pin enforcement mode: smoke in soft-mode first (log-only) for 48h, then enforce with 1% canary traffic.
- Fallback-model readiness: ensure alternative model variants are registered and have verified perf profiles in target regions.
- Evidence packaging: automated bundle script (evidence-bundle.sh) produces: request IDs, routing headers, zone-annotations, and storage location.
- Legal/contract flag check: verify tenant contract flag for "region-exempt" is honored.
- Operator playbook artifact: a single, linkable ticket template that oncall can attach to customer comms.

Telemetry & acceptance signals (what we watch during runway):
- requests_local_pct >= 99.5% for pinned tenants (after 1wk stabilization)
- fallthrough_rate < 0.5% (default) — alert if > 1% for 30m
- latency_p90 by route stays within SLA (compare to baseline)
- evidence_bundle_success_rate (per tenant) > 99%
- reconciliation_delta_count (tenant mapping vs anchor index) = 0

Incident vignettes (run as tabletop; 20–30m each):
1) Zone Evacuation (simulated AZ/region outage)
- Setup: mark eu-west-1 as degraded in routing mesh; force 30% of EU traffic into fallback path.
- Expected: pinned tenants in EU should continue to be routed to EU-anchors (if available) or to the configured fallback with documented evidence.
- Operator steps: enable transparent fallback -> notify legal & account owner -> trigger evidence-bundle -> open incident ticket with template -> postmortem checklist.
- Evidence to collect: pre/post routing traces, routing decision payloads, model-variant used, customer-facing note draft.
- Key checks: no unpinned tenant receives EU data; pinned tenant fallthrough reasons recorded.

2) Misconfigured Pin (human error: tenant mapped to wrong region)
- Setup: manually flip tenant.region to us-east for one EU test-tenant in staging.
- Expected: soft-mode logs discrepancy but does not enforce; if transitioned to hard-mode, enforce rollback path must be reversible.
- Operator steps: detect via reconciliation alerts -> run reconciliation job -> validate evidence bundle -> coordinate fix with account team -> escalate to product if contract implications.
- Comms: short templated apology + description of corrective action + statement of evidence produced.

3) Evidence ingestion failure (storage or packaging outage)
- Setup: point evidence-bundle output to a broken S3-like endpoint (introduce 503s).
- Expected: system retries with exponential backoff, falls back to local queue with retention policy, raise urgent pager if buffer > threshold.
- Operator steps: check queue length, invoke disaster-recovery script to export backlog to temp blobstore, notify legal for audit implications.

Simulation exercise plan:
- Cadence: weekly tabletop for 2 months pre-rollout, then monthly for 3 months post-rollout.
- Roles: facilitator (ops lead), runner (SRE oncall), comms (customer success), legal observer.
- Success criteria: for each vignette, evidence artifacts exist, comm template drafted, and any code/config fixes landed within 5 business days.

Operator quick sequence (what to do in the first 15 minutes):
1) Acknowledge incident in PagerDuty and assign oncall.
2) Run "evidence-bundle collect <tenant>" and push to artifact store; if collector fails, flip to fallback dump.
3) Confirm routing decision via trace_id; if routing deviates, enable emergency fallback flag.
4) Post initial summary in incident channel and tag product/legal/account.

Comms snippets (short, modular) — reuse these in customer and internal updates:
- Initial: "We detected a routing anomaly affecting a subset of tenants; our team is investigating and has enabled fallbacks to preserve availability. We are collecting evidence and will follow up within 2 hours with an update."
- Customer follow-up: "We identified the root cause as a configuration mismatch and have corrected the mapping. No customer data left configured regions; attached evidence bundle #ART-12345."
- Postmortem intro: "Incident impacted pin enforcement for X tenants between T1 and T2; immediate mitigations were applied and a permanent fix was deployed."

Evidence packaging checklist (what we attach to audit):
- manifest.json with tenant-id, timestamp, anchor-region, request-ids list
- routing-traces (compressed) + routing-decision-headers
- operator-notes.txt (who touched what and when)
- reconciliation logs and pre/post mapping diff

Open questions / TODOs:
- [ ] Decide retention policy for evidence bundles (default 90d vs customer-specified).
- [ ] Should we redact full request payloads by default (PII concerns)? Proposal: bundle keeps request IDs and headers; payloads require E-Discovery ticket.
- [ ] Add automated test in staging that flips anchors and asserts evidence bundle generation. (ENG-4578)
- [ ] Confirm legal-approved comm templates for EU / UK customers.

Quick links and references:
- Residency telemetry dashboard: /d/residency-ops-dashboard
- Reconciliation job: job-id=rcn-2024-09-a
- Evidence bundler: github.com/redwood/evidence-bundler (PR #62)

notes:
Informal notes and fragmentary TODOs — expect updates after the next tabletop. Use this doc to copy comm snippets into incident ticket templates.

[Pool thermal grok: incident breadcrumb sketch]
Notes to self - quick chronology:\n\n2025-01-10 09:12 UTC - Pager: dedicated-pool-x had 5x scale-ups then immediate scale-downs, latency spikes to 900ms P95 for hosted-generation route.\n2025-01-10 09:15 UTC - Observed repeated cold-start churn: new containers coming up, warm handshake failing, and then pool autoscaler reducing target.\n2025-01-10 09:22 UTC - Manual intervention: scaled pool target to stable-min=20, paused autoscaler. Latency stabilized after ~3m.\n\nSymptoms observed:\n- Capacity thrash: rapid scale-ups followed by scale-downs within 30-120s window.\n- Warmup time per instance ~45-70s on A100 nodes (kernel load + model mmap).\n- Autoscaler cooldown appears shorter than warmup, causing under-provisioning in steady demand bursts.\n- Occasionally saw device allocation failures (NVML) during hot reattach attempts.\n\nCommands I ran (raw outputs trimmed):\n- kubectl get pods -n dedicated-pool-x --show-labels -o wide\n  -> many pods in ContainerCreating, some in CrashLoopBackOff due to device plugin init timeouts.\n\n- kubectl describe node gpu-node-17 | sed -n '1,120p'\n  Allocatable: nvidia.com/gpu: 8\n  Allocatable memory: OK\n  Events: device plugin reported timeout 2025-01-10T09:05:23Z\n\n- kc exec -n infra autoscaler-7fd5c /bin/sh -c 'ps aux | grep autoscaler'\n  -> autoscaler process healthy, logs show rapid target recalcs triggered by metric bursts.\n\nAutoscaler config excerpt (from cluster):\n- minReplicas: 4\n- maxReplicas: 80\n- scaleUp: stabilizationWindowSeconds: 20  # suspiciously low\n- scaleDown: stabilizationWindowSeconds: 60\n- metrics: customPrometheus (tokens/sec, queueLength)\n\nPromQL probes I ran (timeline around incident):\n- sum(rate(requests_total[1m])) by (pool)\n- histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(latency_seconds_bucket[1m])) by (le, route))\n- pool_warm_start_duration_seconds_bucket -- shows heavy mass in 30-80s bucket\n\nError snippets captured from device plugin logs:\n- 2025-01-10T09:06:12Z ERROR deviceplugin: Allocate failed: nvml: device not ready\n- 2025-01-10T09:06:45Z WARN kubelet: pod \"serve-abc\" is slow to start: CNI wait 12s, device attach 42s\n\nHypotheses (ranked):\n1) Stabilization windows too aggressive relative to instance warmup. scaleUp window 20s < warmup 40-70s -> autoscaler swings up then down when short bursts end before instances finish priming.\n2) Device plugin intermittently failing under burst attach load (nvml timeouts), causing pods to flake and the autoscaler to see them as unsuccessful, lowering desired replicas.\n3) Scheduling churn because pods have strict nodeSelector:nvidia-a100 and limited packing, so bin-packing conflicts cause preemption/evictions during concurrent scaling.\n4) Cold cache (KV cache not primed) amplifies perceived latency, triggering additional scale decisions in feedback loop.\n\nExperiments and what I tried:\n- Experiment A (2025-01-10 09:30) - increased scaleUp.stabilizationWindowSeconds to 120s and observed behavior for 40m. Result: thrash reduced by ~70% but time-to-service for first requests increased slightly when real demand dropped quickly.\n- Experiment B - bumped minReplicas to 12 and paused downscaling for 10m during controlled traffic replay. Result: no device plugin errors observed; latency steady but cost increase obvious.\n- Experiment C - changed nodeSelector to allow nvidia-a40 as fallback for non-latency-critical routes. Result: scheduler placed pods on A40s; KV cache miss rate increased but fewer device attach errors.\n- Experiment D - manual pre-warm: run a bootstrap job that performs dummy inference to populate KV cache on new pods. Observed lower P95 on subsequent real requests but cold-start duration unchanged.\n\nRepro steps (best-effort):\n1) Use replay load generator to push 3x baseline RPS for 60-90s with short quiet windows.\n2) Observe autoscaler behavior and check pool_warm_start_duration_seconds histograms.\n3) Watch device-plugin logs for NVML allocation errors.\n4) Toggle scaleUp.stabilizationWindowSeconds between 20s and 120s to see difference.\n\nTemporary mitigations taken:\n- Increased scaleUp.stabilizationWindowSeconds to 120s cluster-wide for dedicated pools (rolled back on 2025-01-11 14:00 after follow-ups).\n- Raised minReplicas for pool-x to 12 during office hours (manual).\n- Added a probe to detect NVML allocation failures and mark node as \"no-new-alloc\" for 2m to reduce attach pressure.\n\nLonger-term remediation ideas (backlog):\n- Autoscaler: make warmup-aware scaling policy (explicit warmupDuration per pool) so desiredReplicas only considered stable after warmup window.\n- Implement jittered scaleDown policy: avoid simultaneous downscales across similar pools to prevent cascade.\n- Device plugin: collaborate with infra team to improve attach concurrency handling and add exponential backoff retries for NVML errors.\n- Scheduler: relax nodeSelector (fallback tiers) and prefer soft-affinity to reduce packing bottlenecks.\n- Serve runtime: add faster cold-start path that warms only lightweight KV cache to reduce critical path latency for first tokens.\n\nOpen questions / TODOs:\n- Is the NVML failure rate correlated with simultaneous attach attempts per node? [Feature flag experimentation cheat sheet (wip)]
Purpose

This is a tactical, cross-functional cheat sheet for shipping features behind flags with a mix of short canaries and A/B experiments. It’s intentionally practical — quick checklists, thresholds, and who-does-what for the first 72 hours. Not a policy doc; think runbook + experiment hygiene notes.

Audience
- PMs running product experiments
- SRE/Oncall and Observability engineers supporting rollouts
- Feature owners and release engineers
- Solutions/Customer Success for high-impact customer rollouts

TL;DR (two-line summary)
- Use small canaries for safety-critical infra or when latency/regression risk is high. Use A/B for signal-driven product decisions (engagement, retention).
- Always pair a rollout with a monitoring dashboard + pre-registered analysis plan. If p95 latency or error-rate exceed thresholds, rollback immediately.

Quick decision flow (one-page)
1) Is user-facing experience changing perceived quality or cost? -> Yes: prefer canary + quick smoke tests. No: consider dark-launch + metrics bake.
2) Is the change expected to produce directional product metrics (CTR, retention, conversions)? -> Yes: A/B with pre-defined primary metric.
3) Is there potential to affect cost/unit (token cost, GPU seconds)? -> Add cost telemetry and set cost-alerting thresholds.
4) Does the feature touch model outputs (hallucinations, safety)? -> Add human review cohort + manual rollback path.

Roles & responsibilities (practical)
- Feature owner (PM/Eng): writes short rollout plan, primary contact during rollout, owns experiment hypothesis.
- Release lead (Eng): configures flags, ramp schedule, ensures deployment slots and smoke checks.
- SRE/Observability: builds dashboard, sets alerts, monitors first 6 hours and p95 windows.
- Data analyst/ML eval owner: pre-register analysis plan, sanity checks, sample size estimate.
- Solutions/CS: scope impacted customers, prepare comms for customers if needed.

Pre-rollout checklist (must complete before 1% traffic)
- [ ] Feature flag created with clear name + owner + kill-switch.
- [ ] Rollout doc linked in PR and shared in #prod-rollouts.
- [ ] Short smoke test plan and acceptance criteria (example samples).
- [ ] Observability: dashboard with primary metrics, p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, 5xx, rate limiting, token/cost per request, throughput.
- [ ] Alerting: at least one Slack + Pager alert for >= X% error increase and p95 latency regression.
- [ ] Data logging: event markers to identify cohort membership (flag value, variant id).
- [ ] Canary users identified (internal + small external cohort) and communication sent.

Recommended monitoring signals (quant + qual)
- Quantitative signals (instrument and show on single dashboard):
  - p50, p95, p99 latency (inference + end-to-end)
  - Error rate (5xx, model timeouts, downstream failures)
  - Request throughput and concurrency
  - Token consumption and cost per request
  - Rate of safety / content policy hits (if applicable)
  - Traffic funnel metrics relevant to the change (CTR, completions per session, conversion)
- Qualitative signals:
  - Support/CS mentions in last 24h (search #support for topic)
  - Random sample of outputs reviewed by human raters (for model-output changes)
  - Feedback form responses or NPS snippets for major UI changes

Guardrail thresholds (default recommendations — tune per project)
- Immediate rollback if:
  - Error rate increase >= 0.5 percentage points absolute and sustained for 3 minutes AND total requests > 1000 in window.
  - p95 latency increases by > 30% vs baseline for 5 consecutive minutes.
  - Token/cost per request increases > 40% and estimated daily spend delta > $500.
- Automated slowdowns / alerts if:
  - Small regressions (error +0.1pp or p95 +10%) persist for > 30 minutes.
  - Unexpected spike in safety hits or policy flags > 5x baseline.
- Note: thresholds are intentionally conservative for hosted API customers. For internal-only features you may relax thresholds after SRE discussion.

Canary plan (example sequence)
1) 0% -> 0.1% internal employees (smoke) for 15–30 mins. Manual checks + express rollback test.
2) 0.1% -> 1% external users for 60–120 mins. Monitor error / latency and customer signals.
3) 1% -> 5% for 4–8 hrs (or one business day), collect data.
4) 5% -> 25% overnight (if stable), then 50% next day, full ramp after 48–72 hrs of stability.
- For safety-sensitive changes: keep canary windows longer and require two independent SRE signoffs before ramping.

A/B experiment plan (example)
- Hypothesis: short statement tying the change to a measurable metric (primary metric must be defined).
- Primary metric example: percent of sessions with successful completions. Secondary metrics: latency, error-rate, cost per session, retention.
- Experiment sizing: estimate minimum detectable effect (MDE) and set duration to reach power >= 80%. Work with data analyst to compute sample sizes.
- Randomization: use server-side bucketing, log deterministic cohort id. Avoid client-side randomization for mobile clients.
- Analysis plan (pre-registered): specify primary test (two-sample t-test or bootstrapped mean difference for continuous; chi-square or binomial test for rates), covariates to adjust for, and handling of missing data.
- Multiple comparisons: if running many metrics, use FDR control or Bonferroni — highlight the primary metric for decision.
- Early stopping: permitted only for safety signals (use guardrails above) or pre-agreed interim analysis with alpha spending rules.

Experiment interpretation guidance
- Signal != causation if instrumentation is incomplete. Validate cohort markers in logs before reading results.
- Check leading indicators (latency, errors, cost) before final decision even if primary metric shows an uplift.
- If primary metric weak but secondary suggests regression, do not proceed; prioritize user safety/latency.

Communication template (Slack + status doc)
- Channel: #prod-rollouts (post initial ramp and status updates)
- First post must include: feature flag name, owner, short hypothesis, rollout percentage, start time, dashboards (links), rollback threshold, who is on-call.
- Hourly updates while ramping between 1% and 25%, then every 4 hours between 25% and 100%.

Rollback & post-rollback triage
- Kill-switch: flag must be able to cut traffic to baseline variant in < 60s. Practice this during pre-rollout tests.
- Post-rollback immediate steps:
  1) Confirm rollback completed and observe stabilization for 15 minutes.
  2) Gather logs, last-good baseline timeframe, and failing traces.
  3) Convene incident owner + feature owner for 30-min triage.
  4) Decide on next steps: patch + re-rollout, extended canary, or cancel feature.
- Postmortem template: include timeline, metrics at failure, root cause, and next action items (owner + due date). Add link to postmortem in the rollout doc.

Data hygiene and instrumentation notes
- Always log a deterministic cohort id and the active flag value for the request.
- Keep event schemas backward compatible for 30 days post-rollout.
- Add tags for model-version and quantization profile because runtime changes often explain regression.

Practical knobs for model-serving rollouts
- Kernel/quantization A/B test: run small percent of traffic through quantized model variant, monitor correctness metrics + latency/cost.
- Routing policy: prefer region-local fallback to avoid cross-region latency spikes.
- KV cache priming: pre-warm cache on canary cohort to avoid cold-start penalties skewing latency signals.

Example template (paste into PR description)
- Feature flag: ff.feature_name
- Owner: name + PagerDuty handle
- Hypothesis: one-line
- Primary metric: metric_name (how computed)
- Rollout plan: 0.1% -> 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% with windows and criteria
- Guardrails: list thresholds and who to notify
- Dashboards: links
- Rollback contact: name + phone/pager

Open questions / TODOs
- Do we want standardized default thresholds per product line (hosted vs dedicated vs private)? Current thresholds biased to hosted customers.
- Add canned Grafana/Looker dashboard templates for common rollout types.
- Experiment meta-data: should we persist experiment config to Confluence automatically from PR? Discuss with platform team.

Notes to self (short-term action items)
- Create a small checklist generator script that produces the PR template + Slack post shell. (owner: Ben)
- Work with Observability to create a minimal rollout dashboard that can be cloned (owner: Marta).
- Sprint task: document kill-switch test steps and schedule a chaos-window to practice one forced rollback per quarter. (owner: Aisha)

Appendix: example metrics query snippets (high level)
- p95 latency (end-to-end): percentile(latency_ms, 95) grouped by variant, 5m rolling
- Error rate: sum(errors) / sum(requests) grouped by variant, 5m rolling
- Cost delta: avg(token_cost) * request_count_by_variant -> daily projection

End of cheat sheet — this is a living file. Add specific experiment notes below each rollout plan.

Example experiment notes (template filled)
- Experiment: reduce-beam-size-for-embedding-cache
- Start: 2026-02-12 09:00 UTC
- Owner: Noah Patel
- Rollout steps: internal 0.1% for 30m -> 0.5% external for 2h -> 5% for 24h
- Observed: p95 latency -6%, token cost -18%, error rate unchanged. Continue to 25%.
- TODO: add sample of outputs to human-rater queue to validate semantic parity.

If you copy from this doc for a PR, remove the TODOs and add direct links to dashboards and tickets.

The goal is to:\n\n- Define a small surface area of stable variables/outputs we can commit to across providers.\n- Provide a reproducible test harness to validate compatibility and rollback behavior before rolling upgrades to production on Dedicated and Private fleets.\n- Capture experiments, failure modes, and migration steps so SRE and infra teams can run safe rollouts.\n\nContext / constraints:\n\n- Customers sometimes run Redwood Private in air‑gapped or restricted networks; our TF modules must support a narrow set of required outputs and optional extension points.\n- Many downstream repos consume module outputs directly (service accounts, network IDs). Breaking changes must be non‑disruptive.\n- Onprem clusters vary: some use EKS with private endpoints, others are self‑managed K8s (GKE‑like or AKS equivalents). The module needs adapters, not provider‑forced opinionation.\n\nHigh level design decisions (short):\n\n1) Minimum stable contract: keep outputs for: vpc_id, subnet_ids (public/private), cluster_security_group, control_plane_endpoint, cluster_ca_cert, node_role_arn, service_account_oidc_url.\n2) Avoid returning cloud‑provider-specific ARNs in top‑level outputs. [minimize GPU scratch and arena allocations with fused checkpointing and kernel coordination]
description:
Summary: This PR reduces GPU workspace/scratch allocations by combining three complementary changes: (1) a staged activation checkpointing strategy that fuses checkpoint boundaries for contiguous transformer blocks, (2) a reuse-aware arena allocator with tighter bucket sizing and cross-kernel eviction heuristics, and (3) kernel launch coordination to avoid simultaneous peak scratch usage when continuous batching is active. Together these changes reduce observed peak workspace on A100/RTX instances by ~25-35% for long-context generation and batch-heavy workloads, with negligible latency regressions and modest additional CPU memory for checkpoint metadata.

Motivation and background: We have recurring customer reports and internal benchmarks showing OOMs and elevated tail latency when continuous-batching and KV-cache are both in use on constrained GPUs (40-80GB). Investigation (linked ENG-4823) showed that per-kernel scratch allocations plus activation checkpointing peaks overlap in worst-case schedules. Additionally, the existing arena allocator conservatively rounds many small scratch allocations up to large buckets, inflating peak working set. This PR targets the runtime workspace pressure (not model weights or KV storage) to improve headroom for large-context LLMs and autoscaling predictability.

What changed (high level):
- Activation checkpointing: added "fused_checkpointing" mode that coalesces adjacent checkpoints across consecutive transformer layers when safe (no parameter updates and contiguous KV/atten state). This reduces the number of saved activations and consolidates temporary buffers. Implemented conservative alias analysis in runtime/graph/utils to verify fusion safety. Fallback to per-layer checkpointing remains default for models with custom side-effects.
- Arena allocator: introduced reuse-aware buckets. We now track recent allocation shapes and prefer reusing same-sized scratch buffers across kernel types. Bucket sizes reduced (power-of-two floor) and a cross-kernel eviction policy prevents many medium buffers occupying peak simultaneously. Tunable via REDWOOD_GPU_ARENA_PROFILE env var and console settings.
- Kernel coordination: scheduler now batches kernel launches with awareness of their peak-scratch demand. When continuous batching is enabled, the scheduler staggers high-scratch kernels across micro-batches or defers lower-priority workloads to avoid simultaneous peaks. This is an opt-in heuristic controlled by runtime policy and benchmarked to avoid throughput loss.
- KV cache padding: trimmed conservative rounding for KV-cache allocations based on observed sequence-length distributions; padding now uses 8-token granularity instead of 64 for most models, reclaiming workspace in common cases.

Commits (summary):
- feat(runtime): fused activation checkpointing pass + safety checks (authored by Mina)
- perf(memory): reuse-aware arena allocator & cross-kernel eviction (Ethan)
- feat(scheduler): scratch-aware kernel launch coordination and continuous-batch sharding (Soraya)
- fix(tests): add regression tests for fused checkpointing and arena reuse (Rakesh)
- ci: add perf benchmark job for peak-workspace measurement

Files changed (high-level):
- runtime/arena/allocator.cpp (core allocator changes, ~420 additions/120 deletions)
- runtime/checkpoint/fused_pass.cpp (new fused checkpointing implementation)
- runtime/scheduler/scratch_aware_scheduler.cpp (staggering heuristics)
- runtime/kv/cache_alloc.cpp (padding heuristics)
- tests/perf/peak_workspace_bench.cc (new benchmark)
- docs/perf/gpu_workspace_tuning.md (new doc explaining env vars and console flags)
- examples/bench/long_context_config.yaml (example config used for CI)

Small illustrative snippet (allocator heuristic):
"// prefer exact reuse, then floor to pow2 buckets, avoid pre-allocating next higher bucket unless under low-pressure"
"if (recent_shape == req_shape) return reuse_bucket; else return bucket_for_floor_pow2(req_size);"

Testing and benchmarks:
- Added unit tests for fused checkpointing verifying numerical equality for fused vs per-layer (within FP tolerance).
- CI perf job runs long-context generation on A100-80GB and RTX-6000; measured peak workspace reductions: 32% (GPT-like 8k seq, batch 1), 28% (8k seq, batch 8, continuous-batching enabled), and 18% (4k seq, batch 32).

[Hybrid slab arena and adaptive checkpoint scheduler to reduce GPU workspace]
description:
Summary: This PR introduces a hybrid slab-focused arena allocator plus an adaptive activation checkpoint scheduler that cooperates with per-kernel scratch throttling and KV-cache LRU hints to materially reduce peak workspace and overall device allocation for long-context chat workloads. Motivation: customers running 100k+ token sessions and multi-turn chat were hitting OOMs on medium GPUs due to worst-case scratch+arena peaks; previous approaches (pure checkpointing or global arena caps) either increased latency or underutilized GPU memory. The goal here is to reduce worst-case workspace while preserving p95/p99 latency and throughput. What changed: 1) Arena allocator: add slab reservation for transient kernel scratch (slab_reserve_ratio tunable) so short-lived scratch allocations get carved from a temporary slab instead of the global arena; introduce slab eviction heuristics to free slabs when sustained memory pressure detected. 2) Hybrid checkpoint scheduler: new scheduler defers some activation checkpoints from the hot microbatches to colder microbatches within the same request when safe, reducing simultaneous checkpoint buffers; it uses a cheap cost model keyed by sequence-length and layer-flops to decide which layers to checkpoint eagerly versus deferred. 3) Scratch pool throttling: per-kernel scratch quotas that bias kernel selection toward low-scratch variants under pressure; integrates with kernel selector to prefer fused-attention paths that use smaller temporary buffers when sequence-length distribution suggests benefit. 4) KV-cache coalescing: KV manager now coalesces identical prefix KV handles across concurrent requests from the same conversation id to avoid duplicate KV allocations; LRU hinting reduces retention of rarely-reused past-turn keys. 5) Runtime knobs and telemetry: new tunables (slab_reserve_ratio, checkpoint_deferral_threshold, scratch_quota_ms) and metrics (arena.slabs.active, checkpoint.deferrals, scratch.throttled_count) added to Console and traces. Benchmarks: Internal p50/p95/p99 latency changes on rw-llama-7b loadtest with batch=8 and 4 concurrent streams: peak device allocations down 28% (from 9.8GB to 7.0GB), average device footprint down 18%, p95 latency +2.3%, p99 latency +3.8% on worst-case mixed-length traces; throughput unchanged within noise. Safety/perf tradeoffs: some microbatched requests may force checkpoint deferral causing slightly higher recompute on tail cases; knobs default conservatively to minimize recompute for latency-sensitive tiers. Commits: "alloc: add slab reserve allocator and eviction policy"; "sched: hybrid checkpoint scheduler and cost model"; "kernel: scratch quota enforcement + selector hints"; "kv: coalesce conversation kv handles and LRU hints"; "telemetry: arena and scheduler metrics + console panels"; "tests: add unit/integration tests for slab/deferral behaviour". Files changed (high level): runtime/allocator/slab_arena.{h,cpp} - new slab reserve implementation; runtime/scheduler/checkpoint_scheduler.cpp - new scheduler and cost model; runtime/kernel/scratch_pool.cpp - quota enforcement and selector hooks; runtime/kv/kv_cache_manager.cpp - coalescing logic and LRU hint flow; runtime/selector/kernel_selector.cpp - prefer low-scratch kernel variants when quota triggered; console/metrics/arena_dashboards.yaml - new panels; tests/allocator/test_slab_eviction.cpp - unit tests; integration/bench/long_context_memory.yaml - benchmark harness. Small illustrative snippet (updated allocator heuristic): "if (current_pressure > slab_threshold) slab->evict_least_recently_used(); else reserve_from_slab(requested)". Review conversation: Jordan Kim (reviewer) requested clearer invariants around deferral: "How do we ensure correctness when deferring checkpoint writes across microbatches?"; Anika replied: "We only defer within the same parent request boundary and track dependency fences per-layer; added assertion coverage and integration tests to validate tensor liveness across deferral windows." Priya Desai asked for telemetry gating and signal names; Anika: "Added metrics and Console panels and documented tunables in runtime/README.md; default values set to conservative for hosted API." Liam O'Connor raised concern about KV coalescing for multi-tenant Dedicated pools: "Could coalescing leak state across tenants?"; response: "Coalescing keyed by conversation-id + tenant-id; no cross-tenant sharing. Added unit tests and an audit log entry when coalescing occurs." CI status: initial lint failure (allocator header include order), tests flaky on integration bench (timing sensitivity) causing a failed run; fixes applied and CI green on re-run. Rollout plan: feature gated under runtime.tunable.hybrid_checkpoint enabled=false by default for hosted main, enabled in internal perf clusters and Dedicated with opt-in; gradual rollout to all Dedicated pools after two-week soak. Related work: follows ENG-742 and builds on previous arena and checkpoint experiments (see PRs reducing arena/checkpoint footprint) but differs by combining slab-reservation with a cost-driven deferral scheduler and KV coalescing. Merge: squash and merged by Anika Rao; merge commit message: "hybrid slab arena + adaptive checkpoint scheduler - reduce workspace and scratch peaks". Notes for ops: if customers report increased recompute tail, recommend lowering checkpoint_deferral_threshold or disabling hybrid_checkpoint for that pool. Checklist: [x] unit tests added, [x] integration bench added, [x] telemetry panels, [x] docs updated, [x] feature gated for gradual rollout.

release_notes:
Reduced peak GPU workspace by ~28% and end-to-end GPU footprint by ~18% for typical chat workloads; no API changes. Rollout: gradual on Dedicated pools with new arena tunables defaulting to safe limits.

[Reduce GPU workspace and peak memory via arena tuning, checkpointing, and scratch buffer refactor]
description:
Motivation: production LLM inference at large batch and sequence lengths frequently hits GPU workspace/peak memory limits, forcing use of larger instances or conservative quantization. This PR reduces peak GPU allocations and working set by combining three complementary changes: (1) a conservative activation checkpointing path for transformer blocks that trades minimal CPU recompute for up to 25-40% activation RAM reduction at long sequence lengths; (2) a unified arena allocator tuning for per-stream scratch buffers and temporary kernels, reducing fragmentation and per-request overhead; (3) refactoring scratch buffer lifetimes in the CUDA kernel wrappers so scratch allocations are reused across micro-batches inside the continuous-batching loop. Design: activation checkpointing is opt-in per model variant via a new config flag model.runtime.activation_checkpointing: "auto|off|aggressive". The default "auto" enables checkpointing when offloaded KV/cache is enabled and the estimated peak reaches configured thresholds. Arena allocator changes include: a smaller max-block size for short-lived temporaries, bucketized free-lists for 512B-8MB ranges, and a fallback slow-path that reclaims whole-stream arenas on schedule boundaries. Scratch buffer refactor centralizes buffers on the BatchWorkspace object and pins those allocations to per-GPU streams to avoid cross-stream synchronization. We added microbenchmarks and a realistic ChatML workload to the perf suite to validate both latency and throughput under mixed request sizes. Results: on our A100 40GB testbed with batch=8 and seq=4096, peak GPU memory reduced by ~36%, soft latency increase <=3% p50 and throughput steady or improved in ground-truth workloads due to reduced OOM/backoffs. Backwards compatibility and safety: the changes are gated behind feature flags and require model authors to opt into activation checkpointing for small models; we provide an automated suggestion tool in the optimizer that proposes flags based on profiling sample traces. Rollout plan: staged rollout as default for Dedicated customers after two weeks of Canary (this PR includes canary toggles). Checklist: - [x] bench and microbench added - [x] unit tests for arena invariants - [x] smoke tests for continuous batching with scratch reuse - [x] documentation updates (runtime flags + upgrade notes) - [x] performance dashboard panels for memory/arena churn Additional context: this is part of ENG-1972 which targets inference cost reduction for long-context workloads. See linked performance dashboards and linear ticket for traces and flamegraphs.

[TP: kernel fusion + NCCL pipelined overlap + sharded KV cache + continuous-batcher multi-GPU adjustments]
release_notes:
- Multi-GPU tensor-parallel: improved communication/computation overlap and tuned NCCL rendezvous to reduce allreduce stalls
- Fused attention and rotary kernel paths for lower per-token compute on 2/4/8 GPU configs
- Sharded KV cache across TP ranks; reduces peak memory and improves throughput for long context workloads
- Continuous batcher aware of TP topology to form GPU-aware microbatches
- No public API breaking changes; rollout gated behind runtime flag

description:
Motivation: Production TP workloads for long-context streaming showed two related bottlenecks: (1) NCCL collectives blocking critical compute on some sequence-length distributions, and (2) KV cache memory pressure and locking during continuous batching that forced smaller microbatch sizes. This PR attacks both bottlenecks with a suite of coordinated changes: - NCCL rendezvous tuning and pipelined collectives: introduce a lightweight rendezvous/handshake to align NCCL communicator launches across ranks, add opportunistic async allreduce/p2p windows to overlap with kernel compute, and add per-topology backoff thresholds to avoid cascading retries on temporary GPU bus congestion. - Kernel fusion and scheduling: implement a fused attention+rotary kernel path (CUDA) that reduces memory churn and has a smaller kernel-launch overhead; adjust the TP scheduler to prioritize compute-heavy kernels when collective windows are expected so overlap is maximized. - Sharded KV cache: partition KV storage by TP rank with fast remote prefetch for prefix reuse; replace coarse global locks with per-shard lock-free ring metadata to reduce contention. - Continuous-batcher topology awareness: continuous-batcher now tags microbatches with TP-affinity metadata; the router groups requests to form microbatches that maximize local KV hits and reduce cross-rank synchronization. Backwards-compatible runtime flagged rollout: all changes are gated behind runtime flags (tp_optim.enable and tp_optim.kv_shard) with safe fallbacks to previous behavior. Benchmarks: internal perf harness (see commits) shows +22% throughput on a 4xA100 (32k window) synthetic conversational load and up to 18% p99 latency reduction at 8-GPU TP for mixed sequence-length traces. Also measured ~12% lower GPU memory high-water for long-context inference due to KV sharding. Rollout plan: merge to main behind flags -> enable on canary Dedicated pool -> monitor tp-overlap and KV-hitratio dashboards -> wider rollouts. [interstage-sampler-fusion-and-deferred-decode-windowing]
description:
Motivation: continuous-batching and prefill/decode handoff currently incur repeated kernel launches and buffer materialization when sampling decisions are resolved only during decode. This PR introduces two cooperating mechanisms to reduce kernel churn and KV cache thrash: 1) an Interstage Sampler component that computes lightweight sampling hints during prefill and encodes them into a compact hint payload attached to the request context, and 2) Deferred Decode Windowing which groups decode invocations into micro-windows that allow the scheduler to fuse compatible kernels and coalesce KV cache accesses. The changes reduce per-request kernel launches and improve GPU kernel occupancy for medium-length generations.

What changed (high level): implemented an interstage sampler interface in the serving runtime, added a hint-serialization path that travels with the request through scheduler and executor layers, extended the scheduler to recognize hint-aligned requests and opportunistically perform in-place sampling decisions during prefill-to-decode handoff, and introduced a deferred-decode windowing policy that batches short decodes into micro-windows of configurable time/size thresholds. Also added a soft-locking mechanism for KV cache entries to avoid immediate eviction when a prefill indicates imminent reuse. The implementation is careful to keep the public API unchanged; all behavior is guarded by a feature flag (runtime.experimental.interstage_sampler) and rollout knobs (window_size_ms, max_window_tokens).

Design notes: the interstage sampler emits one of three hint classes (greedy, topk-k-prob, temperature-sample-metadata) encoded as a compact enum+payload to avoid bloating network buffers. Deferred windows are sized to prioritize throughput gains while bounding added per-token latency; defaults are 6ms or 8 tokens whichever first. Scheduler-level changes include a kernel fusion planner that merges prefetched logits with decode kernels when hints are compatible, and a KV soft-lock counter with TTL to prevent eviction during immediate handoffs. The approach is conservative by default and falls back to existing prefill/decode handoff semantics if hints are missing or incompatible.

Compatibility and safety: feature-flagged rollout, end-to-end regression tests added (unit + integration + nightly perf suite). KV soft-locks use a bounded counter to avoid permanent leakage; the soft-lock acquires only when prefill declares reuse within the configured horizon. The feature is disabled in Dedicated beta clusters until we've validated SLA impacts.

Benchmarks (summary): measured on v100-equivalent cluster with mixed short/medium workloads: +9-12% aggregate throughput for mixed traffic, ~20% fewer kernel launches per request, 7% lower GPU memory churn during bursts, and median latency unchanged. 99th percentile for tiny single-token generations increased by 1.8–6ms in the worst-case windowing configuration; default windows keep increase under 3ms which is within our latency SLO for non-low-latency tiers.

[Standardize ephemeral workspace creation and autosweeper for feature pods]
description:
Issue summary:
We need a standardized, auditable automation that provisions ephemeral Slack channels, Confluence draft spaces/pages, and temporary Jira groups when a feature pod requests a sandbox workspace. The automation should attach an owner, enforce RBAC, and schedule an automatic review/archival (autosweeper) after a configurable TTL (default 30 days).

Background / why: 
Feature teams frequently create ad-hoc channels and Confluence pages for short-lived experiments. Lack of standardization causes orphaned channels, inconsistent permissions, and audit gaps. Security and Platform would like a predictable lifecycle that reduces noise and improves cost/retention hygiene.

Impact: 
- Cross-pod clutter in Slack and Confluence; difficulty finding active workspaces.
- Manual cleanup burden on Platform and SRE.
- Potential permission drift and audit holes (unknown owners).

Request: 
1) Implement a lightweight self-serve flow (Slack slash command + Jira form) that creates: a named ephemeral Slack channel (private by default), a Confluence draft space or page created from a template, and a Jira group with scoped view permissions.
2) On creation, require an explicit owner (email) and set metadata tags: pod, feature, ttl-days.
3) Autosweeper: after TTL expires, automated job posts a 7-day warning in the channel, then archives Slack channel and sets Confluence space/page to read-only and not searchable. Create a small audit artifact (confluence note / jira task) capturing the action.
4) RBAC/Compliance: integrate with existing role-sync; owners must belong to an org group; deny creation if owner is not in an allowed list for private workspaces.
5) Provide a Confluence runbook and a short onboarding doc for product leads.

Scope and constraints: 
- Must reuse existing Slack-bots infra; do not introduce new long-lived credentials.
- The automation must emit an event to our audit topic (kafka/audit-events) for every create/modify/archive action.
- Default TTL = 30 days; allow override per-request up to 90 days (enterprise exceptions handled via manual process).

Acceptance notes: see acceptance_criteria field.

Operational handover expectations:
- Include a runbook with playbook steps to reverse archive, reassign owner, and override TTL for enterprise requests.
- Provide a migration/cleanup plan for 60-day backlog of orphaned pods (separate follow-up ticket).

acceptance_criteria:
Provisioning flow: ability to create workspace via Slack slash command and Jira form with owner, pod, and ttl metadata recorded.
RBAC enforcement: creation blocked if owner is not in allowed identity group for private workspaces.
Audit events: every create/modify/archive emits a record to kafka/audit-events with workspace id and actor.
Autosweeper behavior: 7-day warning -> archive Slack channel + set Confluence to read-only -> create audit note. Verified in a staging test with ttl=2 days.
Runbook and docs: public runbook created and reviewed by Security and Internal Tools; 1 pager for product leads published in Confluence.
Graceful override: Platform staff can extend TTL via admin Jira action; extension events are audited.

description:
Issue summary:\nWe need a supported self-service flow for creating temporary and long-lived Slack channels that automatically provisions Confluence space skeletons and the minimal Jira project-space permissions. The goal is to remove repeated manual requests to Internal Support for standard project onboarding while preserving an approval gate for security-sensitive channels.\n\nImpact:\n- Teams repeatedly open manual tickets to request: channel creation, Confluence skeleton with page templates, and Jira permission groups. This causes 2-4 day lead times and inconsistent naming/permissions.\n- Risk of over-provisioned access when ad-hoc channels are created without a standard claim process.\n\nBackground and constraints:\n- There are existing templates for Confluence pages in the Ops space but no automated hook for Slack channel creation.\n- We must respect RBAC constraints: only certain users (pod leads) can approve channel owners that get 'project-editor' access in Confluence and 'jira-developers' role in project spaces.\n- Integration must record an audit trail (who requested, approver, timestamps) and create a ticket in the Internal Support queue if manual review is required.\n\nRequest / Acceptance criteria:\n1) A Slack slash-command /new-project that triggers a small modal asking: channel name, channel type (ephemeral|long-lived), owning team, lead (@handle), and requested Confluence skeleton (marketing|engineering|compliance).\n2) If the owning lead is in the "approved project leads" group, the bot should auto-create the Slack channel, call the Confluence API to instantiate the matching skeleton, and provision minimal Jira group memberships. The whole flow must create a traceable internal ticket with links to each created artifact.\n3) If the owning lead is not in the approved group, the flow should route to a 48-hour approval queue (Auto-approve if no action) and put the channel in #ops-approval-watch until approval completes.\n4) All actions must add an entry to the new audit log page under the Ops Confluence space and post a structured message to #support-ops with metadata.\n5) Provide a small runbook for SRE to disable the automation per workspace or region (eu-west / us-east) in case of misconfiguration.\n\nSuccess metrics:\n- Reduce manual channel/confluence/jira onboarding tickets by 60% in 90 days for small projects (<=10 members).\n- Average provisioning time for approved leads < 10 minutes.\n\nAcceptance test steps:\n- Request a new long-lived channel as an approved lead -> verify channel, Confluence skeleton, and Jira groups are created and ticket logged automatically.\n- Request as non-approved lead -> verify approval flow triggers and channel is held in pending state with audit entries.\n\nNotes on compliance and audit:\n- All approval events must write to Confluence audit page and Slack message must include requestor, approver, timestamp, and links to created resources.\n- We cannot auto-grant 'admin' roles; only minimal contributor/edit roles are allowed in Confluence and Jira.\n\nDeliverables requested from Platform/Infra team:\n- A lightweight Slack app and bot manifest with modal UI and permission scopes documented.\n- Serverless automation (preferred) or a small internal service with retry and idempotency keys.\n- Confluence page templates and an Ops runbook for emergency disablement.\n- A short post-deployment validation script that runs in staging before promoting to prod.

[Tag-driven project lifecycle automation: decommission Slack channels, snapshot Confluence spaces, archive Jira projects]
description:
Issue summary:
We need a tag-driven project lifecycle automation that enforces a standardized decommission process for cross-team projects. When a project is marked with a lifecycle tag (e.g., lifecycle:decom-30d) in Jira or Confluence meta, the system should: 1) place the project's Slack channels into read-only mode and postfix the name with _archived-YYYYMMDD, 2) snapshot and store Confluence pages in a compliance S3 bucket (with metadata), 3) create an archival Jira project clone with reduced permissions and move open issues matching criteria, 4) notify project owners and start a 30-day quiesce countdown with opt-out, and 5) emit audit records to the compliance audit log.

Background / rationale:
We have several ad-hoc project shutdowns that are inconsistent: channels left open, docs drift, and missing audit trails. Legal/compliance requested a reproducible, auditable process for project offboarding that preserves data for eDiscovery and reduces clutter in Slack/Confluence/Jira. This automation should be permission-gated and require project-owner acknowledgement before irreversible archival steps.

Impact:
- Internal housekeeping: reduces stale channels and pages.
- Compliance: consistent snapshot and retention metadata for audits.
- Developer experience: avoids losing important artifacts while reducing noise.

Requirements / constraints:
- Non-destructive by default: first step is read-only / snapshot and notification; final destructive actions require explicit project-owner confirmation or 30-day expiry.
- RBAC: only Platform Admins and assigned project owners can opt-out or fast-track.
- Auditability: every action must produce an entry in the compliance audit stream (syslog/Kafka).
- Idempotency: automation should be safe to re-run and support retries.
- Rate-limits: operations must be rate-limited to avoid Slack API throttles.

Acceptance criteria (see separate field):

Related runbooks / references:
- Confluence design stub: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/PLAT/Tag-driven+Lifecycle+Automation+Design
- Slack channel archival best-practices: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/OPS/Slack+Archival+Guidelines


acceptance_criteria:
When a Jira project is tagged with lifecycle:decom-30d, an automated notification is sent to project owners within 1 hour.
Slack channels for the project become read-only and are renamed with _archived-YYYYMMDD but retain history within 2 hours of tag application.
Confluence pages are snapshotted to the compliance S3 bucket with metadata (project key, tag, timestamp, owner) and a checksum recorded in the audit log.
A cloned Jira project (read-only) is created and open issues matching 'critical' priority remain assigned; other issues are moved or closed per policy.
All automation steps emit audit events to /audit/lifecycle with sequence IDs and linkable metadata for eDiscovery.
Project owners can opt-out within the 30-day period via the acceptance flow; opt-out action is recorded in audit log.
Automation respects Slack rate-limits and retries transient failures without inconsistent partial state (idempotent runs).

implementation_notes:
Proposed approach: 1) Add a lifecycle tag recognizer lambda that subscribes to Jira/Confluence webhooks; 2) Enqueue tasks to a lifecycle worker (k8s) that runs sequential sub-tasks with compensating actions; 3) Use immutable snapshotting for Confluence (export HTML + attachments) to S3 and record checksum; 4) Use Jira project export to an archival project with restricted perms; 5) Use Slack SCIM / Admin APIs to set channel to read-only and rename; 6) Emit audit events to Kafka topic 'audit.lifecycle'. Start with a staged rollout for one internal team (pod: infra-ops) in staging region then prod rollout plan with feature flags.
