[Response choreography: latency vs. econ brief (draft)]
Purpose:
This is a working brief exploring 'response choreography' — the set of runtime and client-side choices that change how responses are assembled and released (chunking, partial flush, multiplexing vs dedicated slots) — and how those choices trade off latency percentiles and $/1k-token economics. Goal is to produce a short, actionable set of recommendations for Console defaults and a set of benchmark figures we can include in product collateral (annotated charts in text).

Scope and motivation:
- We focus on interactive chat-style workloads where responses are frequently short (turns <= 64 tokens) but occasionally long (>= 512 tokens).
- Two broad runtime patterns tested:
  1) smallbatch (session affinity, small slot sizes, aggressive KV cache) — optimized for low p50 and p90 for short turns
  2) multiplex (max packing, opportunistic slots, higher batching latency but much better amortized $/token)
- We test three model variants representative of our catalog: rwd-7B-fat (fast, lower quality), rwd-13B-quant (balanced), external-70B-vanilla (higher latency, higher quality).
- Hardware baseline: A100-class dedicated pools (single-GPU serving), and an A10G-like mainstream class for multiplex runs. All runs on Redwood runtime with current kernel-selection heuristics.

Methodology (short):
- Synthetic session generator with mixture: 80% short-turns (<=32 tokens), 18% medium (33-128), 2% long (>512).
- 30m steady-state windows per config, with warmup 5m. Each config repeated 3x; numbers below are median-of-median runs.
- Measured: p50/p90/p99 (ms), tokens/sec (system-level), observed $/1k tokens (amortized infra + GPU time + scheduler overhead).
- Client behavior: streaming allowed; two partial-flush policies tested — eager-flush (emit first non-empty chunk asap) vs flush-on-chunk-complete (emit only when chunk boundary reached).

Annotated benchmark table (compact, numbers are illustrative from runs):

Scenario | Model | Runtime pattern | p50 (ms) | p90 (ms) | p99 (ms) | tokens/s | $/1k tokens
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Short-turn, eager-flush | rwd-7B-fat | smallbatch   | 42  | 78  | 210 | 1,600 | $0.42
Short-turn, eager-flush | rwd-7B-fat | multiplex    | 85  | 190 | 420 | 3,400 | $0.18
Short-turn, eager-flush | rwd-13B-quant | smallbatch | 55  | 110 | 280 | 1,200 | $0.65
Short-turn, eager-flush | rwd-13B-quant | multiplex  | 110 | 260 | 520 | 2,600 | $0.30
Long-turn (512 tokens), flush-on-chunk-complete | rwd-13B-quant | smallbatch | 820 | 1,100 | 1,760 | 260 | $0.95
Long-turn (512 tokens), flush-on-chunk-complete | rwd-13B-quant | multiplex  | 1,150| 1,820 | 3,400 | 640 | $0.40
Long-turn (512 tokens), flush-on-chunk-complete | external-70B | multiplex | 2,400| 3,900 | 6,700 | 180 | $2.90

Quick observations from table:
- Multiplex (max packing) consistently halves $/1k tokens relative to smallbatch for short-turn-heavy traffic, at the cost of ~2x p50 and larger p90/p99 regressions.
- For short-turn latency-sensitive experiences (chat UX where users expect immediate typing-like responses), smallbatch + eager-flush gives p50 ~40–60ms on smaller models which is perceptually instantaneous.
- Long-turn throughput and cost strongly favor multiplexing: amortization across tokens drops $/1k by 2–3x for long responses.
- p99 is the place where user experience and economics collide: multiplexing increases p99 dramatically for short-turns because large packets wait behind long requests unless we isolate them.

Micro-insights and heuristics:
- For PLG/first-time-user flows where perceived snappiness correlates with retention, default to smallbatch for models <=13B with eager-flush for short-turn endpoints.
- For billing-heavy / throughput-first endpoints (embedding-generation, batch summarization, document expansion) default to multiplex and enable session-affinity only as an opt-in.
- Implement a hybrid fast-path: dedicate X% of slots per-GPU to smallbatch-like low-latency serving. Heuristic: allocate low-latency pool proportional to short-turn fraction (e.g., if short-turn fraction >70%, keep 30% dedicated).
- Consider 'adaptive flush' client policy: for first N tokens in a response, eager-flush; for subsequent chunks, switch to chunk-complete flush. This captures perceived snappiness while recovering some batching efficiency on long responses.

Risk notes & caveats:
- These numbers depend a lot on underlying kernel choices and the version of our tensor-launcher; an upcoming kernel patch (runtime/#1429) improves smallbatch p99 by ~12% for 13B — so we should re-run pre-launch.
- Network jitter and client TCP pacing can add 10–50ms to observed p50 depending on region; our runs were in us-west only.
- $/1k is computed with our internal allocation model (infra + amortized GPU-hour price). External customer pricing will differ by margin and commit discounts.

[Quantile-Driven Mini-Buckets and Opportunistic Kernel Fallback]
Summary:

This note proposes a lightweight, production-friendly strategy for handling variable sequence lengths with lower padding overhead and predictable latency: quantile-driven mini-buckets combined with opportunistic kernel fallback and per-bucket KV sharding. The approach is targeted at high-throughput hosted endpoints and Dedicated pools where reducing per-token cost without impacting tail latency is critical.

Motivation and pain points:
- Large variance in sequence length (e.g., short chat turns mixed with long documents) forces large padding if using fixed-size buckets, wasting GPU cycles.
- Fine-grained bucketing reduces padding but increases scheduling overhead, kernel dispatch overhead, and KV cache fragmentation.
- Aggressive compaction can hurt tail latency when long requests miss the faster kernel or when KV locality is lost.
- Existing strategies at Redwood (time-window batching, slot compaction) work well but either keep too coarse buckets or are complex to tune per-model/workload.

Design goals:
1) Reduce average padding overhead by aligning pack sizes to observed quantiles of sequence length distribution.
2) Keep the number of bucket classes small (micro-buckets) to limit scheduling and kernel-selection complexity.
3) Provide a safe, latency-preserving fallback path: opportunistic kernel delegation to a latency-optimized but lower-throughput kernel on tail cases.
4) Preserve KV cache locality through lightweight per-bucket sharding and grace periods to avoid rewarm penalties.
5) Be incremental: can be toggled per-route and rolled out via canary.

Core idea (high level):
1) Runtime observes sequence length histogram in rolling windows (default 60s) and computes a small set of quantiles (e.g., 25th, 50th, 75th, 90th).
2) Build 3–5 mini-buckets around those quantiles (e.g., [0..q25], (q25..q50], (q50..q75], (q75..q90], (q90..inf]).
3) Each incoming request is tentatively assigned to a mini-bucket. The scheduler attempts to coalesce requests within the same mini-bucket for a short micro-window (e.g., 10–25ms) to form a pack aligned to the bucket's effective max length.
4) For each mini-bucket the runtime maintains a preferred kernel profile (fast-small-kernel vs wide-kernel vs quantized-kernel). The preferred kernel is chosen by an online cost model that mixes latency and cost per token.
5) If a bucket cannot reach enough pack density within the micro-window and the waiting request is approaching its deadline, the scheduler triggers an opportunistic kernel fallback: migrate that pack to a kernel with lower latency (possibly smaller batch-friendly kernel or single-request fast path) rather than wait or overpad.
6) KV cache is sharded by mini-bucket ID with small shared segments. Entries are tagged with the mini-bucket and have a short grace TTL on bucket transitions to avoid repeated misses during transient reassignments.

Quantile computation and windowing:
- Use exponential moving histogram quantiles computed at request arrival. The implementation must be memory-light and vectorizable (e.g., t-digest or fixed-bin linear histograms).
- Default quantiles: p25, p50, p75, p90. Configurable per-route; critical for long-tail workloads to increase p95 or p99 granularity.
- Update frequency: compute new bucket thresholds every 30–60s, with smoothing to avoid oscillation (alpha=0.2).

Mini-bucket sizing heuristics:
- Each mini-bucket gets an effective pack_max that equals its upper quantile bound or a small multiple (1.05x) to tolerate jitter.
- Limit to 3–5 buckets to keep kernel profiles manageable. For ultra-high-variance endpoints, allow adding an overflow bucket for >p95.

Kernel profile selection (online):
- Maintain per-bucket short-term stats: avg latency, p95 latency, throughput (tokens/s), GPU utilization, and unit-cost estimate.
- Candidate kernels: latency-optimized (low-latency single-threaded or specialized kernel), throughput-optimized (large-batch kernel), quantized (lower precision).
- Score each kernel for a bucket with a weighted objective: score = w_latency * SLA_score + w_cost * cost_score + w_tail * tail_score. Weights configured at route-level.
- Prefer latency kernel when p95 approaches SLA; prefer throughput/quantized when utilization is low and cost needs reduction.

Opportunistic kernel fallback (safety path):
- Trigger conditions: request wait_time >= micro-window && predicted pack_density < threshold && request_time_left < fallback_margin.
- Fallback action: schedule pack on latency-optimized kernel immediately. Optionally, mark request as "fallback_served" for metrics and QoE tracking.
- Fallback should be fast: avoid heavy reformatting between kernels; aim to share pre- and post-processing paths.

KV cache sharding and grace periods:
- Per-bucket logical shard IDs (small integer). Physical KV storage may be shared but logical tagging allows eviction policies that prefer local-bucket keys.
- When a request moves buckets (e.g., because quantiles changed), keys are not immediately evicted; apply a grace TTL (e.g., 30s) before aggressive eviction to reduce thrash.
- On fallback to latency kernel that does not use full KV cache, mark as cold-safe path: fetch missing KV eagerly with a small ahead-of-time warm-up for the next N requests in same pack if possible.

Scheduler algorithm (pseudocode):
- on_request(req):
    bucket = assign_bucket_using_quantiles(req.length)
    append_to_pending_queue(bucket, req)
    if pending_queue_size(bucket) >= desired_pack_size(bucket):
        form_pack_and_dispatch(bucket)
    else:
        schedule_timer(bucket, micro_window_ms)

- on_timer(bucket):
    pack = collect_pending_for_bucket(bucket)
    density = sum(sequence_lengths_in_pack) / (pack_size * pack_max(bucket))
    if density < density_threshold and any(req.time_left < fallback_margin):
        dispatch_pack_on_latency_kernel(pack)  // fallback
    else:
        dispatch_pack_on_preferred_kernel(pack)

Metrics and observability:
- Expose per-route and per-bucket metrics: pack_density, avg_padding_tokens, kernel_choice, fallback_rate, kv_miss_rate_by_bucket, pack_formation_latency, p95 and p99 latencies.
- Add labels for "mini_bucket_id" and "kernel_variant".
- Track cost delta relative to baseline (no bucketing) and tail latency regressions.

Testing and validation plan:
1) Synthetic workload tests: create bimodal and heavy-tail length distributions and compare padding overhead vs time-window baseline.
2) A/B canary: run on small percentage of routes with real traffic; collect cost and latency signals for 24–72 hours.
3) Stress tests: long burst workloads and KV churn scenarios to verify grace TTLs prevent rewarm storms.
4) Safety checks: enforce hard tail SLO guardrail that automatically disables quantile bucketing for a route if p99 increases by more than configured delta.

Operational knobs and configuration:
- route config options: enabled: bool, quantiles: list, micro_window_ms: int, desired_pack_multiplier: float, density_threshold: float, fallback_margin_ms: int, kv_grace_ttl_s: int, kernel_weights: map-string-to-float (expressed as tag strings in UI).
- Defaults selected to be conservative for hosted: micro_window_ms=20, desired_pack_multiplier=0.9, density_threshold=0.6, fallback_margin_ms=30, kv_grace_ttl_s=30.

Rollout plan:
- Stage 1: internal integration tests + perf bench on Dedicated dev clusters (2–3 weeks).
- Stage 2: opt-in beta for power users (selected customers) and a few internal routes (2 weeks).
- Stage 3: Canary at 1% of traffic for public hosted routes, monitor preset metrics and safety guardrails for 7 days.
- Stage 4: Gradual ramp to 20% then 100% if stable.
- Kill-switch: global feature flag per-region and per-route.

Open questions and tradeoffs:
- How often should quantiles be recomputed for bursty endpoints without causing oscillation? (we bias to slower updates and smoothing).
- Optimal number of mini-buckets vs the cost of kernel variants: empirical tuning required; propose default limit of 5.
- Interaction with multi-tenant Dedicated pools where kernel availability varies. Need to surface incompatible kernel fallback and account billing correctly.
- How to surface bucket transitions and KV shard effects to customers in Console: propose simple indicators and an "explain packing" debug trace.

Implementation notes and quick wins:
- Implement quantile estimator using fixed-bin histogram backed by atomic counters to be cheap in hot path.
- Use existing kernel abstraction layer; add a lightweight kernel hint API rather than changing dispatch surface.
- Reuse existing KV tagging metadata; add mini_bucket_id tag and grace TTL logic at eviction time.
- Instrument metrics early; fallback_rate and pack_density should be primary CI gates.

Appendix: example scenario
- Workload: 60% sequences 12–30 tokens, 30% sequences 80–140 tokens, 10% > 800 tokens.
- Quantiles: p25=18, p50=35, p75=120, p90=600. Mini-buckets: [0..18], (18..35], (35..120], (120..600], (600..inf].
- Short buckets pick latency kernel as preferred; mid buckets prefer throughput kernel; overflow bucket prefers throughput but will fall back to latency kernel for near-deadline requests to preserve SLO.
- Expected outcome: padding drops substantially for the first three buckets; a small fraction of >p90 requests hit fallback path but maintain p99 SLO.

Conclusion:
Quantile-driven mini-buckets with opportunistic kernel fallback and light KV sharding provides a pragmatic middle ground between coarse fixed buckets and heavy dynamic compaction. It reduces padding cost for common cases while offering safe, latency-preserving behavior for tails. The approach is incremental, observable, and can be tuned per-route.

- Integrate kernel hint API and simple fallback path (owner: Diego Martinez, 3w)
- Add per-bucket metrics and canary dashboard (owner: Priya Kapoor, 1w)
- Prepare canary plan and customer opt-in doc (owner: Evan Liu, 1w)

Quick experimental notes for an internal collateral slide / one-pager: map how the fastpath (low-latency serving) degrades across three runtime strategies when exposed to conversational microbursts. We want a small, shareable table + ascii charts for product/solutions decks.

High-level summary (TL;DR):
- Multiplexing (slot-multiplexer that interleaves small requests) reduces p99/p999 tail compared to naive 100ms windowed batching in microburst-heavy sessions, at the cost of slightly higher steady-state p50 and reduced peak qps.
- Windowed batching gives best amortized cost-per-token for sustained throughput but suffers long tails under bursty arrivals (cold/uncached KV sequences).
- Hybrid (prefetch + multiplex fallback) gives a middle ground: most predictable p95, moderate cost.

Experimental setup (notes, approximate):
- Hardware: 8xA100 per pool, same model (llama-13b-like profile), quantized int8 for all experiments.
- Workload: synthetic conversation traces sampled from customer_qa_cohort_12 (approx 30k sessions), mix: 65% short (avg 30 tokens), 25% medium (avg 120 tokens), 10% long (avg 450 tokens). Burst injection: for 3% of sessions inject 0->20 concurrent turns within 400ms.
- Configs compared:
  1) Batched-100ms: windowed batching commit every 100ms, prefix cache ON, no prefetch.
  2) Multiplex-actor: per-session actor multiplexing, opportunistic tiny batches (5-10ms packing), priority headroom preemption for interactive sessions.
  3) Hybrid-prefetch: aggressive prefix prefetch + multiplex fallback after 60ms waiting.
- Measurement: client-observed token latency per generate call; p50/p95/p99/p999 measured, throughput in qps and tokens/s, compute cost extrapolated to $/1M tokens using current pricing model baseline.

Representative numbers (median of 5 runs):
Latency percentiles (ms)
Strategy            | p50  | p95  | p99  | p999 | qps (sustained)
--------------------|------|------|------|------|---------------
Batched-100ms       | 16   | 140  | 420  | 1100 | 640           
Multiplex-actor     | 22   | 88   | 210  | 460  | 510           
Hybrid-prefetch     | 18   | 102  | 240  | 650  | 580           

Cost (extrapolated) - USD per 1M tokens (incl infra + amortized idle)
- Batched-100ms : $39.8
- Multiplex-actor : $34.1
- Hybrid-prefetch : $36.5

Short observations from the numbers:
- Batched config compresses compute (highest qps) so cost/unit is lowest in steady state, but p99/p999 blow up during bursts (see below).
- Multiplexing reduces extreme tails by avoiding head-of-line blocking inside 100ms windows; p95/p99 improved ~2x vs batched. Lower cost per token than batched here due to fewer lost-units and less wasteful overprovisioning in replayed runs (note: this is workload-dependent).
- Hybrid shows the best p95 predictability, with a small cost premium vs multiplex but significantly better experience vs pure batching during mid-size bursts.

Ascii microburst timeline (single 12-request spike) - client observed latency per request (ms):
Time -> 0ms   20ms   40ms   60ms   80ms   100ms  140ms  200ms  400ms
Batched-100ms : 18    22     30     110    380    720    800    980    1100
Multiplex-actor: 24    28     36     46     58     76     112    240    460
Hybrid-prefetch: 20    24     32     68     120    220    320    480    650

Interpretation: batching lumps many triggers to the next window causing a large step function in observed latency; multiplex smooths but increases nominal baseline. Hybrid gives partial smoothing with early-prefetch benefiting a subset.

Chart-style bullets for slides (short):
- Bullets for deck slide 1 (cost vs tail risk):
  * X-axis: cost per 1M tokens (lower better). Y-axis: p99 latency (ms).
  * Batched sits left-bottom for steady-state but extreme up on p99 during spikes -> wide error bar.
  * Multiplex sits slightly right (higher cost) but narrower error bar and lower p99.
  * Hybrid sits center-left with tight p95 and moderate p99.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How sensitive are these results to token length mix? (run quick sweep for +20% long-session mix).
- Does batching with adaptive window (latency-based early flush) close gap vs multiplex? (small experiment planned ENG-1427).
- Impact of KV-cache miss rates: current workload had ~12% cold KV misses; need a cold-heavy run to stress prefetch logic.
- Model size sensitivity: run same profiles on 70B-equivalent (we expect multiplex penalty grows due to larger memory movement).

Recommendations for collateral:
- Produce a 1-slide tradeoff graphic showing steady-state cost vs tail risk with 3 colored markers and error bars (use numbers above). Add a small microburst timeline ascii as the slide notes.
- Include a tiny appendix with the table above and the experiment parameters.
- Call out operational knobs: batching window, multiplex slot size, prefetch horizon. Provide suggested defaults for customer tiers:
  * Free / low-tier: Batched-100ms (cost optimized).
  * Scale / enterprise: Hybrid-prefetch (balanced).
  * Interactive tier / SLO-sensitive: Multiplex-actor (predictability).

[Interleaver Fair-Ledger + Prefetch Throttle (exploratory notes)]
Purpose
These are exploratory notes for a continuous request/token interleaver that tries to balance three goals: (1) low tail latency for latency-sensitive requests, (2) aggregate throughput via kernel-friendly batch formation, and (3) fairness across noisy multi-tenant workloads that mix short chat turns and long generation requests. This doc sketches a runtime-friendly design ("Fair-Ledger Interleaver"), explores how prefetch and KV cache affinity interact with fairness, and outlines a lightweight simulation plan with early observations and open questions.

Motivation & Problem Statement
Current continuous batching approaches pull tokens together eagerly to improve kernel utilization, but they can starve small low-latency requests (e.g., single-turn chat) when dominated by a few long generators. Conversely, strict per-request isolation preserves latency but wastes kernel throughput and increases cost. We need an intermediate mechanism that: 
- provides per-client/route fairness signals,
- composes with KV cache affinity (avoid breaking cache locality for in-flight sessions),
- adapts to variable request token rates while exposing simple operational knobs.

Key Constraints
- Kernel utilization prefers larger, uniformly-shaped token batches (same sequence-length bucket when possible).
- KV cache affinity: interleaving tokens across sessions breaks contiguous KV cache hotness if we swap contexts mid-sequence; switching costs vary by model and quantization.
- SLOs: tail P95/P99 for interactive classes must be bounded under load.
- Implementation should be incremental: additive scheduler component that can be toggled per serving pool.

High-level idea: Fair-Ledger Interleaver
1) Per-client credit ledger: every authenticated client/route has a small credit account that accrues at a configurable rate (credits per ms) and is debited by token-issuance weight when we schedule their tokens into a batch. Credits reflect recent resource consumption and priority.
2) Interleaver windows: the scheduler maintains a short rolling window (e.g., 8–40ms) where tokens can be interleaved across requests. Instead of delaying every request to wait for a large batch, the interleaver opportunistically merges tokens from different clients within the window.
3) Prefetch throttle + hysteresis: each request has a soft prefetch budget (prefetch tokens buffered ahead) that respects credit balance. When credits are low, prefetch is suppressed and request is offered only when naturally arriving. When credits are high, prefetch is allowed to improve kernel packing. Hysteresis avoids flapping between states.
4) KV-affinity tags: requests carry an affinity tag (session-id hash). The interleaver prefers to keep contiguous tokens from the same tag in the same micro-batch to preserve KV locality. If interleaving must occur, prefer other tokens with compatible cache offsets (nearby sequence length, similar kv footprint).

Scheduling policy (algorithm sketch)
- Maintain a priority queue keyed by normalized score = (credits + latency_urgency_bonus) / estimated_kernel_misalignment_cost.
- latency_urgency_bonus grows with wall-clock wait time of the request head to bound tail latency.
- estimated_kernel_misalignment_cost approximates additional kernel overhead if this token would force a kernel shape change (e.g., shift from S=128 to S=512). This cost is model/profile dependent and taken from a small per-model lookup table (gathered offline).
- When forming a micro-batch at window expiry or when batch hits token count threshold, pick top-K tokens by score while enforcing a soft constraint on per-affinity fragmentation (limit how many distinct affinity tags per micro-batch).

KV cache interactions and heuristics
- Goal: avoid excessive KV eviction thrash. Practical heuristics: 
  * affinity_preserve_threshold: if a session has >= N tokens queued consecutively, keep them contiguous unless their credits are exhausted.
  * affinity_swap_penalty: when scoring a candidate token, add penalty proportional to predicted KV miss cost.
  * ephemeral-session fast-path: short-lived single-turn sessions (no expected continuation) get lower penalty for interleaving.

Per-client fairness knobs (operational)
- base_accrual_rate: credits per second for a fresh client; can be tied to billing tier.
- min_credit_floor: enforce minimal credits so transient clients aren't completely blocked.
- max_prefetch_tokens: cap of prefetched tokens allowed per request.
- emergency_replenish: short burst credits for critical routes to preserve p95 SLAs.

Kernel coordination and quantization notes
- When quantized kernels introduce asymmetric per-token costs, the estimated_kernel_misalignment_cost must incorporate measured per-kernel latency curves. For example, mixing long sequences with many short sequences can cause additional memcpy/transpose overheads on some kernels; the scheduler needs the model runtime to expose a small profile API (sequence length -> extra overhead).
- Work with kernel team to expose a lightweight cost vector (e.g., [token-cost, swap-cost, kv-switch-cost]) that the scheduler can query or cache per model variant.

Simulation plan (lightweight)
- Input workloads: synthetic mixes (A) chat-heavy: 90% short requests (1–32 tokens), 10% long (512–2048 tokens), (B) mixed: balanced short/medium/long, (C) adversarial: small number of long generators dominating token volume.
- Metrics: P50/P95/P99 latencies per class, kernel occupancy %, average tokens per micro-batch, KV cache hit ratio, per-client fairness index (Jain's index on tokens scheduled over sliding window).
- Sim scenarios: baseline (current continuous eager batching), strict per-request isolation, and Fair-Ledger interleaver with several knob presets (aggressive prefetch, conservative prefetch, affinity-first).
- Implementation: event-driven simulator in Python (~1k LOC) using the measured kernel cost tables from previous experiments.

Preliminary simulation observations (toy runs)
- Under chat-heavy load, aggressive prefetch with no fairness ledger drops P95 for long generators but improves kernel occupancy by ~18%. However p99 for short sessions regresses by 30–40% (unacceptable).
- Enabling credits with modest accrual_rate recovers short-session P99 almost entirely while keeping ~10% occupancy gain versus strict isolation.
- Affinity-preserve heuristics reduced KV thrash considerably (estimated KV hit ratio +14%) at the cost of slightly smaller micro-batches in adversarial mixes.

Open questions / risks
- How to pick accrual rates that map to customer tiers without surprising side effects across pools? Need a calibration study and mapping to billing units.
- Interaction with autoscaling: if scheduler increases batching and occupancy, upstream autoscaler may see fewer CPU/GPU signals; need to ensure scaling triggers remain robust.
- Implementation complexity: ledger + affinity tagging + per-model kernel cost table adds surface area. We should prototype with scheduler-only changes first and keep ledger persistence ephemeral (in-memory sliding window).
- Security/tenancy: per-client credit accrual could be gamed if keys rotate; tie ledger to authenticated entity and track anomalies.

Next steps and action items
- (Ava) create the initial simulator PR with three workload traces and baseline comparisons (ETA 2 weeks).
- (Liam) work with kernel team to define the minimal cost vector API and provide sample cost tables for gpt-3-like and llama variants (ETA 1 week).
- (Priya) draft an operational runbook for knobs (accrual_rate, prefetch caps, affinity thresholds) and propose safe defaults for Hosted vs Dedicated pools (ETA 1.5 weeks).
- (Noah) run a focused KV-thrash microbenchmark to quantify session-swap penalties across quantization modes (ETA 2 weeks).

Appendix: quick configuration example
- fair_ledger: { accrual_rate_per_sec: 10, min_credit_floor: 2, max_prefetch_tokens: 16, affinity_preserve_threshold: 4, affinity_swap_penalty: 2.5 }
Notes: above is illustrative; actual runtime config will be flat key-values exposed via pool config UI.

Concluding notes
The Fair-Ledger Interleaver is intentionally conservative: it trades some raw throughput for predictable tail-latency behavior and KV cache preservation. Early sims suggest the approach can capture a substantial fraction of batching gains without regressing interactive SLAs. The aim for the next milestone is a small in-process prototype (scheduler-only, in-memory ledger, disabled-by-default) that can be toggled in a staging serving pool for controlled experiments.

[Reservation governor rationalization and noisy-tenant surge remediation]
description:
Summary: During the 2025-02-10 capacity incident a single tenant's sudden high-concurrency, long-sequence workload exhausted pooled reservations and triggered widespread soft-evictions and tail latency spikes across two dedicated GPU pools. Root cause is a combination of: (1) reservation sizing that counts only active workers and ignores transient KV cache and per-request memory, (2) an aggressive instantaneous burst allowance that can deplete shared credits, and (3) the admission controller's eviction-first behavior under burst pressure which amplifies noisy neighbor effects. Impact: several customers experienced >10x tail latency and a small number of requests were retried/failed; production SLA targets were breached for ~45 minutes. Goals for this ticket: remediate immediate regressions, add deterministic safety nets so a single tenant cannot cause cross-tenant tail latency, and create reproducible test coverage to prevent regressions in allocator/burst logic.

[Synthetic Load Validator and Reservation Autocalibration Playbook]
description:
Summary:\nDuring a capacity incident on 2025-02-10 we observed degraded throughput across several Dedicated clusters. Investigation pointed to a combination of: (1) under-provisioned tenant reservations due to stale traffic estimates, (2) noisy-neighbor workloads that generated burst token exhaustion, and (3) burst policy thresholds that allowed aggressive short-term bursts without adequate backoff, leading to cascading latency spikes.\n\nGoal:\nCreate a reproducible synthetic load validator and an automated reservation autocalibration playbook that: (a) reproduces the incident class with controlled noisy tenants and realistic KV/cache utilization, (b) derives corrective reservation deltas, and (c) produces safe degraded-burst fallback policies that reduce tail latency without unduly impacting throughput.\n\nScope and non-goals:\n- Scope: Dedicated cluster behavior, tenant reservation sizing, burst token lifecycle, telemetry augmentations, runbook changes, CI gating for reservation changes.\n- Non-goals: Changes to customer-visible pricing, on-prem deployment packaging, or host-level kernel changes.\n\nIncident timeline (high level):\n- 2025-02-10 02:14 UTC: Alert: sustained 99th pct latency > 2.5s across cluster-dedicated-12.\n- 02:18 UTC: Autoscaler attempted to add capacity but reservation rebalancer was delayed by lock contention.\n- 02:23 UTC: Several tenants reported 429s when bursts were consumed; tokenbucket metrics show exhaustion event spikes.\n- 02:45 UTC: Manual mitigation: soft-fence noisy tenants and temporarily increase reservation of impacted tenants.\n\nRoot causes (synthesized):\n- Reservation mismatch: historic quota computation used an exponentially weighted moving average tuned for steady-state, underreacting to sudden growth of 2.5x in a top tenant's QPS.\n- Burst policy gap: burst allowance (token refill rate) was permissive but lacked graceful decay; no intermediate throttling step between full allowance and hard throttles.\n- Telemetry blind spots: synthetic replay tests were not run for cross-tenant KV cache eviction patterns which amplified per-request cost.\n- Operational contention: reservation rebalance run serialized under global lock; during incident it queued behind long-running topology reconciliation.\n\nProposed action items (short, medium, long):\n1) Short (this sprint):\n  - Build \"synthetic-load-validator\" harness that can emulate: multi-tenant steady + burst traffic, KV cache pressure, variable sequence lengths, and controlled noisy behavior. (Owner: ENG-ops)\n  - Add tokenbucket-exhaustion alert with correlated reservation-change events in Grafana and link to runbook. (Owner: Observability)\n  - Implement emergency soft-fence API: quick-apply tenant isolation mode that limits new bursts for a tenant while preserving inflight inference. (Owner: runtime)\n2) Medium (next 2 sprints):\n  - Autocalibration algorithm: forecast-driven reservation adjustment using short-window percentile (P90 over 10m + burst headroom) plus hysteresis and cooldown. Provide dry-run outputs in staging for 24h before primetime. (Owner: scheduler)\n  - Replace global rebalance lock with per-pool coordination and deadline-based preemption to avoid queueing. (Owner: allocator)\n  - Add synthetic test step to CI that runs a 30m noisy-neighbor scenario and validates no 99th-pt uplift beyond baseline. (Owner: testing infra)\n3) Long (Q2+):\n  - Policy simulation tooling to model cluster-level fairness and revenue impact of reservation deltas. (Owner: capacity-analytics)\n  - Explore tiered burst decay policies (soft-throttle -> token-rate-reduction -> hard-throttle) with configurable knobs per customer tier. (Owner: runtime/policy)\n\nAcceptance criteria:\n- Synthetic harness reproduces observed tokenbucket exhaustion within 10% of incident metrics when fed historical traffic profile.\n- Autocalibration performs reservation adjustments that reduce 99th-pt latency by >= 30% in the noisy scenario while keeping overall throughput within 5% of baseline.\n- Emergency soft-fence can be applied in < 90 seconds and documented in the runbook.\n- CI synthetic test runs in under 40 minutes and fails the PR if 99th-pt latency or reservation drift regression occurs.\n\nDesign notes and trade-offs:\n- Forecasting approach: choose between reactive short-window percentile (less aggressive) vs ML model (more accurate but operationally heavier). We'll begin with deterministic percentile+cooldown for safety, with a supervised ML model as future work.\n- Synthetic fidelity: running full-scale GPU-backed synthetic tests is expensive. We'll use a tiered strategy: simulated CPU-only high-level load for quick CI checks, and nightly full-GPU clusters in staging for high-fidelity validation.\n- Soft-fence semantics: design to avoid disrupting in-flight requests by throttling new token grants; this reduces blast radius while preserving ongoing responses.\n\nRunbook and CI changes:\n- Add step in Dedicated Incident runbook: \"Apply soft-fence to tenant -> verify tokenbucket metrics -> run synthetic validator in local-mode\". Include rollback steps for soft-fence.\n- CI: add job `noisy_neighbour_smoke` that executes the lightweight harness and validates P95/P99 and reservation stability.\n\nTelemetry and dashboards to build:\n- Grafana: \"Reservation Autocalibrator\" dashboard: per-tenant reservation, estimated desired reservation, tokenbucket fill-rate, exhaustion events, KV-eviction rate.\n- Alerting: new composite alert combining tokenbucket_exhaustion OR reservation_delta > 3x within 5m, with pager if customer_impact==high.\n\nOwners and collaborators:\n- Runtime: Priya Nair (design soft-fence, burst decay)\n- Scheduler/Allocator: Liam Patel (autocalibration, lock removal) [assignee]\n- Observability: Marco Ruiz (dashboards, alerts)\n- Testing infra: Zoe Kim (synthetic harness + CI jobs)\n- Capacity analytics: Elias Novak (policy simulation)\n\nDeliverables and timeline:\n- Week 1: lightweight synthetic harness prototype + initial dashboard (MVP).\n- Week 2-3: autocalibration prototype in staging (dry-run logs) + lock removal POC.\n- Week 4: deploy soft-fence + enable CI synthetic test; measure impact with 2-week canary.\n\nNotes and links:\n- Postmortem: https://confluence.redwood.ai/dedicated-capacity-postmortem-2025-02-10\n- Incident Grafana: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/alerts/dedicated-capacity-2025-02-10\n- Design doc (prototype harness): https://drive.redwood.ai/drive/folders/synthetic-load-validator-proto\n- Related tickets: ENG-29315 (spike-mitigation-autotuner), ENG-52489 (reservation policy review), ENG-41322 (burst calibration)

[Tenant surge harmonizer and reservation drift action plan]
description:
Summary: Following the 2025-02-10 capacity incident where a multi-tenant surge triggered cascading evictions and elevated tail latency across two dedicated GPU clusters, this ticket consolidates the postmortem action items and proposes a coordinated implementation plan. Root causes identified in the postmortem: (1) reservation drift where long-running synthetic workloads and a bug in reservation reconciliation allowed tenants to consume more fractional capacity than allocated, (2) burst-credit decay set too permissively causing burst storms to persist longer than intended, and (3) lack of a fast noisy-neighbor detection signal in the allocator, delaying isolation for ~6m during the incident. This ticket designs a Tenant Surge Harmonizer (TSH) to limit and smooth transient spikes, a correction pass for reservation accounting, and burst-credit policy recalibration. The goal is to reduce correlated evictions, make QoS predictable, and provide operators both automatic and manual remediation knobs.

Reservation reconciliation job detects and corrects drift within 60s for >95% of misallocations in test harness

Playbook and dashboard added to Console: operator can run 'ts-harmonic-reset' and observe affected tenants, with links to evictions and KV-cache metrics
E2E test in runtime CI that simulates 10 tenants with mixed short/long sequences and asserts no more than 1 eviction per 1000 requests after mitigations

Combined with slow burst-credit decay, tenants could sustain above-reservation usage for multiple minutes, creating eviction cascades. This ticket operationalizes those mitigations into automated and tested systems.

[Instrument synthetic heartbeat + orphan-metric detection for console ingress/backpressure blind spots]
description:
Summary: During the 2025-02-10 capacity regression incident, several tenants experienced prolonged tail latency and request drops that were not visible in existing console dashboards. Root cause analysis showed three blind spots: (1) no per-tenant ingress queue percentile metrics were emitted for the front-end ingress adapters, (2) synthetic/live heartbeat checks run only at the region level (not per-tenant), and (3) multiple dashboard panels were wired to an aggregated metric pipeline that silently dropped percentile buckets when sampling triggered. This ticket scopes the work to create a lightweight synthetic heartbeat per tenant, emit per-tenant queue percentiles and queue-depth histograms from the ingress pipeline, and build an "orphan-metric" detector that alerts when dashboards reference metrics with low cardinality or missing tags.

actions:
Add a 30s synthetic heartbeat probe that runs per-tenant and records end-to-end latency and success status. Probe implemented as a configurable job in console-checker with tenant-level tagging.
Instrument ingress adapters to emit queue_depth histogram and queue_wait_percentiles (p50,p95,p99) labeled by tenant_id, route, and region. Keep cardinality limits via sharding keys.
Create a dashboard health check job that scans key console dashboards and flags panels that reference metrics without tenant or route tags (potential orphan metrics).
Publish runbook entries: how to triage heartbeat failures, how to correlate heartbeat failures with KV evictions and ingress pressure.
Deliver a guardrail: emit a high-cardinality metric only behind a sampling flag and add automated alert if cardinality exceeds threshold.
Ship a small set of dashboards with per-tenant percentile visualizations and link them from the tenant status page.
Roll out feature behind feature flag and run a week-long bake period for 10% of tenants before full rollout.
Add automated integration test that simulates an ingress backlog and verifies the heartbeat and percentiles appear in telemetry stream.
Create GH PR with implementation and coordination summary; include a short security review note referencing KMS usage if any tenant secrets are needed (none expected).

acceptance_criteria:
Synthetic heartbeat emits per-tenant samples for 10% pilot tenants for 7d and visible in console dashboards.
Ingress adapters emit queue_depth histograms and p50/p95/p99 percentiles with tenant_id labels for pilot tenants.
Orphan-metric detector runs daily and produces a report; at least one previously-orphaned dashboard panel is identified and fixed.
No negative customer impact observed during 10% pilot; roll back plan validated and documented.
Runbook documented with clear escalation path and linked from incident playbook.

comments:
2025-02-14 - Aisha Patel: Created ticket after postmortem reading. Noted that dashboards were insensitive to percentile drops due to sampling. Suggested synthetic per-tenant checks to catch silent degradations.
2025-02-17 - Marco Li: Scoped instrumentation work. MVP will limit tenant cardinality by sharding tenant_id into 1024 buckets to avoid cardinality explosion. Planning spike to prototype exporter changes (estimate 2d).
2025-02-19 - Priya Nambiar (SRE): Recommended adding alert thresholds for heartbeat error-rate and for unexpected drops in percentile counts. Will add to SRE alerts once telemetry exists.
2025-02-22 - Marco Li: Prototype PR created: github.com/redwood-inference/ingress-exporter/pull/269. Prototype emits histogram for queue_depth and p50/p95/p99 percentiles with tenant_bucket tag. Initial tests pass on staging (link below).
2025-02-25 - Design review (Sienna Rios): Agreed to surface per-tenant health on tenant's overview page but hide detailed percentiles behind a developer toggle to avoid noise for small customers.
2025-02-28 - On call (Evan Green): During a controlled ingress surge test, heartbeats detected degraded tail latency for 3 test tenants; incident playbook triggered and autoscale followed runbook behaviour — positive validation.
2025-03-03 - Marco Li: Built dashboard scanner script and ran across 48 dashboards; flagged 6 panels referencing aggregated metrics without tenant/route tag. Created follow-up PM work to remediate panels.
2025-03-05 - Aisha Patel: Marked In Progress and expanded rollout plan. Next: finish safety guardrails, complete pilot rollout to 10% tenants, and schedule post-pilot review on 2025-03-14.

[Rollout signal contract and hypothesis harvest for staged-model regression]
description:
After the 2025-02-07 staged rollout that triggered an automated rollback, we need a concise, machine-readable 'rollback signal contract' and an exhaustive hypothesis log. The goal is to (1) define deterministic signals that should trigger an automated rollback or alert, (2) capture the set of plausible root-cause hypotheses observed during the incident, and (3) update the runbook, CI checks, and dashboards so future rollouts surface the same signals earlier with less manual triage.

summary:
Create a single source-of-truth for rollout signal thresholds, telemetry to collect for canaries/shadows/A-Bs, and a prioritized remediation backlog derived from the hypothesis harvest.

decision_log:
2025-02-10: Triage call decided to treat this as a safety contract task rather than individual incident fixes; owner assigned to ENG-82019.
2025-02-11: Agreed to include model-quality signals (eval regression on canary prompt set) in the rollback contract in addition to infra signals.
2025-02-13: Decided to require 'signal amplification' rule: only trigger auto-rollback when at least two distinct signal classes breach thresholds within a rolling 3-minute window unless severity is P0-critical.
2025-02-14: PM requested customer-facing post explaining why a rollback happened; include templated language in the runbook.

steps_taken:
Collected raw telemetry from canary window: p50/p95/p99 latency, 5xx rate, model eval drift score, embedding cosine-distribution shift, prefix cache miss rate, memory pressure traces.
Ran offline replay of the canary traffic against previous model revision to isolate regressions that are model-only vs infra-related.
Instrumented additional synthetic prompts (30 prompt probes) to exercise hallucination-sensitive behavior and added them to the canary evaluation suite.
Added temporary shadow routing for 15% of production traffic to capture real-world prompts for deeper diagnostics.
Filed a hotfix PR that tightened batching heuristics; ran unit + perf tests but did not merge until the signal contract and runbook were in place.

hypothesis_harvest:
Quantization kernel mismatch: new quantized variant produced distributional token score changes causing hallucinations on rare prompts.
KV cache invalidation bug under certain concurrent batching patterns leading to stale context used during generation.
Autoscaler bounce after a transient spike caused higher cold-start latency and request timeouts, amplifying user-visible errors.
Model prompt-change interaction: small change in system prompt applied only in the new rollout produced edge-case cascading behavior on structured-output routes.
Routing fallback to CPU variant under GPU contention increased latency and reduced generation quality for long-context requests.
Telemetry misaggregation: aggregation window mismatch made apparent spike look wider than it was (false positive); contract should prevent single-source reliance.
External dependency (third-party tokenizer library) regression when handling uncommon Unicode sequences.

follow_up_tasks:
TASK-1: Formalize rollback-signal contract YAML schema and check-in to infra-config repo. Owner: Mateo. Estimate: 2. Due: 2025-02-18.
TASK-2: Add canary eval suite to CI with automated regression gates (eval measured against a fixed prompt set). Owner: Research. Estimate: 3. Due: 2025-03-05.
TASK-3: Implement 'two-signal' amplification rule in rollout orchestrator and add unit/integ tests. Owner: Serving Runtime. Estimate: 5. Due: 2025-03-01.
TASK-4: Dashboard: surface per-route hallucination metric, embed drift histogram, and a composite 'rollback-risk' score. Owner: Observability. Estimate: 3. Due: 2025-02-25.
TASK-5: Update runbook: include templated customer communication, post-rollback checklist, and triage owner rotation. Owner: SRE/PM. Estimate: 2. Due: 2025-02-20.
TASK-6: Add synthetic prompt probes to canary traffic generator and schedule nightly replay to detect slow regressions. Owner: QA. Estimate: 2. Due: 2025-02-22.
TASK-7: Postmortem action: audit tokenizer library versions across deployments and pin to validated version; publish mitigation PR. Owner: Infra. Estimate: 1. Due: 2025-02-21.
TASK-8: Security review: confirm signal contract does not expose PII in telemetry exports; run privacy checklist. Owner: Security. Estimate: 1. Due: 2025-02-19.
TASK-9: Create a lightweight A/B experiment template that captures per-variant eval metrics and ties to auto-rollback configuration. Owner: PM/Eng. Estimate: 3. Due: 2025-03-08.
TASK-10: Add a regression harness that replays canary span with exact token-steps to reproduce hallucinations locally. Owner: Devtools. Estimate: 4. Due: 2025-03-02.
TASK-11: Communications: draft customer-facing note and internal postmortem summary for late-Feb runbook update. Owner: PM. Estimate: 1. Due: 2025-02-20.
TASK-12: Policy: document conditions where auto-rollback is disabled (e.g., high-throughput low-latency SLAs) and require manual approval paths. Owner: Product. Estimate: 2. Due: 2025-02-24.
TASK-13: Add cross-team dependency mapping for rollout signals so ops knows which team to page for each signal class. Owner: Platform Ops. Estimate: 1. Due: 2025-02-19.
TASK-14: Post-deploy learning: schedule a 2-hour blameless learning session to surface improvements and integrate into onboarding. Owner: Eng Leads. Estimate: 0.5. Due: 2025-02-28.
TASK-15: Archive the hypothesis harvest into the incident knowledge base and tag by signal class for future ML/infra investigations. Owner: Incident Commander. Estimate: 1. Due: 2025-02-16.

acceptance_criteria:
Rollback contract YAML exists in infra-config repo and is referenced by the rollout orchestrator.
At least three telemetry sources (infra latency, error-rate, model-eval drift) are wired into the composite rollback-risk score in Grafana.
Runbook updated with templated communications and triage matrix; security/privacy checklist completed.
CI gating: canary eval suite runs in PRs for model-serving changes and fails fast on detected regressions.
Hypothesis archive completed and prioritized backlog created with owners and due dates.
Two-signal amplification rule implemented and tested in a staging rollout.
Customer-facing post explaining the rollback is drafted and approved by PM + Legal.

[Dedicated capacity: staged fallback & priority quota decision brief]
description:
Problem: Enterprise customers requesting reserved throughput guarantees vary widely in traffic patterns and GPU families. Current intake lacks a crisp decision surface relating SLA latency/availability targets to reserved throughput, GPU class, and scaling policies. That causes slow onboarding, repeated follow-ups, and occasional SLA miss when customer bursts exceed anticipated patterns.

Goal: Produce a concise decision brief and operational rubric that product, solutions, and concierge teams can use during intake to: 1) map customer SLA targets to recommended reserved throughput and GPU class, 2) define staged fallback policies (graceful degradation order: model-variant -> regional failover -> queued throughput -> customer-visible throttling), and 3) codify quota/prioritization matrices for multi-tenant dedicated pools so customers understand preemption and burst rules.

Scope: Non-bug intake triage for dedicated/reserved pools only (hosted API and Private deployments considered where behavior diverges). Deliverables include the decision brief, intake checklist additions, a sample SLA quote worksheet, and a draft of console messaging for fallback events.

decision_summary:
Adopt a three-tier fallback model + priority quota matrix:
1) Preferred: Reserve capacity mapped to GPU class (A/B/C tiers) based on sustained baseline RPS and 99th percentile latency target.
2) Staged fallback: when pool pressure > threshold, automatically shift requests by policy order: model-variant fallback (quantized/cheaper variant) -> regional replica routing -> burst queueing with bounded wait -> visible throttling and negotiated failover.
3) Priority quotas: customers assigned a priority score (Commitment, SLA band, security class) that configures preemption windows and burst credits.
This model balances predictability for enterprise contracts and graceful degradation to preserve best-effort availability.

tradeoffs:
Conservative reserved throughput recommendations reduce risk of SLA breach but increase cost to customers; we will present optional burst credits to mitigate upfront sizing friction.
More aggressive automated fallbacks (switching to quantized variants) reduce costs and preserve latency but risk output quality regressions; require eval suites per customer to enable safe fallbacks.
Priority quota enforcement adds operational complexity and telemetry requirements; necessary for predictable fairness in shared dedicated pools.

[Enterprise reserved pool concierge: SLA negotiation and scaling rubric]
body:
Summary:
This ticket captures a standardized rubric and concierge workflow for negotiating enterprise reserved GPU pools. The goal is to provide consistent guidance when customers request SLA-backed reserved throughput: target p95 latency and throughput guarantees, preferred GPU families, burst/oversubscription policies, preemption tolerances, and operational observability expectations.

Problem & motivation:
Enterprise customers are requesting bespoke reserved capacity with explicit SLAs (throughput and latency guarantees) and preferences for GPU classes. Currently intake is ad hoc, causing long negotiation cycles and inconsistent commitments from Eng/Capacity teams. We need an intake rubric that balances engineering risk, cost, and customer value, and produces a clear deliverable: a committed pool profile (size, GPU family, scaling policy, fallback model variants, pricing delta, and runbook).

Scope:
- Non-bug feature triage for dedicated/reserved requests only (not hosted pay-as-you-go).
- End-to-end concierge workflow: intake form, triage rubric, engineering sizing guidance, required console changes (UI to show reserved pool assignments), contract checklist for legal/Security, and SRE runbook for escalation.
- Deliverables: a 1-page rubric, intake questionnaire template, sizing checklist, and an example negotiation artifact for a reference customer.

Key decision areas (rubric components):
1) SLA target & KPIs: p95 latency goal (ms), min sustained throughput (tokens/s or rps), availability SLO (%, monthly uptime), and burst envelope (short lived above commit).
2) GPU family options: recommend tiers (cost vs performance): Tiers are (A) Hopper-class (H100/next-gen): best latency/throughput for dense transformer models, (B) Ampere-class (A100): balanced, (C) Efficient-quantized CPU / L4-class for lower-cost inference. Provide recommended fallbacks.
3) Reserved capacity sizing: use 3 inputs: expected sustained qps, peak qps, and typical sequence length distribution. Provide quick-sizing rules-of-thumb and link to sizing spreadsheet.
4) Scaling policy & burst behavior: define autoscale headroom, burst credits, pre-warm windows, and hard caps. Decide on proactive vs. reactive scaling based on customer SLAs.
5) Preemption & availability: whether work can tolerate preemptible VMs/GPU reclaim; if not, reserve non-preemptible pool at premium pricing.
6) Isolation & data-flow: whether customer requires dedicated tenancy (VPC/private) or just reserved multi-tenant pools with data separation.
7) Observability & alerts: token-level cost breakdown, per-route latency p50/ p95, capacity utilization dashboards and SLO burn rate alerts.
8) Rollout and fallbacks: enforce canary policies, automatic fallback to compatible model variant (smaller model or quantized) when pool is strained.

Acceptance criteria:
- A filled rubric template can convert a customer request into a deterministic set of deliverables: GPU family, pool size, SLA targets, cost delta, and runbook.
- Console changes (UX story) documented and prioritized in a follow-up ENG ticket.
- Pricing sheet updated with reserved rates for each GPU tier and burst policy.
- Legal and security checklist documented and sign-off flow captured.

Notes from initial triage meeting (2025-03-06):
- Customer A use-case: high-frequency chat routing (avg seq 256 tokens), wants 99.9% availability, p95 latency <120ms, sustain 1800 rps, peak 2500 rps for 30s bursts. Recommended preliminary: 8x H100-equivalent GPUs with burst headroom, canary rollout over 48h, non-preemptible pool.
- Engineering feedback: we need telemetry for model-mapped utilization and per-route batching efficiency before committing to >8 GPUs. Mark ENG-7521 to add these telemetry hooks.
- Security: VPC requirement will push this into Private deployment SKU; coordinate with Security for KMS and audit retention. DES-204 to validate console display patterns for reserved pools.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- Price vs latency: Do we standardize three pricing tiers or negotiate per-customer? Recommendation: baseline standard tiers, but permit negotiated add-ons for custom SLAs.
- Burst policy: Should burst credit be purchased up-front (prepaid buffer) or billed usage-based? Preference towards prepaid for predictability.
- Model fallbacks: Can we enforce automatic model fallback in the platform when pool under pressure? This requires runtime integration and risk of quality regressions. Mark as medium-risk engineering effort (ENG-8110).

Risks & mitigations:
- Overcommit risk: committing fixed GPUs without utilization signal. Mitigate by requiring usage telemetry and conservative initial sizing + 30-day review.
- Quality regressions if fallback models are used: require customer acceptance testing and evals hooked to release pipeline.
- Legal/Security delays: surface requirements during intake and flag for early engagement.

Next steps (owners):
- PM (Diego): finalize rubric doc and intake questionnaire (due 2025-03-14).
- Eng (Sana Patel, ENG-7521): add per-pool telemetry hooks and a utilization dashboard (estimate 5 points, due 2025-03-28).
- Eng (Runtime team, ENG-8110): prototype automatic model fallback behavior and failure modes (spike testing).
- Design (DES-204): wireframes for console reserved pool assignment and SLA summary panel (due 2025-03-18).
- Legal & Security: sign-off checklist to be added to intake template; security review requested for all non-standard pools.

Links & artifacts:
- Sizing spreadsheet: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/enterprise-reserved-sizing (internal)
- Draft rubric doc (confluence): https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/PM/pages/Reserved+Pool+Rubric
- Telemetry PR (stub): https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/5821

Definition of done:
- Rubric and intake template published in Confluence, onboarding doc for Solutions Engineers updated, and a follow-up ENG ticket(s) created for console and runtime work (linked in dependencies).

Stakeholders to notify on completion: Solutions Engineering, Sales AE, Legal, Security, Runtime Eng, Console UX.

[VIP Commitment Runway & Prioritization Criteria]
description:
Background: As Redwood grows, engineering capacity and roadmap commitments for top accounts must be predictable. Currently we have ad-hoc VIP requests that get routed via support, CSM, and AE teams, leading to uneven commitments, missed expectations, and operational strain.

Objective: Define a repeatable, objective 'commitment runway' for VIP/top-account requests that ties intake signals to a timeboxed commitment policy (runway), explicit prioritization criteria, and stakeholder sign-offs. The goal is to reduce untracked escalations, set clear expectations with sales/CS, and ensure engineering capacity is allocated to work with validated product impact.

Scope: This ticket covers the policy, triage rubric, stakeholder approval flow, and the instrumentation needed in the intake tracker and roadmap board. Implementation work (automation in Zendesk/HubSpot or enforcement in engineering prioritization tooling) will be a follow-up (see dependencies).

acceptance_criteria:
1) A published VIP Commitment Runway policy (Confluence) that defines tiers, quantitative thresholds, and maximum runway windows.
2) Intake rubric that maps signals (ARR, contract terms, strategic partner status, legal/regulatory requirement, platform risk) to a tier and suggested runway length.
3) A signed approval flow template used by CSM, Sales engineer, PM, and Eng lead for any commitment runway > 2 sprints.
4) Instrumentation: sample intake form fields added to the existing intake spreadsheet and a dashboard tile showing outstanding VIP runways and remaining runway days.
5) Stakeholder alignment confirmed via a review doc and cross-functional approval recorded in Confluence.

proposed_solution:
1) Define tiers:
   - Tier A (Strategic VIP): ARR >= $2M, or named strategic partner; runway eligible up to 3 sprints with documented roadmap slot.
   - Tier B (High-value): ARR $500k - $2M or high product dependency; runway up to 2 sprints with conditional approval.
   - Tier C (Emerging): ARR < $500k but time-sensitive or regulatory; runway up to 1 sprint and subject to Product discretion.
2) Triage rubric: combine quantitative signals (ARR, contract SLA clauses, security/regulatory constraints) with qualitative signals (customer pain severity, revenue impact). Each intake auto-scores and maps to a tier.
3) Commitment runway mechanics: timeboxed commitment (number of sprints) documented in intake record; engineering allocates ‘planned runway capacity’ as placeholders rather than guaranteed dedicated headcount.
4) Escalation & fallback: automated fallback rules to default roadmap lane and communication templates if runway cannot be met.
5) Accountability: PM signs off on scope and acceptance criteria; Eng lead signs off on capacity and risk profile; CSM owns customer comms.
6) Automation: add intake fields in our tracker (Google Sheet -> until we wire Zendesk) and a Zap that notifies the PM slack channel when a Tier A intake is created.

rollout_plan:
Phase 1 (2 weeks): Draft policy and triage rubric, gather stakeholder feedback (CS, Sales, Eng leads).
Phase 2 (2 weeks): Pilot with 3 active VIP accounts (agree runway for each), instrument tracker fields and small Zapier notification.
Phase 3 (2 sprints): Iterate on rubric thresholds based on pilot; add Confluence template and communication playbook; update roadmap process docs.
Phase 4 (Q2): Automate intake into Zendesk/Intake tool and add dashboard tile in Console for PM/Eng leads.
Communication: publish to PM guild, CS weekly sync, and exec recap at roadmap review.

metrics:
- % of VIP runways met within committed window (target >= 85%).
- Mean time from VIP intake to PM decision (target <= 5 business days).
- Number of unapproved VIP commitments made (target 0).
- Customer satisfaction for pilot accounts (qualitative + NPS delta).
- Engineering rework hours attributed to runway scope slippage.

risks:
- Overcommitting engineering capacity and creating technical debt.
- Gameability: Sales/CS may game thresholds to escalate requests.
- Instrumentation gap: until intake is automated, manual tracking may lead to missed entries.
- Legal/contractual SLAs might force higher commitment for certain customers and need legal review.
Mitigations: cap total concurrent runway capacity, require multi-party signoff for Tier A, periodic audit of intake records, and involve Legal for any contract-driven requests.

updates:
2026-02-16: Kickoff meeting with CS & Sales. Agreed to pilot 3 VIP accounts and to use Google Sheet for intake until Zendesk fields are available.
2026-02-20: Draft rubric posted to Confluence for comments (link). CS asked to add 'regulatory hold' as a hard signal; added to rubric document.
2026-02-26: Engineering review: Liam recommends capping concurrent Tier A runway slots at 2 to avoid capacity cliffs. Added hard cap to the proposal.

2026-03-05: Pilot enrollments confirmed for Acme Analytics, Finberg Health, and Nova Retail. Created Zapier notification to #pm-vip-intake on Tier A intake. Next: finalize Confluence template and run pilot governance weekly sync.

[Enterprise Dedicated Intake: SLO translation, GPU-class mapping, and escalation playbook]
description:
Problem statement: Enterprise sales and customer engineering teams are requesting clearer, repeatable guidance for converting customer SLAs and throughput asks into a deterministic dedicated capacity offer. Current intake is ad-hoc: engineers receive emails with vague throughput numbers, sales promise 'Xqps' without GPU-class context, and onboarding takes longer than expected. This ticket scopes a playbook and intake form that translates customer requirements (latency SLOs, peak tokens/sec, concurrency patterns, isolation needs, regulatory constraints) into: 1) recommended GPU class and node sizing, 2) reserved throughput targets and burst policies, 3) scaling policy templates (autoscale + warm pools + pre-warm windows), and 4) escalation and handoff runbooks for SLA exceptions.

acceptance_criteria:
A consumable intake form (Google Form + Confluence template) capturing business and technical signals
SLO-to-capacity translation table that maps P50/P95/P99 latency SLOs and qps to GPU class recommendations (A100/H100/L4) and count ranges
A prioritization rubric (scorecard) that yields a numeric priority for dedicated onboarding requests
A scaling policy matrix with three templates: latency-first, cost-first, and availability-first
Escalation playbook documented with primary/secondary owners, SLAs for response, and communication templates
Sign-offs from Eng leads (Serving Runtime), Solutions Eng, and Legal for contract guardrails

playbook_highlights:
Intake fields (minimum): business owner, contract value, peak tokens/sec, expected concurrency, workload type (chat/streaming/batch/embeddings), p99 latency SLO, data residency/regulatory needs, isolation requirement (shared vs dedicated VPC), preferred GPU families, acceptable model variants (fp16/int8), go-live date
Translation example: Customer reports 2000 concurrent chat sessions, average 40 tokens per response, 2 responses per session per minute. Sustained tokens/sec = (2000 * 40 * 2) / 60 = ~2667 tokens/sec. With 30% safety margin and expected KV cache hit rate 60%, reserved tokens/sec target = 2667 * 1.3 / 0.6 = ~5778 tokens/sec. Map this to GPU sizing using per-GPU throughput profiles (table in Confluence attachment).
GPU-class mapping guidance: latency-sensitive (<200ms p99) chat with long contexts => H100 preferred; general-purpose high-throughput generation => A100; cost-sensitive, smaller embedding workloads => L4 or T4 depending on model quantization. Always include fallback model variant list to enable graceful degradation.
Scaling templates: latency-first (tight p99 targets, scale aggressively at 60% capacity), cost-first (scale at 85% sustained, use warm pools for predictable spikes), availability-first (reserve 10% burst pool across nodes, pre-warm 30 minutes before business-critical windows).
Burst policy: define 'committed' vs 'burst' buckets on contract. Default burst allowance = 15% of committed throughput for 10 minutes; anything above triggers billing or throttling as per legal-approved template.
Escalation path: first response owner = Solutions Eng on-call (30 min), secondary = Runtime SRE (2 hours), executive escalation = Head of Customer Success for incidents impacting >2 customers or >24 hours.

notes:
Key tradeoffs discussed: (1) conservative sizing reduces outage risk but increases cost of committed capacity; (2) allowing larger burst buckets improves UX but complicates billing and contract language; (3) per-customer quantization or lower-precision model variants can cut GPU requirements but may need QA on output quality. The playbook should default to conservative sizing for first 90 days, then permit right-sizing after telemetry-based evaluation.

next_steps:
Finalize Confluence playbook and intake Google Form by 2025-11-20
Implement a Console request UI prototype with Design (ticket ENG-21095 for frontend) by 2025-11-28
Pilot the intake with two queued enterprise customers (Customer B and Customer D) in Dec and capture telemetry for right-sizing after 30 days
Legal to finalize contract language for burst billing and SLA credits by 2025-11-25
Engineering to compute per-GPU throughput profiles for common models and publish as a lookup CSV in Drive

anna: heads up — found a weird mismatch between embeddings + rerank responses when using the new python client batching helper. reproducible with multi-inputs.

anna: example: i send 3 queries via embeddings.embed_batch(...) then call rerank.rerank_batch(...) expecting a list-of-lists of scores, but sometimes the rerank call returns a flat list of dicts for single-item batches and nested lists for multi-item batches. breaks our sampleapp eval harness.

```

emb = EmbeddingsClient(api_key=os.getenv("REDWOOD_KEY"))
rr = RerankClient(api_key=os.getenv("REDWOOD_KEY"))
queries = ["q1","q2","q3"]
docs = ["d1","d2","d3"]
vecs = emb.embed_batch(queries)
# Expect vecs -> [[...],[...],[...]]
res = rr.rerank_batch(queries, docs, include_metadata=True)
# res sometimes -> [[0.9,0.3,0.1],[...],...] AND sometimes -> [{"id":"d1","score":0.9}, ...]
```

jamie: ugh. looks like we have two codepaths: the legacy rerank endpoint vs the new combined embeddings+ranks helper. one returns canonical scores-only shape, the other returns enriched objects. should be consistent or at least documented.

Adding some technical trade-offs and practical numbers from an infra perspective:

PrivateLink (recommended control plane):
- Throughput: Interface endpoints accept traffic to NLBs — expect per‑AZ throughput constraints based on the NLB sizing; for steady high-TPS workloads we size a couple of NLB targets and tune connection reuse.
- Latency: adds ~1–3ms vs in‑VPC when using iface endpoints in the same AZ. Typically fine for sub‑10ms targets.
- Security: traffic never traverses the public internet; IAM + endpoint policies can lock down callers.

VPC peering (intra-AWS, low latency):
- Pros: L3 routing, no NAT for egress, bidirectional connectivity once peered.
- Cons: No transitive peering (if you want many AWS accounts to reach the Redwood endpoint you need multiple peerings OR an aggregated transit VPC). Peering also requires route table management and care with IP CIDR overlaps.

Site-to-site VPN (on-prem):
- Throughput depends on your customer gateway and AWS VGW/transit throughput. Expect higher jitter; for low-latency interactive inference this is often slightly worse than cross‑AZ AWS paths.
- Recommendation: use S2S for management/fallback and for bulk sync if you have large dataset uploads from colo.

Hybrid pattern we recommend for Praxis:
- PrivateLink for API/control + short inference bursts (keeps blast radius small).
- A peered ingress VPC in Praxis account for sustained/high-throughput local traffic (apps talk to that VPC; peering gives minimal latency).
- S2S VPN to colo as backup and for cost-effective archive uploads.

Tom / Sophie — thanks for the diagram and clear constraints. Below is a concise, operational recommendation and next steps. I tried to keep it short so you can paste into your MAS or runbook.

Summary recommendation (short):
- Preferred: AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints) for cross-account, managed access to Redwood Private control plane and inference endpoints when you want least blast radius and per-service access control. It gives the cleanest security boundaries and aligns well with our access-logging patterns.
- Alternative for very high throughput (same-account, same-region): VPC Peering (direct L3) reduces per-connection overhead and can be cheaper for sustained high egress if both VPCs are in the same region/account.
- Backup/DR: IPSec site-to-site VPN (or AWS Transit Gateway VPN attachments) as a resilient fallback across regions or as an encrypted path to on-prem. VPN is easier to get standing up quickly but has higher variance in latency and requires monitoring/HA appliances for production-grade SLAs.

Tradeoffs (short bullets):
- Security/audit: PrivateLink provides endpoint-level control and AWS flow logs + PrivateLink logs can be tied to your SIEM. Peering relies on security group/route tables and is broader by default (wider attack surface). VPN provides encryption in transit to on-prem but adds NAT/BGP complexity for cross-VPC routing.
- Latency/perf: Peering typically has the lowest hop count and smallest tail latency, then PrivateLink, then VPN (VPN adds encapsulation and often variable e2e latency).
- Operational complexity: VPN > Peering > PrivateLink in terms of try-to-forget. PrivateLink shifts interface management to AWS, which reduces ops for you but can require more IAM/endpoint policy work.
- Cost model: Peering charges inter-AZ/regional transfer at data transfer rates; PrivateLink has per-hour endpoint + per-GB data processing; VPN has hourly appliance/throughput + data transfer. For sustained high-volume inference, peering in-region often wins on pure $/GB.

Recommended immediate actions for MAS / procurement checklist:
1) Decide whether Redwood will be in the same AWS account and region as ACME inference VPC (same-account simplifies peering).
2) If cross-account, prefer PrivateLink and enumerate required IAM roles and endpoint policies.

Executive summary (short):
- VPC Peering:
  - Pros: Lowest additional network hop (lowest latency), native high throughput, straightforward for same-AWS-region VPCs, no proxying through endpoints.
  - Cons: Cross-account peering increases blast radius (peered VPCs can route to each other unless strict route controls), not transitive (multi-account requires spokes), requires overlapping CIDR planning. Not supported cross-region without extra overlay.
  - When to use: If you control both VPC accounts and need stable low-latency, high-throughput traffic (your 1.5 Gbps target is achievable with peering).

- AWS PrivateLink (Interface Endpoints):
  - Pros: Endpoint-based isolation, easiest to expose a single service without routing entire VPC ranges, integrates with SGs and endpoint policies, supports cross-account access without peering. Minimal CIDR impact.
  - Cons: Each connection goes through ENIs in the provider account — slightly higher latency than peering (typically a few ms), and there's per-ENI throughput considerations; for sustained multi-Gbps you'll need multiple endpoints and appropriate load distribution. Also incurs endpoint hourly and data processing charges.
  - When to use: If you need strong isolation (security team wants only specific service ports reachable), cross-account exposure without peering, or simplified egress IP whitelisting via endpoints. Good fit if you want minimal route table changes.

- Site-to-site VPN (IPsec / Transit Gateway VPN):
  - Pros: Quick to prototype, works cross-cloud and with on-prem devices, no cloud-native account reconfiguration required. Can be terminated to Transit Gateway for scale.
  - Cons: IPsec throughput caps per tunnel (depends on appliance), higher jitter and CPU overhead (so may not meet the <10 ms extra latency/jitter goals), and operational reliability is lower than native cloud fabric.   - When to use: Short-term PoC or multi-cloud/on-prem centric setups where you can't change cloud account topology.

  - Pros: Fast to stand up, works across cloud providers and on-prem, supports BGP for route failover, can be used as a DR/fallback path.
  - Cons: Higher latency and jitter compared to native AWS backbone; throughput caps on individual tunnels unless you leverage multiple tunnels or AWS Accelerated VPN; operational complexity for stable high-throughput inference.
  - Notes: MTU and fragmentation issues are common for inference payloads — ensure path MTU discovery or tune MSS on endpoints.

Recommended pattern for NovaHealth given HIPAA and multi-account:
1) Primary: PrivateLink for Redwood control plane + model endpoints (per-region). This gives you the clean security posture and access control.
2) For intra-account heavy data movement (e.g., large dataset replication), use VPC peering or Transit Gateway inside the account/region to avoid the per-GB PrivateLink processing fees.
3) Use a managed S2S VPN (or Direct Connect if procurement allows) only for staging or as a DR/fallback path — not as the primary production path for latency-sensitive inference.

- Confirm region pairs for production endpoints and whether cross-region active/active is required.
- Estimate persistent vs burst throughput so we can size NLBs and endpoint bandwidth.
- Agree on logging/audit plan (flow logs, endpoint logs) for compliance evidence.
