[00:01:26] Liam: so we're balancing latency vs quality — we saw quality lift on multi-step answers with 14b in evals, but it wasn't huge for all prompts. can we soften degrade gracefully?
[00:01:40] Maya: yes, that's where soft-pin and shadowing helps. we can do traffic weight 80/20 (primary/backup) and shadow 100% to collect outputs. soft-pin means routing prefers pinned version but still allows fallback if capacity constrained. hard-pin is pinned and locked — no automatic fallback.
[00:02:05] Sophie: what's the emergency swap flow? our SREs want a <5min RTO for customer-facing endpoints.
[00:02:12] Ethan: two options: automated policy-based swap that reroutes by model family on health signals (latency/slo breaches) or manual cutover initiated by Atlas on-call. automated can be 10-30s to shift if using the routing layer, but you need to accept brief partial outputs; manual is slower but safer.
[00:02:34] Ravi: does automated swap keep same request fidelity? will it map completions from 14b to 7b seamlessly?
[00:02:41] Maya: semantic differences remain; you can configure escape hatch to change prompt prefix or increase sampling temp to keep behavior similar. Also important: KV cache warmup — when you swap down to 7b it won't share kv cache, so first N requests may be slower.
[00:03:02] Ethan: also note we can do model-variant alignment — deploy a 14b-compat quant that is tuned to match 7b latency, so the swap delta is smaller. but that takes onboarding time.
[00:03:18] Liam: cost question — if we do automated fallback, will costs spike because of doubled shadow traffic?
[00:03:25] Maya: shadowing adds overhead; in our pilot we did 100% shadow for two days and saw an extra 35% egress compute. we can sample shadowing 20% and still gather quality signal.
[00:03:38] Sophie: security — if we need to swap across regions for capacity, we need to ensure keys stay in our KMS and logs meet sock two and ISO requirements. is that supported in hosted mode?
[00:03:50] Ethan: hosted has region-level options and we can integrate with customer KMS via our private tenant pipeline for Dedicated or Private. for Hosted we offer envelope encryption and bring-your-own-key integrations in certain regions; not all regions yet. note: our compliance docs will call out SOC 2 and ISO 27001 for hosted.
[00:04:15] Ravi: there's a few transcription errors in earlier notes — when you say "K V cash" i think you mean kv cache, just flagging.
[00:04:23] Maya: ya, the auto notes sometimes flop acronyms.
[00:04:29] Liam: okay back to pinning — can we do conditional pinning per route? e.g., pin model A for inference route /cart and model B for /recs?
[00:04:38] Maya: yes per-route pinning is supported, and you can set fallback policies per-route. you can also set a global fallback for the entire customer. routing can be region aware, cost-aware, or latency-aware — you pick the policy.
[00:04:55] Sophie: we like the idea of per-route because cart has stricter latency needs.
[00:05:02] Ethan: proposed approach: pin 14b for /recs where quality matters, soft-pin 14b for /cart with 80/20 fallback to 7b, and schedule a weekly roll-forward window for pin reviews.
[00:05:15] Ravi: what about rollback — can we automate rollback to previous model version if eval regressions appear?
[00:05:22] Maya: we have a version gateway — you can set a canary traffic slice and tie it to quality metrics (bleu-like or custom eval). if the canary drops below threshold we auto-roll back to previous stable version. that's what we did in the demo last month. caveat: automatic rollback needs the previous version still deployed and available.
[00:05:43] Liam: does that require extra reserved capacity? like keep previous versions warm?
[00:05:48] Maya: ideally yes — we recommend a small standby pool or cold start warmers to keep KV cache seeded for the previous version. without warmers, rollback is functional but slower. cost tradeoff vs RTO.
[00:06:06] Ethan: for emergency swap we recommend two options: 1) standby locked fallback — keep 7b pinned on a small reserved capacity pool (warm) for instant swap; cost = reserved. 2) cold fallback with warmers — cheaper but RTO may be minutes.
[00:06:24] Sophie: our budget boundaries: we can accept up to +15% infra cost for standby in peak months, otherwise prefer warmers.
[00:06:31] Ravi: what about model catalog naming? i want clarity so our CI can refer to stable identifiers not friendly aliases.
[00:06:38] Maya: we expose model identifiers and semantic tags. e.g., redwood-14b-quant:v1.3-stable. you can pin by id. we also expose compatible model variants list for automated fallback mapping.
[00:06:54] Liam: any gotchas with private deployments? we may need on-prem V P C and H S M integration.
[00:07:01] Ethan: Private supports HSM/KMS and air-gapped options. note that some runtime optimizations require specific CUDA drivers; our private installer includes kernel checks. for V P C peering we keep control plane in Redwood but can allow private egress to your subnets.
[00:07:20] Sophie: SSO — our compliance folks want SAML and RBAC. do you support SCIM?
[00:07:26] Maya: yes SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning are available for enterprise tiers. RBAC supports route-level roles.
[00:07:34] Liam: let's define concrete thresholds for auto-swap: p95 > 1.2s for 5 minutes triggers a health breach?
[00:07:42] Maya: that's reasonable. we usually set rolling window 5min and require consecutive windows to avoid flapping. can set suppression and cooldown.
[00:07:52] Ethan: i'll capture that as part of runbook.
[00:07:56] Liam: on rollback testing, we want a dry run — simulate swap in staging with traffic replay and measure time to stable. can you provide the tooling?
[00:08:04] Maya: yes we have a traffic-replay harness and tracing hooks. we'll share the harness repo link and instructions.
[00:08:12] Ethan: OK quick alignment on pins today: Atlas will soft-pin 14b for /cart at 80/20 and hard-pin 14b for /recs. Standby: keep a warm 7b pool in region us-west-2 with RTO target 3 minutes.
[00:08:26] Ravi: 3 minutes seems fine. but if the automated swap is possible in 30s we may prefer that — is warming 7b going to block compute for other tenants?
[00:08:34] Maya: on Dedicated you get reserved nodes; on Hosted, warm pools are shared but with isolation guarantees, and you'll see small overhead. we'll quantify in the pricing note.
[00:08:46] Liam: any compliance doc we can send to security?
[00:08:50] Ethan: i'll attach SOC 2 summary, our infra pen test summary, and the Private deployment checklist.
[00:08:58] Sophie: one last bit — during a swap can we annotate logs that show model-version mapping per request for audit?
[00:09:05] Maya: yes each request has model_id and version metadata and we can route logs to your SIEM via the log forwarder.
[00:09:12] Ethan: sweet. i think that's the main set. shall we go through next steps?
[00:09:17] Liam: yes please.
[00:09:20] Ethan: summary/next steps: Maya will run the 24-hour soak for both variants and share heatmaps. i'll send pricing and pilot delta. Atlas to confirm on-call roster and RTO acceptance. we'll schedule a dry-run in staging for emergency swap next week.
[00:09:36] Ravi: thanks, sounds good.
[00:09:40] Sophie: thanks all.
[00:09:43] Ethan: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with artifacts.

References mentioned:

[00:18] Maya Chen: Okay, on the agenda today we wanted to walk through the hit-rate trends after we switched the cohort prefetch heuristic and then talk through prompt reuse for the clinical-dialog flows. Samir, take it away on the dashboard.

[00:44] Rajiv Singh: Wait, are those numbers stable throughout the day or do they spike? We saw some midday drops last Friday.
[00:50] Samir Patel: Good call. The drop corresponds to the longer sessions set — when context grows past 6k tokens the cache effectiveness falls because eviction is more aggressive. We can soften eviction, but that increases memory footprint and maybe cost.
[01:05] Dr. Marcus Hale: When you say soften, like what policy specifically? Time-based TTL or LRU tweak?
[01:10] Samir Patel: Primarily LRU window expansion plus session affinity — we keep a session pin for the top n prefixes per session. We can also do a hybrid TTL for less active prefixes.
[01:20] Lena Ortiz: Hybrid sounds promising. Our workflow is multi-turn followups, so losing long-tail is painful. But we also have strict budget so cost matters.
[01:28] Maya Chen: Side note — this is a good place Redwood's automatic batching and dynamic routing can help: route longer sessions to Dedicated pools we configured for Veridian to preserve latency SLOs while trying to keep unit costs in check.
[01:41] Rajiv Singh: For Dedicated we'd need certs and KMS access; what's the handoff timeline?
[01:46] Maya Chen: We can start provisioning once you sign the pilot amendment; Samir will do an on-prem run first to validate. We'll share the security pack — SOC2, ISO, KMS integration steps and SAML SSO notes.
[01:58] Samir Patel: Back to the data — also noticed prompt normalization errors in about 4% of requests, transcription mismatches where users append timestamps and the tokenizer prevents prefix matching. We've been experimenting with light prompt cleaning and stemming to improve prefix reuse.
[02:14] Dr. Marcus Hale: Hmm, prompt cleaning seems risky for clinical texts — we can't normalize out negations. Need to be careful.
[02:20] Samir Patel: Absolutely, that's why we apply rule-based cleaning that is reversible and don't touch protected tokens. But the tradeoff is more false negatives if we err on the side of caution.
[02:30] Lena Ortiz: Could we instead do soft matching, like fuzzy prefix match with similarity threshold?
[02:34] Samir Patel: Yeah, approximate matching is supported but it's more CPU-heavy; it costs more in the control plane. But it can bump hit-rate for conversational prompts where small variations are common.
[02:45] Maya Chen: Another anomaly — latency tail went up on sessions that hit disk-backed eviction. The 95th percentile jumped from 320ms to 700ms for those requests. That aligns with the midday drop Rajiv mentioned.
[02:58] Rajiv Singh: Disk-backed eviction — is that when the KV overflows to SSD? We've got NVMe but not huge capacity.
[03:03] Samir Patel: Right, we tier to local NVMe as a stopgap. For Dedicated we can pin more GPU memory and avoid spilling. For Private on-prem we'll rely on your hardware sizing. We'll test a large context run to see thresholds.
[03:16] Dr. Marcus Hale: Ok, let's talk prompt reuse strategy specific to our clinical intents: we have templates for triage, diagnosis, and follow-ups. Which ones are easiest to prioritize?
[03:26] Lena Ortiz: Triage and medication-reconciliation flows are top for latency sensitivity.
[03:30] Samir Patel: Great, Lena if you can send top 25 templates we'll build a prefix catalog and pre-warm those keys with the cohort prefetcher.
[03:37] Lena Ortiz: Yep, will do.
[03:39] Maya Chen: Quick practical question — what's the expected delta in cost if we keep more prefixes per session vs reducing eviction? Can you ballpark?
[03:46] Samir Patel: Ballpark: keeping +20% prefixes per session increases memory footprint around 15% and token cost about 4-6% due to extra cache maintenance. But it reduces model tokens consumed by ~18% on the prioritized routes, so net cost could still go down. These are estimates — we'll run the perf job to validate.
[04:03] Rajiv Singh: How about model fallbacks — if primary model is busy do we have automatic fallback to smaller quantized variant? That would change latency/ quality tradeoffs.
[04:10] Maya Chen: Yes, Redwood routing supports automatic fallback policies. You can configure per-route quality thresholds and allow fallback to a quantized variant. We'll demo that in the next call.
[04:21] Dr. Marcus Hale: On data residency, we need audit logs for every inference for compliance. Do you have per-request audit and immutable logs?
[04:29] Maya Chen: Yes, audit logs with optional retention windows. For Private we can push logs to your SIEM via S3/GCS connectors and HSM/KMS for key control. We'll include the log sample in the security pack.
[04:40] Lena Ortiz: There was a small regression we spotted: one route's perplexity increased after the prefix coalescing change. Might be due to over-aggressive coalescing mixing clinical templates. Any quick mitigation?
[04:51] Samir Patel: We can add a safe-list for templates that shouldn't be coalesced and run an A/B canary rollback on that route. Canary is quick, will revert hit-rate but hopefully restore quality.
[05:01] Maya Chen: Let's note that as an action — safe-list those templates and run a canary.

[05:11] Samir Patel: Yes, we'll upload per-token traces with redaction for PII. Expect a CSV and a summarized sheet.
[05:19] Rajiv Singh: About SSO and SAML — our security needs a short window for integration testing. I can carve out Thursday morning.
[05:24] Maya Chen: Perfect; Samir, can you and Rajiv pick a slot?
[05:27] Samir Patel: Yep, I'll ping Rajiv after the call.
[05:29] Dr. Marcus Hale: One more question on caching semantics: how do you handle context window shifts when users edit earlier messages — that can invalidate prefixes.
[05:38] Samir Patel: We treat edits as new tokens and invalidate affected prefix segments; for heavy edit flows we can use a session-level checkpoint so you only re-evaluate from last stable checkpoint. That's part of the session affinity features.

[Edge On‑Prem Stability & Rollout — Weekly POC Check‑in]
summary:
Weekly sync focused on stability after recent kernel upgrade attempt; customer reported intermittent egress errors and higher p99 latency during bursts. Discussed rollforward plan (kernel 2.4 canary), telemetry gaps, MTU and BGP causes, and next steps to run a 12-hr soak and a security deep-dive. Agreement to collect packet captures and to test with continuous batching disabled briefly to isolate KV cache behavior.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-05 15:30 UTC | Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (AsterMed Platform), Liam O'Connor (AsterMed MLOps), Sara Weber (AsterMed Security), Tomáš Novak (AsterMed NetOps)

[00:00] Maya Chen: ok everyone, thanks for joining, we'll kick off, um, quick agenda—stability update, kernel canary plan, telemetry gaps and then actions. Diego, want to start with what we saw overnight?

[00:18] Diego Ramos: yeah, sure. So this morning the canary we pushed to the staging onprem cluster hit a p99 spike during a burst test. The median looked fine but the 99, and sometimes 99.9, jumped. We think it's correlated with node egress retries when the batcher backpressures, so there's a coupling between continuous batching and the KV cache warmup behavior.

[00:40] Priya Singh: to be clear, that was after the 2.3 -> 2.4 kernel bump? Because our patch notes show that, but, uh, original patch was intended to resolve a NIC driver stall.

[00:50] Diego Ramos: correct, this was kernel 2.4 canary. The driver change mitigates stalls under heavy VRF egress, but it also changed NIC ring timing a bit — so MTU boundary conditions pop up. We saw occasional path MTU discovery delays.

[01:05] Tomáš Novak: yeah we saw a ton of ICMP fragmentation messages in the netstack; sometimes BGP sessions would flit, not a hard drop but flapping enough to cause re-route. I can share pcap later.

[01:18] Liam O'Connor: to add, when the re-route happened, Redwood's fallback routing kicked in which is good, but the model requests that hit the fallback variant had a 20–30% higher token latency. That's causing user-surface errors in our staging telemetry.

[01:34] Maya Chen: thanks, that's the exact tradeoff we expected — fallback keeps you available but at the cost of both latency and token economics. The goal here is to find the narrow path: fix the networking so you don't hit fallback for normal traffic while still having the fallback as a safety valve.

[01:48] Sara Weber: security question — when fallback triggers, are audit logs preserved and are we still within our KMS encryption boundaries? We need to demonstrate chain-of-custody for SOC2.

[01:57] Diego Ramos: quick answer: yes, logs continue to be written to the private control plane. There was a small telemetry gap we identified where our sidecar didn't forward some early startup traces — we're pushing a patch to ensure immediate buffer flush on failover.

[02:13] Priya Singh: that's the telemetry gap we noticed. Our retention policy requires immutable logs for 90 days; can you confirm the storage location for those failover logs?

[02:22] Maya Chen: we'll share the exact S3/GCS path and the retention policy mapping. Diego, please include the log key prefixes in the artifact list.

[02:31] Diego Ramos: will do. Also adding, during repro we tried two modes: continuous batching enabled vs disabled. With batching disabled the p99 drops significantly, which points to a batching + KV cache warmup interdependency. There's a possible fix in the canary to pre-warm KV cache for pinned models, but it needs testing.

[02:49] Tomáš Novak: pre-warm how? like priming the KV cache on startup? that could increase memory usage but might stabilize latency.

[02:57] Diego Ramos: yep prime at startup for hot routes, with an LRU expiration tuned to your traffic pattern. We can also reduce batch windows to lower tail effects. There's a balance to keep cost in line.

[03:12] Liam O'Connor: cost is important — remember we're metric-ing tokens and infra separately. If pre-warm doubles memory we may overshoot footprint. We prefer less memory and more deterministic latency, but we'll find the right config.

[03:24] Priya Singh: on the MTU thing — we have a legacy edge router doing 1500, but some internal links are 9000 (jumbo). The fragmentation shows when packets traverse mixed MTU paths. Could that explain the odd retries?

[03:36] Diego Ramos: absolutely. If PMTUD is delayed, TCP will retransmit and that shows as increased service latency. For UDP-based health checks and GRPC keepalives it could look like BGP jitter.

[03:46] Sara Weber: aside from SOC2, we have a compliance ask: we need KMS attestations that keys don't leave our HSM when fallback is used — any variance there?

[03:56] Maya Chen: no variance, KMS calls are made from the private control plane locked into your VPC. Diego, we'll include an architecture diagram with SAML/SAML SSO flows and KMS boundary notes.

[04:07] Diego Ramos: noted. I'll add explicit call paths and audit log samples.

[04:12] Maya Chen: ok, let's run through the canary plan and rollback criteria so we're all aligned — Diego?

[04:18] Diego Ramos: Plan A: deploy kernel 2.4 to two canary nodes in the onprem pool (non-critical serving). Enable continuous batching monitoring, and run synthetic burst tests (10k req/min) for 3 hours, then 12-hour soak if no p99 > target and no egress flaps. Rollback criteria: any sustained p99 > 250ms for > 5 minutes, any BGP session error rate above baseline, or any audit/log gap discovered.

[04:42] Priya Singh: what baseline do we use for BGP error rate? Our normal is <0.2% session flaps per hour.

[04:49] Diego Ramos: use your historical as baseline; we'll set an absolute threshold of 0.5% for the canary window to be safe.

[04:55] Tomáš Novak: also, if we see PMTU blackholes, I'd like to enable TCP MSS clamp as a temporary mitigation while we trace path MTU.

[05:03] Diego Ramos: good mitigation, and we'll instrument the flow to detect PMTUD failures.

[05:10] Liam O'Connor: one more thing — during the earlier run, we saw a small burst where the fallback model served older quantized variant which produced a subtle quality regression. We need to tag that as a user-impact event even if latency stayed okay.

[05:22] Maya Chen: understood — we'll add a quality regression flag to the rollback criteria: any change in ROUGE/BLEU or model output distribution above your guardrail. Diego, can Redwood inject a canary variant that maintains output parity?

[05:32] Diego Ramos: yes, we can pin a canary variant that uses the same quantization settings, but the kernel-level NIC timing may still affect token timing. We need to separate quality deltas from timing deltas in telemetry.

[05:44] Priya Singh: telemetry — currently we don't get per-token timing in our logs; we get per-request latencies. Can Redwood add per-token percentiles for the pilot?

[05:54] Diego Ramos: we can enable token-level tracing in the sandbox. It will increase log volume but we can limit windowed traces — e.g., sample 5% of requests during the soak.

[06:05] Sara Weber: and are those token traces encrypted the same way as request logs? we need to ensure PII not leaking.

[06:11] Maya Chen: yes, same KMS boundary. We'll provide a privacy matrix.

[06:16] Speaker 1: okay so next steps from a networking side — Tomáš will push pcaps and BGP logs.

[06:23] Tomáš Novak: I'll drop a tarball to the secure share, and annotate timestamps where we saw flaps. Expect that by tomorrow morning.

[06:30] Priya Singh: question about the continuous batching toggle — you mentioned disabling briefly to isolate KV cache; can we do a traffic-shift test that toggles batching for 15 minutes?

[06:38] Diego Ramos: yes, we can run runbooks that change the global batching window at route level; we'll do a controlled window and compare p99. Also can do a no-batching run for 30 minutes during low-traffic.

[06:48] Maya Chen: good. Diego, add the exact runbook steps to the doc and I'll send to Priya for approval.

[06:54] Diego Ramos: will do.

[07:00] Liam O'Connor: for acceptance criteria — assuming the 12-hour soak passes, what's the recommended rollout cadence? full pool in 48 hours?

[07:07] Diego Ramos: if soak passes with no alerts and p99 within target, we usually do a staggered 25% increment every 4 hours with automated health checks. With your stricter compliance, we can extend to 8-hour windows.

[07:18] Priya Singh: 8 hours sounds safer. Also, we want a dry-run of the rollback to ensure it is fast; can you simulate rollback in staging?

[07:25] Diego Ramos: yes, simulate both a soft rollback (traffic re-route) and hard rollback (package revert). Soft rollback is usually sub-minute; hard rollback depends on your orchestration but we can pre-place the older kernel package to cut time.

[07:40] Maya Chen: switching briefly to security: Sara, you had a list of SOC2 evidence we didn't provide last week?

[07:47] Sara Weber: right, we still need architecture diagrams with KMS calls annotated, a list of who has HSM access, and proof that logs can't be altered during fallback. Also metadata retention policy.

[07:59] Maya Chen: we'll produce an updated security pack. Diego, include the control plane call-flow and the audit log sample.

[08:05] Diego Ramos: yes. Also note that our private deployment supports customer-managed KMS — if you want HSM retention >90 days we can give options.

[08:13] Priya Singh: for now we'll stick to existing HSM with Redwood-managed rotation, but send options.

[08:18] Speaker 2: minor item — someone asked about competitor notes, why not just use Vertex?

[08:24] Maya Chen: short answer, Vertex is fine but doesn't have our unified rollout and fallback playbook for private onprem with telemetry parity, which is why AsterMed chose Redwood. But we also respect your multi-cloud strategy.

[08:36] Liam O'Connor: ok thanks — one ops question: can Redwood's console emit alerts into our PagerDuty on these specific rollback triggers?

[08:45] Diego Ramos: absolutely. We'll map events to your PD service and can set escalation policies.

[08:50] Tomáš Novak: good — for the pcap I'll annotate which PD alerts corresponded to flaps.

[08:58] Maya Chen: all right, let's capture the definitive next steps — Diego, can you list the artifacts you'll deliver by Friday?

[09:05] Diego Ramos: sure: 1) kernel 2.4 canary runbook and instrumentation (including token-level sampling) 2) updated logging path and sample logs 3) audit diagram + KMS callflow 4) an annotated rollback test plan. I'll push to the secure share and ping Priya.

[09:20] Priya Singh: I'll share VPC peering config, the BGP adjacency history, and the MTU topology map. Expect that tonight.

[09:28] Sara Weber: I'll confirm the SOC2 list and schedule a 30-min security deep-dive for next week.

[09:34] Maya Chen: perfect. Recap: run a 3-hour synthetic then 12-hour soak on 2 canary nodes, collect pcaps and logs, toggle batching for isolated runs, and convene security call.

[09:45] Speaker 1: any blockers?

[09:48] Priya Singh: main blocker is time window for soak — we'll need to align with a low-traffic period; otherwise we can do an overnight soak starting 00:00 local.

[09:55] Liam O'Connor: also team availability for rollback; ops will be on-call tomorrow morning.

[09:59] Diego Ramos: Redwood will be on standby for canary window.

[10:03] Maya Chen: thanks everyone. I'll send minutes and the checklist. Meeting adjourned.

--- End of transcript (many disfluencies preserved; some names auto-attributed)

[01:20] Drew (SRE): yeah, the KV cash - uh cash - sorry, KV cache - got trimmed by the compaction job that ran out of schedule. That made certain requests fall back to full model reloads and we saw tail latency blow out.

[02:05] Priya (VP Product): A few folks raised the question in slack about why Dedicated tenants saw different behavior. Short answer: Dedicated pools had a different eviction window and less aggressive compaction but also more headroom so impact was variable.

[02:48] Speaker 1 (unlabeled): Do we have telemetry we can point customers to? Some customers asked for more granular logs and the audit trail.

[03:15] Clara (VP Ops): We're shipping an observability dashboard that surfaces token-level latency, KV cache hit rates, and kernel-selection events. It's in beta for a small set of Console tenants next week. Link in the follow ups.

[03:58] Marcus: Important note: we are moving to explicit latency tiers in the SLOs. Hosted has default SLOs at p95/p99 latency, Dedicated customers can opt into stricter tail-latency SLOs and Private deployments will be allowed custom SLOs driven by on-prem capacity.

[04:38] Elena: This matters because product and sales need a single story about what good looks like. We don't want sales promising sub-50ms for workloads that are actually long-context with low quantization.

[05:10] Nora (Customer Success): Quick customer anecdote - one customer in finance asked for data residency + private inference and also wanted a weekly SLA report. We told them we're able to create a reporting bundle but need the playbook to standardize the process.

[05:42] Jade (Eng Manager): On the playbook: it's structured around triage, containment, root-cause, postmortem, and customer communication templates. There's also a short ops quiz to ensure folks read it. We tried to keep it short so it's actually consumed.

[Per-request KPI Hydrator and OTLP->Prometheus Deduper]
description:
Background: We currently ingest a mix of Prometheus-style scrapes and OTLP metric streams for inference requests. Downstream KPI consumers (dashboards, SLO rollups, billing) require deterministic per-request metrics (latency_ms, tokens_generated, model_variant, route) with cardinality controlled for tenant scale. Problem: duplicate signals appear when both the sidecar emits a per-request metric and the upstream proxy translates spans into OTLP metrics; we also see partial label mismatches (tenant_id vs org_id) and bursty high-cardinality from debug labels. Goal: implement a lightweight Hydrator component that canonicalizes per-request KPI envelopes, enriches with deterministic identifiers (request_id, tenant_digest), applies label canonicalization, and emits a single, deduplicated stream to Prometheus remote_write and to our metrics lake. The Hydrator will run as a small sidecar/agent in inference nodes and as an ingestion stage in the telemetry pipeline for hosted endpoints.

acceptance_criteria:
Hydrator accepts OTLP metrics and Prometheus packets and outputs a canonical per-request KPI envelope
Deduplication heuristic removes duplicate emissions where request_id matches and timestamps within 250ms
Label canonicalizer maps tenant_id, org_id, customer to a single tenant field; debug labels are filtered by sampling config
Output conforms to prometheus remote_write schema with fixed metric names: r_kpi_latency_ms, r_kpi_tokens, r_kpi_error_count
No >1% increase in pipeline tail-latency after enabling Hydrator in canary
Integration tests cover span->metric stitching, dedupe cases, and label normalization

implementation_steps:
Design Hydrator schema and CEP (canonical envelope prototype) - document in Confluence
Build a minimal OTLP consumer that can parse gauge/counter/summary and map to envelope fields
Implement deterministic request_id extraction and tenant_digest algorithm
Add dedupe window implementation (configurable, default 250ms) with probabilistic memory cap per tenant
Wire outputs to Prometheus remote_write client and to existing metrics-lake Kafka topic
Create a canary deployment flow: edge nodes -> hydrator sidecar -> telemetry-staging -> dashboards
Run load tests with synthetic multi-tenant traffic to validate CPU/memory and dedupe effectiveness
Rollout plan: internal staging -> 5% production (non-critical customers) -> 25% -> 100%
Add monitoring and alerts for hydrator queue length, dedupe eviction rate, and label-loss rate

progress_updates:
2026-02-19: Kickoff — scoped MVP schema, agreed on canonical metric names and minimal field set (request_id, tenant, model, route, latency_ms, tokens, error_flag).
2026-02-25: Design review with PM/Console team — decided to emit both Prometheus remote_write and a compact protobuf envelope to Kafka for downstream analytics. Runbooks drafted for canary rollback.
2026-03-02: PoC implemented — OTLP consumer can parse simple counters and create CEP; dedupe logic implemented using LRU cache per-tenant with TTL. Initial perf shows ~4% CPU overhead on a small node under synthetic load.
2026-03-08: Security review requested — data minimization confirmed (no PII collected); asked to surface KMS-backed tenant_digest option for private deployments.
2026-03-12: Met with Observability team — decided to increase dedupe window configurability and add a probabilistic Bloom filter fallback for very high-cardinality tenants to bound memory. Preparing canary PR.

notes_and_tradeoffs:
Trade-offs: strict deduping risks dropping legitimate rapid re-emissions for retried requests; to mitigate we include a routed_retry flag in envelope to bypass dedupe for known retries. Memory vs accuracy: LRU per-tenant is simple but can OOM under large tenants; chosen design adds tenant-level caps and Bloom filter fallback. We prioritized deterministic request_id extraction over probabilistic stitching to keep downstream billing and SLOs stable.

Integration test harness that replays production traces and validates 1:1 mapping for canonicalized requests
Performance test: sustained 20k req/s per node with sample tenants to ensure <1% pipeline latency regression
Canary observability: compare r_kpi_latency_ms p50/p95 between raw and hydrated streams and validate alerts

[Incremental token latency allocation and cache impact tracing]
description:
Summary: We need fine-grained instrumentation that attributes latency and cost to incremental token emission steps and isolates the effect of KV/prefix cache hits and misses. Current observability aggregates request-level timings which obscures cache economics and prevents per-customer unit-cost reconciliation for sequences with mixed cache behavior.

Goals:
- Emit stable, low-cardinality traces and metrics that break a single request into ordered emission spans (token_index, phase) so we can correlate per-token latency with cache state and kernel selection.
- Surface cache impact: capture whether each emission span was served from local KV, hot remote cache, cache miss (backend recompute), or prefilled prefix.
- Produce metrics streams usable by billing/reconciliation and by console dashboards: per-token latency distributions by model/variant, request-type, and cache outcome.
- Enable sampling that preserves head/tail behavior for long sequences while capping cardinality for high-throughput customers.

Non-goals:
- Not implementing billing pipeline changes in this ticket; this is instrumentation and observability only.
- Not adding new kernel-level timers inside third-party runtimes (we will integrate if they expose hooks).

Design and approach:
1) Trace span model: introduce ordered emission spans named "emit:<i>" where <i> is the token emission index. Each span contains low-cardinality tags: model, variant, host_pool, cache_outcome (hit_local|hit_remote|miss|prefill), emission_phase (kv_lookup|compute|kernel_exec|serialize), token_index_bucket (head/1-16|mid/17-256|tail/257+), and request_id. We will avoid literal token text or token ids in traces.

2) Metrics: For each emission span we will increment counters and record histograms: emit_latency_ms, kv_lookup_ms, compute_ms, kernel_ms, and a gauge emit_cache_outcome. Histograms are configured for high-resolution at head tokens and coarser at tail. Metrics keys are templated to collapse by model and cache_outcome to keep cardinality manageable.

3) Sampling and aggregation: To avoid explosion, full emission-span tracing is enabled for 0.5% of requests by default with deterministic sampling for known customers. We will also provide a per-customer toggle for increased sampling. Aggregation pipeline will roll token_index into buckets and produce daily rollups used by billing.

4) Logging: For sampled traces we will add structured logs linking spans to request-level metadata (customer_id, route, pinned_model). Logs redact any PII and do not include prompt contents.

5) Pipeline and storage: Traces flow into our APM backend (currently X-APM), metrics to Prometheus+THANOS, and aggregated artifacts to the metrics warehouse for further joins with billing traces. We will add a transformation job that tags aggregated token-bucket latency by cache_outcome.

6) Dashboards and alerts: Create console dashboards with breakdowns: per-model emit latency by token_bucket and cache_outcome, and tail-latency P99 per-route. Alerts on spike in cache_miss_ratio or P99_emit_latency exceeding SLOs.

Success criteria:
- Instrumentation emits emission spans for >=99% of sampled requests with correct cache_outcome tag.
- Console dashboard shows token-bucketed latency and cache miss ratio for runtime-1.24 models.
- Aggregated metrics available in warehouse for billing reconciliation jobs.
- No customer-visible latency regression from tracing (<0.5ms median overhead on sampled path).

Implementation plan and milestones:
- Week 1: API design and low-level trace/span schema review with runtime and infra teams.
- Week 2: Add emission spans in runtime codepath with cache_outcome tagging and initial metrics; unit tests.
- Week 3: Hook downstream pipeline (APM + metrics) and create aggregation job; mammoth-run tests on staging.
- Week 4: Create dashboards and run 2-week shadow sampling for verification, then enable deterministic sampling for a set of pilot customers.

Risks and mitigations:
- Cardinality blowup: mitigate with token_index_bucket, emission_phase, and strict label set; enforce cardinality quotas in APM.
- Overhead: keep sampling conservative; ensure timers are lightweight and avoid locks on hot path.
- Data joins for billing: coordinate with billing team to ensure trace IDs are persisted in warehouse.

Artifacts and links:
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/OBS/Incremental+Emission+Tracing
- Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/9421 (WIP)
- Draft dashboard: https://console.redwood.ai/dashboards/token-latency-cache-impact

Next steps: finish runtime PR, add metrics config, wire pipeline transformer, and schedule design review with Security for log redaction rules.

Emission spans emitted for sampled requests with cache_outcome tag present
Metric emit_latency_ms and kv_lookup_ms available in Prometheus for models on runtime-1.24
Dashboard in Console replicates per-token-bucket latency and cache miss ratio
Sampling overhead measured and below 0.5ms median on sampled path
Aggregation job produces daily rollups consumable by billing team

[Token cost attribution pipeline for per-route & per-model billing]
description:
Background: Product and Finance need a reliable, low-latency pipeline to compute per-request token cost attribution and rollups by route, customer, and model. Current billing reports rely on coarse daily aggregates which miss spikes and do not reflect short-lived route-level surges. This ticket implements an always-correct, scalable pipeline that converts per-request telemetry (OTLP spans + per-token logs) into token counts, assigns costing metadata, and emits aggregated rollups suitable for billing, alerting, and cost dashboards.

Goals:
- Produce near-real-time per-route, per-model, and per-customer token usage metrics (1m granularity) labeled for billing and SLO calculations.
- Preserve request-level provenance for sampling/inspectability (store sampled traces with cost metadata).
- Keep downstream Prom/TSDB cardinality bounded via controlled rollups and tenant aggregation strategies.
- Integrate with existing billing engine (billing-aggregator) and Redwood Console dashboards.

Telemetry sources and inputs:
- OTLP traces: span events that mark "generation.start", "generation.token" (for streaming) and "generation.end". Spans contain model_id, route_id, billing_tier, and customer_id labels.
- Structured logs (ndjson) from runtime for per-token events when streaming is enabled (fallback for older runtimes).
- Prom counters emitted from runtime sidecars for token_count_total per model/route (used for reconciliation).

Design approach (high level):
1) Ingest: Collect OTLP traces and structured token logs into the telemetry Kafka topic (telemetry.inference.calls).
2) Enrich: A stream job (Flink) correlates spans and token events to construct canonical per-request objects: {request_id, model_id, route_id, customer_id, token_counts: {prompt, completion, total}, sequence_length_distribution}. Enrichment also applies price per token from product catalog (pull from pricing-service cache).
3) Reduce & rollup: Aggregate canonical objects into minute-level rollups with labels: [customer_id, model_id, route_id, pricing_tier, region]. Emit two outputs: low-cardinality Prom-style aggregates (remote write) and high-cardinality append-only billing events to ClickHouse/BigQuery for audit and dispute resolution.
4) Sampling & retention: Keep 0.5% deterministic sample of full request objects (configurable) with deterministic hashing on request_id -> stored in s3/ClickHouse for 90 days. Aggregates retained per current telemetry retention policy.
5) Backpressure & safety: If the enrichment job lags, write raw telemetry to a hot-journal S3 prefix and emit degraded-mode metrics (degraded_token_rollup=true) to Console with ETA for catchup.

Acceptance criteria:
- Pipeline processes synthetic load (10k req/s, avg 120 tokens/req) end-to-end with <60s delay to minute rollups and 99.9% delivery to Prom remote write.
- Aggregated per-minute metrics exposed as Prom time series with labels model_id, route_id and customer_id (customer_id only for enterprise tenants; for public tenants use customer_bucket label) to control cardinality.
- Deterministic sampled requests available for debugging via Console links in <2 min.
- Billing team validates parity (within 0.2%) vs. existing offline billing on a 24h reconciliation run for three pilot customers.
- Security review completed for PII handling and pricing cache access; KMS usage documented.

Implementation tasks:
- T1: Telemetry schema update: add canonical token events to OTLP span spec and runtime sidecar (PR: github.com/redwood/runtime/pull/4217).
- T2: Ingest connector: kafka topic onboarding + schema registry (avro) (PR: github.com/redwood/telemetry/pull/238).
- T3: Flink enrichment job: join spans/logs -> canonical request object. Metric counters for lag/backpressure. (draft job at infra/flink/jobs/token_attrib).
- T4: Rollup writer: write both remote_write compatible metrics and append-only events to ClickHouse.
- T5: Sampling store and Console integration: deterministic sampler + link to trace in Console UI (frontend task in Console backlog).
- T6: QA/Load tests and reconciliation runs with billing.

Design trade-offs considered:
- Option A: Do full request reconstruction in streaming (chosen) vs Option B: approximate attribution from Prom counters + heuristics. We chose reconstruction to achieve precise per-request billing and dispute resolution.
- Storage: ClickHouse chosen for append-only audit table due to query speed on large volumes. S3 archival used for raw journal.
- Sampling rate default 0.5% to balance inspectability and storage; made configurable per-tenant.

Security & privacy notes:
- Customer identifiers will be hashed for public tenants in Prom outputs and only the billing pipeline has access to raw customer_id.
- Pricing cache access uses service identity with KMS key; support for customer-managed KMS will require a follow-up.

[Chronometer probes for per-subtoken timing and KV-hit chargeback]
description:
Add lightweight per-subtoken chronometer probes in the serving runtime to attribute latency and cost to individual subtokens and KV cache interactions. Motivation: current request-level and per-sequence metrics mask micro-latency sources (KV cache deserialization, kernel-switch overhead, per-layer token emission) that matter for accurate cost allocation and for automatic routing/caching policies. This ticket covers probe placement, span/metric naming, sampling strategy, downstream aggregation changes, and dashboarding for chargeback and regression detection.

implementation_notes:
Instrument four probe points per emission: pre-kv-lookup, post-kv-hit, start-attention-step, end-token-emit. Each probe records monotonic nanoseconds and minimal metadata (model_variant, avx_level, request_origin, trace_id, token_index).
Use a per-thread ring buffer to append probe events and flush as part of the existing request-batched write to the telemetry pipeline to avoid extra RPCs. Buffer entry size target: <= 64 bytes to keep memory pressure low.
Aggregate probes into aggregated spans at 100ms or when request completes, emitting: token_latency_ns, kv_lookup_ns, kv_hit:boolean, kernel_switch_ns. Export via OTLP batcher to our metrics ingestion gateway with a new metrics schema version v2.
Sampling: default 1% uniformly across requests, 100% on flagged canary routes and internal test harnesses. Support adaptive sampling: increase sample rate when per-route 95th latency regresses > 15%.
Data retention: raw probe events retained for 7d in BigQuery for postmortems; aggregated rollups (per-model, per-route, per-hour) retained in TSDB for 90d.
Backwards compatibility: probes are guarded by runtime feature flag 'chronometer-probes'. When disabled there is zero additional metric emission and codepaths are elided.
Overhead estimates from local microbenchmarks: wall-clock additional latency per emission < 15us median when buffered; CPU usage +0.6% on sample workloads. End-to-end network overhead depends on sample rate; at 1% sample rate expected telemetry egress +1.3%.
Security: recorded token text must never be logged. Probes will include only token_index and token_hash truncated to 64 bits. No user PII will be included.

acceptance_criteria:
Runtime emits chronometer spans when feature flag enabled and remains silent when disabled.
Aggregated per-token latency and kv_hit rates are visible in a new dashboard with per-model and per-route breakdowns.
PromQL and BigQuery queries compute per-token cost attribution within 5% of sampled ground truth for synthetic workloads.
Canary rollout exercised on dedicated pool without detectable SLA regressions (latency p50/p95 within 2% of baseline).
On-call playbook updated with queries to triage token-level regressions.
Design doc and PR reviewed by runtime and observability reviewers and merged.

observability_queries:
PromQL: sum by(model_variant) (rate(token_latency_ns_sum[5m])) / sum by(model_variant) (rate(token_latency_ns_count[5m]))  # per-token avg latency
PromQL: sum by(route) (rate(kv_hit_total[5m])) / sum by(route) (rate(kv_lookup_total[5m]))  # kv cache hit rate by route
BigQuery: SELECT model_variant, route, token_index, AVG(token_latency_ns) as avg_ns FROM telemetry.chronometer_probe_events WHERE _PARTITIONTIME BETWEEN DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 7 DAY) AND CURRENT_DATE() GROUP BY model_variant, route, token_index ORDER BY avg_ns DESC LIMIT 100
Sample SQL for chargeback: SELECT route, SUM(CASE WHEN kv_hit THEN kv_lookup_ns ELSE token_latency_ns END) as reimbursable_ns FROM telemetry.chronometer_rollups WHERE ts BETWEEN TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 1 HOUR) AND CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() GROUP BY route

[Hosted API: implement failure grace-window + customer fast-path to contain retry storms during escalations]
description:
Summary: Multiple customers escalated after observing cascading 5xx/timeouts during transient upstream slowdowns. Symptoms included synchronized client retries, spike in outgoing RPC latency, and frontdoor connection pileup. This ticket implements a short 'grace-window' circuit policy and a per-tenant fast-path guard to reduce retry amplification and preserve capacity for prioritized customer bridges during live escalations.

Context & impact: Over the last month several incident postmortems pointed to short-lived backend slowdowns that generated a wave of client retries. Our existing circuit-breakers tripped too quickly for some flows or too late for others; once tripped, fallbacks triggered heavy routing changes that increased tail latency and produced customer-visible 502/504 errors. Customers in P1 escalations need a temporary 'fast-path' that reduces their effective admission checks and prevents them from being swept up in tenant-wide backoffs while we remediate root causes.

Goals: 1) reduce retry amplification during short upstream slowdowns, 2) provide an on-call-safe escape-hatch to steer specific customer traffic to a prioritized admission lane, 3) increase observability so SREs/SEs can make informed in-incident decisions without code changes.

Proposed approach: Implement a multi-part change: (A) Grace-window circuit-breaker semantics: instead of immediately increasing circuit score on the first N failures, apply a 10s sliding grace window that counts only sustained error rates above threshold before tripping. This permits transient spikes to recover without hard-routing changes. (B) Retry-suppression token: attach a short-lived header (X-RW-Retry-Suppress) for internal gateways to suppress client-side hedged retries when we detect amplification patterns. (C) Customer fast-path flagging: add an admission router flag that temporarily lowers queueing thresholds for flagged tenant IDs and routes them to a small warm pool reserved for escalations. (D) Observability/UI: Console endpoint with per-tenant 'escalation mode' marker and a dashboard panel showing grace-window triggers, suppressed retries, and fast-path occupancy.

Root cause hypothesis: client retry storms + synchronous admission policies amplified transient backend latency into service-wide 5xx waves. Existing mechanisms either over-react (trip too quickly) or under-protect high-priority customers.

Trade-offs considered: 1) Longer grace windows reduce false-positive trips but increase the time before we isolate a legitimately failing backend. We chose a conservative 10s default with per-route tunables. 2) Fast-path reduces latency for flagged customers but increases isolation risk; the pool size is intentionally small and subject to autoscaling guardrails. 3) Retry-suppression requires changes across edge and SDKs; we implement suppression opportunistically at our gateways first and later expose SDK guidance.

Progress updates:
- 2026-02-13: Spike implementation and prototype circuit-window logic completed (Arjun). Local integration tests show reduced trip rate on synthetic jittered error traces.
- 2026-02-15: Design review with SRE and Product (notes attached). Decided to use header-based suppression to avoid client SDK changes in the hot path (SRE signoff: Diego Rivera).
- 2026-02-17: PR #4982 opened for admission-router changes and new grace-window circuit state machine (PR link below).
- 2026-02-19: End-to-end staging run with 3 tenants simulating retry storms. Fast-path prevented two tenants from being impacted while non-flagged tenants experienced isolated degradation. Observability panels validated.
- 2026-02-22: Security review: no encryption or KMS changes needed. Security requested audit logs for any fast-path toggles (added).
- 2026-02-24: Canaries ready for controlled rollout to prod-1 region. Preparing runbook and customer communication templates.

Testing plan: unit tests for circuit logic, integration harness with synthetic client retry driver, staging soak with tenant-weighted load, and dark launch of X-RW-Retry-Suppress header on 1% of traffic. Acceptance criteria below.

Rollout plan: 1) Dark launch grace-window in runtime-1.24 canary with telemetry only. 2) Enable retry-suppression header handling in gateways and log toggles. 3) Enable per-tenant fast-path behind feature flag; reserve pool at 2% capacity initially. 4) Runbook: SREs may toggle fast-path for customer on-call; toggles recorded in audit logs. 5) If any regressions, roll back feature flag and revert admission-router configuration.

Customer comms: Draft saved for customer-bridge teams. Template includes symptom explanation, mitigation steps we performed, and a recommended client SDK update timeline for retry-suppression semantics.

Post-incident actions: update SDK docs with recommended retry jitter/backoff patterns, instrument more granular per-route latency percentiles, and create a retrospective for improving route-level defaults.

acceptance_criteria:
Grace-window circuit prevents at least 70% of transient trips in staged test workload without increasing sustained error exposure
Retry-suppression header propagated and honored by gateway; suppression events appear in logs and dashboard
Console shows per-tenant escalation mode and fast-path pool occupancy; SREs can toggle per-tenant flag via UI
Feature flag rollout tested in prod-1 canary for 48 hours with no elevated 5xx rate attributable to the change
Audit log entries recorded for all fast-path toggles during rollout

decisions:
Use 10s default grace-window with per-route override rather than global 30s window
Implement retry-suppression via internal header first to avoid SDK rollouts during initial mitigation
Reserve small (2-5%) warm pool capacity per-region for fast-path rather than unbounded routing priority
Require audit logging for fast-path toggles before rollout to all regions

notes:
SRE recommended additional tracing tags for correlated retry chains (trace.parent_retry_id)
Product requested we expose a read-only escalation status API for customer success teams
Design and Console teams suggested a simple 'Escalation' badge on the tenant dashboard to avoid runbook navigation during incidents

[SCIM: telemetry-driven user expiry orchestration with safe rollback]
body:
Summary: We need a safe, observable orchestration for SCIM-driven user lifecycle expiration (soft-suspend -> final removal) that uses telemetry signals to gate progress and supports idempotent retries, tenant-scoped rate limiting, and admin-initiated rollbacks. This ticket implements the orchestration layer, metrics/audit events, and an operator UI hook so support can intervene during the grace window.

Background: Multiple customers have reported accidental mass-deprovisions when third-party IdPs return stale group deltas or when SCIM delta jobs are retried aggressively. Existing SCIM workers perform deletions and emit basic audit logs, but we lack a standardized state machine and telemetry gates to safely escalate from soft-suspend to permanent removal.

Goals / Acceptance criteria:
- Implement a three-state user lifecycle: ACTIVE -> SOFT_SUSPENDED (tombstone candidate, reversible) -> PENDING_DELETE (finalization) -> DELETED, with configurable grace window per org.
- All state transitions must emit audit events with trace IDs and user/actor/tenant fields (events: scim.user.suspend.requested, scim.user.suspend.applied, scim.user.delete.requested, scim.user.delete.completed).
- Provisioning orchestration must be idempotent: retries from SCIM webhook or background job should not cause double-deletes or inconsistent group membership.
- Add telemetry gates that prevent promotion from SOFT_SUSPENDED to PENDING_DELETE when: recent failures for tenant > 5% over 1h OR audit-sampled restore rate > 0.5% over 24h OR active rollback flag set by SRE/product.
- Tenant-scoped rate limiting for finalization: at most X final deletions per minute per tenant (configurable), with circuit-breaker that pauses finalization on high error rate and surfaces runbook.
- Integrate with Console: admin-facing list of users in SOFT_SUSPENDED with restore button and timeline.
- End-to-end tests + integration test against Okta/OneLogin sandbox and a fault-injection harness.

Proposed design:
1) Orchestration state machine lives in identity-service: lightweight DynamoDB table (or Postgres table namespace) containing user_id, tenant_id, state, state_version, last_updated_at, tombstone_expires_at, pending_ops (dedup token). To avoid race conditions with concurrent SCIM deltas, include an epoch-based state_version and require compare-and-set updates.
2) When SCIM delta indicates user removal, mark SOFT_SUSPENDED with tombstone_expires_at = now + tenant_grace_period and emit scim.user.suspend.applied audit event. Do not remove group links yet.
3) Background finalizer worker scans SOFT_SUSPENDED records whose tombstone_expires_at <= now and attempts to transition to PENDING_DELETE after evaluating telemetry gates. Telemetry gates implemented as queries against metrics store (Prometheus/Influx) and recent audit logs.
4) Finalizer performs tenant-scoped batching and uses a token bucket to limit deletion throughput. Each deletion is recorded with a unique op_id; deletion idempotency achieved by storing op_id in pending_ops and using idempotent delete endpoints to external identity providers.
5) If finalizer sees high error rate or gate triggered, it will pause for tenant (exponential backoff with jitter) and mark a pause_reason in the orchestration table. Admins can resume or rollback from Console.
6) Rollback path: within the grace window, Console can hit an endpoint to move user from SOFT_SUSPENDED back to ACTIVE. For PENDING_DELETE we allow a short undo window (30 minutes) if the finalization job has not yet processed the external delete step. Once external delete succeeded, we emit scim.user.delete.completed and only a manual account-restore (reprovision) is possible.

Telemetry & auditing:
- Metrics to add: counter scim.user.suspend.count{tenant}, scim.user.finalize.attempts{tenant}, scim.user.finalize.failures{tenant}, scim.user.rollback.count{tenant}, scim.user.restore.count{tenant}.
- Histograms: scim.finalizer.duration (ms).
- Alerts: tenant-specific alert when finalize_failures/attempts > 0.1 over 15m (configurable) and global incident if many tenants show elevated failure rates.
- Audit events must include correlation_id (trace id) and link to the Console action event. Store audit events in the existing audit-log pipeline and ensure retention aligns with compliance policies.

Failure modes & mitigations:
- Duplicate SCIM deltas: use dedup token and state_version CAS to avoid double-applying transition; idempotent calls to external IdP.
- Partial external failures (Okta times out): finalizer marks item PENDING_DELETE with last_error and retries with backoff; expose last_error in Console.
- Large tenant blasts: tenant-scoped throttling and circuit-breaker to prevent noisy-neighbor impact.
- Operator mistakes: soft-suspend grace window and explicit restore action in Console.

Migration & rollout plan:
- Phase 1 (canary): implement state machine and soft-suspend path for 5 pilot tenants (low-risk) and enable verbose logging + feature flag.
- Phase 2: add finalizer job behind feature flag; run as read-only dry-run (simulate finalization) for 2 weeks and collect metrics.
- Phase 3: enable finalization for more tenants with conservative rate limits; open 72h rollback window for first 50 tenants.
- Phase 4: full rollout and deprecation of old immediate-delete path.

Testing strategy:
- Unit tests for state transitions and CAS semantics.
- Integration tests against a mocked Okta SCIM server covering success, 429, 5xx, and network failure.
- Chaos test: interrupt finalize worker mid-batch and verify idempotency and correct resume.
- Manual end-to-end with an Okta sandbox tenant and Console restore flow.

Implementation tasks (high level):
- identity-service: orchestration table, API endpoints for suspend/restore/finalize (Diego).
- finalizer-worker: tenant-scoped batching, telemetry gating, circuit-breaker (SRE pairing with Diego).
- console: admin UI for soft-suspended users and restore button (FRONTEND ticket to be created).
- metrics: Prometheus instrumenters + dashboards (Nikhil).
- docs: runbook + runbook play for high-failure tenant (PM/Support).

Links & artifacts:
- Design doc: https://redwood.atlassian.net/l/cp/SCIM-telemetry-expiry (internal)
- Draft schema PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/identity/pull/412
- Example Console mockups: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/SCIM-Console-Mocks

Open questions:
1) Should tombstone_expires_at be tenant-configurable via Console configs or only via org policy? (PM preference is per-tenant config behind RBAC).
2) Where to persist last_error and pause_reason: orchestration table or separate incidents table? Storing with orchestration row simplifies debugging but increases row size.
3) Do we need per-tenant SLAs for finalization latency? current assumption: best-effort within 24h for normal tenants.

Next steps (short term):
- Implement orchestration schema migration and unit tests (Diego) by 2026-02-28.
- Create finalizer skeleton and metric counters in a feature branch (Diego + SRE) by 2026-03-05.
- Schedule review with Security and Compliance for audit retention and event shape (Ava to schedule).

2026-02-22 - Diego: Implemented initial schema migration in branch feature/scim-expiry-schema. PR #412 opened for review. Basic unit tests added.
2026-02-24 - Nikhil Rao (SRE): Reviewed rate-limiter design, suggested tenant token-bucket per region to avoid global contention. Requested integration metrics for per-region error spikes.
2026-03-01 - PM review by Marta Lopez: Asked to make grace window configurable in Console and add an audit checkbox for orgs that require manual approval before finalization.
2026-03-05 - Security review kickoff: Need to confirm audit retention policy and whether audit events include PII; Security requested a scrubbed field list. Assigned to Ava for follow-up.
2026-03-09 - Diego: Finalizer worker prototype completed in staging and ran in dry-run mode for pilot tenant. Observed 0.4% simulated restore events (within acceptable threshold). Preparing canary toggle.
2026-03-10 - SRE: Added runbook draft: scim-finalizer-pause and manual-restore steps. Will refine after first canary run.

[Graceful dual-region session migration and streaming fallback for hosted gateway]
description:
Problem: Hosted API customers experience intermittent cross-region degradations (network partitions, regional GPU congestion). We need a failover model that preserves session/streaming semantics for in-flight connections (websocket/HTTP streaming) while satisfying tenant SLOs and minimizing token cost and user-visible errors. This ticket defines a pragmatic dual-region migration strategy with transparent traffic shifting, streaming fallback mode, circuit breaker integration, and load-shedding knobs for overload scenarios.

acceptance_criteria:
1) New gateway flows can shift traffic between primary and secondary regions for a tenant without requiring client reconnection for short handovers (<=30s grace window).
2) For streaming sessions, implement a fallback that resumes from last acknowledged token when possible, or gracefully completes with a clear error and metrics when not.
3) Circuit-breaker state machine integrates with per-tenant SLOs and can trigger selective load shedding (non-critical routes first).
4) End-to-end tests (integration + chaos) validate that 99% of requests for targeted tenants meet P99 latency SLOs during a simulated regional flapping event.
5) Dashboards surfaced in Console: per-tenant failover events, stream-resume success rate, circuit-breaker triggers, and dropped-token metrics.
6) Runbook updated with step-by-step rollback and escalation paths.

design_decisions:
- Use a dual-active routing table per tenant: primary region + prioritized fallback list.
- For short-lived streaming sessions (<2 minutes) attempt transparent in-band handover using proxy-level buffered tail packets and token-level checkpointing (kv-cache snapshot).
- For long-running streams, prefer a deterministic graceful shutdown: send STREAM_PAUSE event to client SDK via SSE/frame and mark session migratable; if client reconnects within grace window it attempts resume with session ID and last acked token.
- Circuit breaker is tiered: local per-worker CB (fast failure on overload) + regional CB aggregated by gateway (trips based on sustained error/latency percentiles and queue length).
- Load shedding policy: drop or downgrade low-priority routes (embeddings batch jobs, background reranks) before terminating live chat generation.
- Traffic shifting algorithm: weighted gradual shift with sigmoid ramp over 60s by default, with emergency immediate cut to fallback if safety limits are hit.
- Telemetry contract: all handover attempts emit events with reason, duration, session id, resume result, and fallback model variant used.

implementation_plan:
1) Runtime: implement session checkpoint API (kv-cache snapshot + model position) and make it pluggable to the gateway.
2) Gateway: add per-tenant routing table and shift controller; expose config flags to PM and SRE.
3) Streaming layer: implement STREAM_PAUSE/RESUME wire frames and SDK helpers (js/python) to attempt resume.
4) Circuit breakers: hook runtime latency and token-queue metrics to CB engine; expose thresholds as tenant-configurable.
5) Load shedding: implement priority tags on routes and scheduler-level preemption.
6) Tests: unit + integration + chaos harness against simulated region outage.
7) Docs: Console doc pages and runbook.
Implementation owners: Priya (gateway & routing), Liam Chen (streaming layer & SDK), Sofia Martinez (CB & scheduler), Marco (telemetry & dashboards).
Milestones: a) API + gateway prototype (2 wks), b) streaming resume + SDK (3 wks), c) CB integration + load shedding (2 wks), d) E2E tests and rollout (1 wk).

rollout_plan:
- Phase 1 (canary): enable for internal staging tenants only. Monitor stream-resume success and P99 latency.
- Phase 2 (pilot): enable for 3 low-risk customers with high availability needs; run extended chaos (simulated latency spikes, region partition) for 72h.
- Phase 3 (regional opt-in): allow tenants to opt into automatic failover via Console; default off for customers with active regulatory constraints.
- Phase 4 (global): flip default to on for new tenants after 8 weeks of stable pilot metrics.
Controls: kill-switch per-tenant, region-wide emergency revert with 30s abort window.
Communication: pre-rollout notes to SRE, Support, and Sales; blog post with guidance for customers integrating SDK resume flows.

test_plan:
- Unit tests for checkpoint serialization and resume idempotency.
- Integration: gateway + runtime resume under simulated tail-loss.
- Chaos tests: orchestrate AWS/GCP region-level network blackholes and CPU starvation; verify failover logic within safety thresholds.
- Performance: benchmark mem/CPU overhead with kv-cache snapshots under 10k concurrent streams.
- Regression: ensure no change to non-streaming request latencies (<=5% delta p50/p95).
- Acceptance thresholds: stream-resume success >= 85% for short handovers; overall customer-visible error rate increase <= 0.5% during failover windows.

telemetry:
Required metrics and traces to add:
- gateway.failover.attempts (tags: tenant, from_region, to_region, reason)
- gateway.failover.success_rate (tenant)
- stream.resume.attempts, stream.resume.success, stream.resume.latency
- cb.tripped.count, cb.tripped.duration, cb.scope (worker/region/tenant)
- scheduler.shed.count (route_priority)
- session.kv_snapshot.size, session.kv_snapshot.duration
- trace samples including checkpoint hash and last_ack_token
Dashboards: Failover Overview, Streaming Reliability, Circuit Breaker Heatmap, Load-shedding trends.
Alerts: cb.tripped.rate > 10/min for >5m -> page SRE; stream.resume.success_rate < 60% for >15m -> P1 ops.

risks:
- Resume correctness: some model internals (non-deterministic sampling, stateful decoders) may make exact resume impossible leading to duplicate tokens or incoherence. Mitigation: detect non-resumable models and fall back to explicit reconnect with user-visible error.
- Cost: additional kv snapshots and buffering increase memory and network usage; will need quota and throttles for snapshot frequency.
- Complexity: SDK changes required for best-effort resume may slow adoption; provide server-side graceful fallback.
- Edge-case: long-running streams crossing region boundaries with different model variants may degrade quality; add model-variant compatibility checks before migration.

[Sticky session failover and transparent retry attenuator for hosted API during customer escalations]
description:
Summary:
During an ongoing customer escalation (large tenant migration), we observed correlated 5xx/timeouts originating from a combination of: an edge sticky-session behavior that routed long-lived streaming connections to overloaded serving nodes, a mismatch between SDK retry semantics and server-side idempotency protections, and a mis-configured circuit-breaker threshold that caused rapid circuit cycling and retry amplification. Impact: multiple high-value tenants experienced elevated error rates and client visible timeouts for synchronous generation requests and streaming sessions.

Root cause hypothesis (consolidated):
- Edge sticky routing (designed to reduce cold KV cache misses) kept certain tenant flows pinned to saturated inference lanes.
- When a backend hit transient saturation it returned 502/504; client SDK retries (4x aggressive retries with no jitter) caused immediate retry storms back to the same pinned nodes.
- Circuit-breaker thresholds were too aggressive (short window, low request-count floor) causing circuits to open/close frequently, producing more 5xx and resetting warm caches.
- Dedicated vs Hosted difference: Dedicated pools had stronger isolation but shared control plane settings inherited a global retry recommendation that was too aggressive for hosted multi-tenant edge.

Goal / acceptance criteria:
- Mitigate customer-visible errors within the next 72 hours using safe server-side controls and a targeted SDK patch where required.
- Restore graceful degradation so affected tenants see rate-limited or slower responses rather than 5xx cascades.
- Implement long-term fixes (per-tenant hysteresis for retries, sticky routing softening, and aligned idempotency guard) with telemetry showing 90% reduction in tenant-originated 5xx during similar load profiles.

Immediate mitigation plan (hotpatches):
1) Edge-routing soft failover: introduce a short TTL (30s) for sticky session affinity on streaming lanes and prefer regional replica after first backend error. This reduces likelihood retries hit same saturated host. (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/edge-router/pull/1284)
2) Server-side retry attenuator: add request-level transient-retry quota that declines retry attempts when backend error rate or queue latency exceeds threshold; returns 429 with Retry-After when appropriate to signal client backoff. (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/hosted-api/pull/4310)
3) Circuit hysteresis tuning: widen the sliding window and add minimum-open duration to prevent flapping. Roll this as a feature flag for quick rollback. (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/982)
4) SDK advisory patch: publish a minor SDK release (server-side opt-in header to enable safe-retries) and a guidance note to customers to use idempotency tokens for operations with side effects. (SDK release candidate: github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-js/releases/tag/v0.21.3-rc1)
5) Fast monitoring and alerting: deploy a temporary synthetic workload and Datadog dashboard to compare error rates and tail latency pre/post changes. (Dashboard: https://app.datadoghq.com/dashboard/hosted-api/tenant-escalation-synthetics)

Rollout plan:
- Stage any edge/router changes to 10% of traffic for 30 minutes, monitor for error decrease and CPU/queue impacts.
- Enable server-side retry attenuator in passive mode (log decision only) for 1 hour, then convert to active for affected tenants only.
- Release SDK advisory and coordinate support message to the escalated customers; prepare assisted upgrade where needed.
- If any mitigation increases latency beyond SLO by >15% for >10% of customers, immediately rollback via feature-flag.

Postmortem / follow-ups (medium-term):
- Implement per-tenant retry hysteresis with exponential backoff + jitter and server-side enforcement of idempotency token validation for retryable endpoints.
- Replace hard sticky affinity with cache-aware routing that balances cache-warmth vs load fairness.
- Add unit and integration tests that simulate tenant migration bursts and assert no retry amplification.
- Formalize SDK/server retry semantics in the public docs and add a compatibility matrix for Dedicated vs Hosted defaults.

Notes / constraints:
- We must avoid breaking any existing dedicated-customer guaranteed latency SLAs while adjusting hosted defaults. The feature-flag approach helps staged testing.
- Security review: changes do not add new secrets or key flows. Marked not required for this patch (security_review_required=false).

[Burn-rate-driven progressive throttling and per-tenant escalation policy]
description:
Goal: Define a deterministic, burn-rate-driven policy that automatically applies progressive throttling to tenants when their SLO error budget is consumed, and specify per-tenant escalation paths (notification, quota reduction, support-runbook, and optional manual intervention). Scope includes: metric definitions, three-tier burn-rate bands with concrete actions, API behavior during throttling, rollout gating for the policy, and acceptance criteria for production rollout. Out of scope: pricing changes, billing adjustments, and tenant contract negotiations.

background:
We currently rely on coarse, org-level circuit breakers for capacity problems and manual runbooks triggered by alerts. Recent incidents (Jan 2025 spike in chat workloads) highlighted two gaps: (1) tenants can exhaust their error budgets quickly without automated, proportional protection of the global runtime; (2) engineering response is reactive and inconsistent. A burn-rate driven approach integrates SLO consumption into automated mitigation, reducing blast radius while enabling predictable UX degradations.

acceptance_criteria:
Define burn-rate metric based on rolling 1h and 24h error budget consumption and publish formula (number of missing successful requests weighted by traffic vs allowed budget)
Three bands established: Green (burn-rate < 1.0) - no action; Amber (1.0 <= burn-rate < 4.0) - advisory throttling (per-tenant token rate reduction + warning header); Red (burn-rate >= 4.0) - enforced throttling (hard quota reduction, 429 responses for excess, and escalation to support)
Per-tenant throttling must be configurable by tier (free/startup/enterprise) and support an escape hatch for enterprise accounts (manual override with audit log)
Automated notifications to tenant owners, internal SRE rotation, and an incident channel must be triggered at Amber and Red thresholds with distinct runbook links
Telemetry: dashboards show per-tenant burn-rate, throttle actions, and user-visible error rates; metric names and tags defined for ingestion into observability (e.g., metrics: tenant.slo.burn_rate_1h, tenant.throttle.action)
Rollout gating: feature is behind a runtime-flag and rolled out to 5 pilot tenants, then 20, then 100 with automated SLO/latency guardrails at each stage
No increase in global 99th latency beyond defined regression envelope during pilot (regression envelope defined in rollout playbook)
Runbook and customer communication templates published and reviewed by support/solutions engineering
End-to-end acceptance test that simulates tenant traffic pattern and verifies throttle thresholds, notification, and override behavior

decisions:
Use a burn-rate formula that compares observed error budget burn to expected burn scaled by request volume; maintain both 1h and 24h windows for short and medium-term detection
Throttle implementation will be token-rate based at the API gateway level for immediate enforcement; runtime will apply KV-cache hints to preserve model-state where possible
Tiered configuration: default conservative settings for free tier, lenient for enterprise with manual override logged to audit
Expose throttle signals in response headers (X-Redwood-Throttle: none|advisory|enforced) and a tenant-scoped metric to track actions
Progressive rollout controlled by feature flag and an automated gate that checks global error budget and pilot tenants' local SLOs

acceptance_test_plan:
Create a sandbox tenant and generate synthetic traffic that consumes error budget at controlled rates
Verify burn-rate metric calculation matches expected values for 5m, 1h, 24h windows
Trigger Amber band: confirm advisory header, no hard 429s, internal notification created
Trigger Red band: confirm enforced throttling (token rate drop), 429 responses for excess requests, escalation channel pinged, and enterprise override works with audit log
Run pilot with 5 real tenants for 48 hours and measure global 99th latency and SLO regressions; validate rollback if guardrails breach

[Queue admission gates with plan nudging and graceful deprioritization]
description:
Goal: Implement an admission controller for per-tenant request admission that balances free/paid/enterprise lanes using credit-aware scoring and a soft-deprioritization path. The controller must: 1) allocate a short-lived admission score per request using available credits, plan entitlements, and recent latency/error signals; 2) support graceful deprioritization (soft demotion to cheaper model variants or lower-priority queues) rather than hard rejections for improved UX; 3) expose plan nudging hooks (rate-limited upgrade prompts surfaced in responses or analytics) and instrumentation for conversion experiments; 4) play nicely with region selection and model-variant fallback so we avoid cross-region thrash and uncontrolled spin-ups of expensive pools.

acceptance_criteria:
Admission controller calculates an admission_score (0-100) for each request within 5ms median overhead under production load simulation
Requests with score < 30 are routed to a soft-deprioritized path (cheaper quantized variant or background lane) instead of immediate 429s
Quota deduction and replenishment logic prevents starvation: short bursts allowed using a borrow window and payback policy
Telemetry surfaces per-tenant admission_score distribution, demotion rate, and uplift from plan nudges
A staged rollout behind feature flag that can be toggled per-org and per-region without downtime

design_notes:
Admission scoring inputs: tenant_credits_remaining, rolling_token_consumption(1h), recent_p90_latency(region), SLA_tier_weight, active_model_cost(weighted), emergency_override
Score composition strategy: linear blend with configurable weights and an exponential decay on historical debt to prefer recent behaviour
Soft-demotion options: (A) downgrade to quantized sibling model (same capability band), (B) route to background/predictive lane with lower priority and caching, (C) if model-variant unavailable, route to cross-region low-cost replica if latency budget allows
Plan nudging: attach a compact hint header and track nudges_sent per-org to avoid spam; experiment via console opt-in
Safety: fallback to hard rejection only if admission_score < 5 or request would breach critical safety quotas (billing or legal holds)

implementation_notes:
Admission controller will live in gateway proxy as a lightweight filter to avoid extra RPC hops
Use existing credit ledger (ENG-62345) for authoritative balances; add a cache with TTL 2s for hot tenants
Introduce Borrow Window token bucket: allows 1 extra burst per 10s scaled by plan tier; payback enforced by higher future cost multiplier
Expose feature flags via rollout service and support per-org override for Dedicated customers
New metrics: admission_score_histogram, demotion_count, demotion_reason, nudges_sent, borrow_window_uses

testing_plan:
Unit tests for scoring math and edge cases (negative credits, clock skew)
Load tests with synthetic tenants across tiers to validate controller overhead and demotion rates
Chaos scenarios: region outage to validate cross-region fallback path does not route into expensive pools
Canary rollout to 5% of free-tier orgs and 1% of paid-tier orgs, monitor errors and latency for 48h

rollout_plan:
Feature gated behind 'admission-v2' flag
Phase 1: Internal QA and perf benchmarking in staging
Phase 2: Canary to selected tenants + runbook for immediate disable
Phase 3: Gradual ramp with telemetry thresholds to auto-pause rollout
Phase 4: Open to all tenants and enable plan nudging experiments

risks_and_mitigations:
Risk: mis-calibrated scores cause unexpected demotions and customer complaints -> Mitigation: conservative defaults + telemetry + quick rollback flag
Risk: cross-region fallbacks spike egress or expensive GPUs -> Mitigation: per-region budget caps and cost-aware routing policy
Risk: feature inadvertently bypasses Dedicated isolation -> Mitigation: enforced per-deployment policy check and automated integration test
Risk: upgrade prompts create UX friction -> Mitigation: throttle nudges and A/B test content and placement
