[Adaptive streaming retry dampener and tenant signalization]
description:
Summary: Several enterprise customers reported repeated 5xx spikes and downstream timeouts during long-lived streaming requests (chat + tool-calls) that coincided with background tenant maintenance and autoscaler churn. Root cause appears to be an interaction between our front-door retry policy and per-tenant admission signals: when a streaming RPC stalled briefly, the edge retried the request without signaling the backends, which led to duplicate inflight streams, KV cache churn, and cascading timeouts. This ticket implements an adaptive retry dampener for streaming RPCs plus an explicit tenant-level signal to prevent duplicate inflight streaming attempts while maintenance windows or reshard operations are in progress.

acceptance_criteria:
1) New dampener prevents immediate retry for streaming RPCs for a configurable grace window (default 5s) and reduces duplicate inflight streams by >90% in synthetic replay. 2) Tenant signal header is honored by all runtime pools; when set, front-door routing will fast-fail new streaming attempts to a tenant undergoing maintenance. 3) No regression in short RPC latency (95th/99th percentiles). 4) End-to-end test and canary rollout documented and run on dedicated tenants.

implementation_summary:
- Add 'Stream-Retry-Dampener' middleware in edge gateway that tracks streaming call signatures and enforces a short backoff window before allowing a retry. - Introduce optional header 'X-Tenant-Maintenance' emitted by control plane during reshard/maintenance. - Runtime pools check header and surface a 409-fast-fail when maintenance is active; SDKs will surface structured error to enable client-side retry strategies. - Add e2e integration tests that simulate reshard + high fanout streaming to measure duplicate inflight suppression. - Instrumentation: tracing span and metric 'stream_duplicate_suppressed' and dashboard panel.

risks:
- If dampener window too long, some legitimate retries may be delayed causing client-perceived latency; mitigation: window is configurable by tenant tier. - Header propagation requires small control-plane change; mismatch could cause unexpected fast-fails for some Dedicated deployments. - Potential interactions with SDK idempotency tokens for non-streaming calls; tests required.

rollback_plan:
- Rollback edge middleware toggle (feature flag) to restore previous retry semantics. - If header rollout causes problems, disable control-plane emission of X-Tenant-Maintenance for affected region/tenant while monitoring. - Run quick canary downgrade to previous runtime image if downstream regressions detected.

[Adaptive request shaping and priority eviction for regional dependency resilience]
description:
Owner: ENG infra. Problem: downstream stores (Redis user cache, Kafka event store, primary DB) occasionally cross degradation thresholds during regional spikes or partial outages. Current mitigation (global circuit breakers + blunt shedding) causes tenant unfairness and noisy failovers across regions. This ticket designs and implements an adaptive shaping + priority eviction layer in the connection/adapter layer to provide per-tenant fairness, bounded tail latency, and predictable SLO behavior while enabling fast cross-region fallback to read-only degraded modes.

background:
We have repeated production incidents where a regional network blip or a noisy tenant causes connection pool exhaustion against Redis or DB replicas, sending load to fallback regions and cascading increased latency. Existing global shedding is binary and tends to over-shed low-priority traffic instead of protecting high-priority flows. Engineering needs a hybrid approach: shape ingress to dependencies with per-tenant quotas, prioritized admission lanes, and an eviction policy that prefers cacheable or non-critical work. This must integrate with multi-region routing and the rollout/console observability features.

goals:
Limit P99 latency amplification on downstream stores under partial failure to <= 2x baseline
Maintain throughput for high-priority tenant lanes during regional degradation
Avoid full-service cascades when a single downstream saturates
Provide clear telemetry in Console for troubleshooting and post-incident analysis

non_goals:
Replace existing global circuit-breaker architecture (this augments it)
Re-architect Kafka consumer groups — only adapter-level admission & backpressure

proposed_solution:
Introduce an adapter layer component (shaper) sitting in front of each downstream client (Redis, Kafka producer, DB pool). The shaper implements: (1) hierarchical token-bucket for admission: global pool, region pool, per-tenant logical buckets; (2) lane-based priority queueing (critical | normal | best-effort) with size-limited fast-path; (3) priority-aware eviction for cache/write patterns: prefer dropping best-effort cache-priming writes and background indexing tasks; (4) soft-fallback mode where reads degrade to tombstone/TTL-extended cache reads and DB queries are routed to read-replicas with staleness metadata. The shaper emits metrics (admissions, rejections, waits, evictions) and events to Console and integrates with rollouts to allow canary of different thresholds. Admission thresholds are SLO-driven and auto-tunable via closed-loop feedback from observed token consumption and tail latency.

design_decisions:
Use token-bucket over static quotas to allow short bursts while enforcing long-term fairness
Implement lane prioritization in-memory per adapter to avoid extra RTTs to central services
Eviction policy will be pluggable: default 'least-impact' heuristic (evict best-effort cache writes first), with optional tenant-weight overrides
Soft-fallback decisions made locally with config sync from control plane; no control-plane dependency in the fast path
Expose per-tenant admission metrics with tenant hashed ID (non-PII) to Console for cost and SLA attribution

rollout_plan:
Phase A (canary - 2 weeks): deploy shaper to 1 region on read path only for low-risk tenants; monitor P95/P99 and admission rates
Phase B (limited write shaping): enable write-path shaping for canary tenants and observe application errors/retries; tune eviction heuristics
Phase C (regional ramp): extend to 3 regions with tiered thresholds; enable auto-tune feedback loop in shadow mode

[SLO-aware request admission with per-tenant priority lanes and regional failover]
description:
We need an admission controller for incoming inference requests that enforces SLO-driven capacity decisions at two dimensions: per-tenant priority lanes and region-aware failover. The goal is to avoid cascading failures when Redis/Kafka/DB tails spike, and to provide deterministic behavior for tenants with contracted SLOs. The controller will combine token-bucket admission, a fast-path for high-priority tenants, progressive degradation for best-effort tenants, and integration with our regional routing layer to prefer healthy backends or fallback to compatible model variants. This ticket covers the proposal, design, and a production canary implementation in the serving runtime and API gateway.

acceptance_criteria:
1) Admission controller enforces per-tenant rate/tokens with 95th-percentile latency target mapping to admission thresholds
2) High-priority lane (reserved tokens) guarantees minimal queueing for P0/P1 tenants under typical load up to committed capacity
3) Best-effort lane is subject to probabilistic shedding when downstream tail latency exceeds configured quantiles and error budget is depleted
4) Regional failover triggers within 150ms for RPCs routed through the routing layer and falls back to secondary region or degraded response per policy
5) Circuit-breaker trips on sustained 5xx or 99th-percentile latency breaches and traffic is rerouted to warm fallback or model variant; trips are visible in console and triggered automatically by SLO watcher
6) Observability: dashboards with per-tenant admission rate, dropped percentage, latency quantiles, error budget burn rate, and per-region health are available in Console; alerts for >1% shed rate for customers with SLA
7) Canary rollout plan executed with no customer-facing errors and rollback path validated

tasks:
Design: finalize token-bucket parameters and mapping from tenant SLOs to reserved tokens (Asha + Priya)
Runtime: implement admission filter hook in request pipeline and token accounting (Miguel + Ethan)
Routing: add region probe and failover policy in smart router (Lena)
Circuit breaker: implement adaptive burn-window and integration with admission decisions (SRE team)
Metrics: emit per-tenant admission_allowed, admission_denied, shed_reason, token_balance metrics (Telemetry)
Documentation: update runbook and Console docs with shed semantics and SLA notes
Canary: deploy to staging group of 5 customers, observe for 72h, then gradual ramp

decisions:
Use hybrid admission: reserved tokens for committed tenants + shared token pool for burst tolerance
Probabilistic shedding is preferred over blunt reject for best-effort tenants to preserve degraded success cases
Circuit-breaker uses 5min adaptive window with increased sensitivity when error budget < 20%
Regional failover will prefer warm cache replicas before spinning new capacity to keep latency bounds
We will surface 'partial' responses with a standardized header (X-Redwood-Degraded: reason) for degraded cases rather than opaque errors

notes:
Trade-offs: reserving tokens isolates tenants but increases unused capacity; sharing pool improves utilization but needs fairness heuristics
Edge cases: startup storms when many tenants reconnect after region outage — added jitter and token warm-up needed
Compatibility: admission plugin must be pluggable so Dedicated/Private deployments can opt for local policy enforcement
Telemetry cardinality: per-tenant metrics can blow up; we'll roll up to tenant tiers and sample top-K tenants by usage for detailed traces

[Cross-tenant retry amplification investigation and per-tenant adaptive admission control]
description:
Summary:
A recurring spike of 5xx errors and long tail timeouts was reported by multiple customers over the last 48 hours. Initial traces point to cross-tenant retry amplification originating at the edge admission layer: when a subset of tenants hit sustained slowdowns (KV cache misses + CPU-bound kernel path), upstream clients aggressively retried which amplified load and caused downstream queues to saturate. This produced a feedback loop: timeouts -> retries -> queue growth -> more timeouts.

Hypothesis:
- Edge/frontdoor is not enforcing per-tenant inflight limits; bursty tenants can monopolize router threads and downstream execution slots.
- KV cache compaction/eviction during surges is causing expensive cold-path model initializations which increase p95 latency for other tenants sharing the same pool.
- SDK/client retries are too aggressive in the absence of explicit 429/Retry-After signaling and are amplifying transient failures.

Investigation performed so far:
- Correlated tenant-level traces with queue-depth metrics and kernel CPU heatmaps. Observed clear alignment between tenant bursting and server queue growth across multiple AZs.
- Reproduced a scaled-down scenario in staging by replaying recorded production traffic for 3 tenants; confirmed that one noisy tenant can cause >3x p95 increase for co-located tenants.
- Verified no global circuit-breaker was tripping; circuit thresholds are global not per-tenant.

Short-term mitigations (hotfixes):
1) Deploy edge-side short-term admission controller patch (edge-proxy) to apply a conservative per-tenant inflight cap (default 50 concurrent requests) and early-fastfail when reached. This reduces queue churn and gives slow tenants informative 429 responses.
2) Adjust SDK guidance and temporary rate-limiting rules to reduce client retry aggressiveness (increase backoff window + random jitter).
3) Turn on targeted KV cache prefetching for highest-traffic tenants to soften cold-starts in the next 24h window.

Planned long-term fixes:
- Implement adaptive per-tenant admission control in the edge router with token-bucket shaping that adapts to observed p95 latency and retry rate per tenant. The controller will scale quota up/down on a 60s cadence and expose metrics for audits.
- Add tenant-scoped circuit-breakers and a graceful degradation path that prefers lower-cost cache-backed model variants when latency budgets are tight.
- Make retry guidance explicit by returning Retry-After and structured error codes when admission drops are intentional. Coordinate SDK releases to honor Retry-After headers.
- Improve KV cache eviction policy to be workload-aware (favor hot prefixes for stable tenants) and expose cache occupancy by tenant to the console.

Rollout plan:
- Feature-flag the admission control behind a rollout flag.
- Canary: enable for 5 non-critical tenants with high traffic (selected by SEs) for 12 hours. Monitor: per-tenant RPS, p50/p95/p99 latency, 5xx rate, queue depth, retry rate, and customer-visible errors.
- If metrics show regressions, rollback to previous admission thresholds and iterate. Full rollout expected over two weeks after canary if stable.

Testing and validation:
- Unit tests for token-bucket and admission logic.
- Staging replay with >1M requests/hour to verify queue behavior under burst patterns.
- Chaos tests: randomly delay backend response to validate early-fastfail semantics and ensure no client-side deadlocks.

Observability additions required:
- Tenant-level queue-depth and inflight counters on the edge router.
- New SLO dashboard tile showing tenant-top contributors to p95 latency and retry amplification index.
- Alerting: page when a single tenant accounts for >30% of total queue depth for >5 minutes.

Post-incident follow-ups (owners assigned):
- Run a root-cause postmortem (owner: Marco Ruiz) and update runbook to include admission controls and SDK retry guidance.
- Product to review quota defaults and communicate available controls to customers (owner: Linh Nguyen).
- Research/Applied ML to explore cache eviction improvements and prioritized prefix retention (owner: Priya Mehta).

Notes for customer communication:
- Provide transparent explanation: we observed amplified retries causing transient overload; we implemented admission limits and will roll out adaptive shaping to prevent recurrence.
- Offer remediation: temporarily migrate at-risk customers to dedicated pools or increase their reserved capacity while we finish rollout.

Impact: unexpected charge resulted in a negative provisional balance and a customer request for immediate credit and correction. Customer provided invoice PDF and list of deactivated keys for audit.

impact:
Customer-facing invoice shows a non-zero legacy probe surcharge; affects customer's month-end reconciliation and triggers negative provisional balance on an account with dedicated commitment. Customer has paused autopay pending resolution.

Our billing pipeline finalized invoice for period 2026-02-01 to 2026-02-28 on 2026-03-01
Invoice line includes 'legacy probe surcharge - prorated' for hours within the period after key deactivation

[Unapplied provisional credits after cross-currency reconciliation delay caused negative provisional balance]
description:
Issue summary: AtlasInsights reports a negative provisional credit balance on their March invoice preview. Provisional credits that normally apply after hourly postbacks were not applied for a ~3 hour window on 2026-03-09 due to a delayed cross-currency reconciliation job. The reconciliation job runs after postback aggregation to convert usage from customer currency (EUR) to billing currency (USD) and to calculate provisional credits.

Impact: Customer-facing invoice preview shows a -$1,240 provisional balance that is blocking autopay and their finance team from approving the finalized invoice. This has caused a billing hold and manual intervention request from their billing team. No production requests were affected; this is a metering/invoicing discrepancy only.

Environment: prod account for AtlasInsights (org id: atlas-2741), eu-west region. Affected time window: 2026-03-09 02:00 - 05:15 UTC. Affected services: postback-reconciler, billing-reconciler, currency-conversion pipelines.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Query usage postbacks for org atlas-2741 for 2026-03-09 01:30-06:00 UTC in postback DB.
2) Run the local billing-reconciler conversion step with the same postbacks but force the currency conversion step to be skipped (simulate delayed fx-run).
3) Generate provisional credit allocation and preview invoice; observe provisional credits missing for the 02:00-05:15 window leading to a negative provisional balance.
4) Re-run reconciliation with FX rates applied and provisional credits are produced, balance returns to expected positive allocation.

logs:
2026-03-09T05:16:12Z postback-reconciler ERROR: fx-conversion job timeout after 300s; retry scheduled (job id: fx-20260309-281)
2026-03-09T05:20:03Z billing-reconciler WARN: partial-aggregation detected: 9 postback batches missing currency tag eur->usd (agg window 02:00-03:00) (run id: br-790)
2026-03-09T05:45:47Z postback-reconciler INFO: delayed-fx-run completed, 100% of outstanding batches converted (job id: fx-20260309-281-complete)
2026-03-09T06:00:01Z invoice-generator INFO: provisional-credits applied for run br-790-postfix, but the provisional credit application step missed mapping to invoice preview snapshot id: preview-20260309-06-00

investigation_notes:
Initial triage by CS (Maya): validated negative provisional balance on customer invoice preview and collected invoice preview id and sample postbacks.
SRE (Liam): found a delayed fx-conversion job due to transient downstream exchange-rate API timeouts between 05:00-05:15 UTC; reconciler retried and completed at 05:45 UTC.
Hypothesis: delay caused the invoicing pipeline to snapshot preview before provisional credits were merged; a race between invoice preview snapshotting and late-arriving credit allocation (ordering bug in preview snapshotter).
Reproducer: locally re-running reconciler with the same late batches reproduces missing provisional-credit-to-preview mapping (missing preview-merge event).
Risk: If invoice preview snapshots are finalized before reconciliation completes, autopay blocks can occur for enterprise customers during FX or reconciliation delays.

resolution_notes:
Workaround applied (2026-03-11): retriggered invoice preview merge for AtlasInsights with corrected provisional credits; finance confirmed the preview now shows a +$4,560 provisional credit and autopay is no longer blocked.
Code fix (backlog): patch to invoice-generator to retry preview snapshot merge when late credit batches arrive (PR filed: github.com/redwood-inference/invoice-generator/pull/77).
Operational fix (deployed 2026-03-12): postback-reconciler now tags incomplete previews and delays final snapshot for up to 30 minutes if FX job has not completed; rollout verified in eu-west staging then prod.
Follow-up: Add monitoring alert for fx-conversion job latency > 2m (owner: billing team). Owner assigned: Liam O'Connor.

[Decision Breadcrumbs: Chained Routing Context and Per-Hop Metrics for Fallback Explainability]
description:
Summary: Add a compact, human- and machine-readable 'decision breadcrumb' record that captures chained routing context for each inference request. Breadcrumbs should include per-hop timing, policy scores, region/tier decisions, model-variant mappings, and fallback triggers so engineers can reconstruct exactly why a request was routed the way it was and what fallback sequence executed. This ticket scopes the telemetry schema, sampling/retention policy, console integration, and a lightweight ingest path for high-throughput hosted traffic.

Why: Current traces and per-hop metrics exist but are fragmented across services and lack a single artifact that represents the routing chain with normalized fields (scores, reasons, tenant constraints, candidate variants). That makes debugging fallback behavior and root-causing SLO regressions slow, especially when requests cross regions or downgrade model variants for cost/latency. Breadcrumbs will improve incident MTTR, make regression alerts actionable, and enable post-hoc quality analysis for fallback sequences.

Non-goals: This ticket does not implement full request-level payload capture, long-term cold storage of every breadcrumb, or heavy-weight causal analysis pipelines. Those can be follow-ups once core schema and console UI are validated.

acceptance_criteria:
Every routed request includes a decision_breadcrumb ID in existing request traces in staging (sampled) and production (sampling rate configurable).
Breadcrumb record contains canonical fields: decision_id, timestamp, route_hops (ordered list as compact string), per_hop_latency_ms, selected_model_variant, selection_policy, policy_scores (normalized), fallback_reason, region, tier, capacity_tier, and trace_link.
Console shows a per-request breadcrumb panel that visualizes the hop chain and highlights fallback hop with reason and latency.
Alerting rule exists to surface increased fallback frequency or long breadcrumb chain durations across a rolling 5m window for a customer with high SLO risk.
Storage respects PII and tenant isolation: breadcrumbs do not include prompt/response content unless redaction/opt-in is enabled via tenant config.
Sampling and retention controls are configurable with defaults that limit cost for free-tier customers.

implementation_notes:
High-level approach: 1) Define compact breadcrumb schema (string-safe, CSV-friendly for event streams). 2) Inject breadcrumb span/field from routing service at decision points; each hop appends a compact token describing node_id|policy|score|chosen_variant|latency_ms; hops concatenated in order. 3) Emit a final breadcrumb event to telemetry pipeline with decision_id and summary fields; include link to full trace/span ids. 4) Add sampling knobs in routing config (percent, deterministic by tenant hash) and retention tiering upstream. 5) Console: lightweight renderer that expands tokens into human labels and maps chosen_variant IDs to model names via catalog lookup.

Schema (textual representation): decision_id (uuid string), root_ts (ISO8601), hops_token (pipe-separated hop tokens), hops_token example = "node42|region-us-east1|policy-latency|score=0.92|variant=redwood-7b-q|lat=8", fallback_reason (enum: capacity, error, cost_policy, region_unavailable, preempt), selected_variant (string), total_path_ms (int), sampled_trace_id (string), tenant_id (string), redaction_flag (bool). Keep fields flat and short to minimize storage.

Storage/ingest considerations: use the existing telemetry kinesis stream with a new compressed topic for breadcrumbs. Explore protobuf vs compact CSV string; start with compact CSV-in-JSON for rapid rollout. Provide configuration to disable breadcrumbs per-tenant. Privacy: never include prompt text by default.

Rollout plan: 1) Feature branch + unit tests (routing service) 2) Staging deploy with 1% deterministic sampling for selected tenants 3) Console UX behind feature flag and enable to internal prod tenants 4) Ramp sampling and default retention settings 5) Document in runbook and update escalation guides.

comments:
2026-03-05 - Aisha Martinez: Created ticket and initial schema draft. Requested feedback from telemetry and console teams.
2026-03-06 - Rajiv Patel (telemetry): Prefer binary protobuf schema for compactness; concerned about transformation cost in current pipeline. Suggested proof-of-concept with small sample size first.
2026-03-07 - Priya Sengupta (console): UX mockups attached to design doc; recommends adding a condensed latency waterfall and highlighting the hop that triggered fallback.
2026-03-09 - Liam O'Connor: Implementation plan updated to start with compact CSV-in-JSON to reduce infra changes. Added sampling knobs and tenant opt-out.
2026-03-11 - Security review (notes): Ensure breadcrumbs do not contain raw tokens/keys. Must include KMS-protected metadata for tenant-sensitive flags. Security review required flag added.
2026-03-12 - Liam O'Connor: Pushed initial router instrumentation branch; opened PR and linked below. Starting staging rollout (1% sampling) by end of week.

[Console: Rebaseline 'Insight Lenses' MVP — trim telemetry and emphasize actionability]
description:
This ticket captures a scoped-down MVP for the Console insights surface (dashboards + tracing + per-route cost breakdown) focused on surfacing high-actionability signals while reducing telemetry and compute cost. The prior scope attempted to ship a broad set of cards and deep trace exploration; we will cut non-actionable visuals, remove per-token heatmaps, and defer sampling-based tracing to a later iteration. The goal is a minimal, testable surface that meets latency and cost targets while giving product teams clear next steps to remediate regressions.

background:
During alpha reviews we discovered two key problems: 1) too many low-signal cards created noise and lengthened load times, and 2) the initial trace sampling approach required high storage and frontend complexity. Finance flagged potential cost overruns if we shipped full per-token traces and dense telemetry retention. PM and Eng agreed to prioritize actionability: top-line route-level cost deltas, a single aggregated trace preview for failing routes, and a compact set of dashboard cards tied to concrete runbooks.

decision_log:
2025-03-12: Cut per-token heatmap and latency flamegraphs from MVP; retain single aggregated flame preview.
2025-03-13: Endorse 'Actionability Score' as primary sorting metric for insight cards.
2025-03-15: Defer heavy-weight trace sampling (full traces at 100% capture) to post-MVP; implement deterministic sampling + sparse KV cache pointers for preview.
2025-03-18: Lock acceptance criteria and performance SLA for dashboard load under 1.5s for 95th percentile on typical org with <= 500 routes.

scope_in:
Compact dashboard view: 6 high-priority cards (route cost delta, error rate delta, median latency delta, top 5 error messages, active routes by traffic, cost per 1k tokens)
Actionability Score: computed from cost delta, error delta, and recent rollouts; used to sort cards
Per-route cost breakdown: summary table + links to cost explorer (no deep token-level breakdown)
Tracing: aggregated trace preview for top 3 failing routes with single-click link to start full-capture workflow
Rollout guard UI: flag routes with rollout-related regressions and provide quick rollback/redeploy checklist
Acceptance tests and synthetic traffic harness for performance verification
Console telemetry gating: sample rate controls and aggregated retention defaults to minimize cost

scope_out:
Per-token cost heatmaps and dense token-level visualizations
Full trace capture and long-term storage for all routes
Custom dashboard card builder for initial MVP (deferred to phase 2)
Advanced correlation panels (correlate external metrics or APM spans)
Per-tenant deep-cost attribution breakdowns beyond route-level summaries
Real-time streaming of trace spans into the UI (deferred)

acceptance_criteria:
Dashboard load time: median < 700ms and p95 < 1.5s for orgs with <= 500 routes under standard test harness
Actionability: at least 4 of the 6 cards include a documented remediation step or runbook link
Cost delta accuracy: per-route cost delta within ±7% compared to batched billing export over a 24h window
Tracing preview: aggregated trace preview for failing route renders within 1s and links to full-capture workflow
Sampling controls: org-level sample rate can be set to 0.5%, 1%, 5% via console and observed in telemetry within 5 minutes
E2E smoke tests: synthetic traffic triggers insights and acceptance tests pass in CI with no flaky failures > 5%
Security: no new secrets displayed in console and access respects existing RBAC roles
Cost guard: estimated incremental monthly telemetry cost for MVP < $5k for median customer profile

metrics:
Primary: % of flagged insights that lead to an explicit user action within 7 days (target >= 18%)
Performance: dashboard p95 load time target < 1.5s
Cost: incremental telemetry cost vs baseline (target < $5k/month median)
Reliability: tracing preview error rate < 1%
Adoption: number of orgs that enable the insights surface in first 30 days (target >= 25% of early adopters)

rollout_plan:
Staged rollout: 1) internal dogfood across Platform and Core infra teams for 2 weeks; 2) opt-in beta for 10 pilot customers (selected by CS) for 2 weeks; 3) gradual enable 10% -> 50% -> 100% across orgs with monitoring thresholds for cost and error to pause rollout. Each stage includes post-stage retro and a go/no-go checklist for performance and cost impact.

dependencies:
ENG-40211: telemetry sampling API (blocking for sampling UI)
ENG-41602: dashboard card server-side aggregation endpoints
DES-2210: compact card visual design and action affordances
PM-82412: cost-export schema stabilization (for delta calculations)
Security: RBAC review and minor console privileges update

risks:
Underestimating cost of trace previews if previews trigger backend replays; mitigation: rate-limit previews and cache lightweight summaries
Actionability Score may bias toward noisy but low-impact routes; mitigation: manually tune weights and run calibration against historical incidents
Performance regressions for large orgs (> 1k routes) — MVP targets are scoped to <= 500 routes; mitigation: add graceful degradation and placeholder cards for larger orgs
User confusion if deep features are missing; mitigation: clear messaging in UI about 'MVP surface' and links to request features

notes:
Preference is for server-side aggregation over heavy client rendering to keep frontend CPU low. Design suggested progressive disclosure: show compact card then expand to preview. Finance requested telemetry cost simulation during beta; schedule integration with billing reports. Keep full-capture trace workflow gated behind customer opt-in and extra data retention agreement.

[Define rollout plan: feature gate integration + per-model allowlist/denylist + staged region rollout + rollback workflow (kernel auto-selection v2)]
description:
Rollout mechanics for kernel auto-selection v2: wire selector enablement into control-plane feature gates, add per-model allowlist/denylist controls (incl. hot reload), define staged region rollout steps for Hosted (then Dedicated pools), and specify a rollback workflow that oncall can execute quickly during tail-latency spikes or correctness concerns.

Primary goals:
- Safe, reversible rollout (fast kill switch; scoped to region/model/GPU where needed).
- Deterministic gate evaluation (same inputs => same decision) and auditable configuration changes.
- Clear ownership/authority during canary windows (who flips gates, who approves rollback).

Non-goals:
- Implementing the selector itself (tracked in ENG-4822/4823 + PRs).
- Dashboard buildout (tracked separately, but rollout must depend on dashboards being usable).

rollout_plan:
Proposed staged rollout (Hosted -> Dedicated -> Private):

1) Pre-canary prerequisites (before any traffic):
- Gate exists in control plane: kernel_selection_v2_enabled.
- Runtime supports evaluating gate + loading allow/deny lists.
- Telemetry emitted for selection decision + gate reason (sampling ok).
- Perf-canary scenario coverage exists for target SKUs and long-context buckets.
- Rollback tested in a staging region with synthetic load.

2) Hosted canary (region staged):
- Stage A: us-east-1, 1% traffic for allowlisted models only.
- Stage B: us-east-1, 10% traffic for allowlisted models; monitor p95/p99 + error rate + selection distribution.
- Stage C: us-east-1, 50% traffic; add 1 additional region (eu-west-1) at 1%.
- Stage D: 100% of allowlisted models across initial regions.
- Expansion: add remaining regions progressively (1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100%), one region at a time.

3) Dedicated pools:
- Opt-in pilot with 1–2 internal/low-risk Dedicated pools first (known GPU SKUs, stable drivers).
- Customer opt-in by pool: default OFF; allow customers to request enablement via support/onboarding.
- For Dedicated: require explicit model allowlist per pool (avoid surprises with pinned models / special kernels).

4) Private deployments:
- Default OFF.
- Enablement via documented flag + allowlist file; require customer acknowledgement of rollback workflow.
- Provide “force v1” and “force kernel” escape hatches (documented in runbook).

Rollback philosophy:
- Prefer the smallest blast-radius rollback first: disable v2 for a specific (model, gpu_sku, region) combination; fall back to v1 selection.
- If widespread, flip regional kill switch (v2 off for region).
- If systemic, global disable in control-plane + runtime config reload confirmation.

Canary success criteria (minimum):
- No correctness regressions detected by conformance suite.
- p95 latency: no regression > 2% for allowlisted models overall; p99 latency: no regression > 3% (or per SRE guardrail).
- Error rate: no increase > 0.05% absolute attributable to selector changes.
- Selection distribution stable (no unexplained swings in chosen kernels for a given (model, gpu_sku, seq_bucket)).

gate_and_policy_design:
Gate design + evaluation order (deterministic):

Inputs available at request-time:
- model_id (resolved to pinned version where applicable)
- model_family (e.g., llama, mistral, qwen, gemma)
- gpu_sku (normalized: A100-80GB, H100-SXM, L40S, etc.)
- region
- seq_bucket (short/medium/long; prefill/decode regime signal)
- driver/cuda version (if available; otherwise inferred from runtime build tags)

Decision order (first match wins):
1) Hard safety blocks (global): driver/cuda denylist => force v1.
2) Explicit per-model denylist (optionally keyed by gpu_sku and/or region) => force v1.
3) Explicit per-model allowlist (optionally keyed by gpu_sku and/or region) => eligible for v2.
4) Region gate percentage rollout (for eligible set) => v2 for sampled traffic.
5) Default: v1.

Policy constraints:
- Determinism: gate sampling must be stable (e.g., hash(model_id + request_id) with a fixed seed) and documented.
- Auditability: any allow/deny change must be written to control-plane audit logs (who/when/what).
- Hot reload: runtime should pick up policy changes without restart (bounded propagation time target: <5 minutes).

rollback_workflow_definition:
Rollback workflow (operational):

Who can trigger rollback:
- Primary rollback authority during canary: Release Engineering (Connor O’Brien) + SRE oncall (Sean Gallagher / Allison Grant) in consultation with Runtime lead (Hiro Tanaka / Yuki Sato).
- If paging event: SRE can execute emergency rollback immediately and notify Runtime + Release.

How to rollback (in order):
1) Scoped disable: add (model_id, region, gpu_sku) entry to v2 denylist and hot reload.
2) Region kill switch: set kernel_selection_v2_enabled=false for region.
3) Global kill switch: set kernel_selection_v2_enabled=false globally.

Validation steps post-rollback:
- Confirm config propagation (control plane reports effective policy version in each region).
- Confirm telemetry: selection_v2_enabled drops to ~0 for affected slice.
- Confirm latency recovery: p95/p99 returns to baseline within 10–15 minutes (depending on traffic volume).
- Capture incident notes: attach selection traces + exact policy diff applied.

Escalation path:
- If rollback does not recover tail latency, proceed to kernel pinning for the affected model(s) (runtime debug flag / config override) and open incident with Runtime Kernels + Scheduling.

acceptance_criteria:
Control-plane feature gate exists for kernel selection v2 and supports region-scoped percentage rollout.
Per-model allowlist/denylist semantics defined, implemented, and documented (including optional gpu_sku and region scoping).
Gate evaluation order is deterministic and recorded in design notes (including sampling approach).
Runtime supports hot reload of policy changes with bounded propagation time; effective policy version exposed in logs/metrics.
Rollback workflow is written, reviewed by SRE + Release Eng, and validated in a staging environment.
Canary plan includes clear success metrics, rollback triggers, and named owners for gate flips and rollback decisions.

comments:
2026-01-10 (Talia Benson): Kicking off ENG-4826. Need a single source of truth for: (a) who flips the gate, (b) how we scope rollout by model, and (c) rollback blast radius controls. Please propose deterministic evaluation order; SRE asked specifically for replayability in incident reviews.
2026-01-14 (Ethan Park): Control-plane can support: global boolean, per-region boolean, per-region percentage rollout (stable hash), and policy bundles with versioning + audit logs. Need exact matching keys for model_id and gpu_sku normalization so we don’t create cardinality bugs / mismatches.
2026-01-17 (Benji Okafor): Draft decision order: hard safety blocks -> denylist -> allowlist -> percentage rollout -> default off. This keeps us safe when we learn new bad combos mid-canary. Will rely on stable sampling via hash(model_id + request_id).
2026-01-21 (Jordan Lee): Determinism note: request_id is not guaranteed stable across retries depending on client. Prefer hash(model_id + trace_id) if present; otherwise fall back to request_id. Also ensure the same input tuple generates the same decision in replay tests.
2026-01-29 (Aisha Bello): Add explicit rollback triggers tied to p99 and error rate. Suggest: rollback if p99 regression > 5% for 10 min in a slice OR if error rate increases >0.1% absolute. Also: require dashboard panels to be live before Stage B (10%).
2026-02-03 (Connor O’Brien): For runtime-1.21 release train, we need a canary window with named gate operator + back-up. Please include ‘who flips the gate’ and ‘who can override’ in the ticket before we move to In Review.
2026-02-07 (Omar El-Sayed): During early testing we saw long-context tail spikes when seq_bucket misclassifies. [Introduce trace-gatekeeper microburst smoothing to cut tracer overhead and improve tail fidelity]
description:
Background: Tracing hotpath cost has increased with growing QPS and high-cardinality requests. Existing sampling approaches either add too much allocation/CPU on the hot path or lose tail signal needed for incident RCA. Goal: introduce a lightweight "trace-gatekeeper" layer that makes a single, tiny hot-path decision (pass/hold/drop) using microburst-aware smoothing heuristics and a tiny in-memory sketch. Complement this with an asynchronous tail rehydration pipeline that reconstructs high-value traces for post-hoc analysis without increasing steady-state hotpath overhead. Success criteria: 1) Reduce per-request tracer allocations and CPU on hotpath by >= 30% for top-tier services. 2) Maintain or improve tail-event reconstruction recall for top-10 latency clusters (target >= 90% relative recall after rehydration). 3) No customer-visible latency regressions; error budget impact < 1% of baseline.

technical_approach:
1) Trace-gatekeeper inline shim: tiny fixed-size ring sketch + exponential decay window that tracks recent trace score and microburst rate. Decision is a single cache-friendly integer read/update; no heap allocations. 2) Microburst smoothing: use burst-aware thresholding to avoid over-sampling short spikes while preserving sustained slow requests. 3) Hold buffer: small per-shard in-memory fixed ring to hold minimal metadata references (no full span copies). 4) Async tail rehydration: held metadata is used by a background worker to request full spans from the long-form buffer/collector and rehydrate exemplars into S3/Historical store for later queries. 5) Telemetry: add new metrics for gate decisions (pass/hold/drop), hold-buffer occupancy, rehydration success/failure and latency, and estimated downstream recall. 6) Rollout: Canary on internal non-customer inference service, then staged rollout by QPS tier with kill-switch tied to occupancy SLOs.

tradeoffs_and_risks:
Tradeoffs: the gatekeeper errs on conservative holds to preserve tail fidelity which may slightly increase background IO. Risks: poorly tuned decay/window parameters can either under-sample tails or overload rehydration workers. Mitigations: safe defaults from PoC, circuit-breaker on rehydration throughput, and goal-based autoscale for background workers. Privacy: held metadata must avoid PII; design stores opaque tokens only. Security review: not required for initial PoC (security_review_required: false) but will be flagged if holding changes to include request payloads.

rollout_plan:
1) PoC on canary service for 2 weeks (metrics collection): measure hotpath CPU, allocation, and gate decision distribution. 2) Tighten thresholds and add telemetry dashboards. 3) Week-long canary on internal customer-facing route. 4) Gradual rollout to low-impact external services (10% -> 50% -> 100%). 5) Post-rollout: keep rehydration monitor and automated throttles for 2 months. Rollback path: feature flag to disable gatekeeper per-service; emergency kill-switch in control plane.

metrics_to_monitor:
tracer.allocs_per_request, tracer.cpu_nanos_per_request, gate.decision.{pass,hold,drop}.rate, gate.hold_buffer.occupancy, rehydration.requests_per_minute, rehydration.success_rate, tail.recall_estimate, infra.rehydration_queue_latency

[Hopwise decision reasoning with causal-tags for fallback attribution]
description:
Problem: Current routing observability captures which model or region was selected for a request but often lacks a causal trail that explains *why* a fallback model or non-preferred region was chosen. This impedes debugging when requests hit fallbacks that degrade latency or quality.

Goal: Produce per-hop, human- and machine-readable reasoning breadcrumbs (causal-tags) attached to routing decision events so we can: 1) explain fallback choices, 2) correlate SLO regressions to specific decision predicates, and 3) build rollup metrics that attribute latency/cost/quality changes to decision logic rather than downstream infra alone.

acceptance_criteria:
1) Routing decision event emitted for each hop contains a compact causal-tag list (predicate ids, evaluated values, priority score, and policy-version).
2) Fallback events include a top-2 contributing predicates and an estimated SLO impact delta field (ms and cost cents).
3) End-to-end trace can reconstruct hop order and join causal-tags to per-hop micrometrics (p50/p95 token latency, token count).
4) New aggregated dashboards show attribution by predicate and policy-version and can be filtered by customer tier/region/model-variant.
5) Instrumentation must add <5% p99 overhead on routing path in our staging traffic profile.

design_decisions:
Emit causal-tags as a compressed comma-separated token in the routing envelope to avoid schema churn in telemetry pipelines.
Represent predicates by stable short ids (4-8 chars) with a lookup table stored in config-service and versioned per policy rollout.
Attach an estimated SLO delta computed by the router heuristics (heuristic model trained offline) rather than attempting exact downstream simulation in-path.
Sampling: full causal-tags for 0.5% of requests, header-only indicators for 10% of requests, and aggregated counters for all requests to control cost.
Fallback attribution captures both decision-layer causes and immediate resource-availability signals (e.g., capacity-tier-fill, region-constraint) to separate policy-based and capacity-based fallbacks.

[Heterogeneous-bandwidth-aware allreduce fanout with KV-shard coalescing and comm/compute overlap]
description:
Motivation: on mixed-cluster deployments we observed long tail latency and suboptimal throughput for tensor-parallel allreduce when nodes have heterogeneous NVLink/intra-node bandwidths or asymmetric cross-node links. Smaller microbatches and low-latency applications (streaming chat) disproportionately hit these tails.

This PR introduces a bandwidth-aware fanout planner and a KV-shard coalescing pass that together reduce cross-node stalls and improve overlap between communication and compute. It also adds a narrow-copy optimized kernel for strided small-chunk merges and a runtime hook that maps comm streams to physical links based on a link-rate profile discovered at startup.

What changed (high level):
- Fanout planner: builds a minimal spanning fanout for allreduce that avoids slow links and increases per-hop concurrency when it detects bandwidth heterogeneity. The planner prefers intra-node NVLink-RDMA pairs, then high-rate cross-node links, and uses low-rate links only as fallback.
- KV-shard coalescer: groups adjacent KV cache shards into aligned coalesced writes to reduce the number of small allgathers. This reduces per-step launch overhead and amortizes DMA for common prefix cache hits.
- Stride-optimized memcpy kernel: a small, vectorized kernel for <4KB strided copies used by the coalescer; reduces memcpy time by up to 3x in microbenchmarks.
- Stream mapper: startup probe collects link bandwidths (via existing topo_probe) and creates stream->link mappings to route collective streams away from congested links.
- Scheduler tweak: a light-weight scheduling hint that encourages launching compute kernels on the stream that finished the local reduce, improving KV reuse and overlap.

Benchmarks: (multi-node, 8xA100-80GB, TP-4)
- Throughput: +18% median for 512-token workloads with batch size 8; +11% median for batch size 2.
- P99 latency: reduced by 24% for streaming microbatch workloads (<=2 microbatches).
- Small allgather count: reduced by 38% for a realistic prefix-caching trace.
- Overhead: startup probe adds ~45ms to init time on first run; negligible once cached.

Compatibility and safety:
- The fanout planner is opt-in via config flag "runtime.bandwidth_fanout.enabled" (default: true for Dedicated and Private, false for Hosted until canary completes).
- Fallbacks: if topology probe fails or detects homogeneous links, planner falls back to existing balanced tree.
- Unit and integration tests added; new runtime flag is gated behind a feature flag at rollout.

- [x] Unit tests for planner and coalescer
- [x] E2E smoke on CI
- [x] Docs: added runtime flags and rollout notes
- [x] Bench dashboard entry (Linear ENG-4281)

Related: ENG-4219 (heterogeneous link investigation), ENG-4281 (bench dashboard and canary plan).

Notes: this is intentionally conservative in memory use for the coalescer (max 1.5x temporary buffer). We plan a follow-up to expose a memory/perf knob and to extend the stream mapper to NVSwitch-aware topologies.

[opportunistic-collective-coalescer-and-kernel-resynthesis-for-tp-hotpaths]
description:
Context / Motivation: Tensor-parallel inference workloads spend a non-trivial fraction of wall time in many small collectives (alltoall/allreduce) and short-lived kernel launches when sequence lengths and micro-batch packing vary. This PR adds an opportunistic collective coalescer that merges closely-timed small collectives into a consolidated launch when safe, plus a lightweight kernel resynthesis component that generates tuned microkernels for the hot small-sequence paths at runtime. The goal is to reduce NCCL/kernel launch overhead and improve overlap between comm and compute, without changing existing APIs or requiring offline compile steps.\n\nWhat this PR changes (single-string summary): Implement runtime/collectives/coalescer that buffers and coalesces eligible collectives within a configurable window; add runtime/compiler/kernel_resynth which JITs small fused kernels specialized for common (seq_len, hidden) tuples; adjust scheduler to prefer compute-forward stream ordering and to annotate coalesced collectives for KV-cache-friendly ordering; add perf harness, unit/integration tests, and docs.\n\nKey design points: - Opportunistic coalescing window is adaptive: starts at 100us and grows/shrinks based on observed inter-collective gaps and overall SLO headroom. - Safety: coalescer observes token-level dependency metadata; it will not merge collectives across operations that would change correctness (e.g., KV cache writes or model-ordered reductions). - Kernel resynthesis is bounded: compiled kernels are small, cached per-(device,seq_len,hidden) triplet, and evicted by LRU to avoid memory bloat. The resynth path falls back to precompiled kernels on memory pressure or when JIT fails. - Scheduler changes include a heuristic to launch compute-heavy projection kernels on the compute stream immediately and delay non-critical launches until NCCL progress is in flight, improving overlap.\n\nPerformance: Microbenchmark numbers (internal perf-lab, TP-8, A100s, sequence distribution from real prod traces): - End-to-end throughput up to +26% for chat-like workloads with many short sequences (median +18%). - P95 latency reduction on small prompts: ~12–18% depending on batching. - NCCL launch/latency tail reduced by ~30% as measured by collectives/s and avg latency per collective. - KV-cache hit path unchanged; some small improvement (~4%) due to reordered coalesced launches avoiding redundant KV buffer syncs.\n\nCommits (high-level): - Implement coalescer: runtime/collectives/coalescer.cpp/.h, +tests/perf/bench_collective_coalescer.py - Add kernel resynth module: runtime/compiler/kernel_resynth.cpp/.h, +runtime/compiler/Makefile tweaks - Scheduler integration: serving/scheduler/stream_optimizer.cpp - Tests: tests/unit/collective_coalescer_test.cc, tests/integration/tp_end2end_coalesce.sh - Docs: docs/perf/collective_coalescer.md - CI: ci/perf-lab.yml additions + a small windows to disable resynth in GPU-less CI\n\nFiles changed (high-level): - runtime/collectives/coalescer.cpp/h - runtime/compiler/kernel_resynth.cpp/h - serving/scheduler/stream_optimizer.cpp - tests/unit/collective_coalescer_test.cc - tests/perf/bench_collective_coalescer.py - docs/perf/collective_coalescer.md - ci/perf-lab.yml\n\nCompatibility and safety notes: - No API/ABI changes. - Coalescer disabled by default in release builds; opt-in via REDWOOD_COALESCE=1 or per-deployment config in console. - Kernel resynthesis requires a writable tempfs on device; when unavailable the path is a no-op and the runtime uses fallback kernels. - Added extensive unit tests to exercise correctness across heterogenous GPU topologies; we also ran a canary suite on Dedicated clusters (TP-2/TP-8) before merge.\n\nReview conversation (abridged): \n- Ethan Zhao (reviewer): "Nice direction. Two correctness asks: 1) ensure we never reorder collectives that cross KV cache write boundaries; 2) add a deterministic seed for the coalescer's adaptive backoff so tests are stable."\n- Sofia (author): "Addressed both: coalescer tags ops with KV write flags and we added COALESCE_TEST_SEED env var for deterministic behavior in tests. Updated tests accordingly."\n- Priya Nair (reviewer): "Kernel resynth looks promising but we should bound JIT memory. Please add eviction metrics and a hard cap. Also add a guard that disables resynth on preemptible instances."\n- Sofia: "Added eviction metrics (collective_resynth_evictions) and RESYNTH_MAX_CACHE_MB config. Also added a cheap instance-type check to disable on preemptible/spot instances in the resynth manager."\n- Lucas Reinhardt (reviewer): "CI failed on first run due to flaky timing in bench harness. Reran perf CI and added a 2s stabilization sleep in bench harness to reduce flakiness. LGTM after CI pass."\n\nCI summary: - Static checks: passed - Unit tests: passed (collective_coalescer_test, kernel_resynth unit) - Integration: perf-lab required two reruns; first run showed a transient timing flake in bench_collective_coalescer; second run green. - Merge gating: all checks green at merge time.\n\nPost-merge notes and follow-ups: - Created follow-up ENG tasks to: 1) expose per-tenant coalescer tuning in Console (ENG-4902), 2) explore combining coalescer with adaptive batching heuristics (ENG-4916), 3) add TPU-simulated sanity checks (ENG-4920). - Performance dashboards added to Console: new metric group "collective_coalescer" (collectives_coalesced, avg_coalesce_window_us, resynth_invocations).\n\nWhy this is different from previous work: earlier PRs focused on static NCCL tuning, stream prioritization, or KV prefetch heuristics. This change introduces an adaptive, correctness-aware consolidation layer plus an on-host microkernel JIT that together attack the high-overhead case of many small collectives + short kernels. The approach is intentionally opportunistic (runtime opt-in) to reduce blast radius and provide a safe migration path.\n\nNotes for on-call / SRE: - The coalescer can be disabled via REDWOOD_COALESCE=0. - Watch metrics: collective_coalescer.coalesced_rate, resynth_errors, resynth_evictions. - In the unlikely case of deadlock symptoms, set REDWOOD_COALESCE=0 and restart serving workers; safe fallback to precompiled kernels is automatic.\n\nMerge: Squash and merge after final approvals.\n\nEnd of PR description.

Introduce opportunistic collective coalescer and a small-kernel resynthesis path that reduces per-collective overheads on TP workloads; measurable throughput and latency improvements for multi-GPU inference.

[Bandwidth-fair communication splitting and NCCL stream coalescing to reduce tail latency in tensor-parallel serving]
description:
Motivation: In multi-GPU tensor-parallel serving we observed p99 spikes caused by uneven per-slice transfer times and excessive per-op stream overhead on small collectives. This PR implements a bandwidth-fair splitting strategy for large allreduce/allgather payloads plus an NCCL stream coalescer to reduce kernel/launch overhead. Goals: (1) reduce tail latency and jitter for TP workloads without sacrificing throughput, (2) improve overlap of comm/compute by giving the scheduler richer progress hooks, (3) keep changes compatible with existing rollout and comm topologies. Design summary: Introduces a BandwidthFairSplitter that divides a collective payload into shards proportional to measured link-bandwidth and recent throughput per-peer instead of equal fixed chunks. Each shard is mapped to a dedicated NCCL communicator where beneficial; the mapping is adaptive and bounded so we never create more than 4 communicators per tensor by default. To reduce stream proliferation we add a StreamCoalescer that groups small NCCL ops onto a small pool of cuda streams and merges adjacent launches when they share execution properties. The scheduler receives progress callbacks from both splitter and coalescer and provides a lightweight priority token to prefer outstanding comm shards that are blocking compute. KV cache interaction: added a prefetch-aware sync point so that cross-node KV fetch work is placed before low-priority shards to avoid head-of-line stalls when cache misses coincide with large collectives. Continuous batching: micro-batch slicing allows earlier dispatch of high-priority shards while the rest of the batch aggregates, enabling additional overlap. Backwards compatibility: new behavior is opt-in via runtime config flags (tp.bandwidth_fair_split=true, tp.stream_coalesce=true) with safe defaults matching previous behavior. Testing & results: microbench run on 8xA100 (DGX-style), TP=8 and TP=16 across 70B and 8B models. Results: median latency -12% to -18%, p95 -14% to -21%, p99 reduced up to 25% on noisy hosts; end-to-end throughput improved 5-9% on mixed 8B/70B workloads. Perf tests run in perf-canary and benchmark-lab; canary ID: perf/2026-02-22/tp-split-01. Risks & mitigations: communicator creation can add overhead; we cap communicator churn and reuse communicators per-tenant. Coalescing may hide per-op failures so we added stronger error propagation hooks and CI integration. Rollout plan: staged feature flag rollout per-customer, enable in perf canary, then 10% prod, monitor p99 and token backlog metrics. Checklist: [x] design doc updated, [x] unit tests, [x] integration tests in perf lab, [x] canary run, [x] migration safe defaults. Related: ENG-1374 implements telemetry hooks used by the splitter.

[hierarchical-lane-scheduler: opportunistic comm/compute interleaving with soft-priority NCCL lanes]
release_notes:
Introduces a hierarchical NCCL lane scheduler and opportunistic comm/compute interleaving. Default-off behind runtime flag; improves TP throughput and p99 latency in heterogeneous-batch workloads. See ENG-1987 for rollout plan.

description:
Motivation: tensor-parallel workloads experience stalls when collectives and kernel launches contend for GPU resources and when KV cache prefetches interfere with in-flight NCCL streams. This PR implements a hierarchical lane scheduler that classifies NCCL lanes into soft-priority groups and uses opportunistic kernel launch windows to interleave communication and compute while preserving correctness. The goal is to reduce comm-induced stalls, improve kernel packing for small microbatches, and prioritize KV-cache prefetches that unblock the critical path. Summary of changes: 1) scheduler: hierarchical_lane_scheduler module that creates lane classes (control/high/low) and maintains per-peer credit accounting and vacancy windows; 2) nccl: soft-priority lane construction with graceful demotion/promotion heuristics and lane affinity hints on collective enqueue; 3) kvcache: prioritized prefetch queue integration so hot-shard prefetches use high-priority lanes and do not starve reduce/allgather operations; 4) batching: continuous-batcher boundary awareness so the scheduler respects microbatch commit windows and coalesces kernel launches when safe; 5) telemetry: new metrics (tp.lane.waits, tp.lane.promotions, tp.kv.prefetch_blocked) and corresponding console panels for debugging. Design notes: the lane scheduler uses a lightweight token/credit model and a small state machine per-lane to avoid global locks. Promotion is heuristic-driven (time-in-limbo, backlog, peer-progress) and conservative to avoid starvation. All new behavior is gated behind runtime config flags --runtime.experimental.hierarchical_lanes and --runtime.experimental.kv_lane_priority and is off by default in production clusters. Benchmarks: on a mix of 8xA100 TP tests (seq_len=2048, batch=2 microbatching=8) we observed +18% sustained throughput for throughput-bound prompts, 12% reduction in p99 tail latency on short-response workloads, and ~6% reduction in token GPU time cost on mixed workloads. Safety and fallbacks: if NCCL returns transient errors or lane contention exceeds thresholds, the scheduler demotes lanes to round-robin mode and records diagnostic traces for post-mortem. Rollout: staged canary on Dedicated regions for 2 weeks behind feature flag, monitor tp.lane.* metrics and rollback on regression. Implementation detail highlights: - We do not change NCCL kernels; changes are orchestration and enqueue-time hints. - KV cache prefetch now provides an affinity hint so the runtime routes it through high-priority async lanes. - Continuous batcher cooperates with the scheduler by emitting a small token when a microbatch boundary is safe to coalesce. The description below includes commits, diffs, review thread, and CI history for context.

[Credit-based ring pacer and async NCCL progress + KV-cache sharding for TP runtime]
description:
Motivation: TP inference workloads with imbalanced micro-batches frequently hit transient NCCL stalls and KV-cache thrashing when multiple tensor slices contend for allreduce bandwidth. This PR introduces a credit-based ring pacer that smooths outgoing collective launches, an asynchronous NCCL progress helper to reduce kernel blocking in user threads, and a lightweight KV-cache sharding layer to reduce lock contention for hot prefixes. Scope: runtime/tp scheduler and comm stack, small API surface for ops to observe credits, and tests/benchmarks. Changes include a new credit allocator, pacing hooks in the TP dispatcher, an async-progress thread with cooperative polling, and a KV cache shard map with per-shard mutexing and eviction heuristics. Checklist: - Add credit pacer and integrate into TP dispatcher - Implement async NCCL progress and graceful shutdown - Introduce KV-cache sharding and eviction policy tuned for short sequences - Add microbench harness and end-to-end regression test for 8xA100 TP scenarios - Ensure CI and perf traces show regression-free latency and improved p99 throughput Results summary: internal perf runs on 8xA100 reduced end-to-end token p99 by ~18% on a mixed short/long prompt workload and reduced collective queuing stalls visible in tracing. KV-cache hit rates increased on hot-prefix traces by ~12% and per-prefix lock contention is eliminated in the common case. Backwards compatibility: no API changes for customers; runtime knobs exposed via config flags (credit_initial, shard_count, async_progress=true). Rollout plan: staged canary on Dedicated pools; opt-in by default for new Dedicated clusters, off by default for older clusters until nightly perf validation completes. Notes on stability: async progress thread has a conservative polling backoff; integrated with existing shutdown flow to avoid leaks. Referenced issues/threads: Linear ENG-9241 describes production incidents where mixed sequence workloads regressed after recent batching changes; SUP-4482 is the support ticket requesting relief for a customer on Dedicated.

[SAML assertion ordering + session stitching causes transient admin privilege or unexpected permission denial]
description:
Summary: Several customers reported either 'permission denied' errors for users who should have access or, conversely, brief elevated privileges after SSO events. Root cause appears to be an ordering edge in the SAML attribute processing + session stitching flow used by RBAC v2 when multiple identity providers (IdPs) and transient session attributes are present.

What happens today: when a login or assertion arrives we merge assertion attributes into an existing session. The merge path does not consistently apply deny-over-allow precedence and can retain stale transient roles from a prior session if the new assertion arrives with a subset of attributes. In some traces the audit log only records the successful assertion, not the state removed during merge, making post-incident analysis hard.

Why this is bad: customers intermittently receive denied API responses for actions they routinely perform, causing escalations. In other cases elevated privileges linger for short windows, which fails our least-privilege guarantees and is a compliance risk.

Scope: Reproduced on hosted and dedicated (internal prod-like) environments. Affects SAML and some SSO providers that send overlapping group and role assertions and when session TTLs allow stitched merges. Not related to the RBAC policy language itself, but how session attribute precedence and audit writes occur during assertion processing.

repro_steps:
1) Create two distinct IdP assertions for a single user: one with admin-like transient role, another later without that role but with overlapping group attrs. 2) Log in via IdP1 (admin role) and perform actions to confirm admin access. 3) Before session TTL expires, trigger a login via IdP2. 4) Observe session merge: in broken path the old transient role can persist or the new assertion can suppress an allow incorrectly. 5) Capture /api/v1/session and /api/v1/audit logs for the times around both assertions.

acceptance_criteria:
1) Session merge follows deterministic ordering: explicit denies take precedence over allows; transient roles from previous sessions are cleared unless reasserted. 2) Audit logs contain a before/after snapshot for any session attribute changes caused by an assertion merge. 3) Regression tests cover multi-IdP merge ordering and prevent reintroduction. 4) Fix deployed to staging and validated by SE on two customer escalations reproductions. 5) No increase in request latency for assertion processing beyond 5ms median.

implementation_notes:
- Normalize attribute canonicalization early (lowercase keys, canonical group IDs).
- Add a merge strategy that computes resulting role set by: base_roles + explicit_assertion_adds - explicit_assertion_removes, then apply deny-first resolution using policy engine.
- Persist an audit row showing 'session_pre_merge_attrs' and 'session_post_merge_attrs' (JSON string) with reason 'saml-merge' and reference to assertion id.
- Update session store cleanup hook to remove transient roles with source != current_assertion_id.
- Add instrumentation to measure assertion-merge time and capture examples that change effective privileges.
- Coordinate with infra to allow a short feature flag rollout for the safer merge logic.

migration_plan:
Migration is lightweight: new merge logic is backward compatible. For long-lived sessions we will run a one-off pass in staging that scans sessions for conflicting transient roles and emits normalization audit events. A migration script (safe-run) will be added to ops playbook to expire affected sessions for customers with confirmed incidents. Document the script and provide step-by-step rollback in the PR.

qa_plan:
- Unit tests for merge strategy and deny-first resolution.
- Integration tests simulating two IdPs with overlapping attributes.
- End-to-end tests in staging using recorded SAML assertions from customer escalations.
- SE verification checklist to confirm audit entries include pre/post snapshots and assertion IDs.
- Load test to ensure added audit writing at merge path does not degrade latency beyond SLO.

[Investigate and fix RBAC v2 SSO role-mapping race -> permission-denied / over-permissioned audit gaps]
description:
Summary: After RBAC v2 and SSO/SAML group-to-role mapping shipped to a subset of customers, we have two customer escalations that appear to be caused by the same root race condition: (A) users intermittently receive 'permission denied' for actions their mapped role should allow; (B) other customers see a rare over-permission where a transient mapping grants extra admin capabilities. Both cases also show incomplete audit trail entries (missing principal or mapping context) which prevents post-incident forensic analysis.

Background: RBAC v2 introduced a role cache keyed by user_id with an async refresh triggered on login / assertion. SSO/SAML group mappings update the role cache via a listener that applies deltas. We discovered that simultaneous assertion processing + a concurrent mapping-change can result in the request being evaluated against a stale or partially-applied role set. Additionally, our audit pipeline anonymizes some PII for Private deployments; the anonymization step runs before mapping context is attached, causing blank principal/mapping fields in a subset of logs.

Impact: Two paying customers escalated (one fintech tenant, one healthcare tenant) due to either blocked workflows or unintended data access. Customer impact severity: high for the fintech tenant (blocked production flows), medium for healthcare (investigation/mitigation required). We must address correctness and restore trust in audit completeness.

Repro steps (intermittent):
1) Configure SAML group 'eng-admins' -> role 'org:admin' with mapping updates enabled.
2) Simulate concurrent: A) SAML assertion login for user U; B) Mapping delta event that adds/removes group membership for U at the same time (use test harness to send both within ~50ms).
3) Observe token evaluation: sometimes the request handler reads role cache before listener completes -> permission denied. Other times the listener applies an overlapping merge that produces an extra wildcard grant -> over-permission.
4) Check audit log for the request: in affected cases principal_id or mapping_snapshot fields are empty.

Proposed fix (primary):
- Make mapping update and role cache refresh atomic per-principal. Implement per-user update locks (optimistic CAS with versioned role documents) in the role-store so assertion processing either sees pre-change or post-change consistent state, not a mix.
- Attach mapping_snapshot (group->role hash) to the auth evaluation context before any anonymization step; ensure anonymizer preserves mapping_snapshot separately.
- Add a short-lived in-memory dedupe window for mapping deltas to avoid thrash when many events arrive near-simultaneously.

Audit and recovery plan: 
- Add a migration job that recomputes role-cache for affected orgs (api endpoint /admin/roles/recompute) and mark completed on tenant.
- Backfill missing audit entries where possible by reprocessing raw auth traces and adding mapping_snapshot (best-effort). Log backfill results and notify customers.

Testing plan:
- Unit tests for optimistic CAS and versioned role docs.
- Integration tests that simulate concurrent SAML assertion + mapping delta at varying latencies (0ms, 10ms, 50ms, 200ms).
- End-to-end test against Private deployment image to verify anonymization order doesn't drop mapping_snapshot.
- Chaos test on staging with scaled concurrent mapping changes.

Rollout plan:
1) Patch runtime (role-store + listener) in canary cluster; run regression + chaos tests.
2) Deploy to hosted - opt-in customers first (notify CS).
3) Coordinate with Private/Dedicated release owners for patch versions.
4) After 48h monitoring, progressively release to remaining customers.

Observability:
- Add a new metric rbac.mapping_concurrent_conflicts and a trace tag rbac.mapping_version_on_eval.
- Create dashboard card showing rate of auth_evals with empty mapping_snapshot.

PRs and artifacts: 
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/8342 - "role-store: versioned role docs + CAS apply"
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/8361 - "saml-listener: attach mapping_snapshot before anonymizer"
- Integration test harness: github.com/redwood-inference/tests/pull/211
- Incident notes (customer-facing): drive.redwood.ai/esc-2025-11-rbac-sso-01 (private, CS owns distribution)

Acceptance criteria: 
- Auth regression tests pass (no flakes in simulated concurrent scenarios).
- No new customer reports for 7 days post-rollout.
- Audit logs consistently contain mapping_snapshot for >99.9% of auth events in canary.

Follow-ups: 
- Evaluate replacing per-user locks with a lock-free merge algorithm in Q1 2026 (research spike).
- Add documentation on SAML mapping eventual consistency guarantees for Support and Customer Success teams.

Notes: This ticket is P0 due to active customer escalations. Coordinate with CS (Emma Torres) and legal for tenants in regulated industries.

[Customer escalation: SSO group sync led to permission-denied and over-permission edge cases]
description:
Summary:
A high-severity customer escalation with AcmePayments surfaced two distinct RBAC v2 failures after a recent SSO/SAML group sync: 1) users who should have inherited admin-level grants were evaluated as permission-denied (permission denied regression), and 2) in a different sync scenario group memberships were temporarily evaluated as effective-admin for several minutes (over-permission window).

Context and impact:
- Customer: AcmePayments (enterprise Dedicated tenant).
- Timeline: first reported 2026-03-01; reproducible across orgs with certain SAML group claim structures and group-dep mapping.
- User-visible issues: inability to access admin console pages, and in one reported case audit logs showed elevated operations executed by non-admin principals during a sync window.
- Business impact: blocked customer workflows, one escalated incident to account execs, potential compliance risk due to transient over-permission.

Root cause analysis (summary):
1) Permission evaluation race: RBAC v2 permission evaluator runs a two-stage evaluation (group-mapping -> effective-role resolution -> cache write). Under heavy SAML sync load, a batched sync path applied group mapping changes but the effective-role cache eviction and recomputation were asynchronous; some requests hit the pre-update cache and were denied.
2) Over-permission gap: an optimization in the SSO/SAML sync merges membership diffs and applied a short-lived additive grant path before the authoritative replace path finished; combined with an optimistic cache update this allowed a transient state where inherited admin privileges were visible to request paths that check different caches (session vs. real-time).
3) Audit logging omission: batched audit flush optimization suppressed granular grant/deny records when both events happened within the same batch window, causing gaps in the chronological trail for forensic purposes.
4) Mapping precedence bug: a misordered precedence rule in SAML group claim mapping caused groups from multiple IdP mappings to be merged in the wrong priority order, enabling two different grant rules to apply in conflict scenarios.

Scope of work (proposed fixes):
- Fix A: Make SAML group claim mapping deterministic and stable across syncs by enforcing explicit precedence and adding a stable sort on group identifiers before apply. (ENG)
- Fix B: Change permission evaluation to compute effective-role in-place under the sync lock or use a short-lived strong-consistency window: any request during an active sync will either use pre-sync snapshot or block briefly until recompute finishes. This removes the race that caused permission-denied and over-permission windows. (ENG + infra)
- Fix C: Audit logging: stop merging grant/deny audit events within the same batch; instead emit a compressed but ordered event bundle that preserves chronology and actor. Add telemetry to detect missing audit sequences. (ENG + Security)
- Fix D: Migration script: detect and repair inconsistent effective-role cache entries in Dedicated tenants that were exposed by the bug. Run with customer opt-in and provide rollback. (ENG + SRE)
- Fix E: UI/Console change: add an "Effective permissions" inspector for admin pages and a visible warning banner when a tenant is undergoing a SAML sync that may temporarily affect permissions. (Product/Design)

Testing and verification:
- Unit tests for precedence ordering in SAML mapping and for the evaluator lock behavior.
- Integration tests: simulated SAML sync with interleaved reads/writes to reproduce race; verify no transient over-permission and no false denies.
- Load test: simulate 200 org-wide syncs/minute in staging and observe cache consistency and audit emission.
- Canary rollout: staged rollout to 10% of Dedicated hosts, monitor errors/latency, audit gaps, and customer edge cases.

Rollout plan and timeline:
- Patch PRs open now: r/PR-3152 (mapping deterministic), r/PR-3153 (evaluator lock), r/PR-3154 (audit change). Target ship: console-2026.03 (2026-03-20 mainship), backport to runtime-1.19 for active Dedicated clusters if verified.
- Migration window: schedule per-customer migration scripts; communicate via SRE runbook and account teams.

Mitigation for customers while fix is in progress:
- Temporary mitigation for affected tenants: toggle to "sync in replace mode" instead of diff-apply in IdP connector (low-risk but increases sync CPU).
- Support mitigation: advise customers to suspend large group mass-updates during our patch window.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- Strong consistency vs. throughput: holding a short sync lock adds latency for requests during sync — acceptable for Dedicated/Private but should be configurable for Hosted tenants.
- Audit verbosity vs. S3/log retention costs: ordered bundles increase event count slightly; need cost approval from Finance for higher ingestion.
- Whether to auto-run migration across Dedicated tenants or require explicit opt-in.

Next steps (immediate):
1) Merge deterministic mapping PR and cut canary for mapping only (ETA 2026-03-10).
2) Complete evaluator-lock PR and coordinate with infra to allocate canary hosts (ETA 2026-03-14).
3) Run migration job on a single affected tenant in staging and verify.
4) Prepare customer comms and SRE runbook.

- Repro doc (Confluence): https://confluence.redwood.ai/rbac-v2/saml-sync-repro-2026
- Support ticket: SPT-1894 (AcmePayments escalation)
- GitHub PRs: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/3152, /pull/3153, /pull/3154
- Staging dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/abcd/saml-sync-loads
