[SSO assertion precedence causes transient admin shadowing for linked identities]
description:
Summary: A customer escalated that users who authenticate via SSO (SAML) and have multiple linked identities can briefly obtain admin-level privileges after SSO re-auth even though their effective local role should be viewer/editor. This is an RBAC v2 precedence/merge edge case plus an audit-logging omission that makes it hard to trace.

How to reproduce (internal steps):
1) Have a test org with two linked identities for a single account: a local user identity with role=viewer and a SAML identity that asserts role=admin in the SAML attribute.
2) Log in via the SAML identity, then sign out.
3) Trigger a background sync/refresh (session refresh via token exchange) or a second SSO login from the other identity.
4) Observe user surface showing admin access (can access org settings) for ~10-30s before background reconciliation corrects the role.

Observed behavior:
- The UI and enforcement gates briefly allow admin actions.
- Audit logs record a role change event but omit the assertion source and prior_role fields, so forced rollback and root cause analysis were difficult for the customer.
- Secondary effects: console rollout controls used by some customers briefly executed canary rollouts against the wrong user set.

Root cause analysis (summary):
- RBAC v2 merge logic (IdentityRoleResolver) applies assertion-derived role by iterating identities and setting the account role to the last non-null asserted role instead of computing the highest privilege across all identities. Essentially: role = role || asserted_role (last-wins) instead of role = max(role, asserted_role) by precedence.
- When a SAML assertion includes an "admin" group, the code path that writes the transient role update uses an in-memory merge and emits an audit event without attaching the identity_source or raw_assertion fields due to an early short-circuit.
- A separate background reconciliation job (reconcile-roles-worker) corrects the effective role back to the canonical value shortly after, but the window allows authorization checks to pass.

Why this is customer-impacting:
- High-risk privileged access window for sensitive orgs (finance/healthcare customers reported escalations).
- Lack of detailed audit trail prevents security teams from proving whether access was intentional or an error.

Proposed fix:
1) Change IdentityRoleResolver.mergePrecedence to compute effective_role = highestPrivilege(all asserted roles + local role) with deterministic tie-break rules (admin > maintainer > editor > viewer).
2) Ensure every role-change audit event includes: prior_role, asserted_role, identity_source (local | saml | oidc), idp_entity_id, and a redacted idp_raw_assertion pointer (S3 key) for forensic debugging.
3) Add unit tests covering multiple linked identity permutations and an integration test that simulates SAML assertion arrival + reconcile job timing.
4) Add a short-lived feature flag rbac_v2_safe_merge (default off in production) to allow controlled rollout + ability to rollback quickly.
5) Backfill job: detect accounts that have admin tag but whose canonical mapping should not be admin, and place them into a remediation queue (notify customer admins rather than auto-demote).
6) Datadog monitors & alerting: create monitors for spikes in transient role-change events and for audit events missing identity_source.

Deployment plan:
- PR opens -> internal staging (greenhouse) -> canary (10% orgs) for 48 hours -> expand to 50% -> full rollout.
- Add automated smoke tests that execute a simulated SAML response and then run an auth check immediately and after 1 minute.
- Rollback: flip rbac_v2_safe_merge off. Audit event schema change is additive; consumers will tolerate new fields.

Open questions/risks:
- Audit storage cost if we attach idp_raw_assertion pointers at scale. Consider sampling or TTL-based retention.
- Edge case: offline reconcile job timing variance across regions. Need region-aware canary.
- Customer expectations around remediation: do we auto-demote incorrectly elevated users or notify only? Legal/compliance wants notification first.

Related artifacts: PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/redwood-inference/pull/12189
Design doc: https://docs.redwood.ai/confluence/rbac-v2-precedence-cleanup (internal)
Runbook draft: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1RBAC-Runbooks (internal link)
Datadog query snippets in comments below.

Acceptance criteria:
- No transient admin access observed in integration canary tests for simulated multi-identity flows.
- Audit logs include prior_role and identity_source on every role-change event.
- Backfill job finds and surfaces affected accounts to customer admins for approval.
- Code + tests merged and deployed to canary with monitors in alerting state.

[SAML account linking creates transient duplicate principals leading to role bloat and inconsistent deny checks]
description:
Summary: Several customer escalations reported two related symptoms after a recent SSO/SAML attribute sync change: (1) users saw intermittent "permission denied" errors even though they were members of an admin group; (2) in other cases, accounts accumulated extra permissions (role bloat) when SAML-linked identities created transient duplicate principals during rapid provisioning/sync. Root cause appears to be a race between SAML assertion-based linking and the background group-sync job plus ambiguous provenance of role grants in the RBAC v2 model. The system currently merges roles on link without recording source provenance and applies allow-rules before deny precedence resolution in some enforcement paths. We need a fix that prevents over-permissioning, makes audit trails explicit for link/unlink and role merges, and reconciles deny/allow evaluation order across sync paths.

acceptance_criteria:
SAML-based link flow produces a single canonical principal per external identity in >99.99% of test runs (no duplicates in 10k synthetic link attempts)
Background sync and on-assertion linking are serialized or idempotent such that role merges include provenance tags and can be reversed safely
Authorization checks evaluate explicit denies with precedence across all enforcement paths (assertion-time, cached token time, background sync) and no customer can gain an admin role without an audit event recorded
Audit log schema contains event types: saml.link, saml.unlink, rbac.role_grant (with provenance and correlation_id), and saml.sync.conflict and is searchable in Kibana/dashboard
E2E tests covering fast parallel SAML assertions and group-sync demonstrate no permission-denied regressions and no role-bloat in 99.999 percentile of runs

proposed_solution:
1) Canonicalization: compute canonical_principal_id from SAML NameID + tenant-id at assertion handler entry. Use single CREATE/GET DB operation with unique constraint to avoid duplicates. 2) Provenance: extend role_grants table with a provenance string and correlation_id (migration) to record whether grant came from 'saml:assertion', 'saml:sync', 'admin-console', etc. 3) Precedence: change enforcement logic to always check explicit deny flags (deny-list, explicit deny grants) before allow merges; unify evaluation code paths (runtime enforcer + cache layer + background reconciliation) to call a single evaluator function. 4) Safe merge: when merging roles on link, attach provenance, and avoid automatic elevation to admin unless a manual or authoritative source is present. 5) Audit: emit structured audit events on link/unlink and role changes with the correlation_id propagated through the request chain. 6) Mitigation: temporary feature-flag that disables automatic role-merge during SAML sync for affected customers while fix is deployed.

tradeoffs_and_notes:
DB migration to add provenance increases row size and requires careful index planning; estimated migration time 10m-30m on prod primary. We'll add the column nullable and backfill asynchronously to reduce migration window.
Unifying enforcement paths requires touching cache eviction and enforcer code in three services (auth-runner, realtime-cache, background-sync). Risk of regressions — will gate behind canary deploys and increased tracing.
Temporary mitigation (disable auto-merge) increases friction for orgs that expect immediate group changes after SSO; tradeoff accepted to reduce privilege escalation risk.
We may see a small latency increase (~2-5ms p95) when adding provenance propagation and correlation IDs to auth paths; acceptable given security priority.
Security review is required because this changes deny/allow semantics and audit surfaces; coordinate with legal/compliance for customers with strict audit requirements.

implementation_plan:
Week 0: Reproduce with a deterministic test harness that simulates 1000 parallel SAML assertions and background sync operations (owner: Ravi)
Week 1: Add canonicalization DB uniqueness and simple lockless upsert for principal linking; add integration test (owner: Ravi)
Week 2: Add provenance column + migration plan; implement audit event emitters for saml.link and rbac.role_grant (owner: infra+auth)
Week 3: Update enforcer common library to enforce explicit-deny precedence; update cache invalidation logic (owner: auth-runtime)
Week 4: Canary deploy to internal staging, run chaos tests that introduce delayed syncs and dropped assertions; roll back on failures (owner: SRE)
Hotfix: Feature-flag to disable auto-merge for customers reporting incidents; document customer opt-out and rollout steps (owner: Support/PM)
Post-deploy: Run backfill job to populate provenance for recent role grants and run audit-query to validate (owner: data-engineering)
Follow-up: Create a lightweight UI in Console to show link provenance for org admins (next cycle, owner: Console)
Docs: Confluence write-up with sequence diagrams and mitigations; link included below

testing_plan:
Unit tests for canonical upsert and provenance field population
Integration test: simulate 10k parallel SAML assertions against staging cluster with background sync enabled
E2E: role evaluation tests including explicit deny scenarios across cache, runtime and background sync paths
Canary: deploy to 5% of requests plus single-tenant canary for affected customers, monitor audit events and permission-denied rate
Post-deploy: run backfill and run a regression query to ensure no role_bloat events for the last 7 days

Migration risk: adding a provenance column requires careful rollout to avoid long locks on the role_grants table
Regression risk: changing enforcement order could unintentionally block legitimate access if provenance tags are missing for older grants
Customer discomfort: disabling auto-merge may temporarily break onboarding for some orgs
Operational: correlation_id propagation requires updates to multiple services and could be missed in async pipelines

[Simulated cross-region restore scheduler with automated health validators]
description:
Goal: build an automated scheduler that performs simulated cross-region restores for Private (VPC) deployments and validates application health using a battery of non-destructive checks. This ticket covers Terraform hooks, orchestration, and health validators that will be reused in periodic failover drills and upgrade rehearsals.

Scope:
- Orchestrate scheduled simulated restores from REGION-A -> REGION-B in customer-like private VPC stacks using existing Terraform modules (no destructive production data writes).
- Implement a pluggable health-validation framework (API probe, KV cache warm, latency SLO smoke, token-count sanity checks, and example inference test prompts).
- Add IaC lifecycle hooks to trigger stateful snapshots, restore workflows, and optional reconciliation after the simulation completes.

Out of scope: automated cross-account networking reconfiguration, actual DNS cutover for customer traffic, and manual runbook steps for legal/compliance approvals.

Success criteria:
- Scheduler triggers end-to-end simulation in 3 target environments (staging, preprod, canary) with isolated VPCs and no customer data exposure.
- Health validators return PASS/FAIL and a deterministic failure reason for any check; failures written to the Console observability dashboard and GitHub issue created automatically.
- Terraform modules include idempotent hooks and a toggle flag so customers can opt-in to the simulated restore feature when onboarding private deployments.

Extend terraform/private-modules to expose 'restore_simulation' lifecycle hook and variables
Implement health-validation library (http probe, kv-warm, inference-sanity, latency-smoke)
Wire orchestration to Console: emit events, trace IDs, and upload results to the DR-dashboard

Chaos test: inject delayed KV restore and assert failure reason and retry behavior logged

Manual review: security team runs checklist on simulation artifacts before enabling for enterprise customers

[Active-passive DR playbook, backup/restore validation cadence, and scheduled failover drills]
description:
Create an operational playbook and quarterly schedule for active-passive disaster recovery for Redwood Inference. Deliverables: (1) an executable DR runbook for multi-region failover that covers control plane and data plane steps, circuit-breaker and load-shedding behavior during failover, and verification checks; (2) automated and manual backup/restore validation procedures with pass/fail criteria and telemetry dashboards; (3) a recurring calendar of failover drills with scope templates (partial region, full region, control-plane-only) and post-mortem checklist. Goal is to validate that RTO and RPO targets for customer-facing hosted API and Dedicated control planes meet SLOs and to reduce mean time to recover in cross-region incidents.

acceptance_criteria:
1) A published DR runbook in Confluence with step-by-step run commands and escalation contacts; 2) Backup verification job that runs weekly and produces a green/red summary in the DR dashboard; 3) Two scheduled failover drills documented and executed in staging by the end of cycle, with post-drill writeups and action items assigned; 4) Playbook includes circuit-breaker thresholds and load-shedding policies with safe defaults and rollback steps; 5) Restore tests include data integrity checks and end-to-end smoke tests for the hosted API and Dedicated routing layers; 6) SRE and Product sign-off recorded as approvals on the Confluence page.

steps:
Overview:
1) Inventory: catalog all services, data stores, and configuration tied to region-A (primary) and region-B (secondary). Identify stateful components requiring cross-region replication (KV cache snapshots, metrics stores, model artifacts, customer keys).
2) Define SLO guardrails: map services to SLOs (availability RTO, RPO) and define target thresholds for failover and rollback (e.g., if API p99 latency > 5s for > 5min AND error rate > 3%, begin failover evaluation).
3) Circuit breakers & load shedding: set documented triggers; implement per-service levers in runtime to downgrade model flavors, enable aggressive batching, or drop non-essential routes during failover. Include safe-mode toggles in Console.
4) Backup/restore validation: implement an automated weekly job that: snapshot config + artifacts, attempt restore to an isolated "drill" namespace, run schema and checksum verification, run smoke traffic against pinned model version, and publish results to DR dashboard.
5) Failover drill plan templates: (A) Control-plane-only: exercise control-plane failover procedures without switching data plane; (B) Partial traffic shift: shift 10% traffic to secondary for 15 minutes; (C) Full region failover: switch primary->secondary with full DNS and network validation.
6) Communication and escalation: prepare run-cards, pager rotations, and Slack incident channel naming convention. Pre-authorize on-call runbook owners to approve DNS TTL changes and emergency capacity increases.
7) Post-drill: capture timeline, telemetry snapshots, action items with owners, and update playbook. Implement follow-ups as separate tickets (e.g., increase snapshot frequency, fix automation flakiness).

notes:
Design constraints and trade-offs:
- Active-passive keeps primary cold for some stateful components to reduce cross-region replication costs; trade-off is longer restore time for those components.
- For low-latency KV-cache we replicate metadata and warm critical keys during drill windows only. Full continuous replication is costly on GPU-backed caches.
- Load-shedding policy prefers 'graceful degradation' (reduce model size, increase sampling temp) over outright request rejection for paying customers; emergency rejection reserved for system-protecting thresholds.
- Security: KMS keys used for secrets are region-bound; include a step to validate key availability and an approved emergency key-rotation procedure for cross-region restores.
Known risks:
- DNS TTL propagation may cause uneven traffic shifts; include CDN-level routing tests.
- Automated restore jobs can be noisy; always run in isolated namespaces and tag metrics with drill_id.

Overview:
Implement a reusable Terraform-driven generator that composes and schedules end-to-end private VPC 'region flips' for multi-region DR rehearsal. The generator produces opinionated IaC artifacts and a small control-plane job that executes an automated sequence: preflight validations, staged traffic flip (canary -> partial -> full), post-flip health validations, and rollback on failure.

Why this work:
- Current DR rehearsals are manual, brittle, and require deep ops involvement.
- Teams deploying Redwood Private lack a repeatable, auditable mechanism for exercising cross-region restores and DNS/GRP switchover behaviors.
- Automating these rehearsals reduces time-to-detect infra regressions and validates upgrades and configuration changes under realistic load.

Scope:
- Terraform module library that generates a region-flip execution plan for a customer VPC topology (subnets, LB targets, DNS entries, routing policies).
- A lightweight 'flip controller' job (stateless function + small state in SSM/ParamStore) that runs the plan and records events to the Console audit log.
- Health gates that include application-level checks (smoke endpoints), KV/redis cache warm-up checks, and token-level request sampling to ensure ML model RPCs are returning expected latency and error rates.
- Integration with existing rollout features: canary percentages, rollout windows, and automatic rollback policies.

Out of scope:
- Implementing customer-specific model migration logic.
- Full UI in Console (we'll expose a minimal connector; Console work is separate).

Deliverables:
- Terraform module(s): vpc_flip_generator, flip_preflight_validators, flip_dns_sweeper.
- Flip controller: small Lambda/Container job + state schema (ParamStore keys).
- Test harness: synthetic traffic runner and smoke-test checklist that can be invoked by the generator.
- PRD + runbook documenting how to schedule, audit, and interpret flip runs.

Acceptance criteria:
- The Terraform generator can output a complete flip plan for a sample private deployment topology with >= 2 regions.
- A scheduled flip run executes the stages (preflight -> canary -> partial -> full -> post-validation) and writes step-level events to the Console audit log.
- The flip controller triggers automatic rollback when any health gate fails and records failure reasons and metrics to the DR dashboard.
- The flip plan supports a dry-run mode that performs preflight checks without touching DNS or routing.
- Modules include clear inputs for DNS TTL, canary percentage, allowed maintenance windows, and pre-approval tokens.

Implementation notes and trade-offs:
- We will implement the generator as Terraform modules that emit a JSON 'execution plan' using terraform-local-exec; this keeps intent declarative and auditable. Trade-off: introduces a thin imperative step during apply.
- Preflight validators will include both infra-level checks (subnet reachability, route table ACLs, LR endpoints) and application-level checks (smoke endpoints, model RPC latency profiling). Validations should be idempotent and fast (< 60s aggregate) to keep preflight cheap.
- DNS switchover will favor low-TTL records where possible; for customers with constrained DNS control we will support provider-specific API-driven updates (Route53, Cloud DNS).
- For final traffic routing we will use weighted LB or traffic proxy approach instead of IP-level BGP manipulation to reduce blast radius.
- Persistence: minimal ephemeral state stored in ParamStore with a tombstone marker on completed runs for auditability. Consider moving to an internal DR runs table later.

Telemetry and success metrics:
- Per-run: start/end timestamps, per-stage duration, rollback cause (if any).
- SLA checks: post-flip P50/P95 latency vs baseline, 5xx error delta, token consumption.
- Number of rehearsals run per quarter (target > 2 per critical customer).
- Mean time to detect configuration regressions introduced by recent infra changes.

Security and compliance:
- Flip runs must be restricted to specific service principals; Terraform module will accept a DR role ARN.
- All changes are gated behind approval tokens for production-like environments (manual or automated approvals supported).
- Audit events forwarded to customer KMS-wrapped logs where required.

Rollout strategy:
1) Alpha: internal Redwood testbeds (1 customer-like env) — validate generator and controller.
2) Beta: opt-in customers with engineering involvement — iterate on validators and DNS integrations.
3) GA: expose Terraform modules and minimal console connector; document pre-reqs and runbook.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Terraform-local-exec introduces drift if controller changes independently. Mitigation: enforce plan-only dry-run CI job and store generated plans in Git.
- Risk: DNS propagation causing partial traffic mix that breaks model stateful caches. Mitigation: include KV cache warm-up stage and canary traffic sponge to exercise model cold-start paths.
- Risk: accidental double-run. Mitigation: plan locks via ParamStore/LK and tenant-scoped run IDs.

implementation_plan:
Phase 1 - scaffolding (2 sprints):
- Design Terraform module interfaces and example inventory format.
- Implement vpc_flip_generator that produces an execution JSON plan.
- Implement basic flip controller prototype (Lambda) and ParamStore state schema.

Phase 2 - validators & DNS (2 sprints):
- Implement preflight infra validators and application smoke checks.
- Add Route53 & CloudDNS update adapters; implement dry-run locking.
- Add metrics emission to DR dashboard.

Phase 3 - traffic choreography & rollback (2 sprints):
- Implement staged weighting logic and canary runner (synthetic traffic runner).
- Add automatic rollback triggers and post-mortem scaffold.

Phase 4 - Beta + docs (1 sprint):
- Run with 2 opt-in customers and iterate.
- Finalize runbooks, PRs, and Console connector hooks.

testing_plan:
- Unit tests for Terraform modules (plan output schema).
- Integration tests: run generator against test VPC and simulate flip with synthetic traffic.
- Chaos tests: artificially fail health gates and ensure rollback triggers and audit events recorded.
- Load validation: run canary traffic generator with representative token rates and verify latency distributions.

[Orchestrator epoch skew triggered rollback-fallback loop during multi-variant rollout]
description:
During a staged rollout of a multi-variant model promotion, the orchestrator entered a repeated rollback -> fallback loop across two regions. The loop caused transient mixed-serve, elevated tail latency, and a ~45% increase in token cost for impacted customers for ~32 minutes while autoscaling oscillated. This ticket documents the timeline, root cause analysis, actions taken during the event, and permanent mitigations.

impact_summary:
Outage window: ~00:12 UTC to 00:44 UTC on 2026-03-08. Affected: ~12% of production traffic for the deployment (cross-region routes). Symptoms: repeated variant flips, cache churn causing CPU/GPU load spikes, elevated 95/99 p99 latencies, and increased egress costs due to duplicate work. No data loss; no secrets exposed.

timeline:
2026-03-08 00:11 UTC - Canary rollout initiated (2% to variant B)
2026-03-08 00:12 UTC - Orchestrator A (region-1) reports epoch increment and applies new stage mapping
2026-03-08 00:13 UTC - Region-2 does not observe epoch update due to delayed metadata fanout (batching + rate limit). Region-2 controller considers new variant unhealthy and triggers rollback to variant A
2026-03-08 00:14 UTC - Global routing detects mixed serve and applies fallback to fallback-model (costly variant)
2026-03-08 00:15-00:28 UTC - Orchestrator leadership re-election and late metadata fanout cause region-1 to perceive a stale epoch; it reasserts previous stage mapping, flipping variants again. This continues in a loop with approx 30-90s oscillation until 00:44 UTC
2026-03-08 00:44 UTC - Operators manually quiesce rollout, apply fence, and promote a single-source-of-truth config; traffic stabilizes
2026-03-08 01:10 UTC - Post-incident monitoring confirms steady-state and autoscaler damping has recovered

root_cause:
Epoch token propagation and application ordering in the orchestrator is not strictly monotonic under metadata fanout delays and batch rate limiting. A leader applied an epoch increment; another region applied a rollback without the epoch, creating divergent perceived desired state. The orchestrator then performed conflicting actions (rollback vs. promote) leading to a flip/flop loop. Secondary causes: missing global rollout semaphore, insufficient circuit breaker for rapid fallback, and KV cache invalidation policy that caused heavy cache eviction during repeated variant warmups.

contributing_factors:
1) Metadata fanout batching and rate limits introduced >30s propagation lag between regions. 2) No strong fencing: epoch increments are applied but not validated against an authoritative source before making promotion/rollback decisions. 3) Autoscaler responded to transient load spikes, amplifying capacity churn. 4) Lack of a cooldown on rollback-triggering health signals.

detection_and_response:
We detected the issue via rollback alerting (route-divergence) and increased p99 latency alerts. On-call engaged, reviewed orchestrator logs, and correlated epoch numbers across regional controllers. Response actions included pausing the rollout, applying an authoritative config from the control plane, adding temporary traffic pins to stop promotions, and increasing KV cache TTLs to reduce churn.

mitigation_steps_taken:
1) Manual quiesce of rollout and applied single-source-of-truth config (00:44 UTC). 2) Forced epoch reconciliation across regions and restarted the sidecar in region-2 to flush stale route cache. 3) Temporarily disabled aggressive autoscale policies for the affected pool. 4) Increased metadata fanout budget while we validated fixes.

permanent_actions:
Add strict epoch fencing: validate incoming epoch against authoritative control-plane watermark before acting
Introduce rollout global semaphore to serialize promotion/rollback decisions for multi-region deployments
Add cooldown and hysteresis to rollback-triggering health signals to avoid flip-flop on transient failures
Improve metadata fanout: add prioritized fanout for rollout-critical keys + backpressure metrics
Adjust KV cache eviction policy to prefer warm entries for models during rollouts and add an adaptive TTL for cache items created during variant swaps
Add canary-run harness that simulates cross-region propagation delay in CI to catch ordering bugs
Dashboard: surface epoch drift (max - min epoch across controllers) and rollout divergence metric with alert thresholds
Automerge gate: block automated rollouts when epoch drift > threshold or when fanout latency > threshold

verification_plan:
1) Deploy epoch-fencing patch to canary cluster and run synthetic multi-region rollout test (owner: Diego). 2) Run CI rollout harness that injects fanout delays for 48 hours against canary (owner: Priya). 3) Verify dashboard alerts for epoch drift and divergence fire on synthetic tests. 4) After 2 successful synthetic runs without flip/flop, schedule a low-traffic real-world canary with manual oversight. 5) Post-deploy review and sign-off by SRE (Elena).

follow_up_notes:
PM and Design notified; no customer-facing incident page required as impact was contained to some high-volume customers—we'll brief affected accounts via CSMs. We will add this incident as a learning example in rollout runbook and run a war-room simulation in next on-call rotation. Estimate for completion of permanent mitigations: 3 sprints (6 weeks).

2026-03-10 - Diego Ramirez: Collected controller logs and epoch timelines; confirmed out-of-order apply in region-2 due to batched fanout. Preparing patch for epoch validation.

2026-03-14 - Diego Ramirez: Draft PR for epoch-fencing ready; internal review requested. Assigning owners for action items.

[Hot-shard eviction and circuit-breaker misfire during cross-region token surge — postmortem]
description:
During a sustained token-generation surge in EU-West, a small set of GPU shards became hot and triggered aggressive KV-cache eviction. Evictions increased model cold starts and amplified tail latency, which caused downstream heterogeneous circuit-breakers in North America to trip incorrectly due to skewed observed latencies. The result was an extended SLO degradation spanning two regions with user-facing latency and increased cost from repeat cold-starts and fallback routing.

timeline:
2026-02-14T09:12Z - Spike begins: organic traffic from a large customer batch job started ramping EU-West requests (token/sec ~6x baseline)
2026-02-14T09:18Z - Noticeable tail latency increase in EU-West; first internal alert (p99 > 1.8s) fires
2026-02-14T09:21Z - KV-cache eviction rate on shard-gpu-12 jumps from 0.8% to 37% (observed in runtime metrics)
2026-02-14T09:25Z - NA region sees increased SLO error rate due to downstream routing fallbacks; heterogeneous CBs in NA mark backends degraded
2026-02-14T09:27Z - Automated fallback routing routes traffic to secondary model variants causing capacity contention and a second wave of cache thrashing
2026-02-14T09:40Z - Oncall enables emergency short-circuit to stop cross-region failover and limits token window per user to reduce burstiness
2026-02-14T10:05Z - Traffic engineering applies temporary per-customer rate cap; evictions and tail latency progressively recover
2026-02-14T11:10Z - Full mitigation confirmed; post-incident working group formed to investigate root causes and long-term fixes

impact:
User-facing p99 latency increased above SLO for ~1 hour in EU-West with spillover affecting NA routing decisions. Estimated customer-visible requests impacted: ~18K. Cost impact: ~12% uplift in GPU runtime for the hour due to repeated cold starts and fallback traffic. No data loss, but increased error rate (rate-limited fallback responses) and degraded quality for a subset of responses.

root_cause:
A combination of uneven request fanout to a small subset of GPU shards (hot-shard) plus an overaggressive KV-cache eviction policy on those shards led to cache churn and cold-start amplification. Circuit-breaker heuristics in other regions treated the latency signals as systemic, triggering failovers that increased cross-region traffic and reinforced the hot-spot pattern.

contributing_factors:
Shard allocation algorithm allowed concentration of a high-rate customer on 3 GPUs without sufficient affinity spreading
KV-cache eviction threshold (default LRU window) was tuned for median workloads and did not handle repeated short-lived bursts well
Circuit-breaker thresholds used short windows and did not account for heterogeneous cold-start signals (cache miss vs systemic overload)
Fallback routing lacked hysteresis; rapid oscillation caused repeated cold-starts on secondary pools
Insufficient visibility in alerting to correlate cache-eviction metrics with latency signals across regions

immediate_mitigations:
Applied emergency per-customer token rate caps to smooth the incoming burst
Temporarily disabled cross-region automatic failover for affected customers to limit treatment of localized latency as global failure
Increased KV-cache size on the hot shards as a stopgap to reduce eviction rate
Added a short cooldown to the heterogeneous circuit-breakers to require sustained degradation before tripping

long_term_action_items:
ENG-34902 - Shard placement changes: implement affinity spreader to avoid high-fanout packing on <=4 GPUs (owner: Aisha Kapoor, due: 2026-03-15)
ENG-34910 - KV-cache policy: introduce burst-aware eviction policy and adaptive windowing; add targeted unit/e2e tests for short-burst scenarios (owner: Rafiq Hussein, due: 2026-03-22)
ENG-34934 - Circuit-breaker tuning: modify heuristics to label latency signals with cache-miss tags and require multi-metric confirmation before failover (owner: Serena Park, due: 2026-03-29)
ENG-34956 - Routing hysteresis: implement cooldown and maximum failover frequency per-customer to prevent oscillation (owner: Maya Alvarez, due: 2026-04-05)
ENG-34980 - Observability: create composite alert that correlates KV eviction rate, cache hit ratio, and regional p99 latency; dashboard and runbook update (owner: Marco Chen, due: 2026-03-08)
ENG-35012 - Chaos tests: add synthetic short-burst tests to CI that emulate token surges and validate circuit-breaker + routing behavior (owner: Devex Team, due: 2026-04-12)
PM-4125 - Customer communication: prepare summary for affected customers with mitigation steps and recommended client-side retry/backoff patterns (owner: Priya Nair, due: 2026-03-01)

verification_plan:
Deploy KV-cache adaptive eviction A/B to 10% of traffic and monitor p99, cache-hit ratio, and eviction rate over 7 days
Run shard placement change in staging with synthetic multi-customer fanout load for 48 hours before canary in production
After circuit-breaker heuristic change, simulate cross-region latency perturbations to ensure failovers only occur with corroborating signals
Publish new alerts/dashboards and perform oncall walkthroughs with runbook updates

comments:
2026-02-14 12:00 - Marco Chen: Initial incident triage indicates cache churn. Ramp control and temporary disable of cross-region failover helped stabilize.
2026-02-15 09:30 - Aisha Kapoor: Confirmed shard allocation pattern; scheduling follow-up with infra team to prototype spreader algorithm.
2026-02-18 16:45 - Serena Park: CB heuristic proposal posted; will include cache-miss tagging and require >=2 metric violations across a 30s window to trip.
2026-02-20 11:10 - Rafiq Hussein: Draft of adaptive eviction algorithm uploaded to the RFC; perf sims show ~60% reduction in eviction spikes under synthetic bursts.
2026-02-24 15:00 - Priya Nair: Customer outreach drafted; suggested client-side best practices (jittered exponential backoff) and temporary quota safeguards.
2026-02-25 09:00 - Oncall rotation note: add explicit guidance to avoid disabling cross-region failover as first mitigation unless cache evictions are confirmed.

[Unified Inference Consumption Paradigm — Product Overview and Roadmap]
Summary

Purpose: This document defines the "Unified Inference Consumption Paradigm" (UICP) — a product-level model that unifies usage patterns, billing primitives, and operational controls across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments. UICP is intended to reduce customer confusion, improve predictability of unit economics, and create a clear migration path between short-term experimentation and long-term committed capacity.

Audience
- Product managers and pricing owners
- Engineering teams (billing, runtime, routing)
- Customer success and sales (for contract conversations)
- Finance (forecasts and revenue recognition)

Key goals
1) Simplify: present a small set of clearly documented consumption primitives that map to typical customer journeys (prototype -> scale -> enterprise).
2) Align: ensure meter semantics are identical across hosting modes whenever feasible so product analytics and customer invoices match expectations.
3) Optimize: enable feature-level levers (routes, batching, caching) to be surfaced as cost controls customers can apply per-application.
4) Grow: create packaging that reduces friction for upgrades (e.g., credits applied toward reserved capacity).

Core concepts and definitions
- Unit primitives: token-generation-unit (TGU) and embedding-unit (EU). A TGU represents 1k generated tokens of model output (billed at model-profile rates). An EU represents 1 embedding vector invocation.
- Route: a logical endpoint customers configure that maps to a model, routing policy, and cost-slo profile (e.g., route: chat-low-latency).
- Bundle: a purchasable allocation of TGUs/EUs with attributes {term, refundable_credits, route_scoped}. Bundles may be on-demand (monthly) or committed (annual).
- Route-aware bundles: bundles tagged to one or more routes so customers can buy reservations for high-value endpoints without committing for all consumption.
- Effective price: dynamic per-call price calculated from model profile, route-level optimizations (batching, cache-hit-rate adjustment), and bundle discounts.

Illustrative billing example
- Model: open-llama-70B-qk8, baseline rate: $0.020 / TGU.
- Customer purchases a 12-month bundle: 1,000,000 TGUs for $12,500 (effective $0.0125 / TGU).
- Route optimization credit: their chat route has expected 15% KV cache hit; effective per-call cost adjusts to $0.0106 / TGU for that route.

Requirements (summary table)
| Requirement ID | Description | Priority | Owner | Acceptance criteria |
| RQ-001 | Unified meter semantics for TGUs/EUs across Hosted/Dedicated/Private | Must | Billing | All three modes report identical token counts for identical requests within +/-1% observed variance over 7d test window |
| RQ-002 | Route-aware bundle support in billing pipeline and UI | Must | Product & Billing | Bundles can be created that are route-scoped, show remaining usage, and apply discounts on invoice lines |
| RQ-003 | Effective-price telemetry exported to Console & cost API | High | Eng Runtime | Console shows modeled vs actual spend breakdown per-request and per-route for last 30d |
| RQ-004 | Migration flow: credits conversion for upgrades from Hosted to Dedicated | High | Sales Ops | Tooling converts remaining prepaid credits into usable reservation discounts with clear audit trail |

Product capabilities (feature list)
- Consumption catalog: standardized descriptions and example invoices for each bundle type.
- Route tagging and per-route controls in Console (risk controls: max QPS, latency tier, fallback variant).
- Billing API enhancements: purchase, query balance, allocate to routes, and programmatic refunds.
- Effective price estimator: SDK endpoint that returns an estimated per-call cost given model, sequence length distribution, and route config.
- Metering reconciler: daily job to compare runtime counters with billing counters and surface anomalies >1%.

Architecture overview (high level)
- Metering pipeline: runtime -> normalized event stream (token events, embed events) -> aggregator -> reconciler -> billing ledger.
- Route-aware middleware: runtime attaches route metadata to every request that is persisted through the event stream so bundle application is deterministic.
- Price engine: standalone service that calculates effective price and exposes the estimator API to Console and SDKs.

Roadmap and milestones (timeline)
- Q1 2026: design sign-off for UICP; implement token nomenclature and small-scale test harness (owner: Eng Billing).
- Q2 2026: implement route metadata propagation in runtime and telemetry (owner: Eng Runtime).
- Q3 2026: billing pipeline changes: bundles, route-scoped discounts, and UI prototypes (owner: Eng Billing + Console).
- Q4 2026: pilot with 3 customers across SMB and mid-market for route-aware bundles; iterate on legal contract templates (owner: Sales + Customer Success).
- Q1 2027: GA with full billing export compatibility and SDK estimator (owner: Product + Eng).

Rollout plan (canary -> pilot -> GA)
1) Internal canary: enable UICP in staging and a subset of internal customers; run reconciler for two business cycles, verify variance <1.5%.
2) Customer pilot: invite 3 customers representing different personas (startup, platform team, regulated enterprise). Pilot window: 30–60 days with dedicated success engagement.
3) GA: enable self-serve purchase in Console, add documentation and migration guide, publish examples and pricing matrix.

Customer migration and support notes
- Migration path for Hosted to Dedicated: offer automated credit conversion, route export/import tooling, and a migration checklist.
- For Private deployments: offer a local price-engine release that can be run in air-gapped mode and a final reconciliation report to be uploaded to the Redwood billing service.
- Support SLAs: Sales Ops and Customer Success to own conversion disputes for the first 90 days after pilot signoff.

Success metrics and KPIs
- Reduction in pricing-related support tickets by 30% after GA.
- Average time to convert a paid Hosted customer to Dedicated reduces from 45 days to 20 days.
- Billing variance between runtime and billing ledger <1% in production for 95% of customers.
- Net revenue retention uplift via route-aware bundles for mid-market customers by 12% YoY.

Operational considerations and guardrails
- Default fallback: if route metadata is missing, fall back to tenant-level bundle application; log and alert owner team.
- Fraud detection: anomalies in token usage (spikes >10x baseline) trigger an automated hold and a billing review workflow.
- Backcompat: historical invoices continue to reference legacy unit names until archive cutoff (12 months).

Open questions and decisions to make
- Pricing alignment: should effective-price estimator consider GPU-hour equivalent to inform enterprise procurement discounts? (Decision owner: Finance).
- Refund policies: what portion of committed bundles are refundable in the first 90 days? (Decision owner: Legal + Finance).
- Private deployment reconciliation cadence: daily vs weekly for air-gapped customers? (Decision owner: Eng Private Deployments).

Next steps (action items)
- Product: finalize acceptance criteria for RQ-001..RQ-004 by 2026-11-30 (owner: Asha Patel).
- Engineering: create trackable tickets for route metadata propagation and price-engine API by 2026-12-07 (owner: Diego Marquez).
- Sales: select pilot customers and draft pilot contract template by 2027-01-15 (owner: Rina Sato).

Appendix: example CLI flows
1) Create route-aware bundle (example):
   redwood billing create-bundle --name "chat-reserve-100k" --tgus 100000 --term 12m --routes chat-low-latency --price 1250
2) Query effective price (example):
   curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <key>" \n     https://api.redwood.ai/v1/cost-estimator?model=open-llama-70B-qk8&seq=512&route=chat-low-latency

References
- See pricing catalog and token definitions in: /confluence/product-docs/pricing-and-packaging/token-bundle-flex-enterprise-metering-2026-08-20.json
- Related requirements: /confluence/product-docs/requirements/tenant-aware-cost-and-slo-management-prd-2026-11-01.json

Document history
- 2026-01-08: Drafted initial problem statement (Asha Patel)
- 2026-04-14: Added architecture and billing examples (Diego Marquez)
- 2026-11-15: Finalized roadmap and pilot plan; published (Asha Patel)


[Adaptive Token Budgeting and Pricing Modes — Design Spec]
Overview

Purpose: This design spec describes the Adaptive Token Budgeting subsystem and associated Pricing Modes to make per-route and per-tenant token economics flexible, predictable, and SLO-aligned. The goal is to enable customers and internal systems to select tradeoffs between latency, cost, and quality through an explicit budgeting API and backend billing primitives.

Scope:
- Config surface for routes and tenants to express token budgets and pricing mode.
- Runtime enforcement and accounting hooks in the serving runtime to decrement budgets and emit metrics.
- Billing integration that maps budget consumption to invoiceable units and credits.
- UI/Console representation and rollout steps.

Non-goals: internal-only rate limiting (existing quota system remains); deep ML model changes; user-facing experiments outside configured modes.

Background and motivation

Redwood currently charges primarily per-token and via reserved capacity contracts. Customers building latency-sensitive features request more predictable per-route economics tied to SLOs (e.g., 95th percentile latency < 120ms) and per-feature budgets (e.g., chat sessions capped at 1,000 tokens/day). Existing approaches are either too coarse (account-level token bundles) or too brittle (static per-request limits).

Adaptive Token Budgeting introduces:
- Explicit budgets that can be bound to a route, API key, or tenant.
- Pricing modes that change how budget consumption maps to billable tokens (flat token accounting, SLO-backed creditization, and hybrid subscription models).
- Runtime signals (latency, tail, error-rate, model fallback) to dynamically adjust effective spend rates to protect SLOs and cost targets.

Goals and success metrics

Primary goals:
1) Allow product teams and customers to declare per-route/tenant token budgets and pricing mode.
2) Ensure billing accuracy within 0.5% of serving accounting for budgets-enabled routes.
3) Reduce cost-per-request for bursty workloads by >= 12% via intelligent remapping (within 6 months of rollout).
4) Provide tooling to convert current token bundles into budgeting constructs with < 5% migration delta.

Success metrics (sample):
- Percentage of paid requests routed through a pricing-mode (target 30% in 6 months).
- Billing reconciliation delta (target <= 0.5%).
- Customer-reported latency regressions attributable to budgeting toggles (target < 1%).

High-level design

Components:
- Budgeting API (admin): /v1/budgets (create, update, delete, preview)
- Enforcement library: thin runtime hook inside the serving runtime to decrement budgets, consult pricing mode, and emit accounting events
- Pricing Engine: maps accounting events to billing line-items according to mode and rules
- Console: UI to visualize budgets, projected spend, and SLO impact
- Reconciliation service: asynchronous job that verifies usage events against billing tables nightly

Pricing modes (supported):
1) fixed_token: straightforward tokens-in/tokens-out pricing. Accounting event = tokens_consumed.
2) slo_credits: budgets are denominated in SLO credits. Credits are consumed at a variable rate based on runtime signal (e.g., high tail latency -> credit burn increases). Billing maps credits to invoiceable token-equivalents at periodic conversion.
3) buffered_subscription: subscription seat or capacity that provides a discounted effective per-token rate after a fixed monthly commitment; budget prevents overspend beyond allowed burst credits.
4) hybrid: per-route rules that mix modes (e.g., warm path fixed_token, cold path slo_credits).

Configuration model (example)

Config object (JSON example):
{
  "route": "/v1/chat/completions/preview",
  "scope": "route",
  "mode": "slo_credits",
  "budget_amount": 5000,            // units depend on mode (tokens or credits)
  "budget_period": "P1M",         // ISO 8601 period (monthly default)
  "slo_target": {"p95_latency_ms": 120},
  "fallback_policy": "throttle_then_fallback",
  "adjustment_policy": {"latency_threshold_ms": 150, "burn_increase_pct": 50}
}

Config table:
| field | type | description |
| ----- | ---- | ----------- |
| route | string | Route path or matcher |
| scope | enum | route|key|tenant |
| mode | enum | fixed_token|slo_credits|buffered_subscription|hybrid |
| budget_amount | integer | numeric budget for period in mode units |
| budget_period | string | ISO period for budget reset |
| slo_target | object | SLO target(s) used for adjustment decisions |
| fallback_policy | enum | allow|throttle|fallback| |
| adjustment_policy | object | Runtime adjustment tuning parameters |

Runtime enforcement and events

At request completion, the serving runtime will emit an accounting event to the Budgeting topic (Kafka):
- event fields: timestamp, route_id, tenant_id, api_key, tokens_input, tokens_output, model_variant, latency_ms, status, applied_mode, effective_budget_units_consumed

The Enforcement library behavior (pseudocode):
1) Lookup budget config by route/key/tenant precedence.
2) Evaluate adjustment_policy against observed signals (latency_ms, error_rate).
3) Compute effective_consumption = base_token_count * mode_multiplier (mode-dependent).
4) Atomically decrement budget; if insufficient, apply fallback_policy.
5) Emit accounting event and metrics (budget_remaining, burn_rate, last_adjustment).

Mode multipliers (example):
- fixed_token: 1.0
- slo_credits: variable (1.0 -> 3.0 depending on stress signals)
- buffered_subscription: 0.6 (discount factor) until subscription cap reached

API and Console UX

Admin API endpoints (surface):
- POST /v1/budgets  -> create or preview config
- GET /v1/budgets/{id} -> current state and projected spend
- PATCH /v1/budgets/{id} -> change mode/budget/fallback
- POST /v1/budgets/{id}/preview -> simulate N requests and report cost & SLO impact

Console screens:
- Budget Summary (percentage consumed, forecasted burn)
- What-if Preview (simulate different traffic shapes and adjustment settings)
- Billing Impact (translated to invoiceable units)

Telemetry and SLOs

Metrics to emit per budget-enabled route (prometheus names):
- redwood.budget_remaining{route,tenant,mode} gauge
- redwood.budget_burn_rate_per_min{route,tenant,mode} gauge
- redwood.budget_adjustments_total{route,tenant,policy} counter
- redwood.budget_denied_requests_total{route,tenant,reason} counter
- redwood.budget_accounting_delta{route,tenant} gauge (nightly reconciliation diff)

SLO contracts and enforcement policies (recommended defaults):
- p95_latency_ms <= 120 for latency-sensitive chat routes
- error_rate <= 0.5%
- budget_reconciliation_delta <= 0.5% monthly

Billing integration and invoice mapping

Mapping rules (examples):
- fixed_token: invoice line = tokens_consumed * token_rate
- slo_credits: invoice line = credits_converted * credit_conversion_rate (conversion window: daily close)
- buffered_subscription: base_monthly_fee + overage = (committed_tokens*discount_rate) + overage_tokens*standard_rate

Reconciliation and auditing

Nightly job responsibilities:
1) Aggregate accounting events and produce aggregate consumption per budget id.
2) Cross-check against billing ledger; compute budget_accounting_delta.
3) If delta > 0.5%, create an investigation ticket and tag affected customers.

Rollout plan

Phase 0 (pilot, 4 weeks):
- Internal pilot with platform routes only.
- Validation of enforcement hooks and event schema.
- Manual reconciliation checks.

Phase 1 (beta customers, 8–12 weeks):
- Onboard 3–5 customers across use cases (chat, embeddings, reranking).
- Enable only fixed_token and buffered_subscription modes initially.
- Provide migration tool to translate token bundles.

Phase 2 (SLO-backed modes, 12–16 weeks):
- Open slo_credits and hybrid mode.
- Monitor billing delta and tail latency.
- Add UI previews and automated conversion tool.

Phase 3 (GA):
- Full rollout, doc updates, and pricing page changes.
- SLA and support plan updates.

Migration and backward compatibility

- Existing token bundles: migration tool will compute an equivalent budget in fixed_token mode; customers can opt-in to change modes.
- Fallback: default to existing quota system when budget system is unavailable (circuit breaker).

Security, privacy, and compliance

- Budget configs considered customer metadata — include KMS-backed storage for sensitive fields.
- Accounting events contain no PII; API keys are hashed before being emitted to Kafka.
- Audit logs retained consistent with data-retention policy; include export path for compliance customers.

Operational runbook (short)

Common alert triggers:
1) budget_accounting_delta > 0.5% for > 24h -> paging to Billing SRE
2) budget_denied_requests_total spike -> page Platform Oncall (possible config bug)
3) nightly_reconciliation_job_fail -> page Data Platform

Quick recovery steps:
1) For mis-billed customer: run manual aggregate and create invoice credit; revert budgets if rollout caused regression.
2) For enforcement hotpath failures: toggle budgeting circuit-breaker for affected cluster; monitor error rates.

Security review checklist: handled (encryption at rest, encrypted audit trail, role-based UI access).

- Precise conversion algorithm: linear vs tiered conversion rates under stress.
- UI UX: how much control to expose to customers for adjustment policy tuning.

Risks

- Misconfiguration could cause customer downtime (mitigation: preview + safeties).
- Billing reconciliation complexity increases (mitigation: nightly reconciliation and manual override).

[Deployment Surface, Consumption Mapping, and Pricing Implications]
Overview

This document defines a unified view of the Redwood product deployment surface, maps technical consumption signals to billing primitives, and outlines product and go-to-market implications. It is intended for product, pricing, and platform stakeholders who must make consistent decisions about how features are exposed across Hosted API, Dedicated, and Private deployments and how those exposures translate into customer-facing billing and packaging.

Goals
- Reduce customer confusion by standardizing the mapping from technical metrics (tokens, requests, reserved GPU-hours) to billing units.
- Ensure pricing captures meaningful unit economics differences across deployment modes (latency SLAs, reserved vs burst capacity, support tiers).
- Provide a clear rollout plan to phase pricing changes with minimal disruption.

Scope
- In-scope: Hosted API, Redwood Dedicated, Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem). Includes generation, embeddings, streaming, and function/tool calling surfaces. Covers per-request/per-token pricing, reserved capacity contracts, and enterprise licensing models.
- Out-of-scope: Third-party reseller billing, marketplace-specific adjustments that are handled by Cloud Partnerships.

Background and motivation
Over the past 18 months we've added features (streaming, KV-cache sharing, auto-batching cross-tenant pools) whose cost and performance characteristics differ materially by deployment mode. Sales and finance report frequent customer confusion about which features are free or billed and how to estimate monthly run rates. This doc aligns product exposure and pricing primitives to reduce churn and accelerate procurement.

High-level mapping: technical signals -> billing primitives
(ASCII table for quick reference)

| Technical signal / feature | Hosted API billing primitive | Dedicated billing primitive | Private billing primitive | Notes |
|---------------------------|-----------------------------|---------------------------|--------------------------|-------|
| Raw tokens generated | per-token unit (generation/response) | included in reserved capacity; overage per-token at reduced rate | customer-specific (license + metered add-ons) | streaming counts as tokens as emitted |
| Embedding vectors computed | per-embedding unit (per-vector) | included up to reservation; burst at per-vector rate | typically included in enterprise data packages |
| KV/prefix cache hits | transparent to billing (performance optimization) | reserved capacity sizing guidance impacts price | considered in sizing for licensing (reduces required GPUs) | caching reduces effective tokens billed upstream; we credit customers via billing guidance |
| Streaming sessions | same per-token math; additional small "session" fee for long-lived connections | session fees optional; consumed by reserved throughput | included as part of on-prem SLA or optional telemetry package | session fee covers connection infra costs and retention |
| Model variant fallbacks | routed transparently; charged at chosen model rate | fallback to smaller pinned model counted at that model's token rate | customer-defined routing; billing mapped to selected variant | important for cost-aware SLOs |

Requirements and acceptance criteria
1) Product-level: A canonical mapping table (this doc) published and linked in all sales materials. Acceptance: Legal sign-off and one-pager billing FAQ created.
2) Billing system: Instrumentation to produce monthly meter of effective billable tokens and embeddings per customer across deployment modes. Acceptance: daily ledger match within 0.5% against serving telemetry for a 7-day rolling window.
3) UX: Console display of estimated monthly cost given workload profile (tokens/min, avg seq len, embeddings/month, cache hit%) for Hosted and Dedicated. Acceptance: cost estimator in Console returns a stable estimate within ±15% of the billing system forecast for the sample workloads.
4) Pricing: Publish recommended reserved capacity commit bands for Dedicated with corresponding per-GPU/hour and per-token overage. Acceptance: internal pricing approved by Finance and Go-to-market.

Design constraints and decisions
- Single canonical meter: We will use "billable_tokens" as the primary unit for generation/streaming; embeddings remain a separate meter. This decision avoids double-counting across streaming events and partial retries.
- Cache attribution: Cache hits are not billed; however, we will compute and report an "effective_tokens" metric which is billable_tokens adjusted by cache hit rate for modelling.
- Reserved capacity math: Reserved capacity contracts are priced by committed GPU-hours plus a discounted per-token overage. We accept complexity in contracts to preserve predictable unit economics for large customers.
- Private deployments: Pricing is negotiated (license + support + optional telemetry ingestion). We will provide a reference mapping and a standard worksheet to accelerate enterprise procurement.

Pricing primitives and sample formulas
- Hosted API: charge = base_per_token * billable_tokens + embedding_price * num_embeddings + session_fee * sessions
- Dedicated: charge = committed_gpu_hours * reserved_gpu_hour_price + overage_per_token * max(0, billable_tokens - included_tokens) + premium_support_fee (if selected)
- Private: charge = platform_license + optional telemetry_ingest_per_gb + professional_services for onprem_install + annual_support_tier

Sample price table (reference, illustrative only)
- base_per_token (hosted): $0.0009 per token for standard models, $0.0025 per token for large/LLM-XXL
- embedding_price: $0.0001 per embedding vector
- session_fee: $0.50 per long-lived session per month (threshold > 15 minutes continuous)
- committed_gpu_hour_price (dedicated): $6.50 per GPU-hour for reserved A100-equivalent pool at 12mo commit
- dedicated overage_per_token: $0.00045 per token (post-included tokens)
- private: platform_license starting at $75k/year for small deployments; typical mid-market deals range $150k-$500k plus infra costs

Example: estimating a conversational workload (monthly)
- Workload: 200 reqs/min (steady), avg prompt+response 800 tokens, 30 days, no. of minutes per month = 43,200
- billable_tokens = 200 * 800 * 43,200 / 60 = 115,200,000 tokens monthly (approx)
- Hosted cost = 115.2M * $0.0009 = $103,680/month
- Dedicated scenario: customer reserves 8 A100-equivalent GPUs (assume 1 GPU ~ 20k tokens/s average throughput for this model), reserved_gpu_hours = 8 * 24 * 30 = 5,760 GPU-hours
  - reserved cost = 5,760 * $6.50 = $37,440/month
  - included_tokens (profile) = 80% utilization equivalent ~ 80M tokens included; overage tokens = 35.2M * $0.00045 = $15,840; total = $53,280/month + optional support

Operational requirements and telemetry
- Telemetry signals to produce for billing: billable_tokens, embeddings_count, cache_hit_rate, streaming_sessions_open, average_seq_len, model_variant_id, region, customer_tier
- SLOs (billing/data freshness): daily meter generation job must complete within 2 hours after UTC midnight; daily reconciliation test success rate >= 99.5%
- Anomaly detection: alert if daily billed tokens delta > 10% vs 3-day rolling median or absolute increase > 10M tokens; ownership: Billing infra (eng-fin-billing) + Product pricing SME for escalations

Console UX and estimator requirements
- Inputs: expected qps, avg sequence length, percent cache hits, embeddings/month, expected streaming sessions
- Outputs: monthly cost estimate (hosted vs dedicated entry), recommended reserved commitment band, sensitivity visualization (slider for cache hit % and avg seq len)
- Acceptance: estimator must have API and SDK hooks for programmatic usage (Console, Sales quoting tool).

Roadmap and rollout plan (Q3–Q4 2026)
1) Q3 2026 (MVP) — publish canonical mapping and pricing primitive definitions; deliver Console estimator alpha; enable telemetry meters for billable_tokens and embeddings. Owners: Product (Priya Nair), Eng-Fin-Billing (Marco Ruiz), Console (Leah Park).
2) Q4 2026 — roll out Dedicated recommended commit bands; publish dedicated overage math and sample worksheets for Sales; legal and finance approve contract templates. Owners: GTM (Sam Ortega), Finance (Nadia Singh).
3) Q1 2027 — publish Private reference worksheet and standardized license tiers; integrate telemetry ingestion option into Private install docs. Owners: Private Deployments Team (Ravi Patel).

Rollout communication and training
- Sales enablement: 2x 1-hour trainings + one-pager cheat sheet + worksheet for customer estimates.
- Support: runbook for common billing disputes (first look triage + reconciliation steps).
- Customers: update public pricing pages and provide migration guide for customers affected by changed estimation logic.

Migration and compatibility notes
- Historical bills: we will not retroactively re-bill prior months but will re-run estimator for historical windows to show differences and explain driver (cache, batching improvements).
- Customer notifications: any change that affects an active committed contract will be handled under contract terms; recommended changes to contracts will be presented as optional add-ons.

Security, compliance, and privacy considerations
- Metering pipeline must not leak PII. Tokenization and counters run on hashed customer IDs.
- Telemetry ingestion for Private deployments is optional and requires customer consent and an agreed retention policy.

The product will enable SRE, Billing, Product, and Sales teams to reason about unit economics, run experiments, and support commercial conversations with precise, explainable usage data.\n\nContext and motivation\n- Current telemetry captures request headers, trace IDs, and coarse token counts per request. [Unified Capacity Transition PRD: SLO-aligned Consumption and Dedicated Migration]
Executive summary:\n\nThis document defines the product requirements, design constraints, rollout roadmap, pricing impacts, and release notes for the "Unified Capacity Transition" initiative. The initiative enables customers to move from legacy per-token consumption and ad-hoc reserved capacity models to an SLO-aligned consumption paradigm that unifies Dedicated reservations, hosted usage, and private deployments under a single migration playbook.\n\nGoals:\n- Provide a predictable migration path for customers on Dedicated capacity and legacy token billing to SLO-aligned bundles.\n- Maintain or improve customer latency SLOs (p50 <= 45ms for short sequences, p95 <= 250ms for chat workloads) during and after migration.\n- Prevent revenue regressions and make pricing transparent to customers.\n- Reduce operational overhead for account teams via automated migration tooling, billing reconciliations, and clear rollback policies.\n\nNon-goals:\n- This PRD does not change model internals, kernel selection, or per-model performance optimizations.\n- It does not replace existing enterprise contract negotiation workflows; those remain supported.\n\nStakeholders and ownership:\n- Product (owner): Maya Thompson — overall initiative and PRD.\n- Eng Platform: Ravi Singh — migration tooling and rollout automation.\n- Eng SRE: Lina Gomez — SLO validation, monitoring, and incident readiness.\n- Finance: Alisha Verma — pricing modelling and revenue reconciliation.\n- Sales/CS: Account teams (named reps) — customer communications and approvals.\n\nSuccess metrics (90-day post-rollout):\n- 85% of migrated customers meet their pre-migration latency SLOs within +/-10% of baseline.\n- Migration churn rate <= 2% attributable to performance regressions.\n- Average time-to-migrate (from opt-in) <= 14 days for customers with < 200M tokens/month.\n- Net new ARR uplift from SLO-aligned bundles >= 10% for migrated cohort within 3 months.\n\nFunctional requirements:\n1) Migration offer types (API + Console)\n- Offer A: "SLO Starter Bundle" — 99th percentile latency SLO not guaranteed; discounted bundle for low-volume customers.\n- Offer B: "SLO Standard Bundle" — p95 latency SLO guarantee with transparent overage pricing.\n- Offer C: "Dedicated-equivalent Bundle" — reserved capacity equivalence with burst allowance and SLA.\n\n2) Migration UI and API endpoints\n- Console: Guided migration wizard (preview, cost estimate, staging run, apply, rollback).\n- API: POST /migration/estimate, POST /migration/start, GET /migration/status, POST /migration/rollback.\n- API auth: requires account admin role and signed acceptance of new T&Cs.\n\n3) Billing and reconciliation rules\n- Billing engine must support dual-metering window for up to 60 days: customers pay both legacy and new bundle for reconciliation, with credits applied automatically.\n- Financial holdback: 10% of first-month revenue held in escrow to cover performance crediting if SLOs are missed.\n\n4) Observability and quality guardrails\n- Per-account SLO dashboards (latency, error-rate, token consumption, tail-latency breakdown).\n- Auto-escalation: if p95 latency degrades > 20% relative to baseline for 6 consecutive hours, flip to mitigation mode (see Runbook).\n\nNon-functional requirements:\n- Backwards-compatible APIs: endpoints must not break existing key flows.\n- Rollback time target: full rollback under 30 minutes for customers with < 1M QPS-equivalent requests.\n- Storage: migration metadata retention for 365 days.\n- Data residency: migration operations must honor customer's region and VPC constraints.\n\nDesign overview:\n- High-level approach: create a "migration orchestration" service that coordinates cost estimates, staged test runs against a canary route, and final cutover. The orchestration service communicates with: billing, routing, runtime control plane, monitoring, and the console.\n\n- Components:\n  - Migration Orchestrator (service): tracks state machine (estimate -> staging -> validate -> cutover -> reconcile -> archive).\n  - Estimate Engine: runs simulation using historical token traces + model profiles to produce cost and SLO risk assessments.\n  - Staging Proxy: routes a configurable percentage of production traffic to the new bundle variant for validation.\n  - Billing Reconciler: coordinates dual-metering and credits.\n  - SLO Validator: compares live metrics to baseline and flags pass/fail.\n\nAPI contract examples:\n- Estimate request (JSON)\n```\nPOST /v1/migration/estimate\n{\n  "account_id": "acct_123",\n  "lookback_days": 30,\n  "models": ["redwood/gemini-13b", "open/guanaco-7b"],\n  "target_bundle": "slo-standard"\n}\n```\n- Example estimate response (abridged)\n```\n{\n  "monthly_cost": "USD 12,400",\n  "predicted_p95_delta": "+12%",\n  "recommended_configuration": {"burst_capacity": "2000 rps", "quantization_profile": "q3"}\n}\n```\n\nMigration phases and timeline (high level):\n- Phase 0 (Prep, 0-2 weeks): product sign-off, legal T&Cs update, pricing modelling finalized, pilot cohort selected.\n- Phase 1 (Pilot, 2-8 weeks): 5–10 reference customers, staging runs, end-to-end billing validation.\n- Phase 2 (Scale rollout, 8-20 weeks): self-serve console enablement, sales enablement docs, automated reconciliations.\n- Phase 3 (General availability, 20+ weeks): GA launch, public docs, migration incentives sunset.\n\nRollout steps (detailed numbered procedure):\n1. Prepare account profile and collect 30-day telemetry snapshot.\n2. Run Estimate Engine to generate cost + SLO risk.\n3. Present migration plan to customer via Console and Sales.\n4. If customer accepts, create staging proxy and route 1–5% traffic for 48 hours.\n5. Run automated SLO validation. If pass, increment to 25% for 72 hours.\n6. Final cutover window is scheduled; during cutover route 100% traffic and enable Billing Reconciler.\n7. Monitor for 72 hours; if any auto-escalation triggers, run rollback (documented in Runbook).\n8. After 60-day dual-billing window, finalize reconciliation and archive migration metadata.\n\nRunbook: auto-escalation and rollback (engineer-facing):\n- Trigger conditions:\n  - p95 latency increase > 20% vs baseline for 6h.\n  - Error rate increase > 1% absolute for 1h.\n  - Token consumption variance > 30% and billing delta > 15% projected.\n- Immediate actions:\n  1) On-call SRE receives page with affected account_id and baseline.\n  2) Migration Orchestrator toggles staging proxy to previous route.\n  3) Billing Reconciler marks account for manual review and applies interim credits.\n  4) Post-incident triage within 48 hours and customer-facing status update.\n\nPricing and packaging implications:\n- Principle: preserve transparency and provide a clear economic mapping between token usage and bundle capacity.\n- Example pricing tiers (illustrative):\n| Bundle | Monthly commit | Included tokens/mo | Burst | SLA | Overages |\n|--------|----------------|--------------------|-------|-----|----------|\n| Starter | $1,200 | 50M | 500 rps | best-effort | $0.00007/token |\n| Standard | $10,000 | 500M | 5k rps | p95 latency SLO | $0.00006/token |\n| Dedicated-equivalent | $45,000 | 3B | 20k rps | SLA-backed | negotiated |\n\n- Migration credits and incentives:\n  - 30% credit on the first month for pilots.\n  - Volume commitment discounts continue to apply post-migration.\n\nRoadmap and milestones (quarterly themes):\n- Q2 2027: Pilot cohort execution, Estimate Engine MVP, console wizard alpha.\n- Q3 2027: Billing Reconciler beta, expanded pilot, early self-serve flows.\n- Q4 2027: Scale rollout, analytics dashboards GA, CS/sales playbooks.\n\nRisks and mitigations:\n- Risk: Customers experience tail-latency regressions after bundling.\n  - Mitigation: Staging proxy with progressive traffic ramp + canary performance tuning.\n- Risk: Billing reconciliation disputes inflate finance workload.\n  - Mitigation: Automate credits, provide clear reconciliation reports, finance SLA with account teams.\n- Risk: Migration tooling introduces new surface area for incidents.\n  - Mitigation: Circuit-breaker patterns, per-account toggles, and 30-day metadata retention for audit.\n\nDeveloper notes and implementation constraints:\n- Orchestrator state machine must be idempotent; design to tolerate at-least-once events.\n- Ensure all calls to runtime control plane include reason and correlation_id for audit.\n- Migration UI must surface estimated risk categories (Low/Medium/High) and the primary driver (latency, token variance, model mismatch).\n\nPlanned release notes (to be included in product release):\n- Added migration wizard to Console to transition customers to SLO-aligned bundles.\n- New API endpoints: /v1/migration/estimate, /v1/migration/start, /v1/migration/status, /v1/migration/rollback.\n- Billing: dual-metering window support and automatic crediting for migration reconciliations.\n\nAppendices:\nA. Example migration checklist (for CS and Sales)\n1) Confirm customer's legal acceptance and billing contact.\n2) Run Estimate and review predicted p95 delta.\n3) Schedule staging window and collect required runbooks.\n4) Assign SRE on-call for the cutover window.\n5) Validate reconciliation report post-60 days.\n\nB. Example CLI snippet to start a migration (internal tooling)\n```\nredwood migrate start --account acct_123 --bundle slo-standard --staging-percent 5 --contact "cs-rep@example.com"\n```\n\nC.
