[Pinned session reverts during tiered canary: sidecar snapshot desync triggers fallback routing]
description:
Issue summary: During a staged (tiered) canary rollout for redwood-open-gpt-3.5-v1, a subset of tenant sessions that were previously pinned to the promoted variant unexpectedly reverted to the default fallback variant. Impact: customer-visible mixed-model responses for ~3% of requests from Meridian Analytics' production traffic in us-east; increased latency for affected requests due to additional routing and KV cache misses. Timeline: 2026-03-10 09:10 UTC - deploy start for tiered canary; 09:22 UTC - first customer report; 09:30-10:00 UTC - increased 5xxs and quality complaints; 10:15 UTC - Support triage. Observed behavior: some sessions lost model affinity and were routed to a fallback variant; this coincided with sidecar snapshot refresh events on a subset of edge pods. Expected behavior: pin affinity should persist across sidecar snapshot refreshes and control-plane rollouts until explicit unpin or pin TTL expiry. Steps to reproduce: 1) Create tiered canary rollout with staged weights and pin variant for a test tenant; 2) Trigger sidecar config refresh (simulated by restarting sidecar or pushing a SIGHUP); 3) Send session traffic with pinned token and observe routing; 4) Reproduce by toggling edge header rewrite feature flag. Logs & artifacts: edge-proxy logs show header rewrite events at same timestamps as routing flips; sidecar snapshot logs show a full snapshot replace (snapshot_id changed) and an applied config hash mismatch with control-plane; KV cache miss logs for pinned sessions; sample request IDs: rq-0a1f23, rq-0a1f98, rq-0b2c11. Attachments: packet captures and a short trace are in the ticket attachments (internal).

investigation_notes:
Initial hypothesis: sidecar snapshot replace caused pin metadata to be dropped locally on edge pods that applied new snapshot before pin reconciliation completed.
Correlated timing between snapshot replace and a partial control-plane propagation delay (10-14s window) in us-east region.
Found header rewrite rule that migrates legacy session-cookie to new token format; during rewrite the pin-token field was being stripped by an older sidecar build on ~7% of pods.
Reproduced in the staging cluster by applying an older sidecar image plus the header rewrite: pinned token removed on snapshot apply and route fallback triggered.
Checked rollout orchestration logs: canary weight adjust and snapshot distribution overlapped; reconciliation controller did not retry pin sync fast enough when snapshot applied mid-window.
No evidence of model-serving node eviction or GPU preemption; serving runtime healthy for promoted variant.

comments:
Priya Desai (2026-03-10 09:35): Customer reported 'we're seeing different answers mid-session, some requests go to older model' - provided request IDs and sample outputs.
Jordan Ellis (2026-03-10 10:05): Handoff to SRE to check edge snapshot behavior and sidecar versions across us-east; escalated to infra team.
Marcus Liu (SRE) (2026-03-10 11:20): Confirmed sidecar binary mismatch on ~6 out of 90 edge pods in us-east; those pods show snapshot replace events exactly at 09:18-09:24 UTC.
Elena Park (Control Plane) (2026-03-11 08:50): Found a timing edge in the pin-reconciliation backoff; filing PR to add a forced sync when snapshot ID increments during an active pin window.
Jordan Ellis (2026-03-12 07:10): Temporary mitigation applied: disabled header rewrite during ongoing tiered canary for Meridian and kicked a targeted pin-resync job against affected edge pods.
Priya Desai (2026-03-12 08:00): Customer confirmed reduced incidence and reported no further mixed-model responses after mitigation for last 12 hours.
Marcus Liu (2026-03-12 09:05): Pending follow-up: patch sidecar to preserve pin-token on rewrite and add telemetry to detect snapshot-induced pin drops.

root_cause:
A race between sidecar snapshot replacement and control-plane pin-reconciliation caused pin metadata to be stripped on edge pods running an older sidecar build that applied an incompatible header rewrite. The strip led to routing logic treating the session as unpinned, invoking fallback routing to a default variant.

workaround:
Disabled the header rewrite flag for affected tenant during the canary window and ran a targeted pin-resync job against edge pods in us-east. This restored session affinity for affected tenants within ~30 minutes.

resolution_plan:
Short term: keep header rewrite disabled for Meridian until sidecar patch is deployed. Medium term: merge sidecar PR to preserve pin-token across rewrite and add a forced pin-sync when snapshot ID changes; add critical telemetry and an alert on pin-drop rates. Long term: adjust rollout orchestration to avoid snapshot distributions that can overlap with active pin windows or make reconciliation immediate on snapshot increment.

notes:
Customer is on a Dedicated contract; follow-up retrospective scheduled with product and infra teams to update the canary runbook and add explicit guidance about header rewrites during pin-sensitive rollouts.

[Routing fallback loop triggered by model-pin grace-period mismatch during canary drain shift]
description:
Issue summary:
During a scheduled canary drain-shift in us-east the customer's pinned-model sessions began bouncing between the pinned variant and fallback variants, producing a sustained routing loop. The loop caused repeated model switches for in-flight sessions and elevated 5xx and latency for affected tenants.

Impact:
- Multiple tenants on a dedicated pool (OrionMaps) observed mixed outputs and elevated error rates for ~18 minutes.
- Production traffic experienced token-latency spikes (median +120ms) and 502/504 counts increased.

Environment:
- Dedicated capacity pool (dedicated), us-east region, host cluster rp-prod-ded-3
- Canary rollout in progress for model openchat-7b-v2 -> openchat-7b-v2-quant (weight shift 10% -> 50%)

Observed at 2026-03-10T09:12:00Z in customer telemetry and platform metrics.


steps_to_reproduce:
1) Start a weighted canary promote of model variant v2-quant in a dedicated pool (10% -> 50% over 10m).
2) Trigger a graceful drain shift of a hot node (scale down / drain with grace-period 30s) overlapping the canary window,
3) Replay a cohort of pinned session tokens bound to the older variant while the router re-evaluates pin tokens and fallback policies.
4) Observe routing decisions and token logs at the edge proxy and router reconciliation endpoints.

observed_behavior:
Router TTL and pin grace-period are mismatched: pin tokens on edge proxies expired later than router's in-memory pin lease, causing router to consider the session unpinned and route to fallback variant. The edge continued to present a pin token, router accepted the request, then later re-evaluated on health probes and re-routed back to pinned variant — creating repeated switch attempts and a fallback loop.

expected_behavior:
During overlap of drain/shifts and canary weight change, the router and edge proxies should have consistent pin lease semantics so a session remains pinned until a single coherent handoff completes (no repeated switch attempts). Router should not short-circuit pinned sessions mid-request or flip precedence more than once per session lifecycle.

logs:
[09:12:03Z] edge-proxy/rp-edge-12: pin_token_present=""
[09:12:04Z] router/rp-router-4: session=tenant-847 pin_state=EXPIRED_LEASE local_pin=null fallback_selected=openchat-7b-v2-quant
[09:12:06Z] serving-runtime/node-3: healthprobe=failed draining=true; node removed from pool
[09:12:15Z] router/rp-router-4: session=tenant-847 pin_state=ACTIVE leased_to=node-1 route=original_variant
Error excerpts: 502: "model backend connection reset" correlated with immediate prior route flip

investigation_notes:
Hypothesis 1: Router in-memory pin lease shorter than edge cookie grace. When the node drains, router marks local lease expired and re-routes to fallback variant; edge still sends pin token leading to acceptance and later re-evaluation.
Hypothesis 2: Canary-coordinator triggered a background rebalancer that prompted router to aggressively re-resolve pins for cohorts tied to the drained node, amplifying flip frequency.
Findings: Correlation matrix shows re-route events cluster around node drain start and completion. Router config shows pin_lease_ttl=20s, edge cookie grace configured at 90s on the customer's dedicated pool. Canary coordinator re-eval interval observed at 15s causing overlap with router TTL windows.
Partial root cause: Inconsistent TTL semantics across edge/router/canary-coordinator; also missing a request-safety guard that should avoid changing a route mid-request when pin_token present and connection to previous backend was healthy.
Risk: High for any overlapping rollouts and drain operations in dedicated pools where operators tune local grace periods; could cause customer-visible quality degradation and transient errors.

comments:
2026-03-10T09:20:00Z - Support (Anika Patel): Customer reported intermittent mixed outputs after canary promote. Attached request ids and timestamps. Asked for tracing and timeline.
2026-03-10T09:32:12Z - SRE (Diego Ramos): Identified spike in router re-evaluations coincident with node drain events. Pin lease TTL on router ephemeral cache set to 20s while edge cookie grace set to 90s. Hypothesis: lease mismatch leads to flip-flop.
2026-03-10T10:01:45Z - ENG (Maya Chen): Runbook done: pinned session debugging. Gathering router logs and KV cache snapshots. Noted router had aggressive background re-check after node removal.
2026-03-10T11:05:00Z - Support (Anika Patel): Shared customer mitigation: temporarily paused canary weight change and queued further rollouts until fix. Customer accepted workaround pending RCA.
2026-03-12T14:10:00Z - ENG (Diego Ramos): Working on coordinated TTL alignment patch and extra guard to prevent re-route if request has pin_token header and original route succeeded within last 60s.

resolution:
Workaround (applied 2026-03-10T10:15Z): Pause ongoing canary weight adjustments and postpone scheduled node drains for the affected dedicated pool. Instruct customer to avoid concurrent drain+promote windows.
Hotfix (deployed 2026-03-12): Align router pin_lease_ttl with edge cookie grace by default for dedicated pools and add a request-safety guard: if request includes a valid pin_token and the previous route returned a successful backend response within N seconds, do not re-route mid-request. Patch rolled to canary routers with a staged rollout 20% -> 100% over 2h.
Follow-up: Add telemetry alert for pin_lease_ttl mismatch across components and update runbook to require coordinated TTL settings on dedicated pools. Engineering to add an e2e test for drain+canary overlap to prevent regressions. Customer notified and will monitor for 48 hours.

[Edge retry path strips model-pin header resulting in unpinned requests routed to degraded fallback during canary]
description:
Issue summary: After a canary rollout yesterday, IonHealth reported intermittent requests from long-lived sessions being routed to the degraded fallback variant when upstream edge retries occurred. Impact: Customer saw ~0.6% of session requests routed to the degraded model, causing hallucination regressions and a support escalation. 2) Trigger a simulated transient 502 from an upstream node (eg. kill serving worker) so the edge proxy retries the request
3) Observe routed variant in response metadata and request traces

curl -v -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -H "X-Redwood-Pin: tenant123|gpt-redwood-13b-v2" -d '{"prompt":"ping"}' https://api.redwood.test/v1/generate -o /tmp/resp.json

[token-bucket sync failure causes pinned-model fallback during canary rollout]
description:
Issue summary:
During a scheduled canary rollout for redwood-v2-quant (tenant-scoped rollout for Clipr Labs, dedicated tier), a subset of requests that had active model pins were being routed to the fallback model variant. Customers reported sudden quality regressions and mixed outputs for pinned sessions.

Impact:
- ~1.8% of Clipr Labs traffic in us-east was served by the fallback model for pinned sessions over a 27-minute window.
- Customer-visible quality regressions for chat completions and hallucination rate increase reported.
- No broader platform-wide alert; localized to us-east edge cluster dealing with canary cohort.

Environment:
- prod | us-east (edge cluster: edge-us-east-3)
- Customer: Clipr Labs (dedicated capacity pool assigned)
- Rollout: weighted canary 5% -> 10% in progress at time of incident

Steps to reproduce (observed):
1) Simulate tenant with pinned sessions sending steady request rate through edge-us-east-3.
2) Introduced canary traffic by marking subset of hosts as v2-canary and starting rollout.
3) Several edge proxies returned 429/over-quota responses then the routing layer invoked fallback policy even when a model pin existed.
4) After fallback, session responses came from redwood-v2-legacy variant (fallback model) instead of pinned v2-quant.

Observed logs/snippets:
- edge-proxy logs: "token-bucket: local-balance=0, tenant=clipr-123, decision=reject -> fallback-route"
- rate-limiter ec2 metrics: token-sync lag spikes at 03:12:14 UTC; hop-count mismatch between proxies: 3 vs 1.
- routing trace: "pin=yes but local-throttle=true => applied fallback policy"

Initial hypothesis:
- A recent change to token-bucket synchronization (PR referenced below) introduced an infrequent race where bucket-sync daemon fell behind for newly-promoted canary hosts. Proxies with stale token balance interpreted tenant as over-quota and invoked fallback-circuit despite pinned routing decisions. Because local throttle check ran before pin-coherence check in the routing path, fallback took precedence.

Investigation notes:
- Confirmed correlation between token-sync lag and fallback events using tracing (trace IDs attached in comments).
- Replayed traffic against a reproduce cluster with intentional bucket-sync lag; observed deterministic fallback behavior when sync lag > 12s.
- Audit of deployment shows edge-proxy config was updated 2026-03-10 02:50 UTC to change token-bucket sync interval from 5s -> 30s (to reduce DB load) in canary hosts only (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/edge-proxy/pull/462).
- Routing path analysis shows ordering: local-throttle check -> pin-check -> route decision. When local-throttle rejects, routing code sets fallback even if pin-check would prefer original model. This ordering predates recent rollout logic.

Customer communication summary:
- 2026-03-10 03:40 UTC: initial alert from Clipr Labs support contact (noise of mixed-quality responses).
- 2026-03-10 03:55 UTC: Support acknowledged, escalated to SRE and serving-runtime.
- 2026-03-10 04:12 UTC: Temporary mitigation applied and communicated to customer.

Mitigation and resolution:
- Immediate mitigation (03:57 UTC): increased local token balance on affected proxies and forced token-sync to run ad-hoc across cluster (manual kick). This restored normal routing for pinned sessions within ~8 minutes.
- Code rollback (04:05 UTC): reverted canary-specific token-sync interval change so all hosts use 5s sync.
- Hotfix (deployed 2026-03-10 10:30 UTC): added routing guard so model-pin check has priority over local throttle for pinned sessions; local-throttle re-evaluated as a soft-fail (logs counters) rather than immediate fallback for pinned sessions.
- Post-deploy verification: 12:00 UTC automated checks confirmed no pinned-session fallbacks for 24h window; Clipr Labs verified quality restored.

Root cause:
1) Token-bucket sync interval change on canary hosts created out-of-sync local balances.
2) Routing logic evaluated local-throttle before honoring model-pin, causing premature fallback decisions when local-balance was stale.

Follow-up actions (owners):
- edge-proxy (Marcus Reed): strengthen token-sync telemetry and add alert for token-sync lag > 5s (ETA 2026-03-15).
- routing (Lena Zhang): make pin-check highest-priority decision in routing path and add unit/integration tests (ETA 2026-03-18).
- release (Infra Eng): revert any environment-specific throttling config changes without compatibility checks for pin semantics (process update, ETA 2026-03-16).
- SRE (Diego Morales): run a targeted chaos test simulating token-sync lag to validate no pinned fallbacks (ETA 2026-03-20).

Postmortem required: yes (owner: Diego Morales).

[Pinned-session entropy and route reversion after partial canary rollback]
description:
Issue summary: After a partial canary rollback initiated for redwood-7b-v1.2, a subset of tenant sessions that had pinned model versions experienced route reversion to a legacy variant and intermittent mixed responses. Impact: customer saw mixed model outputs for live sessions, some requests routed to an older variant without pin being explicitly changed. Environment: production (dedicated) in us-east-1 for NimbleScribe. Observed starting 2026-03-10 08:12 UTC during canary rollback window.

Expected behavior: pinned sessions should retain their pinned variant during rollbacks, or fall back deterministically to configured fallback policy. Actual behavior: a cohort (~0.8% of active sessions for the tenant) lost pin affinity and were routed to legacy variant (llama2-13b-quant), producing inconsistent outputs and causing a short-term quality regression for customer traffic.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Start with tenant using pinned model redwood-7b-v1.2.
2) Initiate canary promote to redwood-7b-v1.3 for 10% traffic, wait for health probes.
3) Run partial rollback to revert canary at 09:58 UTC (abort promote, commit rollback).
4) Observe session affinity map and edge headers for affected tenant cohort.
5) Reproduce by replaying traffic from recorded session IDs through edge (see attached session list).

investigation:
Timeline reconstruction shows a narrow window where three events coincided: (1) operator-initiated partial rollback commit on control-plane, (2) a burst of health-checks hitting edge sidecars which triggered header sanitizer rule, and (3) control-plane snapshot merge code applied snapshots out-of-order for ephemeral commit IDs. Logs show 'commit-order-mismatch' warning immediately before edge removed X-Redwood-Pin for a subset of sessions. Session lease renewal traces indicated delayed lease refresh due to reconciler holding a lock while merging snapshots. The combination produced transient entropy in the routing decision: sessions without X-Redwood-Pin were evaluated by route-engine and matched fallback variant ruleset that selected a legacy model.

Hypotheses tested: header-stripping during health probes (confirmed), reconciler commit-ordering race (reproducible in staging with canary scripts), session lease TTL renewal delay under lock (observed in traces).

root_cause:
A race during partial canary rollback where control-plane snapshot merge applied snapshots with commit-order mismatch while edge-sidecar health-probe sanitization removed pin headers for requests. The reconciler's commit application path temporarily blocked lease renewals, leading to pin eviction for a small session cohort. Combined, this produced non-deterministic routing and fallback to legacy variants.

mitigation:
Immediate: re-applied pin metadata for affected tenant sessions from control-plane snapshot backups and forced lease renewal. Added a temporary rule to disable header sanitizer for X-Redwood-Pin during rollback windows.
Medium-term: deployed reconciler patch to enforce strict commit-serial application and prevent snapshot reorders. Deployed edge-sidecar patch to treat X-Redwood-Pin as protected header (not removed by health-probe sanitizer). Added metrics/alert to detect header removals and commit-order warnings.

2026-03-10 11:20 UTC: Reapplied pins for 142 affected session IDs (script: tools/reapply_pins.sh --tenant nimble-123 --file sessions.csv).
2026-03-10 13:45 UTC: Disabled legacy header sanitizer rule in prod for edge cluster us-east-1.
2026-03-11 22:30 UTC: Reconciler patch merged and rolled to canary (PR #4203).
2026-03-12 02:10 UTC: Edge-sidecar patch rolled (PR #3891) and protected header behavior enabled.

resolution_notes:
Patch to control-plane reconciler and edge-sidecar released. Backfill script reapplied pins and forced lease renewals. Customer confirmed that mixed outputs stopped within one hour of mitigation. Monitoring dashboards show no recurrence for 48 hours post-deploy. Ticket marked Resolved pending postmortem follow-ups.

[Runtime inference forensics interactive walkthrough - Arcadia Retail]
summary:
Interactive console walkthrough focused on tracing, request-level forensics, and error analysis. Demonstrated request playback, KV cache fallthrough detection, model fallback routing, and SLO/latency breakdowns. Discussed security/compliance needs (SOC 2, SSO, KMS), POC scope, and benchmark run next week.

transcript:
Header: Date: 2027-07-22 15:00 PDT | Duration: 53m | Redwood: Alex Kim (AE), Maya Patel (SE), Diego Ramos (Product) | Arcadia: Jordan Lee (Head of Platform), Priya Banerjee (SRE), Samir Gupta (ML Eng), Lena Ortiz (Security)

[00:00] Alex (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, really glad to be here. quick intro — I'm Alex, AE for the west region, with Maya our solutions eng and Diego from product.
[00:10] Jordan (Arcadia): Thanks, Alex. Jordan here. We're excited to see the console playbook you're talking about — particularly how we can map requests to traces and figure out why some inference calls go sideways.
[00:20] Maya (Redwood): Awesome. Today's plan: we'll show live request playback, how request IDs map to model runs, KV cache hits vs miss detection, and the fallback routing when dedicated capacity is saturated. We'll also show latency/cost per route. Questions before we dive in?
[00:30] Priya (Arcadia): Just to set context — our production inference runs on a mix of hosted endpoints and an on-prem private cluster for regulated SKUs. P95 latency target is 150ms for interactive queries, and anything above 250ms is a problem. We also have strict retention rules — 30 days for request logs.
[00:45] Alex (Redwood): Good to know. We'll show the timeline and filter by retention windows and you can see redactions.
[00:55] [01:00] Maya (Redwood): I'm sharing my screen — opening the Runtime Forensics tab in the console. One note: transcription may spell product names funny — our internal name is Redwood Optimize — sometimes the auto transcript writes it as Red wood Opti. ignore that.
[01:20] [01:30] Maya (Redwood): Ok first, here is a request list. You can search by request_id, user_id, or route. I'm going to pick a request that failed with a model fallback. You can see at 0.00 the initial enqueue, then 45ms later the model 13b was selected, but then we had a KV cache miss and a fallback to a quantized variant.
[01:50] Samir (Arcadia): When you say KV cache miss can you show the indicators? We had an incident where the cache thrashing created huge tail latencies last month.
[02:05] Maya (Redwood): Yep — in the timeline you'll see a green block for 'KV cache hit', yellow for 'prefetch', red for 'KV cache miss' — also a small note that sometimes the transcript or the event name shows as "KV cash" which annoyed me in the logs — transcription issues. But here's the miss, see the spike in token compute after the miss.
[02:30] [03:00] Jordan (Arcadia): Is the miss detection deterministic? Could we get false positives when we do partial key sets?
[03:10] Maya (Redwood): Good question. Detection combines the request prefix fingerprint and the runtime cache lookup. We mark a miss when the runtime had to fetch embeddings/keys from main memory and there's a corresponding delta in compute time. There are heuristics so very short prefixes can look like misses — we annotate those as 'probable miss'. We surface confidence scores.
[03:35] Priya (Arcadia): Are those confidence scores available via API? We need programmatic alerts.
[03:40] Maya (Redwood): Yes — both the console and the API expose the raw events. You can subscribe to cache_miss events and push to your alerting.
[03:50] [04:00] Alex (Redwood): Another critical piece is model fallback routing — when you have dedicated pools full, the smart router will route to a cheaper quantized variant or to hosted lane with a different latency. We'll show an example of an automatic fallback that kept the app alive but at a different latency and quality tier.
[04:20] [04:30] Maya (Redwood): Here's a request where the policy says prefer dedicated, else fallback to hosted low-cost. Notice the quality flag in the trace — we log the model id, quantization, and a quality estimate (we call it Q-score in the console). Note: sometimes the console transcribes Q-score as 'cue score' if audio is bad — ignore that.
[04:55] Samir (Arcadia): How do you capture quality regressions? We need regression detection tied to a set of prompts.
[05:05] Maya (Redwood): We integrate Optimize-style evals — you can pin a prompt set and the console will run diffs when we swap model variants. It generates an alert on semantic drift beyond thresholds. We can wire that to your slack.
[05:20] [06:00] Jordan (Arcadia): Walk me through a real failure scenario — like the one we saw earlier this quarter where certain routes had intermittent 400s and some 502s.
[06:15] Maya (Redwood): Sure — pulling an example. This one shows a 502 returned from the runtime because KV cache backend timed out. In the trace you can see: initial request, cache lookup, timeout event, then fallback model selection, then final return to caller with 200 but with degraded tokens per second. We also keep the raw stderr captured for the runtime error — redacted per retention policy.
[06:40] Priya (Arcadia): Can we see the actual error text? For compliance we sometimes need stack snippets for RCA. 
[06:50] Diego (Redwood): We can surface error snippets but by default they are redacted in the hosted logs. For Dedicated and Private you can enable verbose logs stored in your VPC and integrate with your SIEM. We'll include retention and redaction options in the security pack.
[07:10] [07:30] Lena (Arcadia): On the SOC2 note — do you have audit logs for who accessed request payloads? We need user-level access trails and SSO.
[07:40] Alex (Redwood): Yes — audit trail per token and per-user. We support SAML SSO and RBAC, and KMS for encryption keys. We also integrate with HSM providers if required. We'll send the SOC 2 evidence and the HSM integration notes after the call.
[08:00] Samir (Arcadia): Back to traces — how granular are timestamps? We need sub-10ms resolution for distributed tracing.
[08:10] Maya (Redwood): Our runtime timestamps are microsecond-resolution in the trace, but the console UI shows ms. You can export raw traces in newline-delimited JSON for post-hoc analysis.
[08:25] [09:00] Jordan (Arcadia): One pain point for us is mapping external request IDs (from our frontend) to the runtime request_id. How do you correlate?
[09:15] Maya (Redwood): We have a header mapping — you can pass x-arcadia-request-id and the console will show both ids. You can also configure a mapping rule so the external id is primary in the UI.
[09:30] Priya (Arcadia): Can we add custom tags to filter traces by customer_id or experiment flags?
[09:40] Maya (Redwood): Yep — metadata tags come through the request payload and are indexed. There are size limits and sanitized fields — we'll share the limits.
[09:50] [10:00] Alex (Redwood): Now I want to show the request playback — Maya will re-run the request against a pinned model in a sandbox. This helps reproduce flakies. Maya?
[10:10] Maya (Redwood): Running playback now. You'll see the timeline advance and a side-by-side diff of tokens. Playback supports three modes: exact replay (same input), sandbox with synthetic token seeding, and A/B with two model variants.
[10:30] [11:00] Maya (Redwood): Ok playback finished. Note the difference: the original had a small dropout at token 42 because the runtime retried a failed KV fetch. Playback shows the retry pattern and we annotate the retry type (fast/linear backoff).
[11:20] Samir (Arcadia): Is playback deterministic? If we replay after a model update will tokens differ?
[11:30] Maya (Redwood): If the model weights changed you'll get different tokens. Playback includes a 'model signature' header that pins model version and quantization. For critical repros we recommend pinning an exact model hash in the POC.
[11:50] [12:30] Jordan (Arcadia): What about SLO dashboards — can we slice by customer, route, and model variant?
[12:40] Maya (Redwood): Yes — the console has templated SLO dashboards. You can build custom widgets to show p50/p95/p99 latency, cost per token, and error rate by model. You can also set auto-alerts if p95 crosses threshold.
[13:00] [13:30] Priya (Arcadia): We had an event where batch sizes increased and that spiked latency. Can your console show batch size distribution correlated with latency?
[13:45] Maya (Redwood): Absolutely — sampler events include batch size and GPU utilization. We show a heatmap of batch distribution over time. If you want, we can also correlate with autoscale events.
[14:10] [15:00] Alex (Redwood): Quick tangent — cost controls: token breakdown by prefix vs generation and suggestions for quantization. Diego, may want to add any product notes here.
[15:20] Diego (Redwood): Yeah, we run an Optimize analysis that looks at sequence length distributions and suggests quantization profiles or batching windows. For Arcadia with short interactive queries, we often suggest enabling prefix caching and a medium quant profile to hit latency SLOs while reducing unit cost.
[15:50] Samir (Arcadia): Is the Optimize analysis automated or a manual report? We have 20 routes so manual is too heavy.
[16:05] Diego (Redwood): It's automated — you can run it on historical traces, and it produces recommendations ranked by estimated cost savings and expected latency impact. You can accept them through the console as a change set.
[16:25] [17:00] Jordan (Arcadia): Security again — if we run a private deployment on-prem will we still get the same tracing fidelity?
[17:10] Maya (Redwood): Yes — the private control plane ships with the same agent and the traces are collected locally then optionally mirrored to Redwood's console if you opt in. For air-gapped installs we provide an on-prem analytics bundle.
[17:30] Lena (Arcadia): Do you support field encryption or token-level redaction? We cannot log PII in plaintext.
[17:40] Alex (Redwood): Field-level redaction is supported. You can configure redaction rules and a scrubber pipeline. We also support envelope encryption with customer-managed KMS.
[17:55] [18:30] Priya (Arcadia): Ok, let's talk about the POC: we want to run a week-long benchmark against 500 sample requests, measure median and p95 for dedicated vs hosted fallback, and validate cost numbers. Can we do that?
[18:45] Maya (Redwood): Absolutely. We'll run the benchmark from a dedicated pool sized to your expected concurrency, and then simulate the overload to exercise fallback rules. We'll export the traces and send a benchmark report.
[19:05] Samir (Arcadia): For the overload simulation, can you mimic network jitter and KV backend slowness? That's what caused our last incident.
[19:15] Maya (Redwood): We can add fault injection to the POC harness — introduce artificial latency on the KV layer and on the network. That will surface fallback and retry behavior.
[19:30] [20:00] Jordan (Arcadia): How do you recommend we instrument our app headers to make troubleshooting faster?
[20:10] Maya (Redwood): Send both x-arcadia-request-id and a user_session_id; include route and experiment tags. Also include a short stack trace capture for client errors. We'll share a small middleware snippet — Samir, you'll like it — that auto-injects these headers.
[20:30] Samir (Arcadia): Great.
[20:40] [21:00] Alex (Redwood): Quick note on compliance: we'll redact the actual prompt text in the hosted logs by default, but for the POC we can enable dev-mode which keeps raw prompts in a secure bucket for debugging. This has to be agreed in the security addendum.
[21:20] Lena (Arcadia): We'll want the dev-mode turned off after debugging window. We need an attestation.
[21:30] Alex (Redwood): Sure — we'll include an attestation template.

Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-23
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 57 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE); Jordan Patel (Redwood SE); Ivy Rogers (Redwood CSM); Carlos Vega (CTO, Asterian); Priya Menon (Lead ML Eng); Samir Patel (Full-stack Eng); Lena Ortiz (Security)

[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick agenda — we do a short intro to the hosted API, then Jordan will demo streaming and params, we’ll cover retries and backoff, then peek at the Console Optimize suggestions. We’ll save Qs after each section.

[00:18] Carlos (Asterian): Thanks. high-level goal for us: we want chat responses under 200ms p50 and p95 under 600ms for simple retrieval-ish prompts. also we need to understand data controls — VPC or private options later.

[00:34] Maya: Got it. that latency target is tight but doable for short responses depending on model choice and batching. Jordan — show the simple streaming sample?

[00:48] Jordan (Redwood SE): Yeah, sure. I’ll share my screen — quick code sample in node. so we do a streaming chat request, you see partial tokens arrive as a chunk. this is the way applications render tokens as they come. in the SDK we default to a continuous stream. the payload here — messages array, model spec, and generation params like temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences.

[01:12] Samir (Asterian): Quick q — for interactivity, should we keep temperature at 0.0 for deterministic responses? or 0.2?

[01:21] Jordan: For UI chat where you want deterministic answers, 0 to 0.2 is typical. 0.0 is more deterministic but might be slightly repetitive. also note top_p interacts with temperature, so pick one to tune. we recommend starting with temp 0.1 and top_p 0.9 for most assistant flows.

[02:05] Jordan: Now on retries: the hosted API can surface transient errors — rate limit 429s or internal 5xx. our client libraries have an idempotency token option for generative calls so you can safely retry without duplicate side-effects. for non-idempotent calls we recommend an explicit dedupe layer.

[02:28] Lena (Security): when you say idempotency token, how are those stored? do you persist them in our side only or do you have retention? we need to track for audit logs SOC2.

[02:42] Maya: good q. logs and audit trails are available in Console — request ids, token-level cost and latency. for Private customers with VPC we can offer shorter retention windows and customer-managed KMS for encryption. we’ll share the security pack after the call.

[03:05] Priya: We do a lot of short prompts ~20 tokens, most are retrieval-augmented. how does batching interact with latency for small requests? we’re worried batching will increase tail latency.

[03:22] Jordan: Right — batching gives throughput gains but can add queuing delay. our runtime does dynamic batching where we bound batch wait time; you can configure target latency SLOs in the Dedicated plan. for Hosted, the default is conservative — it optimizes for low-latency for small requests, but for high QPS you’ll see batching kick in. in the Console Optimize tab we also show suggestions: enable prefix caching for repeated context, or configure KV-cache sizing.

[04:10] Carlos: KV cache — is that the same as the keys we store for repetition? i’ve seen docs call it K V cash which confused my team.

[04:18] Jordan: yeah sorry the docs sometimes are abbreviated — KV cache is token-level key-value cache used for decoder-only models to avoid recomputing earlier keys. helps when you have long histories and a lot of repeated prefixes.

[04:41] Samir: can you show us an example of a failed stream and how to recover on the client? we saw partial tokens then connection reset earlier in a POC.

[04:50] Jordan: Sure — demo time. I’ll start a stream and we’ll simulate a transient connection reset. when the socket drops, client should check the last accepted token index, then re-issue a request with an idempotency token and a partial context (or use the server-side KV cache if available). if you can’t resume, fall back to a fresh request but with a conservative backoff. the SDK includes automatic exponential backoff with jitter.

[05:35] Priya: you mentioned idempotency for generation — how do you prevent duplicated completions for say, a billing side-effect?

[05:44] Maya: For side-effects, the best practice is to separate generation from execution. generation is treated as a read; any write or billing action should be done after a deterministic confirmation step. we also support function/tool-calling patterns where the model returns structured JSON which you validate before executing.

[06:12] Carlos: in terms of models — which family should we pick for sub-second p95? our prompts are short but need good factuality.

[06:22] Jordan: Short prompts + high factuality, start with a medium-sized open model in the Redwood catalog tuned for low latency — we’ll recommend two candidates in the follow-up. if you need the absolute lowest latency we can point to smaller quantized variants or Dedicated with pinned capacity. tradeoffs: smaller model = lower cost and latency but may have lower factuality on complex queries.

[06:50] Samir: what about token billing for streaming partial tokens? do you get billed per partial chunk?

[06:57] Maya: Billing is per token emitted; partial chunks don’t change billing semantics. Console shows token counts and cost breakdown per request and per token.

[07:12] Jordan: switching to Console — I’ll flip to the Optimize tab. here you can upload representative prompts and get model suggestions, quantization recommendations, and caching hints. the Optimize tool will flag prompts with high-generation cost and show you where batching or caching can help.

[07:42] Jordan (screen): See this sample run: p50 120ms, p95 580ms on the medium model with 8ms kernel selection overhead. if we enable prefix caching and reduce max_tokens for these flows you can shave 30-40% from p95.

[08:05] Priya: does Optimize simulate our exact prompt distribution, or is it heuristic?

[08:12] Jordan: You can upload traces and Optimize will run against the selected model profile. it’s not a perfect playground but it gives actionable suggestions — like: reduce temperature for template responses, add a 0.2s target batch wait to increase throughput, or recommend quantized weights for Dedicated pools.

[08:45] Lena: Security wise — can we get SSO integration, RBAC, and customer-managed keys mentioned earlier? also audit logs retention policy?

[08:56] Ivy (CSM): Absolutely — we support SAML SSO, fine-grained RBAC in Console and for Private deployments you can bring your own KMS. retention windows can be configured per account for logs; default hosted retention is 90 days, and we have an enterprise add-on for extended retention.

[09:18] Carlos: timeline — we’re hoping to pilot next quarter. what’s a realistic path?

[09:25] Maya: Pilot: sandbox + benchmark this week, then a 2–4 week POC if results look good. if you need Dedicated or Private, that typically takes 4–8 weeks for provisioning and security review.

[09:40] Jordan: quick demo of a retry scenario in code — (reads) send request with idempotency-key, on 5xx do exponential backoff starting at 200ms doubling up to 3s with full jitter. on 429s backoff longer and respect Retry-After header. if you need guaranteed ordering/at-most-once semantics we can recommend a control-plane pattern.

[10:10] Samir: are there built-in client libraries for our stack — node/java/python?

[10:16] Maya: yes — official SDKs for node, python, and java. we also publish curl examples for quick smoke tests.

[10:31] Carlos: Ok, let's do the sandbox. we want the following in the invite: a) sample prompts, b) expected p95 targets, c) security checklist.

[10:39] Maya: noted. I will provision the sandbox and put those items in the ticket. Jordan will run a small latency script and record it. Ivy will attach security docs.

[10:52] Priya: one more technical question — for streaming token resume, do you recommend re-sending the full prompt history? that’s costly if the history is long.

[11:02] Jordan: If you have KV cache enabled, you can resume by sending just the delta and referencing the cache key — avoids re-sending entire history. otherwise you can hybird: send the recent window plus an identifier for the rest and rely on server-side cache where supported. still, if you often need resume, Dedicated gives better cache hit rates.

[11:30] Samir (interruption): lmk if you have a sample of the backoff code — i’ll try it after the call.

[11:34] Jordan: I'll paste the snippet in the ticket — small node example with idempotency and jitter.

[12:05] Maya: quick recap before Qs: 1) we demoed streaming and generation params; 2) discussed retries, idempotency tokens, and backoff; 3) Console Optimize can suggest batching/caching/quantization changes; 4) next steps: sandbox invite, benchmark run, security packet.

[12:28] Carlos: sounds good. two final asks: can we get a short checklist for when to pick Hosted vs Dedicated? and can you include estimated monthly cost for our projected QPS?

[12:40] Maya: yes — Jordan will draft a Hosted vs Dedicated decision checklist and we’ll include a cost estimate for your QPS scenarios.

[12:50] Ivy: I'll schedule the security follow-up with Lena for next week, and add the SOC2/KMS docs to the ticket.

[13:02] Maya: Great — thanks everyone. we’ll send the sandbox invite by EOD tomorrow and target the benchmark run mid-next week.

Notes on transcription quirks: occasional mis-attributions (Speaker 2 vs Jordan), some acronyms spelled out weirdly (K V cache / K V cash), slight stuttering in a few places, filler words retained.

Nadia R: couple of quick notes we see frequently:
- If an intermediate proxy buffers the response (nginx with proxy_buffering on, Cloudflare default), the client won't get chunks until the buffer fills or proxy flushes. That looks like 'partial outputs' behavior.
- If the proxy closes the TCP connection because of an idle timeout, the client gets an abrupt close and then reconnects. Duplicate tokens happen when client doesn't dedupe by `id`/message timestamp.

Ethan L: suggested fixes (short):
- Ensure upstream emits regular keepalives/comments (SSE comment lines) every 15s: `: keepalive\n\n` or a small whitespace chunk so proxies see activity.

- For nginx (important): disable buffering and extend read timeouts. Example config snippet to put in the proxy block: 
```
proxy_buffering off;
proxy_http_version 1.1;
proxy_set_header Connection '';
proxy_set_header X-Accel-Buffering no;
proxy_read_timeout 3600s;
proxy_send_timeout 3600s;
chunked_transfer_encoding on;
```
- For Cloudflare: if used, prefer a bypass for streaming endpoints (page rule to disable caching and response buffering), or move streaming traffic behind an NLB (TCP passthrough) to avoid HTTP buffering. Cloudflare Workers/Stream product can also be used.

[Stream continuity negotiation and fragment handoff for resilient SSE streaming]
description:
Implement a resilient SSE streaming layer that supports graceful fragment handoff between serving workers, a lightweight continuity negotiation handshake for clients, and compatibility shims for older chunk-id-based clients. The goal is to minimize token re-generation on reconnects, preserve function-call/structured-output boundaries across handoffs, and provide clear metrics and observability for resume success rates. This ticket covers protocol design, server implementation changes (handoff markers + soft-state resume tokens), client-facing compatibility headers, and an automated test harness for reconnect scenarios.

acceptance_criteria:
Clients can reconnect after an ephemeral worker restart and resume a stream with <= 2 tokens of duplication in 99% of synthetic reconnect tests
Function call frames (structured outputs) are not split across resumed segments: resumed stream replays any incomplete function-call frame as a single re-emitted boundary or signals a deterministic rewind to the last safe boundary
Backward compatibility header X-RI-Chunk-Compat toggles legacy chunk-id resume behavior for older clients; new default uses Continuity Token negotiation
Fragment handoff is implemented such that ownership transfer between workers does not require client-side changes and adds <1ms median extra latency for in-flight token emission
End-to-end integration tests covering: worker preemption, network flapping, delayed fragment arrival, and cross-zone handoffs are added and pass in CI
Dashboard panels added for resume-success-rate, average replayed-tokens-per-resume, and fragment-handoff-rate; alerts configured for >1% resume failure over 10m

design_decisions:
Use a soft-state Continuity Token (base64) containing a compact sequence window and a checksum instead of exposing raw offsets to clients
A two-way negotiation: client sends last-seen token in reconnect handshake; server validates and either accepts (resume) or responds with a deterministic fallback point and reason
Introduce an internal handoff marker (HND-<seq>) appended to fragment envelopes that workers can emit to identify in-flight handoff boundaries without altering user-visible payloads
To protect function-call atomicity, the runtime will treat any fragment that contains a function-call start without a corresponding function-call end as an unsafe boundary and will rewind to the last safe frame on resume
Legacy support: if X-RI-Chunk-Compat: 1 is present, the server will attempt to reconcile using per-chunk ids and a best-effort replay mode; this mode is opt-in and not eligible for SLA-backed resume guarantees

implementation_notes:
Server: extend existing fragment envelope with fields: continuity_token (opaque), handoff_marker (HND-<seq>), and optional provenance header for worker_id
Worker handoff flow: origin worker emits final fragment with handoff_marker and registers the token in a shared faststore (redis with TTL=1m); new owner verifies and claims the token before emitting further fragments
Reconnect handshake: POST /v1/streams/:id/reconnect with body {last_seen_token: "..."}; response 200 {resume: true, server_token: "..."} or 409 {resume: false, fallback_token: "...", reason: "handoff_mismatch"}
Function-call handling: add fc_id per function-call boundary inside fragment metadata; on resume, if fc_id is open, server will re-emit a close frame or rewind to safe boundary depending on policy
Compatibility shim: X-RI-Chunk-Compat toggles parsing of chunk_id header and engages older resume path; warn in logs when engaged
Observability: emit metrics: resume_attempt, resume_success, resumed_replayed_tokens, handoff_claim_latency, handoff_failures; tag by project, model, region
Testing: extend chaos harness to preempt worker after sending partial fragment, simulate client reconnect with different tokens, and verify deterministic outcomes
Docs: update streaming API reference with reconnect examples for new clients and a migration guide for chunk-id clients

tasks:
Protocol: write formal spec doc and sample reconnect flows (Lucas)
Server impl: add handoff_marker and token registration (Anika)
Runtime: integrate fc_id handling and safe-boundary rewind logic (Ravi)
Client SDK: add reconnect helper and examples for Continuity Token handshake (DX)
Tests: add chaos and deterministic resume tests in CI (QA)
Observability: add metrics and dashboard panels (Infra Observability)
Docs: draft migration guide and API examples (Docs)
Rollout: staged rollout plan and canary with runtime-2.4 (Ops)
Post-rollout: collect resume metrics for 72h and open follow-up if replayed_tokens_per_resume > 3% (PM)
Security review: schedule security review for token MAC design (Security)
Compatibility toggle: add feature flag to control legacy chunk-id path (Platform)
Create runbook for operators to manually reconcile stuck handoff tokens (SRE)

notes:
Initial spike found a race when origin worker cleaned its local cache before registering token in faststore — fixed by ordering commit before cache prune (see PR #4892)
We debated exposing absolute byte offsets vs opaque tokens; chose opaque tokens to avoid leaking internal buffer layout and to make future changes backwards-incompatible-safe
Design reviewed with PM and DX (Priya) on 2026-02-18; agreed to include explicit function-call ATOMICITY section in docs
Security: continuity tokens are not secrets but include a MAC to prevent tampering; KMS signing was considered but deferred (low-risk and higher latency)

[Resilient streaming schema: fallback stubs and idempotent tool-relay semantics]
description:
Problem statement: Clients consuming streamed structured output must be able to make progress even when downstream tool invocations fail or when the network cuts the stream. Current behavior either aborts the emit entirely or leaves consumers with partial, non-actionable payloads. We need a pragmatic contract that ensures predictable consumer behavior, clear retry semantics for function/tool calls, and measurable observability for debugging and economics.\n\nGoals:\n- Define a minimal, deterministic start-of-stream stub that gives downstream services enough schema and provenance to act (routing, caching, UI placeholders).\n- Specify idempotent tool-relay semantics and tokens so tool calls can be retried safely across disconnects and platform failovers.\n- Describe a bounded fallback policy (graceful degradation) that prefers useful partial outputs over silent failures.\n- Provide clear acceptance tests, observability signals, and a canary rollout plan.\n\nNon-goals:\n- Not addressing large-scale protocol negotiation across different client SDK versions (handled in follow-up).\n- Not providing exact cost-optimization heuristics for batching — that remains in Optimize workstream.\n\nDesign summary:\n1) Start stub: for every streamed request the platform must emit a single well-formed stub JSON as the first record (if streaming is used). The stub contains: request_id, schema_version, model_variant, short_status ("in-progress"), required_output_keys (list), and optional resume_token (opaque string). Consumers can use this stub to allocate UI slots or pre-warm caches.\n2) Progressive objects: subsequent items are full or partial records with a 'progress_id' that maps to required_output_keys. Every partial record includes an 'is_final' boolean.\n3) Tool-relay semantics: tool invocation requests from the model are emitted as "tool_call" frames with: tool_name, args_hash, idempotency_key (generated by platform if model doesn't supply), submit_timestamp. The platform will accept tool_call frames and return a tool_call_ack (tool_call_id, status: queued). The platform guarantees at-least-once delivery to third-party tool adapters but provides idempotency semantics keyed by idempotency_key to allow exactly-once logical behavior where tools support it.\n4) Timeouts & fallbacks: each tool_call has a configurable soft_timeout (recommended default 4s) and hard_deadline (default 30s). On soft_timeout the platform emits a "tool_stub" containing minimal expected response shape (per schema) and a recommendation to retry. On hard_deadline the platform emits a tool_error frame with standardized error_code and optionally a replacement stub depending on fallback policy.\n5) Resume & reconciliation: resume_token in stub enables clients to reconnect and request missing progress_ids. Tokens are single-use; platform will accept resume requests up to 24 hours depending on retention policy. Reconciliation includes a delta list describing which progress_ids were completed so client can request only missing parts.\n6) Security & audit: every tool_call frame is logged with request_id, tool_name, op_hash and stored in audit logs. Tool payloads marked sensitive must be redacted in standard logs and only appear in encrypted audit stores accessible to compliance roles.\n\nTrade-offs considered:\n- Emitting stubs increases token count and latency for tiny requests, but greatly reduces error handling complexity for integrators.\n- Idempotency tokens shift some responsibility to model authors; platform can synthesize tokens when absent but will prefer model-generated keys for cross-request deduplication.\n\nSuccess metrics:\n- consumer-visible error rate for streamed structured requests drops by 50% in first month after rollout.\n- resume success rate >= 98% for reconnects within 24 hours.\n- tool_call duplicate execution rate <= 0.5% for tools that support idempotency; platform-initiated duplicates recorded separately.\n

acceptance_criteria:
A1: First-record stub is emitted for 100% of streaming structured responses within 50ms of connection establishment in canary region.
A2: Each tool_call frame must produce either a tool_call_ack or a tool_error within soft_timeout; soft_timeout behavior must be observable via metric 'tool_call_soft_timeout_rate'.
A3: Resume flow: given a valid resume_token clients can reconnect and obtain a delta list; automated e2e test must validate reassembly of a previously interrupted 12-part stream.
A4: Idempotency: when model supplies the same idempotency_key for repeated tool_calls, the downstream tool adapter must receive the operation at most once logically; integration tests simulate at-least-once delivery and dedup is validated by comparing op_hashes in audit logs.
A5: Fallback stubs: when a tool hard_deadline elapses, the platform emits a validated replacement stub conforming to the recorded schema; schema conformance tests assert shape and required keys.
A6: Observability: traces include request_id and any tool_call_id, and logs surface 'resume_token' issuance and use; dashboards show tool_call_latency_p50/p95, resume_success_rate, stub_emitted_rate.
A7: Security: sensitive tool args are redacted by default in runtime logs; security review sign-off required before rollout to production.

test_plan:
Unit: parser/generator tests for stub and tool_call frames ensuring valid JSON and required keys.
Integration: platform <-> tool-adapter harness that injects fail/slow behaviors and validates ack/replay paths.
E2E: client SDK replay test that opens stream, forces disconnect at N=3, reconnects with resume_token and verifies complete reconstruction.
Chaos: simulate platform pod restart during active tool_call and ensure idempotency and resume behavior meet acceptance criteria.
Load: synthetic workload of 10k streaming sessions/hour to verify stub emission rate and latency in canary region.

2025-02-10: Design review — security requested redaction scheme; added audit store requirement. Action: Security to provide redaction spec by 2025-02-14.

2025-02-18: PRD in review; PM requested explicit rollback criteria in case of increased tool duplicate rate post-rollout.

open_questions:
Q1: Retention window for resume tokens — default 24h ok for enterprise customers with long-running clients?
Q2: Should platform synthesize idempotency_keys using deterministic hashing across model revision upgrades?
Q3: What is required behavior for clients that don't consume the stub first (legacy SDKs) — do we need compatibility mode?

rollout_plan:
Canary: 1% of streaming traffic in us-west-2 for 3 days, monitor resume_success_rate and tool_call_duplicate_executions.
Ramp: 10% for 48 hours if canary metrics within thresholds, then 50% for 72 hours.
Full: 100% after 7 days with weekly check-ins for first month.
Rollback: if tool_call_duplicate_executions > 1% or resume_success_rate < 95% for 4 hours, rollback to previous streaming contract and open incident review.

[Geo-harmonized routing and resilient streaming sessions for hosted API]
description:
Goal: Implement a geo-harmonized, session-cohesive failover strategy for the hosted API gateway that preserves streaming session continuity where possible, and provides deterministic graceful degradation (load shedding and circuit breakers) when region capacity is constrained. This ticket covers design, implementation, and rollout of: 1) per-region SLO enforcement and budgeted failover triggers; 2) L7 routing rules with session affinity and KV-backed session continuation tokens; 3) streaming-aware fallback behavior that can degrade to polling or truncated streams; 4) region-level circuit breakers and adaptive load shedding based on latency/error budgets. The end-state should keep most customer sessions alive during partial region outages, avoid cascading latency spikes, and provide measurable SLO spend accounting for failover events.

problem_statement:
We currently route hosted API traffic using a global L7 edge with health checks and simple weight-based failover. This causes two recurring problems: (1) long-lived streaming sessions often drop or restart when traffic shifts between regions because state (session position, prefix KV cache pointers, open SSE/TCP streams) is not portable across gateways; (2) region overload causes latency tails and cascading failures across downstream subsystems before we can safely shed load. We need a resilient flow that preserves session continuity where feasible and degrades predictably otherwise, without violating customer SLO commitments or incurring undue cost.

proposed_solution:
High-level design: 1) SLO and budget model: define per-region SLOs (p50/p95/p99 latency and error-rate) and an explicit Failover Budget token that is decremented when we route requests to non-primary regions. The Failover Budget ties to each customer/tenant and to global platform budgets so we can control cross-customer blast radius. 2) Routing plane: implement a geo-harmonized router component in the edge that uses: - primary region mapping (by geolocation + latency matrix) - consistent hashing-based session affinity for non-stream requests - session tokens for streaming: issue a signed session-continuation-token (SCT) at stream start that encodes the minimal state (KV pointers, prefix checksum, model variant) and can be used to rehydrate the session in another region. Tokens are HMAC-signed and short-lived. 3) Streaming continuity: support two modes: sticky-stream (try to keep stream on original region via sticky routing and long HA keepalives) and portable-stream (if original region unavailable, accept SCT to pick up near last delivered token; if full-consistency can't be met, fallback to best-effort resume or to a truncated/polling mode with clear response headers indicating degraded continuity). 4) Circuit breakers & load-shedding: per-region breakers based on composite signals (95th latency, 5xx rate, queue length, GPU utilization). Breakers have three states: closed, throttled (soft shed by returning 429 with suggested backoff), and open (fast fail and route to fallback region/variant). Load-shedding policies prefer shedding non-critical work types first: embeddings batch jobs, lower-priority tenants, heavy long-context generation, then chat completions. 5) Telemetry & observability: dashboards for SLO spend, per-tenant failover counts, streaming resume success rate, and per-region breaker triggers. 6) Rollout: feature flags, canary to low-volume tenants, emergency off ramp.

technical_details:
Routing mechanics: - Use a global L7 control plane that publishes per-region weight tables and affinity rules to edge routers. - Session affinity uses consistent hashing on session_id or API key + client_ip as a fallback. - For streaming, at stream creation the origin gateway stores minimal pointers to prefix/KV cache entries (opaque IDs) and returns an SCT. The origin also checkpoint-stores the last delivered token index in a short-lived replication log that is replicated to the nearest secondary region cluster with eventual consistency (replication window <= 10s). - SCT format: base64(hdr.payload.signature) where payload includes model_id, variant, prefix_checksum, last_token_index, origin_region, issuance_ts. Signature HMAC using account-level secret. - When a rehydrate occurs, the target region validates SCT, checks for compatible model variants, and rehydrates KV pointers; if pointers missing, we can replay a truncated prompt constructed from the last known prefix checksum and send a warning header to client. - Health signals: integrate runtime telemetry (rt_latency_p95, rpc_5xx_rate, kv_cache_hit_rate, gpu_queued_ms). Composite breaker expression: open_if(rt_latency_p95 > 3xSLO_p95 OR rpc_5xx_rate > 0.02) with manual tuning knobs per region. - Failover decision: incremental policy that prefers local mitigation (throttle, cache bypass, quantized model fallback) before cross-region shift to avoid extra latency tax and SLO spend. - Load-shedding actions must be observable and annotatable per response (headers: X-Redwood-Fallback, X-Redwood-SCT-Status, X-Redwood-Shed-Reason).

tradeoffs_and_risks:
- Complexity: Introducing SCTs and cross-region replication increases code and operational complexity. - Consistency vs availability: portable-stream requires eventual replication and may still lose a small window of in-flight tokens. We accept bounded loss (<= configurable tokens) for availability. - Cost: replicating checkpoints to secondaries and routing extra traffic during failovers consumes cross-region bandwidth and compute. We mitigate via Failover Budget limits and prioritized tenant lists. - Security: SCTs carry session metadata; must be short-lived, signed, and audited. Storing per-session pointers requires lifecycle management to avoid data retention issues. - Edge cases: model variant unavailability in fallback region — we need to degrade model quality gracefully or apply deterministic fallback variants with documented semantics.

acceptance_criteria:
Per-region SLOs and Failover Budget documented and implemented in control plane
Edge router can issue and validate SCTs and route streaming rehydrates successfully in test harness
Circuit breakers trigger and transition through states in response to synthetic load tests
Load-shedding order respects priority table and emits clear headers and metrics
Canary rollout to 5% of traffic shows <2% increase in client-observed disconnects and >80% successful stream resume on cross-region rehydrate
Dashboards show SLO spend and per-tenant failover counts; alerts for unexpected failover spikes

implementation_steps:
Design and document SCT format and security model (Confluence link in links)
Add SCT issuance to streaming pathway and minimal checkpointing in gateway runtime
Extend control plane to publish affinity and failover budget state to edges
Implement per-region composite circuit breakers and soft-shed responses
Add server-side replay/rehydrate logic in secondary region that accepts SCTs
Create telemetry dashboards and SLO spend metrics; add alerts
Canary rollout and iterative tuning based on metrics and customer feedback

incident_playbook:
Step 0: Identify region degradation via composite breaker alert. Step 1: Shift failsafe to soft-throttle for affected region. Step 2: If still degrading, enable cross-region failover for affected tenants within Failover Budget. Step 3: Notify SRE and toggle canary off if unexplained errors. Step 4: Post-incident runbook: capture SLO spend and update global budget policies.

[Progressive Emission Safety Net — PRD for structured output, tool handshake degradation, and streaming checkpoints]
description:
Summary:
This PRD defines the "Progressive Emission Safety Net": a set of behavioral requirements and acceptance tests for structured outputs and tool/function calling when responses are emitted progressively (streaming). The goal is to ensure consumer resilience across partial emits, schema drift, network interruptions, and downstream tool failures while providing clear observability and safe rollback modes.

Goals:
- Define a canonical lightweight handshake and checkpoint envelope for streamed structured output that consumers can rely on for incremental validation and replay.
- Specify graceful degradation modes for tool calls (timeboxed handshakes, replayable call intents, fallback descriptors).
- Provide testable acceptance criteria and telemetry signals to gate rollout.
- Minimize breaking changes for existing API users while enabling stronger guarantees for enterprise customers.

Scope:
In-scope: streaming text and framed structured emits (JSON fragments), function/tool invocation metadata, per-fragment provenance headers, checkpoints (sequence/offset), observable error classification, retry semantics for idempotent tool calls, examples and test harness.
Out-of-scope: model-level generation logic (LLM tokenization internals), SDK surface changes beyond exposing headers, policy/auth changes for tool endpoints (handled by ENG-28012).

Key assumptions:
- Clients can parse newline-delimited frames and accept optional metadata headers.
- Tool endpoints will support an idempotency token on the first handshake.
- Network interruptions may occur; we must provide resume semantics or well-defined finalization messages.

Handshake & checkpoint envelope (informal):
Each streamed frame contains either: a 'fragment' (partial object), a 'checkpoint' (sequence number + deterministic hash), or a 'final' message. Example frame payload (stringified for clarity):

{"type":"fragment","seq":12,"schema":"billing.v2.Invoice","payload":"{\"line_items\":[...]}","prov":{"model_version":"rdw-v1.9","prompt_hash":"abc123"},"idempotency_token":"r-550e8400"}

Checkpoint frame example:
{"type":"checkpoint","seq":12,"checkpoint_hash":"sha256:...","accepted_schema":"billing.v2.Invoice","partial_valid":true}

Behavioral requirements (high level):
- Consumers must be able to validate partial objects using the accepted_schema on checkpoint frames.
- If a checkpoint indicates partial_valid=false, the runtime should attach a remediation hint (suggested fallback model variant or retry policy).
- Tool calls invoked mid-stream must include a call-intent envelope (function name, args preview, idempotency token). The platform must guarantee at-least-once delivery semantics with clear duplicate suppression metadata for idempotent endpoints.

Error modes & degradation policies:
1) Network interruption between fragments: system emits 'resumeable' checkpoint with a TTL and resume token. Clients can request missing fragments via the control-plane within TTL.
2) Tool endpoint unavailable: function-call frame is marked 'deferred'. Runtime retries based on configured backoff; if retries exceed policy window, emit 'fallback' frame with best-effort result and explicit 'uncertain' flag.
3) Schema incompatibility on checkpoint: emit 'schema-mismatch' frame with suggested compatibility actions (coerce-to-string, fallthrough).

Telemetry & observability signals required:
- fragment_emit_rate (per model+route)
- checkpoint_acceptance_ratio (partial_valid true vs false)
- function_call_retries, function_call_duplicate_suppression_count
- resume_requests_per_minute and resume_success_rate
- fallback_emits_rate and customer-facing_fallback_rate

Rollout plan & gating:
- Alpha (internal): enable on canary routes for 2 teams, collect telemetry for 14 days, validate resume success > 95% and checkpoint acceptance > 98%.
- Beta (selected customers): opt-in for enterprise tenants behind Dedicated; require explicit SDK opt-in.
- GA: enable-by-default with feature flag for private deployments; rollout conditional on telemetry gates.

Files & artifacts referenced:
- Confluence PRD: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/STR/Progressive+Emission+Safety+Net (internal doc with spec and sample harness)
- GitHub RFC: https://github.com/redwood-inference/rfcs/pull/218 (handshake protocol proposal)
- Test harness: internal repo rdw/inference-stream-test (unit & e2e scenarios)

Acceptance test plan summary (details below in acceptance_criteria): logs and golden fixtures for checkpoints, intentional failures to verify fallback frames and idempotency behavior, simulated network drop tests to validate resume semantics.


acceptance_criteria:
Checkpoint frames are emitted for any long-running structured emit where payload size > 16KB or after 30s of continuous emission; checkpoint contains seq, checkpoint_hash, accepted_schema.
Client-visible partial_valid metrics: >= 98% of checkpoints in normal traffic must be partial_valid=true in alpha canary (measured over 14-day window).
Resume token lifecycle: resume_token TTL enforced (default 10 minutes); resume API returns missing fragments exactly once per token; resume_success_rate >= 95% in test harness.
Function/tool call idempotency: first-call carries idempotency_token; repeated deliveries within 5-minute dedup window must be recognized by runtime and flagged as duplicate in telemetry but not re-executed for idempotent endpoints.
Deferred function semantics: when upstream tool returns 5xx or times out, runtime emits a 'deferred' then retries with exponential backoff up to policy limit; after exceed, runtime emits 'fallback' frame with 'uncertain':true and documented fallback_reason.
Schema mismatch handling: when checkpoint accepted_schema does not validate payload, runtime emits 'schema-mismatch' frame and attaches a single suggested remediation (coerce, simplify, or escalate) with deterministic ordering.
Observability: all frames emit trace_id and span_id headers; traces link to console-2026.04 UI; token-level cost and latency breakdown show per-frame token counts in Console's timeline view.
Backward compatibility: existing non-streaming clients receive a single 'final' frame equivalent to prior API behavior; no required client changes for non-streaming flows.
Security: idempotency tokens and resume tokens are treated as short-lived bearer tokens and logged only in redacted form; security review signoff required before Beta (security_review_required=true).

2026-03-05: Design review — Sofia suggested a compact 'prov' header for model provenance; accepted. DES to provide compact schema examples by 2026-03-09 (DES-7810).
2026-03-08: PM sync — clarified that fallback frames must include human-readable hint and machine-actionable code. Added telemetry hooks for 'fallback_emits_rate'.
2026-03-10: Security raised concerns about resume_token leakage; assigned to Security to validate token format and TTL. Security review required prior to Beta. Link to security checklist added to Confluence.
2026-03-11: Action items: ENG to add unit tests for duplicate suppression; QA to author e2e scenarios for network drops; PM to prepare customer-facing rollout notes and opt-in SDK flag.
Links: PRD draft (Confluence): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/STR/Progressive+Emission+Safety+Net, RFC: https://github.com/redwood-inference/rfcs/pull/218, Test harness: internal rdw/inference-stream-test

[Progressive traffic taper + session escrow for active-active gateway streaming resilience]
description:
Summary: This ticket implements a progressive traffic tapering mechanism combined with a session escrow layer at the edge gateway to enable active-active multi-region failover for streaming sessions. The goal is to shift traffic between regions with minimal client-visible disruption, preserve in-flight KV cache/state where possible, and provide deterministic fallbacks when capacity or latency SLOs are threatened.

Background: We observed two classes of failures during the last outage: (1) abrupt region drains caused streaming sessions to terminate unexpectedly and clients to retry, leading to double-billing and state loss; (2) overloaded replicas tripped coarse-grained circuit breakers that ejected healthy sessions. Current failover logic is binary (drain now or not) and does not coordinate with session state or streaming handover.

Proposal: 1) Progressive traffic taper: instead of immediate 100% cutover, the gateway will shift traffic using a parameterized taper curve (default: 80-60-40-20-0 over configurable windows). Each step is telemetry gated by SLO headroom, tail-latency, and KV cache pressure metrics. 2) Session escrow: when a session is nominated for handoff, the edge creates an ephemeral escrow record containing minimal rehydration artifacts (session id, last-offset, lightweight summary, pointer to persisted KV snapshot). Escrow is replicated to a cross-region durable store for short TTLs (60s by default). 3) Stream handshake: clients are offered a 2-phase resume token and a graceful short-buffer period where the old region continues to accept and forward tokens while the new region warms caches. 4) Soft circuit breakers: circuit decisions move from replica-level hard ejects to a graded throttling model (token-shed -> priority-degrade -> eviction) driven by SLO budgets and per-session criticality.

Why this is different: The design prioritizes session integrity and streamed-token continuity over aggressive capacity-preserving ejections. It treats failover as a multi-step choreography rather than an instantaneous state flip, reducing duplicate work and improving p99 tail latency during transitions.

acceptance_criteria:
Can shift 1000 concurrent streaming sessions from region A to region B with <=1% session-abandon and <200ms median additional resume latency
Escrow store writes and reads succeed under normal traffic and are garbage-collected after TTL; no escrow leakage after 5 minutes
Tapering steps are telemetry gated: transitions abort within 5s if tail-latency > configured threshold
Soft circuit-breaker phases (throttle -> degrade -> evict) occur deterministically based on configured thresholds and generate incident telemetry
Automated e2e test reproducing a regional capacity overload validates session resume semantics and no double-billing

implementation_notes:
Edge gateway: add taper controller with weighted-shift API and per-route session tagging
Session escrow service: small footprint service (k8s deployment) with cross-region replication using existing durable tier (S3-backed index + 1s-2s replication window)
KV snapshot: integrate with existing prefix/KV cache persistence hooks to write minimal rehydration blobs
Client contract: add resume-token header and backoff handshake; SDKs must be backward compatible (server will support both modes)
Circuit-breaker refactor: replace hard-eject path with phased actions and add hysteresis to prevent flapping

telemetry_queries:
dashboard:edge/taper-controller: query=rate(successful_handoffs[5m]) / rate(handoff_attempts[5m])
alert:handoff-failure-rate: query=hand_off_failures / handoff_attempts > 0.02 for 2m
slo:stream-p99-resume-latency: query=histogram_quantile(0.99, resume_latency_bucket)
pressure:kv-cache-hit-pressure: query=kv_cache_evictions / kv_cache_size > 0.1

rollout_plan:
1) Canary: enable taper controller (read-only) in us-west-2 on 5% of traffic for 24h; collect metrics
2) Small-scale: enable progressive taper + escrow for non-production orgs and internal loadtest harness; run synthetic 2k concurrent streams
3) Regional: enable for low-traffic customer region and exercise telemetry gates
4) Gradual: ramp to 25% -> 50% -> 100% with automated rollback on SLO regressions
5) Post-rollout: run 72h soak and add to chaos playbook for periodic exercises

risks_and_mitigations:
Risk: Escrow store becomes hot during mass failover -> Mitigation: shard escrow keys by session hash and enforce write QPS throttles
Risk: Clients without updated SDKs might not support resume token -> Mitigation: maintain compatibility path where old clients get force-evicted with clear retry guidance and metrics tagged
Risk: Incorrect taper curve config causes oscillation -> Mitigation: add damping/hysteresis and require two-step opt-in for curve changes in prod
Risk: Cross-region replication lag causes stale rehydration -> Mitigation: minimum warmup window and verify KV snapshot freshness before final cutover

qa_notes:
Create synthetic harness to open 10k streaming connections and trigger staged drain; verify resume success rate and session continuity
Unit test escrow TTL GC and replication fences; add property tests for resume-token idempotency
Load test soft circuit-breaker path for 30m at 2x normal traffic to observe graded degradation behavior
