[Kernel auto-selection v2: add model allowlist/denylist rules + hot reload for rollout control]
body:
Context\nKernel auto-selection v2 is landing behind gates for Runtime 1.21. For staged rollout (Hosted first, then Dedicated pools) we need a fast, explainable control surface to enable/disable v2 at a per-model granularity, with the ability to react to incidents/customer escalations without restarting the runtime. This PR adds model allowlist/denylist rules, evaluation precedence, and hot reload behavior for those rules.\n\nWhat this PR does\n1) Allowlist/Denylist evaluation\n- Adds a new rule set: ModelRolloutRules { allow: [Rule], deny: [Rule] } consumed by the v2 selector entrypoint.\n- Rule matching supports: exact model id (including pinned rev), family wildcard, and optional environment/region scoping.\n- Precedence (explicit + deterministic):\n  (a) deny match -> v2 disabled\n  (b) allow match -> v2 enabled\n  (c) otherwise -> fall back to global feature gate (existing)\n- The selector records the rollout decision reason and exposes it to telemetry/logging (without increasing per-request cardinality).\n\n2) Hot reload (no restart)\n- Wires rules into runtime config loader and existing config watcher.\n- Reload is atomic: config is parsed/validated, then swapped; on parse/validation failure we retain the last-known-good rules and emit an error + metric.\n- Includes monotonic config version handling (ignore out-of-order updates) to reduce flapping when the control plane retries.\n\n3) Safety checks (fail closed + guardrails)\n- Validation on load:\n  - Disallow ambiguous rules (e.g., the same exact target in both allow and deny).\n  - Disallow rules that would match everything unless explicitly marked as a wildcard rule (prevents accidental global enable).\n  - Require normalized model identifiers (canonicalization uses existing model registry normalization; rejects unknown/empty ids).\n  - Enforce max rule count to keep evaluation bounded and to protect against config explosion (default 500, overridable for Private with a hard cap).\n- Runtime behavior: if rule evaluation errors (should be unreachable post-validation), v2 defaults to disabled for that request (consistent with correctness-first posture).\n\n4) Metrics + logs\n- Metrics added (names subject to final prefix alignment; see below):\n  - runtime_kernel_selector_v2_rollout_rule_eval_total{outcome=\"allow|deny|fallback|error\", scope=\"global|region|env\"} (no model label)\n  - runtime_kernel_selector_v2_rollout_config_load_total{result=\"success|failure|ignored_stale\"}\n  - runtime_kernel_selector_v2_rollout_rules_count (gauge)\n  - runtime_kernel_selector_v2_rollout_config_version (gauge)\n- Structured log event emitted on config load + on rule evaluation only when debug logging is enabled (not default), including a stable rule_id hash to support incident triage without high-cardinality model labels.\n\nRule syntax (examples)\n- Allow v2 for a pinned model release in canary region:\n  allow: [{ target: \"llama-3.1-70b-instruct@2026-01-30\", region: \"us-east-1\" }]\n- Deny v2 for a family across all regions (temporary mitigation):\n  deny: [{ target: \"qwen2.5-*\" }]\n- Allow for Dedicated environment only:\n  allow: [{ target: \"mistral-large-*\", env: \"dedicated\" }]\n\nTesting\n- Unit tests for precedence + wildcard behavior + canonicalization and max rule count.\n- Config hot reload tests verifying atomic swap and last-known-good behavior on parse failure.\n- Determinism coverage: rule evaluation order is stable across loads; no iteration over map keys without sorting; replay test updated to include rollout decision in snapshot.\n\nOperational notes\n- Intended to be driven by Control Plane gate config (Ethan/Jordan): the runtime only consumes a validated JSON payload and does not depend on CP-specific semantics.\n- Oncall can use this to quickly disable v2 by model during canary, while keeping global gate enabled for other traffic.\n\nFollow-ups (not in this PR)\n- Add dashboard panels for rule match outcomes during canary (tracked separately).\n- Consider adding an optional \"expires_at\" to rules for automatic cleanup (would require CP support + clock source considerations).\n\nReview discussion highlights\n- Noah Patel: Requested explicit statement that deny always wins and that errors fail closed. Implemented + added tests; also removed any non-deterministic iteration in rule compilation.\n- Allison Grant: Flagged metric cardinality risk. Updated metrics to avoid model labels; added hashed rule_id only in debug logs.\n- Ethan Park: Asked for monotonic version handling and clear ignored-stale behavior. Added config_version gauge and a counter for ignored stale updates.\n- Jordan Lee: Asked that policy evaluation remain replayable. Updated replay snapshot to include rollout outcome and reason, and ensured stable rule compilation ordering.\n\nChecklist\n- [x] Adds tests for precedence, validation, and hot reload\n- [x] Adds metrics + logs with cardinality constraints\n- [x] No correctness-impacting changes to kernel selection beyond gating\n- [x] Linked to ENG-4826 and aligned with Runtime 1.21 rollout plan\n\nNotes for release train\nThis is safe to land ahead of canary: default behavior remains unchanged unless rules are provided; on invalid config the runtime keeps last-known-good and v2 remains controlled by existing global gate.

release_notes:
Runtime: Kernel auto-selection v2 rollout can now be controlled via per-model allowlist/denylist rules with hot reload (no process restart required).
Adds metrics and structured logs for rollout rule evaluation outcomes.
Adds safety checks to prevent invalid/ambiguous rules from silently enabling v2.

[Latency regression after runtime-1.22 canary: elevated p99 decode latency correlated with KV compaction activity]
Issue Summary
- During a runtime-1.22 canary expansion in prod (hosted, us-east-1), we observed a statistically significant p99 latency regression on decode-heavy traffic, most visible for mixed sequence-length distributions.
- Regression correlated with elevated KV compaction work (bytes moved + compaction time) and increased allocator fragmentation ratio oscillation.
- Canary was rolled back (feature flag disabled + cohort drained) per guardrails.

Customer Impact
- Customer: Northwind Analytics (enterprise) reported increased p99 latency and intermittent request timeouts during bursty chat traffic.
- Symptoms: p95 largely stable; p99 degraded (notable tail spikes) during bursts and after churn events (rapid session start/stop).
- Scope: Only canary cohort in us-east-1. Control region (eu-west-1) did not show comparable change.

Detection
- 2026-01-29 09:12 PT: SRE alert fired: hosted decode p99 exceeded threshold for canary cohort for 10m.
- 2026-01-29 09:18 PT: Support received escalation via CSM thread referencing prior tail-latency concerns (see SUP-28411).

Environment
- Runtime: runtime-1.22 canary (hosted)
- Canary cohort: ~5% of us-east-1 hosted capacity (dedicated pools not included)
- Traffic pattern: mixed prompt lengths, bursty chat sessions, high cancellation/churn

Evidence / Observations
- Dashboard signals (high level):
  - p99 decode latency: +18–35% vs baseline during burst windows
  - Compaction bytes moved: spiky (peaks aligned with p99 spikes)
  - Compaction time per step: higher variance than staging
  - Eviction counters: low/near-zero (so tail impact likely compaction rather than eviction)
  - Fragmentation ratio: saw sawtooth behavior (trigger threshold repeatedly crossed)
- Trace exemplars (from compaction spans): decode loop shows intermittent stalls where compaction step executed near decode boundary.

Timeline / Comments
- 2026-01-29 09:22 PT (Sean Gallagher, SRE): Confirmed alert corresponds to canary nodes only. Requesting runtime team to validate compaction budget enforcement and whether compaction can run during decode.
- 2026-01-29 09:31 PT (Rafael Mendes, Oncall): Opened incident bridge in #incidents; linked thread: sources/slack/incidents/1767735109.json. Requested latest canary diff + feature flag defaults.
- 2026-01-29 09:40 PT (Sofia Ivanova, Runtime): Suspected scheduler boundary issue: compaction budget being applied but step can still run in an unfavorable phase when queues are shallow (burst recovery) and decode becomes latency-sensitive.
- 2026-01-29 09:55 PT (Allison Grant, Observability): Noted instrumentation overhead increase in the same canary build (compaction tracing spans). Suggested testing with spans disabled to isolate.
- 2026-01-29 10:05 PT (Decision): Roll back canary per hosted tail-latency guardrails. Disable KV compaction feature flag in hosted us-east-1 canary cohort; drain cohort to baseline build.
- 2026-01-29 10:11 PT (Rafael Mendes): Executed kill-switch via config propagation (validated propagation <2m). p99 began recovering within 15m as cohort drained.
- 2026-01-29 10:38 PT (Support): Informed Northwind Analytics we rolled back the canary change and are investigating; requested a 30-minute window of request IDs for trace correlation.
- 2026-01-29 12:10 PT (Samir Qureshi, Runtime): Preliminary hypothesis: compaction relocation step sometimes exceeds time budget due to larger-than-expected copy size when fragmentation is high; budget accounting is per-step but actual move cost depends on page locality. Also flagged potential overhead from tracing spans.
- 2026-01-30 08:45 PT (Runtime): Added follow-up to test: disable compaction spans (keep metrics) and re-run canary in a smaller cohort; additionally adjust compaction trigger hysteresis to reduce repeated threshold crossings.
- 2026-02-03 16:20 PT (Rafael Mendes): Confirmed no further p99 regressions after rollback; customer reports normalized behavior. Closing support incident; tracking engineering fixes under runtime epic/tickets.

Rollback / Mitigation Actions Taken
- Rolled back canary cohort in us-east-1 hosted (KV compaction kill-switch OFF).
- Left fragmentation metrics ON for continued monitoring.
- Paused further canary expansion pending fixes + perf canary pass.

Root Cause (Provisional)
- KV compaction work occasionally executed at an unfavorable time relative to decode scheduling, causing transient stalls that manifest as p99 spikes under bursty mixed-length workloads.
- Contributing factors:
  - Compaction trigger oscillation (threshold crossed repeatedly) causing repeated compaction attempts.
  - Increased tracing span overhead in the same build (amplifying tail effects).

Resolution
- Customer-facing: Regression resolved by rolling back canary (feature flag disabled; nodes drained to baseline).
- Internal: Incident closed with action items assigned; canary expansion blocked until updated perf canary scenario and revised compaction budgeting/hysteresis are validated.

Follow-up Tasks / Next Steps
- Runtime (owner: Sofia Ivanova / Samir Qureshi):
  - Tighten scheduler phase gating: ensure compaction steps never run on latency-critical decode path when queue depth is below threshold.
  - Add hysteresis + cooldown to fragmentation trigger to prevent sawtooth compaction behavior.
  - Verify budget enforcement uses wall-clock + bytes moved with hard stop when approaching decode deadlines.
- Observability (owner: Allison Grant):
  - Add dashboard panel overlay: p99 vs compaction bytes moved and compaction step time.
  - Reduce tracing overhead or sample compaction spans; keep metrics at full fidelity.
- SRE (owner: Sean Gallagher):
  - Update automated rollback condition to consider compaction bytes moved rate + p99 correlation (not just p99 absolute).

External Communication
- Northwind Analytics updated 2026-01-29: rollback performed; performance back to baseline; follow-up planned after next canary with improved guardrails.

References
- Slack incident thread: sources/slack/incidents/1767735109.json
- Oncall procedures draft: sources/slack/eng-oncall/1767660044.json
- Guardrails: sources/confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets/hosted-api-tail-latency-guardrails.json
- Runbook: sources/confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-kv-cache-compaction-runbook.json

[Add kernel selection v2 canary scenarios (v1 vs v2) across GPU SKUs + seq buckets]
body:
## Summary
Adds a new perf-canary scenario pack to compare kernel selection v1 vs v2 under realistic prompt/decode regimes across heterogeneous fleets (A100/H100/L40S). This is intended to be the primary signal for runtime 1.21 staged rollout gating.

## Why
Kernel auto-selection v2 changes decision logic keyed on (model family, seq-length regime, GPU SKU). We need canary coverage that (a) is SKU-aware, (b) buckets workloads in a way that catches long-context tail-latency spikes, and (c) emits stable, actionable alerts when v2 mis-selects.

## What changed
- New scenario group `kernel_selection/v2_compare` that runs each workload twice per target: once with selector v1, once with selector v2 enabled via runtime flags.
- Coverage matrix:
  - Model families: llama (Llama-3.x), mistral (Mistral), qwen (Qwen2.5)
  - GPUs: A100-80GB, H100-SXM, L40S
  - Seq buckets (prefill/decode regimes):
    - short: prefill~512-1k / decode~128-256
    - medium: prefill~4k / decode~256-512
    - long: prefill~16k-32k / decode~128-256 (tail-risk bucket)
  - Mixed workload scenario that alternates short/long to stress regime classification stability.
- Added comparison report that tags results with `selector_version=v1|v2`, `gpu_sku_normalized`, `model_family`, `seq_bucket`, and `workload_id`.
- Added alerting thresholds (defaults) and grouping policy:
  - p95 latency regression: warn at +5%, page at +10% (v2 relative to v1) per (model_family, gpu_sku_normalized, seq_bucket)
  - p99 latency regression: warn at +8%, page at +15% (same grouping)
  - throughput regression (tok/s): warn at -3%, page at -7%
  - error rate (5xx/runtime errors): page if absolute >0.2% or delta >0.1% (whichever is greater)
  - stability guard: suppresses paging if N<30 runs for a bucket (still emits a warn + marks bucket as low-sample)

## Notes on SKU normalization
We normalize provider instance strings into `gpu_sku_normalized` (e.g., `a100-80gb`, `h100-sxm`, `l40s`) to avoid alert cardinality and to match how runtime v2 registry keys SKUs. This is intentionally coarse; MIG and vendor-specific variants are folded into the parent SKU for canary gating.

## How to run
- Local (dev): `perf-canary run --scenario kernel_selection/v2_compare --target local_gpu`
- CI (nightly): `kernel-selection-v2-compare` job
- Ad hoc (pre-canary): `perf-canary run --scenario kernel_selection/v2_compare --target hosted_canary --set selector_v2=1`

## Related
- Runtime changes: redwood/pr-28460 (feature gate), pr-28452 (SKU-aware registry), pr-28439 (seq bucketing)
- Epic: ENG-4821

## Checklist
- [x] Scenarios cover long-context + mixed workloads
- [x] Metrics include selector_version, gpu_sku_normalized, model_family, seq_bucket
- [x] Alert thresholds reviewed with SRE (Aisha/Allison)
- [x] CI runtime < 40 min per target pool (measured on A100)
- [x] Docs added for oncall interpretation + links to rollout dashboards

## Risk
Low. perf-canary only; no production runtime changes. Primary risk is alert noise from low sample sizes or label explosion; addressed via normalization + N threshold.

- perf-canary: add kernel selection v2 comparison scenarios (v1 vs v2) across A100/H100/L40S with short/medium/long seq buckets
- perf-canary: add alert thresholds tuned for selection regressions (p95/p99 + error + throughput) with SKU-aware grouping
- perf-canary: add dashboards links + runbook pointers in scenario docs

[Load shedding: consistent Retry-After + correlation IDs; document client retry contract]
description:
Context: During canary we saw overload responses missing Retry-After on some routes (notably chat completions + a subset of streaming paths), which caused clients to implement ad-hoc retry behavior and in one case a retry storm. This PR standardizes how we emit Retry-After and correlation IDs for overload/load-shedding responses, and adds a short internal "client retry contract" comment block to keep behavior stable across gateway/routing/runtime.

What changes: 1) Retry-After is now set for all overload-class responses emitted by the API gateway (admission control + breaker open + dependency brownout mapping) and for propagated overload errors from downstream services when they bubble back through the gateway. 2) Correlation ID plumbing is tightened: we prefer an existing inbound X-Request-ID (if present), otherwise generate a Redwood request id, and we always return it to clients in both X-Request-ID and X-Redwood-Correlation-ID for a deprecation window. 3) Centralizes overload response construction into a shared helper that sets headers + JSON payload consistently (status, error.code, error.message, retry guidance, request_id). 4) Adds a code comment (internal contract) that documents semantics: when clients should retry, how to treat 429 vs 503 overload, and that Retry-After is in seconds.

Notes/constraints: - Retry-After is emitted as an integer number of seconds (RFC-compliant); we do not emit HTTP-date format. - For streaming (SSE) requests, we only attempt overload rejection before the response is committed; once headers have been sent, we cannot reliably add Retry-After. This PR ensures the admission decision happens before initiating the stream in gateway. - We do not change error codes/status mappings here (see ADR-014); this PR only enforces header + correlation id consistency.

Testing: - Unit tests for overload response helper (header presence, seconds formatting, correlation id behavior). - Integration test covering /v1/chat/completions streaming: overload rejection happens before stream start and includes Retry-After + request id. - Regression test for SUP-2860 reproduction (route missing header).

Rollout: Safe for dark launch; header additions are backwards compatible (additive). Client-visible change is improved consistency (some clients previously saw no Retry-After).

review_conversation:

Christine Wong (author): Yep. Helper only used by overload paths (breaker open, admission shed, downstream mapped overload). Added a guard test to ensure generic 5xx errors do not set Retry-After.

Aisha Bello (review): Please add a metric for missing Retry-After as a canary safety check. We should be able to alert if this regresses.

Christine Wong (author): Added api_gateway.overload.retry_after_missing counter (dimensions: route_group, region, status) and wired it into logging when helper isn't used (should stay at 0). No tenant_id dimension.

Ibrahim Khan (review): For SDKs we key off X-Request-ID today. Returning both X-Request-ID and X-Redwood-Correlation-ID is fine, but we should document the precedence and avoid breaking existing clients.

Christine Wong (author): Updated request_id.ts to prefer inbound X-Request-ID and always echo it back; X-Redwood-Correlation-ID is additive for now. Added comment in helper about deprecation window.

Mina Haddad (review): On routing fallback, we sometimes return an overload from routing with a retryable code. Are we certain Retry-After is preserved when routing returns its own error payload?

Christine Wong (author): Gateway now overwrites/sets Retry-After on mapped overload regardless of downstream body, but preserves downstream error.code/message. Also ensures request_id is our canonical id.

Nikhil Sharma (review): Please keep the "client retry contract" short and explicit. We should avoid promising exact backoff durations.

Christine Wong (author): Tightened language: we only promise Retry-After is present and in seconds; clients should add jitter and cap retries. No guarantees on exact window beyond header value.

release_notes:
Hosted API: overload/load-shedding responses now consistently include Retry-After (seconds) and return a stable correlation ID header for easier client retry/backoff and support debugging.

[Retry-After header missing on some overload (503/429) responses for Hosted API (enterprise tenant)]
description:
Issue summary
Aurora Health Systems reports that when they receive overload responses (503 / occasionally 429) from Hosted API, the Retry-After header is not present on some routes. Their client relies on Retry-After for backoff; without it they either retry too aggressively (risking retry storms) or back off too conservatively (causing request latency spikes and user-facing delays).

Impact
- Affected: production traffic; customer reported intermittent failures during peak periods
- Customer-visible symptoms:
  - HTTP 503 with Redwood overload JSON payload but missing Retry-After
  - Some responses include Retry-After correctly, leading to inconsistent client behavior
- Business risk: customer flagged this as an enterprise requirement for safe overload handling and asked whether this is "expected" during the canary.

Environment
- Product: Hosted API (chat/completions + streaming)
- Regions observed: us-east primary; eu-west noted once
- Tenant: enterprise hosted (Aurora Health Systems)

Customer evidence
1) Missing header example (from customer logs)
- Endpoint: POST /v1/chat/completions (stream=false)
- Response: 503
- Headers: includes x-redwood-request-id, missing Retry-After
- Body: error.code=overloaded, error.type=overload_error

2) Header present example (same client, same day)
- Endpoint: POST /v1/embeddings
- Response: 429
- Headers: Retry-After: 2

Steps to reproduce (internal)
1. Generate synthetic overload by applying a low per-tenant concurrency cap in staging OR run perf-canary burst scenario.
2. Issue requests against multiple routes:
   - /v1/chat/completions
   - /v1/completions
   - /v1/embeddings
3. Observe that Retry-After is only reliably set when admission control rejects at gateway; when overload is returned from downstream routing/runtime path, header may be absent.

Expected behavior
All overload responses that instruct clients to retry should include Retry-After with a stable, bounded value per ADR-014 and overload retry contract.

Actual behavior
Retry-After missing for some overload errors (notably 503) depending on where overload is triggered (gateway vs downstream).

Initial hypothesis
Mismatch between overload error mapping layer (gateway middleware) and downstream overload responses: downstream returns a structured JSON error but does not set headers; gateway sometimes passes body through without applying header normalization.

Notes
This is likely related to the ongoing canary rollout for hosted overload protection; customer is seeing the new overload taxonomy in production.

Customer request: "Please confirm Retry-After will always be present when you return overloaded errors; we need a deterministic backoff signal." Added two example responses to internal notes (redacted).

[Handle overload errors (stable codes), parse Retry-After, and add backoff helper example]
description:
Context: As part of Hosted circuit breakers + load shedding rollout, the API now returns structured overload errors (e.g., 429/503 with stable error codes) and includes Retry-After guidance to prevent retry storms. Previously, the Python SDK surfaced these as generic APIError/HTTPError; clients had to parse message strings and often ignored Retry-After, leading to inconsistent behavior and support load.

This PR makes overload errors first-class in the SDK, parses Retry-After consistently, and adds a small, copy/paste-friendly backoff helper example for docs and customer integrations.

Changes:
- Introduce typed overload errors: OverloadError (base) with concrete subclasses RateLimitedError (HTTP 429) and ServiceOverloadedError (HTTP 503). These preserve a stable `code` (server error_code), `request_id` / `correlation_id`, and an optional `retry_after_seconds`.
- Parse `Retry-After` header into seconds (supports integer seconds and RFC 1123 date formats). If header is present but invalid, keep raw value for debugging and fall back to exponential backoff guidance.
- Prefer structured fields from the JSON payload (error.code, error.message, error.type, request_id) while maintaining backwards compatibility with older payload shapes.
- Add `is_retryable` semantics: overload errors are retryable by default; non-overload 4xx remain non-retryable; 5xx remain retryable unless explicitly non-retryable.
- Add an example backoff helper in `examples/overload_retry.py` demonstrating exponential backoff + jitter and respecting Retry-After.
- Improve error string formatting to include `code` + request_id for Support triage.

Testing:
- Unit tests for Retry-After parsing (seconds, HTTP-date, invalid)
- Unit tests for payload parsing across old/new shapes
- Integration test stub verifying raised exception types for 429/503

Rollout/notes:
- No API surface breaks; existing exceptions still subclass APIError.
- This is meant to pair with server-side Retry-After consistency changes; the SDK will honor it when present and behave predictably when absent.
- Follow-up: once canary is complete, we should reference this helper in the public docs error-handling section (Elliot/Wei).

review_conversation:
Christine Wong: Can we make sure we don’t encourage clients to hammer us if Retry-After is missing? Also confirm we treat 429 vs 503 differently in terms of messaging.

Ibrahim Khan (author): Yep. Default path is exponential backoff + jitter; if Retry-After is present we honor it. Added separate subclasses so messaging can recommend client-side rate limiting for 429 and capacity retry for 503.

Nikhil Sharma: Please include the stable server error_code in the exception and ensure it doesn’t rely on message text. Also: request_id should be surfaced consistently; Support will ask for it.

Ibrahim Khan: Updated parsing to prefer payload.error.code and payload.request_id (with fallback to x-request-id header when present). Added tests for both new and legacy payload shapes.

Dev Patel: Support ticket SUP-2860 mentions some responses missing Retry-After. Can the SDK still provide guidance if header is missing/invalid? Also we should include raw header in the exception for debugging.

Ibrahim Khan: Added `retry_after_raw` (string) when parsing fails, and the helper demonstrates fallback backoff. Error string includes request_id + code + retry_after when available.

Elliot Price: The example is good; can we keep it minimal and link from README rather than embedding too much in docs?

Ibrahim Khan: Agreed; README now links to examples/overload_retry.py.

Christine Wong (final): Looks good. One nit: cap the computed HTTP-date delta at 0 to avoid negative sleeps.

Ibrahim Khan: Fixed and added test.

[Runbook: Hosted Overload Circuit Breaker (Detection, Mitigation, Rollback, Comms)]
## Purpose
This runbook covers how oncall responds when Redwood Hosted API overload protection (circuit breakers + load shedding) is suspected to be:
1) correctly protecting the platform during real overload, or
2) misfiring (false positives / overly aggressive shedding), or
3) partially degraded (inconsistent Retry-After, missing correlation IDs, fallback loops).

It includes detection/verification, safe toggles, rollback steps, comms templates, and post-incident data capture.

## Scope
Applies to Redwood Hosted API request paths where overload protection is enforced:
- API Gateway admission control (tenant/route/model caps)
- Smart Routing fallback-on-overload (model/region)
- Serving runtime admission/backpressure signals (queue depth, token/sec saturation, memory pressure proxies)

Out of scope: Dedicated and Private deployments (different controls and SLAs).

## Quick glossary
- **Breaker**: state machine controlling admission (closed → open → half-open) based on saturation signals and error/latency thresholds.
- **Shed**: explicit rejection/degradation of requests to prevent overload cascades (e.g., return 429/503 with stable error codes + Retry-After).
- **Degradation mode**: policy-driven feature reduction (e.g., lower max_tokens cap, tighter streaming concurrency) to preserve SLOs.
- **Correlation ID**: `x-redwood-correlation-id` header, included in error payload.

## Severity guidance (Hosted API)
Use this to decide paging/escalation and comms.

- **SEV-1**: Multi-region outage, sustained inability to serve, or overload controls causing widespread customer impact (e.g., >20% requests shed across multiple tiers for >10 min) and no stable mitigation.
- **SEV-2**: Single-region major degradation, sustained elevated overload errors for enterprise/critical tiers, or fallback routing not functioning as configured.
- **SEV-3**: Localized overload in one model/route, short-lived spike, or minor misconfiguration with safe workaround.

## Primary detection signals
Check these in the Overload Protection dashboard (see related page) and standard Hosted API dashboards.

### 1) Customer-visible symptoms
- Spike in 429/503 with overload taxonomy codes (examples):
  - `overload.breaker_open` (typically 503)
  - `overload.shed_rate_limit` (typically 429)
  - `overload.runtime_queue_full` (typically 503)
  - `overload.dependency_unhealthy` (typically 503; treat as dependency incident)
- Increased timeouts (client-side) despite shedding being enabled (may indicate missing early admission or stuck half-open).
- Missing/incorrect `Retry-After` headers.

### 2) Platform signals
- **Breaker open rate** by region, route, and model
- **Shed rate** (overall and by tier)
- **p95/p99 latency** (prefill + decode) rising before error spike
- **Runtime queue depth** (prefill/decode), scheduler backlog
- **Token/sec saturation** (model pool) and GPU utilization plateaus
- **Memory pressure proxy / KV cache pressure** increasing

### 3) Alert triggers (common)
- `hosted_overload_shed_rate{region=*} > 5% for 10m` (tune per region/model)
- `breaker_open_events > baseline + 3σ for 5m`
- `p99_latency > SLO threshold` paired with rising queue depth
- `Retry-After missing rate > 0.5% for 5m` (compliance with client retry contract)

## First 5 minutes (stabilize + classify)
1. **Acknowledge the page** and post in `#incidents`:
   - “Investigating possible Hosted API overload / circuit breaker event in <region>.”
2. **Confirm scope**:
   - Which region(s)? which route(s) (`/v1/chat.completions`, `/v1/completions`, embeddings)? which model(s)?
   - Is the impact tier-specific (self-serve vs enterprise hosted)?
3. **Check if the breaker is doing the right thing**:
   - If shed rate increased but p99 latency and timeouts improved/stabilized, it may be working as intended.
   - If shed rate increased AND timeouts still rising, admission may be too late (runtime saturation without early shed) or retries are storming.
4. **Verify error semantics** (spot-check 5–10 events):
   - Response includes: stable `error.code`, `error.type`, message, `x-redwood-correlation-id`, and `Retry-After` when applicable.
   - Ensure HTTP status matches ADR-014 mapping (429 vs 503).
5. **Decide escalation**:
   - Page/loop in based on suspected layer:
     - Gateway admission/policy: **Platform Control Plane/Gateway** (Ethan Park / Amara Diallo)
     - Routing fallback loops/misroutes: **Smart Routing** (Mina Haddad / Ravi Menon)
     - Runtime queue/saturation: **Serving Runtime** (Sofia Ivanova / Lena Fischer)

## Verification steps (avoid false positives)
### A) Determine if overload is real
- Look for:
  - Runtime queue depth rising steadily
  - Token/sec saturation at/near cap
  - GPU utilization high but throughput not increasing (flatline)
  - Increasing prefill time and decode time
- Cross-check if a traffic spike occurred:
  - Request rate, concurrency, prompt length distribution (if available)
  - Large tenant traffic burst (noisy neighbor)

If system is not saturated (queue depth flat, utilization moderate) but breaker opens, suspect:
- Misconfigured policy thresholds
- Bad saturation signal export (stale/NaN)
- Metric aggregation bug (cardinality drop causing wrong rollup)

### B) Determine if a dependency brownout is the trigger
If `overload.dependency_unhealthy` is high:
- Identify dependency: auth, policy store, routing config service, model registry, tokenization service, etc.
- If dependency is failing, treat as dependency incident and consider temporarily enabling more permissive caching or bypass modes only if approved (see Safe toggles).

### C) Check for retry storms
Signs:
- Rising request rate following shed spike
- High `429/503` plus repeated identical requests (same idempotency key or same prompt hash patterns, if logged)
Actions:
- Ensure `Retry-After` is present and non-zero where required
- Prefer longer `Retry-After` under severe overload to dampen retry storms

## Mitigation playbook (choose the least risky first)
### Mitigation priority order
1) **Protect core availability** (admit fewer requests early) 
2) **Preserve tenant isolation** (avoid one tenant taking all capacity)
3) **Enable graceful degradation** (reduce expensive features)
4) **Enable safe fallback routing** (if configured and proven)
5) **Scale capacity / drain traffic** (if available, region-specific)

### 1) Safe toggles (gateway admission + policy engine)
Use these when load shedding is needed or thresholds are too aggressive. Apply changes narrowly (region + route + tier) and with a clear rollback plan.

**Common toggles** (names are representative; see Policy Engine Integration doc for canonical keys):
- Enable/disable breaker evaluation at gateway:
  - `overload.gw_breaker.enabled = true|false`
- Adjust shed response behavior:
  - `overload.response.retry_after_seconds = <int>`
  - `overload.response.force_503 = true|false` (avoid unless directed; prefer taxonomy mapping)
- Tighten tenant fairness:
  - `overload.fairness.per_tenant_concurrency_cap = <int>`
  - `overload.fairness.per_tenant_rps_cap = <int>`
- Reduce streaming concurrency (high cost under overload):
  - `overload.degrade.streaming_concurrency_cap = <int>`
- Reduce max tokens cap (reduce tail latency amplification):
  - `overload.degrade.max_tokens_cap = <int>`

**Procedure (policy change)**
1. Apply to a single region first (or to canary cohort):
   - Region: `<us-east|us-west|eu-central|...>`
   - Cohort: `canary=true` or a small set of tenant IDs
2. Monitor 10 minutes:
   - p99 latency trend
   - shed rate by tier
   - timeouts
   - breaker open/close transitions (ensure it recovers)
3. Expand gradually.
4. Document the exact change in the incident timeline.

**Example (CLI-like pseudo)**
- “Set Retry-After to 15s for overload 503 in us-east for chat completions”
  - `ri policy set --region us-east --route chat.completions --key overload.response.retry_after_seconds --value 15`

### 2) Runtime overload mitigation (if runtime saturation is primary)
If runtime queue depth is critically high and admission is too late:
- Increase early shedding at gateway (preferred) rather than letting runtime thrash.
- If runtime has emergency caps available (coordinate with runtime oncall):
  - tighten batching caps to reduce latency blowups (trade throughput)
  - reduce concurrent decodes
  - temporarily disable expensive features (tool calling / structured output) if supported by policy flags

Follow the dedicated runtime runbook for deeper actions (see related pages).

### 3) Smart Routing: fallback on overload
Use only if:
- Fallback is configured for impacted tenants/routes AND
- Loop prevention is healthy AND
- The fallback target has available capacity.

Checklist before enabling broader fallback:
- Confirm fallback attempt rate and success rate in routing dashboard.
- Confirm no route/model mismatch (compatibility constraints).
- Ensure bounded retries are enforced (avoid request multiplication).

Mitigations:
- Enable fallback for a subset of tenants (enterprise first if contractually required) or for self-serve to preserve overall SLO.
- Prefer same-region model variant first; cross-region only if latency/SLA permits.

### 4) Address missing Retry-After / bad error payloads
If customers are seeing overload responses without `Retry-After` or correlation IDs:
- Treat as SEV-2 if widespread (can cause retry storms and support escalation).
- Workaround (short-term): force a default `Retry-After` at gateway for overload-coded errors.
- Rollback the specific canary/flag associated with response formatting changes.

### 5) If breaker appears stuck open
Symptoms:
- Breaker open rate remains high despite queue depth returning to normal.
Actions:
- Validate signal freshness (timestamps).
- If stale signals: restart/refresh signal exporter component or fail over to a simpler signal.
- Temporarily force half-open probing (if supported) to allow recovery.
- As a last resort: disable gateway breaker evaluation for the affected selector while keeping rate limits (avoid full removal of protections).

## Rollback steps
Rollback should be fast, scoped, and explicit.

### Rollback triggers
- Shed rate increases but p99 latency does not improve within 10–15 minutes
- Enterprise tenants impacted unexpectedly (tier policy violated)
- Fallback attempts spike with low success (or loops detected)
- Retry storms detected after change

### Rollback procedure
1. Identify the last applied change (flag/policy key) and its scope.
2. Revert to the previous value for the same selector (region/route/model/tier/tenant).
3. Confirm within 5–10 minutes:
   - breaker open rate decreases appropriately
   - error mix returns to expected
   - p95/p99 latency stabilizes
4. Add a clear incident note: “Rolled back <key> from <x> to <y> at <time> due to <reason>.”

## Communications
### Internal channels
- `#incidents`: incident timeline + decisions
- `#eng-oncall`: coordination with service owners
- `#support` (if customer tickets are active): what customers will see and recommended guidance

### What to communicate (minimum viable)
- Impacted region(s), route(s), model(s)
- Current error codes/status behavior (429 vs 503)
- Whether Retry-After is present and recommended backoff
- Estimated time to next update

### Customer-facing status update template (status page or support macro)
**Title:** Elevated overload errors for Hosted API in <region>

**Body:**
We are investigating elevated request rejections for the Redwood Hosted API in <region>. During this period, some requests may receive **429** or **503** responses with an overload error code. These responses are an intentional protection mechanism to keep the platform stable.

**What to do:**
- Respect the `Retry-After` header and retry with exponential backoff + jitter.
- Avoid immediate high-concurrency retries.
- If you are streaming or sending very large prompts, consider reducing concurrency or request size temporarily.

**Next update:** <time, e.g., 30 minutes>

### Support handoff snippet (for active tickets)
- “This is a capacity-protection response. Please share the `x-redwood-correlation-id` and approximate timestamp/region/model. Recommended retry behavior: respect `Retry-After`, exponential backoff with jitter, and cap concurrent retries.”

## Data to capture during the incident (for postmortem + tuning)
Capture these as you go (paste into incident doc or #incidents thread).

### Incident header
- Start time (UTC):
- Region(s):
- Routes:
- Models:
- Tiers affected:
- Primary symptom: (shed spike / timeouts / stuck open / missing Retry-After / fallback failure)

### Key metrics (before and after each change)
- Shed rate (%), by tier
- Breaker open events/min
- p95/p99 latency
- Runtime queue depth (prefill/decode)
- Token/sec saturation (if available)
- 5xx/timeouts rate
- Retry-After missing rate
- Fallback attempt rate + success rate

### Configuration deltas
For each change:
- Timestamp (UTC)
- Selector: region + route + model + tier/tenant
- Key changed + old value + new value
- Expected effect
- Observed effect (5–10 minutes later)

### Customer impact highlights
- Top affected tenants (if permitted for internal visibility)
- Number of support tickets opened (link IDs)
- Any enterprise escalation (name + account team)

## Post-incident follow-ups (within 48 hours)
- File issues for:
  - False positives (thresholds too low, bad signals)
  - Missing Retry-After/correlation ID
  - Fallback routing failures or loops
  - Poor tier isolation behavior
- Update the tuning sheet (region/model thresholds) with evidence.
- Confirm SLO/error-budget classification for overload errors is correct for the window.

## Escalation matrix
- **Gateway admission / policy eval issues**: Platform Control Plane + API Gateway oncall (Ethan Park / Amara Diallo; Benji Okafor / Jordan Lee)
- **Routing fallback issues**: Smart Routing oncall (Mina Haddad / Ravi Menon / Elena Popov)
- **Runtime saturation / signal issues**: Serving Runtime oncall (Sofia Ivanova / Lena Fischer / Omar El-Sayed)
- **Dashboards/alerts anomalies**: SRE + Observability (Aisha Bello / Logan Wright / Allison Grant)

## Appendix: Overload error handling reminders (for oncall)
- Prefer explicit overload errors (429/503 with stable `error.code`) over allowing timeouts/ambiguous 5xx.
- Ensure consistent `Retry-After` to prevent retry storms.
- Changes should be scoped (region/route/model/tier) and reversible.
- Tenant isolation is a requirement: avoid global disables that allow a single tenant to dominate capacity.


[Add overload error classification rules (separate from 5xx) for Hosted API SLO reporting]
description:
Context: As part of the Hosted circuit breakers + load shedding rollout, the gateway and downstream services now emit stable overload semantics (HTTP 429/503 + a Redwood error code + Retry-After). Our current SLO classifier treats most 5xx as availability failures, which makes overload-induced shedding look like an outage and obscures the intent of graceful degradation. This PR updates slo-toolkit classification rules so overload errors are tracked separately from generic 5xx while still being visible in dashboards/alerts.

What this changes: Adds a new classifier bucket `overload` and rules to map requests into it based on (1) the canonical Redwood error code (from `x-redwood-error-code` header or JSON body `error.code`) and (2) the overload HTTP status mapping (429/503 with overload code). Removes these responses from the default 5xx classifier so they no longer inflate `server_error` rates. Adds a policy switch to treat `overload` as excluded from the availability SLO calculation for Hosted API (per the updated SLO policy) while still emitting a parallel time series to quantify shed rate.

Signals supported: - Header: `x-redwood-error-code` in {`OVERLOAD_SHED`, `BREAKER_OPEN`, `CAPACITY_EXHAUSTED`, `DEPENDENCY_SATURATED`} - Body: `{"error":{"code":"overload_*"}}` (prefix match) - Status: 429/503 only count as overload when accompanied by an overload code (to avoid misclassifying generic 429 throttles)

Tests/validation: Adds fixtures using payloads from the gateway implementation PRs and validates (a) overload is not counted as 5xx, (b) availability burn excludes overload when `availability.exclude_overload=true`, (c) regression coverage for legacy 503s with no code still count as 5xx.

Rollout notes: This is a non-breaking change to the toolkit. Consumers should pull the latest rule bundle and confirm the new `overload` series is wired into dashboards. Follow-up work will update the default dashboard templates in observability-pack to include the new breakdown.

Refs: - Reliability program: Hosted circuit breakers + load shedding - ADR-014 overload error taxonomy - Related PRs: redwood#18421, redwood#18472 - Linear: ENG-4826 / ENG-4822

release_notes:
- SLO Toolkit now classifies overload/load-shed responses into a dedicated "overload" bucket (instead of generic 5xx).
- Adds policy-driven handling to optionally exclude overload from availability SLO burn while still tracking it as a first-class rate.
- Includes fixtures/tests for 429/503 overload payloads and header-based error signaling.

Aisha Bello: Yep — added an explicit guard: 429/503 are only overload if `x-redwood-error-code` is in the overload set OR body.error.code matches `overload_*`. A plain 429 still goes to `client_throttle`.

Sean Gallagher: Looks good. Add a note that excluding overload from availability is controlled by policy and should match the SLO doc.

[Runbook: Hosted Canary Rollout stuck or traffic split mismatch]
## Purpose
This runbook covers two common incident modes for **Hosted canary rollouts**:

1) **Rollout is stuck** (step not progressing, state machine not advancing, approvals not unblocking, or auto-stop evaluation hanging).
2) **Traffic split mismatch** (observed baseline/canary traffic does not match the configured percentage, or behaves differently by region).

It provides a fast triage path, diagnostic checks, safe mitigations, rollback steps, and escalation guidance.

---

## Scope / systems
**Applies to:** Hosted routes using percentage-based canary split.

**Core components involved:**
- **Console** (customer UI + orchestrator client)
- **Rollout Orchestrator** (control-plane service; rollout state machine)
- **Smart Routing / Data Plane** (enforces split; deterministic cohorting)
- **Policy Engine** (guardrails, approvals, soak-time rules)
- **Telemetry Pipeline** (cohort tagging + metrics aggregation for stop conditions)

**Non-goals:** Dedicated/Private deployments (use the Dedicated/Private rollout runbooks once published).

---

## Severity guidance (SRE)
Use the following guidelines when declaring severity:

- **SEV-1:** Widespread routing impact (many tenants), large latency/5xx increase, or rollout control plane causing sustained customer outage.
- **SEV-2:** Single large tenant impacted (SLA risk), or split mismatch causing repeated auto-pauses/rollbacks with user-visible degradation.
- **SEV-3:** Rollout stuck without service impact (customer blocked but production stable) or split mismatch limited to one region with low traffic.

If in doubt and customer-facing impact is ongoing, escalate severity early; mitigation (freeze/rollback) is typically low-risk.

---

## Safety principles
1) **Prefer freezing/rollback to “debugging in place”** when production health is at risk.
2) **Change one thing at a time**: pause rollout, confirm stable, then investigate.
3) **Avoid cardinality blow-ups**: do not add ad-hoc high-cardinality tags in telemetry during an incident.
4) **Audit everything**: use official endpoints so actions appear in audit logs.

---

## Quick triage checklist (5 minutes)
### Inputs to collect
- Tenant ID / org slug
- Hosted route (route_id) and region(s)
- rollout_id
- Baseline model version/config and canary model version/config
- Expected split schedule (e.g., 1% → 5% → 25%)
- Time window when mismatch/stuck began

### Immediate actions
1) **Check for service-wide incident:**
   - Data plane errors elevated? Control plane elevated? Telemetry ingestion delayed?
2) **Pause rollout if customer impact is ongoing:**
   - Pausing should hold current split (depending on policy), preventing step changes while you triage.
3) If splits are clearly unsafe (e.g., canary unexpectedly at ~100%): **Rollback immediately**.

---

## Symptoms and likely causes
### A) Rollout is “stuck”
**Common symptoms:**
- Step does not progress after soak time.
- Rollout state shows “Evaluating metrics…” indefinitely.
- Approval gate is shown as satisfied in UI, but orchestrator still “waiting”.
- Auto-stop evaluation timeouts; rollout remains “Paused by system” but cannot be resumed.

**Likely causes:**
- Telemetry aggregation delay or missing cohort tags (rollout_id/cohort not present).
- Orchestrator job runner backlog / stuck worker.
- Policy engine denying progression (but UI error not surfaced due to stale validation).
- Region split application failed in one region (partial apply), leaving orchestrator waiting for “applied” acknowledgements.

### B) Traffic split mismatch
**Common symptoms:**
- Observed canary traffic differs significantly from configured percent.
- Split matches overall, but **per-region** mismatch (e.g., us-east OK, eu-west off).
- Mismatch only for streaming requests or retries.
- Canary sees 0% traffic despite non-zero configuration.

**Likely causes:**
- Deterministic cohort key mismatch (unexpected hashing input due to missing user/session key).
- Sticky assignment changes across retries (incorrect retry key usage).
- Multi-region propagation lag (config not yet applied everywhere).
- Data plane caching old route config.
- A/B test or fallback routing policy taking precedence (policy evaluation order).

---

## Where to look (dashboards/logs)
> Replace placeholders with tenant/route/rollout identifiers.

### Recommended dashboards
- **Hosted Rollouts: Cohort Overview**
  - Error rate (5xx), timeouts, p95 latency baseline vs canary
  - Request volume baseline vs canary
- **Smart Routing: Config Apply Health**
  - Route config version by region
  - Apply failures / stale cache counters
- **Rollout Orchestrator: State Machine & Worker Health**
  - Queue depth, job latency, failed transitions
- **Telemetry: Cohort Tagging Coverage**
  - % of requests with rollout_id
  - % of requests with cohort label (baseline/canary)

### Logs to query
- **rollout-orchestrator** (state transitions, stop-condition evaluation results)
- **routing-gateway / smart-routing** (route config version, cohort selection decisions)
- **policy-engine** (deny reasons, required approvals, max step size/soak enforcement)

---

## Diagnostic procedure
### Step 1 — Confirm truth: what is configured vs what is observed
1) **Fetch rollout details** (source of truth = orchestrator):
   - Verify state: DRAFT / RUNNING / PAUSED / ROLLED_BACK / COMPLETED
   - Verify current step target percentage
   - Verify region scope and any partial-apply warnings
2) **Compare to observed traffic**:
   - Look at request counts per cohort over the last 10–15 minutes.
   - Compare overall and per region.

**Interpretation tips:**
- At low volumes, small absolute differences look like large % differences; check confidence intervals and absolute counts.
- Deterministic cohorting can produce slight variance at very low traffic; treat >2–3x deviation (or persistent deviation >15 minutes) as suspicious.

### Step 2 — Determine which failure mode you’re in
Use this table:

| Observation | Most likely area | Next check |
|---|---|---|
| Orchestrator state not changing; UI shows stuck in evaluation | Orchestrator / Telemetry | Telemetry delays; orchestrator worker health |
| Orchestrator progressed step, but traffic doesn’t reflect it | Smart Routing / propagation | Config version by region; routing cache |
| Only one region mismatched | Propagation / region-specific dataplane | Route config apply status in that region |
| Canary traffic is 0% despite >0% config | Cohort tagging / eligibility filter | Cohort eligibility decision logs |
| Canary traffic is ~100% unexpectedly | Routing precedence or config corruption | Policy evaluation order; rollback immediately |

### Step 3 — Check telemetry tag coverage (critical for both auto-stop and “truth”)
- Validate that requests include:
  - rollout_id
  - cohort = baseline/canary
  - route_id
  - region

If cohort tags are missing for >5% of requests, metrics comparisons can be misleading and stop conditions can misfire.

**If missing tags:** treat as a telemetry/data-plane integration issue. Prefer pausing/rolling back and escalating to Telemetry + Smart Routing.

### Step 4 — Check config propagation and cache
- Confirm latest route config version is applied in each region.
- Check for config apply errors or stale-cache counters.

**If propagation lag:**
- Wait a short window (typically 2–5 minutes) if the system is otherwise healthy.
- If lag exceeds 10 minutes or affects high-traffic tenants, mitigate (pause/rollback) and escalate.

---

## Mitigation playbooks
## 1) Safe pause (recommended first action when unsure)
**When to use:** Rollout health uncertain; need to stop automated progression.

**Effects:**
- Stops step progression.
- Depending on configuration, split may remain at current value (most common) or revert to previous safe step (tenant policy dependent).

**Procedure:**
1) Pause rollout from Console (preferred; ensures audit event):
   - Console → Hosted Route → Rollouts → Select rollout → **Pause**
2) Confirm in orchestrator that state is PAUSED and no scheduled transitions remain.
3) Monitor baseline/canary metrics for 10 minutes.

**If pause fails:** proceed to “Kill switch / forced rollback”.

---

## 2) Rollback to baseline (fastest path to safety)
**When to use:**
- Canary causing errors/latency regressions.
- Split is incorrect and sends too much traffic to canary.
- Orchestrator stuck in a state that risks further automated changes.

**Procedure (Console):**
1) Console → Rollout → **Rollback**
2) Confirm rollback target (baseline version/config)
3) Confirm rollback is applied in all regions (config version converged)
4) Validate that canary traffic is ~0% (allow small residual during in-flight requests)

**Procedure (API - for oncall with appropriate permissions):**
- Use the orchestrator rollback endpoint (example):
  - `POST /v1/rollouts/{rollout_id}:rollback`

**Post-rollback checks:**
- Error rate returns to baseline.
- Split in routing logs shows baseline-only.
- Audit log contains `rollout.rollback` event with actor + reason.

---

## 3) Fix split mismatch without rollback (only if impact is low)
**When to use:**
- Split mismatch exists but canary/baseline are both healthy.
- Customer is blocked but no production regression.

**Options (in order):**
1) **Re-apply step / re-sync config**
   - Trigger a “reconcile/apply” action in orchestrator (if available to oncall).
   - Confirm apply ack in every region.
2) **Lower canary percent**
   - If canary is receiving more than expected, reduce target to a safe value (e.g., 0–1%) while investigating.
3) **Pause and hold**
   - Stop changes; coordinate with owner team for deeper fix.

Do not repeatedly “nudge” percentages quickly; it increases confusion and complicates audit timelines.

---

## 4) Kill switch / forced revert (last resort)
**When to use:**
- Orchestrator or routing plane is malfunctioning and normal rollback cannot be executed.
- Wide blast radius incident.

**Action:**
- Disable Hosted canary routing primitive via the rollout kill switch feature flag (per-tenant or global depending on incident).

**Important:**
- Coordinate with Release Oncall / SRE lead before global kill switch changes.
- File a follow-up incident task: kill switch changes should be temporary and explicitly reverted.

---

## “Rollout stuck” deep diagnostics
### A) Stuck in metric evaluation
**Checks:**
- Telemetry ingestion delay (pipeline lag)
- Metric evaluation timeouts in orchestrator logs
- Missing cohort tags

**Mitigation:**
- Pause rollout.
- If health regression: rollback.
- If only evaluation stuck but traffic split correct: keep paused and escalate to Telemetry + Orchestrator.

### B) Stuck waiting for approvals
**Checks:**
- Confirm approver role present for tenant (RBAC).
- Confirm audit event for approval exists (`rollout.approve`).
- Check policy engine deny reasons for step change.

**Mitigation:**
- If UI approval happened but orchestrator didn’t register it: re-approve via Console.
- If policy denies: adjust plan to comply (smaller step size, longer soak) or request tenant admin to change policy.

### C) Stuck due to partial region apply
**Checks:**
- One region reports older route config version.
- Smart Routing logs show apply failures.

**Mitigation:**
- Pause rollout.
- If canary receiving unintended traffic in that region: rollback.
- Escalate to Smart Routing oncall (see escalation section).

---

## “Bad split” deep diagnostics
### A) Validate cohorting inputs
**What to validate in routing decision logs:**
- Hash key inputs: tenant_id, route_id, stable request key (e.g., user_id/session_id if provided), plus rollout_id.
- Stickiness rules across retries and streaming reconnects.

**Common pitfalls:**
- Missing user/session key causes cohorting to fall back to request-id which changes frequently (appears non-deterministic).
- Retry path not preserving cohort assignment.

**Mitigation:**
- If cohorting is unstable: rollback and escalate to Smart Routing.

### B) Policy precedence causing unexpected routing
**Checks:**
- Fallback routing policy may override canary selection.
- Region routing constraints may redirect canary traffic to baseline in some regions.
- Quota/rate limiting policy may shed canary disproportionately.

**Mitigation:**
- Prefer rollback if behavior is not easily explained.
- Escalate to Policy Engine if denies/overrides suspected.

---

## Customer communication guidance (Support + Oncall)
- If customer impact is active: inform Support that rollout has been paused/rolled back and provide ETA for follow-up.
- Avoid blaming “metrics are wrong”; instead say “cohort measurements are being verified” and that rollout safety has been prioritized.
- Provide a short audit-friendly reason for rollback/pause in the incident ticket.

---

## Escalation paths
### Primary oncall (first responders)
- **SRE Oncall:** coordinate severity, comms, incident process
- **Rollout Orchestrator owner:** Engineering Platform (Console backend / orchestration)

### Component-specific escalation
- **Smart Routing / Data plane split enforcement:** Mina Haddad / Ravi Menon (routing oncall)
- **Telemetry / cohort tagging & aggregation:** Logan Wright / Caleb Johnson
- **Policy engine / guardrails / approvals:** Jordan Lee / Benji Okafor
- **Security / audit logging integrity:** Marcus Lin / Kevin Osei

### When to page immediately
- Split mismatch sends materially more traffic than expected to canary (especially >25% when configured <=5%).
- Rollout actions (pause/rollback) fail or do not take effect within 5 minutes.
- Multi-tenant or multi-region routing anomalies.

---

## Evidence to capture (for post-incident)
- rollout_id, tenant, route_id, regions
- Orchestrator state timeline (timestamps of transitions)
- Config versions per region (before/after mitigation)
- Dashboard snapshots (baseline vs canary) around the event
- Relevant log excerpts:
  - routing decision samples showing cohort assignment
  - orchestrator errors/timeouts
  - telemetry lag indicators
- Audit log events for actions taken (pause/rollback/killswitch)

---

## Post-incident follow-ups (create tasks)
Create follow-ups in the appropriate area:
- If stuck due to metric evaluation timeouts: harden retries/backoff and improve UI surfacing.
- If split mismatch due to cohort key instability: add guardrails/warnings when stable key is absent; improve docs.
- If partial region apply: improve reconcile loop and alert on config divergence.
- If policy precedence confusion: add “effective routing decision” explanation in Console.

---

## Appendix: Common commands / queries (examples)
> Commands vary by environment. Use approved internal tooling; do not run ad-hoc DB writes.

### Orchestrator: fetch rollout
- `rwctl rollouts get --rollout-id <rollout_id> --tenant <tenant_id>`

### Orchestrator: pause / rollback
- `rwctl rollouts pause --rollout-id <rollout_id> --reason "Incident mitigation"`
- `rwctl rollouts rollback --rollout-id <rollout_id> --reason "Split mismatch"`

### Routing: check config version by region
- `rwctl routes config-version --route-id <route_id> --tenant <tenant_id> --all-regions`

### Telemetry: validate cohort tag coverage
- Query: `rollout_tag_coverage{tenant="<tenant_id>", route="<route_id>", rollout_id="<rollout_id>"}`
