[Streaming write-stall + TTL regression — hosted API outage postmortem (2026-04-25)]
Summary:

On 2026-04-25 at ~02:12 UTC the hosted streaming API experienced a high-severity outage that manifested as 5xx errors for streaming sessions and extreme tail latency for non-streaming requests. Impact lasted ~43 minutes for customers on affected regions and degraded for another 90 minutes during mitigation rollouts. Root cause: an unintended change to a per-connection TTL/keepalive config combined with an edge buffer write-stall bug in the streaming proxy, which caused head-of-line stalls and backlog amplification under normal traffic spikes.

Impact:
- Scope: ~11% of streaming sessions experienced repeated 5xx (502/504) immediately; additional ~7% of non-streaming requests saw 95th+ latency spikes from 600ms -> 3.2s.
- Customers: 23 enterprise tenants saw visible error rates; a handful of PLG customers reported degraded developer experience. No data loss or model correctness issues were observed.
- Business: Incidents triggered PagerDuty P0 and on-call SREs initiated incident response. External status page was updated.

How it was detected:
- First alert: custom anomaly detector on streaming session error-rate crossed threshold at 02:13 UTC (SRE paging).
- Secondary signals: edge response-time dashboards and increased connection resets observed in edge logs.
- Pager: 02:14 UTC, SRE lead ack at 02:15 UTC.

Timeline (UTC):
- 02:12 — initial spike in streaming session errors; error rate rose from baseline 0.3% to 18% in 2 minutes.
- 02:13 — anomaly alert fires; on-call SRE starts investigation.
- 02:14 — correlating logs show write stall metrics on streaming proxy (high write queue depth).
- 02:18 — quick mitigation: rolling restart of streaming-proxy fleet in affected region, partial drop in errors but tail latency persisted.
- 02:25 — rollback of a recent edge-config change that adjusted connection TTL made at 01:55 UTC. Edge config rollback began.
- 02:35 — error rates fall to ~2%; tail latency trending down but not fully recovered.
- 02:55 — full rollback complete and additional throttling rules temporarily applied; streaming success rates returned to baseline.
- 03:00 — status page updated to reflect mitigation progress.
- 04:30 — follow-up remediation runs and validation; monitoring shows stable behavior. Incident declared mitigated at 04:35.

Root cause analysis (why):
- Primary bug: an existing bug in streaming-proxy write handling where a stalled TCP write (EAGAIN/later drain) could leave per-connection buffers frozen while the proxy's internal queue accounting incorrectly marked the connection as writable. This allowed the proxy to continue accepting streaming state and buffer memory without advancing network writes, producing head-of-line stalls.
- Trigger: a separately deployed edge config tweak at 01:55 UTC reduced keepalive/TTL for upstream connections from 90s -> 10s to aggressively free idle connectors for recent scaling changes. This increased connection churn during normal traffic bursts and surfaced the proxy write-stall bug.
- Amplification: the serving runtime's KV cache prefetch caused more concurrent active streaming sessions per process during a traffic spike at 02:10 UTC, compounding queue depth and memory pressure on streaming-proxy workers.

Contributing factors:
- A config change (edge TTL) was rolled without a targeted canary to measure streaming-specific impact.
- The proxy bug existed in the binary for ~3 months but was low-probability; normal workloads had not triggered it at scale.
- Alerts were configured for absolute error-rate thresholds but not for queue depth or write stall latency in the streaming-proxy.
- Rollback of edge-change required coordination across teams and took longer than expected because the change was bundled with other minor fixes.

Immediate remediation performed:
- 02:18 — rolling restart of streaming-proxy processes to clear stuck write buffers (short-term relief).
- 02:25 — rollback of edge TTL config to previous value (90s).
- 02:55 — deploy temporary traffic shaping: soft concurrency limit per upstream instance and reject-new-session policy for overloaded proxies.

Longer-term fixes and planned actions:
(Planned timeline + owner)
- Fix proxy write-stall bug in runtime and add explicit writeback checks (PR: runtime#657). Owner: Miguel Torres. ETA: 2026-05-03.
- Add unit+integration tests that simulate partial write backpressure and verify buffer accounting. Owner: Juno Kim. ETA: 2026-05-10.
- Update deployment practices: require streaming-sensitive canary (1% traffic for 30m) for edge/TCP-level TTL or connection lifecycle changes. Owner: Priya Raman (edge infra). ETA: 2026-05-01.
- Implement alerting for streaming-proxy write-queue depth and per-connection write latency (new SLI). Owner: Liam O'Connor. ETA: 2026-04-30.
- Run a chaos experiment to model connection churn under reduced TTLs to ensure proxy resilience. Owner: Evelyn Zhang. ETA: 2026-05-07.

Runbook and playbook changes (immediate edits):
- Add a new streaming runbook section: "Detect and mitigate write stalls" including commands for probing write queue depth, safe rolling restart procedure, and temp traffic shaping knobs. Owner: Ana Patel. Actioned: draft added to Confluence, see linked runbook.
- Add step that any edge-level connection/TTL changes must include a streaming-canary approval checkbox. Owner: Priya Raman.

Monitoring & alerts to add/modify:
- New alert: streaming-proxy.write_queue_depth > 500 for > 2m -> P1.
- New alert: streaming-proxy.per_conn_write_latency_p95 > 1s -> P1.
- Adjust anomaly detector to correlate streaming error-rate with write-queue depth before auto-scaling decisions.
- Dashboard: new streaming health panel with per-region metrics: conn churn, write queue depth, buffer memory, and per-second stream accepts.

Customer communication:
- At 02:20 UTC we published a short status page update.
- Post-incident public note to affected tenants drafted and queued for account team review. Owner: Customer Success (cc: Ana Patel). ETA for send: 2026-04-27.

Action items (owner — due):
- Miguel Torres — land runtime fix and coordinate canary release (2026-05-03).
- Juno Kim — add integration tests and run pre-merge CI scenarios (2026-05-10).
- Priya Raman — update edge deployment checklist + canary gating (2026-05-01).
- Liam O'Connor — implement monitoring alerts + dashboard (2026-04-30).
- Evelyn Zhang — run chaos/connection-churn experiment and share findings (2026-05-07).
- Ana Patel — finalize runbook writeup and schedule SRE runbook walk-through (2026-04-29).

Lessons learned / retrospective notes:
- Low-probability bugs can become high-impact when paired with seemingly innocuous config changes (keepalive/TTL tweaks).
- Edge-level changes touching connection lifecycle must be treated as high-risk for streaming customers; they require a streaming-aware canary path.
- Having more fine-grained streaming proxy SLIs (queue depth & per-conn write latency) would have accelerated detection and reduced MTTR.
- Rolling restarts are effective short-term mitigation but we need faster rollback paths for edge configs (decouple TTL change from unrelated cleanup fixes).

Appendix (commands and quick diagnostics):
- Check streaming proxy write queue depth: 
  - curl -s http://proxy-metrics/metrics | grep write_queue_depth | awk '{print $2}'
- Live tail to detect stuck writes: 
  - ssh proxy-node && sudo journalctl -u streaming-proxy -f | grep "write stall"
- Safe rolling restart (recommended): 
  - kubectl rollout restart deployment/streaming-proxy -n hosted-api --selector=region=<region> --max-unavailable=2

[Edge TLS rehandshake cascade — P1 hosted API incident postmortem]
Summary:

On 2026-03-19 between ~18:04 and 18:42 UTC the hosted API experienced increased 5xx rates and elevated tail latency for streaming and short-text generation routes. Impact: ~14% of requests returned 5xx (mostly 502/504) and median p99 latency increased from ~120ms to ~1.8s for affected routes. No data exfiltration. Total customer-facing window ~38 minutes with partial recovery after manual mitigation. Severity: P1 (service degraded, significant customer impact to streaming clients).

What happened (plain English):
An interaction between a recently deployed change to edge TLS session handling and a spike in client connection churn caused our edge proxies to perform repeated TLS rehandshakes. Rehandshakes caused worker thread saturation inside the proxy process and increased time spent waiting on socket handshakes, which in turn delayed request forwarding and caused connection timeouts to upstream compute pools. Several upstream pools returned connection errors under heavy backlog, producing 502/504s.

Detection and timeline (UTC):
- 18:03:42 ALERT: grafana-alert edge-5xx-rate crossed threshold (anomaly detection)
- 18:04:05 Pager duty -> on-call SRE (Arjun) paged
- 18:05:10 Initial triage: spike in SYN/SSL activity shown on edge egress metrics; SYN rate up 3x baseline
- 18:06:00 Observed p99 TLS handshake duration climb from 8ms to 250ms on edge-proxy nodes
- 18:08:20 502/504 spike begins in hosted-api-prod (~12% 5xx)
- 18:12:00 Scoped to region-us-west-2 edge cluster (edge-cluster-7)
- 18:18:00 Mitigation 1: scaled edge-proxy deployment from 12 -> 24 replicas (manual kubectl scale)
- 18:22:30 Mitigation 2: applied transient iptables rule to drop repeated rehandshake traffic from abusive IP blocks (temporary stopgap)
- 18:28:00 Partial recovery noted (5xx reduced to ~4%)
- 18:42:00 System stabilized; monitoring continued for 3 hours

Root cause analysis:
Primary cause: regression in edge-proxy TLS session resumption logic introduced in PR #482 (changes to session cache eviction and new per-connection session ticket behavior). Under high connection churn, session resumption attempts failed more often causing full handshake fallbacks.
Contributing factors:
- Lower-than-expected session-ticket reuse due to the change in how tickets are marked stale (cache TTL miscalculation).
- Edge proxy's thread model prioritized connection accept over completing handshakes, allowing queue build-up of unfinished handshakes.
- No automatic fallback rule existed to route excess TLS-handshake-heavy traffic to a standby proxy tier.

Why didn't auto-scaling catch it sooner?
Horizontal autoscaler targets CPU but TLS handshakes were blocking in user-space and not always reflected as CPU spike (blocked syscalls). The manual scale helped but was slower than an ideal reactive mitigation.

Immediate mitigation steps performed: (what we did during incident)
- Brief: scale edge-proxy horizontally (kubectl scale deployment/edge-proxy -n edge 12 -> 24)
- Blacklist high-rate client IPs at iptables level on edge-cluster-7 to interrupt rehandshake storm
- Re-deployed previous edge-proxy image (rollback to v1.14.3) onto a canary subset of nodes to validate that rollback reduces handshake duration
- Opened traffic steering to fallback region for a small % of traffic (5%) to relieve pressure on us-west-2

Longer-term fixes proposed (with owners and target dates):
- Revert and patch session-ticket TTL logic in PR #482 (owner: Lucia Morales, due: 2026-03-26)
- Add a handshake-duration SLO and alert (owner: Ben O'Neill, due: 2026-04-02)
- Implement backlog-aware autoscaler metric (blocked-fds / handshake-queue-length) (owner: SRE infra team, due: 2026-05-01)
- Build an automatic traffic circuit-breaker that detects excessive TLS-handshake retries and routes to standby cluster (owner: Eng Proxy, due: 2026-05-15)
- Add unit/integration tests for session ticket resumption edge cases and simulate high churn (owner: Applied ML infra, due: 2026-04-10)

Runbook draft (new items to add to edge runbook):
- Detection: add metric `edge.tls.handshake_duration_p99` and alert on sustained >200ms for 3m
- Triage steps:
  1) Identify affected cluster: query grafana dashboard `edge-tps-and-errors` for server/region
  2) Check `ss -ntp | grep ESTAB` and `netstat` for high connection churn patterns
  3) Run `kubectl get pods -n edge -o wide` to find node saturation
- Immediate mitigations:
  - `kubectl scale deployment/edge-proxy -n edge --replicas=<current*2>`
  - `kubectl rollout undo deployment/edge-proxy -n edge --to-revision=<previous>` (if rollback validated)
  - On-call: run `sudo iptables -I INPUT -s <ip> -j DROP` for abusive IPs and log for remediation team
- Escalation: if >10% 5xx persists for >10m, page Eng Proxy and Product (CS) and consider partial traffic migration

On-call notes (commands run / observations captured):
- 18:05 arjun@oncall: ssh edge-cluster-7-proxy-3 -> ran `tcpdump -n -i eth0 'tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-syn) != 0'` and observed SYN burst from ~120 unique /16 ranges
- 18:08 ran `openssl s_client -connect proxy:443 -tls1_2 -msg` and captured repeated FULL handshakes vs session reuse
- 18:15 `kubectl get hpa -n edge` showed no change; HPA configured on CPU only
- 18:18 `kubectl scale deployment/edge-proxy -n edge --replicas=24` (effects visible ~3m later)
- 18:22 set temporary iptables drops on 8 candidate IP blocks (audit ticket JIRA-2021 opened to review)

Lessons learned:
- Testing: Session cache edge-cases were not covered by integration tests that simulate massive connection churn; add load tests that specifically exercise TLS resumption behavior.
- Monitoring: CPU-only autoscaling missed a starvation mode; we need metrics for blocked syscalls and handshake queue depth.
- Runbook: insufficient guidance on when to deploy iptables blocks vs. rollback; add explicit decision tree.
- Release process: any change touching TLS/session-ticket handling should require a canary in low-traffic region for 48h with synthetic churn test.

Action items (owner / ETA / status):
- Lucia Morales — revert session-ticket TTL bug and PR with unit tests — due 2026-03-26 — open
- Ben O'Neill — add handshake-duration SLO + grafana alert — due 2026-04-02 — in_progress
- Arjun Kapoor — update edge runbook with triage and iptables decision tree — due 2026-04-06 — in_progress
- SRE infra — prototype backlog-aware HPA metric (handshake queue length exporter) — due 2026-05-01 — planned
- Applied ML infra — create integration test harness for connection churn and TLS resumption — due 2026-04-10 — planned

- Incident Slack thread: linked_artifacts

[Streaming backpressure / queue saturation - SRE on-call notes]
Quick summary:

- What happened: Between ~2026-04-20T09:14:00Z and 2026-04-20T10:05:00Z the hosted streaming API experienced elevated 5xx rates and end-to-end tail latency spikes for a subset of customers using long-lived streaming sessions. The primary symptom was steady growth in the streaming request-handling queue on edge muxers and a cascade of HTTP 502/504 from downstream worker pools.

- Impact: ~4.2% of production streaming requests returned 5xx during the window, with tail latency P99s for streaming endpoints increasing from ~120ms to ~2.1s for affected regions (us-west-2). A small number of clients saw session disconnects and had to reconnect. No data loss reported; sessions that reconnected resumed normally.

- Detection: Alert: STREAMING_WORKER_QUEUE_DEPTH_HIGH (threshold 1500 msgs) fired at 2026-04-20T09:16:18Z. Follow-up alert STREAMING_PROXY_5XX_RATE_HIGH (5xx > 1%) fired at 09:18:02Z. On-call paged at 09:19.

Timeline (UTC):
- 09:14:00 - first abnormal increase in muxer queue length observed on dashboards (manual exploration by monitoring runbook).
- 09:16:18 - automated alert STREAMING_WORKER_QUEUE_DEPTH_HIGH triggered for us-west-2.
- 09:18:02 - 5xx rate crossed automated threshold. Slack thread created (#incident-streaming).
- 09:20:00 - first mitigation: increased worker_pool size by +25% via autoscaler override (temporary). Partial reduction in queue growth but 5xx persisted.
- 09:28:00 - discovered a correlation: sudden spike in small short-lived reroute requests from a single customer tenant ID (tenant-x) with many concurrent streaming sessions opening and immediately sending high-frequency messages.
- 09:35:00 - enabled per-tenant soft-rate limit on open streaming session creation for tenant-x (throttle to 50 new sessions / minute). Queue growth stabilized.
- 09:45:00 - rolling restart of streaming-proxy pods to clear transient backlog of stalled connections. Short blips of connection reset observed but overall 5xx rate trended down.
- 10:05:00 - incident declared mitigated; monitoring observed normal queue depths and 5xx returned to baseline by 10:12:00.

Initial root cause hypothesis:
- The immediate cause was an unbounded burst of streaming session creations + high message fanout from a single tenant that overloaded the muxer->worker queue coupling. Two amplifiers made the effect worse: (1) an overly permissive per-connection concurrency policy in the edge muxer that allowed many ephemeral sessions to occupy internal buffers; (2) degraded KV cache lookup performance (seen as higher KV latency) causing workers to spend more CPU/latency per message, reducing throughput and increasing queue dwell time.

Evidence supporting hypothesis:
- Grafana: muxer queue depth correlated closely with tenant-x session creation rate (annotation + correlation panel).
- Traces: distributed tracing shows increased time in kv-cache.get (P95 from ~1.6ms to ~12ms) for requests during the window.
- Worker metrics: worker-side CPU increased ~30% and message processing time per-message doubled for affected shards.
- Logs: streaming-proxy logs show many ephemeral connections with small payloads and frequent open/close pattern from the same IP block owned by tenant-x.

Why it became P0-level:
- Existing soft limits for session creation were tuned for steady-growth patterns, not pathological rapid open/close loops.
- Autoscaler for workers reacts to CPU/latency slowly; autoscaling alone cannot prevent queue overflow when processing cost per-message increases sharply.

Immediate mitigations taken (chronological):
1) Manual temporary increase of worker pool capacity (+25%) via aws/gke override to buy time. (Benji)
2) Per-tenant throttle applied to tenant-x streaming session creation (soft-limit, rejected new sessions with 429 until stabilised). (Aisha)
3) Rolling restart of streaming-proxy pods to drop stuck socket state and reduce OS-level connection fanout. (Carlos)
4) Short-term configuration: reduced muxer per-connection buffer retention to 30s (from 2m) to free up memory and queue slots. (Zoe)

Commands & links used during troubleshooting (notes to self):
- kubectl -n streaming get hpa -o wide; kubectl -n streaming scale deployment/streaming-worker --replicas=24
- curl -X POST "https://controlplane.redwood/api/v1/tenants/tenant-x/throttle" -d '{"streaming_new_session_rate":50}'  # temp
- grafana dashboards: streaming/muxer-queues, streaming/worker-latency (use correlation view)
- traces: jaeger/service=streaming-proxy?start=2026-04-20T09:00

Permanent root cause analysis (consolidated):
- Trigger: tenant-x load generator (malfunctioning integration) created many short sessions that produced high fanout and heavy KV cache traffic.
- Amplifier 1: muxer allowed unlimited ephemeral sessions to allocate internal resources (buffers/slots), leading to queue backlog.
- Amplifier 2: KV cache SLO regression during the window (disk/ephemeral node GC on one kv-cluster shard) slowed down worker-side lookups and increased per-message processing time.
- System design gap: lack of effective per-tenant open-session rate limiting and insufficient backpressure propagation from workers to proxies/muxers. Also, autoscaler is reactive and too slow for sudden bursts when processing cost per unit increases.

Proposed runbook changes (draft):
- Add a new incident play: "Streaming: tenant surge/backpressure" with clear steps:
  * Detect: runbook should include tenant-level session-open rate panel and an alert STREAMING_TENANT_SESSION_OPEN_HIGH (per-tenant threshold: 100/min by default).
  * Immediate actions: apply per-tenant soft-throttle (controlplane API) -> if that fails, apply tenant blackhole gate for extreme cases (ops only).
  * If queue depth > X and 5xx > Y, scale worker_pool to N and trigger rolling restart of streaming-proxy in a controlled fashion (30s drain, one AZ at a time).
  * If kv-cache P95 > 10ms, switch the worker-side cache to read-through fallback mode (local LRU) and escalate kv-cluster runbook.
- Implement backpressure channel: worker should surface processing backpressure metrics to proxy (gRPC headers or health flags) so proxy can immediately start rejecting new sessions instead of relying on global queue depth alerts.
- Tune defaults: reduce per-connection buffer retention (default 120s -> 45s) and set a hard cap of 10k ephemeral sessions per-proxy instance.
- Autoscaler tuning: add a burst-mode that can temporarily oversubscribe more aggressively when processing latency increases and queue depth is rapidly rising.
