[Go SDK streaming tool-callback: webhook HMAC signature mismatch after proxy timestamp truncation causing duplicate tool executions on retry]
description:
Issue summary:
NimbleDocs is seeing duplicated downstream tool executions (webhook target receives same tool invocation twice) when a streaming generation triggers a function/tool call. The Go SDK client receives a transient signature verification error from the webhook endpoint on the first delivery, performs a retry, and the webhook ends up executing the side effect twice.

Impact:
- Intermittent duplicate processing of invoices in customer's system (customer reports ~2-3% of requests duplicating over the past 48h).
- Affects production traffic on their Dedicated cluster in us-west-2.

Environment:
- Customer using Redwood Go SDK v0.8.3 with streaming and func_call support enabled.
- Dedicated deployment (customer-owned VPC) with API Gateway + edge proxy (third-party WAF) in front of customer webhook.

Steps to reproduce (as reported by customer):
1) Start a stream with a tool call that posts to https://hooks.nimbledocs.com/rdw-callback
2) We observe the SDK sending callback with headers: X-Redwood-TS, X-Redwood-Signature (HMAC-SHA256).
3) The customer's WAF strips millisecond precision from the timestamp header (X-Redwood-TS: 1678901234 -> 1678901234).
4) Customer server calculates HMAC using original timestamp (with ms) and signature validation fails.
5) Server returns 401 -> Redwood SDK performs immediate retry for callback delivery -> server accepts second delivery and executes tool action.

Expected behavior:
- SDK retries should not cause duplicate side effects for non-idempotent endpoints if the first delivery might have actually been processed (or should include guidance to make webhooks idempotent).

Actual behavior:
- Some webhook endpoints reject the first callback because of timestamp rounding/truncation by intermediaries, causing client retries that lead to duplicate downstream side effects.

Relevant logs (sanitized):
- SDK outbound attempt 1 headers:
  X-Redwood-TS: 1678901234.789
  X-Redwood-Signature: sha256=ab12...
- Edge/WAF observed header rewrite:
  X-Redwood-TS: 1678901234
- Customer server log: "signature mismatch: calculated=cd34... received=ab12..." -> returns 401.
- SDK outbound attempt 2 (retry) headers:
  X-Redwood-TS: 1678901235.102
  X-Redwood-Signature: sha256=ef56...
- Customer server accepts and processes the callback on attempt 2.

Attachments: customer provided packet capture showing header truncation and sample SDK trace token.

comments:
2026-03-12 10:22 - Support (Aisha): Opened with initial triage and requested packet captures and example webhook logs from customer.
2026-03-12 14:05 - Customer (NimbleDocs): Uploaded packet capture showing WAF middleware truncating X-Redwood-TS. Confirmed duplicates occur ~2% of calls.
2026-03-13 09:10 - Eng (Marcus): Reproduced locally by inserting a proxy that truncates timestamp header; observed identical signature verification failure followed by retry leading to duplicate POSTs to origin.
2026-03-13 11:40 - SRE (Lin): Noted that SDK currently includes full-ms timestamp and server-side validation expects exact match — there's no replay cache for callbacks at customer endpoint by default.
2026-03-14 08:12 - Support (Aisha): Proposed mitigations to customer and engineering follow-ups (see investigation notes and resolution).

investigation_notes:
Reproduction steps performed in internal staging: Go SDK v0.8.3 streaming client -> local proxy that truncates X-Redwood-TS to seconds -> origin validates signature with ms precision -> origin returns 401 -> SDK retries with new timestamp -> origin accepts second call. Result: duplicate execution observed.
Root cause: mismatch between the timestamp canonicalization expected by customer's HMAC verification and header mutation by an intermediary. The SDK sends a fresh signature tied to the precise timestamp; if intermediary mutates timestamp before the origin, origin will reject first attempt even though SDK signed original value. SDK then retries and issues a second signed attempt which origin accepts. No deduplication layer on customer's webhook means side effect occurs twice.
Edge case: clock skew on origin could cause legitimate rejections; however packet capture shows clock aligned — truncation is the trigger. WAF (third-party) is rewriting headers for normalization/compatibility and dropping fractional seconds.
Potential SDK behavior change: include an idempotency token in callback body/headers separate from HMAC that downstream can use for deduplication; maintain short-lived replay cache on our callback delivery subsystem (danger: extra state and memory on Redwood side).
Customer constraints: they cannot add a replay cache on origin side easily because their processing pipeline is third-party-managed. They prefer guidance to harden webhook validation logic to tolerate timestamp normalization.
Related internal links: linked SUP-473901 (retry-scope-enforcement-mismatch) may have useful context on header normalization patterns.

resolution:
Workaround provided to customer (2026-03-14):
1) Update webhook signature validation to allow for a configurable timestamp tolerance and to validate HMAC against both raw and truncated timestamp variants when the request originates from known proxies. Example pseudo-logic: accept if HMAC matches signature(timestamp_ms) OR signature(timestamp_seconds).
2) Implement idempotency check on webhook consumer using X-Redwood-Callback-Id header (we recommended customer check this header when deciding whether to execute side effects).
3) As short-term, whitelist Redwood delivery IPs on their WAF or configure the WAF to preserve X-Redwood-TS header without truncation.
Engineering follow-up (internal):
- Action item ENG-11273: Evaluate adding an X-Redwood-Callback-Id header to all SDK callback deliveries (low-risk), targeted for SDK v0.9.x.
- Action item ENG-11274: Investigate a transient dedupe cache in the callback delivery path; document operational cost/limits.
- Action item DOCS-5568: Add guidance to webhook best practices for handling timestamp normalization and idempotency patterns (include signature verification tolerant patterns and sample code for Go/Python/TS).
Status: Workaround accepted by customer. Engineering tickets created and tagged for Q2 prioritization. Keeping this support ticket open while ENG checks feasibility and until docs are published.
Final customer note: NimbleDocs implemented header-tolerance logic and reported a drop to ~0.05% duplicates over 24h after change (2026-03-14 18:30).

[Streaming resume duplicates function-call webhooks when idempotency header is rewritten by edge proxy]
description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports duplicated external webhook invocations for server-side function_call events after a client stream reconnect/resume. The original function call appears to complete on our runtime but the webhook gets invoked twice when the client retries the streaming session.

Impact:
- Customer (NimbusPayments) sees duplicate payment-create webhooks resulting in duplicated downstream jobs (idempotency not respected by downstream).
- Occurs intermittently during poor mobile network conditions when the browser/edge SDK reconnects mid-stream.
- Potential financial impact for customer: duplicate charge attempts and manual reconciliation.

Environment:
- Customer using TypeScript browser SDK v1.12.0 with streaming chat + function_call enabled.
- Dedicated deployment, prod us-east region, API fronted by CloudFront-like edge layer.
- Server runtime: serving-runtime v2.7.3, api-gateway v1.9.1.

Steps to reproduce (reported by customer):
1) Open streaming chat session from mobile web client and trigger a sequence that results in a function_call to the payment webhook (function name: create_payment).
2) Simulate a flaky network (toggle airplane mode) so the socket disconnects during the streaming/chunked response (server had already emitted a function_call and partial response).
3) Client reconnects and the SDK attempts to resume the stream with a fresh resume attempt; SDK sets an idempotency header (x-idempotency-key) on the resumed connection.
4) Observe two webhook POSTs for create_payment within seconds.

Expected behavior:
- Only a single create_payment webhook should be delivered for the original function_call. SDK retries/resume should not cause duplicate downstream side effects when an idempotency key is provided.

Actual behavior:
- Two POSTs reach customer's webhook endpoint. The first is the original in-flight delivery from the runtime. The second comes after the resumed connection and appears to be triggered by a resumed function_call state.

Observed logs (redacted):
- Runtime logs show request traces T-9a7e... and T-9a7e... (same trace) with function_call recorded once, but gateway access logs show two separate incoming streaming requests with different idempotency header values: 
  - req1: x-idempotency-key: "8e4b24f6-7a9e-4c3d-9f2a-aaaaaaa..."
  - req2: x-idempotency-key: "8e4b24f6-7a9e-4c3d-9f2a-1"  (note numeric suffix)
- Edge logs (CloudFront) show header normalization/truncation events when header length > 48 chars; downstream origin receives rewritten header name/value for second request.

Temporary workaround provided to customer:
- Advise customer to include a per-call confirmation token in the webhook payload (client-side generated) and to deduplicate on the webhook receiver while we investigate.
- As an immediate mitigation, asked customer to increase server-side idempotency window and to enable "webhook delivery dedupe" via a short-lived token if possible.

Root cause hypothesis so far:
- Edge proxy is rewriting or truncating the x-idempotency-key header on connection resume (some internal normalization rule at the CDN that appends/truncates long header values), causing our gateway to treat the resumed request as a distinct idempotent scope. The runtime reconciles function_call state but the gateway's idempotency lookup uses the altered key, so the resumed request triggers an additional webhook delivery.

Data points collected / logs attached:
- Access logs and header captures from edge for the two attempts (attached as support artifact).
- Server trace showing single function_call state but duplicate webhook deliveries downstream.
- Customer-provided webhook receiver logs showing two POST requests within 2s.

Proposed next steps / remediation:
1) Short term (0-24h): Document and push the recommended customer workaround (embed client-confirmation token in webhook payload and dedupe).
2) Fix the gateway to canonicalize idempotency keys from either header or streaming-metadata and accept alternate name forms (x-idempotency-key and x-idempotency). Backfill support for keys truncated by edge (map detected rewritten forms to canonical token using a best-effort normalization).
3) SDK change (TS/browser): On resume attempt, include idempotency token in both header and in the first JSON control frame body so origin sees the same token even if an edge alters headers. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/redwood-sdk/pull/842 (WIP).
4) Long term: Add signed confirmation tokens on function_call completion so webhook consumers can validate original call provenance.

Notes:
- This issue is reproducible with a synthetic test using our edge staging where we simulate header truncation; reproduction script and test harness stored on the linked Confluence page.
- We should coordinate with CDN partner to remove header normalization rules for this header or increase header length allowance.


investigation_notes:
Engineering ran correlation of traces across gateway, runtime and webhook delivery. Found mismatch between idempotency header observed at edge vs origin. Confirmed SDK sets a UUID v4 token; edge truncated to 37 chars and appended a suffix in some cases. Reproduced in staging by injecting header-mod rewrite. Eng hypothesis: CDN rule intended to canonicalize headers containing control chars is accidentally mangling long IDs. Next step: file ticket with infra/CDN partner and push gateway fallback normalization. Temporary SDK/console guidance added.

comments:
2026-03-12 09:18 - Sophie Lane (Support): Customer reports duplicate payment webhooks when mobile client reconnects mid-stream. Provided early mitigation: dedupe on webhook receiver.
2026-03-12 11:05 - Diego Martinez (Oncall Eng): Collected edge access logs and runtime traces. Seeing header value rewrite on second request; opening internal ticket INT-1203 to track CDN rule.
2026-03-13 08:40 - Aisha Kumar (SDK Eng): Drafted SDK change to include idempotency token in first control frame body as well as header. PR created: https://github.com/redwood-inference/redwood-sdk/pull/842 (needs review).
2026-03-13 15:22 - Customer (Danielle R., NimbusPayments): Confirmed they received two POSTs; currently deduping at receiver. Asked if Redwood can provide permanent server-side fix because dedupe is operationally expensive for them.
2026-03-14 10:12 - Diego Martinez (Oncall Eng): Reproduced in staging with header rewrite injection. Coordinating with CDN team; recommended gateway change to accept idempotency in streaming body as fallback.
2026-03-14 14:55 - Diego Martinez (Oncall Eng): Next action: ship SDK WIP change as patch release 1.12.1, and create gateway hotfix to map rewritten header forms. Assigned INT-1203 owner: Priya Shah.

1) Add client-generated confirmation token to webhook payload and dedupe on receiver. 2) If using a custom CDN, disable header normalization for x-idempotency-key or increase header length allowance. 3) Use the SDK patch (1.12.1) when released which writes idempotency token into control frame body as well as header.

resolution:
In Progress - mitigation applied. SDK patch and gateway normalization hotfix planned and in review.

[JSON key ordering canonicalization mismatch across SDKs causing funcall duplicates]
description:
Customer reports repeated duplicate function/tool executions when their orchestrator (TypeScript SDK) issues a function call and the downstream webhook (Go service) confirms execution. The duplicate runs occur after automatic retries — confirmations appear to be dropped/mismatched at the Redwood platform because the confirmation payload's fingerprint does not match the idempotency key generated by the original request.

impact:
Acme Health is observing duplicated patient-record enrichment jobs (side effects are non-idempotent) in production. Approx 1.7% of inbound function calls for their busiest route have executed twice in the last 24 hours, creating billing and data integrity issues. Customer has paused a subset of traffic and requests priority help.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Use ts-sdk v1.12.3 to create a streamed chat that issues a function call with a nested JSON payload (objects with 3+ levels and map-like keys).
2) The TS orchestrator computes an idempotency fingerprint and sends the request to Redwood via POST /v1/chat/completions with header 'Idempotency-Key: <fingerprint>'.
3) Redwood dispatches funcall to customer webhook (Go service using go-sdk v0.9.7) and the Go service executes the side-effect, then POSTs the confirmation back to /v1/callbacks with a JSON body that includes the original function response payload and a confirmation field.
4) Observe on retry (either client retry or Redwood retry due to 200->504 transitional path) that the confirmation is not associated with the original Idempotency-Key and Redwood executes the function a second time.
5) Repro is intermittent but increases when payloads include empty arrays and when the webhook's Go runtime serializes the confirmation using encoding/json with default settings.
6) Customer attached minimal repro harness under an anonymized token and logs in their support bundle.


logs:
[2026-03-11T02:14:03Z] INFO dispatch func_call id=fc_4b9a header Idempotency-Key=hash:0x7b3df
[2026-03-11T02:14:04Z] INFO webhook POST /callbacks status=200 body={"result":{"name":"enrich","payload":{"meta":{},"items":[]}},"confirmed_for":"hash:0x7b3df"}
[2026-03-11T02:14:05Z] WARN idempotency confirmation mismatch id=fc_4b9a expected=hash:0x7b3df received=hash:0x1a9c0
[2026-03-11T02:14:05Z] INFO retrying func_call id=fc_4b9a attempt=2

comments:
2026-03-10 15:20 Priya (Support): Opened ticket after customer provided reproduction bundle and sample traces. Noted correlation to nested payload shapes and empty arrays.
2026-03-10 16:05 Rajiv (SRE): Captured request/confirmation pairs from prod and saw fingerprints differ by hash suffix in ~1.6% of cases. Suspect mismatch in canonicalization used to compute fingerprint vs what webhook posts back as 'confirmed_for'.
2026-03-11 09:12 Liam (Eng): Reproduced locally with ts-sdk v1.12.3 and go-sdk v0.9.7 using customer's harness. Observed go encoding/json leaves map key order nondeterministic; ts-sdk was sorting keys before hashing by default.
2026-03-11 10:00 Customer (Acme Health): Confirmed they recently upgraded to go-sdk v0.9.7 and added a middleware that reserializes webhook confirmation using a standard encoder (no key sorting). Asked for mitigation while Redwood teams investigate.
2026-03-12 11:22 Liam (Eng): Submitted initial patch to guava-hash (internal canonicalizer) to add an optional deterministic serializer used by server path for matching confirmations; plan to publish go-sdk patch next.
2026-03-12 14:45 Priya (Support): Notified customer of interim workaround and ETA for SDK patch.
2026-03-12 16:30 Acme Health: Applied recommended mitigation (middleware to echo back original Idempotency-Key header as 'confirmed_for' in confirmation body) and reported duplicate rate dropped to ~0.02%.
2026-03-12 18:00 Liam (Eng): Follow-up - added unit tests and integration test in CI to cover nested-object canonicalization across SDKs.

investigation_notes:
Root-cause hypothesis: mismatch between how the TS SDK canonicalizes nested JSON prior to hashing (it sorts object keys deterministically) and how customer webhook reserializes confirmation payload (Go encoding/json does not guarantee key order). The platform associates confirmations by computing a fingerprint from confirmation body; when ordering differs the computed fingerprint differs and matches fail.
Reproducer: local harness using randomized map insertion order in Go reproduced mismatch ~15/100 runs for deep-nested maps with empty arrays and nulls.
Alternate hypothesis ruled out: network truncation and header splitting were checked and not present in the sample traces.
Related SDK versions observed in traces: ts-sdk v1.12.3 (sortKeys=true), go-sdk v0.9.7 (default encoder), python-sdk v1.3.0 not implicated in initial report but later used by a subset of customer jobs.
Impact severity analysis: Because confirmations are dropped/mismatched the platform retries which causes second execution downstream. This is high-impact for non-idempotent side effects.
Temporary mitigation succeeded when customer echoed Idempotency-Key in confirmation body rather than recomputing fingerprint locally.
Platform-side quick fix: server now computes an additional confirmation lookup using raw header Idempotency-Key if present before falling back to fingerprint-of-body match. Patch deployed to prod us-east (canary) 2026-03-12 05:00 UTC; monitoring shows reduction in duplicate execs in canary zone.
Long-term fix: make canonicalization deterministic across SDKs and publish go-sdk patch to compute identical fingerprint (sort-map-keys prior to hashing) and add opt-in compatibility flags.
Test matrix: must include nested maps, arrays, nulls, and omitempty behavior across Go/TS/Python and across multiple Go encoder settings.
Linked documentation action: document recommended confirmation contract (either echo Idempotency-Key header or use deterministic canonicalization) in function-calling guides.

workaround:
Customer applied a short-term middleware to include the original 'Idempotency-Key' string inside the confirmation payload as 'confirmed_for'. Recommended other customers who see this issue either echo the header in the confirmation or use a deterministic serializer in their webhook.

next_steps:
1) Push go-sdk v0.9.8 with deterministic canonicalizer used for computing idempotency fingerprint (target 2026-03-15).
2) Add server-side best-effort matching by raw header (deployed to canary already), roll to all regions after 48h of monitoring.
3) Update function-calling docs with explicit confirmation schema and sample middleware for Go/TS/Python.
4) Notify customer when go-sdk patch is published and offer hands-on validation for their production webhook.
5) Postmortem runbook item: add integration test to CI covering cross-SDK fingerprint compatibility.

[Console cached query results and trace links resolve to previous API key after customer rotated API key]
description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports that after rotating their API key, Console dashboards and ad-hoc usage queries continue to show results and trace links tied to the previous API key. Clicking trace links from the Console leads to 404s or traces attributed to the old key. This appears to be a cache/staleness problem on the Console/usage-analytics side where cache entries are not invalidated correctly after API key rotation.

Impact:
- Customer cannot reliably link dashboard query rows to live trace anchors (404s)
- Usage numbers in Console may temporarily reflect activity attributed to the old key instead of the new one
- High business impact for this enterprise customer due to audit/compliance reporting needs

Environment:
- Prod environment for BrightHealth AI (org: brighthealth-ai) in us-east-1
- Console version: web-2026.02.14
- Cache-service: redis-cluster-prod-3 (managed), cache-key-prefix v2

Steps to reproduce (as reported by customer):
1) Rotate API key via the Console > API keys > Rotate for org brighthealth-ai
2) Open Usage -> Ad-hoc Query with filter api_key: <new-key> and time range last 24h
3) Observe that panel rows still show request_ids and trace links for requests made with old key
4) Click a trace link -> Console opens trace URL and shows 404 or a trace page with request_id that predates rotation

Observed logs / snippets provided by customer:
- Example request_id seen in Console: req_20260309_7c9f3a8b
- Trace anchor from Console: trace-span-0a1b2c3d (resolves to old-key-owner)
- Customer-side API audit shows calls credited to new key from 2026-03-09T16:12:24Z

Attachments: customer-provided screenshots, session recording, and API audit CSV (uploaded to ticket).

investigation_notes:
03/10 - Triage by Support (Aisha): Verified customer repro steps in a staging replica. Confirmed Console is serving cached rows that include request_id/trace links linked to old API key after rotation.
03/10 - SRE (Diego): Examined cache key format in cache-service. cache-key included api_key_id in v1 but v2 rollout switched to org_id. Observation: rotation job updates api_key table but does not trigger cache invalidation for entries keyed by api_key_id in legacy caches. Some panels still reading from legacy cache prefix (v2 migration not complete across all pods).
03/11 - Eng (Sana, backend): Looked at request routing and link generation. Trace links are generated using stored request metadata pulled from the usage-analytics index. Indexing pipeline attaches original api_key_id as metadata; on rotation, a downstream migration job expected to remap historical entries but task hasn't completed and migration flag is off.
03/11 - Hypothesis: Two independent issues: (1) Console frontend sometimes reads from legacy cache prefix v1 which is keyed by api_key_id and remains stale post-rotation, (2) indexing migration that would remap historical requests to the org-level view hasn't been run for this customer's partition, so trace anchors reference old api_key values and the live trace lookup uses new key leading to 404s.
Relevant traces/logs: /logs/console/cache-debug/2026-03-10.log, /logs/indexer/migration-partition-42.log (partial failures)

03/11 02:32 UTC - SRE manually flushed legacy cache prefix for brighthealth-ai on redis-cluster-prod-3 (keys matching 'v1:org:brighthealth-ai:*'). This momentarily allowed new queries to surface correct request_ids for new key.

03/11 09:22 UTC - Added temporary console guard: panels will prefer live index read when an API key rotation event is detected in the last 24h, bypassing cache for affected orgs. Deployed as emergency feature flag rollout (ff/console/rotation-cache-bypass).
03/11 18:11 UTC - Notified customer of workaround and requested confirmation that trace links now resolve.
Customer confirmation 03/11 19:05 UTC: Reported that trace links are resolving for most rows but a small subset (approx 0.8%) remain 404ing.

comments:
Aisha Patel (Support) 2026-03-10T18:40Z: Created ticket after phone call with BrightHealth AI. Customer needs audit-aligned usage numbers by EOD 2026-03-12.
Diego Morales (SRE) 2026-03-10T20:05Z: I confirmed cache key mismatch; preparing safe flush plan for redis (will do per-org prefixes during off-peak windows).

[Dashboard tile refresh stalls when query cache lock persists, causing delayed trace links and alert delivery]
description:
Issue summary: Several customers reported dashboard tiles in the Console stalling on refresh for up to 30+ seconds. Stalled tiles show a spinning loader; clicking through trace links either returns 404 or times out until the tile finally completes. Impact: Multiple enterprise customers (Streamline AI + 2 others) reported missing alerts or delayed alert delivery tied to dashboard rule evaluation. Environment: prod, us-east, Console version 3.14.2, query-cache-service v1.7.2. Expected behavior: Dashboard tiles should refresh within configured panel timeout (default 3s) and trace links should remain stable. Actual behavior: Tile hangs until a cache lock TTL expires (~25-35s); during that time associated alert evaluations are queued and can miss the evaluation window, causing delayed or dropped alerts.

steps_to_reproduce:
Open Console -> Dashboards -> Organization X -> Panel 'Request Latency (p95)'
Trigger a high-cardinality ad-hoc query (example filter: route:*/batch, user_agent:mobile*)
Initiate a refresh (manual or automatic) while a background compaction job is running on the query-cache node
Observe tile spinner remains for 20-40 seconds; clicking trace link either times out or returns 404 until tile completes

logs:
Selected logs from query-cache (us-east-1) around 2026-03-10T14:02:34Z: 
[query-cache] WARN lock_acquire: key=panel:orgX:queryHash: ttl_override=30000ms owner=compactor-3
[dashboard-renderer] ERROR tile_render_timeout: panel_id=428 path=/dashboards/panel/428 waiting_for=cache_lock
[alert-eval] WARN evaluation_delayed: rule_id=547 queued_for=28000ms
Tracebacks: dashboard-renderer timed out waiting on cache lock; subsequent re-eval succeeded at 2026-03-10T14:03:06Z

investigation_notes:
Hypotheses: (1) Cache compaction/rehash job temporarily extends lock TTL beyond expected values, (2) Lock cleanup job not running due to recent deployment, (3) Dashboard renderer mishandles lock wait backoff. Findings: Replayed compaction schedule correlated with spike in long-held locks on query-cache nodes. Lock TTLs increased to 30s due to regression in compaction job (PR linked). Dashboard renderer waits for lock without exponential backoff and does not surface immediate fallback causing spinner and delayed trace link resolution. Metrics: lock_hold_time 95th percentile jumped from 120ms -> 28s during compaction window. No signs of database contention. Affected customers all in us-east region using org-scoped high-cardinality queries.

comments:
Support (2026-03-10) - Aisha Patel: Customer reports multiple dashboard tiles stalling and missing alerts. Reproduced in prod/us-east. Escalating to SRE and Console owners.
SRE (2026-03-10) - Priya Nair: Observed lock_hold_time spike on query-cache; pointed to compaction PR (https://github.com/redwood-inference/cache/pull/402). Temporarily disabled compaction on us-east to mitigate.
Console Eng (2026-03-11) - Marco Velez: Identified renderer wait loop that blocks for full TTL without fallback. Preparing patch to add fast-fail and fall back to best-effort execution path.
Customer (2026-03-11) - Streamline AI (Ben Carter): Confirmed tiles returned to normal after compaction disabled; reported one missed alert. Requesting postmortem and assurance this won't recur.
Support (2026-03-12) - Aisha Patel: Deployed hotfix to reduce compaction lock TTL and added renderer fallback. Added alerting rule for lock_hold_time > 5s. Marking resolved pending postmortem.
SRE (2026-03-12) - Priya Nair: Follow-up: Re-enabled compaction with adjusted settings; monitoring shows no recurrence in 24h window.

resolution:
Mitigation: Disabled compaction on affected query-cache cluster and cleared stale locks. Deployed hotfixs: (1) query-cache compaction PR rolled back and TTL reduced, (2) console renderer updated to fast-fail after 2s and render partial results with informative tooltip, (3) alerting rule added for lock_hold_time > 5s and an incident dashboard for cache metrics. Follow-up: Postmortem page created, and a small migration scheduled to add lock ownership metadata to improve cleanup. Customer notified and credited for partial SLA impact.

[Postmortem: EU-West capacity shortage and region fallback (2025-03-03)]
h2. Summary
On 2025-03-03, a GPU capacity shortfall in eu-west-1 impacted a subset of Hosted and Dedicated traffic pinned to that region. Mitigation required activating *automatic region fallback* (eu-west-1 -> us-east-1) for eligible routes until additional capacity was brought online.

h2. Impact
* Elevated p95 latency and increased 429/503 responses for region-pinned routes in eu-west-1.
* Customers: 7 Hosted orgs and 1 Dedicated tenant with optional cross-region allowance enabled.
* Duration: ~41 minutes of degraded performance; ~18 minutes of hard errors for the most constrained pool.

h2. Timeline (UTC)
* 09:42: Capacity alert: available_gpu_count < 5 in eu-west-1 pool rw-a100-eu-01.
* 09:48: Saturation exceeded 95% and queue wait climbed > 400ms.
* 09:51: Mitigation: enabled *region fallback* for "chat-default" and "embeddings-default" where customer policy allows cross-region.
* 09:54: Router began directing overflow to us-east-1 for eligible traffic.
* 10:03: Error rate dropped; latency partially recovered.
* 10:23: Added 8 GPUs to eu-west-1 pool; disabled region fallback after stabilization.

h2. Mitigation details
We toggled a router policy flag:
* Primary region: eu-west-1
* Fallback region: us-east-1
* Triggers: saturation > 90% OR 503 rate > 0.5%
* Eligibility: routes not marked "data_residency_strict"

h2. Root cause
A delayed GPU delivery + slow provisioning left the eu-west-1 pool below the forecasted headroom for a scheduled customer load test.

h2. What went well
* Region fallback prevented a full outage for eligible traffic.
* On-call followed the capacity runbook and coordinated with Infra quickly.

h2. What went poorly
* We lacked a clear customer-facing flag indicating whether cross-region fallback was enabled for a tenant.

h2. Action items
1) Add tenant-level UI indicator and API field for cross-region fallback eligibility. Owner: Eng Platform.
2) Improve capacity forecasting for scheduled load tests and Dedicated bursts. Owner: Eng SRE.
3) Add automated comms template for region fallback events. Owner: Incident Response.

h2. References
* Incident ID: INC-2025-0303

[cross-region-gpu-failover-simulation-playbook]
Summary
This playbook describes a reproducible simulation and validation procedure for cross-region GPU failover for Redwood's inference clusters. The goal is to exercise our multi-region routing, model fallback, and capacity-autoscaling behaviors under realistic workload and network-failure conditions without impacting production traffic.

Scope
- Applies to Redwood-managed inference clusters in public cloud regions (AWS us-west-2, us-east-1, eu-west-1) and to Dedicated testing fleets used for canaries.
- Focuses on: routing failure, preemption (spot interruption), regional network partition, and cold-cache regeneration.
- Not covered: durable storage corruption, KMS key compromise, customer-data exfiltration tests. Those are handled by security incident drills.

Objectives and success criteria
- Verify that automatic routing fallback reduces 5xx error surface area to <= 0.5% during the sim window.
- Maintain p90 inference latency within 2x baseline and p99 <= 3x baseline for at least 80% of requests during the simulation.
- Confirm autoscaler ramps to expected capacity within defined timeouts (see thresholds).
- Validate telemetry (traces, logs, SLO burn) is recorded to long-term observability.

SLO & thresholds (baseline values are cluster-specific; replace placeholders)
- Baseline p90 latency: 80ms (threshold during sim: 160ms).
- Baseline p99 latency: 320ms (threshold during sim: 960ms).
- Error budget usage: simulations target <= 5% of monthly error budget per region.
- Autoscaler warmup: new GPU nodes should be Ready within 6 minutes; capacity target achieved within 10 minutes.

Prerequisites
1) Approvals: Incident commander (IC) and infra lead sign-off at least 48h prior. Notify Customer Success for Dedicated customers.
2) Simulation window: choose low-traffic 2-hour window or use isolated canary tenant and staging traffic.
3) Canary workload: synthetic prompt set with realistic token distribution and KV cache warmers.
4) Test cluster: tag a set of GPU instances with "chaos-sim=true" via Terraform variable to avoid impacting production tenants.
5) Observability: Grafana dashboards, tracing, and logs must be configured to retain sim data for 90 days.
6) Playbook owner and stakeholders listed in calendar invite.

Test scenario matrix
- Scenario A: Region outage simulation (BGP + route table blackhole) -> Validate smart routing and model fallback to remote region.
- Scenario B: Spot/preemption flood in primary region -> Validate autoscaler fallback to on-demand pools and model variant downgrade path.
- Scenario C: Network partition between control plane and worker pool (simulate high loss/latency) -> Validate KV cache invalidation and safe reconnect behavior.
- Scenario D: Cold-cache restart (full cache eviction) -> Measure cold-start latency and infer cache warmup policy effectiveness.

Step-by-step execution (high level)
1) Prep and soften traffic:
   - Direct 10–20% of canary traffic to test cluster (route via traffic-router with tag filter).
   - Enable sampling at 100% for request traces to capture detailed traces during sim.

2) Baseline capture (10 min):
   - Capture p50/p90/p99, token throughput, GPU utilization, KV cache hit rate, and autoscaler metrics.

3) Scenario run (ordered):
   - For each scenario, follow numbered sub-steps below. Run one scenario at a time and validate before moving on.

Scenario A (Region outage simulation):
1. Using the network test harness (see Appendix A), apply a route table rule to blackhole egress from the test cluster to regional endpoint (5 min window).
2. Monitor the smart router service: ensure policy routes traffic to next-preferred region as defined in policy config (policy id: routing.priority.policy.v2).
3. Verify that model fallback triggers for incompatible model variants and responses are still served with a compatible model shard.
4. Validation checks: error-rate <= 0.5%, traces show fallback hop, and cross-region egress costs recorded.

Scenario B (Spot/preemption flood):
1. Using the cloud provider API, trigger simulated interruptions for spot instance group tagged "chaos-sim".
2. Confirm autoscaler consolidates workloads onto reserved/on-demand pools and schedules new pods in fallback AZs.
3. Validation checks: new pod Ready time <= 6 minutes, request retry loops follow backoff policy (exponential up to 10s), and no burst of 429s beyond configured throttle (max 2% of requests).

Scenario C (Control plane partition):
1. Use traffic-control (tc) to introduce latency/loss between the control-plane subnet and worker nodes: 150ms added latency + 10% packet loss for 5 minutes.
2. Observe KV cache reauthorization, connection churn, and any model state sync errors.
3. Validation checks: state reconciliation completes within 3 minutes of recovery and no inconsistent model versions are served (version audit log).

Scenario D (Cold-cache restart):
1. Evict KV caches by restarting the cache process on the test fleet or rolling the runtime with an env var (RUNTIME_CACHE_FLUSH=true).
2. Send warmup traffic (see Warmup script in Appendix B) and measure time until 90% of requests hit cache.
3. Validation checks: cache hit rate reaches >=90% within the configured warmup window (15 min), and p90/p99 latencies return to baseline.

Validation checklist (run during and after each scenario)
- Monitoring: Grafana (inference-latency, rps, errors), Traces (distributed spans show fallback), Logs (router decisions).
- Alerts suppressed during sim: document alert IDs and hold with paging duty.
- Cost telemetry: estimate incremental egress and on-demand cost and report to finance tag manager.
- Safety kill-switch: an IC can abort simulation by running:
  - CLI: redwoodctl chaos abort --run-id <run-id>

Rollback and cleanup
1) If any validation fails beyond thresholds, abort using kill-switch and revert any Terraform or network changes immediately.
2) Run rollback tasks in this priority: routing config revert -> restart affected workers -> drain and reschedule canary traffic.
3) Post-cleanup verification: ensure all services are in a healthy state for 30 minutes before re-enabling normal traffic.

Observability and artifact collection
- Required artifacts to capture and attach to the run ticket: Grafana snapshots, Jaeger trace dumps, autoscaler event logs, Terraform plan/apply logs, cloud provider interruption logs, synthetic workload logs, and cost estimation CSV.
- Label all artifacts with run-id and scenario tag (e.g., run-20251018-A).

CI/CD integration and Terraform notes
- Use the chaos-sim Terraform workspace to provision and tag resources. Example variable in terraform.tfvars: chaos_sim_run = "run-20251018"
- All IaC changes must be limited to the test workspace. Do not modify production routing policies in the same plan.
- A helper script generates a dependency graph for affected infra resources; run before any apply:
  - ./tools/infra/dep-graph --workspace chaos-sim --output tf-deps.svg
- When automating scheduled drills in CI, gate the pipeline with approval and an oncall snooze window.

Roles and ownership
- Playbook owner: Priya Nambiar (Infra Reliability).
- Incident commander during sim: assigned from infra-sre rotation.
- Observability owner: Mariana Ruiz.
- Responsible for Terraform and IaC: Platform IaC team.

Post-run review and checklist
1) Postmortem within 3 business days describing deviations from expected behavior.
2) Action items tracked in the infra backlog with SEV, owner, and ETA.
3) Update routing priority and fallback policy if needed.

Appendix A — network test harness example (tc + iptables)\sudo tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay 150ms loss 10%\sudo iptables -I OUTPUT -d <control-plane-ip> -j DROP --wait 300

Appendix B — warmup script (bash pseudo)
#!/usr/bin/env bash
for i in {1..1000}; do
  curl -s -X POST \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"prompt":"Tell a short story about a redwood tree","max_tokens":64}' \
    https://canary.api.redwood.internal/v1/generate &
  sleep 0.05
 done

Appendix C — example Terraform snippet (chaos workspace)
variable "chaos_sim_run" { default = "run-20251018" }
resource "aws_instance" "gpu_chaos" {
  ami = var.gpu_ami
  instance_type = "p4d.24xlarge"
  tags = { Name = "gpu-chaos-${var.chaos_sim_run}" ; chaos-sim = "true" }
}

Notes and safety reminders
- Never run this against clusters without explicit owner sign-off.
- Keep customer-impacting datasets off the test fleet.
- Record and justify any temporary alert suppressions in the run ticket.

Document history
- 2024-02-12: Created (Priya N.)
- 2024-06-05: Added warmup script and CI gating notes (Ethan C.)
- 2025-10-18: Expanded validation metrics and added terraform dep-graph guidance (Mariana R.)

End of document

[Global GPU capacity calendar and drain coordination]
Purpose
-------
This document defines the Global GPU Capacity Calendar and the operational runbook for scheduling, coordinating, and executing node drains and capacity maintenance across Redwood’s multi-region GPU fleet. It standardizes preflight checks, IaC/CI gating, drain sequencing, and post-maintenance verification to minimize customer impact and maintain SLOs.

Scope
-----
- Applies to all production GPU pools (hosted &dedicated) that serve inference traffic: `gpu-allocator`, `capacity-sentry`, `burst-orchestrator`
- Regions: us-west-2, us-east-1, eu-west-1, ap-southeast-1
- Changes covered: kernel upgrades, driver updates, instance image rotation, topology changes, and bulk node retirements

Definitions & stakeholders
------------------------
- Maintenance window: scheduled 2-hour block reserved for non-emergency drains
- Drain lead: oncall eng-infra engineer responsible for coordination during a window
- Rollout owner: service or team owning the change (e.g., runtime, kernel team)
- Stakeholders: Runtime team, SRE, Capacity planning, Customer Success (for enterprise tenants)

Maintenance cadence & global calendar (operational policy)
-----------------------------------------------------
- Safe weekly windows per region (default):
  - US: Tue 02:00–04:00 UTC, Thu 03:00–05:00 UTC
  - EU: Wed 01:00–03:00 UTC
  - APAC: Mon 22:00–00:00 UTC
- Major batch operations (>=10% pool): coordinate 14 days prior, limit to 1 window/week/region
- Emergency windows: ad-hoc; must follow emergency drain protocol below

Maintenance risk matrix (SLO / capacity guidance)
-----------------------------------------------
| Change size | Expected capacity impact | Preflight target | Rollback threshold |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Small (<2% of pool) | Negligible | smoke tests green | auto-rollback on >1% error increase |
| Medium (2–10%) | Minor | full canary traffic for 30m | manual rollback if p95 latency spikes >20% |
| Large (>10%) | Risk of SLO violations | staged rollout + capacity reserve | abort and restore capacity if errors >5% for 15m |

Preflight checklist (runbook)
----------------------------
1. Announce window in #infra-maintenance and to affected customers 72/48/24 hours out.
2. Verify capacity runway: `capacity-sentry` target reserve >= 20% for large changes, >=10% for medium.
3. Terraform plan & diff approved: run `terraform plan -var-file=env.tfvars` and attach plan to change ticket.
4. CI/CD health gates: all dependent CI pipelines pass for the last successful image and the candidate image.
5. Canary provisioning: spin canary pool with new image/config (1–2 instances); run end-to-end suite for 30 minutes.
6. Monitoring baseline snapshot: capture current metrics (p50/p95 latency, 5xx rate, KV cache hit ratio).

Terraform / IaC patterns for safe drains
--------------------------------------
- Use blue/green-friendly node group naming and immutable image promotion. Example snippet for terraform variables and strategy: 

```hcl
variable "gpu_node_pool_strategy" {
  description = "rolling | bluegreen"
  default     = "bluegreen"
}

module "gpu_node_pool" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repo/infra-modules.git//gpu-node-pool?ref=v2.3"
  name   = "gpu-pool-${var.region}-${var.stage}"
  strategy = var.gpu_node_pool_strategy
  desired_capacity = var.desired_capacity
}
```

- Flags to include in CI/CD: `--approve-canary`, `--constrain-drain-concurrency=3`, `--dry-run`
- Locking: use remote-state seat reservation `seat_reservation=true` before applying large-scale changes

CI/CD gating & automation (how changes are promoted)
--------------------------------------------------
- Pipeline stages: plan -> canary-apply -> canary-smoke -> gradual-rollout -> verification -> finalize-apply
- Gating checks (automated):
  - `kube-smoke` pass against canary nodes (latency, qps, error-rate)
  - `alloc-check` ensures `gpu-allocator` has available slots >= requested concurrency
  - `batch-sim` simulates burst traffic for 10 minutes against canary fleet
- Human approval required for Medium/Large changes after canary-smoke

Drain coordination runbook (step-by-step)
--------------------------------------
1. Ownership & communication
   - Drain lead confirms roster and primary backup. Post start time in #infra-maintenance.
2. Verify preflight: confirm checklist items 1–6 are green.
3. Reserve capacity: temporarily increase warm-pool by % reserve if needed: `rwdctl capacity set --pool ${POOL} --reserve 20%`
4. Begin staged drains (concurrency limit = 3 unless emergency):
   a. Select node subset (label `maintenance=true`) 
   b. For each node:
      i. `kubectl cordon <node>`
      ii. `rwdctl drain-node --node <node> --grace-period 120s --wait-for-active-sessions=false`
      iii. Monitor `runtime.request_latency` and `service.5xx_rate` for 5m before moving to next node
5. If any metric breach occurs (see thresholds): pause rollout, scale up warm-pool, or trigger rollback.
6. Post-drain validation: run end-to-end smoke tests, confirm KV cache warm ratio >= 90% for top 10 tenants.
7. Finalize: update terraform state for drained instance group, close maintenance ticket, and publish summary.

Automated rollback & emergency mitigation
---------------------------------------
- Abort conditions (example):
  - sustained p95 latency increase >20% for 15m
  - 5xx rate increase >2% absolute for 10m
  - Pod OOM or executor restarts >3x within 15m
- Immediate actions:
  1. Halt further drains: `rwdctl rollouts pause --project infra`
  2. Restore capacity via warm-pool or fallback to lower-cost model variant: `rwdctl capacity override --pool ${POOL} --type burst`
  3. If required, reverse node changes by reattaching previous instance image via Terraform (see rollback CLI snippet):

```bash
# restore previous image by forcing terraform apply with previous AMI variable
TF_VAR_ami=ami-previous terraform apply -var "force_replace=true" -auto-approve
```

Post-maintenance verification checklist
-------------------------------------
- All nodes in pool show `Ready` and expected kernel/drivers.
- Telemetry: p50/p95 back to baseline ±5%, 5xx at pre-maintenance levels.
- KV cache hit ratio restored to target for top tenants.
- Billing/scheduling sanity: no sustained cost increase >3% over baseline.
- Release notes: short summary posted to #infra-maintenance and ticket closed with links to telemetry graphs.

Monitoring & dashboards to watch
-------------------------------
- Dashboards: `GPU Fleet Overview`, `Capacity Sentry`, `KV Cache Heatmap`, `Per-tenant Latency`
- Critical alerts: `gpu_pool_capacity_below_reserve`, `allocator_p95_surge`, `node_drain_failures_rate`
- SRE runbook for paging: page on-call SRE when any critical alert persists for >10 minutes during window.

Ownership & escalation
----------------------
- Drain lead (oncall) is primary during window.
- If rollback >15 minutes to execute or ambiguity in root cause, escalate to the runtime owner and SRE lead.
- For customer-impacting regressions, notify Customer Success immediately and begin enterprise incident process.

Change log (summary of recent updates)
------------------------------------
- 2024-09-12: Initial draft published.
- 2024-11-04: Added terraform seat-reservation pattern and canary gate `batch-sim`.
- 2025-02-07: Updated global calendar and adjusted rollback thresholds for large changes.

----------


B. Contact matrix
- Runtime lead: runtime-team@redwood.ai
- SRE oncall: pagerduty-sre
- Capacity planning: capacity@redwood.ai

[Cross-tenant GPU Allocation, Fairness, and Preemption Strategy]
Overview

Goal: Provide a clear, operational policy for allocating GPUs across mixed workloads (hosted inference, dedicated reserved pools, background training/batching, and internal experiments) that balances fairness, SLO compliance, and cost efficiency. This document describes the allocation hierarchy, preemption windows, eviction thresholds, terraform config patterns, monitoring/alerts, and an incident runbook.

Context and motivation
- Redwood operates a multi-tenant GPU fleet that must support: hosted API inference (low-latency, customer-facing), Dedicated reserved capacity (contracted throughput), asynchronous batch/embeddings jobs (throughput-optimized), and internal experiments (best-effort).
- Historically we prioritized utilization and spot capacity, which increased customer impact during high demand spikes. This policy formalizes deterministic behavior to reduce customer-facing regressions.

Principles
1) SLO-first for customer-facing workloads: Hosted API and Dedicated pools have top priority to meet latency SLOs.
2) Predictability: Preemption and fallback behavior must be deterministic and observable.
3) Fairness by intent: Teams with reserved capacity keep their guarantees; remaining capacity is apportioned by priority tiers and recent usage.
4) Cost-awareness: Prefer spot/spot-like nodes for best-effort work but provide safe fallbacks.

Allocation hierarchy (high-level)
1. Reserved Dedicated Pools (contracted capacity) — absolute priority.
2. Hosted inference (hosted API / low-latency customers) — SLO backed, autoscaled.
3. Platform critical background work (model-serving warmup, cache rebuilds) — policy-controlled.
4. Best-effort batch (training, large embedding jobs, experiments) — preemptible on demand.

Priority tiers and labels
- reserved: dedicated_capacity (immutable to autoscaler decisions for other tenants)
- hot: hosted_inference (SLO 95p latency target; non-preemptible except in extreme network/region failure)
- platform: platform_maintenance (short windows allowed for maintenance throttles)
- spot: best_effort (preemptible, scheduled lower-priority)

Preemption policy summary
- Trigger conditions: global GPU usage >= 92% in region OR hosted queue latency > configured SLO window for 2 consecutive 30s windows.
- Eviction order: spot -> platform -> hot (only if entire region degraded and no cross-region failover available) -> reserved (never evicted by autoscaler).
- Grace period: 120s default for graceful eviction; 30s for forced immediate eviction during critical overload (emergency).
- Preemption signalling: Pod annotation "gpu-preempt: pending" + SIGTERM delivered to process. Jobs must implement checkpointing hooks.

Concrete thresholds and SLOs
- Hosted API SLO: 95th percentile p99 token latency <= 350ms for standard small models; targeted per-route SLOs defined in dashboards.
- Eviction threshold: region_gpu_utilization_percent >= 92% triggers proactive scaling and eviction window.
- Spot fallback: spot_spare_capacity_percent >= 5% must be maintained during business hours; otherwise batch queue throttles.

Terraform / IaC patterns (examples)
- Module: modules/gpu-pool (variables shown as example). Use the following minimal pattern to create a labeled pool: 

Example: terraform snippet (text)
variable "pool_name" { default = "spot-batch-west-1" }
variable "node_labels" { default = { "priority" = "spot", "region" = "us-west-1" } }
module "gpu_pool_spot" {
  source = "github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-modules//gpu-pool"
  name   = var.pool_name
  labels = var.node_labels
  instance_type = "nvidia-a100-80gb"
  min_nodes = 0
  max_nodes = 80
  preemptible = true
}

Recommended module variables (table-style in text)
- name: string (pool identifier)
- labels: map(string) (applies priority and tenant tagging)
- instance_type: string (gpu instance to use)
- min_nodes: int (autoscaler lower bound)
- max_nodes: int (autoscaler upper bound)
- reserved_for: string (optional tenant id for dedicated pools)
- preemptible: bool (spot behavior)

Scheduler implementation notes
- Service: gpu-scheduler (internal) consults capacity-manager to allocate nodes by label and tenant.
- Cache: the scheduler maintains a per-tenant weighted token bucket used for short-term fairness when contention is present.
- Continuous batching: hosted_inference uses continuous-batching lanes pinned to non-preemptible nodes when latency SLOs require.

Monitoring and alerts (metrics and thresholds)
- region_gpu_utilization_percent (prometheus)
  - warning: 80% sustained for 15m
  - critical: 92% sustained for 2m -> trigger preemption-window workflow
- hosted_queue_latency_ms_p95
  - warning: > 250ms for 2m
  - critical: > 350ms for 30s -> autoscaler scale-up and eviction of spot lanes
- preemption_evictions_count_by_pool > 10 in 5m -> alert on noisy preemption
- spot_fallback_rate: percentage of spot jobs restarted due to evictions

Runbook: handling a preemption-driven customer-impact incident
1. Detection: Pager fires from hosted_queue_latency_ms_p95 critical alert.
2. Triage (first responder): check region_gpu_utilization_percent, autoscaler logs, and recent scaling events in capacity-manager.
3. Immediate mitigation (first 5 minutes):
   - Trigger on-call playbook: run `kubectl get pods -l priority=spot -n gpu-jobs` and cordon top spot nodes if necessary.
   - Scale up reserved pools or hot pools using CLI helper: `ci-infra capacity-manager scale --pool hosted-west-1 --delta +8` (requires approver).
   - If cross-region failover configured for VIP customers, enable fallback routing in gpu-router: `gpu-router set-fallback --from us-west-1 --to us-east-1 --tenants tenant-123`
4. Stabilize (5-30 minutes):
   - Throttle batch queues: set batch concurrency to 25% via queue-admin: `queue-admin set-concurrency --queue embeddings --percent 25`
   - Increase spot fallback margin on spot-autoscaler: `spot-autoscaler update --spare-percent 10`
5. Post-incident (30m+): run full root-cause analysis and a capacity simulation to determine whether permanent pool resizing is required.

Checklist for application owners (must-haves for preemptible workloads)
- Implement graceful SIGTERM handling and checkpointing (/opt/redwood/checkpoint).
- Export `preemption_expected_duration_seconds` metric during graceful shutdown window.
- Use the `priority` node label to opt into expected behavior.

Ownership and responsibilities
- Capacity Manager Team: owns capacity-manager service, terraform modules under modules/gpu-pool, autoscaler rules. (Pager: eng-infra)
- Scheduler Team: owns gpu-scheduler binary, token-bucket fairness algo, and preemption signalling. (Pager: eng-serving-runtime)
- Platform SRE: owns monitoring, alerting, and incident playbooks.
- Tenant App Owners: ensure apps implement the checkpointing hooks and respect node labels.

Rollout plan (4 phases)
1. Canary (2 weeks): apply policy to non-customer internal tenants only (internal experiments). Monitor preemption_evictions_count_by_pool.
2. Beta (6 weeks): include low-traffic customer-facing buckets (non-critical SLAs).
3. Gradual rollout (8 weeks): enable in half of the production pools per region and run mixed-load stress tests.
4. GA (post-metrics review): enforce policy fleet-wide and update IaC defaults.

Testing and validation matrix
- Unit tests: scheduler fairness invariants, preemption order, token-bucket weights.
- Integration: simulate 110% demand with workload generator and assert hosted p95 latency remains within SLO after preemption flows.
- Chaos: run preemption-injector chaos experiments in staging and ensure evicted spot jobs restart with checkpoint.

Examples of telemetry dashboards (links/references)
- GPU Fleet Overview: /dashboards/gpu-fleet-overview
- Per-region preemption heatmap: /dashboards/preemption-heatmap
- Per-tenant utilization and reserved vs used: /dashboards/tenant-utilization

Open risks and next steps
- Cross-region capacity transfer delays can cause brief SLO violations; investigate faster routing updates in gpu-router.
- Some older internal batch jobs lack checkpointing; schedule remediation and apply a kill-switch in 2025-04 to opt them out of spot lanes.

Appendix A: recommended terraform IAM and tagging policy (example)
- IAM roles required: terraform-gpu-admin, gpu-autoscaler-runner, capacity-manager-ci
- Tagging standard: "{\"team\":\"<team-name>\",\"env\":\"<prod|staging>\",\"priority\":\"<reserved|hot|spot>\"}"

Appendix B: sample preemption annotation for pod spec (Kubernetes)

kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: embedding-job-01
  annotations:
    gpu-preempt: "enabled"
    checkpoint-path: "/opt/checkpoints/embedding-job-01"
spec:
  containers:
  - name: worker
    image: ghcr.io/redwood/embedding-worker:stable
    lifecycle:
      preStop:
        exec:
          command: ["/bin/sh","-c","/opt/redwood/bin/graceful_checkpoint --path /opt/checkpoints/embedding-job-01"]

[Cross-account GPU VPC Modules and Network Runbook]
Summary
-------
This document describes Redwood's cross-account VPC topology patterns, Terraform module design for GPU node pools, and an incident runbook for common networking and provisioning failures that affect GPU capacity. Target audience: infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners responsible for Dedicated and Private deployments.

Goals and scope
----------------
- Provide a reusable Terraform module pattern for provisioning GPU node pools across accounts/projects/regions with consistent network/security posture.
- Document cross-account connectivity options (VPC peering, Shared VPC, Transit/Hub, and interconnects) and recommended defaults for Redwood workloads.
- Define SLOs and alert thresholds for GPU capacity and network provisioning.
- Supply actionable runbook steps for incidents that block inference traffic or prevent node pool provisioning.

Architectural patterns (high level)
-----------------------------------
1) Shared-Hub (recommended for enterprise customers)
   - Central network hub (Transit/VPC hub) in the security account that hosts egress NAT, centralized firewall (cloud-native or NGFW), and route propagation.
   - Per-customer or per-environment spoke VPCs attached via Transit Gateway / VPC-SC.
   - GPU node pools live in spoke VPCs with routes to the hub for egress and monitoring endpoints.

2) Shared VPC (GCP-specific option)
   - Host project provides subnets to service projects. Use host-level IAM to restrict who can attach resources.

3) Cross-account peering (fast, limited scale)
   - Direct peering between service and infra accounts for setups with limited regions. Avoid for >10 peers due to operational complexity.

Networking constraints for GPU nodes
-----------------------------------
- MTU: enforce 1460 for AWS ENIs that traverse NAT appliances.
- Multicast: blocked — do not rely on multicast for discovery.
- Maximum routing table size: keep per-subnet route entries <100 to avoid cloud limits.

Terraform module design: gpu-node-pool (example usage)
------------------------------------------------------
Purpose: create node pools or instance groups with correct machine types, GPU accelerators, subnet attachment, IAM binding, and bootstrapping tags for image pipeline. The module must be idempotent and safe for drifted clusters.

Example (pseudo-Terraform snippet)
```hcl
module "gpu_node_pool" {
  source                = "git::ssh://git@internal.redwood.ai/infra/terraform-modules.git//gpu-node-pool?ref=v1.4.0"
  name                  = "inference-gpu-pool-eu1"
  cloud                 = "gcp" # or aws/azure
  region                = "europe-west1"
  zone                  = "europe-west1-b"
  cluster_id            = "redwood-inference-cluster-eu1"
  machine_type          = "n1-standard-16"
  gpu_accelerator_type  = "nvidia-tesla-t4"
  gpu_count_per_node    = 4
  min_size              = 0
  max_size              = 12
  subnet_id             = module.network.subnet_ids["inference"]
  service_account       = "svc-gpu-node@infra.redwood.ai.iam.gserviceaccount.com"
  labels                = { role = "inference", team = "platform" }
  tags                  = ["gpu","inference","dedicated"]
  node_init_script      = file("./scripts/gpu-bootstrapping.sh")
}
```

Important module features (must be implemented)
- Pre-checks for quota availability (GPUs, IPs) with graceful fail message.
- IAM/service account binding automation to reduce manual steps.
- Optional lifecycle "ignore_changes" only for known cloud provider metadata.
- Output the "provision_id" and a small JSON blob with capacity metadata for the autoscaler to consume.

Network and firewall golden rules
--------------------------------
- Egress to monitoring/metrics endpoints (Datadog/Prometheus push gateways, tracing collectors) allowed via TLS to hub IPs only.
- Allow kubelet/proxy ports between control-plane CIDR and node pools (e.g., 10250/10255).
- Block inbound SSH by default; designate bastion subnets with strict ingress ACLs.
- Restrict management plane APIs to management account ranges; use IAM conditions and VPC service controls where applicable.

SLOs, metrics, and alerting thresholds
-------------------------------------
SLOs (platform capacity):
- Node provisioning time: 90% of new nodes become Ready within 10 minutes of create request.
- Scale event latency: 95th percentile scale-out completion < 12 minutes for moderate batches (<= 5 nodes).
- Network path recovery: 99.9% of routes repaired within 6 minutes after BGP flap.

Key alert triggers (examples)
- GPU instance quota exhausted in a region: alert if available_gpu_quota == 0 and pending_pods > 0 for 2m.
- Sustained GPU utilization > 85% across cluster for 5m (scale policy/alert).
- >30% of nodes in a node-pool report NotReady for 3m.
- Transit hub peer down for >1m OR BGP session flapping >3 times in 5m.

Runbook: provisioning failure (node pool create fails)
-----------------------------------------------------
1) Triage and ownership
   - Pager triggers: infra-oncall@redwood.ai -> infra oncall takes lead.
   - Identify the failing stage: quota, IAM, network, bootstrapping script errors.

2) Immediate checks (commands)
   - Check Terraform plan/apply logs in CI: curl -sS "$CI_ARTIFACTS_URL/terraform-apply.log" | tail -n 200
   - Cloud console quotas:
     - GCP: gcloud compute regions describe europe-west1 --format=json | jq '.quotas[] | select(.metric=="GPUS")'
     - AWS: aws service-quotas get-service-quota --service-code ec2 --quota-code L-0263D0A3 --region eu-west-1
   - Instance creation error: gcloud compute instances describe <instance-name> --zone eu-west1-b --format json

3) Common fixes
   - Quota: open quota request with cloud provider using pre-filled template (link in team wiki) and temporarily failover to another region if low risk.
   - IAM: verify the node service account has compute.instanceAdmin (or cloud equivalent) + iam.serviceAccountUser on the SA.
   - Network: ensure subnet has free IP addresses and route tables include hub routes. For Shared VPC, ensure host project allowed subnets list includes the target.
   - Bootstrapping: inspect cloud-init logs (serial port) and check cached AMI/golden image tags. If image is corrupt, roll back to previous image tag and re-run terraform with -target=module.gpu_node_pool.

4) Safe rollback pattern
   - If a large-scale apply introduced regressions, switch autoscaler to conservative mode and run terraform apply -target=module.<control-plane> to re-create control plane artifacts. Coordinate with release manager.

Runbook: network partition affecting inference traffic
------------------------------------------------------
1) Detection
   - Alert: 5xx rate increase on inference HTTP endpoints + cloud network packet drops > 0.5% for 2m.

2) Containment
   - Route traffic to warm standby region via the smart-router (route override) and enable fallbacks in Redwood routing policy.
   - Confirm hub health: check BGP sessions: (example) bgpctl show sessions OR gcloud compute routers get-status <router>.

3) Recovery steps
   - If BGP flap: bounce the affected VRF/peer: gcloud compute routers update <router> --peer-update etc. (follow provider runbook).
   - If route table corruption suspected: re-apply route module: terraform apply -target=module.network.routes -var='apply_validation=false'

CI/CD integration (how infra code is deployed)
--------------------------------------------
- Repo layout: infra/terraform-modules (modules) and infra/envs (env-specific stacks).
- Protected branches: main requires 2 approvers from the infra team.
- Pre-apply checks in pipeline:
  - terraform validate
  - tflint with cloud ruleset
  - policy-as-code (opa/conftest) against allowed machine/gpu whitelist
  - dry-run smoke using a synthetic "plan-checker" job that simulates quota & network pre-checks.

Sample GitHub Actions job (snippet)
```yaml
jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Setup Terraform
        uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v2
      - name: Terraform Init
        run: terraform init
      - name: Terraform Plan
        run: terraform plan -out=tfplan -var-file=envs/prod.tfvars
      - name: Save plan log
        run: terraform show -json tfplan > tfplan.json
```

Secrets and IAM considerations
------------------------------
- Use centralized KMS/Keyring for encrypting bootstrap secrets. Node bootstrap should retrieve secrets via short-lived signed tokens only.
- Avoid long-lived service account keys in CI; use workload identity / OIDC whenever possible.

Ownership and contacts
----------------------
- Network module maintainers: @Ethan Park (primary), @Leah Kim (secondary)
- Provisioning/autoscaler: @Maya Lopez
- Oncall rotation: infra-oncall@redwood.ai (see org rota in team wiki)

Rollout checklist for module changes (major versions)
----------------------------------------------------
1) Create a feature branch and bump module major version (v2 -> v3) in modules repo.
2) Add migration notes and compatibility shims.
3) Run migration test suite against a staging env and record node provisioning times.
4) Coordinate a gradual rollout by tagging 10% of stacks to use new module via feature flag in envs repo.
5) Monitor SLOs for 48h and be prepared to revert.

[rbac policy 'not_in' operator fallthrough grants unexpected access when claim missing in private deployment]
description:
Issue summary: Atlas Retail observed that several service accounts and a subset of human users were granted admin-level routes in their private VPC deployment despite RBAC policies that should exclude them via a 'not_in' expression. Impact: Incorrectly permissive access to admin/config APIs for a small number of identities, risk of configuration changes. Environment: Private deployment (customer-managed control plane), prod-us-east region, customer using SSO via their IdP with claims delivered as JWT to the identity-proxy. Observation window: 2026-03-12 22:30 - 2026-03-13 03:00 UTC. Steps to reproduce: 1) Customer provided a minimal policy that allows action if user.entitlements not_in ["admin", "superuser"] 2) Send request with JWT that omits the 'entitlements' claim altogether 3) Call to /admin/config returns 200 and allowed instead of denied. Expected behavior: Missing claim should be treated as empty set and 'not_in' should evaluate to true for empty set only if semantics intended; policy author expected deny when admin exclusion is required. Observed behavior: Policy evaluator treats missing claim in 'not_in' as a non-match that bypasses exclusion, resulting in grant. Customer impact: Two internal teams escalated (SRE and Platform) and temporarily halted config pushes. No data exfiltration detected.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Customer defines policy: allow if user.entitlements not_in ["admin", "superuser"]
2) Acquire JWT from IdP that omits entitlements claim (token valid for authN)
3) Call admin API route through identity-proxy and observe 200 OK
4) Inspect policy-evaluator logs and request trace (trace_id: trace-20260313-34b9)

logs:
2026-03-13T00:11:45Z authz-eval INFO allow user=svc-ordering token_kid=abcd1234 trace=trace-20260313-34b9 expr='user.entitlements not_in [\"admin\",\"superuser\"]' claim=ABSENT

[Customers in private VPC seeing 403 from IP-based RBAC conditions due to untrusted X-Forwarded-For header from proxy chain]
description:
Issue summary: Several Soteria Health users in a private VPC deployment report sudden 403 Authorization failures when calling Redwood admin APIs. The errors began after an internal network appliance upgrade. Impact: A subset of service accounts and admin users are blocked from performing operations that are gated by IP-based conditional RBAC rules (e.g., allow-listing corporate IP ranges). Environment: Private deployment (customer-managed VPC) fronted by customer edge proxy + Redwood identity proxy in us-east-1. Steps to reproduce: 1) Call admin endpoint with a request proxied through the customer's upgraded edge appliance. 2) Observe 403 with error 'denied by ip_condition'. 3) Repeat from same client but bypassing edge appliance (direct to Redwood ingress) — request succeeds. Expected behavior: Requests forwarded through trusted proxies should evaluate the original client IP and allow access when within allow-list. Actual behavior: Requests forwarded via the customer's upgraded edge appliance are being evaluated with a spoofed/misattributed client IP (X-Forwarded-For appears to contain internal hop IPs first), causing the RBAC engine's IP condition check to fail. Logs/Traces: AuthN logs show valid JWT and tenant; authZ logs show evaluated ip_condition set to "203.0.113.245" (edge appliance) rather than the original client IP. Ingress proxy provenance trace: received X-Forwarded-For: "10.0.0.5, 203.0.113.245". Identity proxy received the same header without a trusted-hop validation. Customer reports appliance upgrade changelog included "preserve-source-ip=false" by default.

comments:
2026-03-13 09:12 - Customer (Soteria): 'All of our automation that runs from on-prem IPs is failing with 403s after our edge appliance update.'
2026-03-13 09:47 - Support (Elaine Park): 'Thanks — investigating. Can you share a request-id and a sample X-Forwarded-For header from a failing request?'
2026-03-13 10:05 - Customer (Soteria): 'Request-id: req-7f3a; X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.5, 203.0.113.245'
2026-03-13 13:20 - Engineering (Marco Ruiz): 'Reproduced in staging by inserting a proxy hop that prepends a private RFC1918 address before the public edge IP in XFF. RBAC engine currently trusts the left-most XFF element as source IP when header present.'
2026-03-14 08:21 - SRE (Ivy Chen): 'We applied a workaround to verify proxy-hop trust and prefer the right-most public IP when intermediate hops are private. Rolling to canary.'

investigation_notes:
Hypothesis: Identity/ingress proxy accepts X-Forwarded-For without validating trust of upstream hop; upgraded appliance now prepends internal hop which pushes client IP to the right, altering evaluation if trust policy expects left-most client. 
Observed authz decision traces: ip_condition evaluated against 203.0.113.245 (edge appliance) not 198.51.100.77 (client) because XFF order changed after appliance rewrite.
Reproduced: Created synthetic proxy that inserts '10.0.0.5' before public IP in XFF; RBAC check fails when trust policy is configured to treat left-most token as client IP. 
Configuration review: Some private deployments configure 'trust-proxy=true' without restricting trusted hops; ingress should validate hop IPs against a configured trusted list or use right-most public IP when private hops present.
Related: linked INT-4219 tracks a planned auth library change to XFF parsing and trusted-hop config; PR opened to ingress-proxy to add explicit trusted_hops and to ignore RFC1918 tokens when selecting client IP.
Risk analysis: If we flip selection logic globally without per-tenant config, some customers who rely on left-most semantics may be affected. Need customer-scoped rollback/feature-flag.

resolution_notes:
Workaround (applied 2026-03-14): Deployed ingress-proxy canary to Soteria's private control plane that 1) validates X-Forwarded-For hop chain against configured 'trusted_hops' and 2) when private RFC1918 hops are present, prefers the nearest public IP for RBAC evaluation. This restored access for affected service accounts. 
Fix plan: Merge PR https://github.com/redwood/ingress-proxy/pull/1124 which introduces tenant-scoped 'trusted_hops' config and a 'xff_selection_policy' parameter ('left-most', 'right-most-public', 'validated-trusted-hops'). Ship as opt-in for private deployments with follow-up migration docs. 
Post-deploy actions: 1) Add runbook instructions to validate edge appliance XFF behavior during upgrades. 2) Notify customers in private tier with IP-based RBAC to review 'trusted_hops' config. 3) Schedule postmortem and update RBAC docs. 
Customer follow-up: Soteria Health confirmed workaround fixed immediate blocking issue and will coordinate with their appliance vendor to preserve original-source-ip semantics or explicitly configure proxy to forward XFF in expected order. 
Closure criteria: Fix merged and enabled in customer's control plane, runbook updated, automated tests added to prevent regressions.

[Claim header normalization causes conditional RBAC role expressions to evaluate false in private deployment]
description:
Customers on the private deployment report sudden 403s for administrative API calls that rely on conditional RBAC rules evaluated against JWT custom claims. Errors started after an ingress edge upgrade in us-east. This ticket tracks the investigation and remediation for Arcana Health (private tenant).

impact:
Multiple service accounts in the customer's private VPC receiving 403 on admin GraphQL routes; blocks operation automation and scheduled model rollouts. Estimated ~20% of ARC tenants impacted in us-east cluster during outage window.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Use service account token with custom claim 'tenant.env' set to 'arcana:prod' 2) Send POST to /admin/graphql route through customer's private ingress 3) Observe 403 with 'rbac:condition-eval-false' in response headers

observed_behavior:
Requests that previously passed RBAC now fail with 403. Request logs show the claim header present but conditional expression in RBAC evaluated to false.

expected_behavior:
Conditional expressions that reference JWT claim keys should evaluate using the original claim key names/values provided by the IdP exchange and preserved through the ingress path.

logs:
- proxy-access: 2026-03-10T08:12:14Z POST /admin/graphql 403 x-request-id=abc123
- auth-service: 2026-03-10T08:12:14Z claim 'tenant.env' found in token payload
- rbac-engine: 2026-03-10T08:12:14Z condition 'claims.tenant.env == "arcana:prod"' evaluated to false (input claims: tenant.Env="arcana:prod")

investigation_notes:
- 2026-03-10: Support reproduced issue with customer's token; confirmed mismatch in claim key casing during header propagation.
- Observed that the upgraded ingress (edge-proxy v3.7.0) started normalizing header names by capitalizing dotted claim keys (e.g., tenant.env -> tenant.Env) when serializing into X-JWT-CLAIMS header.
- RBAC engine uses case-sensitive JSON path lookups for condition evaluation; mismatch causes expression to short-circuit.
- Cross-checked with ingress change log and found PR that touched header canonicalization logic (https://github.com/redwood-inference/edge-proxy/pull/1569).
- Quick test: modifying RBAC condition to use a case-insensitive extractor returns correct allow; however this is not feasible for all customers.
- Correlated timeline with customer report and internal deploys; regression introduced during 2026-03-09 midnight deployment to us-east nodes.

2026-03-10 10:22 - SRE (Tomas Ortega): Found header normalization in edge-proxy v3.7.0. Adding ingress-proxy and rbac-engine owners to this ticket. Tentatively rolling back v3.7.0 to v3.6.8 in a canary to validate.

2026-03-12 12:00 - Customer (Nadia Chen, Arcana): We accepted the maintenance window. Thanks for the quick triage.

root_cause:
Ingress edge-proxy v3.7.0 introduced header canonicalization that changed the casing of dotted claim keys when serializing JWT claims into the X-JWT-CLAIMS header. The RBAC engine evaluates JSONPath expressions in a case-sensitive manner, so tenant-specific conditional policies referencing 'tenant.env' failed when header became 'tenant.Env'.

short_term_workaround:
1) Roll back edge-proxy to v3.6.8 for affected us-east nodes (completed in canary, scheduled cluster rollback).
2) Customer can temporarily rewrite RBAC conditions to use a case-insensitive claim accessor or normalize claim keys in policies.

resolution:
Performed staged rollback of edge-proxy to v3.6.8 in us-east cluster (rolled out 2026-03-11 02:15 UTC). Deployed edge-proxy patch v3.7.1 with preserved claim key casing and unit tests on 2026-03-12 10:30 UTC. Verified Arcana's admin calls succeed post-deploy.

verification_steps:
1) Confirmed admin GraphQL POSTs from Arcana succeed with previously failing service-account tokens. 2) RBAC engine logs show condition evaluation true for claims. 3) Customer executed CI job that previously failed — now green.

follow_up_actions:

- Expand monitoring alert for spikes in 'rbac:condition-eval-false' returns to trigger rollback automation.
- Postmortem scheduled on Confluence: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SUPPORT/pages/142421/2026-03-11+Claim+Header+Normalization+Postmortem
