[Latency-aware Cost Fallback Protocol (LACFP) Design Spec]
Summary:
This design spec defines the Latency-aware Cost Fallback Protocol (LACFP), a server-side policy and lightweight protocol that enables Redwood inference routing to automatically fall back to lower-cost model variants or capacity tiers when latency, cost, or capacity signals indicate it is appropriate. The goal is to preserve user-facing latency SLOs while minimizing incremental cost and providing transparent accounting for customer billing and internal cost centers.

Motivation:
- Customers require predictable latency for interactive workloads (e.g., chat) but also demand cost efficiency.
- Static fallback rules (time-based or simple capacity thresholds) are brittle and cause noisy behavior during transient events.
- We need a shared, auditable protocol that:
  1) reacts to latency and cost signals in near real-time;
  2) guarantees bounded user-impact by enforcing soft/hard fidelity and latency limits;
  3) preserves billable attribution and enables credits/discounting when lower-fidelity fallbacks are applied.

Design goals (must):
- Latency-first: Respect per-route latency SLOs (default 95th pct <= 120ms for token production in interactive endpoints).
- Cost-conscious: Prefer lower-cost variants when they do not violate quality or latency objectives.
- Transparent accounting: Emit events for every fallback decision with cost delta metadata for billing reconciliation.
- Configurable: Support per-tenant and per-route policies with hierarchical inheritance (global -> tenant -> route).

Non-goals (out of scope):
- Model distillation, model training, or quality-aware model retraining.
- Deep content-aware fidelity negotiation (that belongs to the fidelity negotiator PRD).
- Full rewrites of the billing system; LACFP only emits metadata consumed by billing services.

Assumptions:
- Runtime can measure per-request latency to the active model variant and expose aggregated 1m/5m windows.
- Cost-per-token or cost-per-second estimates are available for each variant and capacity tier.
- Each model variant has a compatibility label set (e.g., conversational-v1, embeddings-v2) so fallbacks only target compatible variants.

High-level protocol overview:
- LACFP runs inside the request routing stack. When a request arrives, router evaluates the active policy for the tenant/route and does the following:
  1) Compute expected latency and cost for the request given current telemetry (historical per-variant latency distribution + queue depth).
  2) Evaluate policy rules (latency budget, cost delta threshold, fallback budget).
  3) If policy triggers, select a fallback variant and attach a Fallback-Decision header to the upstream call; emit a fallback event to telemetry.
  4) Billing and credits: tag request with cost-override metadata and store the decision event for offline reconciliation.

State machine and decision logic (simplified):
- States: Normal, SoftFallbacking, HardFallbacking, Stabilizing.
- Trigger signals: 
  * Latency breach probability > P_soft (default 0.25) over 1m window -> SoftFallbacking.
  * Latency breach probability > P_hard (default 0.6) and queue backlog > Q_hard -> HardFallbacking.
  * Cost spike detection: cost-per-token delta > C_threshold (default +50%) -> consider SoftFallback.
- Stabilization: After a fallback, hold policy for a hold_time (default 30s) and require metric improvement across 2 windows before reverting.

Fallback selection heuristics:
- Preferred order: smaller model variant -> quantized variant -> lower-shape instance -> regional shift (if latency permits) -> graceful truncation (session-level fidelity actions handled by fidelity negotiator).
- Only select variants with Compatibility = true for route.
- Respect tenant affinity: if tenant has reserved Dedicated capacity, avoid fallback to shared-hosted unless policy explicitly allows it.

Cost attribution and crediting rules:
- Every decision emits an event payload with: request_id, route_id, tenant_id, timestamp, active_variant, fallback_variant, estimated_cost_delta, latency_estimate_before, latency_estimate_after, reason_tags.
- For customer-facing billing: If fallback reduces cost by >= 10% and the tenant holds a fidelity-safety guarantee, apply a 'fallback-credit' equal to 50% of the cost savings for that billing window (configurable per contract).
- Internal cost centers receive raw cost delta events for chargeback.

Sample cost accounting table (reference):
| Variant | Token CPI (USD) | Avg latency (ms) | Notes |
| small-7b | 0.0008 | 90 | quantized fast path available |
| base-7b-q4 | 0.0005 | 110 | 4-bit quantized variant |
| midsize-13b | 0.0016 | 140 | higher quality, higher cost |

APIs and configuration examples:
- Policy YAML (per-route):

policy: |
  name: lacfp-small-chat-policy
  scope: route
  latency_slo_ms: 120
  soft_trigger_probability: 0.25
  hard_trigger_probability: 0.6
  cost_delta_threshold_pct: 30
  allowed_fallbacks:
    - variant: base-7b-q4
      max_daily_usage_pct: 40
    - variant: small-7b
      max_daily_usage_pct: 20
  hold_time_seconds: 30
  tenant_override: true

- Runtime header injected when fallback applied (HTTP):
  Fallback-Decision: variant=base-7b-q4;reason=latency-soft;estimated_savings=22.4%;credit_tag=fb-50pct

Sample event JSON emitted to telemetry (flattened for ingestion):
  {"request_id":"req_12345","tenant_id":"t_678","route":"/v1/chat","active_variant":"midsize-13b","fallback_variant":"base-7b-q4","estimated_cost_delta_usd":"0.0012","latency_est_before_ms":"160","latency_est_after_ms":"115","reason":"latency_hazard","policy_id":"lacfp-small-chat-policy"}

Backward compatibility and migration:
- Existing per-route fallback rules will be translated into an initial LACFP policy during rollout.
- If runtime does not support LACFP for a capacity pool, the router falls back to previous behavior and emits a compatibility_warning metric.

Rollout plan (phased):
1) Canary (2 weeks): Enable LACFP in a single EU region for internal tenants only. Metrics: false-positive fallback rate < 1%, customer error rate unchanged.
2) Pilot (4–6 weeks): Enable for small set of opt-in customers (20 tenants) across regions. Introduce billing credit hooks in sandbox.
3) Gradual GA (8–12 weeks): Auto-translate legacy fallbacks, expose UI in Console (policy editor), enable for all hosted routes with safe defaults.
4) GA+: Expose per-tenant SLO-driven monetization options and expand to Dedicated routing when tenant permits.

Rollback criteria:
- Error rate increase > 0.5% absolute for a route after rollout.
- Customer support escalations indicating quality regressions (>= 3 within 24 hours).

Telemetry and SLOs to monitor:
- Primary SLO: 95th percentile request latency for interactive routes (target 120ms).
- Metrics to emit: fallback_decisions_count, fallback_rate_per_route, estimated_cost_savings_total, fallback_false_positive_rate, compatibility_warnings, fallout_customer_errors.
- Dashboards: per-tenant fallback summary, per-region stability heatmap, cost-savings ledger for billing reconciliation.

Testing and QA:
- Unit: Decision engine deterministic tests for stochastic triggers.
- Integration: Synthetic load tests simulating queue-backlog and model latency spikes with traffic replay.
- E2E: Billing integration test that validates credit events are generated and consumed by billing pipeline (sanity check: credit and invoice reconciliation end-to-end).

Security and privacy considerations:
- All fallback events contain only tenant and routing metadata; no prompt or response payloads are included in fallback telemetry.
- Fallback decisions stored for at most 12 months by default; retention configurable per tenant contract.

Ownership and next steps:
- Spec owner: Priya Raman (Product – Runtime Economics).
- Implementation owners: eng-serving-runtime (decision engine) and eng-platform (router + telemetry hooks).
- Short-term milestones (Q1 2027):
  * Prototype decision engine in runtime (Spike) — owner: eng-serving-runtime — due 2027-01-30.
  * Telemetry event schema published and consumed by billing sandbox — owner: eng-platform — due 2027-02-10.
  * Console policy editor wireframes — owner: product-ux — due 2027-02-28.

Appendix A — Example debug CLI commands:
- Force a soft fallback test for tenant: redwoodctl routing simulate-fallback --tenant t_678 --route /v1/chat --variant base-7b-q4 --duration 60s
- Inspect last 100 fallback events: redwoodctl telemetry query --filter "event_type=fallback_decision AND tenant=t_678" --limit 100

Appendix B — Open questions for review:
1) Should fallback credits be proportional to realized-line-item savings or based on estimated savings at decision time? Recommendation: start with estimated savings to allow near-real-time customer transparency, revert to realized reconciliation in billing batch.
2) How strict should compatibility labels be for multi-modal endpoints? Recommendation: conservative by default; expose opt-in to relaxed compatibility.
3) Do we allow cross-tenant fallback into Dedicated pools in crisis scenarios? Strong recommendation: no, unless emergency escalation with explicit owner approval.

Document change log:
- 2026-12-10: Initial draft by Leah Chen.
- 2027-01-12: Added cost accounting table and soft/hard trigger tuning (review feedback Marco Rivera).
- 2027-02-03: Finalized rollout plan and telemetry schema (review feedback Anya Patel).

For further discussion, please comment on this page or ping the reviewers listed above.

[Onboarding KPIs Dashboard Spec (TTFS/TTFP + Checklist Funnel)]
## Overview
This document specifies the **Onboarding KPIs dashboard** used to track the Guided Onboarding + “First Production Launch” checklist initiative for Hosted API.

The dashboard answers:
- Are we improving **time-to-first-success (TTFS)** and **time-to-first-production (TTFP)**?
- Where do users drop off in the checklist funnel, and why?
- Are we introducing regressions (e.g., auth/rate-limit/streaming confusion) during rollout?

This spec covers:
- Metric definitions (TTFS/TTFP + funnel/step completion)
- Cohorts and filtering
- Drop-off reason taxonomy
- Alerts (thresholds, data quality, and regression detection)

## Audience
- DevEx, Hosted API PM, Console PM/design: adoption + activation
- Telemetry/Platform: instrumentation integrity + regressions
- Support/CS: early detection of common onboarding failures and documentation gaps

## Scope and non-goals
**In scope**
- Hosted API onboarding funnel + checklist completion metrics
- Cohort breakdowns (feature flag, region, SDK/language, account type)
- Operational alerts for regressions and data freshness

**Out of scope (MVP)**
- Dedicated/Private onboarding KPIs
- In-product guided tours analytics
- Automated remediation suggestions (tracked separately)

## Source of truth and data flow
### Primary datasets
1) **onboarding_events_v1** (append-only)
- Emitted server-side (gateway/control plane) with limited client hints (SDK language/version, streaming enabled)
- Schema governed by: `onboarding-event-schema-v1` and `ADR-2025-02-onboarding-checklist-eventing`

2) **checklist_progress_state** (derived state)
- Computed by checklist progress service using monotonic transitions
- Used by Console to render state; also exported to analytics for funnel reporting

3) **gateway_request_facts** (request outcomes)
- Used to validate “first success” and classify failures (401/403/429/5xx)

4) **usage_metering_facts** (optional validation)
- Used to cross-check that first production traffic corresponds to sustained token usage (helps detect false positives)

### Identifiers
- **tenant_id**: primary entity for funnel conversion
- **user_id**: secondary for debugging individual user flows (dashboard defaults to tenant view)
- **api_key_id**: used only for event correlation; not used as primary cohort identifier

### Data latency expectations
- onboarding_events_v1 ingestion SLO: **p95 < 10 minutes**
- checklist_progress_state export SLO: **p95 < 20 minutes**
- Dashboard “freshness” guardrail: show a banner if last successful ETL/export is **> 30 minutes**

## Definitions
### Time-to-first-success (TTFS)
**Definition:** time from tenant signup to first successful Hosted API inference request.

- **Start timestamp:** `tenant_created_at` (from control plane)
- **Success event (earliest of):**
  - `onboarding.inference.first_2xx` (preferred)
  - Fallback: first 2xx request in `gateway_request_facts` where route is a supported inference endpoint
- **Success criteria:** HTTP 2xx AND request classified as inference (chat/generate/embeddings/rerank)
- **Exclusions:**
  - internal tenants (Redwood dogfood) unless explicitly filtered to “internal” cohort
  - replay/backfill events (events with `is_backfill=true`)
  - requests from health checks or non-inference endpoints
- **Units:** minutes/hours; dashboard shows p50/p75/p90 and distribution

**Edge cases**
- Multiple users in one tenant: TTFS is tenant-level (earliest success across users)
- If `tenant_created_at` missing (rare), drop from TTFS metric and count in “data quality: missing anchors”

### Time-to-first-production (TTFP)
**Definition (MVP):** time from tenant signup to first sustained production traffic signal.

Because “production” is ambiguous, TTFP is defined as the first time the tenant satisfies BOTH:
1) `onboarding.inference.first_2xx` occurred, AND
2) at least **N=3 inference requests** over a **30-minute window**, with at least **1 request not using a known quickstart user-agent tag** (to reduce demo-only noise)

- **Start timestamp:** `tenant_created_at`
- **Production timestamp:** first window end time that satisfies the sustained traffic rule
- **Caveat:** This is an approximation; enterprise customers may validate production readiness through checklist steps rather than traffic.

Dashboard must clearly label this as **TTFP (behavioral proxy)**.

### Checklist step funnel
**Entity:** tenant_id

**Step state model:**
- Not started → In progress → Complete
- State transitions are **monotonic** (no regressions), except via explicit admin reset (tracked)

**Canonical steps (Hosted API MVP)**
1) Create API key
2) Configure environment (set `REDWOOD_API_KEY`)
3) First successful request (2xx)
4) First streaming response (optional but recommended)
5) Configure retries/timeouts (client-side; validated by SDK preset usage tag or explicit console toggle)
6) Review usage dashboard (visited usage page OR usage API called)
7) Set quotas/budgets (tenant quota set OR budget alert configured)
8) Pin model version (model pin set in config)
9) Configure fallback policy (fallback enabled in routing policy)
10) Add observability hook (trace/log correlation header enabled OR tracing integration configured)

**Note:** Steps 4 and 5 are “recommended”; the funnel view supports toggling inclusion of recommended steps.

## Drop-off reason taxonomy
Drop-off reasons are used in a dedicated diagnostic panel. Classification uses gateway facts plus onboarding events.

**Primary reasons (mutually exclusive, ordered):**
1) **Auth failure**: first request attempts contain 401/403, no subsequent 2xx
2) **Rate limited**: 429 occurs before first 2xx OR immediately after first 2xx with no recovery
3) **Streaming disconnect / client abort**: streaming attempted, connection drops before first token OR repeated disconnects (>=3) within 30 minutes
4) **5xx / platform error**: 5xx responses dominate (>50% of attempts) in first hour
5) **SDK misconfiguration**: unsupported SDK version, missing required headers, or repeated 400s with known patterns
6) **Unknown / no signal**: no requests observed and no checklist interactions

**Implementation notes**
- Drop-off reason is computed at fixed horizons (e.g., 1h, 24h, 7d post-signup) to enable comparable rates.
- Each reason must provide drill-down to example tenants (restricted access) and representative error codes.

## Dashboard layout (sections and charts)
### 1) Executive summary
- TTFS p50/p75/p90 (last 7 days vs previous 7 days)
- TTFP p50/p75/p90 (last 14 days vs previous 14 days; longer window due to lower volume)
- Activation rate: % tenants with first 2xx within 24h
- Production proxy rate: % tenants meeting TTFP within 7d
- Data freshness tile (events, derived state, request facts)

### 2) Funnel: signup → first success
- Step conversion funnel (tenant counts + % conversion)
- Time-between-steps distribution (median/percentiles)
- Breakdown by:
  - region
  - SDK language
  - onboarding cohort (feature flag on/off)
  - acquisition channel (if available; otherwise leave as “unknown”)

### 3) Checklist completion funnel
- Completion rates per step (bar chart)
- “Recommended steps” completion (streaming, retries/timeouts) shown separately
- Time-to-complete per step (box plots)
- Admin override rate (how often Support resets/marks complete; used as friction signal)

### 4) Drop-off reasons
- Stacked bar: drop-off reasons at 24h and 7d
- Trend lines for top reasons (auth, 429, streaming disconnect)
- Table of top error codes/messages associated with onboarding failures (aggregated, no payloads)

### 5) Cohort comparison (rollout monitoring)
- Feature flag cohorts:
  - `checklist_enabled=true` vs `false`
  - dogfood/internal vs external
- Incrementality view:
  - TTFS delta (median and distribution)
  - Step completion deltas
  - Support ticket proxy (if available via tag): onboarding-related ticket rate per 100 new tenants

### 6) Data quality & instrumentation health
- Event volume by event_name over time (detect missing emissions)
- % events missing required fields (schema conformance)
- Late events rate (event_time older than ingestion_time by > 60 minutes)
- Out-of-order events detected (should trend toward 0 after race-condition fix)

## Filters and drill-down requirements
### Global filters (apply to all panels)
- Time range (default: last 14 days)
- Tenant cohort:
  - External (default)
  - Internal/dogfood
  - Enterprise-contract (if available)
- Region (cloud region)
- SDK language (python/typescript/go/openai-compat/unknown)
- SDK major/minor version (bucketed; avoid high-cardinality patch granularity)
- Checklist feature flag state (enabled/disabled)

### Drill-down links
- From funnel step → list of example tenants (restricted) with:
  - timeline of key events
  - first error code counts
  - last seen SDK version/user-agent tag
- From drop-off reason → examples + top remediation docs link

## Alerting specification
Alerts are configured in the platform alerting system and should page only for severe regressions; otherwise route to Slack channels.

### Severity levels
- **SEV2 (page)**: likely platform regression impacting onboarding at scale
- **SEV3 (Slack)**: meaningful degradation that needs investigation within 1 business day
- **Info**: data quality warnings, non-urgent trends

### Core regression alerts
1) **TTFS p50 regression (SEV3)**
- Condition: TTFS p50 increases by **>= 15% WoW** AND absolute increase **>= 10 minutes**
- Window: compare last 24h vs previous 7-day baseline (same weekday weighting if available)
- Route: #eng-platform + #devex

2) **Activation rate drop (SEV2)**
- Condition: % tenants reaching first 2xx within 24h drops by **>= 8 percentage points** compared to trailing 7-day average
- Additional guardrail: only fire if new tenant volume >= 200/day (avoid noise)
- Route: oncall (Telemetry/Platform) + #eng-sre

3) **Auth failure spike (SEV3)**
- Condition: 24h auth drop-off rate (reason=Auth failure at 1h horizon) increases by **>= 25% relative** and **>= 3 pp absolute**
- Route: #devex + #support + Platform oncall (non-paging)

4) **429 spike after first success (SEV3)**
- Condition: Among tenants with first 2xx, % seeing a 429 within 60 minutes increases by **>= 5 pp absolute**
- Route: #eng-platform + #product

5) **Streaming disconnect spike (SEV3)**
- Condition: streaming disconnect classification rate increases by **>= 3 pp absolute** in last 24h
- Route: #devex + SDK leads

### Data freshness and integrity alerts
6) **Onboarding events ingestion stale (SEV2)**
- Condition: no new onboarding_events_v1 ingested for **> 20 minutes** OR ingestion lag p95 **> 30 minutes**
- Route: Telemetry oncall

7) **Derived state export stale (SEV3)**
- Condition: checklist_progress_state export job last success **> 45 minutes**
- Route: #eng-platform

8) **Schema conformance regression (SEV3)**
- Condition: % events missing required fields exceeds **0.5%** over 1h window
- Route: #eng-platform; file ticket to emitting service owner

### Alert noise controls
- Alerts should be suppressed during planned maintenance windows (tracked via change calendar).
- Use minimum volume thresholds where applicable.
- All alerts require a runbook link (even if short) and a dashboard deep link.

## Access control and privacy
- Dashboard is **internal**.
- Tenant-level drilldowns are **restricted** to DevEx, Platform, Support leadership, and SRE (least privilege). Default view is aggregated.
- No prompt contents, message texts, or customer payloads are displayed.
- User identifiers shown only when explicitly necessary for debugging and must be accessed via restricted drilldown.
- Retention aligns with `onboarding-telemetry-data-review`.

## Implementation notes (for dashboard builders)
- Prefer derived checklist state for completion panels; use raw events only for instrumentation health and timeline debugging.
- Bucket SDK versions to reduce cardinality (e.g., 1.18.x).
- For TTFS/TTFP distributions, use percentile aggregations with explicit handling of right-censoring (tenants that have not converted yet).
- Annotate key rollout dates (feature flag cohorts, SDK releases) directly on time series charts.

## Ownership
- DRI (data/metrics): **Mei Lin**
- Telemetry platform: **Logan Wright**, **Nadia Rahman**
- Metric definitions/product alignment: **Chris Osei**, **Nikhil Sharma**
- Alerting review: **Allison Grant**, **Sean Gallagher**
- Support consumption: **Dev Patel**

## Validation checklist (must pass before GA)
- [ ] TTFS computed from onboarding event matches gateway facts for a random sample of 50 tenants (>= 98% consistency)
- [ ] Funnel step counts match checklist_progress_state for last 7 days (>= 99% within tolerance)
- [ ] Drop-off reason classifier precision spot-check (>= 90% for auth/429/5xx categories)
- [ ] Data freshness tiles and alerts tested in staging and production
- [ ] Access control verified (aggregate-only by default; restricted drilldowns gated)

## Open questions / follow-ups
- Should TTFP shift from behavioral proxy to “checklist-defined readiness” for enterprise cohorts?
- Do we need separate funnels for OpenAI-compat vs native SDK due to different failure modes?
- Can we join Support ticket tags into the dashboard for a direct “ticket deflection” KPI (requires data sharing approval)?

[P1 Incident Postmortem: Metrics pipeline dropped tracing spans]
## Summary
On 2026-02-25, Redwood Console traces for several services showed missing spans and incomplete request graphs. The underlying services were healthy, but the observability pipeline dropped a portion of spans under burst load.

## Severity
P1

## Customer impact
- Internal impact: on-call and support debugging slowed due to partial traces for ~2 hours.
- No direct serving impact; data plane SLOs were met.

## Timeline (UTC)
- 12:08: First report from on-call: trace graphs missing child spans.
- 12:22: SRE identifies span-ingester backpressure and queue drops.
- 12:44: Mitigation: increase ingester replicas + raise queue limits temporarily.
- 14:05: Drop rate returns to baseline; backlog drains.

## Root cause
The span ingester queue was configured with a low max size and a drop-on-full policy. A parallel deploy increased span volume per request (additional attributes), pushing the queue into frequent drops during peaks.

## Detection
Detected via manual observation; there was no alert on span drop rate.

## Follow-up action items (count these)
1) Add alert on span drop rate (drop_rate > 0.5% for 5 minutes) and page SRE. Owning team: Eng SRE.
2) Add load test to observability pipeline release checklist (span volume burst + attribute size). Owning team: Eng SRE.
3) Add safe defaults and documentation for span attribute limits in the instrumentation SDK wrapper. Owning team: Eng Platform.

## References
- Service: span-ingester
- Dashboard: Observability > Tracing pipeline health


[Runbook: Suggestions API Latency and 5xx Triage]
## Purpose
This runbook covers triage and mitigation for elevated latency and/or 5xx error rate on the **Suggestions API** used by the Redwood Console “Optimization suggestions” beta.

Primary goals:
- Restore availability and latency SLOs quickly.
- Prevent cross-tenant or broad Console impact (UI timeouts, repeated retries).
- Preserve correctness guarantees (RBAC + org/project scoping) while degraded.

Non-goals:
- Deep root cause analysis (capture data for follow-up; open an incident or ticket as needed).

---

## Service / Endpoint Overview
**User-facing surface:** Redwood Console → Optimize → Suggestions

**Backend service:** `optimize-suggestions-service`

**Primary endpoint (internal naming):**
- `GET /optimize/suggestions` (list; paginated, sortable)
- `GET /optimize/suggestions/{suggestion_id}` (details)

**Common query parameters:**
- `org_id`, `project_id`
- `route_id` (optional filter)
- `model` (optional filter)
- `sort` (e.g., `estimated_savings_usd_day_desc`, `risk_asc`)
- `page_size`, `page_token`

**Critical dependencies:**
- Suggestions DB (Postgres)
- Cache layer (Redis) for hot list requests (if enabled)
- RBAC/Authz service and policy store
- Suggestions compute pipeline (produces precomputed estimates + `stale_as_of`)

---

## SLOs, Alerts, and What “Bad” Looks Like
### SLO targets (beta)
These are operational targets for the **API**, not the compute pipeline:
- **Availability:** 99.9% (per 30d) for `GET /optimize/suggestions`
- **Latency:** p95 < 350ms for list endpoint (typical page_size 25)
- **Error rate:** 5xx < 0.2% (5-minute window)

### Common alert triggers
- `SuggestionsAPIHighP95Latency` (p95 > 500ms for 10m)
- `SuggestionsAPI5xxRateHigh` (5xx > 1% for 5m)
- `SuggestionsAPITimeouts` (upstream gateway timeouts elevated)
- `SuggestionsDBPoolSaturation` (connection pool > 90% for 10m)

### User symptoms
- Console Suggestions page spinner/timeouts
- Empty states that look like errors (e.g., “Couldn’t load suggestions”)
- Rapid retries from Console amplifying load

---

## Where to Look First (Dashboards)
1) **Grafana: Suggestions API Health (Overview)**
- Panels: RPS, p50/p95 latency, 4xx/5xx, timeouts, payload size
- Breakdowns: region, cluster, endpoint, status_code
- Link (internal): `grafana://dashboards/suggestions-api-overview`

2) **Grafana: Suggestions API – Dependency Drilldown**
- DB query latency, DB connections, Redis ops/latency, authz latency
- Link (internal): `grafana://dashboards/suggestions-api-deps`

3) **Grafana: Suggestions Compute Lag**
- Compute job success rate, last successful run, lag minutes, stale rows
- Link (internal): `grafana://dashboards/suggestions-compute-lag`

4) **Funnel dashboard (for blast radius / retries)**
- Impressions → expand → error events
- Link (internal): `grafana://dashboards/suggestions-beta-funnel`

---

## Fast Triage Checklist (10 minutes)
### Step 0 — Confirm scope and severity
- Is it **one region/cluster** or global?
- Is it **list endpoint only** or also details?
- Is the issue **latency**, **5xx**, or both?
- Is there a correlated **deploy**, **config change**, or **feature flag ramp**?

### Step 1 — Check recent changes
- Deploys (last 2 hours): `optimize-suggestions-service`, authz service, DB migrations
- Console rollout: Suggestions feature flag ramp, cohort expansion
- Infra: DB failover, Redis maintenance, network incidents

### Step 2 — Identify dominant failure mode
Use dashboard splits by `status_code` and error class.
- If **5xx spikes** with stable latency → likely exceptions, dependency outage, pool exhaustion
- If **p95 latency climbs** with rising DB time → query regression or DB contention
- If **gateway timeouts** dominate → threads blocked, deadlocks, slow queries, downstream timeouts

### Step 3 — Capture evidence for follow-up
- Snapshot graphs (latency, 5xx, DB latency, DB pool)
- Top error messages (from logs)
- A few example request IDs / trace IDs

---

## Logs, Traces, and Key Signals
### Logs (Kibana/Loki)
Filter by:
- `service=optimize-suggestions-service`
- `endpoint=/optimize/suggestions`
- `status>=500`

Look for:
- DB errors: `too many connections`, `timeout`, `deadlock detected`
- Authz errors: policy fetch timeouts
- Serialization/payload errors: response too large
- Pagination token parsing failures (can present as 5xx if unhandled)

### Traces (Tempo/Honeycomb)
Find slow traces and identify which span dominates:
- `db.query` (slow SQL)
- `authz.check` (RBAC latency)
- `redis.get`/`redis.mget` (cache slowness)

### Metrics (names may vary by cluster)
- `http_server_request_duration_seconds{service="optimize-suggestions-service"}`
- `http_server_requests_total{status_code=~"5.."}`
- `db_pool_in_use{service="optimize-suggestions-service"}`
- `db_query_duration_seconds{query_name=...}`
- `authz_request_duration_seconds`
- `redis_command_duration_seconds{command=...}`

---

## Common Causes and Mitigations
### A) DB query regression / N+1 behavior
**Signals**
- p95 increases with DB time; CPU on DB rises; slow query log shows repeated similar queries.
- Latency worsens with higher `page_size`.

**Immediate mitigations**
1) Reduce load:
- Temporarily reduce Console page_size defaults (if configurable via server config).
- Consider throttling list endpoint at the gateway for abusive orgs (avoid global throttles if possible).

2) Enable/Increase caching for list responses (if safe for RBAC scoping):
- Ensure cache key includes `org_id`, `project_id`, filters, and `sort`.
- Keep TTL short (e.g., 60–120s) to avoid confusion and preserve “near-real-time” expectation.

3) If a known regression is identified, roll back:
- Roll back the last deploy to `optimize-suggestions-service`.
- If caused by a query change, prefer rollback over hotfix unless rollback is blocked.

**Follow-up**
- Open ENG ticket and attach the slow query / trace evidence.
- If this resembles the prior N+1 pattern, reference the query optimization work (e.g., “N+1 in suggestions query” fix).

---

### B) DB connection pool saturation
**Signals**
- Elevated 5xx with errors like `remaining connection slots are reserved`.
- `db_pool_in_use` near max; queue wait time increases.

**Immediate mitigations**
1) Scale application pods (carefully):
- Scaling pods can worsen DB saturation if pool sizes scale linearly.
- If scaling, ensure max connections per pod is bounded.

2) Reduce concurrent work:
- Temporarily lower worker concurrency / thread pool if requests are blocking.

3) Gate traffic:
- Pause new beta org enables (feature flag) and/or reduce cohorts.

4) Engage DB on-call if the DB itself is overloaded (high CPU/IO, long locks).

**Escalation trigger**
- Pool saturation sustained > 15m or repeated DB connection errors → page SRE + DB owner.

---

### C) Redis/cache degradation (if enabled)
**Signals**
- `redis_command_duration` increases; timeouts; cache miss rate spikes.
- Latency increases but DB time may remain flat (if app blocks on cache timeouts).

**Immediate mitigations**
1) Fail open on cache:
- Switch cache operations to non-blocking mode / shorter timeouts (config).
- If Redis is causing tail latency, temporarily disable cache reads (keep writes off as well).

2) Reduce cache key cardinality:
- Ensure keys are not including high-cardinality fields unnecessarily.

---

### D) Authz/RBAC dependency latency
**Signals**
- Traces show `authz.check` dominating.
- Increased 5xx due to authz timeouts or circuit breaker open.

**Immediate mitigations**
1) Confirm we are not making per-row authz checks.
- List endpoint should authorize at org/project scope once, then filter results.

2) Enable authz result caching (short TTL) if available.

3) If authz is down: fail closed (no data) rather than serving suggestions without verification.
- Prefer returning a 403/feature unavailable rather than leaking data.

---

### E) Suggestions compute lag / stale data confusion (not usually 5xx)
Compute lag typically causes “stale_as_of” to be old or “insufficient telemetry” states, but can cause backend errors if invariants break.

**Signals**
- Compute lag dashboard shows last successful run too old.
- Errors referencing missing aggregates or null estimate fields.

**Immediate mitigations**
1) Degrade to “stale but serveable”:
- Continue serving last known suggestions with `stale_as_of` intact.
- Do not recompute synchronously on read.

2) Pause compute backfills if they overload the DB.
- Prefer off-peak backfills.

3) If compute job is failing repeatedly:
- Page compute owner (Optimize pipeline) and consider disabling new suggestion generation while serving cached results.

---

## Safe Degradation Options (Preferred Order)
Use these to reduce user impact while protecting safety and trust.

1) **Serve cached / precomputed results with explicit staleness**
- Keep `stale_as_of` visible to UI.

2) **Return partial list with clear UI messaging**
- Example: “Some filters are unavailable right now. Showing top suggestions only.”

3) **Temporarily disable expensive fields** (only if the API contract allows)
- Example: omit confidence bands or verbose explanations if they cause payload bloat.
- Must maintain backward compatibility per API contract.

4) **Feature flag off** for impacted cohort
- If needed, disable Suggestions UI entry point for newly-enabled orgs first.

5) **Hard disable endpoint** (last resort)
- Return 503 with Retry-After and ensure Console handles gracefully.

---

## Step-by-Step: What to Do During an Active Alert
### 1) Acknowledge and assess
- Confirm alert is real (not a monitor glitch).
- Identify affected clusters/regions.

### 2) Stabilize
- If 5xx > 5% or timeouts are high: reduce traffic first (pause cohort ramp, throttle abusive orgs).
- If p95 is high with DB saturation: prioritize DB protection (reduce concurrency, consider rollback).

### 3) Identify top contributor
- Check traces for the slowest span type.
- Check logs for top error signature.

### 4) Apply the smallest reversible mitigation
- Prefer config toggles and rollbacks over code changes during incident.

### 5) Validate improvement
- Watch latency p95 and 5xx over 10–15 minutes.
- Confirm no new regression (e.g., 4xx spike from authz failures).

### 6) Communicate
- Update incident channel with:
  - Current status, suspected cause
  - Mitigation applied
  - Next checkpoint time

---

## Rollback / Feature Flag Procedures
### Backend deploy rollback
- Use standard deploy tooling to roll back `optimize-suggestions-service` to last known good.
- Confirm schema compatibility (no forward-only migrations).

### Console feature flag gating
- If Console traffic is the amplifier, disable Suggestions view for new cohorts first.
- Keep internal dogfood enabled if it’s needed for debugging and is low volume.

Audit expectations:
- Record org IDs enabled/disabled and reason.
- Ensure access changes are logged (especially if involving RBAC scopes).

---

## Escalation Paths
Page in this order, based on evidence:

1) **Eng Platform On-call (API owner)**
- Primary responder for API errors, deployment, caches.

2) **SRE On-call**
- If multi-service incident, gateway timeouts, cluster instability, or broad customer impact.

3) **DB On-call / Infra**
- If DB saturation, lock contention, failover, or disk/IO pressure.

4) **Telemetry/Compute owners**
- If compute lag/failure is causing API exceptions or overload (backfills).

When to declare an incident:
- User-facing 5xx > 1% sustained > 10m for multiple orgs, OR
- p95 > 2s sustained > 15m, OR
- Any suspicion of cross-tenant data risk (immediate incident + security escalation).

---

## Post-Incident Follow-ups (Required)
Within 24 hours of stabilization:
- Create a ticket with:
  - Start/end time, regions affected
  - Primary metrics (p95, 5xx, timeouts)
  - Root cause hypothesis and evidence (logs/traces/screenshots)
  - Mitigation applied and any downsides
  - Concrete prevention items (query fix, caching changes, monitor tuning)

Within 5 business days (if severity warrants):
- Write an incident review summary (or attach to ongoing reliability initiative).

---

## Appendix: Quick Commands
### cURL sanity checks (internal)
- List:
  - `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "https://api.redwood.example/optimize/suggestions?org_id=...&project_id=...&page_size=25" -v`
- Details:
  - `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "https://api.redwood.example/optimize/suggestions/$SUGGESTION_ID" -v`

What to verify:
- Server timing, status code
- Response size
- Presence of `stale_as_of` and stable `suggestion_id`

### kubectl (if applicable)
- Pods:
  - `kubectl -n optimize get pods -l app=optimize-suggestions-service`
- Recent errors:
  - `kubectl -n optimize logs deploy/optimize-suggestions-service --since=10m | grep -E "ERROR|panic|timeout"`

---

## Appendix: Known Edge Cases
- Large orgs with many routes/models can produce heavy list queries if filtering is absent.
- Certain sorts (e.g., sorting by computed savings fields) can be expensive if not indexed.
- Page token parsing errors can cascade into 5xx if not handled defensively.
- Retries from Console can amplify load; watch for sudden RPS step functions correlated with UI changes.

If any of the above is suspected, prefer mitigation via throttling + rollback, then follow up with indexing/query fixes and contract-safe caching.

[SDK call tracing and root-cause playbook]
Overview

Purpose: This playbook describes a standardized approach for instrumenting Redwood SDKs, propagating trace/correlation identifiers, and performing fast root-cause analysis when customer requests fail or show degraded latency. It consolidates client-side examples, server-side expectations, console lookup patterns, and a prioritized troubleshooting checklist.

Audience:
- SDK engineers (Python, TypeScript/Node, Java)
- Backend engineers integrating Redwood APIs
- SREs and support engineers performing customer triage

Scope and goals:
- Ensure every SDK call can be correlated to a single trace or a small set of related traces in Redwood Console.
- Define minimal headers and span attributes to set in SDKs so SREs can diagnose errors without asking customers for payloads.
- Provide a compact runbook for reproducing, isolating, and escalating issues within 30 minutes.

Quick summary (one-line): Include an idempotent correlation_id on every user request, propagate trace/span headers, sample 1% of requests with full debug traces, and attach trace IDs to errors and telemetry emitted by the SDK.

Minimum tracing contract (what SDKs must implement)
1) Correlation headers: every outgoing HTTP request from SDK must set:
   - X-Request-Id: a UUID v4 (string) representing the client request lifecycle.
   - X-Traceparent: W3C Trace Context header (if available) for interoperability.
   - X-Sdk-Client: <sdk-name>/<version> (e.g. redwood-js/1.3.0)

2) Error enrichment: when an error is raised from the SDK to the customer app, the SDK should include the X-Request-Id value and the Redwood-side trace id (if received) in the error metadata.

3) Sampling and debug payloads:
   - Default sampling: 0.01 (1% full traces) for hosted customers to control cost.
   - Force-sampled flag: SDKs expose a debug override (environment variable REDWOOD_TRACE_DEBUG=true) that forces full capture and returns a debug_trace_id in responses for triage.

Header example (HTTP):
X-Request-Id: 8a7dd3e2-6f8b-4ea9-9f0b-2a9c3e5b9f0d
X-Traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01
X-Sdk-Client: redwood-py/2.0.0

Recommended SDK implementation patterns
- Generate X-Request-Id at the top-level SDK API entry (e.g., client.generate_request_id()). Reuse it across retries and sub-requests spawned by the same logical call.
- If the host application provides a trace context (OpenTelemetry or W3C), prefer propagating that traceparent header instead of generating a new trace. Always attach X-Request-Id regardless.
- Avoid including user PII in correlation IDs or trace attributes. Use non-sensitive labels (e.g., user_hash, project_id).

Client examples
Python (requests):
```python
import uuid
import requests

def call_redwood(payload, api_key, force_debug=False):
    rid = str(uuid.uuid4())
    headers = {
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
        "X-Request-Id": rid,
        "X-Sdk-Client": "redwood-py/2.0.0"
    }
    if force_debug:
        headers["X-Redwood-Trace-Debug"] = "1"
    r = requests.post("https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate", json=payload, headers=headers, timeout=30)
    # Attach request id to exceptions for faster triage
    if r.status_code >= 500:
        raise RuntimeError(f"Redwood server error ({r.status_code}), request_id={rid}")
    return r.json(), rid
```

Node/TypeScript (fetch):
```ts
import {v4 as uuidv4} from 'uuid';

async function callRedwood(payload: object, apiKey: string, forceDebug = false) {
  const rid = uuidv4();
  const headers: Record<string, string> = {
    'Authorization': `Bearer ${apiKey}` ,
    'X-Request-Id': rid,
    'X-Sdk-Client': 'redwood-js/1.4.1'
  }
  if (forceDebug) headers['X-Redwood-Trace-Debug'] = '1'
  const resp = await fetch('https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate', {
    method: 'POST',
    body: JSON.stringify(payload),
    headers,
    // keep a short timeout at the application layer to avoid stuck clients
  })
  if (!resp.ok && resp.status >= 500) {
    throw new Error(`Redwood server error (${resp.status}), request_id=${rid}`)
  }
  const body = await resp.json();
  return {body, request_id: rid};
}
```

Server-side expectations (Redwood runtime)
- If incoming request includes X-Request-Id, the runtime must use it as the root-correlation-id for logs, traces, and KV-caches for that request.
- The runtime will return the header X-Redwood-Trace-Id when a full trace was captured for the request. SDKs should surface that id in error payloads.
- Runtime will also echo back X-Request-Id when present to verify propagation.

Common triage flow (30-minute runbook)
1) Gather artifacts: customer request time, X-Request-Id (or approximate timestamp), sample customer payload (if allowed), SDK name/version, region.
2) Search Console: filter by X-Request-Id or time window (+/- 2 minutes). If present, open the trace. Check service span latencies, kernel queue time, and tail token generation time.
3) If no trace found: verify if customer had client-side sampling or wrong header (common root cause). Ask customer to resend with REDWOOD_TRACE_DEBUG=true to force a debug trace.
4) If trace found and error is 5xx: inspect backend service spans in trace for exceptions and logs. Correlate with runtime logs (owner: serving-runtime team).
5) If high latency but no 5xx: check batching layer span and KV cache hit rate; correlate with GPU utilization from gpu-fleet-and-capacity dashboard.
6) Escalate: if issue is reproducible and affects Dedicated/Private customers or violates SLOs, open an Incident and notify eng-sre and serving-runtime on-call. Attach trace ids and representative payload.

Priority lookup table
| Artifact | Where to look | Owner | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---|
| X-Request-Id | Redwood Console / request traces | SRE / support | Best single key for cross-system lookup |
| X-Redwood-Trace-Id | Trace view | Serving runtime | Indicates full capture; include in bug reports |
| SDK logs | Customer app logs | Customer / SDK-team | Ask for SDK debug logs with correlation id |
| GPU metrics | Grafana (gpu-fleet) | Infra / capacity | Helps diagnose batching/backpressure |

Canonical fixes and known patterns
- Symptom: No trace in Console but customer reports error. Cause: client stripped headers (proxies or CORS) or client used custom HTTP client without propagation. Fix: document header requirements in integration guide and add SDK instrumentation tests that assert header presence.
- Symptom: High 95th token latency. Cause: large request sequences hitting longer attention kernels or cache misses. Fix: include request size metrics and advise quantized model variants or lower max_tokens.
- Symptom: Intermittent 502/503. Cause: transient scaling/queue drains. Fix: implement exponential backoff with full jitter in SDKs (recommended default: initial=50ms, max=2s, max_retries=5).

Telemetry and logs to collect when filing a support ticket
- Timestamp (UTC), X-Request-Id, SDK name/version, region, sample payload (if customer consents), client-side logs (including stack traces), any returned X-Redwood-Trace-Id.

Debugging checklist for SDK authors (pre-release)
1) Unit tests assert X-Request-Id exists and is stable across retries.
2) Integration tests using a local proxy record all outgoing headers.
3) Optional e2e test that flips REDWOOD_TRACE_DEBUG=true and asserts the runtime returns X-Redwood-Trace-Id.
4) Add metrics emitted by the SDK for: requests_total, requests_errors_total (label: status_code), request_latency_seconds (histogram).

Escalation and ownership
- Primary owner: eng-developer-experience (SDK telemetry workstream)
- On-call for runtime tracing: eng-serving-runtime on-call (see runbooks/trace-oncall).
- Severity mapping:
  - Sev-1: Reproducible data-loss or SLO breach for Dedicated customer — immediate incident.
  - Sev-2: Widespread >=10% error rate increase for hosted customers — paged to eng-sre.
  - Sev-3: Single-customer sporadic errors — support ticket and scheduled follow-up.

Appendix A: Example support ticket template (copy/paste)
Subject: [Support] Request tracing artifacts for customer <customer-name> – request_id=<X-Request-Id>
Body:
- Time (UTC):
- Region:
- SDK: (name/version)
- X-Request-Id:
- X-Redwood-Trace-Id (if present):
- Sample payload (redacted if necessary):
- Customer logs attached: yes/no
- Screenshots of Console trace: yes/no

Appendix B: Reference commands
- curl example to include headers:
  curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -H "X-Request-Id: $(uuidgen)" -H "X-Redwood-Trace-Debug: 1" -d '{"prompt":"hi"}' https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate

- Small grep to find request_id in logs (SRE):
  rg "8a7dd3e2-6f8b" /var/log/redwood/ -n || true

Appendix C: FAQ
Q: What if a customer cannot share payloads?
A: Request only the minimal redacted payload necessary to reproduce (e.g., token counts, sequence length, prompt shape). Ask them to enable REDWOOD_TRACE_DEBUG for a time window; debug traces are sampled and limited to triage windows.

Q: Is X-Request-Id globally unique across retries?
A: Yes — keep the same id for retries of the same logical call to simplify dedup and tracing.

- Runtime tracing runbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/trace-oncall
- Support triage playbook: /confluence/customer-success-and-support/support-process/triage-playbook

[Progressive Telemetry Degradation and Recovery Contract]
Overview
========

This document defines a standardized contract for progressive telemetry degradation and automated recovery across Redwood Inference services. The goal is to preserve essential SLI evidence and incident detection capability while gracefully reducing telemetry volume and cost when ingestion budgets, downstream backpressure, or operational emergency conditions require it. The contract specifies: ownership, staged degradation levels, metric and trace priority tiers, safe minimum telemetry sets, implementation patterns, recovery and verification steps, and testing/rollback guidance.

Why this exists
---------------

- Telemetry ingestion and retention costs can grow non-linearly under heavy traffic and degraded runtime conditions.
- Naive bulk sampling or blanket retention drops can remove signals needed to detect and triage outages or correctness regressions.
- Operators need predictable behavior: when and how telemetry will be reduced, who is responsible, and how the system will restore full instrumentation.

Scope and applicability
----------------------

Applies to: all production services that emit metrics, traces, and prompt telemetry into Redwood’s central telemetry pipeline (metric names: redwood.*; traces prefixed redwood-trace). This includes hosting plane services, runtime shards, ingress proxies, and the console. This contract does not change data classification or PII handling — those remain under security-and-compliance policies.

Terminology
-----------

- Degradation Event: a condition that triggers telemetry reduction (examples: ingestion backlog > 90% for 10m, telemetry budget burn rate > 120% daily projection, or dependent system outage).
- Degradation Level (L1..L4): predefined tiers describing how aggressively telemetry is reduced. L1 = mild reduction; L4 = emergency minimal set.
- Safe Minimum Set (SMS): the smallest set of telemetry required for incident detection and SLO evidence.
- Telemetry Fence: per-service configuration that defines what can be disabled at each degradation level.

Contract Principles
-------------------

1) Predictability: every service must expose a telemetry-fence config (YAML) that maps degradation levels to actions.
2) Prioritization: telemetry is tiered into Priority A/B/C where A = critical SLO SLIs, B = supporting metrics/traces, C = high-cardinality debugging signals.
3) Conservatism: never drop Priority A signals. Priority B may be sampled. Priority C may be fully turned off at L3+.
4) Safety-first rollbacks: any automated degradation must be reversible and accompanied by health checks that ensure incident detectability hasn’t been lost.
5) Auditability: every change in degradation state must be recorded as an event (redwood.telemetry.degradation_event) with reason, trigger, and operator identity/idempotency token.

Degradation levels and actions (reference)
----------------------------------------

- L0 (Normal): no change. Full telemetry per service defaults.
- L1 (Constrained ingestion): apply adaptive sampling to Priority C and non-essential debug logs; enable batching of events; delay low-importance retention flushes by up to 1 hour.
- L2 (Sustained budget overrun): sample Priority B at 25% and Priority C at 5%; reduce trace span details (keep parent/child but drop heavy tags); truncate or compress large text fields (prompt bodies).
- L3 (Severe pressure): disable Priority C metrics and traces; emit synthesized summary metrics (e.g., p50/p99) instead of full histograms; collapse multi-line logs into single-line headers.
- L4 (Emergency minimal): SMS only. Streamlined set: all Priority A metrics, one representative trace per 60s per service (trace sampling key: redwood.sampling.l4), and aggregated prompt-rate counters (no prompt text).

Safe Minimum Set (SMS) - example
-------------------------------

The SMS for any inference-facing runtime should include: 

- redwood.slo.latency.p50, redwood.slo.latency.p95, redwood.slo.error_rate
- redwood.capacity.available_gpus and redwood.capacity.pending_requests
- redwood.runtime.queue_depth_per_shard
- redwood.telemetry.degradation_state (current L0..L4)
- A single sampled trace per minute containing top-level timing and error tags, per runtime shard
- Aggregated prompt throughput counters: redwood.prompt.requests.total, redwood.prompt.requests.failed

Configuration schema (example YAML)
----------------------------------

services:
  - name: inference-runtime
    owner: eng-serving-runtime
    telemetry_fence:
      default_level: L0
      thresholds:
        ingestion_backlog_percent: 90
        budget_burn_rate_percent: 120
      levels:
        L1:
          sample: 
            priority_b: 80  # keep 80% of B
            priority_c: 20  # keep 20% of C
        L2:
          sample:
            priority_b: 25
            priority_c: 5
        L3:
          disable: ["priority_c"]
        L4:
          sms_only: true

Operator event schema (JSON example)
-----------------------------------

{
  "event_type": "redwood.telemetry.degradation_event",
  "service": "inference-runtime",
  "level": "L3",
  "reason": "ingestion_backlog_percent > 95 for 12m",
  "triggered_by": "autoscaler-policy:ingest-shed-v2",
  "operator_id": "ops-team-rotation-3",
  "timestamp": "2026-05-12T10:04:23Z"
}

Implementation guidance
-----------------------

1) Each service must implement a TelemetryFence component that:
   - reads per-service fence YAML from config-store (S3/consul/parameter-store),
   - exposes an HTTP admin endpoint (/admin/telemetry_state) to report current level and event history,
   - integrates with the central telemetry controller (see below) to receive commands and report audit events.

2) Local enforcement should be as close to the emission point as possible (e.g., SDK instrumentation layer inside runtime binary rather than a sidecar) to avoid excess CPU/networking overhead.

3) Use prioritized sampling for traces: implement deterministic, sticky sampling keyed by service:shard:request_id to maintain follow-up ability. Sampling keys should be reversible to add targeted replays in controlled environments.

Central controller responsibilities
----------------------------------

- Evaluate triggers: ingestion queue backlog, billing burn rate projections, downstream availability signals.
- Compute recommended global degradation level and reconcile per-service fence constraints (do not recommend L4 to services marked as "restricted-sms" without operator override).
- Publish decisions on the event bus and to the audit index.
- Provide a read-only dashboard and API for SRE/owners to approve immediate escalations or rollbacks.

Recovery and verification steps
------------------------------

When a degradation event clears (triggers no longer met):

1) Controller issues a staged rollback to L0 across affected services: L4 -> L2 -> L1 -> L0 with minimum stabilization windows (default: 2m between steps).
2) Each service must execute readiness checks after each step: ensure metric emission for a canonical Priority A metric and at least one sampled trace within 2 minutes.
3) Controller verifies ingestion backlog and budget projection for a stabilization period (default 10m) before issuing the next step.
4) If any service fails a readiness check, controller pauses rollback and notifies owners with remediation steps.

Dashboards and alerts
---------------------

Minimum dashboards every service owner must maintain: 

- Telemetry budget burn vs projection (90/95/100% thresholds)
- Degradation state timeline with event drill-down
- SMS health panel: shows presence/absence of Priority A metrics and their last emission timestamp

Alert rules (examples):

- FIRE: telemetry.ingest.backlog.percent > 95% for 10m -> page oncall + escalate to eng-infra 2nd
- WARN: redwood.telemetry.degradation_state != L0 && any Priority A metric missing for 5m -> slack notify owners

Testing and runbook exercises
----------------------------

- Every service must include unit tests that validate fence config parsing and admin endpoints.
- Create a synthetic traffic test that simulates ingestion-backlog triggers to validate L1..L4 transition behavior in staging before any production rollout.
- Conduct annual "telemetry game day" where SREs and owners practice degrading and recovering one major subsystem. Document outcomes and update fences.

Privacy and security considerations
----------------------------------

- SMS must never include user prompt text or full request bodies unless explicitly allowed by data classification and with appropriate retention exemptions.
- All degradation_event audit records are retained for 90 days in the audit index and surfaced to security for forensic requests.

Ownership and responsibilities
------------------------------

- Service Owners: maintain telemetry_fence config, own SMS definition, respond to degradation events.
- SRE/Platform: operate the central controller, maintain dashboards and alerting templates, run game days.
- Security: review any service-level exemptions that allow SMS to include higher-sensitivity fields.

Rollout checklist
-----------------

1) Add telemetry_fence YAML to config-store for each service.
2) Implement TelemetryFence admin endpoint and test locally.
3) Register service with central controller and run end-to-end staging simulation.
4) Publish dashboards and alert rules.
5) Schedule a canary rollout (10% of traffic) with manual approval gates.

Appendix: Example client-side pseudocode (sampling)
-------------------------------------------------

// pseudocode - deterministic sticky sampling
function shouldSample(service, shard, requestId, priority, level) {
  if (priority == 'A') return true
  if (level == 'L4') return false
  key = hash(service + ':' + shard + ':' + requestId) % 100
  threshold = config.sampleThreshold[priority][level] // e.g. 5, 25, 80
  return key < threshold
}

References
----------

- Telemetry budget and enrichment playbook: /confluence/architecture-and-standards/observability-standards/telemetry-budget-enrichment-playbook-2026
- Incident runbook template: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/runbooks/incident-process
- Data classification policy: /confluence/security-and-compliance/data-residency-and-retention

Change log
----------

- 2026-02-15: Initial published draft (Asha Patel)
- 2026-03-18: Added deterministic sampling pseudocode and SMS examples (Liam O'Connor)
- 2026-05-12: Updated recovery stabilization windows and audit retention (Marta Gomez)


[Operator Simulation Syllabus and Skill Validation Catalog]
Summary

This page defines a repeatable syllabus for platform operator simulations, a catalog of hands‑on labs, and a structured skill validation rubric. The goal is to make oncall readiness measurable and repeatable across teams that operate Redwood’s inference platform. This document is intended for platform operators, platform SREs, and engineers who run or observe incident simulations.

Goals

- Provide a modular curriculum for running platform incident simulations (gamedays) with measurable learning outcomes.
- Teach observable runbook execution, triage discipline, and safe mitigation patterns for LLM inference services.
- Produce a canonical set of lab exercises operators can run locally or in the sandbox fleet.
- Provide an assessment rubric and a retro template so teams can measure improvement over time.

Audience

- Platform operators, site reliability engineers, platform QA, and junior engineers preparing for oncall rotations.

Prerequisites

- Familiarity with platform observability (Prometheus/Tempo/Tracing, internal dashboards).
- Access to the operator sandbox namespace (ask Platform Lab: self‑serve access).
- Basic familiarity with CLI tools: redwoodctl, kubectl, and the internal operator UI.

Curriculum Overview (Modules)

1) Fundamentals: Observability & Mental Models (1 session, 2 hours)
   - Learning objectives: read SLO dashboards, interpret per‑tenant token cost graphs, and map alerts to potential root causes.
   - Topics: SLI taxonomy, token‑cost attribution, KV cache heatmaps, request path call graphs.

2) Controlled Degradation: Prefetch / KV Cache Failure (2 sessions, 3 hours)
   - Learning objectives: identify cache miss storms, run the cache‑drain runbook, and test graceful prefetch fallback.
   - Lab: simulate KV cache shard offline, force synthetic prefix churn, verify fallback to warmset and measure tail latency.

3) Capacity Scarcity: Tenant Eviction and Fairness (2 sessions, 3 hours)
   - Learning objectives: apply eviction thresholds, reconcile tenant credits, and run emergency buydown.
   - Lab: trigger a tenant burst, use the eviction simulator to claim capacity, and execute soft‑eviction.

4) Model Variant Fallback and Quality Regression (2 sessions, 3 hours)
   - Learning objectives: switch model variant rollout safely, validate regression tests, confirm fallback policy works under overload.
   - Lab: flip traffic using canary DSL, validate evaluation prompts, and observe degradation alerts.

5) Multi‑Region Failover and Routing (2 sessions, 3 hours)
   - Learning objectives: verify regional routing policies, practice cross‑region failover, and observe cache warmup costs.
   - Lab: simulate regional partition and run operator‑guided failover.

6) Post‑incident Communication & Retro (1 session, 90 minutes)
   - Learning objectives: run a concise retro using the Incident Hypothesis Canvas, assign remediation actions, and update runbooks/dashboards.

Lab Catalog (practical exercises you can run in the sandbox)

Each lab includes: objective, setup commands, verification checks, rollback.

A) KV Cache Shard Failover (sandbox)
- Objective: validate graceful KV shard handoff and prefix cache rehydration.
- Setup:
  1. Mark node: redwoodctl node taint cache-shard-3 NoSchedule --reason=simulate-failure
  2. Trigger eviction: redwoodctl simulate cache-shard-failure --shard=3 --duration=600s
- Verification:
  - Dashboard: prefix_cache_miss_rate (should spike then converge)
  - Check: curl -sS 'https://sandbox-op/health/prefix-cache' | jq .status
- Rollback:
  - redwoodctl node untaint cache-shard-3
  - Confirm prefix cache steady state in 2–5 minutes

B) Emergency Model Swap (canary then rollback)
- Objective: run a safe model swap when a larger model is causing token cost regressions.
- Setup:
  1. Open canary: redwoodctl canary start --route=model-gen --variant=smaller-quantized:v2
  2. Apply traffic weight: redwoodctl canary set-weight --id=1234 --percent=10
- Verification:
  - Latency SLO: p95 < 1600ms for canary traffic
  - Quality: run 20 eval prompts: redwood-eval run --canary 1234 --suite=smoke-qa
- Rollback:
  - redwoodctl canary abort --id=1234

C) Tenant Burst Eviction Play (operator simulator)
- Objective: practice decision canvas for fair share and tenant buydown.
- Steps:
  1. Launch synthetic load: redwoodctl loadgen start --tenant=synthetic-burster --rps=1200 --tokens=10k
  2. Monitor: tenant_token_consumption_total by tenant
  3. Run eviction: redwoodctl tenant eviction --tenant=synthetic-burster --policy=soft
- Verification: eviction reduces q-length and token burn within 90s

Assessment Rubric (skills to validate during or after a simulation)

- Triage speed: 0–15m (A), 15–30m (B), 30–60m (C), >60m (D)
- Correct diagnosis: root cause identified (yes/no)
- Runbook fidelity: followed documented steps (yes/partial/no)
- Safe mitigation: used non‑destructive fallback first (yes/partial/no)
- Communication: clear status updates every 10–15 minutes (yes/partial/no)
- Postmortem: action items created with owners and due dates (yes/no)

Scoring guidance: A = majority A grades and yes for critical items; simulation certification requires A or B overall.

Runbook & Dashboard Mapping

Use this quick mapping to pick which runbook and dashboards to include in a sim: 

| Scenario | Primary runbook | Dashboards to show | Minimum alert set | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| KV cache failure | cache-drain-and-rebuild-runbook | prefix_cache_miss_rate, cache_rehydration_time, tail_latency | cache_miss_spike > 5x | Cache team |
| Tenant burst | tenant-eviction-and-soft-buydown | tenant_token_consumption_total, queue_length_by_tenant | tenant_token_rate > threshold | Capacity team |
| Model variant regression | model-variant-fallback-runbook | per_variant_latency, eval-passrate | eval_regression_alert | ML infra |
| Regional partition | regional-failover-runbook | cross_region_p95, interregion_rtt | region_health_down | Network infra |

Alerting playbook (during a simulation)

1) Acknowledge alerts and set incident channel: /incident create "Sim: <scenario>" --visibility=private
2) Assign roles: Incident Lead, Triage, Mitigation, Communications.
3) Run triage checklist (5 items):
   a) Confirm symptoms on dashboards
   b) Confirm affected tenants/services
   c) Check for correlated deployments or infra changes
   d) Identify immediate mitigations (fallbacks/evictions/circuit-breakers)
   e) Execute non‑destructive mitigation first
4) Track timeline in the incident channel and log operator commands used.

Retro template (one page summary to paste into postmortem)

- Title: [Sim] <scenario> — <date>
- Participants: 
- Timeline (bullet list with timestamps)
- What went well (3 bullets)
- What to improve (3 bullets)
- Action items (table):
  - Action | Owner | Due date | Status
  - e.g. "Add dashboard to show per‑canary eval passrate" | Marco Li | 2026-02-01 | open

Sandbox safety rules

- Simulations must use the sandbox or designated synthetic tenants. Do not run destructive operations against production.
- If a safe window in canary overlaps production routes, reduce traffic weights to <= 5% and notify the SRE rotation lead.
- All simulations must be scheduled on the platform lab calendar and have an observer from the platform ops team.

Implementation roadmap (next 12 months)

- Q2 2026: Add automated scoring harness that parses incident channel logs and assigns rubric grades (MVP).
- Q3 2026: Expand lab catalog with thermal/spot instance simulations.
- Q4 2026: Integrate skill validation into new‑hire platform onboarding and certify 90% of new oncall engineers.
- Q1 2027: Publish an anonymized simulation results dashboard for leadership and training insights.

Ownership and maintenance

- Document owner: Platform Training (team alias: platform-lab@redwood.com)
- Quarterly review cadence: Platform Training + Eng Platform (quarterly)
- Update policy: update module content after each public simulation with actionable retro items.

Related resources

- Operator runbook writing guide: /confluence/eng-platform/how-tos/runbook-authoring-and-maintenance-guidelines-2025
- Simulation automation playbook: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/platform-gameday-exercise-automation-and-scripting-playbook-2026
- Incident Hypothesis Canvas template: /confluence/templates/incident-hypothesis-canvas

Appendix: Quick CLI cheatsheet

- Open sandbox node taint: redwoodctl node taint <node> NoSchedule --reason="simulate-failure"
- Start canary: redwoodctl canary start --route=<route> --variant=<variant>
- Start loadgen: redwoodctl loadgen start --tenant=<id> --rps=<n>

If you have questions or want to run a bespoke simulation for your team, ping platform-lab@redwood.com and include a brief objective and preferred week.

[Non-ASCII attachment filename charset normalization causes checksum/idempotency mismatch and duplicate function invocations]
description:
Issue summary:
Customer observes duplicate downstream tool/function executions when uploading attachments with non-ASCII filenames (accented characters, composed vs decomposed forms).

Impact:
- Customer reported multiple duplicate webhook/tool invocations for the same user action, causing double-processing in their pipeline and billing spikes.
- Occurred intermittently when clients used different SDKs (Python + Go) or when requests passed through an edge proxy.

Environment:
- Customer uses Dedicated capacity in us-east.
- SDKs: python-sdk v1.8.2, go-sdk v0.9.7.
- Ingress: fast-edge-proxy v2.2 (company-managed), Redwood API gateway.

Steps to reproduce (reported by customer):
1) Use python-sdk to start a streaming request that includes an attachment metadata field filename="résumé.pdf" (UTF-8 composed NFC).
2) SDK computes attachment-checksum header (X-RW-Attach-Checksum) over the filename+payload and sets Idempotency-Key derived from that checksum.
3) A downstream proxy normalizes the Content-Disposition filename to NFD decomposition when rewriting headers.
4) The go-sdk client later retries the same logical request but computes a checksum over a deconstructed filename (NFD) producing a different checksum.
5) Server treats the second request as distinct and re-invokes tool/webhook, causing duplicate side effects.

Observed logs/snippets (customer-provided):
- Request A (python): Idempotency-Key: rw-ck-0a1b2c3d, X-RW-Attach-Checksum: sha1:9f7a4e
- Request B (via proxy, go retry): Idempotency-Key: rw-ck-1d2c3b4a, X-RW-Attach-Checksum: sha1:2b4e9a
- Gateway trace: header-rewrite: filename normalizer applied: decomposed_form=true

Why this is likely happening (initial hypothesis):
- Different SDKs and intermediaries compute hashes over raw bytes of the filename/payload without applying a canonical Unicode normalization form.
- Some proxies or client environments (macOS vs Linux) canonicalize filenames differently (NFC vs NFD), so the checksum and derived idempotency key diverge even though the human-visible filename is identical.

Customer-provided business impact: "Two or three duplicate order events per upload during peak hours; we had to pause processing queues to avoid double fulfillment."

investigation_notes:
Repro notes: Created two clients producing different checksums based solely on Unicode normalization of filename. Hash function is SHA-1 truncated first 6 bytes in current SDK codepath (historical for space constraints).
Root cause hypothesis: Non-canonicalized filename bytes in checksum calculation + intermediary header rewrite/normalization cause mismatched idempotency-key derivation across retries and SDKs.
Why truncation matters: The 6-byte truncation increases collision surface in edge cases; with normalization differences the resulting truncated digest often differs even when full digest similarity would be apparent.
Gateway behavior: fast-edge-proxy rewrites Content-Disposition and normalizes to NFD for legacy compatibility with file-systems; gateway does not currently normalize X-RW-Attach-Checksum header values and relies on clients to match exact bytes.
Security/compatibility note: Changing server-side to accept canonicalized variants must preserve resistance to replay/fraud; avoid loosening verification without stronger checks (e.g., full-hash or signed metadata).

resolution:
Workaround implemented (customer): Set explicit Idempotency-Key at application layer when sending uploads (recommended pattern). This bypasses checksum-derived keys until SDK/gateway fixes land.

Engineering fixes in progress:
- SDKs: python-sdk and go-sdk will normalize filename metadata using NFC before computing attachment checksum and idempotency derivation. PRs created: sdk-python#4123, sdk-go#198.
- Gateway: Added optional header compare that normalizes filename metadata server-side and compares normalized hashes to accept equivalent uploads during rollout (gateway PR #87). Gateway change will not disable strict mode; strict mode remains default.
- Long-term: Remove SHA-1 truncation from idempotency derivation and switch to full SHA-256 base64 token for deterministic idempotency values. Requires client+server rollout coordination.

Post-deploy actions:
- Notify customers of SDK updates and encourage explicit Idempotency-Key usage for critical operations until rollout is complete.
- Add a runbook entry describing how to triage normalization-related duplicate invocations (linked in related_confluence_pages).

Status: Patch PRs in review. Hotfix for gateway accepted behind feature flag; currently testing in staging. Customer confirmed temporary workaround stopped duplicates in observed window.

[Edge HTTP/3 idempotency token fragmentation causing duplicate tool invocations from TS streaming clients]
description:
Issue summary:
Customers using the TS streaming SDK over HTTP/3 through our edge network are observing duplicate external tool/webhook invocations when a request is retried. The duplicates correlate with very long idempotency tokens (generated by the customer) that exceed typical header frame sizes and appear to be fragmented across QUIC frames. Edge proxies sometimes normalize reassembled headers differently on retry paths, leading to the server treating retried requests as new (no idempotency match).

Impact:
- OmniPay reports duplicate payment-notification webhook posts from their orchestration service; duplicates observed ~1-3% of streaming retries in eu-west.
- Potential revenue/customer trust impact; duplicates trigger downstream compensating transactions.

Environment:
- Hosted Redwood API (edge-enabled HTTP/3), prod, eu-west
- TS SDK v1.9.2 with streaming resume/reconnect enabled
- Customer uses long base64-encoded idempotency keys (~420 chars) generated by their orchestration layer

Observed behavior:
- Client sends stream, connection interruption causes SDK reconnect with resume token and retry.
- Edge receives retry but QUIC frame fragmentation causes the idempotency header to be split; after internal reassembly the header string differs (insertion of padding or percent-decoding in path through sidecar).
- Serving runtime does not match previous idempotency record; tool/function calls (webhook posts) are executed again.

Expected behavior:
- Retries that include the same idempotency key should be deduplicated and not cause re-execution of external tool calls when the original attempt succeeded or was in-flight.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Use TS SDK v1.9.2 streaming client pointed at api.redwood.ai over HTTP/3.
2) Provide a long base64 idempotency key (> 380 chars) in x-redwood-idempotency header.
3) Begin a streaming request that triggers a tool/function call (webhook) mid-stream.
4) Simulate a connection interruption (network drop) and allow the SDK to reconnect/resume.
5) Observe webhook endpoint receiving duplicate POSTs for same logical action.

Notes: reproduces reliably when client and edge sidecar MTU/fragment behavior forces header to be split across QUIC frames. Short keys (< 120 chars) do not reproduce.

logs:
- edge-proxy trace: edge-trace=et-20260310-7b4a; request_id=rq-8f3c; header-length=428
- serving-runtime: TRACE:rq-8f3c idempotency_lookup miss (normalized_key=z2F... vs original z2F... padding mismatch)
- webhook logs (customer): webhook_id=wh-1122 timestamp=2026-03-10T15:22:33Z status=200; webhook_id=wh-1122 timestamp=2026-03-10T15:22:41Z status=200 (duplicate)
- pcap attached to internal S3: s3://redwood-internal/pcaps/SUP-975310/quic-frag-2026-03-10.pcap
- Related edge proxy log snippet: "POST /v1/stream 200 idempotency: received-length=428 reassembled-length=430 norm-key=..."

investigation:
Initial triage (Support): confirmed duplicates only when idempotency header length > ~360 chars and when HTTP/3 path used. Customer reproduced with network simulation.
SRE/Edge team checked edge-proxy code path: we discovered an intermediate sidecar (third-party L7) performing percent-decoding of header fragments when reassembling QUIC frames; that decoder will sometimes insert '=' padding characters when fragments align differently on retry. This produces a different canonical idempotency token string.
TS SDK team confirmed that v1.9.2 will automatically attempt resume with the same header value but will resend headers in a new packet set; edge reassembly path difference explains divergence.
We correlated request ids and webhook timestamps; serving runtime records show idempotency store entries keyed by normalized string, so token mismatch leads to new execution.
Interim workaround tested: customer changed idempotency key generation to a short hex digest (64 chars) and duplicates stopped.
Further findings: PR proposed to edge-proxy to canonicalize header values before forwarding (github.com/redwood-inference/edge-proxy/pull/489). A smaller SDK patch to add client-side canonicalization/trim policy is in review (github.com/redwood-inference/ts-sdk/pull/1220).

resolution:
Workaround implemented for customer: advise customers to use <=128 char canonical idempotency keys (hex or SHA256 truncated) until a permanent fix is rolled out. OmniPay applied the temporary change and verified zero duplicates for 48 hours.
Planned permanent fixes:
- Short-term (~72h): edge-proxy hotfix to normalize base64 headers during QUIC reassembly (PR #489 under review).
- Medium-term: TS SDK change to apply a canonicalization and max-length warning at key creation time; publish docs guidance (PR #1220).
- Long-term: add server-side tolerant idempotency matching (hash and canonical fallback) to avoid strict string equality.
Follow-ups: monitor eu-west metrics and roll edge-proxy fix to other regions after validation.
Status: in progress; ETA for edge hotfix 2026-03-14, SDK release v1.9.3 ETA 2026-03-16.

2026-03-10 16:40 - SRE (Anika Bose): Captured quic pcap and saw header fragments; forwarding to edge-proxy owner. Linked pcap to ticket.
2026-03-10 18:12 - Edge Eng (Miguel Torres): Confirmed third-party sidecar percent-decodes fragments differently on reassembly. Proposed normalization fix. Assigned to Miguel for hotfix.
