[Idempotency token re-encoding after HTTP/2->HTTP/1.1 downgrade causes duplicated funcall callbacks]
description:
Customer reports duplicate downstream tool/webhook executions after an intermittent network hiccup. ClearSight observed two identical webhook POSTs for the same funcall within ~10s, despite supplying an idempotency token. The pattern only occurs when requests traverse our edge proxy path that performs HTTP/2 <-> HTTP/1.1 translation (edge-side connection downgrade).

customer_message:
We saw duplicate webhook invocations for the same function call when our clients hit the Redwood endpoint through our CDN-backed edge. This started after a bandwidth spike in their region. We consistently send X-Idempotency-Key header and only expect one webhook per funcall. Can you advise why the dedup didn't work?

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Use Go or Python SDK to initiate a streaming funcall with header X-Idempotency-Key: A1+b/9==token (base64-like with plus and slash)
2) Route traffic through the edge proxy configured to terminate HTTP/2 and proxy to origin over HTTP/1.1 (typical CDN config)
3) Simulate a transient connection reset on the edge (e.g., terminate upstream connection mid-stream) so client retries using SDK exponential backoff
4) Observe downstream webhook receiver logs for duplicated POSTs for the same logical funcall id within rollback window (~30s)
5) Capture raw request headers at edge and origin and compare X-Idempotency-Key values

logs:
edge capture (raw): X-Idempotency-Key: A1+b/9==token
origin capture (after downgrade): X-Idempotency-Key: A1%2Bb%2F9%3D%3Dtoken
downstream webhook received (first): id=fn-98321 payload=... ack=200
downstream webhook received (second, ~7s later): id=fn-98321 payload=... ack=200
sdk debug (go): retry attempt=2 replacing connection, idempotency_header_sent=A1+b/9==token
sdk debug (python): retry attempt=1 header_transport=%22A1%2Bb%2F9%3D%3Dtoken%22 (note: URL-encoding observed)
nginx-ingress log: proxy_protocol backend chunked transfer applied; header rewrite enabled: true

investigation_notes:
Initial hypothesis: dedup table keys differ because edge rewrites/percent-encodes special characters (+, /, =) when downgrading HTTP/2 to HTTP/1.1 or when manipulating header frames.
Confirmed with packet captures: clients send raw token (plus/slash/equals). Edge transforms token to percent-encoded representation when converting header from HTTP/2 pseudo-headers frame to HTTP/1.1 header string in the upstream request.
Go SDK sends header as-is; Python SDK underlying requests library appears to quote/encode header intermittently when connection pooling is torn down mid-stream and a new connection starts over HTTP/1.1 path.
Serving runtime dedup key normalization expects canonical token (raw bytes) and currently treats percent-encoded and raw string as different keys which bypasses dedup check.
Edge configuration has a legacy flag 'encode_non_ascii_headers' set to true for historical infra compatibility; this flag appears to be the culprit for token mutation.
Reproduced locally by toggling edge flag: with encoding flag ON, origin sees percent-encoded token and duplicates observed; flag OFF origin sees raw token and dedup works as expected.

actions_taken:
Scoped to dedicated customer's edge path; created INT-3321 to validate edge config change impact across tenants
Temporarily advised customer to URI-safe base64 their idempotency token (replace +/ with -_) as mitigation while we fix server-side normalization
Added logging in serving runtime to decode percent-encoded idempotency tokens to canonical form for dedup-key lookup as short-term protective measure (feature flagged)
Opened runtime PR to canonicalize idempotency header decoding and normalizing both raw and percent-encoded forms (see related PR)
Requested edge team to evaluate disabling header encoding for idempotency header or to preserve original header bytes during HTTP/2->HTTP/1.1 translations

resolution:
Workaround provided and server-side normalization feature-flag enabled for ClearSight. Pending permanent fix: runtime PR merged and scheduled for deployment in next minor (042). [Retries produce duplicate tool calls due to ephemeral nonce encoding differences across Python/TS/Go SDKs]
description:
Issue summary:
Customer reporting duplicate external tool/webhook invocations when client library retries occur mid-stream. Behavior appears only when clients are using a mix of Python and TypeScript SDKs behind an edge proxy.

Impact:
- Duplicate downstream charges for webhook recipients (MapleHealth integration).
- Partial data duplication in downstream systems; high business impact for patient-scheduling flows.
- Reproducible for customer request flows that include function/tool calling and a short lived ephemeral nonce placed in request headers.

Environment:
- MapleHealth Dedicated deployment in us-east-1.
- Redwood Dedicated pool (g5-2x), private VPC peering.
- SDK versions observed: python-sdk v2.9.1, ts-sdk v3.0.2, go-sdk not used by customer but reproduced by Support.

Steps to reproduce (customer provided):
1) Create a streaming chat session that requests a tool/webhook call (function_call).
2) The client attaches X-Redwood-Nonce header generated by local session code (ephemeral 24-byte nonce, base64 encoded).
3) Trigger a simulated network hiccup: client network drops and reconnects, SDK retry logic replays in-flight events.
4) Downstream observes duplicate webhook POSTs (same payload, different Redwood request IDs).

Observed behavior:
- When the request is retried by TS SDK the nonce header is URL-encoded by the edge-sidecar (plus EOL normalization). Python client sends a raw base64 string. Edge proxy normalizes whitespace/EOL resulting in two different canonical header values across paths; our idempotency normalization path treats them as distinct, so server-side dedupe fails.

Expected behavior:
- Header canonicalization should be consistent across SDKs and proxies such that retries referencing the same logical nonce are deduplicated and tool calls are not duplicated.

Logs & artifacts attached:
- Customer captured request traces (request IDs): r-20260310-82A, r-20260310-82B
- Edge proxy config dump and header rewrite rules (anonymized) attached to ticket.
- Minimal repro scripts from Support for Python and TS included in comments.

Workaround (customer):
- Customer temporarily added a server-side dedupe that hashes normalized JSON body + timestamp window (not ideal).
- Suggested temporary mitigation: client-side avoid mixing SDKs for same session or ensure nonce encoding canonicalization (URL-safe base64) on all clients.

Requested outcome:
- Guidance on canonical nonce encoding and recommended header normalization rules for SDKs and edge proxies.
- Bugfix or doc update to prevent future interop duplicates.

comments:
2026-03-10 09:22 - Aisha Kumar: Filed on behalf of MapleHealth. Provided initial traces and edge proxy rewrite config. Customer reports duplicate webhook POSTs correlated to retry events.
2026-03-10 11:05 - Support Engineer (Aisha): Reproduced locally with python-sdk v2.9.1 against edge-sidecar v1.14. Noticed base64 vs url-safe base64 differences after proxy rewrite. Opening investigation with SDK and edge teams. CC @#support @#edge-proxy.
2026-03-10 14:30 - Customer (MapleHealth SRE, Jonah Lee): We can confirm switching TS client to url-safe base64 reduced dupes but still saw a few. Happy to share repro credentials in DM.
2026-03-11 08:45 - Diego Morales (Edge Team): Observed edge-sidecar had a header normalization feature enabled for HTTP/2->HTTP/1 translation that converts plus signs to spaces on EOL boundaries in our environment. Filing INT-2203 to track patch. Tentative root cause: EOL normalization + header canonicalization difference between SDKs leads to failing idempotency key match.
2026-03-11 10:10 - SDK Lead (Priya Shah): Confirmed python-sdk currently emits standard base64 with padding while TS SDK team adopted url-safe base64 in v3.0.x. We need an SDK compatibility note and possibly normalize encoding in client and server layer. Patch PR created: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk/pull/7890 (adds url-safe base64 helper and tests).
2026-03-12 09:00 - Diego Morales: Added replication notes: reproduced using go-sdk as well when explicitly toggling encoding to standard base64. Edge proxy rewrite rule reproduced behavior with header chunking enabled on HTTP/2.

investigation_notes:
Hypothesis 1: Nonce encoding mismatch (standard base64 vs url-safe base64) across SDKs causes different canonical header values after proxy header normalization.
Hypothesis 2: Edge proxy is performing EOL/whitespace normalization when mapping HTTP/2 header blocks to HTTP/1 downstream which corrupts '+' padding characters, turning them into spaces in certain chunk boundaries.
Reproduction steps performed by Support: run python repro that emits X-Redwood-Nonce=SGVsbG8rK3BhZGRpbmc= then pass through edge-sidecar with HTTP/2 chunk size 8192 -> observe server receives 'SGVsbG8 K3BhZGRpbmc='.
Captured pcap between client->edge shows header split across two HEADERS frames; HTTP/2->HTTP/1 translator glues back and applies linearization causing '+'->space.
Edge team confirmed config flag 'http2_strip_trailing_padding' toggles behavior. Disabling for MapleHealth eliminated observed space substitution in test env.
SDK teams agreed to document canonical nonce encoding: use url-safe base64 (RFC 4648 section 5) without padding for header tokens to reduce exposure to '+','/' and '=' transformations.
Opened PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk/pull/7890 to add helpers and interop tests across python/ts/go and to add a warning in README. Edge team preparing a patch to avoid whitespace normalization at proxy translation layer.
Linked internal ticket INT-2203 to track edge-sidecar config change and rollout to dedicated clusters.

next_steps:
Edge team to deploy config change to MapleHealth dedicated pool in a canary region and monitor for duplicate webhook counts (INT-2203).
SDK teams to land PR #7890 and cut patch releases: python-sdk v2.9.2 and ts-sdk v3.0.3 with url-safe nonce helper and compatibility notes.
Create short KB article for customers: 'Canonical nonce encoding for idempotency headers' and link in SDK docs and support runbook.
After edge patch deploy, ask MapleHealth to toggle back to mixed SDKs and validate dedupe metrics for 48h.

[Edge sidecar rewrites idempotency header into auth body during h2 connection migration, causing duplicate tool calls across SDKs]
description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports duplicated external tool/webhook invocations when their orchestration client retries after transient network errors. The pattern occurs intermittently during high sustained traffic and correlates with HTTP/2 connection migration on the edge proxy.

Impact:
- Multiple duplicate tool executions observed (pay-per-execution downstream cost).
- Customer-facing task orchestration experiences duplicate side-effects (duplicate invoices, double-posted messages).
- Affects multiple SDK languages (Python and TypeScript) in their mixed orchestration stack.

Environment:
- Customer running Redwood Dedicated in prod us-west with reserved capacity.
- SDKs: python-sdk v1.4.2, ts-sdk v2.0.1.
- Edge proxy: internal sidecar (we host) performing auth/token translation and HTTP/2 connection pooling.

Steps to reproduce (as provided):
1) Start orchestration: client opens long-running streaming session to our streaming endpoints from both Python and TS workers.
2) Client triggers model function calling that invokes downstream tool webhooks (POST to customer backend).
3) Simulate transient network interruption (brief TCP reset / container restart on client's side).
4) SDKs reconnect; requests get routed via a different HTTP/2 connection and are multiplexed through the edge sidecar.
5) Observe duplicate webhook/tool calls for the same logical operation ID within ~10s window.

Expected behavior:
- Retries should be deduplicated by idempotency key scope (per-request). A reconnection should not cause a second tool invocation if the original request may have been accepted by the serving runtime.

Actual behavior:
- Edge sidecar rewrites the idempotency header (X-Redwood-Idempotency) from the request header into an auth token blob in the request body for certain connection migration paths. When the header is rewritten into the body, our request routing treats it as missing for connection-scoped dedupe, and the retry is processed as a fresh request, causing duplicate tool invocations.

Logs / Observables:
- Customer-provided snippet from Python worker (timestamps redacted):
  - Sent: POST /v1/streams (X-Redwood-Idempotency: sess-abc-123)

logs_excerpt:
- Edge proxy log: conn_migrate: 0x7f12 -> 0x8a9b, header_promoted_to_body=true, idempotency_header_removed=true
- Serving-runtime trace: request_id=rr-90012, idempotency_key=(none) -> processed as new
- Downstream webhook receipts show two POSTs for the same operation_id within 4s

investigation_notes:
- Reproduced in internal staging by toggling connection pooling behavior on edge-proxy; when header promotion is enabled the serving runtime no longer sees X-Redwood-Idempotency.
- Python SDK and TS SDK set idempotency header correctly; the mutation occurs inside our sidecar before forwarding.
- Root cause appears to be an optimization in the edge-proxy that compresses headers into an auth blob for long-lived multiplexed h2 streams; it was intended to reduce header overhead but unintentionally changes idempotency scope detection.
- Race window: when a retry originates over a different h2 stream that the proxy promotes header->body, the server's dedupe table misses the original key because lookup expects header-scoped key.
- Cross-language note: Some SDK variants include the idempotency token in both header and initial metadata frame; others only send header. Behavior is exacerbated in mixed-language setups where one client sends header-only and the other sends header+meta.

Temporary mitigation attempted:
- Asked customer to enable client-side explicit ack confirmation flow (returning a tool_confirmation token in response) — reduced duplicates but requires app changes.
- Disabled header promotion on the edge-proxy for a subset of flows; duplication stopped for those tests.

Open questions:
- Should idempotency be canonicalized to accept keys from both header and body?
- Do we need to change SDKs to include idempotency token in both header and initial metadata frame for streaming?

customer_impact_details:
Customer reports ~0.6% of tool invocations duplicated during peak; financially material for downstream paid webhooks. Business logic duplicates (double-charges) require customer remediation and manual refunds.

comments:
Support (Aisha): Initial triage - customer reports duplicate webhooks; asked for recent request IDs, timestamps, and SDK versions.
Customer (Spellbound AI): Provided request IDs rr-90012 and rr-90046 plus edge-proxy logs and a small repro script that toggles connection pooling.
Eng (Marco): Reproduced locally by enabling header_promote flag on edge simulator; confirmed serving-runtime sees no idempotency header after rewrite.
Support (Aisha): Noted workaround to disable header promotion at edge; customer confirmed reduced duplicates in canary traffic (10k requests).
Eng (Marco): Created PR to change server dedupe to also read canonical idempotency keys from the auth blob (linked in related_github_prs).
Customer (Spellbound AI): Requests guidance for long-term fix and asks whether SDK updates are required on their side.

resolution:
Workaround applied: disabled header promotion for streaming endpoints in us-west for this customer. Permanent fix plan: update serving-runtime to extract idempotency keys from both headers and promoted auth blobs, and update edge-proxy to avoid in-place header removal for dedupe-sensitive headers.

Rollout notes:
- Hotfix: patched edge-proxy config for affected pool (completed 2026-03-11 04:12 UTC).
- Medium-term: server change in PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/edge-proxy/pull/412 to accept idempotency token from auth blob; will be canaried in staging, then deployed to prod in controlled rollout (expected 2026-03-18).

Follow-up items:
- Update SDK docs recommending inclusion of idempotency token in both header and initial metadata for streaming use-cases.
- Add automated test in CI to ensure edge-proxy header promotion does not strip dedupe headers.
- Postmortem capturing root cause and contributor mitigations scheduled once rollout completes.

[Postmortem: SEV-2 Console rollout UI bug triggered rollback loop (2026-02-22)]
summary:
A Console UI change caused repeated client-side retries on a non-idempotent rollback endpoint, putting rollouts-service into a rollback loop for a subset of deployments.

customer_impact:
Operators could not reliably pause or promote canary rollouts via Console. Some actions displayed as successful but were not applied, leading to confusion and delayed mitigations for unrelated rollouts.

timeline:
19:05 UTC: Internal user reported Console rollout controls unresponsive.
19:10 UTC: Eng on-call saw elevated 5xx and increased write QPS to rollouts-service.
19:20 UTC: Isolated to Console release 2026.02.22.2 with a new retry wrapper.
19:28 UTC: Disabled feature flag for retry wrapper in prod.
19:40 UTC: Rollouts-service write QPS returned to normal; rollback loops stopped.
19:58 UTC: Incident resolved.

root_cause:
The Console’s new retry wrapper treated 409 conflict responses as retryable and retried POST /rollback automatically. The endpoint was not idempotent and could re-trigger rollback actions.

detection:
Internal report and rollouts-service error/QPS alerts.

mitigation:
Disabled the retry wrapper via feature flag and added a server-side idempotency key requirement for rollback actions.

what_went_well:
Feature flag allowed immediate mitigation. Service-level alerts were actionable.

what_went_wrong:
The UI change was not tested against the real rollouts-service conflict behavior; endpoint idempotency was assumed but not documented.

follow_ups:
Document idempotency requirements for rollouts-service endpoints (Platform Engineering; due 2026-03-10).
Add integration tests in Console CI that simulate 409 and ensure no retries on non-idempotent endpoints (Console & Tooling; due 2026-03-15).
Introduce a standard client retry policy library with an allowlist of safe endpoints (DevEx; due 2026-04-01).

[Audit Events: Hosted Rollout Actions (Canary Workflow)]
## Overview
This document specifies the **audit log events** emitted for **Hosted canary rollout actions** in Redwood Console / Platform Control Plane. These events support:
- Customer governance and change control (who changed what, when, and why)
- Incident investigations and root cause analysis
- Compliance evidence (SOX/SOC2/ISO-style change management)
- SIEM ingestion/export with stable schemas and retention guarantees

This spec covers:
1) Event taxonomy (names, when emitted)
2) Standard event envelope fields
3) Rollout-specific fields and diff format
4) Retention and access expectations
5) SIEM export considerations
6) Examples

## Scope
### In scope
- Hosted routes canary rollout workflow actions (create/start/step/pause/resume/rollback)
- Approvals (human approval gates)
- Policy decision enforcement outcomes for rollout actions
- Auto-stop / auto-rollback actions triggered by SLO breaches
- Customer-visible activity timeline events (must be a subset/superset mapping to audit events)

### Out of scope
- Full request-level data plane logs (handled by telemetry and tracing)
- Model output content, prompts, customer payloads (explicitly excluded)

## Event naming and versioning
### Naming convention
Audit event types use the prefix:
- `rollout.*` for rollout lifecycle
- `rollout.approval.*` for approval gates
- `rollout.policy.*` for policy enforcement decisions
- `rollout.autostop.*` for automatic actions based on SLO/health

### Event versioning
- Field schema changes are tracked with `event_version` (string).
- Backward-compatible additions do not require version bump.
- Removals/renames or semantic changes require a version bump.

Current version for this document: **`event_version = "2025-05-06"`**

## Event emission rules
### When to emit
Emit an audit event when:
- A user or system actor **attempts** a rollout action that can modify state or routing behavior.
- The platform **enforces** a decision that blocks an action (policy/RBAC denial).
- A system automation changes rollout state (auto-pause / auto-rollback).

### Attempt vs success vs failure
For state-changing operations:
- Emit exactly one event with `outcome = "allowed"` (success) or `outcome = "denied"` / `outcome = "error"`.
- If a request is accepted asynchronously, emit:
  - `outcome = "allowed"` at acceptance time (and include orchestration identifiers), and
  - a later **state transition** event when the rollout actually changes state.

### Idempotency
- Events MUST include a stable `event_id` (UUID) and `request_id`.
- If an action is retried with the same `request_id`, downstream export should be able to deduplicate.

## Standard event envelope (all audit events)
All events MUST include the following envelope fields.

### Required fields
| Field | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `event_id` | string (UUID) | Unique per emitted event. |
| `event_type` | string | One of the event types defined below. |
| `event_version` | string | Schema version string (e.g., `2025-05-06`). |
| `occurred_at` | string (RFC3339) | When action occurred (server-side). |
| `received_at` | string (RFC3339) | When persisted to audit log store (may differ slightly). |
| `outcome` | string | `allowed` \| `denied` \| `error`. |
| `actor_type` | string | `user` \| `service` \| `system`. |
| `actor_id` | string | Redwood user ID / service principal ID. |
| `actor_email` | string | For `actor_type=user` when available. Use empty string if not available. |
| `actor_roles` | string | Comma-separated roles at evaluation time (RBAC snapshot). |
| `tenant_id` | string | Redwood tenant/org ID. |
| `tenant_slug` | string | Human-readable identifier; do not assume uniqueness globally. |
| `environment` | string | `prod` \| `staging` \| `dev`. |
| `request_id` | string | Correlates across Console, control plane, orchestrator. |
| `source` | string | `console` \| `api` \| `terraform` \| `system`. |
| `ip_address` | string | Best-effort (may be empty for service/system). |
| `user_agent` | string | Best-effort; may be empty. |

### Optional envelope fields
| Field | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `session_id` | string | Console session ID when available. |
| `impersonator_actor_id` | string | If support/admin impersonation is used; must be recorded. |
| `support_ticket_ref` | string | e.g., `SUP-48377` when action initiated as part of support workflow. |
| `region` | string | Control plane region handling the request (not the data plane traffic region). |
| `tags` | string | Comma-separated key=value pairs for export filtering (avoid high-cardinality). |

## Rollout domain fields
Rollout-related audit events MUST include these fields.

### Required rollout fields
| Field | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `rollout_id` | string | Stable identifier for rollout object. |
| `rollout_name` | string | Customer-provided name (if any). |
| `route_id` | string | Hosted route identifier. |
| `route_name` | string | Human-readable route name at time of action. |
| `baseline_target` | string | Canonical baseline target (model version/config ref). |
| `canary_target` | string | Canonical canary target (model version/config ref). |
| `rollout_state_before` | string | State machine state prior to action. |
| `rollout_state_after` | string | State after action (or unchanged for denied/error). |

### Optional rollout fields
| Field | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `traffic_percent_before` | string | Canary percent before action (0–100). |
| `traffic_percent_after` | string | Canary percent after action (0–100). |
| `step_id` | string | Rollout step identifier when applicable. |
| `step_sequence` | string | Human-friendly step number (e.g., `3`). |
| `rollout_plan_summary` | string | Short description of planned steps/soak/guards shown in Console. |

### Diff format (what changed)
When the action changes configuration (guardrails, thresholds, schedule), include:
- `change_summary`: short human-readable description
- `diff`: JSON Patch (RFC 6902) serialized as a string

Rules:
- Do not include secrets, prompts, model outputs, customer request payloads.
- Threshold values are allowed.

## Policy and RBAC decision fields
When an action is evaluated by policy/RBAC, include:
| Field | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `policy_decision_id` | string | Correlates to policy engine evaluation logs. |
| `policy_rules_evaluated` | string | Comma-separated rule identifiers (stable names). |
| `policy_result` | string | `allow` \| `deny`. |
| `deny_reason` | string | Stable, customer-safe error code/message (no internals). |
| `required_approver_role` | string | If approval gate applies (e.g., `rollout-approver`). |

## Event taxonomy
### 1) Rollout lifecycle
| Event type | Emitted when |
|---|---|
| `rollout.created` | Rollout object created (wizard submit). |
| `rollout.started` | Rollout transitions to active execution (initial traffic > 0 or scheduled start). |
| `rollout.step.changed` | Traffic percent changes (manual or scheduled progression). |
| `rollout.paused` | Rollout paused by user action. |
| `rollout.resumed` | Rollout resumed after pause. |
| `rollout.rolled_back` | Rollback initiated and applied (traffic returns to baseline, state set accordingly). |
| `rollout.completed` | Rollout reaches terminal success (100% canary promoted). |
| `rollout.canceled` | Rollout canceled without promotion (traffic set to baseline; terminal). |

### 2) Approvals
| Event type | Emitted when |
|---|---|
| `rollout.approval.requested` | A step progression requires approval and enters pending state. |
| `rollout.approval.approved` | An authorized approver grants approval. |
| `rollout.approval.rejected` | Approval explicitly rejected. |
| `rollout.approval.expired` | Approval timed out/expired (if configured). |

Approval events should include:
- `approval_id`
- `approval_gate_name` (e.g., “Traffic step > 10%”) and `approval_reason`

### 3) Policy/RBAC denials
| Event type | Emitted when |
|---|---|
| `rollout.policy.denied` | A rollout action is blocked by RBAC or policy guardrails. |

Must include:
- `policy_result=deny`
- `deny_reason` (customer-safe)

### 4) Automatic safety actions (SLO breach)
| Event type | Emitted when |
|---|---|
| `rollout.autostop.triggered` | Stop condition evaluation triggers an automatic pause. |
| `rollout.autorollback.triggered` | Stop condition triggers an automatic rollback. |

Auto-stop/rollback events must include:
- `trigger_signal` (e.g., `http_5xx_rate`, `p95_latency_ms`, `timeout_rate`)
- `trigger_threshold` (string)
- `observed_value` (string)
- `evaluation_window` (e.g., `5m`)
- `affected_regions` (comma-separated) when applicable

## Data minimization and sensitive data rules
### MUST NOT log
- Prompts, completions, tool inputs/outputs, embeddings, or any customer payload
- Full request/response bodies
- API keys, access tokens, cookies, session secrets
- Any customer-provided PII beyond what is required for actor identity

### Allowed
- Actor identity and roles
- Route identifiers/names
- Model/version/config references (e.g., `model=llama-3.1-70b`, `profile=throughput-v2`)
- Thresholds and guardrails
- Aggregated metric values used for stop-condition decisions

## Retention and access expectations
### Default retention
- **Customer-visible audit logs in Console:** 90 days (default), configurable via plan.
- **Back-end retained audit store:** 400 days (default) for operational and compliance needs.

### Compliance add-on retention
For tenants with Compliance add-on:
- Back-end audit store retention: **7 years**
- Export stream to customer-controlled storage strongly recommended

### Access controls
- Only tenant admins (and delegated `security-auditor` role where enabled) may view audit logs.
- Support access requires explicit approval and is logged via `impersonator_actor_id`.

## SIEM export considerations
### Export format
- JSON Lines (one JSON object per line) over:
  - Managed S3 export (preferred), or
  - HTTPS push endpoint (customer SIEM collector)

### Ordering and completeness
- Ordering is **best-effort**; consumers must rely on `occurred_at` + `event_id` for ordering.
- Export is **at-least-once**. Consumers must deduplicate on `event_id`.

### Field stability
- Envelope fields and required rollout fields are stable.
- New fields may be added without notice (backward-compatible).
- Deprecated fields will remain for at least 180 days after deprecation notice.

### Cardinality guidance
- Avoid including high-cardinality tags beyond `tenant_id`, `rollout_id`, `route_id`.
- Do not include per-request identifiers beyond `request_id`.

### Recommended SIEM mappings
- Actor: `actor_email`, `actor_id`, `actor_roles`
- Target/resource: `route_id`, `rollout_id`, `baseline_target`, `canary_target`
- Change: `change_summary`, `diff`
- Result: `outcome`, `policy_result`, `deny_reason`

## Examples
All examples below are illustrative. Field presence may vary by source (`console` vs `api`) and feature availability.

### Example: Rollout created

[PRD: Dedicated staged rollouts for reserved pools]
## Summary
Dedicated customers rely on reserved GPU pools for predictable throughput and isolation. Today, upgrading a Dedicated pool (new model version, runtime build, routing policy, or config change) is higher risk than Hosted because it can impact all traffic for that customer at once.

This PRD defines “Dedicated staged rollouts for reserved pools”: a first-class, auditable rollout plan that partitions a Dedicated pool into explicit stages (e.g., 1%/10%/50%/100% or replica partitions) with measurable gates required before promotion. Rollouts must be deterministic, reversible, and consistent across regions and failure modes.

## Background / Customer problem
### What is failing today
Dedicated pool changes currently happen via one of:
- Manual, operator-driven changes with implicit canarying (ad hoc)
- Coarse “flip” changes where the new version receives all traffic
- Customer change windows relying on “try it and pray” rollbacks

This leads to:
- Incident risk during pool upgrades (latency spikes, 429s, OOMs)
- High operational toil (SRE/operator babysitting, unclear stop/go decisions)
- Low customer trust and slower adoption of performance improvements
- Regulated customers blocking on change management and auditability

### Evidence / signals
- Support escalation trend: Dedicated customers request “safe upgrade” primitives comparable to Hosted canaries and A/B rollouts.
- Early beta partitioning tests uncovered a known failure mode: small canary partitions can effectively reduce usable capacity and trigger 429s if not guarded by headroom and routing rules.

Representative customer asks:
- “We need a canary stage with objective stop/go signals (429s, p99 latency, GPU saturation).”
- “If telemetry is missing, we need a safe default and explicit overrides with audit trails.”
- “We need an exportable audit record of who approved and who forced an override.”

## Goals
1) Provide first-class staged rollout plans for Dedicated pools (reserved capacity) with explicit stage definitions and promotion/abort controls.
2) Define and enforce gate criteria using objective signals:
   - error rate, p95/p99 latency
   - saturation/headroom, queue depth
   - GPU health (ECC/throttling/taints), OOM rate
   - request drop/429 rate
   - (where applicable) quality regression metrics
3) Ensure deterministic, auditable, and reversible changes:
   - stage-by-stage promotion
   - automatic abort/rollback when gates fail
   - explicit hold/freeze states
   - clear operator “escape hatches” (force-promote/force-rollback)
4) Integrate into Redwood Console rollouts UX and the policy engine/routing layer so behavior is consistent across regions and failure modes.

## Non-goals (initial release)
- Fully general experiment platform for Dedicated beyond rollout safety.
- Customer-defined arbitrary custom metrics for gating (v1 uses Redwood-defined signals; limited configurability).
- Solving every possible model evaluation workflow; v1 quality gates are optional and limited to supported eval signal sources.

## Definitions
- **Dedicated pool:** Reserved GPU capacity allocated to one customer (optionally multi-region).
- **Rollout plan:** A control-plane object representing a staged change for a pool (target version/build/config), plus stages and gates.
- **Stage:** A partition of pool traffic/capacity receiving the candidate change.
- **Gate:** A set of pass/fail criteria over a time window (and sample size) required to promote.
- **Promotion:** Transition from stage N to stage N+1.
- **Abort/Rollback:** Stop rollout and revert routing/selection to the prior stable target.
- **Hold:** Freeze rollout progression at current stage without reverting (used during investigation).

## Users & personas
### 1) Redwood SRE / Dedicated operator (primary)
Responsibilities:
- Perform safe upgrades of customer pools (scheduled or urgent)
- Respond to incidents and degrade gracefully
- Provide clear audit/compliance evidence

Needs:
- Deterministic rollout actions with idempotency
- Standard gates aligned to SLOs and error budgets
- Clear “what failed and why” evidence
- Fast rollback that does not worsen outage (especially during overload)

### 2) Customer admin / platform engineer (secondary, v1 limited)
Responsibilities:
- Approve changes / align with internal change management
- Monitor performance and be confident that upgrades are safe

Needs:
- Read-only visibility into stages and health
- Exportable change/audit history
- Clear language (no internal-only jargon) for gate results and holds

### 3) Redwood TAM / Customer Success (secondary)
Responsibilities:
- Coordinate design partner rollouts
- Communicate risk, schedule, and success criteria

Needs:
- Simple explanation of stages and gates
- Shareable report of rollout outcomes

## User stories
1) As an operator, I can create a rollout plan for a Dedicated pool upgrade, selecting stage defaults and standard gate templates.
2) As an operator, I can start a rollout and see it progress through stages with objective pass/fail gates.
3) As an operator, I can place a rollout on hold, then resume, with all actions audited.
4) As an operator, I can abort a rollout and automatically revert traffic to the previous stable target.
5) As an operator, I can force-promote or force-rollback in emergencies, with stricter RBAC and mandatory reason fields.
6) As a customer admin, I can view the stage timeline and gate evidence (without internal-only details) and download an audit log export.

## Product requirements
### Functional requirements
#### A) Rollout plan lifecycle
- The system MUST support creating a DedicatedPoolRolloutPlan with:
  - pool identifier(s) (including region scope)
  - change target: model version and/or runtime build and/or routing policy/config bundle
  - explicit stage definitions
  - gate template selection (default per tier) and per-plan overrides where permitted
  - rollback target (previous stable target) captured at start
- The system MUST support:
  - start rollout
  - promote to next stage (manual action; auto-promotion is v2)
  - hold/resume
  - abort/rollback
  - force-promote/force-rollback (admin-guarded)
- All state transitions MUST be deterministic and idempotent. Promote/abort actions MUST accept idempotency keys.

#### B) Stages and partitioning
- Stages MUST support (as decided in stage model ADR):
  - percentage-based traffic split OR replica partitions, depending on pool size and constraints
- Default stage set for v1:
  - 1% → 10% → 50% → 100%
- The system MUST enforce minimum partition size / headroom constraints to avoid starving capacity (e.g., very small pools cannot support a 1% stage).
- For multi-region pools:
  - Stage behavior MUST be consistent across regions (no partial region exposure without explicit operator selection).
  - If a region becomes impaired mid-stage, routing MUST follow safe fallback rules (see Reliability requirements).

#### C) Gate evaluation
- Gates MUST be evaluated using standardized metrics/traces sourced from Redwood telemetry.
- Gate evaluation MUST expose:
  - evaluation window (e.g., 5m/15m)
  - minimum sample size requirements (requests/tokens)
  - observed value(s), thresholds, and pass/fail reasoning
  - missing data / stale data handling state
- Default behavior for missing or stale telemetry MUST be fail-closed for automated “gate pass” (i.e., the system cannot claim a pass without data), while allowing explicit manual override with audit.
- Gate categories v1 (required defaults):
  - Availability/Error: 5xx rate, request failure rate
  - Latency: p95 and p99 end-to-end latency (and optionally TTFT for streaming)
  - Capacity/Overload: 429 rate, queue depth, saturation/headroom
  - Runtime stability: OOM rate
  - GPU health: unhealthy node fraction / ECC-threshold alarms (where available)
- Optional gate category v1 (tier-dependent / design partner only):
  - Quality regression signals from Redwood eval harness (if configured)

#### D) Rollback/abort semantics
- Aborting MUST revert new traffic to the previous stable target as quickly as possible.
- For streaming/in-flight requests, behavior MUST be explicitly defined and consistent:
  - default: in-flight requests remain pinned to the backend they started on; new requests use rollback target
  - operator messaging MUST set expectations (“streams started before abort may complete on canary”) and provide limits/timeouts where supported

#### E) Auditability and RBAC
- All rollout actions MUST emit audit events including:
  - actor identity (human or service principal)
  - action type (create/update/start/promote/hold/resume/abort/force-promote/force-rollback)
  - pool(s), rollout_plan_id, stage (from/to)
  - reason/comment field (required for force actions; recommended for abort/hold)
  - correlation identifiers (request_id/idempotency_key)
- RBAC MUST enforce:
  - standard operators can create/start/promote/abort/hold
  - force actions require admin role and additional confirmation UX
- Audit retention MUST meet enterprise requirements (see linked audit logging spec).

### Console UX requirements
#### Core UX principles
- Make the stage timeline the “source of truth” for what changed, where, and why.
- Prefer clear states and explicit next actions over implicit automation.
- Always provide a safe action in failure conditions (hold or abort) and explain consequences.

#### Required screens/components (v1)
1) **Dedicated Pool → Rollouts tab**
   - List of rollout plans (status: Draft/Running/Held/Aborted/Completed)
   - Search/filter by time, actor, status

2) **Rollout plan detail (timeline view)**
   - Stage timeline with the current stage highlighted
   - Per-stage gate status: Pending / Evaluating / Passed / Failed / Unknown (missing data)
   - “Promote” button enabled only when gates are satisfied (or when force-promote is permitted)
   - “Hold” and “Abort” always available to authorized operators

3) **Gate evidence panel**
   - For each gate: query name, time window, observed value, threshold, region breakdown where applicable
   - Missing data messaging: “Telemetry delayed (last datapoint X minutes ago). Gate cannot be evaluated.”

4) **Change history / audit trail view**
   - Human-readable list of actions
   - Export option for admin users (CSV/JSON)

#### UX copy requirements
- Avoid internal-only metric names where possible; show friendly names with a “details” accordion.
- When a gate fails, show:
  - what breached
  - by how much
  - the recommended next action (hold vs abort)
- Force actions must show a warning and require a reason.

### Reliability and performance requirements
- Gate evaluation must be low-latency and resilient; it MUST NOT introduce a new critical dependency in the routing hot path.
- Stage routing MUST be consistent and deterministic across retries and regions.
- Rollout plan APIs MUST support optimistic concurrency controls to prevent double-promotes.
- Metrics cardinality MUST be bounded (stage tagging must use allowlisted tags; no free-form stage names as labels).

## MVP scope vs V2 scope
### MVP (Phase 1–3)
- Rollout plan object + API: create/update/start/promote/hold/resume/abort
- Default stages (1/10/50/100) with validation for small pools
- Standard gates for Dedicated (latency/error/429/saturation/OOM/GPU health as available)
- Manual promotion (operator clicks Promote)
- Automated gate evaluation (Phase 2), with fail-closed pass semantics + manual override
- Audit logging for all actions
- Console timeline + gate evidence + basic audit trail view
- Runbook and on-call playbook integration

### V2 (post-GA candidates)
- Auto-promotion policies (e.g., promote after N consecutive pass windows)
- Customer self-serve creation of rollout plans (with guardrails)
- More flexible stages (arbitrary number and naming) where safe
- Richer quality gates (per-customer eval suites, regression thresholds)
- Scheduled rollouts (maintenance windows) and change approval workflows
- Advanced multi-region strategies (region-by-region rollout with explicit policy)

## Success metrics
### Product outcomes
- Reduce Dedicated upgrade-related incidents by 50% over two quarters (measured as incidents where root cause is pool upgrade/config change).
- Increase percentage of Dedicated upgrades using staged rollout plans to:
  - 60% within 4 weeks of GA
  - 90% within 12 weeks of GA
- Reduce mean time to rollback for upgrade-related incidents by 30%.

### Operational / SRE outcomes
- Gate failures should be actionable and not noisy:
  - <10% of rollouts end in “Unknown” due to telemetry issues (target after Phase 2 hardening)
  - <5% false-positive gate failures validated by post-rollout review (measured via operator feedback tags)

### Customer outcomes
- Design partners report increased confidence: ≥8/10 satisfaction on rollout safety workflow.
- At least 2 enterprise security reviews accept audit evidence without requiring custom instrumentation.

## Rollout / launch plan
### Phase 0: Requirements + alignment (1–2 weeks)
- Confirm stage model and constraints with Infra/SRE (minimum pool size/headroom)
- Finalize default gate thresholds and evaluation windows per tier
- Finalize audit event schema and RBAC requirements

### Phase 1: Control plane + routing primitives (3–5 weeks)
- Implement rollout plan APIs behind feature flag
- Implement stage partitioning support in routing/data plane (no UI beyond admin tools)
- Manual gates allowed (operator attestation) for early end-to-end testing

### Phase 2: Automated gates + Console UX + dashboards (3–4 weeks)
- Gate evaluation pipeline integrated with policy engine
- Stage-tagged metrics emitted with cardinality controls
- Console timeline and evidence panels
- Standard dashboards and alerts for gate failures

### Phase 3: Dogfood + limited beta (2–3 weeks)
- Dogfood on internal Dedicated pools
- Limited beta: 1–2 design partners
- Iterate on:
  - small pool behavior
  - multi-region impairment handling
  - missing telemetry messaging and override guardrails

### Phase 4: GA
- Enablement playbook and feature-flag ramp
- Docs/runbooks and support readiness
- Post-launch reliability review at 30 days

## Dependencies
- Control plane service for rollout plan persistence and state machine (Platform)
- Routing updates to support stage selection + safe fallback (Routing/Data plane)
- Telemetry tagging and dashboards (Telemetry/Observability)
- Audit logging pipeline and export (Security/Compliance)
- Console backend endpoints and UI components (Console)

## Risks & mitigations
1) **Capacity fragmentation / starvation in small pools**
   - Mitigation: enforce minimum partition size and headroom; allow replica-based partitioning; adjust default stages for small reservations.

2) **Gate false failures from noisy metrics or bursty workloads**
   - Mitigation: minimum sample size, longer evaluation windows for low-traffic pools, smoothing/aggregation rules, and clear “hold” guidance.

3) **Telemetry lag/outage blocks promotions**
   - Mitigation: staleness detection, fail-closed pass semantics, operator override with audit, and alerting on telemetry health.

4) **Metrics cardinality regression from stage tagging**
   - Mitigation: label allowlist, sampling, bounded stage_id format, and pre-launch load tests on metrics backend.

5) **Multi-region inconsistencies**
   - Mitigation: define default “all regions together” behavior; treat region impairment as a gate failure or hold recommendation depending on policy; explicit runbook.

## Open questions
1) Missing metrics behavior: confirm the final policy for “Unknown” state and promotion eligibility (current proposal: cannot pass automatically; manual override permitted with audit).
2) Default gate thresholds by tier: what is fixed vs configurable in v1 (especially p99 latency and 429 thresholds)?
3) Quality gates: which Dedicated customers qualify for optional eval-based gates in v1, and what is the minimum supported integration?
4) Multi-region pools: do we allow region-by-region staged rollouts in v1 (likely no), and how do we message this limitation?
5) Streaming semantics: should we introduce an optional “drain and abort” mode (stop accepting new streams on canary, wait up to X minutes) in v2?
6) Customer visibility: what is the default visibility of rollout plan details to customer admins for Dedicated (read-only), and which fields are redacted?

## Appendix A: Default stages and example gate set (v1)
Default stages:
- Stage 0: 1% (or minimum viable partition based on replica count)
- Stage 1: 10%
- Stage 2: 50%
- Stage 3: 100%

Example gate set (illustrative; final thresholds in gate ADR / SRE alignment doc):
- Error gate: 5xx rate <= baseline + X, over 10m, min N requests
- Latency gate: p99 <= baseline * Y, over 10m
- Overload gate: 429 rate <= Z, queue depth < Q
- Stability gate: OOM rate == 0 (or below tiny threshold)
- GPU health gate: unhealthy node fraction <= H

## Appendix B: Out of scope examples (v1)
- Arbitrary customer-provided PromQL queries
- Simultaneous multi-variant experiments beyond rollout safety
- Automated rollback based on bespoke customer SLOs without standardization

[ADR: Audit Event Delivery Guarantees (Ingestion, Buffering, and Outage Behavior)]
## Status
Published (effective for schema v1 rollout).

## Summary
This ADR defines Redwood Inference’s delivery semantics for audit events and how producers must behave during audit pipeline degradation or outages.

We choose **at-least-once delivery from the audit ingestion service onward** (durable queue → storage/export), and **best-effort delivery from producers to ingestion** with **bounded buffering and retry**. This prioritizes platform availability (admin actions must not routinely fail) while still providing strong audit reliability, clear signals when delivery is degraded, and a consistent customer guidance story (including how to de-duplicate in SIEMs).

## Context
Redwood is standardizing audit logs across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. Customers (especially regulated/enterprise) require:
- Consistent auditability of sensitive actions.
- Reasonable delivery latency to their SIEM.
- Predictable behavior under failure (no silent drop without detection).

Constraints and realities:
- Audit pipelines can degrade (regional outages, backpressure, exporter downtime).
- Some producers are latency-sensitive synchronous request paths (API Gateway, Control Plane) and must not introduce high tail latency.
- Some producers are “operator tooling” paths (Private installer/upgrade) where longer retries and local spooling are feasible.
- At-least-once semantics inevitably introduce duplicates; we must provide an **idempotency/deduplication story**.

## Definitions (for this ADR)
- **Producer**: Any service/tool emitting audit events (API Gateway, Control Plane services, Console backend/admin actions, policy engine, Private installer).
- **Ingestion service** (“audit-ingest”): Receives audit events from producers, validates schema, adds server-side metadata, and writes to a durable queue.
- **Durable queue**: Managed Kafka/PubSub equivalent in Hosted/Dedicated; pluggable in Private (customer-managed or bundled).
- **Audit storage**: Redwood-managed storage for retrieval/export (Hosted/Dedicated) or customer-managed in Private depending on configuration.
- **Exporter**: Pushes events to external SIEM targets (Splunk HEC, Azure Sentinel, Datadog, etc.).

## Decision drivers
1. **Do not break admin workflows** by making audit sink availability a hard dependency in the general case.
2. **Detectability**: if audit delivery is degraded, Redwood and customers must be able to detect it quickly.
3. **Consistency across deployment modes** (Hosted/Dedicated/Private parity).
4. **SIEM compatibility**: flattened JSON, stable identifiers, duplicates possible.
5. **Operational simplicity**: clear retry and buffering rules; avoid per-service bespoke logic.

## Considered options
### Option A — End-to-end exactly-once
Pros: clean semantics, minimal duplication.
Cons: high complexity (distributed transactions/idempotency everywhere), performance cost, brittle failure modes; not realistic across all producers and Private environments.

### Option B — End-to-end at-least-once with blocking (fail closed when ingestion unavailable)
Pros: strong audit guarantee.
Cons: makes audit pipeline a hard dependency; creates major availability risk and potential customer-facing outages for unrelated admin actions.

### Option C — Producer best-effort to ingestion + at-least-once after ingestion (chosen)
Pros: preserves platform availability; still yields strong reliability with buffering/retry and durable queue; easier to operate; duplicates handled via event_id.
Cons: in a total ingestion outage beyond buffering limits, some events may be dropped (but must be signaled and measurable).

## Decision
### 1) Delivery semantics
**1.1 Producer → ingestion: best-effort with bounded buffering + retry**
- Producers MUST attempt to deliver audit events asynchronously and MUST NOT routinely block user/admin requests on audit delivery.
- Producers MUST implement bounded buffering and retry (see “Producer requirements”).
- If buffering is exhausted or the outage exceeds retry policy, producers MAY drop events, but MUST emit internal telemetry indicating drops and MUST surface degradation signals as defined below.

**1.2 Ingestion → durable queue → storage/export: at-least-once**
- Once the ingestion service acknowledges an event (HTTP 2xx / gRPC OK), Redwood guarantees **at-least-once** delivery into the durable queue.
- Downstream consumers (storage and exporters) MUST be resilient and operate with at-least-once semantics. Duplicates are expected.

**1.3 Customer-facing statement**
- Redwood provides **at-least-once delivery** after ingestion acknowledgment and **best-effort delivery** from producers, with explicit detection/alerting when degraded.
- Redwood does **not** claim exactly-once.

### 2) Required identifiers and deduplication
- Every audit event MUST include a globally unique `event_id` (ULID preferred; UUIDv7 acceptable) generated at the producer.
- Ingestion MUST treat `event_id` as the idempotency key for a bounded window.
  - Hosted/Dedicated: ingestion performs best-effort dedupe for repeated `event_id` within **24 hours**.
  - Private: dedupe is best-effort and configuration-dependent; guidance must recommend SIEM-side dedupe on `event_id`.
- Exporters MUST forward `event_id` unchanged.

### 3) Producer requirements (library-level defaults)
All producers MUST use the shared audit library defaults unless an explicit exception is approved.

**3.1 Retry policy**
- Exponential backoff with full jitter.
- Initial backoff: 250ms
- Max backoff: 10s
- Max attempts: 12 (approx. 2–5 minutes depending on jitter)
- Retry only on retryable classes: timeouts, connection errors, 429, 502/503/504.
- Do NOT retry on schema validation errors (4xx) except 429.

**3.2 Buffering policy**
- Default: in-memory queue per process.
- Default capacity: 10,000 events or 10 MB, whichever comes first.
- Drop behavior when full: **drop oldest** (to preserve recency for investigations) and increment `audit_events_dropped_total`.
- Producers MUST emit metrics for:
  - `audit_events_enqueued_total`
  - `audit_events_sent_total`
  - `audit_events_failed_total`
  - `audit_events_dropped_total`
  - `audit_queue_depth`
  - `audit_delivery_degraded` (0/1)

**3.3 Synchronous-path latency budget**
- Producer code MUST not add more than **5ms p99** on synchronous request paths.
- Audit emission should be non-blocking; when unavoidable (rare), it must be behind a short deadline (<= 50ms) and must fail open.

**3.4 Private installer special case (disk spool allowed)
**
- The Private installer/upgrade tooling MAY use a local disk spool (encrypted at rest when feasible) to tolerate longer outages during maintenance windows.
- Disk spool is bounded (default 250 MB) and rotated; if full, follows drop-oldest and emits explicit operator warnings.

### 4) Outage and degradation behavior
We standardize behavior for “audit pipeline degraded” across surfaces.

**4.1 Hosted/Dedicated services**
When ingestion is unreachable or returning persistent retryable errors:
- Continue processing admin actions (fail open) by default.
- Set `audit_delivery_degraded=1` metric.
- Add response header on admin endpoints where appropriate:
  - `X-Redwood-Audit-Delivery: degraded`
- Log an internal structured error (non-audit) with rate limiting.

**4.2 Console UI**
- If the Console backend detects `audit_delivery_degraded=1` for the tenant/region, show a non-blocking banner:
  - “Audit log delivery is currently degraded. Actions are still applied. Some audit events may be delayed.”
- Console actions that mutate sensitive config MUST still emit audit attempts; UI must not attempt to “retry on behalf of audit.”

**4.3 Private deployments**
- If the configured sink/export target is unavailable, the platform MUST:
  - Continue applying changes by default.
  - Surface degradation in operator-visible logs.
  - Provide `redwoodctl private status` indicators for audit pipeline health (when available).

**4.4 Fail-closed is not the default**
- We do not fail closed on audit delivery for general admin actions.
- Any request to fail closed for a specific action category must go through Security + SRE review and be documented as an exception (with customer impact analysis).

### 5) Monitoring, SLOs, and alerting (minimum viable)
- We measure delivery at the ingestion service boundary:
  - **Ingestion acceptance latency** (producer → ingestion ack)
  - **Queue write success rate**
  - **Exporter lag** and **drop/duplicate indicators**

Baseline SLO target (enterprise tiers; subject to tuning):
- 99.9% of accepted events available to exporters within **5 minutes**.
- Drop rate (post-acceptance) < **0.01%** rolling 30 days.

Alerting:
- Page SRE on sustained:
  - ingestion backlog > 10 minutes, or
  - exporter drop rate above threshold, or
  - `audit_delivery_degraded` > 0 for > 10 minutes in a region.

(See runbook: Audit Log Pipeline Incident Runbook.)

## Consequences
### Positive
- Keeps admin/control-plane workflows available even during audit sink incidents.
- Provides clear, consistent semantics to customers and internal auditors.
- Standardizes retry/buffering so teams don’t reinvent (and misconfigure) delivery logic.

### Negative / trade-offs
- Duplicate events are expected; customers must dedupe by `event_id`.
- In extreme outages beyond buffering limits, some producer-originated events may be dropped (but must be measurable and trigger alerts).
- “Best-effort producer to ingestion” means that “100% coverage of sensitive actions” refers to **instrumentation coverage**, not a cryptographic guarantee of delivery under all failures.

## Implementation notes
- Shared audit library MUST:
  - Generate `event_id` if missing.
  - Enforce timeouts and non-blocking behavior.
  - Provide a standard async delivery worker with buffering and retry.
  - Emit the required metrics.
- Ingestion MUST:
  - Validate schema version and required fields.
  - Stamp server receive time.
  - Best-effort dedupe on `event_id`.
- Exporters MUST:
  - Preserve `event_id`, `schema_version`, and correlation fields.
  - Batch with retry/backoff; expose duplicate rate metrics where possible.

## Rollout plan
1. Land shared audit library defaults and metrics.
2. Update ingestion to enforce ack semantics and queue durability.
3. Roll out producers service-by-service; ensure each service exports `audit_delivery_degraded`.
4. Enable dashboards/alerts and run game-day for ingestion outage.
5. Publish customer-facing guidance on dedupe and expected semantics (Support + Solutions).

## Open questions
- Should we introduce a small “fail-closed” allowlist for ultra-high-risk actions (e.g., disabling audit export, breaking-glass RBAC changes) in specific regulated Private environments?
- Should Private bundle a default local durable queue (so producers aren’t directly coupled to exporter availability)?

## References
- Audit Event Schema + Taxonomy ADR (structure and required identifiers)
- Audit Log Events Logging Standard (naming, required context, and cardinality controls)
- Audit Log Pipeline Incident Runbook (mitigation and comms)
- SLO/alert tickets: ENG-4829, ENG-4835

[Private: cross-tenant audit suppression + KMS rotation interaction causing stale SSO attributes and role reconciliation gaps]
description:
Summary: A production customer reported that after a scheduled KMS rotation in their Private deployment, audit events for RBAC and SSO role changes stopped being indexed for ~18 minutes and some users observed stale SSO attributes that prevented role reconciliation. The combined effect temporarily allowed cross-tenant permission checks to rely on stale assertions and suppressed audit visibility for the window. This ticket tracks the urgent investigation, rollback/patch, and follow-up hardening work.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) In a Private environment with KMS envelope rotation enabled and SSO caching turned on, rotate the envelope key via the rotation API.
2) Trigger SSO assertion refresh for an identity provider that uses attribute-maps to generate Redwood roles.
3) Perform RBAC role-change operations (grant/revoke) and perform API calls that should produce audit entries.
4) Observe that during rotation window audit events are dropped from the audit-forwarder and the SSO attribute cache returns stale claims for some requests.

impact_summary:
- Customer-facing impact: High. One enterprise customer reported missing entries in compliance audit exports and transient incorrect role state for a small percentage (~0.5%) of requests during rotation.
- Security risk: Medium-High. Although no confirmed data exfiltration, role-reconciliation gaps increase risk surface and reduced audit visibility violates compliance commitments.
- Affected product: Private deployments (VPC/on-prem), specifically the audit-forwarder + SSO attribute cache + KMS integration path.

investigation_notes:
Initial findings:
- Audit-forwarder drops: During envelope key rotation the audit-forwarder attempted to re-encrypt stored batched events; our retry logic did not handle a transient key ID mapping change and dropped a subset of events when the re-encrypt RPC returned a 403 followed by an unfamiliar key ID.
- SSO cache staleness: The SSO assertion cache uses a TTL plus an invalidation hook tied to the key fingerprint used to sign the session token. The KMS rotation updated the signer fingerprint index before the assertion invalidation finished propagating, creating a mismatch that let stale attributes be served for up to 18 minutes.
- Race condition: A race where role binding reconciliation job queries RBAC state and SSO cache simultaneously; if reconciliation reads before assertion invalidation, reconciliation writes stale role grants.
- Logs: We have matching gaps in audit logs between 2026-03-09T22:11:40Z and 2026-03-09T22:29:55Z on the affected cluster.
- Reproducible locally in a private test harness with simulated rotation timing and VPC network delays.
Evidence: console trace ID=trc_0b1f3c, support ticket #CS-8127, canary logs at s3://redwood-incident-logs/2026-03-09/eng11097/


mitigations_taken:
1) Immediate: Activated a temporary policy to pause envelope key auto-rotation on the affected customer's Private cluster and kicked a manual backfill job to re-ingest dropped audit events from forwarder local buffer.
2) Hotfix deployed: Small change to audit-forwarder retry logic to treat transient key ID mapping changes as retryable and buffer events until a successful re-encrypt. Deployed as hotpatch private-2026.03.1-hotfix. Patch PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/13340
3) Feature toggle: Enabled assertion-cache strict invalidation mode for the affected customer which forces cache miss on key/signer fingerprint drift while we validate the full fix.
4) Customer communication: Security and CSM teams issued an initial incident notice and are scheduling an audit export handoff.


proposed_fix:
1) Audit-forwarder: Harden re-encrypt flow to support concurrent key rotations by using a key rotation map and exponential backoff with non-dropping buffer; add end-to-end acknowledgement for batched events.
2) SSO/Cache: Make assertion invalidation synchronous with KMS signer index updates (or gate rotation completion), and add a short pre-rotation quiesce window where caches are proactively invalidated.
3) RBAC reconciliation: Introduce a reconciliation fence that validates assertion freshness timestamp before committing role changes.
4) Add integration tests simulating KMS rotations with VPC-induced latency, and add a chaos test to the Private CI job.


deployment_plan:
- Stage: apply hotfix to staging cluster and run regression suite (30m)
- Canary: deploy to a single private customer cluster with low activity and monitor for 2 hours (alerts on dropped audit events, SSO stale cache hits)
- Roll: if canary is green, roll to affected customers in waves (5 clusters per wave) with 30m observation windows
- Rollback: rollback script available at ops/runbooks/rollback-audit-rotation.sh; in case of regression, pause rotations and revert hotfix
- Timeline: aim to complete emergency patches for impacted customers by 2026-03-13 02:00 UTC

verification_steps:
1) Run the KMS rotation test harness against patched build and confirm no audit-forwarder drops.
2) Confirm that SSO cache invalidations occur within 5 seconds of signer index change in the test harness.
3) Customer validation: provide regenerated audit export and compare event counts to pre-incident baseline.
4) Add alert for >0 dropped-audit-events per 10m window and ensure it is firing properly in canary.


communication:
- Support ticket updated: CS-8127 (privileged) with steps taken and ETA for re-ingest.
- Incident notice sent to affected customer and security contact.
- Internal: Slack incident channel #inc-priv-kms-11097, briefing scheduled with SOC and CSM at 2026-03-12T10:30Z.

postmortem_followups:
1) Follow-up RFC to standardize KMS rotation semantics with forwarders and caches (owner: Priya Nair, due 2026-04-01).
2) Add permanent integration test coverage in private CI and chaos tests to simulate envelope rotations and signer index drift.
3) Backfill: Complete audit backfill and share compliance-ready export with the customer.
4) Run a tabletop incident with SOC/Support to review detection and SLA communication.

[Assertion TTL regression in private control plane leading to dropped audit events and RBAC stale grants]
description:
Customers (AcmeCorp, FinSoft) reported intermittent authorization failures and gaps in audit logs on private clusters. Root cause: a regression introduced in control-plane token assertion TTL handling (edge case when IdP sends inexact NotOnOrAfter) that caused assertion cache entries to be evicted prematurely and audit emission to be suppressed during rapid KMS envelope rotation. Resulting symptoms: RBAC grants remained stale for up to 10 minutes after assertion refresh, missing audit events for role-bind changes, and failed SSO logins when failover routing occurred. This ticket coordinates an urgent patch, backfill for missed audits, and a release to private clusters with a staged rollout and rollback plan.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Configure private control plane with SAML IdP that omits millisecond precision and uses NotOnOrAfter boundary equal to current time. 2) Enable KMS envelope rotate interval=5m and simulate simultaneous key rotation. 3) Exercise short-lived SSO assertions across two pods behind control-plane HA router. 4) Observe: assertion cache eviction log lines, subsequent denied API calls, and missing audit events in control-plane audit stream (kubectl logs and audit-sink).

mitigation:
Temporary mitigation: increase assertion grace-window in control plane config to +30s and disable automated KMS envelope rotation for affected clusters. Suggested customer communication: instruct affected accounts to pause KMS rotation and apply runtime config change. This reduces risk while patch is developed and tested.

fix_summary:
Adjust assertion time parsing to accept missing millisecond precision and treat NotOnOrAfter equal-to-now as valid for an additional 45 seconds grace window. Ensure assertion cache eviction triggers audit flush before removal. Add guardrails during KMS envelope rotation so audit emission is not suppressed when keys are rotating. Unit tests + integration test harness added for SAML edge-time handling and KMS rotation interplay.

deploy_plan:
1) Merge PRs and build control-plane image with tag cp-fix-assertion-2026-03-14. 2) Deploy to staging clusters for 2 hours with heavy SSO+KMS rotation load tests. 3) Canary deploy to 5% of private clusters (region US-WEST) for 1 hour. 4) Gradually ramp to 100% over 90 minutes, monitoring audit event rates and RBAC success rates. 5) Post-deploy backfill (see backfill_plan).

rollback_plan:
Rollback by reverting image tag to previous stable cp-2026-02-28 and re-enable previous KMS rotation cadence. Automated rollback if error rate > 1% for 5m or audit-event-drop metric increases by >20%.

backfill_plan:
Run audit replayer job that pulls raw request traces and re-emits audit events into customers' audit sinks for the interval 2026-03-09T00:00Z to 2026-03-11T23:59Z. Customers will be notified with summary of records re-emitted and SHA hashes for verification. Backfill job stored results in s3://redwood-backfill/ENG-36277/ and will be throttled per-customer to avoid sink overload.

monitoring_checks:
- increase in audit_event_emit_rate (should return to baseline)
- RBAC_evaluation_denied_rate (should drop to baseline)
- SSO_login_success_rate (should improve)
- control_plane_error_5xx

test_plan:
Unit tests for time-parsing; integration tests in staging with simulated IdP notOnOrAfter edge cases; chaos test that rotates KMS envelopes during active SSO sessions; synthetic traffic validating audit sink delivery. Acceptance criteria: zero missing audit events in 30m staging run; RBAC denied rate <0.1% under load.

regression_cause:
A refactor of the assertion cache input normalization (PR #3930) replaced tolerant time parsing with strict RFC check and removed an audit-flush hook that executed on eviction during KMS rotation. Combined with a KMS rotation optimization that temporarily disabled audit emission, this produced a race condition.

customer_communication:
Draft sent to customer success and account teams. Initial outreach made to affected customers with mitigation steps and ETA for patch. Follow-up scheduled post-canary with confirmed times for backfill. CS contacts: jessica@acmecorp.com, ops@finsoft.example, compliance@nimbushealth.org.

[Certificate rotation race in private control plane causes transient RBAC denial and dropped audit events]
description:
Summary: On 2026-03-09 we received multiple escalations from two private deployment customers reporting short-lived 403s for inference requests and gaps in audit streams during a scheduled certificate rotation window. Investigation shows a race between control-plane certificate chain rotation and the private agent's KMS envelope key rotation. The race caused rolebinding lookups to fallback to cached membership that evaluated to false for a small percentage of requests and simultaneously queued audit events that failed to be encrypted/dequeued resulting in missing audit records for ~6-12 minutes.

impact_details:
Affected surface: Private (VPC/on-prem) control planes running agent v1.12.1-1.12.2 with automated cert rotation enabled. Two customers reported user-facing 403s (authz failures) for ~3-9 minutes during rotation. Audit ingestion lag caused ~1.2k audit events to be dropped or delayed beyond retention window for one customer that had strict compliance ingestion. Root cause thread race between cert hot-swap path and KMS envelope key TTL renewal where the control plane temporarily presented a certed identity that the agent's RBAC cache invalidated, triggering expensive KMS decrypt retries that exhausted the async audit buffer.

reproduction_steps:
1) Deploy private control plane and agent v1.12.2 with auto-rotate enabled and KMS envelope rotation scheduled at 03:00 UTC.
2) Initiate cert rotation (simulate immediate chain replacement).
3) Force heavy auth traffic (100 RPS) and watch for RBAC evaluation hits that miss due to short-lived identity mismatch.
4) Observe audit queue metrics and KMS decrypt error spikes in the agent logs.
Expected: no 403s and reliable audit delivery. Observed: transient 403s and audit gaps.

root_cause:
Two concurrent operations (cert chain hot-swap + KMS envelope rotation) were not serialized. When the control plane rotated certs it briefly served a newly-signed certificate chain before the agent completed KMS envelope refresh; the agent invalidated local RBAC caches and attempted KMS decrypts against a partially rotated envelope metadata set leading to a spike in decrypt failures and audit buffer overflows. The code path lacked defensive retries with exponential backoff and did not persist audit events to a durable store if KMS temporarily rejected decrypt requests.

short_term_mitigation:
1) Immediately disabled automated cert rotation for impacted customers via control-plane feature flag (rolled between 2026-03-09 23:40 UTC and 2026-03-10 00:05 UTC).
2) Applied configuration change to increase agent audit buffer and enable synchronous fallback write to disk for audit events for customers with strict compliance.
3) Contacted affected customers with timeline and requested they extend rotation window while we deploy a hotfix.

remediation_plan:
1) Backport patch to private-agent that serializes cert rotation and KMS envelope refresh (agent v1.12.3). Patch includes: serialized rotation lock, robust KMS decrypt retry with jitter and capped exponential backoff, audit persistence to ephemeral on-disk queue as fallback.
2) Add guard in control-plane to publish rotation-ready signal after confirming agents report successful envelope update.
3) Add end-to-end test for concurrent rotation scenarios and KMS error injection.
4) Ship rollout with canary to two low-impact customers, monitor for 24 hours, then progressive rollout to remaining customers.

rollback_plan:
If v1.12.3 causes regressions: revert feature flag to disable serialized rotation and revert agent to v1.12.2 while re-enabling previous mitigations (increased audit buffer + disk fallback). Control-plane will be set to manual rotation until remediation is verified.

qa_steps:
Unit tests covering rotation lock and retry behavior
Integration test in staging with KMS error injection to validate audit persistence
Canary deployment to two private customers (non-production) and monitor auth 403 rate, audit delivery, KMS error rate
Load test at production-like 200 RPS during rotation window to confirm no auth failures

[Tenant Guard: reconcile SSO session replay + KMS unwrap drift causing audit gaps in private clusters]
description:
Several enterprise Private customers reported missing or delayed audit entries after bulk SSO re-auth events. Root cause traces to a race between SSO session reconciliation (IdP-initiated rebinds) and our async KMS unwrap worker: when a tenant token is rewrapped during a short window, RBAC lookups use the incoming assertion but the KMS unwrap returns an older envelope and the audit-stream emitter drops the event. This manifests as: 1) action accepted by the runtime, 2) no corresponding audit event in the control plane (gap), 3) intermittent permission denial for follow-up requests using the new assertion. Impact spans VPC private clusters with customer-managed IdPs and recent KMS envelope rotation. The bug is regressional relative to the tenant-claim rehydration changes shipped last quarter.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Configure a private cluster with SAML IdP and scheduled KMS envelope rotation. 2) Trigger IdP-initiated SSO session refresh for 10 concurrent sessions. 3) Simultaneously run kms-wrap to rotate envelopes. 4) Observe control-plane audit logs for missing entries for ~10-20% of the requests. 5) Reproduce locally with federation test harness: ./scripts/fed-test --sessions=10 --wrap-window=200ms

impact_summary:
High-severity for customers using Private: gaps in audit trails break compliance controls, SLOs for audit delivery violated, and some tenants see transient RBAC failures leading to customer escalations and an open support ticket per affected org.

mitigation_plan:
Short term: deploy an emergency control-plane patch that serializes claim rehydration and KMS unwrap per-tenant key (hotfix) and add a guard that stalls audit emission until envelope version is validated. Rollout as canary to 3 private customers first. Long term: refactor unwrap worker to be idempotent by envelope-versioning and add end-to-end audit watermarks with retry/backpressure. Also add telemetry: metrics for audit-drop-rate per-tenant and unwrap-latency histogram.

implementation_notes:
- Minimal hotpatch: add per-tenant mutex in control-plane claim-sync path; verify with unit tests and a short e2e scenario. - Avoid global locks to keep throughput. - Use existing tenant-index shard lock. - Add feature flag tenant_guard.enable_strict_unwrap=true. - Ensure flag defaults to on for private clusters that opted into strict security mode.

risks_and_tradeoffs:
- Mutex introduces contention; we mitigate by sharding locks by tenant-id prefix. - Stalling audit emission adds latency to control-plane response; acceptable for private compliance customers but should be limited to canary and behind the feature flag. - Rolling KMS changes may surface related race conditions in dedicated/hosted; test on those planes but do not enable by default.

testing_plan:
- Unit tests for unwrap-version check and mutex acquisition. - Integration test using fed-test harness with simulated IdP and KMS rotation. - Canary: deploy to 3 private clusters (small tenants) and run workload generator for 24h. - Post-deploy: monitor metrics: audit-drop-rate, unwrap-latency, control-plane-error-rate. - Regression: run previous customer-repro scripts from support tickets.

deployment_steps:
1) Branch: eng/tenant-guard-unwrap-hotfix. 2) QA: run integration smoke in staging. 3) Merge and build image tagged priv-2026.03.1-hotfix-1. 4) Canary deploy to 3 customers via control-plane rollout config. 5) Monitor 6h, if stable roll to remaining private clusters over 12h. 6) Flip feature flag globally after 72h stable.

[Priv SSO: hyphenated group mapping failure combined with KMS envelope rotation race (urgent patch)]
description:
Summary: Multiple enterprise Private customers reported login failures and missing RBAC grants after a scheduled KMS envelope rotation and consequent SSO token refresh window. Investigation shows a twofold issue: (1) SAML group attribute normalization code dropped groups containing hyphens when the raw assertion used the dash-delimited format (e.g., 'team-engops'), and (2) a race during KMS envelope rotation caused ephemeral credentials to be reissued with stale role binding references, resulting in dropped audit events for affected sessions. Impact: customers experienced inability to access dedicated/private resources for short windows (30s-2m) and partial missing entries in audit logs for those sessions. Reproduction steps: 1) Configure private cluster with SAML group attributes containing hyphens. 2) Trigger KMS envelope rotation on the control plane during active SSO token refresh. 3) Observe user receives 403 on privileged routes and audit events missing for the failed token refresh window. Root cause: the SAML parser's attribute normalization pipeline used a regular expression that treated hyphenated group names as token separators; when combined with the token re-issuance path triggered during envelope rotation, role binding lookup used the pre-rotation cache key and dropped on miss rather than falling back, resulting in denied authorization and no audit entry. Temporary mitigations applied: 1) Turned on conservative SSO token fallback for impacted customers (config toggle) to accept both normalized and raw group claims. 2) Disabled automated KMS envelope rotation for affected clusters until patch is deployed. These mitigations were communicated to affected customers. Permanent fix plan: 1) Patch SAML attribute normalization to preserve hyphenated group tokens and add comprehensive unit tests (PR: infra#4286). 2) Change role-binding lookup to perform a tolerant lookup that attempts cache miss fallback to authoritative control-plane store and to emit audit entries before returning failures. 3) Harden KMS rotation path so reissued ephemeral credentials are atomically swapped with consistent cache invalidation (introduce a rotation epoch token). Rollout plan: - Patch to be deployed as hotfix to private control plane: rollout in canary (1 region) → staged rollout to remaining regions over 2 hours. - Monitor SSO error rate, authorization 2xx rate, and audit event completeness via dashboard. QA and validation: synthetic SAML assertions with hyphenated groups will be tested against canary clusters during patch window; stress test KMS rotation while simulating concurrent logins. Monitoring: target alert thresholds configured: SSO 5xx spike >50% baseline, RBAC 403 rate >3% of auth attempts for 10m. Rollback plan: if canary shows regression, revert control-plane binary and re-enable previous KMS rotation guard; customers will be notified. Postmortem and follow-ups: will include an exec summary, timeline, and action items (audit log backfill for missing entries where possible). Owner: Sofia Nguyen (ENG); PM liaison: Priya Singh. Estimated ETA for hotfix in prod: within 24 hours of ticket creation.
