[Reserved pool latency drift and elevated timeouts correlated with nightly background maintenance jobs]
description:
Issue summary:
BrightDocs reports elevated p95/p99 latency and intermittent 504 timeouts from their Dedicated reservation beginning 2026-03-09 22:00 UTC. The impact aligns with our cluster nightly maintenance window (22:00-23:30 UTC).

Impact:
- Customer-visible: increased request latency (p95 up from ~120ms to 1.1s, p99 spikes to 3.4s) and 504s for synchronous streaming requests.
- Affects production traffic for BrightDocs' reserved capacity in us-west-2 (dedicated pool ID: dp-56f9).
- Business impact: degraded UX during evening peak for customer; BrightDocs billing tier and SLAs flagged this as P1.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool: dp-56f9 (3 reserved nodes, GPU: A10G equivalent), auto-scale policy: min=3 max=6 scale_cooldown=300s, preemptible=false.
- Node image: node-agent-v2.14.1 (includes nightly maintenance agent).
- Models in use when issue observed: redwood-2.7b (chat), mistral-7b (reranking).

Steps to reproduce / Observed pattern:
1) Customer runs bursty workloads starting ~2026-03-09 21:45 UTC.
2) At ~22:00 UTC nightly maintenance jobs begin (node-agent orchestrates OS package updates, kernel GC, background log rotation and node-level checkpoint consolidation).
3) Within ~5-12 minutes of maintenance start, telemetry shows increased scheduler queue length and longer wait times for GPU contexts.
4) Customers see streaming disconnects and 504s; requests are retried by client at higher rates which amplifies the queue.

Logs / Metrics (examples):
- grafana: https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/serve/dedicated-pool-dp-56f9?orgId=1&from=2026-03-09T21:30:00Z&to=2026-03-09T23:30:00Z
- p95 latency (redwood-2.7b): baseline ~120ms -> spike to 1.1s at 22:07 UTC.
- p99 latency: baseline ~450ms -> spikes 3.4s, correlates with GPU context switch rate increase.
- node_exporter: write_iops spikes on /var/lib/checkpoints starting 22:02 UTC.
- nvidia_smi: transient GPU utilization drop and higher kernel launch latency reported on node-03 which is running the maintenance agent.

Expected behavior:
- Nightly maintenance should not interfere with serving-critical processes on reserved nodes; scheduling should prefer off-host maintenance or drain with graceful workload evacuation.

Additional notes:
- Customer has routing pinned to pool dp-56f9. Failover routing to other pools is possible but not enabled in their config.
- Similar timing pattern has been observed in other reserved pools in us-west during the same maintenance window (see linked issues).

comments:
2026-03-10 02:12 — Support (Aisha Patel): Opened ticket after BrightDocs support call at 23:00 UTC. Collected initial logs and confirmed correlation with nightly maintenance window.
2026-03-10 03:05 — SRE (Marco Li): Confirmed increased queue length and GPU context latency on node-03. Noted disk IO activity on /var/lib/checkpoints concurrent with spike. Hypothesis: maintenance agent performing checkpoint consolidation is contending for CPU/io and causing kernel/GPU latency.
2026-03-10 05:20 — Customer (BrightDocs - Emma Zhou): Provided request traces and mentioned they did not configure cross-pool fallback because they wanted data locality. Asking for mitigation options tonight.
2026-03-10 07:40 — Platform Eng (Diego Morales): Suggested immediate mitigations: 1) disable nightly maintenance on dp-56f9 for next 24 hours, 2) temporarily increase min nodes to 4 to provide headroom, 3) enable routing fallback to regional shared pool. Preparing an autoscaler patch to reduce cooldown acceleration during eviction events.
2026-03-10 09:15 — SRE (Marco Li): Actioned temporary disable of maintenance on dp-56f9 (change-id CHG-7882), increased min nodes to 4. Monitoring for next maintenance window.
2026-03-12 11:02 — Support (Aisha Patel): Customer confirmed improved p95 and no 504s during subsequent maintenance window after mitigations. Follow-up engineering work assigned for root cause and permanent fix.

investigation_notes:
Telemetry aggregated from Grafana and node logs indicates the main contention vector is node-level IO and scheduler preemption during checkpoint consolidation; this increases kernel launch latency observable in CUDA profiler traces.
nvprof sample (node-03, 2026-03-09T22:05): average kernel launch latency increased 6x vs baseline; GPU occupancy transiently drops suggesting CPU-side stalls rather than GPU load saturation.
Autoscaler behavior: min=3, observed burst increased active pods but autoscaler cooldown prevented quick scale up while nodes were blocked by maintenance-related IO, causing queue to back up.
Hypothesis 1: maintenance agent not respecting cgroup/ionice limits, performing high-priority IO on shared checkpoint disk, causing host CPU and I/O contention and delaying serving threads.
Hypothesis 2: node-agent triggers lightweight local checkpoint compaction on same disk backing model cache; compaction uses synchronous fsyncs that block the serving process's pagefault handling, increasing kernel scheduling latency.
Reproducibility: reproduced in staging by enabling maintenance job on a 3-node reserved pool while running a synthetic bursty workload; observed same p95/p99 drift within 6-10 minutes.
Cross-reference: SUP-642113 observed similar p99 patterns but was attributed to vram paging; this ticket differs because we see host IO spikes rather than GPU OOM activity.
Action items taken so far: disabled maintenance on customer pool for 48h, bumped min nodes to 4, queued autoscaler config change (PR referenced) to allow faster scale up when queue depth exceeds threshold.
Next step: instrument node-agent to respect ionice and CPU shares and implement a 'maintenance-drain' mode that triggers graceful evac prior to IO-intensive work.

resolution:
Workaround (applied 2026-03-10): Disabled nightly maintenance on dp-56f9 (CHG-7882), increased pool min nodes to 4 to provide immediate headroom, and offered enablement of routing fallback to BrightDocs. Customer accepted these temporary mitigations.
Permanent fix (planned): 1) Update node-agent to run background consolidation at low IO priority (ionice -c3) and within a cpuset/cgroup that avoids core serving processes. 2) Implement maintenance-drain mode that sets node to cordon and migrates active contexts before heavy IO. 3) Adjust autoscaler thresholds so scale-up can preempt maintenance windows if queue depth rises rapidly. 4) Add a monitoring alert for 'maintenance+queue correlation' to auto-trigger mitigations.
Deployment plan: node-agent change scheduled for canary on 2026-03-18, full rollout 2026-03-25 after performance validation. Autoscaler tuning PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/autoscaler/pull/98 (in review).
Follow-up: Postmortem and runbook update to be published to Confluence (link to be added). Assign owners: Diego Morales (node-agent), Priya Raman (autoscaler).

[Cross-tenant microthrottling causing intermittent throughput collapse in Dedicated pool (us-west)]
description:
Issue summary:
Customer QuantizeAI reports repeated short-duration collapses in sustained throughput on their Dedicated GPU pool in us-west. Over the last 36 hours they observed 3–8 minute drops where tail latency spikes and throughput falls to ~20% of provisioned capacity despite apparently healthy GPU memory and normal average utilization.

Impact:
- Customer report: production batch inference jobs degrade intermittently, affecting SLAs for their end users (timeouts and retries).
- Observable: request success rate drops, streaming connections get disconnected during drops, error rate (5xx) increases by ~4–6x during events.

Environment:

1) Run a steady stream of small requests (avg request size ~150 tokens) from multiple clients across tenants.
2) Add an intermittent burst generator that sends 400 short requests over 30s every 90s.

[Dedicated capacity GPU OOM eviction caused embeddings truncation and SLA exposure for Northfold Financial (post-incident follow-up)]
description:
Issue summary:
On 2026-02-23 at ~12:14 UTC Northfold Financial observed truncated embedding responses (lengths far shorter than expected) and a spike in 5xx errors for requests routed to their Dedicated GPU pool in us-east-1. This coincided with a sharp billing delta reported by the customer and active customer escalation to Support + CSM.

Impact:
- Customer-facing embeddings returned truncated vectors for ~14 minutes for ~8% of requests during the window.
- Several downstream ranking tasks degraded leading to visible product regressions for Northfold's customers.
- Billing meter showed a transient spike due to repeated retries and request replay behavior from the customer side.
- SLA exposure: several requests exceeded latency SLOs; customer flagged as enterprise and requested urgent remediation and credits.

Environment:
- Dedicated capacity (reserved pool) in us-east-1.
- Models: redwood-embed-compact-v1 pinned in customer config.
- Autoscaler set to conservative scale-up (min 2, max 6 GPU workers).

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Send batch embedding request set used in production (payloads ~2k tokens per request).
2) Observe intermittent truncated embeddings and 5xx responses logged by the client.
3) Replaying requests sometimes returned success after a retry.

Raw error snippets / logs:
- "runtime: eviction due to OOM: host node oom-kill, worker pid 11234 exit code 137" (serving-runtime logs).
- SRE dashboard: GPU memory pressure spiked to ~98% on host gpu-03c for the pool; kernel swap activity observed.
- Autoscaler logs: scaling action delayed by 67s due to coordinator contention.

Customer communication template used:
- Initial acknowledgement within 6 minutes. Provided incident short summary and time window.
- CSM called customer within 20 minutes and offered active monitoring and credits pending root cause.


investigation_notes:
12:16-12:25 UTC: Correlated customer traces with serving-runtime telemetry; 137 exit codes across two containers on host gpu-03c. Memory footprint increased with request sequence length.

12:30 UTC: Heap dump analysis (runtime team): rapid growth in KV cache retention for prefix keys during long embedding batches; appears to retain per-request tensors when quantized execution path triggers a fallback allocator.

12:40 UTC: Autoscaler logs show scale decision stalled due to scheduler lock contention (thread stack trace attached in internal ticket). The delay allowed memory pressure to reach eviction thresholds on the single affected host.

12:55 UTC: Observability team: discovered a mismatch between runtime's kernel-selection table and the new compact-embed quantization profile shipped in last week's rollout (release v1.14.2). The mismatch caused a fallback to a less memory-efficient kernel under specific shape/seq-length combos.

Hypothesis: Combined effect of (1) quantization-profile mismatch -> increased per-request GPU memory, (2) autoscaler delay -> slower pool growth, and (3) noisy neighbor on gpu-03c -> host OOM and evictions.

Evidence: PRs and release notes correlate: release v1.14.2 included compact-embed profile updates (PR #2890) merged 3 days prior. Host-specific logs show elevated memory for requests routed to gpu-03c vs gpu-03a/b.


resolution_notes:
Mitigation timeline: 12:34 UTC drained gpu-03c and restarted worker set -> immediate reduction in 5xx and truncation. 12:45 UTC autoscaler temporarily set to aggressive scaling (min 3 -> 5) for the pool until patch applied. Incident window considered closed at 12:38 UTC for customer-visible failures.
Permanent fix: Reverted the problematic kernel-selection fallback path in serving-runtime and updated the quantization profile mapping to ensure memory-efficient kernels are selected for compact embeddings. Patch merged: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/2987 (merged 2026-02-25).

SRE changes: Added a guard in dedicated-manager to avoid draining being delayed by scheduler locks; added an alert for 'autoscaler decision > 30s' which will create INT tickets automatically.

Customer remediation: Applied a goodwill credit for the affected billing window (one hour pro-rated) and offered a private postmortem review with engineers. Customer accepted credit and follow-up review scheduled.

Follow-up action items (tracked in CON-411):
- SEV-A: Backfill unit/integration test coverage for new quant profile -> owner: Priya R. -> due 2026-03-10.
- SEV-B: Improve autoscaler contention metrics & add circuit-breaker -> owner: Alex G. -> due 2026-03-05.
- SEV-C: Run dedicated pool soak test for compact-embed profile at scale -> owner: Ravi P. -> due 2026-03-08.

Customer communication notes: Drafted and shared detailed timeline and root cause (2026-02-25). Customer replied 'thank you for the fast response, please share post-fix soak results' and requested a follow-up call on 2026-03-02.

Closure: Incident marked Resolved after patch rolled to prod and soak results for 48h showed no recurrence (2026-02-26).

[Config surge: aggressive optimizer profile triggered tenant KPIs — mitigation & controlled rollback walkthrough]
description:
Issue summary:
An aggressive optimizer profile (experimental profile 'aggr-prefetch-v3') was enabled for BrightHealth AI tenant in Dedicated capacity. Within minutes we observed P95/P99 tail latency spikes and intermittent 5xx responses for long-sequence streaming requests.

Impact:
- Customer-facing latency increased: 95th latency rose from ~120ms to ~2.7s for token streaming paths.
- Spike in 5xx errors (503/504) and a few OOMs on one GPU node in their Dedicated pool.
- Production traffic was degraded for ~18 minutes before mitigations.

Environment:
- Dedicated GPU pool: dhp-dedicated-us-east-4 (A100s), tenant BrightHealth AI.
- Model: redwood-v2-7b pinned at version 2026-02-18.
- Optimizer profile applied: aggr-prefetch-v3 (changes: prefix KV prefetch enabled + target_batch_size from auto->256 + delayed flush window).

Steps to reproduce (approx):
1) Apply optimizer profile 'aggr-prefetch-v3' via console -> tenant overrides.
2) Send long-sequence streaming requests (~2048 tokens) with concurrent clients at 30 RPS.
3) Observe serving/runtime metrics for request queue length and KV cache hit/miss.

Observed behavior:
- Sustained queue growth on a subset of shards.
- KV cache evictions climbed rapidly; prefetch thrash and increased host<->GPU PCIe traffic.
- Autoscaler did not immediately pick up the pressure due to burst policy thresholds.

Expected behavior:
- Optimizer profile should improve tail latency for typical workloads and not cause sustained queue growth or OOMs.

Logs & metrics:
- Grafana dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/tenant-brighthealth/tenant-serving-overview?from=2026-03-10T14:00:00Z&to=2026-03-10T15:00:00Z
- Error logs sample: request_id=rcq_9f7a, 2026-03-10T14:07:12Z, "kv_cache_eviction_rate=0.86, queue_len=72, gpu_mem_free=1.2GB"
- Node OOM events: kube://dhp-node-17 (oom_kill)

Customer impact note:
Customer reported a critical degradation affecting a staging-to-prod migration gate for a marketing launch. They requested immediate rollback help and confirmation of a safe rollback path that avoids cold-start regressions.

comments:
Support (2026-03-10 14:12 UTC) - Asha Patel: Acknowledged. Opening incident, prioritizing P1. I requested immediate snapshot of optimizer config and tenant traffic split. Asked SRE for node health and autoscaler logs.
SRE (2026-03-10 14:18 UTC) - Jamie Liu: Observed increased PCIe and host memory churn on node dhp-node-17; several pods showing high iowait. Autoscaler didn't scale because average CPU across pool remained below threshold; queue growth happened on per-shard basis.
Customer (2026-03-10 14:22 UTC) - BrightHealth Oncall: We rolled the change back from our side but see residual 5xx on some requests. Need confirmation the profile is fully disabled per-tenant and whether traffic was routed to fallback model variants.
Support (2026-03-10 14:28 UTC) - Marco Ruiz: Confirmed profile unset at tenant override layer. Initiating controlled per-tenant snapshot restore and staged traffic isolation to remove prefetch hooks. Also applied temporary rate-limit to tenant token throughput to prevent immediate re-thrashing.
SRE (2026-03-10 14:40 UTC) - Jamie Liu: Performed a hot-snapshot restore of the last stable optimizer snapshot (2026-03-09T02:12Z) for BrightHealth tenant on 3 affected shards. Evictions fell and queue length returned to normal within 9 minutes.
Customer (2026-03-10 15:05 UTC) - BrightHealth Oncall: Confirmed latency recovered and 5xx reduced to baseline. Thanks. Requesting a short post-incident summary and recommended safe profile rollout checklist.
Support (2026-03-11 09:10 UTC) - Marco Ruiz: Created this ticket to capture the mitigation steps, findings, and recommended preflight checks. Added follow-up tasks for engineering to harden circuit-breakers.

investigation_notes:
Hypothesis: Aggressive prefetch + larger target batch size caused pathological cache churn for long-tail sequence distribution used by this tenant.
Telemetry shows per-shard queue growth rather than cluster-wide CPU pressure—indicates scheduler/placement sensitivity to sequence-length skew.
Autoscaler logic thresholds are average-based and lacked per-shard burst response—contributed to 10-15 minute reaction lag.
No evidence of code regressions in model runtime; related PR (runtime#4821) was experimental flags-only and toggles look correct.
KV cache metrics show increased eviction_rate from 0.05 -> 0.86 during incident window.
One node hit OOM; root cause was combined host memory pressure from prefetch buffers and larger batch kernel memory reservation.
Fallback routing did not trigger because the fallback policy only matches when node health is 'unhealthy' not on per-shard queue thresholds.

actions_taken:
Confirmed tenant override and immediately unset optimizer profile 'aggr-prefetch-v3'.
Applied temporary tenant-level token throughput throttle (reduce to 60% of baseline) to avoid immediate re-thrash during recovery window.
Hot restored optimizer snapshot (2026-03-09T02:12Z) to 3 affected shards to rehydrate stable KV profile and kernel settings.
Isolated routing: drained new connections from 2 noisy shards and rebalanced traffic across spare capacity nodes.
Filed internal engineering ticket to add per-shard queue-based autoscaler trigger (see linked issue SUP-82401).

workaround:
Step 1: Disable tenant optimizer override from Console -> Tenant -> Optimizer Overrides.
Step 2: If 5xx persists, apply immediate tenant token throttle: support API POST /admin/tenant/throttle {tenant_id, pct=60}.
Step 3: Hot-restore last-known-good optimizer snapshot using admin CLI: redwood admin snapshot restore --tenant <id> --snapshot 2026-03-09T02:12Z
Step 4: If node OOM observed, cordon and drain the affected node and restart pods after verifying kernel memory release.

resolution:
Rolled back tenant optimizer override, restored last stable optimizer snapshot to affected shards, applied temporary throughput throttling, and rebalanced traffic. Latency and error rates returned to baseline. Engineering to implement per-shard autoscaler triggers and a per-tenant optimizer gating rule before reintroducing aggressive profiles.

follow_up_tasks:
ENG-1258: Implement per-shard queue-length autoscaler trigger and test under synthetic long-sequence workload.
ENG-1259: Add optimizer profile gating checks in Console UI and disallow 'aggr-prefetch-v3' globally until safety validation completes.
DOCS-77: Publish a 'Safe Rollout' checklist for optimizer profiles (including prefetched memory budget estimation and per-tenant shadow runs).
SRE-404: Update incident runbook to include hot-snapshot restore steps and tenant throttle API examples.

customer_communication:
2026-03-10 14:14 UTC: Acknowledged incident and escalated to SRE. Requested temporary mitigation permission.
2026-03-10 14:30 UTC: Informed customer we were unsetting the optimizer override and applying a short throttle while we restore snapshots.
2026-03-10 15:08 UTC: Notified customer that metrics returned to baseline and recommended waiting 24h before reintroducing changes and to run the preflight checklist.

recommended_preflight_checks:
Run tenant-specific synthetic workload that matches 95th/99th sequence length distribution for 30 minutes.
Estimate KV cache memory impact via 'optimizer-sim --profile aggr-prefetch-v3 --tenant <id>' and confirm < 40% of host spare memory.
Enable profile in shadow mode for 1% traffic for 6 hours and monitor eviction_rate and queue_len per shard.
Ensure autoscaler per-shard triggers are enabled or manual escalation plan is in place.

[Crucible Health: inference latency spike + transient 5xx on /v1/generate (INC-9821)]
description:
Customer escalation relayed by Stephanie Nguyen. Crucible Health reported sudden latency spike and burst of 5xx on inference endpoint /v1/generate beginning ~2026-08-28 07:55 PDT. Reported impact: median latency increased from ~120ms to ~900ms; throughput dropped from ~250 req/s to ~150 req/s for Crucible production key; initial customer-observed 5xx rate ~8% during the window; multiple batches timed out and downstream throttles triggered. Customer had a critical demo at 10:00 PDT.

Immediate hypotheses (serving): autoscaler oscillation under burst + degraded single shard causing head-of-line blocking.

Immediate mitigations executed: emergency scale-up of dedicated pool (target +20% capacity) + temporary concurrency limit increase + drain suspected bad instance(s) + enable routing of new requests to compatible fallback model variant (lower context) to reduce per-token work.

Outcome (updated after investigation): improvements observed within ~9–12 minutes; throughput returned to baseline and tail latency normalized after draining the degraded node(s) and reverting autoscaler policy.

Updated root cause (post-incident): the triggering event was an autoscaler policy update that reduced stabilization/cooldown and interacted poorly with a burst in queue depth, causing scale oscillation. One GPU instance concurrently entered a degraded driver state (intermittent kernel launch stalls rather than a hard OOM), amplifying tail latency and increasing request timeouts which surfaced as 5xx at the gateway. The instance replacement lag plus oscillation extended the incident duration.

Impact (finalized): peak 5xx rate revised to ~6–8% (varied by minute) with ~10–12 minute period of elevated errors; throughput dipped to ~60% of baseline at trough. No evidence of data integrity or security issues.

alex_w: Heads-up — our pass@k smoke test is flaky after the q8 bring-up. Fails ~30% of runs with assert pass_at_5 >= 0.4. Happened on main CI and my local mac with the same container.

priya: repro steps? which model/quant?

alex_w: repro: checkout branch quant-q8, run `pytest tests/evals/test_smoke_metrics.py::test_pass_at_k_smoke -k pass_at_5` a few times. Sometimes passes, sometimes assert fails because exact-match count goes from 2 -> 1 across runs.

jamie: do we still sample predictions randomly during eval? Could be nondeterministic sampling.

alex_w: yep, eval runner uses rng.choice with replace=True in the quick sampling path. snippet from eval/runner.py:
```python
# eval/runner.py (simplified)
def sample_candidates(candidates, k, rng=None):
    rng = rng or np.random.default_rng()
    idx = rng.choice(len(candidates), size=k, replace=True)
    return [candidates[i] for i in idx]
```

lexi: replace=True will allow duplicates which changes pass@k semantics. pass@k (as used in our evals) expects k distinct attempts unless we explicitly use the stochastic estimator from the paper. If duplicates happen pass@k will be biased upward if the best answer repeats.

priya: also saw differences in BERTScore numbers between float32 and float16 quant runs last week. Small float noise pushed some items over the 0.87 threshold. We have several binary decisions that use a strict cutoff.

jamie: so two sources of flakiness: sampling-with-replacement + FP nondeterminism from quantization. both can flip exact-match counts and thresholded metrics.

lexi: quick mitigation proposals:
- make sampling deterministic in CI tests (fixed RNG seed + use numpy Generator seeded at test start)
- change sampling to without replacement for computing empirical pass@k (or explicitly call it sampled_pass@k if kept with replacement)
- normalize predictions before exact-match: unicode normalize, collapse whitespace, strip punctuation? document the exact normalization.
- for thresholded metrics (bert/rouge) use margin epsilon or run calibration over a small heldout set and assert ranges instead of hard cutoffs.

alex_w: agree. for the sampling change I tried this patch locally and it stabilizes the smoke test:
```diff
-def sample_candidates(candidates, k, rng=None):
-    rng = rng or np.random.default_rng()
-    idx = rng.choice(len(candidates), size=k, replace=True)
-    return [candidates[i] for i in idx]
+def sample_candidates(candidates, k, rng=None):
+    rng = rng or np.random.default_rng()
+    # sample without replacement for empirical pass@k (avoid duplicates)
+    k = min(k, len(candidates))
+    idx = rng.choice(len(candidates), size=k, replace=False)
+    return [candidates[i] for i in idx]
```

priya: +1 to that patch. but note: some downstream evaluations intentionally sample with replacement as part of ensemble-style estimator; we should preserve both modes with a flag and name them clearly.

jamie: good point. add param replace=True default False for the eval harness. tests should explicitly set rng=Generator(42) too. and update smoke tests to use deterministic seed.

import unicodedata
import re

def canonicalize_prediction(s):

    s = s.strip().lower()

[Private (On‑Prem) Backup/Restore + Audit Log Retention Guide (Day‑2 Ops)]
h1. Purpose
This page defines the supported backup/restore workflow and audit log retention/export patterns for *Redwood Private (on‑prem / restricted egress / air‑gapped)* deployments.

It consolidates commonly-audited requirements raised by regulated customers (e.g., healthcare) including:
- Encrypted backups with customer‑managed keys (CMK)
- Clear separation of *cluster recovery (Kubernetes/etcd)* vs *application-level restore (Redwood control plane)*
- Long-term audit log retention (7–10 years) with immutability/WORM patterns
- Evidence artifacts for auditors (manifests, checksums/signatures, restore validation reports, exporter gap detection)

h1. Scope and ownership model
h2. What Redwood backs up (application-level)
Redwood Private backups focus on *control-plane state and critical configuration* required for a deterministic redeploy:
- Redwood control-plane configuration database
- Redwood control-plane metadata/state required for tenant configuration and routing policy restoration
- Redwood-managed Helm release versions + values (for Redwood components)
- Redwood CRDs and Redwood-specific resources *as inputs to restore* (see pre-flight requirements)

h2. What Redwood does NOT back up
- *Kubernetes cluster recovery artifacts* (e.g., cluster-wide etcd snapshots) are owned by the customer’s Kubernetes operations practice.
- Request payloads, prompt bodies, and inference content are not included in standard control-plane backups.
- Raw secret material is *excluded by default* (see “Secrets handling”).

h2. Boundaries: etcd restore vs Redwood restore
Use two distinct runbooks:
1) *Cluster recovery (customer-owned)*: recover Kubernetes control plane (including etcd) when the cluster is corrupted.
2) *Redwood application restore (Redwood-supported)*: restore Redwood control-plane state into a *clean/rebuilt* Kubernetes cluster.

Important: Restoring etcd snapshots that include stale Redwood resources can create conflicts (e.g., stale finalizers, CRD/version mismatches). For DR validation, prefer a clean cluster + Redwood restore.

h1. Backup artifact format and integrity
h2. Backup artifact components
Backups are produced as an encrypted bundle with:
- A *manifest* containing: backup ID, timestamp, software version(s), format version, component list, checksums, and restore prerequisites.
- Encrypted payload(s) containing the backed-up control-plane data.

h2. Integrity and tamper evidence
- Each component is hashed; the manifest records checksums.
- As of Private Toolkit v1.8+, manifests can be signed using *Sigstore/cosign (offline key mode)*. (Older deployments may still use GPG signatures; both are supported during migration.)
- Optional policy: store backup artifacts in immutable/WORM storage for stronger tamper resistance.

h1. Encryption model (CMK, air-gap, KMS/HSM)
h2. Envelope encryption (DEK/KEK)
Backups use *envelope encryption*:
- Backup data is encrypted with a *Data Encryption Key (DEK)*.
- The DEK is wrapped by a *Key Encryption Key (KEK)* controlled by the customer’s KMS/HSM.
- Only wrapped DEKs are persisted; DEKs are intended to be ephemeral in memory.

h2. Supported key providers (on-prem)
The Private key provider interface supports:
- On-prem KMS services with an HTTP API via the provider layer
- HSM integration via *PKCS#11* (commonly used for Thales/Entrust setups) where operationally permitted

Notes:
- Exact compatibility depends on HSM policy (wrap/unwrap allowed, key types, network segmentation). Validate permitted operations early.
- Restore requires unwrap access; if the HSM disallows unwrap in the restore environment, restore will fail by design.

h2. KMS/HSM availability behavior
Default posture is secure-by-default:
- If KMS/HSM is unavailable at *backup time*: backup *fails* (default) to avoid producing artifacts that cannot be attested as encrypted under the customer KEK.
- If KMS/HSM is unavailable at *restore time*: restore fails because the DEK cannot be unwrapped.

A “break-glass local key” mode exists for specific non-production use cases, but it is *disabled by default* and requires an explicit configuration flag + logged approval.

h2. Key rotation expectations
Many regulated customers require annual rotation.
- Backups created under an older KEK remain decryptable as long as the ability to decrypt old wrapped DEKs remains available (e.g., KMS key versioning).
- If KEK versions are retired before the retention window, customers must rewrap or re-encrypt retained backups.

Operational guidance:
- Either retain KEK versions for the entire retention period, or schedule periodic rewrap to the active KEK.

h1. Secrets handling (secure-by-default)
h2. Policy
The design intent is: *backup references, not secrets*.
- The backup tooling excludes Kubernetes Secret values by default.
- Backups may include references (secret names, external secret paths, KMS key IDs) needed to rehydrate secrets from the system-of-record.

h2. If secrets exist only as Kubernetes Secrets
If a customer keeps secret material only in-cluster, they must implement a separate secrets DR strategy (customer-owned). Redwood will not silently include secret plaintext in control-plane backups.

h2. “Forbidden resource” validation
As of Private Toolkit v1.8+, the backup verification step checks manifests for forbidden resource types (e.g., Kubernetes Secret payload inclusion). Misconfiguration should fail closed.

h1. Storage targets and retention
h2. Where backups can be written
Backups can be written to:
- NFS (common on-prem default)
- S3-compatible object storage (recommended when immutability/object lock is required)

h2. Retention enforcement
Two layers exist:
- *Tool-level retention* (e.g., keep N days) is available for convenience.
- For regulated environments, prefer *storage-backend lifecycle policies* (harder to tamper with; supports dual-control workflows).

h2. Immutability/WORM patterns
Recommended patterns:
1) Backups: checksums + signed manifest + restrictive write permissions; optionally replicate to immutable storage.
2) Audit logs: export to object storage with immutability/object lock, or export to NFS then replicate to a compliance archive system.

Ownership: Redwood produces the backup/export artifacts and provides supported runbooks; customers own the archival platform and retention configuration.

h1. Restore workflow and validation (auditor-ready)
h2. Restore pre-flight checklist
Before restore, ensure:
- Target cluster is healthy and time-synchronized (NTP). If drift exceeds policy threshold, restore should warn or fail.
- Required CRDs exist at expected versions.
- KMS/HSM connectivity and unwrap permission is validated.

Default drift threshold guidance:
- Warn at >200 ms drift
- Fail at >1 s drift (customer may tune)

h2. Restore validation report
The restore workflow generates a report suitable for audit evidence. Typical fields include:
- Backup ID, backup timestamp, restore timestamp
- Backup format version, Redwood version
- KMS provider identifier (not keys), unwrap success/failure
- Checksums verified (yes/no) + counts
- Components restored + ordering
- Post-restore health checks executed and results

Post-restore validations commonly include:
- Control plane API readiness
- Ability to list tenants and read routing policy configuration
- Auth configuration loads successfully
- Dependency connectivity checks
- Optional smoke inference call (if a data plane is present and policy permits)

h2. Restore drill cadence (recommended)
For regulated environments:
- Quarterly full technical restore drill into a clean cluster (preferred)
- Monthly tabletop review of DR runbooks and access prerequisites
- Staging environment monthly technical drill is common when feasible

h1. Audit logs: export, schema, retention, and gap detection
h2. Audit event scope
Redwood Private emits audit events for control plane actions, including:
- Configuration changes
- Auth changes
- Administrative actions
- System events relevant to control-plane governance

Audit logs do *not* include prompt bodies by default. For PHI-heavy environments, prompt/request logging is typically disabled by policy.

h2. Export modes
Two common patterns:
1) *Near real-time* forwarding to SIEM for short RPO (minutes)
2) *Batch export* to durable storage for long-term retention and immutability

Supported batch export formats:
- JSON Lines (JSONL) with stable fields (timestamp, actor, action, resource, result, correlation IDs)
- Parquet (optional) for long-term cost/performance (where customers standardize on it)

h2. Export reliability and evidence
Exporter includes safeguards and evidence outputs:
- Cursor/checkpointing to avoid pagination gaps
- Metrics (Prometheus-style) including last-exported timestamp, event counts, failure counts
- Optional “gap detection” checks to flag missing windows

h2. Audit log RPO (cluster-loss window)
If audit logs are stored locally before export, cluster loss can create a loss window.
Best practice:
- Stream to SIEM with an RPO measured in minutes
- Run batch exports frequently enough to meet archival requirements

h1. Evidence pack: what Redwood can provide
Redwood-supported artifacts that customers commonly use for audits:
- Supported runbooks for backup/restore and audit export
- Backup job logs including backup IDs, timestamps, and outcome
- Backup manifest per backup (format version, component list, checksums)
- Signed manifest verification procedure (offline)
- Restore validation report outputs
- Exporter metrics and dashboards/alerts (or exported metrics snapshots)

Customer-owned complementary evidence typically includes:
- Tickets/change records showing scheduled execution and approval
- Storage lifecycle/immutability configuration screenshots or policy exports
- Access control/RBAC and HSM policy documentation (separation of duties)

h1. Least privilege and separation of duties
Recommended controls:
- Backup writer service account: minimum required read access + write-only (append-only where possible) to the backup target.
- Restore operator: can run restore workflows but should not directly access KEK unwrap permissions unless policy requires.
- HSM/KMS policy enforces separation: operators can initiate workflows; key custodians authorize unwrap.

h1. Air-gapped/offline bundle considerations
- Offline bundles are delivered as signed artifacts with checksums.
- No external network calls are required during install/upgrade in air-gapped mode.
- Telemetry is optional and should be disabled in air-gapped deployments.

h1. Operational FAQ (common customer questions)
- *Does the backup contain PHI?* Standard control-plane backups should not contain request payloads or prompt bodies. Audit logs can contain identifiers depending on configuration; treat audit archives according to your compliance classification.
- *Do you back up Kubernetes/etcd?* Not as part of Redwood control-plane backup. That is cluster recovery and remains customer-owned.
- *Can we prove backups/audit logs weren’t tampered with?* Use checksums + signed manifests; prefer immutable/WORM storage for audit logs.
- *What happens if KMS/HSM is down?* Backups fail by default; restores fail until unwrap capability is available.

h1. Change log
- 2026-03-10: Updated signatures guidance to cosign (offline) as primary; documented PKCS#11 HSM support; added JSONL+Parquet export options; clarified secure-by-default break-glass behavior.
- 2025-06-18: Added exporter gap detection and Prometheus metrics evidence recommendations.
- 2025-02-25: Initial publication based on regulated customer security reviews (on-prem backup/restore + audit retention requirements).
