[Token Economics & Tier Messaging: buyer-centric playbook]
Purpose
Purpose: give SDRs, AEs, PMs, and pricing owners a compact, high-utility playbook for: metric framing (why tokens), tier structure rationale, discounting guardrails, and quick competitive counters. Use this when drafting seatless proposals or prepping for pricing negotiations.

Audience
- Revenue (AEs, SDRs, Sales Eng)
- Product marketing / pricing
- Solutions engineers / CS for renewals

TL;DR (two-liners for quick copy)
- Why tokens: map price to actual usage so customers pay for what they ship, reduce surprise bills, and make economics explicit across features (chat, embeddings, reranking).
- Tiers: Design to align with buyer metric (dev adoption, production throughput, enterprise risk). Give clear commit incentives: deeper discounts for time-bound committed tokens and multi-region SLAs.

Core messaging pillars (short bullets to reuse)
1) Usage-aligned fairness: Tokens let teams correlate cost directly with value delivered (requests, embeddings, tokens generated) — better ROI visibility than seat or per-model vans.
2) Predictable economics: Commits + token pools convert variable usage into predictable unit economics while preserving scale flexibility.
3) Performance parity across modes: Same token currency across hosted, dedicated, and private — one accounting layer for ops and finance.
4) Operational controls: Budgets, per-route throttles, and token forecasting reduce surprise overages.

Metric-framing: translate technical metrics into buyer language
- Developer / Platform lead: "Tokens let us measure and forecast monthly usage per endpoint and correlate to product launches" -> emphasize fast experiment-to-prod and predictable unit cost.
- Product manager (feature ROI): Tie tokens per active-user feature to revenue uplift tests; show token-per-DIU (daily interacting user) estimates.
- Infra / SRE: Map tokens to GPU-hours and tail-latency budgets; explain commit sizing reduces burst risk and improves capacity guarantees for Dedicated.
- Procurement / Finance: Show token consumption models across scenarios (conservative / expected / aggressive) and equivalent dollar spend; highlight committed discounts and renewal step-downs.

Why token pricing? (talking points + metaphors)
- Analogy: tokens are to LLMs what compute hours were to cloud VMs — metric tied to consumption, flexible across instance types.
- Key benefits: granular visibility, decouples price from headcount (no per-seat friction), supports mixed workloads (short chat vs long generation vs embeddings) under one unit.
- Risk mitigation: token pools + alerting = no bill shock; rolling forecasts and auto-top-ups available.

When tokens are NOT ideal (acknowledge limits)
- Small teams wanting a blunt monthly price with no metering (offer a small fixed monthly package).
- Customers who demand per-user metrics for internal chargeback (we can provide per-route consumption dashboards that map tokens to users).

Tier design rationale (narrative + examples)
Goal: map tiers to buyer journeys and commit-intensity, not just raw token counts. Keep 4 tiers: Trial, Growth, Business, Enterprise.
- Trial: free tier with starter token credit (e.g., 200k tokens) + API keys, basic telemetry. Purpose: low friction eval and embedding experiments.
- Growth: pay-as-you-go with volume breaks and starter committed pool option (monthly tokens, modest discount). Targets: dev teams and early PLG motion.
- Business: for productizing features -> mid-size committed pools (quarterly or annual), feature flags (dedicated routing, higher retention), SLO credits.
- Enterprise: large commits, multi-region SLAs, private deploy options, custom audit/KMS, on-prem connectors and white-glove onboarding. Pricing: highest discounts for multi-year/volume/capacity reservation.

Discounting language & guardrails (sales playbook)
Principles:
- Default is list price; discounts are tied to commitments (term length, token volume, add-on services).
- Avoid ad-hoc % for convenience; anchor discount to a named program: e.g., "Commit Discount" or "Capacity Reservation Credit".
- Protect unit economics: define minimum unit price by tier; discounts must not drop below that floor.

Typical discount bands (guideline, internal only)
- Small commit (monthly, <10k USD): 0–5% (or none)
- Standard commit (annual, mid-size): 10–20%
- Large strategic commit (multi-year, large volume + private): 20–40%
- Additive for prepayment: +2–5% for upfront payment
- Implementation services / migration credits are separate line items, not part of token discounting.

Negotiation scripts (sample language)
- If customer asks for a flat % reduction: "We can wrap that into a Commit Discount — tell me the horizon you want to commit and we’ll map to the right program so you get billing predictability and a pricing break that scales with consumption."
- If procurement asks to move to per-seat: "We can provide per-user chargeback views, but tokens align cost directly with user activity and ensure you don’t pay for dormant seats."
- If concerned about bill shock: "We’ll set a soft cap, push alerts, and create a monthly forecast with you. You can choose to auto-top-up or stay within the committed pool."

Competitive analysis notes (how to counter common alternatives)
- Per-request pricing (competitor): sells simplicity but punishes heavy outputs. Counter: tokens more accurately capture cost variance by output length and model type.
- Per-seat pricing: simple for orgs with steady users but poor for public-facing products. Counter: tokens avoid paying for unused seats and scale with usage spikes.
- Flat model-specific pricing: can be cheaper for some patterns but lacks cross-model portability and makes model upgrades/broad use harder. Counter: tokens work across model variants and deployment modes; routing policies preserve cost controls.

Common objections & short rebuttals
- "We don’t want complexity": "We provide guardrails and default presets (monthly commit templates) so most customers never touch the knobs."
- "How do we forecast?": "Template scenarios + per-route historical metrics -> 3-point forecast (conservative/expected/aggressive) we share during the POC."
- "Tokens feel abstract": "We translate tokens into example calls (e.g., X tokens ≈ 1k chat messages at 80 tokens/msg) and provide a usage simulator in the console."

Examples & worked scenarios (one-pagers to reuse)
- Embeddings-heavy app: show tokens per embedding vector, batch sizing recommendations, projected cost per 10k vectors, compare commit vs PAYG.
- Chat assistant with long context: show average tokens per session, tail sensitivity, recommended commit levels to keep 95th percentile latency within SLOs.

Sales enablement snippets (copyable)
- Email opener: "We price by token so you only pay for what your app generates — commits get you discounts and predictable cost, while pay-as-you-go keeps it simple for early experiments."
- Demo line: "Let me show live how a single query maps to tokens and how the console forecasts month-end spend."

Portal / console features to highlight
- Per-route token dashboards, forecast simulator, commit vs usage visual, alerting/soft caps, token transfer between projects (governance controls).

Implementation notes for PM/engineers (short)
- Billing counter: Tokens should be recorded per model-call with labels for model, route, project, and org. Keep event-level logs for 90 days and aggregated metrics for 13 months.
- Export: CSV/BI connector for finance reconciliation. Provide a "token-to-dollar" monthly summary line for procurement.

Open questions & TODOs
- Define the minimum unit price floor per tier (finance + product to finalize).
- Build a simple usage simulator widget for the console (SE asks).
- Draft 1-pager for procurement that maps token scenarios to CapEx/Opex expectations.
- Finalize the public-facing discount bands and legal wording for SOWs.

Appendix: sample visuals to create (descriptions only)
- "3-scenario forecast" chart: conservative/expected/aggressive token consumption over 12 months.
- "Token anatomy" infographic: show how chat + embeddings convert into tokens and where batching helps.
- "Commit decision tree": asks to guide sales through commit size & term recommendations.

Notes to reviewer
- Please flag any competitive cases we missed (notable vendors using seat or flat-model pricing).
- Prioritize creation of the console simulator; SEs report it short-circuits most pricing objections.

End.

[OpenAI-compat: resilient chunking + tool-signal proxy for Responses v9 (seed passthrough & metadata routing)]
description:
Motivation: Customers using the OpenAI Responses family expect stable streaming semantics, reliable tool/function call signal delivery, and preservation of determinism hints (seed/RNG) and user metadata when we bridge from our internal Responses v9-compatible runtime to the OpenAI API shape. This PR adds a resilience layer that: 1) performs backpressure-aware chunking and reassembly for streaming frames to avoid partial json/toolcall corruption on slow clients, 2) proxies a lightweight 'tool-signal' envelope so function/tool-calling boundaries are deterministic across retries and reconnections, and 3) forwards seed/determinism flags and a subset of user metadata transparently through the compatibility layer.

What this changes (summary): consistent chunk framing and reassembly on the server and client-facing bridge; explicit tool-signal envelope that annotates tool-call start/end + unique tool invocation id; passthrough of 'rng_seed' and 'deterministic' attributes from our Responses request model into the OpenAI-compatible response attributes; metadata routing (user-provided tags/trace id) added to response attributes and to audit logs so downstream services (console, evals) see the same identifiers.

Compatibility notes: We keep the OpenAI-compatible surface stable for existing callers. Default behavior is identical unless callers set determinism/seed or rely on streaming reconnects; in those cases the bridge guarantees idempotent framing (replay-safe chunk markers) and consistent toolcall reassembly. There are small opt-ins: the 'tool-signal' envelope is only applied when callers include a 'enable_tool_signal' flag (default true for our hosted API). For private deployments customers can opt-out via config.

Checklist:
- [x] Server-side chunking + reassembly implementation
- [x] Tool-signal envelope design + tests
- [x] Seed/determinism passthrough plumbing
- [x] Unit tests for corrupted-chunk scenarios
- [x] Integration tests against the openai-compat test harness
- [x] E2E regression test in perf-canary
- [x] Docs + migration note (redwood-docs)

Related: linear/ENG-5272 (streaming reliability for responses bridge), ENG-5319 (toolcall idempotency). See design doc: https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-5272/openai-bridge-resilient-framing (internal).

review_comments:
Liam O'Connor: Overall approach looks good. Two requests: (1) add a short comment in stream_framer explaining the choice of 1KB reassembly window vs dynamic, (2) ensure the tool invocation id is cryptographically random to avoid collisions in multi-tenant setups.
Maya Chen (author): Added comment and switched the id generator to use crypto/rand with fallback to xoshiro for perf-sensitive paths. See stream_framer.go: lines ~78-110.
Sana Patel: The integration test is flaky on Windows CI (timeout on reconnect). Can we increase the reconnect window or make the test use the perf-canary harness?
Maya Chen: Moved the test to perf-canary harness and added retry/backoff stabilization. CI run passed on the rerun: https://ci.redwood.internal/runs/7981
Diego Ruiz: Small nit: audit_mapper should not copy full user metadata into logs. Limit to allowlist [trace_id,user_tag].
Maya Chen: Adjusted audit_mapper to redact non-allowlisted fields and added unit tests to verify.

release_notes:
Bridge for Responses v9: improved streaming resilience with backpressure-aware framing, deterministic toolcall envelope and rng_seed passthrough. Opt-out config available for private deployments. See docs for migration steps.

testing_notes:
Added unit tests for chunk corruption/reassembly, tool-signal replay safety, and seed propagation. Perf-canary scenario exercised reconnects at 50ms/200ms jitter. Manual smoke test performed against hosted API (create streaming chat + forced reconnect) and verified tool call reassembly and seed parity.

security_considerations:
Tool invocation ids are generated with crypto/rand to avoid predictability. We redact non-allowlisted user metadata from audit logs. No new permissions surface exposed by this change.

[OpenAI Responses v9 streaming: tool-signal + backpressure framing (post-merge notes)]
Context
- This doc captures updated notes after the merge of PR #62401 (OpenAI-compat: resilient chunking + tool-signal proxy for Responses v9) and what we learned in the first week of rollout.
- Audience: DevEx + Hosted API + Serving Runtime engineers supporting the OpenAI-compatible Responses bridge.

What shipped (still accurate)
- Backpressure-aware streaming chunk framing and reassembly to avoid partial JSON / partial toolcall corruption when clients are slow or reconnect.
- A lightweight tool-signal envelope that makes tool/function call boundaries deterministic across retries/reconnects.
- Passthrough of determinism hints (seed + deterministic) and routing of a limited set of user metadata (trace/user tag) into response attributes and audit logs.

Key updates since the PR description (newer / corrected)
1) Reassembly window sizing changed
- Original implementation notes referenced a fixed ~1KB reassembly window.
- In production we saw avoidable fragmentation for larger tool arguments (esp. JSON schema + long strings). Follow-up tuning (PR #62544) sets the default reassembly window to 2KB with a capped growth policy (2KB -> 8KB) when the framer detects repeated boundary splits.
- Rationale: keeps memory bounded under high fanout while reducing tool-arg split frequency.

2) Tool invocation id generation finalized (security + determinism)
- We kept crypto/rand for the tool invocation id (as requested in review) for collision resistance in multi-tenant environments.
- Important nuance: for replay/idempotency we do NOT re-randomize ids on reconnect. The id is generated once at tool-call start and then replayed deterministically from the stream state when resuming.
- We removed an earlier idea to use a deterministic hash of content because it risked leaking information across logs and increased accidental coupling to tool argument serialization.

3) Tool-signal enablement behavior changed (compat simplification)
- The PR text mentioned an explicit enable_tool_signal flag with default true for hosted.
- Based on customer confusion in early support tickets, we changed semantics:
  - Tool-signal is automatically enabled when tool calls are present (i.e., when the model emits tool-call events or the request includes tools).
  - There is no per-request enable_tool_signal flag exposed on the public OpenAI-compatible surface.
  - Private deployments can disable via server config: openai_compat.tool_signal_enabled=false.
- Result: fewer “why did my tool-call boundaries change when I forgot the flag” issues; keeps compatibility closer to OpenAI streaming expectations.

4) Seed / determinism naming alignment
- Internally we still accept rng_seed and deterministic on the v9 request model.
- On the OpenAI-compatible request surface we now accept both seed and rng_seed as synonyms (seed wins if both are provided).
- On the response side we do not echo the seed value back (to match common OpenAI patterns). We only preserve deterministic behavior server-side and include a stable system_fingerprint-like field when available.

5) Audit metadata allowlist tightened (privacy)
- The PR description said allowlist was [trace_id, user_tag].
- As of 2026-03-01 we also allow request_id (generated server-side) to help correlate reconnects without copying arbitrary user metadata.
- Final allowlist for audit logs and response attributes:
  - trace_id (if provided)
  - user_tag (if provided)
  - request_id (always generated)
- Everything else is redacted/dropped (including nested metadata blobs).

Rollout notes (what we observed)
- Windows CI flake: fixed by moving the reconnect scenario to perf-canary harness and loosening the reconnect deadline slightly (net effect: fewer false failures, no product change).
- Client reconnection behavior: the biggest practical win is preventing partial JSON parse failures when a reconnect happens mid-tool-args.
- Latency: median unchanged; p99 for very slow clients improved because we avoid repeated parse/retry loops. Slight CPU increase in the bridge (~1–2%) due to additional framing bookkeeping.

Known limitations / open questions
- If a client ignores replay markers and concatenates duplicate frames, they can still produce invalid JSON. We’re compatible with well-behaved clients; we should document the replay marker semantics more clearly.
- We still have a hard cap on buffered reassembly per stream; extremely large tool arguments can hit the cap and produce a controlled error. Need to decide whether we want partial tool-arg streaming support (probably not for v9 compat).

Operator checklist (current)
- Verify openai_compat.tool_signal_enabled=true in hosted envs.
- Verify audit logs only contain trace_id, user_tag, request_id.
- Ensure perf-canary scenario “responses_v9_stream_reconnect” is green before release cut.

Quick reference: linked work
- PR #62401: baseline implementation (framer + tool-signal + seed passthrough + metadata routing)
- PR #62544: reassembly window tuning, docs corrections for tool-signal enablement
- Linear ENG-5272: streaming reliability for responses bridge
- Linear ENG-5319: toolcall idempotency

[openai-bridge: stabilize streamed responses, pass seed hints, and enforce structured toolcall routing]
description:
Motivation: Customers using the OpenAI-compatible bridge reported intermittent stream truncation, mismatched tool/function call boundaries, and a missing surface for seed/determinism hints and URI-level metadata passthrough. This PR stabilizes the streamed Responses compatibility path, introduces a small 'seed_hint' passthrough that maps to our internal determinism toggle, and tightens the function-call routing to prevent partial-tool payloads from reaching backends.\n\nSummary of changes (single-string): Implement streaming chunk integrity markers and a reassembly helper in pkg/openai_compat/stream_repair.go; add a lightweight 'SeedHint' HTTP header and map to request.determinism.seed_hint in api/handlers/responses_compat.go; validate and coalesce tool/function call events in the compatibility layer to ensure a complete call object before proxying; add unit and integration tests that simulate delayed/fragmented SSE chunks; add docs and an example client for the new header and stable reassembly behavior.\n\nWhy this shape: We intentionally keep the compatibility layer idempotent and low-latency: the stream repair is a minimal-state reassembler that only buffers chunks up to a short timeout (configurable) and emits sequence-checked frames to the internal runtime. The seed_hint header is advisory and does not override model-side randomness when a model enforces a different determinism policy; it maps to our determinism hints used by routing and cache keys. Tool/function calls are now validated against a JSON-schema in the bridge before being forwarded to ensure downstream consumers don't get half-formed objects.\n\nChecklist:\n- [x] streaming reassembly helper implemented\n- [x] seed_hint header passthrough and internal mapping\n- [x] toolcall coalescing+schema validation\n- [x] unit tests for stream fragmentation and timeout behavior\n- [x] integration tests with the runtime mock and example client\n- [x] docs and example snippet added to docs/openai-compat.md\n\nCommit summary:\n- 0a1f2b3: pkg/openai_compat: add stream_repair with SeqID checks and CRC guard\n- 1b2c3d4: api/handlers: read \"SeedHint\" header and attach to compatibility request context\n- 2c3d4e5: compat: add toolcall coalescer + JSON schema enforcement\n- 3d4e5f6: tests/integration: add fragmented SSE and toolcall assembly tests\n- 4e5f6a7: docs: openai-compat.md examples and migration note\n\nFiles changed (high-level):\n- pkg/openai_compat/stream_repair.go (new) -- reassembly and validation helper\n- api/handlers/responses_compat.go -- header handling, schema validation, routing hints\n- compat/schemas/toolcall.json (new) -- minimal schema used for bridge validation\n- tests/unit/openai/stream_repair_test.go -- unit coverage for buffer timeouts and bad frames\n- tests/integration/openai/compat_stream_fragmentation_test.go -- end-to-end simulated SSE fragmentation against runtime mock\n- docs/openai-compat.md -- brief section on SeedHint, streaming guarantees, and example client\n- examples/compatible-function-calls.md -- example client flow showing reassembly resilience\n- go.mod/go.sum updates for added test deps\n\nIllustrative snippet (kept small):\n- stream_repair guarantees: each chunk must include a seq_id and either full_frame:true or continuation:true. The reassembler will merge continuations until full_frame:true is seen or timeout. Example pseudo: \n  {seq_id:123, continuation:true, payload:\"...\"}\n  {seq_id:123, full_frame:true, payload:\"...\"} \n\nReview conversation (summary thread stitched into one continuous narrative):\n- Ava Patel: \"Great direction. Can we avoid a global buffer limit that could OOM with adversarial clients? Suggest per-seq window + soft-limit eviction.\"\n- Maya Singh (author): \"Agreed, implemented per-seq window + configurable maxBytesPerSeq (default 256KB) and eviction policy that emits an incompleteness marker downstream for observability.\"\n- Liam Chen: \"SeedHint semantics need to be explicit in docs. Will this change cache keys?\"\n- Maya Singh: \"Docs updated. SeedHint is advisory only; we use it in deterministic routing decisions and as part of cache key derivation when present — noted in docs and tests. It will not force determinism for models that ignore it.\"\n- Sofia Romero: \"Tests look good; please add an integration test where the bridge receives interleaved toolcall chunks from two concurrent sessions.\"\n- Maya Singh: \"Added test (compat_stream_fragmentation_test.go) covering interleaved sequences and ensured per-session seq tagging prevents cross-session contamination.\"\n- Ava Patel: \"LGTM after CI green and a brief changelog blurb.\"\n\nCI summary: Build: pass, Unit tests: pass, Integration tests: pass, Lint: pass. One flaky test (tests/integration/openai/old_stream_retry_test.go) was flaky and unrelated; team filed a follow-up ENG-1501. All relevant checks for this PR passed on the final run.\n\nCompatibility notes and migration guidance:\n- This is additive for users of the OpenAI-compatible Responses path. Clients that already stream will see stronger continuity guarantees; the bridge may emit an explicit \"incomplete_frame\" event for severely fragmented inputs (monitoring surfaced).\n- New header: SeedHint: string. Example: SeedHint: \"seed-20260301-42\". This header will be preserved and surfaced in request metadata and used for cache keys when present. Do not assume it guarantees byte-for-byte determinism with third-party models.\n\nRelease notes (brief):\n- Stabilize OpenAI responses streaming by adding chunk reassembly and sequence checks\n- Add SeedHint header passthrough to support client-side determinism hints and better cache routing\n- Enforce complete tool/function call objects in the compatibility bridge to prevent partial-tool deliveries\n\nFollow-ups:\n- ENG-1501: flakiness cleanup for unrelated old stream retry test\n- ENG-1512: telemetry knobs for counts of repaired frames and dropped seqs\n\nMerge: Squash and merge to main. Merged at 2026-03-01 by Maya Singh.\n\nNotes: kept the bridge changes narrowly scoped to avoid touching the runtime Erlang-style router; this preserves our ability to roll back the compatibility layer independently if any customers see regressions.

release_notes:
Stabilize OpenAI streaming with chunk reassembly and sequence checks
Add SeedHint header passthrough for determinism hints and cache routing
Validate and coalesce tool/function calls in the compatibility bridge to prevent partial deliveries

notes_for_cherry_pick:
No runtime ABI changes; cherry-pick to release/2026-03 if backporting docs and handlers only. See migration guidance in docs/openai-compat.md

[Normalize OpenAI invocation envelope, clarify tool-selection signals, and add stream-resilient framing]
description:
Motivation: Several customers and internal evals showed inconsistent behavior when the OpenAI-compat layer returned tool selection signals (e.g. 'tool_choice' with ambiguous metadata) across streaming and non-streaming modes. This caused duplicate tool invocations, incorrect schema inference, and brittle downstream tool routers in Redwood Dedicated/Private deployments.

This PR introduces a deterministic normalization step for the OpenAI invocation envelope, plus stream-resilient framing for tool/message fragments. The goal is to: 1) make the compatibility layer emit a single canonical selection signal for every invocation, 2) map OpenAI tool schemas into a stable internal schema with minimal changes for existing customers, and 3) make streaming fragments idempotent and re-assemblable at the service edge.

What changed (high level):
- New package: pkg/openai/normalize_invocation.go — normalizer that transforms incoming OpenAI-style responses into Redwood's canonical InvocationEnvelope. It collapses multiple tool signals into one selected_tool hint and preserves tool confidence/metadata in a stable metadata map.
- Tool schema mapper: pkg/tooling/tool_schema_mapper.go — conservative mapping rules for OpenAI 'parameters' -> Redwood typed schema, including type coercion rules and a small whitelist for nested objects.
- Streaming: server/streaming/frame_parser.go updated to add fragment IDs and checksum headers for tool/message fragments. Parser now supports out-of-order fragments and dedup by fragment id+checksum.
- API layer: server/api/openai_adapter.go updated to call the normalizer before routing to tool routing pipeline; updates to response shape sent back to clients to maintain OpenAI wire-compatibility while ensuring a single 'selected_tool' semantic in the internal router.
- Docs: docs/openai-compatibility/invocation-normalization.md with migration notes and examples.

Compatibility notes:
- Outbound API responses remain OpenAI-compatible: we do not change the visible OpenAI fields returned to customers. Internally, however, the runtime will prefer the normalized 'selected_tool' hint to decide which tool to invoke. In the rare case of conflicting tool signals, the normalizer uses (in order): explicit_invocation field, highest-confidence tool_choice, then deterministic fallback to first available tool that matches schema.
- Customers who implemented custom tool routers based on raw tool_choice fragments should migrate to using the new normalized hint or consult the docs which show a 1-line change to switch to the normalized envelope.

Testing and rollout plan:
- Unit tests for mapping rules and type coercions included.
- Integration tests: simulated streaming sessions with fragmented tool metadata; verified idempotent assembler under network reorders.
- Canary rollout: staged to 10% of traffic for hosted API for 48 hours, then to Dedicated nodes behind a feature flag. Private installer includes an opt-in toggle for the first release cycle.

Migration steps for operators (short):
1) Review docs/openai-compatibility/invocation-normalization.md for the mapping table.
2) If you have custom routers, update to read the normalized 'selected_tool' header from the invocation payload.
3) Toggle feature flag if running Redwood Private/Dedicated during rollout.

Related work: links to internal Linear tasks ENG-7421 (tool-selection ambiguity), ENG-7553 (stream-fragment dedup).

Rationale for not changing public wire format: minimize breaking client changes while fixing internal flakiness in tool invocation semantics.

Release notes summary: Normalizes OpenAI invocation envelopes to ensure a single canonical tool-selection signal, improves streaming fragment resilience, and provides safe mapping rules for tool parameter schemas. Operators with custom routing should follow the migration guide in docs/openai-compatibility/invocation-normalization.md.


review_conversation:
Leo Carter (request changes): The mapping looks reasonable but I worry about nested parameter coercions. Can we add a strict-mode toggle for operators who want to reject coercions rather than coerce?
Asha Menon (author): Added a 'coercion_mode' config to tool_schema_mapper with 'permissive' and 'strict' options and documented it in the migration guide. Also added unit tests covering both modes.
Maya Singh (comment): CI initially failed on a flaky streaming test — I saw we added a small sleep in the assembler. Can we avoid sleeps and use deterministic signaling?
Asha Menon (author): Reworked assembler to use a fragment arrival map keyed by fragment-id+checksum and removed the sleep. Tests updated accordingly.
Rui Zhang (approved): Verified canary traces and the duplicated-tool incident no longer reproduces under the test harness. Approving for merge.

release_notes:
Normalize OpenAI invocation envelopes: canonical internal selection hint (selected_tool), stream fragment resilience (ids + checksum dedupe), and conservative tool parameter mapping with a strict/permissive toggle. No public wire-format breaking changes. Operators with custom routers should read docs/openai-compatibility/invocation-normalization.md for migration steps.

[gateway: ingress payload windowing + bounded fncall streaming to reduce memory/latency spikes]
description:
Context: We observed intermittent memory spikes and increased tail latency when many concurrent function/tool calls arrived as large initial payloads (tool params + long messages) on the gateway ingress. These events were correlated with long-lived streaming connections where the proxy would buffer large chunks while waiting for downstream runtime availability.

Motivation: Reduce gateway memory amplification and improve tail latency without breaking existing OpenAI-compatible streaming semantics. We need to limit per-connection and per-route buffered bytes, apply a small sliding "window" for ingress chunk acceptance, and surface clear backpressure behavior to callers and runtimes for graceful degradation.

Design summary: 1) ingress window: implement a sliding byte window per connection that caps buffered, unconsumed bytes to route-configurable max_payload_bytes and a new streaming_window_bytes (defaults: max_payload_bytes=1MB, streaming_window_bytes=128KB for OpenAI-compat routes). The window allows a few small chunks to stream through while preventing a single large upload from inflating memory. 2) fncall streaming bounds: when function/tool calling is detected (via content flags in the OpenAI-compat adapter), the gateway keeps a tighter default window and switches to chunk-prioritization: small chunks (<4KB) are preferred and put through immediately; large chunks are acknowledged with a 429-like backoff signal (X-Stream-Accept: delayed) and reflowed when capacity frees. 3) route-level overrides: new fields in route_defaults.yaml and per-route config to tune both limits and prioritization behavior. 4) observable signals: new metrics (gateway.ingress.windowed_bytes, gateway.ingress.backpressure_count) and a short human-readable reason code in responses when chunks are deferred. 5) compatibility: openai_adapter updated to interpret and emit the new small-chunk prioritization header and to surface a stable fncall handshake when chunks are deferred so SDKs can retry with smaller chunks.

Checklist: - [x] ingress window primitives and tests - [x] route config + defaults - [x] fncall prioritization logic - [x] adapter compatibility changes + unit tests - [x] integration test that simulates many concurrent fncall streams with mixed chunk sizes - [x] docs and release notes

Testing: Added gateway/tests/streaming_integ_test.go that spins up a simulated runtime and opens 300 concurrent streams mixing small/large payloads. Verified memory usage under the new defaults is stable and tail P99 latency drops ~35% in our stress harness. CI initially failed the integration flakily due to a timing assumption; fixed by adding backpressure delay jitter handling and reran checks.

Rollout plan: feature flag gated under "gateway.ingress.windowing.v2". Default enabled on staging, will flip in prod after 48h of staging telemetry. If early signals show increased client errors we will lower streaming_window_bytes for OpenAI-compat routes and push a hotfix to relax prioritization.

Backward compatibility: No breaking API changes. OpenAI-compatible streaming still follows same framing; we add advisory headers and observable reason codes. SDKs are recommended but not required to honor the backpressure headers. Documented behavior in docs/gateway/payload-policies.md.

review_comments:
Diego: Can we make the 4KB small-chunk threshold configurable at route-level? I think mobile clients may prefer 8KB. (resolved: added route override)
Lina: The metric names look fine but add a tag for route.id so we can filter noisy tenants. (resolved)
Samir: Integration test flaked on 2nd CI run, I saw a flakiness because of tight timing; ask authors to add jitter. (resolved)
Asha: responded with implementation notes and added jitter + route tag in metrics

release_notes:
Gateway: add ingress streaming window and fncall prioritization to reduce memory amplification and improve tail latency for streaming function/tool calls. Defaults tuned for OpenAI-compatible routes; route overrides available.

[AWS Marketplace procurement + security FAQ (2026)]
## Overview
This page is the current internal FAQ for answering enterprise buyer questions about purchasing Redwood Inference through AWS Marketplace (public offer vs private offer), and the most common security/compliance questions (SOC 2, encryption/KMS, retention, audit logs, data residency, incident response, and SSO/RBAC).

This content is used by AEs/SEs for deals where the customer prefers AWS Marketplace so spend can count toward AWS commitments (e.g., EDP) and to streamline vendor onboarding.

---

## What customers typically ask for (quick list)
- Why buy via AWS Marketplace (EDP/committed spend, consolidated invoicing) and when to use a private offer.
- SKU fit: Hosted API now, Dedicated capacity later, and when Private (VPC) is required.
- Metering and billing: dimensions (tokens/requests), reporting cadence, and invoice visibility.
- Security questionnaire items: SOC 2 posture, encryption/KMS, retention controls, audit logs, data residency, incident response, and SSO/RBAC.
- Shared responsibility boundaries for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private.
- Onboarding flow: subscription → entitlement validation → org provisioning/linking → first API key → first call.
- Support and escalation expectations for marketplace customers.

---

## Marketplace procurement FAQ

### Q: Public offer or private offer?
**Recommended for enterprise: Private offer.** Private offers allow us to align term length, committed spend constructs, and any deal-specific exhibits (e.g., security addendum, DPA references) while still using Marketplace as the procurement channel.

**Public offer** (pay-as-you-go) is typically used for small pilots or when procurement does not require an order-form-like artifact.

### Q: Does Marketplace spend count toward AWS commitments (e.g., EDP)?
In most enterprise cases **yes**, but eligibility is determined by the customer’s AWS agreement and how the offer is accepted. When asked, we should state:
- We structure offers using standard AWS Marketplace constructs.
- The customer should confirm EDP crediting mechanics with their AWS account team.
- Redwood can loop in our AWS partner contact if needed to validate mechanics for the customer.

### Q: What information do we need to create a private offer?
Provide the customer the intake checklist and collect:
- Buyer AWS account ID(s) that will accept the offer
- Preferred AWS region(s) for processing (and any single-region requirement)
- Requested start date
- Term length (12 months is most common)
- Commercial structure (committed spend target, prepay vs monthly, overage expectations)
- Required legal/security exhibits (DPA, breach notification language, subprocessor references)
- Signatory / procurement contact

**Internal note:** The current intake path is the “AWS MP Private Offer Intake” Salesforce form (ask Deal Desk for the latest link).

### Q: What is the onboarding flow after subscription?
Typical flow:
1) Customer subscribes/accepts the offer in AWS Marketplace.
2) AWS sends an entitlement to Redwood.
3) Customer signs into the Redwood Console and links the Marketplace subscription.
4) Customer creates or links a Redwood org.
5) Customer generates an API key and makes a first test call.

**Entitlement timing (updated):** Most entitlements propagate in **5–20 minutes**. In rare cases it can take longer (up to a few hours) depending on AWS-side propagation.

**If entitlement is delayed:** Customer should contact Redwood support first. We can confirm whether we received the entitlement and can trigger a re-sync using the subscription/entitlement identifier.

---

## SKU + deployment model FAQ

### Q: What’s the difference between Hosted, Dedicated, and Private?
- **Hosted:** Fastest start. Shared infrastructure with tenant isolation controls. Usage-based metering via Marketplace. Best for pilots and many production workloads.
- **Dedicated:** Reserved capacity for predictable throughput and stronger isolation. Often adopted after a successful Hosted pilot.
- **Private (VPC):** Redwood runs in (or is tightly attached to) the customer’s network boundary. Best for strict network controls, VPC-only access, and certain key management/residency requirements.

### Q: Shared responsibility (what we own vs what the customer owns)
- **Hosted/Dedicated:** Redwood operates the service, core security controls, and platform availability. Customer configures org access (SSO/RBAC), API key practices, and application-layer security.
- **Private:** Customer owns more of the network boundary and can own more of the key management and logging pipeline depending on architecture. Redwood still owns application security and platform components we operate.

---

## Security & compliance FAQ (common questionnaire items)

### Q: Do you have SOC 2 Type II?
**Yes.** Redwood maintains a current SOC 2 Type II report.
- We provide access via our trust portal with controlled access.
- For Marketplace reviews, we also provide a security overview packet that maps major controls without distributing the full report broadly.

### Q: ISO 27001?
Redwood is aligned to ISO 27001 control areas and maintains a formal security program. If a customer specifically requires an ISO certificate, route the request to Security/Compliance to confirm the current status and appropriate response for the deal.

### Q: Encryption in transit and at rest (what TLS versions)?
- **In transit:** TLS **1.2+** (TLS 1.3 supported for modern clients where applicable). API and console require HTTPS.
- **At rest:** Encrypted storage layers.

### Q: Do you support customer-managed KMS keys (BYOK)?
**Updated guidance (2026):**
- **Hosted:** Customer-managed KMS is available for enterprise tenants in select regions as an add-on, using per-tenant key configuration (subject to feasibility review). If not available in the target region, the default is provider-managed keys.
- **Dedicated:** Customer-managed key options are available for many Dedicated configurations.
- **Private (VPC):** Customer-managed keys are supported and typically the recommended path when BYOK is a hard requirement.

If asked for a simple statement: “Hosted uses provider-managed keys by default; customer-managed keys are available for certain enterprise configurations; Private/VPC supports customer-managed keys.”

### Q: Do you store prompts and completions? Can retention be set to zero?
We should avoid vague language. Use these points:
- Redwood does **not** use customer prompts/outputs to train models.
- Redwood retains limited metadata required for service reliability, abuse prevention, billing reconciliation, and security investigations.
- **Content retention controls:** Enterprise configurations can disable content logging and minimize content persistence.

**Updated retention guidance (2026):**
- Default for enterprise Hosted is **content logging disabled** unless explicitly enabled for debugging.
- Minimal operational/billing metadata is retained per policy; the retention window is documented in the “Data Handling & Retention” attachment for Marketplace buyers.
- “Retention = 0” should be positioned as “no persistent storage of request/response content,” while acknowledging that transient in-memory processing is required to serve the request.

### Q: Audit logs (what events exist, can we export to Splunk)?
Redwood provides audit logging for admin actions and auth events, such as:
- User invites and role changes
- SSO configuration changes
- API key creation/revocation
- Model deployment/config changes (where applicable)
- Policy/config updates

**Export options (updated):**
- API-based export is supported.
- Standard integrations include export to customer SIEM pipelines (Splunk commonly) and/or customer-owned storage (e.g., S3) depending on deployment and plan.

**Immutability/WORM:** Redwood maintains integrity controls. If the customer requires WORM/immutable retention guarantees, the recommended approach is exporting logs to the customer’s immutable store where they enforce WORM retention.

### Q: Data residency / region restriction (e.g., US-only, us-east-1 only)
- Redwood can support regional processing commitments within the set of available regions for the customer’s SKU.
- If the customer requires strict single-region processing (e.g., **us-east-1 only**), confirm feasibility for the specific SKU and put the commitment in writing (private offer exhibits / order form language) referencing the data handling documentation.
- For Private (VPC), data residency aligns to the customer’s chosen region and architecture.

### Q: SSO / SAML / RBAC
- Enterprise orgs support SSO/SAML.
- Console access is governed by RBAC.
- API keys are scoped and can be managed per org/project practices.

### Q: Incident response and breach notification timelines
Redwood maintains an incident response program with defined severities and notification processes. Specific notification timelines are typically addressed contractually; route strict requirements to Legal + Security/Compliance.

### Q: Subprocessors
Redwood maintains a current subprocessor list and shares it through the security packet/trust portal. Scope varies by Hosted vs Private (Private can reduce reliance on some subprocessors depending on the customer architecture).

### Q: Private connectivity (VPC endpoints / PrivateLink)
- **Private (VPC):** Supported.
- **Hosted:** Generally accessed over public internet with TLS. If the customer has strict network controls requiring private connectivity, position **Private** as the intended solution.

---

## Metering, billing, and FinOps FAQ

### Q: What are the metering dimensions?
Metering is usage-based and expressed in AWS Marketplace dimensions (commonly token-based for generation and embeddings units depending on SKU). The exact dimension names are included in the offer and listing details.

### Q: How quickly does usage show up in AWS billing / Cost Explorer?
**Updated guidance (2026):** Marketplace metering is not real-time. Customers typically see updates within **hours to ~24 hours** depending on AWS billing pipelines.

### Q: Does Redwood provide usage reporting that matches the AWS invoice?
Yes. Redwood provides org-level usage reporting (e.g., by project/model/route) and supports reconciliation with Marketplace billing line items.

---

## Standard next steps for an enterprise Marketplace deal
1) Send the customer the Marketplace security packet and short-form security FAQ.
2) Provide trust portal access instructions for SOC 2 (as needed).
3) Collect buyer AWS account IDs, region constraints, term/start date, and commercial preferences.
4) Draft and route the private offer internally (Deal Desk) and then to the customer.
5) Book a technical deep dive if the customer requests detail on audit logs, retention controls, or entitlement troubleshooting.

---

## Internal escalation and ownership
- Security/compliance questionnaire, SOC 2 access, retention/residency commitments: **Security & Compliance (Naomi Feldman)**
- Marketplace entitlement/provisioning issues and onboarding flow: **Solutions Engineering (Markus Klein)**
- Private offer structure, term/commit mechanics, and procurement timelines: **Account Team / Deal Desk (primary AE: Stephanie Nguyen)**

[Marketplace SKU Catalog v2 (AWS + GCP) — Hosted, Dedicated, Private, Add-ons]
## Overview
This document defines Redwood Inference’s **Marketplace SKU Catalog v2** for AWS Marketplace and GCP Marketplace.

The catalog is designed to:
- Map cleanly to Redwood’s internal billing meters and entitlements (no “special marketplace-only plans” in product).
- Support enterprise procurement patterns (usage-based, commits, reserved capacity, and Private licensing).
- Reduce buyer confusion by aligning names across clouds: **Hosted** vs **Dedicated** vs **Private**, plus add-ons.

This is the source of truth for:
- SKU naming conventions
- Inclusions/exclusions
- Marketplace billing dimensions → internal meters
- Entitlement semantics used by provisioning and metering

---

## Scope
**In scope:**
- Hosted API (usage-based) SKUs
- Dedicated capacity (reserved) SKUs
- Private deployment (license) SKUs
- Compliance + observability add-ons sold via marketplace

**Out of scope (handled via private offers / order forms as needed):**
- Custom model onboarding fees
- One-time professional services
- Complex multi-year ramp schedules (documented in private offer templates)

---

## SKU naming conventions
We need names that work in:
- AWS Marketplace product/offer UIs (title length limits, readability)
- GCP Marketplace listings (SKU + plan naming constraints)
- Internal billing catalog (stable identifiers)

### 1) Human-readable SKU names (customer-facing)
Format:
- **Redwood Inference <Product> — <Plan>**

Examples:
- “Redwood Inference Hosted — Pay-as-you-go”
- “Redwood Inference Dedicated — Reserved GPU Capacity”
- “Redwood Inference Private — VPC/On‑prem License”

Rules:

[Runtime release pipeline: rollback procedure]
h1. Summary
This page documents the standard and emergency rollback procedure for Serving Runtime deployments to *Hosted* and *Dedicated* environments using Redwood release tooling.

h1. Definitions
* *Runtime release tag*: immutable identifier for a runtime build (example: runtime-release-2025.02.01)
* *Hosted*: multi-tenant regional fleets
* *Dedicated*: per-tenant or per-cluster fleets
* *Rollback*: re-pin the deployment to a previous runtime release tag

h1. Preconditions
* You have prod deploy permissions (see Access & Permissions).
* You know the rollback target tag and it is present in the artifact registry.
* For customer-impacting changes, an incident exists OR an emergency change is logged.

h1. Rollback workflow (high level)
# Pause progressive rollout controller
# Pin runtime release tag to rollback target
# Trigger redeploy
# Verify health and metrics
# Document outcome in incident/change record

h1. Hosted rollback (regional fleets)

## Step 1: Pause any in-flight rollout
In #eng-releases, ask the release captain to pause the rollout, or do it directly:
* Command (example):
  `rw-release pause --service serving-runtime --env hosted-prod`

## Step 2: Pin runtime release tag
* Command (example):
  `rw-release set-tag --service serving-runtime --env hosted-prod --tag runtime-release-2025.01.17`

## Step 3: Redeploy
* Command (example):
  `rw-release deploy --service serving-runtime --env hosted-prod --regions us-east-1,us-west-2,eu-central-1`

## Step 4: Verify
Minimum verification before declaring rollback complete:
* 5xx < 0.5% for 10 minutes
* ttft_p95_ms within 10% of 7-day baseline
* gpu_oom_count returns to baseline (or zero)

## Step 5: Lock the tag (to prevent auto-advance)
If the progressive delivery controller is configured to auto-advance, apply the lock:
* `rw-release lock --service serving-runtime --env hosted-prod --reason "Emergency rollback stability hold"`

h1. Dedicated rollback (tenant clusters)

## Step 1: Identify impacted clusters
Use the Console dashboard "Dedicated / Runtime Release Adoption" and confirm the cluster names (e.g., ded-use1-a, ded-euc1-b).

## Step 2: Pin tag per cluster
* `rw-release set-tag --service serving-runtime --env dedicated-prod --cluster ded-use1-a --tag runtime-release-2025.01.17`

## Step 3: Redeploy per cluster
* `rw-release deploy --service serving-runtime --env dedicated-prod --cluster ded-use1-a`

## Step 4: Customer-sensitive tenants
If a tenant has special comms requirements (regulated / premium SLA), coordinate with CS before or immediately after action depending on SEV level (see comms guide).

h1. Evidence to capture
Record these in the incident channel and/or emergency change ticket:
* Job URLs from CI/CD
* Regions/clusters affected
* Old tag and new tag
* Start/end times
* Verification results

h1. Common pitfalls
* Picking a rollback target that is not compatible with the current model set (check model registry notes).
* Forgetting to lock the tag, causing auto-advance to reintroduce the bad release.
* Rolling back only some regions, leaving cross-region routing sending traffic into degraded pools.

h1. Related
* Emergency rollback runbook (runtime-owned)
* Emergency change policy (approvals)


[Emergency rollback: Serving Runtime (Hosted + Dedicated)]
h1. Purpose
This runbook describes how to perform an *emergency rollback* of the Serving Runtime release across *Hosted* and *Dedicated* fleets. It focuses on restoring SLOs safely and quickly while preserving evidence for later analysis.

h1. When to rollback (triggers)
Rollback is appropriate when one or more is true and mitigation is not available within ~30 minutes:
* p95 *time-to-first-token (TTFT)* regression > 30% in 2+ regions for 10+ minutes
* error rate > 2% on generation routes due to runtime (5xx, timeouts, OOM)
* canary cohort shows sustained degradation and traffic shift cannot be halted cleanly
* repeated GPU OOM or kernel crash loops attributable to the new runtime build

*If unsure*: declare an incident and page Runtime + SRE (see incident process) and start preparing rollback steps in parallel.

h1. Preconditions
* An incident has been declared if customer impact is confirmed or likely (see SEV process page).
* Runtime oncall has identified *candidate rollback target* (prior runtime release tag).
* Release engineer or infra oncall is available to execute the pipeline rollback (see CI/CD rollback doc).

h1. Ownership and roles
* Incident Commander (IC): owns the decision to rollback and comms cadence.
* Runtime oncall: validates technical root cause hypothesis and rollback target.
* Release/Infra oncall: executes the rollback in deployment tooling.
* SRE: monitors fleet-level SLOs and regional health signals.

h1. Rollback decision checklist
Before executing rollback, capture in the incident channel:
# Current runtime release identifier (e.g., runtime-release-2025.02.01)
# Intended rollback target (e.g., runtime-release-2025.01.17)
# Blast radius (Hosted regions; Dedicated clusters/tenants)
# Primary symptom (TTFT, throughput, 5xx, OOM)
# Confirm the prior release is known-good (at least 24h stable in prod)

h1. Step-by-step procedure

## 1) Freeze rollout / stop further progression
* If a rollout is in progress, *pause* it immediately (do not continue canary expansion).
* Ensure no automated progressive delivery job will re-advance the rollout.

## 2) Hosted rollback (global fleets)
Follow the CI/CD rollback doc to pin the Hosted runtime to the rollback target, then:
* Roll back in this order:
  # non-critical region (if any still on canary only)
  # remaining canary cohort
  # all regions currently on the bad release
* After each region completes, verify:
  * 5xx rate normalizes
  * GPU utilization returns to expected
  * TTFT and token/s recover to baseline

Hosted verification queries (Console):
* Dashboard: "Hosted Inference / Runtime Release Health"
* Metrics to watch: request_error_rate, ttft_p95_ms, tokens_per_sec, gpu_oom_count

## 3) Dedicated rollback (tenant clusters)
Dedicated rollbacks must consider customer-specific change windows and comms. In emergencies, proceed under the emergency change policy.
* Identify impacted Dedicated clusters/tenants:
  * Check "Dedicated / Runtime Release Adoption" dashboard
  * Confirm whether each tenant is on the bad release
* Execute rollback per cluster using the pipeline rollback procedure.
* For high-sensitivity tenants, coordinate with CS for outbound comms and approvals (see comms guide).

## 4) Post-rollback validation
* Keep the incident open until metrics are stable for 30 minutes (Hosted) / 60 minutes (Dedicated)
* Confirm request latency distributions return to baseline and no new error modes appear
* Ensure autoscaling stabilizes (watch for over-provisioning due to the regression)

h1. Guardrails and common failure modes
* If rollback target also shows elevated OOMs, stop and reassess (may be traffic pattern or model mix).
* If only one model family is impacted, consider temporarily routing to a compatible variant instead of fleet rollback (requires IC approval).
* Avoid rapid flip-flopping between releases; if you must re-roll forward, document the reason and require runtime lead approval.

h1. Required artifacts (for later review)
Capture links in the incident channel:
* CI/CD job link(s) for rollback
* Affected regions / clusters
* Metrics screenshots or dashboard permalinks
* Any customer comms sent

h1. References
* SEV process for runtime regressions (incident roles, paging, timelines)
* Runtime release pipeline rollback procedure (exact CI/CD steps)
* Emergency change policy (approvals and documentation)
* Customer/status comms guide (templates and approval chain)


[Emergency change policy (production)]
h1. Policy statement
An *emergency change* is a production change required to mitigate an active or imminent customer-impacting incident. Emergency changes are allowed to bypass standard change windows and review timelines, but must meet the approval and documentation requirements below.

h1. Examples
* Emergency rollback of a Serving Runtime release
* Disabling a faulty feature flag causing elevated 5xx
* Routing traffic away from a degraded region

h1. Minimum required approvals
Emergency changes require at least one of:
* Incident Commander approval (for an active incident), OR
* SRE oncall approval (if no IC assigned yet)

Additional required approvals:
* If the change impacts *Dedicated* customers with premium SLAs: CS oncall or Account Owner must be notified as soon as practical.
* If the change touches authentication, RBAC, audit logging, or encryption: Security oncall must approve.

h1. Documentation requirements
Within 24 hours of the emergency change:
* Create or update the incident record with:
  * what was changed
  * when it was changed
  * who approved
  * verification results
* Link the CI/CD job(s) and dashboards used to validate recovery

h1. Post-change review
* SEV1/SEV2 emergency changes require a postmortem
* During the postmortem, document why standard change management was bypassed and what guardrails will prevent repeat issues

h1. Interaction with releases
If an emergency change is a rollback:
* Pause progressive delivery
* Pin the release tag
* Lock auto-advance until the incident is resolved

h1. References
* Incident SEV process
* Runtime rollback runbook
* Runtime release pipeline rollback procedure


[Runtime incident customer communications (status page + direct customer updates)]
h1. Purpose
This page describes the required communications for Serving Runtime incidents, including regressions that lead to an emergency rollback.

h1. Who owns comms
* Comms Lead: typically Customer Success oncall (or Support lead after-hours).
* IC approves external messaging for SEV1/SEV2.
* For Dedicated premium SLA tenants, Account Owner must be looped (sales/CS) even during SEV1.

h1. When to post to the public status page
* SEV1: post within 15 minutes of declaration if there is confirmed customer impact in Hosted or multiple Dedicated tenants.
* SEV2: post if impact is user-visible and expected to last > 30 minutes, or if many customers are likely to notice.
* Never post for canary-only SEV3 issues unless instructed by IC.

h1. Required content (status page)
Include:
* What customers observe (symptoms)
* Affected product surface (Hosted API, Dedicated clusters)
* Regions (if known)
* Current mitigation (e.g., paused rollout, rolling back runtime)
* Next update time

h1. Dedicated customer notifications
For Dedicated incidents, in addition to status page (if applicable):
* Email the impacted tenant distribution list and open a support ticket on their behalf (if not already open).
* If the customer has an on-call bridge procedure, ask them to join once we have an ETA or a mitigation plan.

h1. Templates

## Initial status page post (SEV1)
"We are investigating elevated error rates and increased latency affecting the Redwood Inference API in some regions. We have paused the current Serving Runtime rollout and are preparing mitigations. Next update in 30 minutes."

## Update when rollback begins
"We identified a regression in a recent Serving Runtime release and have started an emergency rollback. We are monitoring recovery metrics across regions and will provide an update within 30 minutes."

## Resolved
"The issue has been mitigated and service metrics have returned to normal following a rollback. We will publish a post-incident review."

h1. Approval checklist
Before sending customer-facing comms:
* IC has reviewed the wording
* Do not speculate root cause
* Do not share internal release tags or cluster names unless customer-specific and approved
* If security is suspected, follow the security incident process instead


[memory-pressure-incident-triage-and-recovery-playbook-2026]
Summary:\n\nThis runbook describes detection, triage, mitigation, and recovery procedures for GPU and host memory pressure incidents affecting the Redwood serving runtime. It centralizes observable signals, automated mitigations, manual steps, rollback guidance, and post-incident analysis templates. It is intended for on-call SREs, runtime engineers, and the serving runtime owners.\n\nScope and intent:\n- Applies to production and pre-prod clusters running the runtime (hosted and dedicated).\n- Covers transient memory spikes, sustained memory leaks, KV cache bloat, and OOMs that surface as request failures, elevated tail latency, or node instability.\n- Does NOT replace component-specific leak-fix investigations (those belong in an RCA). This is an operational triage and recovery playbook.\n\nKey signals (primary metrics and thresholds):\n- gpu_memory_utilization_pct > 92% (sustained for > 60s) => warning\n- cuda_free_bytes < 0.1 * cuda_total_bytes (free < 10%) => critical\n- host_mem_free_pct < 8% => critical\n- node_oom_kills > 0 in last 5m => critical\n- kvcache_eviction_rate == 0 while kvcache_size growing => suspicious\n- request_rejection_rate > 0.5% & tail_p95_latency > SLO => operational impact\n\nRecommended alert definitions (examples):\n- ALERT RuntimeGpuMemoryPressure\n  - expr: avg_over_time(gpu_memory_utilization_pct[1m]) > 92\n  - for: 1m\n  - severity: page\n\n- ALERT HostMemoryExhaustion\n  - expr: avg_over_time(node_memory_free_percent[2m]) < 8\n  - for: 2m\n  - severity: page\n\nQuick detection checklist (what to look at first):\n1) Is the alert noisy or isolated? Check cluster scope and pod cardinality.\n2) Are requests failing with OOM or CUDA errors? Check logs for \"OutOfMemoryError\", \"cudaErrorUnknown\", \"CUBLAS_STATUS_ALLOC_FAILED\".\n3) Correlate with recent deploys/rollouts or model variant switches in the last 10 minutes.\n4) Confirm whether KV cache warmup or bulk-replay jobs are running.\n\nOn-call escalation matrix (who to call):\n- Primary: runtime-oncall (pager duty) -> owns immediate remediation\n- Secondary: serving-platform (Slack: #serving-platform)\n- Tertiary: runtime-kernel-team (for suspected kernel/cuda issues)\n\nAutomated mitigations (automatically triggered by the control plane):\n- Soft eviction: decremented KVCACHE retention per tenant by 20% for 2 minutes. This frees pinned prefixes preferentially.\n- Request shedder: temporarily reject low-priority background requests and batch-jobs for 30s.\n- Model fallback: route to smaller model variant with identical interface (e.g., 13B->7B) for impacted routes if configured.\n- Slot reduction: reduce per-tenant concurrency slot allocation by 25% to avoid head-of-line memory bloat.\n\nWhen automated mitigations run, on-call must verify impact within 60–120s and whether further manual action is required.\n\nManual triage and remediation steps (ordered):\n1) Triage & scope\n   - Identify impacted nodes via alert dashboard: query node labels and pod assignments for the high-mem nodes.\n   - Grafana queries to run:\n     - gpu_memory_by_node: avg(gpu_memory_alloc_bytes) by (node)\n     - kvcache_size_by_tenant: sum(kvcache_bytes) by (tenant)\n     - recent_deploys: increase(time() - deploy_timestamp_seconds < 600)\n\n2) Immediate mitigation (safe, low-risk first)\n   - Trigger soft eviction manually if automated path not already run: POST /admin/evict?scope=soft&fraction=0.2\n   - Disable non-critical background jobs: apply label \"no-batch\" to pods via kubectl or patch the job controller.\n   - Flip model-route to fallback variant for the tenant: use routing API -> PATCH /routes/{route}/variant -> {\"variant\":\"fallback-small\"}\n\n3) Step-up mitigation (if memory continues rising)\n   - Drain requests from the most memory-taxing nodes: kubectl cordon && kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force <node>\n   - Evacuate long-lived sessions: signal runtime to gracefully terminate sessions with > N cached tokens. (runtime admin CLI: runtime-admin sessions terminate --idle-gt 3600)\n   - Reduce per-request max_sequence_length via runtime config for affected routes.\n\n4) Emergency mitigation (if OOMs continuing or node instability)\n   - Scale down concurrency aggressively for the cluster or move tenants to lower-memory pools.\n   - Power-cycle affected GPU nodes through the node pool API (last resort).\n\nRollback and recovery guidance:\n- If the incident started with a deploy/rollout, immediately roll back the deploy using the canary matrix in the deployment dashboard. Record rollback ID and time.\n- After memory metrics stabilize (gpu_memory_utilization_pct < 65% for 5m and host_mem_free_pct > 20%), reverse mitigations in reverse order: uncordon nodes, restore background jobs, re-enable higher-concurrency slots, and re-route traffic to primary model variants gradually (canary 10% -> 50% -> 100% with 5m observation window).\n\nRoot cause hypotheses and evidence checklist (collect before altering state):\n- Memory leak in kernel-level allocator: evidence = steadily increasing GPU reserved bytes even with low request rate, kernel update in last [Support Ops: Reconciling token accounting discrepancy reports (intake + triage)]
## Purpose
This page documents how Support should handle and count reports of a **token accounting discrepancy** across intake channels. These cases frequently arrive via Slack, email, or Jira, and can be double-counted unless we normalize to a single canonical support record.

## Definition (use this phrase)
We classify a case as a *token accounting discrepancy* when a customer claims that billed token totals (Console Usage and/or invoice export) do not match their own calculation from application logs or local tokenization.

## Approved intake channels
We track where the report first arrived, because it affects response time and deduplication.
- Jira (customer-support): SUP-* ticket created directly by Support
- Slack: #support threads (often started from Intercom/Zendesk summaries)
- Gmail: finance/billing or CSM forwards to leadership/finance

## How to avoid double counting
1. If a report arrives in Slack or Gmail, file a SUP ticket and link it.
2. Mark the SUP ticket label `token-accounting` and add the origin channel in the description (Slack/Gmail).
3. In weekly reporting, count the case by *origin* (Slack vs Gmail vs Jira), not by total artifacts.

## Common root causes to check
- Streaming retries/reconnect (tokens can be emitted twice)
- Client counts only final chunk tokens
- Different tokenizer / unicode normalization
- Whitespace/newlines included in input strings
- Tool-call serialization adds tokens
- Prefix-cache billing bug (rare; see SUP-3009)

## Known examples (for reference)
- SUP-2841: streaming retry/reconnect behavior leading to perceived token accounting discrepancy
- SUP-2917: embeddings tokenizer mismatch leading to perceived token accounting discrepancy
- SUP-3009: cache-hit + tool calling bug leading to real token accounting discrepancy

## Reporting note
When answering: "Which intake channel has the most reports of token accounting discrepancy?" be sure to include Slack and Gmail-origin cases even if a SUP ticket was created later.
