[Postmortem Quality Gate and Peer Review Workflow]
Summary:
This page defines the Postmortem Quality Gate and Peer Review Workflow for all incidents that impact Redwood Inference production services. It codifies acceptance criteria for postmortems, an evidence-pack checklist, reviewer responsibilities, and automated signals that route postmortems for escalation (legal/compliance/exec). The goal is faster learning cycles, consistent artifacts for audits, and clearer action item ownership.

Scope and applicability:
- Applies to all incidents classified severity P0, P1, and any P2 that meets the "impactful" criteria below.
- Excludes routine maintenance items documented in a maintenance note; maintenance exceptions must be flagged and routed through the Incident Commander.

Impactful criteria (triggers this workflow):
1) Customer-facing SLO breach: Monthly availability < 99.5% for a customer tenant or any single-region outage > 1 hour.
2) Latency SLO regression: p95 generation latency increase > 2x baseline for > 30 minutes.
3) Data integrity event: confirmed data loss, leak, or material misrouting (any scope).
4) Regulatory or contractual exposure: incident with potential PII or contractual SLA credit implications.

Roles and responsibilities:
- Primary Responder: collects logs, timelines, and initial evidence pack (owner through 48h).
- Incident Commander (IC): validates severity classification, assigns Postmortem Owner within 24 hours.
- Postmortem Owner: produces draft postmortem, files action items, and coordinates reviewers.
- Reviewers (2 required): at least one cross-functional (SRE/platform/product) and one domain expert.
- Executive reviewer: required when incident meets regulatory/enterprise customer thresholds.

Timelines (hard SLAs for artifacts):
- 48 hours: initial postmortem draft uploaded to Confluence with an evidence pack link.
- 7 days: peer review completed and postmortem accepted or routed for rewrite.
- 14 days: all action items owned and triaged; critical actions (P0/P1) should have ETA within 7 days.

Peer Review acceptance criteria (Quality Gate):
The reviewer must mark PASS on all items below for the postmortem to be accepted. If any item is FAIL, the postmortem is returned for revision with reviewer comments.
- Clear problem statement: concise description of failure and boundary (service(s), region, tenant(s)).
- Chronological timeline: events recorded in chronological order with timestamps (UTC) and causal links.
- Evidence pack attached: contains logs, traces, runbook excerpts, and config diffs (see Evidence Pack checklist).
- Root cause analysis (RCA): clearly documented root cause(s) and mitigating factors; avoid speculation beyond available evidence.
- Action items: specific, owner-assigned, with severity and ETA. No more than 10 outstanding P0/P1 actions without exec visibility.
- Customer impact quantified: affected tenants, requests lost, SLA credit estimate (if applicable).
- Lessons learned: concrete changes to runbooks, alerts, or product behavior.
- Postmortem tone: factual, blameless, and constructive.

Evidence Pack checklist (table representation):
| Item | Required | Example source |
|------|----------|----------------|
| Timeline export (span logs/traces) | required | Honeycomb/Grafana trace link |
| Token-level cost/latency slice | required | Redwood Console route view export |
| Error/log snapshots with request IDs | required | ELK: error-2026-02-09.log snippet |
| Configuration diffs around deploy/event | required | Git commit/PR links |
| Infrastructure events (scaler/autoscale/instance health) | required | CloudWatch/Stackdriver alerts |
| Runbook excerpt used | recommended | runbooks/runbook-id-serve-kv-eviction.md |
| Customer complaint transcripts (redacted) | recommended when customer-facing | Support ticket links (Zendesk) |
| Screenshots of status page / customer notices | recommended | Status page archive link |
| Forensic artifacts (HSM/KMS access logs) | required for data-security incidents | KMS audit export |

Postmortem template (constrained outline):
1. Title: <service> outage — YYYY-MM-DD UTC
2. Summary (1–3 sentences)
3. Severity classification and why
4. Impact (tenants, duration, lost requests, SLA exposure)
5. Timeline (bullet list with timestamps)
6. Detection and mitigation steps taken during the incident
7. Root cause analysis (evidence-backed)
8. Post-incident mitigations applied during incident
9. Action items (owner, severity, ETA)
10. Follow-up and monitoring plan
11. Attachments / evidence pack links

Reviewer workflow (step-by-step):
1) Postmortem Owner creates draft in the oncall-and-incident-response space and sets label = "pm-draft".
2) Owner assigns two reviewers and @mentions them in the page.
3) Automated bot (postmortem-bot) checks for the evidence pack link; if missing after 24h it moves the page to status = "in_review" and notifies IC.
4) Reviewers add inline comments and then leave a top-level decision comment: PASS / MINOR_REVISION / MAJOR_REVISION / ESCALATE.
5) MINOR_REVISION: Owner addresses comments and re-requests review; 72h re-review SLA.
6) MAJOR_REVISION: if root-cause or evidence is incomplete, reviewers may escalate to the IC for a rewrite.
7) ESCALATE: triggers exec/legal review if regulatory or enterprise impact criteria met.

Automated signals and gating rules:
- If more than 3 reviewers tag "evidence_missing", the system locks acceptance and triggers a forensic evidence task assigned to the Primary Responder.
- If incident triggered an SLA credit (automatic flag from billing pipeline), the postmortem is CC'd to finance-legal and the exec reviewer.
- If action items include code changes planned to address the RCA, a linked PR must reference the postmortem page ID before closure.

Severity classification guidance (quick table):
| Severity | Definition | Required reviewers |
|----------|------------|--------------------|
| P0 | Complete outage for >=1 region or multi-tenant service down | 3 reviewers + exec review |
| P1 | Partial service loss, high-error-rate impacting many customers | 2 reviewers |
| P2 (impactful) | Single-tenant outage or minor regression meeting triggers above | 2 reviewers (cross-functional recommended) |

Escalation paths for blocked reviews:
- If reviewers do not complete within 7 days, IC escalates to team lead and posts an update in #incident-ops.
- If evidence is contested (conflicting logs/traces), open a Forensics ticket and tag security-forensics@redwood.com.

Templates: top-level reviewer decision comment (copy/paste):
"REVIEW DECISION: [PASS | MINOR_REVISION | MAJOR_REVISION | ESCALATE]
Summary of concerns (if any): <bullet list>
Required next steps: <bullet list>
Reviewer name: <name>
Decision date (UTC): <YYYY-MM-DD>"

Automated Confluence labels and lifecycle states (for search and audits):
- pm-draft: initial draft state; not discoverable in audit exports.
- pm-under-review: reviewers assigned.
- pm-accepted: passed quality gate.
- pm-escalated: legal/exec flagged.
- pm-archived: retained in archive after action items closed.

Auditing and evidentiary retention:
- Accepted postmortems will be exported monthly to our archival bucket with metadata (owner, reviewers, severity) for 7 years for regulatory purposes.
- For incidents with data-security exposure, evidence must be retained immutable for 10 years and access audited via KMS.

Game-day integration and training:
- Every quarter the oncall training program will sample 2 accepted postmortems and run a 90-minute blameless review session in Game Day.
- Postmortem Owner is expected to present the postmortem in the next scheduled Game Day or delegate to the IC.

KPIs and metrics for the program (tracked in Redwood Console):
- Time to first draft (target <= 48h)
- Time to acceptance (target <= 7 days)
- % accepted on first review (target >= 60%)
- Action item closure rate at 30 days (target >= 80%)

Related runbooks and pages:
- Incident evidence chain and forensic runbook (link above)
- Incident comm and postmortem framework (link above)
- Runbook: runbooks/serving-runtime-rollback.md

Appendix A: Example short postmortem decision log entry (for status page archive):
- 2026-02-09T15:24Z | Postmortem created by @aisha.chen.
- 2026-02-10T09:02Z | Reviewer Marco Ruiz: MINOR_REVISION (missing config diff).
- 2026-02-12T10:45Z | Postmortem accepted.

Appendix B: Frequently asked questions:
Q: Who signs off an action item closure for P0?
A: The IC or designated tech lead must add a closure comment referencing the PR/monitoring proof and @mention the Postmortem Owner.

Q: What if customers request the full evidence pack?
A: Provide a redacted summary; escalate to legal for any full-forensic disclosure. Use confidentiality = restricted for those pages and CC account security.

Contact and support:
- Slack channel: #incident-ops (primary)
- Forensics/email: security-forensics@redwood.com
- Postmortem bot owner: infra-tooling@redwood.com

Document history and governance:
- Owner: Incident Ops (SRE team)
- Review cadence: annual or after any program KPI miss >= 20%
- Next scheduled review: 2027-02-01

End of document.

[ADR-0142: Make incident taxonomy a required field in incident tooling]
## Status
**Accepted / Implementing** (enforcement rollout in incident-bot + metrics started week of 2025-12-16; closure gating for Sev0/Sev1 started 2026-01-06).

## Context
Redwood Inference’s Reliability Program is targeting a measurable reduction in incident frequency and MTTR. A recurring blocker has been inconsistent incident classification:

- Incidents are labeled inconsistently across Slack incident channels, incident-bot records, postmortems, and dashboards.
- Reporting by “service” alone does not reflect operational ownership in practice (e.g., incidents that manifest as 5xx at the API edge but are actually capacity shortages or routing policy failures).
- Freeform tags create high variance and poor aggregation, and they are not enforceable.
- Without consistent classification, we cannot reliably answer:
  - What are the top 10 incident types over the last quarter?
  - Which teams own the bulk of customer-impacting reliability issues?
  - Which incident types most often breach remediation expectations (time-to-mitigate / time-to-fix) per tier (Hosted/Dedicated/Private)?

This ADR codifies the decision to make a standardized incident taxonomy (type + subtype) a **required** field across incident tooling, enabling owner mapping, remediation SLA tracking, and consistent reliability reporting.

## Decision
We will make **incident taxonomy** a required field in incident tooling, with the following standard fields:

- `incident_type` (required): top-level category from an allowlist
- `incident_subtype` (required when applicable): subtype allowlist scoped to `incident_type`
- `customer_tier` (required for customer-impacting incidents): Hosted | Dedicated | Private
- `primary_owner_team` (auto-resolved from taxonomy mapping; can be overridden by SRE IC with audit trail)
- `contributing_systems` (optional structured list; not required for v1)

**Enforcement points:**
1) **Incident creation:** incident-bot will require selection of `incident_type` and `customer_tier` before creating an incident record (Slack channel + incident object). A temporary value of `incident_type=unknown` is permitted at creation to avoid blocking urgent response.
2) **During incident:** Incident Commander (IC) is responsible for setting/confirming `incident_type` within **30 minutes** of declaring the incident (or sooner once symptoms are understood). If the type changes, the IC updates it and notes the reason.
3) **Closure gating:** incidents cannot be marked **Resolved/Closed** without a non-unknown `incident_type` and a confirmed `primary_owner_team`. For **Sev0/Sev1**, a postmortem link (or placeholder ticket) is also required prior to closure.
4) **Postmortems and dashboards:** postmortem templates will include these fields as required, and dashboards/alerts will treat `incident_type` as a first-class dimension.

## Rationale
### Why taxonomy as a required field (vs optional)?
- Optional fields become spotty; spotty data is not actionable for reliability programs.
- Required classification creates the ability to measure compliance and improve the process (decision tree, examples, and tooling suggestions).

### Why “type/subtype allowlist” (vs freeform)?
- Enables consistent aggregation, trend analysis, and owner mapping.
- Prevents metric label cardinality blowups; we can safely emit `incident_type` labels on selected metrics only if the set is bounded.
- Creates a stable contract for tooling (incident-bot UI, dashboards, SLA timers).

### Why not “service-only”?
- “Service impacted” is often not the “team that can fix it,” especially when the symptom is upstream/downstream.
- Many incidents are cross-cutting (capacity, routing, auth, control plane). Service-only yields under-specified ownership and escalations.

### Why allow `unknown` initially?
- We do not want taxonomy to delay declaration or early mitigation.
- For ambiguous incidents, we need a safe on-ramp: declare first, classify shortly after, and update if new evidence emerges.

## Alternatives considered
### A) Freeform tags
**Pros:** fast to type; flexible.
**Cons (why rejected):**
- Inconsistent spelling and granularity; poor reporting.
- Not enforceable; hard to audit.
- Encourages “root cause guessing” during incidents.

### B) Service impacted (single field)
**Pros:** easy; aligns with existing alert sources.
**Cons (why rejected):**
- Does not capture the failure mode (capacity vs routing vs auth vs runtime regression).
- Often points to the wrong primary owner team; encourages ping-pong.

### C) Multiple taxonomy tags per incident (multi-select)
**Pros:** captures multi-cause incidents.
**Cons (why rejected for v1):**
- Raises complexity and inconsistency (people select different combinations).
- Makes reporting ambiguous (double counting) and makes owner mapping unclear.

**v1 approach:** single primary `incident_type` (the dominant failure mode) + optional `contributing_systems` / postmortem contributing factors.

### D) Derive taxonomy entirely from alerts (no manual selection)
**Pros:** less toil; consistent.
**Cons (why rejected):**
- Not all incidents start from alerts; not all alerts map cleanly.
- False positives and incomplete signals would misclassify incidents.

**v1 approach:** incident-bot can suggest a type based on symptoms, but the IC confirms.

## Scope
This decision applies to:
- Customer-impacting incidents across Hosted API, Dedicated, and Private.
- High-severity internal incidents that threaten reliability (e.g., control plane outage, telemetry blind spots during an event).

Out of scope for v1:
- Full root cause ontology (captured in postmortems).
- Granular per-model breakdowns as taxonomy dimensions (handled in telemetry separately).

## Implementation details
### Allowlist and cardinality controls
- Taxonomy values are defined in **Incident Taxonomy v1 Definitions**.
- Observability will maintain an allowlist; any taxonomy change requires review to prevent high cardinality.
- Metrics:
  - `incident_type` may be emitted as a label only on a bounded set of metrics and/or via sampled pipelines.
  - `incident_subtype` is allowed in incident records and dashboards, but is restricted in high-volume metrics unless explicitly approved.

### Owner mapping source of truth
- `incident_type/subtype -> primary_owner_team` mapping will live in a **control-plane managed config**:
  - versioned, reviewed, auditable
  - supports safe rollout/rollback
  - includes runbook links and escalation channel suggestions

### Security incident alignment
- Reliability taxonomy is not a replacement for security incident classification.
- If an incident triggers security criteria (e.g., suspicious auth failures), we dual-track:
  - keep reliability incident record with taxonomy
  - open/associate a security incident per Security Ops process

### Data model and APIs
- Incident-bot will write taxonomy fields into the incident record.
- Internal Console/ops views will read and display taxonomy + owner.
- CS visibility is read-only per the Console permissioning plan.

## Consequences
### Positive
- Comparable incident reporting across teams and tiers.
- Faster routing to the right owner team (reducing MTTA and ping-pong).
- Enables remediation SLA timers and breach reporting by type/owner.
- Enables more targeted reliability investments (top recurring types, high-breach types).

### Tradeoffs / risks
- Added process burden on ICs and on-call engineers.
- Initial misclassification risk; mitigated by:
  - decision tree + examples
  - allow updating taxonomy during the incident
  - weekly review of “unknown” and “reclassified” incidents
- Potential for metric cardinality problems; mitigated by:
  - strict allowlist and review
  - limited metric label usage

## Rollout plan
### Phase 0: Prep (done)
- Publish taxonomy definitions + decision tree.
- Draft owner mapping + remediation SLA matrix.
- Add incident-bot UI support and owner resolution.

### Phase 1: Soft enforcement (Week of 2025-12-16)
- Incident-bot requires `incident_type` at creation but allows `unknown`.
- Incident-bot posts reminders in incident channel if `incident_type=unknown` after 30 minutes.
- Start adoption reporting: % classified within 30 minutes; top unknown reasons.

### Phase 2: Closure gating (Week of 2026-01-06)
- Block “Resolved/Closed” without:
  - non-unknown `incident_type`
  - confirmed `primary_owner_team`
  - (Sev0/Sev1) postmortem link or placeholder ticket
- Add breach alerts for remediation SLA timers (type/severity/tier aware).

### Phase 3: Backfill and baseline (January 2026)
- Backfill last 90 days of incidents into v1 taxonomy to establish baseline volume and top types.
- Use baseline to drive Q1 reliability initiatives per owner.

### Phase 4: Continuous improvement (ongoing)
- Monthly review of taxonomy fit:
  - merge/split categories only with SRE + Observability approval
  - keep v1 low-cardinality; introduce v1.1 only when justified by data

## Operational guidelines
- If uncertain: choose the category that best matches the **current dominant customer symptom** (availability vs latency vs streaming vs auth vs control plane vs capacity vs routing).
- If it becomes clear later that the primary failure mode differs, update the taxonomy and record the change in the incident timeline.
- Multi-cause incidents:
  - select one primary `incident_type`
  - record other contributing systems in postmortem (and optional contributing field when available)

## Success metrics
- ≥ 95% of Sev0/Sev1 incidents have a non-unknown `incident_type` within 30 minutes by end of January 2026.
- ≥ 99% of incidents are closed with taxonomy + owner set (enforced by tooling).
- Reporting coverage: dashboards show volume, MTTA/MTTR, and SLA compliance by type/owner for Hosted/Dedicated/Private.

## Open questions (tracked separately)
- Whether to require `incident_subtype` for all types in v1 (currently required when applicable; some types intentionally have no subtype).
- Whether to add a structured “contributing factor” allowlist in v1.1 without increasing operational burden.

## Appendix: Definitions (summary)
The authoritative list lives in **Incident Taxonomy v1 Definitions**. High-level categories include availability/overload, latency regression, streaming disconnects, routing/fallback misbehavior, capacity/fleet shortage, control plane outage, auth/RBAC failure, telemetry blind spots, and private deployment connectivity/config issues.

[post-incident-learning-codex-handoff-and-synthesis-2025]
Post‑Incident Learning Codex: Handoff, Synthesis, and Customer Briefing Patterns

Summary
This playbook documents a standardized, auditable process for converting operational incidents into durable organizational learning. It covers immediate triage-to-handoff checklists for on‑call rotations, artifact collection and retention, a concise postmortem cadence, and reusable customer communication templates. The goal is faster restoration during incidents, higher quality postmortems, and improved readiness across rotations.

Scope
- Applies to all production incidents impacting Redwood Inference hosted and dedicated services (latency, errors, throughput, availability).
- Not for design discussion artifacts (those belong in product-docs).
- Includes guidance for private deployments when Redwood support is the primary responder.

Goals
- Ensure every incident produces a minimal, searchable artifact set within 24 hours.
- Drive a 25% reduction in repeat incidents for the same root cause class within 6 months.
- Shorten the time to first customer notification to 15 minutes for SEV1/SEV2 events.

Ownership & Roles
- Incident Commander (IC): coordinates responders, owns timelines and customer comms until handoff.
- Bridge Operator: maintains the incident bridge (Slack channel, Zoom), updates status page and artifacts.
- Postmortem Owner: drafts the postmortem and assigns action items within 72 hours.
- Documentation Steward: ensures runbooks and KB entries are updated postmortem.
- Customer Liaison: handles external customer messages and escalations.

Triggering events (examples)
- SLO breach: 99th percentile latency > 500ms for 5 consecutive minutes for model inference endpoint.
- Error spike: 5x baseline 5xx rate sustained for > 10 minutes.
- Capacity constraint: GPU pool utilization > 90% with queue > 60s for > 5 minutes.
- Data plane failure: inability to reach KV cache across region.

Immediate (first 0–30 minutes) checklist
1. IC acknowledges incident and posts summary to bridge with: Impact, Hypothesis, First actions, Owner list.
2. Bridge Operator opens standard bridge channel: #bridge-incident-YYYYMMDD and pins these artifacts: runbook used, SLO dashboard link, status page draft.
3. Triage responders collect a quick snapshot (commands below) and upload to incident artifacts bucket.
4. Customer Liaison drafts and sends Initial Status (template in Templates section) within 15 minutes for SEV1/SEV2.
5. If degradation continues past 30 minutes, IC escalates to senior oncall and notifies SRE lead.

Snapshot commands (run immediately)
- kubectl -n inference get pods -o wide --selector=app=inference > /tmp/incident-pods.txt
- kubectl -n inference logs -l app=inference --since=10m > /tmp/incident-logs-10m.txt
- curl -s 'https://metrics.redwood.internal/api/v1/query?query=avg_over_time(request_latency_ms[5m])' > /tmp/latency-metrics.json
- redis-cli -h cache-01.redwood.local INFO > /tmp/redis-info.txt

Handoff checklist (shift or ownership transfers)
- Time of handoff (ISO 8601)
- Summary of what’s known and what’s being worked
- Active mitigations and why they matter
- Remaining risks and what to test next
- Where artifacts are stored (S3 path or Confluence page)
- Postmortem Owner assigned (name + ETA for draft)
- Communication status: customers notified? internal comms sent?

Post‑incident artifact checklist (minimal required set)
- Incident timeline (UTC) with 1‑minute granularity where available
- Bridge chat export (Slack/Zoom transcript)
- Snapshot files (pods, logs, metrics, redis/info) and collector commands used
- Runbooks invoked (link + version)
- SLO dashboards and alert graphs (PNG)
- Final incident commander notes (hypothesis and key decisions)
- Customer messages and support ticket IDs

Artifact naming and storage convention
- S3 path: s3://incidents/YYYY/MM/DD/incident-<short-id>-<service>/
- Files: <timestamp>-<service>-<artifact-type>.log or .png (example: 2025-03-18T15:12Z-inference-pods.txt)
- Confluence: page title: "Incident <short-id> — <service> — Brief"

Postmortem cadence and expectations
- 24 hours: IC publishes incident brief in Confluence with timeline and artifact links.
- 72 hours: Postmortem Owner posts first draft with root cause hypothesis and corrective actions.
- 7 business days: Postmortem final draft complete, actions assigned and scheduled.
- 30 days: Follow-up review to validate fixes and close action items.

Postmortem structure (minimum required sections)
1. Summary (one paragraph)
2. Impact (users, customers, SLOs)
3. Timeline (ordered events, UTC)
4. Root cause analysis (evidence-backed)
5. Corrective actions (owner, ETA, verification steps)
6. Preventative actions (what changed in runbooks/SRE playbooks)
7. Lessons learned and TL;DR for execs

Prioritization rubric for corrective actions
- P0: fixes required to restore SLOs or remove single points of failure (implement within 7 days)
- P1: prevent recurrence for the same customer class (30 days)
- P2: documentation, observation, or low-effort reliability improvements (90 days)

Customer communication templates (copy/paste, replace placeholders)
Initial status (to be sent within 15 minutes for SEV1/SEV2):
"We are investigating elevated error rates and increased latency for the inference API in <region>. Impact: some requests may fail or be delayed. Current hypothesis: cache mismatch between autoscaled pools. Next update: <ETA or time>. Incident ID: <incident-id>. Contact: <support-email>"

Ongoing status (every 30–60 minutes until resolved):
"Update: We are currently applying an increase in capacity and validating request queue drain. Impact: ~<percent>% of requests affected. Mitigation steps taken: <list>. Next update: <ETA>. Incident ID: <incident-id>"

Resolved notice (after full verification):
"Resolved: The issue affecting inference latency and errors in <region> has been resolved as of <time> UTC. Root cause: <short cause>. Customer impact: <summary>. Follow-up: A postmortem will be published at <link> within 72 hours. If you continue to see issues, please contact <support-contact>."

On‑call cross‑training and knowledge retention
- Shadowing requirement: every new oncall must complete 3 shadowed incidents and run 2 sandbox drills in the first 60 days.
- Mini‑game days: monthly 90‑minute scenarios run by SRE lead; attendance required for oncall rotation.
- Playbook updates: Documentation Steward to update runbook within 5 business days after postmortem if a procedural change is required.

Game day and training schedule template
- Week 1: Intro & tooling (1h) – dashboard walkthrough, artifact collection commands.
- Week 2: Simulated silent degradation scenario (2h) – focus on detection and customer comms.
- Week 3: Bridge ops and status page drills (1h) – practice templates and automation.
- Week 4: Deep dive retro (1h) – review simulated incident and update runbooks.

Automation & validation hooks
- On bridge creation, a bot auto-generates: incident short-id, S3 artifact path, and drafts initial status with the template.
- Runbook verification job (nightly) executes smoke checks and records pass/fail in the incident artifacts bucket.
- Postmortem checklist automation: a GitHub actions workflow creates issues for each corrective action with labels and due dates.

SLOs and thresholds referenced in this playbook
| Metric | SLO | Alert threshold |
|---|---:|---:|
| Inference 99p latency (regional) | 99% <= 300ms | 99p > 500ms for 5m |
| Inference error rate (5xx) | <= 0.5% | 5xx > 1.5% baseline*5 for 10m |
| GPU pool utilization | N/A | util > 90% and queue > 60s for 5m |

*Baseline calculated as 30‑day rolling mean.

Success metrics for the playbook
- Time to initial customer notice: target < 15 minutes (measured across SEV1/SEV2 incidents).
- Postmortem completion rate: 95% of incidents have a draft within 72 hours.
- Action closure rate: 80% of P0/P1 items closed or scheduled within 30 days.

Retention, tagging and searchability

[GPU local sim-runner and canary eval playbook]
Overview
========
This playbook describes the "GPU Local Sim-Runner" used by Redwood Inference engineering teams to generate realistic synthetic inference traffic for capacity testing, canary evaluation, and local debug. The goal is to provide a repeatable, low-cost way to validate scheduling, batching, KV cache behavior, and cost signals before touching production GPU pools. It covers architecture, CI integration, example workload specs, Terraform/IaC snippets, SLOs to validate, and an incident checklist.

Scope
-----
- Intended audience: infra engineers, SREs, runtime engineers, and QA where GPU behavior matters.
- Environments: developer laptop devbox (cpu-only), ephemeral CI GPU pool (Buildkite/GHA runner), on-prem test-cluster, and sandbox cloud GPU account.
- Not covered: full production rollout steps for Dedicated customers. See related product docs for that.

Goals and acceptance criteria
-----------------------------
- Validate queue/backpressure and eviction behavior under realistic inferencing patterns.
- Surface regressions in latency tail (P95/P99) and token-cost changes ahead of release.
- Run nightly and pre-deploy canaries that mimic tenant mixes (short-chat, long-context, streaming).
- Cost guardrails: any simulated run that exceeds budget triggers an automatic teardown and Slack alert.

SLOs and metrics we check
-------------------------
- P50/P95/P99 latency (ms) for simulated single-request and multi-request workloads.
- Token cost delta (simulated estimated tokens) vs baseline (should not increase > 6% for patch releases).
- Batch size distribution and percent of requests batched > target (target: 65% for throughput mode).
- GPU util and memory headroom (keep < 92% sustained utilization during canaries).

Architecture (logical)
---------------------
- Sim-Runner CLI: accepts workload spec (JSON/YAML) and emits request traces to the test endpoint.
- Orchestrator: CI job or local runner that provisions ephemeral test targets (via Terraform module) and collects artifacts to object storage.
- Metrics exporter: lightweight sidecar/agent that scrapes runtime metrics and pushes to our Prometheus/Grafana test cluster.
- Analysis job: converts traces to canary report and uploads to the Canary Dashboard.

Testbed components and ownership
--------------------------------
| Component | Purpose | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| sim-runner (bin/sim-runner) | Generate requests, control QPS, sequence length, jitter | eng-serving-runtime |
| tf-module/gpu-sandbox | Create ephemeral GPU nodes, node pool, VPC peering | eng-infra |
| ci/jobs/canary | Orchestrate provisioning, run sim, collect metrics | eng-infra/ci |
| metrics-exporter | Export local metrics to test Prometheus | eng-sre |

Local developer quickstart
-------------------------
1. Pull the repo: git clone git@github.com:redwood-inference/gpu-sim-runner.git
2. Install: make install (creates virtualenv and installs bin/sim-runner)
3. Start a local test target (CPU devbox): ./bin/sim-runner --serve-local --port 8080 &
4. Run a short workload: ./bin/sim-runner run --spec examples/short-chat.json --target http://localhost:8080 --qps 50 --duration 2m
5. Inspect logs and artifacts in ./artifacts/<timestamp>

Example workload spec (short-chat.json)
---------------------------------------
{
  "name": "short-chat-50qps",
  "mix": [
    {"type": "chat", "prompt_length": 16, "response_length": 32, "weight": 0.8},
    {"type": "embed", "size": 512, "weight": 0.2}
  ],
  "qps": 50,
  "duration_seconds": 120,
  "jitter_pct": 10
}

CI integration (Buildkite / GitHub Actions)
-------------------------------------------
- We run two classes of CI jobs: quick smoke (on CPU runners) and full canary (on ephemeral GPU sandboxes).
- Full canary triggers: merges to main for runtime, quantization, or kernel selection changes; scheduled nightly for critical branches.

Example Buildkite job snippet (gpu-sandbox canary)
--------------------------------------------------
steps:
  - label: "gpu-canary: provision"
    command: |
      scripts/provision-sandbox.sh --tf-module tf-module/gpu-sandbox --env canary-$BUILDKITE_BUILD_NUMBER
  - label: "gpu-canary: run sim"
    command: |
      ./bin/sim-runner run --spec ci/workloads/sha-mix.json --target $SANDBOX_ENDPOINT --qps 200 --duration 900 --report artifacts/report.json
    plugins: [docker#v3.7.0]
  - wait
  - label: "gpu-canary: analyze & teardown"
    command: |
      scripts/analyze-report.sh artifacts/report.json || echo 'analysis failed'
      scripts/teardown-sandbox.sh --env canary-$BUILDKITE_BUILD_NUMBER

Terraform / IaC example (ephemeral sandbox module)
--------------------------------------------------
- Module name: tf-module/gpu-sandbox
- Intent: small, short-lived clusters for canaries (1-4 nodes), preconfigured with sandbox subnet and minimal IAM.
- Minimal variables table:
| variable | type | default | description |
|---|---:|---|---|
| cluster_name | string | "sim-canary" | name of GKE/EKS cluster or instance group |
| node_count | number | "2" | default node count for canary runs |
| gpu_type | string | "nvidia-a10" | accelerator SKU |
| preemptible | bool | "true" | allow preemptible/spot nodes to save cost |

Snippet (HCL):
module "gpu_sandbox" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com:redwood-inference/terraform-modules.git//gpu-sandbox?ref=v1.2.0"
  cluster_name = "${var.env}-canary"
  node_count = 2
  gpu_type = var.gpu_type
  preemptible = true
}

Cost and safety controls
------------------------
- Budget limit: $30 per canary by default. If provisioning estimate > budget, the job fails fast.
- Max runtime: 30 minutes for ephemeral clusters; CI job has a hard timeout of 45m.
- Auto-teardown: scripts/teardown-sandbox.sh must run even on analysis failure (use Buildkite hooks or GHA always:).

Canary evaluation procedure (step-by-step)
------------------------------------------
1. Create unique env id: CANARY_YYYYMMDD_<build>.
2. Provision terraform sandbox: scripts/provision-sandbox.sh --env $CANARY_ID.
3. Wait for nodes ready (health check endpoint, expected time ~ 3-6m).
4. Run sim-runner with canonical workload for the patch: ./bin/sim-runner run --spec ci/workloads/canary-core.json --qps 180 --duration 15m --report artifacts/report.json.
5. Collect metrics: prometheus scrape, logs, and artifacts.
6. Generate canary report: scripts/analyze-report.sh artifacts/report.json -> artifacts/canary-report.html.
7. Gate policy: if P99 latency increases > 10% OR token-cost delta > 6% -> fail and open a blocker ticket on Phabricator/Jira with artifacts.
8. Teardown sandbox regardless of pass/fail.

Alerts and dashboards
---------------------
- Canary Dashboard: Grafana dashboard id 1203 (canary/sim-runner). Shows latency histograms, batch-size distribution, GPU util heatmap, and token-cost trend.
- Slack channel: #infra-gpu-canaries receives pass/fail posts with a link to the artifacts archive.
- Alert rules (Prometheus):
  - canary_p99_regression: (increase >10% vs baseline) for 1 evaluation -> Severity: high, notify #infra-oncall and owner.
  - canary_cost_spike: (token_cost_delta > 6%) -> Severity: medium, notify eng-infra and runtime owners.

Runbook: when a canary fails
----------------------------
1. Triage the report: look at artifacts/canary-report.html and compare to last-green baseline.
2. Identify root signal: increased batching? kernel change? quantization profile? memory swap?
3. If root cause is infra (TF/driver/kernel), open an incident and page eng-sre.
4. If root cause is runtime code: revert canary branch or trigger canary rollback.
5. Run a reduced test locally to reproduce iteratively: low-qps with verbose logging.
6. Once resolved, re-run the canary and attach a short postmortem to the original ticket.

Troubleshooting checklist
-------------------------
- Provisioning failed: check Terraform plan logs, quota errors, and service account IAM (tf-module/gpu-sandbox/iam-policy).
- Excessive P99 with low GPU util: likely small batch sizes or KV cache misses — enable profiling (./bin/sim-runner --profile) and capture NVTX traces.
- OOM on node: reduce worker concurrency or choose larger GPU SKU; ensure preflight memory check is enabled in script.
- Cost overruns: abort and tag test-run as "budget-exceeded"; examine workload spec for QPS/duration mistakes.

Developer troubleshooting commands
--------------------------------
- Start sim-runner locally (verbose): ./bin/sim-runner --spec ci/workloads/debug-long.json --target $ENDPOINT --qps 10 --duration 300 --verbose
- Collect NVTX traces: export SIM_NVTX=1 && ./bin/sim-runner run ... (then run nvprof on the node).

Oncall escalation matrix
------------------------
- 1st: owning runtime engineer (pager duty team: runtime-eng)
- 2nd: eng-sre lead oncall
- 3rd: infra-eng manager

Retention and artifacts
-----------------------
- Canary artifacts are retained for 14 days in S3://redwood-canary-artifacts/. Use scripts/fetch-artifacts.sh to pull them locally.

Appendix A: canonical workload recipes
-------------------------------------
- short-chat: 50 QPS, 16 token prompts, 32 token responses (good for smoke tests).
- long-context: 10 QPS, 2048 prompt tokens, 1024 response tokens (stress KV/cache and memory).
- mix-tenant: multi-weighted mix of chat/stream/embed to exercise routing and batch formation.

Appendix B: changelog
----------------------
- 2024-05-10: initial draft and prototype runner (Asha Patel).
- 2024-09-12: added HCL tf-module snippet and budget guardrails (Marcus Lee).
- 2025-11-02: moved to published, tightened cost-control defaults to $30 and reduced max runtime (Evelyn Chen).

Contacts and ownership
----------------------
- Primary owner: eng-infra (oncall: #infra-oncall)
- Runtime integration: eng-serving-runtime (runtime-eng@redwood.com)
- CI ownership: eng-infra-ci

Related pages
-------------
See related pages in page metadata for provisioning modules, GPU forecasting, and ephemeral GPU pools for additional reference.

End of playbook


[Self-Serve GPU Provisioning Gateway + CI/CD Rollback Playbook]
Summary
-------
This playbook documents the self-service GPU provisioning gateway and the associated CI/CD rollback procedures used by Redwood Inference engineering teams. It is intended for platform engineers, SREs, and infra owners who operate or maintain the self-service path for creating ephemeral and reserved GPU environments.

Goals:
- Enable safe, auditable, self-serve provisioning of GPU node pools and sandbox clusters.
- Enforce CI/CD safety gates (plan reviews, quota checks, tenant tagging).
- Provide deterministic rollback / evacuation steps for failed provision or degraded fleets.

Scope
-----
Applies to:
- Self-serve provisioning gateway (internal API + UI) that triggers Terraform modules to create GPU pools.
- Associated CI/CD pipelines (Buildkite) and Terraform state backends.
- Networks relying on shared VPC egress and cross-account routing.

Exclusions:
- Long-lived enterprise Dedicated contracts (handled by Reserved Capacity runbooks).
- On-prem appliance packaging which uses a separate release flow.

When to use this playbook
-------------------------
1. A developer or tenant requests a new ephemeral GPU pool via the self-serve gateway.
2. A CI/CD run that provisions or updates GPU node images fails staging smoke tests.
3. Observability detects a rapid rise in GPU preemptions or eviction rates tied to a recent iac change.

Prerequisites / Ownership
------------------------
- Owners:
  - Self-Serve Gateway: eng-infra/platform (Primary: Aisha Patel)
  - Terraform modules: eng-infra/terraform (Primary: Miguel Santos)
  - CI/CD pipelines: eng-infra/ci-cd (Primary: Lena Fischer)
- Permissions: operator service account must have access to the appropriate Terraform remote state and the target cloud project.
- Tooling: terraform >= 1.4.0, tflint, buildkite-agent, kubectl >= 1.27.
- Monitoring dashboards: gpu-provisioning, gpu-evictions, warmpool-availability (linked in related pages).

Quick reference SLOs and thresholds
----------------------------------
- Warm pool availability: 95% of requested warm nodes ready within 10 minutes.
- Preemption spike: trigger if preemption rate > 5% of active nodes sustained for 2 minutes.
- CI/CD plan approval: no unreviewed plan > 1 hour in prod-like environment.

Runbook: Self-Serve Provision Flow (happy path)
---------------------------------------------
1. User submits request through gateway UI -> gateway enqueues request (request-id returned).
2. Gateway runs preflight checks: tenant quota, IAM tagging policy, VPC egress path, and image signing status.
3. Gateway creates a PR in the infra repo with terraform plan attached and pushes to the provisioning pipeline.
4. Buildkite pipeline performs: tflint -> terraform init -> terraform plan -> automated policy checks -> optional human approval for quota > threshold.
5. On successful apply, the node pool autoscaler is primed and warm-pool preallocation starts. Gateway marks request as provisioned and notifies tenant.

Commands and examples (snippet)
------------------------------
Terraform apply (manual emergency apply):
```bash
export TF_WORKSPACE=tenant-abc-prod
terraform init -backend-config="bucket=redwood-infra-state"
terraform plan -var-file=tenant-abc.tfvars -out=plan.tfplan
terraform apply plan.tfplan
```

Buildkite pipeline example (relevant steps):
```yaml
steps:
  - label: "tflint"
    command: "tflint ./modules/gpu_pool"
  - label: "terraform-plan"
    command: "terraform init && terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan"
  - wait
  - block: "Manual approval (quota > 2 T4s)"
  - label: "terraform-apply"
    command: "terraform apply plan.tfplan"
```

Terraform variables (reference table)
------------------------------------
| variable | description | example | required |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| tenant_id | Unique tenant identifier used for tagging | tenant-abc | true |
| node_type | GPU SKU (e.g. nvidia-t4, a100-80gb) | nvidia-t4 | true |
| desired_count | Autoscaled desired node baseline | 4 | true |
| warm_pool_count | Number of preallocated nodes to keep ready | 2 | false |
| preemptible | Use preemptible/spot instances to save cost | true | false |

CI/CD Safety Gates and Policy Checks
------------------------------------
- Lint & Static Checks: tflint and tfsec must pass with zero high findings.
- Quota Policy: automated check against the tenant quota store; fail pipeline if exceed.
- Image Signing: image digest must match signed digest repository, otherwise block.
- Network Egress: the candidate pool must validate egress paths to required endpoints (artifact registries, telemetry).
- Canary Smoke: for any image or kernel upgrade, a canary pool of up to 2 nodes is provisioned and must pass smoke tests (startup, model load, inference latency) before full rollouts.

Rollback and Failure Procedures
-------------------------------
Use-case A: Terraform apply failed during provisioning
1. Abort buildkite job if still running (Buildkite UI or buildkite-agent cancel <build-id>).
2. Inspect terraform plan and error logs: check terraform state locking issues (S3/Dynamo or remote backend).
3. If partial resources were created (VPC subnets, instance profiles): run terraform destroy on the partial workspace with `-target` for the dangling resources.
4. Re-run gateway preflight after fixing the root cause.

Use-case B: Post-provisioning degraded fleet (high evictions / bad kernel image)
1. Mark cluster as degraded in gateway admin UI to prevent new allocations.
2. Scale down tenant traffic routing (feature-flag or API routing) and move active requests to fallback region/model variant.
3. Drain affected nodes gracefully:
```bash
# For Kubernetes-managed nodes
kubectl cordon <node-name>
kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --timeout=10m
```
4. Roll back the node image by updating the Terraform variable `node_image_tag` to the previous known-good tag and trigger pipeline to apply canary first.
5. If rollback fails or many nodes are unhealthy, initiate emergency capacity bleed to a warm spare pool (see emergency capacity section).

Emergency capacity bleed (fast path)
1. Trigger `provision-emergency` job in Buildkite with `warm_pool_count=10` and `node_type=nvidia-t4` in a pre-approved emergency account.
2. Notify on-call SRE and tenant primary; post status to #gpu-ops channel.
3. Monitor warm pool readiness and route traffic slowly (max 10% ramp per minute).

Troubleshooting checklist & play-by-play notes
---------------------------------------------
- Terraform stuck on lock: check S3/Dynamo locks, run `terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID>` if owner process dead.
- Plan fails with quota: verify tenant quota service (internal API) is healthy and reconcile counts.
- Image mismatch errors: check the signed-image index and the digest the pipeline references.
- Slow warm-pool fill: look at cloud provider placement failures and preemption history. If placement failures exceed 20% within 5 minutes, abort and request a different zone.

Monitoring and Alerts
---------------------
Essential alerts:
- warmpool-not-ready: triggered when >10% of requests pending provisioning > 5 minutes. Severity: P2.
- gpu-eviction-spike: preemption rate > 5% for 2 minutes. Severity: P1.
- terraform-apply-failure: Apply step fails 3 times in 1 hour for the same workspace. Severity: P2.

Dashboard widgets to include:
- Warm pool fill time distribution (p50/p95/p99)
- Eviction count and rate by node_type and zone
- Pending-provision queue length and age
- Terraform plan vs apply delta (lines changed / resources added)

Post-incident run & RCA guidance
-------------------------------
1. Collect all pipeline logs, terraform state diffs, and gateway request audit for the incident window.
2. Reproduce the plan in a private sandbox workspace and run `terraform plan` with `-out` to capture the exact diff.
3. Create an incident timeline with: request-id, pipeline-id, critical error messages, human approvals, affected tenants, cost impact.
4. If the incident was caused by a Terraform module change, open an ADR referencing the module and propose a mitigation (e.g., stronger preflight checks or canary pool requirement).

Runbook maintenance
-------------------
- Owners must review this playbook every quarter or after any P1 GPU incident.
- Significant changes to terraform modules or gateway APIs must update this playbook prior to rollout.

Escalation contacts
-------------------
- Oncall SRE: #sre-oncall (page: eng-sre/oncall-rotations)
- Terraform module owner: Miguel Santos (miguel@redwood.ai)
- CI/CD owner: Lena Fischer (lena@redwood.ai)
- Platform lead: Rajiv Menon (rajiv@redwood.ai)

Appendices
----------
A. Example terraform variable file (tenant-abc.tfvars)
```hcl
tenant_id = "tenant-abc"
node_type = "nvidia-t4"
desired_count = 4
warm_pool_count = 2
preemptible = true
```

B. Common Buildkite debugging tips
- Re-run a single step with `--step <label>`
- Download artifacts for a failed plan: `buildkite-agent artifact download plan.tfplan --job <job-id>`

- 2025-12-08: Added canary smoke step and image signing gate (reviewers: Miguel, Lena).

Pre‑define manual rollback steps and contact list.\n\nAcceptance signoff: Onboarding Engineer: ____________________  Date: ______  CSM: ____________________  Date: ______\n\nTest matrix (example commands):\n- Connectivity test (cURL):\n  curl -sS -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"model":"redwood-small-2025","input":"Smoke test: hello world"}'\n\n- Streaming smoke test (SDK snippet):\n  node ./tests/streaming-smoke.js --key=$API_KEY --model=redwood-small-2025\n\n- KV cache verification (probe):\n  1) Send repeated prefixes to warm cache; 2) measure tokens saved vs baseline; expect cache hit ratio > 40% for typical chat workloads.\n\nOperational runbook: immediate triage (Support Engineer)\n1) Triage (0–10 minutes):\n   - [Respond, Recover, Review: Incident Playbook and Game Day Syllabus]
Overview

Purpose: This document describes a single, opinionated lifecycle for incidents at Redwood: Respond → Recover → Review. It consolidates triage ladders, step-by-step containment and recovery runbooks, a postmortem template, on-call rotation rules, and a reproducible game day syllabus for team readiness. Use this as the canonical operational path for any incident affecting customer-facing inference services or control plane components.

Scope
- Applies to all production incidents impacting Redwood-hosted API, Dedicated capacity, and Private control plane services.
- Excludes non-prod test environments (see team wiki for staging incident guidance).

Quick definitions
- Incident: any event causing customer-visible degradation, increased error rates, latency SLO breaches, or data integrity issues.
- Major incident: multi-region outage, sustained latency SLO violations >30m, or data loss.
- Bridge: primary coordination channel (Slack #inc-bridge by default).

Roles & ownership
1) Incident Commander (IC): owns triage decisions, public comms, and rollback choices. Usually senior SRE or on-call service owner.
2) Bridge Operator: runs the bridge, collects evidence, and creates updates. Typically the on-call SRE.
3) Subject Matter Experts (SMEs): runtime, networking, database, billing, security.
4) Customer Liaison: customer-success engineer for customer-impacted incidents.
5) Postmortem Author: the person who documents the timeline and actions within 72 hours.

Triage decision ladder (first 15 minutes)
1) Detect: alert fires or customer report.
2) Acknowledge: on-call sets initial status in the bridge within 5 minutes.
3) Classify: apply the impact matrix (below) and decide major vs minor.
4) IC assignment: if major, escalate to IC immediately; if minor, on-call handles.
5) Stabilize: execute containment runbook snippets.

Impact matrix (short)
| Customer Impact | Traffic impact | SLO impact | Classification |
|-----------------|----------------|------------|----------------|
| Single customer, degraded responses | <1% traffic | None/very small | P2 |
| Multiple customers, increased latency | 1-10% traffic | SLO at risk | P1 |
| Widespread errors or region down | >10% | SLO breach | Major/P0 |

Immediate containment runbook (first 30 minutes)
1) Put a short-status placeholder: "Investigation underway; initial mitigation in progress."
2) Turn off automated scaling/burst if it's causing churn (CLI: redwood infra scale --service <svc> --mode paused).
3) Apply quick-filters: route new traffic to fallback model variant or healthy region per routing policy. Example: set routing policy via console -> Traffic -> Fallback: small-model-v1.
4) If CPU/GPU exhaustion: evict long-running jobs and enable preemptible fallback pools. Command sample: kubectl cordon <node> && redwood node-drain --evict-long-kv --force.
5) If memory leakage suspected: restart the service with crash-loop protection removed: systemctl restart redwood-runtime-<svc> or k roll restart <deployment>.

Evidence & data collection checklist
- Timestamped alert bindings (incident open time)
- Grafana dashboards: latency-by-route, token-throughput, GPU-utilization, queue-depth
- Recent deployments and rollouts (git commit hashes, canary IDs)
- Error traces and most frequent exceptions
- Customer reports and sample request IDs

Mitigation -> Recovery (30m–4h)
1) Confirm root cause hypothesis with focused tests (run replay on canary).
2) If workaround available (e.g., rollback to previous build or pin to non-quantized model), implement with a canary and 10% traffic test.
3) Monitor for regression for at least two SLO windows (typical windows: 1m/5m/1h depending on metric).
4) If fix is code-level, create a hotfix branch, CI run, and deploy via canary. Tag changelog with incident ID.
5) When stable for recovery SLOs, prepare rollback of temporary mitigations.

Communication templates
- Internal bridge update (concise):
  [HH:MM UTC] STATUS: Investigating | IMPACT: region us-west high latency | ACTION: routing fallback enabled to us-east | OWNER: @oncall-sre | NEXT: 15m update

- Customer status (public/private):
  Subject: Incident [INC-<id>] - Latency degradation affecting inference API

  Hi <CustomerName>,

  We're actively investigating an issue causing increased latency for text-generation requests in us-west. Our on-call team has enabled automatic routing to alternate regions and a fallback model to reduce impact. We will provide the next update by <ETA 15m>.

  What we're doing: diverting traffic, monitoring failover, validating results.
  What you can expect: service restored for most requests within 30-60 minutes; a follow-up report will be sent when the cause is identified.

  Incident ID: INC-<id>

  Regards,
  Redwood Inference Operations

- Status page template (short):
  Title: Partial outage: inference API (us-west)
  Impact: Increased latency; some requests may time out
  Update: Investigating; fallback routing applied
  Next update: in 15 minutes

Postmortem template (to publish within 72 hours)
1) Title: Postmortem - INC-<id> - one-line summary
2) Severity: P0/P1/P2
3) Date opened / closed / duration
4) Services affected and customer impact (list customers if high impact)
5) Timeline (table of events with HH:MM UTC, actor, action, outcome)
6) Root cause analysis (clear technical narrative)
7) Mitigations implemented during incident (short-term)
8) Permanent remediation and owners (action, target date)
9) Detection gaps and monitoring improvements
10) Communication review (what worked, what didn't)
11) Follow-ups and acceptance criteria for closure
12) Links to evidence (dashboards, logs, commits)

On-call rotation & handoff rules
- Shift length: 1 week primary (Mon 09:00 UTC -> next Mon 09:00 UTC) for SREs; 4-week rotation for on-call leads.
- Swap policy: swaps must be posted to #oncall-swaps and acknowledged by the replacing engineer at least 24 hours prior.
- Handoff checklist (to be filled in Slack or Handoff doc):
  - Current active incidents (IDs and short status)
  - Outstanding action items with owners
  - Known risky changes scheduled in next 24h (deploys, infra changes)
  - Personal contact preference and escalation path

Game day syllabus (90–120 minutes; bi-quarterly)
Purpose: exercise the full Respond→Recover→Review flow under controlled conditions. Rotate inject owners across teams.

1) Pre-work (30m):
   - 5m brief: objectives and scale of injected failure
   - 10m runbook review: triage ladder & containment runbook reviewed by IC
   - 15m environment prep: pre-populated incidents, synthetic traffic, and test telemetry enabled

2) Active exercise (45–60m):
   - Inject: simulate throttling of control-plane API + region CPU spike
   - Observe: on-call detects via alert and opens bridge (goal: <5m)
   - Respond: assign IC, run containment steps, and roll fallback routing
   - Recover: perform targeted rollback or config change; validate with synthetic transactions

3) Debrief and scoring (20–30m):
   - Runbook adherence (0-10): extent to which steps were followed
   - Communication clarity (0-10): clarity and cadence of updates
   - Time-to-detect, time-to-ack, and time-to-recover metrics captured
   - Improvement actions captured as JIRA tickets tagged game-day/<date>

Game day evaluation rubric (examples)
- Detection (0-5): alert fired and was noticed within 5m (5pts).
- Role clarity (0-5): IC and bridge operator were assigned within 3m (5pts).
- Containment effectiveness (0-10): mitigation reduced customer error rate by >75% in one SLO window (10pts).
- Recovery correctness (0-10): rollback or patch restored service without data loss (10pts).
- Communication (0-5): internal and customer message templates used correctly (5pts).

Runbook governance & change control
- Owners: every runbook must list a primary owner and at least one reviewer.
- Review cadence: owners must review runbooks quarterly and after any relevant production change.
- Versioning: runbook edits must include changelog entry and incident tags when used in a real event.

Operational dashboards & useful queries
- Main dashboards: Service Overview, Latency by Route, Model Token Cost, GPU Utilization, Queue Depth.
- Useful queries (examples):
  - Top error types: SELECT error, count(*) FROM logs WHERE service='inference' AND ts > now()-1h GROUP BY error LIMIT 20
  - 95th latency by route: grafana/latency?panel=95p-by-route

Appendix: SLOs and escalation thresholds
| Service | SLO (p95) | Warning threshold | Escalation threshold |
|---------|----------:|------------------:|---------------------:|
| Text-generation API | 200ms | 120% of SLO for 10m | 150% of SLO for 5m |
| Embeddings API | 150ms | 120% for 10m | 150% for 5m |
| Control plane API | 100ms | 120% for 10m | 150% for 3m |

Escalation matrix (summary)
- P2: notify team slack + on-call (no IC)
- P1: IC assigned, bridge opened, customer liaison notified
- P0 (major): Exec notif (paging), incident war room, external status page update every 15m

Document maintenance
- Owner: Asha Patel (eng-sre)
- Review cycle: annual mandatory review; otherwise update after any game day or major incident.

Related resources
- See also: incident-command-playbook-and-escalation-matrix-2024, incident-metrics-and-evidence-collection-standard-2025
- Templates folder: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/templates

[Incident review: Q1 2025 fallback events (model and region)]
h2. Purpose
This page summarizes all reliability-relevant events in Q1 2025 where Redwood systems *activated automatic fallback* (either model fallback or region fallback) as part of mitigation. This is a review artifact used to validate SLO impact, observability, and policy hygiene.

h2. Definitions
* Model fallback: router selects an alternate compatible model (typically smaller) when primary is saturated or ineligible.
* Region fallback: router redirects traffic to a secondary region when the primary region is constrained.

h2. Events included (Q1 2025)
* 2025-01-12: Embeddings pool saturation; *model fallback* enabled for embeddings-default (us-east-1).
* 2025-02-11: Hosted API latency spike; *model fallback* enabled for chat-default (postmortem INC-2025-0211).
* 2025-03-03: EU-West capacity shortfall; *region fallback* enabled (postmortem INC-2025-0303).
* 2025-03-27: Router degradation in us-east-1; temporary *region fallback* for a single route while load shedding was applied.

h2. Observations
* Fallback mitigations prevented multi-tenant outages, but we still lack uniform customer messaging and per-tenant fallback visibility.
* We need an explicit alerting policy for fallback activation anomalies by route.

h2. Recommendations
1) Standardize a "fallback active" banner in Console for affected tenants/routes.
2) Add fallback_activated_count to default dashboard pack; alert if >3x baseline for 10 minutes.
3) Require a policy review for any change that expands eligibility for region fallback.

h2. Related pages
* Router policy standards (Eng Platform)
* Capacity planning: regional headroom targets (Eng SRE)

[Postmortem: Private VPC egress disruption and region fallback (2025-07-22)]
h2. Summary
On 2025-07-22, a networking change in a customer-controlled VPC (Private deployment) disrupted outbound connectivity to one of the inference subnets. As a mitigation, the customer and Redwood jointly activated *automatic region fallback* to a secondary region for non-residency-bound traffic until routing was corrected.

h2. Impact
* Customer: 1 Private deployment (customer-sensitive).
* Symptoms: intermittent timeouts and 502/504 on a subset of inference nodes.
* Duration: ~2 hours of partial impairment; user-visible errors concentrated in the first 35 minutes.

h2. Timeline (UTC)
* 16:20: Customer reports timeouts on chat endpoints.
* 16:27: Redwood on-call engaged; traces show failed egress from subnet private-inf-az2.
* 16:41: Mitigation: enabled *region fallback* for allowed routes to shift traffic from us-east-1 (primary) to us-west-2 (secondary).
* 17:05: Error rate reduced; customer confirms improvement.
* 18:02: Customer reverted the VPC route table change; primary region stabilized.
* 18:15: Disabled region fallback after validation.

h2. Mitigation details
* Primary region: us-east-1
* Fallback region: us-west-2
* Eligibility: routes not marked data_residency_strict and with customer approval
* Trigger: upstream timeout rate > 0.8% OR node connectivity check failures

h2. Root cause
A VPC route table update inadvertently removed a NAT gateway route for one availability zone, breaking outbound calls required for tokenization and telemetry sinks.

h2. Action items
1) Add a Private deployment pre-change checklist emphasizing NAT/egress requirements. Owner: Eng Private Deployments.
2) Improve health checks to distinguish ingress vs egress failures. Owner: Eng SRE.
3) Add documentation for region fallback prerequisites in Private reference architecture. Owner: Eng Private Deployments.

h2. References
* Incident ID: INC-2025-0722

[Known issue note: KV-cache pressure mitigation via model fallback (2025-06)]
h2. Issue
Under certain prompt distributions (high variance in context length), KV-cache memory pressure can cause abrupt throughput collapse on some A100 pools, leading to queue amplification and increased tail latency.

h2. Symptoms
* Rising GPU memory utilization with frequent allocator churn
* Increasing queue wait time and p95 latency
* Occasional 503 spikes from admission control

h2. Recommended mitigation (temporary)
If you observe KV-cache pressure and cannot immediately reduce context length or reconfigure batching, you may activate *automatic model fallback* to a smaller compatible model for the affected route(s) to maintain availability.

Suggested policy parameters:
* Trigger: queue_wait_ms > 300 OR gpu_mem_utilization > 92%
* Primary: rw-llama-3.1-70b-instruct
* Fallback: rw-llama-3.1-8b-instruct
* Disable once the pool is stable for 30 minutes

h2. Permanent fix
We are rolling out a KV-cache eviction tuning change and improved allocator settings in runtime release rr-2.18.

h2. References
* Runtime profiling playbook: KV cache section
* Related incident patterns: fallback activation during latency events

[Postmortem Writeup Style Guide and Executive Summary Templates]
Purpose
This document defines the standard structure, language guidance, and templates for producing postmortem writeups and short executive summaries at Redwood Inference. Our goal is faster, higher-quality postmortems that surface actionable remediation, respect blameless culture, and provide concise executive-ready summaries suitable for customers and leadership.

Scope
- All incidents that meet the postmortem threshold (see "Incident Triage and Postmortem Thresholds" below)
- Game-day exercises where a formal writeup is required
- Customer-impacting outages and incidents requiring external communication or regulatory evidence

Quick reference: When to write a postmortem
1) Severity P1 or P2 incident that impacts >1% of customers or violates an SLO for >10 minutes.
2) Any incident with regulatory evidence requirements (enterprise customers, data residency, security incidents).
3) Any game day or chaos experiment that requires lessons learned.

1. Required structure of a postmortem page (order matters)
- Title: short, specific, include incident date and primary symptom (e.g., "2026-02-18 — Multi-region KV-cache Eviction Causing 5xx Spike")
- Severity and duration: single line (Severity: P1, Start: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM UTC, End: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM UTC, Duration: 00h00m)
- Executive summary (one paragraph + 3 bullets) — see template below
- Impact summary: number of customers, affected routes, estimated error budget/percentage, and key metrics (e.g., 95th latency, error rate)
- Timeline: ordered, timestamped events (ISO 8601) and short descriptions; include detection, mitigation, and closure events
- Root cause analysis: concise causal chain (not a laundry list) with evidence links (logs, dashboards, traces)
- Mitigations applied during the incident (with timestamps and owners)
- Long-term corrective actions: 90-day plan with owner and target completion date (format: ACTION — OWNER — ETA)
- Verification plan: how we will validate the fix (synthetic tests, load tests, monitoring checks)
- Lessons learned / Preventative measures: short list, prioritized
- Postmortem checklist and artifacts: list of evidence files retained and retention policy
- Distribution list and stakeholder notifications: who was informed and when
- Closure criteria and sign-off: product, SRE, and legal (if required) approval

2. Executive summary template (target length: 3–6 sentences + up to 3 bullets)
- One-line incident description: what happened and when.
- Top-level impact: number of customers or percentage affected, and key metric delta (e.g., "peak error rate 18% (baseline 0.3%)").
- Root cause (one sentence): the proximate failure in plain language.
- Short statement of immediate mitigation and current state.
- Bulleted quick actions: 2–3 highest-priority next steps with owners.

Example executive summary (copyable)
"On 2026-02-18 at 14:02 UTC a multi-region KV-cache eviction path was triggered during a rolling kernel update, causing sustained 5xx errors on text-generation routes for ~72 minutes. Approximately 12% of production requests experienced errors at peak; SLOs for 99th percentile latency and error budget were violated. The proximate cause was a race condition in the cache eviction handler under parallel evacuation; a mis-sized eviction window was exposed by the higher-than-expected GC pressure. Immediate mitigation reverted the kernel update and scaled replicas to drain hot partitions; customer-facing traffic is back to nominal. Short-term actions: 1) Fix eviction race (owner: Sasha) — ETA 2026-03-15; 2) Add synthetic canary for kernel-update path (owner: Infra Team) — ETA 2026-02-28."

3. Blameless language checklist (must be enforced)
- Use facts, not attributions. Replace: "Engineer X deployed a bad patch" with "A patch containing an eviction-window change was deployed during maintenance".
- Avoid "caused by" that implies intent. Use "contributed to" or "exposed".
- Attribute systemic factors (process, tests, monitoring, documentation), not people.
- Include timeline evidence that supports statements.

4. Incident triage and postmortem thresholds (short table in text)
- P1 (complete service outage or major data loss): postmortem required and must be published within 5 business days.
- P2 (partial degradation impacting many customers): postmortem required within 10 business days.
- P3 & below: postmortem encouraged where cross-team learning is likely; product or incident owner can opt-in.

5. Evidence and artifact retention (minimums)
- Full APM trace export for the incident window (retain 90 days)
- Raw logs for implicated services (retain 30 days unless regulatory hold)
- Correlated metrics, synthetic test outputs, and timeline screenshots (retain 180 days)
- Incident bridge recording and decision artifacts (retain 365 days)
- For enterprise customers or regulatory incidents, follow the Incident Evidence Chain runbook for extended retention and legal hold.

6. Timeline guidance (best practice)
- Use ISO 8601 timestamps (UTC).
- Each event row: TIMESTAMP — ROLE — ACTION/OBSERVATION — LINK TO EVIDENCE.
- Distinguish detection vs mitigation events.
- Annotate who made the decision and why (brief rationale).

Sample timeline fragment (text table)
2026-02-18T14:02:12Z — Monitoring — Spike detected: 5xx rate > 10% on /v1/generate — link: grafana/dashboard/err-rate
2026-02-18T14:05:30Z — Oncall — Opened incident bridge (bridge-id) and paged Platform team
2026-02-18T14:12:10Z — Platform — Scoped to kv-eviction logs; identified eviction storms — link: logs/query?id=evict
2026-02-18T14:25:00Z — SRE — Rolled back kernel update in eu-west-1; began draining replicas — link: deploy/rollback/1234

7. Action item format and tracking (required fields)
- Each action must be entered into the action tracker (JIRA) and referenced in the postmortem using JIRA-ID. Required fields in the tracker: Summary, Owner, Risk/Impact, ETA, Acceptance Criteria, Verification Plan.

8. Customer and status-page messaging templates (short, adjustable by severity)
A) P1 public status-page (initial notice)
- Title: "Service disruption affecting text-generation routes — investigating"
- Body: "We are investigating elevated error rates for text-generation routes (v1). Affected customers may experience 5xx errors. Our engineers have opened a bridge and are actively investigating. We will provide an update by [time]."
- Follow-up updates: factual, timestamped, short; avoid technical blame in public messages.

B) P2 customer email (post-incident summary)
- Subject: "Incident summary: Partial degradation impacting inference latency (YYYY-MM-DD)"
- Body: Short executive summary + impact bullets + what we did to resolve + link to full postmortem page + next steps and contact for support.

C) Enterprise sensitive notice (when legal or customer data exposure is suspected)
- Contact: CSM and Legal must be looped immediately using the enterprise incident escalation matrix. Do not send external text until Legal approves.

9. Postmortem workflow and SLAs
- Owner assignment: The incident commander (IC) assigns the postmortem author within 24 hours of incident closure.
- Draft: Author produces a complete draft within the SLA window (5 or 10 business days depending on severity).
- Peer review: Two reviewers (one SRE, one Product) must provide comments within 48 hours.
- Publication: Postmortem page is published and linked from the incident tracker; exec summary is emailed to leadership and attached to the incident.
- Closure: Postmortem is closed only after all action items have owners and an initial verification test is scheduled.

10. Examples: poor vs. improved phrasing
- Poor: "Alice's deploy broke the cache and caused the outage."
- Improved: "A deploy that modified the cache eviction parameters coincided with increased GC pressure; the change was a proximate factor in exposing an eviction race."

11. Game day specific guidance
- If a game day triggers a postmortem requirement, label the page with the game-day tag and include: exercise hypothesis, injected fault, expected outcome, observed outcome, and recommended changes to the runbook.
- Always include a dedicated section "What behaved as expected" to keep the learning balanced.

12. Publishing checklist (confluence-specific quick steps)
1) Create page under /oncall-and-incident-response/YYYY/MM/ with title format above.
2) Paste executive summary at the top and pin the page to the incident tracker.
3) Add labels: postmortem, incident, severity-P1/P2, owner-[team].
4) Attach artifacts (screenshots, recordings) and add evidence links (do not paste large logs inline).
5) Assign reviewers and request comment turn-around of 48 hours.
6) After reviewers sign off, set status to "published" and notify distribution list.

13. Metrics and dashboards to include in every postmortem (minimum)
- Request volume (qps) and error rate time series for implicated endpoints
- 50/95/99/99.9 latency percentiles for inference routes
- Pod/node-level resource utilization (GPU/CPU/memory) for implicated clusters
- Cache hit ratio and eviction counts (if applicable)
- Autoscaler events and queue length

14. Ownership and escalation for postmortem defects
- If a defect spans multiple teams, the service owner nominates the primary assignee; SRE co-owns verification.
- For regressions that impact customers repeatedly, the head of SRE sponsors an incident review (30-day retro) and may escalate to leadership for additional resourcing.

15. Frequently asked questions (short)
Q: Who writes the postmortem?
A: The IC assigns the primary author; typically an oncall SRE or the service owner.
Q: Can we redact internal names before publishing externally?
A: Yes — redact PII and internal-only notes. Use the public executive summary for customers.
Q: How do I request extended evidence retention?
A: Follow the Incident Evidence Chain runbook and open a legal hold ticket via the runbook link.

Appendix: Quick CLI snippets and pointers
- Export traces for incident window (example: jaeger)
$ jaeger-export --start 2026-02-18T14:00:00Z --end 2026-02-18T15:30:00Z --service inference --output ./traces.json
- Query logs (example using our internal logs service):
$ logs query "service:inference AND status:5xx" --start 2026-02-18T14:00:00Z --end 2026-02-18T15:30:00Z --save evict-logs.ndjson
- Snapshot dashboards: open Grafana panel and click "share -> snapshot"; attach link to postmortem.

Contact and governance
- Postmortem process owner: Marcus Chen (SRE) — process@redwood.com
- Escalation: see /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/escalation-lattice-restoration-blueprint-2026 for the escalation matrix and legal contacts.
