[Virtual Smart Card initialization fails post SCCM driver hash rotation on depot-repaired workstations]
description:
Issue summary: After a depot repair where SCCM applied the latest driver bundle (hash rotation deployed 2026-02-17), affected Windows 11 machines intermittently fail to initialize the Virtual Smart Card (VSC) subsystem during first boot post-reprovision. Impact: Users are unable to complete local credential enrollment and SSO flows that rely on VSC-backed keys. This blocks a small number of devs and platform engineers receiving repaired hardware. Environment: Corporate depot images (image-2026-02), machines rebuilt via SCCM task sequence, region: us-east, image applied on repaired hardware. Steps to reproduce: 1) Depot repair -> wipe and SCCM image (image-2026-02) 2) During OOBE, complete local provisioning steps 3) Run onboarding script that triggers VSC initialization 4) Observe failure in credential enrollment Expected behavior: VSC service starts, keys are provisioned, and Windows Hello / SSO enrollment completes. Actual behavior: VSC init fails with device-service errors and the onboarding script times out after 10 minutes. Workaround: Manual driver rollback (see resolution) or skip VSC provisioning and use temporary password until a repaired image is applied.

steps_to_reproduce:
1. Build or take a repaired machine and apply SCCM task sequence image-2026-02.
2. Boot to OOBE and complete account creation.
3. Run corp-onboard.ps1 (included in image) or allow auto-run onboarding.
4. Observe onboarding log at C:\ProgramData\CorpOnboard\onboard.log; VSC steps fail between 'vsc-init' and 'vsc-provision' with timeouts.

logs:
Error snippet from C:\ProgramData\CorpOnboard\onboard.log:
[2026-02-18T09:12:02Z] vsc-init: starting
[2026-02-18T09:12:05Z] vsc-init: failed to load driver package (0x000000E9)
[2026-02-18T09:12:05Z] vsc-init: service start timeout (Error 0x800705B4)
Windows Event ID 7026: 'The following boot-start or system-start driver(s) failed to load: VSCFilter'
SCCM log (smsts.log): 'Driver package hash mismatch - applied package hash 3f7a... expected 4b2c... - skipping signature enforcement check disabled: false'

investigation_notes:
2026-02-18 10:00 - Intake: Depot tech reported 5/23 repaired machines failed VSC enrollment post image apply.
Verified correlation with SCCM driver bundle rotation deployed 2026-02-17 (package id pkg-drivers-2026-02).
Reproduced failure on 2 lab devices (Dell 7440, Lenovo X1) with image-2026-02 task sequence.
Observed smsts reports where driver package hash in manifest does not match local unpacked driver hash on some repaired HW serials -> smsts skipped driver installation causing VSC kernel driver missing.
Hypothesis: SCCM package rotation changed signing metadata; for previously repaired hardware with non-standard NIC/ECU, unpack ordering produced hash mismatch under our cache validation, causing SCCM to skip critical VSC driver (VSCFilter.sys).
Checked driver catalog signing: signatures valid, but SCCM content library record uses pre-rotation hash; cache-renew path can cause stale blobs on depot server nodes.
Temporary reproduction using forcing re-download (ccmsetup /downloadcontent) re-applied drivers and allowed VSC to initialize.
Escalated to Imaging/Provisioning infra (PR #7b3f2c1) to add cache-bust and stronger validation; opened linked infra PR for package rotation checklist.
Risk assessment: moderate. Affects small batch of depot-repaired machines until full cache refresh rolled; potential to block onboarding for returning devices.
Next steps: rollback driver rotation on affected depot pool, trigger content library update on depot SCCM nodes, add validation step to task sequence to verify VSCFilter.sys presence before completing onboarding.
Related runbook page reviewed and flagged for update to include 'verify VSC driver present' check in 2.0 task sequence.

comments:
Aisha Patel (Support) - 2026-02-18 10:12: 'Intake from depot: 5 units failed VSC during initial provisioning. Collecting smsts and onboard logs.'
Depot-Tech (Jason Li) - 2026-02-18 11:03: 'I saw smsts indicate driver package hash mismatch on two SKUs. Forcing content redownload fixed 1 device.'
Miguel Ramos (Assignee) - 2026-02-18 15:48: 'Reproduced locally; creating holdback to rollback package on depot-01. Coordinating with Imaging infra to refresh content library. Attaching repro steps and log snippets.'
Imaging Infra (Priya Shah) - 2026-02-19 09:22: 'Confirmed cache-stale condition on depot-01 and depot-03. Pushing content refresh and scheduling package rollback to previous signed bundle at 2026-02-21 02:00 UTC.'
Miguel Ramos - 2026-02-20 18:05: 'Rolling back package to pkg-drivers-2026-01 on depot-01; 3 devices reprovisioned successfully, VSC init completes. Two remaining devices require manual driver reinstall due to missing VSCFilter.sys in filesystem. Creating follow-up task INT-333215 for manual remediation.'

resolution:
Partial rollback applied to affected depot nodes (pkg-drivers-2026-01); content library refresh forced across depot cluster. Manual driver reinstallation steps added to follow-up INT-333215 for remaining machines. Imaging task sequence will be updated to validate presence of VSCFilter.sys and to force content re-download on mismatch. Long-term: add package-rotation checklist and automated cache-bust in SCCM orchestration PR (see related_github_prs).

follow_up_actions:
INT-333215 - Manual reinstall VSCFilter.sys on two remaining repaired units
Infra PR 7b3f2c1 - add cache-bust and package-rotation validation to SCCM pipeline
Runbook update - include VSC validation step in Depots task sequence (Confluence link updated)
Schedule audit of recent driver rotations across depots to ensure no stale blobs remain

[Temporary courier escort access: dock-badge expiration mismatch and shipping-label discrepancy for overnight GPU crates]
description:
Issue summary:
A third-party courier (Celerex Logistics) is scheduled to pick up two GPU crates (asset tags GPU-1782, GPU-1783) from Redwood's secure warehouse dock at 20:30 on 2026-03-13 (outside normal business hours). The courier was issued a temporary visitor badge token (BadgeToken-CRX-917) via the kiosk, but badge TTL in the building access system expires at 20:00, while dock gate credentials (warehouse shipping system) show a separate allowed window until 22:00. Additionally, the printed shipping labels on the crates do not match the manifest uploaded to the shipping system (manifest references dataset: RDW-RMA-332).

Impact:
- Courier unable to access dock after 20:00 due to building badge TTL, causing potential missed pickup and delayed outbound shipment.
- Security concern: mismatch between physical labels and digital manifest increases risk of asset misrouting.
- Customer-facing SLA risk for an enterprise Dedicated customer awaiting hardware decommission.

Environment:
- Secure warehouse dock, us-west region, building A (on-prem Redwood secure facility).
- Systems involved: facility-access-svc (badge provisioning), dock-gate-controller, warehouse-shipping-app (manifest/labels), Slack #facilities, #security, and #logistics channels.

Requested outcome:
- Extend temporary escort badge TTL to 23:00 for the courier on 2026-03-13 and ensure escort assigned.
- Reconcile physical labels with manifest and reprint corrected labels if required before pickup.
- Document corrective steps and prevent recurrence by aligning badge provisioning TTL with dock window for out-of-hours pickups.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Schedule an out-of-hours pickup in warehouse-shipping-app for 20:30 on a weekday.
2) Issue a temporary visitor badge token from facility-access-svc via kiosk or admin panel (TTL defaults to 2 hours, but building policy overrides to nearest business-hour cutoff).
3) Compare TTL shown in facility-access-svc (20:00) with dock-gate-controller allowed window (22:00).
4) Upload manifest to warehouse-shipping-app and print labels; visually inspect label SKU/asset tag vs manifest entries to reproduce mismatch.

logs:
facility-access-svc audit: BadgeToken-CRX-917 issued at 2026-03-13T18:45:12Z, TTL_expiry=2026-03-13T20:00:00Z, issued_by=Maya Patel
dock-gate-controller: pickup_window for pickup_id RDW-RMA-332 allowed_until=2026-03-13T22:00:00Z
warehouse-shipping-app: manifest RDW-RMA-332 uploaded 2026-03-13T17:02:34Z by logistics@redwood.com; printed_labels_checksum=0x4e7a; manifest_checksum=0x7ac2 (mismatch)

comments:
Maya Patel (Reporter) - 2026-03-13T18:50:00Z: Noticed courier on-site now; issued temp badge token from kiosk, but they reported badge denied at lobby turnstile at 20:05. Escalating to security and facilities.
Security (Ana Rodriguez) - 2026-03-13T19:05:00Z: Lobby access policy enforces building close at 20:00. We can approve escorted entry via manual override if facilities confirms escort. See #security slack thread.
Logistics (Jonas Meyer) - 2026-03-13T19:12:00Z: Confirmed manifest/label mismatch — labels printed from local printer show asset tags GPU-1782/1783 but manifest references GPU-1782/GPU-1829. Suspect localized print spooler cached old manifest.

investigation_notes:
Checked facility-access-svc TTL config: default temp badges inherit building business-hours policy (cutoff 20:00). Override requires manager approval or manual backend extension.
Examined warehouse-shipping-app printing subsystem: print job ID 0x9b21 retained an older manifest when the operator re-uploaded a corrected manifest. The print spooler did not flush previous job because driver service (printer-hub) crashed at 16:47 and restarted, replaying a queued job.
Dock-gate-controller supports gate override commands; manual open by security is permitted for escorted transfers when backed by escort ID and pickup manifest verification.

resolution_notes:
2026-03-13T20:20Z - Liam Chen (assignee) coordinated with Security Ana Rodriguez to perform a manual entry override at 20:22. Courier was escorted to the dock and pickup completed at 20:50.
2026-03-13T20:35Z - Logistics reprinted corrected labels after clearing print spooler. New labels checksum 0x7ac2 matched manifest; physical labels affixed to crates GPU-1782/GPU-1783.
Root cause: two independent system TTL policies (badge vs dock) plus a print-spooler race condition that left stale labels on the crates.
Immediate fixes: (1) Facilities updated temp badge TTL override runbook to include an expedited override flow for after-hours courier pickups, (2) IT scheduled a patch to printer-hub to flush queued jobs on restart and added a pre-print manifest checksum validation step, (3) Logistics to use on-screen manifest -> print checksum confirmation prior to operator sign-off.
Follow-up actions assigned (see linked_issues).

next_steps:
1) Facilities to add a UI toggle for temporary badge TTL extension in facility-access-svc (owner: Liam Chen) — ETA 2026-03-21.
2) IT to deploy a hotfix to printer-hub to flush stale jobs and add checksum pre-print gate (owner: Priya Singh) — ETA 2026-03-18.
3) Logistics to add manifest-vs-label verification step in job checklist and to avoid reusing local print spoolers for high-value shipments (owner: Jonas Meyer) — ETA 2026-03-16.
4) Create a post-incident note in #facilities summarizing the manual override and guidance for escorts.

[SSO auth proxy header collision causes intermittent 401/403 for analytics gateway login]
description:
Issue summary:
Users and SREs reported intermittent 401/403 when logging into the analytics portal and when machine agents call the insights API from app-hosted flows. Errors began appearing after proxy middleware v2.14.0 was deployed to prod on 2026-03-09.

Impact:
- ~8% of analytics-portal login attempts fail during peak minutes (observed 09:00–11:00 PDT).
- Automated ingestion jobs that rely on service-to-service SSO occasionally fail with 401s, triggering retries and delayed dashboards.

Environment:
- Prod (us-west-2) behind identity-proxy fleet (k8s, istio sidecar + custom auth middleware).

Observed behavior:
- Requests that should be allowed by Okta SSO show a 401 from the analytics-gateway.
- When retries succeed, request headers show slightly different casing/order for auth-related headers.
- No broad Okta outage; only services routed through the updated proxy are affected.

First seen: 2026-03-09 08:54 PDT (alerts from support + SRE dashboards).

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Hit https://analytics.redwood.com and start login via Okta SSO (browser redirect flow).
2) Observe the redirect back to analytics-portal with session cookie and Authorization header from identity-proxy.
3) Occasionally receive 401 from analytics-gateway after header verification (reproducible in ~1 in 10 attempts during spike).
4) For service-to-service: curl insights API from an internal host through proxy with valid service token; observe intermittent 401s in the service logs.

logs:
2026-03-10T09:15:12Z identity-proxy[proxy-xx] INFO - incoming request /login - headers: {Authorization: Bearer <redacted>, X-Forwarded-User: 'ethan.park', x-okta-session: 'abc123'}
2026-03-10T09:15:12Z analytics-gateway[gateway-yy] WARN - auth middleware: missing expected header 'X-User-Claim' -> returning 401
2026-03-10T09:15:12Z identity-proxy[proxy-xx] DEBUG - header-normalizer applied canonicalization: 'x-user-claim' overwritten by 'X-User-Claim' mapping
2026-03-10T09:16:40Z insights-api[ingest-zz] ERROR - auth check failed for token validation: upstream returned 401; headers seen: Authorization, x-user-claim

comments:
2026-03-10 09:32 - Support (Aisha): Noted spike in 401s on alerts channel #support. Collected a few failing request ids and sample headers from customers. Asked SRE to triage proxy changes rolled last night.
2026-03-10 10:01 - SRE (Samira): Confirmed recent deployment of proxy middleware v2.14.0 (https://github.com/redwood-inference/proxy/releases/tag/v2.14.0). Noticed new header-normalizer component that rewrites auth header keys to lowercase to fix legacy clients. Rolling back candidate sent to canary for testing.
2026-03-10 11:05 - Eng (Diego): Ran reproduce script from staging; observed header duplication where both 'x-user-claim' and 'X-User-Claim' are present; downstream analytics-gateway validates only 'X-User-Claim' exact case, causing intermittent mismatches when proxies compress/merge headers.
2026-03-11 08:24 - SRE (Samira): Deployed a hotfix to proxy configuration (disable header-normalizer for auth-related headers) to canary cluster. Early canary shows failure rate drop from 8% -> 0.5% for canary traffic.
2026-03-12 14:40 - Reporter (Ethan): Confirming login success rate looks normal for morning traffic. Will monitor for 48h before closing.

investigation_notes:
Timeline and evidence: v2.14.0 introduced 'header-normalizer' that lowercases and deduplicates headers. Analytics-gateway auth middleware performs exact-case lookup for 'X-User-Claim' and sometimes reads the wrong header name when the proxy rewrites ordering/casing. Reproducible in staging when header-normalizer enabled. Root cause: tight coupling between proxy normalization and gateway's case-sensitive header expectation. No Okta token failures observed. Metrics: error budget burn tied to proxy deployment window.

hypothesis:
Header canonicalization in proxy created a race/duplication where downstream service reads the wrong header key; some ingress paths merge headers differently causing gateway to miss the user claim and reject the request. The true fix is to either stop normalizing auth headers or make downstream header lookup case-insensitive/standardized.

mitigation:
Temporarily disabled header-normalizer for auth-related headers in prod proxy config (canary -> full rollout). Added a gateway fallback to check both 'X-User-Claim' and 'x-user-claim' while the full fix is implemented. Rolled out within 3 hours of detection; immediate error-rate improvement observed.

resolution:
Permanent fix implemented: updated proxy middleware to exclude auth and okta-related headers from normalization and added service-side tolerant header reading. Changes merged in PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/proxy/pull/842 and https://github.com/redwood-inference/analytics-portal/pull/191. Deployed to prod with canary stage, then 25% -> 100% rollout over 6 hours on 2026-03-12.

follow_up_actions:
1) Add unit/integration tests for header canonicalization behavior (proxy + gateway).
2) Update runbook entry to include header-normalizer exclusion list for auth headers.
3) Postmortem doc and timeline entry on Confluence (owner: Samira, due 2026-03-19).
4) Audit other services that may rely on exact-case header reads and apply tolerant lookups.
5) Add alert to detect sudden jump in header key variance for auth flows.

[Add RAG session recorder demo + docs for local replay and debugging]
description:
Motivation: debugging RAG flows with tool-calling and adapters is hard because reproducing the exact sequence of model outputs, tool calls, and vector DB lookups is non-trivial. This quickstart introduces a lightweight 'session recorder' that captures full request/response traces (prompts, model outputs, tool calls, KV/cache events, and retrieval hits) and a local replay harness that deterministically replays sessions against a pinned model or a mocked runtime.

What this PR adds (single continuous description):
- session-recorder/README.md: developer quickstart that explains recorder architecture, replay modes (deterministic vs. stochastic), and privacy knobs.
- session-recorder/demo/: small Node/TS demo application that runs a RAG pipeline wired to the recorder. Shows tool-calling to a simple facts service and a mocked vector DB.
- session-recorder/docker-compose.yml: runs the demo + recorder + replay web UI locally for easier onboarding.
- session-recorder/.env.example: runtime switches (RECORD=true, REDWOOD_API_KEY=..., REPLAY_MODE=deterministic).
- session-recorder/test/playback.spec.ts: integration test that records a short session, replays it, and asserts identical event sequence and deterministic outputs when REPLAY_MODE=deterministic and model seed is pinned.
- docs/session-recorder.md: integrated docs for the docs site (how to install, security notes, retention policy and suggested evals).
- assets/session-recorder-diagram.svg: architecture diagram for the README and docs.

Checklist: [x] Demo runs locally via docker-compose [x] Unit/integration tests added [x] Docs and diagram included [x] Telemetry hooks instrumented but opt-in by default

How to try locally (short):
1) cp session-recorder/.env.example .env && fill REDWOOD_API_KEY and set RECORD=true
2) docker-compose up --build
3) Open http://localhost:8080 to start a demo conversation and then press "Record session"
4) Use the replay UI to load recorded session and choose "deterministic replay" to validate behavior

Security & privacy: recordings can include PII. Recorder defaults to redaction of fields matching a small patterns whitelist (emails, credit-card-like numbers) and exposes an opt-in retention TTL. The docs section shows how to plug in a KMS-backed encrypt-on-disk adapter before enabling long-term storage.

Motivation and scope notes: This quickstart is intentionally opinionated: it favors a developer ergonomics-first path (local run, Docker, deterministic replay) rather than a production-grade archival pipeline. It is meant as a developer tool to reproduce bugs, create ground-truth prompt/response pairs for regression tests, and to help SREs triage incidents involving tool-calling and retrieval mismatches.

Related: Linear ENG-8721 (session replay prototype), PM-342 (developer debugging UX), Support SUP-1124 (customer reproducer request).

description:
Motivation: debugging RAG flows is often noisy — developers asked for a way to replay narrow time windows of an agent/session (a few turns, or a particular tool call) without rerunning upstream index/ingest or exposing full production traces. This PR introduces a fractional session replay wizard in the docs playground: a small web UI + backend helper that can load a saved session, let users select a fractional time range or token window, and step through generation + tool calls with deterministic inputs.\n\nWhat this PR contains (high-level):\n- docs/playground guide: new page explaining the replay wizard UX and best practices, with screenshots and annotated flow.\n- interactive playground: embeds a JS replay player that fetches trimmed session JSON and drives a stepper UI.\n- examples: three sample RAG sessions (simple Q/A, multi-tool booking flow, and a failure reproduction).\n- SDK integration example (TypeScript): shows how to produce a session envelope that the replay player consumes.\n- telemetry hooks: small metrics emitted for replay start/stop, fraction selected, and tool-call replayed counts.\n- tests: headless puppeteer test that runs the player in CI and asserts deterministic outputs for the provided sample session.\n\nChecklist:\n- [x] Add docs page and frontmatter with redirect to playground\n- [x] Add replay player JS + minimal CSS and accessibility labels\n- [x] Add three example session JSON files\n- [x] Add TS SDK example + README snippet\n- [x] Add telemetry config for replay metrics\n- [x] Add integration test and CI job entry\n- [x] Add release note entry in changelog\n\nHow it works (short):\n1) A session JSON is a simple envelope: metadata, turn list, tools invoked (with deterministic tool inputs/outputs), and model seeds.\n2) The replay wizard accepts a fractional range (e.g., 0.22-0.37 of the session timeline) or absolute turn indices.\n3) The replay player trims the envelope server-side (so we only transfer the slice) and then replays deterministically in the browser by feeding each step to the local stepper runtime. For tool calls, the player can either show recorded outputs or re-invoke them via a sandboxed stub if the developer opts-in.\n\nBackward compatibility / rollout:\n- The feature is opt-in in the docs playground via a "replayEnabled" flag. No runtime changes required for hosted inference. The SDK example shows how to annotate sessions but does not modify existing production telemetry.\n\nTesting & QA notes:\n- Added puppeteer integration test that loads the player, selects the fractional slice for the multi-tool sample, and asserts the UI step output matches expected recorded outputs.\n- Manual QA: cross-browser smoke for Chrome/Edge and keyboard-only navigation for accessibility.\n\nLinks and references:\n- Example sessions stored under examples/rag/replays/\n- Docs preview: https://docs.redwood.com/rag/playground/replay-wizard (internal preview)\n- Linear: ENG-2149 (design + prototype), PM-1884 (product acceptance)\n\nKnown limitations:\n- Replay currently supports only sessions produced by the new session envelope schema (SDK example included). Older session formats will require a lightweight migration script (tracked in follow-up).\n- Tool re-invocation in sandbox mode is limited to stubbed adapters (do not use with live production tool endpoints).\n\nMerge notes: squash-merged to main. The feature is gated behind the docs playground flag; marketing will be notified before public posts.

[Introduce dependency-aware metadata rollback and excerpted release drafts]
description:
Motivation: onboarding metadata can transitively mutate downstream artifacts (aliases, compatibility hints, affinity tags) which in turn pollutes release notes and can cause confusing churn in model catalogs. This PR introduces two orthogonal features: 1) a dependency-aware metadata rollback engine that uses the model dependency graph to revert only transitive metadata deltas while preserving direct author edits; 2) a chronicle exporter that synthesizes excerpted release drafts highlighting the minimal set of meaningful changes for release managers. Scope: library + CLI + operator hook + small web UI preview. Design summary: we compute a directed dependency graph at ingest time, tag metadata deltas with provenance and a TTL, and provide a selective revert operation that accepts an allowed-provenance whitelist and an impact threshold. The chronicle exporter runs an impact scoring pass against a configurable checklist (latency regressions, tokenizer changes, compatibility tags, dataset license updates) and outputs a compact markdown-like draft suitable for editing or direct publishing to the release pipeline. Backwards compatibility: existing onboard contracts and profile formats are supported; the rollback is opt-in and guarded by feature flag "metadata.rollback.v1". CLI: `redwood-registry chronicle export --model-id <id> --since <tag> --excerpt-only --out draft.md`. Operator hook: `onboard-processor` gains a new step `chronicle-seed` that stores the draft alongside the metadata snapshot. Implementation notes: added an in-memory graph builder with fallbacks to provenance-ledger lookups for large catalogs, lightweight diff/patch applier, new REST endpoints (/api/v1/metadata/rollback, /api/v1/chronicle/export), and a preview renderer used by the console. Tests: unit coverage for graph traversal, integration test for rollback safety (ensures direct author edits are not reverted), e2e export smoke tests. Rollout plan: feature-flag gated rollout to 10% of tenants for 2 weeks, collect onboard audit diffs, then ramp to 100% pending no regressions. See linked Linear tasks for rollout details.

release_notes:
Add a dependency-aware metadata rollback tool and a chronicle exporter that generates concise, excerpted release drafts for model onboarding. Backwards-compatible CLI and operator hooks. No breaking API changes.

[Cafeteria Beanbag and Ambient Noise Guidelines]
Summary

This page documents a lightweight, experimental set of guidelines for beanbag seating and ambient noise considerations in Redwood Inference shared spaces (cafeteria, lounge, and overflow areas). The goal is pragmatic: improve employee comfort and informal collaboration while keeping operational burden low.

Scope

- Applies to: cafeteria, adjacent lounge, satellite huddle areas on main campus and leased offices.
- Does NOT apply to: focus rooms, phone booths, secure rooms, or private customer meeting rooms.

Guiding principles

1. Respect for teammates: conserve shared spaces for implicit consent — assume people nearby prefer moderate noise levels.
2. Minimal ops: prefer low-maintenance furniture and sensors; avoid complex approvals for small purchases.
3. Data-informed: measure and iterate; use a simple decibel sampling process before large rollouts.

Furniture guidelines (beanbags and soft seating)

- Quantity: limit beanbag count per room to 6 units or 25% of casual seating, whichever is smaller.
- Placement: require at least 1.5m clear circulation path; do not block egress or access to kitchen equipment.
- Materials: choose wipeable, flame-retardant covers rated for commercial use.
- Procurement checklist (sample):
  1. Model spec and SKU
  2. Flame retardant certificate (pdf)
  3. Supplier lead time and return policy
  4. Estimated cost per unit
  5. Maintenance plan (wipe schedule)

Ambient noise guidance

- Target levels: daylight cafeteria 45-55 dB typical; lunchtime peaks allowed up to 65 dB for short periods.
- Quiet windows: designate 11:30-12:30 on Tuesdays as a quiet-lunch pilot in one lounge for two quarters and evaluate.

Quick decibel sampling procedure

1. Tools: smartphone with a basic dB meter app (note: consumer apps vary).
2. Sampling: take 6 samples across a 30-minute window during a target time (e.g., Wednesday 12:00-12:30).
3. Record: document median and max values. Store sample note on the facilities ticket with a short comment.

Example CLI-style sample (for reference in case teams use a measurement device):

# pseudo-command for a USB mic logger (example only)
# record 30s segments and write a simple CSV of RMS dB values
# recorder --device /dev/audio1 --interval 30 --out cafeteria-sample.csv

Operational checklist for pilot rollout (one-month pilot)

1. Facilities ops to order up to 4 beanbags for Pilot Location A.
2. People Ops to publish the pilot notice and expectations (quiet windows, cleanup).
3. Facilities to execute sampling on week 1 and week 4 and upload notes.
4. Survey: send a 3-question pulse survey after week 4 (comfort, noise impact, cleanup).

Safety, maintenance, and waste

- Cleaning: wipeable covers weekly; deep-clean monthly.
- Disposal: follow office recycling guidelines; avoid foam landfill where programs exist.

Decision and escalation

- If complaints > 10% of local headcount in pilot area, pause and review.
- Escalation owner: Facilities Lead (email: facilities@example.com).

Ownership and review cadence

- Document owner: People Ops (Aisha Khan).
- Review cadence: pilot review at month 1, full review at month 3.

Related artifacts and references

- See: Office space guidelines (Confluence) for building rules and safety.
- See: Facilities procurement template (Drive) for ordering checklist.

Attachments and sample forms

- Procurement sample checklist (attach to ticket)
- Decibel sampling notes (CSV)

Notes and known limitations

- This is intentionally lightweight and experimental. It is not a binding policy for client-facing meeting rooms or regulated spaces. If a space is used for interviews or customer meetings, revert to formal meeting-room standards.

Revision history

- 2024-11-07 initial draft by Aisha Khan
- 2025-01-15 pilot parameters updated after facilities review

[Family Care & Flexible Leave Framework]
## Overview

This document defines Redwood's Family Care & Flexible Leave Framework (the Framework). It consolidates statutory leave, company-paid caregiving leave, flexible part-time transitions, and short-term schedule accommodations into a single reference so employees and managers can make consistent, humane decisions. The intention is to support contributors through life events while keeping teams informed and minimizing operational disruption.

Key principles:
- Equity: similar personal circumstances should result in comparable support across roles and locations (subject to local law).
- Predictability: clear allowances, notice requirements, and payroll impacts.
- Flexibility: a spectrum of options from remote-first days to formal leaves and role-time reductions.
- Manager + People Ops partnership: managers approve operational feasibility; People Ops coordinates eligibility, pay, and compliance.

---

## Who this applies to

- All full-time and part-time employees of Redwood in North America and Europe.
- Specific statutory entitlements (e.g., EU parental leave variations, US state-level family leave) remain governed by local law; this Framework supplements statutory minimums where permitted.

---

## Family Care & Leave Types (summary table)

Leave Type | Company Allowance (paid) | Typical Notice | Manager action required | Notes
---|---:|---|---|---
Primary parental leave (birth/placement) | Up to 18 weeks full pay for primary caregiver* | 8 weeks recommended | Submit People Ops request; approve transition plan | *Top-up applied after statutory pay where applicable
Secondary parental leave | Up to 8 weeks full pay | 4 weeks recommended | People Ops notification | Can be taken in blocks 
Caregiving leave (serious family illness) | Up to 6 weeks at 100% pay, then unpaid up to 12 weeks | As soon as feasible | Manager + People Ops assessment | May require medical attestation depending on duration
Bereavement | 5 paid days for immediate family; manager discretion for extended absence | As soon as feasible | Manager notification | Extended support through EAP if needed
Flexible schedule (temporary) | N/A (adjusted FTE/pay) | 2 weeks notice recommended | Manager approval + People Ops payroll notice | Examples: 60% FTE for 3 months, compressed workweek
Emergency ad-hoc care days | 10 days/year (paid) | Day-of | Manager notification | For urgent short-term caregiving needs

Notes: this table is illustrative. Local statutory entitlements override company allowance where law requires higher benefits.

---

## Eligibility & How allowances interact with statutory pay

1. Always check local statutory rules first. People Ops maintains a per-region statutory matrix (see related_pages).
2. Company-paid allowances are provided as a top-up when statutory leave provides partial pay. Example: if statutory parental leave provides 6 weeks at 80% pay, Redwood will top to 100% for the first 6 weeks for eligible primary caregivers, subject to maximums above.
3. Eligibility window: generally employees with 6+ months tenure are eligible for the company top-up; exceptions can be approved on a case-by-case basis by People Ops for special circumstances.

---

## Process: Requesting leave or a flexible transition

1. Employee discusses preliminary plan with manager (informal).
2. Employee files a formal request via People Ops portal (HR-Portal -> Requests -> Leave). Provide expected dates, role transition plan (if applicable), and any supporting docs.
3. Manager completes the operational impact form outlining coverage (backfill, shift of responsibilities, product deadlines).
4. People Ops verifies eligibility, calculates pay/top-up, and issues a formal approval or a counter-proposal within 7 business days.
5. If approved, schedule a handover meeting and publish a team coverage plan.

Checklist for employees (submit with request):
- Proposed start/end dates (or flexible schedule parameters)
- Handover document link (see Templates section)
- Point-of-contact for coverage
- Preferred return-to-work arrangements (phased return? part-time?)

Manager checklist:
- Coverage plan and temporary ownership matrix
- Communication plan for stakeholders
- Proposed interim KPIs to track deliverables during transition

---

## Templates & examples

- Handover template (use internal docs template): includes active projects, dependences, expected blockers, emergency contacts.
- Phased return plan example: 50% FTE for first 4 weeks, 75% next 4 weeks, full thereafter; include explicit meeting cadence to reassess.
- Role transition example: temporary product owner assignment, 4-week shadowing period, reassign on-call duties.

CLI example for People Ops portal (internal tooling):
- hr-cli leave request --type caregiving --start 2026-05-01 --end 2026-06-12 --note "primary caregiver for parent surgery"
- hr-cli leave status --request-id 8765

---

## Compensation, benefits continuity, and performance reviews

- Payroll: company top-ups are processed on the normal payroll cycle; changes to FTE must be indicated 2 pay periods before the effective date to ensure accurate deductions.
- Benefits: health, retirement contributions, and stock vesting continue during paid leave. For unpaid leave > 30 days, contribution mechanics are described at People Ops -> Benefits Continuity.
- Performance reviews: time away is not a performance signal. Managers should avoid tying leave to calibration or compensation decisions. When review windows overlap with leave, managers should document performance data from the prior cycle and consult People Ops for fair handling.

---

## Manager guidance: balancing empathy and deliverability

1. Treat leave discussions confidentially and empathetically.
2. Focus on outcomes, not presenteeism: agree on deliverables the team can commit to while preserving the employee's recovery/care time.
3. Use the coverage template to identify minimal viable scope for the duration.
4. Escalate complex cases to People Ops (e.g., high-impact roles, extended leaves, or cross-border complications).

Manager escalation triggers:
- Expected absence longer than 12 weeks
- Unclear backfill path that threatens a major milestone
- Requests for role-level changes or promotions tied to leave periods

---

## Edge cases and cross-border considerations

- International hires: local statutory matrix maintained by People Ops. Some countries mandate longer parental benefits; the company will comply with local law and usually will not reduce by offering U.S.-style top-ups.
- Contractors: contractors are not eligible for company-paid leave but may request scheduling accommodations; invoke Manager/People Ops discretion.
- Role change during leave: coordinate with Talent & Compensation for effective dates and compensation proration rules.

---

## Frequently asked questions

Q: Can I take parental leave intermittently?
A: Intermittent leave is allowed for secondary caregivers in most regions; primary caregiver intermittent leave requires manager approval and a clear handover plan.

Q: Will taking leave affect my promotion timeline?
A: No. Promotions and calibration are based on documented performance outcomes. When relevant, managers should work with People Ops to adjust timelines fairly.

Q: Who covers urgent on-call responsibilities while I’m on leave?
A: Managers should identify a temporary on-call owner in the coverage plan. If the role lacks a clear backup, escalate to the hiring team for a short-term contractor.

---

## Ownership and maintenance

- Document owner: People Ops Benefits (Ava Patel).
- Review cadence: annual (every Q4) or after any major statutory change.
- Escalation contact: people-ops@redwood.com; for urgent manager support: on-call People Ops via Slack #people-ops.

---

## Appendix: quick reference (short bullets)

- Emergency ad-hoc care: 10 paid days/year; notify manager same day.
- Bereavement: 5 paid days for immediate family.
- Primary parental: up to 18 weeks company-paid top-up (see locality matrix).
- Secondary parental: up to 8 weeks company-paid.
- Eligibility: typically 6+ months tenure for company top-ups; exceptions possible.

For any questions not answered in this Framework, open a People Ops case via the HR portal or DM the People Ops lead.

[slo-capacity-escrow-and-priority-ledger-guidelines-2026]
Overview:\n\nThis document defines the Capacity Escrow and Priority Ledger approach: a lightweight, auditable mechanism for translating SLO state and error-budget health into short-term, reversible capacity allocations and traffic-priority rules. The goal is to preserve customer-facing SLOs while minimizing cost and avoiding blunt, service-wide throttles when a service approaches its error budget or experiences capacity pressure.\n\nIntended audience:\n- SREs responsible for on-call and capacity decisions\n- Service owners and product engineering leads\n- Capacity planners and cloud infra engineers\n- Platform automation and tooling engineers\n\nObjectives:\n- Provide a predictable escalation path that maps SLO breach risk to incremental capacity or traffic-slicing actions (the \"escrow\").\n- Make capacity assignments traceable via the Priority Ledger so decisions are reversible and auditable.\n- Reduce noisy global mitigations by enabling fine-grained, per-tenant or per-route interventions.\n- Integrate with existing telemetry (observability pipeline), incident tools, and autoscaling systems.\n\nKey definitions:\n- Capacity Escrow: A temporarily reserved pool of capacity (compute, GPU slots, concurrency tokens) that can be assigned to services in response to SLO risk signals. Escrows are timeboxed and must have an owner and a release plan.\n- Priority Ledger: An append-only record of escrow grants, priority rules (e.g., tenant A = high, tenant B = medium), and the rationale linking grants to SLO/error-budget signals.\n- Escrow Owner: On-call SRE or rotation representative who authorizes and releases escrow grants.\n- Burn Rate Thresholds: Predefined burn-rate ranges for error budget health that map to escalation tiers.\n\nScope and non-goals:\n- Scope: production model-serving and API surfaces, multi-tenant request routers, and autoscaler integrations.\n- Non-goal: This is not an alternative to long-term capacity planning or replacing model version rollbacks. Escrow is for short-term mitigation (4–72 hours).\n\nEscrow lifecycle (high level):\n1. Signal detection — telemetry pipeline flags burn-rate and capacity metrics.\n2. Triage — SRE evaluates affected scopes and decides whether escrow is appropriate.\n3. Request — an Escrow Request is recorded in the Priority Ledger with required metadata.\n4. Grant — Escrow Owner approves a grant, the automation reserves capacity and updates routing rules.\n5. Monitor — continuous evaluation during escrow; mandatory check-ins at predefined intervals.\n6. Release or extend — either automatically release at expiry or extend with explicit authorization.\n\nBurn-rate to action mapping (recommended defaults):\n- Green (burn rate <= 0.5): No action; standard autoscale.\n- Amber (0.5 < burn rate <= 1.0): Conditional preemption — enable conservative escrow pre-allocation for high-criticality tenants; increase monitoring cadence to 15 minutes.\n- Red (burn rate > 1.0): Active mitigation — consider escrow grant (timeboxed), traffic shaping (per-tenant throttles), and targeted rollback of recent risky deploys.\n\nExample Priority Ledger entry (format, as text):\n- entry_id: ESCROW-2026-037\n- created_by: oncall-asia-2026\n- service: inference-api-v2\n- scope: route=/chat, tenant=acme-inc\n- reason: p99 latency spike correlated with model-update; error budget burn rate 1.8\n- escrow_type: reserved-concurrency\n- escrow_amount: 50 concurrency tokens (20% of burst pool)\n- start: 2026-01-12T03:10Z\n- expiry: 2026-01-12T15:10Z\n- owner: Priya Nair\n- mitigation_steps: reduce model size to quantized-8bit variant for tenant; enable prefix-cache; increase sampling for tracing\n- approval: Priya Nair (Escrow Owner)\n- release_notes: auto-release at expiry unless extended\n\nOperational procedure (step-by-step):\n1) Detect and classify:\n   a) Alerting: When p95/p99 latency or error-rate alerts fire, the telemetry runbook enriches the signal with SLO context (remaining error budget, burn rate).\n   b) Initial triage: On-call SRE determines affected boundaries (route, tenant, model) and selects candidate mitigations (escrow, throttles, rollbacks).\n2) Create Escrow Request:\n   a) Use the CLI helper: `rwd-slo-escrow request --service inference-api-v2 --scope \"tenant=acme-inc,route=/chat\" --type reserved-concurrency --amount 50 --duration 12h --reason \"p99 spike post-model-rollout\"`\n   b) The CLI populates a Priority Ledger draft and attaches recent deploy IDs and telemetry links.\n3) Approve and grant:\n   a) Escrow Owner reviews ledger draft and verifies telemetry traces and deploy history.\n   b) If approved: automation triggers capacity-reservation in the pool and applies a routing weight increase for the tenant.\n   c) Automation response includes a control plane event ID; record this in the ledger.\n4) Monitor and enforce:\n   a) Health checks at T+15m, T+1h, then hourly.\n   b) If SLOs improve: consider stepwise reduction of escrow (release 25% every 2 hours) to avoid sudden capacity churn.\n   c) If SLOs worsen or other services are impacted: escalate to incident and consider rolling back the risky change.\n5) Release:\n   a) At expiry, automation removes reservations and routing changes unless extension approved.\n   b) Escrow Owner must add a release summary to the Priority Ledger within 24 hours.\n\nRoles and responsibilities:\n- On-call SRE: Triage, create Escrow Requests, request approvals, and own monitoring during escrow.\n- Escrow Owner (rotation): Approve grants, confirm resource availability, and validate that mitigation steps align with product SLAs.\n- Service Owner: Implement suggested mitigations (e.g., enable caching, reduce sampling), coordinate customer communication if needed.\n- Capacity Team: Ensure escrow pool size is sufficient and report exhaustion risks.\n- Platform Automation: Provide CLI and control-plane hooks to reserve/release and to apply per-tenant routing weights.\n\nTelemetry and tooling integration checklist:\n- Observability: Ensure SLO and burn-rate signals are present in the alert context (remaining budget, current burn-rate, recent delta).\n- Priority Ledger: Append-only store (backed by internal DB) with immutable IDs and human-readable notes. request/response IDs.\n- Dashboards: Live view of active escrows, owner, expiry, and linked telemetry.\n\nExample configuration table (recommended defaults):\n| criticality | default SLO | escrow pool |\n| P1 (high) | 99.9% availability | 30% | 25% | 30m |\n| P2 (standard) | 99.5% availability | 20% | 15% | 60m |\n| P3 (low) | 99.0% availability | 10% | 10% | 120m |\n\nExample CLI snippets and JSON --reason \"p99 latency increase\"`\n\n- Automation payload (POST /api/v1/escrow):\n  {\n    \"service\": \"inference-api-v2\",\n    \"scope\": \"tenant=acme-inc,route=/chat\",\n    \"type\": must have a post-mortem-style summary recorded in the Priority Ledger: reason, telemetry snapshots (SLO graphs, burn-rate), actions taken, customer impact, and recommended follow-ups (e.g., capacity commit, model adjustment, runbook updates).\n- If an escrow was extended more than once or led to >2% revenue impact for any customer, escalate to Reliability Initiative review and schedule a follow-up with Product within 7 days.\n\nSafety and guardrails:\n- Maximum escrow duration: default 72 hours unless approved by a Reliability Initiative lead.\n- Pool exhaustion behavior: if reserve [Operations governance: checklists and approval flows (company-wide)]
Overview

This document consolidates operational checklists and approval flows used across Redwood Inference for: access & permissions, change management, data management, procurement & expenses, vendor management, travel policies, and internal templates. It is intended as a single-pane reference for requesters, approvers, and operational owners. Keep this page linked from team runbooks and the central policy index.

Scope and applicability

- Applies to all Redwood employees, contractors, and short-term consultants unless a specific policy states otherwise.
- Where teams require stricter controls (e.g., Customer Data or Private deployments), the stricter control overrides these general flows.
- This page summarizes processes and provides links to canonical forms and templates. For legal, security, or major financial commitments, contact finance-legal or security teams directly.

Quick reference: responsible roles

- Requester: individual initiating the request
- Manager: direct manager of the requester; first-line approver for low-to-medium risk/expense requests
- Team Lead / Product Manager: functional owner for product-related changes or vendor use
- Security Owner: security reviewer for access to sensitive systems or production data
- Finance Approver: finance-legal reviewer for procurement and expense commitments beyond thresholds
- Procurement Ops: owns purchase order creation and vendor onboarding checklist

Access & Permissions: summary and checklist

Principles

- Least privilege by default. Grant only the permissions needed to perform the job for the expected duration.
- Time-bound access for contractors and change-window tasks.
- Access revocation must be executed when an employee offboards or role changes.

Types of access and approval flow

1) Standard tooling (Slack, Google Workspace, internal wiki):
   - Request via Self-Serve: use the Access Portal.
   - Approver: Requester’s Manager (auto-approved if manager is also an admin).
   - SLA: 1 business day.

2) Production systems and data (internal services, dashboards, S3 buckets):
   - Request via Access Portal with justification and scoped resource list.
   - Approvers: Manager + Security Owner (must sign off on data sensitivity).
   - Duration: max 90 days for broad roles; contractors maximum 30 days without renewal.
   - SLA: 3 business days.

3) Emergency access (incident response):
   - Request: create incident ticket and tag oncall; security owner provides temporary access via jumpbox or short-lived token.
   - Post-mortem: access must be reviewed within 3 business days and formally documented.

Access checklist (requester)

- Identify resources and exact permissions needed (e.g., read-only, write, admin).
- Provide business justification and expected duration.
- Confirm manager approval via the Access Portal.
- For production/data access, attach data classification and any program-level approvals.

Change management: approval matrix and runbook

Principles

- Changes to production or customer-facing behavior require risk assessment, testing evidence, rollback plan, and staged rollout.
- Non-production infrastructure changes should follow automated CI/CD with peer review.

Change categories and flows

- Minor (low-risk config or non-prod code): peer review + CI green -> deploy via standard pipeline.
  - Approver: Peer reviewer or team lead.
  - Notification: Weekly changelog.

- Major (schema changes, infra scaling, runtime config affecting latency or cost >15%):
  - Approver: Team lead + SRE/Platform reviewer + Product owner.
  - Documentation: RFC or short ADR attached to PR.
  - Rollout: Canary -> regional rollout -> full rollout with metrics gating.

- Security-impacting changes (auth, PKI, encryption config):
  - Approver: Security Owner + Platform Lead.
  - Additional: Pen test or design review required for changes touching customer data.

Change runbook template (must be attached to PR)

1) Summary and purpose
2) Impact analysis (affected services, users, data)
3) Test evidence (unit/integration/e2e results)
4) Rollback steps and expected recovery time (RTO)
5) Monitoring plan and key metrics to watch
6) Communication plan (SLACK channel, customer notices if needed)

Data management: classification and retention checklist

Data classification tiers

- Public: Intended for public consumption. No special controls.
- Internal: Company internal information with no customer PII. Standard access controls.
- Restricted: Customer data, regulated data (PCI/PHI), and any PII. Requires encryption-at-rest, access logging, and stricter onboarding.

Minimum controls by tier

- Public: Regular backups optional, retention per team norms.
- Internal: Encrypted at rest recommended, audit logs enabled for critical datasets. Retention default 12 months unless business case.
- Restricted: Encryption at rest + in transit, KMS-backed keys, RBAC, access reviews quarterly, retention aligned with contract/regulatory obligations.

Retention and deletion flow

- Data owner defines retention in the onboarding form.
- Before disposal, present deletion plan and verification steps to Security Owner.
- For customer data deletion requests, follow the customer-data deletion checklist and log actions against the customer SLA ticket.

Procurement & expenses: thresholds, approvals, templates

Approval thresholds (examples)

| Spend type | Up to | Approver | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Routine software subscriptions | $5,000 | Manager | Annual renewals allowed with manager approval |
| New vendor contract (software/hardware) | $50,000 | Finance Approver + Procurement Ops | Requires vendor onboarding and PO |
| Capital / multi-year commitments | $250,000 | VP Finance + Legal | Board notice for multi-year strategic commitments |

Procurement checklist (requester)

1) Complete Procurement Request Form (link in templates section).
2) Attach justification, expected term, vendor contact, and security questionnaire if any.
3) Manager approval.
4) Procurement Ops validates vendor, generates PO, and routes to Finance Approver and Legal as needed.

Expense policy highlights

- Use company card for pre-approved travel and team expenses when available.
- Receipts required for all expenses > $25. Exceptions documented and manager-approved.
- Personal expenses on company card are not permitted.

Vendor management and onboarding checklist

- Pre-contract: Security questionnaire (SOC2 summary or security controls), data handling requirements, sanctions check.
- Contract stage: Contract review by Legal + Data Processing Addendum for restricted data.
- Post-signature: Procurement Ops creates vendor record, generates PO, and sets up payment terms.
- Quarterly: Business owner conducts vendor performance review for strategic vendors.

Vendor onboarding checklist (procurement ops)

- Confirm W9 / company tax docs
- Validate bank/payment details via finance procedures
- Configure vendor in AP system and attach contract copy
- Assign vendor owner and expected renewal cadence

Travel and expense policies: quick rules and booking guidance

- Preferred booking channels: Company travel portal or approved travel vendor to ensure rates and travel insurance.
- Pre-approval: Any international travel requires manager + People Ops approval 10 business days in advance.
- Lodging: Standard room, reasonable upgrades require manager approval.
- Per diem: Follow published per diem rates in template.

Travel safety and private deployments site visits

- For private deployment / on-prem customer visits, fill out the Field Visit Risk Assessment and get Security Owner sign off.
- For travel to regions with travel advisories, People Ops will coordinate emergency contact details and insurance coverage.

Internal templates and where to find them

- Procurement Request Form: /confluence/templates/procurement-request-form (use this for all vendor/contract requests).
- Access Request Form: /confluence/templates/access-request
- Change Runbook Template: /confluence/templates/change-runbook
- Travel Approval Form: /confluence/templates/travel-approval
- Vendor Security Questionnaire: /confluence/templates/vendor-security-questionnaire

Operational cadence and reviews

- Quarterly policy review: People Ops + Finance + Security + 1 engineering representative.
- Annual vendor risk assessments for strategic vendors (top 20 by spend).
- Monthly procurement backlog review with Procurement Ops and Finance.

Escalation paths and SLAs

- Access requests: 1 business day for standard tooling; 3 business days for production/data requests.
- Procurement requests: 5 business days for <$50k requests; 15 business days for complex procurements requiring legal.
- Change approvals: minor changes within team SLA; major changes require 3 business days for cross-team review.

Appendices

A. Emergency access post-mortem template (link)
B. Data classification reference table (link)
C. Standard approval email templates and Slack snippets (link)

Contact points

- People Ops: people-ops@redwood.ai
- Procurement Ops: procurement@redwood.ai
- Security: security-ops@redwood.ai
- Finance: finance@redwood.ai

Revision history

- 2025-08-01: Created by Aisha Patel (initial consolidation).
- 2025-11-18: Added vendor onboarding checklist and procurement thresholds.
- 2026-02-10: Updated access SLAs and change management rollout requirements.



[Performance Regression Policy & Thresholds (Company Standard)]
## Overview
This page defines Redwood Inference’s company-wide standard for:
- What counts as a performance regression vs. measurement noise.
- Minimum sample sizes and repeatability requirements.
- Pass/fail thresholds used by automated perf gating (PR checks, nightly canaries, and release-branch gates).
- Required artifacts and triage expectations when a regression is detected.

This policy is designed to support the “Perf baseline & representative workload suite” program and applies broadly to the serving runtime, kernels, scheduler/batching, and benchmark harness changes.

**Owner:** Observability (Engineering) in partnership with Serving Runtime and SRE.

---

## Scope
### In scope
This policy applies to any change that can affect latency/throughput/cost-relevant behavior for production inference:
- Serving runtime changes (prefill/decode scheduling, KV cache management, batching/backpressure, memory behavior).
- Kernel changes and kernel auto-selection changes.
- Model serving configuration defaults that affect runtime behavior (e.g., quantization profile defaults, attention/kernels toggles).
- Infrastructure and deployment changes that impact perf measurement (driver/CUDA/runtime/container base images, node configuration).

### Out of scope
- Application-level changes outside Redwood control (customer client code).
- One-off research experiments without a run manifest and reproducible harness.

---

## Canonical metrics and measurement boundaries
Metrics and definitions are standardized per **ADR-0172**. Any new metric must be proposed via an ADR update.

### Primary metrics (must-report)
1) **TTFT (Time To First Token)**
- Definition: time from server request acceptance (server-side) to first token emitted by the server streamer.
- Report: p50, p95, p99.
- Notes: TTFT explicitly excludes client receive/render overhead. Client-side measurements must be labeled as such and cannot be used for gating.

2) **TPOT (Time Per Output Token)**
- Definition: average per-token time during decode, measured server-side from first token emission to last token emission.
- Report: p50, p95, p99.

3) **Throughput**
- For generation/chat: tokens/s (server-side) and optionally req/s (if output length is fixed/controlled).
- For embeddings: req/s and embeddings/s (if batch mode is used).
- Report: mean and p95 where applicable.

### Secondary metrics (required when available)
- **Queue wait time** (scheduler): p50/p95/p99.
- **Batch assembly time**: p50/p95/p99.
- **Batch size distribution**: histogram summary (p50/p95 max).
- **GPU memory peak**: max (MiB) per run.
- **Error rate**: fraction of requests failing (timeout, OOM, internal errors).

### Cold vs warm cache requirements
Because caching materially affects cost/latency and is production-relevant, results must be reported as:
- **Cold**: prefix/KV caches cleared for the workload cohort.
- **Warm**: a defined warmup phase and cache retention enabled.

For gating decisions:
- Default gating uses **Cold** unless a workload is explicitly designated “cache-dependent” in the representative suite spec.
- Warm results are recorded and monitored; large cold↔warm deltas are treated as a diagnostic signal (not a failure by default).

---

## Noise model (how we distinguish regression vs. variance)
Performance data has unavoidable variability (GPU clocks, placement, thermal behavior, background IO, kernel selection changes, cache state). This policy uses a two-level model:

### Level 1: Run-level repeatability
A “run” is a single harness execution with a pinned workload definition + seed + manifest.
- Each gated comparison must include **multiple independent runs** (see minimum sample sizes below).
- Runs must include a standardized warmup period and must capture environment details in the run manifest (driver/CUDA/runtime build, kernel selection mode, scheduler policy, node type, region).

### Level 2: Statistical comparison across runs
We compare a candidate (PR branch / release build) against a baseline (golden build tag for a given suite version).

**Default test statistic:** percent change of the run-median metric across repeats.
- For each metric M, compute the median value per run.
- Across runs, compute the median-of-medians for baseline and candidate.
- Compute %Δ = (candidate - baseline) / baseline.

**Confidence / robustness:**
- Use bootstrap resampling across runs to estimate a 95% confidence interval (CI) on %Δ.
- A change is considered “actionable” only if it clears the **noise floor** and breaches warning/fail thresholds with CI support.

**Noise floor (ignore region):**
- If |%Δ| < **2%** for a metric, treat as noise by default (unless the absolute delta is operationally meaningful; see “absolute thresholds”).

**Absolute thresholds (override noise floor):**
- TTFT: **+20 ms** at any percentile is considered actionable even if <2%.
- TPOT: **+0.20 ms/token** actionable.
- Error rate: **+0.10% absolute** actionable.

**Known high-variance environments:**
- If a particular SKU/region cohort is flagged as high-variance (SRE-owned designation), gating requires either (a) more repeats or (b) an isolated fleet window. High-variance designations must be documented and time-bounded.

---

## Minimum sample sizes (gating requirements)
Minimums are chosen to balance cost with statistical power for typical Redwood workloads.

### A. Minimum repeats (independent runs)
- **PR gating (fast path):** 2 runs (same environment), only for “tier-1 smoke” workloads.
- **Nightly canary:** 3 runs.
- **Release branch gate:** 5 runs (or 3 runs across 2 separate fleet windows).

### B. Minimum requests per run (by workload type)
The representative suite defines workload cohorts; use the cohort type to select minimums:

| Workload cohort | Example | Minimum requests/run | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Chat streaming (short prompts, variable decode) | interactive chat | 10,000 | Must include concurrency ramp and steady-state window. |
| Tool/function calling (bursty multi-turn) | burst + idle cycles | 6,000 | Must include burst period long enough to show queueing dynamics. |
| Long-context prefill stress (large prefill, modest decode) | summarization | 1,200 | Prefill dominates; ensure long-context bin coverage. |
| Embeddings high-QPS (small payloads) | embeddings API | 50,000 | Prefer fixed-size payload bins to reduce confounding. |

### C. Required steady-state criteria (per run)
A run only counts if:
- Warmup is completed (standard warmup defined by the suite).
- At least **10 minutes** of steady-state measurements are collected (embeddings may use 5 minutes if QPS is high and variance is stable).
- Error rate is below the maximum allowed (see thresholds). If errors exceed allowed rate, the run is invalid unless the error itself is the regression under investigation.

---

## Pass / warn / fail thresholds
Thresholds are expressed as % change vs. baseline (negative throughput change is regression). Unless otherwise noted, thresholds apply to **cold-cache** results.

### A. Default thresholds (company-wide)
**Latency metrics (TTFT, TPOT):**

| Metric | Warn if regression ≥ | Fail if regression ≥ |
|---|---:|---:|
| TTFT p50 | +5% | +8% |
| TTFT p95 | +8% | +12% |
| TTFT p99 | +10% | +15% |
| TPOT p50 | +4% | +7% |
| TPOT p95 | +6% | +10% |
| TPOT p99 | +8% | +12% |

**Throughput metrics:**

| Metric | Warn if regression ≥ | Fail if regression ≥ |
|---|---:|---:|
| tokens/s (generation) | -5% | -8% |
| req/s (embeddings) | -6% | -10% |

**Reliability guardrails (hard fail):**
- Error rate increase of **+0.10% absolute** or more (e.g., 0.05% → 0.15%) is a **Fail**.
- Any new OOM pattern that did not occur in baseline is a **Fail** (even if latency improves).

### B. CI-aware gating interpretation
A candidate fails gating when **both** are true:
1) The bootstrap 95% CI of %Δ overlaps the fail region (i.e., regression is statistically supported), and
2) The regression clears the noise floor (or crosses an absolute threshold).

If the point estimate is in fail but CI is wide (insufficient power), the result is “Inconclusive” and must be retried with additional repeats or an isolated fleet window.

### C. Workload-specific overrides
The representative suite may specify tighter or looser thresholds per cohort if justified by:
- Customer impact (SLO sensitivity of that cohort).
- Historical variance characteristics.
- Known scheduling/kernels sensitivity.

Overrides must be documented in the suite definition and reviewed by Serving Runtime + SRE + Observability.

---

## Gating tiers and where policy applies
### Tier 0: Developer local (non-gated)
- Purpose: quick iteration.
- Not authoritative; no formal pass/fail.
- Must still emit a run manifest when shared.

### Tier 1: PR perf checks (gated when enabled)
- Runs a reduced workload subset (“tier-1 smoke”), typically on one region + one SKU.
- Goal: catch large regressions quickly.
- Thresholds: use **Fail** thresholds only (warnings are surfaced but do not block merges unless configured by the owning team).
- If PR gating is flaky, SRE/CI may temporarily disable with an incident/issue and an ETA to restore.

### Tier 2: Nightly perf-canary (always-on)
- Runs the representative suite nightly for supported baselines.
- Produces trend charts and variance panels.
- Failures page the owning triage rotation only if configured as “page-worthy” (see Alerting section).

### Tier 3: Release-branch perf gate (blocking)
Required before a serving runtime release is approved:
- Representative suite green under this policy for the release candidate.
- Runs must include the release’s target regions (minimum: us-east, eu-west) and key SKUs for that release.
- Any waiver must follow the exception process below.

---

## Required artifacts (to make results attributable)
All gated perf results must include:
- **Run manifest** (per ADR-0172) including:
  - Runtime build identifiers (git SHA, build ID), container image digest.
  - Region/SKU/node type, driver/CUDA, and relevant runtime flags.
  - Scheduler policy name + config hash.
  - Kernel selection mode + any pinned kernels.
  - Workload suite version + cohort ID + seed.
- **Results export** containing:
  - Metric definitions, aggregation method, percentile calculation method.
  - Raw summary stats per run (not only deltas).
- **Links** to dashboards/traces:
  - Dashboard panel link (TTFT/TPOT/throughput) for the run.
  - Trace/profiling artifacts when a regression is flagged (see profiling playbook).

Any result without a manifest is not eligible for gating decisions.

---

## Alerting and escalation
### What pages vs. what posts to triage
- **Page (on-call):** release-branch gate failures for tier-1 models/workloads; error-rate/OOM regressions.
- **Triage channel only:** warning-level regressions, inconclusive results, or failures in non-tier-1 cohorts.

Routing is managed by SRE in collaboration with runtime owners.

### Ownership on regression
- If the regression is clearly attributable to a PR: the PR author/owning team is responsible for first response.
- If attribution is unclear: Serving Runtime on-call (or designated triage rotation) coordinates bisect.

---

## Exception (waiver) process
Waivers exist to unblock releases when the business impact of delaying exceeds the perf risk, but they must be rare and time-bounded.

A waiver requires:
1) A written justification including affected cohorts/metrics, expected customer impact, and mitigation.
2) A link to the failing run(s) and manifests.
3) Approval from:
   - Serving Runtime Engineering Lead (or delegate), and
   - SRE Integration Lead (or delegate).

Waivers must include:
- Expiration date (default: 14 days).
- A follow-up issue/ticket to remove the waiver.

---

## Triage checklist (standard playbook)
When a regression is detected:
1) **Validate reproducibility**
   - Rerun with the same manifest (same suite version, seed, and environment) if possible.
   - Confirm warmup was applied and steady-state criteria were met.

2) **Check environment drift**
   - Driver/CUDA/runtime container changes.
   - Node type differences, GPU clock/power settings.
   - Placement/isolation differences.

3) **Attribute to scheduler vs. kernels vs. workload**
   - Inspect queue wait time and batch assembly metrics.
   - Compare batch size distributions.
   - Check kernel selection debug dumps (selected kernel, fallback reasons).

4) **Inspect tail behavior**
   - Identify whether regression is p99-only (queueing contention, cache thrash) vs. broad (kernel/runtime change).
   - Use profiling playbook to collect traces for a small reproduction.

5) **Decide action**
   - Fix forward (preferred) or revert.
   - If neither is immediately possible, pursue a temporary mitigation (pin kernel, adjust backpressure guardrails) with an explicit rollback plan.

---

## Change management
- Proposed changes to thresholds, sample sizes, or metric definitions require review by Observability + SRE + Serving Runtime.
- Any change must document:
  - Rationale (variance data, customer/SLO sensitivity).
  - Expected impact on flake rate and compute cost.
  - Backwards compatibility for dashboard queries and historical comparisons.

---

## Appendix: Practical guidance
### Recommended interpretation
- TTFT p99 regressions often indicate scheduler backpressure, queue discipline changes, or prefill/decode overlap issues.
- TPOT regressions often indicate kernel selection changes, KV cache behavior changes, or decode batch inefficiencies.
- Throughput regressions without latency regressions can indicate conservative batching caps or increased per-request overhead.

### Contact / channels
- #eng-runtime (coordination)
- #eng-sre (fleet stability, variance)
- #eng-platform (dashboards)

(If these channel names change, update this page; do not create duplicate policy pages.)

[00:30] Priya: Great. Let's start with a scenario: you have a multi-tenant LLM inference service. Customers have mixed latency requirements; some are small chat responses, some are long-form generation. How would you design the request routing and batching strategy to balance latency and throughput?
[00:50] Jordan: Okay, so first cut, separate by SLO tier — fast-path for low-latency customers, batch-path for bulk. Use an upfront router that tags requests with expected token length and priority. For batching you run continuous batching window, but you also have a max-wait timeout, like 5–10ms for the low-latency tier, and larger for throughput.
[01:20] Samir: When you say continuous batching, are you thinking synchronous queues per worker or a global scheduler?
[01:27] Jordan: I'd go with hybrid — local worker-level queues for micro-batching to reduce cross-host coordination, and a global coordinator for balancing load and moving batches if workers are idle. The coordinator can reshuffle by affinity and memory footprint (KV cache locality).
[01:45] Priya: How would you incorporate KV cache behavior? For large chat histories the KV cache grows — what tradeoffs do you consider?
[01:55] Jordan: If the KV cache (kay-vee cache) is per-model shard, you want to minimize cold-cache misses. Techniques: pin recent active conversations to same GPU, use LRU eviction tuned by sequence length, and optionally offload cold-kv to host memory with on-demand fetching. But that increases latency, so prefer sharding customer affinity.
[02:20] Priya: What about memory-limited GPUs; how would you handle quantized models and cache memory?
[02:28] Jordan: Quantization reduces model size but KV cache still consumes a lot. I'd explore 4-bit quantization for weights and mixed precision for activations. For KV caching, you could compress keys or use 8-bit storage for cached kv pairs; there's a tradeoff with decode cost. Also tiered caching: hot kv stays on GPU, warm kv on fast host RAM, and cold kv in a slower store.
[02:55] Samir: Do you have experience with specific quantization libraries or tooling?
[03:00] Jordan: I've used bitsandbytes for 4-bit and a custom offline quantizer for 6-bit experiments. I haven't used Redwood-specific tooling but I worked on a similar stack at OpenEmbeddings.
[03:12] Priya: Cool. Follow-up: suppose a customer sends 200 concurrent short requests — how does your scheduler avoid head-of-line blocking?
[03:22] Jordan: Use priority lanes and per-customer concurrency limits. Implement fairness via weighted round robin between tenants and preemption for high-priority requests. Also allow small fast-path shards that bypass large batching windows.
[03:35] Samir: You mentioned preemption — how do you implement preemption at the GPU kernel level?
[03:41] Jordan: Full kernel preemption is hard; prefer request-level scheduling: if a queued large batch is waiting, you can reorder queues before dispatch, or split large batches into smaller micro-batches. Use CUDA streams to overlap work where possible, though synchronization is tough.
[03:58] Priya: Let's pivot to a whiteboard: design a scheduler that decides which model variant to route to when capacity is constrained — e.g., you have full-precision, quantized, and distilled variants.
[04:10] Jordan: Okay — objective: maximize throughput while meeting latency SLOs and minimizing cost. Have a multi-armed routing policy that considers: estimated latency on variant, quality delta, customer tier, and current load. For each request compute expected utility = quality_weight*quality - cost_weight*latency_estimate and pick highest utility under SLO constraints.
[04:45] Samir: How do you estimate latency for a given request?
[04:49] Jordan: Use a learned model or empiric histograms: features include sequence length, batch size, model variant, and GPU utilization. Keep online calibration.
[04:58] Priya: Any thoughts on rollback/fallback if quality regressions happen?
[05:02] Jordan: Maintain a canary pool and do shadow traffic to evaluate quality metrics. If regressions detected, fallback to next-best variant and trigger alerts. Also use prompt-level checks where applicable.
[05:15] Samir: Let's surface an ambiguity: how do you measure 'quality' programmatically?
[05:20] Jordan: Use task-specific metrics — perplexity for language models, BLEU/ROUGE for summarization, or cosine similarity for embeddings. For chat, may need human evaluations or downstream signal like user satisfaction.
[05:35] Priya: Good. Quick behavioral: tell us about a time you had an incident in production and how you resolved it.
[05:42] Jordan: At my last role we had a GPU OOM cascade after a recent release that increased sequence-length handling. Root cause was a regression in a padding calculation that duplicated KV entries. We mitigated by throttling ingress and rolling back the deploy, then patched the padding logic and added e2e tests for long sequences.
[06:05] Samir: Nice. Any telemetry changes you added?
[06:08] Jordan: Added a long-tail sequence length histogram, per-request KV size metric, and an alert when average KV per request exceeded threshold.

[06:20] Priya: We're about halfway; let's do a short coding/design exercise: outline an API and data model for a take-home that tests batching logic. What would you ask?
[06:30] Jordan: I'd ask them to implement a simple router that ingests requests with (tenant_id, priority, expected_tokens) and outputs batch assignments with a max batch size and max wait. Provide a simulator of incoming load and assert latency percentiles under different scenarios. Also include unit tests for edge cases like starvation.
[06:50] Samir: How would you validate correctness and fairness?
[06:54] Jordan: Validate with synthetic workloads, check p50/p95 latency per tenant, and enforce per-tenant concurrency caps. For fairness, compute Jain's fairness index across tenants' latencies.
[07:10] Priya: Perfect. Final 10 minutes for candidate questions. Anything you'd like to ask us?
[07:16] Jordan: Yeah — how tightly coupled is the inference runtime to the control plane? Are rollouts handled automatically by the platform or handled by SRE?
[07:26] Priya: Our platform provides routing policies and rollout primitives, but SRE owns infra-level rollouts and emergency fallbacks. Engineers can set policies in the control plane and manage model variants.
[07:38] Jordan: Nice. Also curious about hybrid on-prem/private deployments — do teams usually run the same runtime?
[07:44] Samir: Yes, same runtime with optional private deployment packaging; differences are in networking and key management.

[07:52] Priya: Thanks Jordan. We'll send a take-home exercise; expect it by Tues. Any final notes?
[07:58] Jordan: No, thanks for the thoughtful questions.

[Prefix Caching Architectural Review - Zetta AI (deep dive)]
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-02-18 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes (recorded)
Attendees: Lara Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Patel (Redwood SE), Samir Gupta (Redwood Infra), Alice Romero (Zetta Eng Lead), Daniel Park (Zetta CTO), Priya Shah (Zetta SRE)
